## Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL LIBRARY, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE UP TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THAT HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, CAREFULLY COLLATED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH A NUMBER OF MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND CORRECTED WITH THE GREATEST DILIGENCE; CONTINUOUSLY ILLUSTRATED BY DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE VERY AMPLE EDITIONS PRODUCED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES, AND WITH OTHER WRITINGS OF THE SAME AUTHORS PUBLISHED ONLY SEPARATELY; FURNISHED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ADORNED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY SET OUT WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS WELL AS WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; ENLARGED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, AND ALSO WITH WORKS POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: THE FIRST, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH OF THE FATHERS HAS WRITTEN ON ANY THEME MAY BE SEEN AT A GLANCE; THE SECOND, OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH IT may readily be ascertained which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture. AN EDITION OF THE GREATEST ACCURACY, AND EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS IF ONE TAKES INTO ACCOUNT THE CLARITY OF THE TYPE, THE QUALITY OF THE PAPER, THE INTEGRITY OF THE TEXT, THE PERFECTION OF THE CORRECTION, THE VARIETY AND NUMBER OF THE WORKS REPRINTED, THE EXTREMELY CONVENIENT FORMAT OF THE VOLUMES, CONSISTENTLY SIMILAR THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE WORK, THE LOW PRICE, AND ABOVE ALL THIS COLLECTION—SINGLE, METHODICAL, AND CHRONOLOGICAL—OF SIX HUNDRED FRAGMENTS AND OPUSCULES HITHERTO SCATTERED HERE AND THERE, BUT NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME BROUGHT TOGETHER IN OUR LIBRARY FROM WORKS RELATING TO EVERY AGE, PLACE, LANGUAGE, AND FORM.**

**FIRST SERIES, IN WHICH ARE PUBLISHED THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH, FROM TERTULLIAN TO GREGORY THE GREAT. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical scholarship.**

**THE COMPLETE WORKS OF ST. EUSEBIUS JEROME, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON,**

**after the recension of the monks of the Order of St. Benedict, of the Congregation of St. Maur, and especially of Joannes Martianay of that Order, newly corrected against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; enlarged by very many monuments previously wholly unpublished, and by other works of the holy Doctor published only separately; illustrated with innumerable notes, observations, and corrections; through the study and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, priests of Verona, with the assistance of other learned men in that same city. The latest Parisian edition, revised according to the second edition by the Veronese editors themselves through their later labors, and enriched by recently discovered materials in such a way that the present edition, by its sheer extent alone, setting aside all other corrections, materially surpasses all preceding editions, even the Benedictine ones, by a third part or one-third; prepared and finally revised by J. ## PREFACE

To the edition of Jerome’s works, whose preparation began nearly nine years ago, and which was subsequently delayed somewhat longer than I had undertaken by the difficulties of the times and by private troubles affecting my eyes, I now at last put the finishing hand. If there is any room for an apology before fair-minded judges of my circumstances, I beg that it be granted, and I ask that my studies and labors be met with pardon rather than favor. For I know well what the holy Father himself once alleged on his own behalf: that it is the nature of people of this kind not to be as grateful for what you have given as they are distressed over what you have withheld . . . . . For we praise virtues with less zeal than we censure vices (*Preface to Book XII on Ezekiel*). But let us set this aside. Behold the very book with which our entire collection is brought to a close, and the pledge given to the public is discharged.

This final volume contains the **SPURIOUS WORKS**, that is, writings once attributed to St. Jerome and joined, or even mingled, with the genuine fruits of his genius, but in reality composed by others, not by him. Since it is not presently possible to eliminate them altogether and dispossess them of their ancient possession—for by a kind of right belonging to an illegitimate offspring they are nevertheless attached to him—one task remains for us: to make this family somewhere better out of what is bad, known out of what is unknown, and more orderly out of what is disorganized.

First of all, however, a selection of pieces had to be made; then a judgment had to be pronounced on each. Accordingly, we removed from their place those writings which not only knew their certain and genuine author and bore his name in their title, but also commonly appeared in editions of that author’s works. For, apart from the fact that it is entirely idle and foolish to print a hundred times, out of place, works that you possess in their proper place, and to burden a collection with an unnecessary mass of writings, no one will ever seek them in Jerome, but in their own author; and whatever praise they deserve belongs not to some part of themselves but to the complete body of their works. Indeed, an editor who neglects this appears either unwilling to labor in this branch of learning or at least insufficiently concerned for his own studies and for the usefulness of his readers.

The collected works of Bede, for example, and of Rabanus, which for the most part contain what we have removed from here, are readily available to everyone; why, then, should certain passages from their Commentaries be reprinted among Jerome’s spurious writings? Conversely, works rightly claim a place here which, although they have a certain author, cannot be found anywhere except in the company of Our Author, or which are found elsewhere among other writers in foreign settings and, if you order them to be exiled from here, might easily perish to the detriment of literary scholarship. Of this kind are the enormous Commentaries of Pelagius, a heretic and an especially hostile enemy of Jerome, on the Epistles of Paul—so much so that one is more surprised that they could ever have been counted among Jerome’s works. Most of the others are of the same kind.

There were also many things, both from manuscripts and from other printed books, that had to be transferred here because they were absent from other editions and properly and deservedly belonged to the family of Jerome’s works just mentioned; nor was it tolerable that they should be sought repeatedly in one book after another. Among these are several Epistles, neither insignificant in age nor in reputation, as well as the very ancient *Martyrology of Jerome* and the good—if any book ever was—book called the *Comes*.

Yet the question here is not how good the books we have supplied are, but whether they ought to be brought here and assigned the same household as the remaining spurious works.

After the selection had been made in this way and the material for the volume prepared, it had to be assigned to sections according to the character of the writings themselves. Erasmus once arranged everything into something like five classes. The first contained τὰ ἀμφιβολῶς νόθα (*ta amphibolōs nótha*), that is, works about which it might be uncertain whether they were Jerome’s or not. The second contained the learned ψευδεπίγραφα (*pseudepígrapha*), that is, works falsely inscribed with his name but nevertheless displaying some learning. The third contained works that did not seem worth reading, but were wholly unlearned and childish. The fourth contained works plainly belonging to others and marked beforehand with the names of their authors—for example, the Epistles that Damasus, Augustine, Epiphanius, and others sent to Jerome, as well as Gennadius’s *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers* and certain short works of Rufinus. The last contained writings that did not bear the style of a single author, but appeared above all to have been compiled from Jerome’s writings.

Although Erasmus had preferred to err in favor of assigning this class to the higher section, so that works belonging more properly to the lower order would be referred to the preceding one, he completed it almost entirely with a single Commentary on the Psalms. Nor did he include all these works in one separate volume [Col. 0011], but, following the order of subject matter, he published the Epistles and shorter works separately from the genuine writings in his fourth volume, while in the seventh, eighth, and ninth volumes he mingled the Commentaries with Jerome’s works, merely warning the reader.

Victorius followed this arrangement in its entirety; Martianay followed it in part. He arranged a considerable number of Commentaries, as well as one or two exegetical Epistles, in the appendix to his second volume, containing almost exclusively explanations of sacred Scripture, so that spurious works might supply what was lacking in those places in the genuine treatises of Jerome. He included the remaining enormous mass of Epistles and Commentaries in two sections, distinguished according to the character of the writings themselves, in the fifth—or final—volume of his edition.

But he was content merely to copy the Erasmian model in these matters, making use neither of manuscript codices nor of the more fortunate discoveries and judgments of learned men since Erasmus. He did add one or two new short works: the *Penitential Canons*, attributed to Jerome, and the *Exposition of the Gospels from the Short Proverb*. Yet these writings were of the lowest quality, burdened with so many monstrosities of error and corrupted in so many places, and so devoid of meaning, that he might seem to have served literary scholarship better had he refrained from publishing them. In all other matters he followed Erasmus with blind eyes, scrupulously observed that three-part arrangement, and—what is the central point—without daring to add anything of his own, retained Erasmus’s censures word for word, despite the great advances in learning.

We judged it our responsibility to apply a remedy to this. Accordingly, we examined all the writings—or at least those whose ancient manuscript copies could be found—according to the evidence of those copies, willingly undertaking the arduous labor for the benefit of the reader. Then, after weighing each item, we considered what seemed necessary or useful for restoring the furnishings of Jerome’s household, and what did not.

Above all, it was worthwhile to pronounce judgment on each work; and we undertook this exceedingly difficult task, investigating the style and character of the disguised author until we seemed to have discovered who he was, either by certain indications or by not implausible conjectures. We therefore prepared new censures for each writing, explaining the basis of its composition, assigning each work to its proper author, and finally showing whether the opportunity for the deception arose from a bookseller’s fraud, from chance, or from the recklessness of copyists. We brought the greater part of the authors, who had been almost entirely unknown, into the open light, adorned them in their proper character, and made it possible for them to serve the great Jerome with dignity as well.

We also accomplished other things relevant to completing the entire edition of Jerome’s works in every respect. Most recently we composed a life of St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 0011] This Life seemed to us better placed before the first volume of the holy Father’s works, which is volume twenty-two of our *Patrology.] chiefly from his own writings—nothing is more fitting or necessary for attaining a deeper understanding of the sequence and meaning of his works. Yet all the editions that preceded ours either lacked this distinction entirely or possessed it in a better and greater part. Erasmus and Victorius, in fact, composed not so much a life of the holy Doctor as a panegyrical eulogy of him. Martianay appended no life of his own and did not consider the lives supplied by the praised editors worth much. He later published a *Life of Saint Jerome* in French, as you can see, not in Latin; but he intended it to be issued separately in a special book rather than appended to his edition, and considered it more useful to those devoted to piety than to people eager for learning.

In composing ours, historical truth was our chief concern. Year by year we constructed the sequence of the holy Father’s deeds and writings according to the rules of sounder criticism. Nor was it a matter of reviewing the learned affairs of a private individual; rather, the memory of the more important events and controversies in the Church had to be repeatedly recalled, since during that period he especially upheld its glory. We append shorter lives written long ago by the ancients, whose names nevertheless are unknown, together with observations and notes, and with the addition of other short works belonging to the subject, as the next page will indicate.

At the end we provide an overview of our entire edition, compared with the arrangement of the earlier and Benedictine editions; with its help, each writing of the holy Father may be found at a glance, both in our edition and in those of others. Finally, we provide two general indices, much fuller than those appended to the individual volumes: one of all the matters that seem especially worthy of notice in all Jerome’s works; the other [Col. 0013] of all the testimonies of sacred Scripture that are discussed in those works in passages—as they say—foreign to their original context.

One thing remained: that whatever errors we had made in reviewing the entire body of the works, whether later noted by others or noticed by ourselves, should be corrected in a second revision. This was always our intention, and no one could have earned greater gratitude from us than one who exposed us wherever we had gone astray. We have never been more pleased with ourselves than when we have cast off an error and supplied something better to students of Jerome’s teaching.

As for others, however, two writers arose who rebuked us, differing greatly both in learning and in spirit.

One was a Benedictine of Paris, a man belonging to the order to which he was attached and to which, in every other matter, I myself defer completely. Favoring his cause with extremely misguided zeal—and being angry not so much with me as with a most learned man who was promoting our edition of his own accord in France—he believed that my edition would prove detrimental to the monopoly they claim for themselves in publishing the works of the holy Fathers. He therefore tried to detract from it and, so to speak, trip it up in a special piece of writing, which he inserted into a book of varied and highly disparate contents.

I would dare to wager that he could not have persuaded himself for even a moment to believe any of the things he said against my industry. He seems to have acted because, knowing that no one would take the trouble to learn the matter more deeply, he could meanwhile impose his own account on his readers. I say this, and do not hesitate solemnly to swear that if he had correctly noted anything, I would have wished to include it here, but he found nothing whose knowledge would matter to readers. To answer a detractor neither befits us nor belongs to this place.

The other is both our friend and a learned expert in ecclesiastical antiquity, our own Jerome de Prato. In Dissertation VI on the *Dialogue* of Sulpicius Severus, he takes a position contrary to ours concerning that Epistle of Theophilus which we were the first to bring to light in a Latin translation by Jerome and which we called a synodical letter.

“I almost take it as certain,” he says, “that the recently published Epistle of Theophilus is entirely different from that synodical letter which Jerome says he translated from Greek.”

His reasoning may be summarized as follows: the Epistle clearly came neither from a synod, whether held at Alexandria or on the mountain of Nitria, nor from the Fathers collectively, but was written by Theophilus privately; and it seems to be a general letter, which the holy Father himself elsewhere calls an encyclical, but by no means a synodical letter, which must have been entirely different and which had already been lost long ago.

I shall answer him briefly. If he prefers, I shall grant that when Jerome says he translated Theophilus’s synodical letter from Greek, he did not speak with such precision, but designated one and the same letter by different terms. Then I shall appeal to the force of the arguments that I have assembled in many places on behalf of its authenticity, and by which, unless I am greatly mistaken, I have proved that the letter I first brought to light is none other than the one that the holy Translator calls synodical.

I shall also appeal to the judgments of all learned men to whom these matters are known; finally, I shall appeal to the judgment of my opponent himself, if he turns from the desire to quibble to a fairer examination of the matter itself.

**APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF ST. EUSEBIUS JEROME, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, CONTAINING SPURIOUS WRITINGS**

## PART ONE—EPISTLES. (C, G, S)

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING EPISTLE

[Col. 0013] For a long time now this letter—or rather book—of the most wicked enemy Pelagius has been attributed to the great Jerome, though it is all the more surprising that it should have been so attributed. Bede, *Commentary on the Song of Songs*: [Col. 0014] “Some of our people,” he says, “read this book attentively and rashly believe it to belong to the holy and catholic Doctor Jerome, failing entirely to see that both the sweetness of its soothing eloquence and the perversity of its seductive heresy clearly prove that this little work is not his.”

This is sufficiently learned. For the style plainly shows that it is not Jerome’s, and the doctrine that it continuously insinuates is precisely the heretical dogma of the Pelagians, which the holy Father refutes in his own work at the places indicated from this very writing. For this reason it was subsequently attributed to various writers of that heretical faction, especially to Julian, as the Bede mentioned above believed, and as some manuscript codices assert—notably one of the older manuscripts of the Library of St. Victor. Other manuscripts, according to Martianay’s testimony, had the name of Coelestius written at their head.

But, as we were saying, it was produced by Pelagius’s own pen. This can be known with certainty from Augustine’s book *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 20 and following, and more clearly from chapter 37 of the same book. There Pelagius himself declares that he is the author when, writing in his letter to Innocent, he says:

“Let them read what we wrote in the East to the holy virgin of Christ, Demetrias, and they will find that we praise human nature in such a way that we always add the assistance of God’s grace.”

There are also certain passages from the body of this very Epistle, near the end of chapter 1, which Augustine says Pelagius recognized as his own in his *Epistle to Constantius*. Orosius likewise makes Pelagius its author, except that he notes that another supplied Pelagius with the words. That other person may easily have been Anianus, the false deacon of Celeda, as Jerome calls him in Epistle 143 in our recension: he says that Anianus “feeds most abundantly in order to supply the frivolous words of another’s blasphemy.”

As for the date of the writing, the Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works noted it before us: it was sent in the year 413, when Jerome, Augustine, and Innocent each vied in sending letters to Demetrias as she received the veil of virginity; or certainly in the year 414, after she had withdrawn to Rome. Pelagius here seems to indicate this in chapter 23. See what we have said about the genuine Epistle of Jerome to Demetrias, which is numbered 130 in our edition.

## EPISTLE I. PELAGIUS TO DEMETRIAS. (C, G)

### CHAPTER I.—

If I believed that, relying on exceptional talent and equal learning, I could easily fulfill the task of writing, nevertheless I could not undertake so difficult a work without great fear of its difficulty. Yet I must write to Demetrias, a virgin of Christ, a noble virgin, a wealthy virgin—and, greater than these qualities, one who tramples nobility and wealth beneath the ardor of faith. In proportion to the extraordinary [Al. *insigni*: “remarkable”] admiration her virtue deserves, it is easy for everyone to praise her, but difficult to instruct her.

Who could lack words when celebrating her praise? She was born to the highest rank, brought up amid the greatest wealth [Col. 0015] and luxuries, and suddenly broke free from so many and such varied allurements of this life, by which she had been entangled as though by very tenacious bonds, and exchanged all the advantages of the body at once for the virtue of the soul. She cut down the very flower of her still-budding youth with a certain sword of faith, that is, with the will. Crucifying her flesh with Christ, she consecrated it to God as a living and holy sacrifice, and, for love of virginity, despised the posterity of the noblest blood.

The path of speech is easy and smooth when the abundance of the subject itself kindles the course of the discourse. But we must proceed by another route, since our purpose is to write instruction for a virgin, not praise of her; and not so much to describe the virtues she has already acquired as those she must acquire; [Col. 0016A] and rather to order her remaining life than to adorn her past life.

It is exceedingly difficult to deal with a person in whom the desire to learn is so great and the zeal for perfection so ardent that scarcely any doctrine, however perfect, can be equal to her. For she remembers—and rightly remembers—which riches and glory of the world she has rejected, which pleasures she has renounced, and which attractions of the present life she has finally despised. Therefore she is not content with this common and mediocre manner of living; and since it easily becomes commonplace through association with the multitude, she seeks something new and unusual. She demands something exceptional and singular. She desires her way of life to be as remarkable as her conversion. Noble in the world, she wishes to be nobler before God. She seeks in her conduct things as precious as those she despised in material possessions.

What stream of eloquence could ever satisfy such ardor of a devoted mind, such thirst for perfection? What power of speech, what abundance of words, could ever express how much the virgin is prepared to fulfill in deeds? We must ask pardon, however, since, in adorning the Lord’s tabernacle, we offer a gift according to our strength. Nor do we fear that by writing rashly to a virgin of such nobility we may voluntarily expose ourselves to the bites of envy.

For we write at the request of her holy mother—rather, at her command—and she has demanded this from us by letters from overseas, with extraordinary desire of heart. She readily shows with what devotion and care she has planted a heavenly seed in her daughter, since she is so anxious to have it watered by others. Therefore, removed from rashness and free from ambition, let us devote ourselves to the work we have undertaken. Nor do we distrust [Al. *diffidamus*: “despair of”] the modesty of our talent, which we believe will be aided both by the faith of the mother and by the merit of the virgin.

### CHAPTER II.—

Whenever I must speak about the formation of character and the conduct of a holy life, I usually first demonstrate the power and quality of human nature and show what it can accomplish. From there I begin to encourage the listener toward the forms of virtue, so that it will not be useless to call someone to things he may have presumed impossible for himself [Al. *praesenserit*: “foreseen”; *Numquam enim*: “For never”].

For we cannot enter upon the path of virtue unless hope goes with us as our companion. Indeed, every effort to pursue something is destroyed by despair of attaining it. Since I have maintained this order of exhortation in other short works as well, I think it must be observed especially here, where the goodness of nature should be declared more fully in proportion as the life to be formed is more perfect. Otherwise the mind will be so much more relaxed and slow in pursuing virtue as it believes itself less capable, and, while unaware of what is present in itself, will imagine that it does not possess it.

That reality whose use is desired must always be brought to awareness, and whatever good nature can do must be explained, since whatever it is proved capable of doing must be fulfilled. Let these, then, be laid as the first foundations of a holy and spiritual life, so that the virgin may recognize her powers. She will finally be able to exercise them well once she has learned that she possesses them.

The best incentives of the mind arise when someone is taught that he can do what he desires. In war too, the greatest and most authoritative exhortation is the one that reminds the combatant of his strength.

First, then, you must measure the goodness of human nature from its author—namely, God. Since Scripture reports that he made all the works of the world and everything within the world good, and very good, how much more excellent, do you think, did he make the human being himself, for whose sake he is also understood to have created all things?

When he plans to make him in his own image and likeness [Al. *disposuit*: “planned”], even before he makes him he shows what sort of being he will make [Al. *esset*: “would make”]. Then, when he subjected all the animals to him and established him as their lord—even though he had made many of them much stronger than human beings either in bodily size, in strength, or in the weapons of their teeth—he clearly shows how much more beautifully the human being himself was created [Col. 0017B]. By this very fact he wished him to understand the dignity of his nature, while he marvels at the powerful animals subjected to him.

For he did not leave him naked and without protection, nor did he expose him, weak and defenseless, to various dangers. Rather, although he had made him outwardly unarmed, he armed him better within: with reason, namely, and prudence, so that through understanding and the vigor of his mind—by which he surpassed the other animals—he alone might recognize the Maker of all things, and serve God by the very means through which he ruled the others.

Yet the Lord willed him to be a voluntary, not a compelled, executor of justice [Note: [Col. 0017D] Erasmus, and Martianay following him, omit τὸ ἐκτελεστήν, “the executor,” a word which we have supplied from other books.]. Therefore he left him in the power of his own counsel (*Ecclesiasticus* 15). He placed before him life and death, good and evil; and whatever pleases him will be given to him.

Hence we also read in Deuteronomy: “I have set before your face life and death, blessing and curse: choose life, that you may live” (*Deuteronomy* 30) [Al. *et*: “and live”].

### CHAPTER III.—

From this point you must take care lest that very matter trouble you in which the rash and ignorant crowd stumbles. Therefore do not think that the human being was not truly made good merely because he can do evil, nor that he is constrained by the very force of nature to the necessity of unchangeable good [Al. *astringatur*: “is constrained”].

For if you reconsider the matter carefully and compel your mind to a more subtle understanding, the better and higher condition of the human being will appear to you precisely where it is thought to be lower. In this crossroads of two paths, in this freedom toward either side, lies the dignity of the rational soul.

Here, I say, the whole honor of our nature consists; here its dignity; here, finally, the best people earn praise; here, their reward [Col. 0017D]. There would be no virtue at all in one who persevered in the good if he could not have passed over to evil.

Since God wished to endow the rational creature with the gift of voluntary good [Al. *munire*: “to fortify”] and with the power of free choice, by implanting in the human being the possibility of either side he made it his own to choose whatever he wished, so that, being naturally capable of good and evil, he could possess either and incline his will toward either one.

For he could not otherwise have goodness that was spontaneous unless [Al. *nisi aeque etiam*: “unless equally also”] the creature could also possess evil. The best Creator wished us to be capable of both, but commanded us to do only one—namely, the good—and gave us the capacity for evil solely so that, through our own will, we might make his will our own.

Since this is so, the very fact that we can also do evil is itself good. Good, I say, because it makes the better part of us—the good—stronger. For it makes the will itself voluntary and independent, not bound by necessity but free in judgment [Col. 0018B]. We are permitted to choose, reject, approve, and refuse.

Nor is there anything else by which the rational creature is more greatly preferred to the others than this: while all other things possess only the goodness of condition and necessity, this creature alone possesses also the goodness of will.

But many people, impiously no less than ignorantly, when the condition of the human being is being discussed—for I hesitate to say it—as though criticizing the work of the Lord, assert that he ought to have been made such that he could not do evil at all. Thus the creature says to the one who formed him: “Why have you made me thus?” (*Romans* 9).

And the most wicked of human beings, while pretending not to manage well the very thing they have been made, would rather have been made differently, so that, although they refuse to amend their lives, they may appear to wish to amend nature.

The goodness of nature has been so generally established for everyone [Col. 0018C] that it sometimes reveals and displays itself even in pagan people who are without any worship of God.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] No one is unaware of the answers that St. Augustine and Leo gave to these and other arguments below. It pleases us, however, to quote Bede in one or two places by way of example:

“Whoever among the philosophers,” he says, “did not know Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, could possess neither true virtue nor true wisdom. But insofar as they possessed some taste of any wisdom or an image of virtue, they received all of it from above—not only through the gift of their first creation, but also through his daily grace, who, without abandoning his creature when it does not abandon him, distributes his gifts as he himself has judged, giving great gifts to the great and small gifts to the small.”]

For how many philosophers have we heard of, read about, and ourselves seen who were chaste, patient, modest, generous, temperate, kind, who rejected both the honors and the pleasures of the world, and who loved justice no less than knowledge [Al. *sapientiae*: “wisdom”]? Why, I ask, are such things pleasing in people who are strangers to God? And from where do they have these good qualities, unless from the goodness of nature?

[Note: [Col. 0018D] Bede replies with the following:

“Scripture contradicts this when it says: ‘For not all things can be in everyone, since the son of man is not immortal’ (*Ecclesiasticus* 17:29). This clearly suggests that only when this mortal nature has put on immortality can all the good qualities of virtue be in everyone; and even then they will not come from the goodness of nature, but through the grace of him of whom it is written: ‘that God may be all in all.’

“But the daily proofs of our frailty also show that not everything can be in everyone, since so many are found who, striving with the greatest persistence, are nevertheless wholly unable to attain those virtues which they see others possess.”]

And when we see that the qualities I have mentioned are possessed either all together in one person or individually in different people, while human nature is one and the same in all, they show by their example that everything can be in everyone—whether all qualities are found in all, or individual qualities in individual people.

But if human beings, even without God, show what kind of beings they were made by God, consider what Christians can do, whose nature and life have been instructed for the better through Christ, and who are also aided by the assistance of divine grace.

[Col. 0019A] **CHAPTER IV.**—Let us now come to the secret places of our soul: let each person look more attentively upon himself. Let us ask what our own thoughts feel about this matter. Let good conscience itself pronounce judgment on the goodness of nature [Alt. omits *good*]. Let us be instructed by the household teaching of the soul, and let us learn the good things of the mind nowhere so much as from the mind itself.

What, I ask, is it that makes us either blush or fear at every sin; that displays the guilt of our deed now by the redness of our face, now by pallor; that makes us, with trembling spirit, avoid a witness even in the smallest offenses, and suffer the stings of conscience? Conversely, in every good deed we are joyful, steadfast, and unafraid; and if it is hidden, we also desire and wish it to be made public. Unless, indeed, nature itself is its own witness, since by this very fact it declares its goodness: by disliking evil, and by trusting only in a good deed, it shows what alone becomes it.

Hence it is that, even when the executioner is hidden, the torments of conscience often rage against the author of a crime, and the secret punishment of the mind pursues the concealed offender. After guilt there is no place for impunity, since guilt itself is the punishment [Alt. *becomes the punishment*]. Conversely, an innocent person enjoys the security of conscience even amid the torments themselves; and although he fears punishment, he glories in his innocence.

There is, then, I say, in our souls a certain natural holiness, if I may so call it, which presides, as it were, in the citadel of the soul and exercises judgment between good and evil. Just as it favors honorable and upright actions, so it condemns wicked deeds and, as a kind of household law, distinguishes the various sides of the matter by the testimony of conscience. It does not deceive us by some peculiar ingenuity or by any artificial coloring of arguments; rather, through our thoughts themselves—most faithful and wholly upright witnesses—it either accuses or defends us.

The Apostle mentions this law when writing to the Romans. He testifies that it has been implanted in all human beings [Alt. omits *human beings*] and written, as it were, on certain tablets of the heart:

> “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law, although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts accuse or even defend one another” (Rom. II, 14–15).

All those whom Scripture records as having lived holy lives and pleased God between Adam and Moses made use of this law. Some of them must be set before you by way of example, so that you may easily understand how great is the goodness of nature, once you have recognized that nature taught righteousness in place of the law.

**CHAPTER V.**—Abel was the first to follow this teacher, and he so won the favor of the Lord that, when he offered Him a sacrifice, his offering was so gratefully accepted by God that it stirred his brother to envy (Gen. XXIV and following). The Lord Himself, recalling him as a just man in the Gospel (Matt. XXIII, 33), briefly explained his perfection. For every kind of virtue is contained under the single name of justice.

We read that blessed Enoch so pleased God that God snatched him away from the midst of mortals and transferred him, perfected in the world, from the habitation of the world (Gen. V, 24).

Noah is declared to have been just in his generation and perfect. His holiness is all the more admirable because, while the whole world had utterly turned away from justice, he alone was found just. He did not seek an example of holiness from another; he himself provided one. Therefore, when the shipwreck of the whole world was imminent, he alone among all deserved to hear:

> “Enter, you and your household, into the ark, because I have seen you to be just in this generation before me.”

Before God, however, that person is proved just who is holy both in body and in heart.

Melchizedek is read to have been a priest of God (Gen. XIV, 18). His merit can easily be understood from the fact that he prefigured long beforehand the sacrament of the Lord that was to come, expressed the mystery of the body and blood through the sacrifice of bread and wine, and represented Christ’s priesthood through the figure of his own priesthood. To Christ the Father says:

> “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

And by blessing Abraham, the chief of the patriarchs—who through circumcision is the father of the Jews and [Alt. omits *is*] through faith of the nations—he most clearly displayed the figure of Him who, through His faith, granted blessing both to the Jews and to the Gentiles.

Lot likewise, following the virtue of holy Noah, did not abandon justice amid so many examples of sinners. Just as Noah was not overcome by the example of the whole world, so Lot maintained holiness while that entire region in which he lived [Alt. *had lived*] was sinning against the vices of the multitude. He was, as blessed Peter says, “just in sight and hearing” (II Pet. II, 8); placed among the worst of men, he turned away from their evils both with his eyes and with his ears. Therefore, by a similar example, just as Noah was rescued from the flood, so Lot was rescued from the fire.

What need is there to recall Abraham, the friend of God, or Isaac and Jacob? We can estimate how perfectly they fulfilled the Lord’s will from the fact that, by a special and intimate distinction, He wished to be called their God:

> “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Matt. XXII, 32; Luke XX, 37).

“This is my eternal name and memorial throughout generations of generations.”

Joseph, the Lord’s faithful servant from childhood, is shown to have been all the more just and perfect amid tribulations [Alt. *to have been shown just amid great tribulations*]. First he was sold as a slave by his brothers to the Ishmaelites (Gen. XXXVII, 28), and he was sold by those whom he had seen bowing down to him. Then, handed over to an Egyptian master, he nevertheless always preserved the freeborn dignity of his soul. By his example he taught both slaves and free persons that, in sinning [Alt. *in not sinning; and not*, etc.], status is no obstacle to anyone, but the mind is decisive.

Here, I ask you, pause for a little while, and carefully consider, O virgin, the chaste soul. Joseph the young man is desired by his mistress [Alt. *by a woman*]; he is not enticed into desire—he is asked, and he flees. In this one matter she both flatters and begs, although in other matters she commanded. The love [Augustine: *lover*] of God is not conquered by a woman’s love. A chaste soul is moved neither by the age of youth nor by the authority of the woman who loves him.

After being frequently rejected, the mistress lays closer snares for the young man. In secret and without witnesses, the shameless woman seizes him by the hand and, with more brazen words, urges him toward crime. Even then he is not overcome; rather, just as he answers words with words, so he answers deeds with deeds. For he who had repeatedly refused when asked now fled when seized [Augustine: *is bound*]. Before the Gospel saying had been spoken, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28), he, though provoked by the woman not merely through sight but almost through an embrace itself, did not desire her.

You have admired the virtue of chastity thus far; now look upon his kindness. Before the Prophet said, “Let each person not remember the wickedness of his neighbor in his heart” (Lev. XIX, 18), he returned charity for hatred. When he saw his brothers—or rather, enemies born from his brothers—and when he wished to be recognized by them, he testified to the affection of his love instead of resentment:

> “He kissed each one” (Gen. XLV, 15).

With abundant tears he drenched the necks of those who were terrified and washed away the hatred of his brothers with tears of love. He loved them with genuine fraternal affection both while their father was alive and after his death. He did not remember the pit into which he had been cast because of their murderous intent. He did not consider that their brotherhood had been sold for a price; instead, “repaying good for evil” (Rom. XII, 17), he fulfilled the apostolic command while still under the law of nature.

**CHAPTER VI.**—What shall I say about blessed Job, that most famous athlete of God? After his wealth had been plundered and his estates utterly destroyed; after the sudden death of all his sons and daughters; finally, he fought against the devil with his own body (Job I–II). Everything he possessed externally was taken away, and his external goods suddenly fell from him, so that the things truly his own might shine forth more clearly [Alt. *might shine forth*].

He is stripped of everything, as though of all his clothing, so that naked he may triumph more freely and more firmly, and conquer again, by enduring sufferings, the enemy whom he had previously overcome by bearing losses. Of him the Lord Himself gives this testimony:

> “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth: a blameless man, a true worshiper of God, keeping himself from every evil” (ibid.).

And rightly so. For, as he himself says, he always feared the Lord as though waves were swelling over him, and he could not bear the weight of His presence. He did not dare to despise Him whom he believed always to be present, and he said:

> “I am secure, for my heart does not reproach me throughout my life” (ibid.).

Before the Lord commanded that enemies be loved, he could say:

> “If I rejoiced at the misfortunes of my enemy, if I said in my heart, ‘It is well done’” (Job XXXI, 32).

The Gospel command had not yet sounded, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke VI, 30), and he was already saying:

> “If I allowed the needy to leave my door empty-handed” [Augustine: *without provisions*].

He had not yet read the Apostle’s command, “Masters, grant your slaves what is just and fair” (Col. IV, 1), and yet, confidently, he cried out to the Lord:

> “If I have harmed a servant, if I have injured a maidservant, you know everything, Lord.”

Before the same Apostle commanded the rich not to be high-minded or to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches (I Tim. VI, 17), he possessed riches in such a way as to show that he was rich elsewhere. He said:

> “I did not trust in riches, nor in a precious stone” (Job XXXI, 24).

He proved this not only by his words but also by his actions. When he lost everything, he did not grieve; he said of each thing:

> “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord forever. Naked I came out of my mother’s womb; naked I shall return there” (Job I, 21).

For we show with what feeling we possess something when we lose it; the pain of being deprived exposes the desire to enjoy it. If a person did not possess that desire in deprivation, how could he have possessed it in ownership?

O man evangelical before the Gospel, and apostolic before the apostolic commandments! A disciple of the apostles, who opened the hidden riches of nature and brought them into the midst, showing from himself what we are all capable of; who taught how great is that treasure of the soul which we possess without using it, and that what we do not wish to bring forth, we do not even believe ourselves to possess.

**CHAPTER VII.**—After saying much about nature, we have also displayed and demonstrated its goodness through the examples of the saints. And lest anyone think that the fact that some have been wicked belongs to nature’s fault, I shall use the testimonies of Scripture, which everywhere charge sinners with the offense of their will and do not excuse them on the necessity of nature.

In Genesis we read:

> “Simeon and Levi, brothers, completed their wickedness by their own will” (Gen. XLIX, 6).

The Lord spoke to Jerusalem:

> “Therefore they themselves abandoned my way, which I had set before them, and they did not listen to my voice, but went after the desire of their evil heart” (Jer. IX, 13).

And again the same prophet:

> “You sinned against God, and you did not listen to His voice, and you did not wish to walk in His commandments, statutes, and testimonies” (ibid. XLIV, 10).

Through the prophet Isaiah also the Lord spoke:

> “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall consume you” (Isa. I, 19).

And again:

> “All of you shall fall by slaughter, because I called you and you did not listen; I spoke and you neglected me; you did evil before my sight [Alt. *before the Lord’s sight*], and you chose what I did not want.”

The Lord Himself also says in the Gospel:

> “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. XXIII, 37)!

Where we see willing and refusing, choosing and rejecting, there we understand not the force of nature but the freedom of the will. The volumes of both Testaments are full of testimonies of this kind, in which every good and every evil is always said to be voluntary. We omit them now for the sake of brevity, especially since we know that you are devoted to sacred reading and drink more abundantly from that very fountain.

**CHAPTER VIII.**—Nor do we defend the goodness of nature in such a way as to say that it cannot do evil. We openly acknowledge that it is capable of both good and evil. We merely vindicate it from this injustice: that we should seem to be driven to evil by its fault, when we do neither good nor evil without the will, and when we are free always to do one of two things, since we are always capable of both.

Why are some to be judges and others to be judged, unless it is because within the same nature there are different wills, and because, although we are all capable of the same things, we do different ones? Therefore, so that this may shine forth more clearly, some examples must be brought forward.

Adam is expelled from paradise; Enoch is taken from the world. In both cases the Lord demonstrates freedom of choice. For just as the one who sinned could please God, so the one who pleased God could have sinned. Neither would have deserved punishment, nor the other election, from a just God unless each had been capable of both.

The same is to be understood of the brothers Cain and Abel, and also of the twins Jacob and Esau. We must recognize that the sole cause is the will when merits differ within the same nature.

Noah the just rebuked the world extinguished by its sins in the Flood, and the holiness of Lot judged the crimes of the Sodomites.

Nor is this a small argument for proving the goodness of nature: the fact that those first human beings lived for so many years without any admonition of the law. This was not because God had at any time failed to care for His creatures, but because He knew that He had made human nature such that the law of nature was sufficient for them to practice justice.

Indeed, as long as the use of the more recent nature still retained its freshness, and long practice in sinning had not spread something like a darkness over human reason, nature was left without the law. But when the Lord saw it buried beneath excessive vices and infected with a kind of rust of ignorance, He applied the file of the law to it, so that it might be polished by this frequent admonition and be able to return to its own brightness.

Nor is any other cause responsible for the difficulty we have in doing good [Alt. *seeing good*] than the long habit of vices that infected us from childhood and gradually corrupted us over many years. It afterward holds us bound and enslaved to itself so that it seems, in a certain way, to possess the force of nature.

All that time during which we were negligently instructed—that is, trained in vices—during which we even strove to be wicked, when innocence was regarded as foolishness in comparison with incentives to wrongdoing, now resists us and comes against us. The old habit attacks the new will, and we wonder why, through leisure and idleness, while we were ignorant, holiness should be conferred upon us as though by someone else, when we acquire no habit of goodness despite having learned evil for so long.

These remarks about the goodness of nature have been made hastily, as though in another work. We had to make them in order to pave for you a clearer road to perfect justice, along which you may run more easily once you have recognized that there is nothing harsh or inaccessible in it.

For if, even before the law, as we have said, and long before the coming of our Lord and Savior, some are reported to have lived justly and holily [Alt. *are reported*], how much more should we believe that we can do so after the illumination of His coming—we who, instructed by the grace of Christ and reborn into a better humanity, have been cleansed and purified by His blood and stirred by His example toward perfect justice? We ought to be better than those who lived before the law, and better even than those who lived under the law, since the Apostle says:

> “Sin shall no longer rule over you. For you are not under the law but under grace” (Rom. VI, 14).

[Col. 0024A] **CHAPTER IX.**—And since, as I think, we have said enough about these matters, let us now form the perfect virgin, who, kindled continually by both, may testify through the holiness of her conduct to the goodness both of nature and of grace.

The virgin’s first concern and first endeavor, therefore, should be to know the will of her Lord and to inquire carefully what pleases Him and what displeases Him, so that, according to the Apostle, she may render to God a reasonable service (ibid. XII, 1), and may order the whole course of her life according to His judgment.

It is impossible for anyone to please a person if she does not know what pleases him. It can even happen that, in her desire to obey, she offends the one whom she has not previously learned how to obey. And just as doing the Lord’s will is greater than knowing it, so knowing it comes before doing it. The former rightly precedes; the latter follows in order.

Hence the Prophet says:

> “And you, Israel, do not be ignorant.”

And blessed Paul says:

> “But whoever is ignorant will be unknown.”

And elsewhere:

> “Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is” (Eph. V, 17).

The beginning of obedience is the desire to know what is commanded; learning what you are to do is itself part of obedience.

Know, therefore, that in the divine Scriptures—through which alone you can fully understand God’s will—some things are forbidden, some permitted, and some recommended. Evil things are forbidden; good things are commanded; intermediate things are permitted; perfect things are recommended.

All sin is contained in the first two categories, for in both the command of God is present. To forbid is itself an act of the one who commands.

For righteousness is generally commanded to everyone. The Savior, briefly but most fully comprehending it in the Gospel, says:

> “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. VII, 12).

That is, let us inflict no evil upon others, but render every good thing, because we wish both of these to be observed toward us by others. This judgment binds everyone equally by the force of its command. No one at all may transgress what has been commanded to everyone. It is open contempt of God either to do what has been forbidden or not to do what has been commanded.

The other two matters that follow—one being permitted and the other recommended—have been left to our power, so that we may either use what is permitted with lesser glory or, for a greater reward, reject even what has been permitted to us.

Marriage, the eating of meat, and wine are permitted; but abstinence from all these is recommended as the more perfect counsel. The permission of marriage contributes to the honor of virginity, and the concession of food makes the virtue of abstinence more illustrious.

You have despised, O virgin, marriage that was lawful for you, before it was despised. Burning with love for a greater reward, you vowed to God a virginity that was not commanded but praised, and, following the Apostle’s counsel, you made your law broader.

Entering the arena of the contest, you considered not so much the labor of the race as the prize of victory. You had read, I believe, that Gospel proclamation of perpetual chastity, and the Lord’s own word had kindled you to love the preservation of virginity. He praised Peter’s judgment concerning it by the very greatness and difficulty of the matter, and, promising the kingdom of heaven to voluntary eunuchs, said:

> “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12).

I do not command or impose so great a matter; I offer it. I do not compel anyone to it; I summon them.

Although the saying may appear to concern only men, it is not spoken only to men; the palm of virginity is promised equally to both sexes. And the Apostle says that he has no command of the Lord concerning virgins [Alt. *of God*], but gives advice. Thus he says:

> “Do you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

**CHAPTER X.**—Having therefore followed the counsel of perfection and undertaken the blessedness of a special commitment, preserve the general commandment.

I have said this, and now repeat it: in the matter of justice we all have one common obligation. Virgin, widow, married woman, and persons of the highest, middle, and lowest rank are equally commanded to fulfill the precepts. The person who proposes to do more than the law requires is not thereby released from the law. Indeed, no one ought more carefully to avoid what is unlawful than the one who rejects what was permitted.

Nor does anyone promise to fulfill the commandments so completely as the person who rises above the commandments out of love for perfection. By deciding to do more than was commanded, she shows that the commandment was less than she was capable of doing.

Moreover, if someone professes such great obedience that she willingly listens even to divine counsel, how could she fail to listen to a commandment? One matter belongs to choice [Augustine: *perfection*]; the other to necessity.

Of virginity it is said:

> “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matt. VII, 19).

But of justice it is not said, “Let the one who is able do it.” Rather:

> “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

Consider, I ask, how far a command differs from counsel. There counsel excludes some people; here the command embraces everyone. There a reward is proposed; here a punishment. There it invites you to act; here it threatens you if you do not act.

Distinguishing these matters with the best judgment, observe what you offer and observe what you owe. Rather, since you now owe both—virginity, which you freely offered to God, and justice, which He Himself commanded—pay both in full.

That servant pleases the Lord who voluntarily undertakes some work while still accomplishing what has been commanded; who does not do one thing instead of another, but both; who does not exchange one obedience for another, but adds obedience.

Nor should you be deceived by the examples of those women who applaud themselves for chastity alone and, in order to follow their own desires [Augustine: *pleasures*], reject the will of God. They wish to offer the good of perpetual chastity not together with justice but instead of justice, and to count the reward of virginity as compensation for their sins. They ask impunity as their reward—or, with still more shameless madness, think that they ought to be crowned and preferred to others in the kingdom of heaven, although by transgressing the commandments they have closed the kingdom of heaven against themselves.

Christ says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Let them remember that the foolish virgins will be driven back from the bridegroom’s doors, and that it will be said to them:

> “I do not know you.”

They must be joined to those of whom the Lord Himself says:

> “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and perform many miracles in your name?’ And then I shall confess to them: ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’” (Luke XIII, 26–27).

But you must enter by a very different road. Having trampled underfoot love of the world, always thinking about the things of God, you wish to show yourself an apostolic virgin, holy in spirit as well as in body, awaiting the Lord’s coming. You continually pour the oil of holy works into the lamp of your soul, and, joined to the wise virgins, prepare yourself to go out to meet the bridegroom.

You must flee that broad road, worn down by the procession of the many who go to destruction. You must follow the narrow path of that constricted way which few find, leading to eternal life.

You have already laid aside the greatest impediments, and at your first conversion immediately conquered whatever either delays or turns back the course of spiritual life. You rejected the pleasures of marriage, concern for offspring, the allurements of luxury, the pomp of the world, the desire for wealth, and with Paul you can say:

> “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

What must its perfection be, when its beginning is such? Bring this virtue, this spirit, to the rest of your life as well. By that force of mind with which you drove away the occasions of vice, now reject the vices themselves. Let virginity be adorned with holiness of conduct, and let perfection of life follow a perfect commitment.

Certainly, if secular life had pleased you, you would have taken care that no one should surpass you in wealth, bodily adornment, the pomp [Alt. *abundance*] of all things, or honor. Now, since a different pursuit desires a different life [Alt. *since diversity of pursuits desires a different life*], take care that no one surpass you in living well; that no one excel you in holiness of conduct; that no one be preferred to you in virtue.

In the matters we mentioned earlier, it was not within your power either to surpass everyone or to be surpassed by no one. All those things are sought from outside, and whatever is hoped for from elsewhere is not one’s own. These things, however, are in your power and truly your own. They do not come from outside but are generated within the heart itself.

Those external goods are not found by everyone who seeks them, nor does the one who finds them always retain them, since fortune can both lend and take them away. These goods, however, everyone who seeks finds, and the one who finds them never fears that they will be taken away. These alone are good things, which without the will we neither ever find nor lose.

**CHAPTER XI.**—Here, then, you have grounds on which you may rightly be preferred to others—indeed, here especially. Bodily nobility and wealth are understood to belong to your family, not to you. No one but yourself can confer spiritual riches upon you.

In these matters, therefore, you are rightly to be praised; in these you are deservedly to be preferred to others, since they cannot exist except from you and in you.

Is this the only life that has no contest concerning progress, in which each person need only remain where she began and strive toward nothing greater with any desire for increase? When people are not satisfied with progress in all the pursuits of the world, will it be sufficient here merely to have begun?

We are most fervent in earthly matters and most cold in heavenly ones. Exhibiting the greatest eagerness in small things, we grow sluggish toward greater ones.

It is shameful to consider how great is the fervor in the world, and with what care each human pursuit strives daily toward greater perfection. The ardor for learning is extinguished by no age; rather, to use the saying of a secular author, it is inflamed all the more by age itself. The love of wealth is insatiable, and the desire for honors does not know how to be satisfied. Things destined soon to end are sought without end.

We, however, neglect divine wisdom, heavenly riches, and immortal honors through a kind of sluggish indifference. We either do not even touch spiritual riches, or, if we taste them lightly, immediately think ourselves satisfied.

Divine Wisdom invites us otherwise to her feasts. She says:

> “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Eccl. XXIV, 29).

No one is ever filled by such banquets, nor does anyone ever suffer disgust from satiety. The more each person drinks from them, the more capable—and the more eager—he or she will become.

The Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V, 6).

He wishes us always to hunger and thirst for justice in this life, so that in the future we may be filled by the recompense of justice.

**CHAPTER XII.**—The force of the words themselves must be considered, and we must desire justice in the way that food or drink is desired in hunger or thirst. This must be said generally to all who desire the promises of immortal life.

It is now your responsibility to judge how much you ought to accomplish in your soul, since, out of desire for a greater reward, you have proposed to do more than it is necessary for others to do.

The Apostle, defining Christ’s virgin, separated her far from the married woman and divided the merit of singleness from that of marriage by assigning them different pursuits:

> “The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. VII, 32–34).

The woman who is holy in body and spirit sins neither in her limbs nor in her mind. But sin need not occur only in the matter of chastity; it can occur in any area of justice.

For even if a woman is a virgin in body and a virgin in spirit, yet sins with her hands, eyes, ears, or tongue, how can she be called holy in body [Alt. omits *and*]? Further, if she is infected with hatred, envy, greed, or anger, how does she possess holiness in spirit?

And if a married woman, who thinks through her love of marriage how she may please her husband (ibid. VII, 34), and how much she may leave to her children, and who, bound by various concerns of the world, looks less often toward the will of God, nevertheless cannot excuse herself from sins, what will the virgin do, who, released and free from all the impediments of this world, has entered a kind of school of chastity?

**CHAPTER XIII.**—If, then, you wish your conduct to equal the greatness of your commitment and to be joined to God in every respect; if you wish to make Christ’s easy and gentle yoke still easier and gentler for yourself, now above all devote care to the blessed life.

Now strive so that the warm faith of your recent conversion may always be kindled by a new ardor, and so that, while you are still young, the practice of holy conduct may more easily take root.

Whatever you establish in yourself at first will remain, and the rest of your life will proceed according to the rule of your beginnings. The end must be considered at the very beginning. If you wish to reach that final day in a certain condition, strive already now to be such.

Habit is what nourishes either vices or virtues, and it has the greatest force when it has grown together with a person from the beginning of life. The earliest years are best for forming character. They contain [Alt. *also*] something slow and pliant that can easily be shaped and drawn according to the will of the one who wishes to form it. In almost everything, whatever is tender is accustomed to a pattern more quickly.

Young trees, still scarcely firmly rooted, are easy to bend in any direction while they remain responsive to every movement. Once nature has generally bent them, they are quickly straightened according to the cultivator’s will. Young animals, still [Alt. adds *still*] tender and at the beginning of life, are usually tamed without labor. The more quickly they are weaned from the freedom of wandering, the more easily they become accustomed either to the yoke on their necks or to the bit in their mouths.

Even the study of letters is more readily implanted in tender minds. Whatever first settles in the mind generally takes deep root in the senses.

The same principle has great force in the practice of living well. While age is still pliable and the mind easy to guide, the habit of goodness must be exercised and strengthened through constant meditation. The mind must be occupied with the best things, and the practice of holy conduct must be implanted more deeply.

Then the mind rises to the summit of perfection and, by the benefit of long habit, makes use of its ability to live well. Even as it admires its own virtues, it will somehow think within itself that what it has learned was born in it [Alt. *what it is learning was born in it*].

## Chapter XIV

Consider, I beg you, how much sanctity your grandmother and mother expect from you. They think that you have been born to your family as some new and distinguished light; now they have transferred all the concern of their hearts to you alone and inflame the course of your chosen purpose with remarkable zeal and favor. Since they themselves formed you toward honorable conduct from your earliest age, they now desire to be surpassed by you and consider your victory their own praise. Their outstanding faith toward God shone forth especially in your profession, when, having learned that you no longer wished to marry, although you had already been prepared for marriage, they immediately encouraged you toward what you had chosen with astonishing speed of assent. They strengthened your hesitant decision, appropriate to your age, by the authority of their own will, and made your vow their common vow. Although they have seen many of their family attain the highest rank of distinction, they have never rejoiced over anyone as they have over you. For they had seen nothing so great, nothing so illustrious in anyone. You alone have provided your family with what it had lacked for many generations.

Although the male sex may have produced memorable consulships, and the annals of the highest order may have frequently heard the names of an illustrious family, nevertheless nothing in your family has ever been more distinguished than this honor of yours, which has been inserted not into a bodily register [variant: “belly”], but into the book of immortal remembrance.

When they have received theatrical applause throughout the world, and the delighted crowd has expressed, with astonishing unanimity of acclamation, its admiration for the distinguished achievements of the consuls, the glory of your honor is nevertheless far greater: it has brought joy in heaven and gladness to the angels. Through you, little prostitutes are not enriched, but the virgins of Christ are fed; it is not a hunter or charioteer who grows wealthy, but the poor of Christ who are sustained.

For their consulships, the various provinces of the entire world to which the power of your household extends sent foreign beasts and unknown animals, destined to stain the cruel arena with their own blood or that of human beings. To you, however, chosen virgins are sent, whom you may offer as a most precious gift to God and, by your example, summon to perpetual chastity, so that they may serve not you but God together with you.

The glory of your profession has been made known everywhere by widespread report, and the whole world has exulted at your way of life [variant: conversion] so greatly that what, in their immense joy, people could scarcely yet believe, they seem always to have desired. Because of these beginnings, and because they are deeply captivated by the fragrance of your reputation, everyone eagerly desires to hear something extraordinary about you. Those who have learned the excellence of your departure [i.e. your renunciation] now await your way of life.

Imagine that everyone’s mouths and eyes are now turned toward you, and that the whole world has gathered to watch your life. Take care not to offend, through yourself, the hearts of so many, nor to let them find in you less than they seek.

But why am I speaking to you about human beings, and turning their expectation of you into an exhortation to you? God himself, ruler and Lord of all, watches your contest with the entire army of angels. As you fight against the devil, he prepares for you the crown of eternity and makes the heavenly reward an incentive to victory. Consider what spirit and what courage you ought to display before so great a spectacle, and measure the greatness of the contest by the dignity of those who watch.

## Chapter XV

Therefore, as you enter this contest, let this be your chief concern: first, girded for battle, to conquer the war of destruction by courage, and to swear allegiance to all the commandments of God against the camp of the devil—not merely to avoid what is forbidden, but to fulfill what is commanded.

For it is not enough for you to be inactive in evil if you are inactive in good. The law of God is distinguished by a twofold kind of commandment: it forbids evil and orders good, and it forbids contempt of itself on either side. The servant who does what is forbidden has not alone despised his master; so has the one who has not done what was commanded.

We stated shortly before: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 7:19). Are we flattering ourselves if we are not weighed down by evil fruits, when we shall be condemned if we remain barren of good ones (John 15:2)? In accordance with this understanding, the Father will cut away every branch in the Son that bears no fruit. And the one who hid the talent he had received in a cloth, as a useless and wicked servant, is condemned by the Lord (Matt. 25:30). It is culpable not only to diminish, but also not to increase.

Do not think that any commandments should be despised because they are lighter. The greatest and the smallest have alike been commanded by God, and contempt for any commandment is an insult to the one who commanded it. Hence blessed Paul cries out and teaches: “Do everything without murmuring and hesitation, so that you may be blameless and simple, as immaculate children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation; among them you shine like lights in this world” (Phil. 2:14–15).

## Chapter XVI

Let us pause here for a little while, virgin, and weigh, word by word, the most precious pearls with which the bride of Christ must be adorned.

“Do everything,” he says. We must not choose certain commandments of God according to our own judgment, as though they were ours to select, but fulfill them all without exception. Nor should we despise any of his commandments as cheap and insignificant gifts; rather, in everything we must look to the majesty of the one who commands.

No commandment of God can seem contemptible to us if we always consider its author—“without murmuring and hesitation.” We see lowly and obscure masters openly despised by their little servants, who commonly resist even their smallest commands to their faces. But this is no longer permitted in the case of noble persons; the more powerful the masters, the more ready the servants are to obey. When they give more difficult orders, they are listened to more willingly.

Certainly, at a king’s command everyone is so prepared and drawn up for obedience that they even desire to be ordered. They think not only that they will deserve well if they do what is commanded, but, as though they had already earned what they were ordered to do, they regard service as a benefit, in accordance with the dignity of the one giving the command.

Yet God himself—eternal majesty, ineffable and immeasurable power—sends us the sacred writings and the letters of his commandments, which truly deserve adoration, and we do not immediately receive them with joy and reverence. We do not consider it a great benefit that the command of so great and illustrious a power has been given, especially since the advantage of the one who commands is not sought, but the benefit of the one who obeys.

On the contrary, with a disdainful and negligent spirit, after the manner of proud and wicked servants, we protest to the face of the Lord and say: “It is hard; it is difficult; we cannot. We are human beings, surrounded by fragile flesh.”

O blind madness! O profane presumption! We charge the God of knowledge with a twofold ignorance, making him appear not to know what he made or what he commanded—as though, forgetting human frailty, of which he himself is the author, he had imposed on humanity commandments that it could not bear.

At the same time—shameful crime!—we ascribe injustice to the just and cruelty to the merciful. First we complain that he commanded something impossible; then we judge that a human being should be condemned by him for things that he could not avoid. Thus, which is even sacrilegious to imagine, God appears to have sought not so much our salvation as our punishment.

Therefore the Apostle, knowing that the Lord of justice and majesty has commanded nothing impossible, removes from us the fault of murmuring. Murmuring ordinarily arises when what is commanded is unjust or when the person commanding is insufficiently worthy. Why do we argue uselessly and oppose the fragility of nature to the one who commands? No one knows the measure of our strength better than the one who gave us those very powers. No one understands better how much we can do than the one who granted us the power itself to act.

He who is just could not have wished to command anything impossible; and he who is merciful could not have intended to condemn a human being for what that person could not avoid.

## Chapter XVII

He continues: “So that you may be blameless and simple”—for complete perfection of conduct. This one word could be sufficient, since God also commands that it be sought in the choice of a bishop. For how circumspect and holy is the life that incurs no reproach! Who can be holier than the person who, holding to the virtue of true simplicity, never promises one thing in the heart while lying about another with mouth and face?

“As immaculate children of God.” There is no more powerful exhortation than that by which divine Scripture calls us children of God. Who would not be ashamed and afraid to do something unworthy of so great a father, so that one who is called a child of God might himself become a servant of vice? For this reason it adds, “that we may be immaculate.” It is not fitting that the children of God should bear the stain of sin, since God himself is the source of justice.

“In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation”—that is: although an infinite multitude of sinners surrounds you, and examples of vice are innumerable, you must nevertheless remember your heavenly birth in such a way that, while living among the wicked, you overcome every evil.

“Among them you shine,” he says, “like lights in this world.” We read again in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). Life is compared with the reward, so that those who are to be granted the sun’s radiance in the future may already shine here with a similar brightness of justice and illuminate the blindness of unbelievers through works of holiness.

To this passage the meaning should be applied that the same Apostle explains to the Corinthians: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory, and so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41–42). In the kingdom of heaven there are different dwellings according to the merits of each person. The diversity of works produces a diversity of rewards: as much as someone shines here in holiness, so much will that person shine there in honor.

Now, therefore, direct the gaze of your mind toward complete perfection of conduct, and prepare a heavenly life for a heavenly reward. Let the holiness of the virgin shine before all, bright as a star, and let it display the greatness of the future reward through the newness of her way of life.

Your course in good things is easier, since the habit of evil does not hold your mind captive. Nor are we afraid that vices will delay you from virtues and that the devil’s malignant seeds will destroy Christ’s harvest. For if even those who, through a long practice of sinning, have in some manner buried the good of nature can be restored through repentance, extinguish one habit by another after changing their will concerning their way of life, and become among the best from being among the worst, how much more can you overcome those things by which you have not been overcome? You do not need so much to drive out vices as to reject them. It is certainly easier not to admit them than to lay them aside once admitted.

## Chapter XVIII

Nor are vices so attractive that we ought to prefer them to virtues, since not all of them possess the allure of pleasure, and since most people reject even those that seem sweetest.

Of all vices, there are two that most deceive human beings through the pleasure they provide: gluttony and lust. The more difficult they are to renounce, the sweeter it is to indulge in them.
