Yet we have seen many trample these vices—so troublesome and so dangerous because of their pleasure—in such a way that they remained virgins throughout their lives in complete abstinence.

I say nothing of those who, after a long period of luxury [variant: excess] and an ingrained practice of lust, have devoted themselves to chastity and self-control and transformed both vices through the virtue opposed to them.

Other vices have a very different character. Although they contain no pleasure, they contain a great deal of bitterness; and although they are much easier to avoid, you will rarely find anyone who avoids them.

What pleasure, I ask you, does envy provide to the envious person, whom envy itself tears apart with hidden claws of conscience and for whom another’s happiness becomes a torment? What reward does another person gain from hatred except dreadful darkness of soul and the horror of a disordered mind? With a face and spirit always sorrowful, that person tortures himself through the desire to harm another.

What does rage contribute to the angry person? Agitated by the savage goads of conscience, rage drives the person from all judgment and reason, so that, while angry, he is thought to be insane. Run through each vice in the same way, and you will find as many torments of the soul as there are vices. They can certainly be overcome all the more easily because they entice us with no pleasure.

How much more difficult and harsh it is—to say nothing of the labor of chastity—to abstain from wine and meat, even from oil itself, and sometimes scarcely to take cheap food after two or even three days; to have limbs broken by fasts and vigils, to reject the comforts of the bath, to deny the body necessities, and to impose a kind of force upon nature! Bring the same greatness of spirit to other matters, and see what you cannot accomplish.

But we—shame on us!—through a certain pleasure in sin, show a kind of force of our nature in some things, while in others we become completely sluggish. We who have rejected bodily pleasures for love of the virtues then, through love of vices, take upon ourselves their torments. We yield so completely to our evils that we do not even think they can be laid aside.

What, I ask, is this judgment? What new way of life is this? I confidently undertake difficult things full of labor, yet believe that easier things cannot be done. I conquer the greatest things while being conquered by small ones. I tirelessly overcome lofty and arduous matters, yet fail when I come to level ground. I willingly flee what gives pleasure, yet refuse to avoid what causes torment.

But this belongs to those who, having despised the will of God, seek only what more easily finds praise and quickly becomes famous, while neglecting the good qualities of character that are more private.

You, however, who have trampled the world and its desires so that, after trampling it, you might make for yourself a step by which to ascend to heaven, should not seek the world’s glory. Strive to please the one who is often displeased by what pleases human beings and who will judge the judgments of human beings.

Your abstinence and fasting are all the more pleasing to God when they are offered together with holy conduct, so that what in others are screens for vices may in you be ornaments of virtues.

## Chapter XIX

Consider, I beg you, the very dignity by which you have been honored before God: through baptism you were reborn as a daughter of God, and then, through the consecration of virginity, you began to be the bride of Christ. Each of these honors should urge you to be attentive to your chosen purpose.

There should be no room for negligence where such distinguished things must be preserved. The more precious a garment is, the more anxiously it is guarded from a stain [variant: “A more precious garment is guarded with more anxious care”]. A gem acquired at great cost in gold is possessed with greater vigilance, and in general all great things are kept with great care.

Therefore, if you wish to guard yourself well, you must always reflect on the value of your honor. Each person uses something more carelessly the cheaper he considers it. For no other reason is the name “children of God” so frequently imposed upon us in the divine Scriptures, as when the prophet says: “And I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,” says the Lord Almighty (Phil. 3:17). And the Apostle says: “Be imitators of God, as dearly loved children.” Blessed John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy” (1 John 3:2–3).

He wishes to impress upon us frequently the dignity of the heavenly teaching with which we have been endowed and to make our honor a source of shame concerning sin. Thus the Lord himself, calling us to perfect kindness, says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you,” and again: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:45).

Nothing makes human beings beloved of God in such a way as the kindness of the mind and the goodness that ought to be so abundant in a Christian that it extends even to the wicked. Such a person imitates God’s benevolence, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Rom. 12:13).

Therefore, above all, let it be far from you to harm anyone even in word. Strive to benefit everyone in every way you can, and, without returning evil for evil, repay evil with good, as the Apostle says.

May detraction never proceed from a virgin’s mouth. It belongs to thoroughly base people, and to those who seek their own praise, to make others base, because they think they are praised by another’s criticism. Those who cannot please through their own merit wish to please by comparison with worse people.

I have said too little: not only should you yourself not slander, but you should never believe the person who slanders. This is a very wicked vice, which makes another person appear contemptible. Flee detraction no less with your ears than with your tongue.

Remember Scripture, which says: “You shall not agree with those who disparage your neighbor, and you shall not take upon yourself his sin” (Lev. 19:18). And elsewhere: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue” (Eccl. 28:35).

The listener is an accuser, for he makes the slanderer. If he turns away his ears, contracts his face, and restrains his eyes by refusing assent, then, even while silent, he rebukes the evil speaker, so that the speaker may learn not to say willingly what he has learned is not willingly heard.

Set a sufficiently careful guard over your mouth. There is nothing in us by which we can sin more easily than by the tongue. Hence Saint James declares that the perfect person is the one who does not offend in speech (James 3:2). Scripture says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Wis. 1:11).

Let your tongue know neither how to lie, nor to curse, nor to swear. “The mouth that lies kills the soul,” and those who curse “will not possess the kingdom of God,” according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 5:11). Christ himself forbade swearing when he said: “But I say to you, do not swear at all.” And again: “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matt. 5:34, 37).

The Apostle, briefly cutting away the vices of the mouth, says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. 4:29).

Let a virgin’s speech be prudent [variant: modest], restrained, and rare—valuable not so much for eloquence as for modesty. Let everyone admire your modesty when you are silent and your prudence when you speak. Let your speech always be gentle and peaceful. Let sweetness joined with seriousness and wisdom joined with modesty adorn it. Let the manner of silence and speech be steady, measured, and most pleasing when appropriate.

The mouth of a virgin should never speak when it would have been better to remain silent. She must speak with great caution, since not only wicked speech but also idle speech must be avoided.

## Chapter XX

Let your highest and most complete knowledge be the ability to distinguish vices and virtues. Although they are always opposed to one another, some of them are joined by such a great resemblance that they can scarcely be distinguished at all.

How many people regard arrogance as liberty, accept flattery in place of humility, embrace malice under the name of prudence, and give foolishness the name of simplicity! Deceived by this deceptive and most pernicious resemblance, they glory in vices as though they were virtues.

Although you must separate all these things with the most subtle understanding and pursue every virtue along its proper lines without ever departing from them, you must especially flee counterfeit humility and follow the humility that is genuine, the humility Christ taught, in which no pride is concealed.

Many follow the shadow of this virtue; few follow its truth. It is very easy to wear a somewhat plain garment, offer a more submissive greeting, kiss hands and knees, bow the head toward the ground, lower the eyes, promise humility and gentleness, break one’s speech into a slow and thin voice, sigh frequently, and proclaim oneself a sinner and wretch at every word.

Yet if one is offended by even a slight remark, one immediately raises the eyebrow, lifts the neck, and suddenly changes that delicate tone of voice into an insane shout.

Christ taught us another kind of humility when he exhorted us to imitate him, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). When he was cursed, he did not curse; when he suffered, he did not threaten.

Blessed Peter points out this humility to us: “Be compassionate and humble, not repaying evil for evil or abuse for abuse” (1 Pet. 2:22).

Let all verbal fabrications be removed; let simulated gestures cease, together with the gentle speech that precedes an occasion for testing. Patience under insult reveals the truly humble person.

Therefore, let there never be room in your mind for any vice. Let there be nothing proud in you, nothing arrogant, nothing, finally, disdainful. Before God nothing is more exalted than humility.

He speaks through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest my gaze, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

And let your spirit never blaze into anger, which is the seedbed of hatred. Let such fear of God fill your mind that you do not dare to become angry at all, and let fear overcome anger.

The blessed Apostle, cleansing our soul and preparing it as a dwelling place for God, cries out and says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Eph. 4:31).

## Chapter XXI

Beware of flatterers as enemies. Their words are smooth as oil, but they themselves are darts. By false praises they corrupt unstable souls and inflict a flattering wound upon minds that are too ready to believe [variant: “insert a flattering wound into”].

This vice has grown in our age and has reached its final limit; it can no longer increase. We have all devoted ourselves to this school and discipline, thinking it a duty to deceive. What we ourselves willingly receive from others, we offer to others as a sort of gift. In the hope of receiving praise, we first praise those from whom we wish to be praised.

Often we resist the words of flatterers to their faces while secretly favoring them in our minds, and we consider ourselves to have gained the greatest benefit if we are praised even with false praises. We do not consider what we actually are, but what we appear to others to be. Thus matters have reached the point that, neglecting the truth of merit, we care only about reputation, seeking testimony to our life not from our conscience but from public opinion.

Blessed is the mind that perfectly conquers this vice, neither flattering anyone nor believing the flatterer; that neither deceives another nor is itself deceived; that never commits or suffers this evil.

Let nothing false ever be in you, nothing at all painted over. Consider your conscience, which is certainly always open to God, as though you were living among a multitude. Never hold one thing in your heart and utter another with your mouth [variant: “intend one thing in your heart and present another with your mouth”]. Whatever you are ashamed to say, be ashamed even to think.

It is already known and widely proclaimed how useful and necessary the virtue of fasting and abstinence is for this purpose, especially in those years in which the body contains greater heat. Not eating meat or drinking wine has been praised by the Apostle (Rom. 12:15, 21). Whatever can inflame the body and provide fuel for pleasure must be avoided for love of chastity.

Nevertheless, we do not want you to be burdened by this matter with such great labor that you immediately collapse beneath the load. Many, lacking consideration for the measure of their strength because of excessive fervor of mind, have suddenly fallen, and have almost attained weakness rather than holiness from their chosen purpose.

The best course in everything is moderation, and measure is praiseworthy everywhere. The body must not be broken but governed. Therefore let your fasts be moderate, holy, and simple, practiced with complete humility of mind. Let them weaken the body without elevating the spirit; let a practice intended for humility not produce pride, and let vices not arise from virtue.

“I,” he says, “when they troubled me, clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 35:13). The cheapness of clothing, the meagerness of food, and the weariness of fasting should extinguish, not nourish, pride.

Who would turn a remedy into a wound? Who would harm what is healthy by means of the very things by which what is wounded ought to be healed? Or what hope of salvation will remain if the remedies of the soul become poisons?

## Chapter XXII

Let works of mercy commend the labor of your fasting, and let your abstinence become more pleasing through feeding the poor. The Lord speaks through the prophet: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). In the Gospel of Christ we read: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

But I ask that your grandmother and mother undertake this concern in your place. Let them perform these duties for you. Let them raise your treasure to heaven. Let it be their task to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, receive strangers under their roof, and, in hope of an eternal reward, lend at interest to Christ in the poor—for he said: “Whatever you have done for one of the least of these my brothers, you have done for me” (Matt. 25:45).

As for you, especially while your mind is maturing in its chosen purpose, you must withdraw from all occupations and devote every effort and every concern to the adornment of your character. You must give yourself to these things and occupy your entire mind with them, so that you do not feel yourself to be rich or a mistress.

Remember your nobility only for this purpose: that you may contend with the distinction of your lineage through the holiness of your conduct, and that, together with the nobility of your body, you may advance nobler through the virtue of your mind. Glory more in that nobility which makes people children of God and coheirs with Christ.

If you always look toward this, then, while believing that you possess the greater joy, you will cease to glory in what is lesser. Let all the dignity of your distinguished lineage and the illustrious honor of Anician blood be transferred to the soul.

Let that person be distinguished, exalted, and noble; let that person think that he preserves his complete nobility if he disdains to serve vices and is not overcome by them: “For by whatever anyone is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:15).

What slavery of the mind is more disgraceful or more shameful than when hatred dominates it, or envy reigns in it? What is more shameful than when greed possesses it, anger holds it captive, or the remaining vices claim it for themselves?

No one should flatter himself about the nobility of his lineage if, in the better part of himself, he is a slave. It is much more disgraceful to serve in the mind than in the body.

I think it unnecessary to advise you how sparing and infrequent you should be in going out, since even the secular propriety with which you were trained from childhood has taught you this, and you easily understand that it must be observed much more in this life, where privacy is especially fitting.

I do advise you to impose a definite limit even on the greetings that are to be offered to you in your chamber. They should not be excessive or daily, lest they seem to provide not so much courtesy as disturbance.

## Chapter XXIII

Although you ought to consecrate every moment of your life to divine work, and although no hour at all should be empty of spiritual progress, since you must meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1), nevertheless there should be a fixed and appointed number of hours in which you may devote yourself more fully to God and which may hold you, as though by a law, to the highest concentration of mind.

It is therefore best to assign the morning to this work—that is, the better part of the day—and until the third hour to exercise the soul, daily contending in the heavenly contest, as in the training ground of a spiritual gymnasium.

During these hours each day, pray in a more secluded part of the house, with the door of your room closed (Matt. 6:6). Establish solitude for yourself even in the city [variant: world], and, withdrawing for a little while from human beings, join yourself more closely to God. When you return to the sight of your household, display the fruit of reading and prayer.

For in this solitude you should do nothing more than nourish your soul with divine words and fill it with them as with richer food, enough to sustain it throughout the entire day.

Read the sacred Scriptures in such a way that you always remember that they are the words of God, who commands that his law be not only known but also fulfilled. It is of no benefit to learn what must be done and not do it.

You will use divine reading best if you employ it as a mirror, so that the soul may look upon itself there as in an image and either correct whatever is ugly or adorn what is beautiful still more.

Let prayer frequently interrupt reading, and let the grateful alternation of holy work kindle the soul as it continually clings to God.

Now let the order of heavenly history instruct you; now let the sacred song of David delight you; now let the Wisdom of Solomon educate you; now let the admonitions of the prophets stir you to fear of the Lord; now let evangelical and apostolic perfection unite you to Christ in complete holiness of conduct.

Fix deeply in your memory the things that must be prepared, and preserve them through continual meditation. Frequently review the things that must be matured, so that this divine study and heavenly school may at once adorn the virgin’s character and understanding and hand on to you holiness together with wisdom.

Hence Scripture says: “Those who seek God will find wisdom together with justice.”

Let the reading itself be moderate, and let counsel—not weariness—bring it to an end. Just as immoderate fasts, the fervor of abstinence, and excessive, disordered vigils are condemned as intemperance, and by their very excess produce the result that afterward these practices cannot be performed even moderately, so excessive devotion to reading falls under the charge of intemperance; what is praiseworthy in its proper time becomes blameworthy through excess.

## Chapter XXIV

In general, but briefly and concisely, this must be said: even in good things, whatever exceeds measure is a vice.

Great—very great, I say—and requiring immense zeal is the discipline of a perfect life and consummate wisdom: to know what you should pursue, and in what manner, and to put judgment before every action, doing nothing that you will regret having done.

Within the space of a single hour, one can change one’s practice: fasting, abstaining, singing psalms, and keeping vigil require not so much effort as willingness. When someone begins any of these things, that person is immediately perfect in them as soon as he wills it. Indeed, those who bring the fresh strength of their bodies from the world into their chosen purpose can do these things more easily.

But to change one’s character, to shape each virtue of the mind within oneself, and to perfect it requires great zeal and long habit. Thus many of us grow old in our chosen purpose and do not possess the very things for which we came to that purpose.

Your way of life, however, must be new: remarkable seriousness, patience, gentleness, and devotion. Whatever is holier and more perfect, whatever can commend you more to God and make you greater in heaven, pursue and embrace continually (1 Cor. 7:34).

Nothing should be more richly adorned than the bride of Christ. The greater the one whom you must please, the greater must be your eagerness to please him.

The virgins of the world who prepare themselves for marriage, and who prefer to follow the Apostle’s indulgence rather than his counsel, embracing more readily the remedy for incontinence than the reward of continence, strive with astonishing care to shape themselves so as to please their bridegrooms and incite them more strongly to love them. They enhance the natural beauty of their bodies through the art of adornment.

This is their chief daily concern: to color their faces with suitable cosmetics, entwine their hair with gold, make burning stones from shells an ornament for the head, hang wealth from their ears, adorn their arms and sides with necklaces, and let gems enclosed in gold descend from the neck to the breast.

Your bridegroom requires no less an adornment. After cleansing the whole Church with the bath of saving water and presenting her without spot or wrinkle, he desires each day to make her more beautiful, so that, once cleansed from vices and sins, she may always be adorned with the beauty of virtues (Eph. 5:26–27).

And if he requires this from the whole Church, which includes widows and married women, how much, do you think, does he expect from a virgin, who seems to have been chosen as a more august flower from this most beautiful adornment of the Church?

Therefore assume all the adornment by which you can please Christ. Believe your face beautiful enough for God if you do not strive to appear beautiful to human beings.

Preserve the ornament of your head that you acquired through the sacrament of chrism, when, as a mystery of the heavenly kingdom, a diadem of royal anointing was placed upon you.

The finest ornaments for the ears are the words of God. A virgin’s hearing should be prepared for these alone and should prefer them to the most precious stones.

Let every limb be adorned with works of holiness, and let the entire beauty of a virginal soul shine with the varied brilliance of virtues, like a jeweled necklace.

Then the king will truly desire your beauty and will say to you: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no spot in you” (Song 5:7).

These ornaments I have described will also be your greatest defenses. They can adorn you before God and arm you against the devil, who sometimes enters the soul through some seemingly trivial vice. If the defenses of the virtues do not resist him, he drives us from our place and immediately changes from an enemy into a master.

For this reason Scripture exhorts us and says: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place” (Eccl. 10:4).

## Chapter XXV

From the time when you were first consecrated to the Lord through your profession of virginity, the adversary’s hatred toward you has grown. And since he regards another’s gains as his own losses, he considers himself to have lost whatever he grieves that you will possess. You need great vigilance and great care; and the more anxiously must the enemy be guarded against, the richer you have begun to be with God.

An empty and naked traveler does not fear the ambushes of a robber. A poor man sleeps securely from nocturnal thieves, even if he does not fortify his locks. But a rich man’s possessions constantly make him imagine the robber’s approach, and through continual anxiety they deprive him of sleep at night. Thus your riches also—the heavenly treasure—require this caution and protection. The richer you are, the more vigilant you must be. For whoever possesses more must fear more lest he lose it.

The author of envy does not cease to envy. And he who himself was once cast out by God is tormented by so much greater jealousy when he sees someone more distinguished with God. He who envied Eve the paradise—how much more does he envy you the kingdom of heaven!

Believe me, he now goes about everywhere, eager to devour you, as blessed Peter says (1 Pet. V, 8). He approaches like a roaring lion, or, as a deceitful enemy, examines everything, investigating all the entrances to your soul to see whether there is anything weak or insufficiently guarded through which he might creep in. Now he searches out everything, testing each thing, and seeks a place for the wound. You must carefully anticipate his ambushes, so that you may not be ignorant, with Paul, of his devices (2 Cor. II, 11).

Although the Apostle describes the terrifying powers and principalities of the devil, he nevertheless urges us to battle and discloses the enemy’s force in order to increase the soldiers’ vigilance. For he does not want us to be fearful, but prepared. Finally, he does not advise flight, but supplies weapons:

> “Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having been perfected in all things, to stand” (Eph. VI, 13).

Immediately, as he handed over each instrument of spiritual warfare, he added:

> “Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth; and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in the readiness of the gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, through every kind of reasoning and supplication.”

And since women too may triumph in this warfare, take up these weapons of Paul and, encouraged by so great a commander, confidently anticipate victory. For if you possess all these instruments, you will proceed securely to spiritual battle and will not fear the devil with his entire army.

> “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but they shall not come near you” (Ps. XCI, 7).

That blessed James also, a veteran soldier of Christ, promises us victory in this warfare with no less authority:

> “Submit yourselves to God; but resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. IV, 7).

He shows how we must resist the devil: if we are indeed subject to God, doing his will so that we may also deserve divine grace, we can more easily resist the wicked spirit through the help of the Holy Spirit.

He does not fight against us in open battle, nor engage us face-to-face publicly; rather, he conquers by deceit and fraud, and uses our own will against us. The adversary receives strength from our consent, and, as the saying goes, he slaughters us with our own sword.

An enemy who cannot conquer unless his opponent is willing is a weak enemy. Away from us be despair; away from our hearts let every fear of our adversaries depart. Let us not assist our adversaries, but conquer them. They give advice, certainly, but it is ours either to choose or reject what they suggest. For they do not harm us by compulsion, but by persuasion. They do not extort our consent, but seek it. Thus it is said even to Ananias:

> “Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V, 3).

The Apostle would never have charged him with this if the devil had done it without Ananias’s own will.

Eve too is condemned by the Lord for this reason (Gen. II): because she was overcome by one whom she could have overcome. She would not have deserved to be punished by the Lord for her injustice, though she had been defeated, unless she herself had been able to conquer.

## Chapter XXVI

The first piece of cunning belonging to this most wicked enemy, and an art full of deceit, is to weary inexperienced souls with thoughts and sometimes to bring sorrow concerning their very way of life to minds newly committed to the purpose, so that the soul may easily be deterred from advancing in a matter whose beginnings it has found bitter.

Thus he sometimes inserts such filthy and impious thoughts into the mind that the one being tempted, while believing that what he is thinking belongs to him, judges himself to have been made worse by the unclean spirit in relation to his purpose; and he believes that he possessed a much purer soul when he still loved worldly affairs. For the most cunning enemy wishes to turn the horror of their purpose into despair of holiness for those whom he envies, so that, while sadness besieges them, he may at least hold them back from progress, even if he does not turn them away from their purpose.

For this reason, above all, you must love the study of the sacred Scriptures: the soul must be illumined by divine utterances, and the darkness of the devil must be driven away by the flashing light of God’s word. For he quickly flees from the soul that divine speech illumines, which is always occupied with heavenly thoughts, in which God’s word is constant, and whose force the wicked spirit cannot endure.

For this reason blessed Paul compared it to a sword among the other instruments of spiritual warfare (Eph. V, 17).

[Col. 0041A] It is most useful and excellent for the soul to become accustomed, with ever-watchful and vigilant care, to distinguish its thoughts: and at the first movement of the mind [another reading: “the movement was lacking”], either to approve or reject what it is thinking, so that it may nourish good thoughts or immediately extinguish evil ones.

For this is the source of good, and the origin of sin; every great transgression begins in the heart with a thought [another reading: “the beginning is in thought, which”], which depicts each deed, as it were, on a tablet of the heart before it is performed. Whether it is an action or a word, it is first arranged in order to be produced, and what is going to happen is determined by the counsel of thoughts.

You see how, sometimes in a very brief moment, a person thinks each of these things and fulfills what has been thought; and nothing at all is done, whether by tongue, hand, or the other members, unless thoughts have first dictated it.

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “From the heart of man proceed evil thoughts, adultery, fornication, murders, thefts, false testimonies, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, the evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. These are the things that defile people” (Matt. XV, 19–20).

All your care, therefore, and all your attention must be directed to guarding the heart [another reading: “the guarding of the heart”]. You must especially watch for sin where it usually arises, and immediately resist the first appearance of temptation; extinguish evil before it grows.

For one must not await the growth of something that ought to be feared while it is small, and which is conquered all the more easily the sooner it is resisted. Therefore divine Scripture cries out:

> “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the issues of life” (Prov. IV, 21).

## Chapter XXVII

A distinction must be made between those thoughts that the will favors and embraces with affection, and those thoughts that habitually fly across the mind like a slight shadow, merely displaying themselves as they pass—thoughts which the Greeks call τύποι (*typoi*, “forms” or “impressions”)—or, again, between those thoughts that are suggested to a resisting and unwilling mind, against which the mind struggles and resists with a certain horror, grieving when they are admitted and rejoicing when they are expelled.

In those thoughts that lightly display themselves to the mind and, as it were, reveal themselves while fleeing, there is neither sin nor struggle at all. But in those with which the soul wrestles for some time, against which the will resists [another reading: “pleasure”], the contest is evenly matched. For either we consent and are defeated, or we reject them and conquer, gaining victory from the struggle [another reading: “from the fighting”].

Sin, therefore, exists only in that thought which has given the mind’s consent to the suggestion, which gently cherishes its evil and eagerly longs to break out into action. Even if such a thought, prevented by some accidental circumstance, does not fulfill the will, it is nevertheless condemned by the Lord as a criminal act, as we read in the Gospel:

> “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28).

Before God, to whom all things are known even before they happen, a fully formed will to do something is reckoned as the deed itself.

For this reason you must meditate on the holy Scriptures without interruption—for I often repeat what I always want to be done—and fill your mind with them. By removing the place of evil thoughts, occupy your soul with divine meanings; and show how much you love God by your love of his law.

Thus Scripture says:

> “Those who fear the Lord will seek what is pleasing to him, and those who love him will be filled with his law” (Eccl. II, 7).

Then, perceiving how much wisdom assists you in loving him, and how great the help of the divine law is within you, you will joyfully sing with David to the Lord:

> “I have hidden your utterances in my heart, so that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 16, 31 and following).

The soul must always be stirred by spiritual goads and renewed each day with greater ardor. Perseverance in prayer, the illumination of reading, and the care of vigils—both by day and by night—are its stimuli.

For nothing is worse in this way of life than idleness, which not only acquires nothing new but also consumes what has already been gained [another reading: “what has been prepared”]. The discipline of holy living rejoices and grows through progress; through cessation it becomes sluggish and declines.

The mind must be restored by daily and fresh increases in virtue, and this path of life must be measured for us not by what has passed but by what remains. As long as we are in this body, let us never believe that we have arrived at perfection; for in this way we reach it more surely.

We do not fall back as long as we strive toward what lies ahead. But once we begin to stand still, we descend; and for us not to advance is already to turn back. Let all laziness cease, as well as useless confidence in past labor. If we do not want to return, we must run.

The blessed Apostle, living from day to day for God and always attending not to what he had done previously but to what he ought to do, said:

> “Brothers, I do not consider that I have grasped it. But, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed prize of the heavenly calling of God” (Phil. III, 13–14).

If blessed Paul, the vessel of election, who was so clothed with Christ that he could say, “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20), nevertheless still stretches forward, still grows and progresses, what ought we to do, who should hope that at our end we may be compared with Paul at his beginning?

Therefore imitate him who said:

> “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. [reference incomplete in the supplied text]).

Forget everything that has passed, and consider yourself to be beginning anew each day, so that you do not charge the present day, on which you ought to serve God, with the past. You will preserve what you have sought most successfully if you are always seeking. What has been prepared will suffer loss if you cease to prepare.

## Chapter XXVIII

Perhaps you will say: “The labor is great.” But consider what has been promised. Every task usually becomes light when its reward is considered, and hope of the prize is a comfort in labor.

Thus the hardworking farmer plows a field that has long lain uncultivated and rejoices that he has broken up its rich, idle clods with the violent plowshare; and, remarkably, he draws hope of the harvest from the very difficulty of the work, rejoicing in it.

Thus the eager merchant disregards the sea, daring to look upon the foam of the waves and the violence of the winds. While he thinks of profit amid every labor and danger, he simultaneously forgets both weariness and fear.

Consider, I beg you, the greatness of your reward, if indeed what is immeasurable can be considered. After the soul’s departure, after the destruction of the flesh, after ashes and dust, you, a virgin, are to be restored to a better condition. Your body, entrusted to the earth, is to be raised into heaven; your mortality is to be exchanged for the honor of immortality.

After this, you are to be granted the companionship of angels, to receive the kingdom of heaven, and to remain forever with Christ.

> “What shall you repay the Lord for all that he has repaid you?” (Ps. CXV).

What will you consider difficult under so great a rewarder, whose rewards are so great? Therefore blessed Paul says:

> “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

For what worthy thing can we either do or suffer during this brief time of our life, when it is to be repaid with immortality?

## Chapter XXIX

For this reason the same Apostle says:

> “This momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure” (2 Cor. IV, 17).

Let honors be rejected; let riches be despised. Let our very life also be scorned for love of martyrdom. And even if all these things were not given in exchange for the reward of eternity, they would nevertheless at some point perish.

Even those who always desire to possess them lose them. How many people our memory holds who were established in the greatest honors and riches, yet suddenly fell from that summit of power; and those who, lifted up by pride, thought themselves to be something other than human beings, finally taught us by their end what they had been.

For what is stable in this world? What is firm? What, moreover, is not brief and uncertain and subject to chance? What sort of good is it that you always fear losing, that you either fear will be taken away from you or know must be left behind by you? For even if no accident snatches it away, it must certainly be lost through death.

And if our life were extended for a thousand years, and we reached the final day of our entire lifetime through daily delight, how long, I ask, is something that is erased by its ending? Or what fruit is there in that pleasure which, as soon as it ceases, will seem to you not to have existed?

Come now: turn over in your mind the time of your life that has passed. Will it not seem to you to have been a kind of shadow, what has gone by, and, like a thin dream, will not everything that appears seem uncertain?

A decrepit old man too can feel this, for whom it is fitting to say with the prophet:

> “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass” (Ps. XXI).

## Chapter XXX

If we can say these things even here, where, although this life is brief, it is highly valued because it is present, what shall we say in the future, where, in the greater presence [another reading: “knowledge”] of eternity, everything that has passed is regarded as nothing?

Carefully turning these matters over with yourself, and despising the brevity of this life through contemplation of eternity, despise even the contempt of the world with greater strength of soul; and prepare yourself entirely for that one day on which the world’s glory will come to an end.

That day, I say, which the Savior compared to the flood and which, as the Apostle says, will seize by a stealthy arrival many who have been deceived by false security (1 Thess. V, 2).

Blessed Peter too describes it:

> “The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with a great rush. The elements will be dissolved by heat. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought we to be in holy conduct and devotion, awaiting and hastening toward the coming of the day of God, on which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire?” (2 Pet. III, 10).

It is a recent event—and you yourself heard of it—when, at the sound of the shrill trumpet and the cry of the Goths, Rome, the grieving mistress of the world, shaken by mournful fear, trembled.

Where then was the order of nobility? Where were those fixed and distinct degrees of rank? Everything was mixed together and confused by fear; every household was filled with lamentation, and terror was equal among all. Slave and noble were one. The same image of death was before everyone, except that those for whom life had been more pleasurable feared it more.

If we fear the human hand of a mortal enemy in this way, what shall we do when the terrifying blast of the trumpet begins to thunder from heaven, and at the voice of the archangel—louder than any trumpet—the whole world resounds together? When we see weapons not made by human hands being brandished above us, and the powers of heaven themselves being shaken, as the prophet says:

> “When the Lord comes to make the earth’s inhabited world desolate and to destroy sinners from it” (Isa. XIII, 4),

what fear will then be ours, what darkness and gloom, when that day finds us—though so often and repeatedly warned—still unprepared?

Then, he says:

> “All the tribes of the earth will mourn over themselves, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.”

Then they will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us”; and to the hills, “Cover us”; and to the rocks, “Open yourselves to us” (Matt. XXIV, 30 and following; Luke XXI, 27 and following).

But these things will belong to those who, detained by the various cares of this world, do not think about the world’s end. You, however, for whom the coming of Christ is the meditation of days and nights, and for whom, because of the purity of your conscience, the Lord’s presence is to be desired, you who await the consummation of the age as the fixed time of your reward—you will receive exultation from heaven, not fear.

For then, mingled with the choirs of the saints and accompanied by holy virgins, you will fly to meet the Bridegroom and say:

> “I have found him whom my soul sought” (Song III, 4).

You will no longer fear separation for any period of time, since you are to be granted once for all the glory of immortality and the splendor of incorruption, and you are to be forever with Christ, as the Apostle says:

> “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. IV, 16–17).

Let this, therefore, always be your concern and this your pursuit. Let these things continually be turned over in the virgin’s heart. Let the labor of the whole day be occupied with them. Let nightly sleep be laid down in them [another reading: “the sleep of night”]. Let the soul awaken again to them [another reading: “to this”].

For no labor should seem hard, and no period of time long, by which the glory [another reading: “the gifts”] of eternity is acquired.

## Notice on the Following Letter

I rejoice that I have discovered the author of the following Letter, hitherto known to no one. For it is plainly falsely attributed to Jerome, and the style itself cries out that it differs enormously from Jerome’s. I received from Gennadius who he was; and he proves to have been no writer of the lowest bench, but a disciple of the great Augustine.

Eutropius the presbyter, he says in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter XLIX, wrote two letters to two sisters, handmaids of Christ, who, because of their devotion to chastity and love of religion, had been disinherited by their parents. They were letters of consolation, composed in the manner of books, in elegant and clear language, supported not only by reasoning but also by testimonies from Scripture.

This, clearly, is the title: *To the Daughters of Geruntius, on Despising an Inheritance*. In the text he says:

> “If Christ is the cause of offense, the impious father’s reproach must be embraced, not mourned, lest we withdraw from Christ, to whom that disinheritance commends us.”

And below:

> “Geruntius did not wish to have a share with you in heavenly things; why do you desire a share from his estate?”

Finally:

> “For you, daughters, that disinheritance increased the future inheritance in heaven,”

and other similar statements, which you will understand from the whole context.

The chronological indication also agrees with the period to which that Eutropius is assigned. For, taking Paulinus—plainly Paulinus of Nola, who abandoned the senate, honors, and riches—as a most distinguished example in such matters of despising worldly things, he says that Paulinus “recently went before with his wife (*matrefamilias*).”

This Paulinus finally freed himself entirely from worldly affairs around the year 395. Thus, if you wish to date this Letter about ten years later, or to the beginning of the fifth century, you will come close to the truth.

Moreover, its doctrine is thoroughly Christian and worthy of an auditor of St. Augustine; and it is all the more confirmed by the fact that it praises St. Paulinus so greatly.

Therefore Bellarmine is not to be heard, when it seemed to him that the author was imbued with the poison of the Pelagians and held that it was unlawful for a Christian to possess riches. For even in this respect there is nothing in what he discusses concerning the use of riches that does not seem to have been taken from his teacher Augustine’s *Letter to Hilary of Syracuse*, and it is not far removed from that heretical madness.

# Letter II: To the Daughters of Geruntius

### On Despising an Inheritance

### I

All my thoughts are free for you in affection, even though meanwhile I am separated from you in place. For I seem both to see and to hear you: your love keeps me so completely occupied.

And if you do the same toward one another, then, although it is impossible for this to occur through the flesh, it becomes possible through the spirit, so that the body of two people may become one.

To show, then, that your conversations keep vigil with me, receive what has seemed greater to me, as I reflected more deeply, concerning the inheritance about which you consulted me; for through spiritual matters you have chosen me even as judge of carnal affairs.

I could indeed say, “Who appointed me judge or divider between you?” (Luke XII, 14), if that statement had not proceeded from unbelievers. For the unbelief of the Jews is repelled by this response of the Lord, not inculcated by it.

At one time the Jews themselves, failing to recognize in Moses that visitation of the Lord by which, as his brother’s liberator, he had killed the Egyptian, and wishing on the following day to settle the quarrels and disputes of the brothers, dared to say:

> “Who appointed you ruler or judge over us?” (Exod. II, 14).

Accordingly, the Lord answered them in his own words, so that they might be refuted even more completely if it were revealed that they were falsely seeking the one whom they had rejected, saying:

> “If you believed, surely, you would also believe me” (John V, 46).

But since I too am yours, and I know that you have truly sought the judgment of the one who joyfully killed the Egyptian, and since, while you are on the way, you strive quickly to establish peace with your adversary, we shall leave that sentence to the Jews, to come upon those who uttered it.

### II

To the humble we shall speak of the Lord’s kindness:

> “To you it has been given to know the mystery” (Matt. XIII, 11).

And so, returning to the beginning of our digression, I judge that you ought to despise that inheritance and ask nothing from the judge of the world.

For how can you approach those who do not know the truth even by their own judgment? Pilate, from their council, says to the Lord:

> “What is truth?” (John XVIII, 38).

He was, of course, a judge, and by a fixed law he settled the business and cases of litigants with the balance of justice. But what could he do here if he did not know the truth?

Certainly the Evangelists recount that Pilate was so just that he preferred to release an innocent man rather than punish him; and yet he inquires, as though wishing to learn the truth. For ignorance of the truth produces the act of questioning.

What, then, shall we say? Without doubt, he revealed the empty concerns of mortals and the uniform falsehood of worldly affairs; and he judged that true judgments do not exist where the cases are false, and that, in matters lacking truth, true judgment itself is lacking.

For what shall we reclaim as ours before those tribunals, if, as the Apostle prescribes, we brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away? (1 Tim. VI, 7).

If we brought nothing into this world when we came, and can take nothing away when we depart, then we falsely call something here ours, where almost the whole world is alien to us. What, then, can the judge of the world grant—or restore—to us, if nature has granted nothing?

What can Pilate do, who is rather an interrogator of truth than its proclaimer? What, I ask, except Barabbas, whom the Jews preferred to the God of heaven because they fled to the judge of the world? In this matter the faithless people received not the guilty man but guilt itself.

But let these remarks concern judgment, not the case itself.

### III

As for the case, I not only advise but solemnly urge you: if you have offended Geruntius for Christ’s sake, remain steadfast in that offense. For:

> “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

If Christ is the cause of offense, the impious father’s reproach must be embraced, not mourned, lest we withdraw from Christ, to whom that disinheritance commends us, as it is written:

> “Blessed are you when they persecute you and curse your name as evil because of the Son of Man. Rejoice on that day and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke VI, 22–23).

That offense, whose truth is regretted, has provided this reward.

And if, called to the Lord in the likeness of the Levites, you have killed bodily affections with spiritual swords, what father do you desire? There is one Father for us, who is in heaven; and therefore the Lord is your inheritance.

For what is to be possessed with Christ must be possessed in Christ. Do not return to the dead, you who follow the living.

> “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22).

But if long ago you said, “Father, we do not know you,” in order to keep the Lord’s testament, why do you still seek the testament of the father who rejected you?

This is the sword sent by the Lord throughout the world to separate father from son (Matt. X, 34). This is truly to circumcise nature, which the Jews preserve in form and not in truth, and to circumcise with a stone knife (Josh. V, 4). The rock, however, was Christ (1 Cor. X, 4)—the one who said:

> “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37).

Using this sword, imitate the Levites. Running from the inner person through the camp of your outward self, slaughter for the love of the Lord the affections that meet you. In accordance with the legislator’s command, pass through the first army of virtues and return—namely, pass beyond past things without clinging to the marvels of the world, and, when we first return to the one who sent us into the world, let us do so with the sword at our thigh.

Let us kill those who resist us and delay us—our relative, our neighbor, and our brother—lest through them our pilgrimage be prolonged. And let us do this from gate to gate: that is, lest, when I have pursued my brother at the gate of the eye, the gate of the ear perhaps besiege him, and, having been passed over through one gate, he meet us through another.

For these are the gates of our soul, through which the blandishments of the world descend to it and through which the perceptions of the flesh enter. Unless, after making a broad slaughter, we make a way for the virtues through them by a kind of impiety, we shall never reach the king of true piety.

### IV

When, in devotion to your calling, you have courageously carried this out, Moses himself, praising such an action, will immediately say to you:

> “Today you have filled your hands for the Lord.”

This means the world [another reading: “the age”], which is near and close to you by the condition of flesh and substance. By killing your actions—which are your hands—you have filled them for the Lord, since you have agreed to serve no one except the Lord who commands.

Thus Abraham filled his right hand for the Lord when he did not refuse to commit parricide (Gen. XXII). While he armed it for God against his son, he forgot that he had a son; looking toward the majesty of the command, he did not deign to shrink from the atrocity of the deed.

Hands are filled for the Lord when they are occupied with the Lord’s commands; when, handed over to the Lord’s will, they begin to belong not to a human being but to God; when they do not obey the affection of the flesh but serve the divine command.

Thus Judith, for the freedom or salvation of her fellow citizens, filled herself for God under the appearance of prostitution; unarmed, a woman killed an armed man (Judith XII, 13).

Thus, full of the Lord, triumph over the affections of the flesh. Do not seek the deserter who, even if he should encounter you, would have to be killed by you.

> “Give your cloak to the one who takes your tunic” (Luke VI, 29).

> “May their money perish with them, those who have preferred money to Christ” (Acts VIII, 20).

Once we have departed from Sodom, let us leave everything to the fires. Lot sees the Lord’s anger in the example of his wife, who incurred anger because she looked back.

Geruntius did not wish to have a share with you in heavenly things; why do you desire a share from his estate on earth? And if he despised your glorious things so greatly, why do you not despise his dishonored ones?

Bear patiently, I beg you, the marks of faith, the Christian stigmata, and the poverty of the Church. Bear, I say, the reproaches of the shameless, you heirs of virginity.

Recognize that you have been visited, and glorified by so great a visitation, so that you might not have a share with unbelievers. This world did not recognize you together with your Lord. If you belonged to the world, the world would love you.

Kings of this world do not demand tribute from their sons. In the houses of kings are those who wear soft clothing (Matt. XI, 8). Zebedee does not follow James and John.

Let Geruntius remain in the little boat with the nets, provided that you lie with Christ’s Apostles upon his breast.

### V

> “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke VI, 24).

But for you, daughters, your consolation is owed in the future. For you, that disinheritance increased the future inheritance in heaven. The world itself withdrew what belonged to it from you when it recognized that you were not its own.

Indeed, the rich man is tormented by dreadful flames, while Lazarus reclines in the bosom of Father Abraham (Luke XVI, 25).

And what wonder is it if poor and foreign Abraham bought a tomb on foreign soil from the sons of Heth?

O truth! For I cannot be silent without exclaiming:

> “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI, 33).

A patriarch who was a foreigner bought himself a tomb? What is a tomb? It is a place of rest where, according to the world’s order, the bodies of the dead are placed.

Thus, with understanding directed toward the vows of faith, Father Abraham acquired for himself by faith and contempt of money a place of repose (Gen. XXIII, 17).

Our Paulinus recently acquired this same double tomb for himself and his wife through his riches: they have died to worldly conduct and now rest from worldly works, as the Apostle says:

> “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3).

And again:

> “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ” (Rom. VI, 8).

This is that double tomb: one rest for the outward and inward person. For if a human being consists of two substances, he ought rightly to have a double tomb, so that when either substance has been separated and returned to its own nature, rest may not be lacking to either.

For although a human being consists of body and soul, neither can the soul without the body be called a human being, nor is the body without the soul a human being—although soul and body together are the human being.

But when the name that is properly perfected as a third thing through the blending of its two constituent names has been emptied by their separation, each is assigned its own place of rest, since both live and both die.

For just as, beyond this life, there is another life—that of the blessed—so, beyond this death, there is another death—that of the wicked.

But the difference between this life and death and that life and death is that these belong to nature, while those belong to merits. Thus a double tomb is owed both to nature and to merits.

These householders of whom we have spoken provided themselves with this double tomb: by abandoning the senate, honors, and riches, they seemed dead to those who appear dead even while they live.

Behold one tomb, in which the conduct of the old person, together with the toys of his nobility, is hidden. The other will be when the body itself, which is subject to decay by the law of nature, has been dissolved and returns to the earth, of which it is written:

> “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19),

while the soul rests in refreshment.

For whoever refuses to acquire a double tomb for himself will perhaps have, according to the condition of nature, a place where his mortal body may be buried; but according to the law of merit he will not have a place where his soul may rest.

This has been established in such a way that this death, which is produced by the dissolution of soul and body, stands between two deaths and two lives. For it is necessary that a human being die twice, and life is owed to him twice.

Blessed Paul briefly designated two lives when he said:

> “Godliness is profitable for all things, holding a promise of life, both of the present life and of the future” (1 Tim. IV, 8).

And blessed John showed two deaths in the Apocalypse when he said:

> “Over these the second death has no power” (Rev. XX, 6).

He called it the second because there is also a first.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0049C] But this must be considered with great care and provided for with vigilant attention: whether, before that death which, as I have said, is generated by the separation of soul and body, we would rather die to this world—having, if one may so say, anathematized all its pleasures, which the resources of the world supply to us outside the bounds of vital substance—or only after the natural death that separates soul and body.

Hence it is also called *interitus* (“destruction”), because it goes between them and plunges itself as a third stage between the two substances whose union made the human being, in order to remove that perfect substance. [Col. 0049D] For whoever dies here by not enjoying the pleasures of the world and by crushing the impulses of the body seems to have been buried with Christ (Rom. VI, 11); and if buried with him, then certainly in a tomb, without which burial cannot exist. To this person another death is also owed—the common death that loosens and frees the soul from the bonds of the body—and to that body, likewise, its own tomb and burial are owed. After these two deaths and the double tomb, that blessed and perpetual life follows.

But whoever has gained the whole world here by courting it and seizing it—because here he disdained to put to death the deeds of the flesh—is deservedly said, after that natural death which we cannot escape, to have been enclosed, or rather deposited, in one simple tomb; and in misery he falls into the second death, which is filled both with the eternity of pain and the perpetuity of tears.

[Col. 0050A]

## Chapter VII

These, then, are the two tombs which the exceptional man Paulinus, deeply concerned to imitate the patriarch, sought for himself: one in which he might conceal himself, stripped of the old man together with his deeds; and although he had not yet laid aside his body, might have no carnal things in the flesh; another in which, when the Lord comes to break open his earth and his body has been exposed, he might place his soul at rest.

Thus that father obtained these things for his children, as we have said, by contempt for money: a place in which the rich could not recline with the poor. Here he will receive all the world’s pilgrims, here the needy, here also those disinherited for Christ’s sake by secular wills. Therefore he had no trace on this earth, since no one was found who would follow him.

[Col. 0050B] But now take courage, daughters, who are his trace, you who began not to belong to the earth through him. Obey the will of your father, whose corruption you did not follow: he bought for you from the sons of Heth a tomb which he refused to purchase for himself and for his other children. In their presence you are indeed dead, since you do not retain with them what they possessed while alive in the world. Always give thanks to him who made you have no trace here, so that there you might possess with Lazarus the sign of Abraham. Let him possess money, and you the tomb; let him possess images of food, and you the rest of the Prophets.

## Editorial Notice on the Following Letter

This letter was also attributed to Paulinus, and learned men—and especially the recent editor of his works—thought that its diction came very close to his. [Col. 0050C] Yet, since it contains many things that cannot in any way be reconciled with the history of Paulinus, it has rightly and deservedly been rejected as his.

I, unless—as Erasmus thought—it is foolish to try to guess the author among the great multitude of writers produced by that age, would like it to be attributed to the presbyter Philip. According to Gennadius, chapter 62, he was an excellent hearer of Jerome and wrote very false personal letters, chiefly exhorting his readers to endure poverty and sorrows. Certainly, in all that is set forth throughout the work, nothing occurs to us that is inconsistent with the persons of that Philip and of Marcella, to whom the letter is addressed, or with the sequence and circumstances of events.

Marcella is not, as Lebranius thinks, someone other than the woman to whom Jerome often wrote and whose life he described in the letter in our recension 127, addressed to Principia. To say nothing of other considerations, the Author clearly shows that she is the very same person when, at the beginning of chapter II, he says that he saw her at the time when royal kinship surrounded her household—namely, when the consul Cerealis was seeking her marriage.

[Col. 0050D]

# Letter III: To Marcella

*He exhorts her to endure adversity.*

### I

The love of Christ gave our humility great confidence to write to your veneration. It made you humble in the heart of your devotion and rich in works of blessing. Such a reputation for the holy riches of your faith has gone forth from you that it has reached even us, placed far away, and, through hearing of God’s grace, has fattened our bones like the oil of gladness.

[Col. 0051A] Your goodness has become known to us, because God has caused his face to shine upon you. He separated you from the womb of your kindred and from your land—not by region, but by the spirit of good will—so that from earthly riches he might establish you as his faithful servant among heavenly things, making you a participant in those of whom it is written: “Wise women have built themselves houses” (Prov. XIV, 1, according to the Septuagint).

When we heard these things about your heavenly happiness, we poured out our hearts before God and, feasting in a voice of rejoicing (Ps. XLI, 5), said: “The Lord puts to death, and the Lord gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes rich and poor; he humbles and exalts” (I Reg. II, 6). But because [otherwise: “because”] “the cup is in the hand of the Lord,” “he humbles one and exalts another.” Although this seems to pertain to the whole mystery of the kingdom, it can nevertheless be referred especially to your grace: you were exalted by the great purpose of the Lord’s mercy so that you might be humbled, and humbled so that you might be exalted.

### II

For we are not unaware, venerable sister and blessed daughter, of your former glory in this world. We also saw you at that time when royal kinship surrounded your household, eminent in those honors that are destroyed. For although these too are bestowed by the Most High Lord, since “all authority is from the Lord God” (Rom. XIII, 1), nevertheless they are fleeting and fragile, being enacted under this world, whose form passes away like a shadow.

[Col. 0051B] Therefore we marvel all the more at the grace given to you, and we magnify the Lord in you, who placed you amid the labors of human beings and visited you with the saving rod of a father’s compassion, so that, afflicted in a few things, he might order you rightly in many, as the Apostle testifies: “In this world we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (I Cor. XI, 32).

[Col. 0051C] Hence David also says: “Let the righteous strike me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Ps. CXL, 5). And you have undoubtedly learned, being devoted to spiritual studies, that it is likewise written in Solomon: “For the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves and scourges” (Prov. III, 12, according to the Septuagint). He disciplines every son whom he deigns to receive and prepare for eternal life (II Cor. XI, 39).

[Col. 0051D] The Apostle, too, is neither ashamed nor crushed by this; rather, he glories in it and becomes strong in his weaknesses. To strengthen us by his example, he confesses and proclaims this about himself—even though the ascent to the third heaven had been opened to him, and even though that fiery sword could not exclude him from the entrance to paradise, where he had heard an ineffable secret beyond every tongue. Yet, so that he might not be exalted because of the excellence of his revelations, he relates that he was governed by the restraint of the very Lord by whom he had been glorified to such an extent: an angel of Satan was assigned to him as a thorn in his flesh, that is, as bodily tribulation, and he was salutarily humbled lest he be vainly puffed up. “For this reason,” he says, “I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (I Cor. XII, 8).

### III

[Col. 0052A] Therefore, instructed by such a teacher and guide toward the virtue of patience and the hope of eternal glory, be confident, daughter, as you have begun to be, and glory in your past sufferings, recalling also the words of that same teacher: “For, as one who knows the heavenly mysteries, he faithfully testifies that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

“For tribulation,” he says, “produces patience; patience, proven character; and proven character, hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts” (Rom. V, 30). Rooted in this love, we endure everything.

Therefore David also says: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. XVII, 2, according to the Roman Psalter). Love of the Lord is the strength of salvation, because God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God.

The prophet also knew that the momentary tribulation of this world produces, as the Apostle says, an immeasurable weight of eternal glory. That holy king therefore says in the Psalm, asking to be found worthy to be tested in the furnace of temptations: “Test me, O Lord, and try me” (Ps. XXV, 2).

[Col. 0052B] Again, our psalmist, as though repenting of the glory of this world, confesses when he says: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Ps. CXVIII, 67). And because he was healed by humiliation, he immediately says: “Therefore I have kept your word.”

For this reason the Prophet again says: “Give us help from tribulation.” And: “Vain is the salvation of man” (Ps. LIX, 13). Human salvation is indeed vain when it is thought to exist only in this mortal life, of which it is said to man: “Man is like grass; his days are like a flower of the field” (Ps. CII, 15).

And you, holy daughter, have also been taught by experience to prove the saying: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL, 6–8). “The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord—and he who made it—remains forever,” just as the Lord himself remains forever, who is before all ages.

[Col. 0052C] Therefore it was truly said: “Vain is the salvation of man,” because all things under heaven are vain. Hence you have in the Psalms: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6).

### IV

In what class of human beings he says this, he teaches in what follows: namely, of those who are vainly troubled by love of their riches, which they gape at like blind beasts, endlessly desiring and amassing them, storing up treasures on earth and not knowing for whom they gather them (ibid., 7).

[Col. 0052D] “They will leave their riches to others,” he says (Ps. XLVIII, 12), and after their days have failed in vanity, all of them, carried off to the underworld, will be found not masters but slaves of their riches. They will find nothing in their hands there (Ps. LXXV, 6), because they sent ahead nothing except the merits of eternal punishments.

But that is not the vain salvation of man of which it is said: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. III, 9); and again: “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Ps. XXXVI, 39). Therefore hope placed in God will not disappoint (Rom. V, 5), just as salvation is not vain when it is hoped for in Christ and bestowed by Christ.

### V

Therefore, since you received help from tribulation so that you would not desire the human day or rejoice in the vain salvation of man, glory in the Lord and bless him who granted you understanding (Ps. XV, 7), so that you would not persist in standing in the way of sinners (Ps. I, 1) or remain among the children of this generation, for whom there is no salvation (Ps. CXLV, 3, according to the Septuagint), because they prevail in their vanity and forget the truth.

[Col. 0053A] For while they trust in the abundance of their riches, they do not make God their helper (Ps. LI, 9). But your lot has been assigned in the inheritance of Jacob, and your eyes have been enlightened to recognize the truth, so that you might understand that “a little possessed by the righteous is better than the many riches of sinners” (Ps. XXXVI, 16).

For this reason the merciful and compassionate Lord (Ps. CX, 4), who prepares his devices for such people in order to extend human life, allowed you to be tossed by the waves and winds of this age, so that, having experienced shipwreck, you would thereafter take care not to suffer the same danger. Thus everything you have endured, as you understand, was indeed wounds to your body, but remedies for your soul.

[Col. 0053B]

### VI

Perform your works in the circumcision of the heart, so that your glory may be not from human beings but from God (Rom. II, 29), who casts the powerful down from their thrones, exalts the humble, fills the hungry with good things, and sends the rich away empty (Luke I, 52).

The Lord is a God of knowledge (I Reg. II, 3): see with what great recompense he has changed your glory. He preferred that you become a participant in heavenly things rather than remain until the end among earthly things, so that you might pass from human dignity into the kingdom of God.

Indeed, to many people held captive by the vanity of this age God deigns to offer similar aids for attaining eternal salvation. But most of them, with sound counsels overcome by anxieties about riches and by bodily pleasures [Mart.: most people, spurning sound counsels amid anxieties about riches and bodily pleasures], do not wish to understand so as to act rightly (Ps. XV, 4). They prefer to travel along the broad way of destruction with the many rather than find the narrow path with the few (Matt. VII, 13).

[Col. 0053C] Therefore you, most blessed woman, to whom it has been granted not to be hardened by loving correction but to be corrected; not to glory in riches but to place your hope and your true possession in God; and to be separated from the lot of sinful rich people—whose heart is like mud, since they sink their heart, as their treasure, into the earth—pass over to the lot of the blessed poor, whose form Christ assumed and for whom he became a refuge (Ps. IX, 10).

He declares not the rich but the poor blessed, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V, 3).

[Col. 0053D]

### VII

It is therefore now your task, in great thanksgiving, to confess and sing praises to the Lord. As we have heard, you are adorned in both dress and heart with humility, so that David’s words suit your tongue and your mind: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 71).

You will also be able truly to add what follows immediately: “The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver” (Ps. CXVIII, 72). For you have chosen to place your treasures in the commandments of the Most High.

We too, rejoicing with you, say in the words of the Prophet: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; exult, daughter of Jerusalem” (Zech. II, 10, according to the Septuagint), and forget the evils that arose for you from the goods of this age. You have chosen for yourself the good portion, which will not be taken away from you (Luke X, 42).

[Col. 0054A] No one can take away treasures stored in the bosom of Christ, nor overthrow the house founded upon the cornerstone itself. You did not place your building upon rotten wood, fragile straw, or withering hay, nor upon unstable sand, but upon the immovable foundation that is Christ, “other than which no one can lay another foundation for completion” (I Cor. III, 11). In Christ you began to build with silver, gold, and precious stones.

And because you are completing this building—for it is God’s building (I Cor. III, 9)—that wise architect continues his work in you, teaching you to complete the good course, to forget what lies behind, and to stretch forward toward the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. III, 13), so that you may grasp that for which you were grasped, and receive the crown of righteousness and the diadem of glory from the hand of the Lord.

[Col. 0054B] When that great day begins to be revealed in fire, may your work not be consumed by the testing of the wise fire, but be proved (I Cor. III, 13). May your light not be extinguished, but shine among the brighter stars, among those who will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God (Matt. XIII, 43) and like the moon, perfected forever (Ps. LXXXVIII, 38), whom the sun will not burn by day nor the moon by night (Ps. CXX, 6).

For they will remain in that heavenly city, Jerusalem, to which the Lord himself, as it is written, will be both name and light (Apoc. XXI, 21).

### VIII

Seeing, therefore, and foreseeing in the spirit of revelation that a great harvest of everlasting joys is blossoming for you, we rejoice in the Lord. Rejoicing in your fruits, we sing in a voice of exultant praise: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX, 2).

[Col. 0054C] For his goodness has abounded greatly, surpassing your tribulations, since he has called you to their lot through everlasting joy and a heavenly inheritance, royal honor, and a place among those who judge above.

The sufferings of humility must be endured in this world; they will be repaid to you by God. And meanwhile, blessed woman, console yourself with these words, so that you may forget your former pains and, established with a perfect heart in your present purpose—in which you have raised your hands to saving works—may confidently promise yourself, in festive meditation, perpetual happiness in the good things to come.

[Col. 0054D] In your eager spirit, anticipate yourself in heaven, so that while your body remains on earth, you may already reach Christ in your mind. And while you strive to imitate Christ and cling to his footsteps, laying aside the burdens, obstacles, and fetters by which the rich of this age are held—those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Ps. LXXXVII, 7)—may you, already liberated and unencumbered, accompany the crucified Lord of majesty.

His image can be borne only by one who makes himself naked and dead in this age, so that according to the Lord himself he may say: “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Or, according to the prophet David: “I have become like a dead man among the living” (Ps. LXXXVII, 6), so that, free among the dead, you may say with the Apostle: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

[Col. 0055A] Rejoice, because you have become like the glorious Judith, seeking among the virtues of chastity the rewards of incorrupt widowhood; and like the venerable Anna, persisting night and day in prayer with the purity of fasting.

## Editorial Notice on the Following Letter

This appears to be a fragment from a longer letter or booklet, especially since it lacks an ending and the proper conclusion of the discourse. There is no way to understand from any passage why it is addressed to a virgin sent into exile.
