There is nowhere any sign or trace of her identity, nor any mention of exile, except perhaps in the passage where Noah is mentioned: “Behold, he too suffered the experience of exile.”

As for the author—since it is plainly not Jerome—the style closely agrees with the preceding work, which is why learned men could also have thought this piece to be by Paulinus. By the same reasoning by which I attribute the former to the presbyter Philip, I think this one too may be assigned to him.

# Letter IV, or Consolation to a Virgin Sent into Exile

### I

[Col. 0055B] If God and our Lord Jesus Christ promised security, peace, tranquility, rest, prosperity, joy, and every other kind of delight to his servants and worshipers both in the present and in the future, we would rightly have reason to grieve and weep if we suffered anything contrary in the present life. For, in addition to the inspired pain—which is always more bitter the more suddenly it occurs—the future promise would also be uncertain, frustrated by the anxiety of our present hope.

[Col. 0055C] But since, on the contrary, he foretold that in the present we would suffer anxieties, wars, storms, disturbances, miseries, sorrows, hatreds, and every other kind of hardship and affliction, no one who is secure in the promised prosperity will be troubled by the weariness of the foretold change.

If you have been forewarned, you will possess consolation in the warning itself. And although someone may be extremely distressed by the foretold evil of ill health, he will nevertheless receive that distress not without consolation if he recognizes in it the signs of the health that has been promised.

In the same way, we too are shown to be joyful and glad when we behold the signs of our hope. We receive its confirmation when, through present evils, we already hold future goods in the hands of unwavering faith. For, as it is written, “our salvation is in the time of tribulation” (Ps. CXXXVII, 39).

Therefore whatever it is that seems to signify the greatest joy ought not to produce sadness. He is proud, envious, or disdainful of his own good who is made sad by its proving. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “You will mourn and weep, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI, 20).

[Col. 0055D] The sadness that gives birth to joy must therefore be embraced; its material must not be considered. Often, through the sweetness of the fruit, one takes pleasure in what was bitter at the root.

Again the Lord says: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me; in this world you will have distress” (ibid., 33). What does he mean by saying, “so that you may have peace in me,” and “in this world you will have distress,” except that our belief in his promise should be so great that, while suffering the world’s evils, we believe ourselves to be in perfect peace through confidence in future hope?

[Col. 0056A] Our hope in future things should be so great that we do not feel at all that we are enduring what we suffer, but rather think that we already possess what we believe. For it is written—and from this we recognize that we possess everything in the future: “By hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. VIII, 24).

The Lord therefore desires such stability of faith in us that we judge what we believe to be more certain than what we suffer, and regard what we hope for as more real than what we perceive, so that we do not feel our present straits while we stretch forward with the whole intention of our soul toward future hope.

It is as when a soldier disregards or does not notice the pain of a wound because, with all his senses alive, he seems to think only of victory. Or when someone goes to the baths in winter: first, naked, he patiently endures the harshness of the cold because the warmth that follows consoles him.

[Col. 0056B] Thus certain hope overcomes the thing that is present, so that what is future begins, in a sense, to exist, and what is present ceases to exist.

“In me,” says the Lord, “you will have peace”—that is: what exists in me, who always am, should be firmer for you than what takes place in the temporal world. The world will pass away, and whatever evil is enacted in it will end. But my peace will never be dissolved by any lapse of time.

[Col. 0056C] Elsewhere he says: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come. But when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the distress, because of her joy that a human being has been born into the world. So you now have sorrow, but your sorrow will be turned into joy. Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XII, 21).

### II

For the comparison between present tribulations and future joys, he most appropriately introduced the example of a pregnant woman. Although she knows that the cause of childbirth cannot pass without immense pain, because she longs intensely for children, she disregards the torment of pain while desiring what she loves greatly. She rejoices in the child before she is saddened by the birth, and she does not reject the beginnings of fertility, although she is certain that they will come only through great anguish, because, while considering the greater joy, she embraces the causes of sadness.

[Col. 0056D] So too, in nearly all human affairs, joy can scarcely exist unless sadness has gone before, and the bitterness of preceding pain makes the joys that follow more precious.

Thus health is more valuable when it is recovered after the hardship of illness. From every direction, greater happiness is often reached through the greater necessity of labor. Whoever wishes to possess knowledge of letters cannot attain the joys of learning unless he has undertaken the weariness of study. No one can possess the glory of any learning unless he has first endured the heat of his mind.

Nor can a farmer rejoice in the abundance of crops unless he has first exhausted the earth through much labor. He gathers a greater hope of prosperity the more he knows that he has sweated, and from the labor he has expended he hopes for an increase of abundance.

[Col. 0057A] Indeed, we recognize that this is so in nearly all creatures: a greater fruit is produced where the cause of burdensome bitterness has preceded it. During the seasons of summer and autumn, which serve the crops, the mildness of winter has sometimes brought excessive sterility, while the severity of the cold has often produced the greatest fertility.

Whatever the mildness of spring brings forth loses the hope of abundance. The trees themselves are burdened with a more numerous fruit the more they are restrained by the violence of bitter cold. When timely correction restrains early flowers and does not allow them to rush toward danger, frost provides a useful impediment: what it restrains, it does not suffocate but encloses.

[Col. 0057B] But if the force of the rains has been somewhat too mild, then, to the degree that things first luxuriate in undisciplined haste, they are later left without fruit, since their future strength is consumed at an unsuitable time.

Seeds themselves, cast into and entrusted to the earth, rise more slowly because the icy cold holds them back; they advance with a useful root and are afterward bent down under the weight of more abundant fruits.

For sailors too, an excessively strong and prolonged storm promises a far greater hope of calm. Thus, in almost all creatures, some rejoicing rarely follows hope unless grief has gone before.

Since this is so, we ought to bear it with equanimity even if the storm of a harsher winter of tribulations and pains shakes us, since we will bear a greater fruit of summer in proportion to the severity of the present cold in which we have had to live.

[Col. 0057C] Whatever at its first onset snatches something away to destruction expends the harshness that it might otherwise have reserved. No storm of the rising sea ought to terrify us, since a calm that will never end is also coming to us.

For that is the Lord’s voice when he says: “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and say every evil against you; rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. V, 11–12).

Whoever does not receive the causes of his reward and blessedness with immense joy is certainly suffering either from unbelief or from ignorance. Whatever produces gain should be desired, however bitter it may be; and whatever generates a greater reward should be received with greater joy.

Nor should the accumulation of labor be avoided, since it is an increase of benefits. Thus the eagerness of merchants, for the sake of greater profit, fears neither the sea nor earthly dangers, which sometimes even become causes of loss. For the hope of greater gain, they willingly undertake the hardships of voyages and journeys.

[Col. 0057D] Although the labor is great, it is easily disregarded when one considers not so much its quantity as its usefulness. And if we see that this is done for temporal and uncertain profits, let us consider what we should do for eternal profits that will come without any uncertainty.

For just as their profits are preceded by ambushes and dangers, so our benefits are increased through losses, and happier outcomes arise under danger. Such benefits fear tribulation so little that even death can be despised for their sake. For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV, 16).

### III

[Col. 0058A] But why do I try to summon you to patience in tribulation by human examples or by examples from the present life, when we know that scarcely any saint has passed through the stormy struggle of this age without a storm of tribulation, or endured the hatred and hostility of as many people as he corrected by the dissimilarity of his life?

For one seems to correct another who disagrees with his way of life.

Was not holy Abel, who is found to have preserved innocence and righteousness first in this world, immediately subjected to human hatred—or, what is more criminal, fraternal hatred—and envy, as soon as he pleased God by the acceptance of his unblemished offerings? This was inflicted by his brother, who owed him a greater affection both because of their kinship and for the sake of companionship, since at that time they alone existed in the whole world apart from the ancestors of the human race.

[Col. 0058B] Yet he preferred injustice to be deprived of every consolation rather than be fostered by fellowship discordant with any righteous person—if indeed it is right to call it consolation when the spirit differs as greatly as the life is at odds.

O pitiable Cain! What are you doing? Why do you rush forth in sufficiently cruel and frenzied hatred to shed your brother’s innocent blood? What had your solitary brother done against you? What force had he used? What injury had he committed?

[Col. 0058C] But what greater injury can there be to an unjust man than a life of righteousness? [Perhaps: “the righteousness of life.”] Was the solitary brother displeasing to you for this one reason only: that he desired to please God? You too could have pleased God. Had he excluded you as well? Or did you know God’s love to be so impoverished that he could not love both of you at once?

But when does insane envy perceive this? It always struggles against the good and does not see. In the end, because it could not bear seeing what was just, by killing it made what was more acceptable seem worthless.

Blush, O most pitiable man: by your envy you testify that the one to whom you show yourself harmful is better than you. What hardness of such great cruelty was this, that you did not even reflect upon your solitude?

[Col. 0058D] With what spirit did you later return to that field of fratricide? How did you afterward live alone in the whole world without your only brother? You gained not so much an inheritance through your brother as, because the two of you had been together, you lost the help of shared concern.

What were you turning over in the secrecy of your thoughts when you no longer saw with you the one whom you had been accustomed to have as your only intimate, your only companion, your only associate?

Would it have been more rational if the fury of envy had driven you to turn your criminal hands against yourself, so that the fratricidal weapons would have felt your life rather than your brother’s? No murderer is as cruel as the one who rages against another in such a way that he spares neither himself nor the other.

[Col. 0059A] Why do you deny your crime when God questions you, miserable man? While you think you are excusing yourself, you accuse yourself, so that no reasoning can come to your aid—neither confession nor falsehood. For if you had not known that fratricide was evil, you would not have denied it.

But this is the custom of the sinner: he always wishes to double the evil by denying it, saying either that he did not do what he did, or that he acted from good zeal when it is clear that he acted from evil envy.

And do you think, miserable man, that your crime was hidden from the one who was not ignorant of the reason why your unworthy offering was rejected? He does not question because anything is hidden from him, but so that he may leave you no excuse of ignorance.

For when you deny that you know your brother, you confess what you yourself did, and by suppressing your confession you confirm the gravity of your crime.

### IV

We have set these matters out at somewhat greater length in order to disclose both the evil of envy, whose cruelty cannot be estimated, and the condition of righteousness in the present life, which began at once with hatred directed against it. Nor could it exist even then without much persecution, when it had only one enemy. And if it endured so great a hatred from a single foe that the matter proceeded as far as the destruction of life—if that foe was not just any man but a brother—what must we believe that person can then endure who has so many strangers as enemies, and unless each of the many who cultivate righteousness can hear, through the mass of increased wickedness:

“Come, let us surround the righteous man, because he is useless and opposed to our works” (Wis. 1:12)?

But someone will say: “Whoever wishes to avoid envy should fear becoming known to, or pleasing, many.” Behold, the righteous Abel had no one to whom he might become known or pleasing; yet he could not avoid the hatred of envy. Anyone is mistaken who thinks that envy cannot arise without human friendships, since it persecutes not so much human friendships as friendship with God alone. Therefore not even he who desired to please God alone could be free from the assault of envy. It is enough to incite the goads of envy if it discovers that you please the One beyond whom no other can exist.

Nor do we find that holy Noah possessed in this present life the repose of unshaken security, while, with everyone else wicked, he alone throughout the whole world strove to preserve righteousness; while he built the ark containing the seeds for the renewal of the world; while he prepared himself for the future flood and, with diligent care, announced his faith in the coming inundation; while he gathered food both for himself and his family and for all living creatures, intending, by the merit of his righteousness, to preserve life at the time of death; while, after such a great multitude of human beings, he grieved that he alone with his family remained alive.

But desolate righteousness does not lose its consolation when God is its companion, more festive than every public celebration. Behold, that man too, having suffered exile, with the multitude of human beings destroyed, and although not deprived of every consolation, left almost alone, recognized that he served the Lord greatly. Therefore he did not eagerly seek the empty favor of human consolation, since he possessed in God a more joyful and fuller confidence.

Holy Abraham also—what and how many things did he endure, while alone among all the unbelieving he preserved faith; while he abandoned his homeland and relatives; while he grieved over his wife’s barrenness; while, because of the scarcity of food, he experienced the injuries of exile, now in Egypt, now in the land of Gerar; while he feared death on account of his wife’s beauty; while he mourned her after she had been taken from him; while he did not deserve to bring her forward, because the righteousness of God, the most impartial judge, did not permit it; while he was ordered to inflict a wound on his body through circumcision; while he drove out the son with his mother; while he was tested in beloved Isaac; while he was commanded to be a religious parricide.

Yet the faithful man readily consents to every loss, for whom greater and greater, indeed the greatest, rewards continue to increase, since he is even promised that he will receive a hundredfold.

Isaac himself—by what kinds of temptations is he shaken, while he suffers want of food [Mart. *esse*]; while he experiences the hardships of exile; while, on account of his wife’s excessive beauty, he himself fears—the man worn down by anxiety and afflicted by the very thing that had delighted him, since the beauty of his wife, which had pleased him in security, displeased him in fear; while he suffers the rivalry of the king; while he is not permitted to possess her without provoking envy.

Holy Jacob also suffered many things. First, when, because of the blessing bestowed upon him, he incurred the deadly envy of his brother Esau; when, avoiding Esau’s hatred and indignation, he went alone to Laban; when he served for the sake of a wife; when the sister of his beloved bride was substituted for the woman he did not love; when, at the cost of his first love, marriages were doubled for him by deceit, and again, because of the marriage he had not desired, he was subjected to seven years of service; when he suffered fraud concerning his wages; when, after twenty years of hired servitude, he departed by secret flight rather than by a free decision to leave; when he feared Laban’s pursuit; when he dreaded meeting his brother; when he was horrified at the violation of his daughter Dinah; when he mourned the funeral of his most beloved wife Rachel; when he grieved that his most beloved son [Al. *tac. filium*, “son omitted”] Joseph had been consumed by wild beasts in a bitter death, without the consolation of burial; when he had bestowed his affection upon Benjamin, whom he even thought had been consumed by hatred [Al. *in quem contulerat*, “upon whom he had bestowed it”], and whom he feared he would never see again.

Already exhausted by years and labors, the old and most righteous father groaned.

The most holy Joseph also is afflicted and shaken by many kinds of temptations; to him the appearances of tribulations seemed to have been the seeds of righteousness. For as often as he did anything holy or pious, so often he was compelled to undergo the dangers of unbearable temptations, consenting to righteousness and persevering with hope as his support. Thus we must labor to determine what we ought first to take up in praising him for his righteousness: the perseverance of holiness [Mart. *sanctitatisque*, “and of holiness”], or the strength of patience and steadfastness.

When, in fraternal affection, he told his dream to his brothers, as a brother to brothers, he incurred their envy and hatred—as though he had either pretended to have dreamed it himself [Al. *si*, “if”], or had announced the vision as an indication that they would be subjected and terrified. Then, when he had been sent by his father to them in order to learn of their welfare, he eagerly undertook the journey entrusted to him, so that he might the more quickly satisfy their hatred.

### Editorial Notice on the Following Letter

This work once seemed to Erasmus not unlike the style of Tertullian, as far as one may detect from his fragments. “For,” he says, “it is more affected and somewhat harsh, though it contains weighty thoughts.” Others think—perhaps with still greater appropriateness—that it approaches the wording of the following Letter, which, no one now denying it, belongs to Saint Maximus of Turin, so closely that they almost ascribe it to him with certainty. Although I would not yet dare to pronounce judgment on this matter, I nevertheless incline more toward their opinion: the person who wrote this seems to assume the role of a bishop who says at the very beginning that he is occupied by the religious obligation of the Lord’s affairs, and so forth.

## LETTER V. TO A SICK FRIEND

### I

Although I know with complete certainty that your experience has no need of the consolations, reliefs, and oars of another’s comfort—for you yourself sustain and heal the illnesses and sufferings of your enfeebled body, the numbness of your stiffening limbs, through the happiness of a vigorous and heated spirit, and set them in order by medical method—nevertheless, amid adversity a defense, amid illnesses a remedy, amid cares a consolation, and amid the waves the oar of another’s hand is always sought and desired.

For there is no doubt that the fruit of brotherly consolation is part of the greatest remedies; and it introduces refreshment to weary minds through the sweetness of consolers’ words.

[Note: It formerly read, “with the sweetness of consolation,” an expression also used by Saint Cyprian in the first of his two letters to Donatus; by Aulus Gellius, book XIX, chapter 9; and by Boethius, book II of *The Consolation of Philosophy*. Sidonius likewise uses it in book V, letter 17, as do others. Nor, in truth, should that reading have been altered.]

And even if it does not act upon bodily limbs, it nevertheless composes the person in the recesses and hidden places of the spirit through spiritual devotion, and, like a physician, inserts health; it assists the efforts of exhausted strength under the burden of prolonged pressures, especially since it is written: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted” (Ps. 8:10).

Therefore, since the religious obligation of the Lord’s affairs keeps me so occupied that I have no opportunity to brighten your sufferings by frequent bodily visits, I have decided, as you requested, to ease by whatever consolation letters can provide these long trials of virtue—or rather, to attend to your health—and to advance a mind founded upon Christian virtue toward the greatest strength.

We who strive to seize the spoils of the heavenly kingdoms and the tribute of eternal reward cannot be victors without some form of combat. For virtue that is delicate and inexperienced in battle has never climbed to the palm-bearing summit of victory; nor does he receive a reward for vanquished adversities who judges the utterly worthless life of his own body dearer than victory.

He is not shaken by fear of death for whom life arises from death. It is precious to him even to pour out blood; it is happiness to fight against unhappiness; it is the highest health to endure bitter wounds; he considers even the loss of limbs the greatest gain. And, to say what is last, it is glorious for him, in the very contest, to restore his palm-bearing soul to his creditor.

For it is better, as reason determines, if what is owed to nature is paid by virtue [Mart. *virtute*, “through virtue”]. Therefore, brother, everything must be endured—everything, then—that the Lord has wished to test you through the longest affliction and to appoint for great rewards.

### II

**The Weak Man:** What spirit, its strength already surrendered, could endure these unavoidable misfortunes, the attacks of ruinous calamity, and these hostile illnesses—which, as I see, will now die together with the body itself?

**Jerome:** When a storm finds someone amid the waves, he must necessarily meet and confront the dangers. And although no one willingly suffers or endures danger, nevertheless, under the weight of danger, necessity hardens him.

**The Weak Man:** But another anxiety has been added to me, one that envelops my senses with doubled grief and imposes inexplicable cares through its biting concerns. What troubles me is that, amid such trials and in the struggle with so obstinate an illness, I alone have been made to fight, when I know that others have been corrected by milder blows and have emerged victorious after a brief struggle. Why did the Lord not assign me a contest together with the others? Why did he not chastise me as he chastised the others?

**Jerome:** First, once placed in so arduous a contest, you must not think about lesser things. Lesser battles have lesser rewards. When strong things are commanded to the strong, a stronger tribute of reward follows the stronger man; and therefore a strong man considers it disgraceful to be matched with an inferior.

Great is the one who has conquered great things; it belongs to the greatest devotion to endure the greatest things; it is the mark of immense virtue to overcome immense things. At the king’s court, he excels the others in more eminent merit whom the heat of battles has most greatly disturbed and whom conquered adversities have made victorious.

At last, the reward suited to the quality of the contest is present in the very conflict, appointed according to the victor’s merit. Kings impose military burdens according to men’s strength; physicians provide remedies according to the causes of illness.

The one who must be cured does not tell the physician by what rule he is to be treated. Nor does a soldier choose where he is to be sent, nor a slave choose by what beating he is to be chastised. For what depends upon the judgment of a superior is not in the power of the subordinate.

Therefore, since we are ruled by heavenly authority and dwell amid the manifold miseries of the world in order to be corrected, it is not ours to choose, from the Lord’s authority, either the blows or the other contests by which we are to conquer through endurance—just as it is not the slaves’ right to choose from their masters the kinds of scourging. The permission of the one being beaten never depends upon the will of the one who beats. It belongs to authority to correct; it belongs to one’s condition to submit. It belongs to the king to impose the burden, and to the soldier to endure it.

For nothing unjust is done by that very king who, imposing the sweat of war upon his legions according to their strength, sends the strong to strong tasks and commands what is suitable for the inferior, so that neither the inferior is prevented from contending according to his own strength against a more powerful opponent, nor the more powerful is humbled by the contest of an inferior, with his merits degraded. And while this is done, so that no one is diminished in another’s contest—or at least defeated—he wishes all to be victorious.

Nor is the physician an enemy who strikes in order to remove danger and drives out one wound by means of another. Nor does paternal affection become hostile if it teaches children through the embraces of scourges. For paternal scourges are exercises of harmless devotion.

Therefore, since the chastisement of one who corrects is caused by love, because it descends from devotion, love the striking physician, whose wound is the mother of medicine. For devotion produces nothing impious, so that, embracing virtues, the person spiritually healed may contain the fruit of devotion:

“I am the Lord,” he says, “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32:39).

### III

**The Weak Man:** But you said: “Then devotion strikes?”

**Jerome:** Indeed it does, lest devotion be judged impious if it does not correct the delinquent. Since there is something in a person that requires healing, it strikes in order to heal—just as the physician’s hands, by inflicting many injuries, bring health, not without the patient’s murmuring.

In this same way, under the care of the healer’s blows, amid the very constrictions of grief, we murmur against the Lord as wounded people do against the physician who both heals and causes pain.

Therefore, brother, undertake—undertake—the remedy of endurance, by which you may lighten the burden heavy with temptations and overcome dangers while you suffer them. Let a steadfast spirit console and heal your prostrate limbs. Let virtue rule within the body held captive by anxieties, so that the soul enclosed by dangers may flourish through the freedom of virtue itself—virtue which, in the conflict of temptation, was long ago commanded to prepare itself by the lawful trumpets, and, at the very entrance of the Lord’s service, to arm itself against hostile calamities.

“My son,” he says, “when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1).

Therefore, since temptation is prolonged for our benefit, it is not surprising if its heat falls upon us, as the blessed Peter admonishes and says: “Do not be surprised at the fiery trial that comes upon you, which is taking place for your testing, lest you fall away amid the various waves of the world” (1 Pet. 4:12).

Christian life is shaken and tested by frequent storms, and rejoices and grows through countless pressures. The most blessed prophet Solomon, a man of sufficient renown, testifies and proves this. “Join yourself to the Lord and endure,” he says, “so that your life may increase at the end” (Ecclus. 2:3).

The ship of our life rejoices in agitation; it is disturbed only by calm. Its course is stunned when the winds cease; it is endangered if it is not tested by dangers. For it is uncertain whether he belongs to the Lord whom the pressure that is the mother of glory does not purify by its tossing, nourish by its weight, or test by its chastisement and blows.

Since divine love supplies us with blows and various trials, and, like a physician, provides a remedy from opposites and comes to our aid by causing pain, the one who has not deserved to submit to medicinal wounds does not prove himself to belong to the love of the Lord.

But perhaps you say: “If God is my lover, why then do the scourges of my lover grieve me with severe laceration and disturb me by wounding me? If he who loves me tortures me with embraces of scourges, a false love is now exercising the parts of hatred; let him hate me instead, so that he may not torture me.”

Rather, take care that he not hate you; ask that he deign to love you. For love corrects, whereas hatred threatens punishment. Love is accustomed to offer discipline; hatred, when judgment dictates it, is accustomed to declare guilt.

This hatred is propagated from God into humanity through the birth of the human race. Therefore it belongs to humanity that God hates or becomes angry: he hates when he is offended; he becomes angry when the offended party is not entreated.

The person who makes himself hateful through hateful deeds and refuses to entreat the offended God provokes the Lord to hatred of him. Otherwise, God loves the human being as an artificer loves his work, but hates the evil deeds by which his work is driven into ruin and compelled to fall.

And he who hates evil deeds cannot love the perpetrator of evil deeds, as the most holy Solomon declared: “The ungodly and his ungodliness are hateful to God” (Wis. 14:2).

Therefore, in this world that is passing away as its years decline, whose old age sunset presses down upon and swallows up, it is better to endure medicinal scourges from love of the Lord than, from hatred, to await an incurable wound and lead a condemnable life beneath the thunderbolt of judgment.

It is better to pass through the hands of the physician while enduring a brief torment than to reject the physician and incur a punishment that will torment one through eternal torturers.

Or, if you are still astonished that the medicine of our lover consists in scourges, you should also be astonished that remedies cause pain to those whom the physician loves, since he excludes what causes harm by causing pain.

Certainly, one who seeks to expel harmful things cannot avoid causing pain. Therefore he heals by causing pain, so that the health prepared through grief may be more precious.

If medicine did not lacerate the person to be healed, the merit of health would always take delight in a voluntary wound. If the precious care of harmful remedies did not consist in biting aids, necessity would not force the one requiring treatment into grief.

Therefore care is perfected through harmful remedies, so that health purchased at the price of grief may be held more precious and welcome.

Thus the one who is to be loved cannot fail to be corrected by whatever examination; the one who must be corrected cannot fail to be scourged by the blow of the lover; the one who must be healed cannot fail to be hurt by the healer’s biting treatment.

Why are you amazed that someone expects aid from dangers, when fire and iron are healing him? For many things are healed only after being struck. There are many whom physicians cannot heal without iron.

Those who, entreated through various torments, grant health often administer extremely bitter draughts, when illness requires them, for the sake of a remedy to those who do not thirst for them; these are swallowed not without wrinkling the brow.

For if you observe the face of the one drinking, he drinks sadly and anxiously so that he may live joyfully and safely.

O rational and sufficiently perverse convenience of inconvenient medicine! A person is compelled to drink what he does not thirst for, although sometimes the remedy is precisely what he thirsts for.

And because physicians sometimes prescribe abstinence from food, they lighten the body by imposing a fast, so that they may restore it, renewed from that very weariness, and make it stronger.

They soothe, bind, mend, and heal sudden wounds brought by accident in the camp; by causing grief they bring joy, by tiring they strengthen, and by wounding they heal. For while they bring health to the open wound by joining the edges of the flesh with certain clasps, they promise life through consolation, and restore it through treatment.

But these things are minor compared with what happens among them: without a scalpel, putrefied and weakened tissues cannot be removed, nor dead parts amputated from a living person. Although one limb is amputated not without sensation throughout the whole body, the person nevertheless consents to his losses in order to live.

Among them, sometimes after the skin has been removed, the bones themselves are scraped, lest the entire person, perishing, be scraped away. Among them, at times a worm-ridden, burning abscess is cut open by medicinal iron. Among them, fire burns in order to cool; dust bites and tears in order to heal.

What more is there to say? Under medical devotion a person is greatly tormented so that he may live greatly.

Behold the necessary danger in which faithful torment is a benefit. Certainly, the person whom the physician treats is in danger; but the one whom the physician abandons perishes and is deceived. To the former, although under torment, life is promised; to the latter, hope of living is denied.

Therefore, where necessity requires it, it is better to be in danger than to perish. I consider it better to suffer harm with benefit from inconveniences than to die through the refusal of inconveniences—that is, it is better to be harmed by a remedy than to be unable to be cured.

### IV

I speak of this according to the heavenly physician, and refer it chiefly to spiritual healing, not merely to that healing which, through an art destined to perish, concerns mortal limbs.

It is therefore better for us to be rebuked and chastised by the Lord and healed beneath his blow than to be removed from his medicine as incurable. For God keeps from his sight those whom he sees afflicted by the iniquity of an incurable disease and scattered and dispersed by vices like dust or chaff driven by the force of a whirlwind.

As he himself says in his own voice:

“Let the wicked depart from me, for I do not wish to know their ways; for their lamp has been extinguished, and they will have groaning in their life. For they will be like chaff that flies before the wind, and like dust that is lifted by storms” (Job 21:16–18).

He does not wish to know the ways of those who altogether refuse to follow the way leading to exalted things. For there is one way to the one Lord, to be followed in Christ, which leads through constricting trials into the expanse of long security. To this way alone the palace of heaven is open.

The others, twisted by the winding paths of pleasures, seek a region of flame. Solomon himself testifies and says of them:

“There are ways that seem right to human beings, and at their end there is sadness and pain” (Prov. 14:12).

And along these ways rush those whom the course of an enemy life flatters with deceptive blandishments; those whom deaf time deceives and misleads, whom destruction receives and encloses.

As a storm drives a doomed ship upon the rocks, so unhappy prosperity leads the prone and unstable toward destruction. And just as a sudden fall—whether the slipperiness of marble or the shifting surface of a pavement—twists the protection of the feet from beneath someone walking in confident steps, so a sudden fall must hurl into an irreversible collapse those whom the uncertain path of worldly prosperity and a badly pleasant life lead unhappily.

As the most holy Solomon testifies and cries out:

“Just as one who falls on a pavement, so the fall of the wicked will come swiftly” (Ecclus. 20:20).

These are unquestionably the people who do not deserve to be shaken by the blows of some misery, in whom eternal sickness is nourished, nor to be scourged with the saints when the Lord chastises them—together with whom one reigns after the scourges. David invokes their remembrance in this song:

“They are not in the thoughts of human beings, and they will not be scourged with human beings; therefore their pride has taken possession of them” (Ps. 75:1).

You see, then, that those undeserving of the medicinal scourge are despised, while those who deserve it are chastised in friendship. For God, the parent of all, as a faithful physician toward those entrusted to him and a father toward his children, strikes those whom he loves in order to correct, not to kill.

Therefore blessed is the one who is beaten where the wound is inflicted by love. Blessed is the one whom the remedy of heavenly scourging heals, corrects, reforms, and sets in order, as the blessed and renowned prophet David proclaims and cries out:

“Blessed is the one whom you correct, Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12).

Therefore, since by divine ordinance we are subject to illnesses of differing bitterness and carry a life requiring healing through prolonged calamity, let us endure with equanimity the miseries mentioned above as a test of our virtue.

Let us bear with mental happiness the unhappy and manifold accidents, anxieties, and tears into which we have fallen by being born. For it is not surprising that the life of mortals is so ravaged in the world by the various devastations of frequent evils, in which no one is born laughing, in which no one begins the light of life except with tears.

When our mother’s womb displayed its tent to the world, we learned the world while weeping, as though tasting the first fruits of evils in our first tears.

The prophet Solomon testifies in this declaration:

“I was born, and I received the common air; I fell upon the earth made in the same way. I uttered my first voice, like everyone else, in weeping. I was nurtured in swaddling clothes and with great cares. For no king had any other beginning of birth. One is therefore the entrance into life for all, and similar the exit” (Wis. 7:1–3).

It is necessary that whoever has come must depart once he has lived his life as an exile, especially since Solomon thus declares:

“One is the entrance into life, and similar the exit.”

What prosperity or joy, then, can meet us where we first learn to weep, and where, amid the very cradles of newborn infancy and at the very threshold of life, nothing else about the world meets us except weeping?

We trod the thresholds of the world with weeping; we shall indeed weep as we depart. O narrow and sufficiently anxious span of mortal life, in which the end is named together with the beginning, and we receive our beginning together with the end! The one who has been born has already been seized by death. The dead are witnesses, since they do not deny that they are destined to die.

Therefore, since we have come in order to depart, let us conquer by endurance, as travelers do, whatever happens within the lodging of the world, as though passing through it. Evils imposed upon us are conquered when they are carried with good devotion. For evil does greater harm if it is carried badly.

There, certainly, the work of virtue is needed as consolation—under contemplation, that is, of the heavenly reward—where the end and departure of life are desired in the same way that the safety of harbor is desired at sea.

For who, amid the anxieties of the wandering world and the sufferings of illnesses, would not desire death more than a long and languishing life, when Solomon says:

“Better is death than a bitter life, and eternal rest than continuing sickness” (Ecclus. 30:17).

And elsewhere:

“It is better for you to die than to live” (Ecclus. 40:29).

For death gives rest to every person. Certainly, amid prevailing evils, the end is necessarily desired with thirst.

But just as it was not ours to be born, so it is not in our power to die. Otherwise, if dying rested in our power, not dying would also rest in our power.

Amid our anxieties, therefore, we ask for the rest of death because, amid evils, it is a consolation drawn from good not to remain silent; like sailors, for whom, amid hostile and anxious voyages, it is refreshment to speak of the safety of the harbor. Even if it is not permitted to reach it more quickly, as the spirit desires, nevertheless it is pleasing and sufficiently beautiful to desire the better portion.

But since it is not in our power to possess the better things that arise from death, let us meanwhile, while awaiting what is better, conduct a good contest amid evils.

A good contest is not to yield to evils, but to bear evils through the good of virtue, so that we may be raised and carried into better things born from death, free from illnesses.

Without the guidance and bite of unhappiness, one does not reach the triumphs of immortal glory, because the course toward the harbor is completed through dangers. No one can first be called a triumphant victor unless virtue has won victory for him—virtue that sees everything feared crushed beneath it and, undefeated, drags it away captive.

### V

Meanwhile, the world is like the sea, impatient by nature and swollen even without winds, raising, in the very calm, threatening and terrifying waves. Although its magnitude does not harm those who sit upon it, its harmless vastness nevertheless contains something frightening, and even sailors are often not without fears and blows from the waves.

In the end, no helmsman has ever unfolded all the sea’s recesses in security. And in this world, where we seek the rough and turbulent course of this life, we are frequently touched by threats and causes of evils—especially those whom heavenly service, marked out among the royal camps, has enclosed.

We have already said that the world may be compared with the sea, in which favorable conditions are rare and turbulence dense; one is terrified, one fears, and illnesses too are not absent. The harbor is the sole exit into security.

From this side and that, hostile attacks of calamity rush upon us; but to endure as far as the harbor—that is, to the exit—is the work of virtue.

Amid dangers the helmsman protects and preserves the ship. Amid calamities the ruling spirit governs and directs the human being.

Someone may guide a manageable ship through dangers somewhat moderated; but the ship that is especially awaited and received with greater triumphs is the one that powerfully shakes off the waves driven into a crest by the turbulent current.

The harbor crowd receives this ship with profound joy. Triumphing security receives it.

A soldier established in the army is splendid in his armor. But a sluggish and empty man, squalid in misshapen virtue, who in the field is known neither to himself nor to another, is contemptible. He lacks both praise and rewards.

Therefore danger ought not to be harmful where reward is born. Nor should a soldier be recalled or made fearful where the palm of victory follows.

He is wretched through his own happiness who, amid the misfortunes by which glory is generated, has never deserved to engage in combat. He has not learned his own virtue whom calamity has not tested.

Always lying idle in his enfeebled limbs, the soldier remains ignorant of and unknown to himself if he has never panted amid the glorious heat of burning wars and has never found triumphs through sweat. Nor does the happiness of rewards follow the one who refuses to carry the burden of arms.

Therefore what generates reward must be put into practice, and what produces glory must be desired.

Since, then, we must fight with various darts of temptation, if anything emerges that tests our strength, shakes our limbs, or proves our soul, let us seize it as an opportunity for reward by embracing virtue.

The virtue of the spirit ought to be immovable, and the undefeated strength of an unshaken mind ought to be like a rock in the sea, which nature founded amid the waves: though it is struck frequently by the collision of swelling waters, it is not moved.

Therefore, when adversity drives a person into battle and calamity presses and compels him into combat, let a happy spirit bring him forth armed with the shield of virtue, make him safe and secure amid dangers, show him happy amid misfortunes, joyful amid anxieties, healthy amid diseased sufferings, and, by the dart of endurance, make him victorious once calamity has been conquered.

Disease in the body is overcome if the spirit learns to endure. Therefore, when the body lies weak, greater virtue must be nourished in its hidden recesses, and what neither weariness can shake nor age bend must be prepared.

### VI

Hold fast, then, brother—hold fast the undefeated strength of faith. Hold fast the immovable Christian defense founded upon the firmness of heavenly vigor. Amid languishing and sufficiently rigid limbs, carry unharmed and strong the shield of faith and soul, and you will conquer sluggish and destructive weakness.

Meet evils as they batter you with the barriers of virtue. Conquer while you are struck; for Christian power is nourished by hardships and advanced through adversity.

It belongs to Christian service to be shaken by calamities and tested. It belongs to it to expand happily amid unhappiness and distress, to grow beneath pressures, and, maturing, to trample pressures underfoot.

It belongs to it to nourish its own defense through repeated exercises and to engage in combat with dangers. It belongs to it to sail toward the harbor of perpetual happiness through the raging dangers of the world and, under the blows of medicinal discipline, to reign powerfully through necessity itself.

It is ours, I say, to be raised to the summit of glory through the exercise of calamity and, while evils press upon us, to advance toward good rewards.

Among us weakness or any pressure is evidence of power and, certainly, the mother of virtue bearing the palm. Thus the most blessed apostle Paul, placed amid various blows, different scourges, and stormy assaults in the battle against illness, powerful through infirmities as a heavenly soldier, glories and says:

“Therefore I will most gladly glory in my infirmities, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9); “for this reason I am pleased to glory in infirmities, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am powerful.”

And again: “Whenever I am weak, then I am more truly tested and pleasing to myself in my infirmities.”

And again, when he asked that the thorn of the flesh be taken away from him, he learned that virtue could be nourished in infirmity:

“There was given to me a thorn of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to strike me, so that I might not become exalted. For this I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me. And he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (ibid. 12:7–9).

Virtue, therefore, is never trained by gentler lessons, lest the examples of the greatest virtues perish.

Our ship rejoices in agitation: when it is raised in whirlwinds, when it is struck by raging waves, when this rough journey, with adversities rising up, spares nothing in provoking virtue devoted to continual combat.

For we cannot be happy before the Lord in any other way unless we happen to be cleansed by unhappiness and earthly squalor.

He, however, should be judged wretched and sick who, sodden with pleasures, rolls about and lies amid enticements. Let the person who wanders among the delights of vices, pierced by enervated happiness, know himself unhappy.

Wretched and unhappy is the one who has not been tested by unhappiness. He lacks the reward who lacks the contest. The one who feared the weapons of adverse combat has never deserved to receive the name of victor.

It is certainly characteristic of a prostrate spirit to fear fearful things; it is characteristic of the lowly and inactive to pursue safety. Virtue cast into idleness without combat is an imperfect and enfeebled good.

For vigor lies enervated and weak; the sick spirit lies prostrate; brightness lies obscured. Therefore the bravest soldier must always stand in the battle line, and an opportunity must be sought by which virtue, shaken into action, may shine forth.

To the lover of battles, wounds are ornaments. Therefore, to despise labors and to know virtue, experience through practice is necessary—the nourishment, that is, of chosen strength.

A body is solid, and the mass of its limbs robust, when frequent practice has exercised it. Farmers, in the end, have sinewy strength and hardened hands through constant labor, while, bent over amid thorns and thistles, they seek the fruit through sweat.

The art of navigation—the ship of which a storm has often twisted while it makes for the harbor amid dangers—has learned to cross the waves and fight against the tempest.

A battered army is strong enough to shake off weapons; it seeks victories amid wounds, in order to please its own king.

Runners have agile limbs, and practice has taught and trained them.

What more need be said? No one ascends to more perfect attainments except through the increase of temptations, and the victor seizes the reward.

### VII

Therefore, while at first we endure small and moderate things, we must necessarily learn to bear greater—or even the greatest—things. For the hallmark of our military service is to set one’s step firmly along bright but difficult paths, to travel through hard terrain, and with hard strength to endure the harsh discipline of misfortunes. To heaven our road lies through rough places, [Col. 0069D] narrow passages, difficult winding paths, and remote places—a road not taken by anyone unwilling to be tested. God calls to heaven the bravest soldier; pressures, accompanied by glories, lead him onward, and rewards receive the victorious man who is destined to reign.

Does he meanwhile impose upon us anything abrupt that exceeds the measure of a balanced burden? Does he thrust upon us anything that surpasses the capacity of our strength? The most faithful commander orders a load to be imposed according to one’s abilities. Paul’s proclamation bears witness to and confirms this: “God is faithful,” he says, “and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you are able to endure” (I Cor. X, 13).

Let us therefore believe that we are governed and ruled by the Lord as students are governed by instructors in athletic contests. They impose the greatest labor upon those whom they see surpassing the others in cleverness and ability; [Col. 0070A] and we likewise adjust the burden placed upon the animals subject to our authority according to the measure of their strength: we impose strong burdens upon the stronger, and small ones upon the weaker, so that practice—that nourisher of virtue—may raise and advance them into the greatest vigor of youth and strength.

In this way our beginnings are beaten with light strokes, so that thereafter, out of love for divine virtue, they may prepare their accustomed strength for heavier blows. Although this principle is abundantly supported by divine examples, let us also use an example from worldly life; for it is not harmful to use things belonging to others in the respect in which they are also ours.

Do you suppose that the Lacedaemonians hate their own children, whose character and tender limbs—still ignorant, of course, of labor—they put to the test, and when public whippings are applied, paternal affection itself exhorts them to endure the blows of the scourges bravely? They plead and beg with the children, though lacerated and half-dead, to persevere in offering wounds to wounds.

What wonder, then, if God permits you, as noble children and his own household, to be harshly tested for the sake of nurturing virtue, since he is going to bestow everlasting kingdoms upon the victors? In this way he promises and declares the rewards of labor against every adversity: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). And again: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI, 28).

The brief span of perishable time is the price of eternity. Devotion amid tribulation will be repaid, made fruitful with everlasting fruits. Among us, a kingdom is sought through fruitful captivity, security is purchased through dangers, and rest is acquired through sweat. [Col. 0070C] For, says the Apostle, “virtue is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).

It is certainly more advantageous to be physically distressed by languid conditions than, with sound limbs, to carry a conscience tormented by a blind punishment. Many are sick from their sins precisely because of the soundness of their limbs. While they are free from infirmities, the body must necessarily flow in diseased relaxation and dissolve into a deadly sickness, wickedly driving a man—though outwardly healthy—headlong through vices and forests of error.

### VIII

Do you judge those to be free, or untouched by disease, whom barbarous pleasures have bound? They do not possess a chain, but savage luxury holds them in fetters with biting cruelty. Thus they have fallen into the snares of savage pleasures like birds captured by the deception of bird-catching: the more they try to escape, the more they bind themselves with countless knots [Col. 0070D] and plunge into deeper recesses.

Indeed, those are healthy whom an insane disease envelops and tosses about. Truly unharmed is the person whom God corrects with whatever blow, showing through his chastisement that he loves the human being. “Those whom I love,” says the Lord, “I rebuke and chastise” (Apoc. III, 12). Therefore let no one judge himself healthy who is free either from diseases or from filth and is not comforted by the remedy of infirmity.

Those are wretched who grow numb in the idle tranquility of excessive prosperity. A painted health flatters them in order to deceive and mislead; but an everlasting sickness will seize them, destined later to torment the whole person through an eternal torturer. Their roads are as numerous as the pleasures that come to their aid. Their journey is whatever the accompanying lust dictates amid dangers destined to perish. [Col. 0071A]

Seized by the winding paths of vices that drag them onward, these wretched people roll toward destruction in varied falls, along a most uncertain road from which they will not return. They direct their minds outward like streams, which never return to their own source.

They lead this life, whose companion is death, along prosperous courses, as they themselves suppose; but the final steps are brought to a wholly evil end, when one stands harshly at the last stage. What good does it do to have run successfully through dangers if, after the race, one happens to perish? In vain, finally, does a ship run through a proud and raging sea toward harbor with favorable, friendly waves, if it arrives through shipwreck and the harbor receives what is destined to perish.

It is therefore more advantageous to reach the harbor of glory under the guidance of any pressure than, after completing one’s voyage in a delicate vessel of diseased laxity, to go out into punishments. Often, therefore, poverty is better than riches, ugliness than beauty, insult than praise, servitude than power, weakness than strength, captivity than freedom, and humility than rank.

The illustrious prophet David expressed a song of this kind: “It is good for me, Lord,” he says, “that you have humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances” (Ps. CXIX, 71). It is therefore better to be humbled by the judgment of heavenly discipline than to be condemned with the world, as the Apostle says: “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (II Cor. XI, 32).

Therefore let us endure without complaint whatever is assigned for our benefit out of love for the Lord. It is administered as a remedy by a physician, and as discipline by the Lord. It belongs to the medical art sometimes to heal with fire and iron. What wonder, then, if the Lord, physician of our souls, shakes us with storms, examines us through diseases, and purifies us through calamities? It is an expression of our strength to be purified like vessels through fires and flames, as divine Scripture bears witness and confirms: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Eccl. XXVII, 6). And elsewhere it says: “Gold and silver and iron and lead, and everything that passes through fire, shall be cleansed” (Num. XXXI, 22).

Do vessels say to the potter, “Why do you examine us at the mercy of flames, and burn and test us with consuming fires?” Unless the arbiter of fire declares them most suitable by his judgment, they cannot be put to use. Likewise, unless the judgment or examination of temptations has purified us, we are found useless by the potter of our limbs—he burns us in order to heal us, tests us in order to free us, and afflicts us in order to save us. For nothing is so polluted, so filthy, that it cannot be cleansed from vices by purifications.

Finally, we have often seen people stained by reproach come forth into brightness, and iron covered with rust shine again in its former appearance. We have seen gold and silver purified by the discipline of flame, and trees that had been cut back come alive again in luxuriant growth and be adorned with lovely shoots. We have seen barren things restored to fruitfulness, and the great harvest accompany the exhausted trunk and the remaining root [the reading “extre radicem” is uncertain].

So too in us, whatever was seething under the pressure of sins, whatever was obstructed by the stain of squalid old age, has been driven out by the light of illness. Therefore, brother, the illness of your limbs has restored you to health through medicine. Only the material of your flesh needs the strength of health; and lest it should perhaps afflict you, it is afflicted in a useful manner by disease.

This flesh is what the dog-star of old age strikes in everyone, and what, like grass, withers and is destined to lose its own flower, as it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL, 6–7).

Let us therefore endure with equanimity if the body—which we read will perish like grass, together with its flowers destined to fall—is tossed about, exhausted by afflicting evils. Its health is accustomed to bring illness upon the soul, and, contrary to spiritual advantages, to choose savage and barbarous pleasures. Finally, unbridled flesh has often stripped the soldiers of chastity of their armor. It is therefore for our benefit if we are chastised with long and biting scourges by that very flesh by whose chastity we are assailed.

We foolishly love the flesh; we do not grieve over the soul’s prison and burial. Therefore, despising the fragility of that very flesh, let us seize in the embraces of devotion whatever comes to us as a treasure. For it is fearful for a Christian soldier to wish, like those who rejoice, to remain at ease in tranquility. It is the mark of a cast-down mind to fear the storm; it is the contrary of this not to tremble amid adversities. It is a sign of unhappiness not to know adversity; it is a sign of happiness to know how to confront and fight against adversity.

Since, as we have already said, all the blows by which we are shaken arise from a divine gift, let the person who does not know how to be carried through temptations recognize that he has placed himself outside the love of God, even though the legal trumpet repeatedly impresses this upon our ears in manifold song and says: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deut. III, 3). And elsewhere: “My son,” he says, “do not neglect the discipline of God, and do not grow weary when corrected by him. For whom God loves, he corrects” (Prov. III, 11–12). And again: “Do not despise the correction of the Lord. For he himself gives pain, and he himself gives relief. He strikes, and his hands grant healing.”

### IX

But perhaps you say: “If only, as with others, I were permitted to be tested at intervals, with the hope of health. If only I were allowed to taste some small measure of well-being during whatever interval of recovery. What does it mean that disease should so occupy and remain enclosed in my limbs that it has excluded health, never to return? That this destructive companion should lead my shaken limbs all the way to the end of life, and should itself be led out with them at death? What does it mean that my limbs should be deprived of any sense of health throughout the whole span of life? With cold introduced into the veins, warm vigor has vanished into chill; the walking that nature had granted has been shut out by the torpor imprisoned within. Finally, no journey, however brief, is tasted for the exercise of this wasted body. The knees are not bent in their customary prayers; the uneven arrangement of the fingers, disturbed by inner numbness, is prevented from handling what it usually does. What more need be said? Every bodily function that once normally depended upon the standing positions of the nerves lies enclosed in such coldness. Alas! I alone should have been chastised in this way; I alone should be subjected to such destructive blows and enveloped in prolonged evils!”

I ask you, brother, to restrain these murmurs with the reins of patience and confine your complaining voices in silence, since prophetic consolation addresses you in this way [Col. 0073A] and says: “Join yourself to God and endure, so that your life may increase at the end. Accept everything that comes upon you, and endure in pain; have patience in your humiliation, because gold and silver are tested by fire, but acceptable people are tested in the furnace of humiliation” (Eccl. II, 3–5).

When I review the legal ordinances and songs of the prophets, my ears also receive—unless I am mistaken—excellent sayings from worldly authority, hidden borrowings from divine law which necessarily ought to be inserted into the legal precepts. For it is not harmful to use things belonging to others in the respect in which they are also ours.

Here is the first saying: “Fire tests gold, and misery tests good men.” And elsewhere: “Nothing seems more unfortunate than the person to whom nothing adverse has ever happened. He was not permitted to test himself, since everything flowed for him according to his wishes.” And elsewhere: “I judge you wretched because you were not wretched; you passed through life without an adversary. No one will know what you were capable of—not even you yourself. For experience is necessary in order to know oneself. No one has learned what he can do unless he has been tested.”

And elsewhere: “To be fortunate for a long time and to pass through life without sickness of soul is to be ignorant of one half of the nature of things.”

Let us therefore endure with a joyful spirit the miseries that arise—through which unknown things are learned and happiness is born, and through which virtue too is shaken free and purified—whether because we ought to suffer, or because we are already being held captive. Unless flame adds brilliance to gold, it remains obscure and suffers the shame of dross. Likewise, whoever has not been shaken by trials of misery lies ignorant of the portions of happiness and of his own virtue.

Solomon rightly confirms this in these words: “The one who has not been tested in anything does not know what sort of person he is” (Ibid., XXXIV, 11). Therefore bless the Lord in the time of tribulation, whom you praised in the time of health. Use the songs of the prophetic voice: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIV, 1).

May that voice of the most blessed Job be brought forth from you in constant proclamation, by which exhausted strength is nourished with abundant sustenance and, restored, rises again into renewed vigor: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil? The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

It is therefore sufficiently perverse to murmur against the Lord at the time of testing: either he shakes the pestilential stain of our life with the tossing of hardships in order to free us, or he sifts righteousness in order to crown it; and through the affliction of the limbs, either sin is beaten or righteousness is tested so that it may conquer.

And so, in order to recall to your consolation the palm of ancient testing and your merit, let us use the most righteous examples.

### X

Although it is clear that the merits of individuals differ by long degrees, it is not unjust if we compare the struggle of a Christian person with the contests of victorious righteousness. What you see yourself enduring in this world is moderate if you consider what Job, the Lord’s intimate, was able to endure with the Lord’s permission. God measured it so that it might correspond and be suited to your strength.

First, how could you, who are unequal to him, be equal to the titles of righteousness that followed him? [Col. 0074A] Yet you are struck less than that righteous man, though you are wounded more severely than others. His trials were great, but yours are not lesser. For you yourself are great if you follow a great man.

There was one patriarch Job, an invincible worshiper of majesty, wealthy and rich in the resources of his rank. The Lord himself became the herald of his illustrious merits when, anticipating the instruments of the hostile faction with a proclamation of praise, he said: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is no one like him on the earth—a blameless man, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil deed, remaining in his innocence and in the simplicity of his heart?” (Job II, 3).

Therefore, when he was shaken by hostile arrows with divine permission, and the frequent savage attacks of the robber struck him, he defeated the blows that arose with the shield of patience. Strong in the barriers of righteousness, he confronted the savage forest of approaching evils, full of arrows and crosses.

When the hostile storm stripped him of his possessions, he felt no loss, because he found profit in losses, carrying the Lord enclosed within the recesses of his heart. When sudden force twisted the building at its shaken corners into collapse, he was deprived of his children, yet remained steadfast and immovable in faith.

When his innocent limbs, full of the Lord, swarmed with legions of beasts, and a destructive mass of worms wandered through the tunnels of his wounded flesh, piercing his body with hostile blows, the righteous man fought unharmed within his wounds. The raging hostility that gnawed him with pestilential blows he endured with tranquility of mind until the hostile storms yielded. The righteous man conquered by being beaten; the enemy grew exhausted by striking.

His servants’ service was denied him; your own attendants perform their services for you. Your friends console you by frequent visits and grieve, so that, if nature permitted it, they might perhaps carry this burden with you.

There is one virtue of the mind, brother—only one—which, as though rescuing us from the storms of this life and from the open sea, leads us into the harbor of tranquility. Behold, the day hastens toward sunset in its downward course. Behold, the unclean world rolls toward collapse under the filth of old age. Behold, heaven receives us as victors through the support of death [Al. “you”]. Everything perishes as we escape, and, with its setting already near, is swallowed up never to return.

For us, after the world has been destroyed and the body has died, everything will be healed. We will rejoice in the soundness of our limbs where life will be troubled by no disease. Therefore, brother, let the most excellent spirit within you govern and direct the impeded functions of the body with illustrious leadership, so that this bodily calamity may become a welcome opportunity for virtue.

For no tree is solid or strong unless it is tested by the assault of constant storms, its trunk shaken and bent this way and that, or unless the breath of violent winds frequently strikes it. Through those very afflictions it is tightened and pressed, and its roots, fixed more firmly, strengthen it more securely.

So too we are fortified by the biting scourges of frequent evils as we are stretched out; we are corrected when beaten; we are tightened when struck; and we are rid of our squalor while we are shaken by prolonged falls.

Therefore, amid ever-increasing pains and limbs afflicted by monstrous miseries, let strong and unharmed virtue reign with heavenly vigor, [Col. 0075A] so that adversities may be endured and those things called adversities may become advantages. Amid the very straits, the wise person rejoices and grows through an equal measure of consoling aid, and expands and lives through ambitious reasoning.

Finally, the person who remembers unconquered virtue does not know what he suffers; guided by reason, he has discovered that many have been oppressed by evils and that, through their own evil, they have been increased and nourished by reason as their teacher.

Therefore the consolations of reason are open to you, so that bodily calamity may now be regarded as an advantage, even though the whole mass of the body lies captive. But resurrection will come, restoring you unharmed and reclaiming all the limbs that have been seized within you.

Meanwhile, let your tongue be nourished by daily growth in the praises of the Lord, destined to proclaim the abundance of praise in the heavenly kingdoms. May the Lord cherish you with heavenly medicine and permit you to endure beneath such a burden with unbending [Col. 0075B] virtue.

### Notice concerning the following letter

This is Saint Maximus of Turin’s work, as no one now denies, although Saint Agobard, a ninth-century writer, in Book 1 Against Felix, chapter 20, does not doubt that it belongs to Jerome when he quotes from it the passage that we shall note below in its proper place. “The reader,” he says, “has in blessed Jerome, concerning the same matter, a sufficiently polished and lucid statement, when he was treating that passage of divine Scripture where it is said: ‘I shall place,’ and so forth.”

Erasmus, on the contrary, says: “This letter was indeed the work of an eloquent and learned man, and carefully composed, but it differs so greatly from Jerome’s phraseology that neither could he have imitated the other’s diction, had he wished to do so, nor the other his. In most manuscripts it bore no name; in some, the name Ctesiphon had been added. Nor is there any mention in the letter itself of the person to whom it was written. There is, however, mention of Saint Ambrose and of the discovery of the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.”

## Letter VI. To a sick friend: On the perfect man. (C, G)*

Behold, I write to you again, and I find nothing worthy for your wisdom to read; and what wonder is it if, while you are absent [Al. omits “you”], my intellect grows cold-hearted, as though deprived of the sun, and my mind, estranged from the light and suffocated by the cloud of folly, grows numb, so that I know less the farther I am separated from you?

If, for the present, anything in my speech should please you, it will be granted to me through your prayers. Finally, so that you may recognize all my folly more carefully: after applying that poultice, I also treated my stomach in your absence, though I deserve to suffer worse from it. After your holy ministry and angelic service, I laid hands upon it with physicians, as though there were no prophet in Israel. If anything should happen to me, it ought to have been easier for me to return to you than to think like a pagan; and it would have been better to endure even the labor of the most difficult journey than to be deprived of the precious sight of your presence, so that any compensation would have been preferable to my resorting to the fly-god of Accaron [i.e. Beelzebub].

This is what the world suggested to me in your absence, although, when you were present, it had no counsel over me. You had made me a council of prophets, not an assembly of sirens. But now, with all the senate of folly entering into me to destroy your holy work against me, it deals with me in a fourfold manner.

For it exacts interest from me in your absence which, when you were present, it did not dare to demand, so that you may understand that if I possessed any wisdom according to God while you were with me, what I possessed was yours.

Thus, when Moses was absent, the Israelite people committed fornication (Exod. XXXII, 1); thus, while the Lord slept in the boat, the apostles were thrown into confusion by the storm (Matt. VIII); thus, in the porticoes of Bethsaida, the man who had no one to put him into the pool of saving water was overlooked (John V, 4).

Although here too I perceive another kind of fault: I cared for the little body while the soul was languishing; I nurtured the outer man while the inner man was sick; I helped human things while divine things were in distress. I was bent by the fault of common practice, through which we are all cautious in small matters and negligent in great ones.

This happens because we do not know where true life is. This sun deceives us, this day misleads us, this expanse surrounds us. The world imposes itself upon us while we think that nothing exists beyond the sun, and suppose that light is what we see with our eyes; while we judge the person we see to be the human being; and while we believe that the world makes life, unaware of where the human being is, what the human being is, and what the life of that human being is. If we understood this, we would not live one way after being born one way.

Thus, having abandoned the origin of life, we have also lost the principle of living. First, then, let us hear where this human being of whom we are speaking is.

### I

Since the division itself has raised for us a certain question—[perhaps: concerning the human being] enclosed in this body, which was formed by the hand of God the craftsman from the mud of the earth—understand him to be contained, as it were, in a little vessel, as the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7). This person, infused everywhere throughout the body, has borrowed from the flesh the vital sense that does not fail him.

He rules; he is not ruled. He possesses rather than is possessed, so that he does not receive life but provides it. For when the fluid spirit animates this earthly and sluggish matter, taken up for the use of service, the spirit becomes lord of the body, and the human being is not subject to the body.

Finally, the little vessel of which I spoke lives through his presence and dies when he departs [Al. “because of his presence”]. This visible and perishable body is either the dwelling, servant, or sheath of that inner person. But the one who truly is the human being—since he occupies the second place in the division just made and is himself invisible—must necessarily have all things invisible.

If he is sick, the hands of physicians cannot reach him; if he fails, he is not restored by the juices of herbs. Nothing bodily can enter him. Only something resembling his own substance descends to him: he is healed by a word and recovers through obedience.

Finally, although the man in the church of Laodicea seemed to himself, according to the outer man, to be fortunate, rich, clear-sighted, and well clothed, he is rebuked by the Lord, who says to him: “You do not know that you are wretched and pitiable, poor and blind and naked” (Apoc. III, 17).

Certainly, as I have said, he was regarded as neither unclothed, nor eyeless, nor without riches. But our invisible God saw that invisible man to be in poverty, blindness, and nakedness. He even deigns to persuade him to purchase from him refined gold, a white garment with which he may be most gloriously clothed, and salve with which he may recover his sight.

He therefore has eyes of his own in addition to these bodily ones, which he can either lose or heal. He is also naked beside himself, so much so that he needs clothing. Yet, in a marvelous manner, the Lord, as he himself says, speaks to the patient and commands him to acquire riches from himself.

If he is both naked and poor, with what resources will he purchase that most noble garment or that gold already purified by fire? From where can the expense of such a transaction come? Evidently, if he either fosters the profits of the outer man or, by not using the very things through which he seemed outwardly rich, grows wealthy; and if he blinds the eyes of the body, by which he was carried away in the world’s ardor, through contempt for the corrupted universe.

Thus that invisible human being—who truly, as we have said, is the human being—is raised through contempt for this outer man, clothed through nakedness, and illuminated through blindness.

Thus Jacob, through bodily blindness, discerned not only the positions but also the merits of his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. XLVIII, 14). For when his son Joseph, who was presenting the children mentioned above, judged that Jacob could not even see them before his feet, he realized from his father’s reply that Jacob also foresaw what was to come.
