But just as that inner person makes this outer person live by his own life and animates him by irrigating him from the fountain of his own nature, so in turn the outer person, through the corruption of his deadly material, kills the inner person if he binds him to unlawful desires.

Although one may appear to belong to the nature of the other, each passes into the substance of the victor, so that either the spiritual person makes even the flesh spiritual through his virtues, or the victorious flesh makes the soul carnal.

Finally, when the Lord, angered, considered destroying the human race by the flood, he said: “My Spirit shall not remain in human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3).

And since, of course, we are all clothed in flesh, yet certainly are not “in the flesh” if we do not walk according to the flesh, this also gives rise to the fact that a person is not always designated by this name, “human being.” For according to his virtues or vices he assumes different forms and names.

The Prophet says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule” (Ps. XXXI, 9). There are therefore human beings who, before the Lord, are horses and mules. And the Lord says: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII, 6). There are therefore human beings who are swine.

And again the Lord himself says: “Behold, I send you like sheep among wolves” (ibid., XIX, 6). There are therefore human beings who are wolves; and conversely, there are human beings who are sheep. The Lord also says to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17); and earlier he himself says: “Come after me, and I will make you a fisher of human beings” (Matt. XIV, 19). There are therefore human beings who are fish.

These forms, however, seem to belong to actions, not bodies. The condition of our body is fixed, as is that of all living creatures. But since before God we are judged not according to the condition of our body but according to the merits of our life, it is evident that every human being forms a condition and a name for himself through his mind. This is certainly brought about by either the fault or the virtue of the invisible human being whom we are describing.

It is his fault if, having been subjected, he allows himself to remain subjected; if, contrary to divine disposition, there is domination in servitude and servitude in domination.

But lest I seem—since, having briefly cast down a kind of wall, I have reached the invisible human being in my discussion—to destroy the body altogether, I have not done so and am not doing so. The body possesses so great a sacrament that the Lord came in this very thing, that is, in our fragile and infirm condition.

Rather, I have attempted to show that the life of this outer person consists in the life of that inner person; and again, that the death of the inner person descends from the death of the outer person. When poison has been administered through vices, the outer person has no life from himself; unless he has been irrigated by the inner person, he possesses nothing. Each passes into the nature of the other, as I have said, either infected by vices or cleansed by virtue.

Therefore, since I have now briefly shown both where the human being is and what the human being is, let us examine what the life of that human being is.

### II

For if this worldly life— which regards evil as good and good as evil, and which the whole world follows and honors—is not found in an abundance of riches, nor in the summit of power, nor in the cunning of jurisdiction, nor in the pomp of eloquence, nor in strength made glorious through battles, nor in merchandise increased by changing provinces and wandering from one’s homeland, nor in the allurements of beauty, nor in the pursuit of gifts, nor, finally, in all the things that we see—for all these things perish, and even apart from them one may live happily, according to the world—then true life, venerable life, consists in knowing God, fearing his power, loving his goodness, admiring the world in its creator, despising the one who obstructs us, being content with moderate food as nature requires, and being protected by inexpensive clothing either for the sake of modesty or against the harshness of the season.

It consists in approaching the rest of creation not for its abundance or as a condition of life, but as an aid to this light. For whatever is more than this is from evil.

It consists in loving every human being as a brother, harming no one, serving everyone, and bearing the form of a servant together with the Lord, who, beyond the service contained within us, serves us daily in the world by bringing forth the sun, sending out light, pouring down rains, changing the seasons, and either producing or ripening crops.

For he serves us in the face and abundance of all creation, since he generated everything for our sake. But to return to the duties toward human beings: it consists in clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, visiting the sick, grieving with the sorrowful, burying the dead, possessing nothing as one’s own, but judging all one’s things to be held in common with everyone, and then living more truly for oneself when one is thought to live for others, and storing something up for oneself when one is believed to distribute it to others.

Yet these still concern only the outlines of the outer human being.

### III

The life of the inner human being, however, consists in the knowledge of divine matters—not in knowing through which part of the earth the heaven revolves, nor whether the stars are swept along in the opposite course, nor whether the fullness of the moon produces its increase in the Ocean, nor whether the roundness of the world suspends its sphere, nor whether it encloses it with four more prominent corners, nor whether there is one world or several.

These matters do not tend toward the soul’s benefit and are judged foolish before God. Rather, the inner person lives and is nourished when he is occupied with those healthy thoughts.

What, then, are these healthy thoughts? Without doubt, they arise when our mind remembers its creator; when, as though through a kind of repentance, it venerates and contemplates its maker; when it marvels at his works, intending to see him himself in his works, as blessed Paul says: “His invisible attributes are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, and also his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. I, 20).

That is, they arise when, from the immense visible works of creation, we extend ourselves toward the totality of the invisible Creator; when, by learning through these things that he is immeasurable, we measure him; when, unfolding his height through the gift of the Holy Spirit—for he alone introduces us into the one who is from him, and into all the principles of rising creation—we look upon all the origins of creation as though we had been made before them by him.

They arise when we contemplate the things God made as though he were still making them; when, passing through the whole origin of the world, we become older than we are in age; and when, although all things were made before we existed, we nevertheless regard the nature of everything as though it had been generated through us, because we are joined to its creator. We entered into it not in order to serve it, but in order to rule it.

Separated, therefore, from worldly wisdom, which attributes everything either to chance or to atoms; elevated through divine meditations and separated, by his help, from those who either said that matter had always existed and wanted God to be merely the craftsman of things, [Col. 0079C] or who worshiped these elements themselves as gods, or who introduced families of gods according to sexes, ages, and parts, as though through some populace subjected to the senses—we, distinguished by the Holy Spirit and drawn upward into higher things, live the true life, that is, possess true wisdom, of which this folly is deprived.

Let us remember that the world was made by God from nothing; that all living creatures came forth through God, by the Word as craftsman, although they had not existed by nature; for only he has the right to call into being things that are not as though they were things that are.

Let us remember that the human being himself, for whom so great a possession was prepared, was made in God’s image not by some Prometheus from a story, but by that creator of the universe, who deigned with his own hand to make him from the mud of the earth, so that no part of God’s work might be lacking in us.

This thought, as I have said, is the life of the soul, because the first principle of living is not to be ignorant of the one to whom the soul owes itself: not to worship anyone else in deception; not to adore the services of life as though they were the authors of life; and not to admire the elements so greatly that we judge them unworthy of belief as created things, when the one who produced such wondrous things is more worthy of admiration.

O how majestic [Al. “narrow”] this divine thought is, and how full of life! How greatly it kindles the human being toward every pursuit of goodness! How greatly it commends to him the majesty of his creator, when he considers that nothing else in the whole creation except the human being was formed by the hand of God—not the earth, not the seas, not the heaven, and finally not the stars, so clean, so pure, so bright—but that the human being alone was formed by that hand from a certain mud, a heavier and filthier element, by the right hand whose span measures the heavens; whose handful encloses the immeasurable spaces of the outstretched earth.

Such was the value of his having existed in former time.

[Col. 0080A] **IV.** Let us nevertheless see how much the Creator’s goodness further applauds him. It did not make him from the stars; for if he had been created from them, he would derive his distinction rather from the splendor of his material than from the condescension of his Maker. He would seem lesser in the origin of his body if, made from heavenly things, he had been brought down to the cultivation of the lands, to the earth. It was more glorious for him to be raised from the dust and set above the stars.

Our God, I say, specifically willed that what we are should be his own: that we should owe nothing to matter, nothing to the elements, nothing to any principles whatsoever, whether great or small. If he reviews all these things and, turning his mind inward, considers them, they become more moderate and more limited than our origins. But when, through contact with God’s hand, we ceased to be what we had been, and the nature underlying us was glorified by its transformation of the elements into a new quality of matter by its Maker, and our body began, if one may so call it, to be a new element among the elements of the universe, we immediately became more exalted than all the bodies of the world—not by the substance of our nature, but by the power of the Creator. Through that power, what arose from what lay beneath the other creatures was made ruler over all creatures.

Finally, if you consider the metal of our flesh and body, you will find nothing lower, nothing cheaper, nothing more subject to every injury and suffering. Earth alone among the elements appears to be the servant of the rest: alone she experiences within herself the powers of all things, not without her own loss—whether she is scattered as dust by the winds, or drenched and swallowed by the waves, or baked and devoured by the fires of the stars. Thus a human being might not only be unable to boast that he comes from her, but might even be ashamed of it.

Yet if we contemplate our condition, since it is superior to that of the other living creatures when God brings forth the one formed in his own image, we shall discover that the earth itself is the seed of our body. If there is any perception in her, she might have rejoiced that, because of us—in whom she received the image and likeness of the Creator—she was made happier and transformed into something better than she had arisen. For God’s hand touched her, though she herself did not deserve that touch, since it was made for her sake.

What, indeed, is more splendid than this condition? What could we know more exalted? What has been arranged with such care into limbs? What has been bent so gracefully through its joints? What has been raised so sublimely into the face and eyes? What has been modulated so vocally into words? What has been animated so vigorously in the heart? What is richer in sensation? What is more secret in thought? What is more expansive in speech? What is stronger in intellect? What is more fully equipped in disposition? What is more tenacious in memory? What is gentler in affection? What is subtler in reflection?

Thus it becomes evident that he adorned that first-formed human being, already beautified with every dignity—indeed, that he adorned in this body the condition of his own Son, our God, who was to come at the end of the ages for our redemption. The planter of death envied him even paradise at that time, granted under a law as a most delightful estate, beautified with cultivated plots and planted with rural growth. By deceiving the credulous newness of the first human beings, he secretly infused his poison into our bodies and, through a certain discord of division, dissected the one complete nature of the human being, made from two substances. Thus, although we had one mind—that is, the mind produced by the kinship of soul and body—he brought forth, through corrupted nature, another will opposed to the soul.

Finally, the Apostle also says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and making me captive to the law of sin that is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). And elsewhere: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

**V.** Therefore this Creator of ours, who had made either us for ourselves or the world for our sake, offended by those first human beings, poured out curses upon each of them according as the gravity of their offense required. And although he was angry, he immediately displayed the mystery of our salvation like a merciful father. It would not have been right to think of a remedy for our salvation at any other time than when death had been discovered. Thus, among the more prudent, a physician is summoned at the very outset of an illness, so that, once the source of the disease has been detected, a salutary remedy may more easily be supplied.

Our Lord and Savior, therefore, was not promised only when Isaiah cried: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14); nor only when it was said to Abraham: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. 18:10). For by then it was almost too late, and so many thousands of patriarchs seemed to have died without hope. They could not have had life if they had not hoped that the Lord would come, as the Apostle says: “For we have been saved by hope. Hope that is seen is not hope, but hope that is awaited” (Rom. 8:24). And what kind of hope—or, in the variant reading, how could there have been hope—if it had not been promised?

Rather, just as that beast wiser than all the beasts first tasted death for the first human being, so it was necessary that, already at that time, he should taste the support of the true wisdom of our Lord—which he did. Nor did he cease to proclaim it, lest so great a work of his should seem to have been produced more for ruin than for adornment, struck down by one assault of the enemy without any protection; and lest the one who could overwhelm so great a work by another’s power should be regarded as stronger than the one who, having made his work ineffably superior to all creatures, either could not preserve it or would not restore it.

I say that he defended himself against this reproach. Our Creator and Redeemer defended himself, and at the same time showed that he both could and would do so, since neither the strength of power nor the condescension of mercy was lacking. This is what we ought to adore all the more: that in the very storm of our error he did not stop, but burst forth even more mightily while being provoked; that, where we deserved punishment, the hope of redemption was displayed; and that, amid the bitter danger of shipwreck, the harbor of salvation was opened. Thus, in a new manner, what had been the material of anger began to be the source of mercy.

By a hidden operation he thereby revealed that he wished our weakness to be an argument for his power, and showed how much he loved us when we sinned against him: he could not forget us even after our error; rather, he would redeem us more dearly than he had made us (variant: “than what he had made”).

Let human cruelty now seek out for criminals either private workhouses or public prisons, and, angry, sigh over iron handcuffs and harsh chains fastened to a rigid beam, releasing its ingenuity into manifold punishments. Let every judge, with head held high, prove the purity of his own mind through the danger inflicted upon another—becoming more devoted to cruelty the more remote he is from guilt. For those who are purer of guilt are often more savage toward the guilty. They pursue crimes, or the contagion of criminals, more zealously precisely because they have avoided participation in wrongdoing less carefully and less diligently.

O wretched men, endowed with every kind of blindness, who adorn the good with evil; who exalt self-restraint under the appearance of cruelty; who commend their own cruelty by another’s misery; who support their virtues by the destruction of the wretched; and who applaud the torments of the guilty as though they confirmed the judge’s innocence!

**VI.** But our God, contrary to every hope and almost beyond all belief, drew good from evil out of the riches of his mercy. In his anger he generated and strengthened mercy, and he willed the seed of sin to issue in the fruit of pity. He who ought to have destroyed us because of our transgression promised that, because of his mercy, he would restore us.

At the time when we deserved punishments, he displayed the proof of salvation, so that we might understand how powerful he is in granting favor when not injured, since he grants so much even when angry. Thus, in the first human being, as he spoke, he immediately promised us judicial assistance; immediately he brought forth good things from a good treasury; immediately he proclaimed the mystery unknown even to the angels, which was to be fulfilled at the end of time. To the earthly Adam he promised Adam from heaven.

For when he struck the serpent with a curse suited to its deserts, he commanded it to have earth for food and to crawl upon its belly. And because it itself had brought about that death, he added, saying: “I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and the seed of the woman. She shall crush your head, and you shall watch her heel” (Gen. 3:15).

Do you not consider—do you not perceive—that he was then threatening the same one in Christ? I understand no other seed of the woman at all than that of which the Apostle says: “Made of a woman, made of flesh” (John 1:14). That one who, as the Evangelist says, was thought to be the son of Joseph (Luke 3:23), but was not; that one, namely, who was “the Word made flesh” (Gal. 4:4).

For if we examine the ordinary and natural process of generation, women do not have seed; indeed, no woman conceives without a man. And therefore, since the seed of human generation had already been corrupted in Adam through transgression, a heavenly seed is promised—not, as the Apostle understands it, from the corruption of a man, but from God.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] In Agobard, who cites it as from Jerome, the reading is “and you shall lie in wait for his heel”; then follows what he was already threatening, “and, having taken flesh, the one who, as the Evangelist says,” etc., “the one who is the Word,” etc.]

[Note: In the same source: “that flesh might be made in women, and the elements.”]

[Col. 0082D] When this became flesh in a woman, it also naturally fitted together within the very vessel in which those elements were situated the elements of bodily substance—that is, fluid and blood.

The mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, was promised already in that woman. She was set against the serpent’s enmity: “I will place enmity,” he says, “between you and the woman” (Gen. 3:15). He certainly does not say, “I place”—lest this should seem to refer to Eve. It is the word of a promise, transmitted into the future: “I will place,” he says, “enmity between you and the woman.”

That woman, namely, who would bear the Savior, not the one who would give birth to a fratricide. “I will place,” he says, “enmity between you and the woman”—that is, I will raise up a woman who, rejecting the ease of belief, will not merely refuse to listen to you if you point out the sweetness of the fruit as a way of opening the eyes, or promise that she will become like gods; rather, when Gabriel himself brings the word, she will demand an explanation of the novelty of the promise, saying: “How will this be, since I have not known a man?” (Luke 1:34).

That woman, namely, whom golden modesty made tremble at the sight of the angel, but whom the ardor and steadfastness of faith, unable to slip, made bold to inquire into the matter; and who, in what she had withheld from the one who came to her, showed modesty, yet in what she marveled at the one who promised did not yield.

For, concerned about what was announced, she inquired into it. And the angel did not rebuke unbelief, as he did in the case of Zechariah; rather, he instructed her concerning the novelty of the divine operation, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

Behold the seed of the woman, which was not poured into the womb through the usual agency of the genital organs and the union of the sexes, but was found, with the enclosure closed, in the womb of the undeflowered Virgin.

Finally, when the Prophet promises a new event full of wonder, he expresses it in a new phrase: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Hos. 7:14 [sic]).

Every day, certainly, we see and hear of women conceiving according to the necessity of procreation, but of none is it said: “She conceived in the womb.” For the substance of the future human being, poured out through the man, comes together in the woman; and the woman’s womb is not the beginning of the human being who is to be born, but the receptacle of nourishment deposited there.

Mary, however, was not merely the first but the only woman to conceive in the womb. Her untouched modesty brought forth the conception of the womb without injury to virginity. She alone bore for us what she did not receive from us, as the Lord says: “You are from below; I am from above” (John 8:23). She alone is a mother to her son while remaining a virgin to her husband. Her conception, unknown to virginity, was recognized by childbirth. She alone was called a woman, not by conceiving but by giving birth.

From her, therefore, the promised seed of the woman was produced—the one who, according to his humanity, is our Lord God. He was not infused into the womb but found there, as the Evangelist confirms when he says of Mary: “She was found to have a child in the womb” (Matt. 1:18).

Behold, what had been announced does not depart from the preceding prophetic word: “A virgin shall conceive in the womb”; rather, in the novelty of the mystery it agrees even in the wording. The history of what was done is marked by the same style in which what was to be done had been announced.

[Col. 0084A] The prophet Isaiah says: “A virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isa. 7:14); Matthew reports: “She was found to have a child in the womb.” The outcome answers the very word of the promise. The Evangelist speaks no differently from the prophet, nor is he confused by the difficulty of an unprecedented expression in describing the novelty of the work.

Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? What school produced these men, so that they speak outside customary usage? What instruction displayed a novelty so clearly marked? They do not indicate this by human understanding, because what they speak of is not a human work. Yet they mark a new thing, never before done, in such a way that you understand that, together with a marvelous work, a marvelous expression was also born.

Let us, finally, recall the holy women of the patriarchs and see whether anything of this kind is written of any one of them. We read of Sarah: “And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said, and God did for Sarah as he had spoken to her; and she conceived and bore Abraham a son” (Gen. 21:1–2).

In Isaac, divine favor is shown in these words: “And God heard him, and Rebecca his wife conceived” (Gen. 20:21). And of Jacob’s wives it is likewise written: “And Leah conceived and bore Jacob a son,” and so forth (Gen. 25:12 [sic]).

Certainly of none of these is it written, “She conceived in the womb,” although whatever they conceived they could not conceive outside the womb. But because they knew that they conceived through intercourse with a man, their conception did not occur with virginity preserved.

Mary alone conceived in the womb, with the seminal entrance unopened; she conceived with the womb closed. If we reason correctly about the seed of this conception and consider the divine matters inwardly, that sentence preceded it figurally, at the appointed time—the sentence that consecrated or bound the firstborn by blessings or obligations, when the Lord said: “Everything male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. 13:2; Luke 2:23).

What is this male that opens the womb, when it is not the necessity of childbirth but marital intercourse that opens the wombs of all women? Finally, no virgin is said to be “after a husband”—a designation that seems to belong to mysteries whose future remains closed.

Above, moreover, we showed that Scripture says of Rachel: “And God heard her, and opened her womb, and she conceived.” It certainly does not say first, “She conceived,” and afterward, “He opened her womb”; rather, first it says, “He opened”—so that the husband, having opened the doors of the womb, might enter like one about to sow a field prepared for seed. Finally, it adds, “and she conceived.”

Thus it was not childbirth but conception—or rather, conception that was opened—that was indicated. It was not the woman about to give birth who was designated as she came to birth, but the one who was about to sow what would be born. And if she was opened before conception, since she was opened in order to conceive, then certainly the one who was born much later could not open her while he was said to be about to be born—for he could not even be conceived while she remained closed.

“Everything male,” he says, “that has opened the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” What is this interpretation, which does not seem to have been fulfilled even according to the literal sense?

Jacob fraudulently seizes the place of his first-born brother; he is neither prevented by the order of birth nor condemned for his deception. Joseph’s sons are marked by their grandfather’s blessing in an order contrary to that of birth; the blindness of the one who foresaw the future does not err, nor does the son who warned him bend the right hand of his parent, which watered the younger with the sap of the richer blessing.

All these things are contrary if we suppose that the words refer to those males who are born first from women through male seed and who open their mothers’ wombs. But because that sentence has another inner meaning, such firstborn give way and lose their blessings.

Jesse’s son David, not the first, second, or third, but the youngest of all, is anointed by the Prophet and chosen as king, though more despised than all the others. The law’s sentence concerning the firstborn does not flatter the first or second of them against David, since it would certainly have judged the eldest if it had remembered that they opened their mothers’ wombs. When, then, and in whom do we say that this was fulfilled—something that plainly could not remain unfulfilled?

Who is this woman whose womb the fetus opens, not the husband? Who is the virgin who conceives, who does not cease to be a virgin in order to conceive? Certainly not the woman of whom Scripture says: “Adam knew his wife, and she bore him a son” (Gen. 4:1), but the woman of whom the Evangelist declares: “Joseph did not know her until she bore a son” (Matt. 1:25).

Therefore this was unquestionably fulfilled in Mary. Her womb was not opened by one who violated her virginity, but by the birth that poured forth from it. She bore as a virgin, conceived as a virgin, and became a mother before she became a wife.

From her came forth this male who was truly to be called holy. According to the promise, he opened the womb when he was born—not according to the ordinary custom and nature of things, by the seed of a man when he was conceived.

**VII.** But since we cannot quickly unfold the rich meanings of God, with such masses of Scripture opposing themselves to a single interpretation that it is easier to grow weary than to escape, and since all Scripture is one path through all meanings—a path that no one could traverse in human speech, even if he ascribed angelic wings to mortal tongues—it is fitting to return to the subject at hand. Let us not set sail into the deep in a little boat, lest boldness run into danger; rather, as a consolation for our weakness, let us sail within sight of the shore, so that if anything frightening arises, there may at least be hope of easily holding on to what we see.

We were saying that the Lord is the holy seed of the woman, because according to the flesh he would have no human father; and that he was already hostile to the serpent, whom the Spirit of God, not material fluid, had generated in the Virgin’s womb.

Finally, what follows promises an effect greater than any human one, saying: “She shall crush your head” (Gen. 3:15, according to the Septuagint). Who doubts that, apart from our Lord, no one has crushed the serpent’s head? He alone walked upon dragons and scorpions; he alone led captivity captive.

For what follows—“And you shall watch her heel”—to whom else do we believe it belongs? The heel is indeed the extremity of the foot. And the Lord, after John’s baptism and after a forty-day fast, when he is tempted by that same serpent, already victorious over the third deceit, cries out: “Go behind me, Satan” (Matt. 16:23).

What else does he command him to watch but what has been placed or left behind him, namely, his heel? I have said these things above, and from there our discourse itself has led us to this point: when that inner human being thinks, he appears to live not in this world but above the world, with the Maker of all things and with his own Maker. David says: “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies” (Ps. 119:2).

If it is permissible to say so, this is almost what it means to become God: to meditate on divine things; to have already then revealed the mystery of our salvation.

Hence he says in the Psalms: “In the head of the book it is written of me” (Ps. 40:7). The head of the book is the beginning of Genesis, because all Scripture is one book, and the one of whom it is written is God. We see this promise concerning him at its head; and the head of our life is hope. Therefore the head of the book is the hope of life made through God.

I say that the Creator fulfilled, when the world was already growing old, what he had promised in the first age of the world. Hence the Prophet says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 23:4). The rod is the Lord’s mother, from whom this staff came forth to sustain the world, already weary with age.

Let us therefore retrace the whole history of our redemption: he descended into the Virgin’s womb; through birth he became human; he presented himself on behalf of humanity and made himself, the Creator, into his own creature. He took the form of a servant, but emptied himself by the will of his power, not by any change in the nature of his divinity, through which he could not cease to be what he had been.

He deserved curses in return for salutary miracles. He endured spittle, blows, a crown of thorns, and finally the cross. He penetrated the regions below; on the third day he rose again in the same body that had been fastened to the cross. After death, as a living God, he ascended victorious into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God and will come at the appointed time to execute judgment. Through the Spirit of God he is daily celebrated by the mouths of his saints.

To think on these things is to live. This thought is food for the soul. To fall back or return to these things is to be joined to the Lord; and through them to be humbled with him is to suffer with him, to die with him, and also to be raised with him.

What shall I say about the resurrection itself? Although we are mocked by the nations because of it, we are not separated from Christ—even though many who call themselves Christians exclude the resurrection of the flesh. Let those be without a body to whom it is perhaps granted, if one may say so, to be presented to the Lord in some other manner than the Lord returned to the Father. As for us, let us believe and speak accordingly.

[Col. 0086D] **VIII.** What, I ask, could be more joyful than this thought? What could be more uplifting than this hope? It ought to be fixed and rooted more deeply in our minds that, once we have departed from here, we shall one day return to our bodies; and that the separation of soul and body in the meantime does not make us nothing at all, but prepares us to be restored as better beings through the Spirit of God. For we have learned that, even here, the Lord promised us this pledge.

This body, which by its nature is perishable and weighed down by the merit of its former transgression, will, as divine cursing decrees, go to the earth (Gen. 3:19). After many ages—that is, at the end of the world—even when it has become a tiny fragment of ash, or perhaps no longer exists at all, it will be restored by the same earth that corrupts it into nothing. For the earth itself must be freed from the slavery of corruption, and the body must be renewed into the complete solidity of its limbs and into a condition of beauty and splendor.

Whom would such a thought not delight with wonder? The remains of our bodies, I say—certainly none, or at least very little, however small; nevertheless filthy, and never looked upon by the mind without horror—will be reassembled into their own human being, not so that, as Pythagoras falsely and madly imagined, someone may be believed to exist in Euphorbus, but into his own body and identity: through bones and sinews, through veins, through all the organs of life; not merely piece by piece, but joint by joint.

This is not a narrow hope, since the seeds of all crops and plants return in greater and more beautiful form in their grasses than they were either sown by human beings in the earth or fell there of their own accord.

[Col. 0087B] Who would not rejoice, so to speak, to be sown in the earth, which will return us better than it received us, as the Apostle says: “The resurrection of the dead is sown in corruption, but it will rise in incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:42)?

What possession of present things could be compared with this hope? Or what else could raise us to contempt for death more than this meditation, aroused by divine promises and the voices of the prophets?

What comparable lesson had Cleombrotus of Ambracia learned in Plato’s book, when he did not fear becoming his own murderer and threw himself from a high wall, believing that after death there was no judgment and supposing that all souls, without any distinction of merit, were carried equally to heaven once separated from their bodies?

All held this so firmly as truth, and one cloud of this error so enveloped all the wise men of that age, that Socrates himself—so praiseworthy, as they think—killed himself privately, lest he be killed publicly.

The blessed Apostle had meditated on and understood something very different: what he had received not from human beings but through a revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 1:12); not sheltered beneath the shadowy groves of the Academy, but illumined by heavenly light; not instructed in some literary school among yawning boys, but initiated in the third heaven among resplendent angels. In contempt of the present life he cries out: “For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21).

He does not seek a wall from which to throw himself to death, but Christ the Lord, through whom what is mortal may be swallowed up by immortality. For he understands that death is gain for the one whose future life is with Christ. Without the Lord, however, nothing is useful, even if one gains the whole world, while suffering the loss of one’s soul.

That man, therefore, the vessel of election, believed that through Christ our Lord he would be transformed from this earth, which never returns without increase what it receives, but sometimes with lesser and often with greater interest—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. The Lord himself reads these planted seeds in the Gospel.

From that earth, too, came the truth unknown to Pilate, which none of the rulers of this age saw: “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). From that earth, I say, the Apostle declares that he will be transformed into the body of the Lord’s glory, returning in radiant limbs (2 Cor. 3:18). Through Solomon also Wisdom promises this, saying: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reeds.”

Therefore he confidently burst forth in the words, “For me, to live is Christ,” in which, certainly, whatever merits a person possessed will live, while those who are far removed—as they were ignorant, so also they will be unknown.

Now, if it seems good, let us inquire what that Solomonic sentence promised: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the stubble” (Wis. 3:7; Matt. 13:43).

What does it mean that, to those to whom the brightness of flames is granted, so humble and despised a place is offered in which they may run, so that they seem to diminish in the lowliness of the place even though they have increased in the light of their bodies? What, I ask, does it mean that they will fly among the reeds, compared with the stars, and pass through the wretched plants of the earth in the form of a starry radiance, when it is wholly incongruous to mingle either brightness with reeds or reeds with brightness?

Attend, I beg you, to the words of the divine mystery. Just as he is not concerned with oxen, so he is not concerned with a reed bed; and what does a reed bed do in the resurrection unless it strives to show us through all kinds of forms—whether of animals or of plants—that, as the Apostle says, “all things were written for our sake” (Rom. 15:4)?

Understand that by the images of the reed bed unbelieving and faithless human beings are represented: their bodies pleasing on the surface but inwardly empty of virtues. When the spirit of vanity first inflates them, they imitate the hissing of the serpent, and offspring of vipers attend upon healthy births.

“Sparks,” he says, “in the reed bed.” Thus the saints are among sinners, because not all flesh is the same flesh. “In the reed bed,” he says—that is, in bodies empty of light and destined to burn with another’s brightness, for whom the radiance of the saints will be punishment, since God is a consuming fire and the righteous will come into the image of the divinity.

For God made the human being; “in his own image he made him” (Gen. 1:27). And the Apostle bears witness that he believes the human being will become like him.

Necessarily so. For if he was like God when he was made, he will be like God when he rises again. Whatever now appears unlike the Creator in us has been impressed upon us through the defect of transgression. The craftsman of lies disfigured the living form of truth by swollen deeds and, when he corrupted our minds, inscribed his perversity upon our very limbs. Through the glory of the resurrection, those things wrongly added or diminished will be washed away, and only that which reflects the Maker of all things as in a mirror will shine forth. Thus the one who altered the work will grieve that he has lost his own handiwork, while the human being will at last rejoice to be whole.

Yet, as we have already said, this will not be true of everyone. We shall be in the light only if we are righteous: “For all will indeed rise, but not all will be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51). Distinction among persons will be made according to the diversity of their merits.

Even among the saints themselves there will be some difference in their works, as the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41). What difference, then, shall we perceive among the ungodly or among sinners, some of whom rise for judgment and others for the council of the saints?

And although they are separated at the very time of the resurrection, what shall we say of their appearance and form? As it seems to me, their clothing will not be some woven garment, nor something produced by women’s labor, but will be found in their own merits and prayers. Blessed John shows this in the Revelation, saying that he saw the saints clothed in linen (Rev. 19:14).

And lest we should seek the threads or undergarments of linen and imagine that something material, corruptible, and perishable is being fashioned in the heavens, he added: “The linen is the justifications of the saints.”

Then, as I understand it, what is now hidden beneath the body like a shell will appear on the surface of our bodies. Then, miserable me, each person’s conscience will become his garment. Then the things that each person has built upon that foundation, “than which no other can be laid” (1 Cor. 3:11), will stand forth, so that the one who built what will endure may receive a reward, while the one who built what will burn may suffer loss.

Why should I now mention what follows? It all belongs to the saints: flesh without earth, a body without sensation of pain, a soul without fear, life without end, an age without time, light without night, blessedness without end. I see a human being, and in the human being, God, because “God is all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

Everything that now appears impossible to human beings will then, through the generosity of the everlasting King, be able to be veiled and revealed, liquefied and solidified again. He will become the one whom the disciples did not perceive entering to them through solid and bodily walls and doors, yet whom they all saw standing within before them. And all that the Spirit of God nurtured without this body, the body will accomplish together with the Spirit of God.

Christianity cannot be satisfied with contemplating these things. This is its rest, its delight, its pleasure, its luxury: to go in thought to the seat of God and there to claim for itself a place and a share in that seat—not by presumption of its own, but by the promise of the divinity.

Nor does this seem difficult to it, once it recognizes that its human being already exists there in Christ the Lord. It claims for itself an equal right through kinship with the flesh assumed by God, because we are of his flesh and of his bones. For he is the head of the body, the Church (Col. 1:18); he is the beginning of every principality and power, as the Apostle proclaims: “From him the whole body, compacted and brought forth through connection and joined together, grows into the increase of God.”

What shall I say about the coming judgment and the day of the Lord, desirable to the devout and to be fled by the impious? What shall I say about that fiery flood—not of waters—with the earth smoking, the sea fleeing, and the heaven folded up like a book?

## IX

These things are grievous to the rich of this age, but they are to be awaited by Christ’s poor, for whom the Lord sighs in the Psalm, saying: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise” (Ps. XII).

What shall I say of that immense tribunal of the majesty of the Judge, to be worshiped upon twelve seats, and of the great power granted by the Son, so that in judging they will even have the angelic powers—as though their Creator had subjected them to their authority—when the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge even angels?” (I Cor. V, 3). And what will not be believed to be subjected to those to whom even that spiritual nature of wickedness must be made subject?

What, then, will those do who now glory in offices, who, through terrifying prefectures, fasces, and—as they suppose—everlasting consulships, strive to make themselves equal to God by seizure rather than by nature? What will he do who joins house to house (Isa. V, 3)? He who, after throwing the state into confusion and breaking all the boundaries by which it was enclosed on every side, leaping over mountains, rivers, and seas, wishes, so far as it concerns him, to make one possession of what is the common earth of all; and, extending beyond the breadth of the immense world in the anxious ambition of Alexander of Macedon and spreading himself through innumerable Epicurean worlds, once he has acquired by greed the narrow confines of this world, is credulously inflamed toward another, without considering what his own body can endure, supposing that he will suffer loss of his rightful claim if he does not give credence to his madness?

What will those do who, as though correcting morals, attack and harass the household of the Lord when it lives with greater vigilance and austerity—whether in garments of humble color, or in the dry frugality of food, or in the sober wakefulness that is not given over to idleness—as though it were made luxurious by softer clothing, fattened by more abundant banquets, or drowsing on warmer beds? They do not know that in God’s saints, martyrs, and confessors, his pupil is being struck.

Without doubt they will perish; on that day all their thoughts will perish. At that tribunal neither Lucius Crassus will defend them, nor Marcus Antonius, nor Tullius, more eloquent than those men; for then every tongue of this age will fall silent, and justice alone will be eloquent among its humble country folk. It made the mouths of infants articulate and loosened the tongues of the mute into a new song, and by its mercy acquired for itself a heavenly harmony from its little sheep.

Even if human efforts should cease to celebrate its glory, stones are shown as destined to cry out, to the confusion of the human race. But why have I departed from the subject proposed, as though rebuking mortal wickedness? Why, like a public prosecutor of a uniform evil, have I spared no worldly vices, moved by pity for some? Even if it were the time for judging, I would nevertheless not dare to cast a stone at the adulteress; and even if authority armed me with a purer conscience for the judgment of the innocent, I ought still to await the proper time, as the Apostle teaches—he who did not take judgment away from the saints, but postponed it.

For he says: “Do not judge before the time” (I Cor. IV, 5). He is evidently indicating that the time of the resurrection must be awaited, when, through the glory of incorruption, renewed flesh will stand in wonder before the Judge. When permanence in eternity has already been established, when fear of falling has disappeared, then one will not hesitate to pass sentence on another, once one has deserved to be secure concerning oneself.

But now all things are uncertain, all things totter, as the Apostle says: “Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 3). One who does not know the condition of another easily judges his fall. And what if you have placed confidence in the wretched, so that God may grant it to the blessed? Let us rather praise the rewards of the saints—that is, the true things—than be marked as reckless or untimely, whether because of our conscience or because of the time.

## X

Let us therefore return to those most noble and joyful thoughts of the saints; for nothing is more joyful than for a mortal to meditate upon the inheritance promised to him. Let us place before our eyes the one whom we have mentioned; for it is safer to celebrate what is true than to condemn what is pitiable, although blessed truths cannot be recounted without also speaking of sinners’ misery.

Let us behold, as we have resolved, God’s saints flying everywhere with torches, gripping double-edged swords, and flashing their right hands for vengeance. This is the glory of God’s saints; this is the military service despised in this age, scattered by the tongues of all in their slanders. Here will be the fruit of our patience; here the reward of our endurance.

These are the rewards for the Name amid blasphemers: to have every proud soul and every arrogant human being subjected to them—once the world’s most powerful kings, worshiped throughout the earth, now to be brought forward with iron cuffs and fetters, and their nobles bearing upon their necks and throats the monstrous weights of their chains, to be presented before the splendor of that august tribunal to those whom they once despised, scorned, and mocked.

For the order will be reversed: this age will belong to the luxurious, and the next is to be believed to belong to the wretched. “Woe to the rich, because they have received their consolation” (Luke VI, 24)—to those rich, that is, to whom it will be said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matt. XXV, 35).

To those rich who were unwilling to make friends for themselves from unrighteous mammon; who, when their thoughts overflowed with abundant produce that refreshed no one, planned to build new storehouses for immense harvests; who did not know that they would eat on the following day. Their soul was demanded of them at that time, while a vain solitude occupied a single night, though they had not ceased to heap up treasure or to keep watch over their buried wealth.

From this, poor Lazarus, together with that patriarch who lived as a stranger in the world, rejoices in his resting-place. The rich man, by contrast, burns in everlasting fires; stripped of every dignity and possession, the man once despised as poor implores divine assistance and longs to be touched by the tip of his smallest finger—he whose poverty he had failed to sustain even with crumbs falling from his table amid his rich dishes and abundant banquets.

Since, then, the prescribed judgment is to be celebrated through us—that is, through the saints—vengeance upon nations and peoples has been given to us. When this is considered, what frame of mind is ours? What ardor of spirit? What desire for the future? What contempt for the present? It can more easily be felt than said.

Who is there who, hastening toward these things, does not desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I, 23)? And what great thing is it if death is despised for such great and such splendid blessings—blessings for which this life itself must also be despised? For “whoever loses his life for these things saves it; but whoever saves his life here will lose it” (Matt. X, 39).

Indeed, since many in this world are inflamed by ambition as though by the flames of madness, to such a degree that they spare neither hoarded wealth, nor inheritances, nor even their own children—whom they customarily set forward when accused of avarice—while they purchase prefectures and consular offices, powers which death admits and a successor excludes, what madness is it not rather to acquire, at every expense and even at the cost of life itself, those things that will make the promoted either secure concerning the eternity of life or glorious because of perpetual dignity at the judgment?

## XI

Time urges us, and the place itself suggests it; nor does the subject seem alien, since we have begun to discuss the merits of the saints, that we may refute the blasphemies of utter misery, which seem to belong to this matter.

For there have been people who preferred to bite with slander rather than receive with veneration the outstanding and heavenly powers already at work through the relics of the saints, indeed almost in our own times. They vomit forth against God’s servants that ancient poison of Jewish unbelief which those people once poured out against the Lord himself with viperous tongues and deadly hissing, saying: “By what authority does he do this?” and “Who gave you this authority?”

They repeated to us, who were nearby, what foolish unbelief was saying about the divine and blessed Gervasius and Protasius. While some devise disparagement of them before Bishop Ambrose, they do not fear violating them with sacrilegious speech, making inquiries about the miracles in this fashion:

“What is this? Is it because they are martyrs that they have deserved the gifts of miraculous powers? Why is what was granted to them long ago being exercised only so late? Or, if they did not display these powers at the time when they suffered, how are they now performing them? What is this that they seem now to display? Or did Ambrose make them greater by revelation than the dignity of martyrdom?”

Do you recognize that, although expressed in other words, the same falsehood we have reported as spoken against the Lord has been directed against the martyrs: “By what authority do you do this?” and “Who gave you this authority?” (Matt. XXI, 23)?

It is, I suppose, a lukewarm consolation, born of envy, to ask whether what you see to be divine is divine, and to demand a reason when belief is necessary. And when the Apostle says, “Love believes all things” (I Cor. XIII, 7), who doubts that those who have not applied faith to such great powers are without the love of God? The one who inquires like a tempter denies faith.

“From where does this authority come?” As though it were not manifest that the holy martyrs now perform miracles in the spirit by that authority by which they previously overcame their adversaries in the flesh and in suffering.

Let us set our foot against these people, if it is permissible to say so, sons of the Jews; and just as recently we crushed their ancestor—that is, the Jew who thought himself excessively wise in sacrilege—by the gift of the Godhead, so let us destroy this offspring of blasphemers under a Christian name, through him who said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (I Cor. I, 17). Thus may we glory in a double triumph through the Lord, and may they recognize that understanding of divine matters is founded on Catholic faith, not on worldly wisdom. The Lord warns us: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9). Thus it may become clear that the obscure things of unbelief are open to the faithful, while even the plain things of faith are not perceived by unbelievers.

## XII

Perhaps, in your concern, watchfulness, and life-giving diligence, you ask what that controversy was in which the Lord granted us a trophy over a false Israelite. I shall relate it, and I shall not be silent, since you love to have these matters extend the page for you.

Even if it may seem inappropriate to insert another subject before the earlier ones have been completed, I nevertheless prefer, for your sake, to speak of some things out of their proper order rather than pass over what your prayers have now obtained from me.

One of the enemies of the cross of Christ, among God’s household—and indeed among its teachers—struck at the Lord with a spirit of blasphemy because of the scandal of his nation, which they had taken upon themselves against our Lord, and produced examples from the Law.

Just as his murderous father once tempted the Lord on the pinnacle of the Temple and impudently declared what had been promised concerning him in the Law, so this man, lest his faithlessness seem insufficiently learned or his lie stand exposed without greater authority, said:

“Our prophet Elisha performed more miracles than your Lord Christ. For when you report as a great deed that Lazarus was brought back from death into life (John XI, 14), what more can you say than that a dead man was raised by a living man?

“I will present something that even by your own confession is judged to be true. Our Elisha, already dead, when his bones were laid upon another dead man—the corpse which a crowd, fleeing the approaching band of robbers and abandoning the duty of burial, had thrown beside his body—gave life to the lifeless man. From cold bones and a bloodless body he poured vital warmth into another corpse; and he did not give what he possessed, but bestowed upon another what he himself at that moment did not possess (II Kings XIII, 21).

“I believe that this will seem to you greater than all the other miracles: that a dead man was restored to the living air through a dead man, and that at the very time when he himself was bound by the law of nature, he released another from nature’s law.

“If this surpasses all his works, why should he not be regarded as superior, though we confess him to be a prophet, not the Lord? Or, if you know of anything similar to this, declare it, so that the one who was superior in merit may also surpass him in honor.”

At these words our leaders were stunned. They gave no answer and produced no weapon with which to strike back; almost beneath the empty contrivance and useless battering ram of their adversary they collapsed, so completely that the man who, as they say, ought to have been a fugitive from everyone carried away the glory of victory without a contest.

When this was reported to me, I groaned that such negligence was present among us that we could not even establish the truth, while others were able to thrust falsehood forward in the place of truth. I entreated the Lord—since nothing belongs to us—that he supply his own weapons, by which the disgrace of their indolence might be removed.

“Give me,” I said, “this boaster who says: ‘Our lips belong to us; who is our Lord?’” (Ps. XII, 5). Surely, through him who destroys the boastful tongue, I shall show that the servant is not to be equated with the Lord—although the Jews themselves know that the ancient prophets performed no miracles by their own powers.

Indeed, when Elisha came with the spirit of his master as his inheritance, seeming somewhat arrogant because of the reward of his gifts, even he could not divide the waters except by invoking God (II Kings II, 14).

But I admit that, for the moment, this was his proposed power: that the glory of our faith may be greater if, even while we believe, we crush the tempter.

“What do you say, blasphemer of the Lord?”

“Elisha himself,” he replied, “already dead, raised another dead man by contact with his body.”

Here, fully—as in all things—the prophet’s power rises toward its Lord. When your unbelief fortified the tomb of the Lord Jesus Christ with stones and soldiers guarded the stone, I suppose this was done so that his resurrection would not lack suitable witnesses. For if you wished to believe that he would rise, you knew it.

Then suddenly, when the hinges of the underworld had been shaken, amid the soldiers’ astonishment and the collapse of the rocks, he raised into the light not someone else, but himself.

If these gifts had properly belonged to Elisha, he would have preferred to give them to himself; nor could he provide for another what he himself needed. Indeed, even your ancestors proclaimed that this was greater, when they mocked the Lord on the cross, saying: “He saved others; let him save himself. Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. XXVII, 42).

Therefore we prevail by the judgment of your own people. Your people promised that they would believe if he provided for himself what he had been accustomed to provide for others. Why do you not believe what you admit to be more excellent?

Certainly no one else possessed this authority. Indeed, the Lord himself says of his soul: “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John X, 18).

Review the proud images of your ancestors; unfold again the powers of the patriarchs; find who possessed such authority. Why should I not believe that he can free my soul, who was able to free his own?

Though I intended to say more, memory suggested to me that the volume was growing, and therefore that the course of this controversy should be brought back, since the earlier matter still stands at the door. It is owed its own space, though with tighter reins, still untouched.

And truly, it was not necessary to say much on this point, lest he too grow larger—if he thought he had brought forward something significant and sought victory through a lengthy debate. We have broken not his wisdom, for there was none in him, but his arrogance, of which he had an abundance.

## XIII

Having dismissed this Israelite—or lest he boast that he had engaged us in combat, since what we have said was offered more for the instruction of our own people than for a contest and struggle with those who refuse to believe even when defeated—we must return to the place from which I strayed, having almost severed the paths of thought.

We must go carefully around the sheep of the house of Israel, for if the love of God is in us, “who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. XI, 20).

They must be taught rather than allowed to speak as far as blasphemy, if perhaps they neither retain nor understand what was prophesied. They ask whether the divine power that has now begun to appear in the martyrs is truly divine.

Of what law are the people who ask this? Surely, of the Christian law—which has been so furnished with prophecies that nothing so new or unexpected can break upon our times that a stronger faith may not admire it, or a weaker faith blaspheme it.

The ancient prophets foretold everything up to the Lord. After the Lord, the apostles prophesied whatever remained. Blessed Paul, through the freedom of the Holy Spirit, did not remain silent; he says: “We know in part and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

This does not mean that he is ignorant of everything or prophesies nothing at all—especially since Christ speaks in him—but that he prophesies of the whole from one part and knows the whole from one part. He prophesies to us what he knows belongs to that time which was to come. Whatever he prophesies, he prophesies for the age that is to come. He prophesies the whole, even though he prophesies from one part.

For he prophesies those things whose disclosure the portion of time remaining until the end required. He prophesies from one part, therefore, because part had already been prophesied; and for that reason the prophet knew the things he was prophesying would come.

The fullness of time, as he himself said, has abolished the portions of that prophecy in this manner: “When what is perfect has come, what is in part will be destroyed” (I Cor. XIII, 10)—that is, when, at the consummation of the world, no greater knowledge or further prophecy will need to be sought.

To demonstrate more clearly the power of this understanding, he added: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but then face to face.”

For the present, everything exists through figure and is overshadowed by certain outlines of images, so that the weakness of our flesh and our earthly substance may extend themselves more readily toward the truth of spiritual things; and that vision, shown to it faintly even through a mirror, may produce in it a desire for its own beauty and teach us how great that beauty is in its own substance, since it appears so wondrous even in reflected enigmas illuminated by its light.

Therefore now we behold what is promised through a mirror, but do not possess it on account of the merits of our powers; we marvel at what is shown, but do not yet hold it as something bestowed. Then prophecy and knowledge will cease, and what was promised will be entered into.

For this reason prophecy is always obscure: it is sung at one time and seen at another. What is said, while it is not seen, is scarcely believed to have been foretold.

Thus Isaiah, when he recognized our redemption long beforehand in the Virgin’s womb and displayed it to the people as though it were already present, saying, “Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14), disturbed the age of the unbelieving Israelites by announcing what was both present and future.

The earlier Israelites killed their prophet because they did not see what he revealed; and these later Israelites killed him who had been prophesied to them because they did not receive the prophecy. We must take care that this not also happen among us with respect to God’s martyrs, if our age blasphemes those whom the earlier age persecuted.

And since, as we have said, what was foretold has come, nothing remains to come that was not foretold beforehand, the Lord himself saying: “Behold, I have foretold everything to you” (Mark XIII, 23).

Let us rather see whether these things, which now appear to our eyes as though fulfilled, were ever poured into the ears of our ancestors. Let us see whether one and the same spirit performs all these things (I Cor. XII, 11).

Finally, let us see whether an angel from heaven should preach anything other than what was preached to us—even though the powers of the Lord themselves, which are being performed, bear witness through the tormenting of demons, since Satan does not cast out Satan. For the uniformity of wickedness, formed by an undivided natural association, does not fear loss through an increase of likeness, but gains strength from it.

Indeed, many spirits of depravity had gathered into the form of a single legion [Al.: “the spirit is omitted”], and a confederation of viperous wickedness had formed itself into a mass. Their multitude did not harm them; just as, united in miserable weakness, it acquired strength, so it feared falling, once divided, into the emptiness of an unsubstantial mixture.

## XIV

For the moment, however, let us set aside this line of argument. As we proposed, let us establish that the things we admire in the Lord’s churches and in the cemeteries of the saints must be believed to be divinely wrought, if they have been prophesied.

In this matter, so harsh and difficult and previously treated by no one, we ought to consult the Lord, if we were not afraid that, because of our boldness, we might be rejected as unworthy to approach him. For no one outside the Lord himself can explain what belongs to him.

Indeed, it is astonishing from where miserable people derive such confidence—from where comes such friendly familiarity in addressing the Lord, that we dare to break out in the words: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 3).

Who conceived so great a desire? Who, careless in estimating himself, sighed for such immense vows as to long to touch the Lord’s own mouth face to face?

Would that he deign to kiss us with the kiss of those whom he himself deemed worthy to kiss, so that, standing among the last and the third ranks, we might deserve to draw some measure of knowledge from the lips of those who learned the whole fullness of wisdom from the Lord’s own mouth.

And even if we were supported by the privileges of great merits, examples were set before us like lofty foundations repeatedly laid, to restrain modesty, lest anything indecent or any disordered presumption of frivolity should dare to act.

Who was more chosen than blessed Peter? Who was more lifted up in hope, more free in faith? To him the Lord promised that he would kiss him with the kiss of his mouth, saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” and: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 29).

Yet here Peter, bending himself under a certain weight of modesty, submits the confidence that he possessed in his merit when he was more elevated, and, more modestly, asks questions. At the Lord’s supper he inquires, not on his own behalf, who would betray the Lord, and in humble embarrassment seeks the Lord’s kiss through another’s mouth.

He did have confidence before the Lord, so that he sometimes presumed even upon what was not granted to a human being: as when, with the Lord walking upon the sea, he dared ask that the hardened surface of the waters might likewise support him beneath his feet. Yet he was somewhat less confident in himself and more prudent for us, placing before us, as in a mirror, forms that we might imitate through his conduct.

If, through an intermediary, he cautiously investigates the Lord’s foreknowledge, what is more worthy of instruction than this, or more subtle than this method of consultation?

This is what we must do. Since we possess confidence without any merit, we ought at least to possess the modesty of the example, imitating blessed Peter even in this respect. He showed not only with what humility we should act, but also by what means we may reach what we desire.

Let us seek from him the resolution of this question, which he himself was not ashamed to ask—from him who, reclining upon the Lord’s own breast as though upon the ark of the Old and New Testaments, approached not merely the entrance of certain divine oracles as a diligent inquirer, but entered the innermost sanctuary of the hidden dispensation like a familiar priest.

For this reason he alone saw the Word in the beginning, when the inner sanctuary was entrusted to him to measure, just as the outer altar of the most holy temple is entrusted to others.

May he lead us from that book which he wept to see sealed with seven seals, and over whose opening he rejoiced—not through some false doorway, but through doors standing open—into his own breast of truth.

## XV

Yet, lest we linger while consulting him, he anticipates us in our inquiries and, through the brevity of his foreknowledge, illuminates what he saw would at some point trouble our minds.

For he gives answers, as though he had been questioned, from Patmos—from that place where, once the secrets of heaven had been closed to Caesar, he entered without being an outsider and, driven away from human society, came to know the mysteries of the angels.

For he says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus, which they held. And individual robes were given to them, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers who were to be killed afterward in imitation of them should be completed” (Rev. VI, 9, 10, 11).

O truly divine Apocalypse, revealed deservedly to so great an Apostle at the time of confession, so that endurance might be strengthened when the merits of those who had suffered were shown to him.

Therefore we must not go astray among the leaves of the Sibyls, whose pages struggle with the uncertain evils of the world’s spirits, just as their places are disturbed by the winds of this air.

Behold, the Apostle explains with complete clarity what he possessed and brings light to the darkest question. He had sensed that these things would one day have to be spoken, which a more sinister tongue now hurls, in words artfully softened as with oil, toward the destruction of its hearers and of itself.

Therefore, he says, he saw beneath God’s altar the souls of slain martyrs.

No one questions the faithfulness of the witness; let the testimony be examined, let the understanding of the answer waver, but not the authority of the speaker.

## XVI

First, this must be noted: the Apostle testifies that he saw the souls of slain martyrs, lest, when we begin to discuss their gifts, someone should say that what is now taught to have been granted to the martyrs belongs only after the resurrection.

This is especially supported by the fact that they complain about the delay of judgment. One who is going to rise, not one who has already risen, complains about a delay; for it is one thing to ask to take possession, and another already to possess.

The martyrs’ robes are given to the army; and, as though ungrateful for such great freedom, a great resentment strikes heaven because vengeance is delayed. For their speech rebukes the delay with no slight burden, when they say: “How long, O Lord”—that is: “How long will you not avenge those whom you ought to have avenged immediately?”

“How long, O Lord”—that is: “Are you postponing us beyond the end of the ages?” For the end has already been reached, and you do not speak of our vengeance.

When they say this, they add wondrously: “Will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?”

Therefore the question cannot mean “how long,” if those mortals who persecuted the Lord’s servants with clubs, stones, claws, scourges, lead, iron, wild beasts, and fire are still living upon the earth. “How long” refers to the lengthening of the age: either “how long” means without end, because the persecutors still remain in the flesh; or they have departed this life, even though they dwell on the earth—if “how long” is not misleading.

But the witnesses of truth say nothing false. Therefore what must be sought is interpretation, not faith: the faith is not excluded by obscure expression, but veiled by it.

When they say, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” they do not desire the blood and deaths of those mortals who once raged against them in popular revolt or, supported by tribunals, pronounced capital sentences, since those people still dwell on earth.

Nor is it permissible for the dead to be accused, since, while they were alive, they were defended with these words: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII, 60). For they do not know what they are doing.

If, amid the torments of suffering and the bitter pains of death, anyone prayed so piously for the unjust, the impious, the bloodstained, and the blasphemers; if, at the very time when the extremity of suffering might have stirred those enduring it to curse, prayer was poured out for a human being—who does not understand that the persons being marked were not the minds of the martyrs but those of their persecutors?

It is those whom we must believe still dwell on earth at that time who are being sought—those whom ignorance does not defend; not those who have ceased, by the condition of their natural substance, to dwell on earth and who were long ago excused by the martyrs themselves under the plea of ignorance.

We know who these are: without doubt, the spiritual powers of wickedness and darkness, which still dwell on earth and sinned against God’s servants not through ignorance.

For when they said to the Lord himself, “Why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII, 29), how could they have been ignorant of his servants? They would not have persecuted them if they had been ignorant that they were his servants. Therefore, when they persecuted them, they knew whom they were trying through torments to draw away from their Lord.

And when the blessed martyrs intercede for human beings and defend them by excusing them on the ground of ignorance, it follows that those who knew are held guilty—those who poured the very darkness of ignorance over human beings, whose fury even excuses human impieties.

Who else can we say these are than those who are not even friends to their own people, since they do not allow them to be what is good, and who are enemies even to God’s servants, since they persecute them for not knowing what is good?

## XVII

After the complaint of these holy souls, let us examine what follows. “And individual white robes were given to them,” he says (Rev. VI, 11).

What does it mean that they are clothed again? For earlier, as it is written, they received garments from God, and now they are granted clothing in a twofold freedom.

Since these garments are spiritual, we need not fear that the ones given earlier appear to be external; nor, in fact, has any complaint arisen on that account.

Therefore, since the difference and significance of the garments are not without mystery, we must understand varieties of gifts and the abundance of works, because “one and the same Spirit supplies all things.”

They first receive garments where, through confession, they laid down their bodies—so that, I believe, they might be found clothed rather than naked.

Again they receive other garments after their appeal, or rather after the transformation of such prolonged patience and endurance. When they receive these, who does not understand that they have been infused with a new power along with the new garment, by which they now shine forth and appear?

If they had asked for one thing and received another, they would either reject the gifts or seek more, mocked as they would be. But since it is not God’s way to mock those to whom he has made great promises, and since they do not complain after the second act of generosity, should we doubt that the appearance of the robes given to those who seek vengeance belongs to the consolation of their complaints?

And if this is consolation, what greater consolation could be found than the power by which they pursue demons—that is, their own enemies?

If we compare these robes with our garments, let us seek some other garments as well, so that they may not lack when these are being stored away. But this is absurd, as becomes immediately apparent, because it departs from the true and necessary interpretation.

The complaint arose from the delay of vengeance. The end of the ages—that is, of our age—is at hand; for the ends of the ages have come upon us. To dispel the belief in delay, souls are clothed in robes, lest they be thought entirely naked and without greater protection.

The condition of souls stripped of the body is one thing; that of human beings still living in the flesh is another. For us, sheep’s fleeces and the work of women provide clothing; for them, merits make the garment.

When, therefore, after the martyrs’ complaint, souls are clothed in robes, they are granted divine protection—the protection with which that chosen vessel also desired to be clothed. When Adam had lost this garment, he was found naked even in paradise.

Finally, the work itself indicates what we should understand by the robes. If we believe that the martyrs asked for vengeance, then we believe that, for their consolation, they received something in the meantime. If their complaint was quieted because of the robes, as though they were gifts of clothing, why did the first gifts not also deserve this effect?
