But since, as I have said, the varieties of powers with which the noble souls are divinely fortified are signified by the robes, after the second magnificence they show, in accordance with the form of their petition, what they seem to have obtained against the persecutors who dwell on earth, and what they will still obtain, while those persecutors will kill their fellow servants through a persecution of the same kind, until the predestined number of witnesses is completed.

Here too we must not overlook the fact that this voice of the martyrs came between two periods of persecution, so that it might designate those who blaspheme when they wonder that the martyrs have obtained something new in our time.

For since we see that cruel persecutions have occurred and believe that others are still to come, this intervening time, during which the martyrs who preceded us are rewarded, is our own. And therefore they are now at work—not by virtue of the merit they have always possessed, but by the power they have recently acquired.

### XVIII

Perhaps someone may wonder what it is that they are ordered to await, if the power that will bring judgment upon the demons has already burst forth to the maturity of punishment, and they are instructed to endure the resurrection. Yet this glory had also been promised to them in David’s songs in these words: “They will rejoice in their resting places” (Psalm 149:2). Since they have been buried, they will certainly rejoice. He called their resting places their tombs, from which they will also rise when they have been awakened by the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:15). Their tombs, therefore, are truly called resting places, in which they now rest.

And if “they will rejoice in their resting places,” this was to happen before they rose from their repose—before they rose from their tombs. This has been fulfilled so completely that we can see without hesitation that they rejoice in their resting places. For what other such rejoicing could enter their souls than this: that before the very resting places—that is, as we have said, the tombs—of the saints, their enemies, whom they once believed they had killed, now confess, not without the bitterness of torments, both that those saints are alive and that they are taking vengeance upon them?

These are the things which those garments conferred upon them, garments which a special generosity has repeated. Through them, those who were not named are invoked, those who were unknown are celebrated, and those who were not seen become visible. As we read, they had not possessed these garments until now, but have now begun to possess them.

In this form that woman is praised in Solomon who makes double garments for her husband: one in the patience of suffering, the other in the power of vengeance. It is holy and devout for us to read the passage in this way. Otherwise, we ought not even to speak, lest either our unbelief or our ignorance descend, through blasphemous argument, into the darkness of paganism, when prophecy had gone before precisely in order to bring light to what was to come.

Now it remains that we should believe that the things we have proved and promised are accomplished by divine agency—not merely promised, but also requested. And if they were both requested and granted to none but those who asked, what is surprising if they do not conceal either what they had requested or what they rejoice they received beforehand?

“They demand punishments from those who dwell on the earth”: those whom the accusation has seized, those the power attacks. For those who dwell on the earth are the demons who possess the minds of human beings who possess earthly things. When the martyrs demand that these be delivered to punishments [another reading: “martyria”], they also plead on behalf of those whom the demons had possessed. Finally, they perform even their own miracles in such a way as to exclude the demons from earthly habitation—that is, from human beings possessed by earthly things.

Are we slandering them by asking why the demons are tortured, and taking the side of their enemies? The martyrs rise up against them with an almost envious indignation and complain that they are being allowed to endure for so long a span of ages. Yet we pretend to be surprised at what this means, as though the demons ought not, even in our own time, to pay what they have deserved ever since Adam.

But since this miracle appears to have first arisen at Milan, or to have been granted especially to the good Ambrose above all others, who does not see that our faith was approved by divine testimonies because of the perfidy of the Arians? For when the Catholic faith in Italy had endured intolerable tyranny under Auxentius, at last, when the Lord granted back its ancient freedom, it breathed again precisely at the time when the aforesaid Ambrose was appointed.

Nevertheless, all the glory of heaven, and all the martyrs as well, consented to this same man—plainly for the confusion of his adversaries and for our hope. Although they had long possessed the time to appear, they were seeking a person to whom they might reveal themselves: one to whom they might be revealed in the faith under which they had suffered martyrdom.

Thus Ambrose was granted what had been denied to Auxentius, because what Auxentius blasphemed, Ambrose preached. But although this power of the martyrs is destined to pass through all the provinces—for it must be granted to everyone, without respect of persons, not to Ambrose alone—it nevertheless necessarily first appeared in Italy, which had been dominated by Arian unbelief. For signs are granted not to the faithful but to the unbelieving (1 Corinthians 14:23).

Those who ask the Lord for a sign are unbelievers: the scribes ask, the Pharisees ask; the apostles are silent, believe, and follow. Therefore it is not surprising that divine power works through the tombs of the saints, since even by these remedies the heretical mind could not be healed, so that it might at last follow that bishop to whom it had seen the martyrs themselves, through the gracious revelation of their powers, give their fellowship.

### XIX

Let us now return to the contemplation of the perfect man, from which this abundance first grew before his measure had been filled. This discussion concerns those very meditations of which David says: “Blessed is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

Indeed, once one has entered the forest of the law, it is difficult to separate the subject matter of individual questions. One touches another, as branches touch one another, through the interconnectedness of their precepts, so that what has been begun cannot be explained without beginning with the other.

See how beautiful it is to know this man of ours: to remain unmoved when confronted with such things, to be disturbed by none of the others as though by mere accidents, and to distinguish the kinds of works. Since the demons themselves also act, one must understand their natures; know what is true and what is false; know that this is not to be deceived, not to go astray, not to attribute the things of God to the enemy, nor to assign to God what belongs to the demons; know the times; recognize the signs; know the Lord’s will; and venerate some of God’s wonders with thanksgiving, while avoiding others with the condemnation they deserve.

Even the men of this age praised such a man, as Virgil says:

> Fortunate is he who was able to know the causes of things.

This is a good statement, if he had arrived at it by the proper path, so that it might become evident that he did not understand what he praised. Omitting what is primary, he celebrated what is secondary. In the wrong order he even reversed the task of the wise man: for it is not the causes of things but the Creator of things whom one must seek. Through him, if we have come to know him, we shall enter into the causes of things.

Otherwise, if he is omitted, how can we possess knowledge of the causes of things, when one must first inquire who made them and then why he made them? Once the author of things has been found, we also discover their causes.

This man failed to see the point so completely that he proclaimed as primary the place in which he could have recognized the causes of things. He then added that one should worship the gods, as though carrying out a lesser task. Anyone can recognize that these gods were not the creators of things, since knowledge of things is separated from them as something foreign. Nor ought they to be worshiped if they cannot provide as their first achievement those things which are praised.

They do not know the things whose makers they were not. Finally, after taking invention away from their gods, they assign it to human ingenuity—to those, of course, who excel in wisdom because they do not worship idols. Thus man has become more powerful than their gods, if by a higher act of thought he has reached what their gods do not know.

Yet he commands those to worship the gods who, through their folly, are not fully able to discover the causes of things, whose innermost parts, to use his own words, contain “cold blood.” Our man, however, knows both that worshiping God is the principal wisdom and that he possesses knowledge of the causes of things.

He does not seek to excel through the worldly reasoning of Syracuse’s wise man. Rather, he is taught by the one whom he worships, whom he sought before seeking the causes of things, because the Creator of things precedes the things themselves. He warned him what things would come at what times. No one recognized his arrangement without him who arranged it, because no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.

But, as the Apostle says, “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Corinthians 2:12). Therefore we know his things—not instructed by the words of human wisdom, but by the Spirit of God and through the favor of that Spirit poured over us.

This is the folly of worldly people and the wisdom of those who have been called: always to think in one’s heart, “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 116:12). To have him always in one’s mouth, because he is the Word; to hunger for him, because he is bread. Through his Spirit even to become ecstatic in mind, because he is the cup of the new covenant and the wine from the vine which he had earlier transplanted from Egypt—the vine that was the people of Israel, whose fathers were those from whom the Lord Jesus Christ descended according to the flesh.

To speak of him at all times, because his Spirit has brought us new tongues. What are these new tongues, unless they are to be in the world without possessing the world’s speech: to speak to the people in languages other than the language in which the people are accustomed to speak among themselves?

Moreover, to speak in other tongues also means to confess one God by someone who had been accustomed to confess many gods; and, within our faith, to speak of and profess him as one in new tongues, and to believe in the Trinity.

To love him also, because he intercedes for us; to fear him, because the Father has given all judgment to the Son. To worship him at every moment and to ask from him what we need and what pleases him—him who wishes to be asked, so much so that he shows these words to the one who asks.

He alone loves those who ask him—something new among us. He alone also, remarkably, becomes angry if he is not asked. For it is unbelief to expect nothing from God. One who does not ask for what he judges God able to do believes that God can do nothing.

This is that narrow way, dearest son; this is the small opening through which those laden with burdens do not enter, nor animals weighed down with their loads. These narrow and constricted entrances not only cannot admit shapeless beasts with their burdens; they also thwart the sight even of our own eyes when it is distracted in many directions.

Therefore the Lord says through the Prophet: “Be still, and see” (Psalm 46:9). When will it be possible to enter what, because of worldly occupations, has not yet even begun to be discovered?

### XX

We have completed, in their several divisions, the questions proposed, by showing the outward and the inward man. We have shown what a holy life is, in what activity it consists, with what devotion it must be held, and by what substance it is nourished. We have brought its whole course briefly—if one may say so, more by leaps than by steps, because of our haste—to its conclusion.

Now understand why this man is not also seen by the people of this world, since my verbosity pleases you, though you judge it somewhat carelessly while attending more diligently to divine things.

When the one who first brought the seed of death into us had subjected this world—that is, human suffering—to himself after conquering man, and, with its king already captured, had seized its kingdom beneath his feet and under his dominion; when he used everything in the world as though it were his own cattle and the spoils of his victory; then, lest man should ever seek again the wisdom he had lost or the covenant of life owed to him, he so infected everything with the pigments of his craft that he clothed folly in the color of wisdom and overshadowed death with the allurements of a counterfeit life. Thus those who could not see better things set against evil would not flee from evil.

From that time onward, therefore, the human race has proceeded in this way: folly is regarded as wisdom, as the Psalmist says: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” (Psalm 10:3).

Then what is death is thought to be life; and under the appearance of good, evils deceive, since, in order to defraud the understanding, the power of all good is concealed beneath trickery. Wealth is loved even though it will not follow a person after death. The honor of the fasces, which will fade through succession, is pursued. To have committed an injustice is considered a sign of virtue; to possess another’s property, a sign of power; to ensnare the innocent, a sign of cleverness; not to possess the mind of Christ, a sign of wisdom; to dread the Prophet, a sign of eloquence.

Everything is so full of errors, so suffused with darkness through human minds, as one person attacks another, that the world is wrapped in gloom. Truth is obscured to such an extent that lying in the bosom of death is called blessedness.

When that God, who is always thinking of us and of our affairs, saw that, through the wisdom of the world—with which the world had found accomplices and falsifiers—the wisdom of God had been abandoned, he was pleased, in opposition to the cunning of the deceiver, to employ the innumerable riches of his wisdom and the depth of his knowledge, which no one can investigate.

Accordingly, he veiled his wisdom in what is called folly and concealed his life beneath a kind of obscurity of death, so that no one who had fled the world’s opinion of folly could reach wisdom, and no one who had not held death in contempt could approach his life.

For this reason he sent his Son, our Savior, into man:  he clothed his wisdom in flesh, which is folly. He caused his life to suffer the cross, which is death. Thus, by opposites, he destroyed opposites; and through works unlike those of the artificer’s ancient devices, he shattered the mechanisms of that craftsman, so that, although his deadly marks had been impressed upon some parts, they might be erased by certain saving traces.

But unless we desire this discipline—for “what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians 1:27)—we shall not hold fast to his wisdom. Unless we love this death, which is the cross—for “what is weak in God is stronger than men”—we shall not be able to enter into his life.

What follows, then, except that, abandoning both the wisdom and the life of the world, we allow ourselves to be regarded as fools, and always desire to die with the Lord, so that, in the hope of his coming—which will reveal both matters—we may deserve to possess some share?

Then, when all coverings have been torn apart, everything will be seen as it truly is in every particular. Worldly folly will stand exposed, stripped of the wrappings of false wisdom; and the death of counterfeit blessedness, its covering uncovered, will be revealed as the enemy of all that lives, with its mouth always open and its throat gaping toward the abyss.

Then heavenly wisdom, which is called folly in worldly terms, will enter without the labor of any painstaking investigation into the height of the knowledge of God that lies between; and true life, obscured by no darkness of death, will shine forth through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor for ever and ever. Amen.

### XXI

You see, son, what affliction troubles the mind of one who does not consider these things. I have applied a soothing touch to the little body; if I neglected it, the soul would be stronger, for it becomes weak when the exterior is strengthened.

But may the soul I have described, diseased with the illness of folly, be healed by the frequent prayers you offer—your soul, which, untainted by the crimes of the world, can assist others. For a sick person cannot apply the remedy of his own health to those pierced by sickness, nor can one gasping beneath the height of his wounds heal the wounds of others.

The healthy person will certainly care for the sick; the sighted person leads the blind through dangerous places. Therefore, as a wise man, entreat the Lord for me, that I may become wise in what I have not known; and through your intercessions, as through certain remedies, cause me to be healed.

Someone may criticize me for proceeding in so lengthy and pleasing a discussion that I had no awareness of the inadequacy of my merits, or for suddenly and unworthily ascending the august chair of Moses as a disputant on such subjects.

But I truly did this out of love for you, not out of self-appropriation. For I had read the command addressed to the sinner: he must not dare to recount the Lord’s righteousness with his own mouth.

If, contrary to this prohibition, I have presumed to do so because of my affection for you, your grace will deign to compensate for it: do not bring these little writings, which have not been fully corrected—as is evident from the very letters with which they are written—too readily into public view. And if I could not be modest on my own behalf, as I ought to have been, let your modesty at least spare my modesty.

And since they owe their poor composition to me, let them owe their concealment to you. Farewell, and love us in the Lord, in whom you are loved by us.

## Editorial Notice on the Following Letter

Although, if one’s mind were inclined to conjecture, one or another of the authors of the fifth century who composed letters of this kind might have come to mind as one to whom this work could fittingly be attributed, it nevertheless seemed preferable to place before the learned reader the very arguments by which, using his more fortunate judgment—since it has been established abundantly enough that this letter is not Jerome’s—he may investigate its true author.

The entire context indicates that it is addressed to someone who, after having discharged the dignities of the world, has recently embraced the faith of Christ and been initiated through baptism. He is addressed more than once with a title of honor: “I beg your Prudence,” and so forth. Likewise: “For you, honorable and most beloved father, every cause of tears has been wiped away through a new grace.”

At the very beginning it says: “Do not, because of your low opinion of me, despise the words of the Lord, which, in pious affection, are now offered to you, a little one of the Church, as milk for the nourishment of your infancy’s newness.”

The same point is suggested by what is said near the end, where he is called “son.” For the author immediately adds: “Nor do we speak for this purpose, to court human friendships,” and so forth.

The recipient also seems to have wished to profess himself a monk. Our author continues: “I want you to be a Christian, not merely to be called a monk, and to possess the virtue of your own praise rather than an alien name, which is imposed without reason by Latins living amid the crowd, whereas among Greeks living in solitude it is assigned legitimately.”

The period to which the letter belongs—the end of the fifth century—is indicated by several things, including the statement that the day of vengeance and retribution is imminent and near, and that this is demonstrated by the ruins of the world converging everywhere and by the testimony of Scripture.

Finally, there are certain expressions that seem to suggest the Pelagian doctrine, which Bellarmine maintains the author embraced: “Someone says, if everything is expected from our labor, then grace accomplishes nothing . . . . . . . . But grace indeed freely forgives sins, yet with the consent and will of the believer.”

Then there is the statement: “We are certainly the Church, provided that we have lived without fault and blemish, as is commanded.”

Unless I am mistaken, all these indications point to Faustus of Riez, who, according to Gennadius, chapter 85, wrote a letter of this kind to Felix, prefect of the praetorium.

# Letter VII  
## He Instructs a Friend in Knowledge of the Divine Law

### I

I might attempt to excuse my presumption if both the occasion and the reason, as well as affection, did not protect me; and if I now wished to impress upon your ears words that were more my own than divine.

Furthermore, our exhortation derives confidence from simplicity and power from truth, since it does not arise from uncleanness, error, or deceit. I expressly forewarn you of this, lest, because of your low opinion of me, you despise the words of the Lord, which, in pious affection, are now offered to you, a little one of the Church, as milk for the nourishment of the newness of your infancy, until later, whether by yourself or through others, you are instructed and strengthened with more solid food into a perfect man.

I therefore desire you to know fully what I believe you know in part: that the Lord and Word of God descended from heaven for this reason—that, having assumed a human being from our nature, the human race, which had lain prostrate since Adam, might be raised up in Christ; and that as much salvation might be granted to the new man through obedience as destruction had come to the old through disobedience.

But since obedience and disobedience, as it seems to me, are incorporeal terms, not belonging to bodily matter; and since incorporeal things cannot in any way be generated from corporeal things, it is clear that incorporeal things arise from incorporeal things.

If it is reasonable that incorporeal obedience, which is the remedy for disobedience, is generated from the incorporeal soul, then it is clear that obedience proceeds from the counsel of the mind, not from bodily matter.

From this we conclude that our calling stands in accordance with the graciousness of the one who calls, together with the consent of our own will. Thus the washing received by the believer’s body is obtained more through the benefit of the soul, and the purification of both substances, which is accomplished in water and the word, ought rightly to be brought about by the mind.

But in order to confirm what we have said with manifest proof, let us provide clear examples from Scripture. It is written in the Apostle: “Thus Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, so that he might present her to himself glorious and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:25–27).

He said that the Church is cleansed through water and the word. The Church, of course, is us—provided that we have lived without fault and blemish, as commanded.

Corporeal things are cleansed by corporeal things, and spiritual things by spiritual things. The soul is cleansed by the word and water; the body appears to be washed by water alone.

The soul that remains inwardly in its former filth and desires must fear the Evangelist’s statement: “Blind Pharisee, cleanse first what is within, so that what is outside may also become clean” (Matthew 23:26).

And truly, if our bodies are vessels of our souls, then they will be genuinely clean if they contain within a sincere and pure liquid. Otherwise, even if a cup is golden and most beautiful in its adornment of jewels and brilliance, if it contains poison within itself, does not the deadly corruption of the drink obscure the preciousness of the metal and violate the shining splendor of its appearance?

### II

But lest I depart too far from the purpose of my promise, I shall prove the words of my introductory remarks by the words of the Lord, so that what I say may not be thought to have been invented from human feeling or devised by my own ingenuity, but may appear to have been constructed from divine statements.

In John’s Gospel the Lord says to the disciples: “But you are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 13:10). He did not say, “because you have been washed,” only; rather, “because of the word which I have spoken to you, therefore you are clean.”

He knew that all had been washed, but he did not prove that the inward parts of all were clean, because among them was Judas, who, after the cleansing of water, remained filthy through the wickedness of his mind.

For this reason, although he had previously been washed with the others, he is nevertheless declared unclean by the Lord’s judgment. His example clearly and unmistakably shows that the person receives the grace of God in truth who receives it in the order in which Scripture teaches it.

For if someone believes that he has been reborn bodily through water, but has not been regenerated in spirit through the word, he is deprived of his salvation. The purpose of this heavenly renewal is that, while the body’s condition remains, the old man should be changed into a new disposition of soul.

Otherwise, just as a dirty body remains unclean if it has not been washed with water, so the soul, unless it has been cleansed by the divine word, will remain corrupted by the filth of vices.

Therefore, if by his counsel the body is cleansed by water, for what reason is the greater thing rejected, when the lesser is already being held? It is folly for someone who has perished entirely to wish to be saved only in part.

When he possesses complete salvation within his power, he wishes to be satisfied with half of it; and contrary to the laws of nature, he thinks that he has been saved in body alone, although it is more possible for the soul to live without the body before the time of resurrection than for the body to stand without the soul.

If someone suffers from a disorder in both eyes and both feet, and has the treatment of both members within his power, and, after one foot or one eye has been healed, wishes to prevent the physician from treating the other, would he not, in the judgment both of the physician and of all people, be condemned as someone of unsound mind?

But someone says: “If everything is expected from our labor, then grace accomplishes nothing.”

I do not want anyone, under the pretext of ignorance, rashly to make the grace of God thankless, lest he turn his faith into a stumbling block and make what should be the cause of salvation an occasion of destruction and ruin.

If the reason for this matter is sought with moderation, then it will advance toward life—a matter which presumption might perhaps have driven headlong toward death.

Grace indeed freely forgives sins, but with the consent and will of the believer. Thus Philip proves the matter to the eunuch in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “If you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized.”

By this testimony it is understood that there is no less danger if an unbeliever is baptized than if baptism is denied to one who truly believes. The believer, according to Scripture, is the one who has believed with all his heart.

And if one must believe from the whole stronghold of the heart, so that baptism is granted to faith on the merit of belief, water is not sufficient for the baptized person if it does not reach the believer’s soul in the heart.

And lest the merit of the heart be endangered, he ought to receive the word by which the heart can be touched and cleansed. For if the person who says he has believed is content with water, by which the limbs are washed externally, and does not seek the word in which the soul glories, he will appear to have believed not from the heart, as he ought, but from the body.

No reasoning at all permits us to say that the body alone can possess a particular understanding without the judgment of the mind.

### III

Therefore, trusting in your prudence—which, because of the kindness inherent in it, would not allow anything disorderly to be done, nor permit it to be done to another person—I ask you, for the fullness of your instruction, to read the word of the Lord, that is, the Gospel, more diligently.

From it may you receive a greater knowledge of the light which you have believed in, so that you may know in all things what you are going to do.

For that no one can easily be saved without knowledge of the divine law and heavenly discipline will be proved not by my word but by the divine word.

The prophet Isaiah says: “He who has not learned the righteousness of God will not practice truth” (Isaiah 26:9).

Likewise, on this very subject, in the Book of Wisdom: “And who among the children of men will be perfected? If the wisdom of God is absent from him, he will be counted as nothing. For all people are foolish who do not possess knowledge of the law of God” (Wisdom 7:19).

Therefore, in the Gospel the Lord answered those who were supposing things differently from the truth: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures” (Matthew 22:29). He thereby showed that those who refuse to have the spiritual lamp lit—that is, knowledge of the divine law—are established in the deepest cloud and darkness of matters pertaining to salvation.

Some reject this lamp, and through the Prophet they are rejected by the Lord, as it is written: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you also” (Hosea 4:6).

Therefore, let us by no means abandon ourselves indiscriminately to our own judgment, lest Isaiah cry out against us: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight” (Isaiah 5:21).

The Apostle Paul likewise says: “If anyone thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18); for the wisdom of this world is folly with God.

For this reason it is said to the king of Tyre, who gloried in human wisdom: “The wise will not instruct you”—that is, the heavenly teachings and the wisdom of God.

There is also human wisdom; we do not deny it. But one kind urges us toward life, while another drives us toward death. Human wisdom, which is condemned as folly and defined by the Apostle through the Holy Spirit, is shown to be the gate of death and the material of eternal destruction.

As it is written in the Prophet: “The foolish and the senseless will perish together” (Psalm 49:11). The foolish person is the one who said in his heart, “There is no God”; and the senseless person, although he confesses God with his mouth, did not look to the future in the conduct of his present life.

As it is written: “Better is a poor and wise child than a foolish and aged king who does not know how to provide for the future” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

It is good for a person to be wise, provided that, according to Scripture, he is wise for this purpose: to possess foreknowledge of the future, considering the condition of mortality through the deaths of people who die day by day, and the ruin of the entire world gradually collapsing through successive losses.

But if someone is guided by the outlook of an intention once arrogated to himself, and wishes to be governed by his own judgment rather than by God’s; if, setting aside the divine law, he places his own plans before God’s counsels, let him fear the voice of the Prophet crying out: “Woe to those who despise the law of the Lord” (Jeremiah 28:6). Fear, a pit, and a snare are upon him.

As heavy rain is useless, so those who abandon the law praise impieties; but those who love the law surround themselves with a wall.

“Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1:2), whose mind knows nothing except to ponder the utterances of God’s word. The farther he is removed from earthly thought, the nearer he is to God and heaven.

The divine word rightly both praises him and sets him above the rich in true wealth, saying: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom. For it is better to purchase her than treasures of gold and silver; she is more precious than precious stones.” Likewise: “All gold, in comparison with her, is a little sand, and silver will be regarded by her as clay” (Proverbs 3:13–15).

### IV

But since we have lingered too long in exhorting toward wisdom, lest anyone perhaps think that we are setting the teacher of the law above the doer, contrary to the Apostle, we shall reply in due order that we must first know what has been commanded and what has been forbidden, so that, knowing both, we may observe both.

Otherwise, before knowing the commandment, it is impossible to know what is to be done.

It is sufficiently rash to think that the law of our own will can be enough for us, when we read that even the Apostle was under the law. He himself says: “To those who were without the law, as though I were without the law—not being without the law of God, but being under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21).

And elsewhere: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

Those who have been redeemed by the Father’s mercy through Christ’s passion, and who were redeemed for this purpose—that by observing the rights of their Redeemer they might prepare themselves for the life stored up in heaven—are said to be unable to reach that life in any way unless they carry out the obedience that is required of them, as it is written: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:19).

That means: withdraw from every unlawful thing from which you are forbidden, and approach readily every good thing which you are commanded to do. Do not, by persevering in the desires of your former viciousness, corrupt the faith by which you believed through some remaining love of an old sin; and do not allow the knowledge of God, which has been revealed through the new grace, to be violated by offenses.

The Prophet says: “Falsehood, and not faith, has prevailed upon the earth, because they have passed from evil to evil and have not known me, says the Lord.”

Blessed John the Apostle likewise bears witness, saying: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him” (1 John 2:4).

And again: “Everyone who sins does not see God, nor has he known him” (ibid. 3:6).

Sin consists not merely in one kind of commandment, but in both. The person who neglects what has been commanded certainly sins, but the person who does not observe what has been forbidden sins more seriously.

Sacrifices and vows of offerings will be rejected unless the mind of the offerer is pure and holy. A defiled heart makes an unblemished victim unacceptable, as the Lord says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there,” and so forth (Matthew 5:24).

Obedience to the commandments is more precious than every offering and sacrifice, as the Prophet says: “Behold, I say that obedience is better than sacrifice, and submission than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22).

And elsewhere: “To begin to do what is commanded, things acceptable to God, is better than to sacrifice victims” (Proverbs 16:5).

And elsewhere: “He who keeps the law multiplies his offering. A saving sacrifice is to attend to the commandments, to depart from every iniquity, and to make a propitiatory sacrifice for injustice.”

We ought not flatter ourselves because we have done what was commanded if we sin by transgressing what was forbidden, since the crime of transgression takes away the merit of a good deed.

This is proved not by an assertion of my own judgment, but by examples from both Testaments, where we find that even friends of God, because of the error of a single act of contempt, lost the abundance of their former good deeds.

Thus Adam, after enjoying the familiarity and conversation of God, easily believed the devil who deceived him. Overcome by desire for a single fruit, he lost paradise; and because he presumed, through transgression, to possess one thing, he lost many good things at once (Genesis 1).

Thus Lot’s wife, after the service of the angels, looked back contrary to the prohibition and was suddenly changed into a pillar of salt (ibid. 19:26).

Thus Shemaiah, on the very day on which he had performed miracles through prophetic grace, was thrown down and killed by a lion (1 Kings 13).

Thus the most wretched Judas, after the merit of his election, after the glory of signs, and after apostolic dignity, deceived by his love of a small sum of money, was promised a tribunal in heaven but was caught by a noose on earth (Matthew 25:5).

And lest we think that danger threatens us only through the fraudulent pursuit of other people’s possessions, let us remember Ananias and Sapphira, who were condemned not for desiring another person’s money, but for timidly distributing what was their own (Acts 5:5).

After so many warnings and so many deaths, I ask: from where does such impunity in sinning grow within us? What spirit of presumption works such audacity in our minds that, although we see holy people punished even for light faults, we, committing greater and more numerous offenses every day, believe that we shall remain eternal in the midst of condemnation?

## V.

Although it is never a light matter to despise God even in a small thing—for he regards not only the quality of the sin but also the contempt shown toward his person—for this reason a person must consider not only what is commanded, but also how great is the one who commands. Here that common saying is excluded which those who, in their own judgment, are religious and who seem wise to themselves are accustomed to say to me: “It is enough for us not to commit criminal and serious sins; the omission of lesser offenses is easy.” While they occupy their minds with an animal kind of wisdom, they are ignorant of spiritual understanding and of the practice of divine law—a law that often reveals as sin what does not seem to us to be sin, and makes piety consist in what we regard as an impious deed.

Saul and Jehoshaphat were kings of the people of Israel, and when they showed mercy to those whom God hated, they incurred God’s displeasure through an act of mercy. Phinehas, on the contrary, and the sons of Levi, earned God’s favor by human slaughter and the killing of their own kindred. You see how far the divine judgment differs from human perceptions through our ignorance: sometimes, when we do not understand the dispensation of the heavenly Judge, things seem unjust to us which, through knowledge of the circumstances, are proved to have been done justly and rightly. Again, things that are judged good by our standards often appear to God rejected and displeasing.

Who today, following the example of the father Abraham, would not be judged insane by human standards if he wished to slaughter an innocent son? Conversely, who would not be condemned by human opinion for imitating Uzzah in touching the divine ark? The bishop of the Ephesians, called an angel in the Apocalypse, had kept within his conscience the merit of many sufferings endured for the sake of Christ’s name. But because in those very sufferings he had grown lukewarm from the fervor of his original way of life, when he had moderated his ardor even slightly, he was recalled to repentance. Scripture says:

> “I know your works, and your patience, and that you are able to endure evil people; but I have a few things against you, because you have forsaken your former charity. Remember from where you have fallen, and repent” (Rev. II, 2, 3, 4, 5).

Let us consider how great is the fall of one who despises recklessly, when such ruin is said to lie in the negligence of one who obeys; or what condemnation we should believe the undevoted will suffer, when the devoted received such a reproach. Christ does not love a lukewarm disciple. “Whoever wishes to be my disciple,” he says, “let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI, 24). “You must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations” (Acts XIV, 22). “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you: rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V, 11–12).

## VI.

The glory of the life to come is purchased through the hardships of the present life. For Christians, the banners of the cross are delights; the trophies of our life are won not through pageantry but through misery. In our army, brave men know how to bear reproaches, not gifts. Blessedness in the future is promised to poverty, not nobility.

Shame indeed holds back the senator from following the poor Christ, but let him hear Christ say: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” (Mark VIII, 38). It is disgraceful, among parents who are senators and teachers of grammar, for a scholar humbled by voluntary lowliness for Christ’s sake to be content with simple words. Friends are displeased if, after the refinement of an ambitious appearance, common and ignoble clothing is put on instead. “If I still wished to please human beings,” says the Apostle, “I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. I, 10). And the Prophet says in the psalm: “For God scatters the bones of those who please human beings; they were put to shame because God despised them” (Ps. LIII, 6).

As beneficial as human offense is, through which Christ’s service is found, so harmful is friendship that brings about offense against God, as it is written: “Whoever wishes to become a friend of this world will be constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. IV, 4). Let everyone say what he wishes; for the time being, judging according to the smallness of my understanding, I have decided that it is better for me to be put to shame before sinners on earth than before the holy angels in heaven—or wherever the Lord wishes to reveal his judgment.

Isaiah, a man most noble among his people, who is reported to have been the father-in-law of King Hezekiah, at God’s command laid aside his sackcloth and walked naked. He was not deterred by shame from so arduous a command, but followed God’s order, because he judged that nothing was more honorable for a human being than to obey the Creator.

John the Baptist, noble both in the flesh and in the spirit, chose from childhood a haircloth garment and locusts for food. He was drawn to the glory of this burden neither by consciousness of sin nor by poverty’s deprivation, but solely by the blessedness of the future age. The Apostles already hope, and yet they are accused of being foolish, useless, and of little faith. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Therefore Paul, contemplating the future with the eye of his mind, said: “Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or danger, or the sword?” (ibid., 36). Dangers do not separate them; pleasures separate us. They carry chains though innocent; we carry gold though guilty. They are bound in prisons; we are pampered in dining rooms. They are placed in the stocks, praising God with a pure heart and sincere thought; we, perhaps even in the Church itself, think about lawsuits arising from worldly accusations. And although the grace of the law has been given equally to all, and the punishments of Gehenna or the kingdoms of heaven have been promised, some meditate on riches and others on virtues.

Although it has been said generally to all, “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV, 10; Deut. VI, 13; X, 20), while others serve God faithfully and without ceasing through innocence, mercy, chastity, and fasting, we choose for ourselves adulterous masters whom we wish to serve. For according to the Gospel’s declaration: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34).

And indeed, if I am a lover of money, glory, pride, ambition, or display, while I devote all my zeal and desire to these things, I cannot serve the Lord, because it is written that no one can serve two masters. “You are not your own,” says the Apostle, “for you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 19, 20).

The Holy Spirit mercifully addresses us according to our own condition, knowing that this principle is observed publicly among all [variant adds: people]: a servant is more careful in his master’s work the greater the price for which he was purchased. Thus we should understand how zealous those redeemed by Christ’s blood ought to be in God’s work, and how guilty those should be judged who, although they know that Christ’s blood was given as the price of their salvation, offer greater service to another who contributed nothing.

With what shame, I ask, will one whose entire concern was on earth hope in heaven for the reward of his obedience or labor? The hireling of the world cannot receive Christ’s reward. Every soldier in camp rightly hopes for his ration if he has worked bravely in battle for his fellow citizens. “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X, 7); but it is also fitting that he receive the reward of his work from the place where he has devoted all his labor.

“No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II, 4): these are the Apostle’s words. Therefore I greatly fear that on that day of reckoning, when each person must be repaid according to his deeds before Christ’s tribunal, the reply of the just Judge may be spoken to those who labored more in earthly affairs than in heavenly ones: “Go, if you can; and there, where you served with all your devotion, demand the reward of your service.”

Such is the case of the five foolish virgins in the Gospel. While they occupied themselves with the concerns of worldly vanities, contrary to the order of their profession, they had no oil with which to kindle the true light and therefore remained in darkness.

## VII.

But someone says: “These examples apply to only a few, whom God appointed to this special office, because it is written: ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’” (Matt. XXII, 14).

First I wish to ask and hear from you, whoever you are who propose this: if it is God’s election, and calling is also his, why did he wish to call many when he was going to choose only a few from among the many? Certainly, among two who are called, you wish the one whom God establishes by election to stand, and the one whom God does not fortify by the power of election to fall. But if this is so, then neither good nor evil concerns us on this account; and thus neither guilt will have punishment nor good deeds receive praise.

But to this the Apostle replied: “If that is so, how will God judge this world?” (Rom. III, 6). Furthermore, if you consider only the few [variant: omits “few”] whom you call chosen to be saints, and call those who are called reprobates, how does the same Apostle Paul, at the beginnings of his letters, call those who are called saints? Thus, at the head of the letter to the Romans, he says: “To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called saints” (Rom. I, 7).

If Christ suffered for the few, it is just that the few should keep Christ’s commandments. But if all of us who believe indiscriminately receive in baptism the sacrament of his passion; if we all equally renounce the devil and the world; if the punishment of Gehenna is promised to all who do not live rightly, then we must all with equal diligence avoid what is forbidden and fulfill the commandments.

We know, indeed, that there are many dwelling places with the Father in heaven (John XIV, 2). But the justice of the dwelling places makes the more righteous dwelling places differ, just as the Apostle said that star differs from star in brightness. Yet he compared star with star, not stone with stone, because an earthly stone could not be among the heavenly stars, just as a sinner cannot be among the righteous in the kingdom of heaven.

There are, however, degrees of glory among the righteous in heaven, just as there are degrees of punishment among sinners. But just as one who calls his brother a fool will be tormented by punishments different from those of one who calls him “Raca,” so in the kingdom one glory will belong to the Apostle Paul, who became all things to all people in order to save others, and another glory will belong to the layman who could scarcely build up even himself.

Would that I agreed that there are few who keep God’s commandments. But I fear that there are few who truly believe in God’s judgment. Suppose suddenly, with the sky darkened, the brightness of the sun were denied to our eyes, and clouds gathered over our lowliness so that rains threatened the earth. Suppose, as usually happens when the elements are disturbed, thunder were stirred into the wheel of its chariot, and darts of lightning flashed fearfully before our eyelids on every side. Although such things occur according to nature, we are afraid, we tremble, and, prostrate on the ground, laying aside our pride, we bow our necks.

What will we wretched people do on that day, when the heavens are rolled up with the angelic powers, and the fiery Lord comes in his entirety? When the stars fall from above, the sun is changed into darkness and the moon into blood? When the mountains melt like wax? When the earth burns, the rivers dry up, and the seas become parched? When, contrary to the nature of things, the divinely consumed moisture causes fire to produce dryness in the waters? When sinners say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us”? When people call for death, and when called, it does not come? When dangers are turned into wishes, and people desire what they have always hated?

When that time will be fulfilled which Jeremiah predicts in mournful feeling, saying:

> “I looked upon the earth, and behold, there were no lights. I saw the mountains, and behold, they were trembling, and all the hills were disturbed. I directed my gaze, and behold, there was no human being, and all the birds of heaven were afraid. I saw, and behold, Carmel was a desert, and all its cities were burned with fire before the Lord and before the face of his indignation and wrath; and all things perished” (Jer. XXIII).

## VIII.

But lest these things be believed to have been spoken at the devil’s instigation for terror rather than truth, the future is proved by the past, since such events are repeatedly reported to have occurred because of human sins in the Flood, in Sodom, in Egypt, and in Jerusalem.

The Apostles, who were worthy to foresee this dreadful day for the impious and sinners, were humble and raised the dead; yet we exalt ourselves above all others, although by sinning daily we kill ourselves, paying no attention to our pitiable and feeble nature, which is neither strong in adversity nor ever secure in prosperity.

If food taken immoderately, or drink consumed without restraint, stirs up a slight fever in the body, we lose heart, are distressed, and sigh. At that point there is no concern for the world, none for country estates; no one thinks about his patrimony, no one about the marketplace. Every lawsuit and every profit falls silent in the face of bodily danger.

People run to physicians, and for bodily treatment they promise gifts, gold, and silver. Sometimes even slaves are handed over, and nearly the whole patrimony is either neglected or given away, so that the life destined one day to perish may be cared for. Yet for eternal salvation everyone is exceedingly negligent, everyone greedy. There, where a more ready will and more abundant generosity ought to operate, the whole frugality of the giver is restrained by the tightness of his heart.

Although Scripture says, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (I John II, 15), we desire and love worldly things as though we had brought something with us when we were born into this age, or could take something away with us when we depart from it. No one considers the shortness of time; no one considers the condition of nature; no one reflects or examines the matter; no one considers that everything enclosed within some limit is empty.

But if it happens that, among others visiting the sick person, a cleric, priest, or even a lay servant of God arrives, he is asked to pray. The person who was often despised as worthless is begged, in the time of necessity, to obtain by his prayers a longer lease on life.

Thus, through the circumstance of danger that is feared as near, while despised things are chosen and precious things become worthless, the exchange of that life after death is prefigured: there Lazarus the poor man is received into rest, while the rich man who lived in splendor is said to be tormented in punishments.

And when the Lord, moved either by the appeals of the saints, by the benefit of his creation, or by the physician’s art, restores health through his abundant mercy, everything quickly changes in the opposite direction as forgetfulness follows. Fear is turned into insolence, gratitude into contempt. As though we had never experienced any hardship, or as though we could not be recalled again to such circumstances, we rebel and become arrogant. We neglect the time of life granted for repentance, and instead of washing away our former sins through repentant tears, we multiply sins by refusing to repent.

Let us read the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XXXVIII, 4) and seek in King Hezekiah an example appropriate to this matter. As he was dying, fifteen years were added to his life for the higher life through his own tears and the prophet’s prayers. After receiving the grace of so great a gift, he devoted the time of life granted to him not to sins, pleasures, or luxuries, but humbly and holily to the Lord alone.

## IX.

But since, honorable and most beloved parent, through a new grace every cause for tears has been removed from you, act, take care, run, hasten. Act, so that you may advance in spirituality. Take care lest, as an imprudent and negligent guardian, you lose the good you have received. Run, so that you may not neglect it. Hasten, so that you may grasp it more quickly.

For Paul, already carrying Christ’s chain for the proclamation of the Gospel, said that he had not yet grasped it (Phil. III, 13), although at the sixth hour—that is, in the middle age of the Lord, when he was to work in the vineyard—he was like a fervent and faithful laborer, overcoming the long hesitation and sluggish lukewarmness of others.

While we have time, let us sow in the spirit, so that we may gather a harvest in spiritual things. Let us not pay attention to the chaff, which Christ’s winnowing fan will continually separate from the wheat until the one who is to come comes. And, according to the Prophet’s prediction, let distinction be made between the just and the unjust, and between the one who serves God and the one who does not serve him.

As the Lord also says elsewhere:

> “Behold, those who serve me shall eat; but you shall hunger. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice; but you shall be sad” (Isa. LXV, 13).

May the day of vengeance and retribution—which is proved to be imminent and near by the surrounding collapse of the world and by the testimony of the Scriptures—not find us inert [variant: you]. Let us consider that we are guests on this earth and dwell here like travelers for only the final days. “You are not of this world” (John XV, 19), it is said to us.

Why, then, do we labor over what belongs to another? Why are we disturbed? No one chooses to possess more in a worse and foreign homeland than in his own. We ought to be concerned and careful only about those things that we can transfer with us.

Let the Gentiles pursue earthly things, since heavenly things are not owed to them. Let those who do not believe in the future desire the present. For Christians, let the riches and inheritance be the divinity of Christ. They ought not to be distressed as though they possessed less than others, since they have received the author of all things.

It remains that they honor God, whom they have received into their heart, through obedience; worship him through their works; and always confess him in speech and thought, so that at his coming they may not be punished with the rebellious and contemptuous, but crowned with the saints and those who fear God.

In this matter I beg your prudence not to think that I have dictated these things under the persuasion of some superstition. I want you to be a Christian, not merely to be called a monk, and to possess the virtue of your own praise rather than another’s name. For that name is imposed without justification by Latins living among crowds, while it is properly assigned by Greeks living in solitude.

Receive, then, my son, our discourse with the simplicity and truth with which we have spoken. God is witness that we do not seek human glory, nor do we speak in order to court human friendships, lest by the language of our flattery we deceive both ourselves and others. Nor do we speak so that we may seem to be something among human beings, but so that human beings may deserve greatness before God.

## X.

As for your questions, if I may speak with your permission: because you proposed them rather turbulently, I did not wish to answer simply, since I could not extend the right hand of peace to one who was fighting. It may perhaps also seem out of order to revisit something at the end of the letter. But since among Christians progress is sought more than order, I thought that a few matters which I judge necessary for you should be added, until we discuss in person, if you command it, the other things that disturb you—as they commonly do—once every contention of hostility has been removed.

You said, unless I am mistaken, that by right you return evil for evil and ought to swear with those who swear, because the Lord sometimes swore or returned evil for evil. First, I know that not everything appropriate to the Lord is appropriate to us servants, lest by comparing servants with the master an injury be done to the Lord. Otherwise perhaps we might begin to protest: Why are we not born from virgins rather than from women? Or why do our dead not rise on the third day?

I know that the Lord often swore, although he prohibited us from swearing. We must not immediately blaspheme him rashly because he forbade others to do what he himself did. It can be said to us: The Lord swore as Lord, whom no one prohibited from swearing; but we, as servants, may not swear, since we are forbidden to swear by the law of our Lord.

But lest we be scandalized by his example, from the time when he did not wish us to swear, he himself also did not swear. And just as the matter of swearing has been adequately addressed in a brief discourse, so you can easily see that the same understanding is sufficient for the matter of vengeance. For this is now the time of grace, in which the fullness of perfection has arrived; that was the time of the Law, another the time of the prophets. The Lord says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients” (Matt. V, 21), so that they should not kill; “but I command more perfect things,” which the reader will find arranged in their proper place in the order of the Gospel.

From the time when the Son of God became the son of man; from the time when the old leaven of Jewish tradition became a new dough; from the time when the lamb is eaten not in figure but in truth; from the time when, according to the Apostle, “old things have passed away, and all things have become new” (II Cor. V, 17); from the time when we were commanded to lay aside the image of the earthly man and assume the form of the heavenly one—from that time we live after having died with Christ, and have risen with him through virtues.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Contrary to common belief, this is not a letter, but a homily or treatise of one addressing the people in church; one fact clearly proves that it does not have Jerome as its author. This is especially evident both from the continuous sequence of the discourse and from the following passage in chapter 11:

> “This kind of discussion recently arose in a psalm, and we explained how God brought clouds from the end of the earth. But now we are compelled to discuss it again, so that those who heard may recall fully what they know, and those who were either not present or have forgotten may recognize the context of the discourse, which we have now presented as best we could.”

Indeed, whoever the author may have been, he certainly lived many generations later and occasionally drew certain things from Jerome, as in the passage about the world, which in Greek is called *oikoumenē* (οἰκουμένη), that is, “inhabited”; and in what follows about David, who asks for three spirits in the psalm of confession, expressed in almost the same words as the commentary on the Letter to the Galatians, chapter V, 6. The rest, as Erasmus also noted, contains not even a hair’s breadth of Jerome’s diction, nor any trace of that mind.

# LETTER VIII. On Three Virtues

## I.

The Prophet, taking up, in a certain manner, three virtues of God—strength, wisdom, and prudence—assigned to each its proper work: the earth to strength, the inhabited world to wisdom, and heaven to prudence.

Hear the order of Scripture: “The Lord, who made the earth in his strength, established the inhabited world in his wisdom, and stretched out heaven in his prudence.”

Therefore, in our own earth—for it was said to Adam, “You are earth” (Gen. III, 19)—we need the strength of God, because without it we cannot accomplish what resists the flesh. But when the members that are upon the earth have been put to death, then the spirits obey the will. For according to the Apostle, “By the Spirit the deeds of the flesh are put to death” (Rom. VIII, 13). “The Lord, however, made the earth in his strength.”

But if you come to this earth and consider what is written in Job (Job XXVI), at least according to the most carefully corrected copies—how he established it upon nothing—you will find the strength of God sustaining the balance of the earth at the center of the world.

I shall therefore come to the inhabited world, which in Greek is called *oikoumenē* (οἰκουμένη), that is, “inhabited.” I know an inhabited soul; I know a deserted one. If it does not have God the Father; if it does not have the Son saying, “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23); if it does not have the Holy Spirit, the soul is deserted.

It is inhabited, however, when it is full of God the Father, when it has Christ the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet these matters are expressed differently and variously in Scripture: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are said to dwell in the human soul.

David also asks for three spirits in the psalm of confession, saying:

> “Establish me with a principal spirit; renew a right spirit within me; do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L, 12).

What are these three spirits? The principal spirit is the Father; the right spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit.

We have said this in confirmation of the point that the inhabited world—that is, the inhabited soul—was fashioned in the wisdom of God. “Wisdom will aid the righteous, who has power over ten cities” (Eccl. VII, 20). But the one who rejects wisdom and discipline is wretched, and his hope is vain, his labors senseless and fruitless, and his works useless, says Wisdom, which bears the title of Solomon (Wis. III, 11).

Therefore, let us strive with as much labor as we can, so that our habitation may be raised up by the wisdom of God. For it fell and collapsed from its height when we came into this place of miseries. Our habitation fell after we sinned, acted wickedly, behaved unjustly, and conducted ourselves impiously (Ps. CVI, 6); and after its fall it needs to be raised up.

But if you do not wish to accept this interpretation, let us seek the common fall of the entire inhabited world, and after its fall let God consequently be proclaimed as the one who raises it up.

## II.

Everyone who is in this world fell before the raising up. But if he fell, he consequently had to be raised up; for no one is lifted up without a fall. But if he has been raised up, let us see what ruin preceded it: We all fell through sin in the world. And the Lord, who raises up those who are cast down, lifted us up as we lay fallen. In Adam we all die; and thus the world fell and needs to be raised up, so that in Christ we may all be made alive.

Accordingly, we have handed down a twofold interpretation of “the world.” One concerns how individual souls are either inhabited or desolate; the other, how the whole world likewise fell. And “in his prudence he stretched out the heavens.” Prudence was not fortuitously employed in the stretching out of the heavens. You will also find it said in Proverbs: “The Lord founded the earth by wisdom, but prepared the heavens by prudence” (Prov. III, 19).

There is therefore a certain prudence of God which I do not want you to seek apart from Christ. For everything that belongs to God is Christ: he is his wisdom, his power, his righteousness, his holiness and redemption, and—as I may say for the present—his prudence also. Yet although he is the same in the underlying subject, he is called by different names according to the variety of meanings. “Wisdom” signifies one thing, “righteousness” another. For when he is called wisdom, he instructs you in the disciplines of divine and human matters. When he is called righteousness, he is shown as the distributor and judge of merits. When he is called holiness, that virtue is described which makes those who believe in God holy.

So understand his prudence in the same way: it is doctrine and the demonstration of good, evil, or indifferent things. In this manner, then, the heavens are now said to have been stretched out in his prudence.

But hear how the heavens are stretched out, with prudence stretching them: for he does not stretch out the words of one who pays no attention. He asserts that there is likewise a certain stretching out of words, just as now he speaks of the heavens, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “He stretches out the heavens like a skin” (Ps. CIII, 2).

[Col. 0118C] Our soul also is stretched out, although previously contracted, so that it may be capable of the wisdom of God.

But, to return to the subject: we said that the heavens were made through prudence, and now we affirm that those who bear the heavenly man are heavenly. For if it is said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19), why should it not be said to the righteous person, whose is the kingdom of heaven: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”? Or if, because of the word γήϊνον—that is, “earthly”—it is said to the one who bears the image, γῆ εἶ, that is, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19), why, because of the heavenly one, should it not properly be said to the one who bears the image of the heavenly: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”?

Each one of us has either heavenly things or earthly things as his deeds. If they are earthly deeds, they lead the one who stores them up on earth, and not in heaven, to the earth akin to them. But, conversely, those things that have been done according to virtue carry their treasurer, as he draws near, toward the regions of heaven.

“And he brought out clouds from the end of the earth” (Ps. CXXXV, 7).

A discussion of this kind recently arose in a psalm, and we explained how God brought out clouds from the end of the earth. We are now compelled to treat the matter again, so that those who heard may recall more fully what they know, and those who were either not present or have forgotten may recognize the thread of the discourse that we then presented as best we could.

We said that the saints are clouds. For what is written—“Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Ps. XXXVI, 6)—cannot refer to inanimate clouds; rather, the truth of God reaches those clouds that hear the Lord’s command and know where to bring the rains and from whom to withhold them.

Of these clouds it was said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it rain” (Isa. V, 6). For when the clouds are said to consist of condensed air, if there is no rain the Lord does not order them not to rain upon a vineyard or any region whatsoever; rather, they do not appear at all, as we read in the Third Book of Kings (III Kings XVIII, 44), when, in a time of drought, no cloud appeared, and afterward, according to Elijah’s prophecy, a sign of the coming rain was shown in the form of a man’s footprint. Then, after the cloud had gathered, rain descended upon the earth.

But these clouds, as it were, subsisting mists, are commanded to withhold rain when a soul has proved unworthy of heavenly rain; and it is said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it rain.”

Thus each of the saints is a cloud. Moses was a cloud, and he spoke as a cloud: “Give ear, O heavens, to what I shall speak, and let the earth hear the words from my mouth. Let my words be expected like rain, and let my utterances descend like dew” (Deut. XXXII, 1–2). If he had not been a cloud, he would never have said: “Let my words be expected like rain, and let my utterances descend like dew.” He spoke as a cloud: “Like rain upon the grass and frost upon the hay, because I have invoked the name of the Lord” (ibid., 3).

Isaiah likewise spoke as a cloud: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, because the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I, 2). And because he himself was a cloud, and knew other clouds prophesying with him, he therefore foretold: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it rain” (Isa. V, 6).

But if we already say who the clouds are, let us see how God brings clouds out from the end of the earth. The Savior says: “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all” (Mark IX, 25). Paul kept this commandment and was last in this world, saying: “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as men condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to human beings” (I Cor. IV, 9).

Therefore, if some saint, keeping the commandment of the Lord and Savior, becomes last in this life, he becomes a cloud. And God brought out clouds—not from the ends of the earth, not from consuls, not from commanders, not from the rich, but from the extremities of the earth. “For blessed are the poor, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 2).

Do you see how God brings out clouds and corporeal mists from the extremities of the earth? Therefore, if we wish to become clouds to which the truth of God reaches, let us become last of all, and let us say both in affection and in deed: “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last.”

And if I am not an apostle, nevertheless I may become the least, so that he who brings out clouds from the end of the earth may bring me out as well, and make flashes of lightning into rain.

Those who investigate natural causes say (from Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XIII, chapter 11) that flashes of lightning are generated from the collision of clouds, in the manner of harder flints. When you strike them together—that is, when you collide them with one another—fire, struck out between them, escapes; and thus thunder roars together with the flash of lightning: thunder indicating by its sound the collision, and lightning by the brightness of the light that has been struck out.

If you have understood the example, now consider rational clouds. Moses was a cloud; Joshua the son of Nun was a cloud. If these are placed together, flashes of lightning shine forth from their words. Jeremiah and Baruch were clouds: let them converse with one another, and you will see lightning gleaming.

You too can find in the Holy Scriptures, in this manner, collisions of clouds from which fires are sent forth. To come to the New Testament: Paul and Silvanus came together as two clouds, and behold, the radiance of their Epistles illumines the whole world.

“He made flashes of lightning, and rain, and brought out winds from his treasuries” (Ps. CXXXV, 7).

Are these, then, the winds that blow across the earth in the treasuries of God, rather than their nature being evident as to how and by what principle they subsist? Yet there are certain treasuries of winds, treasuries of spirits: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of fortitude, knowledge, and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord, of strength, love, and charity.

You too can gather these winds from the Scriptures and discover the treasuries of these spirits. Where are these treasuries? Certainly in him “in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. II, 3). They have their dwelling in Christ. From there these spirits arise, so that one may be wise, another faithful, another learned, and another may possess whatever gift of God.

“To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 8).

Therefore he brought out clouds from the end of the earth, made flashes of lightning into rain, and brought out winds from his treasuries. And we think that, according to the mercy of God, we are on our way to encounter these treasuries.

And because there are many treasuries, perhaps, according to the order of those who rise again, there will also be rest in the treasuries of God. What I mean is this: the resurrection of the dead will take place according to certain orders. For the Apostle says: “But each one will rise in his own order” (I Cor. XV, 23), and the orders of those rising again are not mixed together at will. There will be one order in this and that treasury of God, another order in another treasury of God.

Yet all these treasuries have one treasury, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. And just as I possess one most precious pearl through many other pearls, so I come to the treasury of treasuries, and the Lord of lords, and the King of kings, when I have been found worthy to dwell among the spirits residing in God’s treasury.

“For he brought out winds from his treasuries.”

## III.

“Every human being was made foolish by knowledge” (Ps. CXXXV, 7).

If every human being was made foolish by knowledge, and Paul is a human being, then Paul was made foolish by knowledge. “For we know in part,” he says, “and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII, 9). He was made foolish by knowledge, seeing through a mirror and in an enigma, seeing only a certain small portion, and—if it is appropriate to say so—recognizing only the smallest part even of that small portion.

Conversely, understand what it means: “Every human being was made foolish by knowledge.” By comparison with the sins of Jerusalem, the sin of Sodom is righteousness: “For,” he says, “Sodom was justified by you” (Ezek. XVI, 48). Just as the sins of Sodom do not possess righteousness in themselves but are justified in comparison with greater crimes, so, conversely, Paul’s knowledge, compared with that heavenly knowledge and that perfected understanding of election, is reckoned folly.

Therefore every human being was made foolish by knowledge. Ecclesiastes, I think, detected something of this kind and said: “I said, ‘I will become wise,’ and it withdrew farther from me than it was, and it is a deep profundity: who will find it?” (Eccl. VII, 24).

We wish to say something boldly, if permitted: that what descended into the world emptied itself, so that by its emptying the world might be filled. But if what descended into the world emptied itself, that emptying is itself folly, because “what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings” (I Cor. I, 17).

If I had said “the foolishness of God,” how would you, hunters of words and people always devoted to accusation, not sharpen poisoned tongues against me? But Paul, being wise and possessing apostolic authority, dared to say that all earthly wisdom—which was in himself, in Peter, and in the other apostles, and which had descended into this world—is the foolishness of God (I Cor. III, 19).

For in comparison with that wisdom which no earthly place can contain, with that wisdom which is heavenly and exceeds the boundary of the world, what descended to human beings is the foolishness of God. Yet this very foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.

Which human beings? Certainly not fools, but the wise—one may call them the wise of this age, whether rulers or prophets. To these wise men of the age, what we have explained as the foolishness of God is wiser.

We wish to insert something remarkable: the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God, and God made the wisdom of the world foolish—not by making the wisdom of the world foolish in his own wisdom, so that it might be proved to be folly. For the wisdom of God does not deign to descend wholly in order to convict the wisdom of the world; rather, it descended only a little—that is, in the mystery of the Incarnation.

What need was there for what was the foolishness of God to make the wisdom of the age foolish by means of this small and foolish thing of God? For the wisdom of the age was not able to endure within itself the greatness of the wisdom that came into it.

But I shall introduce an example, so that it may clearly be understood how the foolishness of God made the wisdom of the world foolish. Let us suppose for a moment that I, who am thought to know something, enter into a discussion with some foolish and uneducated person who understands nothing and asks nothing requiring subtle argument. Do I need to employ the skill of dialectical art and the acuteness of profound meanings in order to expose this person’s foolishness? Would I not, with the throw of one cheap and modest statement—which nevertheless would appear exceedingly sharp to his understanding—prove him to be foolish and ignorant?
