Thus, to make the wisdom of the world foolish, there is no need for the wisdom of God to descend and wrestle with the wisdom that is below; the foolishness of God is sufficient, because it is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.

My Savior and Lord assumed all these opposites in order to dissolve opposites by opposites, so that we might be strengthened by his weakness, made wise by his foolishness, and, having been introduced in this way, might be able to ascend to the wisdom and power of God, Jesus Christ, to whom are glory, power, and dominion for ages of ages.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Erasmus, whom the sons of critics have followed everywhere, does not hesitate to deny that the person who wrote this was Latin, but says that he was Greek. He bases this, evidently, on the fact that the author says he is “using Latin speech” and, in the manner of babbling infants, is not yet able to form words fully.

But the entire context of the discourse cries out that the matter is quite otherwise, as do the testimonies of Scripture that are immediately praised and are taken from the Latin Vulgate translation. I therefore have no doubt at all that the author himself was Latin, although, for the fraudulent scheme he is undertaking, he pretends to attempt a foreign style of speech.

The conjecture, therefore, concerning Sophronius is irrelevant—whether this means the ancient Sophronius, whom Canisius also approves, Jerome’s friend, who rendered the Psalter and several other works of the holy Doctor from Latin into Greek; or another, later Sophronius, who, around the middle of the eighth century, as we have said, translated the book *On Illustrious Men* into Greek.

Whoever the author of this discourse may have been, he plainly reveals his age by the very subject he treats, and especially by saying that the solemnity of the Assumption of the blessed Virgin is celebrated in the churches. For it is known that this feast began to be instituted only in the eighth century and had not yet gained acceptance in the churches of the West, since at the beginning of the ninth century Charlemagne decreed in the *Capitularies*, Book I, chapter 158, as follows: “These are the festivals in the year, etc. . . . We leave the matter of the Assumption of holy Mary to be investigated.”

# LETTER IX. TO PAULA AND EUSTOCHIUM

## On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

### I.

You compel me, O Paula and Eustochium—or rather, the love of Christ compels me, since I have long been accustomed to speak to you in treatises—to address, in a new manner of speaking, the holy virgins who live with you, using Latin speech, and for the sake of exhortation to deliver a discourse on the Assumption of the blessed and ever-glorious Virgin Mary, in the manner of those who customarily speak declamatorily to the people in churches. This method of teaching I had not yet attempted.

But because I cannot refuse whatever you impose upon me, overcome by your excessive affection, I shall attempt what you urge, with the enthusiasm of infants, in the manner of babblers who eagerly repeat whatever they have heard, although they are not yet able to form words fully.

I do this especially because you compel me to bring it forth for the sake of the simpler members, so that your holy community may have, in Latin speech, something with which to occupy itself in praising her on that day and in devoting itself to divine readings. This is particularly fitting since, on many festivals, the efforts of many holy Fathers have forged such things with marvelous eloquence, and what is said about her is read everywhere, more abundantly, in the divine Scriptures.

For what else do the Gospels proclaim except the Lord being born of the Virgin Mary? And they celebrate with divine praises all his growth, at least for as long as he was in the world.

Moreover, from the beginning of the holy Gospel you learned of the archangel Gabriel speaking with Mary, and afterward you read all the remaining matters more fully. At the manger also, O Paula—your testimony confirms it—you saw the child born amid the swaddling clothes of a new birth and the cries of an unknowing infant’s weeping. In place of wedding songs, you heard the multitude of angels singing, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will,” and you saw the radiant star.

You also believed when the shepherds proclaimed the Gospel. Moreover, with blessed eyes you beheld the Magi bringing three gifts; by understanding those same gifts well, you offered them to God in faith with all your desires. For with those Magi you also adored the child God in the manger.

But perhaps, complaining that I have betrayed you, you will cry out because I have exposed you. To this I reply: if you wished the matter to remain concealed, your conscience being witness, you should not have told me about it beside the manger, where you wept so greatly. To speak the truth, even if I were adjured to do so, I could not altogether remain silent about the praises of Christ—and therefore neither about your praises.

Let your daughters, whom you nourish with milk, question you about this. You will reveal more effectively what I do not know whether you saw in some appearance or certainly in the spirit. Therefore, daughters, press your mother with prayers; knock at the door of the inviting friend, to see whether at last those things may be opened to you which were opened to your mother.

Yet what more should I say about these things? You have learned from the Gospel all the deeds of the Savior, the services of blessed Mary, and the actions of her life. And now what remains, that you should seek it from some teacher?

### II.

Concerning the Assumption of that same blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin—how she was assumed—because your prayer requests this, I have taken care to write to you, though absent in body, what I have offered devotedly while present in spirit. Thus your holy community may have, on the day of so great a solemnity, the gift of a Latin discourse, in which tender infancy may learn to taste the sweetness of milk and to conceive great things from small ones.

May God favor us so that each year this entire day may be spent in praise and celebrated with joy. Otherwise, if that apocryphal work, *On the Passing of the Same Virgin*, should come into your hands, you might receive doubtful matters as certain. Many Latins, out of devotion and a love of reading, embrace it eagerly, especially since from it nothing else can be learned with certainty except that on this day she gloriously departed from the body.

Her tomb is shown to us who look upon it even to the present day, in the middle of the valley of Jehoshaphat, which lies between Mount Zion and the Mount of Olives. You too, O Paula, saw it with your own eyes. A church has been built there in her honor, paved with marvelous stone; and everyone there declares that she was buried in it, as you can know. Yet the mausoleum is now shown to those who look upon it as empty.

I have said this because many among us doubt whether she was assumed together with her body or departed while leaving the body behind. How, or at what time, or by what persons her most holy body was removed from there, or where it was transferred; whether she rose again—we do not know. Yet some wish to assert that she has already been raised and clothed in blessed immortality with Christ in heaven.

Many make the same claim concerning blessed John the Evangelist, her attendant, to whom Christ entrusted the Virgin. For in his tomb, as is reported, nothing but manna is found, and it is seen to spring forth.

Nevertheless, we are uncertain which of these accounts should be judged truer. It is better to entrust the whole matter to God, for whom nothing is impossible, than to wish rashly to define by our own authority something that we cannot prove. The same applies to those whom, according to the testimony of the Gospel, we believe to have risen with the Lord.

But whether they returned to the dust of the earth, we do not know for certain, except for what we read: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose, came into the holy city, namely Jerusalem, and appeared to many” (Matt. XXVII, 52–53).

Some teachers certainly held concerning these people, and even left it in their writings, that the perpetual resurrection had already been completed in them. For they maintain that they would not be true witnesses unless their resurrection too were true.

Hence blessed Peter is also said to have spoken, when he referred to David as a witness: “And his tomb,” he says, “is among us” (Acts II, 29). It is as though he did not dare to say that David himself, or his body, was among us, but only the tomb in which he had been buried. From this they say that David also rose with the other saints, and that therefore his mausoleum remained empty, as Mary’s is seen to have done.

They attempt to affirm the same thing concerning other places in the Scriptures as well: that these people now reign with Christ, having been raised in eternal fellowship. Since nothing is impossible for God, we do not deny that this may also have happened to blessed Mary the Virgin. Nevertheless, for the sake of caution and without prejudice to the faith, it is more appropriate to entertain the matter as a pious desire than to define rashly what is unknown without danger.

### III.

Therefore, let us speak for a while about those things of which we are certain, in whatever sort of discourse may serve your exhortation, the building up of the hearers, and the praise of God’s name, so that reverence may be preserved for the sake of service and devotion increased for the sake of affection.

For this is the Virgin who alone destroyed every heretical perversity; she alone, after God, confirms us in every truth, commends us by her merits, and assists us by her prayers, so that we too may be found worthy of praising her.

If it is asked what she did after the Lord’s ascension, one thing is certain: the holy Virgin remained a virgin in body and mind. The angel Gabriel, as a heavenly bridesman, guarded her undefiled. And the apostle and evangelist John, to whom Christ entrusted her from the cross, preserved the Virgin as a virgin and served her with his own attentions.

This does not mean that that illustrious chorus of holy apostles abandoned her. Among them, after the resurrection, she went in and out and spoke more intimately about the Incarnation of Christ—more truly, indeed, because from the beginning she had learned all things more fully through the Holy Spirit and had seen everything with her own eyes, although the apostles too learned all things through the same Holy Spirit and attained to the whole truth after being instructed.

Although all the disciples revered that blessed Virgin and served her with the affection of love, John nevertheless did so more fully and specially to the end of his life. He received her, who had been entrusted to him, into his own [the text is incomplete], as a son receives a mother. The gracious Master said to him from the cross, “Woman, behold your son,” and then to the disciple, “Behold your mother” (John XIX, 26–27), so that a virgin might remain with a virgin and serve her most devotedly through the care of adoption.

For to whom could the most chaste virginity more rightly be entrusted than to a virgin, so that there might be between them a gracious companionship and a flourishing appearance? Their manner of life would be adorned in turn by the splendor of their chastities.

There was one virtue of virginity in both, but another proportion in Mary: another, indeed, because she was more fruitful, though she herself was the same. She was the same, yet another: for although the incorruption was the same, the fruitfulness of her integrity was far more glorious than virginity.

Therefore, both fruitfulness and virginity in her are wholly divine. Otherwise, according to the natural manner of birth, there is nowhere virginity where fruitfulness is proclaimed, nor fruitfulness where complete virginity is preserved.

For this reason, everything that is said about her surpasses all else, because it is divine and ineffable. Hence the virginity and the fruitfulness of her offspring are an extraordinary novelty, even though what is born is visibly human, from flesh.

Nevertheless, although virginity is much more magnificent in Mary because of the excellence of grace, there is one integrity of flesh and one virtue, which are joined to one another as kindred things.

For this reason John too, in proclaiming whatever Mary bore, commends it in his own eloquence. “In the beginning was the Word,” he says, “and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). This Word, which was in the beginning, which was with God, and which was God, blessed and glorious Virgin Mary herself brought forth from herself, made flesh.

Therefore her virginity was far more sacred, and her fruitfulness—as I may put it—far more ineffable than he could explain in his own speech. Yet the more closely virginity was related to virginity, the more excellent and nearer to the Word was the blessed evangelist than the others.

Thus, whatever the Virgin bore, he set forth more plainly for us and taught, as fully as a human being could through the Holy Spirit.

### IV.

As an example of human life, after Christ’s ascension her manner of life was generally with the apostles until they were scattered. Luke recalls this when he says:

“When they had returned from the Mount of Olives, they came to Jerusalem and went up into the upper room, where Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot, and Judas of James were staying. All these,” he says, “were persevering with one accord in prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers” (Acts I, 12, 14).

Behold, after Jesus ascended, with whom did the Virgin devote herself to the school of the virtues and meditate upon the law of God’s commandments, so that she too might be a model of Christ’s discipline and an example of perfection for virgins? She lived with the witnesses of the holy resurrection, and she herself was a witness. She lived with the senators of heaven within the court of paradise, under the discipline and instruction of the Holy Spirit and of the whole divine majesty.

Blessed Mary is found first among the foremost cohorts of the supreme King, whose life was no longer from the earth, in which Christ was waging war, but from heaven.

Then they are recorded to have gone up into the upper room, where the Passover was celebrated with the greatest dignity. There they remained with Mary the mother of Jesus, united in love, persevering in prayer, until they were clothed with power from on high.

They had already begun to pray, although earlier, while living with the Lord, they had been nourished by virtues and miracles. And they persevered well in prayer, doubting nothing, until they received the gifts of the Holy Spirit that they were seeking.

Imitate them also, O daughters, you who have vowed to remain in Christ’s school. Persevere in prayers, living together in unity, until you can enter the joys of eternal life, into which the blessed Virgin happily entered today, amid the alternating hymn-singing choirs of angels, within the pastures of eternal verdure.

There is the one fellowship of the citizens above; there is the sweet solemnity of the angels; there is, after labors and hardships, the happy and pleasant refreshment of souls.

Today, indeed, the glorious and ever-Virgin Mary ascended into heaven. I ask you, rejoice, because—as I must acknowledge—she has been ineffably exalted and reigns with Christ forever.

Today the Queen of the world is taken from the earth and from the wicked present age. Again I say: rejoice, because, secure in her unfading glory, she has already reached the palace of heaven.

Exult, I say, and rejoice, and let the whole world be glad, because today, through the intervention of her merits, salvation has been increased for all of us. To you also who love her, honor, virtue, and grace are granted in greater measure together with the other holy virgins.

Therefore, beloved, rejoice and praise her. For if we are commanded by prophetic speech to praise God in his saints, how much more ought we, on this celebration of blessed Mary the Virgin, his mother, to exalt him diligently with hymns and songs, to rejoice with praises worthy of God, and to honor him with mystical gifts.

No one doubts that whatever is worthily and solemnly offered to his mother contributes wholly to the glory of his praise. For this reason I am sufficiently afraid—indeed, greatly afraid—that while I desire to comply with your spiritual benefit, I may be found both an impudent and an unworthy praiser.

### V.

Indeed, neither holiness nor eloquence is sufficient for me to praise blessed and glorious Virgin Mary worthily. For, to speak the truth, whatever can be said in human words falls short of the praise of heaven, since she has been proclaimed and praised with divine and angelic praises surpassing all else.

She was foretold by the prophets, prefigured by the patriarchs in figures and enigmas, presented and shown by the evangelists, and greeted reverently and most devotedly by the angel.

Moreover, her nature and greatness are divinely declared by that same angel when he says: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.”

Such gifts were fitting for the Virgin to be endowed with: she was to be full of grace, who gave glory to the heavens, the Lord to the earth, restored peace, gave faith to the nations, put an end to vices, gave order to life, and discipline to morals.

And rightly is the angel sent to the Virgin Mary, because virginity is always akin to angels. Indeed, to live in the flesh apart from the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one.

Therefore, to acquire an angelic life in the flesh is a greater merit than to possess it. To be an angel is a matter of blessedness; to be a virgin is a matter of virtue, since the virgin strives through grace to obtain by her strength what the angel possesses by nature.

Yet both being a virgin and being an angel are the work of a divine gift, not of human effort. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace” (Luke I, 28). And rightly “full,” because grace is bestowed on others in portions, whereas in Mary the fullness of grace poured itself wholly out at once.

This is what David sings: “He shall descend like rain upon a fleece” (Ps. LXXII, 6). The fleece, although it is of the body, knows nothing of bodily passion. So virginity, although it is in the flesh, knows nothing of the vices of the flesh.

Clearly, heavenly rain poured gently upon the virginal fleece. The entire wave of divinity entered into flesh when “the Word became flesh.” Then, through the gallows of the cross, it was pressed out and poured over all the earth as the rain of salvation, granting the drops of grace to human minds.

“The Lord is with you.” A wondrous thing: he was already with the Virgin, though he was sending the angel to the Virgin. God went before his messenger, yet did not depart from God. Nor could he be held by places, who is present in every place and is wholly everywhere, without whom nothing is whole.

Therefore, the Word of the Father, never departing from the Father, deigned to become human for us through his own secret mystery, which he alone knows. Since he assumed the whole of what belongs to a human being, he is wholly human; and since he retained the whole of what belongs to God, the one born from Mary could not be anything other than God.

For God knows and can do all things. Therefore, because this is so, he knew and was able, without corruption of himself, to mingle and unite himself in the Virgin’s womb, so that Christ might be one, God and human being, one person and one substance.

For this reason the Mother of God is rightly greeted by the angel as chosen and prechosen, and is proclaimed full of grace. Truly full, through whom every creature was drenched by the abundant rain of the Holy Spirit.

And therefore the angel first reverences and greets her with profound devotion. He himself marvels at what sort and greatness she possesses whom he greets. For, I confess, this was not a simple or customary greeting, but one worthy of all wonder. It was the conveyance of reverence, the offering of a gift, and the service of homage.

For although grace is believed to have existed in the holy Fathers and prophets, it was not complete to this extent. In Mary, however, came the fullness of all grace that is in Christ, though in another manner.

And therefore he says: “Blessed are you among women,” that is, “more blessed than all women.” Accordingly, whatever curse was poured out through Eve, the blessing of Mary removed in its entirety. Moreover, the birth of Christ poured out grace, which the whole world previously had not possessed.

Therefore, what nature did not have, experience did not know, reason did not understand, the human mind cannot grasp, heaven fears, earth is astonished, and every creature, even heavenly, marvels at—this whole reality is divinely announced to Mary through Gabriel and fulfilled through Christ.

For this reason, I confess that I am unworthy to speak about such a great person and such great matters. I also think that no one would presume to do so except one who has no understanding at all of the greatness of what is being revealed.

## VI

Nevertheless, even if no one is found capable of this, no sinner at all ought by any means to cease from praises, although he cannot fulfill what he feels. Hence, when the divine word was speaking of the sinner in the Psalms, it said: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me”; and immediately it added: “And there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Psalm 49:23)—as though it plainly said: “There is a way of praise to eternal praise that will endure without end; but no one will attain it unless I first point it out.”

Therefore, dearest daughters, because the way of our salvation lies in praises of the Savior, I exhort and admonish you: on this sacred solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God, do not cease from praises. If you are a virgin, rejoice, because you have merited to be what you praise; only take care to be one who can praise worthily. If you are continent and chaste, venerate and praise, because you cannot be chaste from any other source than the grace of Christ, which was present most fully in Mary, whom you praise. If, however, you are married or a sinner, confess and praise nonetheless, since from that source mercy and grace flowed to all, so that they might praise. And although praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, do not cease from praise, because the forgiveness promised to you comes from the same source as that which enables everyone to praise.

Otherwise, unless we strive to praise God in his saints according to the measure of our understanding, how will we be able to praise him, as we sing, “according to the multitude of his greatness”? For we must by no means omit what we shall one day fulfill, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83:5). At times, however, because he is immeasurable, let us accomplish by our desires and the depths of our hearts what we cannot express with our voice or achieve through eloquence: because he is great and good and immeasurable, let us confess with mouth and spirit, for justice and salvation, that he is as great and such as he himself knows himself to be.

## VII

For this reason, I ask, let us all together celebrate with the greatest devotion the feast of the glorious ever-virgin Mary. For this is the splendid day on which she merited to be exalted above the choirs of angels and to go beyond what belongs to the nature of our humanity. Here it is not the substance that is removed, but the greatness of glory that is revealed, when she is raised to the right hand of the Father, where Christ entered on our behalf, having been made high priest forever, into the heavenly palace.

This, I say, is the day on which the undefiled mother and virgin advanced even to the height of the throne; and, raised upon the seat of the kingdom, she gloriously took her place after Christ. Thus the holy Church of God confidently sings everywhere that, concerning no other saint, is it permissible to believe that she has rightly surpassed the dignity of angels and archangels. For although likeness is promised to the saints, reality is denied them. This privilege belongs not to nature but to the grace of the blessed virgin Mary, from whom God himself, both God and man, was born.

Therefore, as virgin and human being, she is greater in merits, not in nature. Hence, even if the other virgins imitate her as far as contempt of childbirth and the service of Gabriel’s new greeting, everything that was thereafter accomplished in her is divine, as the angel bears witness: “For the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

Before this, certainly, the Virgin’s womb, although clean, undefiled, free from the contagion [variant: “thought”] of sin, and holy, was nevertheless still clothed in the lowliness of humanity—so, to speak, like the whitest wool, whitened by its own color. But when the Holy Spirit approached it, it was as though that same wool, stained with the blood of the purple-producing shellfish or murex, were changed into purple. Thus she too, without intercourse, was changed into a mother, so that she was no longer what she had been, but became the truest purple, divinely and most fittingly consecrated for the clothing and glory of the supreme king; thereafter no one was permitted to use her for any feminine purpose except God.

Indeed, to put it this way, blessed and glorious virgin Mary, although she had long been incomparable among all the virgins beneath heaven and could fittingly receive within herself the union of divinity while both natures remained intact, nevertheless, when she was filled with grace, flooded with the Holy Spirit, and overshadowed by the power of the Most High, became more precious in merits, higher in exalted dignity, more beautiful in holiness, and more glorious through the prerogatives of her merits—so that she herself was no longer to be devoted to any uses except divine ones.

Therefore, holiest virgins, although you ought to imitate so great and such a virgin and venerate one so illustrious, it is nevertheless highly fitting—and, insofar as is permitted, in a manner beyond angelic dignity—to extol her with the most worthy praises and joy. As we have said, she has not rashly been exalted through Christ’s grace above the choirs of angels, and today she is proclaimed with the greatest devotion, because our Lord and Savior, born from her in true faith, preceded her into the heavenly places, in order to prepare a place for her in the heavenly dwellings, as he himself promised his disciples.

For this reason the prophet David, once rejoicing, sings to Christ: “His going forth,” he says, “is from the summit of heaven, and his return reaches to its summit” (Psalm 18:7). He ascended, therefore, to resume the same glory—which he had not lost—that he had possessed before the world was made. He ascended and prepared for this most holy and glorious Virgin a place of immortality, so that she might reign with him forever.

## VIII

And this is the festivity of the present day, on which the glorious and blessed woman reached the ethereal bridal chamber. As blessed Mary is incomparable among other virgins, so this festivity is incomparable among the feasts of all the saints; it is even an object of wonder to the angelic powers.

Therefore the Holy Spirit, speaking in astonishment from the person of the heavenly citizens at her ascent, says in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness like a column of smoke from perfumes?” (Song of Songs 3:6). And rightly “like a column of smoke,” because she was slender and delicate, because she had been made thin by divine disciplines, and because inwardly she had been burned as a whole offering in the fire of devoted love and the desire of charity.

“Like a column of smoke from perfumes,” he says, surely because she was filled with many fragrances of virtues. From her there arose a most sweet fragrance, perceptible even to angelic spirits. The Mother of God was ascending from the wilderness of the present age—the rod once sprung from the root of Jesse. But the souls of the elect marveled with joy at who she could be who, by the virtues of her merits, surpassed even the dignity of the angels.

Of her the same Holy Spirit again says in the same Song: “Who is this who ascends,” he says, “like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arranged for battle?” (Song of Songs 6:9). The Holy Spirit is astonished because he makes all those who marvel at this Virgin’s ascent marvel also that, shining like the dawn of a new day, she gleams in her ascent, relying upon and surrounded by many armies of saints.

Hence it is said: “terrible as an army arranged for battle.” She was made terrible by her virtues, like a perfectly ordered army, supported on every side by the protection of the holy angels. “Beautiful as the moon”—indeed, more beautiful than the moon, because now she shines without any waning of her own, illumined by heavenly splendors. “Chosen as the sun,” through the radiance of virtues, because the sun of righteousness himself chose her, so that he might be born from her.

At her funeral, certainly—as far as it is permissible to believe—angels served, and all the heavenly courts rejoiced together. Nor is this surprising, because the honor of his mother belongs to him who was born from her, whom every order of heaven venerates and adores, raised above them with the Father on the seat of the Lord’s majesty.

For we read that angels have often come to the funerals and burials of various saints and rendered service at their obsequies; and that they have carried the souls of the elect to heaven with hymns and praises. Choirs of both sexes are also frequently mentioned as having been heard there singing praises. Moreover—and this is more remarkable—they have sometimes shone with a much greater light, and even while still living in the flesh have for a long time perceived the fragrance of a wondrous odor in that place.

If, then, to revive hope and strengthen at times the faith of those standing by, our Savior Jesus Christ, in order to demonstrate more fully the merits of his own servants, deigned to exhibit such great things through his heavenly ministers concerning the dead, how much more ought we to believe that on this day the armies of heaven came festively to meet the Mother of God with their hosts, surrounded her with immense light, and led her with praises and spiritual songs even to the throne prepared for her long ago, before the foundation of the world!

No one doubts that the whole heavenly Jerusalem then exulted with ineffable joy, then rejoiced with immeasurable charity, and then shouted for joy with every expression of gladness, because this festival, which returns to us annually today, has become for all of them perpetual.

## IX

And not without reason. For it is believed that the Savior of all himself, insofar as it is granted us to understand, came wholly in festal joy to meet her and, with rejoicing, seated her beside himself on the throne. Otherwise, how is he believed to have fulfilled what he himself commanded in the Law: “Honor your father and your mother” (Matthew 15:4)?

That he honored the Father, he himself bears witness when he says to the Jews: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges. But I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me” (John 8:49–50). Concerning his mother, the Evangelist says: “When he returned,” coming to Nazareth, “he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51).

But the nature by which God the Father is honored in himself is one thing, and the nature by which he is subject to his parents is another. Yet in both there is rightly believed to be one and the same Christ, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”: one Emmanuel, that is, God with us.

The catholic faith preserves this union of divinity and humanity without confusion and without division. By understanding it, the natural and substantial concord of unity is recognized, so that neither transformation of one of the two substances into the other nor division is admitted.

To believe thus is to honor the mother of the Lord, who gave birth to God and man for us—not to a man without God, nor to God without man, but to one true Jesus Christ, God and man. Otherwise she could not be called Mother of God, as many heretics have attempted to deny, unless she had truly given birth to God incarnate.

For this reason we rightly confess two births in Christ. One is from the Father, without beginning, timeless, eternal, and coeternal with God the Father. The other is from his mother in time, when, assuming pity and mercy, he descended to us by his own will, born as man and God. Accordingly, according to the truth, he who is always recognized as God is also carried in his mother’s womb.

Hence we truly confess her as *Theotokos*—the Mother of God—and also as *Christotokos*. This does not mean that the Word carried flesh along with himself, or that he had previously been joined to the flesh in question; rather, at the moment when the Word became flesh from the Virgin’s flesh, the substance of divinity and humanity was united in the womb without confusion, so that Christ, God and man, might be one person.

From two natures, without confusion of either, there is found only one Jesus the Lord, remaining God in the form of God, who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), remaining one and the same in the form of the servant that he assumed. For he is wholly God in the flesh of the Virgin from whom he was born, and wholly man.

Hence also the Apostle says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Therefore, daughters, “be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16), so that, through the wisdom of perfect understanding, you may preserve whole and inviolate the ring of your faith and the pearl for which you abandoned everything, lest you lose—God forbid—both the dowry and pledge of the Holy Spirit.

Take the greatest care, then, that the simplicity of the dove, which was in Mary, may be preserved unharmed and inviolate in you. Concerning her Solomon says in the Song of Songs, as though in her praise: “Come, my dove, my undefiled one. For winter has now passed, the rain has gone away and departed” (Song of Songs 2:11). And afterward he says: “Come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” (ibid. 4:6, 8).

She is rightly commanded to come from Lebanon, because *Lebanon* is interpreted as “whitening.” She was whitened by many virtues of merits and made whiter than snow by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, representing the simplicity of the dove in all things. For whatever was done in her was wholly purity and simplicity [Martianus omits: “wholly purity and simplicity”], wholly truth and grace, wholly mercy and justice that looked down from heaven. Therefore she was undefiled, because she was corrupted in nothing.

For she encompassed a man in the womb, as the holy Jeremiah testifies, and received him from no other source. “The Lord,” he says, “will make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah 31:22).

Truly this was new, and a novelty surpassing every novelty of virtues: that God—whom the world cannot bear, nor anyone see and live—entered the lodging of the womb in such a way that he did not become aware of the body’s enclosure; and was carried in such a way that he was wholly God within it; and departed from it in such a way that it was, as Ezekiel confesses, an entirely closed gate.

Hence it is sung of her in the same Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; your outlets are a paradise” (Song of Songs 4:12). Truly she was a garden of delights, in which every kind of flower and fragrance of virtues had been planted. She was enclosed in such a way that she could not be violated or corrupted by any deceitful attack.

She was therefore a fountain sealed with the seal of the whole Trinity, from which the fountain of life flows, in whose light we shall all see light. For, according to John, “he is the one who enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). The outlet of this womb is truly the paradise of all the heavenly citizens.

From this field of the womb the patriarch Isaac, smelling from afar, said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field full, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). Yet those who understand little think that the earlier saints understood less of the mystery of the Incarnation of Christ, although they too were saved by the same grace.

## X

From this it is clear that time did not prejudice the mystery of the united man and God, so that the one who had not yet been born of the Virgin Mary was already present in him through the unity of person from the beginning of the world. This is demonstrated by many indications in Scripture.

Thus the Lord says to the Jews: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58). By these words he clearly showed that he who was speaking had always existed in the mystery of unity. To commend this, he says: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” “Before Abraham came to be” expresses the brevity of humanity; “I am” declares the eternity of nature. In that eternity he indicates that he who was speaking had already existed through the mystery of his incarnation.

The apostle Jude, wishing to make this clearer, says: “Jesus, having saved the people from Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5). Elsewhere Paul says: “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him” (1 Corinthians 10:9). This does not mean that Jesus or Christ had already been born from Mary, but that in that one Son of God the unity of person was already being commended, although hidden in the mystery.

Paul also says elsewhere: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), because certainly whatever God did from the beginning, Christ did wholly through the unity of the mystery. Thus Jesus was already in the Son who led the people out, and Christ was in the one who was tempted, since it is not doubted that he always existed in God through the unity of the mystery.

Otherwise, unless you believe this, either Christ will not be God at all, or, contrary to the prophet, God will seem to be recent. But, lest we be shaken by such accusations, the Scriptures must be searched, in which the unity of person in Christ is commended, since time does not prevent him from always being called one.

Hence blessed Peter, speaking of the fathers, says: “Through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we are saved, just as they also were” (Acts 15:11). The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign God with them. Therefore God is not recent with us either, because the one and the same person was both their leader and our Redeemer through the passion of his flesh: one in his flesh, one in the mystery, and one in spirit.

Reason does not permit us to understand one as the Son of man and another as the Son of God. He is neither limited by time nor separated by passion. Rather, God wholly passes into Christ and Christ into God, so that whatever is the Son of God may be called Christ, and whatever Christ endured in the flesh may rightly be believed to have been endured by God.

Otherwise, if you consider reason and human senses, divinity and human condition could never have come together in this way. Yet they came together in Christ, and one Emmanuel exists from both.

Therefore it seems to me that those who judged either that there were two sons or that Christ was something other than the Son of God could not carefully understand or perceive the height of so great a mystery.

Accordingly, we neither worship nor adore a man separately—which would be impious—but rather God incarnate, who united to himself a proper, living body, so that God the Word became flesh. The unity did not fall upon someone else, but upon himself, who had always been the one and true Son of God.

For this reason we worship and adore no other than the same Son of God. Through the assumed man he was not increased in anything, nor was he diminished or changed in anything by becoming flesh. Therefore the one and same Son is always adored with God the Father: not a new one, not a recent one arising in time, not alien to his nature or kind.

## XI

If it seems new to you that he assumed a man for your sake, know that this had always been with him and in his counsel, that it should happen in this way. Now, when the fullness of time arrived, what had always been accomplished in Christ was accomplished.

The earlier saints were divinely affected by such fragrances and inspired by such prophecies concerning Christ: that he would be born into the world, in whom there would be the salvation of all and the blessing of eternal inheritance.

These are the garments of faith; these are the garments with which the earlier saints were clothed; these are the garments which Rebecca—or rather, the Holy Spirit—kept with himself at home and with which he clothed Jacob, his son.

If they had not been preserved and brought out at home by the Holy Spirit, what wondrous fragrance would the father Isaac have drawn from them, so that, sensing the fragrance of the garments, he said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field full, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27)?

But perhaps someone will say: What does the Holy Spirit have to do with Rebecca, since in many places persons are figuratively understood as representing God? Nevertheless, in Hebrew, *ruaḥ* (“spirit”) is also spoken of in the feminine gender—not because gender is revealed in God, but lest anyone should suspect that, according to the rule of the three languages, the Holy Spirit is understood differently. In Hebrew, as I have said, it is read in the feminine gender; in Greek, lest sex be believed to belong to him, **πνεῦμα** (*pneuma*, “spirit”) is found in the neuter; and in Latin it is determined to be masculine.

The Holy Spirit is rightly understood through Rebecca. Therefore everything that takes place is part of the mystery, so that Christ may be announced through the fragrance of the garments. We all who have been baptized put him on; in him he blessed us not with some blessing, but, as the Apostle says, “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3).

Hence the angel, speaking to Mary, began with a blessing: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:28). Drawing in spirit from afar the fragrance of this one, the father Isaac blessed the son in whom every heavenly blessing blossomed for the world.

The field is rightly called full by him, because the virgin Mary is proclaimed full of the grace of virtues. From her womb the fruit of life shone forth for believers. “And we,” says the Evangelist, “have all received from his fullness, grace upon grace” (John 1:16).

Therefore, daughters, I beseech you, do not receive in vain such great grace, which is in Christ Jesus, in whom God and man are united in one and the same person. Thus Scripture is often read as making man coeternal with God through the union of substance; and then God appears to have suffered together with man, although man is not without beginning and God is not passible.

Yet God is so united to his body that, according to human judgment, no separation can be made between God and man. Lest—God forbid—one Son of God and another Son of man be believed, especially since divine Scripture so joins and incorporates God and man that one cannot distinguish man from God in time, or God from man in passion.

Thus, if you consider time, you will certainly find the Son of man always with the Son of God. If you consider passion, you will always find the same Son of God united and indivisible with the Son of man, insofar as the language of Scripture is concerned, so that man cannot be separated from God by time, nor God from man by passion.

## XII

To make this clearer for you, examine Christ’s own words: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

Who, I ask, is speaking? Christ, certainly. Where, I ask, was he when he spoke these words? On earth, of course. And how does he testify that he descended from heaven before he was born? Moreover, while speaking, he confesses that he is in heaven, and he calls himself the Son of man, although no one could descend from heaven except God. And when he speaks on earth, it was none other than the one and same Christ.

This is the wondrous and astonishing novelty—indeed, the novelty surpassing every novelty—of unity. Unless you observe it carefully, prudent virgin, from the beginning of the holy Gospel, you will seem more to err throughout all divine Scripture than to understand the truth.

It is therefore established that one and the same Christ acted according to both forms, namely, humanity and divinity, and consequently exercised two operations. Each form or nature performed, in communion with the other, what properly belonged to it: the Word doing what belonged to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belonged to the flesh. The Word communicating with it in that same operation, the same one is believed to be both God and man in one substance or person, without division or mixture, and one foreknown identity is proclaimed.

Nevertheless, God the Word is not flesh, although he assumed flesh rationally animated; and he joined this flesh to himself by a natural and substantial union [variant: “the manuscript omits ‘to himself’]. Likewise, the flesh is animated flesh and not the Word, although the flesh of the Word of God was seen and observed.

Hence John says: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen, what we have contemplated, and what our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). Certainly no one can see or handle the true God with his hands except through the mystery of the man united to him.

This union is so wondrous that it cannot be distinguished. Otherwise, how can the Word that was from the beginning rightly be said to be all that the apostles had heard, seen, and handled, unless it was because Christ was one and the same? Accordingly, what they had heard, seen, and handled was the Word of life; and from the two natures there was nothing other than one, according to subsistence or person.

This is why the one and same remaining only-begotten Son is seen undivided in both natures and naturally performs what belongs to both substances, according to the essential quality or natural property inherent in each. If these things belonged to a single, unjoined nature, he would not perform them. But now, since Emmanuel is one, and in him both—God and man—truly performed what belongs to both natures, he acted according to the difference between the things accomplished.

Thus, insofar as he is God, the same one performed what is divine; insofar as he is man, the same one performed what is human, wishing to show that he is both God and man. Therefore the same one performs both what is divine and what is human. It was not one who worked miracles and another who underwent human experiences and suffered passions, but one and the same Christ, Son of God and Son of man, who performed divine and human deeds. Christ possessed these actions commonly, inseparably and indivisibly.

Yet the qualities of the works must be understood, and one must always contemplate toward what the humility of the flesh is raised and toward what the height of divinity bends, so that throughout the entire text of the holy Gospel the flesh may be seen to do nothing without the Word, nor the Word to accomplish anything without the flesh.

Thus, what the Virgin conceives and gives birth to is not without the power of the Word, just as what is born, lying wrapped in bands of cloth and reclining in a manger, is not without the truth of the flesh. Moreover, the one adored by the Magi under the guidance of the star (Matthew 2:11) is divine; yet he is also human when he is taken into Egypt by flight so that he may not be captured.

All the works of power must therefore be considered in such a way that we render to God what belongs to God and to man what belongs to man. For just as there is one who calls Lazarus by the word of his power to come out from the tomb, so the same one is he who wept with human feeling. Everything must be considered in this way, so that the fullness of divinity in Christ may be understood as united to man, and the fullness of humanity as assumed into God.

## XIII

I have said these things for a while, dearest daughters, concerning the faith of Christ’s Incarnation because, as many of the Easterners go about wrapped in their own filth, you ought to be warned lest they wish to obscure you with the language of their darkness or confuse Latin purity with a Greek whirlwind.

For there are wise virgins, and there are foolish ones. Therefore, dearest daughters, imitate the blessed and glorious Virgin whom you love and whose feast you celebrate today on earth. Of her it is said: “But Mary kept all these words” (namely, the things spoken about Christ), “pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:51).

Therefore, dearest daughters, ponder in your hearts what is said about that same Lord in catholic teaching, so that you may preserve the faith intact and venerate his mother as you ought. For there is no other honor due to her except when he is rightly honored who deigned to be born from her.

But I ask all of you, daughters—whether you are daughters or mothers—think more attentively and weigh more carefully by what sorrows the blessed and undefiled virgin Mary was affected after Christ’s ascension into heaven, when everything concerning him had been fulfilled that had been proclaimed by the angels, prefigured by the prophets in many forms and in many ways, declared by divine oracles, displayed through miracles, and revealed through the signs of his humanity.

I ask you, if there is in you any inner feeling of devotion, consider with what love she was tormented and with what longing this virgin burned, as she turned over in her mind everything she had heard, seen, and come to know.

I think that, even if you applied all that belongs to the heart, all that belongs to the mind, and all human strength, it would not be enough to enable you to imagine how continually she burned with the heat of devoted love, by how many impulses of heavenly mysteries she was moved, filled as she was with the Holy Spirit.

For although she loved Christ with all her heart, with all her soul, and with all her strength, she was nevertheless inflamed each day by new affections of longing for him who was absent through his presence. This longing was all the stronger because she was inwardly illumined by divine visitations. The grace of the Holy Spirit had filled her entirely; divine love had wholly set her ablaze, so that there was in her nothing that a worldly affection could violate, but only continual ardor and intoxication with love poured into her.

Christ must be loved by human beings with all the heart, soul, and strength, and must be sought above all things. Yet he had to be loved more ardently by her, since he was both her Lord and her son.

Perhaps, therefore, because of her excessive love, we believe that she sometimes lived in the place where he is said to have been buried, so that her inward devotion might be nourished by pious sights. For that place lies midway between the sites, so that she could visit the traces of his ascension, the place of his burial and resurrection, and all the places where he suffered—not because she was seeking the living among the dead, but so that she might be consoled by seeing them.

Impatient love has this characteristic: it always believes that it can find what it desires. It does not know judgment, often lacks reason, knows no measure, and can think of nothing except what it loves. Love finds no consolation in impossibility and no remedy in difficulty.

Although the blessed virgin Mary was already in the spirit, nevertheless, while she lived in the flesh, she was moved by bodily senses; and therefore she was often refreshed by visiting those places and embraced in the arms of her mind the one whom she had borne.

In the end, love of Christ gave birth to longing; and longing, as it grew, was renewed as though by new ardors, so much so that I believe it sometimes transcended everything, even herself. For impatient love simply cannot fail to see what it loves.

Hence, dearest daughters, all the saints considered everything they had merited to be small if they did not see the Lord whom they loved. Likewise, the venerable blessed virgin Mary sometimes offered an act of holiness that was not unworthy of countless and immeasurable benefits, while, still placed on earth, she could not see the giver of those benefits. Therefore today, dearest daughters, she is raised above the choirs of angels, so that she may see the form and face of the Savior whom she loved and desired with the whole longing of her heart.

## XIV

If there is joy in heaven over any sinner who is converted, how much more should we think that there is exultation in the heavenly realms over the exaltation and glory of so great a Virgin! Her festival is the rejoicing of all the heavenly citizens, especially because her celebration is praise and honor for the Savior.

Therefore, as was said above, we believe that they do not regard only this day as an annual solemnity in her honor, but also celebrate it continually and eternally with rejoicing, gladness, and veneration, worshiping her with every exultation of love and joy.

Not without reason, then, does that whole heavenly city rejoice with and venerate the mother whose son, the king, it adores above itself, before whom the powers tremble and every knee bends.

Concerning her ascent into heaven, the contemplator of heavenly mysteries, gazing with profound wonder, says in the Song of Songs: “I saw the beautiful one ascending like a dove from above the streams of waters.” And truly she was beautiful like a dove, because she displayed the appearance and simplicity of that dove which came upon the Lord and taught John that he was the one who baptizes.

And rightly “from above the streams of waters,” because the Lord had led and nourished her beside the water of refreshment (Psalm 23:2). From it many streams flow forth, watering the whole land of delights and pouring themselves into the garden of pleasure. From these streams the blessed Mother of God, thus continually filled, ascends today exceedingly beautiful and marvelous. Her fragrance was utterly beyond measure, and therefore ineffable.

At the fragrance of this scent the whole heavenly Jerusalem joyfully runs together. Flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her, because all the souls reddened by martyrdom embrace her with the arms of eternal love, and those made white by the splendor of virginity—like lilies nurtured in the valley of humility—surround her, serving her in honor.

Rightly so, because the blessed Mother of God was both martyr and virgin, although she ended her life in peace. The prophet Simeon also testifies that she truly suffered when he said to her: “And your own soul a sword will pierce” (Luke 2:35).

From this it is clear that she was more than a martyr. Other saints, although they suffered in the flesh for Christ, could not suffer in the soul, because the soul is immortal. But the blessed Mother of God suffered in that part which is considered incapable of suffering. Therefore, so to speak, because her flesh also suffered spiritually through the sword of the passion of Christ, she was more than a martyr.

It is clear that because she loved more than all others, she also suffered more, so much so that the force of pain pierced and possessed her entire soul, as testimony to her extraordinary love. Because she suffered in mind, she was more than a martyr.

Indeed, her love was stronger than death, because she made Christ’s death her own. Now flowers of roses surround her, continually admiring her beauty among the daughters of Jerusalem (Song of Songs 5:7). In her the king placed his throne, because he desired her appearance and beauty. For she was full of charity and love. Therefore it follows that after her comes an army clothed in purple and a flock clothed in white.

### XV

[Col. 0138C] If you examine her more carefully, there is no virtue, no beauty, no radiance or glory that does not shine forth from her. And therefore roses rightly surround her, as do lilies of the valleys, so that virtues may support virtues, and beauty may be increased by the adornment of chastity. For every splendor and glory, the more sublimely it is illuminated by its own radiance, the more outstanding it appears in the brightness of whatever is beneath it, and the more exceptionally it is proclaimed.

So too the blessed Mother of God, whose planting shone forth with particular brilliance like a rose in Jericho, and whose virginal purity flashed forth more splendidly, is surrounded by the office of charity, while the radiance of the saints is placed beneath her, so that her splendor and glory may be commended all the more. Raised above the choirs of angels, she is now proclaimed blessed, and now most blessed. For although the nature of angels is higher, their grace is not greater, since they too were saved by gratuitous grace lest they fall.

[Col. 0138D] Hence David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. XXXIII, 6). If all their strength subsists by the breath of his mouth, it is clear that the blessed and glorious virgin Mary, upon whom the Holy Spirit came, and into whom God himself wholly entered—carried, as we must believe, for nine months in the womb—earned greater privileges of virtue and received a grace praised even by the angels. Thus, although their virtue and the firmness of their perpetuity are wondrous, they are more wondrous in Mary, whom the power of the Most High overshadowed: so that what happened in her surpasses every angelic virtue and is a sacrament admirable throughout all ages.

And consequently a greater grace is also henceforth bestowed upon the angels, [Col. 0139A] when all that they venerate and adore above themselves—the Christ, the King and Lord born from that same Virgin—is restored through her. Thus Mary is more venerable to all in proportion as she is more full of grace; and the more the power of the Most High raises her to sublime heights, the more brilliantly she resounds in glory. Since she is full of grace, full of God, full of virtues, she cannot fail to possess fully the glory of eternal radiance, which she received in the fullest measure so that she might become the mother of the Savior.

All the daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed, and queens praised her, because they saw her to be as great as no mortal has fully expressed in words. How much more, then, should they praise God, who made her such and so great that he himself might come to be through her! Hence David says: “And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVII, 2).

[Col. 0139B] Blessed, therefore, is such a great and blessed birth; blessed also is the fellowship of the citizens above and the wondrous unanimity of their charity. There no angel, no archangel envies the glory of the blessed virgin Mary—or, I do not say, of her, but not even the glory of any saint. Rather, each person possesses in the other all that is freely bestowed upon everyone, so that God may be glorified, honored, and adored by all, from all and in all.

There sex, age, and nobility of birth do not distinguish anyone; only the quality of merits does. There “star differs from star in glory,” although all are to be raised in their own order. And if “there is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars” (I Cor. XV, 41), yet there is one glory by which all things are illuminated.

Therefore the blessed Mother of God, who is still proclaimed on earth with such great praises, is rightly believed to have been exalted, glorified, and also made radiant today, as fully as he knows who chose her in his wisdom, by which he ordered all things. And if in the house of the Father there are many dwelling places, we believe that today the Son has provided for his mother a more splendid dwelling than the house he once built for himself, supported by seven columns. In that house, truly, the wedding of the churches of God is prepared, and heavenly things are joined to earthly things. For in that Virgin’s womb virginity is consecrated to the immortal Bridegroom, so that the whole exchange may be heavenly.

### XVI

Therefore, dearest women, celebrate solemnly the feast of the Virgin, who showed you heavenly life on earth, for “those who neither marry nor are given in marriage will be like the angels in heaven.” Nor is it surprising that virginity is compared with angels, since it is joined by a marriage covenant to the Lord of angels. And if every virginity is raised so high as to be compared with angels, how much more the blessed and glorious virgin Mary, who is commended by a singular privilege and is said to possess an immeasurable treasure.

Therefore, beloved, love the one whom you venerate, and venerate the one whom you love. For you truly venerate and love her if you wish with your whole heart to imitate the one whom you praise. This life, which you have professed, flowed to you from heaven; this life, which you embrace, is above the use of nature. The Bridegroom came from heaven, and you must follow him with his mother. Nor is it without reason that you sought the manner of life from heaven, since you asked heaven to give you a Bridegroom.

Therefore let your way of life always be in heaven, since the Word of God whom you love is found nowhere but in the bosom of the Father. Although he is wholly everywhere and is not far from each one of us, yet he is received above only by a chaste heart. “He is near,” Moses says, “in your heart and in your mouth,” provided that you seek him with an upright heart (Deut. XXXI, 11).

“His name is an oil poured out”; therefore, young women, love in your spirit the one who was poured out for you. For you have, holy virgins, a virgin Bridegroom, a lover of virginity and chastity, who therefore chose a virgin mother so that she might be an example of chastity to all, in whom the form of virtue shines forth as in a mirror.

In her, therefore, you have examples of uprightness clearly set forth: what you ought first to choose, what to reject, and what to follow. Her first virtue is the foundation and guardian of all virtues—humility itself—of which she boasts: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke I, 48).

Thus the first incentive to learning is the nobility of the teacher; then comes the excellent reward of labor, the fruit of blessedness. What, then, is nobler than the mother of the Lord? What is more radiant than she whom the Radiance of the Father’s glory chose? What is chaster than she who generated Christ’s body without bodily defilement? Yet she confesses that in her the Lord regarded only humility, which is the guardian of the other virtues.

For she had placed the lofty exercises of her merits in the secure harbor of her station, and therefore she was divinely illumined. Hence the Lord says: “Upon whom shall I look, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2). He fulfilled what he had promised [Col. 0140C] and regarded the humility of his handmaid; hence she has been proclaimed blessed by every generation.

Therefore you too, daughters, if you truly wish to be virgins, pursue humility. Strive to imitate with the love of your hearts the mother of the Lord, who calls herself a handmaid. Strive to imitate with the love of your hearts her humility, which she learned from that very Bridegroom to whom you have devoted yourselves and who taught it from himself. Hence he says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

The blessed Mother of God did not, therefore, learn from her Son and our Lord how to fashion the heavens, create angels, or perform the wonders of divine power. She learned only to humble herself and to gather the other lessons of virtue within the protection of humility. Hence the purity of the individual virtues always remained with her as an unfailing companion, because modesty must be inseparable from virginity, without which true chastity cannot rightly be preserved.

The blessed virgin Mary, therefore, never came forth without the guardian of her modesty. And so, dearest women, if such a great virgin pleases you, let the practice of virtue please you also: her life is the discipline of all, her conduct the rule of the churches; she went before everyone and surpasses all. Therefore any virgin who hopes for a reward from her and implores her help must imitate her example.

I beg you, virgins, and I beg you, widows: imitate Paula, the widowed mother, an example of continence and chastity. Imitate Eustochium, whom you have with you, a virgin and beautiful in perfect integrity. If there is less in them than in the Mother of the Lord—or rather, because there is—[Col. 0141A] you have one who is fruitful in offspring and an everlasting virgin. For just as, in comparison with God, no one is good, so in comparison with the Mother of the Lord no one is found perfect, even though proved by outstanding virtues.

There is one Father of us all, who is in heaven, and one teacher. There is one model of virginity in Mary; you all ought to impress her likeness upon the sculpture of the Holy Spirit, as an image that restores your integrity. For she is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, a well of living waters” (Cant. IV, 12, 15), into which no deceit could break, nor the enemy’s fraud prevail. She remained holy in mind and body, exalted by many privileges of gifts.

Therefore imitate her in conduct, follow her in chastity, and implore her help.

### XVII

If some envious person wishes to accuse me of presumption because I have written these things to you, since I speak in this manner, let him accuse charity and love, for when you asked me, I judged that I could not refuse even this untried task. I preferred to bear the blush of embarrassment rather than fail to carry out your command, since God sometimes seems to obey your prayers. Especially since you have with you women whom it is virtuous to imitate and from whom you can learn, you sought from me affection rather than instruction in praise of this day.

Therefore I ought not to have excused myself out of regard for gravity, lest I fail to share with your devotion what you had commanded. And if I was unable to teach, I nevertheless took every care to exhort you in praise of so great a virgin, so that I might not be absent from you on the day of the festival of the one whom you love. Rather, I might join myself to your prayers and your vows, if in some way, aided by your merits, I might deserve to be raised in spirit with you to those heights which the blessed and undefiled virgin Mary attained.

Behold, today she ascended through humility and bodily integrity to that splendid and radiant throne of the angels, from which intemperance once cast down the illustrious archangels, and pride cast them down. Therefore rejoice, rejoice, I say, because the way to heaven has been opened for you. Although the same things are promised to us, those things are already present to you, since with the angels you preserve incorruption.

Although you belong to this world, by God’s favor you are no longer in this world. For even if the world was worthy to possess you, it could not hold you altogether. Thus blessed Mary is today proclaimed far and wide by all nations, and heavenly blessedness is granted to you who have followed the example of so great a virgin.

You are not troubled by the enticements of the body, nor plunged into ruin by the flood of pleasure, nor inflamed by the heat of the flesh’s incitement. Rather, you delight in angelic imitation on earth, whose equality is promised to you in heaven to come.

Blessed, therefore, are you, daughters—and blessed also are you, widows, who lead a celibate life in Christ alongside the virgins. For, according to the Apostle, having been freed from the law of a husband, they remained so. “She will be happier,” he says, “if she remains thus according to my counsel. For I think,” he says, “that I too have the Spirit of God” (I Cor. VII, 40). He clearly wished to express the difference between the woman who is still bound by the law to a husband and the woman who, having already been released from the bond, is proclaimed more blessed.

And if both are blessed because they are in Christ, nevertheless she is more blessed who has already been released from the bond and pursues heavenly things. Therefore widows are always rightly joined to virgins, as the Apostle says: “The unmarried woman and the virgin think of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit” (I Cor. VII, 34).

In a certain sense the teaching of virginity grows and is strengthened through the examples of widows. Having preserved a chaste marriage with husbands, they teach virgins that integrity should be preserved for God; and that it is almost no lesser virtue to abstain from marriage after having once enjoyed it than never to have known the pleasures of marriage. In both states courage is praised, and the virtue of heavenly life is proclaimed.

Therefore both orders now share kinship with Christ. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. XII, 50): where neither sex, age, nor condition is distinguished, but, he says, “whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

### XIX

Since, therefore, free opportunity is granted to all, dearest women, be what the grace of Christ has called you to be: mothers and brides of Christ; sisters and relatives. For what you could not have by flesh has all been granted to you by grace.

Therefore love the mother of the Lord, who bore for you the immortal Bridegroom. She is also your sister, since she did the Father’s will in order to become a mother; she is related to you not by flesh but by spirit, so that the unity of the Church may be commended and the fellowship of Christ’s body understood.

Hence the Lord says: “I will, Father, since I and you are one, that they too may be one in us” (John XVII, 21). This unity is brought about through the one mediator between God and human beings. Therefore you too do the Father’s will, so that you may be one.

Trim your lamps, go out to meet the Bridegroom, because he is already knocking at the door, and follow his mother if you love her. Prepare and trim your lamps within, since you are daughters of the King. Let all your glory be within, and possess within yourselves what may shine outward, lest during these solemn celebrations your lamps be extinguished before the Bridegroom comes.

For this day’s celebration is rightly observed only with lamps lit within and without. Therefore buy oil while there is opportunity, lest, when the Bridegroom comes, you be found—God forbid—empty. Hence set your minds on the things above, where the blessed Virgin has arrived, and not on the things upon earth. For if you are already what you have vowed to be, your way of life ought to be in heaven.

Direct your mind there; hide your life there until the Lord’s anger passes over, to the place where the blessed Mother of God has arrived today. There you have the Bridegroom, there the high priest, there everything you have sought. Direct your mind there, so that when Christ, the Son of the Virgin, appears at the end of the world, you too may appear with him in glory. Amen.

## EDITORIAL NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

I scarcely doubt—or rather, have no doubt at all—that this sermon is by Fulbert of Chartres. It is certainly attributed to him in a manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 3752, immediately after the Pseudo-Jerome just discussed; and also in another manuscript from Saint-Germain, which contains various unbound works. Yet in both it is entitled not *On the Assumption* but *On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, which was its earlier title.

Finally, it is also found under the name of the same author in other books, according to Oudinus. Sermon 208 in the Appendix to Augustine, which, as the Louvain scholars themselves observe, is attributed to the same Fulbert in most of their manuscripts, consists for the most part of the same fragments and exactly the same words as this sermon. It is therefore easy to see that the earlier homily of the bishop of Chartres was—something customary in this kind of composition—mutilated according to the discretion and understanding of interpolators speaking to the people, and then made to pass successively into other forms.

## LETTER X. On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. (C, G)\*

### I

Knowing that we owe much to our Creator because we were created, and even more because we were redeemed, let us venerate the transaction of our redemption, and let us celebrate, if not with merits, at least with acts of devotion, that most sacred womb from which God, united to a human being, appeared. Let us remember that the darkness of our error was partly dispersed by her radiance. For what human beings had lost through the negligence of our first parents and the defiant arrogance as well as the gluttony [Alt. reading: *regula*, “rule”] of the first mother, the birth of this holy Virgin not only restored after its ruin but also bestowed everlasting gifts.

Therefore let us venerate with every kind of praise the author of salvation, who, when she conceived her Creator from heaven, showed us our Redeemer in the world. And since she is established as the model of our mother, the Church, may she herself frequently look upon it amid the storms of the world; may she herself continually cherish it with prayer amid worldly assaults.

For there is no doubt that she who deserved to bear the price for the liberation of others can bestow assistance upon those who have been liberated. Meanwhile, let our unceasing prayer be directed to the Lord, so that he who, for the honor of his name, entered those entrails that he had sanctified—and which we too rightly venerate with constant devotion—may make beneficial for us, as a remedy, the price by which he gave himself to us through her.

### II

Rightly, therefore, the blessed Mary is raised up by our singular praise, since she offered the world a singular transaction. Rightly she rejoiced even among women when she carried in her chaste womb a singular remedy. She knew the burden of her belly, though she had not lost the modesty of chastity. She marveled at the signs of childbirth, though she had known no defilement by a man.

O wonderfully fruitful virginity, which by a new and unheard-of kind could be called both mother and virgin! She gave birth to the one whom she conceived; she carried the one by whom she herself had been created. For the author of Mary is himself the one born from Mary.

Thus, in an ineffably blessed way, Mary is both mother and virgin. While she brought forth the fruit of pregnancy, she suffered no loss of integrity. In her, heavenly providence so ordered the condition of this affair that she offered obedience to the command all the more because she recognized the honor bestowed upon her by the angel.

The messenger’s announcement did not undermine her faith, for she understood the dignity of the one announcing it, when the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35). She believed what she heard when instructed; once sanctified, she merited what she had believed.

Finally, she raised herself so high toward heaven’s summit that she received the Word who was in the beginning with God—that is, the Son of God—from the highest altar of heaven. When, through the mystical secret of divinity, he joined himself to our flesh and frailty, divinity lay hidden in the human being so that humanity might not perish through divinity. Concealed beneath the veil of assumed flesh, he redeemed the lost more precious­ly than if he had defended captives from an approaching enemy.

Immense is this piety, and a majesty to be proclaimed beyond what speech can express. The girl’s womb was filled by the breath of the Holy Spirit; the unmarried virgin’s womb swelled as the seed of the Word grew. I say that the hidden places of her womb were filled with the fruitfulness of the Holy Spirit, and there was hope in the birth because there had been no pleasure in intercourse.

The most precious mother was astonished, and in silence within herself marveled at the novelty of what had happened. She burned in the heat of thought from the fire, and, struck by the novelty of events, was wondrously amazed. Knowing her own integrity, happy Mary marveled at the abundance of her womb.

O glorious mother, O exalted mother in childbirth, in whose womb the author of heaven and earth is entrusted! Happy were the kisses impressed upon the lips of the nursing child, when, amid the frequent signs of creeping infancy, your true son played with you as a mother, while the true Lord from the Father commanded.

For in conceiving your Creator, you brought forth in time as a grown man him whom you had possessed before time as Creator. Blessed is the childbirth: joyful to the angels, awaited by the saints, necessary for the lost, fitting for the fallen. After many injuries inflicted upon his assumed flesh, he was finally scourged with whips, given gall to drink, and fastened to the cross. To show you to be a true mother and to demonstrate himself to be truly human, he revealed himself by suffering torments.

You, therefore, blessed and glorious Mary, are praiseworthy amid these things. You merited the gift of fruitfulness without losing the assistance of virginity. You are blessed among women. You are privileged above all the choirs of virgins. You follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

You invite the virginal choirs, estranged from the enticements of inciting flesh, through gleaming lilies and flowering roses, to the fountain of everlasting life. In that most blessed region of the blessed, you have attained the dignity of the first rank. You wander with dewy feet amid the delights of paradise and proceed on tender knees among the grassy choirs; with a happy palm you pluck unfading violets.

Joined to the angels who sing without end and associated with the archangels, you never cease to cry out with tireless voice: “Holy, holy, holy.”
