### III

But what can I say, poor in understanding, when whatever I say about you is certainly less than your dignity deserves? If I call you the mother of the nations, you surpass the name. If I call you the form of God, you are worthy of the title. If I call you the nurse of heavenly bread, you fill him with the sweetness of milk.

Nurse, therefore, mother, our food; nurse the food of angels; nurse the one who made you such that he himself might come to be in you. Conception brought you the gift of fruitfulness, and birth did not take away the honor of virginity. Before he was born, he made you the mother from whom he would be born, so that from there he might come forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, [Col. 0145A] so that he could be seen by mortal eyes.

What great condescension this was: that the one who created you should be created from you; that he should be carried by the hands he formed; that he should suck the breasts he himself filled!

What praises, then, shall we offer to God’s charity, and what thanks shall we give him? He loved us so greatly that for our sake he became human; that he chose the mother of a human being; that he entered the womb of our condition; that he endured the insults of a newborn infant and bore all the necessities of human life.

Therefore, giving thanks to our Creator as best we can, let us celebrate with joy the Assumption of the most glorious Mother of God. For it is right to serve her with the highest rejoicing, through whom the signs of virginity blossomed. She herself was a virgin before marriage, a virgin in marriage, a virgin while pregnant, a virgin in giving birth, and a virgin while nursing; and rightly she was called a mother, not through a husband.

For the almighty Son did not in any way take virginity away from the holy Mother by being born—the virginity he had chosen when he was to be born. Let virgins, therefore, rejoice: a virgin bore Christ. Let them think that nothing of what they vowed has been destroyed, because she remained a virgin after childbirth [Alt. reading: this passage is absent up to “she recognized”].

Let widows rejoice as they celebrate the virgin’s feast: Anna, a widow, recognized the virgin mother. Let married women rejoice as they attend the solemnities of the blessed mother: Elizabeth, a married woman, was greeted by the Virgin Mother of the Lord.

Let boys also rejoice who vow continence to the Child. He consecrated the integrity of childhood who brought fruitfulness to his mother without taking away her virginity.

To him be glory throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## EDITORIAL NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Its author is uncertain. Nor can the author be identified from this shorter composition; and even if it could, it does not seem worth the effort for anyone to investigate more diligently. The difference of style is so evident, as Erasmus says, that, whatever its author, it cannot be regarded as Jerome’s.

## LETTER XI. On Honoring Parents

### I

By subjecting children to the merits of their parents, almighty God gave succeeding generations the law of service in their duties, so that they would be compelled by divine command to do what piety ought to have urged them to do. For he says in the Book of Exodus, where it is written: “Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. XX, 12).

Listen, children, to this saving command, and fulfill the precepts of the law with the affection of due love. Serve your fathers, you who will yourselves be fathers; and love your mothers with tender devotion, so that your wives too may deserve to be called mothers.

Let no one wound his father with harsh words; let sweetness not become bitterness. Between parents and children let there be what nature has preserved at the Lord’s command. Let whatever the tongues of children say express affection. Among beloved and closely related persons, let the rights of devotion be preserved. Let children’s mouths say what their parents are pleased to hear.

Let fear mingled with love be shown to fathers, who were the first cause of our birth. Children, offer your fathers what the power of the paternal name compels you to offer; it has been attributed to their merits to such an extent that it demands from you what nature could not command.

Show mothers the reverence they deserve. Serving you through the labor of the womb, they bear the weight of your body and, carrying an unknown infant, render a kind of service to the child about to be born.

At that time a mother does not hunger only for herself, nor does she digest alone the food she has taken. The one hidden within her is nourished by maternal food, and his limbs are fed by another’s consumption, so that the future human being may be filled through another’s bites.

Why should I mention the nourishment itself, and the sweet hardships of tender infancy, which the affection of a nurse endures for her little ones? Why mention the food prepared within the mother, which, flowing from female limbs, is dissolved into milk and bathes weak throats with liquid sweetness?

[Col. 0146B] Compelled by nature, infants take from their mother what they drink; with teeth not yet born, they draw forth with flowing lips what they do not need to bite. Maternal breasts serve their descendants; they serve the very cradles. Hands and backs devoted to the limbs of nursing children receive their grateful bodies.

A mother longs for the little one to grow; she longs soon to see him become older and hastens to place him among the ranks of young men, though he may perhaps never serve her. After so many and such great prior deeds, parents and mother deserve to be served with complete eagerness.

Let what is owed to nature be repaid; let what is owed to posterity also be repaid. Pay what you owe, son, and render your due services in whatever form of service you can, for no one can repay parents what is owed to them.

Humility offered to such persons extends the time of life; by delaying death, it greatly prolongs our life, and in return for the services performed it commends our duties, at the Lord’s command. He loves the name of parents so greatly that he commanded himself to be called Father.

### II

What an irreverent son deserves from the Lord himself is attested by Solomon’s words: “He who insults his father and despises his mother’s old age will be confounded and held in disgrace. The son who abandons his father’s discipline will meditate words of wickedness. The light of him who curses father or mother will be extinguished, and the pupils of his eyes will see darkness” (Prov. XIX).

Listen, son, to the father who begot you, and do not despise your mother because she has grown old. Let the tongue obey the father who begot it, and let no one strike his mother with a cruel word. Do not let the authority of youthful age carry you away, son, but know from whom you were born.

Remember the judgment of Scripture [Ambrosian manuscript: “of holy Scripture”], where, with the Holy Spirit speaking, it is said: “Whoever curses his father or mother shall be put to death” (Lev. XX, 9).

Remember, therefore, that you are what you are because of your parents, whose hands supplied your nourishment. Your throat has not yet lost the taste of milk with which your devoted mother nourished you, pouring it into you and feeding that tongue with the drink of her body.

Render due service to father and mother, who, never recoiling from your dreadful cries, covered your entire body with kisses. Let their well-being be dear to you, since your life is dearer to them than their own. Repay the debt of love with reverent devotion. Repay by your own services what your parents did for the benefit of your cradle.

Parents ought to be considered sweeter for this reason: they cannot be replaced by others. When the law of nature has taken them away, you will be able to find neither another father nor another mother. Once a marriage has changed, a stepfather is not a father, nor can a stepmother fulfill the name of mother.

Therefore let no child strike with insults the author of his own light. Let no one wish adversity upon parents who place their children before their own safety [Ambrosian manuscript: “their own resentments”]. It is an intolerable crime to hear a rude word from that mouth, or to be struck by those hands which love cherishes [two manuscripts: “which love softens”].

Fear the judgment concerning your eyes that the Lord promised to the ungrateful. For he deserves to suffer the penalty of blindness who has looked upon his parents’ faces with a grim gaze and injured filial devotion by raising his eyes against them.

If you have any understanding, children, look upon those venerable faces with the same affection with which they themselves look upon you; cling with sweet kisses to their lips, because you still bear their kisses in your limbs.

It is very easy to serve the old, whom no one feeds by drinking, and no one nourishes with the juice of his own body. Let your parents’ old age therefore be cherished, and let repayment be made for their deeds through your own deeds. Old age has a kind of infancy. Let your children see what they should do, since they will repay you with a similar return.

Imitate the son of the Maccabees, who served his mother when she urged him toward death and willingly undertook the harsh command, lest he offend his mother (II Macc. VII, 20–23). He preferred to join his brothers in death rather than resist his mother’s will.

Thus his mother’s urging was fulfilled in such a way that it made her son a martyr for God and a sharer in his brothers’ crowns. Finally, proving his obedience better by death, he fulfilled his mother’s exhortation; despising this light by dying, he became a companion of the martyrs, so that that brotherhood might be established in an eternal fellowship.

Behold what a mind subject to its mother accomplished. The devoted son was advanced through obedience. Unwilling in any way to injure his mother’s devotion, he accepted everlasting life through suffering. By confessing the Lord, he deserved to be crowned by the Lord with his brothers before the angels.

## EDITORIAL NOTE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

A thoroughly learned and worthy little work, but one which, even apart from anything else, is clearly not Jerome’s from the difference of style. The author also reveals himself as belonging to a later period because he borrows several things from Isidore of Seville, who flourished at the beginning of the seventh century.

Among these are the passages that he reported to the doorkeepers from Book VII, chapter 12, of the *Etymologies*, in almost exactly the same words: “For they, holding the key, guard everything inside and outside; and, exercising judgment between good and evil, they receive the faithful and reject the unfaithful.” Then there are the words concerning the fifth rank, namely the deacons: “As consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of ministry belongs to the deacon.”

Indeed, the possibility that Isidore took these things from our author, though it could easily be proposed as an objection, does not have much appearance of truth. I am readily led to believe, however, that our author lived not long after him—perhaps toward the end of the seventh century or finally in the eighth.

And certainly Hincmar of Reims, who wrote in the following century, not only praises this letter but also regards it as Jerome’s. From this one may infer that the reputation of its writings had already prevailed for a long time. The author of the *Micrologus* also praises it, as do others in subsequent periods.

According to Erasmus, the title varies in manuscript copies. In some it is addressed to Damasus, in others to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, and in some it bears no name. Furthermore, in certain codices it is complete, while in others it is mutilated.

Finally, it is not likely that the holy Jerome, if he had written so substantial a book on so important a subject, would not have cited it somewhere, since he so frequently cites works much shorter and dealing with less weighty topics.

## LETTER XII, OR LITTLE WORK ON THE SEVEN ORDERS OF THE CHURCH
I judge that your holy way of life, which you have in Christ Jesus, is sufficient to open for you the narrow and confined way of understanding that leads to the dignity of the priestly order, since, distinguished by preceding merits and virtues, you have been chosen by God for this office. Although in many cases the grace of Christ is proved without works, and when the merit of one’s way of life ceases, the gifts of God alone bear fruit, nevertheless, because you have been shown to have been chosen by God above others for this purpose—you who both fulfill the works of the Law and remain in grace unto the surpassing charity of knowledge, with the understanding of God speaking with you, your notable thoughts hastening forward—you wish to know what you have become.

I shall disclose to you, as you request, the mysteries of the whole Church, preserving the order and place of its teaching, and teaching what you must observe and in what manner, provided that you do not turn the diligence of a youthful exhorter into an insult, and are not ashamed to be for a little while the lesser while you learn. For, as you see, once the privilege of dignity has been set aside, you have more to ask of us. And what you think you obtained long ago in consecration remains for you to grasp, lest you be found lesser in Christ [Col. 0148B] than meanwhile you are called in the world, and become a useless shepherd of a false title because you did not know these mysteries that lie hidden in the Lord.

Yet, maintaining reason in every discussion and speaking with you simply, we shall show that you ought truly to be a bishop of souls. Thus, having made yourself your own judge, hastening to fulfill what we say and agreeing with us, cast away shame and embarrassment, and choose to be rejected in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.

For Jesus says:

> “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called lords; but you must not be so. Rather, let the greater among you become like the lesser, and the leader like the servant. For who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Among the Gentiles, surely, the one who reclines is greater; but among you it must not be so. Rather, the one who serves. I am among you as one who serves. And because you have remained with me in my trials, I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22:25ff.).

And elsewhere:

> “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be like one of them.”

And elsewhere:

> “Not as one who lords it over the clergy, but as an example to everyone” (1 Peter 5:3).

And elsewhere:

> “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3:16ff.).

Since from him, through him, and in him are all things, to him be glory forever [Col. 0148D]—for our God is one, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom are all things and we exist in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we exist through him (Romans 11:36; 1 Corinthians 8:6).

But knowledge is not present in everyone. For a partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved. Therefore God enclosed all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all (Romans 11:25–32).

Above all, love humility, because pride causes apostasy from God, and pride is the beginning of every sin. For our God, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).

Review all the Scriptures in your mind; read the entire Canon. Keeping the examples of the saints before your eyes, imitate what is good and emulate what is holy. [Col. 0149B] Having become a heavenly Jerusalem for yourself, restore your vows to God. Build within yourself a house and a temple of Solomon; construct the tabernacle and hasten to adorn it more diligently. Enter the Holy of Holies, kindle an unfailing light, and maintain perfection in everything.

Set a guard over your mouth and a door of restraint around your lips. Do not expose your soul to temptation, and let him who guards you not fall asleep. Raise your voice and say:

> “All flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40:6–8).

For the priest of the Lord who brings forth righteousness from his mouth and announces truth to those who seek it is an angel of almighty God.

In every case preserve justice. Do not send away the traveler, the orphan, the widow, the poor, or the little child [Col. 0149C] empty-handed. Store your treasure where your heart also is. Keep peace with all your brothers, as it is written.

Flee the counsels of the wicked, lest, while judging, you be condemned. For it is written:

> “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. But his delight was in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Psalm 1:1–2).

Receive the attentions of the powerful, the acquaintance of the rich, and the services of those who greet you in such a way that you do not sadden the poor or impose upon anyone the weariness of an excuse. Let the book of the Law, as it is written, not depart from your hand, but meditate on it day and night. For it is written:

> “Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the Church of God, just as I also please everyone in every way, not seeking what is useful for myself but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10:32–33).

Before you hear, judge no one; and before the accusation brought against someone has been proved, suspend no one from your communion. For the one accused is not immediately guilty, but the one convicted is criminal. Nor should the injury of innocent brothers be permitted to prevail because of the hatred of individuals. Rather, the fear of the Lord must always be kept before your eyes, and you must know that everything done is owed to God and Christ, not to the present age. For the outward form of this world is passing away, and it is right to obey God rather than human beings, since he knows the past and judges concerning the future.

For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying:

> “Whatever you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Matthew 7:12).

At home, if possible, setting aside concern for your own person and respect for your office, it is fitting for you to be a servant to servants, and thus to teach Israel in all things, so that all who hear you may advance more by your conduct than by your speech. For it is written:

> “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside” (Colossians 4:1).

Let the greeting of many not exalt you. Let the gifts and attentions of the rich not overcome you, because gifts, as it is written, blind the eyes of judges. Let a noble and wealthy matron not have greater standing with you than a poor woman who has professed poverty and begs, nor let a widow deprived of her husband’s support appear equal to one who has a powerful husband in this world.

Judge that you must make yourself impartial toward everyone. Do not defend the poor improperly because of injustice in judgment, nor stand indecently beside the rich because of favor. Or, if you cannot do this, reject the hearing of cases. Be content for yourself with reading and prayer alone. For, as it is written, God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom and harms no one (Ecclesiasticus 4:13).

If you do these things, having been proved useful to God in everything, you will retain perfect priesthood in yourself [Al.: “priesthood” is omitted]. Drive out from the temple of Christ those who sell sheep, oxen, and doves, and overturn the tables of the money-changers, because the house of our Father must not be a house of commerce but of prayer. And what is cast out by the judgment of God ought not to be desired because of the sentence of condemnation, lest we be found reprobate in Christ.

Thus it will come about that, standing in the truth, you may be worthy to know the mystery of the sevenfold Church, which consists, together with its veneration, in the omnipotence of God: that is, in the Father, in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit; in archangels, in angels, in wisdom, and in human beings. If you carefully consider all these things, you will recognize in them the foundations of the entire ordering of the Catholic Church. And through these degrees, if you observe everything that has been written, God will be in your memory, and you will return to your own house.

## I. On the first degree of the Church, which is the order of the gravediggers

The first order among the clergy is that of the gravediggers. Following the likeness of the holy Tobias, they are admonished to bury the dead, so that, while caring for visible things, they may hasten toward invisible ones; and, believing in the resurrection of the flesh in the Lord, they may know that everything they do they perform for God, not for the dead.

It is therefore fitting that the gravediggers of the Church be such as the prophet Tobias was: like him in faith, holiness, knowledge, and virtue. Do not therefore think that the office of gravediggers is insignificant, nor, like the other priests, despise the mystery in the servants of God. Do not show more respect to the servants of various people or to friends than to Christ in the temple, when you offer prayers and honor his members. You ought to share with everyone, not only at the altar but also at home: you ought to dine with everyone and sit simply among your household walls.

If you love the prophet Tobias and imitate his example, if you fulfill what is written, “The one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10:41), beware lest your pride inflict any injury upon this office [Col. 0150D], an injury that a layman, who is lesser than Tobias, would not tolerate.

You ought to exercise judgment concerning the members of God in such a way that you understand the mystery of the Church. For what is called episcopacy is a matter of religion and holiness, not of Roman consulship or legal authority. If you wish to be what you have become, preserve your order and guard your place. Show reverence to the prophet, so that the prophet may serve you. Love the mysteries of God, so that you may be loved by Christ.

Do not unlawfully sadden anyone, nor pursue anyone with unjust hatred, because just as you belong to Christ, so do they belong to Christ; and no one is powerful in this world who would wish one of his servants to be trampled by others.

You yourself, too, if you willingly accept what I am about to say, show honor to all servants because of those whom they serve, and venerate each person according to the power of his master [Col. 0151B]. Tell me, I ask: who is greater than Christ? Or to whom do you owe as much as to him who shed his blood for you, who placed you over his Church, who honored you in all things, and who entrusted to you all the divine mysteries?

Does your Lord God deserve that, after doing these things because of his goodness and mercy, you should debase your fellow servants, dishonor Christ, and think that no one but yourself belongs to the Lord? Do you think that reverence is owed only to you, and that the servants of Christ entrusted to you in their way of life should be treated not as free people in their ministry but as slaves whom you possess in domination?

God condemns these things above all, and bears nothing more grievously than that, while you know that honor must be shown to human beings, you yourself show no honor to God. You would not dare to persecute or harass a servant of a ruler assigned to his army, yet you think that those who are truly servants of God, marked with the true sign of Christ, made free by the grace of baptism, and serving as soldiers through the office of the clergy, should be consigned to rejection and disgrace. Thus, if our correction does not do an injury, you sometimes spare servants more in your conscience than clerics; you love one of them as a native servant, despise the others as foreigners, and prefer to please the world rather than Christ.

For the sake of faith, religion, and the purpose of holiness, a cleric is sometimes compelled to show deference to a servant; and, because he cannot bear the disgrace, the one who is supreme in heaven is judged worthless in the world.

You reject these things rightly, and rightly do not preserve them, if you do not wish to be a bishop, if you despise the kingdoms of heaven, and if you desire to have no fellowship with God. But if you rejoice that you have been chosen by God, if you recognize that you have been made shepherd of the flock and created a priest for the clergy, you must labor lest your own members displease you, lest what belongs to Christ be rejected.

For the Apostle says:

> “Can the head say to the feet, ‘I do not need your work’? For there is one body and there are many members” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

If you are the head, the services of the feet are necessary to you. You yourself recognize that the feet belong to your honor and to the substance of the body. Without them, as you yourself know, you cannot walk. They support you; they move the whole body forward; they direct the head; they make you first. If you destroy them, you will be despised by all the faithful [Col. 0152A], and, having become hateful even to yourself, you will spend an embittered life in this world.

## II. On the second degree of the Church, which is the order of the doorkeepers

The second place is that of the doorkeepers, who hold the keys of the kingdom of heaven, which are given to the patriarchs, because they preside over the gates of Jerusalem. Having judgment between good and evil, they open what no one shuts and shut what no one opens.

Here you ought to consider what diligence must be exercised concerning the doorkeepers of God, and how much reverence you must show toward these members and offices. You cannot enter the temple except through them. For they are appointed in their respective turns to guard everything inside and outside, and, perfect in all things, to receive the faithful and reject the unfaithful.

## III. On the third degree of the Church, which is the order of readers

The third order is that of the readers, which is assigned to God, Christ, and the prophets, according to what is written:

> “Raise your voice and say: All flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40:6–8).

Finally, when our Lord read in the temple, he assumed the form of a reader.

These, then, are the readers who sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. These are the ones who follow the immaculate Lamb wherever he goes, who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins (Revelation 14–15). Their number is that of the angels, and through these offices of holiness they are altogether your equals. And the name “angel” is appropriately applied to the priest, as Scripture says:

> “The priest who brings forth righteousness from his mouth and announces truth to those who seek it is an angel of almighty God” (Malachi 2:1).

## IV. On the fourth degree of the Church, which is the order of subdeacons

The fourth order in the ecclesiastical arrangement is that of the subdeacon. In Ezra they are called Nathinnei, serving the Lord in humility.

For this reason our Lord says to Nathanael in the Gospel of John:

> “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.”
>
> Nathanael answered him, “Master, how do you know me?”
>
> Jesus said, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:47–48).

This was written so that you might recognize his place and arrangement.

For this reason our Lord, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore we are always commanded to pray with bent knee [Col. 0152D]. For “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:14).

For this reason Egypt is struck by fitting plagues from the Lord. This day of departure from Egypt is called the Lord’s Passover, so that, because Christ our Passover was sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), you may recognize the fullness of the entire mystery and sacrament in the offices of these things, and, without intolerable arrogance, not despise those who either receive offerings in the temple of God or, as witnesses of all the sacred mysteries, are also sharers in the sufferings, and so forth.

For these are the first to receive our desires; they test in us our best intentions; they reject the evil ones; they stand ready so that we may be received by God. Just as you recognize their ministries as visibly present, so also consider that their peace and concord are invisibly beneficial, lest you thereafter be unable to offer the body and blood of Christ if, when you come to the altar of God, you have neglected the members of the Church.

## V. On the fifth degree of the Church, which is the order of Levites or deacons

The fifth order is the sacramental order of the deacons. God is their portion. They are forbidden to withdraw from the temple of the Lord day or night. They are the pillar and foundation of truth; they support the Churches of God; they are the altar of Christ, on which the sacraments are accomplished and on which the offering is made.

What, then, as you yourself know, can be more venerable in the temple of God than the altar? Who would not humble himself as he approaches the Lord’s table?

These are the ones whom we read of in the Apocalypse as the seven angels of the Churches (Revelation 1:20). These are the seven golden lampstands [Col. 0153B]; these are the voices of the thunders; these are, in the likeness of Noah, heralds of the righteousness of the sacraments, having neither stain nor wrinkle. Made radiant with the brightness of light, they are able to behold God in all Israel: pure in mind, bright in soul, distinguished by the practice of virtues, endowed with humility, quiet, humble, evangelizing peace, announcing good things, cutting away dissensions, quarrels, and scandals, speaking with God alone, thinking of nothing worldly at all in the temple; saying to father and mother, “We do not know you,” and not recognizing their own sons.

Moreover, Levi, as we read in Scripture, is the priestly tribe and the head of all priests. Without him the priest has neither name, nor origin, nor office. He is called the minister of God, because it is written:

> “Who is greater, the one who serves or the one who is served?” (Deuteronomy 10:8ff.).

As consecration is found in the priest, so the administration of the sacrament is found in the minister. The priest is commanded to pray; the deacon to sing psalms. The former sanctifies what has been offered; the latter distributes what has been sanctified.

Even the priests themselves, because of presumptuousness, are not permitted to take the chalice from the Lord’s table unless it has been handed to them by the deacon. Thus, with the ministry of holiness preceding, the priest is humbled for a little while after the consecration; while showing reverence to the minister, he recognizes how much reverence he owes to the ministry of God. For our almighty God has arranged all things in such a way that the one who believes himself greater is lesser, and the one who appeared lesser becomes greater.

Finally, consider for yourself how true this is. The Levites bring the offerings to the altar. The Levites arrange the Lord’s table. The Levites stand with the priests while the sacraments are blessed. The Levites pray before the priests, so that, if distinction of places is acknowledged in the world, the bishops may see at God’s altar that, if they are proud, the deacons are placed before them. If they love humility, let them recognize that they are greater in the very thing in which they are humble.

Then, so that we may have ears for the Lord, the deacon cries out; he preaches, exhorts, and admonishes, with the priests standing by. Do not lightly regard or carelessly observe this voice that speaks and announces peace, nor think it worthy of condemnation.

It is enough that this order has been granted so much by the Lord: that the priest alone should not appear to do and fulfill everything in the temple. The priest needs the office of the deacon, just as the deacon needs that of the priest. Neither can the rich exist without the poor, nor the poor without the rich.

After the consecration of all the sacraments, after the prayers, after the recitation of the names, after all the mysteries of the Godhead, perfection is again given to the Levites at the altar. As I said above, the deacon hands over the chalice: he is a witness of the Passion, a witness of administration, a witness of humility, so that the one who offered it, lifted up in pride, may recognize that he should expect nothing from the deacon.

Therefore the Levite is perfected in consecration and is no longer blessed like a layman, because he is commanded to possess in himself the perfect holiness of the Lord.

Finally, from all the tribes, in the Book of Joshua, the Levites receive cities (Joshua 21), so that you may understand that there is no class of human beings, no land, no place, and no nation that is not commanded to serve him because of the Lord.

But the priests receive tithes of tithes from the Levites; they are commanded not to give these to them but to receive them. Now, ever since avarice grew in the Churches as it did in the Roman Empire, the law has perished from the priest and the vision from the prophet.

Each individual, according to the power of the episcopal name that he has unlawfully claimed for himself without the Church, turns everything belonging to the Levites to his own uses. He does not claim for himself what is written, but takes everything away from everyone.

The wretched cleric begs in the streets, bound to civic labor, and publicly begs subsistence from anyone at all. And indeed the priestly office is despised by everyone because, abandoned by mercy, he is rightly thought to have fallen into this disgrace.

The presbyter is needy in his seat, the Levite at the altar, the subdeacon in the sacristy, the reader at the reading, the doorkeeper in the temple, and the gravedigger at the burial. Those who are commanded to bury others die of hunger; those who are ordered to show mercy ask for mercy themselves.

And while these things are happening, the priest who has not done this is condemned. He alone lies upon riches; he alone uses the ministry; he alone claims everything for himself; he alone invades the portions of others; he alone destroys everyone.

For if we did everything according to the divine books, nothing visible could be lacking to anyone, and holiness alone would abound in the Church of Christ.

From this, because of the avarice of priests, hatred arises; from this, bishops are accused by clerics; from this, the quarrels of rulers; from this, the causes of desolation; from this, the origin of crime.

For if each person, although commanded to possess this world visibly, were content with his own possession and did not invade the property of another—if he did not take away a poor man’s field, vineyard, anything belonging to his subjects, servants, or produce—how much more must the one who presides over the Church of God preserve justice in all things, claiming for himself only what he knows to be his by right?

Let him not touch what belongs to another; let him not seize what belongs to another; let him make himself equal to the rest. And just as he did not exist in the Church without them, so let him not live without them in the administration of the Church’s ministry.

Certainly, as you yourself know, the one who visibly invades another’s right in this world is accused by the poor and condemned by the judge. So also in the Church of God, when each person loses his allotted support, he cries out to God and is heard by Christ; and the sentence of vengeance is not delayed in this matter if everything is not restored.

For God’s patience seeks prayers and only our return, and by his goodness seeks to save us. But if we do not turn back, if we are hard of heart, if we persist unlawfully in sins unto death, then, as it is written, “God does not have mercy on one who sins continually.”

## VI. On the sixth degree of the Church, which is the order of priests

The sixth is the order of elders, which is given to priests, who are called presbyters. They preside over the Church of God and accomplish the sacraments of Christ.

In blessing, they share the ministries with bishops. No difference is to be believed to exist between them and bishops in the accomplishment of the body and blood of Christ. If circumstances require it, bishops ought to receive the Eucharist previously blessed by presbyters and recognize that they share in Christ and in his fullness.

For if anyone treats this as an insult or thinks that he ought not to receive the Eucharist blessed by a presbyter, he is certainly perverse, believing that the Lord had two bodies: one greater and one lesser—the greater one accomplished by the bishop, the lesser by the presbyter. Such a person divides Christ and does him injury.

Can there, then, be a difference between one baptism and another, so that the one baptized by a bishop is judged holier than the one baptized by a Levite? As you read in the Acts of the Apostles, the eunuch was baptized by Philip the deacon, as it is written:

> “Behold, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?”
>
> And he said, “Nothing, if you believe” (Acts 8:5–6).

For faith is what makes clean, and because it is not the giver but the recipient that makes the difference, it must be believed that baptism is perfect in every soul and that the body of Christ is perfect in every priest.

The one who does not share in the Eucharist of presbyters does not share in Christ; nor does he himself bless the Eucharist, because in the very matter in which he judges, he is condemned. Like Judas the betrayer, handing over the Lord, he brings his own hands upon himself without being compelled and perishes by hanging, because through pride he sins against God.

Nor do I say that, when bishops are present and stand at the altar, presbyters can accomplish the sacraments. But if circumstances should require it—for example, if priests arrive at the church at the very hours when the offering has either not been prepared or cannot be offered—the bishop ought not to reject the Eucharist of presbyters if it is placed upon the altar. It ought to be received because of Christ, since it is the body of Christ, as it is written:

> “You are the body of Christ and members in part. Love covers a multitude of sins. Faith, hope, and love—these three; but the greatest of these is love. Love is patient, love is kind; it does not envy, it is not puffed up, it does not act wrongly. It believes all things and endures all things. Love never fails” (1 Corinthians 12:27; 13:13, 4ff.).

And because it is written, “Let presbyters be honored with double honor, especially those who labor in the word of the Lord” (1 Timothy 5:17), it is fitting for them to preach; it is beneficial for them to bless; it is appropriate for them to confirm; it is proper for them to restore communion; it is necessary for them to visit the sick, [Col. 0156A] to pray for the weak, and to complete all the sacraments of God—especially since it is clear that this custom existed in the East, in Illyricum, in Italy, and in Africa, everywhere, in the times of the apostles.

Only the ordination of clerics and the consecration of virgins should be reserved to the chief priest because of his authority, together with the dedication or sanctification of basilicas, altars, and chrism, lest, if the discipline of the Church were claimed by many, it should dissolve the concord of priests and generate scandals.

For this reason, recently the election of a bishop was also referred to the metropolitan. When supreme power is given to one, this faculty is taken away from others, and even the chief priests begin to suffer the appointment of another priest—not by right but by necessity.

Let no bishop, swollen with the devil’s temptation of envy, grow angry in the temple if presbyters sometimes exhort the people, preach in the churches, and bless the congregations, as it is written.

To one who rejects these things I shall say: if he does not want presbyters to do what God commands, let him say, “Who is greater than Christ?” Or what can be placed before his body or his blood? If a presbyter consecrates Christ when he blesses the sacraments at God’s altar, ought he not to bless the people, when he has even been deemed worthy to consecrate Christ?

As for the virgins of God, although the Apostle says, “I have no command of the Lord concerning virgins” (1 Corinthians 7:25), nevertheless, when reason requires it, if circumstances demand, it is clear that they may be blessed by him, if necessary. For Mary, the mother of the Lord Christ, is the sister of virgins; and the Eucharist is Christ’s body, while Mary is less than the Lord. Yet one must trust the judgment of the chief priest and do what he orders concerning laymen and women.

When you priests unjustly command these things, the priest of God does not rightly lose the office of blessing; he loses the work of his tongue and has no confidence to preach. He is mutilated in every aspect of virtue. He has only the name of presbyter and does not retain the fullness and perfection proper to his consecration.

What honor is this of yours, I ask, O priests, that you inflict losses upon the flocks? For when, through your power, proper care is taken away from the shepherds, a kind of contagion and calamity grows among the flocks; and complain to our God of losses to his patrimony, while you alone wish to exercise power in the Churches.

Finally, the matter of chrism follows the same principle. The proper order of consecration is this: it is evident that the Lord was baptized and anointed by the Father in the likeness of a dove, in the form of chrism, and that the fullness of the sacrament—his body and blood—was shown. Since it is permissible to offer these, it is also permissible to consecrate the remaining things that are in him, because in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

Therefore presbyters, if necessary, can make chrism, because chrism is in his body. Indeed, this rule is still observed by many, and they do these things in many churches. Nevertheless, know that this is my opinion: no injury is to be done to any bishop concerning this, nor am I to impose a law upon one who is himself the law of the presbyter.

From the beginning, as we read, presbyters were commanded to be judges in cases and to take part in the council of priests. For presbyters themselves, as we read, are also called bishops, according to what is written to Titus:

> “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you” (Titus 1:5), and so forth.

You see, then, that a presbyter is called a bishop, and that this is the judgment of the Apostle Paul. Elsewhere, writing to Timothy concerning the order of the Church, he says:

> “It is necessary for a bishop to be blameless” (1 Timothy 3:2), and so forth.

You see, then, that no mention of a presbyter is made here, but that this is the position he calls the episcopate. Elsewhere, writing to Timothy the bishop, he says:

> “Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in chastity” (1 Timothy 4:11–12), and so forth.

Do you understand, then, that the fullness of the priesthood is placed in the presbyter?

And elsewhere he says to the elders:

> “He has appointed you bishops to govern his Church at Philippi” (Acts 20:28).

Certainly, Philippi is one city of Macedonia. And when Paul wrote there to bishops and deacons, whom could he be calling bishops except those presbyters who preside?

Finally, the Apostle John, a bishop, also writes:

> “The elder to the chosen lady whom I love in truth” (2 John 1).

For “presbyter” is the name of age, while “bishop” is the name of dignity. Solomon also says, “Humble your soul to a presbyter.”

But proud priests hate the name “presbyter” in presbyters. They do not wish to be what Christ was: the one who washed the disciples’ feet, who was baptized by John, although John proclaimed that he himself ought to be baptized by the Lord.

For this reason I write these things: if the error of the past cannot now be recalled, at least let humility be preserved in the churches at present, so that presbyters may do in their churches what is done in Rome, in the East, in Italy, in Crete, in Cyprus, in Africa, in Illyricum, in Spain, in Britain, and even in part of Gaul—what is done in all places where humility endures; what is done in heaven—which is greater—where you read that their seats have been arranged. Thus you may despise earthly things and claim nothing for yourself from the conduct of this world.

Look to Jerusalem, the mother of all the saints, adorned with patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and the angels of God. Follow her custom; preserve her mysteries. Let nothing be common to you [Col. 0157D] with those who defend their error by unlawful presumption and say that what is a matter of personal vow is merely a matter of custom.

For if any one of us could recognize the custom of former times, I would prove to you that what I am saying was always preserved in the churches from the beginning, when the apostles were preaching, and that afterward some practices were corrupted through hatred of individuals and others were assumed presumptuously.

But no one is to be condemned, no one judged. Rather, everyone is to be embraced in the gentleness and love of the Spirit [Mart.: “Spirit” is omitted], so that, while they come to know with us the foundations of Christ’s goodness, they may come of their own will to the building of God and be worthy to remain with us at the summit of the temple.

[Col. 0158A] **VII. On the seventh and principal rank of the Church, which is the episcopal order, or that of bishops**

The seventh among these arrangements is the episcopal order; and he who is first and perfect in all things, who is given by the omnipotence of God and in Christ, is the source of all glory and the fullness of virtues, from whom are all things and in whom are all things. For he ordains priests, he ordains Levites, he ordains subdeacons, he ordains readers, he ordains doorkeepers, he ordains gravediggers; holding the reed, he measures Jerusalem; he presides over God’s structure; he shows what each person ought to do; he condemns, he receives, he binds, he releases those who are bound; he possesses the keys of the kingdom of heaven; he opens and closes the throne of God, having nothing above himself.

If he is humble and good, if he is perfect, as it is written, “Be perfect, just as your Father [Col. 0158B] is perfect” (Matt. V, 40); if he observes everything; if he is hospitable; if he is without blame; if he has a good reputation; if he is the husband of one wife—that is, content with his own flesh alone and not seeking the allurements of another’s body; if he has children subject to him in chastity and sobriety—for he ought not to sin in his conduct who is perfect in his election.

His priestly garment is the perfect glory of God. The chrism belongs to him, because he himself is the Christ of Christians—that is, the holy of holies—and the bishop of souls, according to what is written: “Do not touch my christs, and do not malign my prophets” (Ps. 104:15). The highest reverence must be offered to him by all the clergy and by all the people, because the creature does not say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me thus?” Or, “Does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:21).

For the sake of perfection, he is commanded not to think about tomorrow. He is forbidden to be anxious about clothing and food. In all things he is like God, if he does not depart from Christ, according to what is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). While walking in the flesh, he does not wage war according to the flesh. He wishes to be with Jesus alone. He condemns no one; even Judas, knowing what sort of man he was in the Passion, he treats peaceably. He gives a kiss to the one by whom he is betrayed. He suffers for all; he saves everyone.

I can say nothing further about this office, since it is clear that the bishop alone possesses what you previously declared to be consecrated in the clergy. In the others there are parts and members of the virtues; in the bishop the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Thus you are to recognize the Lord in the bishop, and the apostles—who are themselves apostles—in the presbyters. But because it is written, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16), the one who chooses is called the high priest, while those who are chosen are priests.

For God gave all his authority to his disciples, and he wished Moses to be called the god of Pharaoh. And Jesus Christ himself was greater in that in which he appeared in the flesh. This is the mystery of the Church that Ezra described, arranged in five ranks and held by the understanding of our head.

To sight are assigned the presbyteries of the episcopate, according to what is written: “I have appointed you as a watchman over the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17). To smell are assigned the Levites, because, joined to the priests, they are the column and foundation of truth; they are the form of the spirit, and to pure minds they are the odor of life unto life; through all of them the fragrance of sacrifice rises before God.

To hearing are assigned the Nethinim, so that all may hear the divine words and the commands of the priests and the services of the Levites. To speech, which is the tongue, are assigned the sacred singers. To the mouth are assigned the doorkeepers or gravediggers, as it is written: “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140:3).

For by our words we shall be justified, and by our words we shall be condemned. In the mouth of a human being are life and death. Therefore, among the gravediggers the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets; among the doorkeepers are the teachers; among the readers, the prophets; among the subdeacons, the angels; among the deacons, [Col. 0159B] the archangels; among the presbyters, the apostles; among the bishops, God.

Finally, it is written: “First, apostles; second, prophets; third, teachers” (1 Cor. 12:28). Therefore, from the bishop down to the deacon there is an arrangement of the spirit; from the subdeacons down to the doorkeepers, of the soul; and among the gravediggers, of the body.

Thus understand all these arrangements in the Church of Christ as one human being serving God, according to what is written: “You are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in you. If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are” (Ibid. III, 16; VII, 18).

Preach the word of God to everyone, as it is written: “Exhort all; command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17), but to be rich in good works. Let no one despise your youth. Let the book of the law not depart from your hand, but meditate on it day and night (Josh. 1:8).

Above all, care for the poor, because for our sake Christ became poor although he was rich, so that by his poverty we might be enriched. Seek out women who have made profession and those who are truly widows; supply what is necessary to the needy; and do not shrink in any way from the name of pilgrimage. For as long as we are in the flesh, we are away from the Lord.

Avoid younger widows; for when they have grown wanton, they wish to marry in Christ (1 Tim. 5:11). Because of the ancient custom and the danger of the priesthood, do not give your soul into the power of your wife, lest perhaps, placed in paradise like Adam, you be put to shame and, if you sin, lose the law you received; and, conscious of your nakedness, receive confusion of mind and lose the place of consecration.

Your wife is indeed to be loved, but as the Church or the temple of God: you are to pray with her, read with her, abstain with her, and communicate with her at the altar, not in the marital act; you are to live by the spirit, not by the flesh. She ought to venerate you because of the bond of the law, not desire you because of the customary indulgence in sin, since you clearly understand that the use of marriage has been forbidden to you when you recognize that you are a bishop.

Let her rejoice that through this she has Christ, not a husband; that she is with God, not dwelling with a spouse; that within the walls of her household she possesses a domestic holiness. Let her rejoice in the Lord and give thanks to God, because she has been freed from corruption. She should also regard herself as indebted to you, because you hastened to this office; because, with her consent, you were chosen by the Lord; because you settled everything with your family beforehand, as was proper, before accepting the episcopate when asked; and because, separated from your spouse, you remained in the Church.

I am confident that, following your example of good conduct, all will do these things: that, believing in God during their youth, while they despise earthly things they may receive heavenly ones; that, corrected, they may be consecrated to the Lord in all things; and that, having become teachers of the peoples, they may preach to everyone after correcting themselves and be called the salvation of all.

Do not take secular men into the ministry of the Church. Thus the law says: “You must lay hands hastily on no one.” And again: “Let these first be tested, and then let them serve, established as blameless” (1 Tim. 5:22; 3:10). For there are many who, following the wishes of the people, do not observe the discipline of the Church and, without testing their good conduct, choose men who have not been converted.

And, to criticize the custom: they bless sinners for their nobility rather than for their excellent morals, and entrust them with the governance of the heavenly kingdom before they are secure in their earthly conduct—as though God lacked priests, or one who has not yet learned to be chaste through abstinence could fulfill the office of the clergy.

I say nothing of the other lessons of life: that he does not know the books, that he does not know the custom; and that he is called a teacher of the nations or a minister before learning anything, living henceforth by another’s judgment, doing the will in everything not of God but of whomever he happens to serve. He owes obedience to God, who instructs him; he yields for a time and unwillingly accepts the name of disciple while he is a teacher, and becomes less than the least.

The people flock to the Church to hear from the new priest something that will build everyone up and save them all. Perhaps nothing beyond the customary manner is said; he strings together wax tablets, turns over in his mind pages unknown to everyone, and, recognizing all the offenses, employs only the shamelessness of one who makes excuses—and becomes angry at the very thing he is asked to do.

What then, I ask, will your judgment be, Bishop, when, questioned, you have said nothing, and have recognized that women and laypeople enter the Church in search of knowledge and understanding of life?

The meaning of the sacraments, then, and the order of all who are born and descend into the flesh, is this: those who come into the world are sold under sin and are first called servants of idols. For whoever is overcome by someone is assigned as that person’s servant and enslaved to that person’s work; he performs the service whose desire he bears in his mind.

When ignorance prevails, greed reigns, which is the root of all evils, along with the pursuit of idols. This is the evil that is difficult to overcome, because one is held either by the desire to possess or by fear of poverty.

But since the word of prophecy must first be preached in exhortation, it is necessary that the one God be eagerly spoken of and named among them, according to what is written: “The Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4).

These are the people whom we call catechumens: subject to correction, yet possessing free choice toward Christ. For the beginning of holiness is to confess the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, according to what is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

The second rank is that of the Competentes, those hastening toward the grace of God and desiring to become something more than they have been. They are called Competentes—that is, those seeking God’s grace—because they are already useful to God and, by the desire of their wills, seek the kingdoms of heaven, wishing through the supreme mercy to claim God as their rightful inheritance.

They abstain from everything, await the washing, are chaste and sincere, recognize that a limit has been set for their present life, and look toward the order of their future conduct. Thus, serving Christ before they receive him, after receiving the faith of God they may not lose his gifts or render void the grace they wished to serve.

The third order is that of the baptized, in whom Christ is already present, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that all who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ?” (Gal. 3:27).

Therefore, when, freed from paganism, we think about something good, we are catechumens; when we desire what is holy, we are Competentes; when we perform good works, we are baptized and abide with Christ. But if, with the devil opposing us, we are defiled by any stain of sin, penance is appropriate. In the likeness of the divine font, it puts those sins to death and saves us in the body.

When this has been completed, the fourth rank is that of reconciliation, so that we may believe Christ to be the head of our body, since he is the husband of his Church and the head of the woman—that is, of all souls that seek God with their whole mind.

Salt is therefore given sacramentally to catechumens, so that we may understand ourselves to be the salt of the earth—that is, the wisdom of God. “His invisible attributes,” as the Apostle says, “are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Rom. 1:20), and so forth.

Baptism is water, which came forth from Christ’s side at the time of his Passion. There is no other element in this world that purifies all things, that is the drink of everyone, and that gives life to all. Therefore the spirit of life is in the water, and the gathering of the waters received the name “seas.”

The one who is baptized in the font is reborn to Christ, for the font is the origin of all graces. In it are seven steps: three in the descent and three in the ascent. The seventh, which is also the fourth, is “like a son of man,” extinguishing the furnace of the blazing fire, the support of the feet, the foundation of the water; in it the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

That oil and chrism belong to the saints is shown by their silence and by the nature of their richness. The body of the Lord is true and heavenly bread from heaven. His blood is what is written: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John 15:1, 5).

And because there are many members but one body, the nature of the whole world has been crushed into invisible forms and transformed into the brightness of light, and through the baptism of water into truth. Since, according to the appearance of the body, the purity and truth of the will always appear, tested by fire, once all these foods have been completed nothing is lacking to visibility and nothing is lacking to the mystery of God; and the resurrection of the flesh is most clearly confirmed, since the visible things, sanctified by the word and prayer, have become the body of Christ.

If you embrace all these things in truth, understanding God, you perform the work of life and abide in Christ.

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). “To you, God, praise is due in Zion, so that vows may be fulfilled to you in Jerusalem” (Ps. 64:2). For you Christ is a banquet; Christ is joy; Christ is thought; Christ is desire; Christ is reading; Christ is rest. And, after you have conquered everything, you are God over the world and Pharaoh.

If you deem it worthy that I should admonish you, always impress these things upon all your peoples as you are able, remembering me in your holy prayers, so that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea and obtain remission of sins.

For I am confident that you will do more than I say. You recognize that you are my debtor, so that you may not cease to pray to God for me, since, as you graciously commanded, I have performed the office of discussion.

I have not laid down for you a law that you must follow, but, with a favorable pen, I have described what you ought already to be. There is, however, one thing above all others that I ask: since much of what has been written according to your custom appears new to you, may you graciously pardon my presumption.

Do not think that we are publishing any perversity or novelty, but only—if it is permissible to say so—the custom of various provinces. Yet just as I have criticized no one, so I have described no one as deserving condemnation, especially since God has made all the Churches and the apostles preached in all of them.

Nor is it fitting for anyone to strive for discord where, in the debate over ecclesiastical discipline, the one who is defeated wins and rejoices that he has been defeated, for the sake of preserving peace among all.

I, nevertheless, yield to all of you. I praise everything that you do and leave this matter to your minds as an incentive toward what is good, so that, each exhorting the other, you may teach one another about our custom and about contemplation.

Grant me only this special indulgence: that you deem me worthy of your prayers. In obedience for the correction of everything that has been written, I willingly take something upon myself, so that you may know that this was first my own judgment. I have commanded only this to be condemned by everyone: whatever the custom of the Churches or the written testimony of the divine books does not retain.

## Editorial Note on the Following Letter

[Col. 0162D] I think that this letter, or little book, was composed after the year 404, though not long after it, but within approximately a decade. Certainly its final words—“Hence the Roman Church, beautifully animated, without doubt, by the apostolic spirit whose seat it occupies, recently established so severe a judgment that it scarcely considered worthy of penance the woman who had defiled a body consecrated to God by lustful pollution”—clearly refer to that decree of Innocent, Roman pontiff, in his letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 12:

“Likewise, those women who have spiritually married Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or corrupt themselves secretly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the one to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world.”

This decree is assigned, as I have said, to the year 404. Thus, by calling it a “recent judgment,” our author indicates that he wrote not much later than that time.

From this it is also permissible to inquire, not without reason, into the author—since it has been discovered, even before Erasmus, that he was not Jerome—and to distinguish him from others who during that period dealt with a similar subject.

Perhaps he was Paul, or Peter, a presbyter and a Pannonian by birth, who, according to Gennadius, chapter 75, wrote *On the Preservation of Virginity* “for a certain noble virgin dedicated to Christ, named Constantia.” Erasmus testifies that in some copies the title was “To Mautitus’s daughter,” in others “To the daughter of Mauricius,” and in others no name was attached.

# LETTER XIII. Praise of Virginity

## I

How great a blessedness in heaven holy virginity possesses, we learn not only from the testimony of the Scriptures but also from the custom of the Church. Through it we learn that virginity has a special merit, since its consecration is distinctive.

For although the entire throng of believers receives equal gifts of grace and all glory in the same sacramental blessings, virgins possess something of their own beyond the others. From that holy and undefiled flock of the Church they are chosen by the Holy Spirit, as holier and purer offerings, according to the merits of their will, and are offered upon the altar by God’s high priest.

Truly worthy of the Lord is the offering of so precious a creature, and no offering is more pleasing than that which bears his own image. I believe that the Apostle spoke of such people when he said: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1).

Virginity therefore possesses both what others possess and what others do not possess: it holds both common and special grace and rejoices in what I might call the privilege of its own consecration.

Ecclesiastical authority also permits us to call virgins brides of Christ, since it consecrates them to the Lord in the manner of brides. It thereby shows that those who have avoided carnal union are especially destined to have a spiritual marriage, and that those who rejected human marriage for love of him are spiritually and worthily joined to God through the bond of marriage.

In them above all is fulfilled the Apostle’s saying: “The one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

It is a great and immortal achievement, almost beyond bodily nature, to restrain lust; to extinguish by the strength of the mind the flame of desire burning with the torches of youth; to exclude by spiritual effort the force of innate pleasure; to live contrary to the law of the human race; to disdain the consolations of marriage; to reject the sweetness of children; and to count as nothing, in hope of future blessedness, whatever advantages belong to the present life.

## II

This, as I have said, is a great and admirable virtue, and it is not undeservedly destined for an immense reward in proportion to the greatness of its labor:

“I will give to my eunuchs,” says the Lord, “in my house and within my walls a named place better than sons and daughters of Israel. I will give them an eternal name that shall not fail” (Isa. 56:5).

Concerning these eunuchs the Lord repeats in the Gospel: “For there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:12).

The labor of chastity is indeed great, but the reward is greater; its keeping is temporal, but its recompense is eternal. Blessed John the Apostle also speaks of such people, saying that “they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4).

I think this is to be understood as meaning that no place in the heavenly court will be closed to them and that all the dwelling places of God will be opened to them.

But so that the merit of virginity may shine more brightly and its worthiness before God may be understood more clearly, let this be considered: when our Lord and Savior God deigned to assume humanity for the salvation of the human race, he chose no other than a virginal womb.

And to show that such a state pleased him greatly, and to make known to both sexes the goodness of chastity, he had a virgin for his mother while remaining a virgin himself. In himself he offered an example of virginity to men, and in his mother to women, showing that blessed integrity and fullness of divinity were present in both sexes, since whatever was possessed in the Son was wholly present in the mother.

But why do I strive to reveal the excellent and sublime merit of chastity and to display the goodness of glorious virginity, when I know that many have already spoken at length on this subject and established its blessedness by the clearest arguments? No wise person can doubt that the matter requiring the greater labor possesses the greater merit.

Whoever considers chastity to be without reward or of little reward certainly either does not understand it or does not undertake its labor willingly. Therefore those who always disparage chastity are those who either do not possess it or are compelled to possess it unwillingly.

## III

Now, since we have shown, however briefly, both the labor and the merit of integrity, we must keep more careful watch so that a matter founded upon great virtue and destined for an immense reward may not be deprived of its fruit.

For the more precious any form of excellence is, the more carefully it is guarded. Since many things lack their own good unless they are aided by the support of other things—for example, the quality of honey—unless it is preserved and, so to speak, nourished by the protection of wax and the cells of the honeycombs, it loses its natural grace and cannot subsist by itself.

Likewise, the quality of wine, unless it is kept in a vessel of good odor and frequently renewed with pitch, loses the force of its native sweetness.

We must therefore provide more attentively, lest virginity too should require certain things without which it cannot produce fruit, and lest so great a labor should accomplish nothing. For it is believed to be useful in vain if it is possessed without the necessary strength.

Unless I am mistaken, integrity of chastity is preserved for the reward of the heavenly kingdom. It is sufficiently certain that no one can attain that reward without the merit of eternal life. Eternal life can be earned only through the observance of all the divine commands, as Scripture says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. X, 17).

Therefore he does not possess eternal life who has not kept all the commandments of the law; and whoever does not possess life cannot be a possessor of the heavenly kingdom, in which not the dead but the living will reign.

Virginity alone will accomplish nothing for one who hopes for the glory of the heavenly kingdom unless that person also possesses something else to which eternal life is promised, through which the reward of the heavenly kingdom is possessed.

Before everything, therefore, those who preserve chastity and integrity and hope for its recompense from God’s justice must keep the commandments, lest the labor of glorious chastity and continence be rendered void.

No wise person who knows the law is unaware that virginity is above a commandment or precept, since the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice” (1 Cor. 7:25).

When he gives advice about attaining virginity, he does not establish a commandment; by declaring that it is above a commandment or precept, he shows its nature. Therefore those who preserve virginity do more than is commanded.

It will benefit one to have done more than was commanded only if one has done what was commanded. For how will you glory in having done more if you fail to do something lesser? Desiring to fulfill divine counsel, keep the commandment above all. Wishing to attain the reward of virginity, embrace the merit of life, so that your chastity may be rewarded.

## IV

For just as observance of the commandments grants life, so, conversely, transgression produces death. One who through transgression has been assigned to death cannot hope for the crown of virginity or await the reward of chastity while established under punishment.

There are three forms through which possession of the heavenly kingdom is entered. The first is chastity; the second, contempt of the world; the third, justice.

Although these, when joined together, are of great benefit to those who possess them, when separated they can scarcely be useful. Each is demanded not only for its own sake but also for the sake of the others.

First, therefore, chastity is sought, so that contempt of the world may more easily follow, since those who are not held by the bonds of marriage can more easily despise the world.

Contempt of the world is sought so that justice may be preserved, which those entangled in desires for secular goods and in the affairs of worldly pleasures can scarcely fulfill.

Whoever possesses the first form, chastity, but does not possess the second, contempt of the world, possesses it almost uselessly. He possesses the first without purpose when he does not possess the second, for whose sake the first was sought.

If he possesses the first and second but lacks the third, justice, he labors in vain, because the first two are sought chiefly for the sake of the third.

What benefit is there in possessing chastity for the sake of contempt of the world, while lacking the reason for which one ought to possess chastity? Or why despise the things of the world if you do not preserve the justice for whose sake it is fitting for you to possess chastity and contempt of the world?

For just as the first form exists for the sake of the second, so the first and second exist for the sake of the third. If the third is absent, neither the first nor the second will be of benefit.

Perhaps you will say, “Teach me, then, what justice is, so that, if I come to know it, I may more easily be able to fulfill it.” I shall speak briefly, as I am able, and shall use the simplicity of ordinary words. For the subject with which we are dealing is such that it ought not to be obscured by more elaborate speeches of eloquence, but revealed through simpler accounts of eloquence.

What is necessary for everyone in common ought to be demonstrated in a common manner of speech.

## V

Justice, then, is nothing other than not sinning. Not sinning means observing the precepts of the law.

The observance of the precepts is preserved in two ways: by doing none of the things that are forbidden and by striving to fulfill all that is commanded. This is what is said: “Turn away from evil and do good.”

Do not think that justice consists only in your not doing evil, since failing to do good is also evil, and transgression of the law is committed in both respects.

For the one who says, “Turn away from evil” (Prov. 3:7), also says, “Do good.” If you turn away from evil but do not do good, you are a transgressor of the law, which is fulfilled not only in the rejection of evil actions but also in the perfection of good works.

You are not commanded merely not to strip the clothed of their garments, but to clothe those who have been stripped with your own garments. Nor merely not to take away his bread from one who has bread, but willingly to share yours with one who has none. Nor merely not to deny the poor hospitality, but to receive into your own home the one who has been driven out and possesses nothing.

For we have been commanded to weep with those who weep. How do we weep with them if we do not share in their needs in any way or offer them assistance in the matters over which they weep?

God does not seek the unfruitful moisture of our tears. Rather, because tears are an indication of grief, he wishes you to feel another’s distress as your own and, just as you would wish to be helped if you were in such tribulation, so to help another, because of this saying: “Whatever good things you want people to do for you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:12).

For to weep with one who weeps and, when you are able, to offer the weeping person nothing is a sign of mockery, not of compassion.

Finally, our Savior wept with Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, and demonstrated the feeling of immense mercy by the witness of his tears. Works immediately followed as signs of true compassion, and Lazarus, whose death had caused the tears, was restored alive to his sisters.

This was truly to weep with those who weep: to remove the occasions of weeping.

“But,” you will say, “he did this as one who was powerful.” Yet nothing impossible is commanded of you. He fulfilled everything who did what he could.

## VI

But, as we had begun to say, it is not enough for a Christian to abstain from evils unless he also performs the duties of good works.

This is especially confirmed by that testimony in which the Lord threatens that those will be guilty of eternal fire who, although they have done no evil, have not done every good thing:

“Then the king will say to those who are on his left: Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:41–42), and so forth.

He does not say, “Depart from me, accursed ones, because you committed murder, because you committed adultery, or because you committed theft.” They are not condemned and assigned to the fires of eternal Gehenna because they did evil, but because they did not do good.

They are condemned not because they committed what was forbidden, but because they were unwilling to fulfill what was commanded.

Hence one must consider what hope those can have who still do some of the things that are forbidden, when even those are guilty of eternal fire who did not do what is commanded.

I do not want you to flatter yourself on this point if you have not done certain things, since it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (Jac. VIII, 10).

Adam sinned once and died, and do you think that you can live while repeatedly committing the act that, once perpetrated by another, killed him?

Or do you think that he committed some great crime and was therefore deservedly condemned to a harsher punishment? Let us see what he did against the commandment: he ate from the fruit of a tree.

What then? Did God punish the human being with death because of the fruit of a tree? Not because of the fruit of the tree, but because of contempt for the commandment.

Therefore the issue is not the nature of the sin but the transgression of the commandment.
