The one who told Adam not to eat from the fruit of the tree himself commanded you not to curse, not to lie, not to slander, nor to listen to those who slander; not to swear at all; not to covet; not to envy; not to be lukewarm; not to be greedy; to return evil to no one for evil; to love your enemies; to pray for those who curse and persecute you; to offer the other cheek to one who strikes you; not to engage in litigation in secular judgment; if someone wishes to take away what is yours, to surrender it gladly; not to admit into your heart the evil of anger, jealousy, or envy; to flee the crime of greed; to guard against every evil of boasting and pride; to live humbly and gently according to Christ’s example; and to avoid the company of evil people so completely that you do not eat with fornicators, the greedy, those who curse, the envious, slanderers, drunkards, or robbers.

If you despise him in any one of these matters, if he spared Adam, he will spare you also.

Indeed, Adam deserved greater mercy, because he was still new and inexperienced and was restrained by no example of anyone who had sinned before him and died because of his sin.

But for you, after so many teachings, after the law, after the prophets, after the Gospels, and after the apostles, if you wish to transgress, I do not know how forgiveness can be granted.

## VII.

Do you flatter yourself on account of the privilege of virginity? Remember that Adam and Eve sinned while virgins, and that bodily integrity did not benefit those who sinned. A virgin who sins must be compared with Eve, not with Mary. We do not deny that, in the present time, there is a remedy of repentance; but we urge you rather to hope for the reward than to seek pardon. For it is shameful for those who expect the palm of virginity to ask indulgence for wrongdoing, and unlawful for those who have even abstained from lawful things to incur something unlawful.

It is lawful to enter into the partnership of marriage. And just as those women are worthy of praise who, for love of Christ and the glory of the heavenly kingdom, have rejected the marital bond, so those who, not yet devoted to God, make use of the apostolic remedy because of the pleasure of self-indulgence are not to be condemned. Therefore, as we have said, those who abandon marriage reject not unlawful but lawful things. But if such women swear, curse, desire what belongs to others, tolerate listening to slanderers, repay evil with evil, incur the crime of avarice with regard to what belongs to others or to themselves, possess the poisons of jealousy or envy; if, contrary to legal and apostolic ordinances, they either say or think something indecent; if, out of a desire to please in the flesh, they go about elegantly and stylishly dressed, and do whatever else they customarily do unlawfully—what will it profit them to have rejected what was permitted and to practice what is not permitted?

If you wish what you have rejected as lawful to benefit you, take care not to do any of the things that are not permitted. For it is foolish to fear what is lesser and not fear what is greater, or not to avoid what is prohibited after having shunned what is allowed.

The Apostle says: “The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit; but the married woman is concerned with the things of this world, how she may please her husband” (1 Cor. 7:34). He asserts that the married woman pleases her husband by thinking about the things of the world, while the unmarried woman pleases God because she has no concern for worldly affairs.

Let her therefore tell me: the woman who has no husband yet thinks about the things of the world—whom does she wish to please? Will she not begin to be placed below the married woman, since the latter, by thinking about the things of the world, pleases at least her husband, whereas the former can please neither a husband, whom she does not have, nor God?

Nor ought we to pass over in silence what he said: “The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” He says that she thinks about the things of God, not the things of the world, not the things of human beings, but the things of God.

What, then, are the things of the Lord? Let the Apostle say. “Whatever is holy, whatever is just, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good repute, if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline”—these are the things of the Lord (Phil. 4:8). These are the things that holy, true, and apostolic virgins meditate upon and contemplate day and night, without any interval of time.

The kingdom of heaven also belongs to the Lord; the resurrection of the dead belongs to the Lord; immortal incorruption belongs to the Lord; the splendor of the sun, which is promised to the saints, belongs to the Lord, as it is written in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). The many dwelling places of the righteous in the heavens belong to the Lord; the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit belong to the Lord. They think about these things, and they think by what works they may merit the things that belong to the Lord.

The law of the New and Old Testament also belongs to the Lord; in them his holy utterances shine forth. If any virgins meditate upon these things without interruption, thinking about what belongs to the Lord, that prophetic saying may be fulfilled in them: “Eternal foundations upon a solid rock, and the commandments of the Lord in the heart of a holy woman.”

It follows: “How she may please God”—God, I say, not human beings—“so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34). He did not say, “so that she may be holy in one limb,” or “in body alone,” but “so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” A limb is one part of the body; the body, however, is the entire joining together of the limbs. Therefore, when he said “so that she may be holy in body,” he testifies that she must be sanctified in all her limbs, because the sanctification of the remaining limbs will be of no benefit if corruption is found in one. And she will no longer be holy in body, which consists of all the limbs, if it has been defiled by the pollution of even one.

But to make what I am saying clearer and more evident: suppose that she has been purified by the sanctification of all her limbs, and that only her tongue sins, whether by blaspheming or by giving false testimony. Will all the limbs free one? Or will the others be judged because of the one? Therefore, if chastity is of no benefit without the sanctification of the other limbs when there is a fault in one, how much less will the integrity of one be of benefit if all are corrupted by various sins?

## VIII.

Therefore, virgin, I beg you, do not flatter yourself on account of chastity alone, nor place your confidence in the integrity of one limb. Rather, according to the Apostle, preserve the chastity of your entire body.

Cleanse your head of every defilement. For it is a crime, after the sanctification of chrism, to soil it with the color or powder of saffron or any other pigment, or to adorn it with gold, gems, or the appearance of any earthly creature, when it already shines with the splendor of heavenly adornment. For it is a great insult to the divine nature to prefer worldly and secular ornament.

Cleanse your forehead, so that it may blush at human works, not divine ones, and receive that shame which produces not sin but the grace of God, as divine Scripture says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings the grace of God” (Ecclus. 4:25).

Cleanse your neck, so that your hair may not wear golden nets, nor necklaces hang from it, but rather that it may carry those ornaments of which Scripture says: “Mercy and truth will not depart from you” (Prov. 3:3, according to the Septuagint). Hang these upon your heart as though upon your neck.

Cleanse your eyes by withdrawing them from every desire, never turning them away from the sight of the poor, and keeping them free from every cosmetic, directed toward the things of God.

Cleanse your tongue from falsehood, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul.” Cleanse it from slander, oaths, and perjury. Do not think that I have placed the order backward by saying that the tongue must first be cleansed from oaths and then from perjury. For you will more easily avoid perjury if you do not swear at all, so that this saying may be fulfilled in you: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33:14).

And remember the Apostle’s words: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14). But remember even more frequently this command: “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, or curse for curse, but, on the contrary, bless; for to this you were called, so that you might inherit a blessing” (1 Thess. 5:15).

And this also: “If anyone does not offend in word, that person is perfect.” For it is impious that those lips by which you confess, beseech, bless, and praise the Lord should be polluted by the filth of any sin. I do not know with what conscience and tongue anyone can beseech the Lord while lying, cursing, or slandering. The Lord hears holy lips, and he promptly assents to the prayers pronounced by an undefiled tongue.

Cleanse your ears, so that they may give hearing only to holy and truthful words, and never receive obscene, shameful, or worldly speech, nor hear anyone speak disparagingly of another, in accordance with what is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclus. 28:28). Thus you may share in the portion of him of whom it is said: “For he was righteous in hearing and seeing” (2 Pet. 2:8)—that is, he did not sin either with his ears or with his eyes.

Cleanse your hands, so that they may not be extended to receive while folded together for giving; let them not be ready to strike, but sufficiently prepared for every work of mercy and compassion.

Cleanse your feet, so that they may not travel along the broad and spacious road that leads to the splendid things of the world and expensive banquets, but may rather walk upon the difficult and narrow path that leads toward heaven, because it is written: “Make straight paths for your feet” (Prov. 4:31).

Recognize that your limbs were formed for you by God the craftsman not for vices but for virtues. And when you have cleansed all your limbs from every filth of sin and have been purified in your entire body, then understand that chastity will benefit you, and await with complete confidence the palm of virginity.

## IX.

I think that I have explained briefly but clearly what it means to be holy in body. Now we must understand what follows: “and in spirit.” This means that what it is unlawful to do in deed must not even be conceived in thought.

A woman is holy in body as well as in spirit when she sins neither in mind nor in body, knowing also that God is the watcher of the heart. Therefore she strives to keep her soul as well as her body entirely clean from sin, knowing that it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4:23).

And again: “The Lord loves holy hearts, but all the undefiled are acceptable to him.” And elsewhere: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8). I think that this is said of those whom conscience does not convict of any guilt of sin.

I believe that John also spoke of them in his Epistle: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (1 John 3:21–22).

Do not suppose that you have escaped the crime of sin if an act does not follow your will, since it is written: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Nor should you say, “I thought about it, but I did not do it,” because it is also unlawful to desire what is a crime to do.

Therefore blessed Peter also gives this command: “Making your souls chaste” (2 Pet. 1:6). If he had known of no defilement of the soul, he would not have wished it to be purified.

We must also consider more attentively and observe the passage that says: “These are those who have not defiled themselves with women, for they remained virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4). Are they joined to the divine company and traversing all the tabernacles of heaven solely because of integrity and chastity? Or are there other qualities joined to virginity by which they attain the glory of such blessedness?

How can we know this? From what follows, unless I am mistaken, where it is written: “These were purchased from among all as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth; for they are without blemish.”

You see, then, that the virgins are not said to cling to the Lord’s footsteps merely in one limb, but those who, in addition to virginity, lead a life undefiled by every contagion of sin.

## X.

For this reason above all the virgin rejects marriage: so that, being more free from care, she may more easily keep herself from every sin—which is required even of those who marry—and fulfill all the commandments of the law. For if she does not marry yet nevertheless does the things from which married women are also commanded to be free, what benefit is there in not having married?

Although no Christian is permitted to sin, and although all who are cleansed by the sanctification of spiritual washing ought to lead an undefiled life, so that they may be joined to the innermost parts of the Church—which is described as being without stain, wrinkle, or anything of that kind—nevertheless it is much more necessary for a virgin to fulfill this. No husband, children, or other necessity prevents her from fulfilling divine Scripture; and if she sins, she will be able to defend herself by no excuse.

O virgin, preserve the resolve appointed for you with a great reward. The virtue of virginity and chastity is excellent before God, provided it is not weakened by other falls into sins and evils. Recognize your status, recognize your place, recognize your purpose. You are called the bride of Christ. Take care not to admit anything unworthy of him to whom you appear to have been betrothed. He quickly writes a bill of repudiation if he sees even one adultery in you.

Therefore, whenever a woman is betrothed by the tokens of a human engagement, she immediately asks carefully and diligently of the bridegroom’s household members, relatives, friends, and servants what kind of character the young man has. She asks what he especially loves, what he willingly receives, how he lives, by what habits he governs himself, what foods he uses, and in what matters he most delights and rejoices. Once she has learned these things, she regulates herself in every respect so that her service, affection, joy, life, and diligence accord with the bridegroom’s character.

You too, since you have Christ as your bridegroom, ask his household and relatives about the character of your bridegroom, and inquire actively and carefully into what especially delights him. Ask what arrangement of clothing he likes in you and what kind of adornment he desires. Let his closest associate Peter tell you—he permits not even married women a bodily adornment, but a spiritual one—as he wrote in his Epistle:

“Likewise, let women be subject to their husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe your chaste conduct in fear. Let their adornment not be external, in the braiding of hair, or the wearing of gold, or the putting on of garments, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, which is precious in the sight of God” (1 Pet. 3:1 ff.).

Let the other blessed Apostle, Paul, also speak, who, writing an Epistle to Timothy, gives the same testimony concerning the discipline of faithful women:

“Likewise, women should adorn themselves in respectable dress, with modesty and sobriety, adorning themselves not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with what is fitting for women who profess chastity through good conduct” (1 Tim. 2:9).

But perhaps you will say: Why did these same Apostles not command this to virgins? Because they did not consider it necessary, lest such an admonition to virgins should appear an insult rather than a correction. Nor did they ever believe that virgins would be so reckless as to presume to use bodily and earthly ornaments not even granted to married women.

## XI.

Indeed, a virgin ought to adorn and arrange herself. For how will she be able to please her bridegroom unless she comes forth arranged and adorned? Let her certainly be adorned, but with inward ornaments; let her be arranged spiritually, not bodily, because the Lord desires in her not the beauty of the body but of the soul.

Therefore, you who desire Christ to love and dwell in your soul, arrange it with every care and adorn it with spiritual clothing. Let nothing indecent, nothing filthy, appear in it. Let it shine with the gold of righteousness, sparkle with the gems of holiness, and glitter with the most precious pearl of chastity; let it be clothed in the robe of piety.

Instead of linen and silk, let it be clothed and dressed in the robe of chastity and mercy, according to what is written: “Put on, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassion, humility,” and so forth (Col. 3:12).

Let it not seek the beauty of white lead or any other pigment, but possess the whiteness of innocence and simplicity. Let it possess the rose-colored hue of modesty and the red blush of shame. Let it be washed with the heavenly nitre of teaching and cleansed with spiritual washings. Let no stain of malice or sin remain in it. And, lest it ever give off the foul odor of sin, let it enjoy the sweetest ointment of wisdom and knowledge.

God seeks this kind of adornment and desires a soul arranged in this manner.

## XII.

Remember that you are a daughter, according to the words: “Hear, daughter, and see.” And whenever you yourself call God “Father,” you testify that you are God’s daughter. Therefore, if you are God’s daughter, take care not to do anything inconsistent with God the Father, but do everything as a daughter of God.

Observe how the daughters of noble families in this world conduct themselves, to what habits they accustom themselves, and in what disciplines they train themselves. In some there is such modesty, such dignity, and such self-control that, out of regard for human nobility, they surpass the custom of other people; and, lest they brand their honorable parents with any mark of disgrace through their own fall, they have in a certain way made another nature of custom for themselves among human beings.

You too should look to your origin, consider your lineage, and attend to the glory of your nobility. Remember that you are not merely the daughter of a human being, but a daughter of God, adorned with the nobility of divine birth. Conduct yourself so that heavenly birth may appear in you and divine nobility shine forth.

Let there be in you a new dignity, admirable honor, astonishing modesty, remarkable patience, a virginal gait, and the bearing of true chastity. Let your speech always be modest and spoken at the proper time, so that whoever sees you may marvel and say:

“What is this new dignity among human beings? What modesty of shame? What restraint of honor? What maturity of wisdom? This is not human training, nor mortal discipline. Something heavenly shines here in a human body. I think that God dwells in certain human beings.”

And when someone recognizes you as a daughter of Christ, that person will be held by even greater wonder and will consider what kind of Lord he must be whose servant is such a woman.

If, then, you wish to have a share with Christ, you must live according to Christ’s example. He was so far removed from every malice and wickedness that he did not repay even his enemies in kind; rather, he prayed for them.

I do not want you to think that those are Christian souls who—I do not say hate their brothers or sisters, but even—do not love their neighbors with their whole heart, in the presence of the testimony of their conscience before God, since a Christian, by resemblance to Christ, must love even enemies.

If you desire to share the fellowship of the saints, cleanse your heart from every thought of malice and wickedness. Let no one deceive you; let no one lead you astray by deceitful speech. The heavenly court will receive only the holy, the just, the simple, the innocent, and the pure. Malice has no place with God.

Anyone who desires to reign with Christ must be clean from every wickedness and deceit. Nothing is so contrary and nothing so hateful to God as to hate someone or wish to injure someone. Nothing is so commendable as to love everyone. The Prophet foresees and testifies to this when he says: “You who love God, hate evil” (Ps. 96:10).

## XIII.

Take care not to love any human glory, lest your portion be counted among those to whom it was said: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?” (John 5:44). And concerning whom the Prophet says: “Increase evils upon them; increase evils upon the glorious of the earth, so that you may be confounded by your boasting and become a reproach in the sight of God.”

I do not want you to look to those who are virgins of the world, not of the Lord—those who, forgetful of their purpose and profession, rejoice in pleasures, delight in riches, and glory in the origin of their bodily nobility. If they truly believed themselves to be daughters of God, they would never, after their divine birth, admire human nobility, nor glory in having any honored father. If they realized that they have God as their Father, they would not love nobility of the flesh.

Why do you flatter and please yourself with the nobility of your lineage? In the beginning God made two human beings, from whom the entire forest of the human race descended. Worldly nobility is granted not by the equality of nature but by the ambition of desire.

Certainly, through the grace of the divine washing, we are all made equal, so that no distinction can exist among those whom a second birth has generated. Through it, the rich and the poor, the slave and the free, the noble and the ignoble become sons of God; earthly nobility is overshadowed by the splendor of heavenly glory and disappears entirely. Those who previously were unequal in secular honors are restored equally by the nobility of heavenly and divine glory.

There is no place there for ignobility, nor is anyone degenerate whose nobility is adorned by divine birth—except among those who do not think that heavenly things should be preferred to human things. Or, if they do think so, how foolish it is for them to prefer themselves in lesser matters to those whom they recognize as their equals in greater matters, and to regard as placed beneath them on earth those whom they have believed equal to themselves in heaven!

But you, who are a virgin of Christ, not of the world, flee all the glory of the present life, so that you may obtain everything that is promised in the future. Avoid words of contention and the causes of hostility. Also evade the occasions of discord and lawsuits. For if, according to the Apostle’s teaching, it is not fitting for a servant of God to quarrel (2 Tim. 2:24), how much less is it appropriate for a handmaid of God? The more modest her sex, the more modest her spirit ought to be.

## XIV.

Restrain your tongue from evil speech, and place the reins of the law upon your mouth, so that, if you should happen to speak when silence would be sinful, you may take care not to say anything that could be censured: “A stone is a word once it has been cast.” Therefore, a word must be considered long before it is spoken.

Blessed are the lips that never utter what they may later wish to recall. The speech of a modest mind ought also to be modest, always building up rather than destroying anyone who hears it, according to the Apostle’s command: “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for building up in faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. 4:29).

A tongue is precious to God when it knows how to construct words only about divine matters, and the mouth from which heavenly utterances continually proceed is holy.

By the authority of Scripture, deter slanderers of the absent as malicious people. For the Prophet also recounts this among the virtues of the perfect person. If, in the sight of a just person, the malicious person who has uttered blameworthy things against a neighbor is reduced to nothing, you may not patiently listen to another’s disparagement when you do not wish your own to be received from others.

Whatever is contrary to the Gospel of Christ is unjust, if you allow another to suffer something from someone else that you find distressing when it is done to you. Accustom your tongue always to speak about good things, and incline your hearing more toward the praise of good people than toward the condemnation of the wicked.

See that whatever good you do, you do it for God, knowing that you will receive from the Lord only the reward of what you have accomplished for fear and love of him.

Strive to be holy rather than to appear holy, because it is of no benefit to be considered what you are not. It is a double charge of sin both not to possess what is believed about you and to pretend to possess what you do not have.

## XV.

Take greater delight in fasts than in feasts, remembering that widow who did not depart from the Temple, serving God with fasts and prayers day and night. If a Jewish widow was such, what ought a virgin of Christ now to be?

Love the banquet of divine reading more; desire to be filled with spiritual food. Seek those foods by which the soul rather than the body is restored. Flee meat and wine, as fuel for heat and incentives to lust.

And if illness of the body, together with excessive pain of the stomach, should compel you at some point to use a little wine, conquer anger and restrain hostility. Whatever it is that, after repentance has been made, brings shame upon your neighbor, avoid as the abomination of a crime.

The mind that desires to be God’s dwelling ought to be sufficiently tranquil and sufficiently peaceful, alien from every disturbance of rage. God testifies through the Prophet, saying: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Believe that God watches all your deeds and thoughts, and take care not to do or think anything unworthy of the divine eyes. When you desire to perform prayer, present yourself as though you were about to speak with God.

When you recite a psalm, recognize whose words you are speaking, and take greater delight in contrition of heart than in the sweetness of a ringing voice. For God approves the tears of the one singing psalms more than the grace of the voice.

As the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). Where there is fear and trembling, there is not elevation of voice but a grieving spirit and tearful abasement.

Apply diligence to all your actions, because it is written: “Cursed is the person who performs God’s work negligently.”

## XVI.

Let grace increase for you with the years; let righteousness increase with age; and let faith appear more perfect in proportion as it is older. For our Lord Jesus Christ, who left us an example of how to live, advanced not only in bodily age but also in wisdom and spiritual grace before God and human beings.

Consider all the time in which you have not found yourself better to have been lost. Preserve the purpose of virginity that you have begun all the way to the end, because virtue consists not merely in beginning but in completing. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Take care, therefore, not to give anyone an occasion for desire, because your bridegroom is a jealous God. An adulteress against Christ is more culpable than an adulteress against a husband.

For this reason the Roman Church, undoubtedly animated by the apostolic spirit whose see it holds, recently established so severe a judgment concerning such a matter that it scarcely judged worthy of penance the woman who had violated a body consecrated to God by lustful defilement.

Therefore, be a model of living for everyone; be an example; in conduct, lead those whom you surpass in the sanctification of chastity. Show yourself a virgin in every respect. Let no corruption be charged against your head, whose body is intact, so that your conduct may also be inviolable.

And since, as we stated at the beginning of the Epistle, you have been made God’s sacrifice—which certainly imparts its sanctification to others also, and whoever receives it worthily becomes himself a participant in sanctification—so through you, as through a living [Variant: divine] offering, let the other women be sanctified. Conduct yourself toward them in every respect so that whoever encounters your life, whether by sight or hearing, may feel the power of sanctification and understand that so much grace is transferred to that person through your conduct that, while desiring to imitate you, he or she may also become worthy of God’s sacrifice.

## Notice concerning the following Epistle

This work is found in a much longer form, with additions, also among Augustine’s works in the appendix to volume eight, under the title *On the Essence of Divinity*. The editors of the collected works of Augustine also point out that it was falsely attributed in equal measure to many other authors—to Ambrose, Anselm, and Bonaventure.

It also bears various titles: in Anselm, *On the Vestments, Members, and Acts Attributed to God*; in Bonaventure, *On the Essence, Invisibility, and Immensity of God*; in the Vatican and Victorine manuscripts, under Augustine’s name, *On the Essence of Divinity, and on the Invisibility and Immutability of God*.

Finally, the first and largest part of the book is said to contain the entire first chapter of Eucherius of Lyon’s work *On the Forms of Spiritual Understanding*, namely the chapter on the divine names. In an old manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, marked with the letter A and number 48, we found it entitled: *A Sentence of Saint Jerome on the Essence of the Divinity of God, and on His Invisibility and Immensity*.

Erasmus, however, very rightly observed that there is nothing in this work—in its language, its learning, or its spirit—that suggests Jerome.

## Epistle XIV: On Those Things Attributed to God in the Holy Scriptures (C)*

[Col. 0176]

(See Saint Augustine at the place cited above.)

## Epistle XV, or the Creed of Damasus

(See this creed among the writings attributed to Saint Pope Damasus, volume XIII of our *Patrology*.)

## Epistle XVI, or Explanation of the Creed to Damasus

(Since Saint Augustine copied almost the whole of this explanation—which is commonly regarded as the work of Pelagius—in order to refute it in his book *On the Grace of Christ*, see it there, volume X.)

## Notice concerning the following Epistle

The reason why this work was attributed to Jerome may have been what he himself says about himself at the end of Epistle 17 in our recension: “As for the faith about which you were kind enough to write, I have given Saint Cyril the written Creed. Whoever does not believe in this way is alien from Christ.”

That Creed, however, concerned the three hypostases; concerning that controversy, there is not a word in this spurious *Explanation*. Moreover, both the style and the matter themselves proclaim that this is not Jerome’s. Indeed, the manner in which the mysteries are explained altogether persuades us that it belongs to a recent author.

## Epistle XVII, or Explanation of the Faith to Cyril

### I.

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, Creator of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord, our Jesus Christ, his Son, born from the substance of God the Father—which in Greek is called *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), “of the same substance”—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, as the heretics say.

Through him all things visible and invisible were made, both in heaven and on earth. For us human beings and for our salvation he became incarnate, became human, suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit, who proceeded properly from the Father and is true God, just as the Son is.

But the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes those who say that there was a time when the Son had not been born and that, before he was born, he did not exist; or who say that the Son of God was made from nothing, or was created, or is mutable or changeable.

This is a faith concerning invisible things, not visible things. Therefore, when the Arians saw the Savior in the flesh, they thought that his divinity was such as his flesh also was: passible, mutable, changeable, comprehensible, as though fearful, as though ignorant of everything, advancing in age and wisdom, doing nothing from himself, subject, praying to the Father, giving thanks, eating, suffering, weeping, groaning, and resting.

Finally, whatever belongs properly to a creature must certainly be attributed to the Savior’s created flesh, not to his divinity, because Scripture says that he is God and human being.

Therefore, since he is also called human being for our sake, we must not attribute what belongs to the flesh to God, nor regard what belongs to God as proper to the flesh. If anything lesser, unequal, powerless, subject, or humble is spoken of in Scripture, it belongs to his assumed flesh.

Because he was born according to the flesh, and because he lived among human beings for thirty years and more, he truly had to suffer. Therefore, because of the flesh, he is understood to be true human being, and true God incarnate. He suffered in the flesh, in a passible nature, not in his divinity.

For these things that the flesh of the transgressing human being ought to have suffered, God consented to suffer on behalf of human beings through passible flesh, so that we might also perceive in a visible reality the unspeakable power of his divinity foretold beforehand, and, believing in him, attain the riches of his goodness—that is, the forgiveness of sins through his suffering.

## II. What, then, is this evil, that anyone should dare to fail to understand the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ—which he bestowed for our sake by humbling himself so that we might be exalted—with human sentiments and heretical speech, and moreover to nullify it by dangerous blasphemies and deliberately oppose it, when Scripture says: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9)? Let there be, then, nothing greater or lesser in the Son of God—in place, power, knowledge, equality, time, or subjection—when these things are attributed to his divinity, not to his flesh. For if anything greater or lesser, or anything of that kind, is found—apart from the fact that the Father begot the Son, and apart from the fact that the Son was not born from himself but was properly born from the Father, not in time but eternally, not from elsewhere but from his own substance—then perhaps, according to their doctrine, the Father is thought to be either envious or powerless, and is even acknowledged to be temporal. And although Scripture openly forbids and condemns this, how do they themselves worship a temporal God in the same way that the Gentiles worship one? For if he is temporal, he cannot be true; and if he is not true, neither is he capable of all things. And what faith should now be placed in such a God, who once existed when he did not exist, and was born from nothing, when Scripture says: “If you will listen to me, Israel, there will be no new God among you” (Ps. 80:9)?

If, then, he is a new God, he must not be believed to be true. But if he is eternal—for this was the eternal God who spoke through all the saints, who gave the law to Moses on Mount Sinai, who is powerful over all things and knows all things, who appeared to Adam in paradise, declaring to him in a fleshly predestination things that were to come, and who wrestled with Jacob—how could human frailty comprehend him? He accommodates himself to the weaknesses of all and displays different forms: to some in glory, as the cause of universal fear; to others in humility, so that his surpassing goodness might be recognized.

If, then, the eternal Son was begotten from the Father—and he knows all things, is powerful over all things, saves all things, contains all things, judges and creates all things always with the Father and the Holy Spirit—understand, then, that a creature cannot be the true God, nor can a creature save a creature, as Scripture says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:25). Do you see, then, that this belongs more to paganism than to Christianity?

And that he was not born in time but was always born from the Father, the blessed Apostle says: “For from the creation of the world his invisible attributes are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, and so are his eternal power and divinity” (ibid., 20). Do you see, then, that Christ, the Son of God, is not temporal but eternal? That he was always born from the divine substance of the Father, the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “What is born from the flesh is flesh, and what is born from the Spirit is spirit, since God is Spirit” (John 3:6). And that he is the true Son of God, Scripture says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). Again, the blessed evangelist John himself says: “This is Jesus Christ, the true God.” And that he always existed, he himself says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). And that the Son is almighty and the creator of all things, the blessed evangelist himself says: “All things were made through him.”

If, then, all things were made through him, visible and invisible, how does the Savior say before his passion that no one knows the day and hour—not the angels of heaven, nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone? Paying attention, you see that, for the benefit of human beings, he said that he did not know the appointed time, lest people become more negligent. He said this also because of his humility, on account of the passible flesh, since he appeared to human beings as though he were a human being; and for the benefit of all he kept silent, announcing and enumerating the events that were to take place in the world, but not revealing the day and hour to them.

What he kept silent about for our benefit, and in which he humbled himself, we ought not deliberately to repay with ingratitude—not only failing to understand, but also, in the manner of the Jews, judging him to be human and considering him, like the Jews, to share their age, ignorance, and powerlessness. That it was not the divinity that naturally suffered, but the flesh, he himself showed to the Jews when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

And who could doubt that it was God who said this—that is, the eternal Son of God, the living Word of the Father, the wisdom of God, the eternal and everlasting power of God, and the image of the invisible God, born from the invisible and not made? Flesh, however, was made and fashioned, and God was in it; he had also clothed himself with it because of his invisibility and our inability to see. For he was not only within, but both outside and within, in heaven and on earth, containing and filling all things.

Therefore there is nothing imperfect in the Son of God, nothing unequal, nothing powerless, nothing temporal, nothing unknown: all things are true, all things possible, all things immense, all things equal to the Father. The Savior says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). Do you see the Son’s equality with the Father? Since, then, the Son knows the Father, does he not know the ineffable and incomprehensible day and hour that he himself made? Far be this from our minds.

Again, the Savior himself says: “Father, grant them that they may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 6:23). The Son, then, is equal to God in divinity, as the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross” (Phil. 2:6–7).

You see that Scripture does not deny either reality in the Son of God: that which belongs to God—the power of the almighty, who knows all things, fills all things, contains all things, possesses all things, gives all things, judges, saves, and creates—and that which belongs to created nature, that is, to his flesh: suffering, weeping, seeming not to know, seeming unable to do all things, seeming subject, and other things of this kind.

There must therefore be no confusion of these realities, even though mortal nature was joined with immortal God for the sake of our salvation. And this is believed even after the body’s passion: that he remains in it forever, in which he appeared, so that those who crucified him may also behold him, and through the visible material may look upon his divine nature, which is impassible, with their own eyes; so that judgment may visibly reach its conclusion, the hidden knowledge of the mystery may be revealed, and the majesty and goodness of his power may be recognized by all human beings.

## III. We also find in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is the true God, that he properly comes from the Father, and that he is always with the Father and the Son; that he reigns, creates, is everywhere, saves, gives life, forgives sins, fills all things, sanctifies, judges, teaches, knows all things, and dwells within. Like the Son of God, so also is the Holy Spirit a third person, just as the Son and the Father are.

For there are three persons in whom we believe, truly equal: divine and of one substance—that is, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit properly and truly proceeding from the Father and the Son. Understand first, then, that the Holy Spirit properly comes from the Father, as Scripture says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). And the Savior says: “When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will receive from what is mine, because he will glorify me, and when he comes he will announce it to you” (John 15:26).

And immediately, by interpreting these words, the Lord explains, first of all, that the Holy Spirit is a person, saying: “He will receive from what is mine.” And so that we should not think of him as a servant, or a creature, or the Father, he shows that the Spirit is not inferior to the Father. Explaining the words, he says: “For this reason I told you that he will receive from what is mine, because everything that belongs to the Father is mine.”

If, then, the things that belong to the Father belong to the Son, and all the things that belong to the Son belong to the Holy Spirit, nothing is therefore lacking from the Son in all things that does not pertain to his power; there is nothing that was not made by him and that is not governed by his command and direction. Since, then, the Son has power over all things, nothing is lacking from him in any respect.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, has power over all these things, just as the Son does. For the Savior says of the Spirit: “He will judge the world and convict it, and he will teach concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment: concerning sin, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I am going to my Father; concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has already been judged” (John 16:8ff.).

Do you see, then, that the Holy Spirit announces the Son and teaches concerning the Son, while the Son teaches concerning the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit teaches concerning the Father and the Son?

Since the Trinity is therefore true, it is ineffable, invisible, and almighty. It honorably proclaims and announces itself to every creature, visible and invisible, which is unable adequately either to speak of it, marvel at it, comprehend it, investigate it, or grasp it with human understanding as it is.

It is therefore evident that human weakness fails in recounting the glory, majesty, and power of the holy and venerable Trinity. If an account of the glory of this Trinity exceeds the power of narration, how much more will those be frustrated who dare to place between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit either place, time, or any human cause—people who have not only failed to understand what God is, but have not even been able to consider what a human being is?

There is therefore nothing sudden in the Trinity, nothing most recent, nothing temporal, nothing powerless, nothing lesser, nothing unequal. The Trinity is to be venerated, entreated, spoken of as ineffable, investigated, and acknowledged as incomprehensible.

And concerning the faith of invisible things the Apostle says to us: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the examination of invisible things” (Heb. 11:1). For in this the elders received testimony. Again in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God.” And again: “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 1:18; 3:8).

That the Spirit is God, the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Why have you lied to the Holy Spirit, Ananias? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:4–5). He did not say “to the Father and the Son,” but “to the Holy Spirit.” You see, then, that the Holy Spirit is God.

And that he is everywhere, the holy Prophet says: “Where shall I go from your spirit, Lord? Or where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7). And that the Spirit fills all things, as the Son does, the Prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 15:7). And likewise in the Acts of the Apostles: “Thus says the Spirit, commanding: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2). And again the Apostles say: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28).

And in the Book of Kings God says concerning the Jews: “They have reigned, but not through me, nor through my spirit” (Hos. 8:4). And in the Prophets the Lord says: “Israel has stirred up the spirit of the Lord” (Isa. 53:10).

And that the Holy Spirit dwells in a human being just as the Son does, the Apostle says: “Your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who dwells in you.” And again: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 6:19).

And that the Spirit knows all things, the holy Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge in the same Spirit, to another faith, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretations in the same Spirit, to another governance. But all these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing them to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:7ff.).

He did not say “as he is commanded,” but “as he wills,” showing that the Spirit is not a creature but the true God, from God, and that he can do all things just as the Son can.

Therefore the Apostle immediately says: “Just as no one knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit that is in him, so also no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit who is from God. For the Spirit of God searches even the depths of God.”

You see how Holy Scripture announces to us that the Holy Spirit knows all things, is powerful over all things, is everywhere, has created all things, and saves all things.

Hence the Savior also establishes in the Gospel that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven human beings, either here or in the future, saying: “Therefore I tell you: every blasphemy and every sin will be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven human beings, either here or in the future” (Matt. 12:31).

The Jews were surely calling something else blasphemy against the Holy Spirit except the claim that he was not God, or that he did not properly come from God. For we find that the Jews do not dare deny the Spirit; but when they read of him somewhere in the Scriptures, they either understand him as a creature, such as an angel, or consider him to be the Father himself and take the third person as the Father, or they think that God the Father is composite, although the Father is Spirit of his own proper nature.

From this they also think that he consists of another spirit and the Word, although this belongs more to a composite and material thing than to what is truly divine, incorporeal, and simple. This is commonly understood in this way by the Jews, and sometimes by the pagans as well.

For us, then, there is one Father, and one Son of his, the true God, and one Holy Spirit, the true God; and these three are one—one divinity, one power, and one kingdom. Yet there are three persons, not two, not one, not according to revelation, aggregation, or confusion, but with the divine persons always remaining distinct.

Faith in these persons is given in baptism; from them forgiveness of sin is granted, and eternal life is expected without any doubt. Believing truly in this Trinity, the holy and blessed patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs both earned the glory of martyrdom, attained the hope of everlasting life, and received by inheritance the kingdom of heaven without uncertainty.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

The author was writing around the year 378; this ought to be clear from the following statement near the end of the letter: “The year has not yet been completed since the emperor Gratian, betrayed by his own army, was first subjected to shameful captivity and then overcome by a more pitiable death.”

He appeared to learned critics, and especially to Erasmus, to have imitated Jerome’s style, since he supposedly gathered certain expressions and words from Jerome’s letters to Heliodorus and others. To me, however, he seems not merely to have imitated Jerome, or anxiously to have followed him step by step, as is often done, but almost to reproduce Jerome’s very intellect and flavor throughout the entire sequence of his discourse and the construction of his sentences.

Yet this is precisely what troubles me most. For if we calculate the dates correctly, in the year 378 there was not yet, among Jerome’s writings, such a well-formed model from which his style could have been fashioned. Nor was the celebrated letter to Heliodorus itself sufficient for this purpose. If you compare the present letter with it, you will perceive that they agree more through similarity of subject and the character of the writer than through words or sentences borrowed from it. Some of the more striking expressions in that letter, no less than in this one, can likewise appear to have been taken from Tertullian’s book *To the Martyrs*.

Moreover, our author could not have borrowed from other writings of Jerome, which belong to later periods, the corresponding passages that he possesses. To mention one or two examples explicitly, Jerome says in Letter 29 to Marcella, written in 384: “If by chance we do not know something, let it die in a faithful ear without witness, without judge.” Our author has almost exactly the same words near the end of chapter I.

An even clearer example occurs in Letter 128 to Gaudentius, written thirty-five years later, that is, in 413: “Honey is not offered in the sacrifices of the Lord; wax is despised, although it is the dwelling-place of honey, and oil is burned in the temple of God, pressed from the bitterness of olives.” Our author expresses the same thought, along with many other passages that we omit, in such a way that, since it is certain that these passages could not have been taken from those later writings, the two letters seem—if one may judge from this single argument—to be by one and the same author.

Yet I do not for that reason declare this work also to be an authentic product of Jerome. I shall discuss the matter more fully in the preface.

For the present, know that the words beginning “When pelicans find their young killed by a serpent,” which we have separated by inserting a space, are not—as Erasmus thought—from the preceding words, “And so I send you back to Placentia.” They are an excerpt (*ἀποσπασμάτιον*) from another author who wrote about the natures of animals—an excerpt that is neither learned nor in any way relevant to the subject and that seems to have been carelessly appended through the error of those who arrange the pages of manuscripts, as has happened elsewhere.

# LETTER XVIII. TO PRAESIDIUS  
## On the Paschal Candle

### I

“There is no matter,” says the old Comic poet, “so easy that it cannot become difficult if you undertake it unwillingly.” If he thought that an easy matter could be made difficult by an unwilling spirit, what do you suppose I can do with a subject of the greatest importance, one that no eloquence has ever adequately explained?

For whenever people have wished to speak about the praises of the candle, and, as they say, to spread the sails of their genius with full winds, penetrating as though into the depths of the sea and hiding the neighboring shores, the orator’s shouting immediately detains them at the very doors of their speech. There follows a description of flowers and meadows, and words falling gently like a murmuring breeze, while bees are described—how they are born and give birth without sexual union; how, alone among creatures, free from intercourse, they gather their offspring with their mouths, arrange them by their art, and by some vital process insert souls into the little bees, not from their own substance.

Moreover, Virgil’s entire book of the *Georgics* is brought forward. The king flies in and leads the swarm, and the various tasks are described with such noise that you might think yourself present in a military camp.

But when you have heard or read these things, you will praise the eloquence of the orator. To put the matter briefly, I think you remember Quintilian’s controversial case in which a poor man complains, grieving over the death of his bees and the flowers poisoned by an utterly ruthless rich man.

Suppose these things are pleasant and soothe the ear with measured rhythm. What have they to do with a deacon [another reading omits “what have they to do with a deacon”], what with the mysteries of the Church, what with the time of Easter, when the lamb is slaughtered and the flesh is eaten with its bones while the loins are girded; when the bishop is silent, and the priests are reduced, as it were, to the dress of commoners, while the Levite speaks and teaches what he has scarcely learned—and after proclaiming it at the most festive season, is then ordered to observe a silence lasting the entire year?

Do you see how great the matters are? Do you understand that you are asking something difficult? In the same moment both to compose what must be proclaimed and to explain why it has been proclaimed in this way is the most difficult task of all.

For I nearly passed over the point that this subject ought to be discussed in divine rather than human language. Read the Pentateuch; go through the Old Scripture. Nowhere will you see honey in God’s sacrifices, nowhere the use of wax, but lamps shining and little flames fed with oil.

Why should I argue from the Old Testament? Go through the New Books. These, I believe, are the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles, and the Apocalypse of John. Nothing beyond these: is there a candle anywhere? Is it not at the end of the Gospel—[variant: “faith”] that resounds among the seven lampstands and golden lamps—that the bridegroom is revealed as he comes?

To this you will reply: “I asked you to do this precisely because I knew that what I was asking was difficult.”

Every question is lightly resolved, and one answer is returned for another. I too will think that I ought not to do it precisely because you have asked for something very difficult. Nevertheless, lest I delay you with excuses, if we are together in person, you will hear everything that I think, “so that, if by chance we do not know something, it may die in your ear.”

For the person who writes takes many judges upon himself: one man envies and attacks another’s talent. If a single phrase is missing, one person flees as though from a lame little speech. If another’s rhetorical cothurnus rises slightly above him as he speaks, he will bark that the man is not a presbyter but a rhetorician.

### II

Therefore, if you want to bind yourself to me by this service, abandon the delights of Placentia, adopt Abraham’s way of life, leave your native land, and, spurning the cities, withdraw to the deserts, so that you may pray with Christ.

There will indeed be hard, moldy, and perhaps barley bread. But a king does not love a delicate soldier. Jerusalem, which ate fine flour, honey, and oil, is accused of fornication—not because the foods that a father’s kindness permits are evil, but because a soft warrior falls at the very first battle line and cannot endure the sun after the shade; after the linen cloth, he considers the helmet a burden rather than a protection.

And if your mother obstructs you at the threshold as you wish to leave, speak to her in the words of your Lord: “My mother and my brothers are these: those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

If the women of your household, among whom you were raised, begin to make you weep, and the memory of your father’s estate, its very rooms and hidden corners, begins to hold you back—the places in which you were rolled as an infant, played as a boy, and indulged yourself as an adolescent—remember that all those who now dwell in the desert passed through these same routes to the heavenly choirs and followed the same footsteps.

And to shorten a long speech with a brief summary—for a letter ought not to smell of a book—what we advise you to abandon is either small or great. If it is small, do not think it difficult to despise small things. If it is great, greater rewards are prepared for great things.

But you say: “I want first to sell my father’s estate and, after gathering a small amount of money, either to prepare provisions for the journey or to provide myself as sustenance for the poor.”

Here too, hear the Gospel’s judgment: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, come, and follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

It is already several years since you began to serve God. A mind following Christ does not long endure the burden of the world, nor allow itself to be bound by such chains. Rather, you must fear that while the opportunity to distribute your patrimony is being held out, and while you do not wish to sell something of greater value for less, this may become an obstacle to your purpose. Something bought for ten small coins—or even for one—I will gladly accept, provided that no delay hinders me as I hasten to battle.

Matthew, sitting at the tax booth, hears: “Follow me” (Matt. 9:9). Did he first calculate his accounts, return home, endure the tears of his family, and concern himself with selling his properties, so that he could not follow the Lord’s footsteps unless he first freed himself from the burden of the world?

That disciple who first wished to bid farewell to his parents is rebuked by the Savior’s voice. And certainly there is a great difference between him whose brief return home, though he was about to return immediately, is condemned, and you, who for so long have either failed to sell what is yours, although you can do so quickly, or failed to despise it, but see that many things prevent you from acting.

### III

When you have read this, you will flee to Romulus’ refuge and, climbing upon the altar of Comedy, evade the words of your angry Lord.

“You will say: ‘As a deacon, I cannot safely leave the church. I fear that I shall incur sacrilege if I abandon the altars.’”

Good! My friend, I shall demand more of you if, in addition to the life of a monk, you possess some clerical dignity; if, standing in the apostolic order, you distribute Christ’s body daily to the devout people in humble service.

But consider, I beg you, that it is difficult enough to fill the place of Stephen or Paul, to stand in angelic service, and to look down upon the peoples beneath you from a garment falling from above.

A pearl is precious, but it is quickly broken, and once broken it cannot be restored. A ship, although rough and fastened with solid nails, may have planking that does not feel the swelling waves; yet if it sails dangerously, it is quickly pierced. And although with full winds it may reach its destination more profitably, those things that are tranquil are safer. To speak more openly: you say that you receive greater reward if, standing in the middle of the city, you imitate the life of monks.

What you say is true, but it is not so easily fulfilled in practice as in words. To pass over everything else that draws us away from the stricter life, I shall mention something by comparison with which you will understand even what I have concealed—or rather, feared—to say.

Another man cuts his beard evenly and covers his cheerful brow with shining hair falling from above. But if you pursue your hair down to the skin, as we rustic people are accustomed to do, you will provide laughter for everyone. If your tunic is dark, you will even be pointed out by the fingers of passers-by. Take care, I say, that your boots are not tight, lest your legs fail to shine. Unless you are handsome, you will not be able to be holy.

Someone from the nobility invites you to dinner, and everyone attends in festive eagerness. You must either go or refuse. If you go, you must either eat the same foods as they do or different ones. If different, the eyes of the guests will be offended; if the same, your abstinence is ruined. And if you do not wish to go, then, poor man, you will be eaten at the dinner.

At every cup and every wine sweetened with honey, you will be made to drink. One person will mock your face, another laugh at your walk, another at your clothing. Perhaps, imitating the Jews, they will say: “Is this not the son of the carpenter? Are not his brothers and sisters among us?” (Matt. 13:35). “I remember him doing something disgraceful nearly so many years ago, and saying something even more disgraceful.”

Another will call you a thief and an adulterer and pretend that he himself shared in your crime. Every dinner together will resound with such remarks, and the drunken banquet will be dissolved at your expense.

If you abstain from cheap meats and do not frequently visit the baths, then almost every pillar will bear the title “Manichaean” against you. If you reject the flesh of birds and, when your appetite seeks tender doves and plump turtledoves, a sterner master denies them to your throat, the charge of sacrilege will be fastened upon you.

Immediately they will say: “These are the people who despise the creator of the world. Everything was made for our use.” I heard—I testify before the Lord, I am not lying—that a certain man eloquent in matters of his appetite, having learned by rumor that I abstained from more sumptuous foods, said: “Was a pig made so that a man in a toga might deliver a judgment in the senate?” By this remark he wished to condemn me for foolishness, because I thought that I should not consume what was created for human use.

When such things and others like them tear apart a good life in the cities, what will you do, brother, in their midst? You will either submit your neck to vices or to an anathema: that is, either you will pursue what is opposed to continence, or, if you refuse to do so, you yourself will be condemned.

I pass over the frequent greetings, the attentions of married women, and the various enticements by which even the most rigid minds are softened and drawn to shipwreck by a Siren’s song; the fact that the eye is often unwillingly drawn toward every beautiful form; the fact that the ears are struck by obscene remarks. I assert this: even if these things did not exist, you ought to have abandoned lesser matters in comparison with so great a good.

### IV

Add that you are a deacon, but the church will not feel the loss through your departure. Elijah lived in the desert. The choir of prophets followed Elisha. The Lord’s forerunner, John, was raised in solitude and finally came down to the banks of the Jordan for this purpose: to rebuke the crowds flowing together and, recognizing the Pharisees as clerics, to mark them as broods of vipers.

Recently you saw the deserts of Egypt; you looked upon an angelic household. How many flowers are there! How do the meadows bloom with spiritual jewels! You saw the garlands with which the Lord is crowned. May that fire blaze within your breast.

Think of those things daily, ponder them, desire them, and, as though held in a kind of prison, cry out: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged!” And ascending in mind into paradise, you will not be on earth as often as you look down upon the earth.

Our condition is certainly the same as that of those who live in the deserts. We have the same eyes and the same number of hands. We are subject to the same weaknesses—or virtues.

If drinking water troubles you, how many people of greater rank—not merely ignorant of wine and unfamiliar with meat, but sustained only by poured-out legumes—are there? If the baths trouble you, how many rulers of cities, either because of their own guilt or through envy, have been deported to islands and remain without baths, without reward and future recompense?

No one can endure from necessity what he refuses to endure willingly for God.

You will have a cell large enough for you alone. Indeed, you will not be alone: an angelic throng will live with you. As many companions as there are saints. You will read the Gospel, and Jesus will converse with you. You will recite the apostles or the prophets. Could you have such another companion in your conversations?

We are earth and ashes, and at every moment suspended over our salvation, soon to be dissolved into dust. Why do we hesitate to make a virtue of necessity? Certainly we must eventually die, and the vital organs filled with excrement—organs that daily remind us of our degradation—will drag the whole body with them into similar corruption.

How quickly we should leave behind the narrow confines of the world! And if perhaps on account of continence—which nevertheless rarely happens—we begin to suffer stomach pain or burn with fever, let us regard illness as the gate of eternal life and complete victory. For we know, as Scripture teaches, that no one should be called fully blessed before the end of this life.

How many people have been snatched away by sudden death amid great wealth and the insignia of the consulship? Recently the emperor Valentinian, while raging fiercely in council against the Sarmatians and Quadi because of the devastation of Illyricum and threatening the destruction of the entire nation with severity, suddenly collapsed as blood burst forth.

Why should I speak of his brother, whom the fire of Thrace consumed in opposition to royal majesty? The year has not yet been completed since the emperor Gratian, betrayed by his own army, was first subjected to shameful captivity and then overcome by a more pitiable death.

And, to say nothing of these events, even those who have died a common death are joined after death to the same condition as everyone else. How many of them will be compared on the day of judgment with even the least of the monks?

Let us at least follow the little women; let the weaker sex teach us. How many women possessing both wealth and nobility—I do not wish to name them, lest I seem to flatter them—have judged it easy to do what you, through your own fear, have thought difficult, abandoning their possessions and despising their pledges?

Learn this from the poem of the candle. Adorn that light for yourself with varied flowers. Be a bee yourself as well. Imitate Deborah’s victory. Let Barak pursue Sisera together with you, and, once Israel has been liberated, let the song of Judges resound from you, so that you may compose the honey of Christ.

If you prepare your lamp in this way, you will not sleep when the bridegroom comes; you will enter the king’s chamber.

I wished to say more and to hold you with me by such exhortation, but suddenly it was announced that asses had been hired to carry me all the way to Rome. Therefore, unwillingly, I send you back to Placentia, on the condition that you know: whenever you read these words, you should understand that you must come to the place you promised.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] We have separated this material, which had been attached in continuous sequence to what precedes, although it had no connection with it. Most ancient writers boast of the story of the pelican, which is even more incredible.]

When pelicans find their young killed by a serpent, they mourn and beat both themselves and their sides; and when their blood has been shed, the dead bodies revive in this way. When an eagle grows old, its feathers and eyes become heavy. It seeks a spring, raises its wings, and gathers heat within itself; thus its eyes are healed. It plunges itself three times into the spring, [Note: [Col. 0187D] The true Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah 40, says: “We have often stated that the old age of eagles is restored to youth by the changing of their feathers.” Eustathius, in his *Hexameron*, p. 27, has substantially the same account from Pseudo-Jerome, not to mention others.] and in this way returns to youth.

The phoenix is a bird in India. For five hundred years it fills itself with spices from Lebanon and thus builds its nest [Col. 0187B] [Note: [Col. 0187D] This passage should be emended and supplemented from the old Lyon edition as follows: “and thus it builds its nest.” And it gives notice to the priest [Col. 0188D] …] and gives notice to the Heliopolitan priest in the month of Phamenoth or Pharmouthi. The priest fills the altar with branches, and there the phoenix brings its spices and places amber upon the altar. At the first rising of the sun, the phoenix moves its wings; the amber is kindled by the sun’s heat, and thus the spices are burned, and the phoenix itself is set ablaze. On the following day a worm is born from the ashes; on the second day it grows wings; on the third it returns to its former nature, and thus goes back to its own regions.

When a serpent grows old, it loses its sight. If it wishes to return to youth, it fasts for forty days, so that its skin may loosen; then it seeks a narrow opening, so that, as it struggles to emerge, it may cast off the skin of old age. When a snake comes to drink, it deposits its venom in the water, lest the venom, congealed by the water, should kill it. [Note: [Col. 0188D] Isidore, *Etymologies* XII.4: “It is said that a serpent has not dared to touch a naked man.”] It fears a naked man and pursues one who is clothed; yet when it is struck, it conceals its head, where it knows its death lies. A serpent dies if struck once with a reed; but if struck a second time, it is strengthened. In winter it becomes weaker and is overcome by mice. Therefore, before winter, it gathers grain around itself, so that it may have food.

Vipers copulate mouth to mouth. The males disregard death, but the female, during the very act of intercourse—whether driven by great pleasure or foreseeing the danger to come—bites off the male’s head while she swallows the seed and thus kills him. But when she has conceived, her entrails are eaten by the very young whom she has conceived, and they thus kill their mother.

Ants that carry nothing do not steal the burdens of those that do carry. But when they have stored wheat, they divide the grains, fearing that, if rain should come, they might sprout.

If a fox has been hungry for a long time, it rolls about in the dust and pretends to be dead. The birds then come, and while they intend to eat it, they are eaten. A little fox plays with hares and in this way kills them. [Col. 0188A]

The panther resembles the leopard; it is of varied color and gentle. When it has eaten its fill, it sleeps for three days. After the third day it rises and cries out, thereby emitting a sweet odor and summoning all the wild beasts, which are drawn by the scent. It is friendly to all wild beasts except the dragon and the asp.

The sea-turtle is as large as an island. When it rises from the deep, it shows itself in the sea like a rock and does not move from there until men tie their ships to it. When it senses this, it pulls itself into the deep. But when it is hungry, it opens its mouth and gives off a pleasant odor; the other fish gather toward it.

The partridge warms the eggs of another bird after losing its own. But when the chicks have grown, they fly from the nest and return to their own parents, abandoning the parent who deceived them.

Partridges set ambushes for one another. If those who possess them bring them to the forest, they utter a hidden cry; the others come and are caught in nets. They flee the bird-catchers more by their feet than by their wings. If they are about to be caught, they seek a stone resembling them in color and lie there on their backs.

When a vulture begins to lay eggs, it first takes from the land of India a stone called *Instintium*. It is like a nut and has inside it something that moves and produces a sound. The vulture places this beneath itself. It produces many offspring, but only one survives. For when they have no food, they watch one another sleeping and eat one another until only one remains. [Note: [Col. 0188D] Eustathius gives nearly the same account, word for word, of the vulture in his *Hexameron*. He does not call that stone *Instintium*, however, but *εὐτοκίον*, from its supposed power to promote childbirth. Others call it *ὠκυτοκίον*. The stone is the *ἀετίτης*, or “eagle-stone.” Hence, instead of *Instintium*, a meaningless name, or *Eutocium*, I would prefer that *Ocytocium* also be written here.]

The myrmicoleon—“lion” in front and “ant” behind—is born from two animals. Its first food is its mother’s milk, that is, the ant’s. For the mother is nourished on leguminous food like an ant.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 0188C] Novatian wrote a book bearing the same title as this one, as is clear from the catalogue. Nor were there lacking those who attributed this very work to Novatian, although mention is found in it not only of the Manichaean but also of the Arian heresy.

Erasmus says: “Although I admit that this book is not unworthy of being read, its style most clearly declares, if it is anything at all, that it was not written by Jerome.” The title varied in the manuscripts: in some copies it was addressed to Terentia, in others to Therasia. Moreover, in the book itself there is no mention of anything relating either to the author or to those to whom he wrote, although the blessed Jerome ordinarily introduces such matters, especially at the beginning and end. Finally, although it is a substantial work on a well-known subject, Jerome nowhere cites it, whereas he customarily cites his other writings. If a catalogue of Tertullian’s works were extant, perhaps it would be found among his compositions; for its diction is not unlike his style.

# LETTER XIX. On True Circumcision

[Col. 0188D]

## I

In the preceding letter, which your inquiry drew from me and which I sent under your name and that of your sister, I ran rapidly over the meaning of circumcision, because the preparations for my journey, during which it was composed, denied it not only the file of polish but also the completion of the work, although I myself am frightened by the things that are filed smooth. If polished things do not please, my mind is afraid to consider what judgment unformed things deserve. Yet I sent it not to the judges’ benches but to the crown of those who favor me.

Indeed, my judgment would not have appeared unless it had been drawn from the secrecy of modesty by you, as though by a hand of charity. But since I can no longer make it better, I have decided to recall and reconsider with you a word once released: your way of life is an interpretation of circumcision and an exposition of the whole law.

The law seems obscure because there are few in whom it is seen. For God’s word is life, and by living otherwise than life itself, we make God’s word obscure. If we lived that life which alone is life, there would be no need to expound its law; it would be easier to see than to speak, since “the kingdom of God is not in word but in power” (1 Cor. 4:20).

Therefore, in the abundance of our affection, we may discuss with you what we have learned in you, and disclose to you what your life has supplied us, lest it remain obscure. But what new thing are we saying, if either you live what we are about to say, or, in your presence, we speak what we have learned in you? One who remembers what must be remembered does not seek admonitions, and one who is instructed does not investigate what he already knows.

## II

You, most beloved daughter, live by circumcision. Yet I propose to discuss with you why the circumcision of the Jews is not performed on a finger, an ear, or some other part of the body—something that would rightly be called irrational if it had not been instituted by God. Nothing is done by God without reason; nothing happens by chance, as the nations say; nothing in him is left to blind fortune. Those are blind who think fortune possesses any power. God himself is reason, and just as he formed everything with complete rationality, so he commanded nothing to be done by human beings without reason.

For if he arranged the elements that we see with such wisdom that the earth should be this earth, on which the other things move, firm and unmoving; that the channels of the waters should be stored in the higher mountains, from which rivers, flowing widely over great distances, should provide living creatures with water to drink throughout their course; that the sea should not rise beyond its bounds, but should seem, as it were, a belly of liquids thirsting for the waters that flow into it; that the earth should not be covered forever by a perpetual flood from springs that flow eternally, rivers that run without end, or rains that fall continually; and that the sky, beyond the fullness of light in the sun, should shine also with the stars of night, so that no time would be deprived of light—
