if, then, he described these transitory things with such wisdom, although he himself says, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35), that we believe they could not have been otherwise, would he perhaps have permitted human beings themselves, for whom he has devised, ordered, and established all these things, to live without reason? Their adoption is sonship, and theirs are the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; from them also comes Christ according to the flesh, who is blessed forever.

Far be it, then, that he from whom he also willed his Son to arise according to human nature should have established for them a covenant without complete reason. But since it is so evident that everything ordered by God is full of reason that it needs no advocate, let us see why the Lord chose for circumcision that part of the body which is more secret and hidden, or that which the Greeks call *φύσις* (*physis*) and we call *natura*, “nature.” For, as a sign by which he wished his servants to be counted among the descendants of Abraham, he could surely have chosen something placed openly before everyone’s eyes and called by another name—something in which there would have been neither obscurity in the sign nor confusion in the name.

[Col. 0190B]

## III

Both images, however, possessed the reason of a twofold truth. While I explain it, grant me your patience, so that you, who believed that circumcision was absent from your life, may now see your life within that circumcision.

First, consider what was signified by the more secret part of the body. It undoubtedly signified what the Lord later demonstrated: that we should not perform our righteousness before human beings, but secretly before him alone, to whom alone nothing is hidden and whom alone we know to be the rewarder of good deeds.

Our circumcision is not seen here, because it is covered as though by a garment, by the veil of worldly foolishness. Nor should we greatly desire that circumcision be openly exposed to everyone’s gaze, lest the reward of the deed belong almost to those whom we want to see it. The Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

Rather, it must be possessed modestly and discreetly, and veiled according to the image that we clothe with greater honor, so that those who see it do not see it. But let those who search and examine within us confess, in accordance with the Apostle, that those whom they think deceivers are truthful; that those whom they believed to possess nothing possess everything; and that those whom they judged to be dying live forever (cf. 1 Cor. 6:9).

This is the glory of hidden circumcision: the glory of the shameful part, not to be exposed for them to see nor to be a source of shame for us in our own bodies. This is the glorious testimony which those who once rejoiced to hate now desire to love after their conversion.

Therefore we must be Jews not openly in the flesh, but secretly in the heart—not according to the letter but according to the spirit. The letter lies before our eyes; the spirit avoids the carnal gaze, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, praise may be obtained from God and not from human beings.

But let us fear hearing from the Lord: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8). Consider the man who, concerning what belonged to the lips, calls him “Good Teacher,” seeking from the good man what is good. To him the old law—that is, carnal circumcision—was recited as something lying on the surface. When he testified that he had fulfilled it and heard what pertained to circumcision of the heart—“Sell all that you have and follow me” (Matt. 19:21)—he went away sad: utterly wretched, because he refused to follow the one whom he could not deny to be good.

That inner sign, then, is the prefiguration seen in our invisible mind by our invisible God, so that he would not heed the one by whom he was invoked, but would regard the one by whom he was believed in. “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33:16), if righteousness is believed with the heart.

But we falsely claim to believe with our whole heart if we receive honor from human beings. We receive honor from human beings if a trumpet, proclaiming our alms to the people, goes before us, although we are not permitted even to let our left hand know what our right hand does in the service of giving.

We receive honor from human beings if our fasts and abstinence from food are commended to the eyes of the people by a faltering gait that feigns weakness, and if pallor summoned by a gloomy face wins the favor of the crowd; or if the face, raised into an appearance of joy, is brightened by baths; if the head is anointed in the manner of a festival, so that, commending our fasts to God alone, we may say: “We will sacrifice to you willingly, O Lord” (Ps. 53:8).

You see, daughter, that you live what you recognize in the character of that hidden circumcision: outwardly poor, inwardly rich; outwardly without the law, inwardly under the law; avoiding public banquets in the eyes of the people, yet joining the merit of the Evangelist in the esteem of those who invite you.

## IV

But let us at last come to true life itself, that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us see whether he taught and did anything of this kind, since what was made in him was life (John 1:4). Did he too perform circumcision as though in a hidden part of the body, wishing both what he did and who he was to be recognized by human beings?

First, after that heavenly teaching, when he descended from the mountain surrounded by the crowds of admiring people and cleansed the filth of a leprous man (Matt. 8:1), he did not, in accordance with ordinary human custom, desire praise or public acclaim in return for so great a benefit of healing. Conscious of what he was to himself alone, he needed no testimony from his elders. He commanded the man to tell no one of his power. He also wished the secret of the divine Majesty—the mystery of the Incarnation, which he had concealed—to be kept silent by the one who had been healed, lest he seem to seek glory as a human being, though he accepted it in another manner and for a mystical reason.

For he commanded him to show himself to the priest and offer a gift to God. He prescribed the gift that Moses had commanded as a testimony to them, so that, while he remained silent about what he had commanded as the Son of Man, he might carry out the commands of the law which God himself had given to Moses; and so that, while the man he had seen in the flesh was forbidden to praise him, he might nevertheless magnify God in the offering of the gift.

Thus the glory of the Son of Man, forbidden at the entrance, seems to enter through the womb itself, since the one who must not be proclaimed as a human being, to whom the vows of healing must be paid as to God, is not to be celebrated carnally in the corners of the streets but worshiped spiritually in the temple. If, according to his humanity, he seeks nothing, according to his divinity he deserves the glory of divine power.

He adds similar examples so that the truth might be supported by fuller testimony. He asks his disciples who the eminent person among the people is considered to be. They name the prophets. He carefully presses them to disclose what they themselves think. Blessed Peter answers him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). The Lord declares blessed the one to whom flesh and blood had not revealed this, but his Father who is in heaven.

Then Peter is named from the Rock, after he first recognized that cornerstone. Yet, after granting Peter many blessings and powers of virtue, he commands that none of the disciples should say that he himself was the Christ.

What a remarkable reason: he does not wish to have proclaimed what he rejoices to have understood. He loves to be recognized and hates to be displayed, thus practicing the mystery of hidden circumcision. He prefers to be found rather than betrayed, so that his power, not another person’s favor, might reveal him.

Yet another kind of understanding is also present in this command. The Lord forbids them to proclaim the very thing for which he had praised Peter. He would certainly have been offended if, contrary to his will, they confessed what Peter had discerned. If he had wished to grant them freedom to speak, the betrayer might have had a prepared excuse: “You allowed us, your disciples, to disclose you to everyone; it cannot be charged against me if someone came to you with a different intention from the one in which I, your praiser, displayed you.”

But since whatever is forbidden is unlawful, he did not wish to be rightly celebrated by anyone while he was being wrongly betrayed by Judas. Therefore he commands the disciples to tell no one that he is the Christ. The prohibitory sentence extends toward Judas and cuts down the betrayer whom he foresaw, marking by the very word of the command the majesty that the command was meant to signify.

The Evangelist reports it in these words: “Then he commanded his disciples that they should tell no one that he was the Christ” (ibid., 20). And Judas the betrayer said to those who had come with him: “He is the one; seize him” (Matt. 26:48). Obedience turns toward the prohibited word; and, lest forgetfulness provide a pretext for excuse, unhappy memory suggested a sacrilege that had to be carried through, while he himself was betrayed by the very speech with which he guarded against betrayal. Thus a reason that cannot be equalized remains on both sides. The Lord also shows that he must be betrayed in the very act of being betrayed.

## V

But forgive me, because the meaning of God’s word, richer in exposition, has carried me onto another path, although what is suppressed may distress you more than what is disclosed; and you may be more angry that I remain silent about these matters than that I speak at length about them—matters whose judgments of the Lord you desire as though they were gold and precious stones, in which you match honey with the honeycomb, and in which you do not lack even the fullness of your desires, though you may be satisfied.

Let us therefore take another example from the Lord himself, so that, in accordance with the law, “every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18:16). We have said that he did not wish to be disclosed; let us also show that he wished to be seen, so that he would not merely allow others to honor him, but would himself, insofar as possible, diminish the dignity owed to him.

He does not hear and announce the death of Lazarus, his friend (John 12:11). He did this from his divinity—what wonder is it?—so that, while he was visibly present locally as a human being, he might be believed never to be absent in his divinity.

He hastens to Bethany, while the disciples almost murmur, compassion is about to perform a miracle. The sisters of the dead man meet him in mournful clothing, with tearful faces and disheveled hair. He orders them to be of good courage if they believe. He affirms that Lazarus lives, if they will not doubt it. He also sees the crowd accompanying Martha and Mary, which had gathered with them for consolation.

The Evangelist says: “He groaned in spirit and was troubled,” and said, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:33–34). What is this? What is the cause of this confusion? What of this fear? Why does he blush or fear, when the power is about to perform a miracle and divinity is not subject to terror? What is the meaning of this thoughtless inquiry after the tomb? You might altogether believe that it arose from one who was troubled and confused.

That God of ours, who had confidently said to his disciples concerning one absent, “Lazarus is dead,” and who had confidently promised his sisters concerning the dead man, “He will rise again,” now seeks the tomb under some new and inexplicable confusion, as though he alone, who knew and could accomplish all things, did not know where the man had been placed.

But this is not really the case; another meaning is hidden. In his earlier words and promises the divinity had sufficiently revealed itself. A crowd of Jews was present, always hostile to such miracles. Plainly, God would have been exposed if he had not seemed, according to his humanity, to be ignorant of something.

“He was troubled,” he says: that is, the filth of the flesh is mingled with the divinity, which must not be disclosed, and the divinity is recalled under the veil of human ignorance. Thus a spring is troubled when mud stirred up by some accident thickens the purity of its liquid element; while the confusion of the two things is separated, the distinction of their properties is concealed.

For he says, “Where have you laid him?” Here too, troubled before the Jews, he conceals divinity in humanity and overlays the splendor of divinity, amid the radiance of so great a work, with the ignorance of mortality. Thus, although God could be worshiped in the raising of Lazarus, the human being is made insignificant by his ignorance of the tomb.

In this way, while he is seen by the blind and not seen by those who see; while he raises children for Abraham from stones (Matt. 3:9) and causes the children of destruction to stumble against the stone of offense; he carries out the mystery of hidden action: the weak and feeble recognize him, without anyone pointing him out, in order to ask him for the help of salvation, while persecutors and enemies do not know whom they ought to seize unless he is betrayed.

## VI

This is the book written within and without; secret and public; open and covered; visible on the upper pages but invisible on the inner ones, because it is incomprehensible (Rev. 5:1).

It is written within when the Prophet says: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). It is written without when the Evangelist says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1).

It is written within when God says: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44:2). It is written without when Isaiah prophesies: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14).

It is written within when John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). It is written without through Matthew: “Now the generation of Christ was as follows: when his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph.” It is written within: “She was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18). What does “with child” mean? The Word of the Lord, the Word made flesh under the law.

It is written without when the apostles are asked who people say the Lord is, and some answer Elijah, some Jeremiah, and others one of the prophets (Matt. 16:14). It is written within when Peter cries out: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16). Therefore the Lord himself says: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, Peter, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17).

Whose flesh and blood? Was Peter’s own flesh and blood preventing him from being called the Son of God? No, but the Lord’s own flesh and blood: while he was seen as a human being, people did not believe that he was what he was—the Son of God. For it seemed impossible to human beings to believe that he was God when they saw a human being, and that such great majesty, in which the fullness of divinity dwells, which the world itself cannot contain, was enclosed in a little body of contemptible appearance.

He therefore says: “It was not this flesh and blood of mine that revealed to you that I am the Son of God. They do not allow me to be believed to be this. The Prophet had said: ‘And he is a man, and who will know him?’ Evidently those who judge according to human appearance or sight call me either Elijah the prophet or one of the prophets, because they recognize that I am a human being by the appearance of my flesh. But my Father who is in heaven revealed me to you.”

When did he reveal this? At what time did God speak with Peter? “My Father who is in heaven revealed it,” he says—that is, you believed the works that speak of the Son of God.

But, as we were saying, the book is written without when the Lord is hungry; it is written within when he satisfies many thousands of people with five loaves (Matt. 14:20). It is written without when he weeps at the death of his friend (John 11:35); it is written within when he raises the very one for whom he wept.

It is written without when he is fastened to the cross; it is written within when he promises paradise to the robber on the cross. It is written without when, dying according to the condition of human flesh, he gives up his spirit; it is written within when, during his passion, the sun is darkened, the day is hidden, and the earth is shaken.

It is written without when he is buried; it is written within when, on the third day, after the stone of the tomb has been removed, he bursts forth into the light (Matt. 28:3).

It is written without when, showing the wounds of the nails and the spear to the apostles, he also asks for food (Luke 24:40 ff.); it is written within when, among those same apostles, with the doors shut, he appears—although he seemed not to have entered.

Yet, remarkably, although the inner writing of the book is more obscure, the outer writing disturbs human minds more deeply. While they see things that cannot be seen through a human being, they do not see, by a novel inversion, the things that can be seen through a human being.

For the Manichaeans believe what cannot be seen and do not believe what can be seen, although blessed John has marked the invisible and visible God and human being with a brief kind of inscription. He says: “What was from the beginning, brothers, what we have heard” (1 John 1:1). Behold the inner part of that book.

What follows—“and we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have touched concerning the Word of life”—is the outer part of the book, subject to the eyes and hands of human beings, and capable both of being seen and handled.

## VII

The Manichaean is ignorant of this part of the book: he sees the works that are done but does not see the one who does them. He may indeed say, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” but he cannot say, “The Lord is the Son of Man, Lord even of the Sabbath.” With remarkable perversity, they deny what they see and confess what they do not see. They recognize the invisible one in his powers, but they do not acknowledge the visible one in his humanity, although that should have been easiest.

O blindness! O ignorance of truth! O presumption deserving condemnation by every form of reason! These are the people who set themselves above God himself. By believing in this way while established in the flesh, they claim to live spiritually, although they do not believe that God could do what they themselves claim to do.

God is undoubtedly lesser in their judgment if he could not do what they can. For if they, while established in the flesh, can receive another nature, why could he, placed in the flesh, not preserve his own nature—so that he might always be God and, without being mixed with corruption, not begin to be corrupt?

A remarkable argument: it destroys God while honoring him. It requires less power to obtain divinity within an earthly substance than for God to remain spiritually in his divinity.

What, then, shall I marvel at in God, except that, when he deigned to become human, he revealed in the human being that he was God? Not that he ceased to be what he had been, but that he caused flesh to be what God is; that, for the sake of excusing defective matter, he himself remained without defect; that, although he became sin for us, he could not become a sinner.

But here the Manichaean, and again the Arian, grasping the upper part of the book with both hands, fears to open the inner page, as though he would commit sacrilege if God, coming in the flesh, did not lose his divinity. He sees the Lord sleeping in a little boat but does not see him commanding the winds and waves. He falsely claims to attribute divinity to him without the likeness of the Father.

For God cannot be God unless he is like the Father, that is, like God. Yet the ordinary language of every day should have instructed them that he is like the Father, and that the one written without has lost nothing from the inner parts. We are accustomed to approve sons who resemble their fathers in everything, so that we say, “He came forth from his mouth.”

Thus every son, however he may be born according to carnal generation, will nevertheless, if he happens to resemble his father in every respect, be said to have proceeded from his mouth. Who does not see that God the Word, uttered from the heart of the Father and brought forth in the Spirit from no other source than the mouth, is judged, even according to ordinary human understanding, to be like the Father?

When we have understood this faithfully, we shall be able to say that you believe both the things written without and the things divinely recorded within, and that you call them one book. Seeing the whole law written in it, we should not follow the arguments of philosophers and gather truth by conjecture. Instead, let us place the pattern of life before our eyes and marvel at that very tangible reality in which whatever may be obscure will be poured forth.

The Manichaeans, failing to see it in the flesh, and the Arians, failing to understand it in the spirit, have cut apart the united structure of the pages of one book and, in heretical frenzy, torn apart the mediator of the two with hands joined together.

## VIII

But what wonder is it if the subtlety of the concatenation of the book, covered and uncovered, escaped these men, who are excessively wise in each individual page and come from worldly philosophy, when even the Jews, who belonged to him, did not recognize him when he came to his own?

While they ask for a sign from heaven—as though the things he performed by heavenly power for the salvation of the weak and the dead were not heavenly—they were blinded by their own unbelief and deserved, even while seeing, not to see.

The Lord was angered that the operation of divinity should be despised in him, and from the riches of his wisdom arranged that the form of a servant should be regarded as contemptible. To those for whom his divinity had not shone forth through his power, he became in every respect an object of contempt, so that his humanity, as judged according to the world, might appear in him unworthy of reverence.

And since Israel did not receive its Lord in the spirit, why should Judah receive and recognize its brother in the flesh? For it was not fitting that those who overthrew greater things and, while ignorant, committed what they wished to regard as sacrilege should not also knowingly commit murder.

Finally, he promises the sign of Jonah to the unbelieving. And the wretched people, despising themselves, kill the servant of God in one and the same human being, so that the one whom, according to their own law, they had not recognized as God, they might condemn outside their law, in a pagan manner, as a criminal.

Thus he earned the ignoble features of the passion, as though veiled, through the operation of which we were speaking, when he clothed the nature of divinity in the garment of mortality; when, among those ashamed to acknowledge him, he himself is put to shame; when they do not believe that the human being is from God; when, finally, he inclines in himself the human form, contemptible to others, so that he may suffer; when among the disciples he is the Word of God, but among the rulers he is found to be a human being without a word.

Therefore, if the Lord of heaven and earth, whose name is above every name, taking the form of a servant, “did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2:7), and cast himself into despised humanity while deliberately veiling his divinity; if he did not wish to be seen as what could not fail to be recognized, what will it be expedient for human beings to observe under the appearance of hidden circumcision—human beings whom he humbled beyond nature by his example and by his command?

They will act more wisely if, even after doing everything, they say: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what was commanded” (Luke 17:10), rather than, lifted up by presumptuous confidence, asking that one sit at his right and another at his left in his kingdom. Otherwise the Lord whom they were thought to love more will answer them: “You do not know what you are asking” (Matt. 20:22).

He immediately sets before them the fear of his passion, which humbles those exalted according to the flesh. When they boldly ask for it, he rightly says to them: “To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you.”

Did he here confess himself unworthy of power, or testify that nothing was permitted to him, when he says, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22)? “It is not mine to give you,” he says—that is, not to those who ask in this proud, insolent, and presumptuous manner, out of the swelling of the flesh rather than the gentleness of the spirit. For I, who now resist you, am accustomed to give grace to the humble.

Thus, while the Lord teaches by both word and deed those who truly listen to humility, he shows why he wished to have the prefiguration of true circumcision in the secret part of the body.

## IX

I have spoken about the hidden circumcision, insofar as I thought it should be discussed. It remains for us to examine circumcision itself: what figure it represents, and why we are not circumcised in eye and hand, when the Lord says: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out; and if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off” (Matt. 5:29). What such a great prefiguration is contained there, that through one part of the body the whole human being is believed to be circumcised—and although after Christ we do not perform this in the flesh, as the Jews do, nevertheless we are judged to perform it through him in the heart?

Let us come to the heavenly sacraments of our regeneration, so that we may seek spiritual circumcision in spiritual birth. At the very cradles of our faith, at the time when circumcision is celebrated, let us repeat the first cries of our consecrated infancy, and place before our eyes that renunciation by which we are stripped of our foreskins. For just as those who were born carnally into the world were circumcised carnally under the law, so those who are now born through the word for the kingdom of heaven are circumcised from the world by the word.

For this is what we say: that we renounce the world and its pomp, since whatever is in the world is “the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age,” which is not from the Father (1 John 2:16). This, then, is the promise and the circumcision which we do not suffer as slaves, but offer as free persons. We do not celebrate it after we have been born, but offer it as we are reborn. Stripped of every garment in the preparation for baptism, we are clothed only in confession before the eyes of the saints.

We do not cover our natural appearance with a garment of woven threads, destined to be burned, because in the Gospel the tree luxuriant in leaves, when no fruit was found on it, withered. Rather, having rejected the whole nature of the flesh, forgetful of sex, we fear nothing. Nor, fleeing from God, do we hear with that first earthly man, Adam, “Where are you?” (Gen. 3:9); instead, following that second, heavenly man, we hear: “Today I have begotten you” (Acts 13:33).

Thus, through submission to heavenly obedience rejecting the foreskins which Adam the transgressor acquired, we circumcise the nature of our vices. Through the single form of a bodily member, we pursue and cut away all the senses that exercise themselves in foreskin. For we do not cut away nature, but what is excessive in nature, knowing that “whatever is more than this is from evil.”

Thus we attain the Lord’s favor, so that although we are called foreskin according to the flesh—that is, as though naturally covered by a kind of ignorance—we nevertheless, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord. Those who are called circumcision according to the flesh, however, are blinded by veils placed before their faces, lest they look into the law.

The figure of bodily circumcision has therefore been emptied, and has passed wholly into the force of its name, since even foreskin is counted as circumcision. This happens if, after the word of the Lord, we yield to the allurements of this corrupted nature and once again follow the incentives of vice; or if, though uncircumcised in the flesh, we persecute that very nature along with its accompaniments and, by failing to keep the word of the Lord, trample it down.

## X

But whether these things are so, let us question both the father of faith and the author of circumcision, since both kinds of circumcision—the kind pertaining to the mind and the kind pertaining to the body—proceeded from him. He himself will answer us through his deeds whether Jewish circumcision commended him to God, or this circumcision of ours of which we speak.

First he hears from the Lord: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12:1). Under this word, while according to the flesh he was still in foreskin, he circumcised himself from his parents. Breaking away from his homeland and from the whole nature to which he was bound by affection, he follows the word of the Lord as an exile.

Then, from a barren and aged wife—both against the defect of nature and against the condition of failing age—a multitude of descendants is promised him. He does not consider his own body, already dead when he was almost a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of his wife Sarah, whose menstruation had ceased, even if she had not previously been barren. Rather, placing hope upon the promise, he earns justification by believing.

He is therefore chosen before he is circumcised in the flesh. For it was written first: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3).

God therefore commands: “Let every male of yours be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin” (Gen. 17:10). He also added the significance of this matter, lest it remain obscure. For he says: “And it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” A sign pertains to the eyes, so that it might be recognized by those who would not think that he had rejected worldly nature through the word of the Lord. If there were people who did not know Abraham’s faith and the virtue of his action, through the sign, as through an image depicted by some comparison, they might recognize what was true.

Then the Prophet also promises a visible sign to the unbelieving people who refused to believe in God because he cannot be seen, saying: “Your God himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14).

The Jews themselves, when they saw the Lord only in the flesh and denied faith to his works of power, ask for a sign from heaven, plainly so that they might believe if they saw.

God therefore, in accordance with the time, wished that when Abraham’s descendants could, if possible, follow with equal steps the path of their election in faith, righteousness should be marked in this sign. Thus, for the one who had rejected worldly nature from the soul, carnal circumcision would appear in the body, and what was understood inwardly could, as it were, be perceived through what was visible.

In the same way, many things announced by the prophets to the people were first enacted by those through whom they were proclaimed. The Lord, in anger, threatened through the Prophet that the sons of Israel would be led naked into captivity. Certainly, the saying could already have sufficed for a full understanding of the matter. Yet the Prophet himself goes naked among the peoples and displays in himself what he prophesied for others. The crowd sees but does not hear, and in Isaiah’s body recognizes what was to come upon it. The prophet becomes a sign, and while the people are still free, the Prophet experiences the bitterness of captivity.

So Abraham designates in the flesh what he practiced in the mind. Through the name of a member he understands, as it were, the virtue of circumcision—not by this sign expressing the flesh, but the sign of faith.

Finally, after that circumcision of his flesh, if it contained the fullness of righteousness, why was God still seeking greater tests of faith from Abraham? Why was he later tested in his paternal affection, if he already held the supreme blessing in that other circumcision?  
[Alternative reading: “if he already held the summit of blessing in that other circumcision.”]

But since it was not that virtue itself, but its sign, that was commanded, the unique man is asked whether he who had already renounced his homeland and kindred, and had allowed himself to be circumcised, would also spare his son.

When he presented him for sacrifice without grief, through impiety toward his beloved pledge he became exalted above carnal affection. He gains childlessness while contemplating parricide; while he does not spare his only son on earth, he is commanded to count the stars in heaven as his children. The despiser of carnal nature is placed among the nature of the stars, and the scorner of human seed is called the father of the heavenly bodies.

Thus, faithful not to his son but to the commandment, and judging that obedience to the Lord was religion rather than crime, that offering his son to God was sacrifice rather than parricide, he almost deserved to foresee that God had willed parricide to be offered for the testing of his mind, but had not willed it to be carried out.

## XI

From this truth the form of Jewish circumcision was admitted: it was a figure of the name, not of the member.

God wished our nature to be stripped bare in such a way that neither desire burned within us, nor ambition labored, nor carnal affection prevailed, but that the love of God and contempt for present things might strip us of every foreskin.

A certain satirical poet of the Gentiles said: “Integrity is praised—and grows cold.” This testimony is true. No crowd surrounds it, no multitude encircles it, no human being embraces it. In this world, as in a stepmother’s house, it shivers, though covered even with necessities, so long as it has not acquired the garment of its own dignity.

Come, if it seems good, let us traverse the whole path of truth through the deeds of the patriarchs, as though through living footprints, so that we may demonstrate circumcision which sanctifies.

I pass over Isaac traveling as an exile, although this itself consists in the form of circumcision. I also pass over his calling Rebekah his sister rather than his wife because of the ambushes of the Philistines (Gen. 26:7). I leave it to you to judge how great a sacrament this likewise contains.

I say nothing of Jacob, who for two weeks of years purchased the mothers of the twelve tribes through servitude. I omit his sons, whom a certain natural necessity held within the blessing and holiness of their homeland.

I come to Job, who had already fallen into another line of descent from the stock of Isaac, who was not numbered among the twelve sons of Jacob, who was born through Esau, deprived of the first blessing, stripped of the dignities of the firstborn, and found among the princes of Edom to be pleasing to God.

Yet he is tested as to whether he can bear natural circumcision with equanimity. He becomes poor from being rich—but even the men of this world know how to despise that. He is wounded by as many bereavements as he had boasted of successions.

In a strong voice he cries out that, naked of wealth and naked of children, he came naked from his mother’s womb and naked will return beneath the earth; the Lord gave, and the Lord took away (Job 1:21).

O man rejecting the nature of the world, who did not surrender himself to tears, groans, or even darkness, but instead received the losses of his children as aids to his merits! Victorious over his sufferings, even deprived of his senses, he becomes stronger in affection when he is weakened, and in the valley of tears he occupies a tower of glory.

Where are you, O Judaea, in your circumcised flesh alone? Set your foot beside this man and compete in glory. Raise yourself through the proud virtues of your ancestors; gird your side with the blessed names of noble patriarchs, so that in you the ancient virtue of justifications and the splendor of your forefathers may appear.

Job comes forward against you, not ashamed of the authors of his blood, nor falsely claiming through Esau an illicit transmission of blessing. For we know that that inheritance can neither help nor harm, since the Lord says: “The soul of the father and the soul of the son are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:4).

Accordingly, he has hope because he surpasses you in all these things, and he comes forward claiming more for himself from his own virtue, precisely because he promises less from another’s glory.

Finally, Job, stripped of all his possessions, asks for nothing. You sigh for Egypt in the wilderness after the delicacies of manna. The trials of so many evils do not draw him away from the hope placed in God; the allurements of all good things do not summon you to that hope.

Feeling the hand of the Lord, he blessed him in his wound; while you, freed from Pharaoh’s yoke by mighty works, do not submit.

Therefore he is permitted to ask pardon even for the circumcised, while you, as though uncircumcised, are told that the Amorite is your father and your mother a Hittite, so that it may plainly be clear both that he, through the virtues of his deeds, restored to himself the blessing which his great-grandfather had lost, without observing circumcision, and that you, through boasting of circumcision while neglecting the virtues, lost the blessing which Jacob had acquired through his sole subtlety.

## XII

For what will the arrogance of the Jews not claim for itself? This Job, who pleased God, is in a certain sense of my people, and perhaps he was circumcised, since he is descended to this day from circumcised Esau. Yet in this matter it was not circumcision that was praised, but virtue. It is not to be asked whether he lived without foreskin, but to be held firmly that he committed no sin with his lips.

Let us come to the foreigners to whom he appealed, since in the field of divine examples—fruitful with every kind of tree—we do not reckon any tree of ours to have been planted, nor shoots from a vine, but produce.

Let us display foreign glory in Israel, and say that the shoot of blessing flowed from a tree not its own. Let us mention Ruth, so that they may be more greatly confounded in a woman.  
[Variant in the margin: “The shoot of blessing flowed from its own tree; we do not mention Ruth.”]

The prophets promise that from the root of Jesse a branch will come forth for our salvation, upon which a flower would rise—one which alone would exhale the fragrance of a full field for its companions, and which the Father would anoint with the oil of gladness beyond all spices, as a fragrance of ointments.

Yet this Jesse had a grandmother who was not an Israelite, but a Moabite. So much is granted to this foreign woman as no woman from the stock of the patriarchs earns: she receives in her womb the seed of the destined blessing, gives birth to dignity for Israel though she is not an Israelite, and, though herself of another people, raises up the horn of his people through its blessings.

By what, I ask, did she merit this? I believe it was because she said to her mother-in-law: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

O virtue worthy even to be preferred to men! A woman of an uncircumcised people imitates Abraham’s faith, which male circumcision abandoned, and enters upon the merit of justification by foreign footprints, from which the blind inheritance of her ancestors had strayed.

The Moabite despises her gods, while you, Israel, long for foreign ones. She binds herself to the one God, having already forgotten her own gods, while you fornicate after a multitude of idols.

For this reason she is chosen by the Lord; for this reason she becomes an Israelite in mind, not in origin; in faith, not in blood; in virtue, not in tribe. For this reason she is blessed to such a degree that she is called the mother of your prophets and kings.

It shines more brightly than day that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and is invaded, seized, and possessed by those who do violence to it. Justification belongs not to a people but to life, since the uncircumcised enter the court of sanctification through the fruit of uprightness, while those circumcised and born in that same court lose the scepter of sanctification through the shamefulness of their deeds.

## XIII

But let us return again to the blessed blood, as it were, of the twelve tribes, so that in it the shadow of the truth of the ecclesiastical mystery, which preceded it even then, may be demonstrated.

It would take too long to enumerate the forms of all the saints and to recount their deeds, dearest daughter, according to your virtues. What does it mean that Joseph fled naked from the house of the Egyptian king after throwing off his garment? What does it mean that this people crossed the sea, while Pharaoh’s army did not cross it, and that the appearance of flowing nature is changed beneath human feet?

What does it mean that the sea itself should meet the sons of Jacob as they escape Egypt? I leave all these matters for you to examine according to your life and according to the mysteries of the Church, so that, when you behold in Abraham the secrets of the truth of circumcision, you may not marvel at the emptied form of the Jewish sign.

Therefore, since everything must be said briefly lest the discourse become too long, I must enter the whole harvest of the Israelite people and winnow out in it the effect of circumcision itself.

Joshua, son of Nun, who was to inherit the peoples on earth, is first commanded to circumcise all those ranks, as it were, of the divine people. As though the whole wilderness had not already grown white with the bones of the circumcised people through the various blows of their sins!

What, then, did this command accomplish, when it did not heal the guilt of sin? The Lord says: “Make for yourself stone knives, very sharp” (Josh. 5:2).

Why does he take such great care that they not be blunt? “Very sharp,” he says, so that they may not merely cut off some small portion of the body with the sensation of pain, but may finely distinguish the deadly senses of the mind with a thin edge, through much filing and the continual use of the whetstone.

He circumcised in them, if I am not mistaken, their desire for Egypt, their murmuring, their defiance, their fornication with idols, and their habit of sinning, for which their ancestors had felt the Lord’s anger.

Without doubt he also circumcised their fear of the battles set before their eyes. For even before they had seen the promised lands, while Joshua was spying them out, they complained that giants of great strength were there, and feared to engage them in battle.

He also circumcised their eyes, lest they should unlawfully desire foreign marriages, or wish to possess anything in those regions other than the lands themselves.

For they do not die through the Lord’s anger because they are not circumcised, but because they neglect these things. That sign belongs to the one who is blessed; it is not the merit by which one is blessed.

## XIV

All the books are full, and antiquity is full of examples, showing that the Lord is pleased not with the cutting off of some particular member, but with the circumcision of our nature.

In this circumcision even that greatest of all prophets, John, circumcised himself. He is not clothed in soft garments, nor fattened with delicacies chosen for the appetite. In this world he is almost without the world, abandoning all concern for worldly desires. His rough, hairy coverings make the austere man harsh, not elegant. He is filled with food from the earth and with the thin sweat of honey. What other circumcision ought to be sought as greater than this?

Finally, he was the first to recognize not that lamb which the Jews were accustomed to have in the shadow of truth as their Passover, through which the sins of the world could not be abolished, but the true Lamb whose blood would save all mortality. Leaving the ninety-nine sheep, he recognized that the one sheep was carried on the shoulders of the true shepherd, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

This too is remarkable in him: he chose the wilderness to preach the Lord’s coming. He does not speak in temples; he does not speak in the marketplaces. Though he might benefit a multitude by addressing a multitude, he shuns it.

And why is he the voice of one crying out, if the hearer turns away? A multitude is certainly necessary for a teacher. But what multitude is there in the wilderness? Clearly, none.

What, then, will the prophet do, who is a voice, and the voice of one crying out? He chose, I believe, a place not where no one would hear him, but to which he might lead people back from the conduct of corrupted nature, so that, seeing a new life in the Prophet, they might learn to wonder at the divine life and permit themselves to be circumcised from every vice in the wilderness.

The place itself, therefore, is a form of teaching, and the preaching itself is the solitude of virtues. The dwelling-place accomplishes its work: the attentive hearer leaves the crowds of the cities and enters the wilderness, torn away from the contamination of the world as from a theater of pleasures.

Finally, he forbids them to glory in Abraham as their father, plainly because they do not follow his footsteps.

Certainly, if we come to that Jewish circumcision, let us be circumcised as Abraham was circumcised. If we appeal to blood, why are those not called children of Abraham who are his children?

But the father of faith can be father only of believers, and children are recognized not by the sign of circumcision but by resemblance in their works.

Thus, when they were forbidden to boast of Abraham as their parent, it was being shown that they did not possess the sign of his faith, but merely the ancestral sign.

They are rightly called children of Abraham if they answer to the form of their parent not in appearance but in life: if, in accordance with the word of the Lord, even their homeland is not loved, and a son can be killed—since the whole human being who died for us must also die to him with equal love.

## XV

When the aged Simeon said, “Now, Lord, you release your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29), this is certainly a form: whoever sees Christ is already destined to die to the world.

This is circumcision—not still shaded beneath the tabernacle of significance, but hidden under the prefiguration of truth, advancing into the light after being stripped of the image of its prefiguration.

Abraham, the initiator of almost all the earlier mysteries, had shown it when, after the word of the Lord, he acquired from the sons of Heth a place not where he would live, but where he would die.

The Magi also, after worshiping the Lord, lest bodily foreskin be a disadvantage to the glory of any people, circumcised themselves in their affections. With their treasures—that is, with the secrets of their minds opened—they sacrificed the movements of their souls as a gift.

They dug up, as though before the altar of piety and the altar of mercy, those diseases through which we desire, fear, or grieve over anything, so that in gold avarice, in frankincense idolatry, and in myrrh the mortality they loved might be subjected to the Lord.

From him, indeed, its captivity had to be led captive. On this rock, as though dashed against it, the sacred greed for money, the profane superstition of error, and the cherished condition of mortality were to die, as the Psalmist had long before sung concerning Babylon: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:9).  
[Variant: “your little ones” instead of “her little ones.”]

Under these names and offerings of the Magi, that challenger of all divine works is entirely stripped away: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

Who, then, would dare possess gold for himself, if it belongs to the Lord? Who would burn incense to idols, if it belongs to Christ? Who would bury anyone dead, unless he himself were dead, if myrrh already belongs to the living?

Finally, the Lord himself is tempted by the devil, as though through this threefold throw of dice. Continence is endangered in hunger, religious devotion in worship, and life in the plunge from the height.

But he easily overcame everything, because he was the father and king of all the treasures of goodness, the priest of mysteries stored up before the ages, and the one destined to be the resurrection of the dead.

The Magi nevertheless left behind the traces of their former life. Entering upon a new path, empty of burdens but not empty of blessing, they sang: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. 114:7).

There was also that man into whom the Lord entered who is said to have been circumcised from every foreskin of vice. For he gives half of his possessions to the poor, and if he has defrauded anyone of anything, he restores it fourfold.

He was unable to see the Lord while he was rich, until, after climbing the sycamore tree through which the Lord was about to pass, he had risen above the earth in which his heart seemed to be with his treasure.

Then, as though by a kindred necessity, he is recognized by the one about to be crucified when he is seen in the tree, and is called a son of Abraham.

Why is he called this? If he already was one, he needed no testimony. But since not all who were believed to be sons of Abraham were so, this man is recognized as a son through his work, not through his people; through virtue, not through blood.

These are the recognizable marks of the effect of circumcision.

## XVI

Do you now see, daughter—do you now consider—the whole of circumcision drawn out through the form of deeds, as through certain lines of the limbs, and depicted through the diversity of actions as through a variety of colors, yet completed in one summit of justification through degrees of virtue?

You see one person leaving his homeland and not hesitating over parricide; another not caring about the shipwreck of such great wealth, nor weeping over bereavements, but even amid the rottenness of his body sighing over his wife’s sin rather than over his own wound.

You see that woman abandoning her people and gods, not fearing to come into a foreign nation without the support of a man.

You see this man, about to enter the lands of the promise, placing knives not in a sword but making them from stone, so that he might have from himself what iron acquires elsewhere.

You see another preparing the way of the Lord in solitude and making straight paths in the wilderness.

You see yet another praying to be released from the world and preferring the Lord’s peace to the world’s peace.

You see these men stripped of their affections, their manner of life changed through gold, frankincense, and myrrh: those who had come by way of Herod returning by way of an angel.

You see also the man now removing heaps of fraud together with interest, and called a son of Abraham not by the gift of nature but by the support of his deeds.

Thus it plainly appeared that the whole nature of the world had been laid low through the actions of individuals.

[Note: In the latest edition, the seven verses that follow this point are missing.]

## XVII

But since, as though toward the end of a wedding banquet, we have nearly consumed the wine served through the patriarchs and have begun to drink the new wine through the transformation of water, let us also bring forth something from the new wineskins, so that we may judge what they received from what they themselves exude.

The wine boils uniformly through the minds of all the apostles, whose breasts are full of new wine; and the spiritual flood, exceeding bodily measure, does not conceal a glorious intoxication.

For us, however, we must begin with the one from whom the thirst for drawing water began, so that from the magnitude of his desire we may demonstrate the fullness of the sacred infusion: that from one person an equal thirst was poured for his companions, not as an act of stingy divine sobriety.

Behold the illustrious fellowship. Peter raised his august head, the new standard-bearer of the covenant and the first in its creation. Another—I speak without hesitation—is Abraham, perhaps the greater; certainly, as I understand it, not second.

To the one a fertile generation is promised; to the other a generation to be fed is entrusted. From the former those who are to be justified proceed; in the latter those who have been justified are established. Thus what the former hopes for, the latter receives.

To Abraham it is said: “I will make you into a great nation” (Gen. 12:2). To Peter it is said: “I will make you a fisher of human beings” (Matt. 4:19).

To Abraham it is said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3). To Peter it is said: “You shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

To Abraham it is said: “Your seed shall be like the stars” (Gen. 22:17). To Peter it is said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

Thus the former is filled with the fertility of blessed seed, while the latter is summoned beforehand to proclaim the seed itself.

The splendor of the stars is shown to Abraham in place of children, but the kingdoms of heaven are entrusted to Peter, so that evidently the children of Abraham cannot enter them without Peter.

Peter therefore does not glory before the Lord because he was circumcised according to his people, but says: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what will there be for us?” (Matt. 19:27).

What are these “everything” for a man who possessed nothing besides the equipment of the fisherman’s trade? “Everything,” he says—plainly everything that the world presents to desire, which may be called foreskins if they are gathered together for the seductions of sin. They grow back more forcefully if they flatter us with the increase of a deceptive happiness, and they try to wrap around the inner nature of our mind, so that what was given to us as light itself may be darkened by greater shadows.

The Apostle says: “We have left everything and followed you.” In faithfulness to the old example, the virtue of descendants, both late and wonderful, aspires through the first disciple to the new justification. As the images of truth are already almost worn away, Abraham is restored in Peter.

Peter testifies that he has left everything. He does not drift upon the deep; he is no longer occupied with the care of his trade; nor is his sick mother-in-law visited without the Lord.

The whole affection of the unique man is in Christ. He follows him as one who scorns possessions, neglects his former occupation, and forgets kinship. What Abraham was commanded to do, Peter does not conceal that he has already done, so that, by a similar circumcision, he may become heir not only of virtue but also of glory.

“We have left everything and followed you; what will there be for us?” This is as though he were saying: “With all the vices of my former life cut away, while I follow you I have dried out like a wineskin lying in frost. In this world I have chosen nothing besides you with which I might wish to be filled.” This kind of dryness is not without reason repaid by the abundance of the Holy Spirit, through which the Apostle himself recognized in himself the intoxication of the new grace while he was slandered in the languages of unbelievers.

The other apostles too foamed with the fervor of the same new wine and were moistened by the overflowing vintage of a single cluster. Nevertheless, they ran after the fragrance of that nectar in imitation of blessed Peter.

Look at them, a double constellation upon the earth, not without reason called sons of thunder. They abandon boat, nets, and father; they do not hesitate because of concern for food; they do not cling to the uses of their occupation; they do not revere paternal authority. They are unmanned in expenditure, trade, and affection.

What else could they be but people circumcised from the nature of the world—clothed in a dry wave, with a hand dry of money, with a heart not softened by affection, and even with a naked trace prepared from the ship?

I believe that it was in reference to this form that Moses too was commanded to loosen the bonds of his feet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Rom. 10:15)!

Therefore, things that are beautiful in the sight of the Lord must not be concealed, nor should what life loves be clothed for the dead.

This again concerns the tax collector from the toll booth, who condemned profit, rejected his former habit, and exchanged the name of his occupation for the name of faith, so that it might be shown that it was not merely one part of the body, but the very nature of an unjust habit, that had been circumcised from everyone altogether.

I would describe the whole examination of the new calling, were it not that they agree in similar things, and that the diversity of persons possessed the same virtue, while the multitude of human beings, through one contempt for possessions, cut down the nature of the world as though with a sickle.

## XVIII

And since we have brought forward examples in sufficient abundance both from the ancients and from the new, and have furnished the course of the mind, lest it descend through blind night upon the reefs of ignorance, with images of the saints marked out, as it were, by the discourse of heaven’s stars, let us now emerge from the darkness of night and contemplate not only day and the sun, but the light of the sun itself and of the light beneath which one cannot go astray.

The multitude itself seeks the judgment of those others, and amid the abundance of forms a resemblance of flames must sometimes arise, so that often, when sailors are confused and stunned by fear, the evening star may be mistaken for the morning star and the morning star for the evening star.

The solitary brightness of the sun, without an equal companion, is alone to be admired, since even when it appears dimly beneath a cloud, its identity is vindicated by its resemblance if it has shone forth.

Accordingly, since the Lord took flesh and deigned to become human, let us seek whether he did something of this kind, so that, like the sun beneath a cloud, we may admire what shone forth even beneath bodily appearance. Let us set before us someone other than those others, rather than believe that he received anything from elsewhere.

Whom else shall we follow to guide the course of truth, we who, through divine and human faith, sail upon the sea of this world never without fear of shipwreck, except him who, having utterly set aside any likeness to himself, is immense even when he is obscured for us in our flesh?

He cannot even be concealed in name, since the substance of divinity surpasses the nature of mortality. He is not an element, but the power of the elements. In him we hold the beginning, middle, and completion of all things. Through him alone there are the courses of the sun and the year, the arrangements of the stars, and also the changes of the months, since “the old things have passed away, and everything has become new” (2 Cor. 5:17).

And since his star guided the journey of the Magi, what wonder is it if the radiance of his deeds has also furnished us, as though with the treasure itself, with immeasurable brilliance?

Would that, for the certain bestowal of such splendor and light, the weakness of our eyes might be turned away! You say that he would withdraw and conceal himself? No: rather, the heavenly splendor would appear openly to all, provided that the mind, following him with friendly goodwill, turns toward him. In him alone it will find the fullness that it had been gathering drop by drop from individuals.

He is circumcised on the eighth day by his mother, plainly as the human being who had been promised to Abraham himself, when the Lord was teaching about circumcision and saying: “And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant” (Gen. 17:11).

Who can doubt that God’s covenant is in our flesh, since the Lord deigned to be in our flesh? And who would not see that covenant as everlasting, the one celebrated with lyres and psalteries?

Since the discussion of this matter is lengthy, and an abbreviated treatment seems necessary, lest, abandoning the strength of the subject proposed amid an abundance of branches, the unchecked outpouring wander astray—especially since it is more difficult for me to exhaust its nature than to investigate it, and it is quite superfluous to labor with weary arms, although my slender intellect does not adequately support the subject itself—and since it is almost necessary that, while discussing circumcision, we ourselves also be circumcised by certain arguments, the authority of the subject itself provides us with an opportunity to excuse even our lack of skill.

XIX. Returning, then, to the subject at hand, let us question his human self—for we were speaking about the Lord, who was present in the circumcised man. When he was already regarded as circumcised according to the Law, he cries out, as the evangelist bears witness: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air have their nests where they may rest, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII, 20).

I ask: where here is the registration inquiry under Quirinius? Where is Caesar’s edict? Where is the necessity of making a declaration? Where is Joseph’s own declaration? The new arrangement there has nothing for the registrar to find—and rightly so. For the things that have been enslaved to the world do not please the Lord, nor does he claim for himself anything that he wished to remain captive either to Caesar or to the world, teaching that no one can serve two masters.

He is therefore circumcised from the inheritance of Joseph and Mary, and claims nothing for himself from worldly possessions under tribute—he who had said to them: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s things?” (Luke II, 49), that is, in the temple, not in the world; in the mystery of sacrifices, not in the assembly of the wicked; in spiritual paternal things, certainly, for he had no father in the flesh.

Finally, from that temple he drove out the sheep and oxen, overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves (Matt. XXI, 12). Thus he also circumcised the temple itself, which is a figure of his body, from carnal desire, so that a person might understand that these things must be done within his own mind. Nor does he spare his own affections. For the sword with which he circumcised others by teaching—“If anyone loves father and mother above me, he is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37)—he turns upon his own vitals and does to himself what he is going to do for believers when he says: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matt. XXII, 48).

O mystery! The Lord disavows Mary as his mother when she was standing outside the hearing of the word—especially at the very time when the Word was being preached by the Word, and when he was presenting himself to the disciples to be ministered to by them. He made this still clearer later, at the pouring out of the ointment, saying: “But you will not always have me” (Matt. XXVI, 11).

He is therefore angry when she does not choose him as the teacher who must teach life, although he had chosen her as the mother from whom he was to be born a virgin. And why did his mother refuse to enter to him, when even strangers could so easily approach him? For his brothers did not yet believe in him.

Who, I ask, could here put forward an excuse either for favor or for love, when no one surpasses Mary in merit and no one surpasses Christ our Lord in affection? That mother is denied by her son so that that true circumcision may be taught: for the teacher and parent of life ought to live as he taught one should live.

This is that thigh-sword with which the Levites killed their relatives and neighbors, and with which the Lord himself is commanded by the Father to gird himself; that sword which all receive who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; that sword which the Lord sends upon the earth, to separate a son from his father, a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law.

With this sword blessed Paul also circumcised the Church, saying: “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it” (I Cor. VII, 30–31).

Here is the power of all righteousness; here is the principle of circumcision from every fleshly attachment—that is, from parents, brothers, kinships, and relationships by marriage: to love no one more than the Lord, so that, fastened to the Word of God in the likeness of the cross rather than to any worldly actions, we may be instructed to entrust the mother to the disciple.

XX. The matter itself explains why that part of the body by which the Jew supposes himself justified appears to have been condemned to removal, so much so that it was more difficult to impose restraint upon the discourse than to seek out arguments. This, then, is the true circumcision: if, renouncing the world—from which our nature is according to the flesh—and circumcising our parents and whatever causes scandal to faith, even eye, hand, and foot, we follow the Lord naked and alone, weakened also, if possible, truly singing: “For my father and my mother have forsaken me” (Ps. XXVI, 10).

Thus may we deserve to be taken up by the Lord; and, stripped of our bodily nature, may we be clothed more gloriously in the garments of spiritual actions, knowing that “what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” The Apostle says: “And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (II Cor. V, 16)—in whom the world has been crucified for us, and we for the world—so that, when the foreskins on the surface of our manner of life have been cut away, that naked and solitary secret of our generation, which had been covered by superfluities, may appear.

For if God so clothes the grass that exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will he clothe us (Matt. VI, 30), if he sees that we are not small in faith!

Therefore the nature of our body must be circumcised with a stone knife. The Stone, however, is Christ; and his knife is love. As love grows within us, the desires of the world will diminish. Whoever loves him says to his father, “I do not know you”; and, circumcising his own nature, he will not be separated from Christ even in order to bury his dead father.

Having stripped off the old person with his deeds—which is the foreskin—he will see that another nature belongs to the substance of his being: just as the first, earthly man was from the earth, so the second, heavenly man begins to be from heaven. Nor will the person whose nature has been circumcised now say that he has any father except him who is in heaven. Rather, with eyes illuminated by the Lord’s clear command, he will recognize the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power.

All the pleasures of the soul must be worn away; the pursuits of delight must be abandoned, for this is the truth of circumcision, not its figure. We must strive above all that, once everything natural has been cut away, our way of life may tend toward heaven, where Christ is at the right hand of God (Col. III, 1).

This will be true if games, joking, banquets, and almost all familiar conversation are abandoned. And yet those who are circumcised wither, so that it may be believed not that we, who are images of life, are dead to the world, but that the world is dead to us. Nor should any of the things that have been circumcised be allowed to be reattached by the enemy’s artifice.

Rather, let us cry out: “[The Latin is uncertain: ‘The blood of circumcision has settled.’]” So that, when the stone in which the new name is written begins to work within us—a name known only to the one who receives it—we may not fear being slain in the place of revelation. Indeed, let us also credit something to our Lord through love, for there too a kindly laborer is admitted, as we learned above in blessed Peter, the recipient of the new grace.

Let the whole harmony of our faith resound more forcefully, with the strings stretched tight by art: “Because of the words of your lips, O Lord, I have kept to difficult paths” (Ps. XVI, 4).

XXI. Is anything so hard, so unyielding, as to resist nature? Although everything in the world has been made for us by God, we must repel those very things as though they did not surround us, refuse to see them, and reject with a certain exercise of virtue the world itself as it thrusts itself upon us with all its riches and beauties.

With all the senses closed by which vital substance reaches the soul, we must almost become rigid in the likeness of the dead: not be captured by sight, hearing, smell, touch, or taste; not possess bodily nature within the nature of the body; and forget that one is a human being. Yet one must not be held by the very fact that one desires these things, because one truly maintains that one is human; and the more one recognizes oneself, the more one despises oneself.

Moreover, it is hard to renounce present things while one is alive and to hope for future things after life. This bodily nature—as we have said—does not permit such conduct unless it has been circumcised. It readily boasts in its own possessions, seeing that the earth is its own, the seas its own, and the sun and all the stars of heaven serving it. And when will it endure being deprived of earthly things, when it rules even heaven?

Thus, surrounded by the excessive servitude of so many elements, it is led even to forget its own condition. Raised up in contempt over the whole world, it presumes to conquer the elements precisely because they obey it: here by digging trenches in the mountains, there by filling valleys with constructed embankments, here by plowing the seas with massive structures; now by making the dry land fertile through irrigation, now by drying up ponds and marshes, or by clothing fields with planted groves and stripping the ridges of wooded mountains of their ancient forests—so that it scarcely believes itself to be mistress of nature unless it acts in this way.

By the disturbance of that nature, our own nature is agitated by these reflections. It is hard to keep the Lord’s ways, in which strength is expended not through achievements but through losses. What all mortality loves is not sought above us, but life is to be lived beneath us, lest, by thinking ourselves greater than we are, we begin not even to obtain what we are. For if, by this very means, we are willing to despise what we are, we may deserve to be better than we are.

The Lord speaks and confirms the reckoning we presume to make: “Amen I say to you, there is no one who leaves house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive a hundredfold in this time, and in the age to come will inherit eternal life” (Matt. VIII, 8).

By such promises those difficult ways—which must be kept for the sake of the Lord’s word—are softened. In guarding them there is indeed a great reward.

XXII. We are invited by these rewards, although we ought also to have been compelled, since our desire embraces what could have commanded us. Finally, when they said that the word of life was a hard saying, and for this reason all who followed him were troubled and withdrew, he turned to his disciples and asked in anger whether they too wished to depart. He so prefers that we owe him all good things if we are willing rather than command us when we are compelled, as the Apostle says: “For if I do this willingly, I receive a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (I Cor. IX, 17).

This will is the sheath of that thigh-sword. When it has received within itself the love of God—which we have said is the knife—it will deserve to understand that the Lord truly proclaimed: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 10).

For when all superfluous things have been cut away and we have been circumcised from every burden, made thin in the image of a pack-bearing beast, we too truly say with the Psalmist that we can pass through that narrow opening of the needle, whether through ice or even through a liquid and yielding substance. Those who hope to enter through it on horses and chariots will not be able to do so, since even that broad and spacious way will scarcely contain such persons.

Thus divine generosity and liberality, inviting us onward, smooths the steep mountains of toil and the almost wall-like barriers of difficulties by which heavenly things are separated from human things as though by the boundaries of a certain province.

And just as, by the priests’ trumpets, it brought down the walls of that Jericho, so by the voices of the prophets it will overthrow the tower of our destruction, provided that, believing against hope in hope, and with the leaping glance of kindled eyes, we marvel at the promises, to the confounding of fleeting present things, as though already grasped in our hands.

Having been circumcised from this nature and transferred into another nature, let us hold in mind and spirit those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which the Lord has prepared for those who love him.” Among their number is no one except the person who, through the circumcision described above, has been fastened with the Lord to the cross and is always worthy of suffering for his sins.

But the one who did not believe our Lord worthy of such suffering said: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII, 42). While he was still speaking, the Lord himself, ready to hear the petitioner and to console him, as was his custom, deigned in his goodness to say: “Take courage: amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

## EPISTLE XX, OR A REBUKE OF SUSANNAH AFTER HER FALL

(This epistle, which has not been unanimously attributed by the authorities to Jerome, appears in truth, by many indications, more probably to be by Saint Ambrose. Therefore, following the Benedictines, we have already published it among the works of the holy Bishop; see there, vol. XVI of our *Patrology*, col. 365, under the title *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*.)

## EPISTLE XXI, OR AN EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLI (C, G)

(It is also found in Augustine, in the Appendix to volume VI, entitled *Sermon on Psalm XLI, to the Newly Baptized*. Erasmus says: “It appears that this fragment is from the homilies of someone on the mystical psalms; certainly it contains nothing Jerome-like.” See the place cited.)

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EPISTLE

In the Veronese manuscript, which certainly predates the ninth century, it is appended shortly after the sermon entitled *On the Eating of the Lamb*. Erasmus says of it: “It is of the same flour as the homily that immediately preceded it and has the same authorial flavor.”

## EPISTLE XXII, OR AN EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXVII

### I.

In every psalm our Lord Jesus Christ is prophesied and sung. For he himself possesses the key of David, which opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens (Rev. III, 7).

But especially in the hundred and seventeenth psalm, which has now been read in song, the mystery of the resurrection is proclaimed. This psalm begins with confession: in it, those prefigured by the Holy Spirit are called to confess the Lord in praise—the true Israelites; or to the confession of the nations in penitence—the house of Aaron, the true priest, which is in the Church; or, more generally, all who rightly fear God for the many gifts of the Father’s mercy, who did not spare his Son but handed him over for us all: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Rom. VIII, 31–32).

For who among us, considering the things that the Church sings daily in exultation—namely, the passion, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord our Savior—could fail to burst into the cry, becoming one of those little children who rejoiced with the Lord with branches and palms: “O Lord, save us; O Lord, grant prosperity”?

Therefore the victorious one himself, ascending to the Father, commands the angels, saying: “Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess the Lord” (Ps. XXIV, 7).

These are the gates of which, in the twenty-third psalm, the angels spoke to one another, preparing the Lord’s entrance: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.”

But beautifully they are commanded to be lifted and raised on high. For, according to the dispensation of the flesh, and the mystery and victory of the cross, he returns to heaven greater than he had come to earth.

“This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.”

Through this gate Peter entered, Paul entered, all the apostles entered, and the martyrs entered; and every day the saints enter. Through this gate the first thief entered with the Lord.

### II.

Have confidence, and hope for similar things yourselves. For the Apostle himself said: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God.”

This psalm does not say that only the apostles, only the prophets and martyrs, will enter through it; it says, “The righteous shall enter through it.” Whoever therefore acts righteously and deserves to be among the Lord’s righteous should act confidently, hoping in him, because he will enter through this gate.

For the Lord does not seek the blood of those who confess, but faith, for which the blood of believers is poured out. If we have the faith that can shed blood, the shedding of blood will also be reckoned to us.

O truly unhappy Jews! O wretched and pitiable people! You did not recognize that the stone promised through Isaiah, which was to be placed in the foundations of Zion and join both peoples together, was the Lord Savior, the Son of God.

You rejected him while once building the Lord’s assembly and guarding the mysteries of God’s Temple. Rejected by you, he became the head of the corner, and he joined together the first Church, gathered from the people of the Jews, with believers from the nations into one flock and one ministry.
