“This was done by the Lord; it is marvelous in our eyes”: that we, who before the Lord’s passion were without a covenant and lawless, should be adopted as children of God; and that, when the former belt had rotted away, God should weave for himself another loincloth and prepare another people.

### III.

You, then, Jews, possess the Scripture; you read the books, while we believe in the one who is written in those books and worship him. You hold the pages; we possess the meaning of the pages. You fold up the skins of dead animals; we possess the life-giving Spirit.

What could be more marvelous than such a mystery? What could be happier than this day, on which the Lord died for the Jews and rose for us? On which the worship of the Synagogue fell and the Church arose? On which he made us human beings rise and live and sit with him in the heavenly places?

And that saying which he himself spoke in the Gospel has been fulfilled: “And when I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw everything to myself” (John XII, 32).

“This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”

The Lord certainly made all days, but the other days may belong to the Jews, may belong to heretics, and may belong to the nations.

### IV.

The Lord’s Day is the day of resurrection, the day of Christians; it is our day. Hence it is called the Lord’s Day, because on it the victorious Lord ascended to the Father.

But if it is called the day of the sun by the pagans, we most gladly acknowledge this too. For today the light of the world has arisen; today the sun of righteousness has risen, in whose wings there is healing.

Does the sun have wings? Let the Jews answer, and those who understand the Scriptures only according to the letter and are like the Jews.

We, however, say that whoever is beneath the wings of this sun—who said in the Gospel, “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!”—will be safe from the hawk the devil and from the flying eagles in Ezekiel, and all the wounds of his sins will be healed.

### V.

But so that you may know, my brothers, that this psalm was specifically written about the Lord: in the Gospel, as we remember, the children who, when the Savior entered Jerusalem, lifted palms and cried out, saying, “Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest” (Mark XI, 9), took these verses from the hundred and seventeenth psalm: “O Lord, save me.”

In Hebrew it is written **HOSIANNA**.

Therefore the Jews, bearing this impatiently, wish to silence the little children, about whom the Lord spoke through Isaiah: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me” (Isa. VIII, 18).

While the elders are silent and tormented by the bitterness of envy, the little children cry out, and the little children confess Christ. And if they too had been silent, the stones would certainly have cried out—that is, the people of the nations. Of them it is written in the Gospel: “The Lord is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 9).

He signifies us, who were once hard of heart but, now believing in Christ Jesus, have through the Lord himself been adopted as children of Abraham [another reading omits “as children of Abraham”], as children of God almighty, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EPISTLE

Erasmus says: “I do not know whose fragment this is; it is scarcely worthy even of this order. It is so far from being attributable to Jerome.”

## EPISTLE XXIII, TO DARDANUS: ON VARIOUS KINDS OF MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS

### I.

You compel me, Dardanus, to answer you briefly concerning certain kinds of musical instruments, as the matter itself teaches, either by sight or by hearing. I cannot bring other things into clear presentation, because each thing is according to its own nature; but whatever can be narrated will gladly be explained.

First of all, I shall come to the organ, since its cries are reckoned to be greater than these instruments in sound and extraordinary power. It is constructed by joining together two hollow elephant skins and is supplied with the bellows of fifteen smiths. Through twelve bronze pipes it produces a very powerful sound, which it drives forward like thunder, so that it is certainly heard distinctly over a distance of a thousand paces and more. This is confirmed by what is said among the Hebrews about organs whose sound is heard from Jerusalem as far as the Mount of Olives and beyond.

### II.

Most people say that there are two kinds of organ. The first is the one we have described; the other is the one mentioned in connection with the Israelites’ captivity among the Babylonians: “By the rivers of Babylon” (Ps. CXXXVI, 1), and what follows.

All this signifies figuratively and spiritually the Gospel of Christ. It is joined together by two skins—that is, by the severity of the two Laws—through the fifteen bellows of smiths, that is, through the patriarchs and prophets. Through the twelve bronze pipes, that is, through the apostles, it sends forth a mighty sound, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII, 5), and what follows.

It is like thunder—that is, the voice of the Gospel throughout the whole world—as it is written: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI, 19).

Through a thousand paces—that is, the perfect number, the ten words of the Law are fulfilled. Its sound [another reading: “sense”] is in the willows, that is, the Gospel is preached through the labor of each teacher’s lips.

### III.

The trumpet, then, of which it is written in Daniel, “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre” (Dan. III, 15), and what follows, is made in different shapes and forms.

For one trumpet is used for the gathering of the people, another for enlistment, another for victory, another for pursuing enemies, another for the shaking of cities, and so forth.

The customary trumpet is understood by those most knowledgeable about such matters in this way: air is blown into it through three bronze pipes at a narrow opening. At the mouth, through four bronze sound-channels, which produce fourfold voices through a bronze base, it emits an extremely great and powerful roar.

Thus the Gospel, through the threefold confession of the three persons of the holy Trinity, is breathed into the narrow opening—that is, into Christ’s birth and divinity. Through the four sound-channels—that is, the four evangelists—it cries out with an immense voice throughout the whole world, through the bronze foundation of the stability of faith and works, emitting sounds powerfully like the trumpet of assembly.

### IV.

The pipe, moreover, is said by the craftsmen of such things to belong to the mystical art, and is found to be made as follows.

A very broad, square, ductile bronze cylinder, shaped almost like a crown, with a small bronze-and-iron tube joined to it and struck in the middle, is formed upon a tall and spacious wooden frame and fastened at its upper end. One end is lowered below the other, though most think that it does not touch the ground. On each side twelve bronze cylinders hang, fixed in a chain, with twelve pipes placed in the middle.

Thus three cylinders are fixed around each side. When the first cylinder is set in motion, and the pipes of the twelve cylinders placed in the middle are set in motion, they produce together a great cry and an immense crash beyond measure.

### V.

The cylinder with the pipes—that is, the teacher in the midst of the Church—is with the Holy Spirit, who speaks in him. It is fastened to the tall wood—that is, to Christ, whom the wise compare to the tree of life; it is fixed in a chain—that is, in faith—and does not touch the earth—that is, carnal works.

The twelve cylinders are the twelve apostles, with the pipes—that is, with the divine utterances.

The lyre, of which it is written in the forty-second psalm, “I will confess to you upon the lyre, O God, my God” (Ps. XLII, 4), is of a distinctive kind among the Hebrews. It is made with twenty-four strings, which, as the most knowledgeable report, are arranged in the form of the letter Delta, and through the fingers of Pindar it is set in motion with varied ringing notes and strokes in different modes.

### VI.

The lyre of which we are speaking is spiritually the Church. With the doctrines of the twenty-four elders, having a threefold form like the letter Delta, it most clearly signifies the faith of the holy Trinity. Through the hands of the man Peter the apostle, who is its preacher, it is struck into various melodies of the Old and New Testament—differently in the letter and differently in the figurative sense.

### VII.

The sambuca, then, which is an unknown object among the most knowledgeable Hebrews, is found to have existed in ancient times among the Chaldeans, as it is written: “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca” (Dan. III, 15), and what follows.

Among the Hebrews, a trumpet is called *bucca*; then, by diminution, it is called *buccina*. Among the Hebrews, *sambuca* is interpreted as “sun,” as it is written: “Samson, their sun.”

It is therefore called *sambuca* among them because many think it to be the bark of a tree. Through the solidity of honey and the mutability of wind, it can be moved like a trumpet from a tree branch. It is therefore called *sambuca* because it can be made in summer and can last until the season of cold. For, according to ordinary practice, it dries out.

It is a type of those who praise the Lord in good works but, in the season of cold—that is, of tribulations or persecution—cannot praise him because of the infidelity of their life and the abundance of their riches.

### VIII.

The psaltery is called *nablon* in Hebrew, *psalterium* in Greek, and *laudatorium* in Latin. Concerning it the fifty-fourth psalm says: “Rise up, psaltery, with the lyre.”

It has ten strings, as it is written: “Upon the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you” (Ps. CXLIII, 9), and it is square in form.

The psaltery with ten strings—that is, with the ten words of the Law, crushed against every heresy—may be understood as square through the four Gospels.

### IX.

The tambourine can be explained in a few words, since it is a very small object and can be carried in a woman’s hand, as it is written in Exodus: “Mary the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand” (Exod. XV, 20).

It is the small measure of the wisdom of the Old Law in the hand of the Jews.

In ancient times the synagogue also had a simple skin with two bronze pipes. Air is blown through the first, and through the second the sound is emitted.

It is a type of the former people, who had received a narrow understanding of the Law and, through the narrowness of their will to preach, proclaimed all things weakly.

[Note: He understands those skins that peasants still inflate today. They are called *utricularii*, and in Greek ἀσκαῦλαι (*askaulai*). Hence, in place of *chorus*, Salmasius doubts whether *dorus* should be read, for Greek δορός (*doros*) means “skin” or “wineskin.”]

But if I look wisely and carefully at earthly things, they too must be understood spiritually and mystically.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EPISTLE

Casimirus Oudinus thinks that this sermon belongs to Faustus of Riez, arguing that a large part of the sermons attributed among those of Eusebius of Emesa belong to him. In Eusebius it is entitled *Sermon on Easter*. In reality, however, these two sermons have been improperly joined together; the second begins with the words “The benefits of our God,” and we have separated it from the continuous sequence for the sake of clarity of expression.

Erasmus, moreover, says: “You could detect no shadow here of a Jerome-like mind.” In other manuscripts it is prefaced by one title or another.

## EPISTLE XXIV, OR SERMON ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

### I.

“Rejoice, O heaven, and be glad, O earth” (Joel II, 21). This day has shone upon us more brightly from the tomb than it has gleamed from the sun.

Let hell rejoice, because it has been released; let it rejoice, because it has been visited; let it resound, because after long ages it has seen an unknown light and breathed again amid the darkness of profound night.

O beautiful light, which flashed forth from the shining summit of heaven and clothed with sudden brilliance those sitting amid purple streams in darkness and in the shadow of death!

### II.

At once, therefore, when Christ descended, the eternal night of the underworld shone brightly. The groaning of the mourners fell silent; the chains of the condemned, torn apart, fell down; the minds of the torturers stood stunned in astonishment; the entire unholy workshop trembled when it suddenly saw Christ in its own dwellings.

Then the rusty gatekeepers, as Christ descended, muttered among themselves in such words, blind amid shadowy silences and with the shadow:

“Who is this, terrible and flashing with wondrous brilliance? Never has our Tartarus received such a one. Never has the world vomited such a one into our cavern. This man is an invader, not a debtor; a breaker [another reading: “maker”], not a petitioner. We see a judge, not a supplicant; he has come to fight, not to submit; to rescue, not to remain.

“Where, do you suppose, were our companions and gatekeepers sleeping when that conqueror battered the bars? If he were guilty, he would not be so bold. If any sins darkened him, he would never disperse our darkness with his radiance.”

### III.

“But if he is God, why has he come here? If he is human, what has he dared? If he is God, what is he doing in the tomb? If he is human, why does he release captives? Has he perhaps made a treaty with our ruler? Or has he attacked and conquered him as well, and thus passed into our kingdoms?

“Certainly he was dead; certainly he was defeated. Our warrior was deceived in the world; he did not know that this man would bring destruction upon hell.

“O that deceptive cross, which frustrates our joys and gives birth to our losses! Through wood we were enriched; through wood we are overthrown. That power, feared by all peoples at all times, has perished.

“No captive has ever trembled beneath our realm. Behold, the one who was groaning now rejoices. The ancient weeping is no longer heard; no lamentations now resound; every groan of the mourners has fallen silent.

“Do you think he will return without our destruction? No living person ever entered among us; no one was ever so bold; no one ever so terrified the executioners. Never in this black dwelling, blind with perpetual soot, has a joyful light appeared.

“Has the sun perhaps migrated from the world? Yet neither heaven nor its stars obey us—and nevertheless hell shines. What shall we do? Where shall we turn against him?

“We cannot hold our bloody dwellings and maintain the guards of the gates of our cavern. We have entered into evil; we have been unable to darken so great a light; we cannot suppress one endowed with such power. We see our own necks being pressed, and we fear, moreover, our own destruction.

“What have we to do with heaven? We are scourged by fresh blows beyond just punishment. We were content with our night; we were hidden in our caves. Why are we exposed by the sun’s rays? Why are we disturbed by violence? Why are we held captive in our own dwellings?”

### IV.

Then Christ directs his ranks against those cruel ministers of punishments, and with the divine sword cuts down the implacable troops. The savage executioners groan beneath the torturer and waste away, driven by rabid shrieks.

When the strongest entered those caverns of the iron bed, the caverns themselves were bound by the stronger one with eternal chains.

For the Lord himself had promised that this would happen, saying: “No one enters the house of the strong man and plunders his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his goods” (Mark III, 27).

Then the sad and grieving crowds and peoples, wearied by long desolation, hasten together and fall at the feet of their ruler.

### V.

Behold, the apostolic words are proved: “In the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 10).

Then the captive souls, released from their prisons, came forth from Tartarus. In this supplication they lament [another reading: “implore”] the kingdom of heaven:

“At last you have come, most merciful Jesus; now help and spare the weary. Now, Christ, extinguish the savage threats; release the pitiable groans. You redeemed the living by your cross; rescue the dead by your death.

“The world itself had perished with us by a common lot, and all creation hung upon your coming. Our torments sighed for you; this hell always feared you.

“While you are here, release the guilty; when you have ascended, defend your own. While you are here, let all the bars be loosened; when you have ascended, let them not be closed.

“You alone could crush the serpent’s head; you were able to shatter the bronze gates and iron bars. Let the gate be opened, we ask, to those who pray; let kindly light not be absent. And if you return to your body in your majesty, may hell not be deprived of your power.”

### VI.

After the prayers had been heard, after the laws had been settled, after the torturers had been plunged into the pit of the deep abyss, our king today came forth from the underworld triumphant and crowned with laurel. Nor was the white-clad retinue lacking; rather, the entire host of the blessed advanced joyfully with its prince, as it is written in the Gospel:

“When the Lord had risen, many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep also rose with him; and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many” (Matt. XXVII, 52–53).

Let the triumphant one, alive once more, return to his course, so that the whole world may know that Christ has returned from the underworld.

Let believers therefore glory; let all the nations clap their hands, because our king both triumphed in this world and conquered the realms below.

## VII

Although the benefits of our God are great and wondrous, they are nevertheless neither new nor sudden; rather, from the beginning of the world they were both foretold by oracles and prefigured through mysteries. The ancient Testament’s utterances proclaimed the sacred Passion of the Lord from the very beginnings of the world as it was coming into being; and therefore we assert that Christ the Lord, preached and announced to his faithful, appears from those very books and volumes. Without doubt, he rests upon powerful privileges who asserts his case from the adversary’s own documents. It is a splendid victory to entangle the opposing party in his own writings, as though in his own snares; to refute him by the words of his own testimonies; and to overcome one’s rival with his own weapons, so that the arguments of your attacker may be shown to serve your own advantage.

Therefore, in the person of our Lord, just as Eve, the mother of all living, was produced from the rib of Adam, the first man, so from his sacred side and life-giving wound the Church, the mother of all the faithful, is shown to be destined for restoration. In Abel’s type, Abel, though conquered, is slain, and the innocent brother is sacrificed as though by Jewish impiety. This same Lord, in the final age of the world as it grows old, is offered as a victim through the figure of the long-lived father Abraham. At that moment, when the pious father-killer rises to strike the throat of his only son in a new sacrifice, a ram suddenly appeared before his eyes, as the divine word declares: “And Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns among the bushes” (Gen. XXII, 13). “Among the bushes,” it says.

## VIII

Let us inquire what this novelty is: that is, among the multitude of surrounding sinners. “Caught by its horns”: that is, hanging upon the horns of the cross through the nailing of the crucifixion, as we read in another passage: “He has horns in his hands” (Hab. III, 4). This is because the arms of the gallows received his venerable hands. He was reckoned among thorns when the author of innocence and righteousness was mocked with a crown of thorns.

But we must look more deeply into another matter: what does it mean that Isaac is brought by his father to the altar, and that suddenly a ram is substituted for him—not by a changed offering, but by a doubled one? Here the twofold substance of the Redeemer is shown, worthy of worship. For the only-begotten Son of God is offered, and the firstborn of the Virgin is sacrificed.

This too prefigured the marks of the Lord’s Passion: we read that blessed Elisha was laid in a tomb and that, when a corpse thrown in by robbers touched his sacred body, it raised the body of the dead man.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Evidently he read IV Kings XIII, 21 according to the Septuagint. For whereas the Vulgate translates the ambiguous Greek word αὐτῶν and the Hebrew [the Hebrew term is missing in the supplied text] as “certain ones,” and refers it to those who were burying him, this removes every doubt that the man was killed by brigands and buried by those same men. This is the view of our author, Josephus, and the Alexandrian Chronicle, while others diverge into other opinions.]

## IX

Who else was prefigured here except our Lord Jesus Christ, who grants resurrection from death and works life while buried? In the robbers, recognize the world; in the prophet’s powers, recognize Christ the Lord.

Again, throughout the sacred Scriptures, the Passion and resurrection of Christ are most clearly prefigured even in the prophet Jonah’s labors and sufferings. This Jonah—as we do not suppose is unknown to your faith—is prescribed as having borne the type of the Lord. For the Lord himself said: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea creature for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. XII, 40).

This Jonah, I say, is sent at the Lord’s command to proclaim to the Ninevites the offense of heavenly wrath. The prophet, foreseeing that the grim sentence would be emptied through the people’s conversion, flees aboard a ship bound for Tarshish. But when a storm arises and throws the sailors into confusion, he is given over to the waves by lot, and, plunged into the fish’s jaws, is received by the sea creature. But when the fish vomits forth its unharmed burden, he is returned to the earth on the third day.

## X

See how the Lord also appears wondrously in the Old Testament in the form of a servant; see how, in earlier ages, he indicated that he would come according to the humility of a servant’s form. Jonah, destined to proclaim the Lord’s wrath, is sent to the great city of the Ninevites to say: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” And Christ is sent to the city of the world to announce the day of salvation and the appointed time of judgment.

Jonah seeks a ship; Christ, the Church. Jonah is tossed by the waves; Christ is buffeted by the storms of the world. Unless Jonah is given up as lost, the ship’s danger is not calmed. So the Church is not delivered unless it is saved by Christ’s death.

The sailors, though about to cast Jonah away, nevertheless are afraid and say: “Lord, do not place innocent blood upon us” (Jon. I, 14). Does not the sailors’ plea seem to you a confession by Pilate? He who hands Christ over, yet washes his hands and says: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matt. XXVII, 24). How fittingly, through the person of a Gentile, the faith of the Gentiles is proclaimed!

## XI

Jonah therefore says in his prayer: “Take my life, then, Lord, because death is better for me than life.”

Let our Lord Jesus Christ say this to us: “Death is better for me than life”—that is, while living I could not save the one nation of the Jews; let me die so that the whole world may be saved by my death.

The fish received Jonah after he had been plunged into it, but did not allow him to be devoured. The hungry beast guarded the one whom human malice had destroyed. With its entrails full, it suffers hunger, and marvels that it has no power over the prey it has swallowed.

Who is this one who can be seized amid greedy jaws but cannot be consumed? He is food, but not corruption. He is handed over to the depths of destruction and preserved through the service of death itself. Who is this one who enters wholly into the vastest gulfs of danger, and, enclosed beneath an immense and deadly depth, is nourished by living air; who, released into an alien nature, journeys with life into the exile of life; and, surviving death, proclaims the salvation of the world?

## XII

I think this is our Lord Jesus Christ, whom savage death, the insatiable beast, seized as its food and, trembling, held as its captive prey. Although the earth had swallowed him crucified, yet, since it had not found him guilty, it could not hold him condemned; for punishment does not create guilt—the cause does.

It devoured man, lost through the primal origin of the world, as its customary food; but, choked, it recognized that the dignity of this man was great. Therefore the divine word records that it commanded the fish, and that it vomited Jonah onto the dry land: it commanded the beast, it commanded ever-hungry death, it commanded the abysses and hell to restore the Savior to the world.

By “vomited forth,” we must understand that victorious life returned from death’s innermost bowels, and that destruction, wounded and banished, restored him from the deepest recesses of hell.

## XIII

Thus we see that both death and resurrection were most openly prefigured in the prophet’s sufferings. Therefore, when you see what was fulfilled in the servant, do not hesitate to believe it in the Lord.

Since this is so, human being, perceive how great is your worth and weigh what you owe. Perceive how great is your worth, so that at last you may cease to regard yourself as worthless; so that, at least for this reason, you may disdain to submit shamefully to vices, while measuring your nobility by the dignity of your Creator and Restorer.

He has reasons by which he may himself confound you: why should one to whom eternal glory is promised submit with a defeated heart to unworthy masters? Thus, by a double privilege, you who once shone through participation in the divine image are also made precious by the nobility of your exchange.

Therefore, to learn how strong you can be against your enemy, examine your condition: the Lord has granted you free power to defeat within your own members the ruler of this world and to overcome spiritual wickedness. Thus do not think it impossible for you to be transferred into angelic blessedness, since in this world you have overcome angelic powers.

Therefore let not life make you degenerate and despised, you whom either creation or grace proves to have brought forth illustrious; rather, let the faithful blood of Christ raise you confidently toward the heights. For those who see themselves redeemed at a heavenly price should not doubt that they have been prepared for heavenly things.

# Editorial Notice on the Following Epistle

Even in the very ancient Veronese manuscript, which we praised earlier, this sermon and the two that follow, on Epiphany and Lent, are ascribed to Jerome. Erasmus says: “I see that others too have doubted whose homily this is.” I do not pronounce whose it is, although it recalls Leo or Maximus. That it is not Jerome’s is plain.

# Epistle XXV, or Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord

## I

Today the true sun has risen upon the world; today light has entered the darkness of the age. God became man so that man might become God. The Lord assumed the form of a servant so that the servant might be transformed into a lord. The inhabitant and creator of heaven dwells on earth so that the human tenant of earth might migrate to heaven.

O day brighter than every sun! O time more eagerly awaited than all the ages! What the angels awaited, what the cherubim and seraphim and the ministers of heaven did not know—this has been revealed in our time. What they saw through a mirror and in an image, we behold in reality. He who spoke to the Israelite people through Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets now speaks to us through the Son.

## II

See what difference there is between the Old Testament and the New. In the former he spoke through a cloud; to us he speaks through clear skies. There God was seen in the bush; here God is born from a virgin. There the fire consumed the people’s sins; here a man forgives—or rather, pardons—the people’s sins and his servants. For no one can forgive sins except God alone.

Whether the Lord Jesus was born today or baptized today, different opinions are reported in the world, and opinion differs according to the variety of traditions. This is perfectly clear to us: whether he was born today from the Virgin Mary or reborn through baptism, both the birth of the flesh and that of the spirit benefit us. Both are my mystery; both are my benefit.

The Son of God had no need to be born or baptized. For he had committed no sin that needed to be forgiven in baptism. Rather, his humility is our exaltation; his cross is our victory; his gallows is our triumph.

## III

Rejoicing, let us raise this sign upon our shoulders; let us carry the banners of victories and immortal washing upon our foreheads. When the devil sees this sign upon our foreheads, he trembles. Those who do not fear gilded Capitols fear the cross. Those who despise royal scepters, the purple robes of Caesars, and banquets fear the squalor and fasts of Christians.

Finally, in the prophet Ezekiel, when the angel who had been sent had killed everyone and the slaughter had begun with the saints, only those were preserved alive whom the letter Tau—that is, the figure of the cross—had marked.

Let us therefore exult in the likeness of the cross; let us raise holy hands toward heaven. When the demons see us armed in this way, they will be crushed. When Moses held his hands raised, Amalek was defeated; if they drooped even slightly, Amalek grew strong.

[Note: [Col. 0221D] The true Jerome says in Epistle 14 to Heliodorus: “Let the cross’s yardarm be fixed upon the foreheads.” This comparison, like others introduced by the author, may be found frequently among the ancients.]

The yardarms of ships and the horns of their sails fly in the form of our cross. Birds themselves, too, when they rise to greater heights and hang in the air, imitate the cross with outstretched wings. The trophies themselves and the ornaments of triumphal victories are also forms of the cross.

We must have it not only upon our foreheads but also in our hands, so that, armed in this way, we may trample upon the asp and the basilisk, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Editorial Notice on the Following Epistle

It appears to be by the same author as the immediately preceding work. Even without adding anything else, certainly the statement: “Whether the Lord Jesus was born today or baptized today—for different opinions are reported in the world, and opinion differs according to the variety of traditions”—is immeasurably foreign to Jerome’s mind and character. In his Commentary on Ezekiel, Book I, chapter 1, he not only clearly distinguishes the day of Epiphany from the Nativity, but also refutes those who considered them one and the same.

Erasmus says: “I have nothing to pronounce concerning this either, except that it is not Jerome’s.” The headings of the copies are also uncertain.

# Epistle XXVI, or Sermon on the Epiphany of the Lord

## I

The day of Epiphany is so called by a Greek name. What we call an appearance or manifestation, the Greeks call ἐπιφάνεια (*epiphaneia*). This is because our Lord and Savior appeared today in the darkness.

Although he had been born long ago from Mary and had already completed thirty years of age, he was nevertheless unknown to the world. He became known at the time when he came to John the Baptist to be baptized in the Jordan, and the voice of the Father, thundering from heaven, was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

The Father had shown him from heaven by his voice; the Holy Spirit, taking the form of a dove and settling upon his head, wished to demonstrate him also by touch itself, so that no other might be thought by the people to be the Son of God.

What is more sublime than this humility? What is nobler than this lowliness? He is baptized by a servant, and is called Son by the Lord. He comes to the washing among tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners, yet is holier than his own Baptist. He is washed by John in the flesh, and himself washes John in the Spirit.

The waters, which are accustomed to cleanse other things, were cleansed when our Lord washed. The river Jordan, which had been dried up at the time when Joshua led the Israelite people into the promised land, now, when the Lord’s limbs were touched, would, if it had been able, have wished to gather its waves into one place so that it might touch the Lord’s body.

## II

See, brothers, how what was read in the Gospel was foretold earlier in the twenty-eighth Psalm: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” (Ps. XXVIII, 3). For the Son of God said to John: “Allow it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15).

It follows: “The God of majesty thundered,” when the Father bore witness to the Son, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“The voice of the Lord breaking cedars.” For Christ was baptized, and the demons, previously erect and lofty, fell. The Lord cut them down like the cedars of Lebanon; the Lord crushed them like a calf scattering fragments of trees and kicking their trunks in different directions.

And, in contrast, what does he say about the Savior? “And the beloved is like the son of unicorns.” Our beloved Lord and Savior is the son of unicorns, the son of the cross, of whom it is said in Habakkuk’s song: “He has horns in his hands; there he concealed his strength” (Hab. III, 4).

After this beloved one was crucified, what follows in the Psalm was fulfilled: “The voice of the Lord cleaving the flame of fire.” For when he had been baptized and the whole world had been cleansed by Christ’s washing, the fire of Gehenna was extinguished.

“The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness.” The Church was a wilderness because previously it had no children.

## III

At the preaching of Christ, the wilderness was shaken; it labored and gave birth. In a single day an entire people was born all at once, the people that had previously been called the wilderness of Kadesh—that is, the wilderness of holiness.

For that which had not possessed holiness began to give birth to stags and to send forth herds of saints: those who kill serpents and scorn poisons. As these run throughout the whole world and preach Christ’s Gospel, everyone in his temple will say glory to God.

It follows: “The Lord makes the flood dwell.” Let us consider the whole world; let us look upon barbarian nations. Let us also survey the Roman Empire in our minds. Everywhere they believe in Christ; everywhere they are baptized in the name of the Lord. Thus it happens that there is not one baptismal water but, in a certain sense, a flood of baptisms.

Therefore the tabernacle has been completed; this is indicated beforehand by the title of this Psalm, because the Church has been built from living stones. Let us bring to the Lord the sons of God; let us bring him the sons of rams, the apostles and saints. And let us imitate our Savior—for he is called both shepherd and lamb and ram—who is sacrificed for us in Egypt, who for Isaac is held by his horns in the thickets, and let us say:

“The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of pasture he will settle me; beside the water of refreshment he has led me.”

To him are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Editorial Notice on the Following Epistle

The character of the writing, its style, and also the very order it occupies in the editions and in the Veronese manuscript indicate that these five sermons, beginning with the preceding one on the Nativity of the Lord, belong to the same author. Erasmus nevertheless valued this one so little that he says it came very close to being relegated to the lowest class.

# Epistle XXVII, or Sermon on Lent

## I

Just as a soldier is always trained for battle and prepared by simulated blows for real wounds later, so the whole life of Christians indeed requires abstinence, but especially when the enemy is near and the adversary leads an army prepared against us.

The servants of God must fast at all times, but especially then, when we are being prepared for the sacrifice of the lamb, for the mystery of baptism, and for the flesh and blood of Christ. As soon as the devil sees his sheep wishing to withdraw from his own flock, he roars, grows angry, rages, and stirs up his strength against them outside, thinking that whatever is saved for Christ is lost to him, and that whatever is given life in the Church is death to his synagogue.

## II

Therefore, dearest brothers, since by a forty-day fast we are being prepared for the Lord’s sacrament, let us fast for as many days for our sins as the Lord fasted for our transgressions.

After his baptism the devil tempted him. For he did not know that he was the Son of God, and therefore he paid him no attention. Finally, in the temptation, he wants to learn, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread.” And: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matt. IV, 3ff.).

But because he knows that we wish to become sons of God, he tries to defeat us and, like a slippery serpent, entangle our feet so that we cannot ascend to heaven. If that crafty and wicked one dared to tempt the Lord, how much more will he not fear to deceive us? If the ruined vessel resisted the Son of God and its own potter, how much more boldly will it rise against us, who are of a nature inferior to it?

“If the righteous man will scarcely be saved, where will the impious and sinner remain?” (I Pet. IV, 18). This does not mean that our Lord could have been deceived by the devil, but that he assumed the form of a servant, wishing in every respect to provide an example, so that no one might trust in his own holiness when even the one whom temptations cannot overcome was tempted.

## III

We repeat all this, dearest brothers, so that we may beware with an attentive mind lest, after leaving Egypt and hastening through the wilderness for forty days—as though for forty years—toward the promised land, we should desire the meat and pots of Egypt and be bitten by serpents.

We have left Egypt: what have we to do with Egyptian foods? Since we have heavenly bread, why do we seek earthly nourishment? We have left Pharaoh; let us invoke the Lord’s help, so that the Egyptian king may be drowned for us in the baptism of believers. There let his horses and riders perish; there let the roaring army of the adversary be killed.

Let us not murmur against the Lord, lest we be struck by the Lord. Let us not slander our priests; rather, let us fast from vices more than from foods, although an abundance of food is also fuel for vices.

If Aaron and Miriam, murmuring against Moses, experienced God’s vengeance on behalf of his servant, how much more will one of us be punished by divine judgment if he tears apart his superior with a viper’s mouth!

But priests too must simply be on their guard lest they be double-minded and doubt the Lord’s power. If even Moses and Aaron, who seemed to waver at the water of contradiction, did not deserve to enter the promised land, certainly we, weighed down by the burden of sins, will be even less able to cross the current of the Jordan and reach the place of circumcision—that is, Gilgal—if we have caused one of these little ones to stumble.

Therefore, let both the pastor’s labors and the flock’s fruitfulness, both the abundance of the harvests and the farmer’s diligence, be prepared for the Lord’s granaries. With all our strength and toil let us strive to become worthy of the coming of Easter and of the flesh and blood of the lamb Christ Jesus. Amen.

# Epistle XXVIII, or Sermon on the Vigil of Easter: On Eating the Lamb

[Col. 0224B]

This work is also found among Augustine’s spurious writings, in the appendix to volume VI, entitled *On the Vigil of Easter, concerning the Eating of the Lamb*. In the very ancient Veronese manuscript, another work precedes it, with this title: “On the foregoing subject: Moses fasted for forty days and forty nights.” Erasmus considers this work and the immediately preceding one to have the same author.

# Editorial Notice on the Following Epistle

Erasmus says: “This sermon too came from the same workshop, and it belongs to the dearest brothers.”

# Epistle XXIX, or Sermon on the Resurrection of the Lord

## I

I cannot express with my mouth the sermon I have conceived in my mind, and my tongue cannot explain the joy of my heart. But I alone do not suffer this difficulty, though I desire to relate what I feel; you too suffer it with me, rejoicing more deeply in your consciousness than you can express in words.

It seems to me that this day is brighter than the other days; that the sun has shone more brilliantly than usual; that the stars and all the elements rejoice; and that those things which, while the Lord was suffering, had withdrawn and hidden their proper light and had refused to look upon their crucified Creator now attend him—the victor and risen from the dead—with their own radiance and, so to speak, their own service.

Heaven believes; earth believes. And the net that fished the whole world could not hold the Jews.

## II

“This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24).

Just as the Virgin Mary, the mother of the Lord, holds first place among all women, so among all the days this is the mother of all days. I say something new, but something confirmed by the words of Scripture: this day is both one of the seven and outside the seven.

This is the day called the eighth. Hence in certain Psalm titles it is written: “For the eighth.” This is the day on which the Synagogue ends and the Church is born. This is the day in whose number eight souls were saved in Noah’s ark (Gen. VIII, 16). Similarly, Peter says, the Church saves you.

This is the day concerning which Ecclesiastes commands: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. XI, 2). These are the eight steps by which in Ezekiel we ascend to the temple of God.

This is the eighth day, whose mystery also marks the beginning of the eighth Psalm concerning all nations in the faith of Christ: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. VIII, 2).

And why must I repeat countless things? The day would fail me if I wished to explain the whole mystery of this day.

## III

I say only this: the whole grace of the Sabbath and that ancient festival of the Jewish people have been changed by the solemnity of this day.

They did no servile work on the Sabbath; we do no servile work on the Lord’s Day, that is, on the day of the Resurrection, because we do not serve vices and sins. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34).

They did not leave their houses; neither do we leave the house of Christ, for we are in the Church. They did not kindle a fire on the Sabbath; we, on the contrary, kindle within ourselves the fire of the Holy Spirit and boil away every vice of sins. Concerning this fire the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!” (Luke XII, 49). The Lord desires this fire to burn within us—that is, according to the Apostle, for us to be fervent in the Holy Spirit—so that the love of God may not grow cold within us.

They did not travel along the road on the Sabbath, for they had lost the one who said: “I am the way” (John XIV, 6). We, however, say: “Blessed are the undefiled, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 1). And again: “I have chosen the way of truth; teach me the way of your ordinances.”

They crowned the Lord with thorns; but we, if we are precious stones, will crown our Lord. A diadem adorns the head of the rulers of this age; we are placed upon the head of our King for this reason: that we may be adorned by the Head.

They did not receive Christ, and they will receive Antichrist; we have received the humble Son of God, so that later we may possess him triumphant.

Finally, our goat is sacrificed before the Lord’s altar; their goat, Antichrist, spat upon and cursed, is cast into the wilderness. Our thief enters paradise with the Lord; their thief, a murderer and blasphemer, dies in his sin. Barabbas is released for them; Christ is killed for us.

For all these things, dearest brothers, let us sing together with one voice: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24).

## IV

Today Christ, together with the thief, unbarred that fiery sword and the gate of paradise which no one had been able to break through. Therefore today Christ said to the angels: “Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them I will confess to the Lord.” Once opened, this gate is never closed to believers.

From the time when the Lord suffered until the present day, this gate has continually been closed and opened. It is closed to sinners and unbelievers; it is open to the righteous and believers.

Through it Peter entered; through it Paul entered. Through it all the saints and martyrs entered. Through it every day the souls of the righteous enter from the whole world.

There are two gates: the gate of paradise and the gate of the Church. Through the gate of the Church we enter the gate of paradise. We must therefore live in such a way that we are not cast out of that house and, once cast outside, devoured by beasts. Fearing them, the Prophet says elsewhere: “Do not give the souls of those who confess you to the beasts” (Ps. LXXIII, 19).

## V

Behold, now the Lord, standing at the gate of paradise, speaks to us who are in his house: whenever any of the saints has entered—although the devil forbids it, although the enemy accuses, for he is indeed the accuser of our brothers and the hostile avenger—he will not be put to shame when he speaks to his enemies at the gate, as it is said in the hundred twenty-sixth Psalm.

In Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Editorial Notice on the Following Epistle

To say nothing of the craftsman himself, who attempted by such poor devices to make Jerome lie in this epistle, and who is more than sufficiently scourged by Erasmus, I advise you to compare it with Bede’s sermon on this same subject, and with another *Encomium* concerning the chains and Peter’s sword in Metaphrastes.

He also fabricated that little letter of the Emperor Constantine to the Christians of the entire world, which he inserts in chapter 5 and which no other human being knows.

# Epistle XXX, to Eustochium: On the Chains of Blessed Peter

## I

Dearest Eustochium, virgin of Christ, your affection has very frequently asked me to make known to you and to your virgins how the festival celebrated on the Kalends of August in honor of blessed Peter the apostle originated, and why it is observed neither later nor earlier but on the first day of the month.

You report that there are some who believe the apostle Peter was brought out of prison by an angel on this day. Finally, you ask me to explain how the hundred thirty-sixth Psalm suits blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, or whether it was prophesied concerning him.

## II

I must answer the first two questions briefly, so that in the final one I may be allowed to linger.

Whoever believes that the apostle Peter was brought out of prison on this day should read the text of the Gospel’s repeated account and will discover that he has fallen into error. The matter is reported so plainly that it is easy for all readers to understand.

For King Herod, the son of the elder Herod, who had consented to the killing of the Savior, seeking to overturn the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ that was preached through the apostles, “laid hands on certain members of the Church to afflict them” (Acts XII, 1).

This indicates that his efforts were directed against several people. Still extending the branches of his pride, he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, and he undertook to commit this crime specifically during the days of Unleavened Bread. “It was,” he says, “the days of Unleavened Bread.” Those who had killed the Lord and Savior the previous year during the days of Unleavened Bread were striving to destroy the apostle Peter during those same days.

When he had seized him, he placed him in prison, handing him over to four squads of soldiers for guarding, intending to bring him out to the people after Passover.

But “there is no counsel, no knowledge, no wisdom, and no strength against the Lord” (Prov. XXI, 30). “On that very night,” he says, “when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains; and guards before the door were guarding the prison. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood there, and a light shone in the prison dwelling. And striking Peter’s side, he awakened him, saying: ‘Rise quickly.’ And the chains fell from his hands, and he went out, following the angel.”

This is how Peter, imprisoned during the days of Unleavened Bread, was released after Passover—not on the Kalends of August.

## III

But I shall explain how the festival of so great an apostle was devised.

Octavian Caesar had Marcus Antonius as a rival for his empire. He was scarcely able to destroy him through repeated engagements and battles. Cleopatra, his wife, mourning him after his death and burying herself alive, placed asps upon her breasts and chose to die with her husband rather than fall into the hands of the Romans.

Caesar, celebrating his victory over the tyrant, returned to Rome, bringing with him an immeasurable number of captives and the treasures of all the ancient Ptolemies, so that it is known that neither before nor afterward was such an abundance of gold, silver, and gems brought to Rome.

When he entered Rome on this day in triumph for so great a victory and for the firmest peace granted to the whole world, he was called Augustus, whereas previously he had been called only Caesar.

The city was crowned; there was immense joy among the people; the Senate established the matter, and all the Romans confirmed it in writing. It was announced throughout the entire world, to all nations, that Octavian Augustus ought to be worshiped among the gods. And the month that had formerly been called Sextilis in the order of the months was, in honor of Augustus, to be called August.

“We decree that this festive celebration, in honor of the triumph of the Augustan victory, be preserved by perpetual law.”

## IV

Thus matters continued until the reign of the great Constantine, who, after being visited by the holy apostles Peter and Paul through heavenly favor and baptized by Pope Sylvester, became, from a persecutor, a defender of the faith and a constant guardian of Christ’s commandments.

Horrified by the phantoms of these solemnities, he said to Pope Sylvester:

“Until now, Father, as you yourself know, using human laws, I have devoted myself with every effort to observing both these days and the others. But now, since it has pleased the Lord Jesus Christ to make me, a sinner, his servant, it seems wrong to me that I should be exalted by the favorable praises of these celebrations. See, then, how I may dedicate this day to the honor of the supreme God and blessed Peter the apostle.”

When Saint Sylvester heard this, he was filled with joy and gave thanks to God. Then, with the council of his clergy, he answered Augustus:

“There is a prison in which the blessed apostle Peter, laboring for Christ, was bound, and in which he dedicated the sacred font after baptizing many people. Have it cleansed of every impurity, so that, once a church has been built there, the prayers of the faithful may continually be offered to the honor of so great an apostle.”

When Augustus heard this, he became joyful. The place was cleansed, a church was built, and the same pope consecrated it.

## V

Augustus was present there and endeavored to send a message throughout the whole world through couriers, written in these words:

> “We wish it to be known to all who devoutly worship Christ that blessed Peter the apostle, given to us by God as shepherd and prince, should be venerated with the greatest devotion, continually and especially on this day, the Kalends of August, on which we were accustomed to be worshiped by you as a god. May this devout shepherd, by prayers poured out to God, deign to assist us and our empire. Farewell.”

Saint Sylvester established this day as a festival for all the Churches, so that, just as it had been celebrated in honor of an earthly prince, it might be celebrated for the glory of the heavenly key-bearer.

This celebration received the name “of blessed Peter the apostle, at the chains,” because of the sufferings of the chains he endured there, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Rom. V, 20).

This house of chains was made, in this manner, a house of holy prayers.

## VI

I have briefly answered the two questions posed; now I shall turn to the psalm and show whether it is applicable to blessed Peter, so that none of your good desire may be disappointed.

Let blessed Peter therefore address the Lord in prophetic words: “Lord, you have tested me” (Psalm 138:1), because you called me; you knew that I presumed and dared to say, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” But you knew all my thoughts from afar, before I had thought them: you examined my path and my course, and foresaw and tested all my ways, because there was no deceit on my tongue when I said, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew 26:35).

But you strengthened me and placed your hand upon me; you strengthened me by your presence, knowing that I would deny you, and you placed your hand upon me so that tears might follow my sin. Your power from me became wondrous; it was strengthened, and I could not attain to it. I tried not to deny you; I even promised that I would choose death rather than incur the guilt of denial. But your foreknowledge was so strengthened that I could not attain to it.

What shall I do now? I denied the Lord and master—and I did not deny merely a man, as some think. I denied the one to whom I said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” I denied the one whom I had experienced walking upon the waters. I denied the one whom I saw, by his own voice, calling the dead man from the tomb. I denied the one whom, when the heavens were opened, I saw with Moses and Elijah, and over whom I heard a voice from heaven: “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Matthew 17:5). I denied the one who by his touch enlightened the blind, cleansed lepers by his word, expelled demons by his command, and displayed many manifestations of his divinity.

## VII

What shall we do now, Novatian? Shall we lose the apostle Peter, or shall we receive him when he returns to Christ? Behold, Christ receives him; will you cast him out? But Paul cries out against you: “If God justifies, why do you condemn?” You say: “Believe that the baptized must not be helped when they repent.” Behold, the repentant apostle is helped—he who is the bishop of bishops—and a greater rank is restored to him as he weeps than was taken away from him when he denied.

To demonstrate this, I point out that none of the apostles received the name “shepherd.” For the Lord, after his resurrection, granted the power of this title to the penitent Peter alone; and to Peter, who had denied him, he gave the authority that he alone had possessed. Thus it was shown not only that he had recovered what he had lost, but that by repentance he had acquired much more than he had lost by denial.

The good teacher established this example in his chosen disciple, so that every disciple of Christ should be whole-hearted and should repent if it should happen that he sins; nor should he allow the harmful condition to diminish within him. But the one who is overcome so much more quickly is cleansed so much more quickly.

## VIII [Col. 0229B]

Certainly, all holiness leads to God, and every sin leads to the devil. Since we have been placed under a good Lord, how can we believe that the possibility of going to the devil has been granted to us while the possibility of returning to the Lord has been denied?

I add something further. Certainly God does not wish a human being to withdraw from him through sin, and he wishes every sinner to come to him. If what God does not wish could happen, how much more can what God does wish happen! Therefore the thought of sin was not prohibited by God through nature, but through command, so that the struggle of labor might fall upon him and the reward arise from the contest. For God wished to leave human beings the toil of their work, lest he prevent the reward in any part of their striving.

## IX [Col. 0229C]

Certainly no one is unaware that there are two peoples, of the good and of the wicked. We call those who believe good, and those who do not believe utterly wicked. Those who do not believe are under the devil, and those who believe are under God.

A great proclamation indeed is yours: you call the devil’s servant to yourself, while driving God’s servant away from yourself—as though you wished God to gain what he does not have and lose what he does have. In this way you reckon God’s riches according to whether he can raise the dead but cannot save the sick. For unbelievers are dead, while believers, although they are sinners, live in their infirmity.

And if our Savior has—in fact, because he has—the power to raise the dead, how can he lack the power to cure whatever infirmities there may be? You blaspheme him on both sides when you deny repentance its effect. If you teach that he can cure every infirmity but that he does not wish to do so, you accuse him of impiety. If you should perhaps say that he wishes to do so but cannot, you exclude him from divinity, so that on both sides, as you are condemned, you deny yourselves his mercy, when you claim that the perishing household of God cannot be helped.

## X [Col. 0229D]

Having spoken thus far with the Novatians, let us return to the repentant apostle, who wept most bitterly and said: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? I know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God; this knowledge was not revealed to me by flesh and blood, but by your Father who is in heaven.”

Where shall I flee, when I know you to be God and have acknowledged you as omnipotent? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. For there you descended especially through your passion, while by your power you are present there, as everywhere generally.

“If I take my wings at dawn”—that is, before the light. In this passage he uses “wings” for thoughts, which by sudden flight are everywhere: in heaven, on earth, in the abyss, and wherever the seas end. “If, therefore,” he says, “I go there before the light of your resurrection, wherever inaccessibility usually conceals a fugitive, so that I may be able to go there, your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me as a fugitive.”

Here he placed “before the light” before the Savior’s resurrection, because the whole age was in darkness while the Lord lay in the tomb. It was during this time that Peter’s repentance was taking place. He also says: “Perhaps darkness will trample me,” and in his three denials he recalled that, if he fled, three regions of escape were closed to him: heaven, hell, and the farthest parts of the sea.

Therefore denial is darkness, and flight is the trampling of darkness. Fearing that, once seized by those very darknesses, he might be trampled underfoot—as though, submerged beneath his evil deeds, he might be given over to the works of darkness, enduring perpetual torment, continual tears, and eternal pains—he describes how the darkness of this death, by which we die bodily, is trampled underfoot. But if, he says, I die, I shall not be trampled by darkness; rather, I shall reach the delights of the saints.

## XI [Col. 0230B]

“The night itself is my illumination in my delights.” There I shall have Christ, my light, who does not suffer the darkness of night; in whose presence night will be illuminated like day.

This is what we sing and believe, taught by Peter the Apostle as he proclaimed it. As his darkness is, so also is his light. For darkness does not make all creatures blind. Indeed, all wild animals, and also the beasts that roam by night, suffer no blindness from the night. There are also birds that fly during the night.

From this we learn that nature did not grant all animals eyes from the Creator that are incapable of seeing in darkness. For God established nights for human rest, so that the human race might be provided with quiet. Therefore the darkness belongs to the one to whom the light belongs—a point which Manichaeus denies. He himself is also the creator of our bodies, contrary to the claim made by those who say that Peter was unrepentant.

## XII [Col. 0230D]

“You possessed my reins, and you received me from my mother’s womb.”

For just as by the mouth, when we speak, and by our work, when we perform some action, we reveal the thoughts of our heart, so what we think is generated in the reins before it is disclosed by speaking or acting, according to what we say to God in another psalm: “For you possessed my reins.”

He will say: “For nothing in me was so hidden from you that you considered not only what had been thought, but also saw what was to be thought in the reins.”

“You, Lord, who received me from my mother’s womb”—so that you know whatever I may at some time have sinned from my birth in the half-articulate, babbling words of infancy. In this too I shall confess to you, because you have been made wonderfully terrible. Your works are wondrous, and I saw them with my eyes; and as you brought them about, I came to know them.  
[Al.: “and as you, Lord Jesus Christ, brought them about, I came to know them.”]  
And my soul knew them exceedingly well.

What I have believed is within me—not on the surface of words, but within, in the innermost parts of my soul—and that this is so is not hidden from you. Indeed, even my mouth is not hidden from you, that is, the mouth which you made in secret. If, therefore, even my mouth is not hidden from you, although you willed it naturally to be hidden, how will what you commanded to be made manifest in the heart be hidden from you?

## XIII [Col. 0231A]

We are led to higher matters when we treat of the bones and substance that lie in the lower parts of the earth. The meaning here is that, when the day of resurrection arrives, wherever my bone may be, and even if my substance is in the lower parts of the earth, your eyes will see my unfinished form, because it will rise at the mere sight of your eyes.

In the book of resurrection all who are born are written down, all who are formed day by day, and there is no one among them who is not written in that book. In this book I have no beloved and honored except your friends alone, O God, for their dominion has been strengthened exceedingly. Indeed, you promise that they will share in your eternal reign.

Nor should we listen to the heretics who say: “The world ought not to have continued through the one who foresaw that human beings, through their sins and crimes, were destined for the eternal fire of Gehenna.” If you think that it ought to have happened in this way, you will judge that provision was made more for the guilty than for the saints. For if the world had been recalled from its passing away, none of the saints would have shared in the kingdom; and while provision was made for the wicked, so that they would not come to destruction and would not perish according to the merit of their wickedness, the good would have received this sentence: that they should not even receive temporal life, though eternal life was owed to them.

But let us, with the prophet, rejoice with the saints of God, and, with the apostle Peter, remember the friends of the Lord with the honors due to them. Their number is so great that they are known to have multiplied beyond the sand.

But what will happen when the Lord kills sinners—when he kills Nero and, after him, all the bloodthirsty men who killed the saints of the Lord?

## XIV [Col. 0231D]

If your God, O heretics, had followed your counsel, so that Nero, Diocletian, and the other killers of the saints should not perish, he would neither have made apostles nor caused martyrs to be born. There would have been one judgment for the just and the unjust, and one sentence would have overtaken them all, by which all would seem to have been punished before they were born.

But you, men of blood, withdraw from us—you who say that they received their cities in vain; that is, that they were made mortal without cause, and that everything perishes together with the world, so that destruction itself is equal for all.

It is not so. All are written in the book; all will rise. But to some there will be given the fragrance of life unto eternal life, and to others the fragrance of death unto perpetual death. Those to whom these words are addressed will arrive there: “Did I not hate those who hated you, O God, and did I not waste away because of your enemies?”

Peter speaks these words, and the Church pronounces them in Peter: “With perfect hatred I hated them, and they became enemies to me.”

And after these people have been anathematized, he says: “Test me, Lord, and know my heart—what I think about you, what I believe about you. Question me, and know my paths. Let your concern be for your Church, for your sheep, and for your shepherds; and see whether there is any way of iniquity in me.”

The way of iniquity is the devil, who offers himself to unbelievers and heretics for walking in it. “And see,” he says, “among your people, lest there be anyone in whom the way of iniquity may provide a path for errors.” Excluding the way of iniquity, lead me into the eternal way, so that the gates of death and hell may not prevail against me, according to your word, Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# Editorial Notice on the Following Letter

Dacherius published this work, as though it had not previously been made public, in volume III of the *Spicilegium veterum scriptorum*, from an excellent manuscript of Saint-Germain. The scholars who later revised Dacher’s collection did not notice that it had long been counted among the works falsely attributed to Jerome.

In that manuscript it is mutilated in several places through the carelessness of the copyist, though otherwise it is not without correction. Its chief merit is that, from the title it bears in the manuscript—“of Nicetius, bishop, concerning the Vigils of the Servants of God”—we can distinguish its true author.

This Nicetius is the bishop of Trier, whom Sidonius Apollinaris praises with the highest commendation, being also, as they maintain, related to him by marriage; whom Gregory of Tours praises in chapter 17 of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers* and in book X of his *History of the Franks*; whom Venantius Fortunatus praises in book III, poem 9; and whom others likewise praise. His holy memory is finally recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 7 January.

The work is also attributed to the same man in other celebrated manuscripts of the Vatican Library, cited by Holstenius and Sirmond, although the learned men there may have read *Nicetae* instead of *Nicetii*, either because the letters had faded through age or because of a preconceived opinion. They also thought that the famous Nicetas, bishop of Dacia, frequently praised by Saint Paulinus, was intended.

Apart from the great authority of the Saint-Germain manuscript, two distinguished letters of the Nicetius in question, recorded in the Councils of Gaul under the years 563 and 565, also persuade us that this is genuinely his work: one addressed to the emperor Justinian, the other to Chlodoswintha, daughter of Chlothar. So too does another treatise entitled *On the Good of Psalmody*, which displays exactly the same style, doctrine, and spirit.

There are also other works among these writings falsely attributed to Jerome which, if I may state honestly what I think, breathe the same diction and character: evidently the works of a bishop instructed from childhood in monastic disciplines and thereafter devoted to the holy instruction of the people entrusted to him.

Erasmus was therefore exceedingly rash when he said that he had retained this treatise in this order, as though he were considering his own modesty more than the treatise’s merit. Saint Isidore of Seville was not at all ashamed to reproduce almost word for word an entire chapter—chapter 21—of his *Ecclesiastical Offices* from this work.

# Letter XXXI, or Treatise on the Observance of Vigils (C, G)*

It is worthy and entirely appropriate, brothers, indeed most fitting, that we should now speak and deliver a discourse concerning the holy Vigils, when the vigil itself is demanded of the watchful.

[Note: In Dacherius: “A good, worthy, and holy matter, and entirely appropriate”; shortly afterward, “to deliver a discourse,” when the nocturnal labor itself is being carried out; and, “Night is blind and the necessary darkness for bodies,” etc.]

Behold, night is the darkness of the body, which holds not only human beings but all living creatures in sleep, so that, their strength restored through slumber, they may remain awake and endure the labors of the day.

God is good: he so provided and so ordained that a person going out to his work and continuing in his labor until evening should have an appointed period in which to rest from harsh labor and great fatigue.

[Col. 0233A] Therefore he made the day for work and the night for rest, and for this, as for all things, we ought to give thanks to him who provided it.

We know, however, that many people, either to please their superiors or to benefit themselves in some particular way, set aside a portion of the night for some task and count as profit whatever they have been able to accomplish by stealing it from their sleep.

[Note: From the words “Solomon praises” through the end of the following period, the intervening material is missing from Dacher’s edition.]

Solomon praises the woman who diligently works at her allotted tasks and spinning by lamplight (Proverbs 31:13). He also added that from this praise for her husband at the gates and great glory arise.

If, then, in the case of bodily implements—that is, things necessary for food or clothing—a person who keeps vigil is not blamed but rather praised, I confess that I marvel that there are some who consider holy vigils, so fruitful in spiritual work and so rich in prayers, hymns, and readings, either superfluous, idle, or—what is worse—inopportune.

[Note: In Dacherius: “How much more ought we to observe and love the fruitful holy vigils . . . so that we may receive a reward from the Lord God. Indeed, there are people who criticize these things, but they are alien to the Catholic faith and religion. Yet it is not surprising—for how could the impious and profane . . .”]

## II [Col. 0233B]

If there are people alien to our religion who think in this way, it is not surprising. For how can religious practices please the profane? If they pleased them, they would be ours, since we know that we are Christians.

But if those who are ours are offended by the salutary practice of vigils, then—to suspect nothing worse of them—they are either lazy, sleepy, or, what comes closest to these, old or infirm.

If they are lazy, let them be ashamed, because Solomon’s words resound for them: “Go to the ant, O lazy one, and imitate its ways” (Proverbs 6:6ff.).

If they are sleepy, let them awaken, as Scripture proclaims: “O lazy one, how long will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, sit for a short time, doze for a little while, and fold your hands over your breast for a little while. Then poverty will overtake you like a traveler, and want will come swiftly like a good and nimble runner.”

[Note: In the plural in Dacher’s edition: “But if they are old, who compels them to keep vigil? Yet, even without compulsion, they ought to keep vigil because of their age.” Then: “and to pray to the Lord God more earnestly.” They ought therefore to keep vigil sitting if they are unable to stand. This material is treated only as part of the following period—“And if you cannot stand,” etc.—up to “is fitting for vigils,” which is entirely absent there. Later, again in the plural: “But if they are infirm,” etc., coherently. Finally: “Let them also commend those who keep vigil, so that through their prayers they may . . .”]

If you are old, who compels you to keep vigil? Yet even without compulsion, you keep vigil because of your age. And if you cannot stand and consider your incapacity, you ought not to call young and strong people back to your own sluggishness; because of the various temptations of youth, they ought to discipline themselves with more devoted vigils.

## III [Col. 0234A]

But if you are infirm in your limbs, do not criticize what you cannot do. Rather, in accordance with the Prophet, water your bed with tears as well, and say: “Thus I remembered you upon my bed” (Psalm 62:7).

Also instruct those who keep vigil to help you with their prayers, so that, aided by the Lord, you may sing upon your bed of pain and may one day deserve to say: “In the morning I shall meditate upon you, because you have been my helper” (ibid.).

[Note: Dacherius adds: “from religion”; shortly afterward, “we ought not to envy but to rejoice with those who are able.” As one who consents to wickedness shares in its punishment. A little later, *coronat affectus* is printed incorrectly for *coronat effectus*.]

Otherwise it is foolish and very foreign to religion that, because we ourselves cannot run, we should disparage those who run well. Even if we cannot do so, we ought to rejoice with those who are able.

For just as through consent to wickedness one shares the punishment of those who commit it, so one ought to hope for a share in glory through consent to goodness. One person is crowned for his achievement; another is gladdened by his pious intention.

## IV [Col. 0234B]

Nor should it seem burdensome or difficult even for delicate bodies [Al.: “or infirm bodies”] to set aside some portion of two nights each week—namely, Saturday and Sunday—for the service of God.

This is, as it were, a purification of the five days, or of the nights, during which we grow heavy through the stupor of the flesh [Al.: “through carnal stupor”] or yawn amid worldly activities.

[Note: For *oscitamus*, Dacher’s edition has the two words “we rejoice, being preoccupied.” Shortly afterward: “the confusion that leads to sin.” Then, in the plural: “If you are holy, love vigils,” etc., continuing below, “so that, striking your breasts, you may cry out more frequently to the Lord, saying with your whole heart: From hidden faults,” etc.]

Let no one, therefore, be ashamed in the good pursuit of holiness, since the wicked are not ashamed when carrying out their shameful deeds. Scripture rightly presses upon us in Proverbs: “There is a shame that leads to sin” (Ecclesiasticus 4:25). To be ashamed in a good work is sin; just as not being ashamed when doing evil is ruin.

If you are holy, love vigils, so that by keeping watch you may guard your treasure and yourself remain in holiness. If you are a sinner, take greater care to be cleansed through keeping watch and praying, while you cry out more frequently with a beaten breast: “From my hidden faults cleanse me, Lord, and spare your servant from those of others” (Psalm 18:13).

For the one who already desires to be cleansed [Al.: “purified”] from hidden faults must necessarily cease to take pleasure in being defiled by these miseries.

## V [Col. 0234D]

The matter requires, dearest brothers, that we say a little about the authority and antiquity of vigils, and about their very usefulness.

For any labor is more willingly undertaken if the usefulness of that labor is set before one’s eyes. The devotion to vigils is ancient, a familiar good among all the saints.

The prophet Isaiah finally cries out to God: “My spirit keeps watch for you from the night, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isaiah 26:9).

David, consecrated with royal and prophetic anointing, sings: “Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out and by night before you” (Psalm 87:2). And in another psalm: “I remembered your name at night, Lord, and I kept your law” (Psalm 118:55).

[Note: The material that follows here for six complete lines, up to “to stand before,” is missing from Dacher’s edition.]

But perhaps he sang these words while lying on his little bed. Some lazier people have thought it sufficient if each person merely prays or murmurs a psalm in his bed.

That too is good: to remember God always and everywhere is salutary. But that it is better to rise and stand before the divine presence, receive from the same Prophet another utterance, which indicates the time, place, and posture of the one praying: “In the nights,” he says, “lift up your hands toward the holy places and bless the Lord” (Psalm 133:2).

And lest you suppose that only the evening hours are called “night,” he adds: “At midnight I rose to confess to you concerning the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118:62).

You have both the precise time for rising and the attentiveness of how one should confess to God.

## VI [Col. 0235B]

As I continue to consider the intention of the saints, something greater and more laborious presents itself—something beyond the condition of human nature is suggested—when I hear the same Prophet singing:

“If I ascend upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131:3ff.).

[Note: The same edition has: “Who would not be astonished at such devotion of spirit in the love of God?”]

Who would not be astonished at such love of God and devotion of spirit, that he entirely forbade himself sleep, without which human bodies certainly fail, until the king and prophet should find a place in which to build a temple for the Lord?

This ought firmly [Al.: “boldly”] to admonish us: if we ourselves wish to be the Lord’s place and desire to be regarded as his perpetual dwelling and temple, as Paul declares when he says, “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16), then, as far as we can, let us love vigils by the example of the saints, lest it be said of us, as it is sung:

“They have slept their sleep, and found nothing in their hands” (Psalm 75:6).
