Rather, let each person say already with rejoicing: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived. For it is good to confess to the Lord and to sing to your name, O Most High, to proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth throughout the night” (Psalm 76:3ff.).

[Col. 0235D] The saints sang and left writings of this kind—so many and so great—so that we, their descendants, might be stirred by corresponding examples to celebrate, even at night, the vigils of our salvation.

## VII [Col. 0236A]

But let us move from the ancient to the new, from the ministers of the Law to the ministers of the Gospel; let the observance of vigils also be confirmed by the New Testament.

Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, a widow serving the Lord with continual prayers and fasts, is read in the Gospel not to have departed from the temple day or night.

[Note: In the same place, “she did not depart from the temple.” In the Gospel it is read that the shepherds . . . From there we supplied the missing word “to see.” Shortly afterward, “If they had kept watch,” instead of “If they had not slept.” Then two words, “be to men,” and afterward the entire period beginning, “But know this,” etc., are omitted. It also reads: “He taught them to keep watch not only by his words, but also confirmed it by his example.” Finally: “He spent the night not for himself, but so that we might know what all ought to do. And he himself rebukes Peter,” etc., with the intervening material shortened through the copyist’s carelessness.]

Those most holy shepherds, while keeping nightly vigils over their flocks, deserved both to see angels in splendor and to hear first of all that Christ had been born on earth.

Moreover, does not the teaching of the Savior, with complete diligence, rouse his hearers to keep watch? In the parable of the good sower he says [Al.: “teaches”]: “While people were sleeping, an evil man came and sowed weeds over the wheat, and went away” (Matthew 13:25). If they had not slept, perhaps the evil man could not have sown the weeds.

Or again, when he says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands; and be like people waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding. Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching. And if he comes in the evening,” he says, “or at midnight, or at the cockcrow, and finds them watching, they are blessed. But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. Therefore you also be ready, because at an hour you do not expect, the Son of Man will come” (Luke 12:35ff.).

He taught vigils not only by words, but also by example. For the Gospel testifies that “Jesus was spending the night in prayer” [Al.: “in the prayer of God”] (Luke 6:12). The Lord spent the night not for himself, but so that his poor and weak servants might know what they ought to do, when the Lord, rich in all things and needing nothing, endured the night in prayer with the utmost strength.

Likewise, at the time of his passion, he rebukes Peter, saying: “Could you not watch with me for one hour?” (Mark 14:37). And he now says to all: “Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.”

These words and examples of this kind—tell me, I ask you—whom could they not awaken even from deep sleep, a sleep very like death?

## VIII [Col. 0236D]

Instructed by these discourses and strengthened by these teachings, the blessed apostles themselves kept watch and commanded vigils.

Peter is awakened at night by an angel in prison, and when the angel himself opened the iron gate, Peter reached the house of Mary, where many were gathered—not snoring [Al.: “sleeping,”] surely, but praying.

In his own Epistle he says: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” [Al.: “to swallow up”].

Paul and Silas are remembered as having prayed in the public prison around midnight and sung a hymn while the prisoners listened. Suddenly, when the foundations of the prison were shaken by an earthquake and the doors were opened of their own accord, everyone’s chains were loosed.

[Note: Dacher’s copy omits *sponte*; shortly afterward it has *sunt subito soluta*. The remaining material that follows, nearly twenty lines from “The same apostle Paul” through the end of this section, is likewise omitted by Dacher’s copy. Instead, for this immense lacuna, it has only the following: “Thus the blessed apostle Paul exhorts the Thessalonians concerning the practice of vigils, saying: ‘Watch and stand firm in the faith; be strengthened and act courageously.’” These words appear to have been distorted by the copyist from the following context, because he had before his eyes a mutilated exemplar at a place where the name and testimony of the apostle Paul recur and where such errors were liable to arise.]

The same apostle Paul, about to depart from Troas, continued teaching until midnight, with many lamps burning in the upper room. A young man named Eutychus, overcome by sleep while Paul was prolonging his discourse, fell from a third-story window and was taken up dead. Life was immediately restored to him, and Paul continued speaking until dawn; then, under God’s guidance, he departed.

How fully and abundantly the same apostle exhorted people to practice vigils! Writing to the Thessalonians, he says: “Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night. But we who belong to God, let us be sober” (1 Thessalonians 5:6ff.).

And he concludes wonderfully: “Whether we watch or sleep, let us live together with him.”

To the Corinthians he says: “Watch, stand firm in the faith, be strengthened, act courageously” (1 Corinthians 16:13).

So too he writes to the Ephesians: “Praying at all times in the Spirit” (Ephesians 6:18; the printed citation reads “Job. VI, 18”).

And, setting forth an example of watchfulness among his list of virtues, he boasts to the Corinthians of the fruit of his many vigils.

## IX [Col. 0237B]

This is sufficient concerning the antiquity and authority of vigils. It remains, according to the promised order, to say something about their usefulness [Al.: “to present something of their usefulness”].

Yet their usefulness can be experienced more readily through practice than described in the speech of one who talks about it.

[Note: Dacher’s edition has “by tasting”; it omits the words “as it is written”; afterward it reads “how great the modesty of the heart” instead of “how great the burden of the heart.” Shortly afterward it reads: “which holy visitation gladdens all the limbs of the one keeping watch.” It is altogether more correct to read “chastity is strengthened” rather than “charity is strengthened.”]

For it seems that one must taste it, because “the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 99:5), as it is written. Therefore whoever has tasted understands and feels how great a burden is laid down from the heart through keeping watch, how great a stupor of the mind is shaken off, how great a light illumines the soul of the one who watches and prays, and what grace and visitation gladden all the limbs.

Through keeping watch, every fear is excluded, confidence is born, the flesh is disciplined, vices waste away, charity is strengthened, folly departs, prudence approaches, the mind is sharpened, error is dulled, and the devil, the head of crimes, is wounded by the sword of the Spirit.

What is more necessary than this usefulness? What is more advantageous than these gains [Al.: “these holy gains”]? What is sweeter than this delight? What is more blessed than this happiness?

The Prophet also bears witness. At the beginning of his psalms, when describing the blessed man, he placed the summit of his blessedness in this verse: “If he meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.”

Daytime meditation is indeed good.

[Note: In the same edition: “daytime prayer is good, but nighttime meditation is much more pleasing and effective, because . . .” Then: “Night is secret, night is quiet and suitable for those who pray, most excellent,” etc.; and, with the sense gathered together, it presents the whole person before the divine presence. Conversely, the material that follows for approximately twelve lines—from “Therefore the devil, a clever imitator of divine things,” through the end of this section and into the following passage where it says “unless he knew them to be pleasing to God”—is missing from that edition. The sense is expressed in this way: “Therefore know that vigils are pleasing to God for the celebration of blessing. Only, dearest brothers, he who keeps watch . . .”]

But nighttime meditation is more effective, because during the day various necessities make themselves heard, occupations distract the mind, and divided concerns disperse the understanding.

Night is quiet; night is private. It offers itself as an opportunity most suitable for those who pray and most fitting for those who keep vigil, while it presents a person, freed from bodily occupations, with a collected and attentive mind before the divine presence.

Therefore the devil, always a clever imitator of divine things, just as he gave his worshipers fasts and virginity, empty baptisms and futile rites, imitating this holy practice as well, has added nocturnal sacred observances and vigils to his banquets.

## X.

Hence, then, let our faithful, if they are not stirred by the example of their own people to hold sacred vigils, recognize, when they observe the contrary practice of the Gentiles, that such vigils are not alien to the affairs of God: the wicked one would not imitate them for the purpose of deception unless he knew that they were pleasing to God for the blessing of those who celebrate them.

Yet, beloved brothers, let the one who keeps vigil with his eyes keep vigil also in his heart; let the one who prays with his spirit pray also with his mind. For [Note: Dacherius: “because it is not sufficiently useful to keep vigil with the eyes while sleeping in the mind”; then: “It must also be taken care above all that the hearts of our watchers are not burdened by an excess of food or drink.” Shortly afterward: “For a certain man said,” and so forth, in the following section. “I, as one about to celebrate a divine mystery,” and shortly afterward, “so that, restored and unencumbered,” and so forth. Finally: “For there are also vigils that come from the evil one, as it is read in Proverbs: ‘because,’ and so forth ... But let such vigils be absent, and far absent, from this assembly; rather, let them be ...”]

It is utterly useless to keep vigil with the eyes while the mind sleeps. On the contrary, Scripture testifies in the person of the Church: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

Care must also be taken that the breast of one who is about to keep vigil is not burdened by an excess of food or drink, lest, belching up indigestion and drunkenness, we become not only distasteful to ourselves but also be judged unworthy of the grace of the Spirit. For a certain outstanding man among the shepherds said: “As smoke drives away bees, so indigested belching turns away and casts off the gifts of the Holy Spirit.”

## XI.

Therefore, since we are about to perform a divine ministry, we must prepare ourselves beforehand through abstinence, so that, unburdened, we may keep vigil more freely. Let every evil thought also be driven away, lest our prayer become the prayer of one who keeps a wicked vigil, as it is written, “into sin.”

For there are also vigils that come from the evil one, as it is read in Proverbs: “Why has sleep been taken away from their eyes? For,” he says, “they do not sleep unless they have done evil” (Prov. 4:16). Let such vigils be absent, brothers—let them be absent from this assembly. Rather, let the breast of those who keep vigil be closed to the devil and open to Christ [Note: In the same author: “so that what we utter with our lips ...”; and: “our vigils are acceptable to God.” At the end, statements concerning their holy usefulness are likewise sufficient. The following is immediately appended: “But concerning the devotion of hymns and psalms, how pleasing and acceptable they are to God, I would have said something, however little, except that a more extended treatment would require another volume, which, with the Lord’s favor, will be presented in the following reading.” In fact, another work follows in that edition: “The same Bishop Nicetius’ Treatise on the Benefit of Psalmody.”]

so that we may hold in our heart the one whom we utter with our lips. Then our vigils will be acceptable; then our all-night vigil will be salutary, if our ministry is offered before the divine gaze with fitting diligence and sincere devotion. Let this suffice concerning the authority, antiquity, and usefulness of vigils. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Nothing, as Erasmus truly says, appears in this letter to belong to Pammachius or Oceanus. He rebukes those whose piety he is otherwise always accustomed to praise. Finally, by what indication can one detect that it was written to two rather than to one?

## LETTER XXXII. AN EXHORTATION TO PAMMACHIUS AND OCEANUS

### I.

One who invites an Ethiopian to the baths, even if he does not remove that man’s blackness, certainly at least receives money for himself; and although he does not rejoice in the other man’s whiteness, he nevertheless rejoices in his own profit. In the same way, without doubt, one who admonishes the disobedient with divine words, even though he does not remove the sins of the one who resists, nevertheless gains for himself a reward from the ministry of true charity.

But do I say this because I despise you? Do I speak because perhaps I do not love you? I answer in the Apostle’s words: “God is my witness” (Phil. 1:8)—that this is what I do and will do. I do not despise you, but I grieve that signs of unbelief, not of faith, appear among my own, because I recognize in you Jewish testimonies, not Christian ones. For, “though seeing, you do not see; and though hearing, you do not wish to hear.”

I am about to say something severe. I am troubled on both sides. I fear offending those who hear, but I fear still more those who despise admonitions. Those who pretend not to hear the word of God are considered worse than idols. Idols indeed have ears, but no will; they do not hear, touch with their hands, or grasp.

### II.

Hence, in comparison with wicked people, idols are better, because they neither covet with their eyes nor run about through things contrary and hostile to God. And, being naturally deaf, they are rightly judged better than the disobedient. Let the Prophet speak, if I lie. Let David speak, who did not deny that such people should be compared with serpents: “Like the deaf asp,” he says, “that stops its ears so that it may not hear the voice of the charmer” (Ps. 57:5).

And let them see whether those who, through the cunning of their craftiness, pretend not to hear what they hear by nature are not rightly compared with serpents. Can those be called Christians who even lose the name of their first humanity? Behold, Jeremiah says: “Their ears are uncircumcised; they cannot hear this” (Jer. 6:12). Not because they cannot hear, but because a will hostile to nature has imposed this inability: through the long practice of vice, their native dispositions have been corrupted by an adverse habit and have fallen into evil works.

Even vessels full of clay cannot receive or retain the liquid of a pure element. A thorny field, unless it has first been cleared by the labor of the cultivator, does not nourish the seed cast into it but chokes it. So also the mind filled with the enticements of worldly cares cannot sustain the divine word unless it has first cut down within itself, with the evangelical sickle, the cares of the world themselves and the sources of every sin.

For the present, perhaps I seem to some, with God overlooking it, to sin less; but that day will come when our deeds must be displayed as though painted on a tablet.

### III.

Oh, how much better it would have been for them on that day if, in this life, they had lacked both the sensation of their limbs and the strength of their organs! And how many there will be there who are without speech and mute, yet will then be happier than the talkative. How many shepherds will be preferred to philosophers; how many peasants to orators; how many dull-witted people to Cicero’s cleverness!

Holy Job, devoted to his glory amid temptation, cried out in his pain: “Why is light given to one in torment? Why were knees joined to me? Why did I suck the breasts? Why was I not dead in the womb? And why, as soon as I came forth from the womb, did I not immediately perish?” (Job 3).

If this was said by God’s friend in the light, what will his enemies say in darkness? If he groaned whom fever burned, what will he do whom Gehenna consumes? If he grieved that his knees had been joined, though his feet had always run in the love of God, what will he say whose feet never stood in truth? He was displeased that he had lived after being born from the womb, although he had lived well, because a worm destined to die was eating him. What will those who live badly do, whom eternal fire and the worm that never dies await?

“This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John 6:61). This was said by those disciples who left Christ’s footsteps in the Gospel and, having been scandalized by the divine word, preferred to love the world rather than God. Their belly is their god, and they do not wish to hear the practice of fasting.

For the word of chastity is an offense to the lustful, as the Prophet says: “The straight way is an abomination to a wicked man.” Isaiah also declared long ago that Christ would become a stone of stumbling to unbelievers.

I cannot flatter, lest I deceive my brother and lest Solomon’s saying strike me also: “The words of flatterers are smooth, but they pierce the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. 18:8). A physician is not faithful if, before the corruption has been cleansed, he applies a scar over the wound. We cannot always give milk, because you must not always remain little children.

### IV.

Tell me: how many years has it been since we were regenerated in Christ? Let each person consider how much he has advanced from that time in the heavenly age. I do not know how parents can be pleased with children who are five or ten years old if they remain in the same smallness in which they were born. What, then, must be said of us, whom the reckoning of time finds not merely small but abortive?

“It is written of Christians: They go from strength to strength.” Let us see whether we are Christians. What virtue has been added to us since we were regenerated in Christ? What humility in prosperity, what patience in adversity, what joy in tribulation, what contentment amid losses, what forgiveness in offenses, what chastity when lust presents itself?

Some pass daily from virtue to virtue; we pass from weakness to weakness. Some become better from moment to moment; we often become worse, as though we were not awaiting the same judge. We are foolish if we have believed in one Savior of believers and do not believe that there will be one judge. The Apostle speaks of one faith, one baptism, one Church, one God.

### V.

Thus the person who is wicked today is worse tomorrow; the person who is greedy today is greedier tomorrow. A year ago, one estate had been enough for my greed; now, perhaps, a fifth is not enough. Formerly my mind stretched itself toward possessing ten solidi; now a hundred have begun to seem small.

And while true Christians, true children of God who go from strength to strength, rejoice in the opportunity for virtue if they lose something, I cannot dine secure unless I have taken what belongs to another.

What are you doing, blind greed? Why are you cruel toward a little one? Why are you savage toward another’s child? Are you overturning the order of nature or of religion? You have already placed at the feet what ought to have been at the head. Insensible gold rules equally over all.

And what, I ask, is that thing—or what kind of thing is it—that turns us away from God? What and how great is the splendor by which the splendor of the true sun is lost to me? Gold and silver are carefully refined mud drawn from sand and ore; and, as the Prophet says, gold is a wood of stumbling, because, when the judgment of the mind has been overturned, through gold a person is enslaved to lust. He acquires solid coin by the same craft by which he loses his soul; he gains the emperor’s image and loses the image of Christ.

Do you wish to know how destructive is the love of possessing and the love of seeking money? Through this Judas betrayed the Savior. Certainly, whenever such a great crime is heard or read, we all recoil from it. As far as we can, we condemn the impious disciple—and through our ignorance we pierce ourselves with our own sword.

### VI.

How many Judases among us condemn Judas? How many, when through greed they hand over their own souls to eternal torments, become at once betrayers and slain victims?

Do we think, brothers, that the prophets proclaimed in jest, that the apostles spoke with laughter, or that Christ uselessly threatened judgment? But where punishments intervene, there are no jokes. If they suffered in jest, let it be believed that they spoke in jest.

Isaiah is cut apart with a saw. Daniel is given over to lions. Paul is beheaded with the sword. Peter is hanged on a cross, after the example of the Lord. And all this happened so that through their teaching they might recall us from sins.

But I fear that divine gifts may be reckoned against the disobedient, and that what was given here for salvation may contribute to punishment at the judgment. I fear that our faith is more a matter of joking than theirs was, both their faith and their words. I fear that we may not be saved through joking, and that just as we enter the Church through laughter, so he may laugh at us, as it is written: “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them” (Ps. 2:4).

There is much that could be said, but disgust on your part—which makes my speech harsh and uncultivated—and the conclusion of the manuscript put an end to my labor. I say one thing that I desire: since you are Christians, you ought to love heaven, not earth; to obey the word of God more than the devil; and to fear eternal judgment more than human beings.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Truly, Erasmus says, this letter in its entire character resembles the same author as the preceding one. In most manuscripts I found it without a title, with no indication either of to whom it was written or by whom.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO A CERTAIN PERSON WHO WAS DOING PENANCE IN THE WORLD

### I.

I rise to address you as a man whom I know to be faithful. My rebuke hastens toward you, whom I perceive to be proud.

You claim to repent, yet you live wholly in the world. You claim to repent, yet you take up again what you had vomited out. You claim to repent, yet, while following the works of the devil, you pass over the Lord.

I desire to know what you repent of. I do not know what your repentance is. You claim to repent, yet, while girded with the justice of God, you have put pride over it. You claim to repent, yet, while following another’s flesh, you are so exhausted that you are like a dog returning to its vomit, like a hungry dog, or like a pig overcome by heat and lying prostrate in the mud of the earth.

I cannot find what your repentance is. I walked to the place of repentance, but I did not find your repentance there. You who had abandoned the world are found there again. You who had laid aside the pride of the flesh lower your shoulder so that you may carry it again. You who had turned your back on greed turn back to meet it once more. You who had given vanity its remedy [perhaps: its repudiation] return again to its favor. You who had fled the pomp of the world have fallen again into its hands.

Yet you walk proud and with your neck held high, unaware that it is written: “What did our pride profit us, and what did honor with boasting bring us?” Again it was said: “All those things passed away like shadows” (Wis. 5:8–9).

### II.

You remember that you were faithful when you were renewed through the water of baptism, as it is written: “Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove your wickedness from your souls” (Isa. 1:16). He urges those people to wash; but although you were clean, you have become filthy.

You cannot now be washed again, as Peter says to the Lord: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.” He replies: “One who has been washed once does not need to be washed again” (John 13:9–10).

If, however, you wish to be cleansed again, give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you. For almsgiving is what cleanses every impurity. Humble yourself in everything, and you will find grace before God. Be submissive, and entreat him; do not imitate the wicked in doing evil. For those who do evil will be destroyed.

Pray to the Lord daily with tears, if perhaps your sins may be loosed. For “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

Remember the son who was in a distant land and, living wantonly, spent his substance on prostitutes. Then, becoming humble, he returned to himself and said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger? I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:17ff.).

When the father saw the humility of his son, exhausted as he was by extreme poverty, he was moved by mercy. For his humbled son he killed the fattened calf.

Remember, therefore, son, that Christ died for you, having previously been the fattened calf. His elder son, however, was saddened. “Why was Christ killed, who was the fattened calf?” But his father rebuked him, saying: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But you ought to rejoice, because this son of mine was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

O how blessed is the people for whom Christ died! What joy the Father bears when what was dead comes to life and what was lost is found!

### III.

Behold, you have now been made healthy. Do not sin, lest something worse happen to you. Consider, therefore, from where you have fallen; mourn and do penance. Otherwise the Lord will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.

Remember, son, that Christ left the ninety-nine righteous and sought the one sinful human being; and, having found him in a trackless place, carried him back on his shoulders.

Or remember that woman who had lost a drachma—that is, the Church of sinful people—and lit a lamp—that is, Christ, who is the light of justice. When she found the coin in the dung, she summoned her friends or neighbors—that is, the Churches—to rejoice over the sinful person who had been found; then, having raised him from the dung, she placed him with the leaders of his people—that is, with the apostles and prophets.

Behold what repentance does for the sinful person: while lying in dung, he is found among the leaders.

I call a person repentant who groans day and night and redeems his sins through almsgiving. I call a person repentant who mourns because he has done evil and asks the Lord that he may not again do what he committed. I call a person repentant who does not follow his desires and restrains himself from his own will. I call a person repentant who loves what he formerly neglected and forgets what he had done.

Let what is good cling to you, and let what is evil be erased. If you do not repent, you will fall into the hands of the Lord according to his greatness. “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15), as it is written: “I abandoned evil and sought good.”

Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance, and do not say: “I have sinned; what sad thing has happened to me?”

### IV.

Do not add sin upon sin and say: “The Lord’s mercy is great.” Know, however, that mercy and wrath come from him.

Return to the Lord and mourn, saying: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Ps. 50:6). “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance, Lord” (Ps. 24:7). Do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn away in anger from your servant. You are my helper; do not abandon me, Lord, nor despise me, my saving God (Ps. 26:9).

Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me (Ps. 50:13). Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you. Deliver me from the lion’s mouth, and turn my eyes away so that they may not see vanity.

Make your face shine upon your servant, and save me in your mercy. I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame. Do not hand me over to those who afflict me. Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings.

I have made my sin known to you, and I have not hidden my iniquities. I will confess to you, Lord God, with my whole heart. Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me; on whatever day I am afflicted, incline your ear to me.

On whatever day I call upon you, answer me quickly. Give me a sign, Lord, for good, so that those who hate me may see and be put to shame. Forgive me, Lord, so that I may be refreshed before I depart and be no more.

### V.

Behold the repentance of a person who humbles himself. How will one who groans in such a manner not obtain forgiveness? Who would not hear him and be moved? For “the one who humbles himself will be exalted, and the one who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity? It is better for you not to make a vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.

You call yourself repentant, yet you delight in the lust of the flesh. Your sins do not cease to walk about, yet you say that they are sitting still.

But God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my justice and take my covenant upon your mouth? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you. When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. Sitting, you slandered your brother, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block.

“You did these things, and I was silent. You wickedly supposed that I would be like you. I will rebuke you and set you before your face. Understand this, you who forget God, lest he suddenly seize you and there be no one to deliver you. A sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him my salvation” (Ps. 49:16ff.).

### VI.

Behold what sort of threat the Lord makes against the sinful person. You who say and assert that you repent—where is your repentance? It has been excluded by pride and contempt; you have neglected to follow God.

Listen, son, and withdraw your foot from the world, which you renounced. Repent, therefore, of all the pomp of iniquity. Seize the faith that you previously lost when you consented to the devil and to darkness, leaving behind your Lord, who is light.

Remember, son, what this means: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). The Lord will have mercy on you if, when you read these things, you do them and follow repentance through obedience.

But if you repent with your whole heart, if you keep the Lord before your eyes, if you abandon the abyss of the poisonous cup and take up the cup of salvation, if you meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, if you cast all your care upon him, then you will rejoice and exult in the Lord, because you have conquered the evil one.

Then your reward will be abundant in heaven, because you have labored in the work of the Lord in this way. Then the Lord will be your helper on the day of judgment. Then you will stand with great confidence at the Lord’s right hand with his saints, and he will say to you: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you, which my Father who is in heaven prepared for you” (Matt. 25:34).

But to the unjust it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.” There the fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die. Then the righteous will go into eternal life, but the ungodly and sinners into eternal fire (ibid., 41, 46).

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Erasmus calls the author of this letter a person of prodigious stammering. Nevertheless, it does not seem to us inferior in rank or ability to several of the preceding letters.

## LETTER XXXIV. ON THE VARIOUS KINDS OF LEPROSY

### I.

Admirable is the examination of the divine ordering: God commanded with great wisdom, careful knowledge, and reason what he wished to be presented and brought before him. For he established that the various kinds of human character and nature should be governed by different statements of precepts.

To some he depicted an imaginary work of the law, as though under the color of truth. To others he revealed the body of truth itself. For those whom he judged still wrapped in the darkness of the world, and not yet capable of grasping what was genuine and solid, he whispered, as it were, through a subtle examination, with the order of observance suspended. But to those whom he recognized as capable of understanding the complete song of proclamation, God sounded forth the perfect harmony of a solid voice.

Hence the ancient law is portrayed through figures and riddles. Since the weak sight of the Jews is dulled and they do not possess the light by which to behold the bright strength of knowledge, it is necessary that the color of figures be applied in various forms. For to them the rewards of virtues are promised under the veil of hope, and the marks of sins are branded upon the body. Through these, some are strengthened, while others are transferred.

The present reading requires that we bear this kind of discourse, for it describes various kinds of leprosy to be detected in different substances. One kind of leprosy is shown on walls, another is marked on the human body, another on vessels, another on clothing, and another is designated in the warp. Then there are the frequent and varied skins assigned to the site of such a wound.

What shall I say? There are as many kinds as there are colors: one pale, another foul, another red. Moreover, if human beings are polluted by leprosy, which is implanted in nature through its defect, what do those do who are weighed down by more serious diseases of the body?

### II.

But come, let us now examine the kinds of leprosy, so that we may recognize and approve the causes of their cures. “If,” he says, “there is leprosy white or red, or foul, or pale; or if it is flowering,” he says—that is, spreading over the whole body.

For there is a detestable leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all. There is also one that can be cleansed easily. Another is adventitious; another is found to be innate. Unless all these things are understood spiritually, they do not admit a simple rational interpretation.

For divine Wisdom placed the depth of its law, in this extreme region of the world, like a temple consecrated in its name, within the walls of another city. Although its construction and work may appear magnificent, the inner entrance is not opened to everyone. Many admire the ornaments of its outward forms, but they cannot open the entrance to its inner knowledge.

### III.

Therefore divine favor must be entreated, so that, when we knock, the entrance to understanding may be opened to us.

The priest of the temple is therefore commanded carefully to inspect the various kinds of leprosy and to detect their appearances or colors through fuller examination. Leprosy, then, is said to be recognizable by its colors, which nevertheless clearly pertain more to the sin of the soul than to an apparent bodily disease. For different colors indicate different stains of the mind.

When pale leprosy is seen, a faith of the soul that is languishing and sick is signified. When red leprosy is detected, the mind is recognized as inflamed by fury and anger and spattered with the blood of murder. When it is white, the disguised and falsely clean conscience of heretics is condemned.

### IV.

But one kind of leprosy is said to arise on the head, another in the beard. For there are heretics who appear to blaspheme God the Father alone, such as Manichaeus, who not only denies that he is the maker of the world but also professes him to be the author of evils. These are the people who appear to carry leprosy on the head. For, as the Apostle says, “the head of a man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3).

Those who carry leprosy in the beard, however, are those who appear to blaspheme the Son. For Christ, at his first coming, was adorned with the manhood of a mature man, living the age of a fully grown person, as if at thirty years of age.

But if, he says, it is foul and livid, what else does it designate except something livid and accursed with the marks of lividity? If the leprosy is black, it is marked, of course, by the smoke of idolatry and the odors of sacrifices.

But if, he says, the leprosy is flowering and covers all the flower of the pollution from head to foot, it shall be judged by the priest’s sight. For the priest will see, and behold, the leprosy has covered the entire skin of the body; and the priest shall cleanse him from the pollution, because it will be changed to white.

### V.

In this leprosy, which he describes as white and flowering, he detects various crimes in various ways. For when the pleasure of worldly life is regarded as white and flowering, then a serious contagion of vices spreads through the body. The stains of either greed or lust become visible.

But he says that this leprosy can quickly be cleansed. For the crime of greed can easily be cured by one who turns to the Lord and supplies what he possesses as nourishment for the needy, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

He will also be able to cleanse lust quickly if, through frequent fasts and abstinence, he restrains the body. But in all these cases the Lord commands that a cure be applied through the priest. For he says that there is a leprosy cleansed by offerings of sacrifices; another that water washes away more easily; and another that is cleansed when placed outside the camp. He also asserts that there is a leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all.

### VI.

The crimes of the more serious sins are therefore gathered according to the figure. Some are committed before baptism, yet are washed away through the grace of baptism. Others are committed after the washing of baptism; whether they are greater or lesser sins, the priest’s judgment nevertheless cleanses them.

For whatever small offense there may be can be entirely absolved by the priest. More serious offenses must be cleansed by the discipline of ecclesiastical rule and by prayer. Those that are incurable are reserved for God the judge.

Hence in this passage he says that each person ought to offer a sacrifice according to the kind of cure he requires—that is, each person, according to what he recognizes himself to have done wrong, whether through carnal desire, idolatry, perjury, or lying, understanding himself to be stained by vices as by leprosy, must not cease to sacrifice to God as far as he is able.

But he says that there is a kind of leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all, and therefore such a person is commanded to be expelled outside the camp. This is truly the crime committed against the Holy Spirit, namely blasphemy, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32).

### VII.

Divine Scripture also added that there is leprosy in vessels, leprosy on walls, leprosy in clothing, and leprosy in the warp. But how leprosy can exist in these things I completely do not know, since, lacking life, they must also lack sensation.

But I think that when leprosy is said to be in the walls of a house, the faithlessness of heretics is signified. For what is not polluted where the blasphemy of adulterated doctrine is preached? Therefore the priest is commanded to cleanse this leprosy from the walls, so that the doctrine of Catholic truth may drive away the stained words of heretics.

When leprosy is said to be in vessels, the sins of one’s own body are indicated. The Apostle compares human bodies to vessels: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7).

But how can leprosy exist in the warp unless the warp signifies the soul of the faithful person? When it is twisted by temptations, like a spindle twisted by the fineness of threads, it is bound together by the solidity of stronger virtue.

### VIII.

Thus the soul stands upright like a very dense warp, while the bodily senses lie beneath the warp like the weft. Therefore he also indicates that leprosy exists in the weft, because it signifies some sins of the body and others of the soul.

But what are the two year-old lambs, the small cake of oil, or the two [Note: The text says [Greek term uncertain/omitted], which means birds, little birds, sparrows; in Greek, *ornithia* (ὀρνίθια). And indeed, why would Moses have said “clean hens,” since a hen certainly belongs to the category of clean animals? This, however, is how Origen once interpreted it; nor did that exposition seem incongruous to others among the chorus of the Fathers.]

hens, which are commanded to be offered for the cleansing of leprosy?

In the two lambs, the two comings of Christ are signified. We must believe in these before we can deserve to be cleansed from the leprosy of sins: one coming, when he came and suffered; the other, when he will come in glory.

“But let him offer a calf,” he says. Through this kind of animal he demonstrates that the nations are to be subjected to the yoke of Christ’s cross.

The two hens appear to indicate the soul and the flesh. “You shall kill one hen,” he says, “wash the other with water, and let it go.” The flesh, certainly, is commanded to be killed in the Passion; but the soul, which by nature appears to be subject to eternal death, is to be released from crimes after being washed with the water of baptism.

### IX.

“But also cedar wood,” he says. No one is unaware that this kind of wood is imperishable. Therefore, through the cedar he wished an incorrupt mind and steadfast faith to be displayed. Hyssop, however, indicates prayers and supplications. Scarlet, moreover, plainly manifests the glory of martyrdom.

“Let the one who is of modest means offer what he can,” he says. That is, if someone has not attained all the riches of heavenly gifts, he may nevertheless bring to God, even if it is little, the service of his devotion.

If someone was unable to observe virginity, let him at least preserve the chaste bed of one marriage. Or if someone was unable to carry away the trophy of martyrdom, let him preserve himself unconquered for God through the protection of flight.

“And let him offer,” he says, “a small cake of oil”—clearly, the grace of mercy. Even if he was unable to carry before him the brightest torch of holiness, let him at least not extinguish the lamp of faith.

You see, therefore, beloved brothers, that no poverty of spiritual grace is so insignificant that it cannot offer God some offering of holiness as a sacrifice.

## II.

Since, then, it has been demonstrated in every way that scrutinizing the divine Scriptures is not only free from danger but also exceedingly useful, let us examine that Gospel parable which concerns a father and two sons (Luke 15). For this one matter is the reason that the comparisons concerning the sheep and the woman were previously recited in connected order. The question, therefore, is who that elder brother is who preserved the portion of his father’s substance given to him—half of the whole—and chose to live an inseparable life with his father. And who is the younger, who, having likewise received his substance from his father, departed into a distant country and, after squandering all the resources belonging to his share there, was reduced to poverty and compelled to feed another’s pigs?

But let us not omit the quality of his repentance, nor the father’s prompt forgiveness and restrained compassion. When the son returned, the father did not reproach him for the frivolity of his former departure [Al. *praeterit*, “of his past departure”] or for the disgraceful waste of his substance; rather, he mercifully received him as he came, went out to greet him, kissed him with rejoicing, rested upon him as he embraced him, and slaughtered the fattened calf for a feast in celebration of his recovered son. At this the elder brother, moved with sorrow, says to his father, “etc.”

The exposition will make clear to your understanding these matters, which have been arranged by sections. Before everything else, it is necessary to inquire into the reason why—and with what intention—the Savior adapted such parables to the Jews: what he wished to demonstrate by them. For if the reason for these comparisons becomes clear to you, then it will easily be discerned whether what we understand from them accords reasonably with the truth. [Col. 0249C]

## III.

There are, then, some who say that these two sons signify the angels and archangels, or the entire heavenly host. They identify the younger with the human being who departed on a distant pilgrimage when he fell from heaven and paradise to earth; and they adapt the interpretation as though it referred to the knowledge of Adam’s fall or condition.

This interpretation does indeed appear pious. I do not know, however, whether it is true. Someone may ask: Why not? Because the younger son came to repentance of his own accord, remembering his father’s former abundance, as the sequence of the reading indicates. The Lord, however, when he came, called the human race to repentance, although humanity had not thought of returning of its own will to the place from which it had fallen.

Furthermore, if the elder son is the choir of heavenly angels, as was said above, how does he grieve at the return and salvation of his brother and at the slaughter of the calf, when the Lord says in the same Gospel that there is joy in heaven among the angels over one sinner who repents? [Col. 0249D]

## IV.

Let us therefore examine the meaning of this parable—not to criticize that other interpretation, but rather to place alongside it, for your judgment, what we understand, so that you may decide whether the two interpretations agree.

We are now explaining the reason that the Lord’s speech itself supplies, introducing this parable on the basis of the preceding matter, as we have said, while identifying the persons represented in these several parables. The Jews were murmuring and burning with envy because they had seen our Lord Jesus Christ receive sinners, feast with them, and welcome tax collectors as they eagerly attended to the Savior’s teaching. [Col. 0250A]

The Lord, therefore, observing this insolence of the Jews, since they were criticizing him, begins with that first parable about the shepherd. Leaving the ninety-nine sheep behind, he went in search of the one that had gone astray. He then adds another parable about the tenth drachma, which a woman finds within her house after lighting a lamp and searching through it when the coin has been lost.

Next follows this parable about the two sons, as he constructs the sequence of these comparisons according to the economy and order of divine providence. Since he himself is the prince and author of our salvation, and, beginning to save and restore to perfection the human being who had been deceived and lost through the devil’s treachery—namely, to restore him to the hundredth place, in which the fullness of perfection is counted—he begins the comparison from this point.

He then introduces the woman’s person as well: reproving the Jews, but instructing the Church. Like a shepherd who loves the wandering sheep, he diligently seeks the human being. He calls him a drachma because of the resemblance to royal coinage: figuratively, in the drachma, which is a kind of money, the image and inscription of the heavenly King has been engraved as upon a coin.

The woman therefore searches for that drachma, and, after lighting a lamp and cleaning the house, finds it. This means that the human being, illuminated by the word and mercy of God, recovers the glory of his nature, in which he was made in the image of his Creator. He had lost this glory when the house of his heart was darkened by sins; but, with his faculties restored, he finds it again. He rejoices with joy because he has wiped away all the uncleanness of his inner chamber through the practices of disciplined devotion, and has shaken off, cleansed by prayers and reproofs, the filth of the soul contracted from worldly affairs and anxieties. [Col. 0250C]

## V.

In accordance with what was said above, he next adds the parable presenting the comparison of the two sons. As I understand it, this is not about the transgressing Jews, nor about the gentiles who were lost, but about his own people, who are restored to salvation through patience and whom he calls the younger son.

Seth, Enos, and those younger than them, who from Eve up to the human coming of the Savior appeared righteous because they lived according to the justice of the Law: these, then, are meant. Therefore, when he speaks of the younger and the elder, he is not referring to chronological order but to the quality of their pleasures. He places the one who had been deceived and gone astray—not voluntarily, but through another’s trickery—before the other, comparing him to a sheep, that is, to an irrational animal, and thus to an imprudent human being. He applies the shepherd’s care to him, seeking the lost sheep and carrying it back once he has found it.

To the one who uses the freedom of his own will and recognizes from where he has fallen, he offers the benefit of repentance and return. Hence there is this distinction among the parables mentioned above, according to the persons or dispositions of sinners: the father does not seek out the son who is traveling abroad, but receives the repentant one; the shepherd seeks the wandering sheep, which does not know how to return wisely, and carries it back upon his shoulders. [Col. 0250D]

## VI.

Let us now see whether the things signified accord with this interpretation. Scripture says that the father divided his substance equally between his two sons. What substance does this evangelical father divide among his spiritual sons except understanding of wisdom and knowledge of good and evil—those true and everlasting riches of a soul living well?

This father gives his riches equally. No one is born either righteous or sinful. Rather, that portion of rational substance which comes from God is given equally to all at the first birth of human beings. In their subsequent way of life, however, each person is found to possess more or less of this substance, as the negligent abandon their natural goods through the difference of their wills, while the diligent preserve them.

One person, remembering and understanding the things he has received from the Lord God the Creator, believes that they belong to his Father and therefore guards them as his father’s property. Another, judging that his possessions belong to him from himself, abuses them as though he had the license of private ownership and will soon be deprived of his resources after squandering them.

In these matters the freedom of the will is both described and clearly displayed—the freedom that God the Creator specially added to the rational soul. [Col. 0251B]

## VII.

See, then, how this father neither restrains the one who wishes to depart nor takes away the power of free will; nor does he compel the other, who wishes to remain, to leave. Otherwise, if he had cut away from them the freedom of their own will, he might appear rather to be the author of the many evils that would later befall them through their own fault.

Thus he gives to the one who asks, because the cause of our poverty and offense proceeds from us, not from God. Having received his portion, the younger son, it says, “went away into a distant country.” By “distant” he expressed not an interval of place but a deviation of the mind. Whoever has fallen into forgetfulness of God is truly said to be a stranger far from God.

Conversely, worldly conduct makes a person not merely a traveler abroad but alien to the Lord. In brief: those who journey away from the world are presented before the Lord; likewise, those who remain among earthly things are exiled from heavenly realities.

Finally, Cain “went out from the presence of the Lord and became a wanderer” (Gen. 4:16), not because some place existed outside God’s sight, but because in his mind he had been separated from the Lord’s regard and, because of his murder, cut off from God.

Knowing, therefore, that we had wandered in this kind of exile through great ignorance, the most blessed Paul says: “You who were once far away have now been brought near” (Eph. 2:13).

That younger son undertakes this kind of departure and consumes the substance of his portion from his father’s inheritance. Deprived, of course, of spiritual riches—that is, of God’s providence and understanding—he is compelled to feed pigs. This means that he nourishes filthy and unclean thoughts in his soul, so that he may eat the irrational foods of a depraved way of life.

These things are indeed sweet to one who lacks good things, because every work of fleshly pleasure appears sweet to the perverse. Yet this is the deception of desire and the corruption of life, which not only gives the soul no virtue or strength but utterly weakens and destroys it.

Scripture designates such foods, as it were swine’s food—foully sweet, in accordance with what they are—the enticements of the flesh, under the name of pods. [Col. 0252A]

## VIII.

And so, after departing from his father and setting out on a distant pilgrimage, after consuming in a foreign land the resources mentioned above, enduring everything he deserved, and afterward being constrained by the necessity of his evils—that is, by hunger and poverty—he repents of his error.

He realizes how he has harmed himself: he had passed, not by a judgment of his own will, but away from his father to strangers, from home into exile, from riches to almsgiving, and from abundance to hunger. Remembering this place of servitude and misery, he begins to think about returning and, reflecting within himself, says:

“I will say to my father: I have sinned against heaven and before you. Receive me as one of your hired servants.”

Scripture shows by this that the father should not be understood as a human being but as God. For the penitent suppliant not only names heaven in his confession of sins, but also says, “before you.” God alone is present before all sinners. No sins meditated upon even in the heart can be hidden from him: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. 7:10).

Yet for us, in this passage, heaven is understood as our Lord Jesus Christ. To him the gentiles who, living in the darkness of unbelief, blasphemed, now converted to faith and confessing the truth of God, rightly say in repentance for their error: “I have sinned against heaven and against you.”

For whoever sins against heaven—which, although it is above, is nevertheless visible and subject to the moon—is the one who sins against the human being whom the Son of God assumed for our salvation. Accordingly, he sins against the Father God, who observes all things. [Col. 0252C]

## IX.

When the father sees the son thus reflecting, recovering his senses, and returning from the distant region through the humility of confession, he rejoices, runs to meet him, embraces him, and kisses him.

Here divine love for human beings is openly described. For what else does the father’s running to meet him mean except that, because sins hindered us, we were unable by our own strength to reach God? He, however, who is powerful enough to reach the weak descended to us.

The same is expressed through the events concerning Zacchaeus. He had desired to see the Lord and, for this reason, climbed a tree. The Lord anticipated him, saw him, and called him; immediately the Lord promised that he himself would turn aside to Zacchaeus’s house to dine there.

See how Christ, foreseeing the faith of one who would believe, carefully seeks him hidden in the tree and overshadowed, as it were, by the darkness of sins, like a lost sheep. He calls the man who hesitates to come, receives him when he comes as though upon his own shoulders, and enters the house of the sinner who did not dare to invite the Lord but nevertheless desired a saving blessing. He shares his meal, showing by visible grace an invisible sanctification: God, in his wisdom, enters familiarly into the heart of the believer and shares the sacrament with the believer. [Col. 0252D]

## X.

Thus, when the father meets the returning son, he pours himself upon his neck and, weeping over him, rests upon him. He kisses his mouth, through which the penitent’s confession, issuing from his heart, had come forth—the confession that the joyful father had received.

Then he immediately orders the first robe to be brought out and restored: that is, his former glory, which he had lost after being stripped by the devil’s deception. He also orders a ring to be given—either the seal of the saving symbol, or rather the emblem of betrothal and the pledge of those nuptials by which Christ betroths his Church, when every repentant soul is joined to Christ through the ring of faith.

He commands sandals to be placed on his feet: either to protect his footsteps for running the course, so that he may walk firmly along the slippery path of this world; or so that, with the mud of fleshly contagion excluded by the Gospel sandals, he may preserve and direct clean feet in an unstained way of life; or on account of the mortification of the members.

For in Scripture the course of our life is called a foot. A sandal is also applied as a figure of mortification, because it is made from the hides of dead animals. [Col. 0253B]

## XI.

He also adds that the fattened calf should be slaughtered and presented at the feast. Without a doubt this signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the Father gave as a sacrifice for our salvation, and whom he calls a calf because of the offering of his immaculate body.

He rightly called him “fattened,” because he is rich and abundant in nourishment for infants, so that he may be sufficient to send up to God, for the salvation of the whole world, the fragrance of sweetness and the savor of sacrifice, and to intercede for all.

For this reason it was also said mystically that the Father gives this calf to others to be sacrificed, while he himself rejoices and feasts upon the sacrifice of his calf. For “the Father so loved this world that he gave his only Son for its salvation” (John 3:28).

The Father himself, therefore, did not sacrifice him, but handed him over to others to be sacrificed. For when the Father sent him, the consenting Son suffered at the hands of human beings. The Creator himself, who is nourished by our faith and rejoices and takes delight in the sacrifice of his Son for us, rejoices at the return of his Son and feasts upon the acquisition of the believing people. [Col. 0253C]

## XII.

Seeing the Father’s joy, the elder son becomes sorrowful. His person is to be compared with those laborers who likewise murmur against the Lord in the Gospel after working in the vineyard, because, although they had been exhausted by a full day’s labor, he had made those who came at the twelfth hour equal to them in the payment of their wages.

The creator of all things says to them: “If I am good, why are you evil?”

That those who come at the twelfth hour are those who will be saved from the gentiles, John openly declares: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). It seems to make no difference whether it is called the twelfth hour or the last hour. [Col. 0253D]

## XIII.

Who are those who murmur and who have borne the labor and heat of the whole day, except those who performed the righteousness of the Law and paid the due of the ancient servitude?

See how plain are the words spoken by the Father, so that they appear to have been spoken by those who lived under the Law. What does the one who comes from the field mean except that he signifies one who comes from the works of the Law, boasts in them, and counts them as long-standing labors?

Hence he says: “I have never transgressed your commandment, and you have never given me a kid so that I might feast”—that is, you have not given me a sinner for our repose.

For, he says, “the one who does the things of the Law will live by them; the one who does not do them will be punished by them.”

But for this man who has committed fornication, you have given even that fattened calf, he says—that is, your beloved Son, as we said above.

What, then, does the Father answer him? “You are always with me, but it was necessary to rejoice over this one, who had perished and has been found, who had been dead and has come to life again.”

By this saying he plainly shows the human being who has fallen away from life through sin and, having become liable to punishment, has been put to death; but who, through a saving return by repentance, has come back into adoption as a son.

He also shows the good person who has remained in goodness as continually possessing the paternal inheritance.

Therefore, if you have sinned, O human being, hasten to reconcile yourself to God by freeing yourself, so that through the reward of your sweat and worthy repentance you may recover what, having been given to you by grace, you lost.

May God grant that you, remaining steadfast in faith, may rather be fellow heirs of our Lord Jesus Christ, because this is the glory and virtue, with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Labbé, in his *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, p. 43, thought this author to be Valerius Maximus. Yet that he is a Christian author is clear from the testimonies from Scripture which he cites and from the fact that he professes to address a Christian. In a manuscript of the monastery of Lyra he is called Valerianus, and the letter itself is entitled “Dissertation.” If that is his true name, the author called himself Valerius because, in imitation of Valerius, he compiled a certain medley of memorable sayings and deeds.

## LETTER XXXVI. VALERIUS TO RUFINUS: THAT HE SHOULD NOT TAKE A WIFE

[Col. 0254C]

### I.

I am forbidden to speak, yet I cannot be silent. Cranes foretell the changing storms of heaven; owls and horned owls, birds of ill omen, mournfully cry out beforehand the approaching severity of winter. And you mock if I give true predictions of an impending loss. Therefore I am forbidden to speak: I am an augur of truth, not of pleasure. I love the nightingale and the blackbird, which announce the joy of a gentle breeze in pleasing harmony; and especially Philomela, which, with all the abundance of delight, brings the season of desired pleasantness to its fullness.

Unless I am mistaken, you love parasites and comedians, who whisper sweet enticements beforehand; and especially Circe, who may pour over you joys full of longed-for sweetness with the fragrance of her perfumes, so that you may be deceived, become a pig or an ass. I cannot be silent. The ministers of Babylon offer you honeyed poison; it enters pleasantly, delights, and wins over the impulse of your spirit. Therefore I am forbidden to speak. I know that in the end it will bite like a serpent and inject a venom unequalled by any antidote; therefore I cannot be silent. You have many most eloquent persuaders of your pleasure, all directed to your ruin; I alone am the tongue-tied herald of truth, whom you loathe. Therefore I am forbidden to speak.

### II.

The voice of the foolish goose is rejected. Among swans only the learned give pleasure; yet the goose taught the senators to save the city from fire, their treasures from plunder, and themselves from the weapons of their enemies. Perhaps you too, being prudent, will understand with the senators that the swans are making music for your destruction and the goose is clamoring for your safety. Therefore I cannot be silent.

Consumed wholly by your desire and seduced by the nobility of a handsome face, unhappy man, you do not know that what you seek is a Chimera; or you vow not to know that that three-formed monster is made attractive by the distinguished face of a lion, is stained by the foul belly of a goat, and lies in ambush with the poisonous tail of a serpent. Therefore I am forbidden to speak. Ulysses was delighted by the harmony of the Sirens. But because he knew the voices of the Sirens and Circe’s cups, he constrained himself with the bonds of virtue so as to avoid the abyss.

### III.

But I, hoping in the Lord, add that you will be an imitator of Ulysses, not of Empedocles, who, overcome by his philosophy—or, not to say melancholy, that is, black bile—chose Etna as his mausoleum and applied to the ancients the parable which you hear. Therefore I cannot be silent. At last, your fire is stronger because the opposing party assents to you; I fear that heat by which you are inflamed against me, lest the greater draw the lesser to itself. And therefore I am forbidden to speak. Yet I shall speak by the spirit through which I am yours.

### IV.

Let the fires be weighed in any equal or unequal balance. Let the danger to my life be considered: whatever you do, whatever you judge, indulgence must be granted me, since through the impatience of love I cannot be silent. The first wife of the first Adam, after the creation of the first human being, broke the first fast through sin. By transgressing the Lord’s command she gave birth to disobedience, which will not cease, before the end of the world, to assail women, who will always tirelessly draw into consequence what they have inherited from their mother.

### V.

Friend, a disobedient wife is an insult to her husband. Beware: truth, which cannot deceive, says of blessed David: “I have found a man after my own heart.” Yet he was grievously cast down by love of a woman, from adultery into homicide, lest scandals ever come alone. For every iniquity is rich in abundant companionship, and whatever house it enters, it hands over to be defiled by its reproaches.

### VI.

Friend, Bathsheba was silent and did no evil; nevertheless she became a spur to overthrow for a perfect man and the sting of death for an innocent husband. Will she be innocent who contends in eloquence like Delilah with Samson, and in beauty like Bathsheba, when this woman’s beauty alone triumphed even against her will? Unless you are more a man after the Lord’s heart than David, believe that you too can be cast down.

### VII.

Solomon, the sun of humankind, the treasury of God’s delights, the singular dwelling-place of wisdom, darkened by the thick ink of shadows, lost through love of a woman the light of his soul, the glory of his house, and the fragrance of his reputation. Finally, bent before the Baals, he was changed from the Lord’s Ecclesiast into a member of the devil, so that he seemed to be hurled down a yet more grievous precipice than Phoebus in Phaethon’s fall—Phoebus who, from Apollo, became Jupiter’s herdsman for Admetus. Friend, unless you are wiser than Solomon—which no one is—you are not greater than one who can be bewitched by a woman. Open your eyes and see.

### VIII.

The best woman, rarer than a phoenix, cannot be loved without the bitterness of fear, anxiety, and frequent misfortune. But evil women, whose swarms are so abundant that no one is free from their malice, when loved punish loving, and devote themselves to affliction even to the division of body and spirit.

### IX.

Friend, the philosophical maxim is: “See to whom you give.” The ethical maxim is: “See to whom you give yourself.” Lucretia and Penelope, along with the Sabine women, bore the standards of chastity and won trophies with a very small company. Friend, there is no Lucretia, no Penelope, no Sabine woman. Fear them all. Scylla, Myrrha, and Phaedra entered battle against the Sabine women, followed by great crowds, packed with an army of every vice; and they brought groans and sighs, and finally made hell for their captives.

### X.

Friend, lest you become prey among robbers, do not sleep while passing through them. Jupiter, the earthly king who was also called king of heaven, because of the singular vigor of his body and incomparable elegance of mind, was compelled to bellow after Europa. Friend, behold: she whom goodness exalted above the heavens can compel you to bellow, unless you are greater than Jupiter, to whose greatness no other was equal. Phoebus, who with the rays of his wisdom first illuminated the circuit of the whole world, so that he alone was worthily distinguished by the name of Sun, was made foolish by love of Leucothoe, to his own disgrace and her destruction; and, altered for a long time by an eclipsing alternation, he was often deprived of his own light, which the whole world universally needed.

### XI.

Friend, lest the light that is in you become darkness, flee Leucothoe. Mars, who deserved to be called the god of warriors because of the familiar frequency of his triumphs, in which the ready vigor of mind is especially displayed, was bound with Venus by Vulcan, fearing nothing for himself, with chains invisible indeed but perceptible nonetheless. This was to the applause of the satyrs and the laughter of the heavenly court.

### XII.

Friend, at least consider the chains which you do not see and already feel in part; rescue yourself while they can still be broken, lest that lame and ugly smith, whom neither a god’s table nor a goddess’s bed has deemed worthy, bind you to Venus in his fashion and make you, like himself, ugly and lame—or, what I fear still more, bandy-legged. Then you will be unable to have the cloven hoof that saves; but, bound to Venus, you will become a pain and a mockery to those who see you, while the rest applaud themselves. Pallas was rejected by the false judge of the goddesses: she promised not to please, but to benefit.

Friend, do you judge in the same way? For I see you already, with a fastidious mind, running through everything you read at full speed, attending not to the arguments but waiting for rhetorical figures. You wait in vain, until this muddy stream has flowed away, so that, when this foul water has withdrawn, pure waters may irrigate you. For the streams must indeed resemble their source, whether muddy or clear. Thus the defect of my speech expresses the ignorance of my heart, and the goitrous incompetence of my diction offends your delicate mind. Conscious of this weakness, I would gladly have turned aside from dissuading you; but because I could not be silent, I have spoken as I could.

If I had as much power of style as I have purpose in writing, I would send you words so elegant and so nobly joined in marriage that each separately and all together would seem to bless their author. But since you owe me everything that love, still naked and unfruitful—not to say barren—can deserve from all things, lend me meanwhile a patient ear while I unfold what I have entangled. Do not demand from me an orator’s purple dye or cosmetic white, which I confess and lament that I do not know; accept instead the intention of the writer and the truth of the page.

### XIII.

Julius Caesar, whose greatness the world found too narrow, on the day when cruel Atropos dared to destroy his noble son, humbly bent his ear at the doors of the Capitol to Tugillius, who was offering humble yet almost divine maxims. Had he also bent his mind, they would have inflicted upon him the penalties which he himself inflicted. But you incline your ear to me, the herald of your writings, as an asp does to spells; you apply your mind as a boar does to barking; you are appeased like the *dipsas* [variant: “serpent”] when the sun has been inflamed by Cancer. You look after yourself as though Medea were despised; you pity yourself as the sea pities shipwrecked people. That you restrain your hand is reverence for royal peace.

Friend, the tamer of the world humbled himself, though not fully, before his faithful servant; he almost withdrew his foot because he almost obeyed, and almost yielded because he almost listened [variant: “heard”], but not completely. His great humility did him no good because it was not complete. What does your savage inhumanity, your unbending harshness, and the terror of your brow profit you? Why do you rush unarmed of your own accord into the ambush of robbers? Humble yourself; yield. But do so after the manner of him who humbled the whole world to himself, and listen to your friend. If you think Caesar erred because he did not trust Tugillius, hear and heed also what happened to others, so that their injury may benefit you. For correction recommended by examples is harmless. I do not know in what refuge you are safe or in what sanctuary you grow numb. Caesar found the Persians merciless and did not return; if ever you escaped such a training-ground, you found the pious impious.

### XIV.

Phoroneus, the king who did not begrudge publishing the treasures of laws to the peoples, but first gilded the studies of the Greeks, said to his brother Leontius on the day he entered upon the path of the universe: “Nothing would be lacking to my highest happiness if I had always lacked a wife.” Leontius replied: “And how does a wife hinder?”

But he said [variant: “he says”]: “All husbands know.” Friend, would that you had once been a husband and no longer were, so that you might know what hinders happiness.

### XV.

The Emperor Valentinian, eighty years old and still a virgin, when he heard on the day of his death the proclamations of the triumphs, in which he had been most frequent, recalled, said that he gloried in one victory alone. Asked which one, he replied: “That I conquered my most wicked enemy, my flesh.” Friend, he would have departed this world without glory had he not resisted it bravely—the flesh with which you have made a compact of familiar assent.

### XVI.

After divorcing Terentia, Cicero refused to marry, saying that he could not devote himself equally to a wife and philosophy. Friend, would that your own mind, or at least your tongue, would give me this answer, so that by speaking you might deign to imitate the prince of eloquence and give me even a vain hope.

### XVII.

Cannius of Gades, a poet of gentle and pleasing eloquence, was reproved by the Carthaginian Livy, a grave and married historiographer, because he enjoyed the love of many women, in these words: “You cannot share in our philosophy while you are shared by so many. Tyre does not love Juno with that liver which many vultures tear apart in many pieces.”

[Note: Here he perhaps confuses the Carthaginian Livy with Livy of Padua. For Cannius of Gades, often mentioned by his contemporary Martial, is said to have visited Livy of Padua, not the Carthaginian. Jerome, *Letter* 58 to Paulinus, is correct: “We read that certain nobles came to this Livy, flowing with the golden fountain of eloquence, from the furthest bounds of Spain and Gaul.”]

Cannius replied: “Whenever I am weary, I rise more cautiously; if I am oppressed a little, I draw breath again more eagerly; the alternations of nights make days more cheerful. But perpetual darkness is like hell. Thus the early lilies, delicate in the warmth of the spring sun, frolic with fuller joy amid the varying breezes of Eurus, Notus, and Zephyrus; but Libs, thundering down upon them with a single blast, brings about their downfall. Thus Mars, with his testicles broken, reclines as a guest of the gods at the heavenly table, from which the uxorious Mulciber is bound far away by his own rope. Thus many threads bind more lightly than a single chain. Thus pleasures are for me a consolation from philosophy, as they are for you.” Friend, I approve the words of both, but the life of neither. Yet many diseases, interrupted by intervals of health, harm less than one languor that does not cease to afflict with irremediable pains.

### XVIII.

Pacuv(i)us, weeping, said to his neighbor Arrius: “Friend, I have in my garden an unlucky tree, from which my first wife hanged herself; afterward my second, and now my third.” Arrius replied: “I marvel that amid so many successes you have found tears.” And again: “Good gods, how many losses that tree has hanged for you!” And a third time: “Friend, give me also cuttings from that tree, which I may plant.” Friend, I fear that you too will have to beg for cuttings from that tree when they can no longer be found.

### XIX.

Sulpicius felt where his own shoe pinched him, when he separated from his noble and chaste wife. Friend, beware lest the shoe pinch you and cannot be pulled off.

### XX.

Cato of Utica said: “If the world could exist without woman, our intercourse would not be without gods.” Friend, Cato spoke only what was true and known; nor does anyone curse the mockeries of women unless he has been mocked, experienced them, and knows the punishment. Therefore one ought to trust those who speak with complete truth. They know how pleasure pleases and sin stings. They know that the flower of Venus is the rose, because many thorns lie hidden beneath its purple.

### XXI.

Metellus replied to Marius, when he refused to marry his daughter, rich in dowry, distinguished in beauty, illustrious in lineage, and fortunate in reputation: “I would rather be mine than hers.” Marius replied: “On the contrary, she herself will be yours.” But Metellus said: “On the contrary, a husband ought to belong to his wife.” For it is a logical principle: subjects will be such as their predicates permit. Thus the wit of Metellus’s saying turned his back away from burdens. Friend, if one must marry, it is indeed not advantageous. Yet let love be the reason, not wealth. Choose a wife’s face, not her clothing; her character, not gold; and let the wife marry you, not the dowry. Therefore, if it can in any way be done, you will be able to be the predicate, so that you do not take envy from the subject.

### XXII.

Lais of Corinth, distinguished by the prerogative of beauty, deigned to embrace only kings and princes. Yet she attempted to share herself with Demosthenes the philosopher, so that, once the miracle of his known chastity had been dissolved, she might seem by her beauty to have moved stones as Amphion did with his lyre; and she gently drew him on with blandishments. When Demosthenes was already softening toward the marriage-bed, Lais demanded from him one hundred talents for her consent.
