Looking up to heaven, he said: “I do not buy repentance at so high a price.” Friend, would that you too direct the keenness of your mind toward heaven, so that you may escape that which I have bought at the price of repentance.

### XXIII.

Livia killed her husband, whom she hated too much; Lucillia killed hers, whom she loved too much. The former voluntarily mixed aconite; the latter, deceived, administered madness as a love-potion. Friend, these women strove with contrary wishes. Yet neither was cheated of the end of feminine deceit, and indeed of her own evil. Women walk by varied and different paths; through whatever windings they wander and whatever trackless ways they deviate, there is one outcome, one goal for all their paths: the single head and meeting-place of all their differences is malice. Take from their example this lesson of experience: a woman is bold in everything she loves or hates, and artful when she wishes to harm—which is always and frequently; when she prepares to help, she harms. Hence it happens that she often harms unwillingly. You have been placed in a furnace: if you are gold, you will come out purer.

## XXIV.

Deianira clothed the Tirynthian man in an undergarment and avenged herself upon the monster’s slayer by means of the monster’s blood; and she brought upon herself tears for what she had contrived as a source of joy. My friend, this woman knew and saw Nessus pierced by Hercules’ weapon; nevertheless she believed Nessus concerning Hercules, and, as though not willingly, clothed the man whom she ought to have clothed in an undergarment with destruction. Woman is of unsound and headlong mind, always acting without deliberation: she considers whatever she wants—and whatever is not expedient—to be pre-eminent; and just as she desires to please above all, so she has resolved to place her own pleasure above everything.

Alcides completed twelve inhuman labors. By a thirteenth, which surpassed all inhumanity, he was overcome. Thus the strongest of men, as much to be mourned as lamented, fell dead—he who had borne the citadel of heaven upon his shoulders without a groan. Yet who, among so many thousands upon thousands of persistent and anxious sinners, has ever been saddened by an unending refusal? Or who has steadfastly cut short the words of one making a request? Her answer has the savor of favor; and however harsh it may be, you will always find in some corner of her words some hidden fuel for your petition. Whatever she denies, no woman utterly refuses.

## XXV.

Gold broke into the defenses of Acrisius’ tower and dissolved Danaë’s chastity, fortified by many a rampart. My friend, just as incest rained down from heaven upon the maiden who had triumphed over the earth, so the lowly never deceives her, whereas the exalted conquers her. Thus the North Wind overturns the tree that the Favonian Wind never moved.

## XXVI.

The Lycian virgin, advancing toward old age and steadfastly distinguished by the privilege of a reputation for chastity, at last conceived under the apparition of Apollo and gave birth to Plato. My friend, what vigilance had preserved inviolate, illusion through a dream deflowered, so that every rose-garden may always be stripped of its purple by some storm. Yet if anything here is good, it is good that Plato was like his father in wisdom, and that he became like the foremost father in name and divinity.

## XXVII.

My friend, are you more astonished or more indignant that in parables I suggest to you that the Gentiles are to be imitated: idolaters by a Christian, dogs by a lamb, and, finally, the wicked by a good man? I want you to resemble the resourceful bee, which draws honey from the nettle, so that you may take honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone.

I know the superstition of the Gentiles, but every creature of God possesses some model of what is honorable. Thus He Himself is called at one time a ram, at another a lion, at another a worm; yet unbelievers do many things perversely. Nevertheless, certain things that had perished with them they have caused to abound as fruit in us.

And if they possessed leather girdles for the sake of cleanliness, without hope, without faith, without confession, without charity, then surely, if we are asses and swine, or resemble brute animals in some inhumanity, by what merit of faith, hope, or charity shall we be found worthy—when you see the prophets, and especially that one of purified heart whom only the eyes can behold?

They afflicted themselves with many efforts through devotion to their arts, without any prospect of future blessedness, but merely so that they would not have ignorant souls. What, then, is illumination and a lamp for our feet, and a light for our paths, except for eternal life?

## XXVIII.

Would that you choose her; would that you read her; would that you bring her into your bedchamber, so that the King may bring you into His. Long ago you plowed her with the flowers of your spring. She awaits from your age that you produce grapes; do not, to her injury, take another, lest, when you have done so, you be found at vintage-time to be a wild grape.

I do not want you to become the bridegroom of Venus, but of Pallas. She will clothe you and adorn you with precious jewels; she will clothe you in a wedding garment. These nuptials will glory in Apollo as their bride’s attendant; their Fescennine verses will befit the cedars of Lebanon.

Stilbon, married, had devoutly conceived the hope of this long-desired solemnity.  
[Note: This seems to be that philosopher who, having lost his wife and children, rejoiced that he then possessed all good things within himself.]

But in fear, this entire reading was composed because of this matter.

## XXIX.

This entire eloquent discourse hastens toward this end. Here lies the severity of this dissuasion; here it is wholly armed, and you feel its barbs hardened with much steel. The surgeon’s hand is harsh, but healing. This speech is harsh, but healthy. Would that it were as useful as it is devout.

My friend, I impose upon you, as you say, a strict rule of life. Let it be so. For narrow is the way that leads to life, and there is no level path by which one travels to complete joys; indeed, even to moderate joys we make our way over rough ground.

Jason heard that to reach the Golden Fleece he would have to travel across a sea still untouched, deflowered by no ships or oars, and through bulls and sulfurous fires, and past the watches of a poison-filled serpent. With sound judgment, though not with pleasant means, he went and returned, and brought back the desirable treasure.

Thus humility of a stubborn mind accepts the wormwood of truth; diligent service makes it fruitful; the usefulness of perseverance brings it to fruition. Thus the South Wind, the cupbearer of the rains, sows the seed. The North Wind, the broom of the roads, consolidates it. The West Wind, producer of flowers, advances it into abundance. Thus harsh beginnings are rewarded with a sweet ending. Thus the narrow path leads to spacious palaces; thus the confined track leads to the land of the living.

## XXX.

But lest I keep you suspended at the cost of much time, so that greater testimony may win your belief, read Theophrastus’ little golden work and Medea of Jason [Alt. Nason], and you will find scarcely a few things impossible for a woman.

My friend, may almighty God grant you not to be deceived by feminine deceit, and may He enlighten your heart, lest, with bewitched eyes, you proceed toward the place I fear.

But lest I seem to have written Orestes—  
[Note: It is plainly an allusion to that verse of Juvenal, *Satire* 1: “Orestes written and not yet finished on the reverse.”]

Farewell.

# LETTER XXXVII, OR A DIALOGUE UNDER THE NAMES OF JEROME AND AUGUSTINE

## On the Origin of Souls

### I.

Since among you the purest springs of heavenly eloquence and the streams of every branch of learning overflow, and since a soundness firm as the summit holds all your members together in a stable condition, I am astonished in mind and wonder why you deem the trickle of an island stream worthy to be drunk, while you heal the bodily surfaces that are sick.

Therefore I shall present what I have borrowed from the fountains of the Greeks to those who thirst, and shall bring the clearest Latin waters to the hidden places of your heart. [Alt. “I shall prefer.”]

### II.

Origen, then, who wrote no book specifically on the soul, mentions the soul in his catalogue of ecclesiastical teaching and says the following:

[Note: Origen holds this view in the prologue to the book *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). The passage is given here in these very words of Rufinus, and is repeated in another work, *On the Deity and the Incarnation of the Word*, addressed to Januarius, book I, chapter 2, among the spurious works of Augustine, vol. VIII.]

> Concerning the soul, however, whether it is derived from the transmission of seed, so that its rational principle or substance is contained within the bodily seeds themselves, or whether it has another beginning—and, if so, whether it is generated or ungenerated—or certainly whether it is inserted into the body from outside or not, this is not distinguished by sufficiently clear teaching.

Likewise, in the book which he wrote on the Apostle’s Epistle to Titus, he says:

> If anyone should inquire into the nature of the human soul, since ecclesiastical rule has transmitted neither that it is derived from the transmission of seed nor that it is more honorable and more ancient than the structure of bodies, for this reason many have not been able to understand that the nature of the soul ought to be conceived otherwise. Yet those who have appeared to think or argue otherwise are regarded by some with suspicion, as though they were introducing something novel.

The same Origen admits this in the works mentioned above. So too Eusebius of Caesarea and the martyr Pamphilus, Basil, Gregory, Didymus, and Rufinus likewise maintain in their writings that all souls are of one substance, immortal and rational, possessing free choice and will, and that they must also be judged according to what they have done in this life. Yet they say that souls were made by God, who created and established all things.

Whether they were made long ago all together, or now individually as each person is born, they say that it is not dangerous to hold either of the two opinions. Athanasius, Hilary, and Ambrose, however, assert that souls are created at the moment when the bodies of women, already prepared in the womb and formed, are present, and that they are inserted into the already formed body.

### III.

Now those who affirm that souls come by transmission and are sown together with bodily seed—if, as some of them are accustomed to assert, they say that the soul is nothing other than the breathing-in of God’s Spirit, namely, that which God is said to have breathed into Adam at the beginning of the making of the world, professing that it is of God’s own substance—how will they not appear in some manner to assert something contrary to the rule of Scripture and to the reason of piety?

For if the soul sins and is of God’s substance, then it is God’s substance that sins; moreover, it must also be subjected to punishment for sin. They do not see that they likewise incur something absurd: it necessarily follows that the soul dies together with the body and is mortal, if it has been sown, formed, or born together with the body.

### IV.

Moreover, those men—Apollonius, Tertullian, Pompeius, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Apollinarius—who say that God made one soul from no pre-existing substances, namely the soul that was first made in Adam, and that the souls of all human beings arise from Adam, and that, unquestionably according to bodily succession, the transmission of souls is also produced: what else do they themselves demonstrate except that souls are mortal?

For if, just as all other animals arise from seed alone, we likewise hold this concerning human beings, so that together with the body the soul is poured forth in the same seed, what shall we say about those who are still imperfect and are miscarried from the womb, and who sometimes perish even before the seed has been received into the natural receptacles of the vessels?

In such cases, there is no doubt that the souls which had been naturally joined to the seeds were likewise extinguished and destroyed together with them.

### V.

Therefore, whether souls come from the Lord’s breathing-in or from the one soul that was first made, if they receive their origin together with bodies according to their reasoning, it is necessary that they be corrupted together with the bodies.

For either that which is still corrupted in the womb has taken no part at all in a rational and immortal soul—and the theory which asserts that the soul was sown together with the bodies through the transmission of seed is thereby rejected—or, if it has taken part in such a soul, necessity compels them to confess that the soul is mortal.

Our faith certainly does not accept this, since the Lord declares that the souls of the dead both held conversation in the underworld, and that Lazarus was rejoicing in the dwelling places of the blessed, while the rich man was burning in flames.

### VI.

Indeed, not only divine books but also the books of philosophers are full of the teaching that souls are immortal. Cleombrotus of Ambracia had learned that this was so in Plato’s book, in which Socrates conducts the discussion. He did not fear becoming his own murderer and threw himself down from a very high wall, both asserting that no judgment remained after death and supposing that all souls, without any distinction of merits, were carried equally to heaven after the body.

They held this so firmly as truth, and one cloud of this error enveloped all the wise men of the age, that even the teacher of the murderer—whom they regard as so praiseworthy—killed himself privately so that he would not be killed publicly.

So too Cato, after reading by lamplight Plato’s book that teaches the immortality of the soul, drew his sword and struck his exposed breast once and again.

### VII.

Let us return, moreover, to those most noble discussions of the saints—not woven in the dark little groves of the shadowy Academy, but illumined by heavenly light.

The blessed Jerome, following both the holy martyr Victorinus and most Catholics, indicated that he believed souls to be made rather than propagated, in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

The holy Augustine too is seen to defend this opinion in about eight volumes. Yet when he endeavors to explain original sin and the punishments of little children who die without baptism, he is found inclined—both by his own arguments and by testimonies of Scripture—to maintain that the soul was made in Adam and that the souls of all human beings arise from it, as in the passage: “The souls that entered Egypt with Jacob and came forth from his thigh.”

### VIII.

The blessed bishop Gaudiosus, a most ready physician of souls and bodies and, in our own times, himself a martyr, had conversed familiarly with us concerning these assertions. Throughout the whole course of his speech he employed the clearest proofs in their support.

But Saint Ambrose, whom we have already mentioned above among apostolic men, says:

> I consider it dishonorable that souls should be generated together with bodies, so that soul should be born from soul, which is not even compatible with the soul itself. Or, if certainly individual souls were made by heavenly power and the others were born from them, it may seem credible that the others were born from the one soul of Adam. But this is not fitting, because it was possible only for God that the simple should generate, and it was not granted to others—something so mystical in the case of the Savior—that it should be thought incredible not only by Gentiles or Jews, but even by those who call themselves Christians.

> For the Photinians reject this faith; they do not believe that God generated. For if, at the time when the body is sown, the soul is generated from the soul, we read that a rib was taken from Adam; yet we do not read that a soul was born from a soul. But if the rib carried a soul with it, then it was not born but removed as a portion [Alt.: “if”]. Yet not even this is written.

[Note: The words “is generated from soul, from Adam” are absent from a recent edition.] For the prophet Zechariah says, among other things: “Who forms the soul of man within him.” Isaiah too, agreeing with them, says: “Thus says the Lord God, who made you and formed you in the womb.”

> Therefore, if the soul is formed in the womb, it is given to an already formed body. When it fills all the limbs of the body, it is said to be formed within the body; just as water, though without a shape, appears shaped when poured into a vessel, so the soul, although by nature incorporeal and simple, is formed within the body, giving life to each of its limbs.

> Moses indeed transmitted this more explicitly, saying: “If anyone strikes a woman who has conceived and she miscarries, if the fetus has been formed, let him give soul for soul; but if it has not been formed, let him be fined money”—so that he might prove that the soul is not present before the form.

> Therefore, if it is given to an already formed body, it is not born in the conception of the body together with seed by transmission. For if soul exists from soul together with the seed, many souls perish each day when the seed, through some kind of discharge, fails to advance toward birth.

### IX.

But if we first look back, we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us contemplate Adam’s making. In Adam an example was given, so that from him it might be understood that the soul was received by an already formed body.

For God could have mingled the soul with the clay of the earth and thus formed the body. But this reasoning fails, because the house first had to be constructed and then the inhabitant introduced.

The soul, certainly, because it is spirit, cannot dwell in what is dry; therefore it is carried in the blood. When, then, the outlines of the body have not yet been joined together, where will the soul be? Does it wander outside for as long as it waits to be inserted, when reason teaches that it is given in such a way that the soul does not wander idly outside the body?

But let those who think otherwise say from whom it is given: from the male or from the female? [Supplement: “From the female.”] It does not fit, because the example is different. They propose that both the rib and the soul were given from the man; yet we have shown this to be weakened by many arguments.

Thus it may perhaps seem that it is given from the woman, especially on account of the Savior, whom we know to have been born from a woman, without sexual union, from the Holy Spirit. If they believe this, they grant more authority to women: they transfer the authority of the man to the woman.

For although they say that the origin of both body and soul is from the man, they turn around and say that what is superior—the soul—is from the woman, while what is inferior—the body—is from the male, although it is clear that the order of the example transmitted by God cannot be changed.

Therefore, let those who assert that souls are propagated from one soul, and are not made by God in bodies each day according to the example of the first man, be anathema.

**Augustine.** Holy brother Jerome, since I am consulting you about matters I do not know, I ask God to grant that this may be fruitful for us [Alt.: “I ask that you may will it to be fruitful for us”]. Although you are much older in age than I am [Note: The same edition reads: “Although you are much older than I am in age, nevertheless, etc.”], even I, now an old man, am consulting you. Yet for learning what is necessary, no age can seem late to me. For although old men are more suited to teach than to learn, it is still better to learn than to be ignorant of what they should teach.

**Jerome.** Blessed Pope Augustine, if you please, let us play together in the field of Scripture without causing one another pain. Do not, then, measure us by the number of our years, nor reckon wisdom by gray hairs; rather, reckon gray hairs by wisdom, as Scripture bears witness: “The gray hairs of a man are his prudence.” Do not, I say, weigh faith by age, nor think me better for that reason, because I began to serve in Christ’s army earlier.

**Augustine.** Then accept what I ask to have disclosed to me, and do not hesitate to discuss it. The question of the soul troubles many people, among whom I confess that I too am one. I shall not keep silent about what I hold most firmly concerning the soul.

**Jerome.** You measure us by your virtues, and, being great, raise up the small. You take the last place at the banquet so that you may be advanced by the judgment of the master of the household. But I confess that I wish to do so, and I prefer to strive for it. I decline the role of teacher and promise to be a companion [Alt. “by replying”]. To the one who asks, it is given; to the one who knocks, it is opened; the one who seeks finds. Let us learn on earth what our knowledge may retain in heaven.

**Augustine.** I am also certain that the soul fell into sin by no fault of God, by no necessity imposed by God or by itself, but by its own will. Nor can it be liberated from this body of death either by the power of its own will, as though that were sufficient for it, or by the death of the body itself, but only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

**Jerome.** The soul is immortal, invisible, and incorporeal. I say this in comparison with the denser substance of our body. I say that it will certainly be punished and experience punishment when it has received its former body, so that it may be punished together with that with which it sinned.

**Augustine.** Human conception is said to proceed in such a way that during the first six days it resembles milk; during the following nine days it is converted into blood. Then, during twelve days, it becomes solid; during the remaining fifteen days it is formed until all the limbs have their complete outlines; and from that point onward, until the time of birth, it increases in size.

**Jerome.** Just as you do not know the way of the spirit and soul entering the infant, and do not understand the variety of bones and veins in the womb of a pregnant woman—how the human body is varied from a lowly element into different shapes and limbs, and how from the same seed one part becomes soft in the flesh, another hard in the bones, another pulses in the veins, and another becomes firm in the sinews—so you will not be able to know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.

**Augustine.** Concerning the incarnation of the soul, I desire to know which opinion should be chosen: whether the other souls are propagated from that one which was first given to the first man; whether new souls are now made for each individual; or whether souls already existing somewhere are divinely sent or spontaneously slip into bodies.

**Jerome.** I remember your little question concerning the state of the soul—or rather, the greatest ecclesiastical question: whether it has fallen from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen think; whether it is from God’s own substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus, and the mad heresy of Priscillian suspect; whether souls, once created, have long been stored in God’s treasury, as certain churchmen foolishly believe; whether they are made daily by God and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the Gospel, “My Father is working until now, and I am working”; or whether they are propagated, as Tertullian, Apollinarius, and the greater part of the Westerners assert, so that just as body is born from body, soul is born from soul and exists under a condition like that of living creatures.

**Augustine.** You certainly hold that God now makes each soul for each individual who is born. To prevent the objection that God completed all creatures on the sixth day and rested on the seventh, you appeal to the testimony of the Gospel: “My Father is working until now.”

**Jerome.** What ambiguity is there in the statement, so as to provide an occasion for different interpretations? It is established, and there is no dispute about it.

**Augustine.** Teach me, then, I ask, what I should teach; teach me what I should hold. And tell me: if souls are made individually for each person now being born, where do they sin in infants, so that they need the sacrament of Christ and remission of sin, since they sin in Adam, from whom sinful flesh has been propagated? Or, if they do not sin, by what justice of the Creator are they bound by another’s sin? For they are inserted into mortal limbs propagated from that source, so that, unless the Church comes to their aid, condemnation overtakes them, although it is not within their power to obtain the assistance of baptismal grace.

**Jerome.** Sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the uterus; they have spoken falsehoods. As soon as they were born, they lay under sin, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the pattern of the one to come.

There is also what is written in the book of Job: “Will man be clean before God, or will a man be blameless in his works? If he does not trust his servants, and finds something perverse even in his angels, how much more in those who dwell in houses of clay,” of which we too are made from the same clay!

For no one is without sin, even if his life should last only one day. If the stars are not clean in God’s sight, how much more are the worm and corruption, and those who are held liable by the sin of Adam, who offended!

**Augustine.** I ask you: how is this opinion defended, according to which souls are believed not to be made from that one soul of the first man, but, just as that one was made for one person, so individual souls are made for individuals? I think I can easily refute the arguments raised against this opinion. One such argument is that, if God completed all His works on the sixth day and rested on the seventh, how can He still create new souls?

If we reply to them with what you cited above from the Gospel—“My Father is working until now”—they answer: “Working” means administering what He instituted, not instituting new things.

**Jerome.** This passage, to the unlearned who lack meditation, practice, and knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, seems at first sight to flatter your opinion. But when examined, it is easily resolved. When you compare the testimonies of Scripture with other testimonies, so that the Holy Spirit may not appear contrary to Himself according to the character of places and times, you must follow what is written: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of Your cataracts.”

I see where your assertion is headed, but this must be discussed later, lest, while we mix questions with questions, we leave our listeners with an obscured understanding.

**Augustine.** It is true that He rested from instituting things that did not exist; and it is also true that He continues until now to work not only by governing what He made, but also by creating more abundantly not something which does not yet exist, but something which He had already created.

Thus, whether in this way or in any other, we escape the objection concerning God’s rest from His works, so that we do not, on that account, refuse to believe that new souls continue to be made—not from that one soul, but just as that one was made.

As for the question why He makes souls for those whom He knows will soon die, we can answer that the sins of their parents are thereby either exposed or scourged.

**Jerome.** I know that I once wrote what I thought about this in my little works against Rufinus, in the pamphlet which he gave to the holy-memorial Bishop Anastasius of the Roman Church. In it, while he tried by a slippery, foolish, and deceitful confession to mock the simplicity of his listeners, he mocked his own faith—or rather his faithlessness.

**Augustine.** In your book against Rufinus you stated that some people slander this opinion because it seems unworthy that God should give souls to adulterous conceptions. From this they try to establish that, on the basis of merits acquired in a life before the flesh, souls may justly be brought as though to the prison-house of this world.

This does not trouble me, although I think of many arguments by which such a slander can be refuted. Your own reply is an elegant comparison: there is no defect in the wheat because it is said to have been stolen, but in the one who stole the grain; nor should the earth therefore have failed to cherish the seeds in its bosom because the sower cast them with an unclean hand.

Even before I read this, the objection concerning adulterous offspring caused me no difficulty in this question, when I considered generally that God makes many good things even from our evils and wicked sins.

If the creation of any animal, when considered by a prudent and devout observer, arouses ineffable praise of the Creator, how much more does the creation not of just any animal but of a human being!

If the reason for creating is sought, no answer can be given more quickly or more appropriately than this: every creature of God is good. And what is more worthy than that the good God should make good things which no one but God can make?

These and other arguments that I can produce, and as I can produce them, I set forth against those who try to weaken this opinion, according to which souls are made individually in the same way as that one soul was made.

**Jerome.** Antonius, that outstanding orator whose praises resound in Cicero, says that he saw many eloquent men but not yet a single truly eloquent one. Therefore do not play with me with the flowers of orators rather than with your own, by which the ears of the unlearned and of children are usually deceived. Simply say what you think.

**Augustine.** When we come to the punishments of infants, believe me, I am oppressed by great anxieties, and I find absolutely nothing to answer. I do not speak only of the punishments of that condemnation after this life, to which they must necessarily be dragged if they depart from the body without the sacrament of Christian grace. I speak also of those very sufferings that occur before our eyes in this life, causing us grief. If I wished to enumerate them, time would fail before examples did.

They languish in sickness, are tortured by pain, tormented by hunger and thirst, weakened in their limbs, deprived of their senses, and harassed by unclean spirits. It must therefore be demonstrated how they can justly suffer these things without that cause being their own evil.

For it is not permissible to say either that these things occur without God’s knowledge, or that He cannot resist those who cause them, or that He acts or permits them unjustly.

**Jerome.** You employ different testimonies of Scripture concerning the same question in theatrical tricks, like those who bring forth one and the same man as Mars and Venus by changing his variety of roles, so that the one who had previously walked stiffly and savagely is afterward softened into feminine tenderness.

**Augustine.** When I sense that you are angry, I shall do nothing other than ask your pardon.

**Jerome.** I ask you to listen patiently. We are seeking not victory over an adversary, but truth against falsehood.

**Augustine.** Just as we rightly say that irrational animals are given for the use of superior natures, even though those natures are vicious—as we see most clearly in the Gospel, where pigs were granted to the demons for their desired use—can we rightly say the same of a human being?

He is an animal, but rational, although mortal. There is a rational soul in those limbs that pay the penalty through such great afflictions. God is good, God is just, God is almighty; to doubt this at all is sheer madness.

Let the cause, then, of the many evils that occur in infants be stated. When adults suffer such things, we are accustomed to say either that their merits are being tested, as in Job, or that their sins are being punished, as in Herod. Concerning certain examples that God wished to make manifest, other obscure matters are left to human conjecture—but this concerns adults.

What shall we answer concerning infants? Explain it, if there are no sins in them to be punished by such great penalties. For certainly at those ages there is no justice to be tested.

**Jerome.** The Preacher first of all devoted his mind to seeking wisdom and, extending himself beyond what was permitted, wished to know causes and reasons: Why are infants attacked by a demon? Why do shipwrecks engulf the just and the impious alike? Do these and similar things happen by chance or by God’s judgment? And if by chance, where is providence? If by judgment, where is God’s justice?

**Augustine.** Teach me, then, what we ought to say and think, so that the account of new souls, made individually for individual bodies, may be clear to us.

**Jerome.** You seem forgetful and, as though nothing had been said above, are returning along the same lines of argument. This has already been examined at length.

**Augustine.** I am asking for the cause of the condemnation of infants. For if new souls are made individually for individuals, I see no sin in this age of life; nor do I believe that God condemns any soul which He sees to have no sin.

Or should we perhaps say that in an infant only the flesh is sinful, while a new soul is made for it, and that, by living according to God’s commands with the assistance of Christ’s grace, it can acquire the merit of incorruption by taming and subjugating the flesh itself?

**Jerome.** Let us strive to remove from the Church a most destructive heresy, which always pretends to repentance so that it may obtain the power to teach in the Churches, lest, if it reveals itself in the clear light, it be expelled and perish outside.

**Augustine.** The cause must be sought and stated why souls that are newly created for each person are condemned if infants die without the sacrament of Christ. That they are condemned if they depart from the body in this condition is testified both by Holy Scripture and by the holy Church.

Therefore, if the opinion concerning the creation of new souls does not oppose this most firmly established faith, let it also be mine; if it does oppose it, let it not be yours.

I do not want it said to me that this opinion should be supported by what is written: “He who formed the spirit of man within him,” and, “He who forms their hearts individually.”

Something exceedingly strong and unconquerable must be sought—something that does not compel us to believe that God condemns any souls without any fault.

For perhaps “to create” is equal to, or even greater than, “to form”; yet it is written: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” Nor can the soul therefore be thought in this passage to desire to be made before it existed.

Accordingly, just as something already existing is created through the renewal of righteousness, so something already existing is formed through the confirmation of teaching.

Nor does what is written in Ecclesiastes confirm this opinion, which we want to be ours: “Then the dust will return to the earth as it was, and the spirit will return to God who gave it.”

Indeed, this gives more support to those who think that all souls come from one. They say: Just as the dust returns to the earth as it was, yet the flesh of which this is said does not return to the man from whom it was propagated, but to the earth from which the first man was made, so the spirit propagated from the spirit of that one man does not return to him, but to the Lord by whom it was given to him.

But because this testimony sounds so much in their favor that it does not appear entirely contrary to the opinion I wish to defend, I thought it necessary merely to bring your prudence to its attention, lest you attempt to rescue me from these difficulties by such testimonies.

For although no one can make something true by wishing it to be true when it is not true, nevertheless, if it were possible, I would wish this opinion to be true, just as I wish that, if it is true, you might defend it with perfect clarity and invincible force.

**Jerome.** You have presented testimonies which are not taken from some other passage of Scripture but are complete in their own books: “Let the dust return to its earth, from which it was taken; and let the spirit return to God who gave it.”

For this reason those who think that souls are made together with bodies, and not by God but by the parent of bodies, are sufficiently laughable. Since the flesh returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it, it is clear that God is the parent of souls, not human beings.

**Augustine.** I do not wish to examine the opinion that all souls are made from one unless necessity requires it. Would that the opinion we are now discussing, if it is true, might be defended by you in such a way that this necessity would no longer exist.

Although I desire, ask, ardently long, and await that the Lord may through you remove my ignorance of this matter, nevertheless, if—God forbid—I should not deserve this, I shall ask patience from our Lord.

**Jerome.** According to the blessed Apostle: “Let each one abound in his own understanding”; one person indeed thinks this, another that.

Certainly, whatever could be said, and whatever could be drawn from the fountains of the Holy Scriptures by a lofty intellect, you have set forth and discussed. But I ask your reverence [Alt. “modesty”] to allow me for a little while to praise your intellect.

We discuss these things among ourselves for the sake of instruction. But our rivals, and especially heretics, when they see that we hold different opinions, will slander us, claiming that these differences arise from bitterness of spirit.

For my part, I have resolved to love you, honor you, receive you [Alt. “accept you”], admire you, and defend your words as though they were my own.

Augustine. Those who assert that souls are propagated from the one soul that God gave to the first man, and thus say that they are drawn from their parents—if they follow Tertullian’s opinion—plainly maintain that souls are not spirits but bodies, and that they arise from corporeal seed. What could be said more perversely than this?

[Col. 0271A] Jerome. Let those who say that souls existed before they were born, and that they are not made daily by God for the body according to the pattern of the first man, be anathema.

Augustine. Who denies that God is the creator and maker not merely of one soul but of every soul, except one who most openly resists his utterances? For without any ambiguity he said through the prophet: “I have made every breath” [*omnem flatum*]—clearly wishing souls to be understood.

Jerome. The Lord says in the Gospel: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Great is the dignity of souls, since each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel appointed to guard it. Let the faith already stated suffice for us, and let our speech at last come to an end. Behold, with God’s favor, I have done what you demanded—or rather, what I was able to do: I have brought the account of the soul, according to the pattern of the first man, and the Savior’s word, that it is made daily by the Lord God and given to an already formed body, through its entire course, briefly indeed, more by leaps, if one may say so, than by steps, because of the haste, all the way to its conclusion. According to the poverty of my little intellect, I have presented it with complete clarity through all the teachers of the Church, especially by having Augustine and Jerome, those two books of richness, stand beside me, with a golden candlestick to the right and left, like the two lights of heaven. Restoring to them sayings discovered in very many of their little works through my diligent vigilance and shrewd investigation, I have made them speak as though present, taking turns.

What is so upright, what so true, what so Catholic, [Col. 0271C] what clearer than the sun, more useful for the instruction of all—or, certainly, against the heretics who rage against us with hostile minds—what so irreproachable? Therefore, by firmly following the instructions of Catholic men, you will be found to be their just heirs, and necessary ones as well. You, who excel in Latin eloquence, will be preferred to the wiser; and, as I stated in the preface, you will overflow not so much with the abundance of dripping liquid as with the richness of inundating rivers, watered by the streams of the saints.

## Notice concerning the following letter

This title frequently occurs among medieval writers for homilies. From its very first words, Oudinus recognizes it as belonging to Faustus, bishop of Riez, who until now has lain concealed under the name of Eusebius of Emesa. It is also found printed among [Col. 0271D] his homilies.

## Letter XXXVIII, or Homily on the Body and Blood of Christ (C, G)*

### I

The greatness of heavenly benefits exceeds the limitations of the human mind. Therefore divine providence ordered that what reason, overcome by the magnitude of these realities, could not contain within us, devout faith should conceive, and that steadfast belief should nourish understanding.

Since, then, on account of Adam’s transgression we were held subject to our origin and to death, God, looking down from on high, repaired the gift of redemption according to the nature of our captivity, from which we had become grievous debtors. That is, he offered, in place of the death that was owed, a death that was not owed, because neither did we have the means by which we might live, nor did he have the means by which he might die.

He therefore took material from our mortality, so that, by the immortality bestowed by him, life might die for the dead. And because he was going to remove the body he had assumed from our eyes and carry it up to the stars, it was necessary for him on this day to consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that what was once offered as the price might rightly be worshiped continually through the mystery. Since redemption for the salvation of human beings was proceeding daily and without weariness, the offering of redemption was also to be perpetual; and that enduring victim was to live in memory and always be present in grace.

It is the true, unique, and perfect sacrifice, to be apprehended by faith, not by outward appearance; not to be judged by the sight of the external human being, but by the inward affection. Hence the heavenly authority rightly confirms [Col. 0272B]: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56).

### II

Let every ambiguity of unbelief therefore withdraw, since the one who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness of its truth. For the visible priest, by his word and with hidden power, converts visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26). And with the sanctification repeated: “Take,” he says, “and drink; this is my blood.”

Therefore, just as at the command of the Lord who ordered them, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waves, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into being from nothing, so in spiritual sacraments the power supplies an equal potency to the words, and the effect serves the reality.

Consider, then, how great and worthy of celebration is the power of divine blessing, and how it ought not to seem new or impossible to you that earthly and mortal things are changed into the substance of Christ. Ask yourself, since you have already been regenerated in Christ.

### III

Not long ago you were alien to life, a stranger to mercy and to the way of salvation; inwardly dead, you wandered in exile. Suddenly initiated into Christ’s laws and renewed by saving mysteries, you passed into the body of the Church, not by seeing but by believing. From being a son of perdition, you deserved, through hidden purity, to become an adopted son of God.

Remaining within a visible measure, you became visibly greater than yourself without any increase in quantity. Although you were yourself and the same person, you came to exist in a very different way through the stages of faith. Nothing was added outwardly, yet everything was changed inwardly; and thus the human being became a son of Christ [Col. 0272D], and Christ was formed in the human mind.

Therefore, just as without bodily perception, after laying aside your former degradation, you were suddenly clothed with a new dignity; and just as those things that God healed in you when they were damaged, washed away when they were polluted, and cleansed when they were stained were not entrusted to your eyes or bodily senses, so, when you approach the venerable altar to be nourished by heavenly foods, behold, honor, and marvel at the sacred body and blood of your God. Touch it with the mind; receive it with the hand of the heart; and, above all, take it in by an inward draught.

### IV

If that manna of the old law, of which it is written, “He rained manna upon them to eat,” tasted to each person according to what his desires had craved; if what was taken was one thing and what was seen another; if that taste was invisibly formed in the senses of each person; if, therefore, that manna of the old law, falling from heaven with manifold sweetness, surpassed the natural quality and appearance of its kind; and if the dispenser’s provision had fashioned its creature with varied diversity, so that taste might supply what sight did not know—because, according to the desire of the recipient, the novelty and excellence of that food arose; because that honeyed gift of the rain, and the manifold service of the dry shower, refreshed each person with different and unfamiliar flavors—since these things are so, let what appetite accomplished there be accomplished here by faith.

As the food there tasted in the body, so here let God advance through belief in the breast. As we read: “A person will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Psalm 63:7). Therefore, what delight achieved there in the throat, let blessing effect here in the senses. For recognizing and receiving the sacrifice of the true body of the Lord, let the very power of the consecrator strengthen you; and let him who was then concealed in figure under the manna be manifested to you now in grace.

### V

That he himself was prefigured in the form of that manna, the Prophet also clearly shows when he says: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:25). And what is the bread of angels except Christ, who satisfies us with the food of his love and the light of his glory?

And he gives this bread, as the Prophet says: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much.” For since at first it is granted in the law from the Lord’s Day and denied only on the Sabbath, Christ was already then shown to be received by the Church, to which he consecrated the Lord’s Day of resurrection [Col. 0273C], while it was commanded that he be denied to the synagogue, to which observance of the Sabbath belonged.

Since the seventh day is punished by the withholding of the heavenly bread, concerning which the ancient narrative says: “Neither did the one who had gathered much have too much, nor did the one who had prepared little find too little,” this is because reception of the Eucharist consists not in quantity but in power. The body of the Lord, when dispensed by the priest, is as much in the small portion as it is known to be in the whole. When the Church of the faithful receives it, it is shown to be as full in each person as it is complete in all.

From this meaning the apostolic statement is derived: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little” (2 Corinthians 8:15). This cannot be understood of ordinary bread. If we were to set such bread before hungry people, it would not reach each one in its entirety, since each person would take his share piecemeal and in fragments. But when this bread is received, individuals have no less than all together: one receives the whole, two receive the whole, and many receive the whole without diminution. The blessing of this sacrament knows how to be distributed, but does not know how to be consumed by distribution.

### VI

We also see the form of this sacrament expressed in the pages of the Jews. For in Genesis we read of Melchizedek: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham. And he was priest of God Most High” (Genesis 14:18 and following).

While circumcision to come is blessed by one who was uncircumcised—that is, by a Gentile—the glory of the Church is proclaimed; and the people acquired from the Gentiles are placed above the unfaithful synagogue. The genealogy or origin of this Melchizedek remained unknown to that age; and by the offering of bread and wine he prefigured this sacrifice of Christ, concerning which the Prophet declares: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

### VII

Moses too, speaking of that mystery, signifies wine and blood under one designation, and in the blessing of the patriarch displays the Lord’s Passion much more clearly, saying: “He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Genesis 49:11).

Observe how clearly the creature of wine is called the blood of Christ. And learn from the Lord himself, who bears witness, what further inquiry you ought to make concerning this twofold form: “Unless,” he says, “you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

This testimony is most clear and powerful against the blasphemies of Pelagius, who, seized by impiety, presumes to assert that baptism is to be conferred on little children not for life but for the kingdom of heaven. For under these words of God, by which the Evangelist declares, “You will not have life in yourselves,” it is plainly to be understood that every soul lacking the gift of baptism is deprived not only of glory but also of life.

### VIII

That this wine of the Lord’s blood must be mixed with water is shown not only by tradition but also by the very manner of the Passion. From his sacred side blood and water flowed when it was struck by the lance, just as the Prophet had long before foretold: “He struck the rock, and the waters flowed.” And the Apostle says: “They drank from the rock that followed them” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

You see that whoever drinks from Christ’s grace is followed by Christ’s mercy. But in Solomon we read that this same God had been foretold: “Wisdom,” he says, “built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1)—that is, he assumed the body of a human being, in which the fullness of divinity dwells. “She hewed out seven pillars,” because the blessing of sevenfold grace filled him; “she sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine in the bowl, and prepared her table.” And in what follows: “Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you.” Thus we read that wine was mixed with water.

### IX

Let us now inquire why the Lord wished the two to be mixed. When, at the wedding feast of the Jews, wine—that is, faith among them—was failing, it is said: “The wine was failing,” because the vine denied its fruit. Of this it is said: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isaiah 5:4)—hence also the thorny crown was placed on the Redeemer’s head.

When the Lord, at the time of the wedding—that is, when the bridegroom joined himself to his Church in the paschal exultation—changed water into wine, he plainly prefigured that multitudes of the Gentiles would come through the grace of his blood. For that peoples are signified by waters is disclosed in the sacred writings, as it is written: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations and languages” (Revelation 17:15).

Thus we observe that the figure of the Gentiles is represented in the waters, while the blood of the Lord’s Passion is shown in the wine. And so, when water is mixed with wine in the sacraments, the people faithful to Christ are incorporated into him and joined to him, united with him by a kind of bond of perfect love, so that they may say with the Apostle: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?” (Romans 8:35), and what follows.

God, having received sanctification, is also mingled with the human being; faith in the sinner pours into him an inclination toward righteousness and the mercy of devotion.

### X

Moreover, in the fact that we know bread to be made from numerous grains of wheat, we recognize that the unity of peoples is signified. For just as grain, brought to its white appearance only by the care of the one who cleans it and by the labor of the mill, is gathered through water and fire into the substance of one bread, so diverse peoples and different nations, coming together in one faith, become from themselves one body of Christ.

The Christian people, like innumerable grains of wheat purified and sifted by faith among sacrilegious nations, are separated out. They are gathered together as the tares of unbelievers pass away; and, instructed by the two Testaments, they shine like grain prepared by the double labor of the mill. They are changed by their native whiteness into the dignity of their first origin, and through the water of baptism or the fire of the Holy Spirit become the body of that eternal bread.

### XI

Therefore, just as grains cannot be separated from the union by which the bread is made, and just as water mixed into wine cannot now return to its own substance, so all the faithful and wise, who recognize that they have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and Passion, ought to be joined to their head as inseparable members through observance of the faith and the most ardent devotion.

They must be so united that they cannot be separated from him by will, by necessity, by any ambition for earthly hope, or finally even by death itself. Let no one doubt that the primary elements of creation can, by the command of divine power and through the presence of supreme majesty, pass into the nature of the Lord’s body, when he sees that the human being himself has been made the body of Christ by the work of heavenly mercy.

### XII

Just as anyone who comes to the faith of Christ, before the words of baptism, still remains bound by the debt of the past, but, once these words have been spoken, is immediately stripped of every dreg of sin, so, when creatures to be blessed with heavenly words are placed upon the sacred altars, before they are consecrated by the invocation of his name, the substance there is bread and wine; after the words, it is the body and blood of Christ.

What wonder is it, then, if what he was able to create by a word he can convert by a word once created? Indeed, it seems a lesser miracle if what he is acknowledged to have fashioned from nothing, once fashioned, he is able to change for the better.

Consider what can be difficult for one for whom it was easy to form the human being from the material of clay; to clothe him with the image of his own divinity; to recall him again from the underworld; to restore him from destruction; to repair him from dust; to raise him from earth to heaven; to make an angel from a human being; to make the human body conform to the body of his glory; and to exalt his creature into fellowship with his kingdom.

Thus, he who assumed the body of our frailty may assume us into the body of his immortality. May he deign to prepare us by holy works for that glorious resurrection—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## Notice concerning the following letter

Oudinus maintains that this too belongs to Faustus of Riez, a man laboring under Semi-Pelagianism, whom he seems, here as elsewhere, to have insinuated into the work deliberately. Besides, this treatise lacks a proper conclusion and appears to be a fragment of a longer work.

## Letter XXXIX, or Homily on the Gospel of Matthew

### I

The holy Evangelist teaches us that, when enduring the necessity of want, we ought to seek out a friend for assistance, and that what is lacking for the refreshment of another ought to be borrowed from someone else. He wished the petitioner to be so persistent in asking that he would not cease knocking at his friend’s door during the night, nor hesitate to rouse him while he was resting. Indeed, by causing annoyance, the petitioner was to obtain through shamelessness what friendship would not grant, and through his importunity to extort the sharing of bread that human kindness would not secure.

For he says: “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight?” (Luke 11:5), and so forth.

### II

According to the literal sense, this seems to persuade us not to cease troubling a friend who is resting at midnight, whose room is closed and who is asleep. But if we turn our attention to the spiritual meaning, we shall find that the Lord gave this command not harshly but usefully.

For after teaching the disciples the Lord’s Prayer, he added this parable so that we might understand that we ought to be importunate friends—not by demanding something, but rather by praying: that is, not striking Christ with a bodily hand, but knocking through spiritual prayer.

He himself is our friend, if we live rightly. For who is more friendly to us than the one who redeemed us at the price of his blood? He, I say, is friendlier than all, who, although he is Lord, deigns to be a friend, saying to the Apostles: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15).

### III

We must therefore knock incessantly at the door of this friend, trouble him during the night hours, and be so persistent that we may even be judged importunate. But let us not fear offending him by this importunity, because with the Lord this importunity is opportune.

A shameless plea is more acceptable to him than secure presumption. That is, the one who anxiously prays insistently merits more than the one who, relying on confidence, carelessly neglects to pray. For he also says, “If he persists in knocking.” The one who perseveres therefore deserves to receive what he says more clearly elsewhere: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13).

Frequent prayer is therefore of little benefit to one who at some point ceases.

### IV

We must therefore always ask and knock without interruption, lest a prayer already offered prove useless if it does not reach the end with the same constancy with which it began.

“I tell you,” he says, “even if he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him.” Great is the perseverance which, though importunate and troublesome to God, is nevertheless more friendly than a friend.

For what is denied to a friend is earned by perseverance. To the one, he refuses because of confidence; toward the other, he is moved by persistence. To the one who knocks familiarly he does not give freely; toward the one who prays stubbornly he shows compassion.

### V

Let us therefore knock at the Lord’s door not only through faith but also through perseverance, so that it may be opened to us. Let us knock at midnight, lest the heavy sleep of sins overtake us while we ought to keep watch, for it is written: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12:37).

The Apostle asks that this door be opened to him, beseeching assistance not only through your prayers but also through his own, saying: “That a door may be opened for me to speak the mystery of Christ” (Colossians 4:3). He desires, with the door opened, to receive those sacramental loaves by which the hunger of the Gentile people, hungering to know the Lord, may be satisfied.

Let us therefore also knock at this door and pray perseveringly, so that we may deserve to receive from it the bread of wisdom and knowledge. For unless we take nourishment from that source, we cannot refresh the desire of this brotherhood by our own speech.

### VI

Alternatively, this man may be understood as any Christian who understands only the faith of the Trinity, and who does not know what is necessary unless someone else teaches him.

His friend, as we have said, is Christ. When it says that he goes to him at midnight, this means at the final time, and says to him, “Lend me three loaves,” it is as though that soul were saying to Christ: “Lend me the faith of the Trinity, and make me understand how I ought to act.”

“My friend has come to me from a journey,” as though he were saying: “My understanding has traveled through different regions, and on returning to me it is empty. I have no spiritual nourishment to set before him unless you teach me the faith of the Trinity, hope, love, and everything I should give him; nor do I have anything with which to teach him.”

“Do not trouble me,” and so forth. He delayed the desire, but did not remove it, so that we might seek more earnestly and hold more firmly what we have found.

When he says, “My children are with me,” it is as though the omnipotent Lord Christ were saying: “My holy ones, whom I willed to be with me, are already with me. I cannot rise and give you anything.” He therefore denies the request in order to test the perseverance of anyone.

And when he says, “If he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs,” so too the Lord Jesus, the friend and brother of Christians [*our brother* omitted in some copies], will grant without difficulty whatever anyone asks in his name, provided that he asks faithfully and importunately through continual prayer. As the following passage also says:

### VII

“I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” That is: ask the Father, seek the Son, knock upon the Holy Spirit. Or: ask with your thoughts, seek with your words, knock with your works. Or again: ask in faith, seek through works, and knock through knowledge; and behold, everything will be opened to you.

“Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?” (Matthew 7:9). It is as though he were saying: The one who asks the Lord for love and affection is not given hardness of heart.

“Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?” (ibid., 10). By the fish faith is understood, and by the serpent unbelief. It is as though he were saying: If you ask the Lord for faith, he does not give you unbelief.

“Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” It is as though he were saying: If you have true hope in God, or if you conceive a holy thought in your heart, you need not fear receiving contradiction or the malicious accusation of snares from the Lord.

“If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who fear him?” (ibid., 11).

It is as though he were saying: If you, carnal human beings, distinguish between good and evil and do not wish anyone among you to receive evil from your hand instead of good, how much more will God, who created all things and made the human being in his image, faithfully grant good things to one who asks him?

“I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). What do we understand by fire in this passage except the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord sent upon the earth to burn away vices and sins, to kindle souls through love, and to illumine them?

## Notice concerning the following letter

Although no one will deny that the author of this letter, when compared with Jerome, falls far below his talent and dignity, yet he will not approve Erasmus’s criticism—wholly unjust, as on other occasions—when he calls him a most shameless pettifogger, spouting rather than speaking, and babbling whatever comes into his mouth. Victor of Cartenna, bishop of a city in Mauretania, treated this very subject; as Gennadius testifies in chapter 77, he wrote for a certain Basil a consolatory book on the death of a son, fortified by the hope of resurrection and thorough instruction.

## Letter XL. To Tyrasius: A Consolation on the Death of His Daughter. Jerome to Tyrasius, blessed and beloved

### I

I received the letter of your charity, in which I learned that your spirit was troubled with grief at your daughter’s falling asleep. I chiefly wondered at nothing else than that the strength of a Christian heart had failed you in the matter of one who had been taken away, so that you bent your mind toward grief. I am astonished that the wall of faith, which hope of the resurrection and the heavenly kingdom ought to have enclosed, was pierced by the wounds of bereavement. Hope never agrees with grief, nor does faith ever feel any loss whatever.

Do we believe that the dead rise again, and yet mourn? What would we do if God commanded only that we die, without resurrection? Surely his will alone ought to suffice as consolation, before which we are commanded to place no affection. He who created her took away what he had given. Who is there who should mourn what he had received only for a time? He had lent her to you, for you to possess her for however long he wished, so that, when he wished, he might take her away again. He who deigned to receive what was his own took away nothing of yours. It was fitting that the creditor should receive back what was entrusted to him; and nothing is fitting for a borrower except to give thanks to his creditor. Thus we read the most devout utterance of Job, which we should follow: “The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

### II

This, then, was no slight consolation against mourning: no one ought to grieve when he has returned another’s property, because it was not right for what was needed by its Lord to be retained by someone else. Another providential consolation is added to meet the darts of bereavement. We ought to have mourned those departing from the world if we did not feel the world’s hostility against us; yet we mourn the benefits of the Lord, who knows what he grants to our weakness. Whoever grieves for one asleep would have wished that person still to be in danger, and would have wished to see the miserable one labor amid the waves of the present life. She has escaped such and so great storms of life, so many assaults of the devil, so many battles of the body, so many disasters of the world. And do you shed tears, as though you did not know what you yourself endure every day?

### III

For this reason the Lord admonishes his Apostles, saying: “If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father” (John 14:12). Certainly he wept over Lazarus dead, but he did not shed your tears. The promiser of resurrection could not teach grief, lest he make the faith which he taught into unbelief. He grieved for Lazarus, not as one asleep, but rather as one about to rise; and he wept for him because he was compelled, for the sake of others, to call him back to the world. The Lord groaned while giving him this life, which you grieve has been taken away. Your tears contend against his tears, and your love does not accord with his love. This weeping has no piety. He did not wish to restore to labors the one he loved; and you believed that you loved her, though you wished still to grant her the torments of labor.

Besides, if you think that he grieved for Lazarus himself, he would not previously have allowed him to die, since he was able to repel death; or at least he would not have wept, since he afterward had power to raise the dead man. It is therefore apparent that he was moved for this reason alone: he was compelled to recall his dearest one anew to a hostile life, for the sake of some who would believe and others who would be put to shame in their unbelief. Finally, he then continued, saying: “Therefore, Father, that they may believe that you sent me,” he said with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43). And it came to pass.

### IV

Rejoice, then, at what compelled him to weep, lest you at least seem to envy the blessings of one asleep. She passed from a foreign world to her own Lord, and migrated from a hostile homeland to heaven. The Apostle similarly reminds us, saying: “As long as we are in this world, we are pilgrims from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6). No one, therefore, ought to cause us grief when he has deserved to return from pilgrimage to his own country, especially when he is known not to return empty and void, having gained the profit of Christianity, for which he descended to the commerce of the world.

“But,” you say, “I am troubled by no doubt whatsoever concerning the heavenly promises; I am only agitated by separation from the sleeping one, bereft of the consolation of a loving pledge.”

### V

This, blessed one, is without doubt an excuse of human frailty, which cannot defend unbelief. For if human beings could not bear desolation, parents would never at all let their children leave them. They complain that those who die have deserted them, yet entrust their living children to foreign lands, either for honors or for business; and they are glad to live their whole lives apart from their affections, provided that they may obtain what they wish to gain through their children. They travel abroad in order to go to palaces; they sail to acquire the pursuits of rank, or to settle some matters of inheritance with labor and danger. They urge all who depart, and do not allow those whom they love to remain idle with them.

Yet that they may reach the palaces of heaven, the pursuits of Christ, the honor of eternal life, and the inheritance of everlasting possession in safety, no one gladly rejoices that his children depart from him. To acquire sins, both parents from children and children from parents rejoice to be separated, at the devil’s prompting. To receive pardon, they are unwilling, when God calls, to be separated from one another. Thus it is evident that we grieve for anyone whom we seem to lose not according to reason, but rather display a proof of unbelief.

### VI

Believe me: in all things unbelief alone grieves. And just as faith cannot know what it should grieve over, so unbelief alone is found to be the handmaid of sorrows. For if we call them asleep, we must surely believe that they sleep, and regard them not as dead but as resting, according to the Lord’s saying: “Everyone who believes in me, though he die, lives” (John 11:25). If any physician promised you this, you could surely deny no joy whatever to his promise. But now, because Christ the maker and raiser promises it, you are not ashamed to mourn her, as though you judged a physician more faithful and more powerful than Christ in making a promise.

### VII

“But,” you say, “I mourn my abandoned old age: I ought rather to have gone before my children, so that I might not remain amid labors.” Whenever spiritual goods are under discussion, nothing carnal at all ought to be set before one’s eyes. I declare that a better thing has happened to you, for I perceive in your case not carnal but spiritual happiness. You say that you have been worn down in old age by the death of your pledge; I, on the contrary, prove that you have been relieved. The Lord has rather cut away from your old age the anxiety which tormented you while she was alive, lest your daughter perish. Surely you now believe her, dead to the world, to be alive with God, rather than alive here but dead.

Rejoice that you will deserve to follow your Christian daughter, and that, following her, you may rejoice to embrace her again in heaven. She has not deserted you but gone before you. You have sent your nourishment ahead to Christ. If you shun grief, you may be reckoned to have offered your pledge to God. After Abraham, hold to the second degree of his vow if you cannot attain the first: so that you may at least rejoice in her removal, which he did not hesitate to offer. From him the Lord asked; from you he took. He obeyed the command; you should consent to the will. He tested Abraham as devoted to himself through an unlawful law of nature; through the lawful condition of mortality, let him at least mark you as religious. In this respect you will be able to prove yourself a Christian.

### VIII

Let our unbelief be ashamed, since it is unwilling to be subject to God even together with the Gentiles. The outcome of death is common to us and them, yet we surpass their sorrows with our own sorrows. What would we do if something peculiar were demanded of us? To our shame, Gentiles often despise sorrows even when they are carried off not to heavenly promises but to the punishments of Tartarus; and do we mourn those going to heaven? Consider what such a Christian will afterward deserve, who strives neither to imitate the examples of the saints nor to possess the contempt of the Gentiles. They despise grief through despair; we do not even attempt to despise it through hope. They fearlessly entrust their children to mortal human beings for service; and we hesitate in sacrilegious spirit to consign both their children and our own to our God, to be saved, as though we judged condemnation among human beings safer than with God. Christians are unwilling even to accompany one of their children to blessings with their congratulations; Gentiles do not hesitate to surrender them to evils.

### IX

Finally, we ought to be compelled to change our minds even by the happiness of our own dying persons, lest our desires begin to resist their desires. Be devout at least because of the wish of her who has escaped, if you cannot be so for your own sake. Rejoice because you know that one who shares your blood has pleased Christ, especially since you ought to bear the Lord’s will in this matter, which you cannot oppose. And since this event is common to all, grief is vain when it seems neither the first nor the only such grief.

### X

“But,” you say, “no anguish of mind concerning my own desolation [variant: consolation] torments me; rather, human affection moves me for the little children left behind by the dying woman.” Nor is it permitted for a Christian mind to be moved, lest it resist Christ’s commands. What difference does it make at what time, or what kind of children, she left behind—children whom we are commanded by the Lord to hate for the sake of devotion? By dying she has now left her own soul safe in peace, lest in persecution she might be unable to leave it with her own death. She will aid in the world those whose mother she has in heaven. And he who helps the mother will certainly also help her children.

XI. Finally, consider whether anything ought to be conceded to grief [Col. 0281D] when the mind can be wearied without any remedy. He who grieves ought to grieve wisely, lest he lose without cause what he grieves over. But now we must take up arms against mourning, so that our hope may gain the victory. Above all, let us rejoice that God has chosen to receive him. Then, since this is common to us all in the world, let us add our own particular consolation: that we are being led to rest. What follows is the completion of every joy: that, when the Lord restores us, we shall be given back to one another in the resurrection. The Apostle promises this:

> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus [Col. 0282A] (I Thess. IV, 12–13).

I have sent you these words, blessed one, out of our common affection. In every other respect I know that you are well and that you console others. Bereavement will not find a heart that can be pierced, if you do not cease to arm [Al. love] others against it.

**EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER**

Erasmus says: “In certain copies this is inscribed as addressed to Oceanus; yet it ends in the manner of a homily.” It bears the stamp of the same author as the preceding letter, since it is neither learned nor in any way redolent of the spirit of Jerome.

## LETTER XLI. TO OCEANUS, AN EXHORTATION ON ENDURING INSULTS

### I

I have learned that you are enduring insults of various kinds and manifold tribulations, with certain people plotting against you [Col. 0282B]. I grieve at the cause of this only if you reject these things; but if you accept them willingly, I rejoice. For in this Christ’s faith is shown in us, fear is discerned, and death is manifested, if for love of him we gladly subject ourselves to insults and temptations.

Nor ought this to be contrary to us, but pleasing: to suffer even a little for the one who endured greater things for our salvation—especially since we know that the kingdom of heaven is not attained without various temptations, as it is written:

> We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations (Acts XIV, 21).

If, then, through many tribulations the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened to some, it is certainly closed to those who are unwilling to endure even a little.

### II

Therefore we ought to endure the various kinds of temptations with an even spirit, through which we are promised that the heavenly gate will be opened to us [Col. 0282C]. The blessed apostle James exhorts and teaches us what sort of people we ought to be in tribulations when he says:

> Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations (James I, 2).

Thus it is sufficiently perverse and contrary that we should be wearied by any sadness in matters in which we are commanded to have joy rather than mourning. The same apostle says elsewhere:

> Blessed is the man who remains steadfast in temptations, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him.

See, then, how much temptation benefits a person: through it he obtains blessedness and a crown. But we must understand what he means when he says, “For when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” [Col. 0282D]. He calls those tested, and loved by God, who have persevered in temptation for the sake of his name; to them the crown is rightly promised. But he calls those rejected and unworthy of any reward of life whom no cause of temptation has afflicted.

### III

Therefore we too ought to rejoice in temptations and endure them, so that, having been tested, we may be crowned with the reward of eternal life. The Lord himself also declared this in his Gospel, saying:

> Blessed are you when they curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you on account of righteousness. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven (Matt. XXIII, 11).
