Who, after such a pronouncement, would not allow himself to be tested? Who would not desire to be persecuted by people for the sake of righteousness [Col. 0283A]? Who would not wish to be afflicted? Who would not desire to be cursed, so as to deserve to be praised by Christ’s voice and rewarded with a heavenly and abundant recompense?

Would that, for the sake of my Lord’s name and righteousness, the whole crowd of unbelievers should persecute and afflict me! Would that this entire world should rise up in reproach against me—provided only that I might deserve to be praised by Christ and hope for the reward of his promise!

Temptation, then, is welcome and desirable when its reward is hoped for from Christ in heaven; nor is a curse grievous when it is transformed into divine praise. Let us therefore endure being tested for a little while in this life, so that afterward we may receive an eternal reward in exchange for temporal temptation.

### IV

Let us also patiently and gently [Al. lightly] endure the insults and disparagements of people, so that we may be worthy of the Lord’s praises [Col. 0283B]. For if we seek human praise, we lose divine praise. Whoever is praised by people is blamed by Christ, as it is written:

> Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation. Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh and rejoice now, for you will mourn and weep. Woe when all people bless you (Luke VI, 24 ff.).

See, then, how grievous and troublesome human praise is, since the Lord threatens it in this way. People, animal and earthly, love only what is temporal and earthly; and whatever they love, they seem to praise. Of them it is written:

> Every animal loves its own kind;

and thus every person, according to his kind, praises wealth, banquets, riches, and those who take pride in costly and luxurious clothing—all of which the holy Law forbids and condemns [Col. 0283C].

### V

But those who, compelled by love and fear of the Lord, cast all these things aside and present themselves as holy according to the order of the Law, the wretched and miserable—blinded by the excess of their own evils—mock and deride. It is not enough for them that they are unwilling to mourn their own sins; they also mock and ridicule those who appear to mourn, whom they ought to imitate.

But the time will come when their laughter will be turned into mourning—those whose laughter now consists in our lamentation—and when they will grieve that they had been rich, those who now shamelessly insult Christ’s poor. Scripture speaks of them:

> Then the righteous will stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors. Seeing this, they will be shaken by terrible fear [Col. 0283D] and, at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation, will say within themselves, repenting and groaning from anguish of spirit: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made the object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. How, then, are they now counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints?” (Wis. V, 1 ff.)

Therefore we did not stray from the way of truth, nor did the light of righteousness shine for us, nor did the sun rise for us. We grew weary in the way of wickedness and destruction and traveled through difficult wastelands while we did not know the way of the Lord. What did our pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All these things passed away like a shadow.

### VI

If only the proud and rich would grieve over these things now, and those who mock others would, while there is still time, weep over themselves as well! Then they would not have to groan at the time when no groaning or weeping will accomplish anything. The blessed apostle James is seen to indicate that time when he urges and admonishes the rich to mourn in the present, saying:

> Come now, you rich: weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths, your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire. You have feasted and nourished your hearts in luxury on the day of slaughter (James V, 1 ff.).

For he knew that whoever wept in the present time would not weep in the future. The Lord himself also says this [Col. 0284B]:

> Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted (Matt. I, 5).

“Those who mourn,” he says, “in this time will afterward be comforted by Christ.” But to those who laugh it is said:

> Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn.

### VII

But let no one think that the Lord threatens all who laugh indiscriminately, since Scripture says elsewhere:

> But the wise man will laugh silently (Eccl. I, 29).

There is, therefore, laughter without guilt, and there is laughter in guilt. The laughter of the wise contains no crime. But that laughter is unworthy which mocks the saints and those who present themselves to God. I think this is what is meant by:

> Whoever mocks the poor provokes to anger the one who made him.

But who is this poor person, whose mockery provokes the Lord to anger [Col. 0284C], except the one who despised human and earthly riches so that, as a poor man, he might please him whom, as a rich man, he could scarcely have pleased?

The Lord rightly becomes angry with those who do not fear mocking him because he became poor for their sake. The scribes and Pharisees mocked Christ because he had despised riches, as it is written:

> When the scribes and Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard these things, they mocked him.

We too have our scribes, and we also have our Pharisees, who now mock Christ’s disciples for despising riches, just as those others mocked the Lord and Master.

### VIII

But we must say to them what was said to them at that time:

> You are those who justify yourselves before people. For what is exalted among people is an abomination before God (Luke XVI, 15).

We ought not, therefore, to be frightened by the laughter or mockery of certain people [Col. 0284D], since we know that the Lord himself was mocked by such people. Rather, we should exult and rejoice if we endure all those things which our Lord first endured, since we shall also receive a reward for the very mockery.

For nothing is inflicted upon us for Christ’s name without a reward. See, then, how blessed and happy are those for whom even the laughter of fools contributes to salvation. For the Lord so loves those who love him and so honors those who fear him that he does not allow them to be mocked without recompense; for their mockery he grants vengeance in return.

### IX

Therefore, wise and holy soul, take care that you are not frightened by the tales of foolish and unbelieving people, so that you may fail to do what belongs to the Law. The tales and laughter of people will not be able to free us from the fires of Gehenna [Col. 0285A], but the fear of Christ and righteousness will.

I do not want you to be confused in this respect either if, for Christ’s name or work, perishable and vain people disparage you—people whose happiness itself brings them destruction. Rather, rejoice and be glad, knowing that a reward has been stored up for you even for this disparagement.

For it is sufficiently unjust and impious if you do not allow yourself to be disparaged for the sake of his name, when he endured so much for your sake. How grievous it is not to endure for the Lord everything that may come in this life—losses, disparagements, suspicions, slanders, or anything else—when he, although he was God and the Son of God, endured human insults and injuries for your salvation!

He is very far removed from him who is not even willing to endure slanders. For how can we say that we love him if we are prepared to endure nothing for him [Col. 0285B]?

### X

But if true love for him is in us, we consider whatever is inflicted for his name, however grievous, to be insignificant, and we say: “These things that we suffer are small; he endured greater things for our life. Nothing worthy is inflicted upon us for his name.”

If we remember his own saying, we shall understand this. For he says:

> A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord (Luke VI, 40).

If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his household members!

Therefore, if we are Christ’s disciples and members of his household, we ought to embrace and willingly endure insults and slanders, and bear with an even spirit everything which our teacher and Lord endured for us.

### XI

But whoever does not wish to endure these things should not claim to be his disciple, servant, son, or member of his household. He—the innocent, undefiled, untouched one, in whom no stain of sin could be found—of whom the Prophet had foretold:

> He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Isa. LIII, 10; I Pet. II, 22),

was brought before the judgment seat by the wicked as the most atrocious criminal, on behalf of us sacrilegious sinners committed to eternal punishment; he was beaten with scourges and mocked with spitting. And we are ashamed to be put to shame on his account, although he endured so much for us!

He was not ashamed, for our salvation, to offer his back to blows, his face to spitting, and his cheeks to slaps. Are we ashamed, for his sake, even to hear a light insult? Rather, let us rejoice and be glad if, for his great sufferings and for our salvation, we endure even small things [Col. 0285D].

### XII

What hope, moreover, is there for us if we are ashamed to hear blasphemy or endure anything for the sake of him who descended from heaven to earth for us and humbled himself in order to exalt us?

Although he was immortal, he consented to die so that he might free us from the snare of eternal death. He was crowned with thorns so that we, who had formerly stood thorny and fruitless, might produce the fruit of a good tree. He was given gall and vinegar to drink so that in us there might no longer be either the bitterness of gall or the harshness of vinegar. He became the Son of Man so that he might make us children of God.

See, then, whether we ought to be ashamed to endure anything for his sake. Truly that soul is blessed and worthy to be compared with the angels [Col. 0286A] which is willing to endure, for Christ’s name and work, as much as he endured for us.

### XIII

Besides, there is great danger to righteousness in being ashamed to live according to the example of him who was not ashamed to endure our unrighteousness. Moreover, if we weigh calmly the very thing by which someone seems unjustly to disparage us, we are proved to be praised rather than accused.

For what else do they do when they speak truthfully about the saints except mention what we do: that we fast, abstain, and live soberly; that we no longer delight in pleasures and banquets; that we despise riches and do not glory in costly clothing; that we are not at all held captive by desire for gold; that we do not acquire silver; and that we despise everything which human vanity seems to embrace?

There is no room here for shame, no entrance for embarrassment [Col. 0286B]. Rather, those ought to blush and be confounded who desire the things that displease the saints.

### XIV

Let drunkards, gluttons, unjust people, robbers, adulterers, and all who glory in their own evils blush—them whom the fire of Gehenna awaits and for whom eternal punishments are prepared.

But those who do the Lord’s will ought not to be ashamed, since there are no works of shame in them. How unworthy and perverse it is that the righteous should be ashamed of good things while sinners glory in evil!

Let the soul devoted to God therefore beware lest the laughter of foolish people or the most empty speech of stupid men confound it and draw it back from its purpose, in which it ought to progress toward what is better with each passing day.

Let it beware lest anyone withdraw from the fear of Christ or tear himself away from his love, for whose sake he has despised all the glory and pomp of the world, for whom he has compared nothing worthy of repentance, whom sons prefer to parents, fathers to children, and the continent to marriage [Col. 0286C].

### XV

May the love of Christ grow daily in us; may faith grow, because a great reward awaits us for the love of God—provided only that a mind once devoted to his worship and work does not withdraw from it, lest it be told:

> I have this against you: that you have abandoned your first love (Rev. II, 4).

Hence it is certain that we ought to please not people but Christ, and that we ought to seek not human praise but divine praise.

What does it profit us if those people praise us for whom it is sinful to please? And what harm is it if those people blame us whose blame does no more good than their praise does harm?

Let us listen rather to what that chosen vessel, the teacher of the nations, says, and let us be urged by his example not to desire to please people:

> If I wanted to please people, I would not be Christ’s servant (Gal. I, 10).

Therefore there is no doubt that those cannot serve Christ who desire to please people rather than Christ. For the present, then, let us be content to displease people, provided that we please Christ.

Nor let us delight in the praises of those who praise no one except people like themselves. Rather, let the prophets and apostles praise us; let Christ praise us in his Gospel. Then we shall truly be happy if we have deserved to be praised by such people. For we shall be praised by the voice of all of them if we preserve whatever the Lord appears to have commanded through the apostles and prophets [Col. 0286D].

### XVI

Therefore, while everyone disparages and all censure us, let us be sober, holy, humble, and chaste, and let us always pray to God with faithful heart, so that he himself may always be in our mind and his Law always in our heart, so that we may speak with the prophetic voice:

> In return for their love of me, they disparaged me, but I prayed for them (Ps. CVIII, 4).

And elsewhere:

> I humbled my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me. I made sackcloth my clothing, and I became a byword to them (Ps. XXXIV, 13).

And again:

> My knees became weak from fasting, and my flesh grew weak for lack of oil. I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads. Help me, Lord my God (Ps. CVIII, 24 ff.).

You see, then, that all the prophets and saints have always endured the mockery of people for this reason: because they wished to serve God faithfully. The Apostle says this too:

> The saying is trustworthy. For this reason we labor and are reviled, because we hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all, especially of believers.

### XVII

Why say more? Let us, as we have often said already, complete the course which we began in the fear of God. Let us be an example to others in the love of God, taking care that no one can criticize anything frivolous or vain in us, but rather everything grave and modest, since the life of a Christian is placed before all as in a mirror.

Even if such a person stumbles in some small matter, he is immediately said to have fallen, and more is said about him than is seen. Let us therefore be wise, serious, and tranquil. Let our tongue never speak vanity, never speak of human works, but meditate without interruption on the Law of our God [Col. 0287C].

Then, if someone who is an enemy of his own salvation should arise and mock, slander, and ridicule us, let us not only refrain from fearing these things but rather rejoice.

### XVIII

And in this respect let us console ourselves to some extent, if we deserve to live more hated by the world than by Christ. Let us also beware of walking indecently and restlessly, as the holy Apostle warns when he says:

> I ask you to withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us (II Thess. III, 6).

When all these things have been guarded by us entirely through our own virtue, whoever thinks that we ought to be disparaged should remind us of the prophetic saying by which the Lord encourages those afflicted for the sake of his name:

> And you, son of man, do not fear them, nor be afraid before them, because they will rage and gather against you. You dwell among thorns and in the midst of scorpions; do not fear their words and do not be afraid before them.

And elsewhere he says:

> Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart is my Law. Do not fear the reproaches of people, and do not dread their blasphemies, for like a garment they will fail for a time, and like wool the moth will consume them. But my righteousness remains forever, and my salvation throughout all ages.

Above all, this must be observed: we must not wish [Al. prefer] to preserve the praise of another rather than Christ’s, so that we too may be able to say with the Prophet:

> With you is my praise in the great assembly (Ps. XXI, 26).

And again:

> I have become like a portent to many, and you are my strong helper.

And again:

> They will curse, but you will bless. Those who rise up against me will be confounded, but your servant will rejoice in you (Ps. CVIII, 28) [Col. 0288A].

### XIX

I have briefly pursued these matters for the consolation, in the fear of God, of devoted minds, insofar as the weakness of my talent allowed. Now it remains for the devoted mind to do something more than our smallness is sufficient to advise.

Greet all who love our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the almighty Father, be praise, power, and glory with the Holy Spirit, now and always and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

No one can fail to perceive that this Letter is later in date than Sulpicius Severus, whom the author names honorifically [Col. 0288B] and whose Life of Saint Martin he praises. As regards its style and subject matter, it comes so close to the character of the little work entitled *On the Singularity of Clerics*, which is found elsewhere and especially among the spurious writings of Saint Cyprian, that it may easily be seen to have been modeled upon that work as a pattern. Compare them with one another; and if that work is rightly assigned to around the thousandth year, when that dispute was especially fierce in the West, you will understand what judgment ought to be formed concerning this Letter.

## LETTER XLII. TO OCEANUS: ON THE LIFE OF CLERICS

Sophronius Eusebius Jerome sends greetings to his Oceanus.

### I

You asked me to explain briefly how clerics ought to live in this mortal life [Col. 0288C]. For this reason many rivals await me with curses, because I do not keep silent about the truth. Nevertheless, my dearest, let us take our beginning from the Apostle, who says:

> The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance. If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work. For a bishop must be irreproachable, sober, chaste, kind, well-ordered, hospitable, able to teach, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not given to wine, one who governs his own household well (I Tim. III, 1 ff.).

And so forth. He comprehends everything that must be avoided when he says “irreproachable.”

### II

How, then, will one person rebuke another when he who has received authority to teach is himself blameworthy? For the life of a bishop ought to be a model for clerics. From the bishop, the other ranks of clerics learn how they ought to live in this mortal life.

Priests ought to present themselves as examples for imitation, so that others, especially younger men who have attained the lower ranks, may rise through the life and example of priests.

I think you must take particular care over this: the first temptations of clerics are frequent visits from women. This sex makes clerics blameworthy. What have you truly to do with women, when you converse with the Lord at the altar?

Everyone will severely tear you apart in public—the country people, ploughmen, and vine-growers in the fields—if, contrary to the disposition of the faith, you insist on living with women. And since, as I think, you desire to be found irreproachable, use a good testimony.

Were there women in the company of the apostles? Do not allow virgins to live with you, even those who are related to you. Love them, arrange for them externally, and visit them frequently together with the service of clerics, lest, while you enter secretly and alone, you stain your reputation [Col. 0289A].

### III

This too must be added: if you were taking a wife, the Law would not prohibit you from living with a fellow servant. For men are promoted to the governance of the priesthood with the consent of their wives, especially since the Apostle’s Letter contains this command:

> A husband of one wife is to be chosen for the honor of the clerical office.

But you are not bound by such salutary commands in the same way. Married men are admonished differently from virgins when they undertake the burden of ecclesiastical ministry.

The association of women with clerics is commanded to be maintained by no means whatsoever. Woman is the door of the devil, the path of iniquity, the sting of the scorpion, and a harmful species: when she approaches, she provokes and kindles fire. With her blazing fire, a woman strikes the conscience of the man who lives with her and burns up the foundations of mountains.

I judge that, if women live with men, the devil’s snare will not be lacking; from such a snare he has hunted sin from the beginning. Lust subdues iron minds.

> If someone binds fire in his bosom, will his garments not burn? Or if someone walks over burning coals, will he not burn his feet?

### IV

Believe me: a person cannot dwell with the Lord with his whole heart if he is joined to the visits of women. But you say:

> Whoever walks simply walks confidently (Prov. X, 9).

Good and clever. But you ought to have a good testimony from those outside (I Tim. III, 7) [Col. 0289C]. Even if you walk rightly before God, you must nevertheless provide what is good before people, because the children of darkness are more cunning than the children of light.

When you do not cut off this sex from yourself, you give your accusers an opportunity; you have handed yourself over to the bites of slanderers if you do not abandon the companionship of *agapetae*.

“You are kind”—I rejoice. “You are chaste”—that is false. If someone notices a cleric living with women, he does not believe him to be chaste. If you seek chastity, why do you live with women?

Love in your mind the woman whom you see conducting herself well; do not frequent her with bodily attention. It is not soft clothing that makes a cleric or a priest, but the chaste intention of the mind. For this preserves in you the devotion proper to your office. A reputation for good work preserves this glorious honor.

Priests, and likewise the other ranks of clerics, ought, as was said above, to be separated from women [Col. 0289D].

### V

If, then, you think that on account of kinship you cannot dismiss them by any means, remember Tamar, who was corrupted by her brother Amnon. This is precisely what I am pursuing, dearest: wherever there is life under one tent, the pleasure of the flesh is not easily removed. When two people are together, one desires what the other desires; even if he cannot speak of it, he is nevertheless tempted.

The removal of the man therefore establishes the defenses of chastity, builds camps in better places, and safeguards the honor of modesty [Col. 0290A].

The Virgin Mary, Mother of the Lord, too could have remained with the company of the apostles, if it had been permitted. After the temptation of persecution, Thecla is forbidden by Paul to proceed with him to Antioch [Note: [Col. 0289D] Formerly, with an incongruous meaning, the text read “after the temptation of the suffering at Antioch, she is forbidden by Paul,” and so forth. We have restored “to Antioch,” correcting the punctuation as well.]. No soldier goes to war with his wife.

### VI

I do not begrudge your affection; let enduring love for chaste virgins be yours. Then you will place merit in what is good and improve your reputation if you establish communities of girls.

I think it fitting that you should come every second week to visit and bless the community. But do not come alone, lest gossipers stain you by tearing you apart with their tongues. Neighbors desire to scrutinize another person’s life, not their own.

Therefore receive the instructions of my words worthily, and read sweetly the admonitions of humility which, with fraternal affection and with the pen commanding [Note: [Col. 0290D] I would rather have this read “with the pen hastening.” The true Jerome says somewhere “with a temperate pen.” The author here has borrowed much from what follows.], we have expressed [Col. 0290B].

### VII

Now, so that the priest of the divine altar may not be blameworthy, I shall explain, insofar as the Lord grants, a few matters from the remaining testimonies of the Apostle. The preceding reasons that have been stated should suffice.

But lest anyone less perceptive think that the Apostle spoke only about bishops, I am pleased to recall what was commanded to Timothy concerning deacons and what was commanded to Titus concerning presbyters.

Yet the preceding statement must not be passed over without explanation:

> The husband of one wife (I Tim. III, 2).

Both the new and the old commandment judged that a priest should be chosen in this way, because many bishops have admitted bigamists to the ministry and assert: “She was a concubine; this one is a wife,” as though the same sordid relations were not practiced with the one who is called a wife as with the other [Col. 0290C].

Or, because he did not draw up marriage documents, was the desire for another man’s wife absent? By no means is it fitting for bigamists, or for those bound in the chains of concubines, to undertake the ministry of the priesthood.

It is written and prescribed in Leviticus what sort of priests ought to be chosen, as you have it:

> And the Lord said to Moses: “Let a priest take a virgin as wife from among the offspring of his fathers. But he shall not take a widow, an abandoned woman, or one who has been left by her husband.”

I have heard well that, when the Lord instructed Moses, not even a bigamous wife should be suitable for a priest, lest she pollute the honor of the priesthood. Just as he commands the husband of one wife, so he commands the wife of one husband.

If, then, a cleric is monogamous but his wife is bigamous, do not admit him to the ministry. He has taken a bigamous woman as wife. The same Apostle gave these instructions to Titus concerning the ordination of clerics [Col. 0290D].

### VIII

And since the book now awaits its conclusion, let us return to the point from which we digressed. Even if two or three handmaids of God are living together, it is not fitting for the priest to enter to visit them alone.

If anyone does not observe these instructions, he is the enemy of his own soul. But if, after our admonitions, some cleric seeks to love *agapetae* more than Christ, he should be summoned according to synodal rule, and the commands of the Fathers defined at Nicaea should be read to him.

But if he flees the assembly and abandons what has been stated [Col. 0291A], we have achieved the greatest gain. Otherwise, if he neglects it, such a person must be anathematized by the Church of Christ.

Women who live with men produce thorns, and they strike the hidden places of minds with a sharp blade. Alas for the sacrilege! It is painful to say, but it ought not to be passed over: these women vowed to marry Christ, not clerics.

### IX

So where does this new kind of wives without marriage come from? And what does it concern us that we do not cease to defame this practice? Let us stop the sword.

It is a good honor in the Church if women remain far from the company of men. Solitude makes a monk or cleric, not public association.

What delights you about virginal conversation? Why do you frequently visit consecrated women contrary to the faith, whether in church or in public itself?

When they see those whom they love, they extend tender words of greeting with smiling eyes. Then, after they have greeted them, if they see the men of God pass by them more quickly, they judge them to be contemptuous of them and become angry.

Then arrangements are made to satisfy the deserted woman; after the satisfaction, a meal is prepared, as though a new joy were being arranged. Amid the cups they utter reproachful words of contempt; he, however, pretends to lament, as though introducing a kind of sin.

Read what sort of person a solitary ought to be, as Jeremiah described him. He says:

> He will sit alone and remain silent, because he has raised himself above himself. It is good for a man to have borne the yoke from his youth (Lam. III, 27–28).

And because Jesus, having left the apostles, went alone to pray; and the angel likewise found Mary alone in her inner chamber, not speaking with an *agapeta*. She trembled at a man’s entrance.

You who are a furnace of wickedness, what do you desire from a man by being greeted so frequently [Col. 0291C]?

### X

Do you not know that you destroy two reputations at once: your own and that of the cleric, whose life ought to adorn the Church of Christ?

It is an undisciplined custom and a fictitious calamity of delicate conversation. But if you wish to practice hospitality, you have your sisters: they ought to be invited to your house and welcomed there, not clerics.

What I have said will contribute to your edification, holy virgin. In the *Life of the Most Blessed Martin* we read that Sulpicius recalled how Saint Martin, while passing by, wished to visit a certain virgin distinguished in conduct and chastity. She refused, however, and sent him a gift of hospitality. Looking out through the window, she said to the holy man:

> “Pray there, holy Father, because I have never been visited by a man.”

Saint Martin gave thanks to God that she had guarded her chaste intention, being imbued with such customs; and, blessing her, he went away rejoicing [Col. 0291D].

### XI

Let what has been said about women suffice up to this point. Since the matter of virgins has been completed, let us pass on to the rest.

The Apostle commands that a cleric to be ordained should be hospitable. By this command the patriarch Abraham and Lot received angels, because they loved hospitality among the other virtues. In the same way Onesiphorus received Paul, the fountain of teaching.

Let these examples be yours to imitate, and do not allow a resident or traveler to pass by without eating bread with you.

The Apostle next says, “Not a striker.” For he does not describe a boxer [Col. 0292A], but one who does not strike the consciences of individuals. Rather, he must be gentle, and so forth.

He must govern his own household well. It will be exceedingly dreadful if the household of a cleric is disparaged. The priest’s reputation among the people will be harmed when the public speaks badly of his relatives.

Above all these things the Apostle commanded clerics to lay the foundations of a good reputation, so that the testimony of good works might be confirmed by a chaste affection.

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER
Many are the so-called *homobiotic* letters of this kind, which falsely claim Jerome and Damasus equally as their authors. We have included them here, adding one or two that were previously unpublished, since nearly all seem to bear the same author’s stamp. I would be wasting time were I to preface each one with the individual arguments by which its forgery is exposed. This one is sufficiently and abundantly refuted by that single passage concerning Chrysostom which, if I may pass over it, makes it certain that, had Jerome ever praised Chrysostom, he had been elected presbyter at least two years after Damasus’s death, and had only then begun to explain the Scriptures in commentaries or homilies addressed to the people. Moreover, is that passage really Chrysostom’s, in his work on Matthew? Certainly nothing similar can be found in his genuine commentaries. Yet the impostor was not content to shelter his rubbish beneath the shadow of Jerome’s name: he fabricated the very response, or decree, of Damasus that Gratian presents in *Decretum* 10.1.15:

> “We entirely forbid this custom, which appears to be growing against the holy Catholic Church: that the offerings made within the holy Church should ever, in any manner, be retained under the authority of laymen,” etc.

Compare the pronouncement of each, and you will discover that they came from one and the same craftsman.

## LETTER XLIII. TO DAMASUS  
### On the Offerings of the Altar

[Note: Although it has commonly been attributed to Jerome, it is nevertheless worth noting that his name appears neither in the printed editions nor in the manuscripts we have seen, whereas it is customarily supplied in other works of this kind. We presented another pseudo-Jerome letter to Damasus, concerning the Canons of the Gospels, in the preceding volume, p. 665.]

### I

Let your holy authority know, venerable pope, that concerning the question which you proposed to your client and about which you sent a suitable response by letter—that is, concerning the loaves offered on the altar by the faithful, and who ought by right to use them—I have taken care to write back to you briefly, insofar as I have been able to investigate the matter with the foremost teachers of the Church. The reliable witnesses whom I have summoned to corroborate this matter are Gregory of Nazianzus, the admirable teacher; Cyril; Athanasius; Theophilus; Anatolius; John Chrysostom; Eustathius [or Eustachius]; Eusebius the chronicler; and our own Hilary. All of them, with one voice and in complete agreement, like true instruments of the Holy Spirit, judge that those who have transferred the loaves of the offerings for lay use ought to be struck by the sword of anathema, since they belong entirely to the priests—unless, perhaps, laymen receive them from the priest’s hand for the sake of religion and blessing.

Our fathers established this not only concerning the loaves in the Church, but concerning everything offered upon the altar, saying and teaching that it is a great sacrilege, and that wherever it occurs it is done with wholly diabolical presumption. It is also utterly intolerable to the holy Church that such a practice should remain without the punishment prescribed by the holy Canons.

### II

Accordingly Chrysostom, in his commentaries on Matthew, where the disciples were plucking ears of grain with their hands on the Sabbath and the Pharisees were reproving them, says:

> “If it was not permitted David and his men, still living under the shadow of the Law, to eat the loaves of the Presence when, driven by hunger, he asked Abimelech for loaves, how now, when the Gospel shines forth, should laymen be persuaded to seize for their own use the offering of loaves offered to God?”

The Apostle likewise says: “Those who serve the altar partake of the altar.” Therefore, since priests customarily pray for all whose alms and offerings they receive, with what face do laymen presume either to eat or to give to others the offerings that Christians present for their sins, when they themselves ought not to pray for the people? For this reason, glorious pope, it is necessary to place those presumptuous persons under perpetual excommunication, so that the others may be afraid and such things may no longer be done in the Church.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTERS

Godefridus Henschenius is said to have been the first to print these letters. They are also found, in most manuscripts—and not in manuscripts of contemptible antiquity or quality—prefixed in the place of a preface to the book *On the Men of the Roman Pontiffs* under the name of Damasus. He certainly regarded them as genuine writings of Damasus and Jerome and argued with all his strength to convince others of this. Now, however, everyone perceives that these near-rubbish and trifles differ less from base counterfeit coins than from the style and learning of those most learned Fathers. Schelestratius deliberately charges and refutes them in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, Dissertation III, chapter 3; Papebrochius does so in the *Propylaeum*; and others do so in various places. Oudinus attributes them to Damasus of Porto, an author near the end of the ninth century, about whom more will soon have to be said. We have included them here first, so that nothing bearing the name of Jerome might be absent.

## LETTER XLIV. Jerome to the Most Blessed Pope Damasus

Our humility begs the glory of Your Holiness that, in accordance with the authority of the apostolic see, which we know to be governed through Your Holiness, you may deign to recount briefly and in order for us the acts and deeds accomplished from the principate of the blessed apostle Peter up to your own times—namely, what was done in your see—so that our humility, learning and recognizing the matter, may know which of the bishops of the aforesaid see deserved to be crowned with martyrdom, or whether anyone is known to have transgressed the canons of the apostles. Pray for us, most blessed pope.

[Note: Lambecius reads from the manuscripts of the Caesarean library: “so that, according to the order of the apostolic see, which we have learned is governed by Your Holiness”; then *pontificatu* instead of *principatu*; and “that you may deign to relate the deeds accomplished in your see down to our times.” Finally, he reads: “that those who deserved among the bishops may recognize,” etc., or “those who, on the contrary,” etc.]

## LETTER XLV. Damasus, Bishop of the City of Rome, to the Presbyter Jerome

(This is found among the apocrypha in the appendix attached to the works of Pope Damasus, volume XIII of our *Patrology*, column 441.)

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

This letter itself deprives itself of all credibility. I do not adequately understand what its author means; such is the ignorance displayed in his pronouncement. Nevertheless, I see where it is aiming, and I have almost no doubt that this letter, attributed to Damasus, as well as the following one attributed to Jerome, had the same author: namely, that notorious craftsman of falsehoods, Isidore Mercator—or, more truly, the Sinner. Among the decrees falsely attributed to the holy Pontiff, the following appears eighth in Sarazani’s collection, plainly fabricated from these letters:

> “Then Saint Damasus also established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the Churches. He further commands that at the end of every psalm there be added: ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, and is now, and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.’”

These decrees, as well as the Acts from which they were excerpted, although Baronius accepts them under the year 384, are wholly false; Father Coustantius demonstrated this above all others. We too shall add certain observations when examining the following letter. Erasmus reproaches this forger—not without learning—for failing at least to avoid calling someone a priest who was not a bishop, since in that age priests were not called anything but bishops. “Then,” he says, “I marvel that he did not, by the same operation, call him a cardinal, since that word was still unheard of in those times.”

## LETTER XLVI. DAMASUS TO JEROME

(You may regard this letter as belonging wherever we indicated that the preceding one should be considered.)

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Damasus was not the author of the doxology that was to be added at the end of every psalm during singing; still less was Jerome its promoter. This alone enables you to understand clearly how splendidly the author of this letter lies. The latter point is proved by Cassian, *Institutes of the Coenobites* II.8, where he says:

> “We have nowhere throughout the entire East heard that, when one person is singing, all those standing by join in the final phrase of the psalm with a shout, ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’”

Jerome, however, was living there. The former point is proved by Canon 5 of the Council of Vasio, held in 529, from which it is clear that in Gaul it had not yet become customary to append to the verses of the doxology the words “As it was in the beginning,” etc. Certainly, if Damasus had instituted this nearly 150 years earlier, it is unreasonable to believe that that Church had neglected it for so long.

There is no time to pursue the remaining points; scarcely a single sentence fails to betray the author of the lie. Erasmus says:

> “Who would not immediately detect the impostor from the salutation itself, unless he prudently closed his eyes? ‘Jerome, suppliant to Damasus of the apostolic see of the city of Rome.’ I ask: when did Jerome ever offer such a greeting? Then how elegantly he enters upon the matter! ‘I have read the letters of your Apostolate requesting…’ and the rest that follows is so foolish and so cold that, by comparison with it, Jovinian himself—whose childishness Jerome attacks with so many witticisms—might appear to be a Cicero.”

Nevertheless, so that we may conceal nothing, we found this letter in a very ancient manuscript, marked in the Vatican, formerly the Palatine Library, as number 187, and compared it most carefully with Sarazani’s edition. In that manuscript there follows immediately, without any sign of division, the long fragment concerning the order and authors of the psalms, which we too append, since it may be regarded as part of the letter, whatever its character, especially because it lacks the proper conclusion that has been published up to now.

## LETTER XLVII. JEROME TO DAMASUS

To the most blessed Pope Damasus of the Apostolic See of the city of Rome, Jerome, suppliant.

### I

I have read the letters of Your Apostolate requesting that, because of the weariness of the Romans, I should hasten to interpret the Psalmist while singing according to the simplicity of the Septuagint translators, so that wherever obscurity hinders, the sense may be rendered more openly and in Latin.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript, together with Sarazani’s edition, reads “your”; then it has “the Psalmist who is to be sung,” whereas the other reading is “those who are singing”; and for “let me interpret” it reads “let him hasten to interpret.”]

Your client therefore begs that you command this voice of the psalm-singers to be sung day and night in the Roman see, and that at the end of every psalm, whether at the morning or evening hours, the order of Your Apostolate should require the addition:

> “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, and is now, and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”

[Note: The same edition inserts “of praise,” and shortly afterward reads: “let it be declared in your mouth with equal fellowship.”]

Command that this hymn be joined to every psalm, so that the faith of the 318 bishops of the Council of Nicaea may also be proclaimed through the united voice of your mouth. Whenever God and man are sung—or spoken—in an honorable voice, let “Alleluia” always be attached to all the psalms, so that at night they may commonly respond in every place.

[Note: The same edition omits “psalms,” then reads “during the nighttime”; together with the Palatine manuscript it reads “from the holy Resurrection until,” etc. Finally, instead of *quinquagesima*, which the cited edition omits altogether, other books read *quinquaginta*—that is, “let it be completed over an interval of fifty days.” Long ago, as Coustantius also noted, someone complained to Pope Gregory I that he preferred Greek customs to Roman ones, specifically because he had caused the *Alleluia* to be said at Masses outside the season of Pentecost. In a letter sent to John, bishop of Syracuse, Gregory replied: “It is reported that the saying of ‘Alleluia’ here—not in the Royal and Colbertine manuscripts—was brought from the Church of Jerusalem through the tradition of the blessed Jerome in the time of the blessed Damasus. And therefore we have rather curtailed that custom in this matter.” The greatest men, Cardinal Bona in *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 16; Tillemont, volume VIII, p. 420; Coustantius in the cited place; and others, debate the meaning of these words, which I believe contain an error, arguing on both sides. As for what concerns us, those who maintain that Isidore Mercator, finding an opportunity in Gregory’s words, fabricated this letter, certainly speak more nearly to the truth. Nevertheless, since Gregory repeats a tradition—or even a decree—from the time of Damasus, I should like some account also to be taken of this point. What Coustantius gathers and repeats from the Benedictine Rule, well known and familiar to Gregory, does not, in my judgment, sufficiently satisfy me. The reading we noted, *quinquagesima* rather than *quinquaginta*, and indeed the different sense that arises from it, also seems somewhat opposed to the proposed explanation.]

In the Church, however, let it be ended after the Resurrection and up to holy Pentecost; but during the interval of fifty days, on account of the novelty of holy Easter, let this word of praise be sung in the *Aleph*, which in Greek is called a *prologue* and in Latin a *preface*.

[Note: Sarazani’s edition adds: “so that this voice…” and, after the word *Aleph*, “which is *Alleluia*, praise to you alone, which in Greek…” But I have not been fortunate enough to understand adequately what these words mean. What follows from this point was copied from the Palatine manuscript, which continues the text, as we noted above.]

### II

When David, the son of Jesse, was in his kingdom, he chose four men to compose psalms: Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun. Thus they recited eighty-eight psalms and two hundred *diapsalmata*; and Abiram struck the lyre with King David.

After forty years the Ark of the Lord was brought back from Azotus to Jerusalem, having remained in the house of Aminadab. David placed it upon a new wagon and brought it to Jerusalem. Seventy thousand men were chosen together from every tribe of the children of Israel. From the tribe of Levi 287,000 men were chosen. From among them these were appointed as the first leaders of the singing: Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun. To each of them were assigned seventy-two men acclaiming the praises of songs to our Lord. One carried a cymbal, another a *cinyras*, another a lyre, and another a curved trumpet, rejoicing.

### III

In the midst stood King David himself, holding the psalter. The Ark of the Lord went before the choirs, together with white calves for the sacrifices. The whole people followed behind the Ark.

There are therefore 150 psalms of David, the son of Jesse, king of Israel. According to the wording and titles of the Scriptures, they have been arranged as follows. Nine were composed by David himself; thirty-two have no superscription; seventy-two are “of David the king”; eleven are of Asaph; twelve of Jeduthun; four of the sons of Korah; one of Zechariah; one of Haggai; two of Moses; and two of Solomon the king.

All the psalms of David, the son of Jesse, king of Israel, thus end in the number 150. The arrangement itself contains seventy-five *diapsalmata*, twenty-one *Alleluia* psalms, and fifteen Songs of Ascents. The remaining psalms are recited according to their own titles, as they are contained in the text of Scripture.

The first psalm is assigned to no one, and belongs, according to its history, to everyone. Who else, then, is understood to be its fullest subject except the Firstborn of God? Therefore no superscription was needed: by mentioning Christ, the first psalm serves to explain the true person of Christ. Yet all the psalms are understood almost entirely not according to their own history, but according to prophecy. For all the psalms that are written—David himself belongs to the mysteries of Christ, because David himself is called Christ—belong to Christ.

Now we have explained the origin of all the psalms, and we explain how the Hebrews divide the Book of Psalms into five books. The first book extends from Psalm 1 through Psalm 40. The second extends from Psalm 41 through Psalm 71. The third extends from Psalm 72 through Psalm 88. The fourth extends from Psalm 89 through Psalm 105. The fifth extends from Psalm 106 through Psalm 150.

May Your Beatitude pray for us, most blessed pope.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Everyone perceives that this letter, the one that follows it, and indeed the narrative appended to them concerning the Nativity of Saint Mary, belong to one and the same architect of fables. To avoid delaying you by reciting the arguments, consult those who charge and refute them as false: Baronius, under the year 388, no. 101; John Molanus, *On Pictures*, chapter 21; and, among more recent writers, Fabricius in volume I of the *Apocryphal Code*. We shall also make use of his recension and notes, so that we may not seem to be repeating work already done.

## LETTER XLVIII. CHROMATIUS AND HELIODORUS, BISHOPS, TO JEROME

(This letter is found among the writings attributed to Chromatius, volume XX of this Library, column 369.)

## LETTER XLIX. JEROME TO CHROMATIUS AND HELIODORUS

To the holy and most blessed lords Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, Jerome, the least servant of Christ, sends greetings in the Lord.

### I

A man who digs earth rich in gold does not immediately seize everything that the torn-open trench has brought forth. Before he lifts the glittering weight with a vigorous stroke of the iron, he spends his time turning over and suspending the clods—and especially when he has not yet increased his profits.

A difficult task has been imposed upon me, since Your Beatitude has commanded me to do what even the holy apostle and evangelist Matthew himself did not wish to have written openly. For if this had not been secret, he would certainly have added it to the Gospel that he published. Instead, he made this little book sealed with Hebrew letters; he published it to such an extent that a book written in his own hand, in Hebrew letters, is possessed by very religious men, who in turn received it from their predecessors through the succession of time. They have never handed this very book over to anyone for translation, but have related its contents in different ways.

### II

It happened, however, that this book was published by a disciple of Mani named Seleucus—who also falsely wrote the deeds of the Apostles in a fabricated account—and provided material not for edification but for destruction; it was approved in a synod to which the ears of the Church rightly ought not to have been open.

Let the bite of the barking critics now cease. We have not added this little book to the canonical Scriptures; rather, to expose the deceit of heresy, we are translating the writing of an apostle and evangelist. In this work we obey not so much the pious commands of bishops as we confront impious heretics. It is therefore the love of Christ that we shall satisfy, trusting that they will assist us by their prayers—so that through our obedience they may be able to attain the holy infancy of our Savior.

## LETTER L  
### On the Nativity of Saint Mary

[Note: It is also entitled *The Gospel of the Nativity of Mary*.]

You ask me to write back to you what I think of a certain little book that some people regard as concerning the Nativity of Saint Mary. I therefore want you to know that many false things are found in it. A certain Seleucus, who wrote the sufferings of the Apostles, composed this book. But just as he spoke truthfully about their virtues and the miracles performed through them, while lying about much of their teaching, so here too he fastened together many untrue things from his own heart.

[Note: He seems to claim that he is translating Seleucus’s book from Hebrew; but it is more correct to distinguish the two matters: Seleucus’s book is rejected as filled with impious additions, while the other Hebrew book is approved as containing nothing destructive, though not as canonical or genuinely Matthew’s.]

Therefore, as it is found in Hebrew, I shall endeavor to translate it word for word. It is clear that the holy evangelist Matthew composed this same little book and placed it at the beginning of his Gospel, sealed with Hebrew letters.

[Note: This should be read as referring to the preface, as is added shortly afterward.]

Whether this is true I leave to the author of the preface and to the faith of the reader. For I pronounce these things doubtful and therefore do not affirm them as plainly false. But I say openly what I think no believer will deny: whether these things are true or fabricated by someone, great and holy miracles preceded the sacred Nativity of Saint Mary, and the greatest miracles followed it. Therefore, without jeopardizing their faith, those who believe that God is able to do such things may believe and read them without danger to their souls.

Finally, insofar as I can remember, following the writer’s meaning rather than his words, and now walking along the same path without following the same footprints, nor returning to the same road by every little detour, I shall attempt the style of the narrative. I shall say nothing other than what is either written there or could have been written in sequence.

[Note: Perhaps: “I shall moderate it.”]

### II

Accordingly, the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, descended from the royal stock and family of David, was born in the city of Nazareth and brought up at Jerusalem in the Temple of the Lord. Her father was Joachim; her mother was called Anna.

[Note: The paternal household was from Galilee and the city of Nazareth. Her maternal lineage was from Bethlehem.]

Their life before the Lord was simple and upright; among human beings it was irreproachable and devout. For they divided all their property into three parts. One part they devoted to the Temple and the Temple’s servants; another they distributed to pilgrims and the poor; the third they reserved for the needs of their household and for themselves.

[Note: The word “servants” has a barbarous flavor, as do six hundred other expressions in this work.]

Thus dear to God and devout toward human beings, for approximately twenty years they lived in a chaste marriage at home without producing children.

[Note: This vow shows that “chaste marriage” in the preceding words should not be understood as complete abstinence. Perhaps those who said that this narrative was composed in imitation of the accounts concerning Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, were not mistaken.]

Nevertheless, they vowed that if God should perhaps grant them offspring, they would dedicate the child to the service of the Lord. For this reason they also used to visit the Temple of the Lord every year at the individual festivals.

### III

It happened that the festival of the Dedication approached.

[Note: The Jerusalem Dedication is celebrated around the winter solstice. This festival is mentioned in 1 Maccabees 1 and John 10:22.]

Joachim therefore went up to Jerusalem with some of his kinsmen. At that time Isachar was the high priest there.

[Note: In the pseudo-Jacobite *Protoevangelium*, Reuben occupies the place of the high priest Isachar; but Josephus and reliable writers worthy of faith say not a word (*gry*) concerning either of the two.]

When he saw Joachim among his fellow citizens, together with his offering, he despised him and rejected his gifts, asking why he presumed to stand among those who had children when he himself was childless. He said that gifts could by no means appear acceptable to God from one whom he himself had judged unworthy of offspring, since Scripture says:

> “Cursed is everyone who has not begotten a male in Israel.”

[Note: The Greek words are found in John of Damascus, who calls it a “legal ordinance” (*nomikon prostagma*), *On the Orthodox Faith* IV.25: “Cursed is he who does not raise up seed in Israel.” Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*: “Cursed is the barren woman who has no seed in Israel.” In this pseudo-Gospel “male” is used for “seed,” by a figure of emphasis—Greek: *kat’ exochēn*. Alternatively, the two clauses may need to be joined: “Cursed is every male who has not begotten.” Otherwise, Mary’s parents, who brought forth Mary, would not themselves have begotten a male. Yet you will look in vain for these words in Scripture, although among the blessings one reads in Exodus 23:26 and Deuteronomy 7:11, “There shall be neither barren nor sterile in your land.” Also in the Greek edition of Isaiah 31 at the end—Jerome says to Pammachius, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, that the Hebrews mock these words—one reads: “Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and relatives in Jerusalem.”]

He therefore said that Joachim must first be released from this curse by the begetting of offspring, and only then come before the Lord with offerings.

Struck by this insult and covered with great shame, Joachim withdrew to the shepherds who were with their flocks in the pastures. He did not wish to return home, lest perhaps his fellow tribesmen, who were present together and had heard this from the priest, should mark him with the same expression of reproach.

### IV

After he had been there for some time, one day, when he was alone, an angel of the Lord stood beside him with immense light.

[Note: Angelic apparitions are generally accompanied by light, which is called the “glory of the Lord” in Luke 2:9, and likewise below in chapter IX. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 79.5, reports that an angel appeared to Joachim in the desert and announced Mary’s birth.]

When he was troubled at the sight, the angel who had appeared to him restrained his fear, saying:

“Do not be afraid, Joachim, nor be troubled by my appearance. For I am an angel of the Lord, sent by him to you,

[Note: Compare Acts 10:4: “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.”]

to announce to you that your prayers have been heard and that your alms have risen into his presence. For he has indeed seen your shame and heard the reproach of barrenness wrongly cast upon you. God is the avenger of sin, not of nature. Therefore, when he closes someone’s womb, he does so in order that he may open it again more wonderfully, and so that it may be recognized that what is born is not the work of lust but a divine gift.

Was not Sarah, the first mother of your people, barren until her eightieth year? Yet in the final period of her old age she bore Isaac, to whom the blessing of all nations had been promised.

Rachel too, who was so pleasing to the Lord and so dearly loved by holy Jacob, was barren for a long time; yet she bore Joseph, not only the lord of Egypt but the deliverer of many nations that were destined to perish from famine.

Who among the leaders was stronger than Samson or holier than Samuel? Yet both had barren mothers.

Therefore, if reason does not persuade you through my words,

[Note: That is, through the many examples I have brought forward. Earlier editions wrongly read: “persuade you to believe.”]

believe that delayed conceptions and long-deferred births are usually more wondrous.

Accordingly, your wife Anna will bear you a daughter, and you will call her name Mary. She will be consecrated to the Lord from infancy, as you have vowed, and she will be filled with the Holy Spirit while still in her mother’s womb (Luke 1). She will neither eat nor drink anything unclean. Her way of life will not be among the external crowds of her people, but in the Temple of the Lord, so that no one may even suspect or say anything sinister about her.

As she advances in age, just as she herself will be wondrously born from a barren woman, so, incomparably, as a virgin she will give birth to the Son of the Most High, who is called Jesus. According to the etymology of his name, he will be the Savior of all nations.

And this will be a sign of what I announce to you—Greek: *sēmeion*, “sign,” as in Lactantius II.12. When you reach the Golden Gate in Jerusalem—the eastern gate of the court—you will find your wife Anna there. Now she is anxious about the delay of your return, but then she will rejoice at the sight of you.”

After saying this, the angel departed from him.

### V

Then he appeared to his wife Anna and said:

“Do not be afraid, Anna, nor think that what you see is a phantom. For I am that angel who brought your prayers and alms into the presence of God. Now I have been sent to you to announce that a daughter will be born to you. She will be called Mary and will be blessed above all women.

From her birth she will immediately be full of the grace of the Lord,

[Note: *Kecharitōmenē*, “full of grace,” which Luke also uses at 1:28. The Syrian translator likewise uses the Greek word. Before Luke, the word appears in Sirach 9:8 and 18:17. The interpretation given by Ambrose and certain other ancient writers—“full of grace,” meaning “full of Christ”—does not fit the angel’s intention very well.]

and she will remain in her father’s house for the three years of her weaning.

[Note: Likewise in the *Protoevangelium of James*, chapter VIII. Evodius, in Nicephorus II.3, also says that she was presented in the Temple at the age of three.]

Afterward, dedicated to the service of the Lord, she will not leave the Temple until the years of understanding.

[Note: That is, until the years at which a person begins to understand what evil must be rejected and what good must be chosen—Isaiah 7:15; John 3:11. Writers not only of the later age but also of the best period often use adjectives ending in *-bilis* with an active sense.]

There, serving God with fasts and prayers night and day, she will abstain from everything unclean. She will never know a man. Alone, without precedent, without stain, without corruption, without sexual intercourse, a virgin will bear a son, a handmaid the Lord; and in grace, in name, and in deed she will give birth to the Savior of the world.

Therefore rise and go up to Jerusalem. When you reach the gate called Golden because it is gilded,

[Note: Josephus, *The Jewish War* V.14, testifies that the Eastern Gate was more abundantly adorned with gold and silver than the others, although those too were gilded.]

there, as a sign, you will meet your husband, for whose safety you are anxious.”

When these things have happened, know that what I announce will undoubtedly be fulfilled.”

### VI

Accordingly, in obedience to the angel’s command, each of them proceeded from the place where they were and went up to Jerusalem.

[Note: Into the Temple; compare Luke 18:31.]

When they reached the place designated by the angelic prophecy, they met one another there. Then, rejoicing in their mutual encounter and secure in the certainty of the promised offspring, they gave due thanks to the Lord, who exalts the humble (Luke 1:52).

After worshiping the Lord,

[Note: To the town of Nazareth. It is said that after Mary’s birth, when Anna had lost her husband Joachim, she married two further husbands, Cleophas and Salome. Concerning this, John Gerson, *On the Nativity of the Virgin Mary*, volume III, p. 59, cites the following three verses:

> Anna married three men: Joachim, Cleophas, and Salome;  
> From these husbands Anna bore three Marys:  
> whom Joseph, Alphaeus, and Zebedee married.  
> The first bore Jesus; the second gave James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas;  
> the third gave James and John.

But the silence of the ancients, and the fact that Salome is a woman’s name, not a man’s, as in Mark 15:16, show that this tradition deserves little credence.]

they returned home, certain and joyful, awaiting the divine promise. Anna conceived and bore a daughter, and, in accordance with the angelic command, the parents called her name Mary.

### VII

When the cycle of three years had revolved and the time of weaning had been completed, they brought the little virgin to the Temple of the Lord with offerings. Around the Temple, according to the fifteen psalms,

[Note: Ezekiel 40:6 and following, and Josephus, also mention those fifteen steps. The assertion here that these steps were beside the Temple, corresponding to the same number of psalms—or were steps of ascent around the Temple—is found in the Talmud and confirmed by Kimchi and other Jews. Christian Fathers frequently mention them. The Greeks call these psalms *ta proskyria*, “the psalms of approach,” because the first of them begins, “To the Lord in my distress…”]

there were fifteen steps of ascent. Since the Temple had been established on a mountain—the mountain of Moriah—the altar of burnt offering, which stood outside, could be approached only by steps.

[Note: Although the Law prohibited ascending to the altar by steps, Exodus 20:26, learned men investigate how this can be reconciled with Jewish custom and Ezekiel 43:17. The most probable explanation is that Ezekiel understood the altar to have several sloping approaches by which the priests could reach the pavement and surrounding area of the altar without steps.]

Accordingly, the parents placed the blessed little virgin Mary on one of these steps. While they removed the garments they had worn on the journey and clothed themselves, according to custom, in more elegant and cleaner garments, the virgin of the Lord climbed all the steps one by one without anyone leading or lifting her by the hand, so that you would have thought that, in this one respect, nothing was lacking in her from a mature age.

The Lord was already accomplishing something great in the infancy of his virgin, and by this miracle he was indicating in advance how great she would be.

[Note: It is asked how a girl of three years—Jacob the Jew, *On the Temple*, p. 21, says that the steps were half a cubit high and wide—could climb them.]

After the sacrifice had been celebrated according to the custom of the Law, and after she had fulfilled her vow,

[Note: Some trace the custom of making a vow of virginity to the daughter of Jephthah. Many Christian theologians affirm that Mary made such a vow, among them Petavius, *On the Incarnation* XIV.4.]

they left the Virgin within the precincts of the Temple to be raised there with the other virgins.

[Note: Epiphanius, *Ancoratus* 60, says that firstborn children, both male and female, were customarily consecrated in the Temple and brought up there until the age of puberty.]

They themselves returned home.

## VIII.

As the Virgin of the Lord advanced in age, she also progressed in virtue; and, according to the Psalmist, “her father and mother abandoned her, but the Lord took her up” (Psalm 26:10). [Note: The *Protoevangelium of James*, in addition to its frequent accounts of angelic intercourse, also relates that she was nourished by an angel.]

For she was visited daily by angels; daily she enjoyed the divine vision, which guarded her from every evil and caused her to overflow with every good. [Note: Evodius says the same thing in Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 3. But the *Protoevangelium of James* says that she was only twelve when she was betrothed to Joseph.] Thus she reached her fourteenth year, so that not only could no one invent anything blameworthy about her, but all good people who knew her judged her life and conduct worthy of admiration. [Note: This high priest is called Zacharias in the *Protoevangelium of James*.]

At that time the high priest publicly announced that the virgins who had been placed in the Temple and had completed this age [Col. 0302B] should return home and attend to marriage according to the custom of the nation and the maturity of their age. While the others readily obeyed this command, the Virgin of the Lord Mary alone replied that she could not do so, saying that she had devoted both herself and her parents to the service of the Lord, and, moreover, had vowed her own virginity to the Lord; she did not wish ever to violate it by knowing any man in the manner of intercourse. [Note: Thus they understand Mary’s words at Luke 1:34, “I do not know a man”—that is, “I will not know a man.”]

But the high priest, placed in great perplexity, thought that the vow could not be broken, since Scripture says, “Vow and pay” (Psalm 75:12); [Note: That is, so that the more mature Virgin might remain in the Temple throughout her entire life. Gregory of Nyssa, in Book III of his *Oration on the Day of the Lord’s Nativity*, says that neither law nor propriety allowed a woman to remain among the priests in the Temple and to be seen in the holy buildings: “It was neither lawful, and at the same time the dignity of the matter was not fitting.”] yet he did not dare to introduce a custom unfamiliar to the nation. He therefore ordered that, for the festival which was approaching, all the leading men from Jerusalem and the neighboring regions should be present, so that by their counsel he might learn what ought to be done in so doubtful a matter. When this had been arranged, it was unanimously agreed that the Lord should be consulted about the matter.

While everyone was applying himself to prayer, the high priest, according to custom, approached to consult God. Immediately, in the hearing of all, a voice came from the oracle and from the place of the mercy seat, declaring, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah, that they must seek the man to whom that virgin should be entrusted and betrothed. For it is clear that Isaiah says:

> “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:1ff.).

According to this prophecy, therefore, he declared that all those from the house and family of David who were eligible for marriage and were unmarried should bring their rods to the altar. Whichever man’s rod, after being brought forward, should produce a flower, and upon whose top the Spirit of the Lord should settle in the form of a dove, was the man to whom the virgin should be entrusted and betrothed. [Note: This is drawn from the account in Numbers 17, with the addition concerning the Holy Spirit settling, in the form of a dove, upon the rod—an addition occasioned by Matthew 3:16.] [Note: The *Protoevangelium of James* calls them “the widowers of the people”; Epiphanius, in the *Ancoratus* 60, says, “widowers and unmarried men from each tribe.”]

## IX.

Among the others there was Joseph, an aged man from the house and [Note: Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 51.10, calls him “an old man of eighty years, more or less.” The true Jerome, in Book II on Matthew, rejects as drawn from the ravings of the Apocrypha the claim that Joseph had been a widower and had previously fathered sons and daughters.] family of David. When all the others brought their rods forward in due order, he alone withheld his. Since nothing corresponding to the divine voice had appeared, the high priest thought that God must again be consulted. The answer was that the one who had been designated to betroth the virgin was the only one among those selected who had not brought his rod.

Joseph was therefore identified. When he had brought his rod, and a dove descending from heaven had settled upon its top, it became plainly evident to everyone [Note: Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 78.7, has “lots compelling him to this”—that is, lots forcing him to it; he repeats the point in the *Ancoratus* 60.] that the virgin was to be betrothed to him.

After the marriage rite had been duly celebrated according to custom [Note: That is, the betrothal ceremony in which, according to solemn custom, the names of the bridegroom and bride were inscribed on tablets in the presence of the assembled people, as Philo testifies in *On the Special Laws*. From the time of betrothal until the taking of the bride, an interval was customarily allowed.], Joseph departed for the city of Bethlehem in order to arrange his house and procure what was necessary for the wedding. But the Virgin of the Lord Mary returned to her parents’ home in Galilee with seven other virgins of the same age, nursed with her, whom she had received from the priest. [Note: I have written “nursed with her” (*collactaneis*) in place of the printed reading “companions” (*collectaneis*); for it means virgins who, at the same time as she, had been brought to the Temple after weaning.]

## X.

During those days, namely, at the time of her first arrival in Galilee, the angel Gabriel was sent to her by God to announce the Lord’s conception to her and to explain the manner or order of that conception. When he entered, he flooded the room in which she was staying with an immense light. Then, greeting her most graciously, he said:

> “Hail, Mary, most favored virgin of the Lord; virgin full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you above all women; blessed above all human beings born until now.”

The Virgin, who was already well acquainted with angelic faces and was not unfamiliar with heavenly light, was neither frightened by the angelic vision nor astonished by the greatness of the light; she was troubled only by his words. She began to consider what kind of greeting this could be, so unusual, what it might portend, and what its outcome would be.

The angel, anticipating this thought through divine inspiration, responded:

> “Do not be afraid, Mary, as though by this greeting I were concealing anything contrary to your chastity. For you have found favor with the Lord, because you chose chastity. Therefore, being a virgin, you will conceive without sin and bear a son. He will be great, ruling from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. [Note: From Psalm 72:8. The Jews themselves interpret this hymn of the Messiah.] And he will be called Son of the Most High, because he who is born humbly on earth reigns exalted in heaven. The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. For he himself is King of kings and Lord of lords, and his throne is forever and ever.”

At these words of the angel, the Virgin, not disbelieving but wishing to know the manner of it, replied:

> “How can this happen? For since, according to my vow, I do not know a man, how can I bear without the addition of male seed?”

The angel answered:

> “Do not suppose, Mary, that you will conceive in the human manner. Without intercourse with a man, you will conceive as a virgin; you will give birth as a virgin; you will nourish as a virgin. For the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you, against every heat of lust. Therefore what will be born from you will alone be holy, because, alone conceived and born without sin, it will be called the Son of God.” [Note: Anastasius of Sinai, *Sermon on the Annunciation of Mary*: “She carried him in the womb without union; she gave birth without marriage.” Hence the familiar formula: “Virgin before childbirth, virgin in childbirth, virgin after childbirth.”]

Then Mary, extending her hands and raising her eyes toward heaven, said:

> “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”—for I am not worthy of the title “mistress”—“let it be done to me according to your word.”

[Note: Here the words of Pseudo-Jerome begin, up to “let us proceed to the account.”]

It may perhaps be tedious and wearisome to some if we wished to insert into this little work everything that we read to have preceded or followed the Lord’s birth. Therefore, passing over what has been more fully written in the Gospel, let us proceed to relate those matters that are treated less fully.

## XI.

Joseph, therefore, coming from Judea into Galilee, intended to take the virgin betrothed to him as his wife. For three months had already passed, and the fourth was approaching, from the time she had been betrothed to him. Meanwhile, as the womb of the woman about to give birth gradually began to swell, she began to reveal herself as pregnant. [Note: In Athanasius’s homily *On the Census of the Holy Mary*, Joseph is introduced as protesting bitterly about this matter with his betrothed, volume II, p. 650. The same account appears in the *Protoevangelium of James*.] Joseph could not remain unaware of it. Entering more freely in the manner of a fiancé and speaking with her more familiarly, he discovered that she was pregnant.

He therefore began to burn inwardly and to waver, because he did not know what course he ought chiefly to take. He did not wish to expose her, because he was righteous (Matthew 1:19), nor to disgrace her by suspicion of fornication, because he was compassionate. Thus he considered secretly dissolving the marriage and dismissing her privately.

While he was thinking about this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying:

> “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid”—that is, do not wish to entertain suspicion of fornication concerning the virgin, or to think anything sinister; nor be afraid to take her as your wife. For what has been conceived in her, and now troubles your mind, is the work not of a man but of the Holy Spirit. For the virgin alone will bear the Son of God for all, and you shall call his name Jesus, that is, Savior; for he will save his people from their sins.”

Accordingly, Joseph took the virgin as his wife in accordance with the angel’s command; yet he did not know her, but, chastely providing for her, kept her under his protection.

When the ninth month from the conception was already approaching, Joseph set out for the city of Bethlehem, from which he came, taking his wife and the other necessities with him. When they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son, as the holy evangelists taught, our Lord Jesus Christ (Luke 2:6), who, with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages.

# NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

The entire texture of the discourse proclaims an author of a much later period. Erasmus says: “There is not even the slightest trace of Jerome in this Letter; rather, it has something barbarous and modern about it.”

# LETTER LI. TO PAULA AND EUSTOCHIUM  
## On the Virtue of the Psalms

### I.

Because you, my sweetest daughters, asked me, trusting in the hope of God’s mercy, to set apart various psalms in sequence, indicating on which occasions they should be sung, I in turn asked you to pray to the Lord our God for me, that by his gift he might deign to grant me the ability by which I could undertake your holy request, or, with his own gift, complete it. Hoping in his mercy, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant understanding to my humility, I considered it necessary, in obedience to the will of our Lord, to comply with your most holy request.

If, in this work, grace has been fully granted to us, give thanks for everything that has been said to our almighty Lord, praying for my humility—he who even commanded a she-ass to speak what the Lord himself willed.

### II.
