Although all the psalms, when properly examined, contain almost the whole of divine law, nevertheless, by the gift of God, and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, in confession of the Trinity, we have set out separately which psalms properly belong to the individual feast-days of the Lord our Savior, the Son of God.

We have indicated which belong to the Nativity; which to the holy Epiphany, that is, to the Lord’s baptism or the day of the star’s manifestation; which to the Thursday before the Lord’s Passion; which to the Passion itself; which to the Easter of the Resurrection of our Lord and Redeemer; which to his Ascension into heaven; which to his Advent; which concern the future judgment; and which concern the eternal city, in which Christ our Lord gathers his saints to himself, from the beginning of the world to the end of this age, so that they may reign with him in the eternal heavenly kingdom—he who is the holy, triune and one, eternal God.

We have also indicated which psalms are to be used in supplication to the Lord God in the litany, which should be sung by penitents, and which should be said on the birthdays of the saints. You will find the remaining psalms, which are to be read daily.

### III.

Nevertheless, all the psalms may be sung in sequence every day throughout the year, according to the custom of churches and monasteries. But you who read this should consider that one psalm pertains to many holy days, and that psalms addressed to God are repeated in various ways on each day. For there is a psalm that may be sung everywhere. There are others that pertain to the character of a single day, with attention being given to what sort of person is involved, whether religious or lay.

As for the psalms spoken on the Thursday before the Passion, or during the Lord’s Passion itself, and those chosen for the birthdays of the saints, we have dealt with them in the same way regarding the prophetic canticles, so that they should not be sung indiscriminately on the days mentioned above; whoever reads will find which ones should be said on which day.

For greater works: Psalm 77.  
For catechumens and the elect: Psalm 24.  
During fasting: Psalms 19, 34, and 72.  
For baptism at Easter: Psalm 64.  
For lamentation: Psalm 131.  
For the assembly of the brethren: Psalm 132.  
For blessing: Psalm 133.  
That praises may be poured out before God: Psalm 9.  
That a person may repent: Psalm 50.  
Concerning steadfast faith: Psalm 10.  
For admonition: Psalm 108.  
That you may exercise the eye of chastity: Psalm 1.  
For vigils in bed: Psalm 6.  
Concerning justice: Psalm 14.  
For upright prayer: Psalm 85.  
For communion with all people, or with the poor: Psalm 40.  
For the Nativity of the Lord: Psalm 109.  
Concerning the Trinity, so that a person may not fear: Psalm 9.  
Concerning the snares of heresies: Psalm 3.  
For admonishing one’s neighbor: Psalm 4.  
Concerning hope in God: Psalm 22.  
Concerning belief: Psalm 10.  
For prayer in a person: Psalm 30.  
Blessing upon rulers: Psalm 20.  
Concerning love of the law: Psalm 26.  
Concerning the tribulation caused by enemies: Psalm 25.  
That creation may praise the Creator: Psalm 102.  
Concerning martyrdom: Psalms 44 and 50.  
Concerning persecutors: Psalm 82.  
When you enter among foreigners: Psalm 81.  
Prayer over a field: Psalm 83.  
Prayer at night: Psalm 90.

# LETTER LII. TO AUGUSTINE

*(In the Benedictine edition it is placed last among the letters of Saint Augustine, with this summary: “An anonymous writer to Augustine—not Jerome, as is clear from the style, although it has been published among Jerome’s letters as number 50—indicating that he is deeply grieved because he did not find Augustine together with Severus in the city of Leges, and explaining how much affection he bears him.”)*

# LETTER LIII. OF GUIGO, FIFTH PRIOR OF THE GRANDE CHARTREUSE, TO THE BROTHERS OF DURBON  
## On the Spurious Letters of Blessed Jerome

[Note: It was first published by Mabillon in volume I of the *Analecta*, and in the appendix to the works of Saint Bernard. We have transferred it here as a critical preface to the writings attributed to Jerome.] [Note: The author flourished around the middle of the twelfth century; one therefore admires all the more the man’s intelligence and keen judgment in those barbarous times.]

To the most beloved friends and brothers in Christ, Lazarus, prior of Durbon, and the others serving God in the same desert, Guigo, called prior of the Chartreuse, eternal salvation from the Lord.

Among the works of Catholic men that they have labored to produce for the instruction of the faithful, and that our own smallness has also endeavored to collect or correct, we have brought together into one large volume the letters of Blessed Jerome, as many as we could find from every source, purged, insofar as God granted us the ability, of falsehoods.

From these we removed certain letters that, either from the writings of other teachers or from the difference of their style and arguments, we discovered to be unworthy of the name of so great a man. Among them is the letter entitled *To Demetrias*, which begins: “If, relying upon the highest intelligence and equal learning …” Blessed Augustine, in his work *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin against Pelagius*, says that this letter belongs to Pelagius, although he needlessly inserts and refutes certain passages from it in his own treatise. [Note: Incorrectly printed as “frustra” in Mabillon, perhaps through a typographical error.]

To this may be added the letter *To Titianus on the Death of His Daughter*, which begins: “I have received the writings of your charity”; the consolatory letter *To Oceanus*, beginning: “The reproaches of various people, the manifold tribulations”; the letter *To the Widow*, which begins: “Our humility has great confidence in writing”; and the letter *To the Virgin, or To the Daughter of Mauricius*, which is found under both titles and begins: “How great is the blessedness in heavenly things.”

Likewise, *On the Fall of a Virgin, or On Penance, to Susanna*—both titles are found in different manuscripts—which is attributed to authors so diverse that it should be adorned with the name of none of them. In some books it begins: “I think the crime is slight”; in others: “What are you doing, soul? Why are you troubled by your thoughts?”

Also, *To Desiderius, on the Twelve Readers*, composed by someone unknown as a mockery of teachers; and *To Celantia*, beginning: “It is a celebrated saying of Scripture.” This last is written in a somewhat nobler style, but even so is unworthy of Blessed Jerome.

Finally, there is the *Disputation on the Origin of the Soul*, presented as a dialogue between Blessed Jerome and Augustine. Although many passages are taken from their writings, it is nevertheless false, both because those teachers never spoke with one another face to face and because that same question has never yet been clearly settled either by them or by other adherents of the Catholic faith. This disputation is found beginning: “When among you the heavenly eloquence of the purest fountain …”

So that the letters of the aforesaid teacher may not appear to the ignorant to have been reduced in number without reasonable cause, place these letters of our smallness at the beginning.

Farewell. Pray for us.

# PART TWO: WRITINGS OF VARIOUS KINDS

# ON THE FORMS OF THE HEBREW LETTERS

[Note: There can be no doubt that whoever the author of this description may have been falsely counterfeited Jerome’s name and pen; he is immeasurably distant from Jerome’s intelligence and learning. Nevertheless, the work itself seemed worthy of publication, since it represents the form of the Hebrew letters and, so far as I know, is older than those previously published and even than the Murnacian alphabet preserved by Montfaucon.]

*(From a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library at Milan.)* (G,S)*

There are two forms of the Hebrew letters: one ancient, used by the Samaritans; the other later, used by the Jews. For this reason, when Israel was taken captive and led away to Babylon, the king of the Assyrians ordered that, so that the land of those people mentioned above would not remain deserted, Assyrians should dwell there in their place.

Esdras has handed down to us in his writings that these are the Samaritans who preserve both the custom of their homeland, worshiping fire, and the Jewish commandments. The Jews themselves call these people “Samaritans” in their native language, which means “guardians.”

When Cyrus ruled the Persians through the Medes, after removing Astyages, the king of the Medes and his own grandfather, and transferring the entire kingdom to the Persians, he released all the Jewish captives. When they returned, they became mixed with the aforementioned Assyrian Samaritans, who appeared to be Jews. Therefore, so that they might be separated from them, Esdras, the teacher of the law, devised and transmitted to them another form of letters, while preserving the same force of the letters; the Jews still use these letters today.

The Hebrew letters handed down through Moses are therefore twenty-two. Their names are these:

[The list of names is absent from the supplied text.]

The lines are written for us generally from right to left, ending on the left-hand side. For this reason we have also placed the letters in this same manner.

# CATALOGUE OF CERTAIN WORKS

Which some of the ancients, whether authors or manuscript codices, praise—though falsely—as works of Saint Jerome.

## Book on the Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart

It is mentioned in Letter I of the Church of Lyons, on predestination, against the three letters of the monk who had raised that question; he is said to have supported his opinion by the authority of Saint Jerome in the *Book on the Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart*. The letter was written around the year of our Lord 855 and appears in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. Rabanus also cites it in his letter to Hincmar of Reims, published by P. Sirmond in volume II, p. 992.

Saint Jerome himself seems to have given occasion for the composition of such a work in his commentary on Isaiah 63, where he says: “It is said that God hardened Pharaoh’s heart … This question Paul discussed most carefully in Romans, and we touched upon it in one of our works”—namely, the letter to Hedibia, question 10.

## On the Consanguinity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

In manuscript codex no. 48 of the Library of Saint Mark in Venice.

## On Three Virtues

Peter Abelard cites it in Book I of his *Christian Theology*, in the edition of P. Martène, volume V of the *Monumenta*, p. 1175.

## The Alphabet of Aethicus, Translated from Greek into Latin by Jerome

Rabanus cites it in the book *On the Invention of Languages*, volume VI of the works, p. 333; it is also found in an old manuscript from the Hautin Library, cited by Du Cange in the appendix to his *Greek Glossary*.

The author does not seem to be anyone other than Aethicus Ister, a Christian writer after the time of Constantine the Great, nor does his book seem to be anything other than that cosmographical description which others attribute to the rhetorician Julius Honorius, according to Cassiodorus’s testimony.

“For Aethicus,” says Salmasius in his notes on Solinus, “is another person: an Istrian sophist, whose work, translated from Greek by Jerome and not yet published, is contained in an old book in the Thuane Library.”

Martin Opitz likewise says: “Hister, or Iste, called Aethicus, was a very ancient writer, whose *Cosmography*, translated in fragments from the Greek by Jerome, is in the Thuane Library at Paris and also in my possession, written in a very ancient hand.”

Indeed, the title of the book itself reads in several manuscripts: “Here begins the book of Aethicus, issued by philosophical oracle, translated into Latin by the presbyter Jerome from the *Cosmography and Writing of the World*.”

Nevertheless, it is enough to examine the little book published by Simler from the Pithoean manuscript to understand immediately, from its style and composition, that it was by no means rendered into Latin by Jerome. It is written in a more than barbarous manner, filled with the most foolish nonsense and fables, and teaches very many things about the creation of the world, marvels, and other matters that could not possibly have been approved by the holy Interpreter.

Finally, it is not even Aethicus’s work, since it repeatedly praises the philosopher Aethicus Ister by name.

## The Cycle of Saint Jerome

In an ancient codex no. 547 of the Library of Saint-Germain.

## A Way of Life for Holy Virgins

This is a compilation of sayings drawn from various writings of Jerome on the subject. It is found in a very old manuscript of the cathedral church of Saint Peter in the Vatican.

## On the Heresies of the Greeks, Jews, and Christians

It ends with the Tritheists. It is found at the end of another manuscript of the *Book of the Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs*, from the same library of Saint Peter. See the *Index of Heresies* published by the distinguished Menard in Paris in 1617.

## Of Saint Jerome: On the Fear of the Last Judgment and the Transience of This Life

It begins: “Therefore you fear sufficiently, lest on that day of tribulation …” A treatise consisting for the most part of sayings of Jerome gathered from here and there. I have the manuscript book; it is neither of the latest age nor without distinction.

## One Letter of Jerome and Another of Mansuetus the Bishop on the Secret of Christ’s Incarnation

So reads the oldest catalogue of books prefixed to Vatican Palatine manuscript no. 57.

## Glosses Translated According to the Hebrew Truth by the Aforementioned Jerome

From the same catalogue.

## Exposition of the Psalms

Whether of all the psalms or only of part of them; homilies on several passages of Scripture also frequently occur in manuscripts, the enumeration of which would be lengthy.

[Col. 0312A] ## Commentary of Saint Jerome on the Apocalypse of the Apostle John

Thus it is entitled in an ancient catalogue of the Library of the Monastery of Pomposa, which is said to have been compiled in the eleventh century by Henry the cleric. It begins: “John, whose name is interpreted as ‘the grace of God,’ represented the figure of Christ.”

The Latin translation of Victorinus’s commentaries on the Apocalypse is also repeatedly attributed to Jerome. As for the preface to Anatolius that is placed before them, even critics of great reputation still doubt whether Jerome is its author.

## A Slavonic Translation of the Bible, and Likewise a Hieronymian Slavonic Alphabet

Those who attributed these works to Jerome—writers and critics of Illyrian affairs who were by no means contemptible—were mistaken, having misunderstood Jerome’s words, “I gave [them] to men of my language.”

# [HOMILY TO MONKS]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING HOMILY

This collection consists of sayings, chiefly those concerned with properly establishing the life of monks, compiled from Jerome’s letters and books by some diligent person. We encountered it in a very ancient manuscript of especially good quality in the Vatican, numbered 140. It seemed sufficiently important that it could be published among the spurious writings, with some benefit to readers, especially since it appears to pave the way for the *Rule of Monks*, a work of the same spirit and character.

# TO MONKS
[Col. 0311B] Some hasten toward heavenly things and desire what is above; others, gazing greedily upon earthly filth, possess no nourishment of truth. If anyone has a virginal soul and is a lover of chastity, he ought not to be content with mediocre things, which quickly grow stale and wither when the scorching heat has arisen; rather, let him pursue perfect virtues, so that he may possess everlasting light. Let us strive to learn on earth those things whose knowledge will endure in heaven. No one who is about to renounce the world can sell well what he has despised. If you desire to follow Christ, and your possessions are in your power, sell them; if you have none, you have been freed from a great burden. For he has given everything to God who has offered himself. He easily despises all things who continually thinks that he is going to die.

A wanton age often condemns shameless old men. Sudden heat prevails over long duration. For many, by living long, carry their own funerals, and, like whitewashed tombs, are full of the bones of the dead. Blessed is the person who, reading the divine Scriptures, turns words into action; and, following the naked cross naked, with pure hands and a spotless heart, glories in being poor both in spirit and in possessions. No one can possess virtues and riches at the same time.

Whoever wishes to be perfect should flee the crowds of people, the duties of greeting, and banquets as though they were chains of pleasure. For monks, food should be plain and taken in the evening. Let them regard vegetables and legumes, and sometimes even little fish, as the greatest delicacies. Whatever is not perceived through the throat should be for him the equivalent of both bread and vegetables. Let the monk pray frequently and, with his body bent, raise his mind to Christ. Let him keep frequent vigils, often sleep with an empty stomach, and meanwhile flee as enemies the whisperers, the ostentatious, and the flattering flatterers.

Let the monk, in the humility of his clothing and with his spirit puffed up, not seek the company of worldly people; let him avoid it. What need has he to see more often what he has despised being? Let the monk possess the simplicity of a dove and plot no deceit against anyone; let him also possess the cunning of a serpent, lest he be undermined by the treachery of others, because it is not far removed from vice either to be able to deceive or to be deceived.

Let the monk who has offered his substance to Christ beware lest he recklessly squander it—that is, lest he give the property of the poor to those who are not poor—and, according to the saying of a very prudent man, lest generosity perish through generosity.

Whoever begins to serve the Lord should diligently watch for all the devil’s snares, so that, like a cautious and attentive helmsman, he may know on which shore the pirate lying in wait for chastity is stationed; where avarice, the root of all evils, is Charybdis; and where Scylla is, with the dogs of slanderers. And let him consider how often, while secure in the midst of calm, we are overwhelmed by the Libyan sandbanks of vices, and how many poisonous creatures the desert of this age nourishes.

If the merchants of this world endure many dangers to reach uncertain and perishable riches, and preserve for a short time what they have acquired amid many dangers and at the risk of soul and body, what must the merchant of Christ do, who, having sold everything, seeks the most precious pearl; who, having sold all the resources of his substance, buys a field in which he may find a treasure that neither thief nor robber can take away?

Whoever wishes to be a monk should concern himself neither with his own nation nor with household property, but with his soul. The dirtiness of his clothing should be evidence of a pure mind; a cheap tunic should prove his contempt for the world.

Beware of entering without a teacher upon a road you have never traveled, lest, turning aside in another direction, you suffer error, and walk either farther or less far than necessary, becoming exhausted by running or falling asleep through delay. Those should be teachers of others who have learned the appearance of their way of life over a long period, who were the least of all so that they might become the first of all. Neither hunger nor satiety ever overcame them; they rejoice in poverty, and their clothing, speech, face, walk, and instruction are lessons in virtue.

A religious person ought not to live among women, lest he see by day what he contemplates by night. The monk’s senses should be watchful, lest they lie open to vain thoughts. Let him love knowledge of the Scriptures, and let him not love the vices of the flesh.

Let the monk live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the company of many, so that he may learn humility from one and patience from another. Let one teach silence, another gentleness. Let him not do what he wishes; let him eat what he is ordered to eat; let him have as much as he has received; let him pay the measure of his labor. Let him be subjected to one whom he does not wish to obey. Let him come to bed tired and fall asleep while walking, and let him not be compelled to rise before his sleep is complete. Having suffered injury, let him remain silent.

[Col. 0311C] Let him fear the superior of the monastery as the Lord and love him as a parent; let him believe that whatever the superior commands is salutary for him, and let him not judge the decision of a superior, whose duty is to obey and fulfill what has been commanded. As Moses says: “Hear, Israel, and be silent.”

Some profess that they renounce the world only in clothing and by verbal profession, not in their possessions. Changing nothing of their former way of life, they increase their household property rather than diminish it. They retain the same servants’ duties, the same banquet equipment, and, amid crowds and swarms of attendants, solitary men claim for themselves the names of officeholders.

Most monks cannot abandon their former trades and business dealings. Instead of pursuing food and clothing, as the Apostle commanded, they engage under the title of religion in unjust commerce, seeking greater profits than worldly people, and die rich with full purses—those who had lived as though they were poor.

Whoever strives to make progress should not consider what evil others do, but what good he ought to do. If, while living in a monastery, you desire to become a cleric, conduct yourself so that you may attain the merit of such a life: namely, that you stain your youth with no filth of lust; that you come forth to the altar of the Lord like a virgin from the bridal chamber; and that, while possessing a good reputation outside, women may know your name but not know your face.

Learn for a long time what you are to teach, and do not trust your flatterers; indeed, do not readily lend your ear to mockers. Thus holy men hasten by spontaneous devotion toward the prize of the heavenly calling, just as powerful horses, harnessed for a race with the charioteer leaning above them, hold their course, not waiting for the blows of lashes but burning at words of encouragement.

Do not seek things greater than your strength, because it is better to proceed safely in humble circumstances than to sway on uncertain footing in lofty ones. God rejoices when wealthy converts give their possessions to the poor; when burning gems, which previously covered their necks and faces, fill the bellies of the needy; when silk garments and gold stretched into threads are changed into soft woolen clothing by which cold is driven away, not clothing by which ambition is strengthened; when virtue consumes the furnishings of luxury; when doors that formerly spewed forth crowds of greeters are besieged by the wretched.

[Col. 0311D] Happy is the person who walks accompanied by this army; happy is the person who is whitened by their filth.

The first virtue of a monk is to despise human judgments and always to remember the Apostle, who says: “If I still wished to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.” However renowned an honor may be, it becomes worthless in the eyes of the crowds, and among good men the dignity itself becomes disgraceful when many unworthy people possess it. Hence Cicero spoke excellently of Caesar: when he said that certain people were adorned, he meant not that he honored them, but that the ornaments themselves were disgraced.

Great demands are always placed at the discretion of those who hear, as in the saying: “If you wish to be perfect”; and elsewhere concerning eunuchs: “Let him accept it who is able.” Necessity is not imposed, so that free choice may obtain its reward.

[Col. 0312B] The wisdom of Christ is sanctification and redemption. Christ is both redemption and price: Christ is everything, so that whoever has abandoned everything for Christ may find one thing in place of all things. When someone has professed religion, let him strive not merely to offer money to Christ but also himself. Let him imitate the Son of Man, who came not to be served but to serve. For skin for skin, and everything that a person possesses, he can give for his life.

“But touch his flesh,” says the devil. The ancient enemy knows that the contest is more a matter of continence than of gifts. What is external is easily cast away. The internal battle is more dangerous: let us tear apart what has been joined, let us cut apart what has been united. For if we offer wealth to Christ together with our soul, he will gladly accept it. But if we give what is outside to God and what is within to the devil, the portion will not be equal; and it would be said to us: “If you offer correctly but do not divide correctly, have you not sinned?”

[Col. 0312C] When a nobleman has been converted, let his conversion be an occasion not for arrogance but for humility, knowing that the Son of God became the son of man: however far he may humble himself, he will not be humbler than Christ. For even if he walks with bare feet and is clothed in a coarse tunic; if he makes himself equal to the poor and graciously enters the cells of the needy; if he is the eyes of the blind, the hands of the weak, and the feet of the lame; if he himself carries water, cuts wood, and builds the fire—where are the bonds? Where are the slaps? Where are the spittings? Where are the scourges? Where is the cross? Where is death?

The first virtue of monks is this: that they flatter themselves about nothing in their profession and nothing in their continence, but that humility be their competition, and whoever is last be considered first. Neither excessive fasting nor immoderate fullness should be condemned. Let no one judge another, lest he be judged by the Lord, for each person stands or falls before his own Lord.

[Col. 0312D] Solitude is especially to be sought by the monk, and residence in the city is to be avoided: to be seen and to see, to greet and to be greeted, to praise and to slander, to hear and to speak, and unwillingly to endure the greetings of so great a multitude of people—all these things are alien to the purpose and repose of monks. For he says: “We see those who come to us, and we lose our silence; or we do not see them, and we are accused of arrogance.” Sometimes we return the visit to those who visit us; we go to the doors of the proud and enter through the gilded doorposts amid the tongues of biting servants.

There are holy stones that roll across the earth; smooth, polished, and round, they resemble the courses of wheels. Concerning such stones the Prophet commands that obstacles be removed, lest the feet of those walking stumble against them. Those walking there are to be understood as travelers and passersby who hasten through this world toward the heavenly dwelling.

[Col. 0313A] The person who wishes to lead a secluded life is blameworthy if, while his body lies hidden in a closed cell, his tongue wanders throughout the world. A religious person should beware of living where he must daily either perish or be overcome. For it is safer to be unable to perish than not to have perished while remaining beside danger.

Amid banquets and the enticements of pleasure, lust subdues even minds of iron. Chastity is difficult to preserve amid delights. One who is polished in every respect displays a filthy mind.

If a cleric or layman says to a monk, “Why are you going to the desert? Stand in the battle line; resist your enemies armed, so that after you have conquered, you may be crowned,” let him answer: “I admit my weakness. I do not wish to fight in hope of victory, lest I should at some time lose my victory. If I flee the sword, I have avoided it; if I stand, I must either conquer or fall. But why is it necessary to abandon certainties and pursue uncertainties? Death must be avoided either with a shield or with one’s feet. You who fight can both resist and conquer. When I flee, I do not conquer in the matter from which I flee; rather, I flee so that I may not be conquered.”

There is no security in sleeping beside a serpent. It may happen that it does not bite me, but it may also happen that one day it does bite me. For this reason we avoid the crowds of cities, lest we be compelled to do what nature does not so much force us to do as pleasure does.

[Col. 0313B] Luxury is the mother of lust, and pleasure in the organs of generation follows a belly distended with food and irrigated by draughts of wine. And, to put it this way, the order of vices should be changed according to the order of the limbs.

Nobility and riches are great not for those who possess them but for those who despise them. Worldly people welcome those who are powerful through these privileges. We, however, praise those who despise such things for the sake of the Savior; and, strangely, those who possess them we consider of little account, but if they refuse to possess them, we proclaim them.

Amid the hands of enemies and the harsh necessity of captivity, nothing is more cruel than separating parents from children. Frequently, at the command of Christ’s grace, faith itself in a certain sense imposes this against the laws of nature. Rather, it seeks it joyfully and despises love of children through a greater love in the Lord.

The flesh of a wanton youth must be broken by frequent and repeated fasts, for it is better for the stomach to ache than the mind. Let no foul or wanton speech ever come from a monk’s mouth, for by these signs a lustful mind is revealed, and through the outward person the vices of the inward person are displayed.

The measure of religion is whether the poor and strangers—and with them Christ—are known to share one’s table. Whoever wishes to lead a perfect life should flee, as a kind of plague of pleasures, a cleric who is a merchant, a poor man who has become rich, and an obscure man who has become famous. For the worst conversations corrupt good manners.

Let us avoid soiled [Al. dark-colored] clothing just as much as white clothing. Adornment and dirtiness must be avoided in the same way, because one smells of luxury and the other of glory.

It is praiseworthy not to go without a linen garment, but to have no money for linen garments. Otherwise it is ridiculous and full of disgrace to boast, with a purse stuffed full, that you have neither a handkerchief nor a neck-cloth.

[Col. 0313C] Let neither the rustic and merely simple brother consider himself holy because he knows nothing, nor the learned and eloquent man deem holiness to lie in speech. Of these two imperfect alternatives, it is far better to have holy rusticity than sinful eloquence.

Whatever intoxicates and overturns the state of the mind, let us flee in the same way as poison. I do not say this because creation is condemned by us, since the Lord was also called a drinker of wine, and Timothy, whose stomach was suffering, was permitted to drink a little wine. In drinking, we take account of age, health, and the qualities of bodies.

If I burn without wine—if I burn with youth and am inflamed by the heat of my blood, and am of a vigorous, well-nourished body—I will gladly abstain from the cup in which wine is consumed.

A fat belly does not produce a subtle understanding. Impose on yourself as much fasting as you can bear. Let fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, and not superstitious.

What benefit is there in abstaining from olives and seeking certain troublesome and difficult foods? Let the whole cultivation of the gardens be consumed: dried figs, pepper, nuts, dates, fine flour, honey, and pistachios, so that we may not eat ordinary bread as food.

Others, contrary to the nature of things and of human beings, refuse to drink water or eat bread, but consume delicate little soups, crushed vegetables, and beet juices—not sipping them from a cup but from a basin.

[Col. 0313D] The strongest fast is bread and water; but because it carries no glory, and because we all live on bread and water, it is called a public fast.

Beware lest you hunt after people’s whispers, lest you exchange God’s displeasure for the praise of the crowds [Ms. my]. “If I still pleased people,” says the Apostle, “I would not be Christ’s servant.” Let the person who has become Christ’s servant cease to seek to please people.

Through good report and bad report, to the right and to the left, the soldier of Christ advances. He is not exalted by praise or broken by blame; he does not swell with riches or shrink through poverty; he despises both joy and sorrow. The sun does not burn him by day, nor the moon by night.

What are you doing, monk, in your father’s house? Where is the rampart, where the trench, where the winter spent beneath skins? Look: the trumpet sounds from heaven; look: the armed commander comes forth with the clouds to wage war against the world. Look: the two-edged sword proceeding from the king’s mouth cuts down everything in its path, and you come forth from your chamber to the battle line, from the shade into the sun.

A body accustomed to a tunic cannot bear the weight of a breastplate. A head covered with linen refuses a helmet; a hard, rough handle irritates hands softened by leisure. And so, even if your mother displays the breasts at which she nursed you, with her hair scattered and her clothing torn; even if your father lies across the threshold—step over your father and hasten with dry eyes to the banner of the Cross. In this matter, to be cruel is a kind of piety.

The day will come—yes, it will come—when you return victorious to your homeland, when, as a crowned man, you walk in the heavenly Jerusalem. Then you will receive citizenship with Paul; then you will claim, with your parents, the rights of that same city. Then you will pray even for me, who urged you to conquer.

[Col. 0314A] Scripture commands obedience to parents, but whoever loves them above Christ will lose his soul. The love of Christ and fear of Gehenna easily break these bonds. The enemy holds a sword in order to kill me, and I am to think about my mother’s tears? For my father’s sake I am to abandon the military service, when for Christ’s sake I owe him no burial, although I owe everything to Christ’s cause?

This ram of piety, by which faith is shaken, must be blunted by the edge of the Gospel: “My mother and my brothers are those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Luke VIII, 21). If they believe in Christ, let them favor me as I am about to fight for his name; if they do not believe, let the dead bury their own dead.

Our adversary, like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, prowls about; and you, sheltered beneath the shade of a leafy tree, take soft sleep, soon to become his prey.

[Col. 0314B] From there avarice attempts to break in; from there my belly wishes to be my god instead of Christ. Lust compels me to drive away the Holy Spirit dwelling in me, to violate God’s temple. The enemy, I say, whose names are a thousand and whose arts of doing harm are a thousand, pursues me; and I, wretched man, shall consider myself victorious while I am being captured.

Let the perfect servant of Christ possess nothing except Christ; otherwise he is not perfect. And if he is not perfect, although he previously promised God that he would become perfect, he lies: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom I, 11).

A monk has no honor in his own homeland, and where there is no honor, there is contempt; where there is contempt, there is frequent injury; where there is injury, there is indignation; where there is indignation, there is no peace; where there is no peace, the mind is often led away from its purpose.

[Col. 0314C] But where something is taken away from one’s devotion through unrest, the result is diminished by what has been taken away; and where it is diminished, it cannot be called perfect. From this calculation arises the conclusion that a perfect monk cannot exist in his homeland. But to refuse to be perfect is to sin.

O desert of Christ, blooming with flowers! O solitude in which those stones are born from which the city of the great King is built in the Apocalypse! O wilderness rejoicing in God as a familiar companion!

What are you doing, monk, in the world, when you are greater than the world? How long do the shadows of roofs weigh upon you? How long does the prison of smoky cities enclose you?

You fear poverty, but Christ calls the poor blessed. You are frightened by labor, but no athlete is crowned without sweat. You think about food, but faith does not feel hunger. You hesitate to place your limbs, worn out by fasting, upon the bare earth, but the Lord lies beside you.

Your head is rough with dirt and your hair unkempt, but Christ is your head. The infinite vastness of the desert frightens you, but walk in paradise in your mind: whenever you pass there in thought, you will not be in the desert.

Your skin becomes rough for lack of baths, but whoever has once been washed in Christ does not need to wash again. And, to hear the Apostle’s answer briefly concerning everything: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII, 18).

[Col. 0314D] You are a delicate soldier if you wish to rejoice here in the world and afterward reign with Christ. Honor your father, but only if he does not separate you from the true Father. Know the bond of blood to last only so long as he recognizes his Creator.

It is grievous that people do not seek eternal goods, which are certain, but hope in uncertain temporal things—things which you see many people not possessing, and which, when they have possessed them, they have lost.

If someone says, “To whom do I leave such great riches?” I answer: “To Christ, who cannot die.” “Whom do I have as heir?” you ask. “The very one whom I have as Lord.” Your father will be saddened, but Christ will rejoice; your household will mourn, but the angels will rejoice with you.

Let your father do what he wishes with his substance. You belong not to the one from whom you were born, but to the one to whom you were reborn, who redeemed you at the great price of his blood.

In Christians, beginnings are not sought but endings. Paul began badly but finished well; Judas’s beginnings are praised, but his end is condemned by betrayal.

In the servant of God, what is sought is not the adornment of the body but the vigor of the soul, which becomes stronger through the weakness of the flesh.

[Col. 0315A] Nothing inflames the body and tickles the sexual organs so much as undigested food and convulsive belching. Whatever is a seedbed of pleasures must be avoided as poison.

Therefore, frugal food and a belly always hungry are preferable to three-day fasts. It is much better to take a little every day than enough only rarely. The best rain is that which gradually descends upon the earth; a sudden and excessive downpour overturns fields headlong.

When you eat, think that immediately afterward you must pray and at once read. Do not seek verbal polish in a monk but purity of soul. For among religious people it is a great solecism and vice to narrate or do anything shameful.

[Col. 0315B] What deserves reverence is not wordy rusticity but holy simplicity.

This mortal life is a racecourse: here we compete so that elsewhere we may be crowned. The devil does not seek unbelievers, nor those who are outside, whose flesh the Assyrian king burns into bones; rather, he hastens to snatch people from the Church.

According to the prophet Habakkuk, his food has been chosen. He wishes to overthrow Job, and, having devoured Judas, he seeks power over the Apostles.

Do not allow thoughts to grow in your heart. Let nothing Babylonian, nothing of confusion, grow within you. While the enemy is small, kill him. Let wickedness be struck down in the seed, for it is impossible that it not arise in the human mind through the familiar warmth of the marrow.

He is praised and proclaimed blessed who, when his thoughts begin, kills them and dashes them against the rock; and the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians X, 1).

[Col. 0315C] If a monk falls, the priest will pray for him. Who will pray for the priest’s fall? The loss of the flock is the shepherd’s disgrace.

Your Blessedness’s question was a disputation: questions ought to be posed in such a way that the answer furnishes the way forward. The person whose speech is destroyed by his conduct will lose the authority to speak.

The priest’s blameless conduct without speech benefits as much by example as it harms by silence. For the rabies of wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s staff.

Violence belongs to the wicked and to banqueters, not to priests. For in wine there is luxury; in luxury, pleasure; in pleasure, immodesty.

A person who is not going to die is killed in order to live.

# RULE OF MONKS COMPILED FROM THE WRITINGS OF JEROME

[Col. 0319]

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING RULE

The inscription itself identifies its author: Lupus of Olmeto of Seville, who faithfully and successfully set forth teachings drawn from Jerome’s writings for the restoration of his own community. He lived, as he himself says, at the beginning of the fifteenth century and professed as a brother of the monastery of Saint Mary of Guadalupe of the Order of Saint Jerome; afterward he was appointed what they call its prior general.

He apparently himself entitled this work of his *Flowers*, in which he aptly and suitably connected the more notable sayings of the Holy Father concerning monks. While he was still alive, Pope Martin V approved it by his letters under the title *Rule of the Monks of Saint Jerome*.

After the editions of Erasmus and Victorius, Brother Pius Rubeus of Piacenza revised it and published it at Como in 1621 under the title *Flowers*, adding many complete chapters and truncating several others that seemed to him alien to Jerome. He performed a service of some value by appending to each chapter references indicating the locations of the sentences. We have sometimes used this work as well, although we have followed the place and number assigned to the genuine, not spurious, writings of the Holy Father in our edition; we did not follow the same method for the latter.

Our intention, however, was to revise and restore not the work that we said Rubeus had interpolated in so many places, but the copy of his Rule that had until now been taken from Lupus of Olmeto’s work and placed at the end of the volume of Jerome’s works. We also compared it with a manuscript codex of the Library of the Trinity of the Mountains in Rome, and corrected it in quite a few places.

[Col. 0319]

# RULE OF MONKS COLLECTED FROM THE WRITINGS OF JEROME BY LUPUS OF [Note: [Col. 0319C] Martianus incorrectly calls him Lupus of Oliveto.] OLMETO. (C,G)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0319A] Most dear brothers, I cannot utter with my mouth the speech that I have conceived in my mind, and my tongue cannot express the joy of my heart. Yet this is not suffered by me alone, who desire to tell what I feel; you too suffer it with me, rejoicing more in your conscience than expressing yourselves in speech.

Nothing is happier than a Christian, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised; nothing more laborious, since he is daily in danger of his life; nothing stronger, since he conquers the devil; nothing weaker, since he is overcome by the flesh. There are many examples of both conditions. The thief believes upon the cross and immediately deserves to hear: “Amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise.” Judas, however, falls from the height of apostleship into the Tartarus of perdition; and neither the intimacy of the banquet [Al. common fellowship], nor the dipping of the morsel, nor the favor of the kiss restrains him, so that he might not betray as though he were merely a human being the one whom he knew to be the Son of God.

We have indeed abandoned little things; we possess great ones. What Christ promised is repaid with a hundredfold return.

[Col. 0319B] We say these things not so much to you as to others under your name, so that, first of all, we may teach you, son, that you have begun great things, that you pursue lofty things, and that, trampling upon the impulses of youth—indeed, of puberty—you are climbing the step of perfect maturity.

For you know that our teaching holds to the path of humility, and that by walking through the lowest places we ascend to the highest. Therefore the Holy Spirit must be invoked by me, so that he may defend this matter through his own meaning and by my mouth.

We do not seek the field of rhetorical eloquence, nor the snares of dialecticians, nor do we search out Aristotle’s thorny thickets. Rather, we flee to the gravity of the sacred Scriptures, where there is true medicine for wounds and certain remedies for sorrows.

[Col. 0319C] Because memory is fleeting, however, and you wish all that we have said to become a little commentary, so that reading may console forgetfulness, I have therefore thought that a few things which I judge will be necessary for you should be appended.

Our speech is directed toward this: that, since our labor is one, our reward also may be one. For those sailing across the Red Sea—which we should desire to see the true Pharaoh drowned together with his army—reach the great city amid many difficulties and dangers. On both shores dwell wandering peoples, indeed the fiercest beasts. Always anxious, always armed, they carry provisions for the entire year; everything is full of hidden rocks and extremely treacherous shallows.

[Col. 0320A] The point of these remarks is clear. For if the merchants of the world endure so much to reach uncertain and perishable riches, and preserve, at the risk of their souls, what they acquired amid many dangers, what must the merchant of Christ do, who, having sold everything, seeks the most precious pearl; who, having sold all the resources of his substance, buys a field in which he may find a treasure that neither thief can dig out nor robber take away?

[Note: [Col. 0319D] See what we said about this word in the cited letter [Col. 0320D] to Rusticus.]

We must therefore know what has been commanded and what forbidden, so that, knowing both, we may observe both. Otherwise, before knowing the commandment, it is impossible for us to know what is being done.

I say these things not from a whole ship or with intact cargo, like someone ignorant of the waves, but, having recently been cast upon the shore by a shipwreck, I announce them in a timid voice to those about to sail.

Nevertheless, with all the affection of my mind, I devote myself to you; but [Al. “devote themselves.” Therefore] I beg you to support my efforts with your prayers, so that the Lord [Col. 0320B] and Savior may answer on behalf of the cause [Note: [Col. 0320D] Others insert, “with his own meaning, by my mouth.”]

[Col. 0320C] It is therefore your task that action follow the will. It is mine to wish; it is the result of your prayers that I may be able. But what is mine will never be mine without God’s help: God always gives, and is always going to give; nor is what he once gave sufficient for me unless he gives it continually.

For if the persistent petition of a woman bent the judgment of a harsh judge, how much more do diligent appeals move a father’s heart? Know, however, above all that nothing is more important to us than to preserve Christ’s rights, not to move the boundaries of our fathers, and always to remember the Roman faith praised by the apostolic mouth.

[Col. 0321A] ## CHAPTER ONE: On Obedience

[Col. 0321B] Receive, then, son, our teaching with the simplicity and truth in which we have learned [Al. “say”], because we do not seek human glory—God is witness—nor do we speak for the purpose of courting human friendships, lest by the speech of our flattery we deceive both ourselves and others. Nor do we speak so that we may seem to be something among human beings, but so that human beings may deserve much in the sight of God.

This, then, is the whole thing that I wish to explain to you while taking you by the hand. And [Al. adds “indeed”], to confess simply the movement of my mind, we are now examining the beginnings and morals of a monk.

If, therefore, you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: that is, withdraw from every unlawful thing from which you are forbidden, and approach readily every good thing that you are commanded to do.

Look to the holy man Pammachius and to Paulinus, a presbyter of the most fervent faith. They offered not only their riches but themselves; against the devil’s evasion they consecrated to the Lord not skin for skin, but their flesh, bones, and souls. By both example and speech—that is, by deed and word—they can lead you to greater things.

Are you noble? So are they, but nobler in Christ. Are you rich and honored? So are they—or rather, from rich and honored men they became poor and without glory, and for that reason richer and more renowned, because they became poor and dishonored for Christ.

You despise gold? Many philosophers despised it as well.

[Col. 0321C] For it is not enough for a perfect and consummate man to despise wealth, scatter money, and throw away what can in an instant both be lost and be found. Crates of Thebes did this [Note: [Col. 0321D] Martianus, following Erasmus, omits “Crates of Thebes did this.”]; Antisthenes did it; many did it, whom we read to have been most vicious.

The disciple of Christ must offer more than the philosopher of the world, that creature of glory and saleable slave of popular favor and rumor.

It is not enough for you to despise riches unless you also follow Christ. The Lord desires you yourself as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God: you, I say, not your possessions.

And God reminds us through various trials, because Israel is instructed by many wounds and pains, and “the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves”; “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews I).

[Col. 0322A] But if you give yourself to the Lord, and, perfect in apostolic virtue, begin to follow the Savior, then you will understand where you have been and how last a place [Al. “foreign”] you have held in Christ’s army.

Fear the superior of the monastery as the Lord, love him as a parent. Believe that whatever he commands you is salutary; and do not judge the decision of one who is greater, whose duty it is to obey and carry out what has been ordered, as Moses says: “Hear, Israel, and be silent.” Do not teach yourself, [Note: The same books omit these words, “and enter the road without a teacher which you have never entered before.”] and do not enter, without a teacher, upon a road which you have never entered before. No art is learned without a master. Even dumb animals and herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Among bees [Variant: riches] there are rulers; cranes follow one another in an ordered formation; there is one emperor, one judge in a province; Rome, from the time it was founded, could not have two brothers as kings together, and was dedicated through parricide [Variant: fratricide]. In Rebecca’s womb Esau and Jacob fought battles. The bishops of the churches are each subject to his own authority, as are the archpriests, the archdeacons, and every ecclesiastical order. In a ship there is one pilot, in a house one master, and in any large army the signal of one commander is awaited.

And, not to weary the reader by repeating more, all this argument tends toward one point: to teach you that you must not be left [Variant: dismissed] to your own judgment, but must live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the fellowship of many, so that you may learn humility from one, patience from another; that one may teach you silence, another gentleness; that you may not do what you wish; that you may eat what you are ordered to eat; that you may wear what you have received; that you may discharge the allotted measure of your work; that you may be subjected to one to whom you do not wish to be subjected; that, tired, you may come to your bed, [Note: And here the same books are silent: “and sleep while walking.”] and sleep while walking, and before your sleep is complete be compelled to rise. Occupied with so many duties, you will have leisure for no thoughts of your own; and while you pass from one task to another, as one work succeeds another, you will retain in your mind only what you are compelled to do.

For obedience is more precious than every offering and sacrifice, as the Prophet says: “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and hearkening than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). And elsewhere: “The beginning of the good way [Variant: life] is to do according to what has been commanded [Variant: the commands that have been received] before God, rather than to offer sacrifices” (Proverbs 16:5). And elsewhere: “He who keeps the law multiplies the offering; a saving sacrifice is to attend to the commandments and depart from every iniquity” (Sirach 35:1). Nor should we flatter ourselves over having carried out commands if we sin by transgressing what has been forbidden, since the guilt of transgression removes the merit of a good deed.

This is proved not by an assertion of my own judgment, but by examples from both Testaments, where we find that even friends of God, through the error of one act of contempt, lost the abundance of the good works they had previously performed. Thus Adam, readily believing the devil who deceived him, after intimacy and conversation with God, was overcome by desire for a single fruit and lost Paradise. And because he presumed to possess one thing through transgression, he lost many good things at once. Thus Lot’s wife, after ministering to the angels, looking back contrary to the prohibition, was suddenly changed into a pillar of salt [Note: Martianus has “contrary to destruction,” incorrectly].

What spirit of presumption is this, which works such audacity in our minds that, although we see holy men punished even for slight faults, we believe that we, sinning daily in greater and more numerous matters, will remain untouched in the midst of condemnation? [Note: Other books read: “eternal.”] Yet it is never a small thing to hold God in contempt even in something insignificant; for he looks not only to the quality of the sin, but also to the contempt shown toward the person. Therefore one must consider not only what is commanded, but also how great is the one who commands.

Here the common saying is excluded which religious people—and those who seem wise to themselves—usually utter to me: “It is enough for us not to commit criminal and serious sins.”

The omission of lesser offenses is easy. While they fill their minds with animal wisdom, they are ignorant of spiritual understanding and of the practice of divine law, which often shows something to be sin that does not seem to us to be sin, and which makes impiety out of what we display as an act of piety. Saul and Jehoshaphat were kings of Israel, and when they showed mercy to those whom God hated, they incurred God’s displeasure in an act of piety (3 Kings 15). Conversely, Phinehas and the sons of Levi earned God’s favor through the killing of human beings and the slaughter of their own people. You see how greatly the divine judgment differs from human perceptions through our ignorance: because we do not know the dispensation of the heavenly Judge, things may sometimes seem unjust to us which, through knowledge of the circumstances, are proved to have been done with complete justice and propriety. And again, things which in our judgment are rightly approved often appear before God to be rejected and displeasing.

Who, following the example of the father Abraham, would wish to slaughter an innocent son (Genesis 22), and would not be judged insane by human opinion? Conversely, who, imitating Uzzah in touching the Lord’s ark (2 Kings 6), would be condemned by human judgment? Let us therefore consider how great is the downfall of one who rashly despises, since such ruin is said to lie in the negligence of one who obeys; or what condemnation we should believe the disobedient will suffer, since the obedient suffered such rejection.

Christ does not love a lukewarm disciple. “Whoever wishes to be my disciple,” he says, “let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” Blessed, therefore, are those souls which have bent their backs to receive upon themselves the Word of God as their rider, and which endure his reins, so that he may turn them wherever he wishes [Note: Other printed books omit: “and guide them with the reins of his commands.”]. For when a master gives an order, it is a sign of obedience if the person, lowering his head, listens; but if he turns his back, it is a sign of contempt.

## CHAPTER II. On the Three Classes of Monks Living in Egypt

And since we have mentioned monks, and I know that you gladly listen to what is holy [Note: Earlier editions read “what has been done,” incorrectly], lend me your ear for a little while. There are three classes of monks in Egypt. The first are the coenobites, whom they call *Sauses* in the local language and whom we may call those who live in common. The second are the anchorites, who live alone in the deserts and are so called because they have withdrawn far from human beings. The third class is called the Remoboth, the worst [Variant: most terrible] and most neglected class, and one which in our province is either the only class or the first.

These live together in pairs or groups of three, and not many more, living according to their own judgment and authority. They contribute to a common fund portions of what they have earned, so that they may have common food. Very many [Variant: very much] of them live in cities and fortified towns; and, as though holiness were an art rather than a life, whatever they sell is priced higher. Quarrels often arise among them, because, living on their own food, they do not tolerate being subject to anyone. In truth, they are accustomed to compete in fasting and to turn the matter of secrecy into a contest.

Among them everything is affected: loose sleeves, boots that billow out, a coarser garment, frequent sighs, visits to virgins, and slander of clerics. And whenever a feast day arrives, they gorge themselves to the point of vomiting.

Having therefore driven out these as so many plagues, let us come to those who are more numerous and live in common—that is, those whom we said are called coenobites. Their first bond is obedience to their superiors and doing whatever they order. They are divided into groups of ten and of one hundred, so that one tenth man presides over nine men, and one hundredth man in turn has ten superiors under him. They remain separate, in separate cells [Note: Rubeus reads: “but with the cells joined together,” as does Victorius]. Until the ninth hour, as is prescribed, no one goes to another, except the deans whom we have mentioned, so that, if someone happens to be wavering in his thoughts, he may be consoled by their conversation.

After the ninth hour they come together. Psalms resound, and the Scriptures are recited according to custom. When the prayers have been completed and everyone has taken his seat, the one in the middle, whom they call the Father, begins to speak. While he is speaking, such silence prevails that no one dares look at another or clear his throat. The speaker’s praise is found in the weeping of his listeners. Tears silently roll over their faces, and grief does not even break out into sobs. But when he begins to proclaim the coming kingdom of Christ, future blessedness, and coming glory, you may see them all, with restrained sighs and eyes raised to heaven, saying to one another: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?” (Psalm 54:7).

After this the assembly is dismissed, and each group of ten goes with its father to the table; they serve in rotation each week. There is no noise during the meal; no one speaks while eating. They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables seasoned only with salt. Only the old men receive wine. [Note: The same edition incorrectly reads: “with whom meals are often taken by the children,” etc.] With them, meals are often taken by the children, so that the worn-out age of some may be supported and the beginning strength of others not broken.

Then they rise together and, after a hymn has been sung, return to their stalls, where each one speaks with his companions until evening and says: “Did you see this man and that one? How much grace there is in him! How great his silence! How measured his walk!”

If they see someone ill, they comfort him. If they see someone fervent in the love of God, they encourage him in his zeal. And because each one keeps watch at night in his own cell apart from the public prayers, they go around to the individual cells and, placing their ears nearby, carefully investigate what they are doing. If they find someone slower than the rest, they do not rebuke him; concealing what they know, they visit him more frequently, and by beginning first they encourage him to pray more, rather than forcing him.

The work assigned for the day is recorded and reported by the dean to the steward, who himself each month gives an account to the father of them all, with great fear. The food prepared is also tasted by him [Variant: tasted beforehand]. The fast of the entire year is uniform, except during Lent, when alone a stricter life is permitted. [Note: Victorius and others read: “From Easter to Pentecost.”] From Pentecost the evening meals are changed into midday meals, both to satisfy ecclesiastical tradition and not to burden the stomach with a double portion of food.

Let me come to the third class, those whom they call anchorites. When they leave the coenobia, they carry nothing further into the deserts except bread and salt. Paul was the founder of this life, Antony its illuminator, and, if we ascend to earlier times, its chief was John the Baptist. The prophet Jeremiah likewise describes such a man, saying: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth” [Variant: the words “of the Lord” are absent]; “he will sit alone and be silent, because he has taken the yoke upon himself, and he will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches, because the Lord has not rejected him forever” (Lamentations 3:27ff.).

At another time, if you wish, I will explain their labor and their manner of life in the flesh but not according to the flesh. Now let me return to the subject. It is good to obey superiors and submit to prefects; after the rules of the Scriptures, to learn the course of one’s life from others, and not to use as one’s teacher the worst teacher of all—namely, one’s own presumption.

## CHAPTER III. On Chastity

“Put to death,” says the Apostle, “your members which are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:5). Hence he later said confidently [Note: Other editions read: “later, considering, he said”]: “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me.” Whoever has put his members to death and has walked through the image of night will not fear saying: “I have become like a leather bottle in the frost” (Psalm 118:83). Hence the same Apostle disciplined his body and brought it into subjection, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified. Speaking in the person of the body, on behalf of the human race, inflamed [Variant: burning] by passions, he said: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” And again: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For the will to do good lies near me, but I do not find the ability to do it” [Note: Erasmus and other printed books omit the word “find”]; “for I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I do not wish.” And again: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

Therefore, after the most diligent vigilance over your thoughts, you must take up the weapons of fasting and sing with David: “I humbled my soul with fasting” (Psalm 34:13). Look at your mother in such a way that through her you are not forced to look at other women whose faces may cling to your heart, leaving a silent wound beneath your breast. Know that the maidservants who serve her lie in wait for you; for the lower their condition, the easier the fall. I therefore want you, for these reasons, not to live with your mother, and especially so that you may neither grieve her [Variant: her herself] by refusing the delicate foods she offers nor, if you accept them, add oil to the fire; and so that among the constant company of girls you may not see during the day what you will think about at night. Do not stain your youth with any defilement, so that you may proceed to Christ’s altar like a virgin from the bridal chamber, and possess a good reputation among outsiders.

Although others may judge the remaining virtues—wisdom, courage, justice [Variant: temperance], humility, gentleness, and generosity—conscience alone knows chastity, and human eyes cannot be reliable judges of it. Let women who know your name not know your face. John the Baptist had a holy mother and was the son of a high priest; yet he was conquered neither by affection for his mother nor by his father’s wealth, so as to live in his parents’ house at the risk of his chastity. He lived in the desert, and with eyes longing for Christ he did not deign to look at anything else. A rough garment, a leather belt, locusts for food, and wild honey: everything was prepared for virtue and self-control.

Thus pleasure overcame the martyr whom torments had not overcome. At last, inspired from heaven, he spat out his tongue, which had been severed by a bite, into the face of the person who kissed him; and so the magnitude of the ensuing pain took away [Variant: overcame] the sense of lust. [Note: Rubeus adds from Book II, Against Jovinian, chapter 7: “The touch of other bodies and an excessively ardent desire for women are close to madness.”] For just as someone who touches fire is immediately burned, so a man senses his own nature when he touches a woman and recognizes the difference of the sexes. [Note: For what follows, beginning “And how,” Rubeus’s edition substitutes the following from Book 3 of the Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 8: “Conscience cannot be concealed by the face and eyes, since a luxurious and wanton mind shines in the face, and the secrets of the heart are revealed by the movement and gestures of the body.”] How, then, will one be able to restrain lust who cannot restrain either his hand or his tongue?

Nor should the feet of women ever wear down the threshold of your little lodging. See that you do not remain under the same roof [Variant: “or”]. Do not trust in chastity preserved in the past. For you cannot be holier than David, stronger than Samson, or wiser than Solomon. Always remember that a woman drove the inhabitant of Paradise from his possession. When you are ill, let some holy brother assist you. For I know of some who recovered in body but began to grow ill in spirit. The person whose face you frequently attend to is dangerously serving you. If, nevertheless, a widow or virgin is visited by you, never enter her house alone. Do not sit alone with a woman alone, without an observer or witness. Let your confidence in conversation be such that when another enters you do not become frightened or ashamed. [Note: Conversely, this section, “For the face is,” is absent from that edition.] For the face is the mirror of the mind, and silent eyes confess the secrets of the heart.

Have as companions men whose association will not bring you disgrace. Let them be adorned not by clothing but by character, and let their dress proclaim chastity. Evil conversations corrupt good morals. Avoid every suspicion; and whatever can plausibly be invented, avoid beforehand lest it be invented. Frequent little gifts, handkerchiefs, ribbons, garments applied to the face, food offered and tasted, and flattering, sweet little letters have no place in holy love. [Note: We have restored this passage according to Rubeus’s copy. Previously it was preceded by “Hear me,” and was then read with another meaning: “and Christ is my desire,” which was also foreign to Jerome’s intention.] “My honey, my light, and my desire.” We blush at all the delights, charms, laughable courtesies, and other absurdities of lovers in comedies, and detest them in worldly people; how much more in clerics and monks, whose priesthood is adorned by their profession and whose profession is adorned by their priesthood?

I do not say this because I fear such things either in you or in holy men, but because in every profession, rank, and sex there are good and evil people, and the condemnation of the evil is the praise of the good. See what benefit restraints provide: they draw us back from vices, introduce us into the choirs of the virtues, and make us dwell in Christ, the most beautiful mountain. [Note: Rubeus substitutes other material here through the passage “If your foot causes you to stumble.” It is enough for us, however, to have provided one or two examples of such interpolations.] As long as you are in your homeland, regard your cell as Paradise; pluck the varied fruits of the Scriptures.

Use these as your delights; enjoy their embrace. If your foot, your eye, or your hand causes you to stumble, cast it away. Spare nothing, so that you may spare your soul alone. “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her,” says the Lord, “has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Who will boast that he has a pure heart? The stars are not clean in the sight of the Lord; how much less human beings, whose life is a time of testing?

Woe to us wretched people: as often as we desire, so often we commit fornication. “My sword,” he says, “has become drunk in heaven”—how much more on earth, which produces thorns and thistles. The chosen vessel, in whose breast [Variant: mouth] Christ resounded, mortifies his body; yet he sees the natural heat of the flesh opposing his own resolve, so that he is compelled to do what he does not wish. And you imagine that you can pass without falling or being wounded unless you guard your heart with every care?

Especially since many, although continent, are angry, drunk, insolent, proud, more puffed up by continence, violent, abusive, greedy, fearful, and highly pleased with themselves, so as to display their continence—as though they asserted that they had supplied material for incontinence.

But the truly continent person is the one who withdraws every function of the members from evil passions and restrains his thoughts from all wickedness. Yet the more numerous the things that attack chastity, the greater are the victor’s rewards.

For when I was young and the deserts of solitude enclosed me, I could not bear the incentives of vice and the heat of nature. When I broke them through frequent fasts, my mind seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I placed myself under the discipline of a certain brother who had believed as one of the Hebrews, so that after the refinements of Quintilian, the gravity of Fronto, the eloquence of Cicero, and the elegance of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice hissing, breath-filled words. My conscience—both mine, who endured it, and that of those who lived with me—bears witness to how much labor I expended there, how often I stopped, and how, through the determination to learn, I began again. And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I gather [Variant: reap] sweet fruits.

The first temptations of clerics are therefore approaches to women. Woman is a harmful species, the door of the devil, the path of iniquity, the sting of a scorpion. When straw comes near, it kindles fire; with fiery flame woman strikes the conscience of the man who lives with her and burns up the foundations of the mountains. I judge that if women live with men, the devil’s snare will not be absent. “If someone binds fire in his bosom, will his garments not be burned?” Believe me: one who is joined to women’s approaches cannot dwell with the Lord with his whole heart.

But you say: “Whoever walks innocently walks confidently” (Proverbs 10:9). Well said and cleverly put; but one must have a good reputation among those outside. Even if you walk rightly before God, good conduct must nevertheless be provided before human beings, because the children of darkness are more cunning than the children of light. When this class of association is not cut off by you, you give room to those who criticize you, since you have handed yourself over to the bites of slanderers. For amid the enticements of pleasure, lust subdues even iron minds. It suffers a greater hunger among virgins, since it thinks everything sweeter that it does not know.

The stories of the pagans tell that sailors were driven headlong onto the rocks by the songs of the Sirens, and that at Orpheus’s lyre trees, beasts, and the hardness of stones were softened.

Chastity is also difficult to preserve amid banquets. A shining skin displays a filthy mind. Although some may think it a greater virtue to despise pleasure when it is present, I consider it safer to remain ignorant of what you seek. The removal of the man, therefore, establishes the weapons of chastity and builds the camp of modesty in better places. After her temptation and suffering at Antioch, Thecla is forbidden to travel together with Paul. No soldier goes to war with his wife. Women living with men make thorns grow; they strike the hidden thoughts of the mind with a sharp blade [Variant: wound them]. No one therefore walks safely among serpents and scorpions.

For lust always leaves regret behind. It is never satisfied, and when extinguished it is rekindled; it grows through use and diminishes [Variant: “and diminishes” is absent], and it does not obey reason, since it is driven by impulse. Hence virginity is happier in that it does not know the incentives of the flesh; widowhood is more wretched [Variant: more anxious] in that it recalls former pleasures in the mind. To a lustful man, the word “chastity” is an offense.

Those who live in a monastery and are numerous together should never go out alone. From a flock of doves, a hawk frequently separates one, which it immediately attacks and tears apart, filling itself with its flesh and blood. Sick sheep leave their flock and are devoured by the mouths of wolves. Let your departure into public be rare; seek martyrs in your own room. You will never have a reason to go out if you always go out only when necessary. Let another’s wound be our warning. When a diseased person has been scourged, a fool will become wiser.

For we see that even things which people consider beneficial to themselves, by God’s will, are turned into destruction. In calm weather a storm arises; nothing is secure when God opposes it. It is also natural for each person, in his own danger, to hope more from someone else.

If you ever sense the outer man sighing for the flower of youth, and after eating, when the sweet procession of lusts has shaken you as you lie in bed, seize the shield of faith, on which the flaming arrows of the devil are extinguished. “All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” (Hosea 3). Although it is difficult for the human soul not to love something, since our mind is drawn by affection toward whatever it encounters, let the love of the flesh be overcome by love of the spirit. Let desire be extinguished by desire; whatever is diminished there, let it increase here.

Do not allow the thought to grow. While the enemy is small, kill it; let wickedness be crushed in the seed. Hear the Psalmist: “Blessed is he who dashes his little ones against the rock” (Psalm 13). It is impossible for a movement of feeling and the heat of the marrow [Variant: “the innate heat of the marrow,” etc.] not to rush into the human mind. Yet the person who immediately kills his thoughts as soon as he begins to think is praised and proclaimed blessed, dashing them against the rock. “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Pure faith allows no delay. When a scorpion appears, it must immediately be crushed.

The devil’s flaming arrows must therefore be extinguished by the cold of fasts and vigils. You are mistaken, brother—you are mistaken if you think that a Christian ever does not suffer persecution. You are attacked most of all when you do not know that you are being attacked. No one is supported by such firmness that he may safely rely on his stability, since the Apostle says: “Let the one who stands take care lest he fall”; for no one is secure when an enemy army is besieging him.

For our adversary, like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, prowls around (1 Peter 5:8); and do you think there is peace? “He sits in ambush with the rich and in secret places, so that he may kill the innocent” (Psalm 9). What we have said about lust let us apply to avarice and to all the vices which solitude avoids. And for this reason let us avoid the crowds of cities, lest we be compelled to do what nature does not so much force us to do as our will.

## CHAPTER IV. On Poverty

Once a rich young man boasted that he had fulfilled everything commanded in the Law. To him the Lord says in the Gospel: “One thing is lacking to you: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me.” The man who said he had done everything could not overcome riches in the first contest. Hence the rich enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty, since it desires inhabitants who are unencumbered and supported by the lightness of wings.

“Go,” he says, “sell”—not part of your property, but everything you possess—and “give,” not to friends, relatives, kinsmen, wife, or children. I will add something more: you will reserve nothing for yourself out of fear of poverty, lest you be condemned with Ananias and Sapphira; rather, give everything to the poor, and make friends for yourself from unrighteous mammon, who may receive you into eternal dwellings, so that you may follow me as Lord. “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29).

O what blessedness—to receive great things for small ones, eternal things for brief ones, things that live forever for things that die, and to have God as one’s debtor! In the Acts of the Apostles, while the blood of our Lord was still warm and faith was still fresh and fervent among believers, everyone sold his possessions and brought their prices to the feet of the Apostles, to show that money must be trampled underfoot; and distribution was made to each according to his need.
