Hence Ananias and Sapphira, timid stewards—rather, double-hearted ones—were condemned because, after their vow, they took away as though it were their own what they had vowed, and reserved for themselves a portion of property that already belonged to another, fearing hunger, which true faith does not fear. They deserved immediate punishment, not through cruelty of judgment, but as an example for correction.

Sell, therefore, everything that you have and give it to the poor, not to the rich, not for luxury but for necessity. Whether he is a priest, a relative, or a kinsman, consider nothing else in him except his poverty.

As is customary in the Egyptian and Syrian monasteries: those who have vowed themselves to God, renouncing the world, trample underfoot all the world’s delights. Would that what we renounce to the world were a matter of will, not necessity, so that poverty might possess the glory it sought rather than the suffering imposed upon it. Otherwise, in view of the miseries of the present age and the swords raging everywhere, he is sufficiently rich who does not need bread, and he is exceedingly powerful who is not compelled to serve.

Many build walls and lay foundations beneath churches; marbles shine, ceilings glitter with gold, and the altar is adorned with gems, while there is no discernment among the ministers of God. Let no one object to me that the rich man in Judea had a temple, a table, lamps, censers, bowls, and other things made of gold. These things were approved by the Lord at the time when priests were offering sacrifices and the blood of animals was the redemption of sins, although all these things had already come beforehand in symbolic form.

But now, when the poor Lord has consecrated the poverty of his own house, let us think of the cross, and let us consider riches to be dirt. Is this a time for you to dwell in paneled houses—that is, houses ornamented and furnished—and things which are intended not so much for use as for pleasure? So says the Prophet. For my dwelling, in which were the Holy of Holies, the cherubim, and the table of the Presence, will be watered with greater abundance: it will become desolate in solitude and will be scorched by the sun. What benefit is there in glittering with gems while Christ is dying of hunger in the poor [Variant: is in danger]? What you possess is no longer yours; it is a stewardship entrusted to you. Beware lest, like a once-faithful and renowned steward of your own possessions, you accept another’s money for distribution.

That Crates of Thebes, once an exceedingly rich man, when he was going to Athens to study philosophy, cast away a great weight of gold. He did not think that he could possess virtues and riches at the same time. Yet we, laden with gold, follow the poor Christ; and, under the pretext of almsgiving, clinging to our former wealth, how can we distribute another’s possessions faithfully when we preserve our own so anxiously? You understand what I am saying. For the Lord has given you understanding in all things: “Except for food, clothing, and evident necessities, give nothing to anyone, lest dogs eat the bread of your children.”

Therefore consider carefully lest you squander Christ’s property imprudently—that is, lest through immoderate judgment you give the property of the poor to those who are not poor, which is an equal act of sacrilege. According to the saying of a very wise man, let generosity perish. There are also those who give little to the poor in order to receive more, and under the pretext of almsgiving seek riches. This should be called hunting rather than almsgiving. In this way beasts, birds, and fish are caught. A little bait is placed on a hook so that the purses of matrons may be dragged out.

But we, humble and very poor, neither possess riches nor deem ourselves worthy to accept what is offered. Country people do not buy balsam, pepper, or dates. “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptations and the devil’s snare and into many desires.” Especially because the age desired by everyone promises us, in empty hope, not the near death owed to mortals by the law of nature but spans of years. No one is so broken in strength or so decrepit in old age that he does not think he will live at least one more year.

But what am I doing? With the ship broken, I am discussing its cargo. We do not understand that Antichrist is drawing near, whom the Lord Jesus will destroy with the breath of his mouth.

A young man may die quickly, but an old man cannot live long, especially since, by comparison with eternity, everything we suffer in the world may be called one day—not a day of dwelling but of pilgrimage. For we are changed every day, yet we believe ourselves eternal. This very thing of which I speak, which I write, which I read, which I correct, is taken from my life. As many points as the clerk writes, so many losses of my time there are.

For all riches arise from injustice: unless one person loses, another cannot find. Hence the common saying seems to me most true: “A rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.” You see people cross seas, keep watch before the doors of the powerful, and endure everything that the condition of slaves scarcely endures, in order to gather riches and obtain some position of distinction. And after they have attained this, they surrender themselves to luxury, pleasures, and every iniquity, so that what avarice gathers, luxury may consume.

These people, therefore, become a dwelling place for demons in return for their labors. Those who ought to be the temple of God become the tents of Ethiopians. After they have grown rich and climbed by right and wrong to the highest rank, then their conscience will always fear death and always fear judgment; and at the slightest fever, like thieves in prison, they will sigh over eternal punishments.

But the rich who have entered the kingdom of heaven, using their riches for good works, have ceased to be rich and should rather be called God’s stewards than rich men. I beg you, therefore, do not seek the profits of the world in Christ’s service. Flee a cleric who is a businessman, one who has become rich from poverty and distinguished from obscurity, as though he were a kind of plague. Especially since I know that you have renounced the entire world and, having cast away and trampled underfoot riches, devote yourself daily to prayer, reading, and fasts.

Clerics cannot be managers and stewards of other people’s houses and estates when they are commanded to despise the resources of their own wealth. The evil of avarice must also be avoided altogether—not merely so that you do not desire what belongs to another, for public laws also punish this, but so that you do not preserve your own things, which are alien to you. “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another,” he says, “who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16).

But you say: “I am a delicate young man, and I cannot work with my hands. If I reach old age, if I begin to fall ill, who will take pity on me?” Hear Jesus speaking to the Apostles: “Do not worry in your heart about what you will eat, nor about what you will put on your body. Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. X). If clothing is lacking, let these words be set before you. If you hunger, listen to the beatitudes concerning the poor and the hungry. If some pain afflicts you, read what the Apostle says: “For this reason I am pleased with my infirmities” (II Cor. XII, 9).

But as for the fact that, abandoning military service, you castrated yourself for the sake of the kingdom of heaven: what else does this mean than that you have pursued the perfect life? The perfect servant of Christ possesses nothing apart from Christ. Or, if he possesses anything apart from Christ, he is not perfect. Therefore, to conclude: if you are perfect, why do you desire your paternal property? The Lord thunders in the words of the Gospel: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matt. VI); and does anyone dare to make Christ a liar by serving both mammon and Christ? Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought to walk as He walked (I Thess. IV, 1). He is abundantly rich who is poor with Christ. For the servants of God, who serve their Lord day and night, who, placed on earth, imitate the way of life of angels, and speak nothing except what pertains to the praises of God, are content with food and clothing; they regard these as riches, wishing to have no more—provided that they preserve their calling. Otherwise, if they desire more, they are judged unworthy even of what is necessary. Whatever can protect our bodies and assist human weakness—those whom nature brings forth naked—this alone should be called a tunic.

If, therefore, you wish to be what the prophet is, what Christ is, give to the poor what will sustain their need, not what will increase their wealth. And if you have anything more than is necessary for your food and clothing, spend it; know that you are its debtor. For the one who tries to retain more than is necessary for himself is convicted of stealing what belongs to another [Martian. tac. *ultra*, “more than”]. Clerics, too, who can be supported by their parents’ goods, commit sacrilege if they accept anything from the poor. For the ancient enemy knows that the struggle is more against continence than against money. What clings externally is easily cast aside; the inward battle is more dangerous.

Zacchaeus was rich; the apostles were poor. Yet, so far as riches were concerned, they abandoned nothing, while in their will they abandoned the whole world. If we offer our wealth to Christ together with our soul, He will gladly receive it. But if we give what is outward to God and what is inward to the devil, the division is not equitable. I do not want you to offer only what a thief can steal, an enemy seize, or confiscation remove; what, like waves and billows, is occupied by masters succeeding one another; what, willingly or unwillingly, you will leave behind at death. Offer what no enemy can take from you. To lay down gold belongs to beginners, not to the perfect; to offer oneself to God belongs properly to Christians. For no one bears the image of the Crucified unless he has made himself naked and dead in this world. Scripture supplies countless examples teaching that avarice must be avoided.

I shall relate something that happened not many years ago. One of the brothers, more frugal than greedy, unaware that the Lord had been sold for thirty pieces of silver, died leaving one hundred solidi, which he had acquired by weaving linen. A council was held among the monks—for about five thousand lived in that same place in separate cells—to determine what should be done. Some said that the money should be distributed to the poor; others, that it should be given to the Church; some, that it should be sent back to his parents. But Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the others whom they call the Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, decreed that it should be buried with him, saying: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII). Let no one think that this was done cruelly. Such terror seized everyone throughout Egypt that leaving behind even one solidus was regarded as a crime.

Avarice is the root of all evils; therefore it is also called by the Apostle the service of idols. The Lord certainly will not kill the righteous soul with hunger. “I was young, and now I am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25). Elijah is fed by ravens serving him. The widow of Sarepta, herself hungry and destined to perish that night with her children, feeds the prophet; and, wondrously, when the jar is filled, she feeds the one who had come to be fed. The Apostle Peter says: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you: rise and walk in the name of Jesus.”

But now many, even if they are silent in speech, speak through their deeds: “I do not have faith or mercy; but what I have—gold and silver—I do not give you.” Hear what Jacob asks: “If the Lord is with me and keeps me on the way by which I travel, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear” (Gen. XXVIII). He asked only for what was necessary. Hence the thieves also said to Saint Hilarion: “What would you do if thieves came to you?” He answered them: “Naked, I do not fear thieves.” They replied: “You can be killed.” “I can,” he said, “but I am not afraid, because I am ready to die.” Those who marvel at the signs and wonders he performs should also marvel at his incredible abstinence, knowledge, and humility.

For my part, I marvel at nothing so much as his ability to trample glory and honor underfoot, because it is difficult to surpass glory by virtue and to be loved by those whom you surpass. Since, therefore, you rejoice in Christ’s freedom and are almost upon the rooftop, you ought not descend from the roof to retrieve your tunic. Do not look back, nor let go of the plow-handle once you have taken hold of the plow. Rather, if possible, imitate Joseph and leave the cloak of the Egyptian mistress behind, so that naked you may follow the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel: “Unless someone takes up his cross and follows me, he cannot be my disciple” (Matt. X). Cast off the burden of the world. Do not seek riches, which are compared to the burdens borne by camels [Al. *pravitatibus*, “depravities”]. Naked and light, fly to heaven; do not let the weights of gold depress the wings of your virtues, so that you may fill the purse which the Lord commands to be emptied.

If, therefore, those who possess estates and riches are commanded to sell everything, give it to the poor, and then follow the Savior, your dignity ought not to seek out what it may distribute. That poor widow in the Gospel, who put two small coins into the treasury, is preferred to all the rich because she gave everything she had. You, too, therefore, should not seek what you might distribute, so that Christ may recognize you as His most courageous recruit, so that the father may gladly meet you as you come from a very distant land, give you a robe and a ring, and slaughter the fatted calf for you.

## CHAPTER V. On the Benefit of Poverty

The poor man should be comforted in such a way that he knows that greater goods are to be considered in poverty. First, that God has provided for him beneficially. He should understand that God foresaw and considered his weakness, and knew that he could not carry the burden and anxiety of riches. Next, he should know how many temptations and dangers he has passed through by virtue of poverty, since abundance is often its opposite. One passes more quickly and without hindrance to the riches of the soul in poverty; certainly, let him consider how many evils he has escaped. He is free from envy, rivalry, ambushes, deceit, pride, contention, and all those things which riches commonly produce for human beings in this world. For through the flowing away of possessions and the abundance of resources the soul is loosened; the vigor of the mind is weakened, and the strength of the body is enervated. But in poverty there are no wanton banquets or shameful drinking bouts: everything is sober, everything strict, everything humble but not degraded, because all is filled with a pure conscience and virtue; it is not overflowing with external possessions.

A person does not easily approach the riches of the soul—that is, the virtues—when he is rich in this world. For when the Son of God says that it is more difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, He plainly implies that it is easier for the poor man, lest the poor person think himself excluded from God’s care. The Prophet testifies, saying: “I made both the poor and the rich; my care is equal for all.” For God is not a respecter of persons. He does not profess to care only for one who flourishes in the riches of the world, but sustains care for everyone, including the poor. He will reward whoever He finds humble in riches or patient in poverty; the distribution and service, as it were, of the entire human body is sought in each of its members.

Consider that the human being is one body, but has many members. Are all of them an eye, or a foot, or the other members? Rather, as the Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says in faith and truth (I Tim. II): “To those members which are less honorable we assign greater honor.” And just as the virtue of each member is demonstrated in its proper order and function, so in the body of the whole human race poverty and riches are placed as lesser and greater members, so that God’s kindness may be proved by His judgment.

The poor man ought to rejoice and give thanks to God because, freed from many bonds of inheritance, he is not burdened on the day of testing by the shackles of possessions. The disciple follows the Lord more easily when free and entangled in no bonds. Let him also show, insofar as he can, just mercy toward the needy. For just as a person is made righteous by frugality, so the one who distributes to inferiors and to those who have nothing should not fear that he himself will fail, since he possesses the readiest willingness for holy service. He will lack nothing. Let him not desire to become rich in this world, lest he acquire many evils for himself, as the glorious Paul says and urges: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (ibid., VI).

Indeed, if by true faith and for the sake of salvation he believes that heavenly riches should be sought and acquired for himself—riches which each person obtains and takes up through mercy and other good deeds—then eternal things must be preferred to temporal, lasting things to fleeting, things of security to things of anxiety, things free from danger to dangerous things, and what is glorious to what is dishonorable. Since Christ said, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI), I believe no one can doubt that those for whom heavenly things are being prepared will not lack an abundance of necessary earthly goods. Therefore, in accordance with these admonitions, let the rich be restrained and the poor be lifted up. The powerful, the noble, and the rich find it difficult to believe God; and it is even more difficult for those who are eloquent. Their minds are blinded by riches, resources, and luxury; surrounded by vices, they cannot see virtues.

Blessed, therefore, is the person who glories not in riches, wisdom, worldly power, or eloquence, but in the sufferings of Christ. Nothing is more wretched than to despise God for the sake of money. Therefore, if you notice someone always or frequently speaking about money, consider him a shopkeeper rather than a monk.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Correction and Instruction of a Superior

The rector, suppressing his own honor, should assign equal treatment to upright-living subjects [Note: [Col. 0335] The word *deputet* was absent. These words are taken from commentaries on the Lamentations of Jeremiah falsely attributed to Jerome.] and should not fear to exercise the rights of justice toward the perverse. For it is clear that nature generated all human beings equal; but by the variety of their merits, the order of guilt has placed some beneath others. Negligent rulers of the Church of God are also censured, because through their carelessness all the beauty of the Christian people perishes, when they do not strive in meditation on divine law, in the practice of piety, or in the exercise of sacred virtues. The teaching of teachers is sweet only when teaching and life agree together. Nor should they think that peace has been restored to their churches by their own knowledge and wisdom, but by God’s help. If they preserve their rank, they are the house of God and, as it were, an angel of the Lord. But if they wish to appear more knowledgeable than others, they eventually reveal that they do not hold to the rule of truth.

A teacher also corrects the disciple whom he sees to possess a more ardent intellect. For if a physician ceases to treat, he despairs. It is no small merit before God to raise children well. It is also the duty of superiors to recognize the sweat of those who labor, to extend a hand to the fallen, and to show the way to those who have gone astray. But do not glory in having many disciples. The Son of God taught in Judaea, and only twelve apostles followed Him. The whole people applauded the teaching of the Pharisees. A disciple injures his teacher if, through his negligence, he destroys the teacher’s commands and labor.

Therefore there should be no diversity of punishment where the sins are equal. Show favor to no person, however powerful or noble he may be; if he has sinned, correct him. For confusion is followed by disgrace; disgrace by correction; correction by consolation; consolation by salvation. True friendship ought not to pretend not to notice what it perceives. It is not cruelty to punish crimes for God’s sake, but piety. Yet nothing more cruel, nothing more wretched, can be found than to be unwilling, through fear of one’s own death, to defend the salvation of one’s children.

When you teach in the Church, let it be not the shouting of the people but their groaning that is aroused; let the tears of your hearers be your praise. The presbyter’s speech should be seasoned with the reading of Scripture. Hence the Apostle commands: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt.” If it becomes tasteless, it is thrown outside and loses the dignity of its name. For just as the Lord’s victory is the triumph of His servants, so the teacher’s learning is the progress of his disciples. Unless the head [Al. *cerebrum*, “brain”] is healthy, all the members are diseased.

When there is no teaching in the churches, we shall understand that chastity is perishing, continence is dying, and all virtues are passing away, because people have not eaten the word of the Lord. Scripture is useful to those who hear it when it is not learned apart from Christ, when it is not proclaimed without the Father, and when the preacher does not communicate it without the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0337D] Previously, *non probatur* (“is not proved”) stood here, and immediately afterward *non jam insinuat* (“does not now insinuate”).]. But it is difficult to find a worthy herald of Christ’s virtues—one who, in announcing them, seeks not his own glory but the glory of the One whom he preaches.

It is also disgraceful to preach Jesus crucified, poor, and hungry while stuffing one’s own body and to proclaim the doctrine of fasts with reddened cheeks and swollen mouths. Therefore, let your deeds not contradict your speech, so that when you speak in the churches each person may silently answer: “Why do you yourself not do what you say?” Even a thief can denounce avarice. Let the priest’s voice agree with his mind. For how can the ruler of a church remove evil from its midst if he has fallen into the same offense? With what freedom does he rebuke the sinner when he silently answers himself that he has committed the very things he rebukes? He loses the authority to teach when his conduct destroys his speech. And there is that saying of Tully: “The chief point of the art is to teach what you do.”

I have always revered not wordy rusticity but holy simplicity. Whoever says that in speech he imitates the apostles should first imitate their virtues and life; in them, the greatness of their holy name excused their simplicity of speech. Ecclesiastical dignity does not make a person a Christian; nor is it easy to stand in Paul’s place or hold Peter’s rank, since they now reign with Christ. Beware lest the angel of the Lord come and tear apart the veil of your temple and remove your lampstand from its place.

Therefore, if you are going to build a tower, calculate the expense of the work to come. Just as it is not being in Jerusalem but living well in Jerusalem that deserves praise, so let us first act and then teach, lest the authority of our teaching be destroyed by chaste deeds. For the world is full of eloquent speakers and declaimers. They speak about what they do not know; they teach what they have not learned. They become teachers though they were never disciples.

Do not rush too quickly into writing, carried away by light-minded madness. Learn for a long time what you are to teach, and do not, with the rashness of certain people, teach what you do not know; first learn what you are going to teach [Al. *dicturus*, “going to say”]. For whoever neglects to hear and understand the words of the wise repeatedly does not know how to govern his own life; how much less can he benefit the governance of others? Therefore, it is fitting for you to be a servant to servants. In all things teach in such a way that whoever hears you may advance more through your way of life than through your speech. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.

But let us not immediately submit to the judgment of the multitude; rather, having been chosen for leadership, let us recognize our measure and humble ourselves beneath the powerful hand of God. Truly, nothing is uglier than a furious teacher, when he ought to be gentle and learned. Instead, with grim face, trembling lips, wrinkled brow, and unrestrained insults, he shouts amid tumult, his face changing between pallor and redness. Through his savagery he draws those who have gone astray not so much toward the good as toward evil, driving them headlong. For not everyone who becomes angry is habitually irascible; rather, that is the person who is repeatedly overcome by this passion. There are also many who teach what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful profit, who overturn entire households and think that piety is a source of gain. It often happens that we engage in controversies over the law not out of a desire for truth but out of vainglory, wishing to be considered learned by our hearers. Let us therefore hasten with steady step to the teachers, wear their thresholds smooth, and regard the commands of virtue and the mysteries of Scripture as eternal bonds.

## CHAPTER VII. On Solitude

Indeed, to speak frankly about the movement of my mind: considering both your purpose and the ardor with which you renounced the world, I think there is a distinction of places. If you leave cities and the crowds of cities, live in a small field, seek Christ in solitude, and pray alone on the mountain with Jesus, enjoying only the proximity of holy places, then you will be free of the city without abandoning the purpose of a monk. I am not speaking of bishops or clerics, whose case is different from that of monks. Clerics feed sheep; I am fed. I am speaking of the monk who laid the price of his possessions at the apostles’ feet, teaching that money must be trampled underfoot, and who, living humbly and privately, always despises what he once despised. For it is the height of folly to renounce the world, leave one’s homeland, abandon the cities, profess to be a monk, and live abroad among great populations [Al. *periculosius*, “more dangerously”].

Since you ask me fraternally by what road you ought to proceed, I shall speak to you openly. If you wish to perform the office of a presbyter, or if the work or honor of a bishopric attracts you, live in cities and fortified towns, and make the salvation of others a gain for your soul. But if you wish to be what you are called—a monk—what are you doing in cities, which certainly are not habitations for the solitary but for the many?

Each calling has its own leaders. Roman commanders should imitate Camillus, Fabricius, Regulus, and Scipio. Philosophers should set before themselves Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Poets should emulate Homer, Virgil, Menander, and Terence. Historians, Thucydides, Sallust, Herodotus, and Livy. Orators, Lysias, the Gracchi, Demosthenes, and Tully. And to come to our own sphere: bishops and presbyters should have the apostles and apostolic men as examples; possessing their honor, they should strive also to possess their merit.

But let Paul, Antony, Julian, Hilarion, and Macarius be the leaders of our vocation. And, to return to the authority of Scripture, Elijah is our leader, Elisha our leader, and our commanders are the sons of the prophets who lived in fields and solitudes and made tabernacles for themselves near the streams of the Jordan. Among them also are the sons of Rechab, who did not drink wine or strong drink and lived in tents. They are praised by the voice of God through Jeremiah, and it is promised to them that a man standing before the Lord will never fail from their lineage.

Interpret, then, the name “monk”: this is your name. What are you doing among the crowd when you are solitary? Your situation is not the same as that of others. “No prophet has honor in his own country.” For where there is no honor, there is contempt; where there is contempt, frequent insult; where there is insult, indignation; where there is indignation, no rest; where there is no rest, the mind is often drawn away from its purpose. And where something is taken away from diligence through unrest, the thing diminished becomes less. Where there is less, perfection cannot be claimed.

From this calculation arises the conclusion that a perfect monk cannot be in his own country. But to refuse to be perfect is to sin. As for where I now am, I do not know not only what is happening in my homeland but even whether my homeland still exists. Indeed, I am not permitted even one corner of the desert; every day I am asked to prove my faith, as though I had been born again without faith.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Praises and Benefit of the Desert

What, then, are you doing in the world, brother, when you are greater than the world? Do you fear poverty? Christ calls the poor blessed. Are you terrified by labor? No athlete is crowned without sweat. Are you thinking about food? True faith does not fear hunger. Do you fear striking your limbs, worn out by fasts, against the bare ground? The Lord lies beside you. Do you dread the unkempt hair of your dirty head? Christ is your head. Does the infinite vastness of the desert terrify you? Walk through paradise in your mind; whenever you ascend there, you will not be in the desert.

O desert blooming with the flowers of Christ! O solitude in which those stones are born from which the city of the great King is built in the Apocalypse! O desert rejoicing in God with intimate familiarity—and so forth! To this also applies the Apostle’s saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

Why, then, are you a Christian with a timid heart? The Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head; you measure broad porticoes and immense spaces of buildings. While you await an inheritance in this world, you cannot be Christ’s co-heir. The desert loves the naked. A body accustomed to tunics cannot bear the weight of armor. A head covered with linen refuses a helmet. A hand softened by leisure is roughened by the hard mattock.

“But why,” you ask, “do you go to the desert?” Surely so that I may not hear you or see you, so that I may not be stirred by your fury or endure your battles, so that the eye of a prostitute may not capture me, and so that a most beautiful form may not lead me into illicit embraces.

You will reply: “This is not fighting but fleeing. Stand in the battle line; armed, resist your adversaries, so that after you have conquered you may be crowned.” I confess my weakness. I do not want to fight in the hope of victory, lest someday I lose the victory. If I do not flee, I must either conquer or fall. Why is it necessary to abandon certainties and pursue uncertainties? Death must be avoided either by the shield or by the feet. You who fight may be overcome or may conquer. When I flee, I do not conquer what I flee; I flee so that I may not be conquered. There is no security in sleeping beside a serpent: it may happen that it does not bite me. Flight is an indication not of faithlessness but of prudence, so that we do not needlessly offer ourselves to dangers.

Recently you saw the deserts of Egypt. You looked upon an angelic community. How many flowers are there! How the meadows bloom with spiritual jewels! You saw the garlands with which the Lord is crowned. Let that fire burn in your breast. Think of it, dwell upon it, contemplate it [Al. *desidera*, “desire it”] every day, and, as though confined in a prison, cry out: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX). Ascending to paradise in your mind, you will not be on earth as often as you have despised earthly things.

Certainly, our condition is the same as that of those who live in the deserts: we have the same eyes, the same number of hands, and are subject to the same weaknesses and virtues. If drinking water troubles you, how many nobles—not merely know nothing of wine, but are ignorant of meat—and are sustained only by poured-in [Al. *infuso*, “infused”] legumes? If baths concern you, how many rulers of cities, deported to islands either for their own guilt or through envy, remain without baths, without eternal reward or perpetual recompense? No one can be unwilling to endure from necessity what he refuses to endure willingly for God.

You will have a cell large enough to contain you alone. Indeed, you will not be alone: an angelic multitude will be present, as many companions as there are saints. You will read the Gospel; Jesus will converse with you. You will repeat the words of the apostles or prophets. Could you have such another companion through your own conversations? We are earth and ashes, continually anxious about our salvation and destined at every moment to dissolve into dust. Why do we refuse to make virtue out of necessity? Certainly, we must die someday. Let us quickly leave behind the narrow confines of the world; and if, perhaps because of continence—which nevertheless rarely happens—we begin to suffer stomach pain or burn with fevers, let us regard the illness as the doorway through which we enter eternal life. How many have been snatched away by sudden death amid immense wealth and the insignia of the consulship [Al. *tabulas*, “tablets”]!

Why, then, do we desire the crowds of cities, when we are defined by solitude? For me, the town is a prison and solitude is paradise. Avoid also the company of worldly people, especially the powerful. Why do you need so often to see those people whose contempt made you begin to be a monk? Solitude makes a monk, not public life.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Danger of the Solitary Life

We are now also examining the conduct of the monk who has placed Christ’s yoke upon his neck. First, we must consider whether you should live alone or with others in a monastery. I approve of your having the fellowship of holy people, lest you enter without a guide upon a road you have never traveled, immediately turning aside in one direction or another, exposed to error, walking more or less than necessary, becoming exhausted through running, or falling asleep through delay.

When someone is placed in solitude, pride creeps in. If he fasts for a little while and sees no human being, he thinks himself a person of some importance. Forgetting from where and to where he has come, he wanders inwardly in his heart and outwardly with his tongue. Against the Apostle’s will, he judges another’s servant [Al. *suos*, “his own servants”]. He extends his hands wherever gluttony demands; he sleeps as long as he wishes; he fears no one; he considers everyone beneath him; and he is more often in cities than in his cell. Among the brothers he pretends modesty, though he is jostled amid the crowds of the streets.

What, then? Do we condemn the solitary life? Not at all, since we have often praised it, although, as has been said, the solitary life is dangerous: those withdrawn from the company of human beings may become exposed to filthy and impious thoughts; filled with arrogance and haughtiness, they may despise everyone and arm their tongues by slandering either clerics or monks. But we wish soldiers of this kind to emerge from the training ground of monasteries—men whom the harsh rudiments of the desert do not frighten, who have displayed the pattern [Al. *speciem*, “appearance”] of their way of life over a long period, who have been the least of all so that they might become first of all, whom neither hunger nor satiety has ever overcome, who rejoice in poverty, and whose clothing, speech, face, and gait are instruction in virtue.

How often, while established in the desert and in that vast solitude which, scorched by the heat of the sun, provides monks with a harsh dwelling, I thought I was taking part in Roman delights! I sat alone because I was filled with bitterness. My misshapen limbs, clothed in sackcloth, were dreadful to behold, and my squalid skin had taken on the appearance of Ethiopian flesh. Every day there were groans; and whenever approaching sleep overcame me despite my resistance, I struck my barely joined bones against the bare ground. As for food and drink, I say nothing: even the sick monks there used cold water, and to have received anything cooked was considered luxury.

Yet I, who because of fear of Gehenna had condemned myself to such a prison, living only with scorpions and wild beasts, often found myself among choirs of girls. My face grew pale from fasting, while my mind burned with desire in my cold body; and [the phrase *ante hominem suum* is uncertain], though the flesh was already half-dead, only the fires of lust were boiling. Thus, deprived of every aid, I threw myself at the feet of Jesus, drenched them with tears, wiped them with my hair, and subdued my rebellious flesh through weeks of hunger. I am not ashamed [Al. *depudesco*, “I am not embarrassed”] of my misfortune; rather, I mourn that I am not what I once was.

I remember crying out and frequently joining day to night, and not ceasing to beat my breast until tranquility returned at the Lord’s rebuke [Al. *imperante*, “command”]. I was even afraid of the cell itself, as though it were conscious of my thoughts. Angry and severe with myself, I penetrated the deserted places alone. Wherever I saw hollow valleys, rugged mountains, or sheer cliffs, there was the place of my prayer; there I established the prison of my most wretched flesh [Al. the words *collocabam*, “I established,” are absent]. And, as the Lord is my witness, after many tears, after fixing my eyes upon heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be present among the ranks of angels, and joyfully sang: “After you, we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I, 3).

I shall also relate something else that I saw in Egypt. There was a Greek youth in a coenobium who could extinguish the flame of the flesh neither through continence nor through any magnitude of labor. The father of the monastery saved him when he was in danger by the following stratagem. He ordered a serious man to harass the youth with quarrels and insults, and after inflicting the insult, to be the first to come and complain. Witnesses were summoned, and they spoke in favor of the man who had delivered the abuse. The youth began to weep at the falsehood. The father alone carefully tried to oppose his defense, lest the brother be overwhelmed by excessive grief.

What more need be said? A year passed in this way. When it was over, the youth was asked about his former thoughts and whether he still suffered any distress. “Father,” he replied, “am I not permitted to live, and yet should I desire to fornicate?” If he had been alone, what helper would have enabled him to overcome? “Two are better than one,” and if one falls, the other will support him. “A threefold cord is not easily broken,” and a brother helping his brother will be exalted.

I have seen some who, after renouncing the world, changed nothing of their former way of life except their clothing and the profession [Al. *promissione*, “promise”] of their voice, not their actions. Their household property increased rather than diminished. The same servants’ services, the same banquet preparations—and they claim for themselves the name of solitary. Others, though poor and of modest means, think themselves learned; like display dishes, they proceed into public so that they may exercise their dog-like eloquence.

There are also those who, through the dampness of their cells, immoderate fasts, weariness of solitude, and excessive reading—while their ears resound day and night—are turned toward melancholy. They need the fomentations of Hippocrates more than our admonitions. Many cannot give up their former trades and business dealings; changing only their names, they conduct the same commerce as shopkeepers. They pursue not the food and clothing commanded by the Apostle, but profits greater than those of worldly people; under the title of religion they practice unjust gains, and the honor of the Christian name makes more frauds than it endures.

And what one may be ashamed to say, but must say so that at least in this way we may blush at our disgrace: while publicly extending our hands, we conceal gold beneath rags; and, contrary to everyone’s opinion, we die rich with full purses, though we lived as though poor.

When you are in a monastery, you will not be permitted to do this. As the habit gradually grows upon you, you will begin to want what at first you were compelled to want, and your labor will delight you. Forgetting the past, you will always pursue what lies ahead, considering not what evil others do but what good you ought to do. Do not be led by the multitude of sinners [Note: [Col. 0343D] In Rubeus these words, “nor let the crowd of the perishing trouble you,” are absent.], nor let the crowd of the perishing trouble you [Col. 0343C], so that you silently think: “What, then? Will everyone who lives in cities perish? Look, they enjoy their possessions, serve the Church, go to the baths, and do not reject perfumes; yet they are spoken of by everyone.”

I have already answered this, and I answer briefly again: in the present little work I am not discussing clerics but instructing a monk.

## CHAPTER X. On the Danger of Living in Cities
Consider, I beg you, how difficult it is to fill the place of Stephen or Paul and to stand in the angelic ministry. [Note: [Col. 0343D] These words are taken from the letter addressed to Praesidius, which is counted among the spurious letters. Rubeus and others therefore add, from its context, the words “and to look down upon the peoples lying beneath from a shining garment above.” A little later they also have: “nor feel the waves and the ship’s planks.”] A precious pearl is quickly broken, and once broken cannot be restored. A ship, even if it is unsophisticated, fastened with solid nails, and does not feel the swelling waves, is quickly pierced if it sails dangerously; and although, with full winds, it may reach its destination more profitably, nevertheless those things are safer which are also peaceful. I shall speak more plainly: you say that you receive greater reward if, while remaining in the middle of the city, you [Note: [Col. 0344D] The same books read: “the life of monks is …” These are true, etc.] live as a monk; and what you say is true, but it is not fulfilled in practice as easily as it is expressed in words.

For if someone of the nobility invites you to dinner, certainly you must either go or refuse. If you go, you must either eat the same foods or different ones. If different, the eyes of the banqueters are offended. If the same, abstinence is lost. But if you decide not to go, poor man, you will be devoured at dinner over every cup and wines sweetened with honey: one person will mock your face, another ridicule your walk, another your clothing; and perhaps, imitating the Jews, they will say: “Is this not the son of the carpenter? Are not his brothers [Al. add. “and sisters”] among us? I remember him doing that shameful thing almost so many years ago, and saying something still more shameful.” Another will call you a thief and pretend that he shares your crime [Al. “adultery”]. Every dinner will echo in the same way, and the drunken banquet will break up at your expense.

And if you abstain from every kind of meat and do not frequently visit the baths, then indeed the label “Manichaean” will be written across every column. If you refuse to eat birds, and deny the appetite that longs for tender doves and fat turtle-doves, the charge of sacrilege is fastened upon you; and immediately they say: “These are the people who condemn the Creator of the world. Everything was made for our use.” I heard—God is my witness, I am not lying—that a certain man eloquent in matters of his appetite, when he learned by rumor that I abstained from more delectable foods, said: “Was the pig made for a man in the toga to deliver a senatorial opinion?” By this he plainly condemned me for folly, thinking that I did not consume things created for use.

And if your tunic is dark, you will even be pointed out by the fingers of passers-by. Thus, unless you are handsome, you cannot be holy. When such things and the like tear apart a good life, what are you doing in the midst of them, brother? You will submit your neck either to vices or to an anathema—that is, you will pursue things opposed to continence. Or, if you refuse to do so, you will be condemned in due course [Al. “you yourself will be condemned”].

I pass over the frequent greetings, the attentions of married women, and the various allurements by which even the most rigid are softened [Al. add. “in spirit”], when they are dragged toward shipwreck by a siren’s song. But this I affirm: even if these things did not exist, nevertheless, in comparison with so great a good, you ought to abandon greater things. Since we find such abundance in heaven, let us grieve that we sought small and perishable things on earth. Ambition, power, the greatness of the city, being seen and seeing, greeting and being greeted, praising or disparaging, listening or speaking, and even seeing such a multitude of people, at least unwillingly, are alien to the purpose of monks and to quiet. For either we see those who come to us, and lose our silence; or, if we do not see them, we are accused of arrogance. Sometimes, in order to return the favor, we go to proud doors and, amid the tongues of servants who gnaw at others, enter gilded doorposts. But in Christ’s villa, as we have learned [Al. omits “as we have learned”], everything is rustic. Therefore, because of our occupations, either we must close the door to ourselves, or abandon the study of the Scriptures, for whose sake the doors ought to be opened.

Invited by these considerations, many philosophers abandoned the crowds of the cities and their suburban gardens, where there was irrigated land, leafy trees, the murmuring of birds, a spring rippling like a mirror, and many attractions for the eyes and ears—lest through luxury and an abundance of resources the soul’s strength should grow soft and its chastity be violated. For it is useless constantly to see the things by which you were once captured and to expose yourself to things of which you can hardly deprive yourself. Those whom the prison of the world encloses are dragged to ruin, now by anger, now by avarice, now by lust, now by the incentives of other vices.

[Col. 0345B] Therefore the soul’s pleasures must be trampled down and the pursuit of delights abandoned, because this is the reality of circumcision, not merely its figure. We must strive above all that, after natural things have been cut away, our conduct may tend toward heaven. This will happen if games, jokes, banquets, and almost all familiar conversation are abandoned, and the things that are circumcised wither: not by sight, not by hearing, not by touch, not by taste, or [the text is uncertain] “will seize in the nature of the body a corporeal nature not to possess.”

[Note: [Col. 0345D] For the following words down to “Therefore,” Rubeus substitutes different wording so that, he says, the sense of the words, which is not very clear, may be more apparent. At the end we have supplied only the word “were” (*fuimus*) from the manuscript. Moreover, for “or it will seize” (*aut capiet*), the continuous sense appears to require: “not be seized by taste, and in nature,” etc.]

For if we wish to despise what we are, we deserve to be better than we were. Therefore let us not rashly offer ourselves to dangers, but, as far as lies in us, avoid ambushes.

## CHAPTER XI. On Abstinence, Especially from Meat

Our Savior says: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21:34). Moderate and temperate food is useful both to body and soul. Do not seek the warming treatments of baths, you who wish to extinguish the body’s heat through the cold of fasts; let the baths themselves be moderate, lest excess weaken the stomach and, demanding greater replenishment, issue in indigestion, which is the parent of lust.

For physicians who have written about the nature of human bodies—especially Galen in his books entitled *On Healthy Things* (Greek: περὶ ὑγιεινῶν), concerning the bodies of children and young men and of men and women of mature age—say that these bodies boil with inborn heat, and that foods harmful to these ages are those that increase heat; they say that it contributes to health to take cold things in food and drink. Conversely, for the elderly, who suffer from phlegm and cold, hot foods and old wines are beneficial. The comic poet too, whose purpose is to know and describe human character, said: “Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.”

Know, therefore, that nothing is so beneficial for Christian youths as eating vegetables. The heat of the body must be tempered with cooler foods. For we seek not the appearance of the body but the vigor of the soul, which becomes stronger through the weakness of the flesh. This is why some who pursue a chaste life collapse halfway along the road: they think only of abstaining from meat and load their stomachs with legumes, which, taken moderately and sparingly, are harmless. And to say what I think, nothing inflames the body and tickles the genital members so much as undigested food and violent belching. Whatever is the seedbed of pleasures, consider poison.

Eating meat is a seedbed of lust. And I am not speaking only of meat: among legumes too, those that cause bloating and are heavy must be avoided. Sparse food and an empty stomach are preferable to three-day fasts. It is much better to take a little every day than to take enough only rarely. The best rain is that which descends gradually upon the earth. A sudden and excessive downpour rushes headlong and overturns the fields. Restoration of strength, therefore, should avoid satiety. It is of no benefit to carry an empty stomach for two or three days if it is then overwhelmed all at once, if fasting is balanced by satiety. At once the mind grows sluggish when filled, and, watered by the body’s moisture, it produces thorns of lust. [Note: [Col. 0346D] Rubeus reads: “Watered earth produces thorns,” etc.]

There are also many who are sober with respect to wine but drunk with the abundance of food. All who pursue drunkenness are called sons of Belial. For a belly seething with unmixed wine easily [Al. “quickly”] foams over into lust. Thus Noah uncovered his thighs through drunkenness. Lot, whom Sodom had not conquered, was conquered by wine. A full belly also speaks easily about fasting. But whoever desires Christ and feeds upon his bread does not greatly inquire with what expensive foods he may make dung. Whatever is not perceived after passing the throat becomes the same as bread and legumes. Everything for which people labor in this world is, as it were, consumed by the mouth, worn down by the teeth, and handed over to the belly for digestion; and it affords pleasure only as long as it is held in the throat. When it has passed into the bowels, there is no longer any distinction among foods.

Nor do we say this because we deny fish; but just as we prefer virginity to marriage, so we prefer fasting to satiety. Yet do not think that you abstain from meat merely because you reject the flesh of swine, hares, deer, and four-footed animals. These are approved not by the number of their feet but by the pleasure of their taste. We know that the Apostle said: “Every creature of God is good, and is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy IV). But he also says: “It is good not to eat meat” (Romans XIII). Let those who serve the flesh eat meat. Let the intestines of those whose ardor foams over into intercourse be filled with meat.

But as for you, let nothing be so necessary to you as persevering in fasting. Let pallor and filth be your jewels. Therefore, when you say to me, “Why was the pig created?” I shall immediately answer you, like children arguing: “Why were vipers and scorpions?” Nor will you judge God to be the maker of superfluous things, since there are very many beasts and birds whose flesh your jaws reject. But lest this seem contentious and arise more from dispute than from truth, listen: pigs, boars, and the remaining animals were created so that soldiers, athletes, sailors, orators, miners, and all others assigned to hard labor might have food—those who require bodily strength, who carry weapons and provisions, who weaken one another’s limbs with fists and kicks, who pull oars, whose sides are strong for shouting and speaking, who overturn mountains, and who sleep under the open sky [Al. “in sweat”] and in the rain.

But what is that to us, whose conduct is in heaven? Our religion trains and follows not an athlete, sailor, soldier, or miner, but a seeker of wisdom who has dedicated himself to the worship of God and knows why he was created, why he lives in the world, and toward what place he hastens to depart. Hence the Apostle also says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (1 Corinthians XII); and: “Though our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians IV); and: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians III); and: “Do not make provision for the flesh” (Romans XIII). We can live without four senses—that is, without sight, hearing, smell, and embrace. But without taste and food it is impossible for the human body to subsist.

Reason must therefore be present, so that we take such and so much food that the body is not burdened and the soul’s freedom is not weighed down. For one must eat, walk, sleep, digest, and afterward the incentives of lust are sustained [Al. “must be restrained”] by swollen veins. Our senses are indeed gates through which the world’s blandishments descend into our soul and through which the perceptions of the flesh enter. Unless, after making a great breach, we make a way for virtues rather than for impiety, we shall never be able to reach the King of piety.

Let each person say where he suffers [Al. “what he wishes”]; I speak of my own conscience. I know that abstinence has harmed me when interrupted and benefited me when resumed. Let us therefore not take foods that we either digest with difficulty or regret having eaten at great cost and lost through much labor. Vegetables, fruits, and legumes are easier to prepare; they do not require the skill and expense of cooks, and they sustain the human race without care when taken moderately, because they are not devoured greedily. What lacks the stimulus of gluttony is digested more easily. No one is burdened with one or two foods, and those inexpensive, until the belly swells—as happens through the variety of meats and the delight of flavor, when dishes steam with varied aromas and, once hunger has been satisfied, drag people captive to their own consumption. Hence diseases too are aroused by excessive satiety. Many remedy the impatience of their appetite by vomiting, and what they have shamefully put in, they expel still more shamefully.

After Christ came at the end of the ages and turned the omega back to the alpha—that is, the end back to the beginning—so that, as in the first age, we are not circumcised, are not permitted to give a writ of divorce, and do not eat meat, Hippocrates teaches in the *Aphorisms* that thick and corpulent bodies which have reached the measure of their growth, unless they are quickly reduced by bloodletting, produce paralysis and the worst kinds of disease [Al. “break out into…”]. For this reason reduction is necessary, so that they may again have room in which they can grow. Nature does not keep bodies in one condition, but either makes them grow or diminish; nor can an animal live unless it is capable of growth.

Hence that most learned interpreter of Hippocrates, Galen, says in his *Exhortation to Medicine* that athletes, whose life and profession consist in fattening, cannot live long or remain healthy. Their souls, he says, are so wrapped in excessive blood and fat as in mud that there is nothing subtle, nothing heavenly in them; they think only of meat, belching, and the gluttony of the belly. Diogenes maintains that tyrannies, the overthrow of cities, and hostile or civil wars are stirred up not for a simple diet of vegetables and fruits, but for meat and the delicacies of banquets.

And what is astonishing, Epicurus, the advocate of pleasure, filled all his books with vegetables, fruits, and cheap foods, saying that one should live in this way: [Note: [Col. 0347] Rubeus omitted these words through carelessness: “because meats and elaborate banquets are prepared with immense care and misery.”] because meats and elaborate banquets are prepared with immense care and misery, and involve greater pain in obtaining them than pleasure in consuming them. Drinking and eating should not arouse the ardor of luxury but extinguish thirst and hunger. Those who eat meat also need the things that are [Al. “are not”] meat. Those who use a simple diet, however, do not require meat.

[Col. 0348C] We cannot devote ourselves to wisdom if we think about the abundance of the table, which requires excessive labor and care. Nature’s necessity is quickly satisfied; cold and hunger can be driven away with simple clothing and food. Luxury and variety in banquets are incentives to avarice. If anyone thinks that he can enjoy an abundance of food and drink and still have leisure for wisdom—living amid luxuries without being held by luxurious vices—he deceives himself. Our sense thinks about what it sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches, and it is drawn toward whatever captures it through pleasure. It is difficult, indeed impossible, for those overflowing with riches and pleasures not to think about what we are doing. Some falsely pretend that, with faith, chastity [Al. omits “and chastity”], and integrity of mind preserved, they can indulge in pleasures, although it is contrary to nature to enjoy an abundance of pleasures without pleasure. The bodily senses are like horses running without reason; the soul, like a charioteer, holds the reins of those running.

Great is the soul’s exultation when, content with little, you have the world beneath your feet and fortify yourself against all its power, banquets, and lusts—for which riches are acquired—with cheap food, compensating for them with a coarser tunic. Take away the luxury of banquets and lust: no one will seek riches whose use is either in the belly or beneath the belly. A sick person does not recover health except through thin food and a disciplined diet. By the foods through which health is recovered, therefore, it can also be preserved; let no one suppose that illnesses are aroused by vegetables. But if vegetables do not provide the strength needed by those who are born and nourished on meat, why does a wise man and philosopher of Christ need such strength as athletes and soldiers require—strength which, once he possesses it, may provoke him to vice? Let those think meat appropriate to health who wish to abuse lust and, sunk in the mire of pleasures, always burn for intercourse. For a Christian, health without exceptional strength is necessary [Al. “health without excessive strength”].

Nor should it trouble us if followers of this purpose are rare, since good, faithful, chaste, and continent friends are rare, and virtue is always rare. We read of some who, suffering from joint disease and the humors of gout, were reduced through the confiscation of their property to a simple table and poor foods, and recovered. They had been deprived of the anxiety of managing a household and of the abundance of banquets, which break both body and soul.

Horace mocks the appetite for foods that, once consumed, leave regret. But even among the cheapest foods, satiety must be avoided. Nothing so clouds the mind as a full and burning belly, twisting this way and that, breathing out belches and blasts of wind. What sort of fasting, or what sort of restoration after fasting, is it when we are distended by yesterday’s banquets and our throat becomes a latrine’s passage? While we seek the hunger of a prolonged fast, we devour as much as the night of scarcely another day can digest. Therefore it should be called not so much fasting as gluttony and a stinking, burdensome digestion.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Abstinence of Philosophers, Ancient Priests, and Other Saints

Dicaearchus, in his books *On Antiquities* and *Description of Greece*, reports that under Saturn, when the earth produced everything, no one ate meat, but all lived on grain and fruits, which the earth produced of its own accord. Chaeremon the Stoic, also a most eloquent man, relates concerning the life of the ancient Egyptian priests that, setting aside all worldly business and cares, they were always in the temple and contemplated the natures and causes of things and the courses of the stars. They never mixed with women; they never saw relatives and kin, not even their children; and from the time when they began to serve divine worship, they always abstained from meat and wine because of the delicacy of their senses [Note: [Col. 0350D] Rubeus adds: “and dizziness of the head.” The same writer shortly afterward has: “They rarely ate bread,” etc.], and especially because of the incitements to lust that arise from these foods and this drink. They did not eat bread, lest they burden the stomach; and whenever they ate, they took crushed hyssop with their food, so that by its heat they might digest the heavier food. They knew only oil in vegetables, and even that in small quantity, to relieve nausea and the roughness of the throat.

“What shall I say,” he says, “about birds, when they avoided even eggs and milk as meats? They said that one of these was liquid flesh and the other blood with its color changed.” Their bed was woven from palm leaves. A sloping footstool, oblique on one side, they placed on the ground beneath the head as a pillow. Sustaining a fast of two or three days, they dried out, through severe moderation of diet, the bodily humors that arise from idleness and from staying in one place.

Josephus too, in the second history of the Jewish captivity and in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities*, describes three sects of the Jews: Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes [Al. “Essaeans”]. He praises the last of these extravagantly, because they always abstained from wives, wine, and meat and had transformed daily fasting into their nature. Concerning their life and food [Al. omits “and food”], the very learned Philo published a separate volume.

Eubulus relates that among the Persians there were three classes of Magi, the first of whom, the most learned and eloquent, took nothing more as food beyond flour and vegetables. Orpheus too, in his poem, utterly detests the eating of meat. I would also recount the frugality of Pythagoras, Socrates, Antisthenes, and the others for our humiliation, if it were not both lengthy and in need of a work of its own—so that those who either do not know or despise the poverty of the Apostles and the harshness of the cross might at least imitate the frugality [Al. “poverty”] of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0350C] I come now to what Asella, after twelve years of labor in her own sweat, chose, seized, held, began, and completed. Shut within the narrow confines of a single cell, she enjoyed the breadth of paradise. The same ground was both her place of prayer and her place of rest. She regarded fasting as play and hunger as restoration. And when it was not the desire to eat but human weakness that drew her to food, she provoked hunger more than she extinguished it with bread, salt, and cold water. She worked with her hands, knowing that it is written: “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians III). Thus she reached the age of fifty without stomach pain, without suffering from any disorder of the viscera, without the dry ground breaking her recumbent limbs, and without skin roughened by sackcloth contracting any foulness or dirt. Sound in body and sounder in soul, she considered solitude a luxury and found a monks’ desert in the turbulent city.

For Paul also, the palm supplied food and clothing. And lest this seem impossible to anyone, I call Jesus and his angels to witness that in the desert adjoining Syria and the Saracens I saw a monk who, shut in for thirty years, lived on barley bread and muddy water. Another was sustained each day by five dried figs. Therefore, if the Lord gave me the choice, I would much rather choose Paul’s tunic with his merits than the purple robes of kings together with their kingdoms [Al. “punishments”].

Yet what have we, animals of the belly, ever done like this? If the second hour finds us reading, we yawn, rub our faces with our hands, hold our stomachs, and, as though after great labor, return to being occupied with worldly business.

I pass over the lunches by which the burdened mind is weighed down. I am ashamed to mention the frequency of greetings, by which either we ourselves go daily to others or wait for others coming to us. Then people turn to conversation; speech is worn away; those who are absent are torn apart; another’s life is described; and by biting one another we consume one another. Such is the food that occupies us and sends us away. When our friends have departed, we calculate accounts. Now anger puts on a role for us; now excessive anxiety anticipates something destined to last for many years. Nor do we remember the Gospel’s saying: “Fool, this night your soul is required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12).

Nor, in saying this, do I condemn the foods that God created to be used with thanksgiving; I assert only that for the young they are incentives to pleasure [Al. “I remove pleasure”]. Neither the fires of Etna, nor Vulcan’s land, nor Vesuvius and Olympus burn with such heat as the marrow of youths filled with wine and inflamed by banquets. Avarice is trampled by most people and laid down together with the purse. [Note: [Col. 0351D] The words “Silence imposed corrects a cursing tongue,” omitted by Rubeus, amend the preceding sentence; Rubeus transferred them elsewhere.] An imposed silence corrects a cursing tongue; bodily grooming and the style of one’s clothing can be changed in the space of a single hour. All other sins are external, and what is outside can easily be cast off. Lust alone is implanted within and, by a certain law of nature, longs to burst forth into intercourse. It is therefore a great virtue and a work of vigilant diligence to overcome what you were born as and to live in the flesh without living according to the flesh.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Temperate Fasts

Take upon yourself as much fasting as you can bear, for people’s stomachs differ. Some delight in bitter foods, others in sweet, others in sharper, others in mild [Al. “gentle”] foods. Therefore we do not impose immoderate fasts upon you or an excessive abstinence from food, by which delicate bodies are immediately broken. The philosophers also hold that virtues are moderate, and that things exceeding measure and proportion are counted among vices. Hence one of the seven wise men said: “Nothing in excess.” I know that in both sexes, because of excessive abstinence, the health of the brain has been disturbed in some people, especially those who lived in damp and cold cells, so that they did not know what they were doing or where they should turn, what they should say or what they should keep silent.

You should therefore fast in such a way that you do not tremble or scarcely manage to breathe, but so that, with the body’s appetite weakened, you do nothing less than usual in reading, psalmody, or vigils. Fasting is not perfect virtue but the foundation of the other virtues, as well as sanctification and chastity, without which no one will see God. For Christ reckons everything according to the will of the soul. Long and immoderate fasts are especially displeasing in tender years—fasts joined to whole weeks and accompanied by a prohibition of oil and fruit in food. Experience has taught me that when a little donkey becomes tired on the road, it seeks side paths. The instruction concerning perpetual fasting is this: sufficient strength must remain for a long journey, lest, running at the first station, we collapse halfway through.

But in Lent the sails of continence must be spread and all the reins of the charioteer loosened for the hastening horses, although the condition of secular people differs from that of monks. A secular person during Lent digests the gluttony of the belly and, living like a snail on its own juice, prepares a little reservoir for future banquets and fattening. A monk should release his horses during Lent, so that he may remember that he must always be running. A completed labor is greater; an unending one must be more moderate. There we breathe again; here we proceed perpetually. Yet eat in such a way [Note: [Col. 0352D] Other books add: “that you may always be hungry”] that immediately after food you can read, pray, and sing psalms. Therefore let your fasts be chaste, simple, moderate, and free from superstition.

But what good does it do not to eat oil while seeking the troubles and difficulties of other foods—dried figs, pepper, nuts, palm fruits, fine flour, and honey? The whole cultivation of the gardens is disturbed so that we may not eat ordinary bread; and while we pursue delicacies, we are drawn away from the kingdom of heaven. Nor, if you have fasted for two or three days, should you think yourself better than those who fast. You fast and become angry; he eats and perhaps flatters to one’s face [Al. “to one’s face”]. You digest the distress of mind and the hunger of the belly by fasting [Al. “by quarrelling”]; he is nourished more moderately and gives thanks to God.

Hence Isaiah cries out every day: “I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord.” And again: “On the days of your fasts your own desires are found, and you goad all who are under your power. You fast for judgment and strife, and strike the humble with your fists. Why do you fast for me?” (Isaiah LVIII). What sort of fast can that be whose anger does not merely last through a night, but remains until an entire moon has passed?

Considering yourself, do not glory in another’s downfall but in your own work; nor set before yourself as examples those who, making provision for the flesh, calculate the revenues of their estates and the daily expenses of their households. The eleven Apostles of Christ were not broken by Judas’s betrayal; nor, when Philetus and Alexander suffered shipwreck, did the others stop their course of faith (2 Timothy II). You must also avoid the banquets of secular people, especially of those who swell with honors. For a fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.

Aesop’s fable teaches that a mouse with a full belly cannot pass out through a narrow hole. For all the handsome, curled, carefully arranged-haired men, or those with red cheeks, whom you see belong to Jovinian’s herd; [Note: [Col. 0353D] Rubeus reads: “Indeed, they grunt among his pigs.” Shortly afterward he omits the psalm verse “Alas for me,” etc.] among them the swine grunt. Those of our flock—sad, pale, dirty [Al. “made dirty”], and, as though strangers in this world—though they may lack speech [Al. “though they are silent”], speak by their clothing and gesture: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged.”

Hence sackcloth and fasting are weapons of repentance [Note: [Col. 0354D] Martianaeus incorrectly reads: “and other sins.”] and aids for sinners. And if one of two necessary things must be removed, I would rather choose fasting without sackcloth than sackcloth without fasting. But those to whom repentance is prescribed appropriately join sackcloth to fasting. What is applied to the heel does not heal the eye. Through fasting the passions of the body must be healed; through prayer, the diseases of the mind. Thus fasting shows that we are going to paradise, from which we had been cast out through satiety. For fasting heals the wounds of the offender and sanctifies those who have been healed.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Contemplation, Prayer, and Reading

If you wish to be a monk, not merely to be seen as one, care not for your household property, which you began this life by renouncing, but for your soul. Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Let body and mind alike be stretched toward the Lord. In the eagerness of your spirit, let your mind run ahead to heaven, so that while you remain bodily on earth, you may already reach Christ in thought [Al. “may hasten yourself”].

Accustom yourself also to rise at night for prayers and psalms, to sing hymns in the morning, to stand in battle array at the third, sixth, and ninth hours like a soldier of Christ, and, after lighting the lamp, to offer the evening sacrifice. Let the day pass in this way; let night find you laboring. Let reading follow prayer and prayer follow reading. Especially those things that the saints do, they do in God’s sight, and they receive fuller knowledge of God; they are more completely imbued with divine teachings.

For if a sick man burning with fever asks for cold water and says to the physician, “I am suffering, I am tormented [Al. “burning”], I am dying; how long, physician, shall I cry out and you not hear me?”—and the wisest physician replies, “I know at what time I ought to give what you ask; I do not pity you now, because this mercy is cruelty, and your will asks for what is against you”—so our Lord, knowing the weights and measures of his mercy, sometimes does not hear the one who cries out, in order to test him, provoke him more strongly to ask, and, as though refined by fire, make him more just and purer.

When rising at night for prayer, let indigestion not produce a belch, but emptiness. For a certain outstanding shepherd said: “As smoke drives away bees, so undigested belching turns away the gifts of the Holy Spirit.” A belch properly means the digestion of food and the expulsion into air of digested food. Therefore, just as a belch bursts from the stomach according to the quality of the food and a breath of good or bad odor is an indication, so the thoughts of the inner person produce words, and “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” The righteous person, eating, fills his soul. When he has been satisfied with sacred teachings, he brings forth from the treasure of a good heart the things that are good.

Read more frequently, and learn as much as possible; and, while you hold the book, let sleep steal upon you, so that the holy page may receive your falling eyes. Although the Apostle commands us always to pray, and even sleep itself is prayer for the saints, nevertheless we ought to have appointed hours of prayer, so that if we are detained by some task, the appointed time itself may summon us to our duty. Let no food be taken before prayer has been offered. Let no one leave the table without returning thanks to the Creator. As we leave our lodging, let prayer arm us; as we enter, let prayer meet us before we sit down. Let the little body not rest before the soul has rested [Al. “been fed”].

At every act and every movement, let the hand make the sign of the cross. On Sundays let time be devoted [Al. add. “only”] to prayer and reading. Indeed, at all times they should do this after completing their little tasks. Every day let something be learned from the holy Scriptures [Al. “let something be recited”]. Care must also be taken to celebrate a solemn day not so much with an abundance of food as with exultation of spirit, since it is very absurd to wish to honor with excessive satiety a martyr whom you know pleased God through fasts.

Priests too ought to pray for all whose alms and offerings they receive. Let divine reading frequently be in your hands and prayers be frequent, so that all the arrows of thought with which youth is usually struck may be repelled by such a shield. For it is difficult, indeed impossible, for anyone to be free from the vices of disturbances. Frequent reading and daily meditation are usually more a labor of the mind than of the flesh. For just as what is done with the hand and body is completed through the labor of hand and body, so what pertains to reading is more truly the labor of the mind. Letters do not follow the purse; yet they are companions of sweat and labor, partners of fasts, not of satiety; of continence, not of luxury. Hence a certain disciple of Origen said that he had never taken food in Origen’s presence without reading and had never fallen asleep unless one of the brothers was reciting the sacred Scriptures.

When eating, let them cover their heads with their hoods, so that they do not look at one another while eating; and let no one be permitted to speak while they are eating. Therefore, when you have eaten, consider that immediately afterward you must pray and read.

Source/review notes: All canonical source column boundaries from 0355A through 0365D are retained at their associated translated passages. The saved substantive corrections were applied; inherited uncertainty in the final flower metaphor remains explicitly marked.

Fix for yourself a set number of verses from the holy Scriptures. Return this task to your Lord. Do not grant your limbs rest before you have filled the basket [Al. *palladium*] of your breast with this weaving. After the holy Scriptures, read the treatises of learned men—only those whose faith is known—for learning produces fear, while ignorance produces confidence. Yet Scripture will benefit the reader only if what he has read is fulfilled in practice.

[Col. 0355A] Therefore delight in the treatises, intellects, and books of those whose devotion to the faith does not waver. Read the others in such a way that you judge whom you should follow. Beware all apocryphal writings; and if at any time you wish to read them, not for the truth of their doctrines, know that they are not by those whose names are written in their titles, and that many corruptions have been mixed into them. It is a mark of great prudence to seek gold in mud. For what has Horace to do with the Psalter, Maro with the Gospels, Cicero with the Apostle? What fellowship has light with darkness? Therefore do not read philosophers, orators, or poets, nor find rest in their reading.
