Nor should we flatter ourselves if we do not believe what has been written in them, since another person’s conscience may be wounded and we may be thought to approve what, while reading it, we do not reject. Far be it, then, that from a Christian mouth should sound “Jupiter Almighty,” “By Hercules,” “By Castor,” and other expressions that are more monstrous than divine names.

[Col. 0355B] But now we see even priests of God, abandoning the Gospels and the Prophets, reading comedies; singing [Al. attempting] the amorous words of Bucolic verses; holding Virgil in their hands; and wishing to make into a voluntary crime what is a necessity in children. The knowledge that belongs to piety is to know how to read the Scriptures, to understand the Prophets, to believe the Gospel, and not to be ignorant of the Apostles. Nor should we think that the Gospel consists in the words of Scripture, but in its meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of its phrases, but in the root of its reasoning.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] In Rubeus: “to know the Law, to understand the Prophets,” and so forth.]

If you do not understand something, or if you are uncertain about something in the Scriptures, ask one whom his life commends, whose age excuses him, [Col. 0355C] and whose reputation does not condemn him. Or, if there is no one able to explain it, it is better to remain safely ignorant of something [Al. *to be safely silent*] than to learn it at peril. Remember that you walk amid snares. I would rather that modesty remain with you for a little while than that your case be endangered. Yet whoever asks about something he knows—not from a desire to learn, but from a zeal to discover whether the person who will answer actually knows it—approaches like the Pharisees, not as a disciple but as a tempter. Many detractors, too, while scrutinizing the words of sacred eloquence more than they ought, fall into a carnal interpretation.

In the divine Scriptures and books, it is better to leave obscure passages as they are than rashly or wrongly to imitate something you do not understand. [Col. 0355D] There are also some who, with wrinkled brow, lowered eyebrow, and carefully weighed words, claim for themselves the authority of teachers—not because they themselves know anything worthy of such arrogance, but because simple brothers seem, by comparison with them, to know certain things less well. It also sometimes happens that, when someone has a small amount of knowledge, he becomes puffed up with pride and ceases to learn [Al. *and to read*]. Gradually, because nothing is added, something is subtracted, until he remains utterly empty of learning: the iron that was sharp becomes blunt.

[Col. 0356A] And now to dread the Prophet is said to be eloquence; not to have the mind of Christ, wisdom; to have done an injury, courage; to possess another’s property, power; to ensnare the innocent, cleverness; to despise the humble, nobility. Thus everything is full of errors, and truth is obscured to such an extent that lying in the embrace of death is called blessedness.

[Col. 0356A] For our part, we approve nothing except what is ecclesiastical and what we are not afraid to say publicly in the Church. Yet this is how we customarily proceed in these matters. When we read philosophers, when books of secular wisdom come into our hands, if we find anything useful in them, we turn it to our own doctrine. But whatever is superfluous—about idols, love, and concern for worldly affairs—we scrape away, strip it bare, and cut it off with the sharpest iron, like the edge of a fingernail.

[Col. 0356B] I shall relate to you the history of my own unhappiness. Many years ago, when I had for the sake of the kingdom of heaven castrated myself from my home, my parents, my sisters [Al. *sister*], my relatives, and—what was more difficult than these—from the habit of richer food, and was setting out for Jerusalem to serve as a soldier, I could not do without the library that I had assembled at Rome with the greatest care. And so, miserable man that I was, I fasted in order to read Tully. After frequent vigils through the night, after tears that flowed from my inmost vitals in remembrance of past sins [Al. *after the remembrance of past sins had drawn them forth*], Plautus was taken up in my hands. Whenever, returning to myself, I began to read the Prophet, his language seemed uncultivated. And because my blind eyes could not see the light, I thought the fault lay not in my eyes [Col. 0356C] but in the sun.

While the ancient serpent was thus mocking me, near the middle of Lent a fever that had penetrated to my marrow invaded my exhausted body. Without any respite—and what is scarcely credible to say—it consumed my wretched limbs so thoroughly that I barely clung to my bones. Meanwhile my funeral was being prepared, and, while the warmth of my living soul had already grown cold throughout my body, my breast alone, still warm, continued to palpitate. Suddenly I was carried away in spirit and dragged before the tribunal of Christ. There was so much light there, and such radiance from the brightness of those standing around, that, thrown upon the ground, I did not dare to look upward.

Asked about my condition, I replied that I was a Christian. But the one presiding said: “You are lying. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also” (Matthew 6). At once I fell silent; [Col. 0356D] and amid the blows—for he had ordered me to be beaten—I was tortured more severely by the fire of conscience, repeating to myself that verse: “But in hell, who will confess you?” (Psalm 6). Nevertheless I began to cry out and, lamenting, to say: “Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me!” This voice continued to resound amid the lashes.

At last those who stood nearby fell at the feet of the presiding judge and begged him to grant pardon to my youth and give my error an opportunity for repentance [Al. *grant my error a reprieve*], intending thereafter to exact punishment if I ever again read books of pagan literature. I, constrained as I was in such a desperate predicament, [Col. 0357A] and willing even to promise more, began to swear an oath. Calling upon his name, I said: “Lord, if I ever possess secular books, or if I ever read them, I have denied you.” After these words of my oath I was released and returned to the world above. To the astonishment of everyone, I opened my eyes, drenched in such a flood of tears that even unbelievers might have been convinced by my grief.

Nor had that been a mere sleep or empty dream, by which we are often deceived. That tribunal before which I had lain is my witness; that dreadful judgment, which I had feared, is my witness. May it never happen to me again that I fall into such an examination. [Note: [Col. 0357D] More correctly in other books: “I confess that I had bruised shoulders,” and so forth.] For I confess that my shoulders were full of wounds; that I felt the injuries after sleep; and that thereafter I read the divine writings with as much zeal as previously I had read mortal literature.

[Col. 0357B] Besides the order of psalms and prayer—which you must always practice at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, toward evening, at midnight, and in the morning—determine how many hours you ought to devote to memorizing holy Scripture and how much time to reading it, not as a burden but for the delight and instruction of the soul. When you have completed these periods, and concern for the soul has frequently roused you to bend your knees, either put together what is to be woven or inspect what has already been woven; correct what is faulty and decide what must be done. If you are occupied with such a variety of tasks, your days will never seem long. Rather, although they are stretched out by the summer suns, they will seem short if some work has been left undone [Al. *if nothing has been left undone*]. By observing these practices, you will save yourself and others, become a teacher of holy conduct, and make the chastity of many your gain.

[Col. 0357C] Recite the psalm according to your order, seeking not sweetness of voice but the disposition of the mind, as the Apostle writes: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” [Al. *the word “disposition” is omitted*] (1 Corinthians 14). For he had read the command: “Sing wisely” (Psalm 14). In Scripture, a cry is not of the voice but of the heart. Can God really be bent by a multitude of words, as a human being can? God is to be prayed to not with words but with the heart. The singing of seven [Al. *five*] psalms with purity and serenity of heart and spiritual cheerfulness is better than the chanting of the entire Psalter with anxiety and sadness of heart. Let the singer also be driven out as harmful; and thrust out from the house the flute players, female harpists, and suchlike—almost deadly—songs of the sirens [Col. 0357D] [Al. *the choir of the devil*].

The soul that is to become the temple of God must be educated in such a way that it learns to hear and speak nothing except what pertains to the fear of God. Let it not understand shameful things [Al. *shameful words*]; let it be ignorant of worldly songs. These matters must not be despised as though they were small, since without them greater things cannot stand. Greek history tells how Alexander, the most powerful king and conqueror of the world, could not free himself from the faults with which he had been infected as a little boy, both in his conduct and in the gait of his tutor Leonidas. [Col. 0358A]

The songs of poets, secular wisdom, and the pomp of rhetorical speech are therefore food for demons. All these things delight people by their own sweetness; and while they captivate the ears with verses flowing in a sweet rhythm, they also penetrate the soul and bind the inmost parts of the breast [Al. *bind them*]. But once they have been produced with the utmost zeal and labor, they give their readers nothing except empty sound and the noise of words. No nourishment of fullness, no refreshment of justice is found there. Those devoted to them persist in hunger for truth and poverty of virtues.

[Col. 0358B] For me, the concern is not what Aristotle teaches, but what Paul teaches. He adorns God’s doctrine who does what is suited to his own condition; conversely, he brings it into disgrace when he is dissatisfied with his condition. A monk has the duty not of a teacher but of one who mourns—mourning either himself or the world—and who fearfully awaits the Lord’s coming. Knowing his weakness and the fragile vessel he carries, he fears offending, lest he stumble, fall, and be shattered. He should know that he is a monk not by talking and wandering about, but by keeping silent and sitting. Let your speech also be silent and your silence eloquent, and let your gait be neither hurried nor slow.

Whenever anyone enters for communion, let him approach wearing only his hooded garment. Let those who wish have their wealth, drink from gem-encrusted vessels, shine in silk, and delight in the applause of the people; yet through various pleasures they cannot overcome riches. [Col. 0358C] Our riches are to meditate on the law of God day and night, to knock at the door, [Note: [Col. 0357D] Rubeus and others add: “not finding it closed, to receive the breads of the Trinity, and, with the Lord going before, to trample the waves of the world.”] and to trample the world as we go before it.

Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves and assume perfect vigor, so that amid the darkness and confusion of errors the light of Christ may appear in the knowledge of the night. Let our day also have a protecting cloud, so that under these guides we may be able to reach the holy land. For what is better than learning? What is sweeter than discipline? What is more delightful than the Lord? Let Christ be our banquet; Christ our reading; Christ our rest [Al. *“rest Christ” is omitted*]; Christ our thought. For what life can there be without knowledge of the Scriptures, through which Christ himself is also recognized? What foods, what honeycombs are sweeter than knowing the wisdom of God?

The wise person is never alone: he has with him all who are and have been good; [Col. 0358D] and his free mind can be carried wherever it wishes. What he cannot do bodily, he embraces in thought. And if there is a lack of human company, he speaks with God; he is never less alone than when he is alone. For the first wisdom is to have been rid of folly; but no one can be rid of folly unless he has understood it. [Note: [Col. 0358D] The same books read: “This is the true wisdom of man: to know that one is imperfect, and, so to speak, [something] of all in the flesh …” A little later: “It is no small thing to know what you do not know.”]

True wisdom, however, is to know that one has recently been made; and, so to speak, in the flesh the perfection of the righteous is imperfect. Yet it is little to know what you do not know; [Col. 0359A] it is the mark of a prudent person to know his own measure. Whoever does not know it will fall all the more deeply to lower things the greater things he seeks. [Note: [Col. 0359D] Previously it was incorrectly read “will be placed.”]

Let us therefore learn on earth what knowledge may remain with us in heaven.

## CHAPTER XV. On Vigils

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Almost everything contained in this chapter is excerpted from the letter or treatise *On the Observance of Vigils*, which we printed above in this volume and showed to have been falsely attributed to Jerome; on the authority of manuscripts we established that it belongs to Nicetius, bishop of Trier.]

It is worthy, brothers, and entirely fitting and appropriate, to speak and deliver a discourse now about holy vigils, since the very keeping of vigil is required of the watchful. Behold, night is darkness for bodies; it holds not only human beings but all living creatures in sleep, so that, their strength restored through slumber, living beings may endure the long labor of the day [Al. *daytime labors*]. Good is God, who so provided and so ordered matters that a person going out to his work and laboring until evening should have an intervening period in which to rest from harsh labor and great fatigue. [Note: [Col. 0360D] It was previously read less well: “he granted that he should rest.”]

[Col. 0359B] We know, however, that many people, whether to please their superiors or to gain some particular advantage for themselves, set aside a portion of the night for some little task and count as profit whatever they have been able to accomplish by stealing it from their sleep. Solomon praises a woman who diligently works at her allotted tasks and spinning by lamplight (Proverbs 26). He also adds that from this praise for her husband and great glory arise at the gates. If, then, one who keeps vigil over bodily necessities—that is, things necessary for food and clothing—is not reproached but rather praised, I confess that I am astonished that there are some who consider holy vigils, so fruitful in spiritual work and so fertile in prayers, hymns, and readings, either superfluous, idle, or—what is worse than these—inconvenient.

[Col. 0359C] If people alien to our religion think this way, it is certainly not surprising. For how can religious practices please the irreligious? If they pleased them, they would be ours, since we are Christians. But if they are our own people who are offended by the salutary practice of vigils—so that I suspect nothing worse of them—then they are either lazy, sleepy, or, which is closely related, old or infirm.

If they are lazy, let them be ashamed, for Solomon’s proverbs ring in their ears: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and imitate its ways” (Proverbs 6). If they are sleepy, let them awaken when Scripture cries out: “O sluggard, how long will you sleep? When will you rise from sleep? You sleep a little, sit a little, doze a little, and clasp your hands to your breast a little.” If you are old, who compels you to keep vigil? Yet even without compulsion, you keep vigil according to your age. And if you cannot stand but consider your incapacity, you should not call young and vigorous people back to your torpor. Because of the various temptations of youth, they ought to discipline themselves with more determined vigils. Athletes are stronger than their trainers, and yet the weaker man gives the command while the stronger one fights. This is especially so because even holy people fall if they are negligent, while sinners recover their former state if they wash away their filth with tears.

[Col. 0360A] I say this so that those who descend may not frighten you, but may provoke those who ascend. Nothing is easier than for an idle and sleeping person to discuss the labor and vigils of others. But if you are weak in your limbs, do not criticize what you cannot do. Rather, in accordance with the Prophet, water your bed with tears and say: “If I remembered you upon my bed” (Psalm 62). Join yourself to those who keep vigil, so that they may help you with their prayers; then, assisted by the Lord, you may sing upon your bed of pain, and may eventually deserve to say: “In the morning I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper” (ibid.). Otherwise it is foolish and wholly inappropriate that, because we cannot run ourselves, we should disparage those who run well. Even if we cannot do so, we ought to rejoice with the strong. For just as, through consent to wickedness, one shares punishment with those who commit it, so through consent to goodness one may hope to share in glory. One person is crowned for his deeds; another is gladdened by his devoted intention.

Nor should it seem burdensome or difficult even for delicate bodies to devote some portion of two nights each week—that is, Saturday and Sunday—to the service of God. This is, as it were, a purification of the five days or nights during which we grow heavy with carnal stupor and yawn over worldly activities.

[Col. 0360B] [Col. 0360C] Let no one be ashamed of the good pursuit of holiness when the wicked are not ashamed to perform shameful deeds. Scripture therefore rightly presses the point in Proverbs: “There is a shame that leads to sin” (Ecclesiasticus 4:25). To be ashamed in a good work is sin; just as not to be ashamed in doing evil is ruin. If you are holy, love vigils, so that by keeping watch you may guard your treasure and yourself grow fervent in holiness. If you are a sinner, take greater care to be cleansed by keeping vigil and praying, while, beating your breast, you cry out more frequently: “Cleanse me from my secret faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Psalm 18).

One ought to taste and perceive that the Lord is sweet, as it is written. Whoever has tasted understands and feels how great a weight is laid down from the breast by keeping vigil, how much mental stupor is shaken off, how great a light illumines the soul of the one who keeps vigil and prays, and what grace and visitation gladden all the limbs. Through vigilance every fear is driven away; confidence is born; the flesh is disciplined; vices waste away; charity is strengthened; folly departs; prudence approaches; the mind is sharpened; error is blunted; and the devil, the source of crimes, is wounded by the sword of the Spirit.

[Col. 0360D] What is more necessary than this benefit? What is more advantageous than these gains [Al. *more beneficial*]? What is sweeter than this love? What is more blessed than this happiness? The Prophet himself bears witness. At the beginning of his psalms, describing the blessed man, he placed the fullness of his blessedness in this verse: “If he meditates on the law of God day and night” (Psalm 1).

[Col. 0361A] Daytime meditation is indeed good, but nighttime meditation is more effective. During the day, necessities make a disturbance, occupations distract the mind, and a double concern disperses the senses. But night, secluded and quiet, presents itself as suitable for those who pray and most fitting for those who keep vigil, while it places before the divine presence the sense freed from bodily occupations, collected, and attentive—the whole person concentrated [Al. *entirely attentive*].

Care must also be taken that the breast of one who is about to keep vigil is not burdened by an excess of food or drink, lest, belching up indigestion and drunkenness, we be not only unpleasant to ourselves [Al. *the addition “unpleasant to ourselves”*] but also judged unworthy of the grace of the Spirit. Therefore, as though we were about to enjoy a divine service, we must prepare ourselves beforehand through abstinence, so that, unburdened, we may keep vigil more freely.

[Col. 0361B] Evil thoughts must also be driven away, lest the prayer of one who keeps evil vigil become, as it is written, a sin. There are also vigils that come from wickedness, as we read in Proverbs: “Sleep has been taken away from their eyes; for,” he says, “they do not sleep unless they have done evil” (Proverbs 4:16). Far from this gathering—far from it—be such vigils. Rather, let the breast of those who keep vigil be closed to the devil and open to Christ, so that the one whom we sound forth with our lips we may hold in our hearts. Then our vigils will be acceptable; then our all-night observance will be salutary, if our service is offered before the divine gaze with appropriate diligence and sincere devotion.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Clothing

Wear a dark tunic; let a cheap tunic demonstrate contempt for the [Col. 0361C] world—provided only that your mind does not swell with pride and that your clothing and speech do not disagree. For a cheap and dark garment is itself an indication of a silent spirit: “Those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.” Have such clothing as drives away the cold [Note: [Col. 0361D] This was lacking: “with which the cold may be driven away.”], not clothing that exposes the bodies dressed in it; let it be neither clean nor dirty, and not conspicuous by any distinction. For neither affected filth nor elaborate cleanliness is suitable for a Christian.

But take care that even this does not generate pride in you—that you despised the world’s pride. Let no secret thought creep in, so that, having perhaps ceased to please in gold-embroidered garments, you try to please in dirt. For we brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away.

But now you may see many people cramming wardrobes with clothes and changing tunics every day, yet still unable to overcome the moths. And one who is more religious than you strips off a single garment while dragging clothes from full chests. Parchments are stained purple; gold melts into letters; books are clothed with jewels; and Christ dies naked before their doors. A dark tunic becomes less dirty when it lies on the ground. Let the woolen belt be completely pure in its simplicity and able to bind the garments rather than tear them. Let there always be the same clothing: [Col. 0362A] cleanliness neglected, an unadorned garment, and adornment itself without adornment. Let the softness of feathers not warm youthful limbs.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Manual Labor

Do not let your mind be idle amid various disturbances. If these settle in your breast, they will dominate you and lead you into the greatest sin. Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. If the Apostles, though possessing the authority to live from the Gospel, worked with their hands so as not to burden anyone, and provided relief for others, from whom they ought to reap material things in return for spiritual things, why do you not prepare something that will serve your own needs?

Either weave a little basket from rushes, or plait a basket from supple branches. Let the ground be dug; [Col. 0362B] let the garden plots be divided by straight boundaries. When seeds of vegetables have been sown or plants set out in rows, let channels of water be led to irrigate them. Graft unproductive trees with buds or shoots, so that after a short time you may gather sweet fruit. [Note: [Col. 0361D] According to the Greek Proverbs, chapter 6; this passage is not found in the Latin translation.] Build beehives for the bees to which Solomon’s Proverbs send you; and learn, in their small bodies, the order of monasteries and royal discipline.

Let linen nets also be woven for catching fish. Let books be written, so that the hand may work for food and the soul be nourished by reading. For “every idle person is in his desires.” [Note: [Col. 0361D] This passage is found only in Proverbs 13 according to the Septuagint.] The monasteries of the Egyptians observe this custom: they receive no one without labor and work, not so much because of the necessity of food as for the salvation of the soul. Let the [Col. 0362C] mind not wander into destructive thoughts and, like fornication-practicing Jerusalem, spread its legs to every passerby.

Nor should you cease from work because, by God’s favor, you lack nothing. [Note: [Col. 0362D] In Rubeus, after the passage omitted here down to “you must labor,” it continues: “so that, through the opportunity of work, you may think of nothing else …”] Rather, you must labor with everyone so that, through the opportunity provided by work, you may think of nothing except what pertains to the service of the Lord. To speak plainly: even if you have distributed all your wealth among the poor, nothing will be more precious before Christ than what you yourself have made with your hands. Through sweat and great labor we shall reach the abundance of fruits.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Praise of Religion and the Call to It

You are indeed building monasteries, and a great number of holy men throughout the islands of Dalmatia are supported by you; but you would do better if you yourself lived as a holy man among the holy. It is difficult—indeed impossible—for someone to enjoy both present and eternal goods: to fill his belly here and his mind there; to pass from delights to delights; to be first in both worlds and appear glorious in heaven and on earth.

As for your claim that those who use their possessions and gradually distribute the proceeds of their estates to the poor act better than those who sell their possessions and [Col. 0363A] give everything away at once, let the answer come not from me but from the Lord: “If you wish to be perfect, go …” (Matthew 19). Nor should monks be drawn back from their purpose by a viperous tongue and most savage bite. You argue and say: “If everyone shut himself away and fled into solitude, who would celebrate the churches? Who would win secular people? Who could exhort sinners to virtue?” By this reasoning, if everyone were foolish along with you, who could be wise? If all were virgins, there would be no marriages and the human race would perish.

But virtue is rare, and it is not sought by many. Would that all were what the few are! Of these it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20). Therefore, even if a little nephew hangs upon your neck; [Col. 0363B] even if your mother, with disheveled hair and torn garments, displays the breasts by which she nursed you; even if your father lies across the threshold—step over your father and fly with dry eyes to the standard of the cross. In this matter, the only kind of piety is to be cruel.

The enemy holds a sword to kill me; shall I think about my mother’s tears? You are delicate, dearest brother, if you wish to rejoice with the world here and afterward reign with Christ. Affection compels us to do many things. While we look to the closeness of our bodies, we offend the Creator of both body and soul. Whoever loves father or mother more than Christ is not worthy of him [Al. *of God*]. Thus a disciple who desired to go to his father’s burial was forbidden by the Savior’s command. How many monks, while showing pity to father and mother, have lost their own souls? [Col. 0363C] It is not permitted to be defiled over father or mother—how much less over brother, sisters, cousins, household members, or slaves! We are a royal and priestly race (1 Peter 2). Let us look to that Father who never dies and who, by dying while alive, gave life to us who were dead.

The only reason for showing piety is where there is no carnal relationship. Honor your father, provided that he does not separate you from the true Father. Know the bond of the flesh only so long as he knows his Creator. Otherwise David will immediately sing: “Forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty, for he is the Lord your God” (Psalm 44). Great is the reward for forgetting one’s parent, because the king will desire your beauty.

For miserable parents, and Christians whose faith is incomplete, commonly hand over to religion sons who are deformed or disabled in some limb because they cannot find them worthy of marriage. But if you desire to be perfect, go out with Abraham from your country and your kindred, and go where you do not know. If you have possessions, sell them and give to the poor. If you have none, you have been freed from a great burden: naked, follow the naked Christ. The undertaking is arduous, great, and difficult, but the rewards are great. Any labor is more readily accepted when the benefit of that labor is placed before one’s eyes. Even to those who sail, [Col. 0364A] a hope of prolonged calm is promised by a very great and enduring storm [Al. *“the ship”*].

Let us, then, follow even women; let the weaker sex teach us. How many women, powerful in both wealth and nobility—I do not wish to name them, lest I seem to flatter them—after abandoning their resources and despising their children or pledges (*pignora*), judged easy to do what you consider difficult because of your own fear! Therefore possess the simplicity of the dove, so that you plot no deception against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so that you are not overthrown by the treachery of others. For a Christian, it is not very different in the matter of fault whether he is able to deceive or to be deceived.

But let those women adorn for you, from many different flowers, a light for this purpose [the wording is uncertain]. When the snake comes to drink, it deposits its venom in the water, lest the venom, congealed in the water, [Col. 0364B] kill it. It fears a naked man and pursues one who is clothed [Note: [Col. 0363D] These words, “it pursues one who is clothed,” were lacking; although we supplied them from the spurious letter to Praesidium, as also, a little later, the word *once*]; but when it is struck it conceals its head, knowing that its death is there. If a serpent is struck once with a reed, it dies; but if it is struck a second time, it becomes stronger. In winter it grows weaker and is overcome by mice. Therefore, before winter, it gathers food around the grain fields to provide nourishment for them.

When the snake grows old, it loses its sight. If it wishes to return to youth, it fasts for forty days so that its skin may loosen; then it seeks a narrow opening, so that, as it struggles to emerge, it may shed the skin of old age. When pelicans find their young dead [Al. *killed*] by a snake, they mourn, strike themselves and their sides, and, after shedding blood, revive the bodies of the dead with it. [Col. 0364C] When the eagle grows old, its feathers and eyes become heavy. It seeks a spring, raises its wings, and gathers heat into itself; thus its eyes are healed. It plunges three times into the spring and so returns to youth.

Many things are said in Scripture that seem impossible, yet are true. Say nothing is impossible where the power of the Most High is present. Think nothing of human frailty where the fullness of divinity is present. But why do I try to urge you toward the yoke of the Lord of the present life by examples, when we scarcely know of any saint who passed through the stormy struggle of this age without tribulation and storm [Al. *the storm of tribulation*]?

A warrior either disregards or does not feel the pain of wounds while, with all his vital faculties, he seems to think only of [Col. 0364D] victory. And one who goes to the whales in winter first patiently endures the severity of the cold naked, because the future warmth consoles him. And for every creature, some rejoicing for God’s sake follows difficult hope only after sorrow has gone before it. [Note: [Col. 0363D] Here, following Rubeus, we have supplied the little word “hope,” although it comes from a spurious letter to the Virgin in exile. Immediately afterward, where the text says “we scarcely feel,” Rubeus has “we do not feel at all,” and so forth.]

Let there therefore be in us such faith in the future that we scarcely feel ourselves enduring what we suffer, but rather judge that we are already obtaining what we believe.

[Col. 0365A] How great, moreover, is the reward with God if people do not hope for payment in the present! With how much sweat an empty inheritance is sought! The pearl of Christ could have been bought at a lower price. The end of your military service will be a kingdom not of earth and time, but of eternity and heaven. Nothing, my son, can or ought to be preferred to him who is the true Lord, the true Father, and the eternal commander. To whom could we more rightly devote our life than to him from whom we received it and to whom we owe it to the end, since by his gift we live? Therefore, if we prefer to serve Caesar rather than Christ, afterward we shall be transferred not to Christ but to hell.

We must therefore prefer neither affection nor homeland, honors, nor riches, because it is written: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7); and, “Those who have loved this world will perish with the world.” Let us serve him who grants those who serve him the glory of life in its fullness and an everlasting sharing in divine knowledge. For no earthly king is lord of the whole world, but Christ is king of the whole world, because all things were made through Christ (John 1). And because “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11), the violence pleasing to God is that which harms no one and rests upon the injury of no one. Extend your hands toward this seizure [Al. *turn your hands toward it*], which contains no crime and brings salvation.

[Col. 0365B] Our carnal ties, the dearer they are, the more they torment and exhaust us. Consequently, the mind never rests so securely in carnal affections that it is free from torment: it either loves [Col. 0365C] its relations while fearing to lose them, or hates bad relations while wishing to lose them. In either case it is always subject to the misery it must endure. Change your life for the better, then, so that you may begin to serve the eternal God [Al. *King*] and have God as your protector.

There are nevertheless many who come to salvation not through fear of punishments but through desire for blessings and promises. Nothing is more worthy than that a human being should imitate his creator and, according to the measure of his own will, carry out the work of God. For whoever wishes to eat the kernel must break the nut. The Apostle says: “It would indeed have been better for a man to enter marriage and walk on level ground than, while striving toward higher things, to fall into the depths of hell.”

## CHAPTER XIX. On Praise, the Avoidance of Detraction, and the Dangers of This Life

[Col. 0365D]

Do not believe your praisers; indeed, do not willingly lend an ear to those who mock. Every false commendation pursues profit and seeks human glory, so that advantages may arise through glory. Let the entrails of the hungry praise you, not the sumptuous banquets of those who belch; for the flattering flatterer is an enemy. We are led by a natural evil. We readily favor our flatterers, although we reply that we are unworthy and a warm blush suffuses our faces; nevertheless, inwardly the soul rejoices at its own praise. But truth does not love corners, nor does it seek whisperers. Praise torments the just and exalts the wicked; yet while it torments the just, it purifies them, and while it gladdens the wicked, it reveals them to be rejected.

Do not slander anyone; nor think yourself holy because you tear others apart. We often accuse what we ourselves do, eloquent against ourselves, inveighing against our own vices while judging the eloquent in silence. Never attach yourself to such people, lest you incline your heart to words of wickedness (Ps. 140), and hear: “Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against your mother’s son you placed a stumbling-block” (Ps. 49). And more plainly in Ecclesiastes: “As a serpent bites in silence, so also does one who secretly slanders his brother” (Eccl. 10). But you say: “I myself do not slander; when others are speaking, what can I do?” (Ps. 108). We put forward such excuses “to excuse excuses in sins.” Christ is not deceived by cleverness. It is by no means my judgment, but the Apostle’s: “Do not err: God is not mocked”; he sees what is in the heart, which we do not see in the face (Gal. 6).

Solomon says in Proverbs: “The north wind scatters clouds, and a sad face the tongues of slanderers” (Prov. 25). For just as an arrow, if shot against hard material, sometimes returns upon the one who shot it and wounds the one who wounded, according to the saying, “They became for me a crooked bow” (Hos. 7); and elsewhere: “Whoever throws a stone on high, it falls back upon his own head” (Eccl. 27); so also the slanderer, when he sees the face of the listener become sad—or rather, of one who is not listening at all, but blocking his ears so as not to hear a judgment of blood—immediately falls silent: his face grows pale, his lips remain fixed, and his saliva dries up. Hence the same wise man says: “Do not mingle with slanderers, because their destruction will come suddenly; and who knows the ruin of both?” (Prov. 24)—that is, both of the one who speaks and of the one who listens to the speaker. And Timothy is told: “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter” [another reading adds: “quickly”]. “But rebuke the one who sins before everyone, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5). One should not readily believe an accusation against a person of mature age, whom both a past life defends and the title of dignity honors. If, then, you want me, as a delinquent, to be corrected, rebuke me openly; only do not bite me secretly. “Let the righteous chastise me in mercy and rebuke me. Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140). For, in comparison between two evils, it is the lesser evil to sin openly than to pretend and feign holiness.

[Note: Previously it was less correctly written that sinners ought sometimes to be rebuked, etc.]

What benefit do your wounds bring you if I am wounded? Is it a comfort to one who has been struck to see a friend dying beside him? What benefit is it to me if you report my evils to others, if, while I do not know it, you wound another through my sins—or rather, through your slanders—and, while recounting them eagerly to everyone, speak to each person as though you had told no one else? This is not correcting me, but satisfying your own vice. For the Lord commanded that sinners should be rebuked privately, or with a witness present. And if they refuse to listen, the matter should be reported to the Church, and those who persist in evil should be regarded as being “like pagans and tax collectors.”

[Note: “Sinners” was formerly read less correctly: “that sinners ought sometimes to be rebuked,” etc.]

For minds educated in liberal studies are more easily overcome by shame than by fear; and those whom torments do not conquer are sometimes conquered by embarrassment. Yet it is much better to correct sins through fear of punishments than to submit to divine judgment through hope of prosperity. For one who does not perceive God through benefits will perceive him through punishments.

Moreover, it is a great sin to hate the one who corrects you, especially if he corrects you not out of hatred but out of love. Every chorus is united against us, and every bench is barking; even members of our own order are joined to them—those who are gnawed and who gnaw: talkative against us, mute on their own behalf, as though they themselves were something other than monks, and as though whatever is said against monks did not rebound upon the clergy, who are the fathers of monks. The loss of the flock is the shepherd’s disgrace, just as, conversely, the life of that monk is praiseworthy who venerates the priests of Christ and does not slander the rank through which he became a Christian. For when we bestow benefits even upon our enemies, by our goodness we overcome their malice, soften their harshness, and turn an angry mind toward goodwill [another reading: “toward gentleness”].

Nor will the one who strives to please God alone be free from the infection [another reading: “assault”] of envy. For envy pursues not so much human friendships as God’s justice alone. The envious person is tortured by another’s happiness, since virtue is always exposed to envy. It is also difficult for one whose companion is justice to escape reproaches; indeed, if anyone wishes to live devoutly, the wicked immediately blaspheme him with mockery. It is also the custom of the slanderer [another reading: “sinner”] always to try to make his evil sprout by denying it, and to say either that he did not do what he did, or that he acted from good zeal. It is no wonder, then, if unclean swine grunt against me, a little human being, and trample pearls under their feet; nor is it surprising that envy has found one who is removed from cities, the forum, lawsuits, and crowds, and lives hidden away. Heretics love me so much that they cannot be without me. I will omit persons; one must answer only with facts and charges.

It is of no benefit to a person who curses to curse back, or to bite one’s adversaries in retaliation, since it has been commanded that evil must not be repaid with evil. Therefore we seek not victory over an adversary, but truth against falsehood. Nor should we fear to incur the hatred of certain people. For we ought to please not human beings but God. But know that I have never spared heretics; rather, I have labored with every effort to make those who were enemies of the Church my enemies. Thus I patiently endured my own injury; I could not endure impiety against God. Dogs bark for their masters; do you not want me to bark for Christ? False rumor is quickly suppressed, and later life judges earlier life. Indeed, no one can pass through the course of this life without the bite of human beings.

The wicked take comfort in attacking the good, while they think that the guilt of sinners is diminished by the multitude of those who sin. But the fire of straw soon subsides, and the overflowing flame gradually dies when its fuel fails. For if rumor lied in the past year, or if it certainly spoke the truth, let the vice cease, and the rumor will cease as well. The first virtue of a monk is to despise human judgments. Therefore I will not fear human judgment, since I shall have my own Judge. Neighbors desire to examine not their own life but another’s. Yet one who is a friend judges even crooked things as straight. There have been clever men skilled only in slander, who wish to display themselves as learned by tearing apart everyone’s life. But nothing is closed to God, and darkness shines before him.

Nevertheless, flee those in whom there may be suspicion of evil conduct, and do not have this saying ready: “My conscience is sufficient for me; I do not care what people say about me.” Certainly the Apostle took care to provide what was good not only before God but also before human beings, lest through him the name of God be blasphemed among the nations; nor did he wish to be judged by an unbelieving conscience. “If food causes my brother to stumble,” he says (Rom. 12), “I will never eat meat.” Therefore remove the occasion from those who want an occasion. For whoever dissents from another’s conduct seems to rebuke that person.

So also, after we had built a monastery in this province and constructed a lodging beside it—for fear that Joseph, even now, coming with Mary to Bethlehem, might find no lodging—we are overwhelmed by such crowds of monks flocking together from the whole world that we can neither abandon the work begun nor carry what is beyond our strength. Therefore, because what is said in the Gospel has happened to us—that we did not first calculate the expense of the tower to be built—we were compelled to send our brother Paulinianus back to his homeland, so that he might sell the half-ruined little estates that had escaped the hands of the barbarians, as well as the ashes of our common parents, lest, by abandoning the ministry begun for the saints, we provide laughter for slanderers and rivals.

Thus everything is full of dangers; everything is full of snares. Desires incite, enticements lie in wait, profits flatter, losses frighten. The tongues of those who speak against us are bitter, and the mouths of those who praise are not always truthful. One person rages and hates; another deceives through his service. It is easier to avoid a quarrelsome person than to evade a deceitful one. A forest grows up so that it may later be cut down; therefore a field is sown so that it may be harvested. The world is already full, the earth cannot contain us, wars cut us down daily, diseases carry us away, shipwrecks swallow us, and nevertheless we slander and quarrel.

You also see the most ignorant people flourishing in the Church. Because they have cultivated boldness of face and acquired a nimble tongue, while not considering what they say, they consider themselves prudent and learned—especially if they have gained the favor of the crowd, which is more easily stirred by lighter words. Conversely, you see a learned man lying hidden in obscurity, enduring persecutions, and not only failing to enjoy favor among the people but wasting away in poverty and want. These things happen because the recompense of merits is not here, but in the future.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the prohibition of oaths, vengeance, lying, and foolish speech

For you said, unless I am mistaken, that you rightly ought to repay evils with evils and swear with those who swear, because the Lord once swore, or repaid evils with evils. I know first of all that not everything appropriate to the Lord is appropriate to us servants, lest, by comparison with servants, injury seem to be done to the Lord. Otherwise we might perhaps begin to protest: why are we born not from virgins but from other women? Or why do our dead not rise on the third day? The Lord, I know, often swore, although he prohibited us from swearing. We must not immediately blaspheme him rashly on this account, saying that the Lord forbade others what he himself did, because it can be said to us: “The Lord swore,” as the Lord whom no one forbade to swear. But for us, as servants, it is not permitted, since we are forbidden to swear by the law of our Lord.

Yet, so that we do not suffer scandal from his example, from the time when he wished us not to swear, he himself also did not swear. And just as this brief statement is sufficient to settle the question of swearing, so you can readily see that the same meaning is sufficient for the matter of vengeance: for the present is the time of Grace, in which the fullness of perfection has arrived; another was the time of the Law, and another that of the Prophets, as the Lord says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’” (Matt. 5). “But I command more perfect things,” which the reader will find arranged in their proper place in the order of the Gospel (Matt. 13).

From the time when the Son of God became the son of man; from the time when the old leaven of Jewish tradition became a new kneading; from the time when the lamb is eaten not in figure but in truth; from the time when, according to the Apostle, the old things passed away and all things became new; from the time when we were commanded to lay aside the image of the earthly person and assume the form of the heavenly; from the time when we died together with Christ; from the time when we rose together with him through virtues—do not learn to swear, and consider lying sacrilege.

Everyone, therefore, must be admonished to avoid perjury carefully, not only at the altar or over the relics of the saints, but also in ordinary speech. For everything that does not build up those who hear turns into danger for those who speak. Truth can indeed be shut up and bound; it cannot be conquered. It is content with the small number of its own followers and is not frightened by the multitude of its enemies. Human beings, even when just, can sometimes conceal certain things temporarily for their own salvation and that of others. Let us therefore consider what we say, because we shall have to give an account for every idle word on the day of judgment. An idle word is one spoken without benefit to either the speaker or the hearer.

By foolish speech I understand not only that of those who recount shameful things in order to provoke laughter and, through feigned stupidity, mock more thoroughly those whom they desire to please, but also that of those who are considered wise in the world and, debating physical matters, say that they have clearly comprehended the sands of the shores, the drops of the ocean, the extent of the heavens, and the point of the earth.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On patience, reconciliation, and not mourning the dead

Now we must speak of patience and its benefits. Patience is endurance of every injury and suffering, and sufficient waiting for all things without haste. Whoever understands and possesses it bears contrary and grievous things in life and contains all good things. It has hope as its sister, and all good things are its kin. For it endures willingly because it hopes, and by hoping it tolerates. What is not hoped for is borne impatiently. Patience carries every virtue through when hope is recognized as going before it, or when hope follows as the fruit of patience.

It rejoices in faith as its mother, and has God, conscience, kind, and relationship as its rudder. Hence glorious witnesses are produced: they are found full of faith, solicitous through fear of God, disciples of self-restraint, children of hope, with patience as their guide. Then they become fellow heirs of Christ, imitating him through the virtues of patience even unto death.

Therefore, when you have suffered injury, be silent; conquer anger through patience. Holy love has no impatience. Gentleness is disturbed by no passion, and especially is not broken by anger or fury. Whoever possesses it will attain the blessedness promised by the Lord’s voice, so that he may possess the earth—that is, command and rule his own body. Nothing intoxicates so greatly as disturbance of mind. There is a sorrow that leads to death; there is an anger that does not accomplish God’s justice and, being close to fury, makes the mind powerless over itself, to such an extent that the lips tremble, the teeth chatter, and the face changes color with pallor. True joy of mind sometimes alleviates bodily pains. But if mental distress is added to bodily sickness, the infirmity is doubled. The Apostle also says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

What shall we do on the day of judgment, when the sun has set over an anger not of one day but of so many years? Therefore let savagery grow mild, let anger become gentle, let them forgive one another their faults, and let the demander of vengeance not be the one who asks for pardon. It is a great offense to refuse to appease one who has been offended, although, as long as we dwell in the tent of this body and are surrounded by fragile flesh, we can moderate and govern emotions and disturbances but cannot cut them off. Therefore the Psalmist says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4). For to become angry is human, but to put an end to anger is Christian. Hence someone—Archytas, speaking to his steward—said: “I would already have killed you with blows, had I not been angry.” Thus they are called just, because they carry out all their works patiently.

It is much better for your stomach to hurt than your mind, and for your step to falter than your chastity. Nor should the remedies of repentance immediately flatter us; they are the remedies of the unfortunate. A wound that is healed through pain must be guarded against. We cannot know the evils of sickness until health has followed, and vices demonstrate how much good virtue contains; light becomes clearer by comparison with darkness.

But let us consider what that ethical psalm says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Ps. 118). No one can say this except the one who magnifies the Lord in everything he suffers and, attributing it to his own merit, glories in his mercy amid adversities. For it is necessary that whoever says he believes in Christ rejoice in all Christ’s judgments, saying: “I am healthy; I give thanks to the Creator. I languish, and in this I praise the Lord’s will. For when I am weak, then I am stronger” (2 Cor. 12); and the strength of the spirit is perfected in the weakness of the flesh. For strength of body is weakness of soul.

The Apostle also suffers something he does not wish to suffer, for which he entreats the Lord three times, but he is told: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” Why, then, should what must at some time be suffered be harsh?

Do we grieve when someone dies? For this reason we were not born [Note: Previously, with an affirmative sense: “we were born.” A little further below, in the passage “For our death is sin,” Rubeus omits the passage.]—in order to remain forever. Let the dead person be mourned, but the one whom Tartarus devours, in whose punishment eternal fire blazes. For our death is sin. But we, whose departure is accompanied by a multitude of angels, whom Christ comes forth to meet, should be more burdened if we dwell in this tent of death.

Moreover, do you not fear that the Savior may say to you: “Are you angry because your brother has become my son? Are you indignant at my judgment, and by rebellious tears do you wrong the one who possesses him? You deny yourself food, not from devotion to fasting but from grief. I do not love this frugality. These fasts belong to my adversary. I receive no soul that is separated from the body against my will. Let foolish philosophy have such martyrs; let it have Zeno, Cleombrotus, and Cato.” If you believed that your brother was alive, you would never mourn that he had migrated to better things. For just as there is another life of the blessed beyond this life, so beyond this death there is another death of the impious.

Against the harshness and most cruel necessity of death, we are raised by this consolation: that in a short while we shall see those whom we grieve as absent. For death is called not death but a falling asleep and sleep. We should rather grieve for ourselves, who stand daily in battle, are stained by the vices of sins, and receive wounds.

Yet far be it from our faith to say that there is any wound without consolation, since the Prophet proclaims: “Is there no physician in Gilead?” (Jer. 8). For God allowed you to be tossed by the waves and winds of this age so that, having experienced shipwreck, you might thereafter take care not to be endangered in the same way. Thus everything you have suffered, just as you understand them to be wounds of your body, are remedies for your soul. The short span of life is compensated by eternal remembrance.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### On enduring tribulations and reproaches

We must enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations. “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and say every evil thing against you: rejoice, therefore, and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matt. 5). The glory of the future life is compared with the hardships of the present life. Especially because it is not the one who suffers, but the one who inflicts injury, who is miserable. Hence, for Christians, the banners of the cross are delights; the trophies of our life are won not through pageantry but through miseries. In our army, strong men know how to bear reproaches, not gifts. For Christ’s bonds are voluntary and are transformed into embraces.

But if someone is weak in body, and lacks wisdom, he does not overcome the contests of the adversary—especially since we possess free will—but is nourished by God’s help itself. Future blessedness is promised to poverty, not to nobility. Shame indeed holds back the senator, lest he follow poor Christ; but let him hear Christ: “Whoever confesses me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will confess [another reading: “put to shame”] him in the glory of his Father, with the holy angels” (Matt. 8). It is shameful, among senatorial parents, to be cast down through voluntary humility for Christ. Friends are displeased if, after the adornment of ambitious dress, plebeian and ignoble garments are put on instead.

“But if I pleased human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10), says the Apostle. And the Prophet says in the psalm: “For God scatters the bones of those who please human beings; they are confounded, because God has despised them” (Ps. 52). As good as human offense is, through which Christ’s servitude is found, so harmful is the friendship that offers offense to God, as it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

Let each person say what he wishes. For my part, judging myself according to the smallness of my understanding, I have decided that it is better to be put to shame before sinners on earth than before holy angels in heaven, or wherever he may wish to reveal his judgment. Hence Isaiah, a man most noble among his people, who is reported to have been the father-in-law of King Hezekiah, at God’s command laid aside his sackcloth and walked naked. He was not deterred by shame from so difficult a command, but followed God’s order, because he judged that nothing was more honorable for a human being than to obey his Creator.

John the Baptist, noble both in flesh and in spirit, chose sackcloth as his clothing from childhood and locusts as his food. He was drawn to the glory of this burden neither by consciousness of sin nor by the lack of poverty, but solely by the blessedness of the future age. Hence even the apostles are accused of being foolish, useless, and of little faith.

Let them therefore bring forward the Apostle Paul, whom, whenever I read him, I seem to hear not words but thunder. Contemplating future things with the eye of his mind, he said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8). Dangers do not separate them; pleasures separate us. They carry chains though innocent; we carry gold though guilty. They are bound in prisons; we are indulgent in banqueting rooms. They are placed on the rack, praising God with a pure heart and sincere thought; we perhaps, in the very Church, are thinking about accusations from the forum.

Although the grace of the Law has been given equally to all, and Gehenna or kingdoms have been promised [Note: Previously read incorrectly: “or the promised rule,” etc.], some meditate on wealth and others on virtues. Though it was said generally to everyone, “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,” while others serve God faithfully and without end through innocence, mercy, chastity, and fasts, we choose adulterers for ourselves, whom we wish to serve. For, according to the Gospel’s judgment, “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). Indeed, if I am a lover of money, glory, pride, ambition, or pomp, while I devote all the zeal of my will to these things, I cannot serve the Lord. For it is written that no one can serve two masters. “You are not your own,” says the Apostle. “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6).

The Holy Spirit properly confronts us on our own grounds, knowing that among all human beings this is observed in public practice: a servant is more cautious in the master’s work in proportion as he was acquired at a greater price. Thus we understand how energetic those ought to be in the work of the Lord who have been redeemed by Christ’s blood, and how guilty those ought to be judged who, although they know that Christ’s blood was given as the price of their salvation, offer greater service to another who has provided nothing.

I ask: with what shame will he hope for the reward of his obedience or labor from heaven, whose entire concern has been on earth? The world’s hired laborer cannot receive Christ’s reward. Every soldier in camp rightly expects [another reading: “looks for”] his rations if he has labored bravely in battle for his fellow citizens. And indeed, the laborer is worthy of his wages. Yet no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself (1 Tim. 2)—these are the Apostle’s words.

Therefore sorrow that gives birth to joy must be embraced, and its material must not be considered; for often we enjoy through the sweetness of the fruit those things whose bitterness at the root we shuddered at. Whoever desires to possess knowledge of letters cannot attain the joys of expertise unless he has undertaken the hardships of learning; nor can anyone possess the glory of any instruction unless he has first endured the heat [another reading adds: “of the mind”].

When the enemy, finding us deprived of God’s help, attacks us and leads us captive, let us not despair of salvation, but arm ourselves again for battle. It may happen that we conquer where we were conquered, and triumph in the same place where we were once captives. For if the Lord helps the miserable, we have salvation; if he despises sinners, we have a grave.

Anticipated death is much more grievous than death inflicted. For this purpose we labor and risk ourselves in the warfare of this age, so that we may be crowned in the age to come (Matt. 5). Nor is it surprising to believe this about human beings, since the Lord himself was tempted. Scripture also testifies concerning Abraham that God tempted him (Gen. 22). For this reason the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in tribulation, and knowing that tribulation produces endurance; endurance, testing; testing, hope; but hope does not disappoint.” It is also written: “For your sake we are put to death all day long, and we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 5). But there is great consolation in misery when someone placed amid torments knows that prosperity will follow.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On fear of the last judgment and the decline of this life

Therefore I greatly fear that on that day of tribulation, when each person must be repaid according to his deeds before Christ’s tribunal, the response of a just judgment may be spoken to those who have labored more in earthly affairs than in heavenly ones: “Go, if you can, and there demand your reward where you served with complete devotion.”

Such is the case of the five foolish virgins in the Gospel. While they occupied themselves with the concerns of worldly vanities contrary to the order of their profession, they had no oil with which to kindle the true light and remained in darkness. For consider: if the sky were suddenly overshadowed, the sun’s brightness were denied to our eyes, and rains brought forth for our humbling threatened the earth; if, when the elements are disturbed as usual, thunder were driven around the wheel of its chariot and afterward bolts of lightning flashed terribly before our eyes—although such things occur by natural custom, we are afraid and tremble, and, bending toward the earth, with pride laid aside, we submit our necks.

What shall we miserable ones do on that day, when, the heavens being rolled up, the fiery Lord will come in his entirety with the angelic powers? When the stars fall from above, the sun is changed into darkness and the moon into blood? When the mountains melt like wax? When the earth burns, the rivers dry up, and the seas are dried against the nature of things, as divine fire consumes the moisture within them and produces aridity in the waters? When sinners say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us”? When people call for death, and death, though summoned, does not come? When disasters are turned into wishes, and people desire what they have always hated?

When that time is fulfilled of which Jeremiah speaks with mournful feeling, saying: “I looked upon the earth, and behold, there were no lights; I saw the mountains, and behold, they were trembling, and all the hills were shaken; I stretched out my gaze upon the air, and behold, there was no human being, and all the birds of heaven were afraid. I saw, and behold, Carmel was a desert; and all the cities were burned with fire at the face of the Lord and at the face of his indignant wrath, and everything perished” (Jer. 4).

But lest these things be believed to have been spoken at the devil’s suggestion for terror rather than truth, future things are proved by past things, since such events are reported to have occurred because of human sins in the Flood, in Sodom, in Egypt, and in Jerusalem. Yet that day will come when this corruptible and mortal nature will put on incorruption and immortality. Then, at the sound of the trumpet, the earth with its peoples will tremble, and you will rejoice. When the Lord judges, the world will bellow mournfully; tribe will strike breast against tribe. Once most powerful kings will tremble with bare chests. Venus will then be exhibited with her offspring. Fiery Jupiter will then be brought forward, and foolish Plato with his disciples; Aristotle’s arguments will not help him.

Then, rustic and poor, you will exult and laugh, and say: “Behold my crucified God; behold the Judge who, wrapped in swaddling clothes, wailed in a manger. This is the son of a laborer and a wage-earning woman; this is the one who, God made man, was carried in his mother’s lap and fled into Egypt; this is the one clothed in scarlet; this is the one crowned with thorns. Look, Jew, upon the hands you pierced; look, Roman, upon the side you opened. See whether the body is the same as the one you said the disciples had secretly carried away at night.”

Oh, how many virgins, and how many men whose chastity was defamed, will be crowned by God the Judge! [Note: Other manuscripts add the incomplete phrase: “the hoped-for chastity of how many, on the day of judgment, from honorable repute—of how many, etc.”] Oh, how many would have benefited on that day if they had lacked in this life the sensation of their limbs and the strength of their inner parts! And how many there who are speechless and mute will be happier than the talkative! How many shepherds will be preferred to philosophers, how many peasants to orators, and how many dull-witted people to Cicero’s arguments [another reading: “subtleties”]!

For when we come before Christ’s tribunal there, we know that neither Job, nor Daniel, nor Noah will be able to plead for anyone, but that each person will carry his own burden.

Therefore, whether you read, sleep, write, or keep watch, let Amos’s trumpet always sound in your ears. The apostles who were found worthy to foresee this dreadful day for the impious and sinners were humble, raising the dead; while we exalt ourselves above everyone, although by sinning we kill ourselves daily, without considering our frail and pitiable nature, which is strong in adversity and never secure even in prosperity.

If food is taken excessively or drink consumed immoderately, producing a slight fever in the body, we cast down our soul, are distressed, and sigh. Then there is no concern for worldly affairs, none for estates; no one thinks about his patrimony, no one about the forum. All accusations and all profits come to rest in danger to the body. People run to physicians, and for bodily treatment they promise gifts, gold and silver; sometimes even slaves are handed over. Almost the entire patrimony is either neglected or given away so that care may be taken of a life that will someday perish. Yet for eternal salvation every person is utterly negligent, every person greedy!

There all frugality is restrained by the tightness of a generous spirit, where a more ready will and more abundant liberality ought to act. Though Scripture says, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world,” we desire human things and love them as though we had brought something with us when we were born into the age, or could take something away with us when we depart from the age. No one looks to the brevity of time; no one to the condition of nature; no one considers or reflects that everything enclosed by some limit is vain. For times slip away: leaving the past behind, they hurry toward the future. Yet the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain.

When they have planned everything for thirty years, a slight fever arrives and removes all their plans. For just as grass, green in the morning and flowering, delights the eyes of those who behold it [Note: Other copies add: “and blooming with its own flowers it delights,” etc.], then gradually withers, loses its beauty, and passes into hay that must be crushed, so the appearance of human beings is fresh in children, blooms in young men, and flourishes in men of full maturity; then suddenly, as it grows old, the head turns white, the face becomes wrinkled, and the skin, once stretched, contracts.

Sickness and hunger also bring this about, so that a face at first exceedingly beautiful passes into such ugliness [Note: Others add: “so that love is changed into hatred”]. Yet whoever remembers daily that he is going to die despises present things and hastens toward the future. But the more we are afflicted in this age by persecutions, poverty, the power of enemies, or the torments of diseases, the greater rewards we shall obtain in the future after the resurrection. Therefore he will be found secure on the day of judgment if no offense against God is found. We ought to be concerned only about these matters. Let the gentiles pursue earthly things, to whom heavenly things are not owed. Let those who do not believe in the future desire the present.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the virtue of humility and simplicity, and avoiding a puffed-up spirit

Take care not to hunt after the little rumors of people, and not to exchange offense against God for the praise of the crowds. Through good and bad reputation, on the right and on the left, the soldier of Christ proceeds; he is not lifted up by praise, nor broken by blame. He does not swell with riches, nor shrink through poverty, and he despises both joys and sorrows. For it belongs to a just and courageous man neither to be broken by adversities nor raised up by prosperity, but to remain moderate in both.

I do not want you to pray in the corners of the streets, lest popular applause break the straight path of your prayers. I do not want you to enlarge your tassels and display your phylacteries, or, while your conscience resists, surround yourself with Pharisaic ambition.

[Col. 0376D] Faithful reader, you understand with me what I am keeping silent about, and what by keeping silent I speak more forcefully. How much better it was to carry these things in the heart than on the body, and to have God as one’s supporter rather than the eyes of men! For although we may be free from other vices, to bear no stain of hypocrisy is the privilege either of no one or of very few. But just as the humility of one who makes supplication earns rewards, so the pride of one who is confident [Al. contemptuous] is abandoned by God’s assistance.

But you, brother, recline in the lower place, so that when one of lesser rank comes, you may be ordered to ascend higher. For over whom, says the Lord, will my spirit rest [Col. 0377A] except over the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?

But do you wish to know what adornments the Lord seeks? I have wisdom, justice, temperance, and fortitude. Enclose the heavens with these defenses; let this four-horse chariot carry you, as Christ’s charioteer, swiftly to the goal. Nothing is more precious than this necklace, nothing more distinguished by such variety of gems: on every side [Note: [Col. 0377D] According to Aput Rubeum and others, “you are adorned, girded, and protected,” and “let them be an ornament,” etc.] let them be for you beauty and adornment, protection and defense.

It is the opinion of the philosophers that the virtues adhere to one another; and the apostle James teaches that whoever lacks one lacks them all. And just as there are four virtues [Note: [Col. 0377D] In the same place: “the four shields of the virtues: wisdom, justice, [Col. 0378D] temperance, fortitude.”] by which we fight and are protected, so there are four vices by which we are struck by the enemy: folly, injustice, lust, and fear; but wickedness has no limit.

Rectitude and simplicity are also related to one another [Col. 0377B] and cannot be separated. The simple, humble, and unlearned person who cannot comprehend the secrets of wisdom will nevertheless, if by living he follows the examples of the wise, rightly be counted among the wise. For it is better to do small good deeds with charity and without knowledge than to shine with great virtues mixed with discord. Lofty things stand more dangerously and what is high falls more quickly.

But it is evident that every creature, even when it has attained perfection, nevertheless needs God’s mercy, and possesses complete perfection by God’s grace, not by merit. Nothing pleases God so much as simplicity and innocence. Therefore the Holy Spirit appeared among birds only in the form of a dove, because of its simplicity [Col. 0377C]; among four-footed animals, in the form of a sheep, because of its gentleness.

You must also avoid this especially carefully: being seized by the ardor of empty glory. When you give alms, let God alone see it. When you fast, let your face be cheerful, lest the passing crowd stop to look at you and you be pointed out with a finger. Do not wish to appear excessively religious, nor more humble than necessary, lest by fleeing glory you seek it. For many who avoid witnesses to their poverty, mercy, and fasting wish by that very act to please because they despise pleasing; and, astonishingly, praise is sought while it is being avoided.

In the other disturbances by which the human mind rejoices and grieves, hopes and fears, I find many who are free from them. From this vice, scarcely anyone has been free.

Therefore do not seek glory; and when you are without glory, you will not grieve. For whoever humbly accepts the words of one rebuking him already has forgiveness for the fault he committed close at hand. It is more serious to complete an evil deed than to commit it. Yet it does not require such great virtue to endure an injury inflicted by others as it requires the Lord’s great grace to be gentle and tranquil and unable to inflict injury.

Nor am I warning you not to boast of riches, not to pride yourself on nobility of birth, or not to place yourself above others. I know your humility; I know that from genuine feeling you say: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up” (Psalm 130). For it is utterly foolish [Col. 0378A] to teach someone what the person being taught already knows.

Let not your voice, deliberately weakened as though fashioned by fasts, be thin and failing. There are some who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting. As soon as they see someone, they groan, lower their eyebrows, and, with their face covered, scarcely uncover one eye to see. They wear a dark garment and a sackcloth belt, and their hands and feet are filthy; but the belly alone, because it cannot be seen, is burning with food.

That psalm is sung daily to such people: “God has scattered the bones of those who please themselves” (Psalm 52). They pretend sadness and prolong what are supposedly long fasts with food secretly eaten at night. I am ashamed to say the rest, lest I seem rather to attack than to admonish. All these are arguments of the devil.

Imitate rather the one whose pallor comes from fasting, whose alms are given to the poor, whose service is rendered to the servants of God, whose humility is evident in heart and clothing, and whose speech is moderate in all things [Col. 0378B]. Give yourself also to the one whose speech, appearance, and gait are instruction in the virtues. Do not aspire to a buskined eloquence, nor, like children, pile up clever little maxims at the ends of sentences.

I have touched on these matters in passing so that, content with the ears of the educated, you may not greatly concern yourself with what the gossip of the unlearned boasts about your talent, but may daily drink the marrow of the prophets. Since you began to be of patrician birth among monks, let this not be an occasion of pride for you, but of humility [Note: [Col. 0378D] Alternatively, “knowing the Son of God made the son of man. For …”], so that you may imitate the Son of Man, who did not come to be served but to serve.

For the more humble you are, the more exalted you are: a pearl shines amid filth. However far you cast yourself down, you will not be humbler than Christ [Col. 0378C]. Therefore, although I am conscious of many sins and speak daily in prayer on bended knees, “Do not remember the sins of my youth, Lord” (Psalm 24), nevertheless, knowing the apostle’s saying, “Lest, being puffed up with pride, you fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3), and what is written elsewhere, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), I have tried from childhood to avoid nothing so much as a swollen mind and an upright neck, provoking God’s hatred against itself.

For I know that my teacher, the Lord and my God, said in the humility of the flesh, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11). And earlier, through the mouth of David, he sang, “Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness” (Psalm 131). And elsewhere we read: “Before glory a man’s heart is humbled, and before ruin it is exalted.” For nothing, as we have often said, is as dangerous as the desire for glory, boastfulness, and a swollen mind conscious of its virtues.

Therefore it is more important to lay down the mind than the clothing. It is more difficult to be without arrogance than without gold and gems. Thus a shabby little cloak, a yellowish tunic, bodily filth, and feigned poverty are of no benefit if by your deeds you destroy the dignity of your name, if amid filth and want you do not avoid sins. A testimony is trustworthy when it has no reason to lie. For from the one who is trusted more, more is demanded. “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6).

Let no one applaud himself merely for bodily chastity, since even an insult against a brother is the guilt of murder. The world falls, yet the upright neck is not bent. Riches perish, yet avarice does not cease. How many hasten to gather what will again be seized by others!
