## CHAPTER XXV. On the Humility of Christ, Whom We Ought to Imitate

[Col. 0379A] Christ [Note: [Col. 0379D] From the spurious writings, except for the passage which we commend, nearly all these excerpts are taken from the Letter to Damasus. So too is the greater part of the chapter which follows.] is baptized by a servant and called the Son by God. He comes to the washing among tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners, and is holier than his baptizer: he comes from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross in the tomb to the underworld [Col. 0379B], and from the underworld he returned victorious to the heavens.

Let us therefore imitate our Savior, because he himself is called the gentle and humble shepherd, the lamb and the ram. He was sacrificed for us. He is held by Isaac by the horns in the thicket. Nothing is more exalted than this humility. The creator of the heavens was born at Bethlehem, in this small cavity of the earth. Here he was wrapped in swaddling clothes; here he was seen by shepherds; here he was shown by a star; here he was worshiped by the Magi. In Christ’s baptism is our exaltation; his cross is our victory; his gallows is our triumph.

When the devil sees the washing and the sign of the cross upon foreheads, he trembles. Those who do not fear golden capitols fear the cross. Those who despise royal scepters, the purple robes of Caesars, and the banquets of Christians nevertheless fear filth and fasting [Col. 0379C].

For Christ commands that none of the disciples should say that he is the Christ. A marvelous arrangement: he does not wish to be proclaimed, though he rejoices in being understood; he loves to be recognized and hates to be displayed. He prefers to have been discovered rather than betrayed, so that his virtue, not another’s favor, might reveal him.

What greater clemency could there be than that the Son of God should be born the son of man, endure the discomforts of ten months, await the coming of birth, be wrapped in swaddling clothes, be subject to his parents, mature through each stage of life, and, after insults of words, slaps, and scourging, become for us even a curse upon the cross [Al. omits “for”], so that he might free us from the curse of the law? “He became obedient to the Father unto death” (Philippians 2), so that he might accomplish in deed what earlier he had entreated in the person of the mediator, saying: “Father, I will that, just as I and you are one, so they may be one in us” (John 17).

Since he had come for this purpose—to overcome with ineffable mercy what was impossible for the law, because no one was justified—he summoned tax collectors and sinners to repentance. Hence something new and wonderful among us: the Lord alone loves those who ask him, and alone becomes angry if he is not asked. At the very time when punishments were deserved, God is shown as the source of salvation. We can understand how valuable it is to please one who has not been injured, when one who has been angered grants so much.

Let us also love Christ and always seek his embraces; then everything difficult will easily appear so, and we shall consider everything long to be brief. And what the blessed Mother of God did not learn from her Son was how to fashion the heavens, create angels, or perform the wondrous signs of divinity, but only how to humble herself and gather the other lessons of virtue within the keeping of humility.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Justice and Uprightness of Life

Let us now discuss justice, which is the most equitable distribution of individual things and persons. Whoever possesses it, and whoever adheres to it, orders his life properly and preserves it without disturbance; he maintains equity in all things. He knows what he owes to God, what he must not withhold from the powers of this age, what he should retain for himself, what belongs to his neighbor, and what he should grant or appropriately assign to strangers.

For it is just to worship and love God with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s strength; to honor the saints and one’s equals, and to pay tribute to the authorities; not to be proud, but rather gentle and humble; to love one’s neighbors as oneself; not to pursue strangers and enemies with hatred, but with love; to be subject to those who precede us or are older in age.

For even the Lord, although he was Lord of all, was baptized by John, who was greater among those born of women, since he was earlier than him in human birth; and thus he declared that all righteousness was being fulfilled. From this mercy obedience to God is born.

[Col. 0380C] Whoever is found in all these things is rightly said to remain in Christ, because all these things are Christ himself. The glorious Paul instructs and teaches us about Christ, saying: “He was made for us by God justice, and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1). Elsewhere also: he is mercy and peace and love, which the Greeks call *agapē* (ἀγάπη).

For if an unjust person follows justice, he denies injustice. If a foolish person follows God’s wisdom, he denies folly. Wisdom, fortitude, temperance, and chastity benefit only those who possess them; but justice benefits others and the wretched. It knows neither father nor brother, but knows the truth; it accepts no person’s status and imitates God.

Learn, therefore, to do good. Virtue must be learned. Nature’s goodness alone is not sufficient for justice unless one is trained by suitable disciplines. Justice must therefore be learned, and the thresholds of teachers must be worn down. But the secular judge, having accepted bribes, condemns the innocent and frees the guilty. The same may sometimes be said of the leaders of the Church: because of bribes they tear apart the law and do not bring judgment to its conclusion.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Faith, Hope, and Fear

If faith, as the apostle Paul says, “is the substance of things hoped for” (Hebrews 11:1), which we hope for, and the proof of things we do not see, then one ought to believe and trust that God is able to fulfill what he promises, and to transfer one’s hope into the future. Then, with complete faith, one will easily be able to attain what has been promised.

Faith places all these invisible things before our eyes. Entering into it, we abandon all things belonging to the devil, the powers of this world, and these darknesses; with confidence we approach God. For it is necessary to believe and hope for what God has commanded, while we reject what the devil had implanted.

Hope follows faith; therefore let us speak of hope itself. Hope is the expectation of all future things that we possess in faith, by which we are saved. The apostle Paul writes: “For by hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8:24). What does someone hope for if he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.

This hope contains fear—not that fear which anyone who lives in faith must forget and cast out, but the fear that is one of the spirits with which Jesus is filled, as Isaiah testifies: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the spirit of judgment and godliness shall rest upon him, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:1).

It is that spirit of which David sings, saying: “Fear the Lord, you his righteous ones” (Psalm 33:10). Hence they are made blessed, as the same witness declares, saying: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” This is the fear that is pure and chaste. For David says, “The pure fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10).

[Col. 0381C] There are therefore two kinds of fear: one to be desired, the other to be avoided. The desirable fear is the admonition and safeguard of all the things that we believe or hope for. We fear judgment because we hope; and we fear the Lord because we believe him to be a strong judge. For true life is to know God, to fear his power, and to love his mercy.

Fear is the guardian of the virtues; security is easily led to a fall. If you have fear, you will be attentive; and if you are attentive, the lion will not be able to enter the folds of your sheep. This applies either to those set over churches or to the guardian of the soul.

The cautious and fearful person can avoid sins for a time. But whoever is secure about his own justice resists God [Note: [Col. 0381D] Previously it read: “resists concerning his justice, and of that person,” etc.], and, deprived of his assistance, lies open to the enemy’s snares. Human frailty is never safe; and the more we grow in virtues, the more we must fear lest we fall from lofty places.

If, according to Ecclesiastes, the root of wisdom is fearing God, what is its fruit except seeing God? The person who loves the good does it not unwillingly, under compulsion, or from fear of the laws, but in order to receive a good reward for his deed.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Charity and Peace

Let us now turn to charity, because it is greater than all things [Col. 0382A]. Paul acknowledges this among other things: “These three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13).

Love is therefore a bond of souls, a chaste and sincere charity without rivalry: the fulfillment of all commandments, the brief summary of all precepts. Whoever possesses it possesses everything; without it, one remains imperfect in other things.

And so that your wisdom may recognize how powerful charity is, we read the Lord’s answer in the Gospel when he was questioned: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matthew 22:37).

Do you see that the whole law hangs upon this one thing? Whoever possesses it may truly already be called God and the Son of God; by this alone he can become like God.

Consider the person who loves God: does he hope, does he fear, does he trust? No; he simply loves. Paul says, “When God loved the world, he sent his only Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to condemn sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3).

He places charity above all things, saying: “Even if I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I give my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, I am nothing.

“Charity is patient; charity is kind; charity does not envy; it is not puffed up; it does not act improperly; it is not provoked; it does not bring disgrace; it does not seek its own interests; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over injustice, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things; charity never fails” (1 Corinthians 13).

Nothing is difficult to those who love, and no labor is hard to those who desire it. Yet only that love is commendable which is joined to God and to the virtues of the soul. There is nothing that one who loves perfectly will not endure.

But whoever does not possess clemency and is not clothed with compassion and tears, though he may be spiritual, has not fulfilled Christ’s law. Hence it is read that when the blessed John the Evangelist was an old man at Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0381D] Other books read: “when he remained there into extreme old age and could scarcely …” They add shortly afterward: “Finally, the disciples and brothers who were present, weary because they had always heard the same thing, said, ‘Teacher, why do you always say this?’ He replied with a saying worthy of John: ‘Because it is the Lord’s commandment, and if it is done, it alone is sufficient.’”], and could scarcely be carried among the hands of his disciples, he used to say nothing else at each gathering except: “My little children, love one another.”

When the disciples asked why he always said this, he replied that it was the Lord’s commandment, and that if it were done, it alone was sufficient. But I beg that the friend who is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve not be lost together with the eyes [Note: [Col. 0382D] The same books read: “lest he lose the friend and my things”—the final word is uncertain.]. For friendship that can cease was never true. True friendship [Al. charity], the more it increases in number, grows by that much in strength, without jealousy.

Turn therefore from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it [Col. 0383A]. Unless we hate evil, we cannot love good. Rather, good must be done so that we may turn away from evil. Peace must be sought; let us flee wars. Nor is it enough to seek it unless, once found and fleeing from us, we pursue it with every effort. It surpasses all understanding; in it is God’s dwelling, as the prophet says: “His place has been made in peace” (Psalm 75).

Hell therefore divides brothers. Whatever separates brothers must therefore be called hell. Through harmony small things grow; through discord even great things collapse. Accordingly, the pursuit of peace is beautifully named, in accordance with the apostle’s saying, “Pursuing hospitality” (Romans 12), so that we may not invite guests with a mild and customary expression, or, so to speak, merely with our lips, but may hold them with the whole ardor of our minds, as though they were taking away with them something from our profit and advantage [Col. 0383B].

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Refreshing the Sick and the Poor

If someone begins to fall ill, let him be transferred to a more spacious room and be cared for with such service by the elders that he will seek neither the luxuries of cities nor a mother’s affection. Let no one be permitted to say: “I have no tunic, cloak, or mat woven from reeds.” Let the steward regulate everything so that no one lacks whatever he requests [Al. adds: “so that no one does not have”].

Serve the brothers; wash the feet of guests; provide refreshment for the poor and the brothers [Al. omits “provide”]; distribute the expense with your own hand. For whatever the clergy possess belongs to the poor, and their houses ought to be common to everyone. They must therefore watch over the reception of strangers and guests.

Solomon teaches that one must devote oneself to works of mercy and not trust in one’s own strength, but ask help from God. Suppose that you make yourself equal to the poor, that you graciously enter the cells of the needy, become the hands of the weak, carry water, cut wood, and build the fire. But where are the chains? Where are the slaps? Where are the spittings? Where are the scourges, the gallows, and death?

And when you have done all these things I have mentioned, you are surpassed by Eustochium and Paula. I say this not because I doubt anything about the ardor of your mind, but because I am urging one who is already running and increasing the fervor of one who is fighting fiercely.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Repentance and the Mercy of God

Seize the opportunity, I beg you, and make a virtue out of necessity. What is sought in Christians is not the beginning but the end. Paul began badly but finished well. Judas’s beginning is praised, but his end is condemned by betrayal.

Although God does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he be converted and live, he nevertheless hates the lukewarm, and they quickly make him nauseated. To the one to whom more is forgiven, that one loves more.

Hence that prostitute who loved Christ, baptized in the Gospel, was saved by her tears and by the hair with which she had previously ensnared many, wiping the Lord’s feet (Luke 7). She did not have curling headdresses, nor clattering little shoes, nor eyes darkened with soot-like makeup [Col. 0384A]. For the more disgraceful she had been, the more beautiful she became.

At last she weeps at the cross and prepares perfumes; she seeks him in the tomb and questions the gardener [Note: [Col. 0383D] Others add: “Do you recognize the Lord?”]; she goes to the apostles and announces that he has been found. They doubt; she trusts (John 20).

For the crime of sin is not so much condemned as the swift conversion praised in the speed of repentance. Nor would God compel people to repent if he were not going to grant forgiveness to those who repent. Nothing is so opposed to God as an unrepentant heart. This alone is the crime that cannot obtain forgiveness—especially since he is not unjust, so as to forget a few good deeds because of many evils.

Indeed, God is angry about nothing in the way he is angry when a sinner grows proud and, standing upright and rigid, is not bent into weeping and does not ask for mercy [Col. 0384B] for his offense. Nothing so offends God as an upright neck after sins and contempt arising from despair.

Therefore do not despair of forgiveness because of the greatness of your crimes: great repentance [Al. mercy] will wipe away great sins. For God does not wish to inflict punishments, but to frighten those who will suffer them. He himself calls people to repentance so that he may not do what he has threatened.

There is none among the demons who spares. They will all come hastening to seize their prey; a wind is before their face. Whatever they see, whatever comes before their countenance, they will desire to burn and destroy.

But no one should, through patience with God’s goodness, contend that his sins will go unpunished, nor suppose that God is not offended because he has not yet experienced him as angry. Indeed, God’s anger is great when he does not become angry with sinners. Hence in Ezekiel he says to Jerusalem: “Now I will no longer be angry with you; your jealousy has departed from me.”

Yet in truth God is not angry with human beings, but with vices; and when these are not present in a person, he does not punish him at all.

God’s anger has its measures: how much, for how long, for what causes, and against whom it is directed, according to what is written: “You will feed us with the bread of tears in measure.”

The person who considers himself wretched therefore obtains mercy from God. For God, who cannot be overcome by any power, is nevertheless overcome by the prayers of the tax collector.

For as long as you know that you have wandered, and as long as you have sinned, humble yourself before God for that same length of time, and make satisfaction to him in the confession of repentance. For one who is a sinner, stained by some defilement [Col. 0384D], cannot be called a member of Christ’s Church, nor be called subject to Christ.

Since we have gone astray in youth, let us amend ourselves in old age; let us join groans and unite tears, confessing our fault simply. For whoever, after falling into sins, turns to true repentance will quickly obtain forgiveness from the judge of mercy, because before God the measure of sorrow is worth more than the measure of time, and the mortification of vices more than abstinence from food.

Yet a great sin is expiated by great and prolonged torments, and the guilt must be balanced by the punishment of the present law [Col. 0385A]. Thus a great sin needs great mercy. For God has shut all things under sin so that he might have mercy on all (Romans 11:32).

But the word is taken up in vain [Al. “repentance”] if the deeds remain. Yet, lest I draw this out longer, take a few things in place of many; in them it is not so much order that is sought as progress.

Act, then: beware, run, hasten. Act, so that you may progress in this spiritual life. Beware, lest through careless and negligent guardianship you lose the good you have received. Run, so that you may not be negligent. Hasten, so that you may grasp it more quickly.

For many have begun; few have reached the summit. May Christ grant you to hear, to be silent, to understand, and thus to speak.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Conclusion Bringing the Rule to an End

[Col. 0385B]

Since human nature is such that truth is bitter and vices are considered pleasant, as the apostle Paul says, “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth” (Galatians 4:16), and since the Savior’s words seemed harsh, so that many of the disciples went back, it is not surprising if we also offend many by criticizing vices.

Nevertheless, I have determined to cut off the nose of what stinks; let the person with swollen glands beware. But what concern is this to you, who understand that you are innocent? Let no one criticize us for praising or censuring certain people, since in rebuking evil persons there is correction for the rest, and the praise of the best spurs the good toward the pursuit of virtues.

As you know, we have been occupied with the reading of the Hebrews and have acquired rust in the Latin language [Col. 0385C], so much so that even when we speak, a certain non-Latin rasp intrudes. Therefore forgive our dryness. And “if I am unskilled in speech,” says the apostle, “yet not in knowledge” (2 Corinthians 11:6). He lacked neither, but humbly denied one of them. We lack both, because we have lost even what we possessed as children and what was pleasing to applause, and we have not attained the knowledge we desired, in accordance with the Aesopian fable: while pursuing great things, we also lose the smaller.

My speeches, whatever I say, will not be prolonged any further. Therefore I admonish you and, weeping and groaning, solemnly charge you: while we run the course of this world, let us not be clothed in two tunics—that is, in a divided mind [Al. faith]; let us not be weighed down in our feet by shoes, that is, by burdensome works; let not the burdens of riches press us to the earth; let us not seek the help of a staff, that is, of secular power; let us not wish to have Christ and the world at the same time; but let eternal things succeed brief and fleeting ones.

I also beg you who are faithful to preserve our life and conduct in such a way that you neither suffer scandal yourselves in it nor cause scandal to others. Let there be among you the greatest diligence and the greatest caution, lest anyone polluted enter this congregation of saints, lest any Jebusite dwell among you.

May the Lord Jesus crush Satan beneath your feet; and may Christ our almighty God protect you unharmed and flourishing in a long life. May the Holy Spirit also deign to grant us that, having become doers of his commandments in this age, tested in the struggle of this life and found faithful, enlarged by spiritual fruits, we may deserve to be joined to the heavenly choirs [Note: [Col. 0385] Previously it read: “that by these things we may deserve to be joined,” etc.]. To him be glory and dominion, with the same Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0385]

# APPENDIX TO THE FOREGOING RULE

## APPROVAL OF MARTIN V, SUPREME PONTIFF

[Col. 0385C]

Martin, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lupo of Olmeto, general prior of the order of monks of Saint Jerome: greetings and apostolic blessing.

### 1.

A pious affection arouses and moves us, so that, following with constant paternal affection the purpose of sincere devotion by which you strive, through contemplation, to imitate the teaching and monastic life of the glorious Saint Jerome, we may grant a kind and favorable assent to your just and honorable wishes. Through these wishes, the regular and monastic observance under which that saint himself is known to have offered his devoted service to the Most High in this world may be propagated in the Church of God and duly venerated.

### 2.

Some time ago, among other matters brought to our hearing, it was reported that you and several other brothers commonly called of Saint Jerome, living under the Rule of Saint Augustine, inflamed by zeal for devotion and for the fruit of a better life, desired to live more strictly and perfectly than such a rule prescribed, and in the true monastic state which Saint Jerome himself is said to have professed and observed in common with his monks and brothers.

And just as you bore the name of that saint, so you desired to imitate his life, rule, and works. At that time, judging this purpose worthy and consonant with reason, we granted you, among other things, full and free authority by other letters of ours—whose contents we wish to be regarded as expressly included in the present document—to receive, whenever it seemed appropriate to you, as the rule of life in monasteries, in place of the said Rule of Saint Augustine, the rule contained and set out in a certain letter addressed to Eustochium and the nuns, which begins, “The body, growing cold in its limbs, is inclined …” [Col. 0386D], and which, as was asserted, had been directed to them, and which the said Saint Jerome was then said by many to have published and composed among his other letters. This is more fully contained in those same letters.

### 3.

But since, as a petition recently presented to us on your behalf stated, some people doubt whether Saint Jerome himself published the said letter [Col. 0387A], you consequently have accepted the norm of life handed down in it, as stated above, only as statutes of the same order and not hitherto as a rule.

Instead, having prudently established a firm foundation for the institution of the rule of that saint, you have extracted, compiled, and reduced as though into a single body, under specific headings, various passages containing the true teaching of religion and the monastic life from the different letters and treatises published by the said Saint Jerome and approved by the Church.

This was the monastic life which that saint, together with his monks and brothers, observed in common throughout his life and until the time of his death, insofar as concerns the principal elements of the monastic state and life, and which he admonished certain others to observe.

Under these headings you and many other monks and brothers of the said order propose and desire, with the permission of the Most High and with the support of the apostolic favor granted to you in this matter, henceforth to live and remain, and to receive these materials as a rule [Col. 0387B].

### 4.

On your behalf we have been humbly petitioned that, out of apostolic kindness, we might deem it fitting to grant you, your successors as general provosts, and all and each of the priors, monks, brothers, and persons of the said order, present and future, who may wish to live in it and serve the Most High, the power and permission to receive, in place of the said Rule of Saint Augustine, that which has been extracted and compiled by you into this manner of life and form of a rule, and to profess the said Order of Saint Jerome.

### 5.

Therefore, rightly praising and approving this praiseworthy regular and monastic observance of the said Saint Jerome, observed by him in his life, and ardently desiring that it be raised and observed in the Church of God as a monastic order; also concurring with favorable assent in the pious and sincere purpose of your devotion, and inclined by these petitions: to your discretion, the teaching and monastic institutions of the same Saint Jerome, as they have been extracted, compiled, and reduced by you, the Lord inspiring you, from the same letters and treatises as stated above, without alteration of their meanings; in place of the Rule of Saint Augustine and of the statutes contained in the aforesaid letter, for reception as the monastic rule of the order of hermit monks of the said Saint Jerome, whose profession you yourself have made; and for receiving that life into such an order, and that rule of the same saint by the aforesaid priors, monks, brothers, and persons desiring to live under it [Col. 0387D].

6. We likewise wish and decree by these presents that they, and you, are henceforth entirely absolved from observance of the said Rule of Saint Augustine and of the statutes received by you according to the said epistle of [Tepescens?], although confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See. We further wish that the provisions expressed in the said letters should in this respect assist you and otherwise remain in force, and we grant you by the authority of these presents full and unrestricted power to deliver and publish them for observance. We wish and decree by the aforesaid authority that, after you have delivered and published this rule as stated above, you, the priors, monks, brothers, and persons of the aforesaid order shall thereafter be bound to make, profess, and live according to it their principal religious vows.

7. You and your customs must likewise be conformed both to the same rule and to the doctrines and institutions contained in a certain epistle sent by Saint Eusebius, a disciple of the same Saint Jerome, to Damasus, bishop of Porto, and to Theodore, Roman senator, concerning the life and teaching of the religious life, as well as the death and miracles of Saint Jerome himself; and also to what the same Saint Jerome, when he was at the point of death, left to his monks concerning regular observance, integrity of life, and holiness.

8. Nevertheless, so that the rule of this kind, which you are to receive and deliver to the other monks, may not appear excessively burdensome or onerous to anyone, we wish and grant you by the same authority that, if the priors, monks, brothers, and aforesaid persons, or any of them who have received this rule, should at some time, because of human frailty or infirmity, or for any other reason, be unable to observe it, or the institutions and teaching contained in the epistle of the same Saint Eusebius, as exactly as they are handed down therein, they shall not on that account be bound by the guilt of mortal sin. Rather, their superiors shall proceed against them only by an appropriate bodily punishment, and a salutary penance may be imposed upon them according to their excess and transgression and the measure of their fault; this penance they shall be bound humbly to accept and fulfill.

9. You and your successors, the superiors of the said order of monks, may also continue to govern and rule those among the aforesaid priors, monks, and brothers who have already professed the order itself under the said Rule of Saint Augustine, but who, because of such infirmity or for any other reason, feel themselves unable to observe this Rule of Saint Jerome, or who otherwise do not wish to accept it, under the rule, observance, and regular obedience under which you have hitherto ruled and governed them. They may likewise remain under those provisions and serve the Most High.

10. With them, and also with those who henceforth in due course profess according to the Rule of Saint Jerome, you or others may, by the aforesaid authority, dispense from the individual provisions contained in the same rule whenever some circumstance mentioned above, or another reasonable cause apparent to you or to them, should exist; or you may otherwise consult and provide for the salvation of their souls as may be expedient. Concerning these matters, we grant you and your successors full and unrestricted power by the tenor of these presents.

11. We further decree by the aforesaid authority that, after this rule has been delivered and published by you as stated above, it shall possess the force of perpetual stability and shall be inviolably observed, according to its content and effect, by all who willingly wish to profess under it their principal vows. The foregoing notwithstanding, and notwithstanding the Apostolic Constitutions, as well as all those provisions in the said letters which we have wished not to obstruct, and all other contrary provisions whatsoever.

12. Therefore, let no one at all be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution, statute, will, and grant, or rashly contravene it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at the Church of the Holy Apostles, on the Ides of March, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

## A Second Bull of the Same Martin V, Supreme Pontiff

Martin, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.

1. Although we willingly devote the efforts of our solicitude to the salutary direction and advancement of the condition of all Christ’s faithful, over whom we exercise the care of the apostolic office, we nevertheless pursue with more devoted affection those whom, having cast aside worldly enticements, diligently serve the Lord of virtues in a spirit of humility. Therefore, whatever we discover to have beneficially proceeded toward stabilizing their purpose under the observance of true religion, we willingly strengthen with apostolic protection, so that it may remain firm and unimpaired.

2. Recently, indeed, the beloved son Lupus of Olmeto, general superior of the order of the Hermit Monks of Saint Jerome, explained to us that some time ago he himself, together with many other professed members of the order of the same Saint Jerome, then living under the Rule of Saint Augustine, inflamed by the zeal of devotion and for the sake of a better life, desired to live more strictly and perfectly than this rule prescribed, and in the true monastic state which Saint Jerome himself is said to have professed and observed in common with his monks and brothers. Since they bore the name of that same saint, they also desired to imitate his life, rule, and works.

For this reason, toward a more stable foundation for such an order, Lupus himself had extracted from various epistles and treatises issued by the said Saint Jerome and approved by the Church certain passages containing the true teaching of religion and the monastic life which that saint, together with his monks and brothers, observed in common throughout his life concerning the principal elements of the monastic state and life, and which he urged certain others to observe. He had compiled these passages and reduced them, as it were, into a single body under specific headings. Under these headings he himself, and many other monks and brothers of the said order, proposed and desired thereafter to live and remain, and to receive them as a rule.

We therefore, judging this purpose worthy and consonant with reason, rightly praise and approve this regular and monastic observance which Saint Jerome himself practiced during his life. Desiring with intense longing that it be raised up and observed as a monastic order in the Church of God, we granted the same Lupus full and unrestricted power, by other letters of ours—which we wish to be regarded in these presents as though their tenor were expressly set forth—to deliver and publish, in place of the Rule of Saint Augustine, as the monastic rule of the order of the hermit monks of the said Saint Jerome, the teaching and monastic institutions of that same Saint Jerome, extracted, compiled, and arranged by Lupus from the said epistles and treatises, as stated above, and to receive the aforesaid life of the same saint into such an order, and to deliver the rule of that saint to the priors, monks, brothers, and aforesaid persons wishing to live under it.

We likewise wished and decreed that they, and those whom Lupus himself would receive after they had made their principal vows according to the same rule, should henceforth be entirely absolved from observance of the Rule of Saint Augustine, and should observe the new rule. By the same letters we granted power that, after Lupus had delivered and published this rule as stated above, he himself, together with the priors, monks, brothers, and persons of the aforesaid order, should thereafter be bound to make, profess, and live according to it their principal vows of this religion; and that the rule, once so delivered and published, should possess the force of perpetual stability.

3. But since, as the petition recently presented to us on behalf of the same Lupus stated, although he later, prudently intending the salutary institution, solidity, and growth of the said monastic order, had assumed, erected, and received into this order the aforesaid monastic life of Saint Jerome, together with his monastic teaching and institutions, as they had been extracted, compiled, and arranged by Lupus from the aforesaid epistles and treatises, as stated above, by force of the said letters and in place of the said Rule of Saint Augustine, and had delivered and published the rule itself to the priors, monks, brothers, and persons of the order wishing to live under it, so that it might be inviolably observed according to its content, and had decreed that it be observed; and although the priors, monks, and brothers had professed their principal vows according to this rule into the hands of the said Lupus, and thereafter, using it, were ruled and governed according to it, and had accepted it as their rule, praising and approving it as the true monastic teaching of Saint Jerome, and according to it were also ruling and governing the monasteries of the same order of monks—

4. nevertheless, the same Lupus doubted that the assumption, erection, reception, delivery, publication, and decree, together with the other foregoing acts, could subsist for certain reasons. On behalf of the said Lupus we were therefore humbly petitioned that, in our apostolic kindness, we might deign to add the strength of apostolic confirmation to the assumption, erection, reception, delivery, and publication, and to the other foregoing acts, for their firmer continuance.

5. We therefore, who with intense longing desire the propagation of religion and the increase of divine worship to flourish in our time, inclined by these petitions, hereby confirm by apostolic authority and from our certain knowledge the assumption, erection, reception, delivery, and publication, and the other foregoing acts, as well as the rule itself, as it will be described below, and everything contained in it, individually and collectively, together with everything arising from it, accepting and approving them as ratified and pleasing. We strengthen them with the protection of this present writing, supplying all defects, if any should perhaps have intervened in them.

6. Nevertheless, establishing and also ordaining that henceforth Lupus himself and his successors, the general superiors, priors, monks, brothers, and professed members, as well as the convents and monasteries of the said order of the Hermit Monks of Saint Jerome, those now existing and those that will exist in the future, shall profess their three principal religious vows; shall also be ruled and governed by the said Lupus and his successors, the superiors; and shall be bound to live according to this rule, its content and effect, its aforesaid reception, delivery, and publication, and the other regular institutions of this order.

7. We further wish and grant, for the purpose of reassuring the consciences of the professed members of this order and for their greater peace of mind, that if any of these professed members should fail, because of human frailty or infirmity, or for any other reason, to observe the said rule, or any of its provisions, as exactly as they are handed down therein, they shall not on that account be bound by the guilt of mortal sin. Rather, their superiors may impose upon them, according to their transgression and the measure of their fault, a salutary penance, which they shall be bound to accept and fulfill. The Apostolic Constitutions notwithstanding, and the statutes and customs of the aforesaid order and of all other orders whatsoever, even those strengthened by an oath, apostolic confirmation, or any other firmness, and all other contrary provisions whatsoever.

8. The tenor of this rule, word for word, follows, and is as follows: “Dearest brothers, I cannot utter with my mouth the discourse which I have conceived in my mind,” and so forth; at the end of the same rule it is added:

9. Therefore, let no one at all be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation, strengthening, petition, statute, ordinance, will, and grant, or rashly contravene it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at the Church of the Holy Apostles, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the thirteenth year of our pontificate.

## Rule of the Nuns

It appeared wholly unworthy to learned and upright men that this should be attributed to Jerome. Certainly, there is no aspect in which one can praise the compiler’s diligence. (G)

## Prologue

With his limbs growing weak, his body inclining toward the earth from which it came, and now an old man with a wrinkled brow, almost a prodigy of nature, your servant, beloved daughters in the Lord and most sacred virgins of Christ, Lady Eustochium and the rest, is urgently moved by pious devotion in the affection of charity toward you, who have been gathered in the house of the Lord for the Lamb’s new nuptials under the resolve of obedience, chastity, poverty, and religion.

Thus, for a little while forgetful of the age of his trembling hand, he undertakes in this little book, through the service of the pen, to teach minds prepared for good a norm and rule—of living for God rather than the world, for the spirit rather than the flesh, and, what is arduous, not for oneself—gathered from the life of Christ and the apostles and from the holy fathers, the anchorites whom, wandering for seven years through the caves of the deserts, I found not without admiration and instruction, and worthy to be commended for observance and imitation; as his tongue had long been accustomed to teach by a living voice.

O happy affection! O desire worthy of commendation in the Lord! You who fear that, when the teacher’s tongue fails through old age and the common end of life, you may fall—although that fall is ready for those who walk presumptuously and without fear on the way of God, in which as many adversities lie hidden as there are moments of time—may learn that your piety asks that, seeing the dangers portrayed for you and the means of remedy, your mind, ever inclined to evil from the beginning of rational and animal youth, should walk along safe paths.

O prudent counsel, to exchange speech for writing, and what passes easily for what will remain for a long time! O just and holy exhortation, and wholly deserving of the benefit of being heard!

But, devoted daughters, although what you ask of your father is just and holy, your father’s age denies it and his insufficiency forbids it, even though charity urges him on. His fluttering eyes stare in darkness, and his unsteady hand, shaken by the frenzy of nature, shrinks from undertaking youthful labors. Nevertheless, the ardor of charity continually urges him not to spare the labor from which so great a fruit is gathered. I would not have thought to pluck this fruit among you, who are better instructed by the Scriptures concerning the Lord’s will—let me confess something flattering, though true—unless so great a labor were being undertaken to instruct others who will follow in the course of time.

Let charity therefore conquer this duel—the charity that conquered the Invincible One himself, so that he might die immortal for us. Yet this victory is hoped for in vain amid such natural impossibility unless the devoted prayers of his daughters are present. God obeyed such prayers so greatly in ancient times that he even repented of what he had first promised while threatening them, although he cannot repent.

## Chapter I. On the Charity and Unity to Be Preserved

What manner and rule of living for God must first be undertaken by sisters established in a monastery? Christ alone, the author and teacher of this purpose, instructs everyone in his reply to one who asked. “If you wish,” said the same teacher to the one asking these things, “to enter into life, keep the commandments.” And when he asked which commandments they were, he immediately explained: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, mind, and strength, and more than yourself; and your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 5:43). On these two commandments hangs everything that belongs to the Law, and everything that the prophets and holy men have examined.

And attend carefully, I ask you, dearest daughters, who desire to enter with all your affections into the life which is truly life—for those living in the world have no life, but death—and who, by God’s help, have already entered upon the path which no one enters in order to live for God without the commandments of charity.

For this reason the apostle Paul does not glory in the tongues of angels and of human beings, nor in knowledge of the mysteries of God, nor in the spirit of prophecy, nor in austerities of the flesh, nor even in works of almsgiving, although piety is effective in all things, provided that charity is not absent.

Charity alone, therefore, makes a person live for God; it makes the religious; it makes the monks. Without it, monasteries are Tartarus and their inhabitants are demons. With it, they are paradise on earth, and those dwelling in them are angels.

Therefore, my beloved daughters, even if long fasts wear you down, an ugly black garment deforms you, and a long sequence of offices and works is woven together, if charity is absent within, you have not yet reached the lowest step of religion. For this reason, dearest daughters, the journey toward the summit of apostolic perfection must begin here.

But since charity is relational, and affection toward one person cannot properly be called brotherly love, it is necessary that there be several who love one another through charity, so that the prophet’s words may be fulfilled: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1). Wisdom sufficiently confirms this, saying: “A brother who is helped by a brother is like a fortified city” (Proverbs 18:19). And again: “If two lie together, they will warm one another; but if one walks and falls, woe to him alone, because he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:10).

For this reason, the life of solitaries, which I have experienced sufficiently, is exceedingly dangerous and arduous. Even if it is good and very often close to God, it is nevertheless not as secure as the life of those dwelling together in the bond and affection of love and charity—those who assist one another when they falter amid temptations and provide one another with the services of piety and charity. But certainly, if brothers or sisters do not dwell together in unity, it is no longer good but evil. Nothing divided is good.

Moreover, according to the philosophers, everything possesses goodness to the extent that it possesses the unity belonging to its nature. Even if each individual thing created in the whole structure of the world is good in itself, it is not perfect unless it is joined to the others. For this reason, at the beginning of the world God saw that everything he had made was very good.

Therefore, dearest daughters, since in the apostolic life you have been gathered together from the world in your bodies, let there be one heart and one soul in the Lord, just as we read of the apostles and of the apostolic men themselves in the Acts: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in the Lord.” Certainly, no life is worse than to dwell together in body but not in mind. Truly unhappy are those in whom there is not one will but differing wills.

Let there therefore always be among you one affection, one will, one sisterhood, one harmony of conduct, one joy, and one sorrow, so that what pleases one may not displease another, and at what makes one rejoice the other also may grieve. In this way you will be able to possess the religious purpose if you dwell with one mind in the house of God. This is truly the life of God, not of the devil; truly a monastery, not hell; truly a religious life, not a diabolical one.

## Chapter II. On Possessing Nothing as One’s Own

Let that Gospel example of the most foolish man always stand before the eyes of your minds: he built his house with the greatest effort, but when the rivers rose, the winds blew, and the rains poured down, he lost everything as it collapsed, because it had been built on sand.

Nor is this surprising, dearest daughters: nothing firm or stable can long remain in something mobile. That foolish man builds on sand who, in the apostolic life and the religious vocation, seeks temporal riches. Attend carefully to this, daughters: here lies every danger, here destruction, here eternal death.

Those who have already renounced everything they possess, who have left behind everything they had in the world and have come by vow, under a promise of oath, to imitate Christ the poor man, who has nowhere to lay his head, must possess nothing temporal or earthly apart from Christ alone. They must not even desire, retain, or seek what they have already abandoned.

For this reason Christ commands the apostles not to carry a purse, a bag, or money in their belts, so that the followers of their life may understand from this that nothing private is permitted in monasteries. Certainly not a tunic, except the one worn out of necessity; not a shoe, nor any other, even the smallest, possession.

Yet even if Christ and the apostles kept certain things given to them for the sake of necessity, no individual was permitted to regard any of them as his own. Rather, that most wicked traitor and thief, carrying the money box, carried everything in it as the common property of the whole congregation, and, as the common minister, provided for the needs of each.

Instructed by this, the apostles and believers after Christ’s ascension said that nothing at all was their own; everything was common among them, and it was distributed to each according to each one’s need.

So also you, dearest daughters, even if you may possess something temporal for food and clothing—for these two things fully suffice for a Christian—none of these things should belong to any one of you. Everything should be common and distributed as is fitting, even to the smallest girls.

## Chapter III. On Choosing Sisters to Receive and Administer the Goods of the Monastery

Therefore I adjure all of you and each one of you before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge everyone, not to allow gold, silver, or quickly passing money to seduce any of your hearts; and not to let any one of you attempt, with Ananias and Sapphira, to lie to the Holy Spirit, from whom nothing is hidden, by retaining for herself any temporal possession, however small, beyond those things carried out of necessity—and not even those without the abbess’s permission.

Let the terrifying judgment of their death always frighten you. For it is written that, because of their death, great fear came upon the whole Church, and all who heard it were afraid.

The naked Jesus seeks naked friends and brides. If you should perhaps wish to follow him while desiring or seeking something temporal, burdened by its weight you will not be able to follow him naked.

For this reason the poor in spirit are called blessed, so that it may be understood that it is not enough to leave behind all temporal things in the world and approach the poverty of the monastery if the wretched mind desires what it abandoned. The eyes of the Lord regard affection more than wealth. It is better to remain in the world with the other rich, devoted to riches, than to desire those same riches while poor in the monastery.

Therefore I wish, exhort, and admonish you, dearest daughters, that this observance remain perpetually in your monastery: namely, that no one at all dare touch or in any way retain, even for an hour, money, a coin, or anything however small, even if it has been sent by a mother or sister.

Let sisters be chosen, either according to the practice of the apostles, by the common vote of the abbess and the others each year; or, if it appears proper and useful, let two or more sisters of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, be confirmed. Let this task be assigned to them: that they receive all revenues, both of the house and of the individual sisters, and faithfully administer from them what the sisters need.

Let them also take care that neither murmuring arising from parsimony nor arrogance arising from abundance find a place among the sisters. Let no one be given more or less than another, according to the life of the apostles; let each be given according to what necessity requires, not according to preference, so that one may not be needy and another overflowing, but each may be moved to praise God by an appropriate provision.

Moreover, those to whom this labor of piety has been entrusted should arrange matters so that every month, or every week, or every day, they are prepared to render a detailed account in the chapter before the abbess and the assembly of sisters, both of what comes in and of what is spent. Let this be done at least once a month, so that they themselves may not be suspected by the sisters of theft, and so that negligence may not provide them with an opportunity to carry out their duty badly.

## Chapter IV. On the Community and Humanity to Be Preserved

Thus, thus, brides of God, bind your bridegroom Jesus to minds cleansed of earthly contamination, for he does not tolerate anything earthly dwelling with him.

Thus, thus, apostolic women, throw away your bags and purses, so that neither money-pouches hang at your sides nor keys are needed; so that the outward signs themselves may show that nothing is possessed within except Jesus, and that nothing is locked away which has been devoted to the use of all.

The Gospel forbids you to have double garments, so that you may learn to possess only what supports nature, and not what feeds moths. If any garments remain, let them be locked in one place, so that from them whatever sister needs may be clothed.

Let no preciousness or superiority in clothing ever display one woman as a mistress and another as a servant. Rather, let equality exist in everything among those who, married to one bridegroom and professed by a common vow, have made this commitment.

I ask you: let not the daughter of a king seek to surpass the daughter of a soldier in earthly splendor within the fellowship of Christ and the apostles. For Christ does not set the noble Bartholomew before Peter, the humble fisherman; indeed, he entrusts to the fisherman the principate of the monarchy of the whole world.

Spiritual life has no need of bodily dignities, and Christ does not seek the pledges of the flesh in his marriage. In the world, let the daughters of kings marry their equals, and let the daughters of soldiers seek precedence and honors. But in the monastery, having forgotten their people and their father’s house, let them seek glory in the Lord alone, and rejoice that they have been taken from the greater precipice of the mountain into the apostolic life.

Therefore I admonish you, daughters, that whatever duties the mother of the monastery imposes upon you, you fulfill with willing hearts. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Let the noble not be ashamed of humble tasks, nor refuse them, but let them hear the wise man: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.” Let them also hear what Christ determined for the apostles when, at the Last Supper, they were debating these displays of human rank: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not to be so; rather, let the greater among you become as the lesser, and the leader as one who serves” (Luke 22:25).

But lest the teacher’s doctrine be cheapened by contrary action, he immediately adds, concluding the matter with a question based on comparison: “For who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves” (ibid., 27).

Let the human mind, which is the vilest dung and vapor lasting only a little while, blush to exalt itself and, refusing the duties of the house, desire to be served by the other sisters. For Christ, whose generation no one can recount, did not come to be served but to serve. And at the Last Supper, washing the feet of his disciples, he left this example of humility to his own.

## Chapter V. On Avoiding Simony in Receiving Sisters

Let your community shudder even at hearing of the detestable heresy of simony, which nuns, through a common depravity inspired by the devil, are accustomed to commit. Let the punishment of Gehazi and the wickedness of Simon terrify you.

May the voice of Peter, the vicar of Christ, speaking to Simon, never depart from your ears: “May your money be with you unto perdition.” For you think that the gift of God can be possessed with money. “The gift of God is the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:20).

It is common among merchants that a sale is exchanged for something better. The simoniac asserts that money is more valuable than the gift of God when he exchanges the latter for it.

When sisters come to you, receive them into the holy nuptials of Christ freely. Let holiness be preferred to money; let goodness of life be sought, not nobility of flesh and not worldly usefulness. Let no agreement or expectation that disturbs purity of mind precede their reception.

Wisdom proclaims blessed the one who shakes his hand free of every gift, who has not pursued gold and does not hope in money, which overturns judgment.

If any sister desires to remedy the poverty of others from her own abundance, let her, according to apostolic practice, place before the feet of the sisters everything she possesses in the world. Renouncing all that she had in the world as she enters, let her become like one of the least. Once ownership has been removed together with possessive affection, let everything she brings be handed over to the chosen administrators of the house, so that they may distribute from it according to each one’s need.

Let the woman who has given her possessions to the monastery not murmur if she is not provided for at greater expense than the others who came from poverty. Nor should she exalt herself and, with her neck held high in the manner of women, reproach the others by saying that she brought so much from her own resources.

The poor sister has brought more if, on entering, she abandoned the desire to possess than the one who brought many gifts but carried in pride. Rather, let her glory in the fact that riches, which ordinarily plunge their possessors into death, did not prevail against her, and that things which are evil in common use have been made good for her through the assistance of the sisters.

Otherwise, it would have been better for her to remain in the world with her riches and be condemned with a small punishment than, after leaving them and coming to the monastery, to be led to hell with a greater punishment because of the pride that arose.

The poor also should humble themselves: those who, because of their poverty, were unable to contribute anything toward the support of the house, just as the others did. Let them give thanks to God in humility, because although previously they could not live in the world, through the labor of others they have what suffices for them, just as the rich do.

It is indeed astonishing how wretched is the condition of many people. There are some who are lowly and despised in the world, who exhaust themselves beyond their strength through daily labor in pursuit of the most meager food, and who are scarcely filled with a few beans and turnips together with coarse barley bread. But when they come to Christ’s table and undertake Christ’s service, forgetting their poverty, they seek finer fare than soldiers accustomed to magnificence.

Let none of these things therefore have a place in the life of Christ and the apostles. Let all be content with what is provided, lest they perish through murmuring. If the administrators provide abundantly, let the sisters receive what nature requires, but let them not exceed the limits of necessity. If they provide little, let each learn with the Apostle to serve the Lord in hunger and thirst, in poverty, nakedness, and cold, so that, having taken up the cross, she may follow Christ, denying herself.

## Chapter VI. On Obedience to Be Shown to Superiors

I wish you, dead to the world, its vices, and its desires, to crucify the flesh with Christ; and you who, by your own vow, have already begun to castrate yourselves under the purpose of perpetual virginity and chastity, to be buried with Christ in the monastery as in the hardness of stone.

According to the decree of Peter, the supreme pontiff after Christ, who by the Lord holds the authority to bind and loose, let your purpose of being raised with Christ in glory be so firmly established by devotion that your entire faith and hope may be in God.

Discipline your souls in the obedience of charity and the love of sisterhood, loving one another attentively with simple love and heart.

Nothing, I think, is more foolish or more intolerable than for strangers and newcomers to command citizens; for one to present oneself as a guide of a journey in a place unfamiliar to oneself; and, according to the inclination of one’s will, to wish to teach about paths, the safety of the journey, and the shortest route.

Such a thing would appear monstrous to sailors; and one would certainly never reach the harbor if, concerning the direction and steering of a ship, whichever oarsman wished were allowed to command according to his own desire.

No city, no kingdom, not even the smallest house would long remain standing in the countryside if it lacked someone to whose will obedience was rendered.

For this reason Pope Peter himself, who wished to instruct the apostolic life of religion as he had learned it from his teacher, explains more clearly how the soul is disciplined in the obedience of charity and the love of sisterhood:

“Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17).

And so that no shield of excuse might be taken up, he applies it generally to everyone under the specific name of preeminent rank: “Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters” (ibid., 18).

And lest the wickedness of superiors be brought forward, which often gives subjects cause for a great fall, he adds: “Not only to the good and gentle, but also to the crooked.”

But lest it perhaps appear difficult for human will to deny itself and take up the cross, he sets before it the reward of obedience, by which every labor, even a burdensome one, becomes sweet: “For this is grace.”

O happy and abundant grace! In obedience the summit of the virtues is enclosed. For it leads a person by a straightforward path to Christ. Not only is the mind excused from rendering an account to God concerning those subject to it, but it is not even obliged to render an account of itself. O supreme freedom, by obtaining which a person can scarcely sin!

## Chapter VII. On the Governance of the Abbess
Attend carefully, my most beloved lady Eustochium, to how heavy a burden is placed upon your shoulders: you are bound before the divine tribunal to render an account concerning the souls of those subject to you, their bodies, their words, and their conduct. Take care, I beg you, that not even the slightest suspicion of evil arise from you, lest you scatter those whom you strive to educate. Give your sisters commands so ordered and so conformed to reason that even depraved and proud minds may be encouraged toward the paths of obedience. Let your speech be so sweet, so gentle, that it does not provoke the fury of harshness but breaks it once it has arisen. Toward the disobedient, let your spirit be manly and steadfast, so that every feminine softness may withdraw from your midst.

Let the brambles be cut away at the very beginning of their growth, lest, growing too luxuriantly, they suffocate the seedlings. For nothing is more dangerous in a ruler than a misplaced humility in correcting proud and insolent subjects. In difficult matters always listen eagerly to the wishes of each sister when they are being considered; yet do not rely upon the will of any one person. Nevertheless, if something useful is proposed, do not consider the person who proposed it. For God chose the weak things of the world, so that he might confound the strong (I Cor. I, 27). In matters undertaken for the common good, do not seek and retain only your own will unless the greater number of the prudent daughters commend it by common consent. It is characteristic of proud and foolish minds to use only their own counsel. No one’s will should be heard amid murmured words and in a hidden place; rather, in the presence of everyone, it should be permitted to speak and to listen with complete charity.

If the greater number of the sisters disagree with your own conception, do not wish to oppose everyone by yourself. In the carrying out of affairs, let fury, hatred, envy, and mockery withdraw so completely that nothing may be recognized except peace, charity, love, and mutual support, so that the Holy Spirit alone, the author of what is to be done, may inspire better things. Among you, whom charity unites together, let there be no sort of feminine disorder, so that the air resounds on every side with laughter and voices and the ears of those listening are terrified by the uproar; rather, stand with complete modesty: while one speaks, let the others be silent. Nor should one interrupt another out of eagerness to speak and thus impede the speaker.

## CHAPTER VIII. On reverence and subjection toward the abbess

For this reason I exhort, admonish, and beseech you, most beloved and dearest daughters, who have already died and been buried with Christ; who, having despised the flesh together with its glory, and having learned that all flesh is grass and its glory like the flower of grass (Isa. XL, 9), have been reborn into the newness of life through the Spirit—not from corruptible seed but from incorruptible seed, through the word of the living and abiding God [Col. 0400A] forever: live as foreigners and resident aliens, abstaining from all carnal desires that wage war against the soul; subjecting yourselves in complete obedience, fear, and reverence to your superior mother; so that no one may be permitted altogether to will or refuse anything except what the abbess of the house has commanded to be done. Let nothing seem burdensome or intolerable if it does not accord with one’s own will, when it has been commanded. The truly obedient person, who for Christ’s sake is deprived of every exercise of personal will, knows nothing difficult and nothing unjust.

Remember, most beloved, that when you entered religious life you renounced before Christ every freedom to will or refuse anything except what those acting in his place should ordain concerning you. For you obey Christ most firmly when you strive to obey the superior mother placed over you. Then you are more pleasing to Christ the bridegroom, to whom, when you were betrothed, you vowed your complete fidelity, and under whose marriage covenant you swore that you would admit no other lover; and you more swiftly deserve to be led to the bridal chamber and bound in every delight by sweet embraces, when you strive to obey his commands in the person of his representative. For the honor shown to the representative redounds to God. Thus the law of marriage commands: the bride is to be under the law of the bridegroom. Always emulate one another in this emulation of God: let each strive eagerly to surpass the other in obedience. Therefore there is no monastery, no religious community, no monks, where obedience is lacking among subjects toward the superior. A body is exposed to destruction when its members disagree with the head.

## CHAPTER IX. On correction and the general accusation of offenses on Friday

A stubborn, presumptuous, and proud woman in your holy community, who disdains being subject and by her quarrels and disputes provides a scandal to the sisters’ peace and displays an example of disobedience to them, is to be chastised with severe and frequent fasts when she resists the commands imposed upon her. If fasts do not chastise her pride, let it be subdued by beatings, humiliations, and severe disciplines, so that she may learn with Peter that unless she obeys the superior—or rather, Christ in him—she will have no share with Christ in the kingdom of Christ and God, even though the commands may appear unusual and not consonant with reason. But if her untamed pride still refuses to obey, let her be expelled with the apostate angels, since she will have no share in the kingdom.

O unhappy pride of life, which, in order to fulfill the pleasures of the flesh, renounces the inheritance of heaven that it was destined to obtain through Christ! She is not yet living for God, nor has she yet reached the path of religion and the marriage with Christ, if she has not become so simple and pure that whatever is commanded to her through the superior mother she believes has been conveyed by an angelic mouth. Let each one consider herself happier than the others when she is placed before the rest in labors.

Let no sister be ashamed, each Friday—the day on which the Savior endured reproaches and death for humanity at the hands of humanity—to examine her life before the entire assembly of sisters, to accuse herself with her own mouth of offenses committed against the commandments and the rule, and to undergo discipline. In this way, a mind stirred to reflection may, through the goad of accusation and words, take care not to commit shameful things deserving accusation. Nevertheless, let neither the hidden thoughts of the heart nor hidden sins be disclosed on this account; these ought to be confessed only to priests. Let only those things be disclosed that contradict public commands and provide the sisters with examples of sinning. But if anyone, whether through pride or shame, neglects to accuse herself, let anyone else be permitted to expose such an offense of hers, so that disobedience and pride may in no way take root in your holy garden, from which they cannot easily be uprooted. But if, in the manner of women who know how to keep nothing hidden—in fact, who reveal things by chattering before they know them—she has disclosed anything of this kind outside the boundaries of the monastery, let her undergo the gravest penalty, so that through punishment she may be taught the discipline of silence.

## CHAPTER X. On the extraordinary lives of the holy Fathers whom he found in the desert

I shall relate to you certain things about some most holy men, no less to be imitated in practice than heard, so that examples of good deeds and the humility of obedience—which, when absent, renders everything built in the structure of the spiritual edifice vain, since it lacks the foundation of the virtues—may instruct your minds, and the frequent remembrance of the deeds of the saints may form your religious life and virtue.

While for seven years I traveled through the caves of the deserts, visiting the holy Fathers who lived there, angels standing upon earth as though in heaven, through constant exertion on the journey, the arduous hardships of their manner of life, and countless other afflictions, I compiled a little book about their extraordinary life and conduct, which I myself observed clearly, so that it might be for you like a lamp on a lampstand for meditation upon religion and life. Nothing was so dear or so eagerly sought by the monks as that which could be found in those who commanded them.

Indeed, I must not be silent about the great charity and great humility possessed by those holy minds. Seeing this, I forgot every hardship and weariness of the journey and almost thought that the deserts, so detestable and inhospitable to human nature, had been transformed into paradises. It is wondrous to hear, but blessed to behold: charity had so transformed the hearts of holy men into godlike creatures that the flesh was almost unaware of flesh. Yet John says that everything in the world is either the desire of the eyes, the desire of the flesh, or the pride of life. For their simple and humble hearts rested so firmly upon the traces of obedience and humility that the opinion of certain philosophers seemed almost to be confirmed in them—those who hold that there is only one soul in all human beings. For the abbots and Fathers knew how to will absolutely nothing except what their subjects willed; and the subjects tried to fulfill commands before they had been issued, striving, as it were, by certain indications to prophesy the will of the one giving the command.

## CHAPTER XI. On the vanity of worldly knowledge

O holy foolishness, which deserves to carry people born for labors in the world over into glory, rescued from punishments! This most learned foolishness Plato did not learn at Athens; nor Aristotle, nor Anaxagoras, nor the crowd of the other worldly wise men, who are fools, acquire it. Certainly I, the wretched Jerome, did not imitate this foolish wisdom before I endured the holy blows. Yet, to reveal my own misery, before I reached the age of twenty the city of Rome had already chosen me as its chief teacher in nearly all the liberal arts. I had not yet entered the schools of the Holy Spirit; still blind, I could not yet reach the discipline of holy truth. Neither the Academy nor, certainly, the learned Rome possessed gymnasia that resounded with this holy foolishness, which the desert preserves.

Yet it was not without labor that you learned your foolish wisdom, Plato. The world could not contain you as you pursued the wisdom of the world, traveling through the territories of diverse nations, peoples, and regions amid infinite hardships and innumerable labors. Nevertheless, you did not know how to find throughout the whole world the end of your most foolish wisdom—the highest good toward which the inclination of your nature directed you—which these holy peasants, fleeing that wisdom, found hidden in the deserts.

And you too, Aristotle, prince of foolish wise men, pay attention. Although, without doubt, you were a great prodigy and extraordinary marvel in all nature, into whom nearly everything that the human race is naturally capable of seemed to have been infused, nevertheless the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God (I Cor. III) if charity does not shape it, if the intellect is not taken captive into faith, and if the heart is not inclined to the service of Christ—Christ who is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the pagans, but for us who believe, honor and glory. In him alone the Apostle glories: “Let the one who glories,” he says, “glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I).

## CHAPTER XII. On readiness to fulfill commands

Nothing is more honorable, nothing more glorious, most beloved, than the service of Christ. It is surely to be preferred to the exalted position of emperors, to royal dignity, and to every glory of the world.

Among the others whom I saw in the desert, there was a certain learned monk who, by the command of his elder Father, wishing to increase the fruit of his charity and humility and to provide younger men with an example of obedience, carried upon his shoulders twice each day, for three miles, a very large stone, undoubtedly heavy for human shoulders. Compelled by no other necessity, he had already done this for eight years. But if one asked what was going on in his mind, this may perhaps seem strange to our proud mind, which has not yet reached the perfection of this holy foolishness: a children’s game and an idle task.

I call God to witness that, when I questioned him earnestly, I found in him such simplicity and humility that from that moment I began to live the monastic life. For he completed this unusual task on every successive day so devoutly, eagerly, and cheerfully that after completing it he seemed to himself to have gained every glory. Indeed, he was not satisfied with the weariness of this task and almost troubled his Father to impose new labors and works for him to complete in the interval.

Why do I wander through individual examples? There is no need to explain everything that the monks continually practice in similar matters. Among all, this is the chief and celebrated rule of discipline throughout Egypt: they accept no one for the completion of every labor and the undertaking of every task unless he is obedient and humble. Thus, when the flesh is subdued by hardship, it may not have leisure for empty thoughts and pleasures through idleness. Hold firmly to this: idleness is the mother of every desire, impurity, and sin.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the works to be performed by the sisters

Learn daily in the monasteries, daughters, this holy foolishness and foolish wisdom, which the holy peasants in the desert teach you. Do not be wise about subtle and lofty things; leave them to the proud and puffed-up people of the world, so that afterward they may begin to learn that “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life,” and that God chose what is despised and weak. Enter this school often; on every day and every night learn a new lesson from it. Let neither leisure, torpor, nor laziness make you lukewarm and cold in the service of God.

Let your body, always wearied by duties, prayers, holy manual work, and other labors, seek rest and refreshment, not pleasure. But take especial care that no work of vanity be handled by you. The person who touches anything unclean, or a dead thing, is considered unclean. No gilded purses, no belts, and not even gloves—things all desired by frivolous and proud minds. Let a heart dedicated to God shudder at knowing such things. Rather, let sacred books rest upon your knees, whether you are reading or writing; or let the cultivation of gardens be practiced, or some other holy and useful work, so that the spirit, refreshed by a kind of relaxation, may be kindled more powerfully toward divine fervor.

Imitate the deeds of the saints that you read about, adapting them to your own purpose. Be willing to imitate what you praise and to follow what you desire. Conduct yourselves well among the nations, so that, from the fragrance of the reputation of your holiness, even the hearts of the wicked may be moved toward holy desires. And in that which depraved peoples disparage about you, as though you were evildoers, let them glorify God because of your good works. For this is the will of God: that you should silence the ignorance of foolish people.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the office and power of the abbess

Take care, whoever you are who preside, I beg you, lest you be lifted up by the office of governing, so that you command illicit, unsuitable, intolerable, or disturbing things to those subject to you, lest the prophetic saying apply to you:

“What has happened to you, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies? You have grown old in a foreign land; you have been defiled with the dead; you have been counted among those who are in hell. You have abandoned the fountain of wisdom. For if you had walked in the way of God, you would surely have dwelt in peace upon the earth” (Baruch III).

For those who, in the administration of government, demand honors and personal advantages do not walk in the way of God.
