Turn these matters over frequently in the secret place of your mind, and write with an iron stylus upon the flint of your heart what the Lord, whose place you occupy toward those subject to you, taught the apostles when they were arguing which of them was the greater, on the day before he was to depart from them. And although it was said earlier, hold what was related again more firmly in your heart:

“The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not so; rather, let the one who is the lesser among you become like the greater, and the leader like the one who serves” (Luke XXII).

Learn, therefore, from the teacher the office entrusted to you, lest in your representation you exceed the limits of the authority given to you. You will certainly not become a mistress but a minister, for there is one Lord. And if the remaining sisters obey you as Christ’s steward and representative, power has not been given to you for this reason so that you may exalt one sister and depress another among the sisters and daughters as you please. Rather, carefully investigate what is enjoined upon you by the founder of the government.

The care and administration of all the monastery’s affairs and of the sisters are entrusted to you, so that, while the others sleep, this office may teach you to spend many nights sleepless and to take on the spirit of a younger person in providing what is useful and necessary for the house. Thus not so much honor as burden is imposed upon you. And if you act as is fitting, you will obtain a much greater reward.

## CHAPTER XV. On the danger of preeminence and dignity

Do not flatter yourself, I beg you, concerning the Lord’s compassion, by which he mercifully tolerates sinners in their sins for so long. Even if his patience is prolonged, the vengeance is no less to be feared; indeed, it is harsher in proportion to the length of time that preceded it in enduring. Therefore, if you act otherwise than you ought, fear the danger, and do not fear it less merely because you have not immediately encountered divine judgment. For your Lord, who has placed you as steward over his sheep and in his vineyard, wishes to demand from you an account of each one, even of hidden things. And if you defraud him of anything, he commands that you, sold to the devil, be placed in the prison of the outer hell, where there is eternal weeping and gnashing of teeth, so that all the pain and punishment that can be imagined may be expressed in them until you have repaid the entire debt.

But if you perhaps trust that you can repay the debt, O foolish woman! For even for the smallest offense all human beings together have nothing with which to repay, unless the one to whom restitution must be made himself wishes to forgive it. Blessed, therefore, and more secure are those who are subject, rather than those who preside; those who are served rather than those who serve.

Nevertheless, the proud mind of human beings, careless of danger, always seeks advancement to greater dignities and is terrified only after the deed, by the descent; for the higher the ascent, the harsher the descent. But perhaps you consider descent uncommon. I shall speak as one firmly taught by experience—and by no small amount of it: a person rarely ascends through the steps of dignity without descending much more grievously.

Yet, even if I depart from my purpose, I do not wish to pass over in this little work an example that I learned as true from a certain holy old man who related it to me in the desert.

When a certain young man, chosen for a holy purpose and way of life, was selected for the exalted office of bishop—than which no other office can be imagined as more burdensome or dangerous—he prudently went to a certain uncle of his, a holy man and full of prophecy, in a desert cell, to consult him about the matter. After hearing his nephew’s account, the holy man answered his questioner not with words but rather with signs. He did not wish, by dissuading him, to oppose the Apostle, who praises one desiring the episcopate for a good work; nor, by encouraging him, to expose the young man to danger.

The old man therefore ordered the young man to climb onto a large square disk, violently raised above the ground by feet, and to roll himself on his back four times along each of the disk’s four sides until the time of his fall. Then, when a fall was imminent, if another revolution followed, he ordered him to roll himself once more beyond the top of the disk. When the nephew replied that, out of fear of falling, he could not do so, the old man immediately made him climb down and roll for a long time across a broad level surface. When both of them became weary of the repeated rolling, the old man said:

“Rise and go wherever you wish. Do what seems safer to you.”

The young man, disdaining this, departed and reported the event to another holy old man, thinking his uncle had been raving. From the latter he was instructed about the danger of preeminence and renounced the election, so that he might retain what was safe. Shortly afterward, when he left the world by a blessed death, he appeared joyful and glad to his uncle.

“Father,” he said, “I give you thanks for dissuading me from the episcopate. For know that I would now be numbered among the condemned if I had been numbered among the bishops.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On the order to be observed in the abbess’s works

For this reason, my lady Eustochium, I have said these things: so that you may perceive how great a danger you are exposed to, and how much prudence you must exercise in walking in the way of God, lest, abandoning the paths of justice, you be seized by the enemies with which everything is filled; and, led into a foreign land and defiled with the dead, you be miserably counted among those who are in hell.

I wish you to learn where wisdom is, where strength, where prudence, where length of life and sustenance, where the light of the eyes and peace are, so that you may understand the way of discipline and lead those subject to you along the way of peace and discipline. When you are dying, let your daughters mourn, not rejoice; but while you command what is just and holy, let all rejoice in obeying you with equanimity. Let neither relatives nor kindred be so exalted that the others become envious. Carnal affection, harmful in many ways, must not be entertained among holy minds. Love all equally, therefore, with charity and spiritual affection, as daughters. When the time requires correction, correct all alike in their omissions, as though they were unknown to you.

But always remember mercy in anger, so that no consideration may move you toward cruelty through rage or hatred. Yet do not keep your hands slack in punishing crimes, lest, through impunity, permission to sin be granted to the sisters. Do not rush according to your own pleasure to undertake difficult matters concerning the monastery and the sisters; rather, let the judgment of the more numerous and better sisters always be added, lest you be accused as guilty and as a destroyer of the monastery’s goods.

Do not be quick to believe everyone who speaks. For lightness in believing signifies a shallow mind. Let no one find you with an unbridled tongue, immodest in your eyes, gluttonous, or drunk. Adorn yourself with virtues and fortify yourself with good conduct, so that you may be ready to teach all by the work and example of holiness and life; so that everyone may regard you as an example of the virtues; and so that, secure in the administration of the ministry entrusted to you, you may be able to meet the Lord and render an account to him for each person.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the bishop’s jurisdiction over the sisters

The sex you bear is exceedingly weak, fragile, and changeable if left to its own judgment. Even if the spirit is virtuous, unless it is ruled and continually directed, it is quickly cast down from its holy purpose. You know this by experience in Eve: how easily she gave her assent, at the devil’s suggestion, against the divine command. The sorrow of childbirth and the lowliness of her condition themselves bear witness to it. Certainly, none of your virtues would be lasting, and nothing would be without grave danger, if you yourselves were responsible for your own care.

Therefore let your bishop, to whom the governance of the Church has been entrusted, whom God has appointed as a watchman in his vineyard, a shepherd of sheep, a director of the flock, and a guide of the people and populace, of the city and parish in which you dwell, cherish you with particular guardianship, nourish you with the pasture of holy teaching, and exercise special care before God for your souls, since the whole city has been entrusted to him. Let everyone obey him devotedly and with equanimity, as though obeying God. Let both the superior and the subjects venerate him as father and as a zealous guardian of the virtues. Let the law he has established for you in the way of God be observed. If any sister is unbridled, transgresses discipline, and is incorrigible by the superior, let her be corrected, chastised, and punished by him.

Let both she herself and the abbess recognize this staff of direction and rod of discipline, together with the others, whenever she deviates from the paths of justice. Twice or more each year, let an open account be rendered to him concerning the monastery’s goods and the condition, life, and conduct of the sisters, so that he may no longer be able to remain ignorant of the sheep whom he has undertaken to govern. Let nothing difficult be sold, bought, or undertaken in the monastery without his consent.

When the abbess of the house dies, let the one whom the common will of the sisters has chosen as mother and abbess of the monastery be blessed by him, and let him betroth her with a ring in Christ’s place, in a true [Col. 0407A] marriage, if she is found suitable for the office. The manner, entrance, and condition of sisters to be received must in no way escape his attention. If anything doubtful in the faith, anything obscure, or anything dangerous occurs in the way of God, let him explain it; let him instruct you in every form of modesty and in the virtue of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the order to be observed between the bishop and the sisters

Let familiarity not be excessively close, nor conversations suspicious. Even if he is a spiritual father, and even if the bishop is holy, he is nevertheless a human being, a weak creature. What is cherished and useful is lost very quickly unless it is strongly guarded. Let the devil find nothing at all in this holy association, lest destruction arise from the very source from which governance and guidance are expected.

Let all be treated equally. Let no carnal affection, but only spiritual love, intervene—and let it not be excessively close. For the beginning of a spiritual work, if mature foresight is absent, is accustomed to be followed by something carnal. I shall not conceal the truth: as often happens, the unhappy frailty of the female condition, under fervor of spirit and excessively close charity—unless a grave restraint is placed upon the mouth so that no one sins with the tongue—if it enjoys freedom of speech and intercourse, immediately gives birth from spirit and charity to lust, most shameful in deed and most wretched to mention.

Therefore, most beloved, I exhort you, admonish you, and command you: since you have been betrothed to Christ in marriage, to whom you have vowed all the fidelity of your chastity, and to whom you have promised under oath that you would acknowledge no lover besides him, seek to avoid the face of any man, even if holiness adorns him, even if he were equal in merits to John the Baptist. Do not be permitted to bind yourself to him in fervent affection even for a day. Believe one who has experience: nothing is more dangerous to a man than a woman, or to a woman than a man. Each is straw; each is fire.

I shall speak boldly, alas! The temples of God, the vessels of the Holy Spirit, and buildings dedicated to God become brothels unless they are guarded with diligent care. So noble a deposit, so precious a treasure, the irrecoverable honor of chastity, is taken away if the ever-watchful devil is able to fasten his gaze through the narrowest crack of any foolish affection.

Therefore let the heart be guarded with every care. Let watchmen be appointed upon the walls of Jerusalem all day, and let them not sleep at night, lest the thief enter, lest he carry away spoils that can never be recovered [Col. 0407D].

## CHAPTER XIX. On appointing a presbyter superior to the sisters after the bishop

A mind spread over many concerns cannot attend to individual matters. The bishop cares for everything; he is a human being, and cannot be present in every place or know several matters at once. Therefore, lest absence provide security for wrongdoing, have as superior after the bishop a holy priest whom holiness commends, whom learning equips, and whom age and life make such that even among wicked and dissolute people no sinister reputation could attach to him.

Let him represent the bishop among you; let him preach; let him correct all; let the house’s secrets be disclosed to him alone; let everyone rely upon his counsel. Let the opinions of different people in the sisters’ assembly not establish different sects or different rites, so that whatever one condemns another may approve. When a house is divided in this way, its peace, quiet, and charity themselves depart.

Believe me: a crowd of priests and religious men who surround women expel all holiness from their association. Let the bishop be informed of whatever must be done for the common good and whatever holy matter has arisen that must be arranged, since he is divided among many concerns and cannot continually attend to one person alone in everything.

Let each sister confess hidden offenses every month, or more often, either to the bishop, to the superior priest alone, or to whomever he entrusts with this duty. Strengthened by the sacred communion of the Lord’s body, let them enter bravely to fight the camps of demons. In this life nothing is stronger or more health-giving than this: that immediately after an offense has been committed, the remedy of confession should not be delayed. Physicians also testify that the illnesses of every disease are removed from the body if help is given at the beginning, when they first arise.

But if, mindful of human frailty, the priest himself should appear to be bound to any sister by an improper familiarity, let what cannot be removed without evil and scandal not be allowed to arise. If necessary, let him be corrected by the bishop. But if, once corrected, he is unwilling to bring his undertaking to an end, let him be removed, even if he should be extremely useful or necessary in that place. No usefulness by which danger to souls is feared should prevail. Instead, let a holy successor be appointed, commended by long chastity and a blameless life.

## CHAPTER XX. On the order to be observed by the sisters toward men, especially in speaking

Let the unchaste feet of any man never tread the thresholds of the monastery. Let your ears never be soiled by a voice announcing the impurity of a disordered mind. Every woman’s voice is an ignited arrow of the devil, and the reverse is also true. Therefore the Psalmist, groaning, begs that his soul be delivered from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue. Then, adding why he asks so earnestly to be delivered, he says: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation.” A man’s lips offer poisons to a woman. Unless she is wary of the deceptions of a deceitful tongue, how powerfully the devil wounds the miserable heart with the arrows of temptations, together with the heat of lust! These are the windows of death; unless they are closed, terrible death immediately enters.

Whatever a man’s condition may be, let him either never appear, or, if seen, let his appearance terrify your sight like a dreadful monster. Therefore I wish, most beloved, that if necessity requires you to speak with a man, a veil drawn across the small window cover the face of one or the other, so that what may not be desired may not be permitted to be seen.

Let holiness claim no excuse for itself. Holy David is captured by looking. Dinah went out in order to see and, having been seen, was corrupted. There would be countless examples of this, which I leave to you to ponder repeatedly. Why do I wander through many examples? Almost every syllable of Sacred Scripture cries out; almost every movement of our own bodies instructs us that victory is not to be hoped for in this struggle except through flight. Let no one dare to resist the forces of temptation out of confidence in strength, for unless one flees, one will quickly fall.

In communal life, therefore, let there be no private conversation. Secret little conversations are not free from suspicion.

For this reason I command that no sister dare speak with any outsider without the presence of several holy sisters and of the abbess, or especially of another superior of the house. The only exceptions are those things said to the priest in confession. Such words are often accustomed to produce many seeds of evil.

If it can be avoided, let there be no mention of a man among you. Beyond what can be believed, the devil rejoices when the memory of men remains in a virgin heart. No poison is more harmful to a woman than affection for a man, whatever its cause. Alas, the unhappy condition of your sex! Even a holier woman than can be expressed in words, if she clings to a man however spiritual, is at last inclined by natural impulse toward wickedness if virtue fails in the man.

I am reluctant to recount everything I know. Even terms of “sonship” and “motherhood,” by which men and women use one another under the appearance of the spirit, are devices of the devil and signs of eternal death.

I forbid you, under anathema and the penalty of eternal death, all little gifts and suspicious little letters—everything that announces lust. Let the utmost diligence be applied so that no letter of any kind leaves the boundaries of the monastery unless the consent of the abbess and the sisters has been given. And if necessity requires it, and the seriousness of the matter demands it, let episcopal permission or the counsel of a priest be present. Let any woman found guilty of this be subject to the gravest penalties.

## CHAPTER XXI. On avoiding fabricated and harmful conversations

All the holy Fathers teach, among other things, that frequent contact with the crowd is exceedingly harmful to the servants of God. In much speaking, sin can never be absent. The human tongue, rash in passing judgment, generally does not cease to gnaw away at the lives of the absent.

Some of a very wicked kind among the spiritual, failing to attend to the fact that God gave all judgment to his Son concerning the life and conduct of all human beings—and, what is more, concerning the conscience, whose hidden things are known only to divine knowledge—think that they are permitted to judge, bringing forward the statement that “the spiritual person judges all things.” Alas, filled with an unclean spirit, what are you trying to remove the speck from your brother’s eye when you continually carry a beam in your own?

Sad hypocrites disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. With long beards, hair sprinkled with ashes, garments broken, rough, and deformed in every way, flattering conversation, and fabricated words, they display themselves as holy; and, like whitewashed walls, they sow sects of error among little women.

Finally, those who speak while blackening a person’s life and reputation together—these are all instruments of the devil. The most unfortunate kind of women are caught by the hook like fish and led to the slaughterhouse like animals. Overly insolent women always desire fabricated things; they always demand words prepared in advance; they seek out lies and are never weary of new stories. They delight in omens, magic arts, and the incantations of demons.

If some people utter such things, they are fed as beloved sons, spiritual fathers and brothers—or, to speak more accurately, as concubine-keepers and corrupters of mind and belly—with carefully prepared dishes and delicate foods; expensive wines are not lacking. Often, from the stolen labors of men, and amid drunken feasts and throats belching with intoxication, they proclaim the sweetness of the spirit. Again and again that saying of the Apostle is put forward: “All things are clean to the clean.” It is shameful and wrong to speak of such people. Yet I wish to expose all the devil’s arts to the servants of God, so that nothing may be lacking that could be guarded against.

## CHAPTER XXII. On silence and observing the appointed days and hours
Thus, beloved brides of God, drive all these things far from you; recognize the devil as their ruler. Among yourselves, never discuss another’s life. Leave every judgment to the divine tribunal. Acknowledge your own sins; weep over your offenses. Let the life of every person appear to you as an example of holiness. Consider yourselves worse than everyone, so that purity may cling to your minds to such a degree that it would be improper even to think—and wicked to believe—that anyone could sin because of you.

If you hear anyone speaking ill of another, flee far away and dismiss her as you would a serpent, so that, overcome by shame, she may learn to keep silent about the deeds of others. It is often the custom of certain little women—usually, or indeed always, chatterboxes—to keep nothing secret of what they hear. [Col. 0410C] Rather, they say what they often do not even know, and know nothing of how to keep silently what might cause scandal. Thus they either utter harmful words here and there, sow discord, or incite others whom they hear to slander; or they confirm curses, so that they are held guilty of a twofold offense. In this community of God’s handmaids, let every feminine weakness be driven out. Let this word of James be repeated frequently in your hearts each day: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his own heart, his religion is worthless.” Holy religion, therefore, cannot exist among the talkative, who are unable at any time to be silent or to abstain from useless words. For this reason, instructed by the holy fathers in the desert, they observe sacred silence with the greatest diligence, as the cause of holy contemplation.

[Col. 0410D] I do not doubt that I have found many who for seven years had uttered absolutely no word to another person, knowing that the Lord cannot be found in agitation. Therefore, dearest daughters, I wish that in your community, three times or more each week, except on feast days, it be altogether forbidden to speak—unless some especially useful and necessary urgent matter requires it—whether together among yourselves or with others outside. On all the days when speaking is permitted, both as a remedy and for the sake of salvation, you must not devote every hour to words that can scarcely be uttered without sin. Rather, let this inviolable observance prevail: every night, after the Hour of Compline has been completed and until after Mass, and from Terce until None, sacred silence is to be observed, [Col. 0411A] so that opportunity may be given for the tongue to praise God and useless words may be utterly cut off. In the choir of the church prepared for divine praises, in the dormitory, refectory, cloister, and chapter house, it is never fitting to speak, except about those things for which these places are appointed in the praises of God. Thus both the time and the place of your religious life may already proclaim holiness, instill compunction in the talkative, kindle holy desires in those entering your fellowship, and move their affections toward heavenly things.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Restraining the Tongue in Speech

The apostle James would never have placed the proof of religious devotion in restraining the tongue, dearest daughters, unless he had known with certain evidence that death and life are in the power of the tongue. For, as he indicates, with it we bless and curse God. Therefore, after saying many things about the tongue, he draws a general conclusion from all that he has said: “Whoever,” he says, “restrains his tongue, that person will be blessed in his deed.” Behold: blessedness is placed in restraining the tongue, so that it may be understood that God—who is our blessedness—cannot be possessed and contemplated amid excessive talk. The tongue is restrained when, since by its own fault it is always inclined toward lies (and hence people are called liars, and the children of men are called vain), it is either subjected to silence, lest it dare to break forth into what displeases God, or exercised in goodness, so that it may offer divine praises.

[Col. 0411C] Thus, dearest and most beloved daughters, when opportunity is granted for you to be blessed, tame your tongues, lest they turn to quarrels, lest they resound with disputes, contentions, brawls, and scandals; lest they reveal oaths, blasphemies, insults, and displeasure toward others. But if, at the devil’s instigation—for he is always sowing discord—even a slight disagreement should arise among the sisters, let the wickedness be struck down at once and utterly by the abbess, or by the bishop, or by the provost of the house at its very beginning, so that the setting of the sun may not find anger in the house of God, anger may not turn into hatred, and the house of peace may not become a tavern for drunkards. Drive out lies as though they were hell itself. Let divine offices or words from the sacred books always be brought forward, both among the sisters and [Col. 0411D] among visitors.

If at any time little women begin chattering about their husbands, their children, clothing, or the vanities of the world, as is their custom, let their words immediately be cut short; let idle and harmful speech at once yield to divine conversation. If divine matters cannot be introduced into such a conversation, let the window be closed in their faces as a sign of hatred for the offense, and let swift departure attest to the holiness within. Thus let nothing enter through the body’s exterior senses to trouble the mind with thoughts when it is being presented to divine contemplation. The mind rarely thinks of anything that the external senses do not transmit. These are the windows; these are the doors. If they are not closed, entrance is open to death, and death enters only disastrously.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Avoiding the Company of Men

[Col. 0412A]

Believe me, dearest daughters—believe an old man who has experienced almost everything: your external senses cannot be closed amid the tumult of men. If a color is placed before the eye, the eye cannot fail to see it; likewise, the ear cannot fail to hear sounds. Therefore, in silence and quiet, perverse thoughts are avoided—thoughts that separate us from God. For this reason I exhort and admonish you to wish to hear the words of holy minds alone, and to be permitted to look upon only chaste and honorable faces, worn by holy fasts. Let a man appear rarely; let mention of a man be rare, so that your young girls may scarcely know the male sex. Certainly, let no male animal cross the boundaries of the monastery, so that every occasion for speaking about men may cease. Let such chaste and pure words resound from holy mouths in every conversation that thoughts of the manner of generation and the birth of young women remain hidden from your hearts. This is truly the devil’s chain. If you remove it from among you—by not extending even a finger to investigate everything out of curiosity, by ceasing to speak of what is not useful, and by not allowing your will, through prolonged silences, to find an opportunity for speaking useless words—then your light will arise in the darkness, and your darkness will be like midday; and the Lord will grant you a rest such as this world does not know. Your soul will be filled with splendors that minds darkened by the gloom of the age cannot grasp.

Happy, therefore, is the soul that, spurning the world’s turmoil and passing beyond the prison of the body, can be illumined by some ray of that highest and incomprehensible [Col. 0412C] light. So sweet and delightful is this consolation that all earthly things are immediately despised. Death, feared by every living creature on earth, is desired for the sake of glory, so that one may be permitted to behold more clearly what, glimpsed for a brief hour, is felt to be so pleasurable and delightful. Act in this way, therefore, dearest daughters; fulfill what you have professed. Rejoice, because you can. You are not troubled by men, by children, by concern for household goods, or by any other marital burden. Flee the company of men in such a way, and drive out all worldly things so completely, that nothing taking place in the world may reach you. Let Christ alone, your bridegroom, enjoy your close embraces. Alone with your one bridegroom, converse with him either through sacred readings or through holy meditations, and let him converse with you.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Services of the Handmaids Who Seek Food and Necessities for the Sisters

[Col. 0412D]

Your bridegroom is exceedingly jealous, dearest daughters; he absolutely does not permit his brides to be brought out in public, lest they be desired by lovers of the world. He always wishes to play alone; he always desires to remain alone with his brides alone. He wishes to admit no one as a companion in consolation; he distrusts everyone and confides in no one. Your bridegroom is so arrogant, so proud, that if you seek another lover, he immediately withdraws; he is so headstrong that he immediately dissolves every marriage. Therefore, my ladies, because you are brides of my Lord, guard yourselves for him with every protection, lest so sweet a bridegroom be separated from you. Let Dinah, who went out to see the daughters of that region, always make you cautious of that danger. Remain in your monastery as in a bridal chamber with your bridegroom.

Let it be permitted to none of you at all to pass beyond the boundaries of the monastery. This is the law, the rule, the complete profession for all of you: once one of the sisters has entered, let her never be permitted to leave, if it can be avoided. Nor should those women who wear the religious habit and are known to be bound by a vow to the monastery go through the city and villages seeking food and necessities. Rather, while remaining outside in some part of the enclosure, let them provide with complete holiness and modesty whatever you need, receiving with Martha a share in the reward. [Col. 0413B] I wish such handmaids to be present that, from the conduct of their lives and their habit, the inner holiness of the monastery may be proclaimed. But if they go out to obtain the household necessities, let them not wander through the villages in gossip, nor through the houses of married women at drinking parties. Let them perform every good work, so that their ministry may not be blamed. Let the sisters who remain inside be forbidden to converse with them in secret chatter, lest something from outside enter that could cause harm. Let the abbess of the house exercise constant care over all these women, lest they themselves do what is unbecoming to holiness. Let them be bound by the laws of observances and fasts, and let transgressors be subjected to the rod of discipline. If, in their perversity, they refuse to be corrected, let perversity have no place in the fellowship of holiness, and let the rotten member be cut away from the holy body.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Sweetness of Contemplation of Divine Things

Therefore, my daughters and ladies, brides of my Lord, remaining inside, let them sense nothing except the devout Jesus. Let them alone possess this paradise, where, in sweet and joyful repose, they may contemplate the ineffable Trinity in the sacred writings; let them join the angelic choirs and mingle with their sweet melodies by singing the divine mysteries in the Church. Let the obedience of the holy patriarchs and ancient fathers shape the mind. Let the oracles of the prophets kindle the heart through sweet meditation toward blessed promises. Let the apostolic teachings of faith disclose all the mysteries.

[Col. 0413D] Let the book of the Gospels always be held in the hands like a mirror. Let the holy martyrs teach you to trample underfoot all the world’s adversities and the storms of this billowing sea, together with every diabolical trick and the assaults of demons. Let the precious devotion of confessors bind your affections to constant contemplation of divine things. Let the wondrous conduct of the holy monks instruct the regular life. Let the most precious Virgin of virgins, together with the other holy virgins, continually teach you to break every softness of the sex and preserve the resolve of holy virginity.

O happy fellowship! O happy are you, if you are not ungrateful for so great and such a gift. Truly most fortunate are you if you yourselves recognize your dignity: joined in marriage as beautiful queens to the King and Lord of all, you merit to possess him, if only you wish it—him whom the angelic spirits long to see. O ineffable glory! In a fragile body you can behold God. Here, I beg you, let your mind be vigorous. Let one day pour forth the word to another, and let one night make this knowledge known to another night. Strive here to take part in the angelic choirs and the fellowship of the saints, so that afterward, at your departure from the body, they may come to meet you joyfully and gladly as acquaintances. If you do this, nothing will be sweeter or more delightful to you than to take part in these banquets and be filled with these foods. Once they have been tasted, all earthly things appear bitter. Then truly the enclosure of the monastery, which bores wandering and errant minds, will be reckoned by you the height of glory; and leaving the monastery’s boundaries will be considered a necessity rather like death.

Therefore, daughters, believe the old man who counsels you devotedly from experience. If you have once tasted how sweet the Lord is, you will be able, when you draw near to him, to hear him say: “Come, and I will show you every good thing.” Then he will show you such things as are known only to minds accustomed to them. I know what I am saying, dearest daughters. For—to speak of my own foolishness—I, a little man so despised and so insignificant in the house of the Lord, while still living in the body, often took part in the choirs of angels. For weeks I sensed nothing bodily; then, after perhaps many days, restored to the body and foreknowing future things through the vision of God, I wept. What happiness did I have while remaining there? What unspeakable delight did I feel? The Trinity itself, which I beheld, is witness, by I know not what manner of vision. The blessed spirits themselves who were present are witnesses. My conscience is witness: I myself enjoyed such great blessings that the weakness of my body does not know how to express how many or what kind they were.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Enclosure of the House

A heart filled with worldly concerns cannot aspire to the sweetness of such contemplation. It must die to the world and cling to God alone through such profound meditations and desires. Thus, when a grain of wheat falls into the earth, unless it dies, it always remains alone, just as it fell; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Likewise, dearest daughters, to leave one’s father’s house and worldly garments and to assume the name of a monk benefits a person very little if the miserable mind still desires, through its affections, the things that are in the world and seeks again in longing what it had abandoned. For when Lot went out of Sodom with his daughters and wife, the angels commanded them not to look back at what they had already left behind as they traveled. His wife, however, in the manner of women who always seek what is contrary, disobeyed the command and was immediately turned into a pillar of salt.

Let this teach you by what punishment those must be punished who desire the vanities of the world in monasteries. They become insensible pillars of salt, so that they can no longer feel anything of the sweetness of heavenly contemplation; instead, they remain in the bitterness of the world, living for the world. [Col. 0415A] Therefore, dearest daughters, choose your monastery as your tomb, where, having died with Christ, you may remain buried there until, rising with him, you appear in his glory. Finally, great care must be taken lest someone enter by night to steal the precious treasure hidden in the tomb. Here and there thieves dig, attempting by countless tricks to steal what is kept inside. Therefore let the tomb be guarded by the bishop, whom God appointed the first guardian in his vineyard. Let it also be guarded by the presbyter-provo​st, who acts in his place there, lest anyone enter carelessly or proceed to make a diminution.

Let the enclosure be surrounded on every side with such fortified walls that scarcely even birds may gain entrance. Let the walls rise so high that it be permitted not only to no one on foot [Col. 0415B] but even to no one’s eyes to discover what takes place inside. Let the doors be firmly secured with locks. Let the bishop arrange the keys, so that no one may enter or leave without his consent unless she possesses the wedding garment. There should be one or more small windows, according to the bishop’s arrangement, so tightly enclosed on every side with iron bars that scarcely even a finger can gain access. Through these windows, at the appointed hours, or on occasions of necessity, edification, or recreation, let the sisters be permitted to converse together in holy words with holy widows and other women whom the habit of their clothing and their gentle, modest faces make worthy of reverence. At forbidden and suspicious hours, let the small windows remain closed. Let the abbess of the house, or another holy sister, keep the keys, lest a raven go out through the window from the ark. Believe me: here one must fear for the treasure because of the terror of night—because of the arrow that flies by day, the business that moves through the darkness, the assault, and the demon of midday. Let these hours always be suspect to chaste minds.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Detesting Precious Garments

Let this prophetic saying never be uttered about you: “Their daughters are adorned and decorated like the likeness of a temple.” They are whitewashed on the outside like tombs, which gleam outwardly with gold; within, however, they are most shameful and unclean, full of the corpses of the dead. Such women are not daughters of Christ the King, but daughters of Tyre. They are caught by, and ensnare, the rich of the people through gifts and the shamelessness of their expressions. Such is the most defective inclination of women. They always place their glory in clothing, in gold, in precious stones, and in outward ornaments. Their natural lust is not enough for them; they seek opportunities to satisfy it. Without doubt they desire the eyes of men, while contemplating gold and gems, eventually to become fixed upon their faces, so that by the gestures of their eyes they may more easily incite them to the fire of lust.

Why, common prostitute, do you glory in pearls and gems? What concern is silver and gold of yours? Why do you exalt yourself in the beauty of cloth? Is not all flesh ashes and hay—or, to speak more truly, a mass of rottenness, food for worms, and most fetid dung? What in you is worthy of wonder, what worthy of praise, spectacle for boys? Even if the preciousness of gems and metals is praised—the preciousness that nature has entrusted to itself—are you nevertheless not always recognized as ash, hay, and unclean dung produced from unclean seed? O, if you wished to look upon yourself, most worthless of women, how ashamed you would be of the body that you adorn with such elaborate care! You are either equal or inferior to beasts of burden and the beasts of the earth. What you have to glory in is within, not outside. In this vessel, so shameful, you hold a treasure that you ought to cultivate with the greatest diligence and preserve with the greatest care. The earthen vessel is of no concern to you, even if its exterior form is ugly, provided that what lies hidden within is noble and beautiful and what is kept inside is whole.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Danger of Ambition in Clothing

Therefore, dearest daughters, who are brides and daughters of the eternal King—whose kingdom will not be corrupted or taken from him—let all your glory be inward. Sit at the right hand of the bridegroom in clothing not outward but inward, gilded with the gold of charity, with golden borders—that is, with the precepts of charity. Let your garment be surrounded on every side with variety, so that nothing may be lacking in its ornaments of virtue. Let myrrh, drops of perfume, and cassia come from your garments, so that other young women may run from the world toward the fragrance of your virtues and your life. Take delight in this honor of yours, daughters of the eternal King. Your King and bridegroom will desire this beauty of yours. Thus you will remain with him in the bridal chamber in joy and exultation. Then sons will be born from you, who will fill not the earth but heaven, whom the Father will appoint princes over all [Col. 0416C] the earth.

But if ambition for outward garments should delight you, if, having left the pomp of the world, the house of the devil, and the congregation of the wicked, you had not completely forgotten your people and your father’s house, exalting yourselves either on account of the dignity of your parents, or your fleshly lineage, or such fleeting vanities—mere vapors of the earth, as is customary among the inhabitants of the earth—then the most powerful King, rising immediately, girded with a double-edged sword upon his thigh, will drive you, wounded on every side by his right hand, out of his tabernacle. Then his sharpest arrows will pierce your hearts with bitterness, because “the rod of his direction is the rod of his kingdom.” Afterwards, cast out from the house of your Lord, everyone will mock you and say of each one of you: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, who did not make God your helper but trusted in your vanity: sit now beside the rivers of Babylon; weep and hang your instruments upon the willows, while you remember from where you were expelled. For you who used to sing a song of praise and joy now weep, led away to a foreign land.”

## CHAPTER XXX. On Consideration of the Final Day of Judgment

Therefore, dearest ladies, with the Apostle consider yourselves in this world to be refuse and filth, so that you may please your bridegroom. The pomps of the world are no concern of yours, since in baptism you renounced the world, the devil, and their pomps; [Col. 0417A] you later confirmed this under promise of an oath when you entered your religious life. Let there never be any conversation among you about the nobility of lineage or the ancestry of the flesh. Let the daughter of a king and the daughter of a peasant be equal in the service of God. All of you together possess one nobility and one dignity through your bridegroom. Go out continually beyond the camp with Christ, so that with Christ you may be crucified to the world and to vices, bearing his reproaches with him; and, for love of him, let the labor of the house’s duties appear sweet.

Do not dispute about the greater rank of duties, but about the devotion and affection with which they are to be undertaken. Never let murmuring, never the sound of shameful words, never the noise of quarrels resound among those dead to the world. Buried corpses never quarrel with one another in their tombs, [Col. 0417B] never blaspheme, never contend. Likewise, dearest daughters, lulled into the sleep of quiet and peace, await your bridegroom and judge. Await the great and terrible day of judgment—the day of wrath, the day of calamity—when heaven and earth together will tremble, all the powers of heaven will be shaken, and the angels, together with all the saints, will tremble. Then the circumstances of each person’s life will be examined, and their merits will appear. Let that terrible trumpet always resound in your ears: “Rise, dead; come to judgment.” Behold, the King comes with mighty power; he wishes to demand an account from everyone, certainly even for the smallest thoughts, certainly even for light and idle words. If you are not prepared to render an account of each one, you will be thrown into the outer prison. You will hear the Judge say: [Col. 0417C] “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Seeking Humility in Clothing

Alas for the most unhappy heart, the most unfortunate mind, which does not meditate daily upon that day of judgment, so terrible; and if it does meditate upon it, it is utterly foolish if it desires anything from the world and its pomps. Let none of these things pass from you on any day or at any hour. Let every wall of the house and every corner display this day, painted before your eyes. If this reading is not neglected, then the humility of clothing, which bores foolish little women, will delight you. Then rustic and shabby cloth will be preferred to purple and fine linen. Then coarse and rough head coverings will be valued above silks. Certainly, there will be such ugliness in the sheepskins (melotes) and such thickness in the cowls, with hoods prepared in such crude workmanship, that if the garments of worldly women were here, the artisans’ entire craft would quickly perish.

These things, dearest daughters, are fitting for nuns: not tight sleeves, precious and elaborate fabrics, or eyebrows veiled with a delicate covering in women who possess, rather than merely feign, the heart of prostitutes. I do not consider such women nuns, but the worst prostitutes and the vilest harlots. Precious and elaborate ornaments in tombs are not needed for the corpses of the dead. Monuments have no need of such things; the stones of the monastery do not desire the glory of garments, which cannot be possessed without great sin. Soft garments should be left to the actors and players of the kings and princes of the world. It befits John to be clothed in camel’s hair. Let it therefore be a shame to bear the name of religion while displaying oneself as an actor through the cultivation of clothing. Therefore, dearest daughters, since you are dead to the world and have utterly trampled it underfoot, I wish you to go forth in clothing so ugly and unadorned that, if impure eyes were permitted to look upon you, laughter rather than evil thought would be provoked. I certainly admit that those who boast of preserving chastity while pursuing seductive elegance in clothing are lying. Let your cloth, even if white and bright, nevertheless be coarse and cheap, so that its color may exhibit the inward brightness of chastity and its plainness contempt for earthly things. This is the glory of nuns; this is the devotion of religious minds; this is the mark of the brides of the eternal God; this is the sign of those dead to the world and buried with Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Seeking Austerity in Bedding

Married women and widows who remain in the world should be occupied with many and laborious concerns. Every day, engaged in frequent service, let them be saved with Martha through works of piety: serving Jesus in the poor, breaking their bread for the hungry, bringing the needy and homeless into their houses, covering the naked, and devoting themselves to works of mercy—works so fruitful and good that it is impossible for them not to please God and turn away his anger. Let them undo the bonds of wickedness; by loosening bundles, let them break every burden.

But you, dearest daughters, who, with Mary, have chosen the better part—or rather, the best—sit continually beside the feet of Jesus, turning over the volumes of sacred Scripture in holy readings. Wash his feet with the continual tears of compunction and joy, charity and devotion, focused upon the sweetness of contemplation. Wipe them with your hair, driving out from your hearts through it every superfluity of earthly things. Hear from the mouth of Jesus the word that passes through hearts like a two-edged sword, cutting the framework of the members even to the division of spirit. This word will be sweet to your throats, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. This is the word through which all things were made; this is the word that the centurion’s devotion sought, so that his boy might be healed. Only those who hear it know the sweetness of this word. The sleepy and those devoted to laziness cannot hear it.

Therefore, dearest daughters, I wish you to lie each night in your cells upon a short and hard bed, not upon feathers or soft bedding, but either upon straw or litter, or rather in wooden chests than in beds, so that your disciplined limbs may dread the bed rather than desire it, and the necessity of approaching sleep may compel you more than your will. Thus, because of the hardness, let brief and light sleep take hold, so that the mind, lulled to sleep, may not be tormented by the customary illusions of the night.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Matins and the Manner of Saying the Divine Office

[Col. 0419A]

Let midnight prepare you for the nightly vigil of Matins. Let the sound of the bell find none of you sleeping. It should not be uncertain whether someone was overcome by drowsiness, but rather whether by ecstasy of contemplation. After prayer has been offered in their cells, let the sisters come individually to the church in the profound quiet of midnight and awaken their beloved bridegroom with the praises of Matins, so that he may rise to their aid. Let the psalms and sacred readings be delivered distinctly and alternately, so that the angelic spirits may not be provoked to laughter by collisions, gaps, or barbarisms. Let the sound of their voices always be measured, attentive, quiet, and sweet, so that no pomp and no carnal delight may have a place in the divine [Col. 0419B] proclamations; instead, let the highest devotion pour forth frequent sighs and tears.

Let slowness and speed be so maintained in the manner of speaking that neither weariness nor impediment of the tongue may arise. Let no words whatsoever, however useful, ever be spoken among those singing the psalms. Rather, let what is being handled outwardly be carefully ruminated inwardly in the secret chamber of the mind. It is of no merit to pray the divine offices with verbal excess while the wretched mind wanders around the things taking place externally. Once the praises of Matins have been completed, let sleep not seize you even then, lest the response of the bridegroom to the petitions of the brides be delayed. Immediately in the chapter house, with the sisters attentive and devoted, let a devout reading from the holy books disclose, according to the will of their Lord, whatever must be done. Thus let illusions and the phantoms of demons that would deceive sleepers depart. Immediately let another very brief reading follow, concerning matters relevant to instruction in the apostolic life, treated in whatever style in the present little work, so that each day the pious mind, as though nourished by a small morsel, may desire sweetness, not be held back by distaste, and think greatly of small things. Let the readings be followed by confessions of offenses according to the regular disciplines, before the abbess of the house and the other sisters.

Let whatever has been done against regular observances and obediences be brought into public view, so that nothing may henceforth pass uncorrected and unpunished, and so that the mother and sisters may not be unaware of each person’s condition. Thus, through both shame and the discipline imposed by the mother, each one may be made prudent for the future. Outside the chapter house, however, let it be anathema ever to disclose any of these matters by any word or sign. With this conclusion, therefore, let the holy night depart, closed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Order for Saying Prime, Terce, Sext, and None

Let the day of salvation begin with the praises of Prime. When these have been completed, let the mysteries of holy Mass, through the presence of the bridegroom, gladden the hearts of the brides, intoxicate them with charity, and satisfy them with the nourishment of devotion and faith at the saving banquet. Afterwards, let there be time for each one either to pray, to read sacred volumes, or otherwise to perform holy work. Then let those who are educated instruct the young novices in the evangelical life, holy conduct, the duties of the household, and regular disciplines until the hour of the meal. Meanwhile, let food be prepared by which their bodies may be refreshed for the yoke of penance.

Let the mind never be given leisure, lest at some time illicit thoughts and impulses tickle the mind. If they should begin to rise in any way, let them be struck down at once in their beginning, lest weeds grow together with the wheat. Let whatever is wrongly conceived vanish through labor or manual work. Let the sister approach a holy sister, so that what is impure may be driven out through holy conversation. It is exceedingly safe to have a faithful and just friend to whom whatever lies hidden in the secret recess of the heart may immediately be disclosed. For a person often cannot have sound judgment in her own affairs.

When the hour of the meal arrives, at which nature compels the body to receive what is owed to it, on ordinary days let the praises of Terce and Sext first be devoutly offered to God. Afterwards, with complete modesty and with the abbess’s blessing given beforehand, let them take food, and let one group serve. Once the others have eaten, let those who served eat as well, and let others serve them. When the time of fasting has made the meal later, let the sacred mysteries of Mass be anticipated by Terce, Sext, and None. On other days, let None be said at the appointed hour after the meal, when the sun is already in the middle of its course and displays midday.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Foods and the Order of Eating

[Col. 0420C]

When the appointed hour brings you together for the meal, let the skill of cooks shine forth as little as possible in your food. Let it be hunger, not the nobility of foods, that stimulates the appetite. Let no stimulants of lust be served, but only what can extinguish hunger. Let either legumes or vegetables be seasoned with oil. Let meat be allowed only by the abbess’s permission for the weak and sick; otherwise, let the monastery be unaware of what meat tastes like. After fasts, let eggs and dairy products be permitted by favor to sisters weakened by fasting and on the principal feast days.

Let foods that arise and live in the waters be known rarely, except for small fish. Let the horrible crime of gluttony—the mother of lust and executioner of chastity—have no share among God’s handmaids. Therefore, let there be such sobriety and such moderation in taking food that the stomach complains rather than rejoices. Let the stomach have no need of medicines for digestion; let a belch be produced by emptiness rather than excessive fullness. Let there be no need to loosen the belt, so that the mind may not be delayed from meditations on God through gluttony and the body may not require medicines. Let eating always be ordered and composed in its manner. Let there not be such speed in taking a dish, nor such rapid chewing of the morsel, that suspicion of gluttony might rightly arise. It is not the food in eating but the shameful manner that is often to be censured. For excessive greed often causes great sin even with beans and barley loaves. Let greedy and wandering eyes not roam here and there over those reclining at table, marking this or that person as eating more or less. Let no one’s mind be occupied with counting the number of diners.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Sobriety and Fasting

Wine, in which there is lust, should also be regarded by Christ’s brides with suspicion, as poison. Let the languor of the stomach and the weakness of an afflicted nature provide relief, rather than pleasure or gluttony. But if necessity itself almost compels its consumption, let either wine that is weak in itself or wine so mixed with water be offered as a drink that a head filled with fumes may in no way produce ridiculous [Col. 0421B] or childish words. Drunkenness is considered sacrilege, especially in a woman, but infinitely more so in the bride of the Lord. Noah’s uncovering of his shame and Lot’s incest because of drunkenness should teach you caution, and should always make you fearful and ever watchful. Truly believe that the person who habitually uses wine carries fire in her bosom.

By no means, I beseech you, should even the slightest word be spoken among women dead to the world, who have renounced every pleasure for Christ, about the dreadful crime of gluttony or the uncleanness of drunkenness. Gluttony and drunkenness provide both the cause and the occasion for weakness of soul and body. Therefore medicinal fasting should remove every illness and bestow every strength and grace. Let the lawgiver teach you this: [Col. 0421C] no one is given the law until the Lenten fast has first been completed. Elijah, strengthened by bread baked under ashes, went fasting for forty days to Mount Horeb, the mountain of God. But what strength the sacred fast contains, investigate from your bridegroom: after completing a forty-day fast, he conquered the devil’s temptation. Let the men of Nineveh not be silent; by fasting they escaped a common destruction and changed God’s irrevocable sentence. Imitate these examples, dearest women, but attain them wisely, lest the Lord say: “This is not the fast that I have chosen.”

Discipline your members, but do not kill them. Let fasting not cause such shame that it becomes a scandal to others; let the sacred readings not be omitted because of headache and bodily weakness, nor the prayers fail, [Col. 0421D] lest it become necessary to abandon contemplation. Let each woman apply to herself, through fasting, a remedy for her salvation. Let the body be broken by fasts; let it be chastised in the cell with blows. If it desires anything unlawful, let abstinence be increased and the severest disciplines applied, until it becomes so humble and gentle that it claims nothing harmful for itself and demands nothing that you do not wish. Let the mistress rise up and rule in everything; let the servant be subjected, subjugated, and trampled underfoot. But if the servant repeatedly raises herself against her mistress, let her be cast out, stripped, wearied, and humbled according to desire. If, however, you wish to torment the quiet body beyond its strength and beyond what is fitting, it will cast you, in its indignation, into a pit of indiscretion. For nothing can possess virtue when indiscretion produces it, imprudence imposes it, and lack of foresight teaches it. [Col. 0422A]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Readings at the Table

The Lord’s words are so sweet to a healthy palate that, once tasted, they never become wearisome. Because of their pleasantness and sweetness, they always generate new appetites. It is fitting for you always to taste them. At no time should you cease from prayer. The Apostle teaches you always to pray, since you are not obliged, like married women, to refrain from prayer for a time because of the enticements of the flesh. Therefore pray always as far as you are able, so that while the body is being nourished with food, the soul may be filled with reading. It is not proper even for secular people to consume food at the same time as they belch out empty words. [Col. 0422B]

Each week, the sister appointed for the purpose should read to those eating a sacred reading from the Old and New Testaments, and from the deeds and sayings of the saints. Then let each woman’s sober mind be intent upon the sweetness of God’s word; let her sigh anxiously when prophetic or historical speech displays God’s severity toward the wicked. Let her be filled with immense joy when God’s kindness is announced toward the good. Let hope breathe again when it is shown, by promise or deed, that pardon can be extended to penitents. Let faith be lifted up when God is shown faithful in his promises. Let charity be kindled when, through so many privileges and gifts arising from Christ’s birth, life, passion, and resurrection, our humanity is endowed and our lowliness exalted. Let words not resound, [Col. 0422C] but groans; not laughter and guffaws, but tears. Let the hands not be occupied with useless cuttings; rather, let breasts be beaten in remembrance of sins. Driven by these reins, savage greed for food does not exceed the limits of sobriety; drunken excess does not enter the doors of the belly; and finally, burning lust does no harm.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Sisters’ Tasks after the Midday Meal

After food has been taken, one must not then turn to stories. Rather, following Christ’s example, let them rise with praises of God to give thanks and offer hymns to God in the church. Then, in complete silence, so that the sacred reading may bear fruit and what has been related may be inscribed upon the mind, let each woman reread and reinforce it privately, [Col. 0422D] or meditate in the church upon what she has learned, until together, on ordinary days after the midday meal at the ninth hour, they have celebrated worthy praises in the church; or, if the midday meal has preceded the ninth hour on fasting days, until the little bell is rung in the cloister. Meanwhile, if the shortness of the nights, the season, and the needs of nature require it, after a little while in which there is reading or prayer after the midday meal, those who wish may briefly refresh their bodies in quiet rather than sleep, so that they may be made stronger for their labors.

After the rest, when the ninth hour has passed or the little bell has been rung, let the devil find nothing idle, lest access to the heart be opened to empty desires. [Col. 0423A] Let one of the sisters copy books, so that both her hands may be filled with labor and her mind with divine nourishment. Let another sew the sisters’ cowls, tunics, and melotas. Let another plant vegetable seedlings in the little garden, so that, as they grow, they may provide you with food. Let another scatter seeds. Let the garden beds be watered so that they become suitable for the seeds. Let fruit-bearing trees be grafted onto unfruitful ones, so that skill may overcome the power of nature. From observing these visible things, let the mind rise to meditate upon the invisible things of God. Let admiration for divine power arise in the seed, from which, out of something so small and so dry, a creature of such size, greenness, and beauty is formed. From admiration let devotion grow, and from devotion elevation of mind, so that the little garden itself may now become an oratory, and insensible creatures proclaim the greatness of their Creator. [Col. 0423B] But above all, care must be taken lest your hands dare touch anything that could be adapted to frivolous uses.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Evening Hours and Compline

Let the serpent of bad habits and every idle word be driven from your midst. Never let laughter, never let a guffaw, proclaim a frivolous heart. Let every act of the body be so holy and modest that it displays the holiness of the mind. Indeed, the outward person is an indicator of the inward person. Let the evening hour find you holy in your labor and holy in your work, battling the devil; at that hour God is to be praised in the church with holy offices.

If the celebration of a festival or excessive weakness permits a common, brief refreshment of the body, prepared for necessity rather than pleasure, [Col. 0423C] let the evening praises be offered to God earlier than on the other fasting days, so that the praises owed at the final hour of the day may neither be omitted nor curtailed in any respect because of the evening meal. After the evening meal has been completed—or, if it is omitted, after a short interval—the sisters should be summoned by the little bell to the church, according to the demands of the time. There a devout reading should be given, either from the deeds of the saints or from other wonders of God. Let the praises of Compline follow it, so that minds strengthened by these things and nourished by divine food may not fear to confront the nocturnal fantasies and hidden deceits of the devil, nor be afraid to fight. Thus, as the day rises from divine services, let it end in divine praises.

After Compline, let nothing other than silence be heard, [Col. 0423D] so that the sisters, quiet and completely withdrawn from bodily senses, may mentally ruminate upon what they heard in the divine reading earlier and retain it in their hearts. Meditating on these things, let each woman go to her cell, having received the mother’s blessing and wearing the religious habit, and, if nature requires it, let her arrange herself in bed for rest. But if the demon begins to pursue a sleeping woman whom he had feared while she was awake, if he sends illusions or sets shameful things before her thoughts, as soon as the bride of God perceives this, let her rise, and let swift watchfulness promptly drive away laziness and sleep. Immediately let her oppose to the devil the dreadful and terrifying sign of the cross, invoke the help of her beloved bridegroom, and the jealous bridegroom, who guards his bride with exceeding zeal, will immediately rise to help his bride. [Col. 0424A] He will surround her with a shield, so that she will no longer fear the terror of the night. Then a thousand will fall at her side and ten thousand at her right hand, nor will they come near her. Finally, he will command his angels to guard her in all her ways, lest she perhaps strike her foot against a stone.

## CHAPTER XL. On Maintaining Charity toward Sick Sisters

The flesh of God’s bride should not accept the luxury of baths. Their use is not suitable for chaste bodies. We ourselves have experienced sufficiently, every day, how great a fire of lust burns in our members, even when, as far as possible, its fuel is removed. He is exceedingly foolish and senseless who, preparing material for a fire in order to kindle it, does not wish it to burn. Such things are appropriate for miserable little women when they are endangered by the travail of childbirth. Nevertheless, if extreme necessity benefits a sick woman, it should be done with every honor of chastity preserved and with complete modesty. In other circumstances, it is sacrilegious for servants of God even to think of such things.

Above all, let this be carefully maintained among you: toward sick sisters, let every care of hospitality be shown with complete solicitude, and let services of complete and total compassion be provided. If danger requires it, let them immediately consult a sober and chaste physician, free from every suspicion; and whatever he prescribes as conducive to health should be done kindly, with every household necessity set aside. If necessities are lacking, let the monastery’s possessions be sold, lest any temporal consideration hinder works of mercy.

[Col. 0424C] Let no rule concerning food, drink, or bedding bind a sick or weak woman. Nevertheless, care must be taken that the greed of gluttony does not seek its own comforts under the cover of illness, and that illness, under the appearance of holiness, does not wear down the body with abstinences beyond its strength, lest the body, broken by a double goad, fail before the just Judge and accuse the impious community of murder. Let prudent and holy sisters be appointed as guardians for the sick; let them carefully anticipate the dangers that may threaten the sick, so that nothing adverse may occur in any way. I beseech you, let those who serve them not make their burdens heavier. Let them always think of Christ hidden in the sick sister; let them always think that they themselves may in the future need such care. Let that law of nature always be held firmly in the bosom of the mind: that a person ought to provide for others what he would himself demand from them. I beseech you, let murmuring not corrupt the works of hospitality; rather, let what ought to be done be done with complete gentleness, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “Pursuing hospitality, with one another in charity without murmuring.”

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Authority of the Bishop and the Superior concerning Observance of the Rule

Behold, my lady Eustochium and the other most beloved daughters of Christ, an old father and one already near death—being a hundred years old—has sent you, with devoted affection, the apostolic life written in a rough and coarse style on these little sheets. Let each of the daughters, through constant meditation, behold in this eternal mirror, through this riddle, the path of happiness in the present life. Let the coarseness of the bark not cause contempt for seeking the marrow. Let an unskilled and rustic manner of speech not produce disgust. Such things befit poetic tales. The work of piety and of complete truth does not require to be read with the rhetorical pomp of orators. These matters belong to the young. Each day, as from a delightful dish, take a morsel from these writings. Do not swallow it, but chew it with great deliberation, moving it from side to side in your mouths, so that you may be able to sense its sweetness.

For I confess to you that, if diligent meditation is practiced, from what is written here things will arise for you such as the human tongue does not know, although this work too is imperfect. For no constitution, however holy, just, and long prepared, is so complete that it will not suffer many defects in the future or at some time require correction. Therefore, if anything in this little rule of apostolic life and religion requires dispensation, correction, or alteration, I entrust it to your bishop or to your superior, the holy presbyter, so that he may dispense, alter, and correct it according to the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, dearest daughters, live holy days. Be joined to Christ in a nuptial bond, so that, when the bridegroom comes at midnight to summon you to the wedding, he may always find you prepared, with your lamps not empty; and so that, while seeking oil outside, you may not, like foolish women, be denied entry to the bridal chamber because of your delay. Help the old age of your devoted Jerome with your holy prayers.

[Col. 0425]

# PENITENTIAL CANONS  
*(C, G, S)*

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK

Martianaeus first appended these Penitential Canons to the spurious writings of Jerome, from a manuscript codex of Saint Andrew near Avignon, which, as he himself says, is four hundred years old. They are excerpts—as no one will fail immediately to perceive—from various compilations of canons. They sometimes agree κατὰ λέξιν (“word for word”) with those decrees that are falsely attributed even to Pope Eutychianus, and also with those included by others in the books they call Penitentials. No one who wishes to compare them with those works—which are certainly very numerous—will waste his labor.

Martianaeus says that these canons require much examination and correction. We have transcribed them here as they are found in the manuscript codex, correcting only a considerable number of the ancient copyist’s errors. Nor are canons of this kind so important that they deserve to be examined more carefully and illuminated with notes by us.

## PENITENTIAL CANONS

[Col. 0425]

### Concerning a Drunken Bishop and Concerning a Presbyter and Deacon

[Col. 0425B]

If any bishop or other ordained person has the vice of drunkenness as a habitual practice, let him either stop or be deposed. If a monk vomits because of drunkenness, let him do penance for twenty days. If a presbyter or deacon vomits because of drunkenness, let him do penance for forty days; if he abstains, let him do penance for six days. But if it is because of illness, or because he has abstained for a long time and it is not customary for him to eat or drink much, or because of joy at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, or the commemoration of one of the saints, and then he has taken no more than the amount decreed by the elders, it is not harmful. If a bishop orders it, it is not harmful to him, unless he himself does the same. If a faithful layman vomits because of drunkenness, let him do penance for fifteen days.

But whoever becomes drunk against the Lord’s prohibition, if he has a vomit of satiety, let him do penance for six days in water, or for twenty days without fat. If a layman, without wine, wickedly makes another drunk, let him do penance for forty days. Whoever vomits from satiety: [the text is corrupt]—in penance, as for a sacrifice, seven days. If it is because of illness, there is no offense.

If anyone, being a bishop, commits homicide, let him do penance for fifteen years and be deposed; and let him end his life by wandering as an exile throughout all his days. Let a presbyter do penance for twelve years, three of them on bread and water, and be deposed. A deacon, ten years, three of them on bread and water. Let a cleric or layman do penance for seven years on bread and water, and let him not presume to rise to priestly honor. But if he has performed his penance well, let him be reconciled.

Likewise, if anyone consented to the commission of homicide and it was carried out, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. But if he wished to do it and was unable, let him do penance for three years. If anyone unwillingly commits homicide, let him do penance for five years, three of them on bread and water. If anyone kills a bishop or presbyter, let the king decide what is to be done. Whoever kills a monk or cleric is subject to the judgment of the bishop. Let him abandon arms and serve God, or do penance for twelve years.

If anyone kills a person in anger, let him do penance for ten years. But whoever does so in revenge for a father or brother, let him do penance for three years. If he makes compensation to the relatives, let him do half that period. If a layman kills another out of hatred and does not wish to lay down arms, let him do penance for seven years without meat and wine. If anyone kills a person while fighting with the king, let him do penance for forty days.

If a mother kills her son, let her do penance for fifteen years, and let her never receive communion except on Sunday. If a poor woman kills her son, let her do penance for seven years. If anyone strikes another in anger and draws blood or disables him, let him compensate him with labor and seek a physician. If he is a layman, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water. If a cleric, two Lents. If a deacon, seven months. If a presbyter, one full year. Let children who strike one another do penance for seven days; if adolescents, forty days.

If anyone suffocates his own infant, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water, and abstain from lust during the period of penance. If anyone causes a woman to lose her conceived child, let him do penance for two years, one of them on bread and water. If a woman voluntarily aborts, let her do penance for three years; if unwillingly, three Lents.

Women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, and those who act so as to expel what they have conceived, [Col. 0426D] the ancients decreed should do penance until the end of life. Now, however, it has been determined more humanely that they should do penance for ten years. A woman who conceives and kills her child in the womb before forty days shall do penance for one year. If after forty days, she shall do penance as for homicide.

A father or mother who kills his or her child before baptism shall do penance for nine years, but with counsel. Those whose infants die without baptism through negligence shall do penance for three years on bread and water. If an infant, sick person, or pagan entrusted to a presbyter dies without baptism, the presbyter shall be deposed. If it was the parents’ negligence, let them do penance for one year.

If anyone voluntarily cuts off any member of his own body, let him do penance for three years, one on bread and water. Eunuchs, if the operation was performed by others, may be advanced in the clergy; but if they castrated themselves, they are in no way to be advanced. If a presbyter castrated himself, let him be deposed.

[Col. 0427B] If anyone provides guidance to barbarians, let him do penance for fourteen years, provided that he has not caused a slaughter of Christians; but if he has, then, having laid down his arms, let him live for God, dead to the world, until death.

If anyone commits fornication as the Sodomites did, let a bishop do penance for fifteen years, five of them on bread and water, and let him be deposed from every office; let him end the days of his life in exile. But if he is elderly or sick, let him do penance imprisoned in confinement and darkness all the days of his life. Let a presbyter do penance for twelve years, two of them on bread and water, and be deposed. Let a deacon and monk do penance for seven years, two of them on bread and water, and be deposed. Let them end their lives in exile. Let a cleric and layman do penance for ten years, one of them on bread and water.

Those written above shall never sleep with others and shall never presume to approach the rank of priesthood. During the years of their penance, let them abstain from wine and meat. Except when illness occurs, in which case this is relaxed until recovery. Let them merit communion at the end of life. But if they have performed their penance well, let them be reconciled and admitted to communion.

If anyone fornicates with a woman consecrated to God, let a bishop do penance for fifteen years, five of them on bread and water, and be deposed; let him never return to priestly honor. Let a presbyter do penance for twelve years, three of them on bread and water, and be deposed. Let a deacon and monk do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water, and never approach priestly honor. After completing penance, let them be reconciled to communion.

If anyone fornicates with his mother, let him do penance for twelve years and never receive communion except on Sundays. If anyone [Col. 0427D] fornicates with another man’s wife, let a bishop do penance for twelve years, with an unspecified portion of them on bread and water [the printed reading is corrupt: “ut ex his”]. Let those written above be deprived of communion; after completing penance, let them be reconciled. For they must never presume to approach the priestly orders.

If anyone fornicates with a widow or another man’s betrothed, let a bishop do penance for twelve years, three of them on bread and water; and let both bishop and presbyter be deposed.
