Not “in sleep,” because the angel came to him repeatedly in dreams. Not “once,” because one cannot understand the mystery of God all at once.

### Joseph, son of David

That is, the prophecy was fulfilled in Joseph through David: “From the fruit of your womb,” and so forth.

### Do not be afraid

That is, love and rejoice in your wife—not in a nuptial union, nor in the act of begetting [possibly “coition”], but in cohabitation. He called her “your” wife so that Joseph would believe that she had conceived not from another man but from the Holy Spirit.

### She will bear a son

That is, so that his joy in the son might be greater, as is customary among human beings.

### And you shall call his name

This too was said for his rejoicing.

### Jesus

And he would have said “Savior”: “He will save his people.” He did not say “all,” but only those who believe in him, from their sins—that is, from what no other physician could accomplish.

Now all this took place—that is, what the angel said—so that what had been spoken by the Lord might be fulfilled, that is, through the prophet Isaiah concerning Christ. Here it is treated only according to the letter:

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall call his name Emmanuel.”

This name is therefore interpreted [possibly “left uninterpreted”], because in both languages it is said to mean “God with us”: that is, God and man are one in faith.

He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him. This shows that he was worthy to see the vision of the Lord, because he did as the angel commanded him.

### And he did not know her until she bore her son

“Until” is used here to mean “never.” In the Law, “firstborn” is said of the one who first opened the womb—not one followed by other children, but the one who is born first.

Christ is called firstborn for three reasons: in the resurrection from the dead, from Mary, and from created beings.

### When Jesus therefore had been born

Here he confirms three things: place, time, and person.

### In Bethlehem

This was fitting because Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread,” so that the living heavenly bread might be born there. “Judah, look toward Bethlehem of the nations.”

### In the days of Herod the king

This refers to the kings and leaders of Judea, as it is said: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been promised; he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

He called Herod “king” in opposition to the Jews because they said at the cross, “We have no king except Caesar.”

### Behold, magi came from the East

Since the East is where he is sought, they are said to come from the East. He himself leads us to himself.

They came to Jerusalem because “from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

### Saying, Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?

That is, king of those who confess.

They add the reason when asked, “Who told you?”: “For we saw his star in the East.” The star is mute but luminous; light leads to the Word.

It says “his star,” not the star of heaven and earth. It did not belong to them, but to the Son of God. There was neither before nor afterward anyone like Christ in the flesh. Therefore the star led them, heavenly beings, to the heavenly one. It was not another creature, but a mute one, so that a mute thing might lead the mute to the mute.

They were offering gifts, they who had worshiped idols.

### When King Herod heard this, he was troubled

That is, through envy, lest the child should overcome him and his sons; or all were afraid lest things should not go well for them. A righteous king, when he is among an unrighteous king’s people, does not become equally dear to another king’s companions; or they were troubled for this reason, so that they might please the king.

Literally, too, trouble is a manifestation of evil: an evil eye is troubled at the rising of the sun.

### And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people

That is, hoping that when they had arrived he might receive counsel, as God says: “Ask your father, and he will announce it to you”—your elders, who will tell you: the fathers, chief men, elders, and scribes.

### Where Christ was to be born

He did not say, “Where has he been born?” or “Where is he?” But they said, “In Bethlehem of Judea.” In words they say what they deny by their deeds. The blind grope like Isaac seeking Jacob. Though they neglect to go, they point out the one whom they show to be worshiped.

The three magi signify the three sons of Noah. With their three gifts, they signify the worship of the Trinity.

### Then Herod, secretly calling them

Here the historical account breaks off. Since he privately learned from them the time of the star, opinions differ as to when the magi came. Some say after one or two years; others say that they found him not in Bethlehem but in Egypt. And if they came within twelve days, how could the Persians from a distant land, or those from Havilah, Arabia, or Kedar, have come within twelve days? But God can accomplish this, at whose word rocks fly and mountains move, for whom it is natural that what he commands should happen.

Nevertheless, he carefully learned from them the time of the star—that is, so that he might know at what time it had appeared. Perhaps he thought that the son had been born from him or from his lineage.

### When they had heard the king, they departed

When he sends them to seek Christ, he must be obeyed; when he orders them to return to him, he must be disregarded.

When he was leading the Savior up to a high place, the Savior refused, while he himself did not refuse. But when he sent him downward and ordered him to worship him, Christ refused according to the Law: “You shall worship the Lord your God,” and so forth.

Thus, when they go out, they know how to depart; they do not know how to return.

### And behold, the star that they had seen, and so forth

It is uncertain where the star hid itself while they had gone away. There was some human planning involved, because the Lord hides things from our hearts so that they may also be sought.

Is the star faith, or the Law? The compunction that leads us to Christ preceded them. When they came to Christ, the star led them; for the star did not lead them to Herod. Herod signified the devil, because one who departs from the devil’s suggestion goes to Christ with the star of faith.

### When they saw the star, they rejoiced, and so forth

This is because it is customary for everyone to rejoice when destruction is found. For this reason he showed them a child greater than his mother.

### And entering the house, and so forth

Was it a house or an inn?

### And falling down, they worshiped him

Previously they had worshiped the star; the creature ceased while the Creator was worshiped.

### And opening their treasures, and so forth

Gold was for the king, frankincense for God, myrrh for the tomb.

Whether one offered gold, another frankincense, and the third myrrh is not known. Nor is it explicitly stated whether each one offered three gifts; both possibilities are understood figuratively.

They do not disagree, because the three faithful are one, and the three fruits are united: the thirtieth, the fortieth, and the hundredth. The thirtieth is faith in the Trinity, the fortieth the perfection of active life, and the hundredth contemplation of eternal life.

Each offered three things: through gold, a pure conscience; through frankincense, upright prayer; through myrrh, the mortification of the will. Likewise, the three gifts are holy thought, a good word, and a perfect work.

The star appeared only at his birth, just as the dove appeared at his baptism. When the star went before them, it was not far from the earth.

### And having received an answer in a dream, and so forth

They received it in a dream, with their eyes closed, so that they might worship the invisible and incomprehensible God and so that, while awake, their eyes might not be opened toward creatures but toward the Creator.

### That they should not return to Herod

That is, after repentance, they should not return to the devil.

### They returned to their own country by another way

The country signifies paradise. He returns by another way who reforms his entire life and comes from wickedness to holiness.

### When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord, and so forth

Gabriel is called “the strength of God.” It was fitting that the strength of God should strengthen the weakness of humanity.

Alternatively, the angel approaches us when we have withdrawn from Herod the devil.

### Flee into Egypt

Flight shows victory, just as Jesus son of Nave did when he said, “Divide yourselves and flee until the citizens come out; afterward turn back, and you will conquer them.” Christ first fled until he defeated the devil behind him.

Thus Joseph fled from his illustrious mistress in Egypt, and afterward he himself became king over Egypt.

### Until I tell you

This shows that one must not always flee the devil, as the apostle Paul says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”

### Night

This shows that the darkness of the letter of the Law withdrew and remained among the Jews after Christ, even to the present day.

### Until the death of Herod

He waits—that is, three years. This signifies that the Gentiles will believe in the Trinity. Yet he did not continue until the death. Herod indicates the Jews, who come to Christ after the death of the letter of the Law.

### Out of Egypt I called my son

At first Moses and Aaron summon Christ.

### Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi

Here the prophecy is fulfilled: “This dragon whom you formed for mockery of them.”

He sends and kills all the boys so that he might find the king who had been born. Here he is mocked still more: those whom he thought dead he sent alive into paradise.

### From two years old and under

That is, from the past year and the following one, because the term “infancy” includes two years.

### A voice was heard in Rama, and so forth

Rachel is interpreted as “a sheep seeing God”; Rama means “lofty.”

Rachel signifies the Church, which weeps in the valley of tears for those whom it has lost—those who sinned beforehand—and does not wish to be consoled because they are not Christians.

Rachel was the mother of Benjamin; alternatively, this is because she died and was buried in the place where the children were killed.

### They are dead, and so forth

This is therefore a synecdoche: the part is used for the whole.

### He came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth

That is, “flower of purity.” It was fitting that he should dwell there who said, “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

Archelaus means “a lion investigating”; Nazaraeus means “holy.”

### Rise, take the child and his mother

First, rise from the earth—you who abandon earthly things. Then he commands him to take the child, and afterward the mother. First, love God; afterward, your neighbor.

Archelaus signifies heresy: those who think they are what they are not, and who are blind.

### In those days

This should not be referred to King Archelaus, but to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, because in that year the word of the Lord came to John. Before Christ, there was the voice before the Word, the lamp before the sun, and the flower before the fruit.

### Repent

Do not work outwardly, because “works” are said to be external to the body; act upon the inner person, and let the action proceed from the heart. True repentance is to lament what has been lost and not to commit what must be repented of.

### For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near

That is, baptism, or the Gospel of Christ, martyrdom, or the Church.

### The voice of one crying in the wilderness

John’s threefold manner of crying concerning Christ in the wilderness is as follows. First, when he is far away: “Salvation is far from sinners.” Second, to the deaf: “Like a deaf asp,” and so forth. Third, in indignation: “Your anger has been provoked.”

“In the wilderness” means that the Jews were without law, without a king, without a priest, and without prophecy.

Just as a friend loves to join a bride to her bridegroom, so John joined the Church to Christ. For this reason he is called the friend of the bridegroom.

John wore a garment of camel hair. He was born in fasting and had the clothing and food of fasting. This was fitting: since he taught repentance, he should first fulfill it in himself, so that everyone who preaches the word might confirm it by example.

John’s camel-hair garment signifies the Church of the Gentiles, or the riches of those whom Christ gathered and made into the Church.

The belt signifies the mortification of vices. It was around his loins because fornication occurs there, between men and women, at the navel.

His food was locusts, very wretched birds. They signify the Jews, who use the letter of the Law like locusts. Wild honey signifies the sweet words of God, or the Jews who received the sweet preaching and came to Christ.

### Then Jerusalem and all Judea went out to him, and so forth

“Judea” is used for its inhabitants. Jerusalem, “vision of peace,” signifies the peaceful who come to Christ through confession.

Jordan means “descent” and signifies those who descend in humility to Christ.

### And they were baptized in the Jordan

This shows that they came to baptism through descent, in humility.

### Confessing their sins

This shows that one must confess sins before coming to communion.

The Pharisees are “the divided,” or they are called Sarabaites. The Sadducees are those justified in their own eyes.

### And he said to them, Brood of vipers

The same poison is only on the tongue. For the Pharisees and Sadducees pretend to be vipers that kill their fathers and mothers: they killed their mother, the synagogue, and their fathers, the prophets.

### Who showed you, and so forth?

That is, “Who?” not in the sense of possibility, but of difficulty, since it is said, “Bear good fruits.” This means: put away every vice; or, “Bear fruit worthy of repentance,” that is, let the one who has two tunics give one to the person who has none. Whoever acts unlawfully must abstain from unlawful things.

### God is able from these stones, and so forth

They were stones because they worshiped stones, although many of them afterward came to faith in Christ.

Alternatively, they are called stones because they are heavy, hard, and cold in faith.

### The axe has been laid

That is, the Gospel has been laid at the root of the trees—that is, at the Jews.

The axe consists of iron and wood; thus Christ consists of divinity and humanity.

The roots signify thoughts; the trees, sinners. Alternatively, the roots signify sons and the trees their parents.

### Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down

That is, it shall be divided from the Church.

### It shall be cast into the fire

That is, on the day of judgment.

### He who comes after me is mightier than I

This refers not only to John: Christ is mightier than all. He is mightier because he baptizes in the Holy Spirit and in fire.

### To carry his sandals

For this reason I cannot fully explain his incarnation.

### He himself will baptize you with fire

That is, in judgment, or in the Holy Spirit and fire.

### Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and so forth

This means just judgment. “In his hand” means in his power. The threshing floor means the world or the Church. The wheat means the holy; the granary, the kingdoms of heaven. The chaff signifies sinners, because chaff is light, is carried by the wind, and is consumed by fire.

Thus sinners themselves preserve the fire, because the fire does not fail unless the wood fails.

### Then Jesus came to Galilee to be baptized, and so forth

Christ came to John: the bride kisses the bridegroom, because John is the bridegroom through the Church. Here it says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Alternatively, Christ was baptized by John so that a servant would not excuse himself from being baptized by his Lord, and so that the Lord would not disdain to be baptized by his servant.

### I ought to be baptized by you

Through this event John recognized Christ among the many, when the Jordan fled from him and the mountains exulted, because creation recognized the Creator.

He therefore came to John to cleanse the waters and to be manifested through the Holy Spirit.

There are four reasons.

### Let it be so now

That is, until both had been baptized: Christ by the waters, or by martyrdom, until it came to you.

### To fulfill all righteousness, and so forth

That is, the law of nature or the written law, because it was customary among them to honor elders.

This concerns Christ’s baptism, so that they would not distinguish John’s baptism from Christ’s baptism.

Water washes and extinguishes; for this reason baptism took place through water. Thus John washes and extinguishes sin, gives life, and satisfies [the passage is corrupt and its sense uncertain]. Thus baptism [the text is defective]. And because they are baptized through two substances—that is, water and the priest’s voice—the visible and invisible, body and soul.

### He ascended from the water

This signifies afterward ascending through good works and descending by the step of humility, because Jordan is called “descent.”

### Behold, the heavens were opened

That is, baptism was revealed. Heaven is opened to each person after Adam’s fault.

### And he saw the Spirit descending like a dove

This shows that it was only in the form of a dove, because the Spirit received a body from the air. The likeness of a dove was made for this purpose; it had not existed beforehand.

The Spirit came upon Christ in the form of a dove because a bird is gentle; likewise Christ is gentle and without blemish.

Alternatively, the dove has seven forms, signifying the sevenfold Spirit. Therefore the Spirit came in Christ through a dove, just as the star existed neither before nor afterward.

Or this was because the Son was in a body. Just as human beings could not have endured the presence of the Son of God without a body, so they could not have endured the Spirit without the form of a dove.

Why did the Spirit appear over the apostles in fire and over Christ in a dove? Literally, this is to be explained as showing [the distinction].

### And a voice came from heaven

Here the Trinity is compared. The voice of the Father speaks of the Son; the Spirit is represented by the dove.

### This is my beloved Son, and so forth

The first son, Adam, had displeased; in Christ, the Father was pleased.

### Then Jesus was led

That is, he was led by the Holy Spirit into the desert after baptism. This shows that the devil is conquered through fasting and prayer. We too must be led into the desert away from vices, so that we may conquer them.

### To be tempted by the devil

That is, so that he might conquer the devil.

### For forty days and forty nights

This was so that heretics would not say that he had eaten during the night.

The number forty signifies that Moses fasted forty days on the mountain, and Elijah forty days; that he was with his disciples forty days after the resurrection; and that the Flood lasted forty days. Through these things he was to erase Adam’s sin.

### Afterward he was hungry

This indicates the true human being, so that the devil might be deceived concerning his birth.

### The tempter approached

That is, as a fish tests the hook and is caught. The one who conquered the first human being through the appetite now is conquered by the second through abstinence.

### If you are the Son of God, command these stones, and so forth

By etymology, bread comes from feeding. The devil wanted to see whether Christ could do this from a stone.

Or, mystically, the devil’s food is stone-like and hard people, hardened in sin. But the one who produced wine from water and water from rock could have done this if he had wished.

### Man does not live by bread alone, and so forth

That is, a human being would not have lived if God had not wished it; and if he had eaten bread, he would have lived, while if he had not eaten bread, he would nevertheless have lived if God had willed it, just as Moses and Elijah lived for forty days.

The word of God is life for the soul, that is, eternal life.

### In the holy city

That is, Jerusalem.

### Upon the pinnacle of the temple

That is, upon the wall of the enclosure of the ark. This signifies exaltation.

He did not allow himself to be tempted by the head, just as he allowed himself to be crucified by a member through Pilate.

The devil first imposed these three temptations upon Adam: through appetite he said, “Taste”; through vainglory, “You shall be like gods”; through greed, “Knowing good and evil.”

He again tempted Christ through these three: through appetite, “Make bread from the stone”; through vainglory, “Throw yourself down”; through greed, “I shall give you all these things,” and so forth.

But the one who leads him into the abyss through the word of preaching shows that the devil is conquered through these three.

Here he shows the true God and the true human being: the human being whom the devil tempts is God, whom angels ministered to.

The forty days signify ten percent of the years, so that, just as we ought to give tithes from all things, we should also strive to give God a tithe of the days of our life.

### He will command his angels concerning you, and so forth

The devil presented this as though he had conquered Christ by an example, just as Christ conquered him by his own example through Scripture.

But the devil does not correctly understand that psalm concerning Christ. Jesus says to him, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” He says this: Since I am the Lord your God, why do you tempt me?

### And he showed him all the kingdoms of the world

That is, gold and silver.

### I shall give you all these things, and so forth

The one who worships the devil truly falls. Any monk who serves a ruler for the sake of payment gives himself over to the devil.

### Go away

That is, your kingdom now—or, in judgment, into hell.

### You shall worship the Lord your God, and so forth

Through three examples from Deuteronomy, which signifies the Gospel—that is, the repetition of the Law—the Lord conquered the devil.

It also signifies the temptation of David and Goliath. The five stones signify the five books of Moses; with one of them he killed the devil, that is, with one book as with a stone.

The three temptations mean suggestion, delight, and consent. Christ was tempted only through suggestion, because suggestion originates from the devil.

### When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee

That is, he departed from the Jews and went to the Gentiles; or, leaving the synagogue with its Law, he established the Church and the Gospel.

Galilee is called “volubility.” He came to those who turn from evil to good. And because he came for the healing of a girl and healed a woman on the way, it signifies the synagogue and the Church.

### Leaving the city, he came to Capernaum

The very beautiful village signifies the Church.

Nazareth is called “flower,” because fruit comes from a flower. Capernaum means “village of richness”: light illuminates, and richness is without blood.

This shows that Christ came from the flower of the letter of the Law to the fruit of the richness of the Gospel of light—that is, of knowledge.

[Note: The words “in the borders” concluded the immediately preceding section.]

### In the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali

Zebulun is called “dwelling of beauty”; Naphtali is called “forgetfulness.”

This shows that whoever forgets his sins dwells in beauty.

### Beyond the Jordan, and so forth

Because of fear of the nations and peoples, this one remained in the field during the night.

### He saw a great light

As it says, “A light has arisen for those who sat in darkness”—that is, in ignorance of sins. The light that arose for them is Christ.

### Repent

That is, pour wine into the wound.

“For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near”: that is, pour oil into the wound. It gives consolation, because in the Old Testament animals were sacrificed, while in the New each person will offer himself to the Lord.

### He was walking

This shows that we are in the present world as people passing through it, not loving it.

### Beside the sea

This means beside worldly flesh. The Sea of Galilee is the same as the lake of Gennesaret, the salt lake, the Sea of Tiberias, and Lake Cinnereth.

### He who comes after me, and so forth

That is, to draw souls from the sea of sin to the shore of eternal rest.

Since fishermen customarily have a boat and a net in the sea, so the apostles have the Church, the Gospels, and the world; the fish are human beings. Casting nets into the sea means preaching in the world.

### They left their nets and their father and followed him

The father likewise signifies the devil; the nets, the dwellings and affairs of the world.

Peter and Andrew cast their nets into the sea. This shows that the Lord chose some who desired and clung to worldly things.

James and John repaired their nets in order to cast them into the sea. This means that he chose others who desired to cling to worldly things.

Who of these four left more? Peter and Andrew left more, because what they possessed was their own; for the other two, it was not their own.

### I will make you, and so forth

He changed their inclination, not their occupation. With these four there is the first chariot. Now they are sent into the Church two by two, as in Noah’s ark.

The pairs of animals signify the four virtues: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

The people were called by three vocations. The first was through John, to friendship: “Behold the Lamb of God.” The second was to belief, when John said, “Jesus performed this first sign in Cana of Galilee, so that his disciples might believe in him.” The third calling was to the apostleship: “Come after me,” and so forth.

### Jesus went around all Galilee, and so forth

Just as Gideon conquered the Philistines, so Christ conquered demons.

“Teaching” means the things that belonged to the Law; “preaching” means the Gospel.

Every sickness means that he was the physician of the people—that is, of Israel. Sickness refers to the body; infirmity to the soul.

### And his fame went throughout all Syria

That is, among all the nations.

### All who were afflicted

That is, they were insane because of many sins, or because of bad faith.

And because they had demons—that is, idols were believed in within the soul.

### Lunatics

That is, people thought that illnesses arose from the rising of the moon.

### They brought him paralytics

That is, those who were sluggish in doing good.

### Great crowds followed him

First, disciples, for the sake of faith; second, the sick, for the sake of healing; third, experts in the Law, to criticize; fourth, the poor, for the sake of almsgiving; fifth, women, so that they would not despair; sixth, children, as he said, “Let the children come.”

### The Decapolis

That is, those who observe the words of the Law.

And from Jerusalem—that is, those who, seeing peace, followed Christ—and from Judea—that is, those who followed Christ through confession.

### When Jesus saw the crowds

Likewise, four crowds followed Christ, and these same four follow the Church.

The first come to Christ through fear and love; likewise they come to the Church.

The second come because of desire for food or drink.

The third come through envy, so that they may have something to accuse.

The fourth are the teachers.

Christ had three places of refuge in which to escape the crowds: on the mountain, in the desert, and in a boat upon the sea. He leaves these three to us: to ascend into the height of the commandments; to enter the desert and abandon vices; and to enter into the unity of the Church.

The boat signifies the Church. It has a helmsman and sailors, and water that is cast about outside the boat. These are the bishops, the laborers, and those who perform the ministries within.

Three things threaten the boats: danger in the waves, in the wind, and on the rock. Thus the Church is endangered by the waves of the devil’s temptations, by the wind of sins, and by the rock of false brothers.

When he ascended the mountain, he signified theory—that is, contemplation. When he descended, he taught practice—that is, action.

And when he sat down, this indicates that his incarnation had not appeared openly, because one who sits protects his body with clothing.

[Editorial notes: [Col. 0535D] The copyist had added in the margin, as is equally credible, one deleted word, perhaps *amarum* (“bitter”); Martianay later intruded these words into the text and was content merely to enclose them in parentheses. We correct quite a few similar matters below. [Col. 0535D] Perhaps *iniqua* was formerly written in place of *in qua*, which gives no sense. [Col. 0535D] Martianay read, without sense, *dixit et* as two words in place of *dixisset*. We silently emend other, slighter matters. [Col. 0536D] Martianay wrongly read *donec pronum quam dicitur*, also adding the gloss “perhaps before”; of these, we have deleted the latter and restored *never* in place of the former to the true reading. [Col. 0536D] *Qui* was read in place of *quia*, and *ubi* in place of *ibi*. Nor is the following context free of errors, many of which we have removed, especially faults of punctuation. [Col. 0536D] It read *nec non illis bene esse, Rex*, etc.; there are many similar examples below, occurring almost every third verse. [Col. 0537D] Earlier it read *ut scissent*. Shortly afterward supply “the devil,” or something similar, where it says, “for when he led the Savior on high,” etc.; the author observes that the devil is signified by the name Herod. [Col. 0537D] The author wrote *perditione inventa*, however extremely barbarously. Many things above and below are corrected which there is no leisure to record. [Col. 0538D] We have restored, as far as possible, a sense wholly absent from Martianay’s edition: “Night here shows that the darkness of the letter of the Law withdrew among the Jews after Christ, even to the present day. Until the death of Herod: he waits,” etc. In what follows, almost countless other lesser matters are corrected. [Col. 0539D] These passages were astonishingly corrupted: “in the wilderness of John Christ’s threefold manner of crying occurs . . . second, to a deaf person, as with a deaf asp,” etc.; then, “the Jews were, and those who love join a bride,” etc.—to say nothing of other faults of punctuation and orthography, which distorted the whole context and sense, and of the complete absence of any distinction between the words of Scripture being expounded. [Col. 0540D] It is plain that some word is missing and that another sense should be read; so also shortly afterward, where it says “baptism [by] sea,” a passage which I do not wish to reconstruct by conjecture. [Col. 0541D] The passage and its sense are corrupt; but I do not wish at all to attempt what cannot safely be emended. [Col. 0541D] Earlier it read *Deuteronomio*, “which signify the Gospel.” [Col. 0542D] We pass over slighter matters.]

The disciples came to him—that is, body and soul. And opening his mouth—that is, he who opened the mouths of the prophets. Blessed are the poor in spirit—that is, those who are poor for the sake of the Holy Spirit, although they could be rich. Blessed are the meek—that is, those who repay no one evil for evil; for they shall possess the earth, of which it is said, “I believe that I shall see,” and so forth. Blessed are those who mourn now: he does not say this of every kind of weeping, but of the three kinds that the world ought to have: first, weeping for one’s own sin; second, for the sin of one’s neighbor; third, from love of heaven. Tears have three qualities: bitter, for not weeping over sin; hot, for grieving over the sins of one’s neighbor through the heat of charity; and [uncertain: *jacent a coelo*, “they lie/fall from heaven”], for weeping out of love for him.

Tears are shed for three reasons: in remembrance, through fear of the future, and because of pilgrimage.

[Note: [Col. 0543] Perhaps “pleasing to heaven”; but I do not care to guess, nor would it be worthwhile. We silently correct innumerable other passages.]

Blessed are those who hunger, and so forth—that is, the person for whom whatever good he does is not enough, unless he wishes to do more. They shall be filled—that is, in the kingdom of God. Blessed are the merciful—that is, those who have pity are freed from misery and will go to heaven with their gift. Blessed are the pure in heart—that is, those who have a pure heart, untouched by any consciousness of sin, because God, who is pure, looks upon the pure in heart.

Blessed are the peacemakers—that is, in four relationships: between God and a human being, between a person and his neighbor, and between a person and his friend. One must hate the vice and love the person.

Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness—that is, in Christ. These eight beatitudes pertain to the eight persons who were in the ark, and who ought now to be there, because seven women had one husband, Christ—that is, in the resurrection. These eight beatitudes are fulfilled in Christ. Blessed are the poor in spirit: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Blessed are the meek: “Learn from me, for I am meek.” Blessed are those who mourn: “When he saw the city, he wept over it.” Blessed are those who hunger: “My food is to do the will of my Father.” Blessed are the merciful: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” Blessed are the pure in heart: “Be holy, for I am holy.” Blessed are the peacemakers: “I give you my peace,” and so forth. Blessed are those who suffer persecution: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.”

You are the salt of the earth: that is, the apostles and teachers are meant; “of the earth” refers to this world. But if the salt has lost its savor, and so forth. If a teacher has gone astray, how is he to be corrected? Salt gives flavor and kills worms. Let it be thrown out and trampled by people—that is, let them go outside the Church and be reckoned among the Gentiles. You are the light of the world—that is, just as hidden light is revealed and illuminates darkness, so you must illuminate the darkness of sins. Alternatively, just as the sun always remains in heaven, so you must remain there.

A city cannot be hidden—that is, the Church, upon a mountain, that is, upon Christ. Nor do they light a lamp—that is, the apostles and teachers—and put it under a bushel, that is, under fear or love. The apostles have four likenesses: salt, sun, lamp, and city. Upon a lampstand—that is, the Church—so that they may shine for everyone who is in the house, that is, in the Church or in the world. So let your light shine—that is, your teaching or good works—and let them glorify your Father, that is, through your benefactions.

Do not think that I came to abolish the law: that is, whatever work was done, he himself fulfilled it. When the children of Israel sinned, Moses and Levi took three swords for vengeance against them; Christ did the same when he said, “I came not to bring peace, but a sword.” And “to fulfill” means to supply what was lacking, because the old Law commanded that anyone who committed adultery be punished; now it is not abolished but fulfilled when it says, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth; and again, “For every idle word they will give an account on the day of judgment.” Behold, I did not come to abolish the law, but to increase what the old Law had not said.

[Col. 0545D] Amen I say to you. Amen means “truly” or “faithfully.” One iota—the name of a letter, which with a single stroke becomes the letter *deca* [Greek δέκα, “ten”]—means the ten words of the Law; among the Greeks it is a letter, whereas we have called it “one.” One stroke, one point: literally, it means the smallest letter; figuratively, the least commandments of the Law. Until all things come to pass, because what was least in the Law becomes full of mysteries: the iota is the old Law, the stroke the New.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] He seems to be speaking of the letter iota, which is also the Greek sign for the number ten. But the text is so corrupt that, although we have corrected six hundred other passages up to this point, here we dare change only ι to κ.]

Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments—that is, whoever teaches a great deal but fulfills very little. The Pharisees strain out a gnat and swallow a camel: that is, they proclaim lesser matters to others but themselves commit greater ones. He will be called least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church. Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees: because they taught great things but did little, or because they rejected some commandments of the Law: what they did not love they did not say, and what they loved they did say.

You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not kill”: that is, the Law is not abolished. Whoever is angry with his brother—that is, anger in the heart without words—will be liable to judgment, that is, on the day of judgment. “Racha” means “empty” or “vain.” “Fool” means “without a brain”; he will be liable to the fire of Gehenna—that is, Gehenna is a double punishment because it punishes both soul and body.

If you offer your gift at the altar, and so forth: go and be reconciled to your brother—that is, if you offer a gift, a prayer, an oblation, or yourself for communion, you must never come to the Church until you have been reconciled to your brother. Leave your gift there: how will this be fulfilled? He rebukes both parties alike. If the brother is nearby, well and good; if he is far away, one must nevertheless reconcile oneself to him in one’s mind, in accordance with what has already been said: to have peace with all people.

Be well disposed toward your adversary—that is, the Gospel—while you are on the way with him, that is, in this life; or toward your adversary the devil, so that you do not do what he suggests to you, lest your punishment for your sin increase. If an infant asks for a sword, do not hand him something with which he might stab himself; in this way you are in agreement with him. Lest your adversary hand you over to the judge—that is, lest the law of the Gospel hand you over to Christ the judge—because you did not consent to the Gospel, to the minister, that is, the angel who sends souls into punishment, into prison, that is, into hell.

You will not come out from there—that is, because no one comes out of hell until he has repaid the last quadrans; “until” is understood as “forever.” A quadrans is a fourth part of a coin, given as payment for washing, or it is used for a very small sin. To repay the quadrans means to be sent into hell; or it is so called because a human being was made from the four elements. You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not commit adultery,” that is, “You shall not commit fornication.” Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her: there are two kinds of desire. The first is one in which, even if opportunity follows, the intention does not lead to the act; the second is completed if opportunity is available. Adultery is committed both in body and in heart.

[Col. 0546D] If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. That is, your ruler or teacher: tear him out, that is, separate him from yourself, if he has hindered you from serving God. He is one of your members; that is, it is better for your ruler to perish than for you to go to hell with him. The eye means your desire, because through it the body is sent into Gehenna. The right hand means a minister or your anger. If it causes you to stumble, that is, if it is dear to you, cut off the hand—that is, the evil work.

Do not swear—that is, do not commit perjury. “Do not swear at all” means never to swear, nor by heaven, because it is the throne of God. Otherwise, “yes” means “yes,” and “no” means “no”: the word spoken in the mouth and in the heart. Anything beyond this is from evil, that is, from the unworthiness of the person who is not believed.

An eye for an eye—that is, do not repay evil with evil. If someone strikes you on the right cheek—that is, if a heretic strikes you in the dogma of a false Scripture—offer him another dogma from divine Scripture, for his life. Whoever wishes to take your tunic—that is, to strip away the accusation that people know against you—let him have your cloak as well, that is, give him a confession of the accusation of which you alone are conscious. If someone forces you to go one thousand paces, go with him another thousand—that is, when you have gone out from the body, go also in mind. Give to the one who asks you—that is, to the one who questions you, give him an answer; or give alms to the poor.

[Col. 0547B] It was said to the ancients, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” How does this accord with the statement that he did not abolish the Law? He rightly fulfills it, because in the Old Testament he says that the enemy—the devil—is to be hated; here, however, he speaks of both. We love our enemies in three ways: with the heart, the one who hates us in his heart; by doing good, the one who persecutes us by his actions; and by praying in words, for the one who accuses us in words. When you are slandered—that is, falsely accused. So that you may be sons of your Father, and so forth: it is as though someone had carried gold or silver to us, and if he had cursed us and struck us, we would love him; and when those things had failed, and we too had failed, life is therefore promised without end. He who makes his sun rise, and so forth, and sends rain upon the just, because the whole world is contained in both: in the sun, dry and hot; in the rain, moist and cold. The world was made from these four elements. Thus we must give our enemies food and drink, clothing, and a word of love.

For if you love those who love you, and so forth. A publican is so called because he sins publicly, or because he administers public affairs. “Ethnics” means Gentiles. Be perfect—that is, fulfill these things perfectly in almsgiving, fasting, and prayers; do not appear before people, that is, do not perform good works for human praise.

When you give alms—that is, give to a priest, a poor person, and an enemy. “Hypocrite” means a pretender. They have received their reward—not God’s. Let your left hand not know—that is, vain glory; your right hand means doing everything for God. Enter your room—that is, the hidden places of the heart—with the door shut, that is, against vain glory.

[Col. 0547D] Do not speak at excessive length—that is, do not make many petitions or speak many words, nor ask God through loudness of voice. For the Father knows what you need. Therefore pray in this way: “Our Father”—that is, let us live on earth in such a way that we may have a Father in heaven. We show charity and brotherhood when we say “our.” The emperor says this, and the beggar; the master and the servant say it together: “Our Father.” Therefore those who have one Father are brothers. Let the master, then, not disdain having as a brother his servant, whom the Lord Christ wished to be a brother. And let us act so that we may be able to become heirs of the Father; for human law also makes sons heirs.

“Hallowed be your name”: here we ask that it be hallowed in us, that is, in our works; for his name is always holy. “Your kingdom come”: just as children desire their father’s kingdom, so we pray that he may reign in us and not the devil; he, and not sin—whether this means the Church or the Gospel.

“Your will be done,” and so forth. Just as the angels serve in heaven without guilt, so may we; or just as in souls, so in the body; or just as among Christians, so among heretics; just as in the Church, so in the Synagogue; just as in righteousness, so in sin. Let them be converted, so that your will may be done in them.

[Col. 0548B] “Our daily bread”: that is, every day until the end of the year; “today” means always; “bread” means Christ. We ought to act so that we may receive him daily as a remedy. “And forgive us,” and so forth: here we make a pledge with God: if you forgive, you will be forgiven.

“And do not lead us into temptation”: as you led people astray in the flood, or those in Sodom, or Pharaoh into the sea; or into the devil’s temptation, or the snares of human beings.

“But deliver us from evil”: that is, from the devil, from sin, and from an evil person. These seven prayers are like the seven graces of the Holy Spirit. Four are common to everyone; three petitions concern heavenly things: “Hallowed be your name,” “Your kingdom come,” and “Your will be done.” Four concern this present life.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] The text here was disordered by the words “the seven graces of the Holy Spirit,” which had been added to the following isocolon, along with the word “he prayed,” interrupting the sense.]

When you fast, and so forth, they disfigure their faces. That is, they alter their appearance so that they may be seen by people to be fasting. Anoint your head and wash your face—that is, give to your neighbor what you wish to give to the Lord, who is your head. Do not store up treasures on earth—that is, in heaven—lest rust, that is, vain glory, or anger, moth, envy, or pride, thieves, demons, gold, the senses, the world, and clothing destroy them; for food means divine preaching.

The lamp of your body means your teacher or ruler; “body” means the inner person. If it is simple, it is directed toward one thing. No one can serve two masters. Where your treasure is, and so forth: he will hate one—that is, the one who is not good to him—and love the other, who is good to him. This means despising the devil and loving God. Whoever serves riches serves the devil. “Mammon” means riches, or it is the name of the devil.

Is not the soul more than food? That is, the person who gives lesser things to God and greater things to the devil. Look at the birds of heaven, and so forth. It is the custom of birds to fly upward and sing, and when they desire something on earth, they receive it from the Lord. So human beings ought to think about heavenly things and praise God; and when they need food, they receive restoration from the Lord on earth.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] It originally read “citizens.” We were forced to substitute “let them lay down the burdens they carry” for the monstrous wording that follows, “let them lay down the gate faith palasticas II.”]

How much more will your Father, who is good by nature, give good things to those who ask him—that is, faith through charity. Enter through the narrow gate, where sinners will not fit unless they lay down the burdens they carry. The two—that is, love of God and of one’s neighbor. The two lamps: the Gospel above and the old Law below; whoever offends there does not enter. How broad the gate, and so forth: that is, those who serve riches and their own will.

Beware for yourselves—that is, beware of false teachers. In sheep’s clothing—that is, in the appearance of a good teacher—are ravenous wolves, who seize souls for destruction. By their fruits—that is, by their works—you will know them. Do they gather grapes from thorns—that is, from heretics—or figs from thistles, that is, a spouse from heretics? A good tree is a good person; a bad tree is a bad person who performs evil works.

Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” and so forth. He speaks of those who love to stand praying in corners. But the one who does the will of my Father—that is, who keeps the commandments. Many say to me, “Lord”—that is, there are many who enter through it. “I never knew you”: that is, the good person, or heretics. “Depart from me”: that is, those who hope that there is no remission of sins. Everyone who hears my words, and so forth: the person who does not act against the preaching will be compared to a wise man who built his house upon rock—that is, upon a good work—so that rain might not enter upon him, that is, heretical doctrine; rivers mean the persecutions of heretics; winds mean demons. Clouds receive rain from the sea; heretics receive doctrine from the world. And the house did not fall—that is, the person who stands upon faith in Christ does not fall.

And everyone who hears my words and does not do them: that is, in the Law there was a custom that no one who was unclean could remain among the people; and if he received health, he was to show himself to the priest, and a gift was offered for him: two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Along with these, according to the rite, there was hyssop wood, with scarlet thread at the top of the wood; the blood of one bird was sprinkled upon this wood, and upon the other bird, which was then released into the air. The wood is the cross of Christ; the scarlet is his passion. One must go to martyrdom through the passion of Christ, and our blood must be sprinkled upon his cross, so that it may ascend to the Church after the passion of our body in martyrdom.

For a testimony to them: that is, so that he would not have abolished the Law, or so that they might see that he had been cleansed from leprosy. The centurion represents teachers; the contracted paralytic boy signifies the human race enclosed in sins. Jesus found three mysteries in the centurion. First, humility, when he said, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Second, faith, when he said, “Only say the word and he will be healed.” Third, prudence, when he said, “I am a man under authority.” Jesus marvels at the centurion—that is, he found in him wisdom, by which he had been instructed through divine preaching.

From the east they are converted—that is, from infancy; from the west, that is, from old age; from the south, from youth; from the north, that is, from the power of the devil. They come to faith and recline—that is, they dwell there. Why with only three? That is, because of forgiveness. Those who desire will weep there; there will be the gnashing of teeth for those whose god is their belly. Peter’s mother-in-law, suffering from fever, means the Synagogue’s uncertainty.

He touched her hand: he supplied help. When the fever had left her—that is, unbelief ceases—she ministered to him, that is, she blessed him. “Toward evening” indicates the end of the world. Demons mean sins; foxes mean unbelieving people; birds mean rich people. He does not lay his head where there is no faith. “Let the dead bury their dead” means the body burying the soul; alternatively, it means when a sinner praises a sinner.

The boat means the Church. Movement and waves mean temptation. He was asleep means incarnate or crucified. The wind means sudden temptation. The demoniac represents a Gentile people, a nation in unbelief. The tombs are bodies. “He does not pass along the way” means that through Gentilism he does not pass into the kingdom. The herd of pigs represents people before conversion, drowned in the sea, that is, in the depths. The shepherd represents philosophers.

He rose—that is, he was healed—and returned to his house, that is, to the first creation. The bridegroom is Christ; the bride is the Church; the children of the bridegroom are the apostles. Rough cloth means the teaching of the Gospel; torn cloth means old people. New wine and old wineskins mean new preaching given to old people. The ruler represents the prophets or patriarchs. This girl is the Synagogue. Jesus took the girl’s hand, that is, he gave her assistance. The plentiful harvest means hearts prepared; the reapers are teachers.

Not two tunics means neither a double mind nor double confidence in the New or Old Testament. No sandals means no testimony of evil people; nor a staff means not strength, but patience. Peace returned means the reward received. Dust means defilement. It is this because dust hinders in three ways: it binds the feet, obscures the eyes, and soils the garments. The crucified serpent hides its head: that is, the crucified apostles do not deny Christ. Persecutions are heresies. From one city to another means through the individual questions of the books.

Nothing is covered that will not be revealed: that is, the passion of Christ and of all teachers. What I say in darkness—that is, to the Jews—say in the light, that is, in the Church. Two sparrows mean body and soul, or Christ and Barabbas. For an assarion—that is, faith. Through the sword: this means the word of preaching. Alternatively, the two sparrows mean the two Testaments. The assarion is Christ. To separate father from son means the faithful from the unfaithful. He takes up the cross—that is, crucify yourself. To stumble in Christ means to deny Christ. A reed shaken by the wind means flattering people, empty and without fruit.

The kingdom of heaven suffers violence: that is, one reaches the kingdom of God through the crucifixions of the flesh and through repentance. He himself is Elijah, who is John, because the same spirit that was in Elijah at the second coming was in John at the first coming. The children sitting in the marketplace are the prophets. “We sang to you, and you did not dance”: that is, we announced your coming, and you did not believe. “We lamented, and you did not mourn”: we announced repentance to you, and you were afraid of confession.

There are four kinds of praise: “I will confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven”; that of faith, “I believe in God the Father”; that of martyrs, “Whoever confesses me before men”; and that of sinners, “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” You have hidden these things from the wise—that is, from those who use the wisdom of this world—and revealed them to infants, that is, to disciples.

The call is made in four ways in the New Testament. “Come to me, all who labor”; in the Old Testament, “Come, children, hear me”; in the future, “Come, blessed ones.”

The yoke is a light teaching for those who are willing, but heavy for those who are unwilling. Perfection is understood in three ways: that of disciples, through baptism; that of sinners, through remission; and that of Jews, through the renewal of the New Testament.

The sown fields—that is, the harvest—signify the old Law. The Sabbath is the rest of the New Testament. The disciples plucking ears of grain means drawing testimonies from the Old Testament to confirm the New; rubbing them with their hands means expressing them in a spiritual sense. The man with the withered hand represents avarice: eager to receive, miserly in giving. Let the one who used to steal learn to give. He stretched out his hand—that is, after his heart had been cleansed, it was restored. This signifies conversion to faith.

The smoking flax means the hearts of the Gentiles prepared for faith. The man who was demoniac, mute, and blind signifies the human race. In the house he bound the strong man: Christ bound the devil. His vessels are the hearts of the Gentiles.

Brood of vipers: “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” Through the viper he represents the Synagogue; the brood is the Jews. Just as a viper kills its mother, so the Jews killed Christ, who is the wisdom and mother of all. An evil and adulterous generation: the same people, abandoning the Lord and clinging to idols.

The Queen of the South came from the ends of the earth: she signifies the Gentiles. To hear Solomon’s wisdom means the teaching of Christ. An unclean spirit goes out from a person—that is, from the Jews—and travels through dry places, that is, through the Gentiles. It returns to its house, that is, to the Jews, and finds it swept clean, that is, by ancestral traditions. It takes with it seven spirits more wicked than itself: these are all their days turned toward evil works. Entering the house—that is, the hearts of the persecutors—because they persecuted Christ and the prophets.

Mother and brothers mean the Synagogue and the Jews. Standing outside means outside the Church. Seeking to speak with you indicates the future conversion of the Jews to the faith. Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. This is understood in two ways: from heaven into the world, and from the Jews to the Gentiles. He went up into a boat—that is, into heaven. The crowds at the shore signify the present life.

He spoke in a likeness, that is, in parables. The one who sows is the preacher; the seed is the word of God. Beside the way means the person who hears the word of God and does not understand it. Upon rocky ground means the person who hears the word of God and receives it but, when temptation comes, denies it. Among thorns means the person who hears the word but lets it be choked by riches. On good soil means the person who hears and understands.

He produces a thirtyfold crop: this represents the order of married people who follow God’s commandment. The sixtyfold crop represents the order of widows who persevere in the Lord. The hundredfold crop represents the orders of martyrs, monks, or virgins.

To the one who has, it will be given: this represents the apostles; those who have Christ will also be given understanding. And from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away: this represents the Jews; the Law they possessed will be taken away from them. Seeing they do not see: these are the Jews, who saw with their eyes but did not believe in their hearts. Hearing they do not hear: this represents the cares of the body; they heard but did not understand because of their hardened hearts.

The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. The one who sows is the Son of Man; the seed is the word in the hearts of believers; the field is the world. The weeds are wicked sons, that is, workers of iniquity. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age; the reapers are angels. Why is it called a bundle? Because people are not all judged equally, but adulterers with adulterers and all like with like, equally.

The mustard seed signifies Christ. The man who sows is God the Father; the field is the world. It is the smallest of all seeds: this signifies Christ, rejected by the Jews. When it has grown—that is, when he has risen—it becomes a tree, that is, he ascends to heaven. Its branches are the apostles; the birds in its branches are the saints, who despise earthly things and desire heavenly things.

Alternatively, the mustard seed is the word of the holy Gospel. The man who sows is Christ; the field is the world. It is the smallest of all—that is, preserved in the hearts of the faithful because of the wisdom of philosophers. It becomes a tree—that is, it rises above all worldly wisdom. Its branches represent the explanations of the individual teachers; the birds are lovers of knowledge, receiving from the seed the doctrine of the Gospel.

The woman means wisdom. She hid it in the flour—that is, in the hearts of the faithful. The three measures represent the three sons of Noah. Until the whole was leavened—that is, until the Gospel had been preached throughout the whole world.

The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. The treasure is Christ or wisdom; the field is the Church or the divine Scriptures. He sold everything—that is, he abandoned worthless or earthly things—and bought the field, that is, the kingdom of heaven.

The merchant is the person who seeks divine teaching. He found one pearl—that is, the wisdom of Christ—and sold everything, that is, his vices.

The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea. The net represents the word of preaching; the sea is the world; gathering fish of every kind means the whole human race.

He hears the word of God beside the shore—that is, near the end of the world. The master of the household is Christ; the scribes are teachers; the apostles are [uncertain: implied in the source]. He came to his homeland—that is, to the Jews.

The tetrarch means the fourth part of a kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0551] It read *inita*, perhaps instead of *quinta*, although that too is false. We have rewritten it as “fourth” so that the truth of the matter may be clear. Besides this, we correct innumerable other passages, too tedious to note individually, throughout the entire context, so that there is scarcely a line to which we have not applied a physician’s hand.]

He bound John and sent him into prison: this signifies the end of the old Law. Herodias represents the Synagogue. The girl danced at the banquet: this represents the Gentiles dancing before idols. John’s head on a dish signifies the body of Christ on the altar; his head in the hearts of believers was given to the girl, that is, to the Church from the Gentiles. She brought it to her mother: this indicates the future conversion of the Jews.

Those who followed were on foot. He showed that a person must follow God not with [uncertain: *anteguis*] money, but through his own labor. He healed the sick—that is, he washed them from sins and idols. The hour had already passed: this means the letter of the Law. The five loaves are the five books of Moses. The two fish are the two Testaments, or the two orders, namely priests and prophets, or the two books of Joshua.

The crowd reclined upon the grass—that is, upon dry hearts—or reclined upon vices. And taking the loaves and looking up to heaven, he withdrew the understanding; he broke them—that is, he expressed the history of the Law in a spiritual sense, and understanding appeared; he blessed them—that is, he multiplied them.

The twelve baskets full mean the twelve apostles, filled with holy doctrine. Why are women and children not counted like men? Because children are unable to struggle against their vices; likewise women, because their sex is imperfect.

He ordered them to go up into the little boat—that is, into the Church—and to go ahead across the strait, that is, from the Jews to the Gentiles.

A person is called in four ways: first by nature, second by kinship, third by nation, and fourth by affection. A human being is described in four ways. What is said may be good and said well: “Repent,” and so forth. It may be evil and said badly: “His blood be upon us.” It may be good and said badly, as when it is said of the blind man, “Are you the only disciple of him?” Or it may be evil and said well, as when the Apostle says, “I handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved.”

When evening came, he was alone: this signifies the end of the world. He came alone to redeem the human race.

The boat was in the middle of the sea: the Church in the middle of the world. It was tossed by the waves: it suffered persecutions. The contrary wind is the devil. Jesus came during the fourth watch of the night: this signifies the fourth Law, that is, the Gospel.

Jesus walking upon the sea means trampling upon the bitterness of the world. Peter walked upon the waters, upon the bitterness, or trampling upon the vices of sins. When Peter was sinking into the sea, this means doubt of faith; thus everyone who doubts in faith sinks into sin. Jesus stretched out his hand and seized him: he gave him the help of faith.

These are the four Laws: the first in nature; the second, the Law of the letter; the third, that of the prophets; the fourth, that of the evangelists.

When he had crossed over—that is, when he had passed over—they came to the land of Gennesaret, that is, from the Jews to the Gentiles. They brought him those who were ill, that is, those serving idols.

The Canaanite woman represents the primitive Church. Her daughter afflicted by a demon means the Church of the Gentiles corrupted by idols. The girl was healed from that hour: this signifies the conversion of the Gentiles from the hour when they believed in Christ.

“I was sent only to the sheep who had perished from the house of Israel”: this indicates that, bodily speaking, he was sent to the Jews; alternatively, all who believe in the God of Israel are called sheep. To take the children’s bread means the teaching of the Jews. To give it to dogs means the Gentiles. The little dogs eat—that is, the Gentiles receive the crumbs, the lesser commandments.

“I have compassion on the crowd”: this shows that God is wholly merciful. They have remained with me for three days: this represents faith in the Trinity. They have nothing to eat: they have no word of preaching. I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way—that is, lest they perish on the way of error in the present life, because faith without works is dead.

The seven loaves represent the *heptaticum* [Greek ἑπτάτευχος, “sevenfold”], and the few fish represent the order of the prophets or priests. Reclining upon the ground represents the more perfect, who have already trampled their vices. The seven baskets represent the seven teachers of the Holy Spirit.

Pharisees means “divided”; Sadducees means “justified.” A clear sky means the resurrection of Christ. A red sky means the shedding of blood. A gloomy sky signifies the passion of Christ. A flashing storm signifies persecution.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees—that is, of their teaching. Simon means “obedient”; “son of Jonah” means “son of the dove,” which is interpreted as the Holy Spirit. Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you—that is, father and mother did not show it to you.

The gates of hell are the sins of human beings. The keys of the kingdom of heaven are the power of binding and loosing; they will be opened through repentance.

Jesus said that he would suffer many things at the hands of the elders and scribes, thereby showing his passion and resurrection. He says to Peter, “Go behind me”: this signifies that he himself was crucified. “After me, let him deny himself”: that is, let him despise the pleasure of the flesh. Whoever loves pleasure loses his own soul; here “soul” is used for pleasure. Whoever loses his soul will find it. A person loses his soul in two ways: through martyrdom and through the denial of the body. He will find it in the kingdom of God. He gives an exchange for his soul who crucifies his flesh and nourishes his soul.

After six days, already on the seventh, he showed the ages of the world; the seventh is understood as rest. Peter, James, and John represent the whole Church. He leads them onto a mountain, that is, into the kingdom of God.

His face shone like the sun: this means the saints in the glory of the Father. Alternatively, the Old Testament shone forth into the New. His garments were white as snow: this means the gathering of all the faithful. Through Moses he represents the letter of the Law; through Elijah, the order of the prophets. Christ with the disciples represents the New Testament.

A dark cloud means the letter of the Law. A bright cloud means the preaching of the Gospel. A rain-bearing cloud means the preaching of the apostles, who produced the fruit of repentance after Christ’s ascension.

When he came to the crowds—that is, when he descended into the world—a man fell on his knees. He represents the order of the prophets, who prayed for themselves as for the Church. His son was a lunatic: this represents the people of the Gentiles worshiping idols. He falls into fire—that is, into desire—and repeatedly into water, that is, into lust.

Move from here, from the Jews to the Gentiles: “Go to the sea,” that is, to the Gentiles. “Cast a hook,” that is, the word of preaching. The fish that first comes up, [Note: [Col. 0555D] Perhaps *coronarium*, namely gold, the tax that was paid to emperors or to the Roman magistrates of the province [Col. 0556D]. But there is no time for conjecture. Several things below have been emended wherever it could safely be done.] shows the *cornemium*: in its mouth you will find a *stater*, that is, confession of faith, humanity and divinity. “Give it to them for me and for you,” that is, faith for me and an excuse for you. The little one enters the kingdom of heaven, that is, not little in age but pure in mind; hence the Apostle says, “Be infants in malice.” Whoever causes one of these to stumble, that is, either by bodily injury or by turning him away from the faith. “Let a millstone be hung,” that is, the care, or the circuit, of this age, “around his neck,” in the labor of the age; “let him be drowned” [Col. 0555B] “in the sea,” that is, in the world. Your hand, that is, your parent; your feet, that is, your minister; your eye, that is, your bishop, or priest, or teacher and elder. “Do not despise one of these,” lest you act against their innocence. The sheep that strayed signifies the human race; the shepherd is Christ; the sheep left in the mountains signify the orders of angels who dwell in the heavenly places.

“If your brother sins, rebuke him between yourself and him”: so that the disclosure of the sin does not occur and reproach does not arise against the brother; “tell it to the Church,” that is, to the congregation of the faithful. “A heathen,” that is, a Gentile, and a publican is one who sins publicly. Let not their image be hateful to you, but their deeds. “If two agree,” that is, flesh and soul. If flesh agrees with the soul, the one who asks receives through faith.

[Col. 0555C] “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” The one who owes ten thousand talents is the one who sins against God. The one who owes a hundred denarii is the one who sins against his brother; the fellow servants who judged are the angels. When Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed for Galilee, that is, at the end of the world, from the Gentiles to Judaea.

A man leaves father and mother: this shows that Christ leaves the Father in heaven; yet he leaves him in such a way that he does not abandon him. The mother is the synagogue. “He will cling to his wife,” that is, Christ to the Church. “The two will be one flesh”: this shows that Christ is the head, while the body is the Church. The wife is abandoned by her husband, that is, when someone departs from Christ, then he joins himself to heresy in a single crime. Four souls perish, [Col. 0555D] that is, the one who dismisses his wife without legitimate cause, and the one who marries the dismissed woman. “It is difficult for a rich man to enter,” and so forth: he speaks of those who possess under the power of greed. The eye of a needle is called the small gate of Jerusalem. In another way, the eye of a needle signifies confession of faith or repentance; the rich are called the Jews, and the camel the people of the Gentiles. In a third way, the eye of a needle signifies Christ’s Passion; the camel is the one who bears the sins of the human race. “In the regeneration,” that is, through the resurrection.

“The last will be first, and the first last.” The last were the people of the Gentiles; the Jews were first, [Col. 0556A] but became last. So it is with Peter and the thief; so with the infant and the old man. “The master of the household hired laborers for his vineyard”: the father is Christ; “early morning” signifies the beginning of the world; the laborers are keepers of God’s commandments; the vineyard is the Church; in the old vineyard, the Law, or the synagogue; the daily denarius, eternal life. “In the marketplace,” that is, in the world. At the first hour Abel came; at the third hour Noah and his sons; at the sixth hour Abraham came; at the ninth hour Moses and David came; at the eleventh hour the people of the Gentiles came. In another way: the first hour is infancy; the second hour adolescence; the sixth, youth; the ninth, old age; the eleventh, extreme old age. At whatever hour a person turns back and groans with all his heart, he receives the daily denarius. “When evening came,” that is, at the end of the world. The steward of the vineyard is Christ. Those who murmured [Col. 0556B] are the Jews, saying, “We have borne the burden of the day,” that is, bearing the Law and the prophets.

Jericho is interpreted as “moon”; it signifies the decline of the people. The two blind men signify the Jews and the Gentiles; sitting beside the road means the present life near its end. Jesus’ passing by signifies that through his incarnation and humanity he passed through the world; Jesus’ standing signifies his divinity. “When he drew near Jerusalem,” that is, when he came into the world. Bethphage means “house of the mouth,” or “of the jaw.” The Mount of Olives means “the name of three lights,” namely, refreshment from labor, consolation in work, and knowledge of the true light. “The village that is opposite you” means Jerusalem, which resisted the law of the Gospel. “Untie it and bring it to me” shows the conversion of the Jews or the Gentiles through the preaching [Col. 0556C] of the apostles. “The Lord has need of it”: he needs nothing other than faith. “To Zion,” that is, to the watchtower. “The daughter of Zion comes,” that is, the congregation of the faithful. Through the garments he signifies doctrine. “They made him sit upon them,” that is, Christ in the hearts of the faithful. “They spread their garments on the road” shows the conversion of humility. The branches from the trees signify the doctrine of the Gentiles. The crowd that goes before signifies the Jews; the crowd that follows signifies the Gentiles. “Hosanna”: “Save me,” or “Save”; just as you save the Jews, save the Gentiles also; just as you save the angels, save the human race also.

In another way, the branches from the trees signify simple teachers who, through the simplicity of their teaching, cut off the doctrine of the fathers like young shoots. Jesus entered the temple, that is, the Church. He cast out the sellers and buyers, that is, those who sell and buy the gifts of the Holy Spirit, baptism, or any consecration. The chair signifies doctrine; the table signifies the commandments of the Law; the children crying out in the temple signify the children in the Church. “Leaving them, he went outside” shows that the Jews were left behind; he went to the Gentiles. Bethany means “house of obedience.” He stayed there, showing that Christ remains in the heart of the obedient. He returns to the city, showing that at his first coming he came to the Jews. Why did he hunger except for the faith of the Jews? The fig tree signifies the synagogue; “beside the road” means according to the letter. He found nothing on it but leaves, that is, the substitution of the Jews [Col. 0557A] and of the teachings of the fathers. The withered fig tree shows the synagogue without repentance. “The mountain,” that is, Christ. “Take this away,” that is, from the Jews; “throw it into the sea,” that is, into the hearts of believers.

The man who had two sons: the man is Christ; the two sons are the Jews and the Gentiles. Which of them did the Father’s will—the one who said “I will go” and did not go? This signifies the Jews. And the one who said “I will not go” and went? This signifies the people of the Gentiles, who acted through confession of faith.

The master of the household planted a vineyard: the man is God the Father; the vineyard is the synagogue. He surrounded it with a hedge, that is, with the protection of angels. The winepress is the temple, or martyrdom; the tower in the middle signifies the doctrine of the Law; the cultivators are the teachers. When the time of the fruit drew near, that is, the coming of Christ, the servants sent are the prophets. The first whom they killed was Jeremiah and Isaiah; the one whom they stoned was Stephen. [Note: [Col. 0557] It seemed preferable to remove from here the monstrous wording “es me Bart,” or whatever it was, which interrupted the sense.] They cast him outside the vineyard, that is, outside Jerusalem, onto Mount Calvary. “This vineyard and other cultivators” signifies the Church of the Gentiles, who render fruit, that is, confession of repentance and faith. The stone is Christ, cut from the mountain without hands, that is, without human action or intercourse, from the mother without seed, from the Father without time. “He became the cornerstone,” containing two walls: this signifies the New and Old Testaments, the Jews and the Gentiles. “Whoever falls upon that stone will be broken”: this signifies the Gentiles being broken upon Christ, moving from unbelief to faith, broken upon him, that is, into humility. “But upon whomever the stone falls, it will crush him”: this signifies the superstitious Jews.

[Col. 0557C] The king who made a wedding feast for his son: the man is God the Father. Through the wedding he signifies the union of Christ and the Church. Just as Eve was redeemed from Adam’s rib, so the Church was redeemed from Christ’s side; and just as Adam came forth from virgin earth, so Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. He sent his servants, that is, the patriarchs; again he sent others, that is, the prophets. The prepared meal signifies Holy Scripture. The slaughtered bulls signify those who shed their blood for Christ; the fattened animals signify the fattened offerings. “They went away to the farm,” that is, into greed. Others went into business, that is, into the world, as the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.” The rest seized his servants, showing the assault of persecution. He said to his servants, that is, to the apostles. The wedding took place, that is, the hearts of believers were joined to Christ through the love of charity. “Go out to the crossroads,” that is, to the Gentiles. They gathered the good and the bad, showing the present life. The king entered among those reclining, showing the Second Coming. The man without a wedding garment signifies charity, as it says, “Faith without charity is dead.”

The woman—that is, the synagogue—through seven husbands: the *Heptateuch* is understood. The dead woman signifies the dead letter, passing from the Old Testament into the New. “In the resurrection, whose wife will she be?” That is, she will belong to the Church of Christ. “The Lord said”—that is, God the Father—“to my Lord”—that is, to Christ—[Col. 0558A] “until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”: this shows that he humbled the Jews and the Gentiles through patience beneath his feet, so that the persecutors might be punished through vengeance in the future. “Upon Moses’ chair,” that is, upon his doctrine. Phylacteries are the ten words of the Law, written on a small scroll, which the Pharisees carried on their foreheads.
