“Jerusalem, Jerusalem”: the repetition shows the feeling of grief; just as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings—beneath the spirals of her feathers, that is, with her wings raised—so Christ spread his palms on the cross in order to gather his children, as the Song of Deuteronomy declares: “He spread his wings and took them up upon his shoulders.” “Behold, your house will be left desolate”: this shows that they were abandoned by their law, their prophecy, and their priesthood. “You will not see me [Col. 0558B] until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’”: this shows that at the Second Coming every creature will see him, and all the tribes of the earth that pierced him will mourn over him. “Not one stone will be left here upon another”: this shows the dispersion of the Jews. “Then many will be scandalized”: this shows that, because of the magnitude of the persecution, they will deny Christ. The abomination signifies the statue of Antichrist placed in the temple; desolation means consummation. “Those who are in Judaea,” that is, in the confession of faith, should flee to the mountains, that is, to the doctrine of the apostles. He who is on the roof, that is, in the contemplative life, should not descend into the house, that is, into the active life. He who is in the field, that is, in the preaching of the Gospel, should not take up his tunic, that is, should not return to his former way of life.

[Col. 0558C] Woe to pregnant women, that is, to those desiring the property of others; woe to nursing women, that is, to those carrying out deeds in practice. Through the wilderness he signifies persecution; through the Sabbath, the end of the world. “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather”: the body is Christ; the eagles are the souls of the saints. In another way, at the resurrection each soul will take up its own body. Through the sun he signifies the preaching of the Gospel; through the moon, the Church; through the stars, the saints or preachers. “The powers of heaven will be shaken”: this means the ranks of angels coming to judge. “The sign will appear in heaven,” that is, the cross of Christ. Through the trumpet he signifies the sound of the angels. “Two will be in the field,” that is, in the preaching of the Gospel: one will be taken, that is, the one who completes the preaching in action; the other will be left, that is, in the work of righteousness. “At the mill,” in the world; the two women grinding signify the Catholic Church and the Church of the heretics.

The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps, that is, in the resurrection, their bodies. They are virgins because they did not deny Christ. The five wise ones signify those who labored for the kingdom of God; the five foolish ones signify those who acted for the reward of human praise. To grow drowsy is to become weak before death; to sleep is to rest in death. Midnight signifies error, or negligent security. “I do not know you,” that is, “I do not know your good works.”

[Col. 0559A] The man going away is Christ; he went abroad, that is, from the world to the Father. He called his servants, that is, the teachers; he gave them his goods, that is, the doctrine of the Gospel. The five talents signify the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Through habit he used to move them so that they might convert transitory matters to the eternal. Thus it is said of sight, “Turn my eyes away,” and so forth. Of hearing: “Hedge your ears, and let them not hear tongues of blasphemy.” Of smell: “We are a pleasing fragrance to God among those who are being saved.” Of taste: “Do not curse, but bless.” Of touch: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but labor with his hands, so that he may give also to the needy.”

Thus ten talents are produced. The two talents signify understanding and action. Whoever has these, fulfills them in examples and teaches in words, saves [Col. 0559B] himself and instructs others. Thus the talent is doubled. The one talent signifies understanding. He hid it in the earth, that is, the one who teaches the preaching of the Gospel for earthly things. “After a long time,” that is, at the end of the world. “You reap where you did not sow,” that is, where there was no preaching. “Take the talent,” that is, understanding; give it to the one who doubled it in good works. The five senses, as the Apostle says, are a law for themselves, showing the work of the Law in their hearts. Whoever has faith and charity will be given understanding and the working of virtues; whoever does not have them, even what he has will be taken away from him. That is, whoever has faith but does not have charity: the faith itself will die in him. Majesty means power and dignity. [Note: [Col. 0559D] The word “kids” was missing, and other things below had also fallen out; these have been supplied. The remaining matters emended throughout would have to be noted at nearly every [Col. 0560D] line.] The kids are the Jews; the sheep, however, are the peoples of the Gentiles. The right means prosperous or straight; the left, adverse or punitive, because with God there is nothing left-handed.

When he was in Bethany, that is, in the house of obedience—here “house” is used for the world—the woman signifies the future Church. The alabaster signifies the human body; through the ointment he signifies the faith of confession. The head of Christ is God the Father; “reclining,” likewise, is Christ above the Church. “You will always have the poor”: spiritually, those who need doctrine; or bodily, those who need food. “You will not always have me”: this shows him according to the flesh. Joseph was sold into Egypt for twenty pieces of silver, so that he might satisfy bodily hunger; Christ was sold for thirty pieces of silver, for the sins of human beings and the hunger of faith. “Opportunity” means a suitable time. Through the unleavened bread of sincerity he signifies sincerity of mind. “I will drink it with you in the kingdom of my Father,” that is, in his members; “in the kingdom,” that is, in the Church. “I will strike the shepherd,” that is, Christ; “the sheep will be scattered,” that is, the apostles. “I will go before you into Galilee”: this means that, leaving the Jews, he went to the Gentiles.

“If it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” that is, the Passion. He said this according to the part of the flesh. Through the sword he signifies the divine word. He cut off the ear, that is, the hearing of the Jews was cut off, so that he might cleanse impurity. Though scourged, he held fast, so that he might free us from the scourges of sins. Just as Adam extended his palm toward the tree of life, so the Jews extended their palms against Christ; therefore Christ also extended his palm toward the tree of life. In this way the Jews extended their palms against the wood of the cross, so that he might free us from every goad. Through the cockcrow he signifies the refreshment of the Holy Spirit. Bound and led away, so that he might loose the bonds of our sins.

*Corbana* in Hebrew, *Gazophylacia* in Greek, is called in Latin “the treasury of riches.” Through the shedding of Christ’s blood the human race was redeemed. Through the price of his blood, a field was bought for the burial of strangers. Hyrus [Note: [Col. 0560D] I do not know what this is supposed to mean, nor do I wish to conjecture.] Pompeius is; Barabbas was led into the desert, that is, into hell; the other was sacrificed, that is, Christ for the sin of human beings. They stripped Christ, that is, he was stripped away from the faith of the Jews. They clothed him in a scarlet cloak, that is, Christ was clothed in the faith of the Gentiles. In another way, through the scarlet cloak he signifies the shedding of his blood, or martyrdom. They stripped the cloak from him and clothed him in his own garments: this shows the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world.

The soldiers divided his garments among themselves: this bears the figure of the Gospel, whose teaching they divided among themselves. Through the tearing of the veil he signifies the tearing apart of the kingdom of the Jews. In another way, the veil was torn: this shows the tearing of the letter of the Law through the revelation of the Holy Spirit; or, through Christ’s ascension, the heavens were torn open for the human race. The earth was shaken, showing the grace of God, moved from the Jews to the Gentiles. The rocks were split: [Col. 0560C] these are the hearts of the Gentiles, split open for faith. The tombs were opened, that is, hearts were opened to faith.

The tomb, that is, the Church from the Gentiles. “New” shows that the word of God had not previously been preached to the Gentiles. The tomb cut out in the rock shows the Church cut out from the hardness of paganism. The stone rolled to the entrance of the tomb shows hardness in the hearts of the Jews.

The evening of the Sabbath, that is, the end of the world. The first day of the Sabbath signifies the day of the resurrection. The stone being rolled away signifies the hardness of the Jews being rolled away in the future. Through the brightness he signifies terror; through the whiteness of the garment he signifies the consolation of correction. “In Galilee, on the mountain,” signifies the movement from the Jewish people to the Gentiles.

## The Gospel According to Mark

[Col. 0560D]

“The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God”: in saying “Son of God” he shows his birth according to divinity. According to the flesh he shows him when he says, “Behold, I send”—that is, the voice of the Father—“my angel,” that is, John, “before your face,” that is, the forerunner of Christ, making him known. The voice is John’s, crying out; Christ is the one announced. “In the wilderness” signifies the Jews, abandoned by the Law, the kingdom, and the priesthood. “Prepare the way,” that is, your hearts or deeds. “Make his paths straight” [Col. 0561A] means the thoughts of your hearts. Through the baptism of water he signifies the washing of body and soul; the baptism of repentance is the remission of sins.

He came into the house of Simon and Andrew, that is, to the Jews. Rising very early shows the coming of Christ and the beginning of the New Testament. He went into a deserted place, that is, to the Jews; and there he prayed, that is, there he preached.

He could not enter the city because of the crowd. Through the paralytic he signifies the human race; through the bed, the body. He was carried by four: these are the four elements from which the human being is constituted, or the four orders of the Gospel, or the four virtues of the soul, namely, courage, justice, prudence, and temperance. Courage is to fight against [Col. 0561B] vices; justice is to love God with all one’s heart and one’s neighbor as oneself; prudence is to provide for the future; temperance is to set a limit to all anger. They uncovered the roof, that is, revealing the history of the Law. They lowered the pallet, showing the letter of the Law stripped bare and the meaning of the Gospel made manifest.

He commanded them to serve him in the boat, that is, to preach in the Church. He went up onto the mountain, signifying his ascent with the flesh into heaven. He is the one who thunders; the sons of thunder are the apostles; the clouds are the prophets; the rain is preaching. The lamp under the bushel signifies one who teaches for the sake of worldly greed; under the bed, it signifies the obscurity of sinners. “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed”: the hidden things of the Jews’ Law, which have been revealed to the Gentiles.

The man who sowed [Col. 0561C] signifies the teacher; what he sowed is the divine word; in the earth, in the hearts of human beings; sleeping, that is, unknowingly. Through the night he signifies adversity or ignorance; through the day he signifies prosperity or ignorance; and again, through the day, prosperity or knowledge. Through the shoot he signifies compunction of heart; through the grass, faith in works; through the ear, perfection of action; through the full grain in the ear, the completion of works; through the sickle, the cutting off of the present life and the consummation of the age.

Leaving the crowd of Jews, he went into the boat, that is, into the Church from the Gentiles. Other boats were with him, that is, the various churches of the heretics. Through the storm of wind he signifies persecutions against the faithful. The waves sent in order to fill the boat signify the persecution of Antichrist, so savage that many come close to denial. Those beloved by God persevere in faith. Christ’s sleeping in the stern signifies the testing of the faithful during persecution. They awaken him, that is, they invoke him for help in persecution. There was a great calm, that is, after the persecution of Antichrist and after the resurrection.

The man who had an unclean spirit signifies the human race. Breaking chains shows the Gentiles transgressing the law of their nature, or the teaching [Col. 0562A] of the philosophers. Likewise, it signifies the Jews breaking the letter of the Law or the prophecy. He cut himself with stones, showing the people of the Gentiles worshiping stones.

The seated man, clothed in faith in Jesus, shows one clothed in faith and charity; “in a sound mind” means with a pure and sincere mind. He had spent his substance on physicians, that is, he had placed all his faith, conduct, and hope in philosophers. He sent them two by two, showing the two Testaments, so that they might preach the same thing everywhere; likewise because charity does not exist with fewer than two. Through the staff he signifies consolation or discipline, as Paul says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with a spirit of gentleness and consolation?” Wearing sandals, for three reasons: because of thorns, that is, because of the entanglement of riches or the anxiety [Col. 0562B] of the world; because of cold, that is, because of desire of mind or unbelief; because of serpents, that is, because of the teaching of heretics. Not having two tunics means not having a double mind, nor doubting between faith and unbelief, nor a double confidence in the New or the Old Testament. It is not like hypocrites, who seek praise from human beings. Through the supper that is not followed by a meal he signifies the consummation of the age, which, when Christ came, saw its consummation. “The hour has already passed,” that is, the letter of the Law; hence he says, “The old things have passed away, and behold, new things have come to be.”

The boats in the middle of the sea signify the Church amid the fluctuation of the world. Jesus alone on the sea signifies that he alone was born on earth without sexual contact. The contrary wind shows [Col. 0562C] the persecution of the devil against the apostles after Christ’s ascension. He wished to pass them by, showing that he was testing them. Gennesareth is interpreted as “a suitable harbor.” He went into the region of Tyre and Sidon, that is, to the Gentiles; he entered the house, that is, the world.

He did not wish anyone to know, showing humility. He could not remain hidden, that is, because his works are always manifest. Through the woman the primitive Church is understood. She fell at Jesus’ feet; the apostles are meant. “First let the children be filled,” that is, the Jews, so that they may receive the commandments of the law of the Gospel; and if they judge the kingdom of God unworthy, then let the Gentiles receive it. He found the girl lying on the bed, that is, he found her in the former condition [Note: [Col. 0561] You may readily supply “of her body,” or something similar. Since there was an empty space in the original, we have not wished to fill it.] of her body.

Through the deaf and mute he signifies the human race. He was deaf because he did not hear God’s commandments; he was unable to speak because he could not render a confession of praise and did not possess a confession of faith. He led him away from the crowd, showing a withdrawn life, because in withdrawal a person always recognizes the blindness of sins and returns to the former way of life of good nature. He put his fingers into his ears, that is, into his heart; and he opened his mouth, in the confession of faith. Looking up to heaven shows that all should render praises to God. He groaned for the sins of the human race that were manifest in the world. In another way, [Col. 0563A] he did this to give us an example, so that we might ask God with supplications.

Through the blind man he signifies the human race. Those who brought him to Jesus signify the teachers. Taking him by the hand means that he gave him the capacity for action. He led him outside the village, showing withdrawal into the contemplative life, or departure from the former way of life. Spitting upon his eyes: through the spittle he signifies Christ’s incarnation, through which the human race was illuminated. By laying on his hands, he gave the help of action.

“I see people like trees”: here he offers an example of humility, so that no one may be lifted up because of virtues, but may consider himself smaller and lower than everyone. Again he laid his hands upon his eyes, and they were opened, [Col. 0563B] showing that he opened human hearts so that they might see the knowledge of God clearly and believe without doubt. “He was restored,” that is, to good works.

He sent him to his house, that is, he recalled him to the former state of worldly nature. Christ’s descent from the mountain shows his descent from heaven. Here the disciples bear the order of the prophets or patriarchs. The crowds asking them show the coming of Christ: the crowds were seeking the Law from the prophets and patriarchs. “They will salute him”: here he understands salvation on account of humility.

The one who brought his son bears the order of the patriarchs. The son signifies the human race. Through the foam he signifies pride; through the gnashing of teeth and the wasting away, he signifies greed. The disciples could not cure him. Here the disciples bear the figure of the patriarchs, because neither the prophets nor the patriarchs could cure the human race, unless Christ came and redeemed it with his blood, as the prophet says: “A brother does not redeem”—that is, Moses through the Law—[Note: [Col. 0563D] The sense was the opposite: Moses redeemed through the Law. Then, when another section had begun, “A man”—that is, Christ—had been written. The matter itself cried out for the place to be restored in continuous speech, as we have done: “A brother does not redeem,” that is, Moses through the Law; [Col. 0564D] “a man will redeem,” that is, Christ. We silently corrected innumerable other things.] “a man redeems,” that is, Christ.

“From childhood” means from the first age of the human race. The father of the child said, “I believe; help my unbelief”: this shows that he said, “If faith is lacking, increase it.” “Tearing him greatly” shows that when the devil sees that he will be driven from the earth at the end of the world, then power is given to him to do as much as he wishes on account of God’s elect. When he sees himself expelled from each person through confession and repentance, he then stirs up vices and the most savage assaults against them. “He became like a dead man”: here he offers an example of the purified person, that is, one who through confession and repentance mortifies himself. Here Jesus appears to have performed two miracles: he cured him of a demon and raised him as though dead. Thus he raised the human race from the death of sins and freed it from bondage to the demon. Through the millstone the circuit of the world is shown; through the ass, the uncleanness of sins.

To be plunged into the sea means to humble oneself in sackcloth through repentance, or to perish in one’s own sin, because it is lighter to endure punishment for oneself alone than to cause [Col. 0564A] others also to be driven from the kingdom of God. Through the worms he signifies those who repent late: punishment continually consumes him, because, while he had time, he did not amend. “Everyone will be salted with fire”: through fire the kindling of the Holy Spirit is understood, because just as all flesh perishes without salt, so every person without knowledge of the word of God becomes foolish. “Have salt in yourselves,” that is, have the wisdom of God within you. They come into the region of Judaea, showing that the Jews will return to faith in Christ in the future.

Beyond the Jordan, that is, to the grace of baptism. “Let the little children come to me”: here the little children bear the figure of the Gentiles; the disciples who forbade them bear the figure of the Jews. Camels cannot pass through the eye of a needle unless their burdens are laid down. So the Jews cannot enter the kingdom of God unless they lay down the burden of sins or riches. What did Peter leave, when he said, “We have left everything”? This shows that the person leaves much who places himself after himself. “He will go before them,” that is, he will go before his sheep by his examples. Through the cup he signifies the Passion; through baptism, the mortification or sleep of the Church.

Just as Adam sinned in three ways—he desired, transgressed, and acted proudly—so Christ was three days in the tomb. Likewise, and for this reason, a person is plunged three times beneath the water of baptism. Hence the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism; for we were baptized into his death.” “Whoever wishes to be first among you will be the servant of all”: here he signifies the teachers of the Church. The blind man bears the figure of the Gentiles. He sat beside the road, that is, beside the faith.

[Col. 0564C] He cried out to Jesus, “Have mercy on me.” The moral sense is this: when we devote ourselves to prayer, then the crowd—the phantom—rebukes the minds of the faithful, so that they may be silent, while they wish to exclude us from prayer, though we persevere. Then Jesus, standing beside us—for standing belongs to divinity, while passing by belongs to humanity—commanded them to call him, that is, through the preaching of the apostles. He calls the Gentiles to faith. He threw off his garments, that is, his former way of life. Leaping up means moving from ignorance to knowledge, from unbelief to faith.

“You will find a colt tied up”: this shows the Gentiles bound by the guilt of sins, “on which no one has sat,” that is, where no teacher had preached. “Untie it and bring it to me,” that is, bring it to faith through preaching.

[Col. 0564D] He saw the fig tree, showing that the faith of the Jews was far from Christ. “It was not the season for figs,” that is, it was not the season for the Jews to believe, because they judged themselves unworthy of the kingdom. He did not allow a vessel to be carried through the temple, that is, through the hearts of the faithful. [Note: [Col. 0564D] It is worth reporting the passage as it stood: “because they judged the kingdom, he did not know how to transfer the vessel, which [was] the hearts [of the faithful]”; I do not know whether more faults could have been contained in fewer words. [Col. 0565D] “He does not wish,” and so forth.] Christ does not wish any work to be done or carried through except what is holy. “To hand it over to the cultivators,” that is, to guard the Law. The winepress is the temple of Solomon; in another way, it signifies martyrdom. The vineyard is the synagogue; the hedge signifies the protection of angels. The tower is the Law. “They cast him outside the vineyard,” that is, from the Jews to the Gentiles. In another way, it means from the city of Jerusalem to Mount Calvary.

The widow put in two coins, which make a quadrans; through these he understands the human being as a quadrans, who offered himself to God. “Whatever you ask for, believing in prayer, will be done for you”: how, then, does Saint Paul say, “Three times I asked the Lord concerning the thorn, and it did not depart from me”? The devil asked to tempt Job, and God allowed him. Paul was not heard, so that through that thorn he might be crowned; the devil was heard, so that through his temptations Job might be crowned. Therefore the Apostle says, “We do not know what we should ask for,” except Christ, who intercedes for us.

“Nation will rise against nation,” that is, pagans [Col. 0565B] against Christians. Morally, flesh against soul; the kingdom of the devil against the kingdom of Christ; the vices of the flesh against the spirit of good action. Earthquakes mean movement from unbelief to faith, that is, the body or soul hearing the word of God. “Standing because of me as a testimony to them” means: if they believe your testimony, it will be for them unto life; and if they do not believe, it will be for them unto punishment.

“No one knows the day or the hour except the Father”: he shows this according to the part of the body, because the body of Christ is the Church. When he says, “You do not know the time,” he means the departure of each individual or the consummation of the age.

The man who went abroad is Christ, who went from the world with the flesh into heaven. He left his house, that is, the Church, to the teachers of each work, that is, of each grace and virtue. Through the doorkeeper he signifies the bishop or teacher. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Here a portion of the sacred text seems to have fallen out, [Col. 0566D] which he is explaining, or perhaps the very word “late.” At the beginning of the following section, where it says, “He broke the alabaster,” the text previously read “Trusting,” and so forth.] “Late in the evening fire and sulfur rained upon Sodom from heaven”; at midnight Egypt was struck in its firstborn; in the morning Sodom was overturned, and its smoke rose up to heaven. “Lest he come suddenly and find you sleeping,” that is, in ignorance or in the security of negligence.

He broke the alabaster, signifying Christ’s body wounded on the cross. Through the ointment the confession of faith is shown. The head of Christ is God the Father. He was seeking an opportunity to hand him over, showing that the suitable time had arrived for the destruction of the Jews, or of Judaea, and for the redemption of the Church. “On the first day of unleavened bread,” that is, on Thursday. The unleavened bread of sincerity became the Church. “Passover” is spoken of in four ways: from the world to the Father, from the Jews to the Gentiles, and for us from unbelief to faith, and from death to life.

A man carrying a water jar (*languena*) represents the apostles, or their successors and baptizers, through whom baptism is effected; the jar signifies the baptism of the Trinity. To eat the Passover with his disciples shows that he was with his disciples among the Jews; otherwise he eats in his members, which is the Church. By the upper room (*coenaculum*) the higher way is indicated; by the large couch the breadth of the Church is shown. The lamb sacrificed in Egypt signifies that, in the New Testament, the mystery of Christ’s body and blood was sacrificed, and that the old sacrifice of the Jews—namely, the blood of goats and bulls—has passed away. For our sacrifice, which is called the wine of Melchizedek, was offered when Abraham returned from the slaughter. Their questioning him individually shows that no one should rely upon his own conscience. Leaving the linen cloth, he fled from them naked: this signifies the abandonment of the malice of the Jews; his naked flight shows that the apostles, stripped of Jewish superstitions, went away to the Gentiles. Peter warmed himself at the fire: this signifies the apostles’ lukewarmness, his own denial, and the unbelief of the Jews.

“They will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” [Col. 0566B] shows that Stephen saw him; Saul also saw him when he was struck down on the road; and many others saw him. Pilate is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammerer”: he who forms, but is not formed. Thus persecutors form the souls of the righteous for the kingdom of heaven, while they themselves remain unformed by the grace of God. The Lord took upon himself a crown of thorns in order to wash away the thorns of our sins; hence it was said to Adam: “Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you.” When he says that Jesus was crucified at the third hour, he shows that he was judged so as to be crucified; at the sixth hour he was raised upon the cross. “Eli, Eli, lamma sabactani”—that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me”—shows that he was forsaken in respect of the flesh, not according to divinity, because the unity of power remains. He abandoned the flesh of the Son for an hour in the Passion, so that through his proper Son he might have adopted sons [Col. 0566C].

“As a sponge full of cavities with vinegar”: so the Jews were full of superstitions and bitter teaching. Joseph represents the primitive Church from the Gentiles. He bought a linen cloth; by the price of the linen cloth he signifies the confession of faith; by the linen cloth he signifies the mortification of the Church, or the grace of those baptized. The body of Jesus wrapped in a new linen cloth signifies the Church surrounded by Christ and the restoration of regeneration. By the tomb and the linen cloth he signifies the altar on which Christ’s body is placed. Alternatively, he signifies the Church, those who received Christ through faith in their hearts, either to eat his body and take his blood. The rock is Christ.

The tomb hewn in rock signifies the Church [Col. 0566D] built from Christ’s side. He rolled the stone to the entrance of the tomb: this signifies Christ hidden in the Law and the Prophets; by the stone rolled away he signifies the history of the Law, with Christ revealed in the New Testament. “He is not here”—that is, he is not among the Jews, but among the Gentiles. “Go, tell his disciples and Peter”: he names Peter because of his denial, so that he might not despair, and because of the primacy of the apostolate.

Mary, from whom he had expelled seven demons. By the seven demons he signifies that her whole life had been defiled, because the cycle of seven days runs its course.

“Preach the Gospel [Col. 0567A] to every creature”—that is, to every human being—because a human being shares something with each of the other creatures: with angels, understanding or discernment; with animals, sight and sensation; with trees, life. A tree lives through its greenness, and so also a human being through youth; with stones, being, because believing human beings are also like stones.

“They will cast out demons,” either spiritually or bodily; “they will speak in new tongues,” either in new or in different languages. The new tongue is the preaching of the Gospel. “They will pick up serpents”—that is, serpents’ venom, or the teaching of heretics. “If they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them”: neither will the teaching of heretics harm them. “They will lay hands on the sick”—whether bodily or spiritual.

We read of three who were taken bodily from the world into heaven. The Lord was raised by his own power, because he was neither begotten through intercourse nor himself begetting through intercourse, but was born of a virgin. Enoch was taken away because he begot through intercourse. Elijah was carried off in a chariot because he was begotten through intercourse, though he did not beget through intercourse, since he remained a virgin.

## ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

Luke—he himself rising up—was a Syrian by nation, an Antiochene, a physician by profession, a disciple of the apostles, and a follower of Paul, serving God without blame. He never had a wife. He died at the age of eighty-three in Bithynia, full of the Holy Spirit, and was buried in Constantinople. In Achaia he wrote the Gospel in the Greek language. Matthew wrote for believing Jews; Mark for penitents; John for the perfect; Luke for believing Greeks.

“There was in the days of Herod,” and so forth. Here he completed the order: he names the king and the region in which he was, the priest, his people, and his wife. “Of the course of Abijah”—that is, “in the days of the Lord.” Zacharias is interpreted as “mindful of the Lord.” The angel of the Lord appeared to him at the right side of the altar, showing that, because he was mindful of the Lord, the mystery of God was revealed to him. Abijah is interpreted as “father of the Lord.” It was fitting that, during the time of his service, this one should have been begotten who would preach the Lord the Father. Elizabeth is interpreted as “the fullness of my God.” She represents Mary, who was full of God. “And both were righteous before the Lord,” not before human beings, because formerly barrenness was a curse under the Law [Col. 0567D]. “Walking in all the commandments”—that is, they observed the whole Law.

They had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both continued in their days. Therefore these two causes are mentioned [Note: The text read “two causes”; it recalls that the testimony would have been greater, etc.]: the power would have been a greater testimony. Zacharias entered the temple—that is, Christ entered Mary. The people pray: that is, the people first ask Zacharias for freedom from captivity. The angel appeared to him; it does not say “came,” because he had already been there. Zacharias was troubled—that is, because the Jews would be troubled when Christ came [Col. 0568A]. “Your prayer has been heard”—that is, more than you asked. You asked for the liberation of the people, and the Forerunner has been given to you. “And many will rejoice at his birth,” because after destruction they will rejoice in eternal life.

“For he himself said, ‘Behold, the Lamb of God,’” and so forth: he goes before Christ; he is baptized before him; he preached before him; he was seen before him; he was born before him; and he died before him. There were six reasons, because there were six months between them. “I am Gabriel”—that is, “the strength of God.” Elizabeth conceived; it does not say “from Zacharias,” but “he knew his wife,” because the will of desire had failed in them. She hid herself because of modesty, to test whether what she had conceived was true: for five months—that is, five thousand years of the world, or the five books of Moses.

“To take away my reproach”—that is, the reproach of barrenness and of conception in old age—“among human beings,” because it was not a reproach before God. Just as Gabriel was sent by the Lord in the sixth month to a city, so Christ was sent in the sixth millennium of the world. Joseph is interpreted as “savior,” the one who saved Egypt from famine; or [Note: The text read: “It was, ‘Egypt from famine or Mary, blessed, etc.’”] Mary, blessed—that is, from the flesh of Christ. She was troubled because she did not know whether what the angel said referred to the past or to the future. “The Holy Spirit will come upon you”: “Spirit” is the name of every grace when it is breathed in. How did Mary recognize what the angel said, or, since she was full of the Spirit, did she know what the angel had spoken to her? “The power of the Most High will overshadow you”—that is, he hid you in Egypt by flight. “Your kinswoman” is said because Elizabeth was from the tribe of Levi [Col. 0568C], that is, from the tribe of God. “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord,” as he says, “the son of your handmaid.”

She went into the hill country with haste, because everyone who wishes [Note: Supply “whoever wishes,” or something similar. More serious difficulties occur below, which we partly correct. This is one of that kind.] to fulfill God’s will ought to hasten. The infant leaped in his mother’s womb: the Son honored the Son, just as the woman honored the woman. She cried out with a loud voice. It was fitting, since it was said of John: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.” “John is his name.” Why did he not say, “John will be”? Because he was called by the angel before he was conceived. “And they marveled”—that is, at the agreement between father and mother. “Blessed is the Lord our God”: Zacharias asked for the liberation of the people, and the Forerunner was given to him; thus he praised the goodness of God. “He raised up a horn of salvation”—that is, Christ, because a horn is neither flesh nor bone. So also Christ is neither bone nor flesh [Col. 0568D], but only divinity.

“The child grew”—that is, bodily. This first census was made, that is, for the Romans, because Julius first ruled the Romans but did not hold the whole world; after him Augustus ruled, and after Augustus Tiberius. In the time of Augustus and Tiberius Christ’s time was completed for his baptism, because in the fifteenth year of Augustus’s reign Augustus and his son Tiberius came together in one chariot to their city. After they had [reading uncertain: *adsuerunt*] the Lamb of the world, he shows that in his reign the one who would reign over the whole world would be born, and that the Father had unity of will with his Son [Col. 0569A].

At that time a bronze-colored circle appeared around the sun. This shows that he was born in the time of the one whose power, beauty, light, and wisdom would surround every power—first beauty, light, and wisdom. At that same time a fountain of oil flowed from the rental lodging-house all day until evening. This shows that he was born in the time of the one from whom a fountain of oil would flow—that is, spiritual anointing—throughout the whole Gospel to the end of the world. Augustus represents the Father; Tiberius, the Son. The census was made so that the king might know the number and greatness of the people.

“Under the governor of Syria” [Note: “Governor of Syria” was written instead of “from Persia,” etc.; and “that each should register” (*profiterentur*) instead of “that each should prophesy” (*prophetarent*), etc. It is not possible to report everything; in truth, the entire treatise required correction with the eraser.] He shows the place from which Christ came. “That each should register in his own city”: he shows that no one outside the Church should render a census to God. He was placed in a manger—that is, Christ’s body upon the altar [Col. 0569B]. The ox and the ass in Christ’s manger show the Gentiles and the Jews sharing upon the altar. The place in the inn—that is, a house between two walls with two doors—represents the Church between paradise and the world. The army of soldiers shows the commander Christ being followed. The shepherds spoke. It was fitting that shepherds should speak; it was fitting that shepherds should give testimony concerning the true Lamb. “Let us go across to Bethlehem”: he shows us not to look backward, nor to the right nor to the left, but only toward Christ. They found Mary, Joseph, and the infant: through these three the world was healed.

Mary kept all these words—that is, what the angel had said to her. “When the eight days were completed, so that he might be circumcised”: in the eighth beatitude he shows the Passion of Christ, when it is said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” [Col. 0569C]. Christ’s circumcision on the eighth day signifies the blood of the martyrs until the day of judgment, or because he fulfilled the Law and did not abolish it. “When the days of her purification were fulfilled”: twelve days were prescribed for a male child, and thirty for a female child in the Law, so that a woman might not enter the Church. “A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons”: through the fierceness of the turtledove he signifies prudence like that of the serpent; through the dove, simplicity. The pair signifies that a person should offer himself wholly to God. “A revelation to the Gentiles”—that is, the glory of faith. “Behold, he is appointed for the fall”—that is, for those who do not believe—and “for the resurrection” of those who believe in him; “and for a sign”—that is, the Gospel. “I have come to separate a man against his mother,” and so forth, as he himself says, “Who is my mother?” “Blessed is the womb that bore you,” and so forth: that many might think good thoughts, since Mary alone is not the mother of Christ [Col. 0569D].

“And a sword will pierce your own soul”—that is, the word of God, or the Passion of Christ. She had lived with her husband for seven years—that is, the synagogue with the Heptateuch. “She did not depart from the temple”—that is, the Church ought not to depart from heaven. “The child grew”—that is, bodily. “And he was strengthened”—that is, in spirit. When he was twelve years old—that is, the twelve tribes that came to Christ—they found him after three days: the father, that is, the Church, and the mother, that is, the synagogue, who sought him [Col. 0570A] through the three Laws; and they did not find him except through the Gospel. “And he was subject to them”: he shows that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.

From the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the first king and first governor mentioned at Christ’s birth, that is, while they had not yet begun to teach, a fourth ruler, the tetrarch, is now mentioned, when he came to preaching and baptism. The king signifies Christ, and the four tetrarchs show the four Gospels. The two priests signify the two Laws. Through the number six the world was made. The first king among the Romans shows the unity of the Roman kingdom; the fourth tetrarch over the Jews shows the division of the Jewish kingdom. “The word of the Lord came upon John”: “Go and preach baptism.” “Every valley shall be filled”—that is, Jews and Gentiles. “The mountains and hills shall be brought low”—that is, whoever humbles himself shall be exalted. “The crooked shall become straight”—that is, let the lustful become chaste. “And the rough places into level ways”—that is, let the proud become humble. “Every flesh shall see the salvation of God”—that is, Jews and Gentiles, men and women.

He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. This shows that no one should forget the Church in which he was nourished. “He rose to read”: here he shows that, if something has been revealed to a younger person, an elder should remain silent—that is, the Evangelist and the Pentateuch. Peter also rises in the midst of the disciples. “He stood”: he shows that what must be preached should not be repaid. “Because he has anointed me”—not with common oil, but with spiritual oil—“to preach good news to the poor,” that is, “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; “and release to captives” [Col. 0570C]—to the Jews from Pharaoh, and to the Gentiles from the devil; “sight to the blind”—that is, to Jews and Gentiles; “to set free the broken”—the Jews, by fashioning clay, and the Gentiles, by worshiping idols; “the year of the Lord”—because a year has four seasons, he shows the four evangelists; and the twelve months show the twelve apostles; “and the day of recompense”—that is, the day of judgment. Literally: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears.”

“There were many widows in Israel”—that is, the Church. Elijah signifies Christ. Naaman the Syrian signifies the Gentiles. The daughter signifies the synagogue. Gehazi signifies the Church. “Having a demon”—that is, by believing in idols. “What have we to do with you?”—that is, torments for us, glory for you. “Beside the lake”—that is, beside the Law. “Two boats”—that is, two Churches [Col. 0570D]. “Put out into the deep”—that is, Christ ascending into heaven. “Having labored all day, we caught nothing”—that is, through the old Law we brought no one to life. “They filled both boats”—that is, he converted through the Church and the synagogue—“so that they began to sink”: that is, a person who cannot bear either riches or poverty. “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man”: this shows that the Lord did not depart, because he does not abandon true humility.

“Do not be afraid”—that is, let the sinner not fear the physician. “The word about him spread all the more”—that is, the word of healing and teaching [Col. 0571A]. When he prayed, he showed the contemplative life; when he sat, he showed the active life. Through the tiles—that is, through divinity—“rise and walk” shows the resurrection of all. He went up onto the mountain to pray and descended to the crowds: this shows the contemplative and active lives united in one.

Four beatitudes are read because the four cardinal virtues are contained in them [Note: Perhaps the author was hunting for some play between the words *cardinales* (“cardinal”) and *cordis* (“of the heart”). These verbal monstrosities require an Oedipus; it would scarcely be worth the labor to restore them.]: “caudes,” which in Latin is said to mean “of the heart.” These four gentle things are shown as the four parts of the world. Likewise, the eight refers to the eight souls who were in Noah’s ark, through whom he signifies the whole human race. “Your reward is great in glory”—that is, for preaching, persecution, and endurance. “Their fathers did these things to the prophets”—that is, they hated them, reproached them, and cast out their names [Col. 0571B].

“Woe to you who are rich!” because you have your consolation, and you do not give thanks to God, but to your riches. “Woe to you when people bless you”—that is, your enemies [Note: We supplied here the words required from the sacred text, “Woe to you who are rich.” Again, at the third verse after this, where it says “that is, your enemies,” a passage of Scripture seems to have fallen out. Finally, the reading we restored as “hoping for nothing in return” formerly stood as “despairing of nothing.” We pass over other omissions, which are innumerable.]. “Expecting nothing in return”: what you have, give, so that you may receive your reward from the Lord in glory.

“Can a blind man lead a blind man?”—that is, can a foolish person teach a foolish person? “Both will fall into a pit”—that is, into destruction. He went into a city called Nain. This shows that, after healing the sick man, he raised the dead, because sickness precedes death. “The only son of his mother”: Adam is carried from the earth by four things—that is, by the four elements from which the human being is made. The place is touched by God—that is, the wood of the cross—because Adam perished through wood.

A person is carried by earth when he thinks only about earthly things, or when he is sick and cannot walk. He is carried by water when he thinks about indulging in lust, or when, because of excessive cold, his body cannot be touched. He is carried by air when he does everything for human praise, or when, because of illness, he cannot breathe. He is carried by fire when, because of excessive fever, he cannot be touched.

The Lord raised three dead persons: the only son of his mother, the daughter of the ruler, and Lazarus. The first was in the house—that is, in thought; the second at the gate—that is, in speech; the third from the tomb—that is, in deed. “The one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he”—that is, Christ, because angels were born: “You made him a little lower than the angels.” Nevertheless Christ is greater than John, reigning with the Father. “Wisdom was justified by her children”—that is, the people and the tax collectors justified God.

An alabaster vessel of ointment—that is, the body together with faith. “Standing behind”: after the Lord’s ascension. “Beside his feet”—that is, beside the apostles. “She bathed them with tears”—that is, inward charity in God. “With her hair”—that is, giving surplus food and clothing. “She kissed his feet”—that is, having peace with everyone. One owed five hundred denarii—that is, the sins of the Gentiles committed through the five senses [Col. 0572A]; another owed fifty—that is, the sins of the Jews. This woman was Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had been expelled. “Who is this who forgives sins?”—that is, divine power and might. This Mary represents the Church, from which he expelled seven vices, corresponding to the seven days in which a person sins.

A certain man—that is, the people of the Gentiles—had lived for many years, that is, from the beginning of the world. He wore no clothing—that is, no faith—nor did he remain in a house, that is, in the Church, but among tombs—that is, in the habit of sinning. Chains and fetters signify the law of nature and the written Law. “Sitting”—that is, in faith after baptism; “clothed”—that is, in immortality; “at his feet”—that is, at the apostles’. He dismissed him and said, “Return to your house”: this shows that we come from the contemplative life to the active.

A woman—that is, the Church—had a flow of blood, that is, the law of nature, for twelve years—that is, two ages. She touched the fringe of his garment: she believed in the least commandment of Christ. “Who touched me?”—that is, who believed in me? “Power has gone out from me”—that is, toward the one proved to have faith. Peter, John, and James signify faith, hope, and charity. The father signifies the bishop; the mother, the Church; the villages and cities, servants and masters. They told him what they had done. “The day began to decline”—that is, to become night. “Dismiss the crowd”—the Jews. “You give them something to eat”—that is, preach to the Gentiles. “He blessed”—that is, the Gospel; “he broke”—literally. “The Son of Man must suffer many things”—that is, die. Those sailing from a state of security, through the danger of the voyage, saw tranquility after danger: his departure signifies suffering many things [Col. 0572C].

On the following day—that is, in the second Law—a man from the crowd cried out—that is, Abraham. “An only son”—that is, the whole human race. “Suddenly crying out”—that is, becoming angry. “And it dashed him”—in flattery of one’s neighbor. “It tears him apart”—that is, in despair. “With foam”—that is, with foolishness. “The hand upon the plow”—that is, the work upon the Gospel. “Backward”—that is, in the world. The plowshares signify charity. The four oxen signify the four evangelists.

The Lord appointed another seventy disciples, just as Moses chose seventy elders from the twelve tribes: that he might unite the seventy languages, which had been divided through pride, into one language through humility. “Two by two”: animals in the ark and two disciples for preaching signify charity; they show the New and Old Testaments, body and soul, man and woman, and the two disciples.

“I send you as lambs among wolves”: I am the shepherd, you are the sheep; the wolves are the scribes and Pharisees. “The demons are subject to us”—that is, what was not in the Law is in the mouth. “Over serpents”—that is, over the pagans, because the serpent does not kill but pours out the poison of its teaching—and “over scorpions,” whose tail and head are equal and kill. This is the same devil, who wishes to deceive at the beginning and at the end.

A man was going down—that is, the world, which is called accursed—to thieves, that is, demons. “They stripped him”—that is, of good faith. “They beat him”—that is, they made him sin. “They left him half-dead”—that is, with a living body but a dead conscience and soul. The priest signifies Aaron; the Levite, the tribe of Levi with its Law; the Samaritan, Christ, who is from the outskirts of Samaria. He himself is interpreted as “guardian,” because the Lord, who guards the little ones, is Christ God.

“He bound up his wounds”—that is, through repentance he restrained his sins. “He poured in oil and wine”—severity and gentleness of Scripture, reward and punishment. “Upon his own beast”—that is, upon his own body, because through his Passion he led the human race to the inn [Col. 0573B], that is, to the Church. He gave two denarii to the innkeeper—that is, the two Laws to the order of teachers. “Whatever more you spend”—that is, whatever through your diligence you do from the teaching of human beings—“when I return,” that is, for judgment, “I will repay you.”

Martha signifies the active Church. Mary signifies the contemplative Church, which always hears Christ’s words. Martha said that her sister should help her, because the active life needs the contemplative life to assist it. “Friend”—that is, a teacher. “At midnight”—that is, at an inconvenient time. The three loaves signify faith in the Trinity. “My friend”—that is, another person doing penance—“has come from the road,” that is, from the world. “I have nothing to set before him”—that is, I do not know how to teach him. “The door is shut”—that is, the door of heaven, which charity alone opens [Col. 0573C]. “My children are with me”—that is, the heavenly virtues. “What is outside and what is inside”: he made the body, and he himself made the soul. “Give alms, and everything is clean”; and if you do not give, everything you possess is unclean.

“Do not fear, little flock”: these are the Jews [Note: We deleted here the word “they said,” which disturbed the sense.], because they believed that the poor man was accursed in the Law. “Let your loins be girded”: he signifies chastity. “Let your lamps be burning”—that is, good works. “So that when he comes”—that is, in suffering—“and knocks”—that is, when the soul passes through death—“they may open immediately”—that is, to be always ready. “Passing by, he will serve them”—that is, after judgment, eternal life.

“I have come to cast fire upon the earth”—that is, charity. “Those Galileans” signify the eighteen upon whom the tower fell—that is, the Holy Spirit, because he is said to have been sent from Siloam [Col. 0573D; Note: In place of *Siloam*, the name of the place where the tower fell, the earlier text had *silva* (“forest”), which made no sense.]. “Let it alone this year also”—that is, the Gospel. “I will dig around it”—that is, I will preach. The basket of manure signifies confessing sins. “In the future”—that is, on the day of judgment.

The woman signifies the human race. “A spirit of infirmity”—that is, in faith and work. “Eighteen years”—that is, the two Laws, or those who did not fulfill the ten words of the Law and did not believe in the resurrection, which takes place on the eighth day. Through three sixes he shows that she was infirm before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. “Bent toward the earth”—that is, earthly desires. “Unable to look upward”—that is, because she did not seek heavenly things through repentance [Col. 0574A]. “He called her to himself”—that is, through confession. “He laid his hands upon her”—that is, good examples. “She was healed”—the hope of healing. “The first day of the week”—that is, the future rest.

“Tell that fox”—that is, Herod, because the devil is an animal who dwells within and destroys the vineyard. Thus Herod the devil destroys the vineyard, as it is said, “You transplanted a vine from Egypt.”

A man with dropsy signifies the human race, the fornicator. “He took hold of him and healed him”: he shows that the assault of fornication is healed. The man signifies God the Father. The great supper signifies the Gospel. He invited many—that is, the Jews. He sent his servant—that is, Christ into the flesh. “Everything is ready”—that is, the things prophesied concerning Christ. “I bought a farm”—that is, because of avarice I did not come to Christ. “A yoke of oxen”—that is, pride; alternatively, the yoke of oxen signifies the five senses, or the five books of Moses. “I married a wife”—that is, lust. “The poor and the weak”—those who recognize their sins. “Go out into the roads”—that is, to the Gentiles. “Compel them to enter”—that is, through confession.

“To build a tower”—that is, to follow Christ. “The cost”—that is, renouncing the world. “What king”—that is, the apostles. “To engage in war”—that is, the recompense of works. “Against another king”—that is, against Christ. “With ten thousand”—that is, with the works a person perceives. “With twenty thousand”—that is, with works that are hidden and manifest. “He sends an embassy”—that is, by showing mercy and giving alms. He asks for the things that make for peace: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord.”

“Upon the earth”—that is, among riches. “Into the dunghill”—that is, into poverty. A certain woman signifies riches. A lighted lamp signifies the Gospel. The drachma found in the house signifies a sinner converted in the Church.

A certain man signifies God the Father. The two sons signify the Jews and the Gentiles, because the Law was first given to the Jews. “Give me my portion”—that is, the present life. “He divided his substance”—that is, he gave freedom of choice to both peoples. “He went away into a distant country”—that is, away from God. “Living riotously”—that is, worshiping idols. “A severe famine”—that is, a famine of the word of God. “To one of the citizens”—that is, to a philosopher. “In his own country”—that is, in the world. “To feed pigs”—that is, he lived like pigs. “From the pods”—that is, to fill the belly without becoming fat. The pigs signify fools.

“The hired servants of my father”—those who are lower servants of God—“are filled with bread,” that is, with teaching. “I have sinned against heaven”: those who say this have the devil as their father, the one who sinned in heaven. “Moved by mercy”—that is, he came in the flesh. “To his servants”—that is, to the apostles. “The first robe”—faith, which Adam lost. “The ring”—the cross on the forehead. “The sandals”—the Gospel. “The fattened calf”—Christ from the two Laws. “He was dead”—that is, Adam. “He came to life again”—that is, through baptism. “He had perished”—that is, in despair. “He was found”—that is, in hope.

The elder son signifies the Jews [Col. 0575A]. “In the field”—that is, in unclean desire. “Music and dancing”—that is, prophecy and the Gospel. “The two servants”—that is, Isaiah, and so forth.

Lazarus was a beggar. He gives the name of the poor man but not of the rich man: good people are written in heaven, but evil people are not. “Full of wounds”—that is, of sins. The rich man signifies the Jews; the poor man, the Gentiles. The dogs signify teachers who heal wounds through the tongue. “In Abraham’s bosom”—that is, in rest. “Buried in hell”—that is, in the letter. “Lifting up his eyes”: the Jews had eyes, that is, they were good in their way of life up to Christ. He saw Abraham. Thus it will be after judgment concerning hell: they will see the kingdom of God so that they may suffer a greater punishment because of a greater joy.

“The tip of his finger in water”—that is, those who give small alms. “I am tormented in this flame”—that is, in his own punishment [Col. 0575B]. “A great chasm”—that is, the confusion of all things, or the old Law. “You received good things in your life”—that is, you did good and received your reward. Lazarus received evil things because he did not receive punishment for his evils during his life. “Five brothers”—that is, the five books of Moses; they observed the sign. “If someone rises from the dead”: this happened when Christ rose, and others from among the Jews believed.

“If the millstone”—that is, if the Gentiles [Note: The original leaves a space unfilled here.] are like a mill-horse that does not see the one whom it serves, so the philosopher teaches philosophy, which benefits him nothing but the holy Church. “Increase our faith”—that is, while you increase the commandment.

This mulberry tree signifies the Gospel, which announces the red cross of Christ, just as the mulberry is red: “Be uprooted”—that is, from the Jewish people—“and be planted” among the Gentile people, that is, as a mulberry tree. Its first fruit is white, afterward red, and finally black. So also the devil, while he was a white angel, became black on the occasion of Adam and red in the murder of Cain and Abel.

The two women grinding show the two Churches, or the two Testaments. The judge and the widow, from those who are only partly full, and he will have patience with them, but they will not always remain silent. Two men went up: one magnified his holiness and lost it; the other magnified his sins, and they perished. “I fast twice on the Sabbath”—that is, without food and without a woman.

“What shall I do to inherit eternal life?” As was said above, the kingdom of God belongs to such people. Thus Nicodemus was likewise considering how a person can be born again. “You shall not kill,” and so forth: why did he say these things? Because he himself fell through them. “When he drew near Jericho”—that is, when he came to the Incarnation [Col. 0575D].

A man named Zacchaeus was a Jew and signifies the Jews. His name is interpreted as “justified,” just as the Jews justify themselves. “Because of the crowd”—that is, of riches and vices. “In a tree”—that is, the cross. “Half of my goods”—that is, half of my property. “I give to the poor”—that is, “break your bread for the hungry.” “And if I have defrauded anyone, I will repay fourfold”: this is said in the Law concerning souls, and in the Gospel concerning every creature.

A nobleman signifies Christ. He went away to a distant country [Col. 0576A]—that is, to heaven—“to receive a kingdom for himself”—that is, the heavenly kingdom—and to return for judgment. The ten servants signify the whole human race. The ten minas signify the ten words of the Law. His citizens signify the Jews.

“They sent an embassy”—that is, the killing of the apostles. The first servant and the second signify the order of the apostles. The mina of each servant signifies Scripture, and he found each one like himself. “The stones will cry out”—these are the Gentiles. The Jews were silent. “He wept over it”: he shows that we should weep for our sins. “They will surround you”: the Romans surrounded it. “On every side”—that is, within and without [Note: The text read *alterum* as one word, in place of “to the ground”; but the following corresponding clause also contains an error. At the end of the section, where it says “I will give you a mouth and wisdom,” the earlier text had “Therefore, from you, them,” etc. Similar errors occurred every third verse, and it is tiresome to report them all.]. “To the ground”—that is, into hell. “The son”—that is, the virtues. What he did by day, he overturned at night.

He entered the temple because he entered the temple on the Lord’s Day. They sought to destroy him. He shows the nine servants who were not rejected in their ministries. A certain man signifies God the Father. He planted a vineyard—that is, the Jews. The tenants signify the legislators. He himself went away to a distant country—that is, he left everyone to the freedom of his own choice. The first servant signifies Isaiah; the second, Jeremiah; the third, Daniel. “Outside the vineyard”—that is, outside Jerusalem. “What will the lord of the vineyard do?” “He came and destroyed them”—that is, the evil man destroyed the evil ones. “It will be crushed”—that is, by the cross he will crush his desires. “He will grind him to powder”—that is, in the vengeance of the cross.

“Nation will rise against nation”—that is, a nation against the Romans. “Kingdom against kingdom”—that is, others against the Romans. “Terrifying things”—that is, chariots were heard in the air. “There will be signs,” as there was above Jerusalem a star with a fiery sword. “They occur in testimony”—that is, from the Jews [Col. 0576C] to the Gentiles. “I will give you a mouth and wisdom”: in Moses it is said, “God showed you wisdom.”

A hair from the head will not perish, that is, through mortality. Jerusalem will be trampled, that is, idols will be worshiped in it, until the times of the nations are fulfilled, that is, until the Jews are converted at the end of the world. Signs in the sun, that is, the letter. The sound of the sea, that is, the Sodomite Sea has been made, and will cast its fish upon the land. Coming in the clouds of heaven, that is, in the prophets and apostles. The fig tree and the trees, that is, the synagogue and human beings. Teaching in the temple by day, that is, he labored with the Jews; at night on the Mount of Olives, that is, he rested with the nations.

A man carrying a jar of water, that is, Moses and John the Baptist. The upper room, that is, the Church. The bed, that is, faith in the Trinity. Until the kingdom of God is fulfilled, that is, the great ministry. Two cups, one with water, the other with wine, that is, with a mixture of water and wine in the cup. Wine with water signifies the Passion through baptism. Did anything fail you when he was with them in the flesh, that is, when he commanded them not to concern themselves with the world? But when he separates himself from them, they are to have a single faith. Let him buy a sword, that is, the Law. Two swords, that is, the two Laws.

[Col. 0577A] The Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power: “The Lord said to my Lord,” and so forth. In a white garment he sent him back to Pilate, that is, in faith in the Trinity. He came to the nations, to the people of Israel. They became friends, that is, both peoples came to the faith of Christ. Herod signifies the people of the nations; Pilate, the Jews. Leviathan [Note: [Col. 0577D] The Author seems perhaps to be hinting at something concerning the revolt of Barabbas; but since it is not presently possible to restore the passage, from several such examples that we have left untouched you may infer the extent of the innumerable other corruptions that we have corrected.] “densi seduna” [uncertain]; Barabbas is called the son of the devil. Weep over yourselves, that is, over your own nation. Then they will begin to say, that is, the people of Israel. Say to the mountains, that is, to the patriarchs; to the hills, that is, to the prophets. Forgive them, that is, let them drink the blood which they have shed, so that those who are vessels of wrath may become vessels of mercy. They do not know what they are doing; and if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty, because they acted through ignorance. Today you will be with me in paradise, that is, whoever follows Christ has no darkness [Col. 0577B] but the light of life.

Joseph, that is, the people of Israel. Aromatics and ointments, that is, faith, hope, and charity. The first day of the week, that is, the Gospel, which shines through the night of the Old Testament. The women were the first to see the resurrection. It was fitting that salvation should first run through those by whom death had first come running.

And behold, two men stood there: in Matthew, one angel; in Mark, a young man; in John, two angels; in Luke, two men. This means that the women made many journeys and that the visions were different—or, alternatively, that [they are] in one [account, uncertain]: again, one vision, though the Evangelists’ accounts differ.

The linen cloths lying alone show that bodies have no need of clothing after the resurrection. Wondering within himself, that is, wondering that the garments had been left behind.

[Col. 0577C] Two of them were going: this signifies the nations, because he appeared to those who were outside just as he did to those who were inside. The village, that is, the world. Jerusalem, that is, the heavenly city. A stadium, that is, an eighth part of a mile. Sixty stadia indicates the number of days in which the world was made. The name of the village was Emmaus. And he pretended that he was going farther, that is, to the nations. They recognized him in the breaking of the bread but did not recognize him while they were hearing the preaching. He vanished from their eyes: this shows that we cannot delay in contemplation; and he was farther from them when they did not recognize him, that is, because we can remain longer in the active life, while he opened the Scriptures to us.

Peace be with you: now he gathers them into one peace. Why did he not rise and ascend in one place? Because honor descended from Jerusalem to the nations.

[Col. 0577D] Here the Lord fulfilled what he himself said: “Pray for those who persecute you.” He forgave them.

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

In the beginning was the Word, that is, because all things begin and end in him. The Word of the Father, the Son with God, because the Son is always with the Father. The Word was God, that is, the Son was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made: these are the idols. What was made—in him was life; that is, all things live in him before they come to be. Life was the light of human beings: Christ is both light and life.

[Col. 0578A] The light shines in the darkness, that is, among the Jewish people through the Law and the prophets. The Jews did not recognize him. He was the true light that enlightens every human being, and so forth. The true light enlightens by being born, being nourished, and living; through the grace of the baptism of the Holy Spirit it enlightens understanding.

He came into the world, and the world did not recognize him, that is, the Jewish people. A foreign part, a certain part, recognized him. He came to his own, to his own people according to the flesh, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God. Through faith they were born from him by the renewal of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, that is, through the assumption of flesh. We saw his glory, that is, through his Transfiguration and his resurrection.

[Col. 0578B] He who comes after me: this indicates birth according to the flesh. He was made before me, that is, all things were made through him; and because he existed before me, from his fullness we have all received: by being born, being nourished, and living—grace in place of grace, the grace of the Old Testament in place of the grace of the New Testament.

Likewise, through faith and charity; through the letter of the Law, or through prophecy. Three modes: through the grace of baptism, grace eternal. The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, that is, in his heart or in his secret place.

John confessed that he was not the Christ; he did not deny that he was Christ’s forerunner. Alternatively, this indicates the New Testament. And I did not know him: John shows that he did not know that through Christ’s baptism the world had been redeemed, although he did know that he was the Son of God and had been born in the flesh.

[Col. 0578C] Rabbi, where are you staying? That is, in what doctrine are you moved, or what do you teach? Come and learn my doctrine, because he wishes everyone to come to him. They remained with him that day: this indicates the New Testament, or the present life. The tenth hour signifies the evening of the world.

On the following day he wished to depart for Galilee, that is, after his resurrection, to the nations. Under the fig tree, that is, under the letter of the Law, or the synagogue. The heavens opened, that is, to the human race. Angels ascending and descending, that is, in the ministry of Christ.

On the third day a wedding took place, that is, the third Law. The wedding signifies the union of the Church with Christ. Mary, the mother of Jesus, at the wedding signifies the synagogue. Jesus and his disciples signify the Church. The wine failing, that is, the failure of the letter of the Law.

My hour has not yet come, that is, the time of Christ’s Passion has not [Col. 0578D] yet come. Six water jars, the six ages. Into wine: Christ. The steward signifies John, showing that John tasted the Passion before Christ. The water made into wine signifies the transformation of the Old Testament into the New.

Alternatively, the water signifies John’s baptism, and the wine Christ’s Passion; likewise, the wine signifies Christ’s blood, as he himself says: his blood is true drink. The command to preserve the good wine signifies the mystery—the mysteries of the Old Testament.

By the sheep-sellers he indicates the teachers who sell sacred gifts; by the sheep he indicates ordinary human beings. A whip made from [Col. 0579A] cords, that is, vengeance for various sins, by which they are expelled from the Church.

Jesus did not entrust himself to them, that is, on account of the condition of the flesh. Nicodemus came to him by night. By night he indicates the letter of the Law, or the ignorance of the heart, so that it might be enlightened by the light of the knowledge of God.

We know that you have come from God: this indicates those who received Christ through faith. Flesh is born from flesh and blood so that it may live bodily in the world; then the soul is ineffably reborn from the Holy Spirit so that it may live forever.

The Spirit breathes where he wills, that is, he enlightens whomever he wills, as the Apostle says: “Whoever adheres to Christ is one spirit.” You hear his voice: this indicates the enlightenment of the ear of the heart. Hence the prophet says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me.”

What we know [Col. 0579B] we speak; what we have seen we testify. What we say we know: this indicates the modes of speech, whether the whole Trinity, or Christ together with the apostles and prophets. We testify, that is, we give testimony. You do not accept our testimony, that is, you do not believe our preaching. Christ descended from heaven by assuming flesh.

No one has ascended into heaven except Christ, with the tree, that is, the Church. Just as the serpent was lifted up in the desert, so Christ was lifted up on the wood [Note: [Col. 0579D] For “wood” the reading was “Lebanon.” Immediately afterward another passage was redundant before the words “through sight”; then “they were being freed” stood for “they will be freed,” with no sense, or with the contrary sense. Many other matters above are corrected.] of the cross. Just as those struck by serpents were freed by looking at the bronze serpent, so the person struck by the devil who believes in Christ’s Passion will be freed.

He came into the land of Judea, the land of confession. To Aenon, that is, the name of the place where they sacrificed their sons and daughters [Col. 0579C] to demons, from which it received the name Gehenna. Near Salim, which is interpreted as “peace,” and which they called Jebus, from which they received the name Jebusites. For John was not yet in prison: this indicates that the completion of the letter of the Law had not yet occurred.

He must increase, but I must decrease: the one who was thought to be a prophet was found to be a prophet. What I have seen and heard, according to divinity, this he testifies. According to divinity, no one accepted his testimony. Here the whole is put for the part. Likewise, believe, because God is truthful.

He had to pass through Samaria: this indicates that, just as he preached to the Jews, he would also preach to the nations. A farm, that is, a field; a spring for flowing, a well for drinking.

Jesus, wearied from the journey: this indicates that he came through the Incarnation above the history of the [Col. 0579D] letter of the Law. Through the sixth hour the faith of the Samaritans is understood, because they were fervent. The woman, that is, the synagogue. To draw water, to learn the history of the letter of the Law. Jesus asks to drink, that is, he asks for the woman’s faith. The well is deep, that is, the depth of the mystery of the Law.

A spring of water leaping up to eternal life, that is, the preaching of the Gospel bubbling forth from the mouths of the apostles or of believers. Five husbands signify the five books of Moses. And the one whom you now have is not your husband: this indicates the book of Joshua.

She left her water jar, that is, her former way of life. She went into the city: this indicates the [Col. 0580A] primitive Church, as if going to the nations or to the people.

Lift up your eyes, that is, the eyes of faith. The fields are white, that is, the hearts of the faithful. Those who sowed are the prophets; those who reap are the apostles.

He remained with them for two days, that is, after the two Testaments had been handed down to the Jews. He went to Galilee, that is, to the nations.

Here it is understood alternatively that those who have died bodily will hear his voice in the future and will be raised. As the Father has life in himself, so also the Son. What is said—“he gave to the Son”—is said with respect to the condition of the flesh.

Those who have done good deeds will rise to the resurrection of life, that is, whoever judges himself rises. Alternatively, those who have died in sins live through conversion by faith to life; those who have done evil here rise to judgment.

When he says, “I can do nothing of myself,” he indicates the condition of the body. [Col. 0580B] As I hear, I judge; and my judgment is just. I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me: here he puts the will of the Father for the members.

If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true. As Solomon says: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth.” Nor do they ever hear his voice: this indicates unbelievers who did not receive his preaching.

He went up onto the mountain with his disciples, that is, attempting to ascend to the higher life. Philip, that is, for testing, not for destroying.

Five loaves: the five books of Moses. Through the barley the harshness of the letter of the Law is understood. Much grass indicates the perfection of the people. So that nothing may be lost of what remained, that is, do not send doctrine where it does not build up.

He went up alone onto the mountain, that is, to the Father. [Col. 0580C] The disciples went down to the sea, that is, to the nations. They got into the boat, that is, into the Church.

Darkness came, that is, as the world grew toward evening, or the onslaught of persecution after Christ’s Ascension. Rowing, that is, taking refuge in Christ.

Jesus walking upon the sea, that is, trampling the vices of the world. The crowds getting into the boat and seeking Jesus show that all should seek Christ through their own labor.

“Manu” is said among the Hebrews, from which it received the name manna. Among the Latins this is living bread, or the body of Christ transformed in the mystery.

A person is raised in three ways: from unbelief to faith, from sin to repentance, and bodily on the last day, unto the resurrection.

I live because of the Father: this indicates the divine nature. The Feast of Tabernacles [Col. 0580D], that is, the construction of tabernacles.

You go up to the feast; I do not go up. You, whom the world delights, go up; I will not go up, because I am not of the world.

In the middle of the feast Jesus went up to Jerusalem, while the zeal of the Jews was burning most intensely. My teaching is not mine; and if it is mine, how is it not mine? It is mine insofar as it proceeds from my mouth to them; it is not mine because what I have heard from the Father, these things I speak to you.

Alternatively, according to the flesh it is mine, but according to divinity it is not mine.

I performed one work, and you are all amazed. I made the whole person sound on the Sabbath: this means the [Col. 0581A] whole human race in the New Testament.

Do not judge according to appearance, that is, do not accept the person of a human being. You do not know where I am from, that is, according to the flesh.

I am with you a little longer: this indicates the time until the Passion. You will seek me and will not find me, that is, bodily. And where I am, you cannot come, that is, through unbelief, unless through faith.
