On the last day of the feast, that is, once the Jewish festival had been completed: let the one who thirsts come and drink, that is, let the one who thirsts for the word of God come and drink the teaching of the Gospel.

Rivers from the belly, that is, doctrine from the heart. Living waters will flow, that is, the preaching of the Gospel, which grants everlasting life.

For Jesus had not yet been glorified: this indicates the glorification of the Passion and resurrection. [Col. 0581B] They returned, each to his own house, that is, to his own wickedness.

A woman caught in adultery signifies the synagogue, which adulterated the Law of Moses, having followed it with the traditions of the fathers [“is” supplied], or the Church from the nations, which, abandoning God, fornicated with demons.

Those who bring her into the midst signify the Jews, who are accusers of the Church of Christ. Moses commanded us to stone such women; what do you say? They tested him for two reasons. If he had said, “Stone her,” they would have said to him, “He does not do what he teaches; send her back to us.” If he had said that she should not be stoned, they would have said, “He is contradicting the Law.”

Jesus, bending down, that is, coming from the Father’s seats into the world to redeem the sins of the human race. He wrote on the ground with his finger: this indicates their sins. [Col. 0581C] He raised himself up in order to raise those who were walking in sins. Bending down again, he wrote on the ground: this indicates the woman’s forgiven sins.

Jesus alone remained with the woman in the house, that is, with the Church in the world.

Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness: this indicates not merely the steps of the feet but the inclination of the heart. Not in darkness, that is, of ignorance, nor in the darkness of sins, but he will have the light of life, that is, the light of knowledge and everlasting light.

I have many things to say and judge concerning you: this indicates that, if you believe, I will teach you many things; and if you do not believe, I will speak many things for your defense.

He was a murderer from the beginning, because through pride he killed himself. Alternatively, he killed the first human being, whom God had created immortal, and made him mortal; [Col. 0581D] and through his suggestion Abel was killed.

Who among you will convict me of sin? Whoever is from God hears God’s words, that is, whoever understands and does them.

You are a Samaritan and have a demon: here he tacitly agreed with what was not true and could not be possessed; but he did not deny what was true.

I do not seek my own glory. There is one who seeks it and judges: God the Father. I do not seek it as hypocrites do, who judge unjustly.

Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day. He saw it and rejoiced, that is, he saw faith in the spirit, and he saw him in the persons of angels. He saw three and greeted them as one when he said: “Turn aside, my [Col. 0582A] lords, to the house of your servant, if I have found favor in your eyes.”

Amen, amen, I say to you: the doubled “amen” has a twofold meaning, “truly” or “faithfully,” announcing the New and Old Testaments.

Before Abraham was, I am: this passage concerns divinity. They took up stones to throw at him, that is, because they had stony hearts. Jesus hid himself: this indicates that he was hidden from their hearts. And he went out of the temple, that is, from the Jewish people. Jesus passed through their midst, that is, he went to the nations.

He saw a man blind from birth. The blind man signifies the human race. Neither did this man sin nor his parents, so that you may understand the statement “he did not sin” in this way: Adam, created first to see evil, had his eyes closed when he transgressed God’s commandment. He kept his eyes open to evil and closed them to good. [Col. 0582B]

What, then, do the parents signify except the human race and the instigators of vices—or are the vices themselves signified?

I must work, that is, preach, while it is day, that is, while I am in the world. Night will come, that is, the persecution of the apostles, or the persecution of Antichrist. Night is when no one can work, that is, after each person’s departure from this life.

He spat on the ground, that is, the Incarnation of Christ. He made mud and anointed my eyes: this shows that, just as he first formed the human being from the mud of the earth, so through that same substance of mud he reformed the human race.

Go and wash in the pool of Siloam: this demonstrates baptism. The parents signify the devil or vices. They said, “He is of age; let him speak for himself”: this indicates one who did not wish to confess the man as Christ.

We do not know where this man is from: this indicates that they did not know his divinity.

[Col. 0582C] For judgment I came into this world: this indicates that whoever hears the word and receives judgment has received it for condemnation.

So that those who do not see may see: this indicates the nations, which did not receive the Law. And those who see may become blind, that is, the Jews. Those who saw through the Law became blind because they did not believe in Christ.

Whoever does not enter through the door signifies bishops who enter through rewards, not through the calling of God or of the people. They are shepherds of sheep who act for the profit of souls, not from worldly ambition.

To him the doorkeeper opens. The first doorkeeper is John, Christ’s Forerunner. [Note: [Col. 0581D] Perhaps the reading should be “the second doorkeeper,” with “doorkeeper” in place of “Scripture.” In place of “he calls by name” there was a reading that made no sense, “called named”; we mention these matters incidentally, taking the opportunity to do so, for we silently correct six hundred other errors of this kind.] The second doorkeeper is divine Scripture.

He calls them by name, that is, “The Lord knows those who are his.” He leads them out, into doctrine or into the kingdom. He goes before them, that is, he first did the example that he taught. He goes before them into the kingdoms of heaven; or, alternatively, all good teachers go before them by their examples.

They hear my voice, that is, my doctrine. They do not follow a stranger, that is, the faith and doctrine of heretics.

All who came were thieves and robbers, that is, false prophets, who existed and will exist in the time of Antichrist.

If anyone enters through me, he will be saved: whoever is saved through the doctrine of Christ will enter the Church through repentance. And he goes out, from the present age into the kingdom of God. Alternatively, “go out” means going forth to conquer the heretics.

The thief comes only to kill and destroy. [Col. 0583A] These are the orders of priests who enter for the sake of shameful profit, not for the profit of souls.

I came so that you may have life, that is, my doctrine; and have it more abundantly, that is, eternal life.

The hired man is one who teaches for earthly profit. He sees the wolf and flees, that is, the devil or a heretic.

I have other sheep that are not of this fold: he indicates the nations. There will be one shepherd, that is, the Church and Christ. This is the cornerstone between the middle of the wall, which makes both into one.

I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again: this indicates the condition of the flesh.

What my Father has given me is greater than all: this indicates that Christ, or the Spirit of God, is greater than all the works of the world.

I said, “You are gods.” [Col. 0583B] This is said in three ways: essentially, of the one who always exists, that is, God; nominally, “you are gods”; falsely, demons or idols are called gods.

He went away across the Jordan, that is, to the nations, where John first baptized, and he remained there: this indicates the Church.

Lazarus signifies the Jews, because the Jews were weak in the faith of Christ. Martha and Mary signify the doctrine of good Jews.

This illness is not unto death: this indicates that those who are dead to human beings live to God. He remained there two days, that is, the two Testaments.

Let us go again into Judea: this indicates the faith that will return to the Jews through Elijah and Enoch at the end of the world.

There are twelve hours in the day. The day is Christ. The twelve hours are the twelve apostles. If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble. In the day, that is, in the doctrine of Christ or of the apostles, he does not stumble into sin, because he sees the light of this world, that is, he sees [Col. 0583C] Christ through knowledge.

If anyone walks in the night, he stumbles. By night are understood the darkness of sins or the ignorance of the heart.

I was not there: this indicates the presence of the flesh. He knew that Lazarus had died, that is, because he knows all things.

First, in the house of the ruler of the synagogue; second, the son of the widow at the city gate; third, Lazarus from the tomb. In the house, that is, in the heart; at the gate, that is, in the mouth; in the tomb, that is, in a deed. Through these same things a person dies, and through these same things he will be raised.

When Martha heard that Jesus had come, she went to meet him. Here Martha signifies the Church, which met Christ through faith. Mary sat at home: this indicates the contemplative life.

Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live, whether bodily or, if dead in sins, through repentance. [Col. 0583D] Everyone who lives and believes in me—that is, whoever here lives in good works in Christ—will not die forever.

Jesus wept: this shows that, as true God and true human being, he provided an example of compassion.

His hands and feet bound: this indicates the bonds of sins. His face bound with a cloth, that is, the veil over the hearts of the Jews. Untie him, that is, through the preaching of faith.

The greater the signs the Jews saw, the more they were blinded.

They will take away the place and the nation. The Romans possess the place, Jerusalem, and the nations that have been dispersed throughout the regions.

The ruler spoke the reason: “It is better for one man to die than for the whole nation to perish,” because he had the ministry of God at hand and spoke this by the Spirit of God, so that he might gather into one the [Col. 0584A] children of God who were scattered throughout the whole world.

Martha served: this indicates the active life. Lazarus reclining with Jesus signifies the Church.

Mary took a pound of ointment. Thus, too, the whole world is understood as the hearts of the faithful. Through the ointment, the fragrance of confession. Mary signifies the Church. She anointed Jesus’ feet, that is, through the confession of repentance.

The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. Thus, too, the whole world was filled with the Passion and resurrection of Christ.

When the crowd heard that Jesus had come, they took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus. This indicates that, at the second coming, three are snatched into the air with the Lord after the resurrection.

He found a donkey. [Col. 0584B] Through the donkey he indicates the people of the nations. He sat upon it, that is, through the confession of faith.

Do not fear your destruction, because your Savior has come, daughter of Zion: this indicates the congregation of the faithful from Jews and nations.

The whole world went after him, because through his Passion and resurrection he redeemed the whole world from sin; and it followed him.

They approached Philip and asked him to see Jesus. This indicates the nations converted to the faith through the preaching of the apostles.

The grain of wheat bears the figure of Christ. If it dies, it produces many grains. So also Christ [Note: [Col. 0583] Supply “by his death,” or something similar; the space is blank in the original.] [lacuna] multiplied his Church.

I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again, that is, you glorified him in the resurrection of Lazarus; glorify him again in his own resurrection.

The ruler of this world is cast out, [Col. 0584C] that is, the devil is expelled from his power over the world through the Passion of the cross.

Walk while you have the light, that is, while you have Christ with you bodily and spiritually, lest the darkness overtake you, that is, the darkness of ignorance and the persecutions of sins.

He hid himself from them, that is, bodily or spiritually.

Lord, who has believed our report? “Who” is used either because of rarity or because of difficulty. The report is faith, which we have heard through the Holy Spirit. The arm of the Lord is the Son of God. To whom has it been revealed? That is, to some part: revealed from the Jews, revealed from the nations.

Whoever believes in me, not only according to my humanity but according to my divinity; or, alternatively, not only in me but also in the Father, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me.

Whoever sees me sees the one who sent me—as though he had plainly said: Whoever has seen me to be a true human being and believes me to be true God sees the Father also according to divinity.

I did not come to judge but to save the world: this indicates that through the shedding of blood he would redeem the world.

I loved you because I was in the world. He loved them to the end. He gave an example so that all might remain in God’s truth to the end.

When the supper had taken place, this indicates Christ’s Passion. Just as a meal does not take place after supper, so Christ, after suffering once, does not show himself as going to suffer again.

Rising from supper, he indicates our Passion, resurrection, [Col. 0585A] or Ascension. He lays aside his garments: this shows that his garments had to be removed at the cross.

*(The capitulation begins.)*

He took a linen cloth and girded himself with the linen cloth, that is, his mortification. He poured water into a basin: this indicates the grace of baptism. He began to wash the feet of his disciples and to wipe them with the linen cloth.

By the washing of the feet the baptism of the apostles is understood; by the wiping with the linen cloth he indicates the wiping away of sins through Christ’s Passion.

You shall never wash my feet: he said this, terrified with fear. If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me: this indicates that whoever has not been washed through baptism and through the confession of repentance will have no share with the Lord.

He took his garments: this again indicates that he will return to the Jews at the end of the world.

A servant is not [Col. 0585B] greater than his lord, nor is an apostle greater than the one who sent him: that is, I suffer, and you will suffer. Alternatively: if I humble myself even to your feet, so must you humble yourselves before everyone.

He will lift up his heel against me: the heel is the extremity of the limb.

And through the morsel Satan entered into him, that is, as the Apostle says, whoever receives the Body of the Lord and his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment.

I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. In the Old Testament it is said: “You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy.” The Lord says: “Love your enemies.” This is the new commandment.

Let not your heart be troubled: here he preaches to the apostles concerning his Passion. Believe in God, and believe in me, because I am the Son of God.

[Col. 0585C] Believe that in my Father’s house, that is, in the Church, there are many dwellings, that is, just as understanding is divided within one human being, so in the Church, which is the body of Christ, there are many graces.

I go to prepare a place for you, that is, I will prepare life for you, as the Apostle says: “We have an advocate with the Father who intercedes for us.”

I am the way, the truth, and the life. Christ is the way without error; he himself is the truth without falsehood and the life without death.

From now on you know him and have seen him, that is, they knew him with the eyes of the body and knew him with the eyes of the heart, according to divinity, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

He will do greater works than these, that is, because Christ healed the woman through the fringe of his garment, while the apostles will heal the sick through their shadow.

*(The Passion ends.)*

I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete. Through the Spirit received twice, the love of God and of one’s neighbor is understood.

The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, that is, whoever loves the world does not receive him.

I will not leave you orphans, that is, I will not leave you according to divinity.

On that day you will know, that is, in the future, or in Christ’s resurrection.

I am in the Father, that is, according to divinity. You are in me, because you are my members. And I am in you, that is, in the love of your hearts.

I will reveal myself to him, that is, to those who believe in divinity.

We will make our dwelling with him, as he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I also,” and so forth.

[Col. 0586A] I give you my peace, that is, just as I patiently endure all things, so you have patience. I leave you my peace, that is, just as I suffered, so you will suffer.

Not as the world gives do I give you peace. The world gives interrupted peace; God gives eternal peace.

The ruler of this world comes to me and finds nothing in me, that is, the devil came to the cross and found no sin in the Lord. He sought to seize him and was seized by him.

As the Father commanded me, so I do. The Father sent him to shed his blood for the human race, and so he did.

I am the true vine, from which blood and water flow; and my Father is the farmer, that is, the cultivator of the Church. You are the branches, that is, the apostles or the faithful of the Church.

Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so [Col. 0586B] each person bears no fruit unless he remains in Christ.

In this my Father is glorified: that you may bear the first fruit, that is, just as I have made preaching and Passion fruitful, so you should do likewise.

As the Father loved me, so I loved you, that is, just as the Father sent me to preach and to suffer, so I send you.

Greater love has no one, and so forth. Love is stronger than death. I suffer for you through love, and you suffer for the Church.

I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father, that is, the commandments of the Gospel.

I chose you from the world, that is, from worldly actions. You are not of the world, that is, because you do not love the world.

As Solomon says: “Such is the adulterous woman who, when she has eaten, wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done no evil.’” [Col. 0586C] She represents the Church from the nations, which through confession cleansed itself from the impurity of sins.

You have been with me from the beginning, that is, from the beginning of the preaching.

If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, that is, he will cause the one who does not believe in me to believe through the preaching of the Gospel.

Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged. He will convict concerning sin, that is, so that through your preaching they may be converted to repentance.

Concerning righteousness, so that just as one loves one’s neighbor, one may also love God with the whole heart.

Concerning judgment, so that whatever you wish people to do for you, you also may do for them. For this is the Law and the Prophets.

A little while, and you will not see me, that is, while I lay in the tomb. Again a little while, and you will see me, that is, through the resurrection.

The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will speak openly to you about the Father, that is, through the resurrection.

On that day you will ask in my name, that is, because I am ascending to the Father and rising again through power.

The Father loves you because you love me.

I leave the world and go to the Father, that is, in the presence of the body; for according to divinity he does not leave the world.

You have tribulation, that is, persecution from worldly people. I have conquered the world, that is, I have bound the strong one in the world, who is the devil.

The hour has come, Father, to glorify your Son—that is, through the resurrection—so that the Son may glorify you—that is, so that through the Son they may be converted and believe. I have glorified you upon the earth [Col. 0587A], that is, I have made you known to all. I manifested your name to the people, showing that according to his divinity he was with the Father, and bodily upon the earth. Those whom you gave me were yours: in foreknowledge they were yours from the beginning. You gave them to me, that is, for instruction; and they kept your word, that is, they remained in the faith. I pray for them, not for the world, because God knows who are his. All that is yours is mine, and what is mine is yours. And I have been glorified in them, that is, I have been manifested among those same nations, because they believed in me. I am in the world bodily, and I am not in the world bodily; and for them I sanctify myself, that is, through martyrdom and resurrection. The glory that you gave me I have given them, that is, the divine commandments.

He went out with his disciples across the torrent [Col. 0587B] of the Kidron, signifying the force of persecution. Jesus again passed over with his disciples, that is, from the world to the Father, and from the Jews to the nations. They came with lanterns and torches, that is, they themselves kindled a punitive light. They led him to Annas—Annas is interpreted “the grace of God,” because he had received the office of high priest by the grace of God—but she appeared as the doorkeeper who introduced Peter into the courtyard; this signifies the primitive Church. He reproached him because he had said that he was the Son of God. Certainly, he did not regard it as robbery to consider himself equal to God, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant.

Jesus carrying his cross gave an example, as he himself said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and so forth. Two thieves were crucified with [Col. 0587C] Jesus. The one who remained in his unbelief signifies the Jews; the one who confessed signifies the nations. It was written in the inscription, “King of the Jews,” that is, king of those who confess.

They made four parts of Jesus’ garments: the four soldiers signify the four Evangelists. The divided garments signify the preaching, the incarnation, the passion, and the resurrection, which they proclaimed in the four regions of the world. But the seamless tunic, woven from the top, shows that the divinity in the Father and the Son is inseparable. “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be”: this shows that Catholic men do not tear apart the unity of the divinity.

“Woman, behold your son”; to the disciple, “Behold your mother.” Here he entrusted the virgin to him, so that he might preserve her undefiled. They did not break Jesus’ legs, that is, in accordance with what had previously been prefigured [Col. 0587D] by the lamb in Egypt: not raw, nor cooked in water, but roasted only by fire. This signifies Christ’s passion. The staff in the hand signifies Christ’s cross, from the world to the Father. “You shall not break any of it” shows that Christ’s cross was not to be broken. They pierced his side with a spear, so that Scripture might be fulfilled: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.”

Blood and water came out. Just as Eve was taken from Adam’s side, so redemption for the Church came out of Christ’s side: remission through the blood, baptism through the water. The two disciples running—Peter and John—signify two peoples running: the Jews through the letter of the Law, the nations through the law of nature.

John ran ahead more quickly, saw the linen cloths lying there, [Col. 0588A] and did not enter. The Jews, through the Law and the Prophets, saw that Christ was to come, but did not receive his coming. Peter came afterward; he saw the linen cloths and entered. This signifies the nations, who believed in Christ’s coming, or in his teaching. The linen cloths signify Christ’s incarnation; the napkin signifies the mystery of his divinity. The napkin was not with the linen cloths, but separately, wrapped up in one place. This shows that the divinity is far removed from human senses, in one place—that is, in the universal Church. Then the other disciple, who had first come to the tomb, also entered; this signifies the Jews returning to the faith at the end of the world. The angels sitting at the head and at the feet signify the beginning and the end.

Mary said, “I do not know where they have placed him.” This signifies according to the flesh [Col. 0588B]. She loved the world and believed through faith. What Mary said signifies the thought behind the utterance: through love of one’s neighbor a person comes to know God. Jesus said, “Do not touch me,” that is, in your heart. “I have not ascended to you,” according to his divinity.

The disciples fished all night and caught nothing. The fishermen signify the ancient teachers; the night shows that before Christ’s coming no one attained perfection through the preaching of the ancient Law. When morning came, this signified that Christ’s coming had taken place. “Cast the net on the right side,” that is, direct the preaching toward the nations.

Peter was naked, that is, they were naked of faith in Christ. He girded himself with his tunic, signifying the faith of the Church. He cast himself into the sea, that is, into the waves and bitterness of the world through love of Christ. The other disciples came in a boat, that is, in the Church, treading down the world’s turbulence. They saw coals, and a fish, and bread laid out: the fish signifies faith, the coals the warmth of charity, and the bread the divine word. They dragged the net to land; by the shore he signified the end of the world. It was full of large fish, that is, the fullness and greatness of the Church through the remission of sins. Through the number three he signified the Trinity. The net was not divided or torn, that is, the Church will be incorrupt in the future. Jesus ate after the resurrection, signifying the true incarnation of the body, so that believers might believe.

Jesus said, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” This signifies that, just as he had denied him three times, so he should confess the faith of the Trinity three times. “Feed my sheep,” that is, in the Church. Jesus entered through closed doors, showing that he entered through closed doors [Col. 0588D] into the womb; likewise, after the resurrection all the saints put on a spiritual body and can enter everywhere without fear. Hence he remained whole and incorrupt in marriage. Three witnesses attest this statement.

The disciple whom Jesus loved: the second miracle was what Jesus did at Cana of Galilee, bringing forth wine from water. The marriage ceremony shows John’s virginity, because a bride was joined to him. This is the testimony in which Jesus entrusted his mother to John. Mary signifies the Church; John, preeminence. Just as John was a virgin in marriage, so he remained incorrupt in death. John relates a genealogy according to divinity, whereas the others relate one according to humanity. John speaks of divinity: “In the beginning was the Word.”

This disciple lay upon Jesus’ breast, [Col. 0589A] and the knowledge of divinity that had been in Jesus’ breast passed to John through the joining of the two breasts. A tree grafted into another produces the fruit of the tree in which it is planted.

If, according to the order of the canon, this book ought to have been placed before Matthew, then its placement last is because the earth was sanctified first, then water, and finally fire, since fire is brighter and more subtle. Likewise this corresponds to the two Laws, namely, the old and the new. The old was given first, but the new is brighter and greater, because it distinguishes what is heavenly and is more abundant. This is what pertains to the Gospel of John, as has been stated above.

[Col. 0589]

COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK (C, G, S)

PREFACE

[Col. 0589A] “Every scribe who has been instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.” But I am like a poor little widow putting two small coins into the treasury, sending nourishment from my poverty to my poor little students who hope for food from the poor woman. From the table of the rich I send these crumbs, which my little dogs eagerly demand with the Syrophoenician woman.

Moreover, being anxious and possessing no gold or silver, no precious stones, I shall offer, if I can, skins of hyacinth-blue [Col. 0589B] from heavenly things, not earthly ones. With God’s help I shall endeavor to convey something about the natural sense—that is, the history of Mark the Evangelist—or about the mystical interpretation, as my predecessors have handed it down.

For this reason, I think, those treating this Evangelist pass him over untouched: because he relates almost the same things as Matthew, although they are distinguished by certain particular testimonies, so that one wing may touch the wing of another living creature, and one wheel may follow another on the same path, and so that, with their faces turned toward one another, the holy living creatures may behold one another.

In the first canon Mark is accompanied by Matthew, Luke, and John. In the second, by Matthew and Luke. In the fourth, by Matthew and John. In the sixth canon, like two rings on a bar, Matthew and Mark are always joined—that is, in forty-seven [Col. 0589C] sections. In the eighth canon he is accompanied by Luke, that is, in thirteen sections. In his own material, which I intend to explain as best I can, he proceeds through eighteen sections individually. Taken together, these are two hundred and thirty-five sections.

Mark the Evangelist of God, Peter’s disciple, a Levite by birth and a priest, wrote this Gospel in Italy. Taking the beginning of his Gospel from the words of the prophets, confirming John, Christ’s forerunner, by the testimony of Malachi—that is, of the angel—and designating the Word made flesh by the voice of Isaiah, he established the beginning of evangelical preaching. He found in the word of the voice what he had lost among the consonants, that is, in the genealogies of God and man.

Therefore, at the outset he begins to preach wholly from the perfection of Christ’s age, and does not labor [Col. 0589D] over the birth of the infant, since he speaks of the perfection of the Son of God. Yet by presenting the fast of the legal number, the defeat of the devil, and the ministry of the angels, he comprehends great things in brief.

He was the first bishop of Alexandria. It was necessary to know his work in its several parts, to arrange within oneself the sayings of the Gospel, to understand within oneself the discipline of the Law, and to discern the divine nature in the Lord’s flesh.

He sows after Matthew; he roars like a lion; he flies like an eagle; he speaks as a man; he sacrifices as a priest; he irrigates like a river; he blossoms like a field; he burns like wine. For Christ, of whom he speaks, is a man in being born, a calf in dying, a lion in rising, and an eagle in ascending.

There are four qualities from which the holy Gospels are woven: precepts, commandments, testimonies, and examples. Justice consists in the precepts, charity in the commandments, faith in the testimonies, and perfection [Col. 0590B] in the examples.

Such are these precepts: “Then Jesus commanded his twelve disciples: Do not go on the way of the nations,” and so forth. This means turning away from evil.

These, however, are the commandments in which it is said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” This means doing good and fulfilling charity.

The testimonies are those that stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses. For example: “John bears witness about me, but I have a greater testimony than John. The Father himself, who remains in me, bears witness about me. And the works themselves that I do bear witness about me; and I bear witness to the truth.”

Examples are those by which people imitate Jesus when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle,” and so forth; and, “Be perfect,” that is, merciful, “as your heavenly Father is perfect”; and elsewhere: “For I have given you an example, so that you also may do likewise.”

The verses of the Psalmist harmonize these four qualities when they say: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes.” History chiefly contains the precepts. And elsewhere: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad,” because whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the whole Law. Again: “I have understood your testimonies,” for it is not given to everyone to understand the testimonies. Hence elsewhere he says: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful,” because testimony requires faith of the mind more than the eyes of the flesh.

Fourth: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves,” that is, the examples of our judgments should be justified in the same way as we have found them in God’s judgments. Hence the same person, seeing this elsewhere, says: “I feared your judgments.” For by the judgment with which we judge, judgment will be passed upon us.

In these four qualities are fear, faith, hope, and charity. We begin through fear; through faith we preserve what we begin; through hope we are raised up; through charity we are brought to completion. For the end of the commandment is charity.

These are the four months that Christ foretold before the harvest when he said: “Are there not four months until the harvest?” Thus through God’s precepts, commandments, testimonies, and examples, after judgment we too may harvest ripe fruits with joy [Col. 0591A]—fruits whose seeds of repentance we cast upon the earth in the tears of fear—and may carry our sheaves of charity and reap them with joy in heaven.

CHAPTER ONE

“The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God, as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you. A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

Κατὰ Μάρκον—“According to Mark.” The Gospel through which came the redemption of the faithful and the blessedness of the saints: for the four are one, and the one is four. The four Gospels are established as possessing many virtues.

For what is stronger than saving souls that could perish through the vices of their errors? As the prophet long ago, moved by the Holy Spirit, unveiled in Psalm 67: “The Lord will give the word to evangelizers with many powers.”

The order of the verse is as follows, and it is fittingly inserted into this work: the Lord will give many powers to the apostles who proclaimed his word with venerable confession, when they were granted the power to heal crowds of the sick.

Εὐαγγέλιον, in Greek, is proclaimed in Latin as bona annuntiatio, “good announcement.” Properly, it concerns the kingdom of God and the remission of sins. Hence it is said: “Repent and believe the Gospel, and the kingdom of heaven will draw near.”

Jesus Christ means “the anointed Savior”: in Hebrew, JESUA; in Greek, Σωτήρ; in Latin, Salvator. MESSIAS is Hebrew, Χριστός is Greek, and unctus is Latin for “anointed.” He is called both king and priest, since Christ the king is born from the line of David and is foretold by the words of prophets of Levitical lineage.

Hence it follows: “A voice crying in the wilderness,” and so forth. The voice is John. Through that voice the Lord Jesus cried out to the Jews that among those born of women no one was greater than he.

A cry is ordinarily made to the deaf who are far away, or in indignation. This certainly happened to the Jewish people, since salvation is far from sinners and they stopped their ears heavily, like deaf adders; they deserved to hear indignation, wrath, and tribulation from Christ.

The voice and cry are made in the wilderness because they were deserted by the Spirit of God, like an empty and swept house; deserted by the prophet, the king, and the priest. Hence John and Jesus seek what was lost in the wilderness. Where the devil conquered, there he is conquered; where man fell, there he rises again.

“Behold, I send my angel.” The voice of the Holy Spirit—πνεῦμα ἁγίου—speaks through Malachi to the Father concerning the Son, who is the face of the Father, through whom he was recognized. The angel is interpreted as “messenger,” because he announces beforehand what concerns Christ.

“After me comes one who was made before me, who will prepare your way.” The way of the Lord by which he enters human beings is repentance, through which God descends to us and we ascend to him. Hence angels are remembered ascending and descending to the Son of Man.

“Prepare the way of the Lord”: this means, repent and preach. Hence παρασκευή, “preparation,” is said of the day before the Sabbath, that is, repentance before the future rest. From this the preaching of John and Christ begins: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near,” because on the seventh day God rested from all his works.

We must erase seven vices through repentance, as though they were evil kinds, so that afterward, having rested, we may possess the desirable land. “Make his paths straight”: the paths that we have bent by turning to the right and to the left.

Now God commands us, walking along the royal road, to love our neighbors as ourselves and ourselves as our neighbors. For whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.

Whoever loves himself and does not love his neighbor turns to the right. Whoever hates himself and loves his neighbor turns to the left. Many do good but do not correct well, as Eli did. Many correct well but do not act, as did the scribes and Pharisees who sat upon the chair of Moses.

Hence the beak of the turtledove is commanded in the Law to be turned back toward its wings, lest the beak be separated from the work and our work be divided from our speech.

The paths follow the road, because moral commandments are explained after repentance, according to Mark. The road is prepared through faith, baptism, and repentance. Straight paths are made through austere signs: a garment of haircloth, a leather belt, locusts as food, wild honey as drink, and a very humble voice. Hence it follows:

“John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. And all the region of Judea and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.”

John is interpreted as “the grace of God.” The account begins from grace. Hence it follows: “Baptizing,” for through baptism grace is given, by which sins are freely forgiven. Hence it is said: “What you have received freely, give freely.” And the Apostle says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves: it is the gift of God, so that no one may boast.”

“And preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.” What is completed through the bridegroom is begun through the friend of the bridegroom. Hence catechumens—that is, instructed persons—begin through the priest and are anointed by the bishop.

Now the bride is brought in by the bridegroom’s friend; thus, through the boy Isaac, Rebecca is led forth veiled in a white garment.

“And all the region of Judea and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.” “Confession and beauty are before him,” that is, before the bridegroom.

Hence the bride leaps down from the camel, when the Church now humbles herself after seeing the true Isaac, Jesus Christ, at whose birth God caused Sarah to laugh. Thus it is said to Mary, who is “princess with God”: “Blessed are you among women.”

Jordan is interpreted as “the descent of another.” There sins are washed away. For after the ark crossed the Jordan, it passed over foreign stones into a foreign land; with one part flowing down into the sea, the other part, swollen in the form of a mountain, was raised up.

So we, once alienated from God through pride, are humbled through the symbol of baptism and raised to the heights, because “whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” But the part that flows into the sea becomes bitter, when the ark of God—that is, the body of Christ—does not benefit those who have not been cleansed but changes them for the worse.

It follows:

“John was clothed in camel’s hair and had a leather belt around his waist; and he ate locusts and wild honey, and he preached, saying…”

The prophet’s clothing, food, and drink signify the entire austere life of preachers and signify that future nations are to be joined, inwardly and outwardly, to the grace of God, which is John.

The camel’s hair signifies the rich of the nations; the leather belt, the poor who are dead to the world; the saw-toothed locusts, the wise of this world, who leave dry straw for the Jews, drag mystical grains with their legs and inhabit thickets in the heat of faith; and the wild honey signifies the faithful, prepared by inspired fires from an uncultivated forest and plunged [reading uncertain]. All these things are taken from the grace of the Gospel, in which there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

“One mightier than I is coming after me.” Who is mightier than grace, through which sins are washed away? Surely the one who forgives sins seven times and seventy times seven.

Grace comes first, indeed, but it forgives once through baptism. Mercy, however, toward the wretched extends from Adam to Christ through seventy-seven generations and reaches one hundred forty-four thousand.

“Of whom I am not worthy, stooping down, to loosen the strap of his sandals.” Grace alone, stooping in baptism, is not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandals, that is, the mystery of the incarnation of God.

The heel is the extremity of the body. At the end, therefore, the incarnate Savior is present for righteousness. Hence the prophet rightly says: “I will extend my sandal over Edom.” For unless knowledge of the Spirit is joined to it, no one investigates through the grace of remission the mystery of Christ’s incarnation: how the Word became flesh; from where Christ’s flesh, soul, and spirit take their beginning, so that he may be wholly true man without sin and true God in true God; how he is true God in true God without beginning—the same Son of Man who is in heaven—and how, coming forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber—that is, from the virgin womb—he left it closed.

Hence, when the true bridegroom arrives, the house of the unshod man is called the house of John, who says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.”

Hence the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove. To him the Song of Songs is sung: “My bride, my friend, my nearest one, my beloved, my dove.”

The bride is represented in the patriarchs; the friend in the prophets; the nearest one in Joseph and Mary; the beloved in John the Baptist; the dove in Christ and the apostles, to whom it is said: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

It follows:

“I baptize you in water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”

The river of God is always full, always equal. Of it it is said: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God.”

What difference is there between water and the Holy Spirit, who was borne over the waters? Water is the ministry of man; the Spirit is the ministry of God. Hence it is written: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” It says “over,” not [Col. 0594A] “under.”

Just as the soul is more excellent than the body that it governs, so the spirit is higher than the soul. Yet the Spirit remained upon him. This is Christ’s anointing according to the flesh, of which it is said: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

Oil cannot be beneath water; likewise, the Creator cannot be beneath the creature. Oil rises from the bitterness of its root and grows at the top into nourishment for light, medicine for wounds, and refreshment for the hungry.

From what does Christ’s bodily anointing arise? From the bitterness of the passion, and it reaches the glory of the resurrection. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus,” and so forth, “unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,” because the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.

“And it happened in those days that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately, as he was coming up from the water, he saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him. And a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.’ And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness. And he was in the wilderness forty days and forty nights, and was tempted by Satan. And he was with the beasts, and angels ministered to him.”

Mark the Evangelist, desiring the springs of water like a deer, leaps through level and difficult places; he merely grazes the peaks of the meadows and carries palms at the summit. Like a honey-bearing bee, he briefly tastes the flowers of the field, in which the fragrance of the true Isaac is suggested.

Therefore he relates Jesus coming from Nazareth of Galilee to baptism, received in the Jordan from John; immediately ascending from the water; seeing the heavens opened; seeing the Spirit descend like a dove and remain upon him; the Father’s voice coming from heaven and being well pleased in the beloved Son; the Spirit driving him into the wilderness; his being tempted by Satan for forty days and nights; his being with the beasts; and his remaining there while angels ministered.

This order is to be followed by us morally according to Christ’s example, as we hasten toward the fellowship of the angels. Jesus first demonstrated it by his deeds before teaching it by his voice.

Thus, drawn from the instability of the world and from the fragrance of the flower of a wavering will, we run with the young women after the bridegroom. Through the mysteries of baptism, we are washed by the grace of remission from the two fountains of love, of God and neighbor; and as we ascend in hope, we behold heavenly mysteries with the pure eyes of our hearts.

After this, with a contrite and humbled spirit, we receive the Holy Spirit descending with a simple heart upon the meek and remaining with unfailing charity. And the Lord’s voice from heaven is directed to us, beloved of God: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

Then the Father is well pleased in us with the Son and the Holy Spirit, when we become one spirit with God. Hence the Son intercedes with the Father for us, saying: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are one.”

Then the Spirit drives us into the wilderness, where we are to be tempted for the period represented by the number forty by Satan, so that endurance may produce testing in us, testing hope, and hope charity, since “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities,” and so forth.

Then the beasts will be at peace with us, when in the ark of our soul we are made gentle with clean and unclean animals, and when we lie down with lions as Daniel did; when the spirit is not against the flesh and blood, nor the flesh covets against the spirit.

After this, the ministering angels who always behold the face of our Father in heaven are sent to us, to give answers and consolations to vigilant hearts, saying: “Your prayer has been heard”; and, “Do not seek Jesus the Nazarene”; and, “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise”; and, “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree that is in the paradise of my God.”

It follows:

“After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God and saying: ‘The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God will draw near.’”

After we have received grace for grace, carnal things are beheaded and spiritual things are given life; when the shadow ceases, the truth is present. John is in prison, the Law in Judea, Jesus in Galilee, and salvation among the nations, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Poverty succeeds an earthly kingdom; the kingdom everlasting is granted to the poverty of Christians. Hence the Lord says: “My kingdom is not of this world.” For every earthly honor is compared with thin water’s foam, smoke, or a dream.

It follows:

“Repent and believe the Gospel. And passing beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother casting nets into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.’ And immediately, leaving their nets, they followed him. And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were also mending their nets in the boat; and immediately he called them. And leaving their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, they followed him.”

“For unless you believe, you will not understand.” The sweetness of the fruit compensates for the bitterness of the root; the hope of profit delights amid the dangers of the sea; the hope of health mitigates the pain of medicine. Whoever desires the kernel breaks the nut. The one who wishes to cling to eternal good practices repentance. Those who have deserved to reach the palm of forgiveness can worthily proclaim Christ’s praises.

After this, four fishermen are called and sent: Simon and Andrew, James and John, leaving their nets, their father, and their boat with the hired men. By this four-horse chariot we are carried to the heavens, like Elijah. Upon these four corners the first Church is built. By these four Hebrew letters—that is, the Tetragrammaton—the Lord’s name is recognized by us.

By a similar example they are commanded to hear the voice of the Lord who calls, to forget the people of vices and the house of ancestral tradition, which is folly before God; and to abandon the spider’s web in which empty air held us, almost fallen like gnats; and to reject the boat of our former way of life.

For Adam, our ancestor according to the flesh, is covered with dead skins. Now, having put off the old man with his deeds and following the new man, we are clothed with Solomon’s skins, with which the bride boasts that she has been made beautiful.

Simon means “obedient”; Andrew, “manly”; Jacob, “supplanter”; John, in Latin, sounds as “grace.” By these four names we are joined to the Lord’s company: by obedience, so that we may be heard; by manliness, so that we may fight; by supplanting, so that we may persevere; by grace, so that we may be preserved.

For unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. These are called the four cardinal virtues: through prudence we obey; through justice we act manfully; through temperance we tread upon the serpent; through fortitude we merit God’s grace.

Occupied with the cares of the brothers, I was unable to explain Mark the Evangelist as I wished. But imitating him, I touch briefly upon his distinctive features; and, like Ruth, I gather ears of grain and clusters of grapes belonging to Christ after the reapers, for Naomi, who has been widowed. Would that through this poverty of mine I might reach the banquets of Boaz, committing a praiseworthy theft!

Mark, arranging the sayings of the Gospel in himself—not in themselves—does not follow the order of the history but preserves the order of the mysteries. Hence he relates the first virtue on the Sabbaths, saying:

“And they entered Capernaum; and immediately, on the Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and taught them. And they were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.’ And Jesus rebuked him, saying: ‘Be silent and come out of the man.’ And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. And they were all amazed, so that they questioned one another, saying: ‘What is this? What is this new teaching? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.’ And his fame immediately spread throughout the whole region of Galilee.

“And immediately, coming out of the synagogue, they entered the house of Simon and Andrew with James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law was lying sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And approaching, he raised her up, taking her by the hand; and at once the fever left her, and she ministered to them.

“When evening came, after the sun had set, they brought to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons.”

Capernaum is interpreted as “the village of consolation”; the Sabbath as “rest.” The man with an unclean spirit is the human race, in which uncleanness reigned from Adam to Moses.

“For those who sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law.” The one who knew the Holy One is commanded to be silent, since although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but instead served the creature rather than the Creator. The spirit, convulsing the man, came out of him.

As salvation draws near, temptation draws near. Pharaoh, released from Israel, pursues Israel; the contented devil rises to cause scandals.

Peter’s feverish mother-in-law is washed by the second virtue, and, when he takes her by the hand, she is healed. The fever signifies intemperance. From this fever we, the sons of the synagogue, are healed by the hand of discipline and the raising up of desire; and we minister to the will of the one who heals us, who declines from us toward evening.

“And the whole city was gathered at the door, and he healed many who were afflicted with various illnesses. And he cast out many demons and did not permit them to speak, because they knew him.

“And rising very early, he went out and departed into a deserted place, and there he prayed. Simon and those who were with him pursued him. And when they found him, they said to him: ‘Everyone is seeking you.’ And he said to them: ‘Let us go into the neighboring villages and cities, so that I may preach there also; for this is why I have come.’ And he was preaching in their synagogues and throughout all Galilee, and casting out demons.

“And a leper came to him, begging him; and kneeling, he said to him: ‘If you will, you can cleanse me.’ Jesus, moved with compassion, stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him: ‘I will; be cleansed.’ And when he had spoken, immediately the leprosy departed from him, and he was cleansed. And he sternly warned him and immediately sent him away, saying to him: ‘See that you say nothing to anyone; but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded as a testimony to them.’ But he went out and began to proclaim it and spread the report of the matter.”

The gate (*janua*) of the kingdom is, morally, repentance together with faith, which brings salvation amid various illnesses. For the world-city languishes under various vices. Hence the leper is cleansed by the third virtue: he begs the Lord’s will on bended knee, for he does not desire the sinner’s death, but that he should turn and live.

Our leprosy is the sin of the first man. It began at the head, when he desired the kingdoms of the world. For the root of all evils is greed. Hence Gehazi, pursuing avarice, is covered with leprosy. But when this is shown to the priest according to the order of Melchizedek, it is cleansed by an offering, when he says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.”

It follows concerning Mark’s distinctive material.

So that he could no longer enter the city openly, but had to remain outside in deserted places; and people came to him from everywhere. Certainly Jesus was not manifested to all who serve with broad and smooth praises and their own pleasures, but to those who go out with Peter into the open country and into the deserted places that the Lord chose for prayer and for restoring the people—those who abandon the delights of the world and abandon everything they possess, so that they may say: “The Lord is my portion.” The glory of the Lord, however, is manifested to those who come together from everywhere—that is, across level and difficult ground—and whom nothing can separate from the love of Christ.

## CHAPTER II

After some days he entered Capernaum again, and it was heard that he was in the house. Many gathered there, so that there was no room, not even by the door; and he was speaking the word to them. And they came to him bringing a paralytic, carried by four men. Since they could not bring him before him because of the crowd, they stripped away the roof where he was; and, having opened it, they lowered the pallet on which the paralytic was lying. When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: [Col. 0598A] “Son, your sins are forgiven.”

Some of the scribes were sitting there and reasoning in their hearts: “Why does this man speak in this way? He is blaspheming. Who can forgive sins except God alone?” Jesus immediately knew in his spirit that they were reasoning in this way among themselves, and he said to them: “Why are you reasoning about these things in your hearts? Which is easier: to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your pallet, and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—“I tell you: Rise, take up your pallet, and go to your house.”

And immediately he rose, took up the pallet, and went away before them all, so that everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying: “We have never seen anything like this.” And he went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd came to him, and he taught them. As he was passing by, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him: “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him.

When he was reclining at table in Levi’s house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples; for there were many who followed him. When the scribes and Pharisees saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus heard this and said to them: “The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. They came and said to him: “Why do John’s disciples and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” And Jesus said to them: [Col. 0598C] “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them; then they will fast, in those days.

“No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the new patch tears away from the old, and a worse rent is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine will be spilled and the skins will be ruined. Rather, new wine must be put into new wineskins.”

And once again, when the Lord was walking through the grainfields on the sabbath, his disciples began to go ahead and pluck the ears of grain. The Pharisees said to him: “Look, why are your disciples doing on the sabbath what is not permitted?” And he said to them: “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the bread of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except the priests, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

And he said to them: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the sabbath.”

In the fourth virtue, four men come carrying a paralytic on a pallet. Offended by the crowd, they strip away the roof. Through their faith the paralytic’s sins are forgiven; he carries the bed on which he had been carried and goes to his house before everyone.

Paralysis is a type of the body: the sluggish person lies in the softness of the flesh, possessing a desire for salvation; but through the body’s inertia and double-minded thoughts, as though his limbs had been weakened, he stumbles. Four men carry him—namely, the four virtues mentioned above—to the tiles of divinity and wisdom, exposed in the house of Christ’s flesh. To him the duty is assigned of carrying the flesh that had been carrying him, so that by another way he may return more fully to his own region.

After this comes the sinner Levi son of Alphaeus. Levi means “added” (*appositus*): having abandoned the tax booth of worldly business, he follows only the word that says: “Whoever does not renounce everything that he possesses cannot be my disciple.”

## CHAPTER III

And he entered the synagogue again. There was a man there who had a withered hand, and they were watching him to see whether he would heal on the sabbath, so that they might accuse him. And he said to the man who had the withered hand: “Rise and stand in the middle.” Then he said to them: “Is it permitted on the sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save a life [Col. 0599B] or to destroy it?” But they were silent.

Looking around at them with anger, grieved at the blindness of their hearts, he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. The Pharisees went out and immediately took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.

Jesus withdrew with his disciples toward the sea, and a great multitude followed him from Galilee and Judea, from Jerusalem, Idumea, and from across the Jordan. A great multitude also came from the region around Tyre and Sidon when they heard what he was doing. And he told his disciples to have a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they should crush him. For he healed many, so that all who had afflictions pressed upon him to touch him.

And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, saying: “You are the Son of God.” And he sternly charged them not to make him known.

In the fifth virtue, there was a man with a withered hand, to whom it is said: “Stretch out your hand.” He signifies the avaricious, who, unwilling to give, wish to receive—who wish to plunder and not to distribute. They are told to stretch out their hands: that is, let the one who was stealing steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his own hands at what is good, so that he may have something to share with those in need.

And he went up the mountain and called to himself those whom he wished, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve to be with him and to send them out to preach. He gave them authority to heal illnesses and to cast out demons. He gave Simon the name Peter; and James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James he named Boanerges, which means “sons of thunder”; and Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him. [Col. 0599D]

It is customary for divine Scripture to speak allegorically: while saying one thing, it intends another to be understood. You will frequently find this placed in the Gospels. But it is necessary for us to apply such exalted matters to our understanding in such a way that we nevertheless discern everything according to the truth of the history.

For Christ alone is spiritually the mountain. The mountain has been briefly praised by us, but is rich in the quality of heavenly things: from it living waters flow; milk is prepared for the salvation of little ones; spiritual richness is recognized; and whatever is believed to be supremely good is established in the grace of this mountain, which is the mountain of mountains and of the saints, and which daily invites them to itself from their present troubles.

Those who are exalted in merit and in word are called to the mountain, so that the place may correspond to their lofty merits, to be twelve with him. “The Lord loved the beauty of Jacob”; and when the Most High divided the nations and separated the sons of Adam, he fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel, so that they themselves might be upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Authority was given to them, which the Son received from the Father according to the flesh, so that they might do the works that he himself did, and do works greater than these.

And he gave Simon the name Peter. From obedience he ascends to recognition: “For to the one who has, it will be given, and he will abound.” And James, who has all the desires of the flesh cast down beneath him; and John, who received by grace what others possess through labor. And he gave them the name Boanerges, which means “sons of thunder.” Their sublime merit on the mountain deserves to hear the thunder of the Father, who thunders through the cloud concerning the Son: “This is my beloved Son.” Through the cloud of the flesh, may they themselves scatter the fire of the word like lightning into the lands, since God makes lightning into rain, so that mercy may extinguish what judgment inflicts. Hence the prophet says: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

And Andrew, who in manly form exerts force against his own destruction, so that he may always have within himself the answer of death and his soul may always be in his hands. And Philip, who is the mouth of the lamp, who can illuminate with his mouth what he has conceived in his heart. The Lord gave him the opening of an illumined mouth.

We know that this manner of speech is proper to the divine Scriptures, when the names of the Hebrews are assigned to some mystery of meaning. The Evangelist now inserts this with great insistence, as though speaking in the person of God.

And Bartholomew, who is the son of the one who suspends the waters. And who is the son of the one who suspends the waters, except the one who said: “And I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it”? The name “son of God” is acquired through peace and love of the enemy. For “blessed are the peacemakers, because they will be called sons of God”; and “love your enemies, so that you may be sons of God,” and so forth.

And Matthew, who means “given,” to whom it is granted by the Lord not only to obtain the remission of sins but also to be enrolled among the number of the apostles, so that lion and ox may eat together and wolf may feed with lamb.

And Thomas, who means “abyss.” For many who know the deep things of God do not bring them forth, as Paul says: “I know a man,” and so forth, up to “things which it is not permitted for human beings to speak.”

And James the son of Alphaeus, that is, “learned” or “of the thousandth.” A thousand fall at his side and ten thousand at his right hand. Another James is the one whose struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual wickedness.

And Thaddaeus, who means “little heart” (*corculum*), that is, a cultivator of the heart, who guards his heart with all vigilance. For God is seen through purity of heart, just as an image is displayed through clean glass.

And Simon the Cananaean, who is also called the Zealot. Simon is interpreted as “one who places sorrow.” For blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted. He fulfills a threefold mourning who seeks future consolation: he laments his own sins with David and Mary; he weeps with those who weep, with Paul; and he weeps greatly with John, who said: “And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book and break its seals.”

He is called a Zealot whom zeal for the house of God has consumed, like Phinehas the priest, so that the shaking may cease.

And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him, who does not erase his sin through repentance, nor is it erased through remembrance. Hence it is said of him: “Let the sin of his mother not be erased. Let them be continually against the Lord.”

Judas means “confessing” or “glorious.” Iscariot, however, means “memory of death.” There are many confessors in the Church who are proud and glorious, the first of whom was Simon Magus, then Arius and the other heretics. Their mortal memory is therefore commemorated in the Church so that they may be avoided.

These are the twelve distinctions among the apostles and preachers, who keep watch three by three and four by four around the Lord’s tabernacle and carry the holy words of the Lord on the shoulders of their own works, so that they may carry one tabernacle with many dwelling places to the promised land. The example of one humbles them all into fear, so that the fall of that Lucifer may preserve the angels and the wise man may not glory in his wisdom; rather, “let the one who glories glory in the Lord.”

And they came to the house, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread. When his own people heard this, they went out to seize him, for they were saying: “He has lost his mind.”

The scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying: “He has Beelzebul,” and: “By the ruler of demons he casts out demons.” Having called them together, he spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house cannot stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but has come to an end.

“No one can enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his house. Amen, I say to you: all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven the sons of men, however much they may have blasphemed.”

Here Mark specifically relates that Jesus came with his disciples to the house. He also records that the crowds gathered again, so that they could not eat bread, and that the disciples thought he had gone mad, because the scribes who had come from Jerusalem were saying: “He has Beelzebul.”

“As the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are the ways of the Lord exalted above our ways.” For this is why the one who hears and suffers has come, the one who says to us: “Blessed will you be when people curse you,” and so forth, up to: “Your reward is in heaven.”

The house to which they come is the primitive Church. The crowds that prevent the eating of bread are sins and vices, because the one who eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Hence the Lord is turned into madness when he says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” and so forth, up to: “You will not have life in yourselves.”

[Col. 0602A] But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of an eternal offense, because they were saying: “He has an unclean spirit.” He does not deserve to perform repentance so as to be received—the one who, understanding Christ, was saying that he was the ruler of demons. For the one who has not released the final farthing of the word before the end of life is never released from prison.

For eternal life is founded upon the four parts of the denarius, so that what you believe in your heart you confess with your mouth; what you confess you fulfill in your works; and what you have fulfilled you do not cease to teach. For “the one who does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

And his mother and brothers came. Standing outside, they sent word to him, calling him. The crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him: “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.” He answered them and said: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” Looking around at those who were sitting around him, he said: “Look, my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.”

Thus we may know that we are his brothers and mother if we fulfill the will of his Father, so that we may be his co-heirs—he who distinguishes not by sex but by deeds.

## CHAPTER IV

Again he began to teach beside the sea. A very large crowd gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat on the sea, while the whole crowd was on the land beside the sea. He taught them many things in parables, and in his teaching said to them:

“Listen. Behold, the sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell beside the road; the birds of the air came and ate it. Other seed fell upon rocky ground, where it did not have much soil; and it sprang up immediately because it had no depth of soil. When the sun rose, it was scorched, and because it had no root, it withered. Other seed fell among thorns; the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no fruit. Other seed fell upon good soil and yielded fruit, growing up and increasing; it produced one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold.”

And he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

When he was alone, the Twelve who were with him questioned him about the parable. And he said to them: “To you the mystery of the kingdom of God has been given; but to those outside, everything is presented in parables, [Col. 0602D] so that they may see and not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest they should ever turn and be forgiven their sins.”

And he said to them: “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The one who sows sows the word. These are those beside the road, where the word is sown: when they hear it, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts.

“And likewise, these are those sown upon rocky ground: when they hear the word, they immediately receive it with joy; but they have no root in themselves and are temporary. Then, when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, they are immediately scandalized.

“Others are those sown among thorns. These are the ones who hear the word, but the anxieties of the world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires concerning the rest enter in and choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.

“And these are those sown upon good soil: they hear the word, receive it, and bear fruit—one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold.”

The place of teaching indicates that the hearers were bitter and unstable. Therefore he speaks to them in parables, so that they might seek what they did not understand and, through the apostles whom they held in contempt, learn the mystery of the kingdom, which they themselves did not possess.

That the sea signifies this world is already known through frequent reading: it is bitter in taste and disturbed by the waves of vices. Yet they could have been rescued from it by the Lord himself, who changes bitter things into sweetness, turns sorrow into joy, and transforms detestable illnesses into salvation.

A parable is a comparison of differing things made under another likeness, according to the manner of providence, so that those who could not grasp heavenly things might receive what they heard through earthly comparisons.

The word *parabola* (παραβολή) is Greek and means “likeness” or “comparison,” when we indicate by certain comparisons what we wish to be understood. Thus we call someone “iron” when we wish him to be understood as hard and strong; and we compare someone swift to the winds or to birds.

What is contained in the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit is this: the Law, the Prophecy, and the Gospel. The mystery of the kingdom, displayed on the mountain in the mouth of three witnesses—that is, Moses, Elijah, and Jesus—consists in this.

And he said to them: “Does a lamp come in order to be placed under a bushel or under a bed? Is it not to be placed upon a lampstand? For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor has anything been concealed that will not come into the open. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

And he said to them: “See what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you. For to the one who has, it will be given; and from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.”

The lamp is the word concerning the three seeds. The bushel that covers it is the hearing of the disobedient. The lampstand is the apostles, whom the Lord’s hidden and concealed word illuminated. It is the parable of both seeds. It comes into the open when it is expounded by the Lord.

And he said: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.” For according to the measure of faith, understanding of the mysteries is distributed to each person; and more is added when virtues are also added to knowledge. “To the one who has, it will be given”: that is, the one who has faith will have virtue, and the one who has the work of the word will have understanding of the mystery. Conversely, the one who does not have faith falls short in virtue, and the one who does not have the work of the word lacks its understanding. And the one who does not understand has already lost his hearing, as though he had not heard.

And he said: “The kingdom of God is as if a man were to cast seed upon the earth, and sleep and rise night and day, while the seed germinates and grows, though he does not know how. For the earth produces fruit of itself: first the stalk, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”

Mark properly took up this parable as following the preceding ones. We know that the divine Scriptures generally display heavenly mysteries through earthly comparisons, as the entire body of the Gospels demonstrates.

The kingdom of God is the Church, which is ruled by God and itself rules human beings; it tramples contrary virtues and vices, as does the centurion who has soldiers under him.

The man who casts the seed is the Son of Man; the seed is the word of life; the earth is human hearts. The man’s sleep is the death of the Savior. The seed rises night and day. After Christ’s sleep, the number of believers grew more and more in faith through adversity and prosperity; and it increased in works, though he did not know it.

This is a figurative expression, very frequent in the divine Scriptures: it makes us ignorant of who will bring forth fruit to the end, while it says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

“For the earth produces fruit of itself,” while God awaits our will, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
