First, the stalk: that is, fear. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Then the ear: that is, tearful repentance. Then the full grain in the ear: that is, love. For “the fullness of the law is love.”

And when it has produced the fruit, he immediately sends the sickle, because the harvest is present.

And he said: “To what shall we compare the kingdom of God, or with what parable shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, is smaller than all the seeds that are in the earth. But when it has been sown, it grows up and becomes greater than all the garden plants, and it produces large branches, so that the birds of the air can dwell under its shade.”

And with many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear. But without a parable he did not speak to them.

The sickle is death or judgment, which cuts everything, because the harvest is present—that is, the consummation of the world—in which the righteous will rejoice, those who sowed in tears.

This seed is again likened to a grain of mustard seed, which is very small in fear but great in love, which is greater than all garden plants, because God is love. Also: “All flesh is grass.” And: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables.” It bears the branches of mercy and compassion. Under its shade the poor of Christ, who are the creatures of heaven, delight to dwell.

But privately he explained everything to his disciples. And on that day, when evening had come, he said to them: “Let us cross over to the other side.” Leaving the crowd, they took him with them just as he was in the boat; and other boats were with him. A great windstorm arose, and the waves were beating against the boat, so that the boat was already being filled.

They were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost recess of wisdom, because, having removed the tumult of evil thoughts, they remained in the solitude of virtues. For wisdom is found in a time of leisure. Then they came to the sea and were troubled by the waves.

And he was in the stern, sleeping upon a cushion. They woke him and said to him: “Teacher, does it not concern you that we are perishing?” He rebuked the wind and said to the sea: “Be silent; be still.” The wind ceased, and a great calm came about. And he said to them: “Why are you afraid? Do you still not have faith?”

They were filled with great fear and said to one another: “Who, then, is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

The stern contains the living within the skins of the dead, wards off the waves, and is strengthened by wood—that is, by the cross and death of the Lord. The Church is saved.

The cushion is the body of the Lord, to which divinity is inclined like a head. The stern is the beginning of the Church, in which the Lord sleeps in bodily death, because “he who guards Israel will never sleep.”

He rebukes the wind and the sea so that they may be silent, concerning which it is said: “You rule the power of the sea,” and so forth. The wind and the sea are demons and persecutors. He says to them, “Be silent,” when he restrains the decrees of wicked kings as he wills, because “it does not belong to man to direct his steps.”

The great calm is the peace of the Church after oppression, or contemplation after the active life.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0605B] And they came across the sea to the region of the Gerasenes. When he had come out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit met him from the tombs. He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no one could any longer bind him, even with chains. For he had often been bound with fetters and chains, but had broken the chains and shattered the fetters, and no one could subdue him.

Always, day and night, he was in the tombs and in the mountains, crying out and cutting himself with stones. When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and worshiped him. Crying out in a loud voice, he said: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” For Jesus was saying to him: “Come out, unclean spirit, from the man.” And he asked him: “What is your name?”

In the sixth virtue, the one who had his dwelling in the tombs is healed; no one could bind him, neither with chains [Col. 0605C] nor with fetters. No one could subdue him. He was crying out in the mountains and in the tombs and cutting himself with stones.

This is the utterly desperate people of the nations, whom the Apostle enumerates: proud, arrogant, unclean, bloodthirsty, idolatrous, shameful, bound neither by the law of nature, nor by God’s law, nor by human fear.

And he said to him: “My name is Legion, because we are many.” And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region. There was a large herd of pigs feeding there near the mountain. The spirits begged him, saying: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.” And Jesus immediately gave them permission.

The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed violently down into the sea and was suffocated in the sea. Those who were tending them fled and reported it in the city and in the fields. The people went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and saw the man who had been possessed by the demon sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

Those who had seen it told them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and about the pigs. And they began to beg him to leave their borders. As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed by the demon began to beg him to let him remain with him. But Jesus did not allow him; rather, he said to him:

“Go to your house and to your people, and announce to them how much the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.”

He went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed.

When Jesus had crossed over again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea. One of the rulers of the synagogue, named Jairus, came; when he saw him, he fell at his feet and begged him earnestly, saying:

“My daughter is at the point of death. Come, lay your hands upon her, so that she may be saved and live.”

And he went with him, and a large crowd followed him and pressed upon him. A woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, who had endured much at the hands of many physicians and had spent all that she possessed without gaining anything, but had rather grown worse, when she heard about Jesus—

Legion, that is, ten thousand, refers to those who fall at the Father’s right hand, which is Christ. To this demon the herd of pigs is entrusted, and it has no use except that, together, in the abyss—that is, in hell—it may be drowned without any regard for mercy through the violence of untimely death. Many who had been tending them flee from them.

For when a fool is scourged, a wise man becomes wiser. And they beg Jesus to leave their borders, as Peter says: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am unclean.” Let them not touch the ark of God, like Uzzah.

The healed man is sent to his house and preaches in the Decapolis, while the Jews are converted from the Roman kingdom, those who depend upon the Decalogue only in its letter.

After this Jairus the ruler of the synagogue comes, because when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved. Jairus is interpreted either as “illuminating” or “illuminated”: that is, the Jewish people, having laid aside the shadow of the letter, are enlightened and illumined by the Spirit. Falling at the feet of the Word—that is, humbling himself before the incarnation of Jesus—he asks on behalf of his daughter.

The one who lives for himself makes others live. Abraham, Moses, and Samuel ask on behalf of the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers.

In the seventh virtue, a dead woman is raised. But on the way, a bleeding woman touches the fringe from behind. She had lost her health and her resources through physicians who accomplished nothing.

On the seventh day God rested from all his works. When the dead woman within is raised, she is half-alive amid the crowds. The flow of blood causes sterility; hence it is said to the Church of the nations: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth.”

She came among the crowd from behind and touched his garment. For she was saying: “If I touch even his garment, I will be saved.” Immediately the source of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she had been healed of the affliction.

At once Jesus, knowing in himself the power that had gone out from him, turned toward the crowd and said: [Col. 0606D] “Who touched my garments?” His disciples said to him: “You see the crowd pressing upon you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” He looked around to see the woman who had done this.

But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell before him and told him the whole truth. He said to her: “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace, and be healed of your affliction.”

While he was still speaking, people came from the ruler of the synagogue’s house, saying: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?” But Jesus, hearing the message that was spoken, said to the ruler of the synagogue: “Do not fear; only believe.”

He did not allow anyone to follow him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, [Col. 0607A] and he saw the commotion, those weeping and wailing greatly. Entering, he said to them: “Why are you disturbed and weeping? The girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him.

But he put them all out, took the girl’s father and mother and those who were with him, and entered where the girl was lying. Taking the girl by the hand, he said to her: “Talitha cumi,” which is translated: “Girl, I say to you, arise.”

Immediately the girl rose and walked about. She was twelve years old, and they were astonished with great astonishment. He strictly ordered them that no one should know this, and he said that she should be given something to eat.

That is, after the resurrection. She touches the fringe, as though it were the cymbals and pomegranates that hang from the edges of the tunic of the high priest. The cymbal signifies confession; the pomegranate signifies the willingness for martyrdom and the brightness—or unity—of virtues.

To the girl it is said: “Talitha cumi,” that is, “Girl, arise.” To the ruler of the synagogue it is said: “Your daughter has died.” But Jesus said: “She is not dead, but sleeping.” Both are true: she is dead to you, but to me she is sleeping.

The girl was twelve years old, and the woman had suffered for twelve years. The sins of unbelievers become apparent at the beginning of the faith of believers. Hence it is said: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

## CHAPTER VI

And he departed from there and went to his own country, and his disciples followed him. When the sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue. Many who heard him were astonished at his teaching, saying:

“Where did this man get all these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him, and such mighty works performed by his hands? Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?”

And they took offense at him.

And Jesus said to them:

Then, going to his own country, Jesus is called the son of the carpenter. This too is mystical: the carpenter is the one who fashioned the dawn and the sun—that is, the first Church and the one that follows—for in their figure the woman and the girl are healed.

“For a prophet is not without honor except in his own country, among his own relatives, and in his own house.” And he could perform no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands upon a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled at their unbelief. He went around the villages in the surrounding area, teaching.

And he called the Twelve and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over unclean spirits. He instructed them to take nothing for the journey except a staff: no bag, no bread, and no money in their belt, but to wear sandals and not to put on two tunics.

And he said to them: “Wherever you enter a house, remain there until you leave that place. And whoever does not receive you or listen to you, when you leave there, shake the dust from your feet as a testimony to them.”

They went out and preached that people should repent. They cast out many demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them.

Lowliness often accompanies one’s origin, as in the question: “Whose son is Isaiah?” But the Lord regards humble things and recognizes lofty things from afar.

Then the twelve apostles are sent out, and authority is given to them to teach the commandments, so that word and deed may accompany one another; and along with invisible promises, visible mighty works may shine forth. When they anointed the sick with oil, they strengthened the weakness of faith by virtue.

And King Herod heard—for his name had become well known—and he was saying: “John the Baptist has risen from the dead, and therefore powers are at work in him.” But others were saying that he was Elijah; others, however, were saying: “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets.” It is not permitted to hide a lamp beneath a bushel.

When Herod heard this, he said: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead.” For Herod himself had sent for John and seized him and bound him in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, because he had married her. For John was saying to Herod: “It is not permitted for you to have your brother’s wife.” Herodias, however, was plotting against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not. For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and he protected him; and when he heard him, he did many things and listened to him gladly. And when a suitable day came, Herod made a banquet on his birthday for the leading men, tribunes, and foremost persons of Galilee. And when the daughter of Herodias herself had entered and danced and pleased Herod, and also those reclining with him, the king said to the girl: “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” And he swore to her: “Whatever you ask, I will give you—even half of my kingdom.” When she had gone out, she said to her mother: “What shall I ask for?” But she said: “The head of John the Baptist.” And when she had immediately entered hurriedly before the king, she asked, saying: “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” And the king was distressed because of his oath, and because of those reclining with him he did not want to disappoint her; but he sent an executioner and commanded that his head be brought on a platter. And he gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard this, they came, took his body, and placed it in a tomb.

By irony Herod is expressly called a seducer. The head of the Law, which is Christ, is cut off from his own body—that is, from the Jewish people—and given to a gentile girl, that is, to the Roman Church; and the girl gives it to her adulterous mother, that is, to the Synagogue, which will believe at the end. John’s body is buried, but his head is placed on a platter: the letter is covered by the earth, while the spirit is honored and received upon the altar.

And the apostles, returning to Jesus, reported to him everything that they had done and taught. They return to the place from which the rivers flow. Those who have been sent always give thanks to God for what they had received.

And he said to them: “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place.”

And this is particularly characteristic of Mark. He leads those whom he has chosen away by themselves, so that, while living among the wicked, they may not attend to wickedness—as Lot in Sodom, Job in the land of Uz, and Obadiah in the house of Ahab.

“Rest a little.” For there were many coming and going, and they did not even have time to eat. And going up into the boat, they departed to a deserted place by themselves. Many saw them going and recognized them, and on foot they hurried there from all the cities and arrived before them. And when Jesus went out, he saw a great crowd and had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. And when it was already a late hour, his disciples approached him, saying: “This is a deserted place, and the hour has already passed. Dismiss them, so that they may go into the neighboring farms and villages and buy food for themselves to eat.” And answering, he said to them: “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him: “Shall we go and buy bread for two hundred denarii and give it to them to eat?” And he said to them: “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said: “Five, and two fish.” And he commanded them to make everyone recline, group by group, on the green grass. And they reclined in groups of hundreds and fifties. And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, and broke the loaves, [Col. 0609B] and gave them to his disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among all, and they all ate and were satisfied. And they gathered up the fragments that remained—twelve full baskets—and also what remained of the fish. Those who had eaten were five thousand men. And immediately he compelled his disciples to get into the boat, so that they might go ahead of him across the strait to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the people. And after he had dismissed them, he went up onto the mountain to pray. And when it was evening, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he alone was on the land. And seeing them laboring at the rowing—for the wind was against them—around the fourth watch of the night he came toward them, walking upon the sea, and he wanted to pass them by. But when they saw him walking upon the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out. For they all saw him and were troubled. And immediately he spoke with them and said to them: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.” And he went up to them into the boat, and the wind ceased. And they were exceedingly astonished within themselves. For they had not understood about the loaves, because their heart was blinded. And when they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesareth and moored there. And when they had gone out of the boat, they immediately recognized him. And running through that whole region, they began to carry about on pallets those who were ill, wherever they heard that he was. And wherever he entered villages, farms, or cities, they placed the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment.

As birds in the branches of the mustard plant: the saints have little rest here, and long labor. But afterward it is said to them that they should rest from their labors. For there were people coming and going, [Col. 0609D] and they did not have time to eat in Noah’s ark. The animals that were inside were struggling to get outside, and those that were outside were bursting inside. So indeed it happens in the Church: Judas withdrew, and the thief entered. As long as there is departure from the faith, the Church has no rest, without sorrow. Rachel, weeping for her children, refused to be comforted. This is not the banquet at which the new wine is drunk. When will the new song be sung in the new heaven and on the new earth, by new people? When this mortal has put on immortality; when, with five loaves and two fish, five thousand people will be fed at the evening of life; and when the twelve baskets, filled with fragments by the eighth power, are gathered up; when they sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. What are the fragments? Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. When will the remnant be saved from Israel? When shall we see face to face what we read as written in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning Christ? Therefore, after the fourth watch of the night, Jesus restrains the swelling of the sea, walking upon it, and says: “Take courage; it is I,” because we shall see him as he is. Then the wind ceased, with Jesus sitting in the boat and reigning in it—the boat that is the universal Church. It follows:

And as many as touched him were saved. When will pain and groaning flee?

## CHAPTER VII

And the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around him. And when they saw some of his disciples eating bread with common hands—that is, unwashed hands—they found fault. For the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding to the tradition of the elders. And when they come from the marketplace, unless they have been baptized, they do not eat. And there are many other things that they have received to observe: washings of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and beds. And the Pharisees and scribes questioned him: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with common hands?” But he answered and said to them: “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.’ For abandoning the commandment of God, you hold to the tradition of men: washings of pitchers, cups, and many other things like these you perform.” And he said to them: “You set aside the commandment of God very effectively in order to observe your tradition. For Moses said: ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever curses his father or mother must surely die.’ But you say: ‘If a man says to his father or mother, “Corban”—that is, “Whatever benefit you might receive from me is a gift”—’ then you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, nullifying the word of God through your tradition, which you have handed down. And you do many other things like this.”

And calling the crowd to him again, he said to them: “Hear, all of you, and understand: nothing outside a person that enters into him can defile him; but the things that come out of a person are what defile a person. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” And when he had entered the house away from the crowd, his disciples questioned him about the parable. And he said to them: “Are you also so lacking in understanding? Do you not understand that everything external that enters a person cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but his belly, and goes out into the latrine, cleansing all foods?” But he was saying that the things that come out of a person are what defile a person. For from within, out of the human heart, evil thoughts proceed: adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. All these evils proceed from within and defile a person.

And rising from there, he went away into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And entering a house, he wanted no one to know, but he could not remain hidden. For a woman, as soon as she heard about him—whose daughter had an unclean spirit—entered and fell at his feet. For the woman was a gentile, Syrophoenician by race, and she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. And he said to her: “Let the children be filled first. For it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she answered and said to him: “Indeed, Lord, for even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.” And he said to her: “Because of this saying, go; the demon has gone out from your daughter.” And when she had gone to her house, she found the girl lying on the bed and the demon gone out.

The Pharisees’ excessive barking is blunted by the fork of reason—that is, by the rebuke of Moses and Isaiah—so that we may conquer those who oppose us and the heresies with the words of Scripture. Their seeing the disciples eat with unwashed hands signifies the future communion of the nations. The Pharisaic purity and baptism are barren. The apostolic communion, though unwashed, extends its branches as far as the sea—which is the greater fault. But the Pharisaic tradition concerning tables and clean vessels is not to be handled; it must be cut off and scraped away. For often the commandments of God yield to human traditions.

After this sign, the Syrophoenician woman, whose daughter had an unclean spirit, entered and fell at his feet. For she was a gentile woman; she begs for the daughter who is our mother, the Roman Church; and, born demonic, she is the barbarian nation of the West, whose faith made a sheep out of a dog. She desires to receive the crumb of spiritual understanding, not the bread broken according to the letter. The faithful, prudent, and humble person merits what she asks.

[Col. 0611C] And going out again from the region of Tyre, he came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, between the boundaries of the Decapolis. Here Mark specifically narrates the tenth power. Tyre is interpreted as “narrowness,” signifying Judea, to which the Lord says: “The bed has been made too narrow; the short covering cannot cover both,” so that he may transfer himself to other nations. Sidon is interpreted as “hunting”; it is our wild and untamed nation. And he came to the Sea of Galilee, which is “fruitful turning,” between the boundaries of the Decapolis, which is interpreted as “the commandments of the Decalogue.” The Savior is led by the apostles to save the nations; when the young man asked him what he should do, he replied: “You know the commandments.”

And they bring him a deaf man who could hardly speak. The human race is enumerated through its many members, as though one man were consumed by various maladies: in the first-formed man he is blinded while seeing; he becomes deaf while hearing; while smelling, he is made to sneeze; he becomes mute while speaking; he becomes crippled in the hand while extending it; he is bent over while being raised upright; he becomes dropsical while desiring; he becomes lame while advancing; he is covered with leprosy while being stripped naked; he is filled with a demon while seeking divinity; he dies by death while boldly excusing what he committed through disobedience.

And they begged him to lay his hand upon him. Many righteous men and patriarchs longed and desired that the Lord would become incarnate.

Taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears. He who deserves to be healed is always led away from turbulent thoughts, disordered actions, and undisciplined speech. The fingers that are put into his ears are the words of the Spirit, concerning whom it is said: “This is the finger of God,” and, “The heavens are the work of your fingers.”

And spitting, he touched his tongue. The spittle from the Lord’s flesh is divine wisdom, which loosens the bond of the human race’s lips, so that it may say: “I believe in God the Father almighty,” and so forth.

And looking up to heaven, he groaned. That is, he taught us to groan and to raise the treasure of our heart toward heaven; through the groaning of inward remorse, the empty joy of the flesh is cleansed, as it is said: “I roared from the groaning of my heart,” and so forth.

And he said to him: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened.” For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosened, and he spoke correctly. His ears were opened to hymns, songs, and psalms; his tongue was loosened so that he might pour forth the good word, which neither threats nor blows can restrain, as the Apostle Paul says: “I am bound, but the word of God is not bound in me.”

And he commanded them not to tell anyone. He taught that one must not glory in powers, but in the cross and in humiliation.

But the more he commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it, and they were astonished still more, saying: “He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.” A city set upon a mountain, visible from every side, cannot be hidden. Humility always precedes glory.

## CHAPTER VIII

In those days, when there was again a great crowd and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples and said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd, because for three days now they have remained with me and have nothing to eat. And if I dismiss them fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way. For some of them have come from far away.” And his disciples answered him: “From where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?” And he asked them: “How many loaves do you have?” They said: “Seven.” And he commanded the crowd to recline on the ground. And taking the seven loaves and giving thanks, he broke them and was giving them to his disciples to set before the people. [Col. 0612D] And they set them before the crowd. They also had a few small fish, and he blessed these and commanded them to be set before the people. And they ate and were satisfied. And they gathered up what remained of the fragments: seven baskets. Those who had eaten were about four thousand, and he dismissed them.

And immediately, getting into the boat with his disciples, he came into the district of Dalmanutha. And the Pharisees came out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven and testing him. And sighing deeply in spirit, he said: “Why does this generation seek a sign? Amen I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.” And dismissing them, he got into the boat again and went across the strait.

And they had forgotten to take bread, and except for one loaf they had none with them in the boat. And he instructed them, saying: “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” And they were discussing among themselves, saying: “It is because we have no bread.” When he realized this, Jesus said to them: “Why are you discussing that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Do you still have your heart blinded? Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand? How many baskets full of fragments did you gather?” They said to him: “Twelve.” “And when I broke the seven loaves for the four thousand, how many baskets of fragments did you take up?” And they said to him: “Seven.” And he said to them: “How do you still not understand?”

And they come to Bethsaida, and they bring a blind man to him. By the eleventh power, the seven loaves are broken for four thousand fasting people, and a few small fish are blessed; and seven baskets full of fragments are taken up. The seven loaves are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The four thousand are the year of the New Testament with its four seasons. The seven baskets are the first seven churches. The fragments of the loaves are the mystical understandings of the first week. The blessed little fish are the books of the New Testament, because after rising the Lord asks for a portion of a roasted fish, and offers his disciples a fish placed upon burning coals in the catch of fish.

After this they come to Bethsaida, which is interpreted as “house of the valley.” What else is this but the world, which is the valley of tears? By the twelfth power they bring a blind man who sees neither before nor behind—that is, one who was, who is, and who will be.

And they begged him to touch him. And taking the blind man by the hand—who is touched except the one who is pierced with remorse? [Col. 0613C]—he took the blind man by the hand so that, weeping, he might lament the blindness of his heart, as Jeremiah lamented the overthrow of the city of God, that is, of his own soul.

He led him outside the village, and spitting upon his eyes and laying his hands upon him, he asked him whether he saw anything. That is, he led him away from proximity to the wicked, for evil conversations corrupt good morals. And spitting upon his eyes, so that by the breath of the Holy Spirit he might see the Lord’s will; laying his hands upon him, he asked him whether he saw anything. Through the Lord’s works he sees his majesty. For from the greatness of creation the Creator is recognized.

And looking up, he said: “I see people, but they look like trees walking.” Then again he laid his hands upon his eyes, and he began to see; and he was restored, so that he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his house, saying: “Go to your house.” That is, considering all people superior to himself and judging himself unworthy, like David, to be called a man—rather, a dead dog and a single flea. Again he laid his hands upon his eyes, so that he might see everything clearly; that is, through visible works he might understand invisible things and things that the eye has not seen, and might contemplate with the clear eye of his soul its state after the rust of sin, with a pure heart. For: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” And he sent him to his house, so that he might see in himself what he had not seen before. For a person who despairs of salvation does not think that he can accomplish at all what, once enlightened by hope, he can easily complete. And he says to him:

[Col. 0614A] “And if you enter the village, tell no one.” And Jesus and his disciples went out to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he questioned his disciples, saying to them: “Who do people say that I am?” They answered him, saying: “John the Baptist; others, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” Then he said to them: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered and said to him: “You are the Christ.” And he sternly ordered them not to tell anyone about him. That is: Always recount your blindness to those near you, not your power, as Paul says: “I who was formerly a blasphemer and persecuted the Church of God.”

And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, be killed, and after three days rise again; and he was speaking the word openly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter, saying: “Get behind me, Satan, because you do not understand the things of God, but the things of men.” And calling the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them: “If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake and for the Gospel will save it. For what does it profit a person to gain the whole world and suffer the loss of his soul? Or what can a person give in exchange for his soul? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

As a skilled helmsman anticipates a storm in calm weather and wants his sailors to be ready, so the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to follow after me, let him deny himself”—that is, let one become another through another. After the confirmation of the cross, the glory of the resurrection is shown. Hence follows the thirteenth power.

## CHAPTER IX

And he was saying to them: “Amen I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God coming in power.” And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain apart, by themselves; and he was transfigured before them. And his garments became shining and exceedingly white, like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make white. And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were speaking with Jesus. And Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here; and let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” For he did not know what he was saying. For they were terrified by fear. And a cloud came, overshadowing them, and a voice came from the cloud, saying: “This is my most beloved Son; hear him.” And immediately, looking around, they saw no one else with them except Jesus alone.

And as they were descending from the mountain, he commanded them not to tell anyone what they had seen, except when the Son of Man had risen from the dead. After six days he was transfigured on a high mountain before his disciples, so that those who had seen with their own eyes the glory of the future resurrection would not fear the reproaches of the cross.

[Col. 0615A] And they kept the word to themselves, questioning what “when he has risen from the dead” meant. And they asked him, saying: “Why then do the Pharisees and scribes say that Elijah must come first?” He answered them: “When Elijah comes, he will first restore all things. And how is it written concerning the Son of Man?—that he should suffer many things and be despised. But I say to you that Elijah has also come, and they did to him whatever they wished, just as it is written concerning him.” This is particularly characteristic of Mark: when death has been swallowed up in victory, they will no longer be remembered, nor rise up into the heart, when the Lord removes the filth of the daughter of Zion and takes away every tear from the face of the saints.

And coming to his disciples, he saw a great crowd around them and scribes arguing with them. And immediately, when all the people saw Jesus, they were astonished, and they were afraid; and running up, they greeted him. There is no rest for a human being under the sun. Envy always kills the little ones, and lightning strikes the great mountains. Some come to the Church with faith; others, envious, come with arrogance. And the people, seeing him, were astonished, and they were afraid. There is no fear in love. Fear belongs to servants; to be astonished belongs to fools.

And he asked them: “What are you arguing about among yourselves?” And one of the crowd answered and said: “Teacher, I brought my son to you, who has a mute spirit. Wherever it seizes him, it throws him down; he foams, grinds his teeth, and becomes rigid. And I told your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” He answered them, saying: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you? Bring him to me.”

And they brought him. And when it saw him, the spirit immediately convulsed him; and falling to the ground, he rolled about foaming. And he asked his father: “How long has it been since this happened to him?” The Lord knows, yet he asks so that confession may bring forth salvation and the murmuring of our heart may be released through pious words, as in: “First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.”

Then, by the fourteenth power, one of the crowd brings a son possessed by an unclean spirit, and the rest follows. The disciples could not cure him, but the Savior cured him. The unbelief of both parties hindered salvation. The spirit tears apart the one who foams, grinds his teeth, and becomes rigid. The sinner foams with envy and foolishness; he grinds his teeth with anger; he becomes rigid through sloth. The spirit tears him apart as he approaches salvation, which is its favored food, drawing those whom it desires into its belly through terrors and losses, as it did with Job. Jesus asks how long this has been happening.

But he said: “Here the gentile people are signified, among whom from birth the useless worship of idols grew, so that in foolishness they might sacrifice their children to demons.” Hence it follows:

“From childhood, and often it has thrown him into fire and water in order to destroy him. But if you can do anything, help us and have mercy on us.” For some among the nations worshiped fire, others water.

But Jesus said to him: “If you can believe”—here he indicates the freedom of the will.

“All things are possible for one who believes.” And immediately the boy’s father cried out with tears and said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” What are “all things” except those things that are asked for in the name of Jesus—that is, of salvation—with tears? The boy’s father was saying: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” Our belief, like a tongue furnished with a beak, is weak unless it stands supported by the strength of God’s help. Faith with tears obtains the desired requests, as in: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”

And when Jesus saw the crowd running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it. From this point Mark gives his distinctive account. The Lord’s rebuke is his power.

“Deaf and mute spirit, I command you.” God imputes to the spirit what the devil does to the human being: though that man never heard or spoke, the sinner fully hears and speaks.

[Col. 0616B] “Come out of him, and never enter him again.” And crying out and greatly convulsing him, it came out of him. When it leaves a person, it never returns if he has fastened his heart with the bolts of humility and love and has secured the door with a fortification. Therefore the prophet says: “Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me.”

And he became as though dead, so that many were saying: “He is dead.” But Jesus, taking him by the hand, raised him, and he arose. For when they have been healed, it is said to them: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Therefore the infirmity of Christians is not death, but a likeness of death.

And when they had entered the house, his disciples questioned him privately: “Why could we not cast it out?” And he said to them: “This kind can come out by nothing except prayer and fasting.” And departing from there, they were passing through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know. But he was teaching his disciples and saying to them: “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him; and after he has been killed, he will rise on the third day.” But they did not understand the saying, and they were afraid to question him.

Foolishness belongs to the luxury of the flesh and is healed by fasting and prayer. Anger and sloth are driven away by prayer. The appropriate medicine must be applied to each wound. What is applied to the heel does not heal the eye. Bodily passions must be healed by fasting, and the diseases of the mind by prayer.

And they came to Capernaum. Capernaum means “village of consolation.” The interpretation accords with the preceding saying, in which he says: “And after he has been killed, he will rise on the third day.” A grain of wheat dies so that it may be gathered in greater abundance; if it does not die, it remains alone.

And when they were in the house, he asked them: “What were you discussing on the way?” But they were silent. For on the way they had argued among themselves about which of them was greater. And sitting down, he called the twelve and said to them: “If anyone wishes to be first, he will be last of all and servant of all.” And taking a child, he placed him in their midst. And when he had embraced him, he said to them: “Whoever receives one of these children in my name receives me; and whoever receives me does not receive me, but him who sent me.”

John answered him, saying: “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, one who does not follow us, and we forbade him.” But Jesus [Col. 0617A] said: “Do not forbid him. For there is no one who performs a power in my name and can quickly speak evil of me. For whoever is not against you is for you. For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you belong to Christ, amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward. And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone drawn by a donkey were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off.”

On the way they had been discussing leadership; the discussion is similar to the place. For leadership is entered into in one way and abandoned in another; as long as it is held, it slips away; and it is uncertain in which dwelling—that is, on which day—it will end. Therefore he says: “Whoever wishes to be first should be a servant like a child.”

[Col. 0617B] “It is good for you to enter life maimed”—that is, without desiring leadership—

“than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire.” The two hands are leadership and pride. Cut off pride while retaining humble leadership.

“Where their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.” And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is good for you to enter eternal life lame than, having two feet, to be thrown into the Gehenna of unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out. It is good for you to enter the kingdom of God one-eyed than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the Gehenna of fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.

The worm is the belated conscience. The fire is punishment without completion. Therefore it is said through the prophet: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled for yourselves.”

For everyone will be salted with fire. It is wonderfully said: What is seasoned with salt wards off the worm of decay. But what—namely, salt sprinkled upon flesh—consumes everything; this was done according to the Law with the sacrifices that were burned upon the altar. Therefore it was commanded that salt be offered with every victim and sacrifice. Salt is the sweetness of wisdom, and fire is the grace of the Holy Spirit. Everyone will be salted with fire, because every elect person is seasoned with wisdom, so that he may become a worthy victim for God’s altars. Therefore he rightly adds:

“And every victim will be salted with salt.” For that person is truly the Lord’s victim who, cleansing body and soul from vices, consecrates himself to God through the love of the Holy Spirit. He is not sprinkled with salt but consumed by fire when not only the contagion of sin is driven away, but also the pleasure of the present life is removed, and the whole mind sighs for the manner of life to come. Hence: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” And: “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies,” and so forth.

The altar of God is the heart of the good; the victims and sacrifices are the good works of the faithful. Salt is present in every sacrifice, because no good work exists without wisdom. Fire consumes sacrifices upon the altar; with this fire he himself baptized us, with the Holy Spirit and fire. Fire refers to tribulations. This concerns the preceding words, where the members that cause stumbling are commanded to be torn away, because to be salted with fire also means to be exercised by temptations, and for the love of Christ to deny ourselves those beloved persons and neighbors who are close to us. For every victim will be salted. The Lord’s victim is the human race, which is salted here by the reasoning of wisdom, while the corruption of blood—the custody of decay, that is, the mother of worms—is consumed, and there it is tested by purifying fire.

“Salt is good. But if salt has become tasteless, with what will you season it?” Tasteless salt is the person who loves leadership, who does not dare to rebuke and confess lest he be expelled from the synagogue, loving human glory more than God’s.

“Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.” Let the saltiness of correction be tempered by love of neighbor, and let the salt of justice season love of neighbor.

And in the house his disciples again questioned him about the same matter. [Col. 0618B] And this is particularly significant: repeated knowledge of the word produces not disgust but hunger and thirst, as in the saying of Wisdom: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still.” Once tasted, the honey-sweet sayings of wisdom yield a many-sided flavor when examined more carefully. When the Lord rains down manna to be eaten beneath the sun, melting like wax and yielding softened words, it is as in the saying: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” It is hardened by fire, as in: “Bread strengthens the human heart.” It is made rough for harsh things, as in: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

## CHAPTER X

And rising from there, he came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. And crowds gathered around him again, and as he was accustomed to do, he taught them again. And the Pharisees approached and questioned him whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife, testing him. But he answered and said to them: “What did Moses command you?” They said: “Moses permitted us to write a bill of divorce and to dismiss her.” Jesus answered and said to them: “Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote this commandment for you. But from the beginning of creation God made them male and female. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

The Pharisees questioned him whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife, testing him. Again, after a little while:

And when they were in the house, his disciples again questioned him about the same matter [Col. 0618D]. And he said to them: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her. And if a wife divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.”

And they were bringing little children to him so that he might touch them. But the disciples rebuked those bringing them. When Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them: “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them; for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven. Amen, I say to you: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will not enter it.” And embracing them and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them.

And when he had gone out onto the road, someone ran up and knelt before him, asking him and saying: “Good Teacher, what must I do to receive eternal life?” But Jesus said to him: “Why do you call me good? [Col. 0619A] No one is good except the one God. You know the commandments: You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not defraud; honor your father and mother.”

But he answered and said to him: “Teacher, I have observed all these things from my youth.” Jesus looked at him, loved him, and said to him: “You lack one thing: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” But he was saddened by this saying and went away grieving, for he had many possessions.

And Jesus, looking around, said to his disciples: “How difficult it will be for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God!” The disciples were astonished at his words. But Jesus answered again and said to them: “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God for those who trust in money! It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle [Col. 0619B] than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

They were even more astonished, saying to one another: “Then who can be saved?” Jesus looked at them and said: “With human beings it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God.”

And Peter began to say to him: “Look, we have left everything and followed you.” Jesus answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now, in this present time—houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields, together with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them; they were astonished, [Col. 0619C] and those following were afraid. Taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes and the elders; they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the gentiles. They will mock him, spit upon him, scourge him, and kill him; and on the third day he will rise.”

And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him, saying: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask.” He said to them: “What do you want me to do for you?” They said: “Grant that one of us may sit at your right hand and the other at your left in your glory.”

But Jesus said to them: “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” They said to him: “We can.” Jesus said to them: [Col. 0619D] “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized you will be baptized; but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to grant, but is for those for whom it has been prepared.”

When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John. Jesus called them and said to them: “You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it is not so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to become great among you will be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you will be the servant of all. For the Son of Man also did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

That is, concerning the state of marriage, as the following chapter indicates. And he says to them: “Whoever [Col. 0620A] divorces his wife, and so forth.” But when Mark says, “His disciples questioned him again,” it was not the disciples who questioned him first, but the Pharisees. The second question, however, was put again by others—that is, by the apostles—about the same matter concerning which the Pharisees had questioned him.

And they come to Jericho. Jericho is interpreted as “moon” or “anathema,” which is fitting for one approaching the Passion. For the decline of Christ’s flesh is the new moon of the heavenly Jerusalem. Hence, leaving Jericho, they approach Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace.

And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a very large crowd, Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, a blind man, was sitting beside the road begging. The blind man is illumined by the fifteenth virtue. The blindness that has come upon the Jews in part will be illumined at the end, when he sends them the prophet Elijah. “Begging beside the road”: whoever preserves Scripture but does not fulfill it is hungry, begging beside the road.

When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” Through the merits of the patriarchs, the Jewish people are illumined. The Lord, merciful and compassionate, is present to them: illuminating the blind, raising up the fallen, loving the poor, and preserving the strangers.

Many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” Sins and demons silence the cry of the poor, whom the Lord heard. But he cried out even more. As the battle grows heavier, hands must be raised with a cry to the stone of help—that is, to Jesus the Nazarene [Col. 0620C].

And Jesus stood still and commanded him to be called. And they called the blind man, saying to him: “Take heart; rise, he is calling you.” How fitting is the order of salvation: first we hear, then we cry out, afterward we are called, and finally we rise. We hear through the prophets, cry out through faith, are called through the apostles, rise through repentance, are stripped of our former garment through baptism, and are questioned according to our will. Hence what follows:

He threw off his garment, sprang up, and came to him. And Jesus answered and said to him. He is said to spring up stripped of the old man, like a young deer leaping over the hills, springing over the mountains: casting off sloth, contemplating the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles on high, he stretches himself toward things above.

[Col. 0620D]

“What do you want me to do for you?” Jesus, considering his eager will, rewards him with the fulfillment of his desire. Hence elsewhere he also says: “Whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

But the blind man said to him: “Rabboni, that I may see.” He asks one thing from the Lord: he seeks to see the will of the Lord, and then, seeing, to visit his temple. Hence what follows:

Jesus said to him: “Go, your faith has saved you.” And immediately he saw and followed him on the road. The blind man was begging on the road that says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” This is the narrow way that leads upward to the heights of Jerusalem and Bethany, to the Mount of Olives, which is the mountain of light and consolation.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0621A]

And when they were approaching Jerusalem and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives—which is the vision of peace, in which happiness remains fixed and immovable, and which, according to the apostle, is the mother of all who believe and live well in Christ—

he sent two of his disciples and said to them: “Go into the village opposite you, and immediately upon entering it you will find a colt tied, on which no human being has yet sat. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it,’ and he will immediately send it here.”

They went and found the colt tied outside before the door, at the crossroads, and they untied it. The disciples of Christ are called and sent in pairs, because charity does not exist with one alone, as it is said: “Woe to the one who is alone,” and so forth. Two lead the Hebrews out of Egypt. Two carry the cluster of grapes from the holy land. Thus leaders should always join work and knowledge; two should bring forth the commandments from the two tablets; they should be washed and wash others from the two fountains; they should carry the Lord’s ark with two poles; and between the two cherubim they should know God, singing psalms in spirit and mind.

They lead the colt, tied and untamed; they untie and tame it. It is the gentile people, tied before the door of faith by the bonds of their sins, standing at the crossroads and wavering in the freedom of choice between life and death.

Some of those standing there said to them: “What are you doing, untying the colt?” They told them as Jesus had commanded them, and the people let them go. And they brought the colt [Col. 0621C] to Jesus—as though they were saying: “Who can forgive sins?”

And they put their garments on it—that is, through the sacraments of baptism they bring the first robe of immortality.

And he sat upon it—that is, he began to reign in it—so that sin might not reign in wanton flesh, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

Many spread their garments on the road. Who are the feet, except those who carry, and the last ones whom the apostle appointed for judgment? Even if they are not below, where the Lord sat, they are nevertheless instructed by John together with the soldiers.

Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. Both those going before and those following cried out, saying: “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name [Col. 0621D] of the Lord; blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming; hosanna in the highest.”

This pertains more to prayer and sacrament than to necessity. “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree”: narrow at the roots, broad in flowers and fruits, because they are the good fragrance of Christ; and they spread the road of God’s commandments with a good reputation.

Those going before are the prophets, and those following are the apostles, so that “the abyss calls to the abyss”—that is, one law calls forth another. “Hosanna,” that is, “save,” they say in the highest and in the depths, so that the righteous may be built up upon the ruin of the angels, and those on earth and beneath the earth may be saved by him who is blessed, conquering and coming in the name of the Lord—that is, of his Father, since the Son received his name from the Father, and the Father from the Son.

[Col. 0622A]

And he entered Jerusalem, into the temple. After looking around at everything, since it was already evening, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve. The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, he was hungry. Seeing a fig tree from a distance with leaves, he went to see whether perhaps he might find something on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And answering, he said to it: “May no one ever again eat fruit from you.” And his disciples heard this.

And they came to Jerusalem. When he had entered the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. He would not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple. And he taught, saying to them: “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it [Col. 0622B] a den of robbers.”

When the chief priests and the scribes heard this, they sought how they might destroy him. For they feared him, because the whole crowd was astonished at his teaching.

Jesus enters the temple; in the evening he goes out to Bethany with the Twelve; in the morning he comes to Judea; and at the evening of the world he visits us. The hungry Lord, desiring the salvation of human beings, saw from a distance a fig tree adorned with leaves but not with fruit—that is, the synagogue clothed in human commandments and swept clean with superstitions—and he denies it fruit forever.

Then he entered the temple and drove out the sellers and buyers and overturned the tables and seats—that is, those who sell honor and buy ranks. For it is written according to Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” But you have made it a den of robbers, according to Jeremiah [Col. 0622C].

And when evening had come, he went out of the city. As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree dried up from its roots. This is also to be understood literally. Leaving darkness behind him, he went out from the city—as the sun goes out—to another city that is benevolent and obedient. When they returned in the morning, they saw the dried fig tree. The sun sets and the sun rises: light is taken away from the scribes and shines in the apostles. The fig tree dried up from its roots is the synagogue, beginning with Cain and the others from whom all blood is required, from Abel to Zechariah.

And Peter remembered and said to him: “Rabbi, look, the fig tree that you cursed has withered.” And Jesus answered and said to them: “Have faith in God.” Peter recognizes the root that has withered and been cut away; in its place succeeds the beautiful, fruitful olive tree, called by the Lord [Col. 0622D]. Hence what follows:

“Amen, I say to you: whoever says to this mountain”—that is, to Christ, who is the mountain growing from the stone cut without hands—

“‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart but believes that whatever he says will happen, it will be done for him. Therefore I say to you: whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will happen for you.”

This happened when the apostles said: “We are rightly transferred to the gentiles, because you judged yourselves unworthy of hearing the word of God.” The text continues:

“And whenever you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins.”

Mark, in his customary manner, has included the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer in one prayer. For the one to whom everything has been forgiven—what more will he ask than that he persevere in what he has obtained?

And they came again to Jerusalem. As they were walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders came to him and said: “By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority to do them?”

Jesus answered and said to them: “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from human beings? Answer me.”

They reasoned among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From human beings’—” [Col. 0623B] they feared the people, for everyone held that John truly was a prophet. And answering, they said to Jesus: “We do not know.”

They are darkened by envy of the lamp, as it is said: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with shame.”

And Jesus answered and said to them: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” Here God is overthrown together with the perverse.

## CHAPTER XII

And he began to speak to them in parables: “A man cultivated a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit, built a tower, and leased it to tenants; then he went abroad. At the proper time he sent a servant to the tenants to receive from them some of the vineyard’s fruit. But they seized him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent another servant to them; they wounded him in the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and they killed him; and many others, beating some and killing others.

“Still having one son, his beloved, he sent him to them last, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But the tenants said to one another: ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ And seizing him, they killed him and cast him outside the vineyard.

“What then will the lord of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture:

‘The stone that the builders rejected,
this has become the cornerstone;
this was done by the Lord,
and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

They sought to seize him, but they feared the crowd. For they understood that he had spoken this parable against them [Col. 0623D]. And they left him and went away.

Then they sent to him some Pharisees and Herodians, to trap him in his words. They came and said to him. The man is God, who is called Father by a human affection. The vineyard is the house of Israel. The fence is the protection of the angels. The pit is the law; the tower is the temple; the tenants are the priests. God’s journey abroad is the freedom of our will. The servants sent are the prophets. The fruit of the vineyard is obedience.

Of the prophets, some were beaten, some wounded, and some killed. The beloved and last son is the Only-Begotten. “They will respect my son”: this is said ironically. “They cast him outside the vineyard,” that is, outside the people, saying: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon.”

The vineyard is given to others—that is, to those coming from the East and West, [Col. 0624A] the South and the North, and reclining with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God.

This is the rejected stone, which the corner bears, joining the lamb with bread in the pure supper, bringing the old Testament to an end and beginning the new. This performs wonders in our eyes, like topazion [topaz].

Then they question him with honeyed words and surround him like bees, carrying honey in their mouths and a sting on their backs, saying:

“Teacher, we know that you are truthful and do not care about anyone; for you do not look at people’s faces, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?”

Knowing their deceit, he said to them: “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius, that I may see it.” They brought one, and he said to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said to him: “Caesar’s.”

Jesus answered and said to them: “Then give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him.

And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if someone’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, his brother should take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

“There were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died without leaving offspring. The second took her and died, and he too left no offspring; and the third likewise. All seven took her, and they left no offspring. Last of all, the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.” [Col. 0624C]

Jesus answered and said to them: “Is this not why you are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven.”

For evil thoughts are sunk into the depths of the earth, because they come out from there and are again rolled about in the same mire. This clearly happened to the Jews when, blaspheming, they wallowed in the blood of the innocent Christ.

He answered those who possessed Caesar’s image: you, who have received a coin stamped with Caesar’s image, willingly return yourselves to God. The light of God’s countenance, not Caesar’s, has been marked upon us.

“And the Sadducees come to him,” and so forth. We shall discuss this question elsewhere; here we are not concerned with another’s error. But that human beings will be like the angels of God means that no one there dies and no one there is born—neither infant nor old person.

The barren woman who left no offspring from the seven brothers and died last signifies nothing other than the Jewish synagogue, left as though dead by the sevenfold Spirit, who filled the seven patriarchs. They did not leave her the offspring of Abraham, which is Jesus Christ. Although a child was born to them, he was nevertheless given to us gentiles. This woman was dead to Christ and will not be joined in the resurrection to any of the seven patriarchs.

For the number seven signifies the totality of the perfect. Thus, conversely, through Isaiah it is said: “Seven women shall seize one man”—that is, seven churches, whom the one Lord loves, reproves, and chastises, and who worship him with one faith. [Col. 0625A]

These are the seven baskets full of fragments of bread. The breads are the words of the Holy Spirit, while the baskets are the churches. Jesus blessed and broke these loaves, and his disciples distributed them to the crowd, when on the seventh day he blessed all his works, resting in them.

Thus, when light was made on the first day, which is wisdom; and the firmament on the second, which is understanding; and the dry land on the third, which is counsel; and the luminaries were kindled on the fourth, which are virtues; and birds and fish were made on the fifth, which are knowledge; and a living soul on the sixth—that is, the human being made in the image of God, which is piety—on the seventh day, through the spirit of the fear of the Lord, which remains holy forever and ever and fills the world, the holy Church is filled, having neither spot nor wrinkle.

But why is the sevenfold Church—that is, the perfect Church—filled with fear? Because “the righteous will scarcely be saved,” and he prays: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight.”

Hence the Spirit sang the psalter according to these seven qualities, recalling in it what our negligence brought forth; what diligence sought; what divine providence bestowed; what the enemy’s instigation robbed; what slippery forgetfulness removed; what human frailty introduced; and what unconsidered ignorance deceived.

We find all these seven affections expressed in the Psalms, as in the following:

1. “He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity.”
2. “I rose early and cried out.”
3. “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”
4. “My enemies have surrounded my soul.”
5. “I have been forgotten like one dead from the heart.”
6. “For my loins are filled with mockery.”
7. “Do not remember, O Lord, the sins of my youth and my ignorances.”

The sevenfold Spirit cleanses and illumines these affections, so that seven lamps burning from the south may drive away the northern darkness in the Lord’s tabernacle.

The spirit of wisdom repels negligence in the slothful. The spirit of understanding reasonably seeks diligence. The spirit of counsel wisely discovers divine providence. The spirit of strength courageously restrains instigations. The spirit of knowledge does not allow slippery forgetfulness to remain long and wholly. The spirit of piety mercifully forgives human frailty. The spirit of the fear of God ardently burns away and completely fills unconsidered ignorance.

Wisdom builds the house. Understanding finds the helm. Counsel makes good distinctions. Strength possesses the soul in patience. Through knowledge, the riches of faith and salvation are acquired. Through piety, the prosperity of the present and future life is established. Through fear, humility is preserved and every sin expelled, because the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

But concerning the dead, that they rise, have you not read in the book of Moses, at the bush, how God spoke to him, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. Therefore you are greatly mistaken.

In this is your likeness: in the bush the fire burned, but did not consume its thorns. So my word inflames you, yet it did not take up your thorns, sprung from the curse, when it said: “The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” By naming God three times, he indicated the Trinity. “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” By repeating one God, he signifies one substance. Those live who claimed the portion they had chosen; those are dead who lost what they had claimed.

And one of the scribes came up, having heard them disputing, and seeing that he had answered them well, questioned him about which commandment was first of all.

Jesus answered him: “The first commandment of all is: Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.”

What is this question of the problem, common to all experts in the law, except that the commandments are arranged differently in Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy? Hence he introduced not one commandment but two. For from these two breasts, raised upon the bride’s chest, our infancy is nourished.

And the scribe said to him: “Well said, Teacher; you have spoken truthfully, for there is one God, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

Jesus, seeing that he had answered wisely, said to him: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And no one dared to question him any longer.

And Jesus answered and taught in the temple, saying: “How do the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself said in the Holy Spirit:

‘The Lord said to my Lord:
Sit at my right hand,
until I place your enemies
as a footstool for your feet.’

Therefore David himself calls him Lord; so how is he his son?” And the great crowd heard him gladly.

And in his teaching he said to them: “Beware of the scribes, who wish to walk in long robes, to be greeted in the marketplace, to sit in the foremost seats in the synagogues, and to have the places of honor at banquets; they devour widows’ houses under the pretext of lengthy prayer. They will receive a more severe judgment.”

Why is the one who comes cunningly not far away? Ignorance is farther from the kingdom of God than knowledge. Hence above he said to the Sadducees: “You are mistaken,” he said, “because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.”

And Jesus taught them in the temple—that is, he spoke openly about himself before them, so that they would be without excuse, and so that fire might kindle the dry examples of the scribes and Pharisees, who wish to walk in long robes.

And Jesus sat opposite the treasury—that is, the place where wealth is guarded.

He watched how the crowd put bronze coins into the treasury, and many rich people put in much. But when one poor widow came, she put in two small coins, which is a quadrans.

Calling his disciples, he said to them: “Amen, I say to you: this poor widow has put in more than all those who have put into the treasury. For they all contributed from what they had in abundance, but she, from her poverty, put in everything she had—all her livelihood.” [Col. 0627A]

Who are the rich, except those who bring forth from the treasure of their heart things new and old—the uncertain and hidden things of the wisdom of both Testaments? And who is the poor woman, except I and those like me, who give what I can and desire to explain to you what I cannot?

God considers not how much—as you have heard—but from what source. Anyone can offer a quadrans. This is the cake of bread in Leviticus, which is ready willingness. Why is it called a quadrans? Because it consists of three things: thought, word, and deed.

When he says that she put in all her livelihood, all the pleasure of the body consists in livelihood. Hence it is said: “All the labor of a human being is for his mouth.”

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0627B]

And as he was leaving the temple, one of his disciples said to him: “Teacher, look at the kinds of stones and the kinds of buildings!” Jesus answered and said to him: “Do you see all these great buildings? Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.”

And as he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew questioned him privately: “Tell us, when will these things happen, and when will all these things begin to be fulfilled?”

Jesus answered and began to say to them: “See that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will deceive many. When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be afraid; for these things must happen, but the end is not yet.
