For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be earthquakes in various places and famines. These are the beginning of sorrows.

“But look to yourselves. They will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them. And the Gospel must first be preached to all the nations.

“When they lead you away and hand you over, do not deliberate beforehand about what you will say; rather, say whatever is given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.

“Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his child; children will rise against their parents and put them to death. You will be hated by all on account of my name. But whoever endures to the end will be saved.

“When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be—let the reader understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. The one on the housetop must not come down into the house or enter it to take anything from his house. And the one who is in the field must not turn back to take his garment.

“Woe to those who are pregnant and those nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For those days will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of creation, which God created, until now, nor will there be again.

“And if the Lord had not shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days.

“Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘Look, there he is,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. You, therefore, keep watch. See, I have foretold everything to you.

“But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars of heaven will fall, and the powers that are in heaven will be shaken. Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.

“Learn a parable from the fig tree. When its branch has already become tender and it has put forth leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, at the doors.

“Amen, I say to you: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.”

He enumerates for the disciples the calamity of the final age—that is, the destruction of the temple together with its people and its letter. Concerning this it is said that not one stone will be left upon another [Col. 0628B]—that is, the testimonies of the prophets will not remain upon those to whom the Jews applied them, as in the cases of the Apostle, Ezra, Zerubbabel, and the Maccabees. Everything he enumerates should be hoped for rather than expounded.

False Christs and false prophets; nation against nation and kingdom against kingdom; earthquakes; the beating of preachers; the preaching of the Gospel to the ends of the earth, so that before the judgment the Church may cry out: “From the ends of the earth I have cried to you, O Lord.”

Members of a household rising against members of the household; the abomination in the temple; flight into the mountains, so that the one who has climbed to the heights may not descend to the depths.

Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath—that is, lest the fruits of your work come to an end with the end of time. For winter brings the fruit to an end, while the Sabbath signifies time.

Great tribulation and shortened days for the sake of the elect, lest the wickedness of this age change their understanding, as is said concerning Noah.

After these things the sun will be darkened over frozen hearts, as in winter; the moon will not shine in the clear weather of dissensions; and the stars will fall from their light when scarcely any seed of Abraham remains, to whom the stars are likened. The powers in heaven will be moved to the anger of vengeance when they are sent by the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with power—he who earlier descended like rain upon Gideon’s fleece, in humility.

And he will gather the elect from the four winds, like wheat winnowed from the threshing floor of the whole earth.

This parable of the fig tree is a prophecy. The leaves that have appeared are present words; the summer that is near is the day of judgment. On that day each tree will reveal what it had within: whether something dry, to be burned, or something green, to be planted in Eden with the tree of life, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations—that is, the words by which it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth. The text continues:

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father.”

“Watch.” What does it mean when he says, “neither the Son”? Concerning him it is said: “The Father is greater than I”—that is, his body placed on earth, which is the Church.

“Watch and pray, for you do not know when the time is. It is like a man who went abroad, left his house, and gave his servants authority over each task, commanding the doorkeeper to keep watch. Therefore watch, for you do not know when the master of the house will come, whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at the crowing of the cock, or in the morning, lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping.”

Vigilance is the work of the mind before the death of the body. The man going abroad is Christ’s body raised into heaven, leaving his house, which is the Church. Giving his servants authority over each task means the eight talents according to Matthew, or the ten minas according to Luke. And he commands the doorkeeper to keep watch—that is, the one who preaches, to whom it is said: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, I will require his blood from your hand.”

“Therefore watch,” and so forth. “In the evening or at midnight,” when the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed, lest he find you sleeping. For the one who sleeps attends not to true bodies but to phantoms, and remains empty and wakeful concerning the things he had seen in dreams. Such indeed are those whom love of the world carries away during life and abandons after life: what they dreamed, they regarded as certain.

The text continues:

“What I say to you I say to all: Watch.” This either concludes the discourse, so that the final command addressed to all may be heard through the first.

## CHAPTER XIV
It was Passover and Unleavened Bread two days later. Now let us sprinkle our book with blood, and the thresholds of the houses, and let us encircle the house of our prayer with scarlet thread, and hold scarlet in our hand, so that we may bind Sarah; so that we may be able to expound the red heifer slain in the valley. “Passover” is interpreted as “passing over”; but *Phase* means “sacrifice.” In the sacrifice of the lamb and the people’s passage through the sea—or through Egypt—the passion of Christ and the redemption of the people from hell [Col. 0629C] were prefigured. He visits us after two days, that is, at the age of the full moon, Christ perfected, so that we may eat the flesh of the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world without any darkened part, in one house, which is the one chosen Church, his mother, the catholic Church; shod with charity and armed with virtue, let us eat, saying: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.”

And the chief priests and scribes were seeking how they might seize him by deceit and kill him. They were saying, however: “Not during the feast, lest perhaps there be an uproar among the people.” And when he was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper and reclining at table, a woman came bearing an alabaster vessel of precious spikenard ointment; and when she had broken the alabaster vessel, she poured it over his head [Col. 0629D].

From rulers iniquity has gone forth in Babylon. For when the head has been killed, the whole body is weakened. Hence wretched people do what their leaders contrive. They avoid the feast day, which suits them. For there is no festivity for those who have lost life and mercy. Jesus came to Bethany. The young stag of the deer always returns to its bed; that is, the obedient Son asks from us obedience to the Father even unto death. Simon the leper signifies first the unbelieving world, and afterward the believing one. The woman with the alabaster vessel signifies ecclesiastical faith, which says: “My nard gave forth its fragrance.” *Pistica* nard is so called, that is, mystical and precious. The house filled with fragrance is heaven and earth. The broken alabaster vessel is carnal desire, which is broken at the head, from which the whole body is joined together. As he reclined, that is, humbled himself, so that the faith of the sinful woman might touch him—faith which rises from the feet to the head and descends from the head to the feet, that is, to Christ and his members [Col. 0630A].

But some were indignant within themselves and saying: “Why has this waste of ointment been made? For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they were grumbling against her. But Jesus said: “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her?” Through synecdoche, one is spoken of in place of many, and many in place of one. They said within themselves: “Why this waste of ointment?” The one lost from salvation finds perdition, and in the fruitful fig tree obtains the snare of death. This ointment could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor. Under the pretext of avarice, he speaks of the mystery of faith. For our faith is bought for three hundred denarii, that is, by the ten senses tripled through body, soul, and spirit, so that, taking upon ourselves, like Gideon, the number of three hundred men, we may destroy the camp of the Philistines, poor in spirit, with our broken jars, trumpets, and lamps; and so that, like Abraham with three hundred men, we may divide the spoils at evening. It follows:

“She has done a good work toward me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me.” What she had, she did. Whoever believes in God is reckoned to him as a work of righteousness. For it is one thing to believe him, and another to believe in him, that is, to cast yourself wholly upon him [Col. 0630C]. What she had, she did. Let us not hope to obtain from elsewhere what we possess within ourselves.

“She has anticipated anointing my body for burial. Amen I say to you: wherever this Gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

And Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went away to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. When they heard this, they rejoiced and promised to give him money. And he was seeking how he might hand him over at a suitable opportunity.

And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, the disciples said to him: “Where do you wish us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” And he sent two of his disciples and said to them: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him. And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says: Where is my dining room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he himself will show you a large upper room furnished and prepared. There make preparations for us.” And his disciples went out and came into the city, and found it as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

That is, before the one who would exclude him came. Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve: one in number, not one in merit; one in name, not one in divine status; one in body, not one in mind. Hence the Bridegroom sings to the Bride: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.” The eye and the lock signify the virtue of wisdom, since it is said to Judas together with the others: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom”; and, “I gave you power,” and so forth [Col. 0631A].

He went to the rulers: “After he went out, Satan entered into him.” Here night indicates knowledge to night. Every animal is joined to one like itself. Mary runs to the apostles, so that day may pour forth the word to day; and Judas to the Jews, so that night may communicate knowledge to night. They promise money and lose life—the life he himself received when he lost life. He was seeking an opportunity. An opportunity for deceit is never found without punishment, whether here or there. He promises to betray him, just as his master the devil had earlier said: “I will give you power over all this.” And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, which are eaten with bitterness: Unleavened Bread for us is our redemption, while bitterness is the Lord’s passion.

The disciples say: “Where do you wish us to go?”—so that we may direct our steps according to God’s will. The Lord indicates with whom he will eat the Passover, and in his customary manner sends two, as we explained above. And he says: “Go into the city,” and so forth. The city is the Church, surrounded by the wall of faith. The man who meets them is the primitive people. The jar of water is the law of the letter. Follow the one who leads upward, to where Christ’s dining room is. Hence Rahab commands the spies not to go through the low places, but to proceed through the heights. The large upper room is the great Church, in which the Lord’s name is proclaimed, furnished with a variety of virtues and languages, as in the passage: “Clothed in variety,” where the Passover is prepared for the Lord. The master of the house is the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted his house, so that there might be one faith under one shepherd.

When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve. And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said: “Amen I say to you, one of you will betray me, the one who eats with me.” They began to be sorrowful and to say to him individually: “Surely it is I?” He said to them: “One of the Twelve, who dips with me into the dish. The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written of him. But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

And while they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, and said: “Take; this is my body.”

The evening of the day indicates the evening of the world. For around the eleventh hour the last arrivals come, who receive the first denarius of eternal life, because before the cross Abraham was in hell, and after the cross the thief was in paradise. While they were eating he said: “One of you will betray me, the one who eats bread with me.” For while falsehood is condemned, truth is nevertheless confirmed, so that what is said might be fulfilled: “He who ate my bread magnified treachery against me.” All are touched, so that harmony may be produced on the lyre; all the strings, properly stretched, answer with a harmonious voice: “Surely it is I, Lord?” One who had been careless and attached to money said: “Surely it is I, Rabbi?” And he says to them: “One of the Twelve.” The wolf separates the sheep that it seizes. The sheep that leaves the fold is exposed to the wolf’s bites.

“The Son of Man goes; but woe to the man through whom he will be betrayed.” Many do good things, like Judas, but it profits them nothing at all. It would have been better for him if he had not been born: hidden in his mother’s innermost womb, it is better not to exist than to exist for torment. Jesus took bread and, blessing it, broke it, transforming his body into bread, which is the present Church: received in faith, blessed in number, broken in sufferings, given in examples, and taken in teachings. He forms his blood into the cup, mixed with wine and water, so that by one we may be cleansed from guilt and by the other redeemed from punishments. For by the blood of the lamb houses are preserved from the angel’s blow, and by the water of the Red Sea enemies are extinguished—these are mysteries of the Church of Christ [Col. 0632A].

And having taken the cup and given thanks, he gave it to them. By grace, not by merits, we have been saved by God.

And they all drank from it. And he said to them: “This is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many. Amen I say to you, that now—”

A blessed drunkenness, a saving satiety: the more abundantly it is taken, the greater sobriety it deigns to bestow upon minds. Judas also drank, but he was not satisfied, nor did the fire of eternity extinguish his thirst, because he receives Christ’s mysteries unworthily. Here the blemish in the moon is shown, which is never erased. The Church is rightly compared to the moon, which does not possess its own splendor, but receives light from the sun in appointed ways—that is, from Christ, who remains forever. For there are people in the Church whom no sacrifice cleanses, but foolish thought leads into guilt; they have mixed themselves with the stench of muddy cruelty [possibly: credulity]. For the blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many, does not correct everyone.

“I will not drink from the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” Here he changes only the sacrifice, but does not change the time, so that we may never celebrate the Lord’s supper before the fourteenth moon. Whoever celebrates the resurrection on the fourteenth moon celebrates the Lord’s supper on the eleventh moon—something never found either in the Old Testament or in the New.

And when the hymn had been sung—that is, the Lord’s praise, as in the psalm: “And they will praise the Lord who seek him, and they will eat him, and all the fat ones of the earth will worship.”

They went out to the Mount of Olives. And Jesus said to them: “You will all be scandalized because of me this night, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.”

On the Mount of Olives Jesus is seized, and from there he ascends to heaven, so that we may know that from the place where we keep watch, pray, and are bound, without resisting on earth, from there we ascend to heaven. “You will all suffer scandal.” All fall, but not all remain lying there. Will one who sleeps not also arise again? To fall is carnal; to lie there is diabolical. It is written: “Strike the shepherd.” The prophet Zechariah asks for the Lord’s passion. The Father answers: “I will strike the shepherd,” at the prayers of the holy beings below. The Son is sent and struck by the Father—that is, he becomes incarnate and suffers. The sheep are scattered when the shepherd is seized; resurrection is promised so that hope may not be extinguished.

But Peter said to him: “Even if all are scandalized, yet not I” [Col. 0633A].

And Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you: today, on this night—” Even a bird without wings attempts to fly high, but the body weighs down the soul, so that through fear of human death the fear of the Lord may be overcome or conquered.

“Before the cock gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times.” But he spoke still more: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And all likewise said.

And they come to an estate called Gethsemane. And he says to his disciples:

The cock crows, and Peter denies him three times. Who is the cock, the messenger of light, if not the Holy Spirit? By his voice in the prophets and apostles, we are roused from the triple denial by which we denied that we knew God; terrified by the voices of servant girls, we are awakened to the most bitter weeping after our fall—we who thought wrongly about God, spoke wrongly to our neighbors, and acted wrongly toward ourselves [Col. 0633B]. And he came to the estate of Gethsemane, that is, “valley of richness,” where fat bulls surrounded him and many calves encircled him.

“Sit here until I pray.” And he takes Peter, James, and John with him. The one who is separated in prayer is separated in passion, because he prays while they sleep, oppressed by the fatness of their hearts.

And he began to be fearful and distressed. And he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful unto death. Remain here and keep watch.” And going forward a little, he fell upon the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him, and he said: “Abba, Father.”

We are taught to be fearful and sorrowful before the judgment of death, since of ourselves we cannot say except through him: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” And he said: “Abba, Father.” He speaks in Hebrew and Greek, because there is no distinction between Jew and Greek [Col. 0633C].

“All things are possible for you. Take this cup away from me; yet not what I will, but what you will.” And he came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter: “Simon, are you sleeping? Were you unable to keep watch for one hour?” To the end he does not cease teaching us to obey our fathers and to place their will before our own. He found them sleeping. As they sleep in mind, so also in body.

“Keep watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” And going away again, he prayed, saying the same words. And when he returned again, he found them sleeping. For their eyes were weighed down, and they did not know what to answer him [Col. 0633D]. And he came a third time and said to them: “Sleep now and rest. It is enough. The hour has come. Behold, the Son of Man will be betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise; let us go. Behold, the one who betrays me is near.”

And while he was still speaking, Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and scribes and elders. His betrayer had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him and lead him away carefully.” And when he had come, immediately approaching him, he said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. But they laid hands on Jesus and seized him.

One of those standing nearby drew a sword, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear [Col. 0634A]. And Jesus answered and said to them: “As against a robber, have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me? Every day I was among you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.”

The one who neglects to pray enters into temptation. The disciples sleep three times, and three times the praying Lord awakens them. The threefold sleep signifies the three dead whom the Lord raised: the first in the house, the second on the way to the tomb, the third from the tomb. The Lord’s threefold watch teaches us to have three persons in our prayer, and to ask forgiveness for past, future, and present things.

Judas came with swords and clubs. Whoever despairs of God’s help relies upon the power of the world. He gives the sign of a kiss with the poison of deceit, just as Cain offered a treacherous and rejected sacrifice. Hence they place wine mixed with vinegar on the cross. And they seized Jesus. Here Joseph is present, bound and sold by his brothers, and iron pierced his soul. One drew a sword and cut off the servant’s ear. Peter’s preaching cut off hearing of the kingdom from the Jews.

Then his disciples, leaving him, all fled. Then was fulfilled what is said: “You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances from misery.”

But a certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen garment over his naked body, and they seized him. But he, abandoning the linen garment, fled from them naked.

And they led Jesus to the high priest, and all the priests and scribes and elders assembled. But Peter followed him from afar, even inside the courtyard of the high priest [Col. 0634C], and sat with the attendants by the fire and warmed himself.

But the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death, and they did not find any. For many were giving false testimony against him, but their testimonies were not consistent.

This is peculiar to Mark. Just as Joseph, leaving his cloak behind, fled naked from the hands of the shameless woman, so whoever wishes to escape the hands of the wicked should abandon in his mind the things that belong to the world and flee after Jesus. And the priests and scribes assembled. Then there is a gathering of bulls among the cows of the peoples.

Peter followed from afar. A man double-minded is unstable in all his ways. Fear draws back; charity draws forward. In the courtyard, with the attendants, he warms himself by the fire. The priest’s courtyard is the worldly circuit; the attendants are demons [Col. 0634D]. The fire is carnal desire. Whoever remains with these cannot weep for sins.

The chief priests sought false testimony against Jesus. Iniquity lied against itself, as the queen did against Joseph and the priests against Susanna; but fire without fuel dies out. And their testimonies were not consistent. What is varied is considered uncertain.

And certain men rose up and bore false testimony against him, saying: “We heard him say: ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands.’” And their testimony was not consistent.

And the high priest rose into the midst and questioned Jesus, saying: “Do you answer nothing to the things these men allege against you?” [Col. 0635A] But he remained silent and answered nothing. Again the high priest questioned him and said:

It is the custom of heretics to draw a shadow from the truth. He did not say what they say; rather, he spoke a similar word about the temple of his body, which he raised after three days. The high priest rose and questioned Jesus; but he remained silent. He himself is our God and Savior, who brought salvation to the world and in his goodness came to the aid of the human race. Like a sheep he is led without a voice to slaughter, and he was silent and kept quiet concerning good things. Christ’s silence acquits Adam’s defense.

“Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” The one whom they awaited from afar, they do not see when he is near. As Isaac, with his eyes dimmed, does not recognize Jacob beneath his hands, but sings from afar of things to come concerning him [Col. 0635B].

But Jesus said to him: “I am,” so that they might be without excuse.

“And you will see the Son of Man.” The priest questions the Son of God, but Jesus answers concerning the Son of Man, so that here we may understand that the Son of God is the same as the Son of Man, and that we must not make a quaternity in the Trinity, but that the human being is in God and God in the human being.

“Sitting at the right hand of Power,” that is, reigning in everlasting life and in divine power.

“And coming with the clouds of heaven.” He ascended in a cloud; with a cloud he will come. That is, in his own body alone, which he assumed from the Virgin, he ascended; and with the many-formed Church, which is his body and his fullness, he will come to judgment, as it says according to Matthew: “When the Son of Man comes, and all the angels with him,” and so forth [Col. 0635C].

But the high priest, tearing his garments, said: “What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemy. What does it seem to you?” And they all condemned him as liable to death.

And some began to spit upon him, to cover his face, to strike him with blows, and to say to him: “Prophesy.” And the attendants were striking him with slaps.

This is the ephod, in which they had honor; the Jews lost it. Here Samuel is present, with his garment torn from Saul’s hands in the kingdom. Gentile soldiers do not tear Christ’s tunic, but the priests tear the dignity of their own priesthood. And they condemn him as liable to death, by which guilt he might release our guilt; by the veil of his face, remove the veil from our hearts; by the spittle he received, wash the face of our soul; and by the blows with which he was struck on the head, heal the head of the human race, which is Adam [Col. 0635D]. By the slaps with which he was struck, the highest praise of him, he would applaud with our hands and lips; hence: “All nations, clap your hands.” By his cross he would release our torment; by his death he would kill our death. When the form of the serpent kills the serpent, because serpents are swallowed up by the serpent made from the staff. Hence he himself says through the prophet: “I will be your death, O death, and your sting, O hell.” His reproaches removed our reproach. His bonds made us free. From the thorny crown of his head we have gained the diadem of the kingdom. By his wounds we have been healed. By his burial we have risen. By his descent into hell we have ascended to heaven [Col. 0636A]. Here honey is found in the mouth of the dead lion. Foreseeing all these things, the prophet said: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?”

And while Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s servant girls came. When she saw Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said: “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” But he denied it, saying: “I neither know nor understand what you are saying.” And he went out before the courtyard, and the cock crowed.

Again, when the servant girl saw him, she began to say to those standing nearby: “This man is one of them.” But he denied it again. And after a little while those standing there said to Peter again: “Truly you are one of them, for you are also a Galilean.” But he began to curse and swear: “I do not know this man whom you are speaking about.” And immediately the cock crowed a second time [Col. 0636B]. And Peter remembered the word Jesus had said to him: “Before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times,” and he began to weep.

Peter, without the Spirit, yielded to the servant girl’s voice; with the Spirit, he yields neither to rulers nor to kings. The first servant girl is stumbling; the second is consent; the third man is action. This is the threefold denial, which the remembrance of Christ’s word washes away through tears. The cock crows for us when every preacher arouses our hearts to repentance and compunction. We begin to weep when we are kindled within by the spark of knowledge, and go out from what we had been.

CHAPTER XV

And immediately, early in the morning, the chief priests, with the elders and scribes and the whole council, taking counsel [Col. 0636C], bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate. And Pilate questioned him: “Are you the king of the Jews?” But he answered and said to him: “You say so.” And the chief priests accused him of many things. Pilate questioned him again, saying: “Do you answer nothing? See how many things they accuse you of.” But Jesus answered nothing further, so that Pilate was amazed.

Now on the feast day he was accustomed to release to them one of the prisoners, whomever they requested. There was one called Barabbas, who was imprisoned with the rebels, who had committed murder in the insurrection. And when the crowd had gathered, he began to ask as he always did for them. But Pilate answered them and said:

Here Samson is present, that is, “their sun,” for whom the sun set at midday. Delilah is interpreted as “bucket”; she is the synagogue, which, like a bucket, does not retain clear liquid, but collects unclean refuse. Our Samson here lays low innumerable bands of Jews and demons with the jawbone of his word, and opens for us who thirst the fountain of everlasting life—that is, for his body.

The chief priests stirred up the crowds to ask for Barabbas and crucify Jesus. Here two goats are present: one *ἀποπομπαῖος* (*apopompaios*), that is, the scapegoat, released into the wilderness of hell with the people’s sin; the other killed as a lamb for the sins of those who have been set free. The Lord’s portion is always slaughtered; the devil’s portion, who is their master, is driven headlong, unbridled, into Tartarus.

It follows:

“Do you wish me to release to you the king of the Jews?” For he knew that the chief priests had handed him over out of envy. But the chief priests stirred up the crowd so that he might release Barabbas to them instead. Pilate answered them again and said: “What then do you wish me to do with the king of the Jews?” But they cried out again: “Crucify him.” Pilate said to them: “For what evil has he done?” But they cried out still more: “Crucify him.”

But Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them and handed Jesus over, scourged, to be crucified.

The soldiers led him inside the courtyard of the praetorium and summoned the whole cohort. They clothed him in purple, placed upon him a crown of thorns that they had woven, and began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!” And they struck his head with a reed, spat upon him, and, kneeling, worshiped him. And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and clothed him in his own garments. And they lead him out to crucify him.

Pilate offered many opportunities to free the Savior. First, by setting a robber alongside him; then by asking: “What then do you wish me to do with the king of the Jews?” And when they had answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately agree, but, following the prompting of his wife, who had sent him word, as Matthew said, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man,” he replied: “For what evil has he done?” By saying this, he acquitted Jesus.

The soldiers clothe him in purple, and so forth. He is stripped of his garments, that is, of the Jews. He is clothed in purple, that is, in the gentile Church, gathered from the rocks of the sea. Again, when it causes scandal, he is stripped at the end and clothed once more in the Jewish people. For when the fullness of the gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

And they lead him out to crucify him [Col. 0637C]. Here Abel is led by his brother into the field to be killed. Here Isaac is present with the wood, and Abraham with the ram caught in the thicket. Here Joseph is present with the sheaf dreamed of in his lap and the long tunic stained with blood. Here Moses is present with the staff and the serpent suspended on the wood. Here is the cluster of grapes carried on the wood. Here Elisha is present with the wood, seeking the axe-head that had sunk into the depths; it floated toward the wood—that is, the human race, which fell from the forbidden wood into hell and, through the wood of Christ’s cross and the water of baptism, floated toward paradise. Here Jonah is present, cast from the wood of the lot into the sea and into the belly of the whale for three days.

And they press into service a certain passerby, Simon of Cyrene, coming from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they bring him to the place Golgotha, which is interpreted as “Place of the Skull.”

Some are remembered because of the merits of their fathers; others because of the merits of their sons. This Simon, who carries the cross under compulsion, is remembered because of the merits of his sons, who were disciples. By this we are admonished in the present life that parents are helped by the wisdom of their children, just as the Jewish people are always remembered because of the merits of the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles. From the bitterness of the root arises the sweetness of the olive. Hence through Jeremiah it is said to Judea: “The Lord called your name a luxuriant olive, beautiful, fruitful, and fair.”

“To carry his cross” [Col. 0638A]. When they read: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” he became cursed in order to carry away the curse. Simon, who carries the cross under compulsion, is the one who labors for human praise. People force him into this labor, which neither fear nor love of God compels him to undertake.

What is the very shape of the cross except the square form of the world? The East shines from the summit; the Bear is held on the right; the South stands on the left; the West is fixed beneath the feet. Hence the Apostle says: “So that we may know what is the height and breadth and length and depth.” When birds fly toward the heavens, they assume the form of a cross; a person swimming through the waters, or praying, is carried in the form of a cross. A ship is driven across the seas by a mast resembling a cross. The letter T is depicted as the sign of salvation and of the cross.

And they bring him to Golgotha, which is interpreted as “Skull.” The Jews report that when the ram was sacrificed in place of Isaac, it was sacrificed at this place on the mountain, so that there he might be beheaded—that is, so that Christ might be separated from his flesh, namely, from carnal Judea [Col. 0638B].

And they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, but he did not accept it. And they crucified him.

By this vinegar the lethal juice of the fruit is wiped away. And he did not accept it—that for which he suffers. Hence it is said of him: “What I did not steal, then I restored.” And they crucify him. Here salvation is fastened to the wood; death was first fastened to wood. The first wood is the wood of the knowledge of good and evil. The second wood is for us the wood of good alone and the tree of life. The extension of the first hand toward the wood grasped death; the extension of the second found life, which had perished. By this wood we are carried across the billowing sea to the land of the living [Col. 0638C].

They divided his garments, casting lots over them to see what each should take. The Lord’s garments are his commandments, by which his body, the Church, is covered. They are divided among the soldiers of the nations, so that there may be four orders with one faith: married and widowed, superiors and separated. They received by lot the undivided tunic, which is peace and unity, seamless in the form of a royal ring.

Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him. This Mark has truly and properly added, for at the sixth hour darkness covered the earth, so that no one could move his head. For Mark rises from the thirtieth fruit to the hundredfold: from the third hour of the cross to the third hour of the resurrection after three days. The thirtieth fruit is on the cross; the sixtieth in hell; the hundredfold in paradise [Col. 0638D].

And there was an inscription of the charge against him: “King of the Jews.” This is prefigured in the headings of the psalms: “Unto the end: Do not destroy.” And this was in three languages: “MALACH JEUDIM,” “King of the Jews”; Βασιλεὺς ἐξομολογητῶν, “King of those who confess.” These three languages were joined together in the title of the cross, so that every tongue might recall the Jews’ faithlessness.

And with him they crucify two robbers, one on his right and the other on his left. And the Scripture was fulfilled that says: “And he was reckoned among the wicked.”

And those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah, you who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself by coming down from the cross.”

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him among themselves with the scribes, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” And those who were crucified with him reproached him.

And when the sixth hour had come, darkness occurred over the whole earth until the ninth hour.

Truth was reckoned among the wicked: he left one on the left and took up the other on the right, as he will do on the day of judgment. From the same crime, they receive different destinies. One precedes Peter into paradise; the other, Judas into hell. A brief confession acquired a long life, while blasphemy, having come to an end, is punished with eternal punishment.

Here the young goat of Judas is bound to the vine. Here the *ἀναβολαίον*, that is, the cloak, is dipped in the blood of the grape; here the kid tears apart the vineyard.

Blaspheming him and shaking their heads: death is sent upon the heads of the wicked when the bonds of hell are raised up as far as the neck, which is the neck of the human race. “Come down from the cross,” so that he would not accomplish the salvation he had begun.

Later they saw rising from the tomb the one whom they had not believed able to descend from the cross’s gibbet. Where now is your unbelief, Jews? While he was still alive you were saying: “If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross.” I appeal to you yourselves; I seek judgment from you yourselves: how much more marvelous is it that a dead man can rise than that one still living should wish to come down from the cross! You asked for small things, while greater things would follow. But your unbelief could not be healed by signs far stronger than those you requested. Here all turned aside; together they became useless.

When the sixth hour had come, darkness occurred over the whole earth [Col. 0639C]. Here Noah is present, drunk and stripped naked, covered by heaven and earth with a dark cloak and mocked by humanity. Here blood dripped from the wood.

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani,” which is interpreted: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

And some of those standing nearby, hearing this, were saying: “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” But one ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, placed it around a reed, and gave him drink, saying: “Leave him; let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.”

Hence this psalm is written for the morning assumption, by which Christ is led to the cross. These are the proper words of the Son of Man; hence it follows according to Luke: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” [Col. 0639D].

At the ninth hour the lost tenth drachma is found, the house having been overturned. But one of them ran and found a likeness of them: a hollow, weak sponge, dry and suitable for fires. He fills it with vinegar, that is, with malice and deceit, concerning which it is said: “I planted you as a choice vine of Sorek; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine? I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced thorns.”

But Jesus, uttering a loud cry, expired. And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. And when the centurion who stood opposite saw that he had expired after crying out in this way, he said: “Truly this man was the Son of God.”

For when the flesh had been weakened, the divine voice grew strong, which says: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them [Col. 0640A] I will confess to the Lord,” while we, who are from the earth, die with a low voice or without a voice. But he who descended from heaven expired with a raised voice. The veil of the temple is torn, that is, heaven is opened.

The centurion said: “Truly he was the Son of God.” The last are now made first. The gentile people confess; blinded Judea denies, so that an error worse than the former may come upon them.

There were also women looking on from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, as did many other women who had gone up with him to Jerusalem.

When evening had already come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea arrived, a noble member of the council, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God. He boldly went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Pilate was astonished that he had already died; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had already died. When he had learned this from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.

Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the linen cloth, and placed him in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock; and he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was placed.

Just as the female sex is not excluded from salvation through the Virgin Mary, so it is not rejected from knowledge of the mystery of the cross and resurrection through the widow Mary Magdalene and the other mothers.

Joseph comes late on the day of Preparation, from Arimathea—which is interpreted as “the one who lays down”—in order to lay the body in the tomb. He is a noble member of the council, himself awaiting the kingdom of God. He enters to Pilate and asks for the body of Jesus. Joseph buys a linen cloth, wraps the body in the linen cloth, and places it in the tomb that had been hewn from rock. He rolls the stone against the entrance of the tomb. The Marys watch where he is placed.

All these things correspond to the Jewish people, who at the end come to believe. They are ennobled by faith, so that they may be children of Abraham. They lay aside despair and await the kingdom of God. They enter among the Christians in order to be baptized.

This is signified by the name Pilate, that is, “hammerer,” meaning one who subdues the iron nations so as to rule them with an iron rod. He asks for the sacrifice, which at the end is granted to penitents as provisions for the journey, and to the pure in heart and dead to sins. He wraps it in the protection of faith, establishes it with the covering of hope, and encloses it through works of charity. For the end of the commandment is charity.

Those who look on from afar are the elect, who are the stars of the sea—when, if it is possible, the elect will be scandalized.

## CHAPTER XVI

When the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint him.

Now, with the bride and the young women who run after her, we sprinkle the book and the chamber of our mind with fragrant spices. Now the king brings us into his storerooms. Now the beloved Mary rises: winter has passed, the rain has gone away; flowers have appeared on the earth; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. The flowering vines have given their fragrance. The bridegroom returns from the shade beneath which he sleeps at noon.

After the sorrowful Sabbaths, the blessed day shines forth, holding primacy among the days: the first light shining upon it, and my Lord rising in triumph and saying: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”

Very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen, and they said to one another: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” Looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away.

“Very early” is what another Evangelist calls “at dawn.” Dawn is between the darkness of night and the brightness of day. At that time salvation came to the human race, to be revealed by this fortunate proximity, after the manner of the sun: when it rises with the approaching light, it sends ahead the rosy dawn, so that, through the grace of its splendid brightness, the prepared eyes may be able to see when the time of the Lord’s resurrection has shone forth.

Then the Church might sing the praises of Christ with its whole voice, following the example of these women, when he gave courage to the human race through the example of his resurrection, when he bestowed life and poured in the light of faith.

The sun rises after the setting of the body. Here the eagles gather around the body. The mothers and the apostles see the stone rolled away, which is the law of death, as though it were saying: “Where, O death, is your sting?” and the rest.

For it was exceedingly large. Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished.

He also touches infants in the womb: the groaning of all, and burdensome to all. Entering the tomb, they saw a young man—not an old man, not an infant, but one joyful in age, as it is said: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth,” which is not truly here, since it is mingled with old age.

He is sitting at the right hand of Power, that is, reigning in prosperity. This young man displays the form of the resurrection to those who fear death. He is clothed in a white robe, which is true joy, once the enemy has been driven away and the kingdom attained, and once the King of peace has been sought, found, and never abandoned.

“And they were astonished,” that is, at what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man”—what God has prepared for those who love him.

He said to them: “Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, the crucified one. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter.”

“God is love.” Therefore there is no fear in love. Why should those women be afraid who had found the one whom they sought?

“You seek Jesus of Nazareth.” The bitter root of the cross has vanished; the flower of life has burst forth with its fruits—that is, the one who lay in death has risen in glory.

“Behold the place.” Mortality is shown to immortals for the thanksgiving that is owed, so that we may understand what we have been and know what we shall be.

“But go, tell.” The women are told to announce it to the apostles, because through a woman death was announced, while through women life, rising again, was announced.

“And Peter”—the one who judged himself unworthy of discipleship when he denied the Master three times. Past sins do not harm when they are no longer pleasing.

“For he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you.”

But they went out and fled from the tomb. For fear and terror had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, because they were afraid.

When Jesus had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and announced it to those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. When they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe.

After this, he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking, going into the countryside. They went and announced it to the others, and they did not believe them either.

A brief statement in syllables, but an immense promise in its scope. There is the fountain of our joy and the prepared origin of eternal salvation. There the scattered are gathered, and those broken in heart are healed. There you will see him, not as you saw him before.

But they went out and fled. This is spoken of the future life: “And pain and groaning will flee.” Before the resurrection of all, the women imitate what they will do after the resurrection: they flee from death and terror.

They said nothing to anyone, because only those who have deserved to see the mystery of the resurrection for themselves see it. Hence, according to John, it follows: “But Peter ran to the tomb, so that he himself might see what he had heard.”

When Jesus had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons, because prostitutes and tax collectors go before the synagogue into the kingdom of God, just as the thief went before the apostles.

Those who have not yet seen weep and mourn, but after a short time they will be comforted. For: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.”

And they, when they heard, did not believe. Faith here is engaged in labor, living the active life; there, after contemplation, it reigns through vision. Here we behold the image through a mirror; there we shall see the truth face to face.

Hence it follows: “After this, as two of them were walking,” that is, laboring, “he appeared in another form.” When they announced it, they were not believed, since, like Moses, they saw something that was not sufficient for them.

Therefore Moses says: “Show me yourself.” Forgetting his flesh, he asks in this life for what we hope for in the future life after this one.

Finally, while the eleven were reclining at table, he appeared and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen.

This was so that all the witnesses might recount to everyone what they had commonly seen and heard. He reproves unbelief so that belief may follow; he reproves the hardness of a stony heart so that a heart of flesh, full of charity, may follow.

Hence it is that crowds of martyrs willingly desire the death of this age, because they know that through this temporal destruction they will live forever.

And he said to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

Now, for the first time after receiving the Spirit, as though vessels of clay had been strengthened through fire, they are commanded to preach “to every creature,” that is, to the whole human race, which shares something common with every creature: angels, cattle, trees, stones, fire and water, heat and cold, moisture and dryness. For the human being is called the lesser world.

The Lord Jesus, who descended from heaven to free the nature of our weakness, also ascended above the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father.

It must be considered that in the divine Scriptures you will often find “heavens” spoken of in the plural, although we read: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” while “heavens” and “earths” are nevertheless read in the plural. This manner of speech is widely used, so that, by a kind of linguistic irregularity, we speak of singular things in the plural and plural things in the singular.

As for the East, which the psalmist mentions, the Evangelists are silent. It signifies Jerusalem, which is situated in the regions of the East. Therefore, while the apostles were looking on, the Lord ascended into the heavens.

The earth is full of many miracles, where the faith of believers is instructed more by deeds than by readings.

Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be well.

And indeed, after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.

In the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, Mark recounts the signs of believers, agreeing with Matthew and Luke.

## [Col. 0643] PREFACE

Falsely attributed to the blessed presbyter Jerome, on the Gospel according to Luke. (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0643B] Luke, a Syrian by nationality, from Antioch, a physician by profession and a disciple of the apostles, afterward followed Paul until the completion of his life, serving the Lord blamelessly. For he never had either a wife or children. He died in Bithynia at the age of seventy-four, full of the Holy Spirit.

When the Gospels had already been written—by Matthew in Judea and by Mark in Italy—he wrote this Gospel in the regions of Achaia, under the prompting of the holy Spirit. He himself also indicates at the beginning that other accounts had been written before his.

Beyond what the order of the Gospel’s arrangement required, the chief necessity of his labor was this: he had to work first for the Greek believers, presenting in every prophecy the humanity of God’s Christ, who was to come in the flesh, so that they would not remain absorbed in the desire for the Law by paying attention to Jewish fables, or fall away from the truth after being led astray by heretical fables and foolish enticements.

Next, by presupposing the birth in the beginning of John’s Gospel, he indicated for whom he was writing the Gospel and in whom he was chosen to write, bearing witness that the things begun by others had been completed in him.

For this reason, after the baptism of the Son of God, he was granted authority to begin again from the human birth, proceeding from the perfection of the generation fulfilled in Christ, so that he might show to those who sought an explanation through whom he had entered—through Nathan, the son of David—by admitting the succession of a generation returning into God, the inseparable God.

Thus, by proclaiming Christ in all things, he would make the perfect work of humanity return to itself through the Son, who through his father David opened the way for those who were coming in Christ.

For this reason, Luke was not undeservedly also granted authority, in his ministry, to write the Acts of the Apostles: so that, with God filled with God and the son of perdition extinguished, the number of the Lord’s elect might be completed by the prayer made by the apostles themselves.

And thus Paul would bring the apostolic acts to completion, for as long as the Lord had chosen him, though he was kicking against the goad.

Although it would have been useful for us to explain this to readers and seekers of God point by point, nevertheless, knowing that the farmer who labors ought first to eat from his own fruits, we avoided public curiosity, lest we seem to have shown God less to those who desire him than to have exposed him to those who find him wearisome.

## [Col. 0643] COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE HOLY PAUL

### ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING COMMENTARIES

No one among educated men will fail to judge that the following commentary on Paul’s thirteen Epistles—once wrongly attributed to Saint Jerome—is the very work that Saint Augustine, both elsewhere and in Book III, chapter 1, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, and Marius Mercator in his *Commonitory* on more than one occasion, as well as Cassiodorus and the author of the *Praedestinatus*, testify to have been composed by Pelagius.

Indeed, this is almost conclusive evidence of the matter: the passages that they quote from that work of Pelagius, since it was infected with the poison of heretical doctrine, and then attack, occur in this commentary in almost exactly the same words. This is especially true of those passages taken from chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans, which differ from the printed text by scarcely more than can be attributed to the freedom of copyists.

We carefully compared each of those passages there; to reproduce them here would be lengthy. The true conclusion, therefore, is that these books not only do not have Jerome as their author, but are, rather, by sure indications, the offspring of his bitterest enemy and of an enemy of the Catholic faith.

Nevertheless, some qualification must be added to this assertion, lest it be concluded from it that the text transmits Pelagius pure and unaltered. Since the commentary once appeared to contain good teaching and was not everywhere unlearned, devout men took care to protect readers from the passages that insinuated heresy more than others. They interpolated some passages with sounder wording and cut out others completely.

Let the following serve as evidence. Mercator copied these passages, but they are now missing:

“But those who hold a different opinion concerning the transmission of sin attempt to attack those who defend its transmission in another way. ‘If,’ he says, ‘Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe, since the Apostle says that through one person people are delivered—indeed, even more than through one they previously perished.’

“Then they say: ‘If baptism cleanses that ancient and deeply rooted sin, those born from two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin. For they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess at all.’

“Moreover, they add: ‘If the soul is not transmitted by descent, as indeed it is not, but only the flesh has the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves the punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from the mass of Adam, should bear another’s ancient sin; since it is not reasonable that God, who forgives personal sins, should impute one belonging to another.’”

These passages, I say, have been erased from our copies for no other reason than that they broke out into open heresy. Other similar passages evidently suffered the same fate.

Furthermore, it had been believed for thirteen centuries that the work belonged to Pelagius. A clear testimony to this matter is found in the account of our Veronese writer John—called a deacon by Panvinio, but, according to Pastrengo, John the presbyter and mansionarius—in a history not yet published, which is in our possession.

“I myself,” he says, “John, saw the commentary of the aforementioned Pelagius on the Epistles of Paul. Although he explains many things well and elegantly, he nevertheless subtly pours in the poison of his heresy.”

Moreover, this preface is unknown to the manuscripts of better quality.

## COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE HOLY PAUL

### PREFACE

[Col. 0645A] Your letter, hurriedly brought to me, Saint Heliodorus, compels me, now that my body is growing old and my strength is failing, to labor through toil and concern over the sacred books. You compel me to do this in the Epistles of blessed Paul, which were brought forth and expanded through the testimony of the Holy Spirit with such great knowledge of the preacher and such a great refinement of righteousness, both for preaching and for teaching, that we do not hesitate to compare or even equate them with the Old Testament and the teaching of the Gospel.

For he himself, when the Holy Spirit revealed it to him, understood this when he asserted that he had been caught up to the third heaven, whether in the body or outside the body—that is, as far as the third law, of the Old and New Testaments.

“In the body or outside the body” means neither through the law of nature nor through the law of the letter, but through the Holy Spirit, who was given last to the least of all the apostles through Jesus Christ our Lord. Through him we have access to this grace in which we stand and boast.

You will discover that we have explained these matters simply and in brief statements. Indeed, all wise people interpret and preach his Epistles with greater magnificence.

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0645A] Paul.

We ask why Paul writes, since he was previously called Saul. We should believe that he did this according to the custom of the saints, who, as they progressed in virtue, were called by changed names, so that they might be new even in name—for example, Abraham, Sarah, and Cephas.

Alternatively:

Paul. Just as the names of other saints in both the Old and New Testaments—Abraham, Peter, and the rest—were changed in accordance with the progress and increase of their merits, so Paul, progressing in grace, changed his own name.

A servant of Jesus Christ.

He begins as a servant, showing us an example of humility, as an imitator of the one who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death; therefore God also exalted him.

This man too, through his first faithful service, merited the apostleship. Again, it is not according to fear but according to love, as he himself says: “I live, yet it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me.”

[Col. 0645C] Called as an apostle.

He was now called for this purpose: to be an apostle. Again, he shows that he was not only called to the grace of apostleship, but also set apart for the preaching to the Gentiles, as he himself recalls: “We are apostles to the Gentiles, but he himself to the circumcision.”

He was therefore called by Christ to apostleship, but set apart for preaching to the Gentiles, to show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance.

Set apart.

As the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have chosen them.”

For the Gospel of God.

“Gospel,” in Latin *bona annuntiatio*, means “good announcement”: namely, of the birth of Christ, his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets.

He shows that he is preaching no other Christ than the one whose Gospel the prophets had promised from Jerusalem would come.

In the holy Scriptures.

He asserts that the prophets themselves were God’s prophets and that they had sung beforehand in those holy Scriptures about Christ.

Indeed, this entire passage is directed against the Manichaeans, where he says that the Gospel had previously been promised through God’s prophets and in the holy Scriptures; and that Christ, according to the flesh, was created from the line of David—that is, from the Virgin Mary—according to what Isaiah had foretold.

Concerning his Son.

Many are sons by grace; this one is so by nature. His birth in the flesh is also found to be unlike that of others, because he was born from a virgin.

[Col. 0647A] Who was made for him from the seed of David.

Made through the Holy Spirit.

According to the flesh.

By adding “according to the flesh,” he excludes both Photinus and Arius. For if he was made according to the flesh, then he was certainly not made according to the substance of the Word.

Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power.

By saying “in power,” he shows that his conception was not ordinary according to human nature, but that he was brought forth from a virgin without male seed.

Then he adds:

According to the Spirit of sanctification.

He shows that his creator is the Holy Spirit. Again, so that he himself might hold primacy in all things, he was predestined according to the Spirit of sanctification to rise before all others through the power of incorruptibility and to open the way of resurrection for the children of God.

Concerning them he himself says: “Because they are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection.”

From the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord.

Not of all who rise, but of those who belong to Christ; in Christ himself there is the form of resurrection.

Through whom we have received grace and apostleship.

Grace in baptism; apostleship when he was directed by the Holy Spirit. “Apostle” in Greek means “one who is sent” in Latin. Again, he says in the proper order that, having received grace, he merited the honor of apostleship.

For obedience to the faith.

He shows that the grace of the Gospel is to be preached to those who obey.

Among all the Gentiles.

He received apostleship so that they would obey not the Law but faith.

[Col. 0647C] For his name.

We act in place of his name, as he says: “As the Father sent me, I also send you.” And again: “Whoever receives you receives me.”

Among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ.

And among you, that is, among the Romans, we have received apostleship.

To all who are in Rome, beloved of God.

That is, to all believers, whom God loves equally without respect of persons, whether Jews or Greeks.

Called as saints.

They were made saints by God’s calling, not by merits. Again, he says “saints” because he was preaching to those who possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

Such is his greeting everywhere, so that he both recalls God’s benefits in us and wishes them to remain complete in us: for our sins have been forgiven by grace, and we have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son.

He also reminds us that we ought to be peaceful, having received one and the same grace.

First, I give thanks to my God.

By nature, God is the God of all; by merit and will, he is the God of a few, as “the God of Abraham”; accordingly, here he names him as his own God.

Through Jesus Christ for all of you.

That is, not for the Jews alone.

Because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.

He shows how the faith of the Romans is known to all the churches. Or certainly, that the same faith which the Romans hold is preached throughout the whole world by the apostles.

Again, he wisely praises them in order to provoke them to progress. Or because it was a marvel to the whole world that the Romans had believed, since they had been possessed by excessive worship of idols, so that they served the gods of all the nations they had conquered.

Yet we should also simply believe that he praised their faith, whose devotion is now being demonstrated.

For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son.

That is, I serve with my whole heart and ready devotion. For if I do this willingly, I have my reward.

Or he has here called the Word “spirit,” as in the passage: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.”

That without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers.

Here he shows that he will say everything out of love, so that he may be heard more freely; and he gives an example of praying without ceasing.

Asking.

That by God’s will I may at some time reach you. For I do not have a prosperous journey unless the will of God, who knows all things, directs me there, so that I may have some fruit.

Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, we read that those who wished to go in one direction were sent in another. Or according to what James says: “If God wills and we live, we will do this or that.”

If somehow, at last, I may have a prosperous journey, by God’s will, to come to you.

He shows that everything he did was carried out according to God’s will.

For I desire to see you.

Here he shows how he had praised them above, who needed a portion of spiritual grace in order to be strengthened in something.

That I may impart to you some spiritual grace for your strengthening.

Paul says that he wishes to strengthen the Romans, who hold the faith through Peter’s preaching—not because they had received less from Peter, but so that their faith might be strengthened by the testimony and teaching of two apostles.

That is, to be mutually encouraged among you through the faith that is in one another, yours and mine.

So that through our common faith we may encourage one another.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you.

You could have heard this from the brothers who travel among you.

And I have been prevented until now.

He shows that he has been occupied by the necessity of preaching the Gospel and therefore has not yet been able to go to Rome.

Again, “prevented” is understood as “occupied,” since he has been preaching in other provinces, as he himself explains at the end of his Epistle, saying: “For this reason I was very much prevented from coming to you.”

So that I may have some fruit among you.

He calls the reward for his labor “fruit.”

As also among the other Gentiles.

“Which I have,” is understood.

I am a debtor to Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish.

By “the wise,” he means Greek philosophers; by “barbarians,” the foolish.

Therefore, as far as depends on me, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are in Rome.

“To you who are in Rome”: he wishes to preach equally to the foolish, as well as to the Greeks.

[Col. 0649A] For I am not ashamed of the Gospel.

He rightly says that he is not ashamed of preaching the cross, which is the power of God for salvation to those who believe.

This also subtly censures the pagans. They are not ashamed to believe that their god Jupiter, because of empty lust, was transformed into irrational and insensible animals, yet they think that we ought to be ashamed to believe that the Lord was crucified for the salvation of the lost human race. In the one case there is dreadful disgrace; in the other, admirable piety and power.

At the same time he also touches on those heretics who shrink from these things as unworthy of God—namely, that he should put on humanity and hand himself over to suffering for the salvation of the human race—not understanding that nothing is more worthy of the Creator than to care for the salvation of his creature, especially since he himself, being as it were incapable of suffering, cannot feel this injury to nature.

For it is the power of God for salvation.

There is no greater power than that which, after conquering death, restores life to the lost human being.

To everyone who believes.

Although it appears to unbelievers to be weakness.

To the Jew first and to the Greek.

Either because it was just that, just as Abraham, believing, was saved from among the Gentiles through his first faith alone, so the other believers should be saved.

Or because God ought to have provided the fulfillment of the Testament that he, being truthful, had promised through the Law.

For the righteousness of God is revealed in it.

He shows that the faith of the preaching can be strengthened from the faith of each one of us.

[Col. 0649C] From faith to faith.

Either because the Jew is justified from faith, and the Gentile in faith. For this reason he explained it in this way, to avoid the fault of a bad formulation.

As it is written.

Not from works of the Law.

But the righteous person lives by faith.

He says this because without faith—that is, without hope of the reward of good works—no one can perfect the virtues. So he himself also teaches this when he bears witness in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Without faith it is impossible to please God. For whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.”

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.

If, as the Manichaeans say, the God of the Old Testament is asserted to be cruel because he brings vengeance upon sinners, how can the Apostle say here that the God of the New Testament inflicts vengeance on ungodly people?

This demonstrates that the God of the New Testament and of the Old Testament is one and the same.

Again, he begins to speak concerning the Gentiles and says that the wrath of God is revealed through the Gospel, or through the testimony of nature. For people know that both benefits and punishments are to be expected from heaven.

Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings.

There appear to be three forms of ungodliness.

The first and greatest is against God, committed either through blasphemy or through idolatry.

The second is against parents, whether through injury or contempt. Thus it is written in Leviticus: “If anyone lies with his father’s wife, let him die the death; both have committed ungodliness.”

The third is against strangers, as in the passage: “And you have forgiven the ungodliness of my heart.”

There are many other examples, which it would take too long to enumerate.

Or all ungodliness is to be referred to the various forms of idol worship, so that ungodliness appears to concern injury against God, while unrighteousness seems to pertain to all sins.

Of those who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness.

Unrighteousness, by confining the truth of God’s name within unworthy matter, causes pain.

Again, they sin knowingly: having recognized the truth of God, they act unjustly.

Because what can be known of God.

He shows how every human being, possessing natural understanding, recognizes that the invisible substance that works various arts and disciplines in all things must be pursued.

By this same example the invisible God is made manifest to human beings through the works that he has done and continues to do. At the same time, the mind of the Trinity is displayed: in it he generates the Word implanted in himself and possesses inseparably the Word born from himself as Wisdom.

Again, what can naturally be known about God is that he exists and that he is just.

It is manifest in them.

In their consciences. For every creature bears witness that it knows God and judges that it was made by another, whose will it must obey.

If God is the supreme and greatest being, invisible, incomparable, incomprehensible, and beyond estimation, and if he is above all things—that is, if nothing can be placed before him or made equal to him in greatness, brightness, or power—then it is clear that this cannot belong to any creature, since every creature is seen by the eyes, grasped by reason, and judged by estimation.

But no creature is greater than all others in every respect, because all surpass one another in some way. One does so in size, such as heaven and earth; another in brightness, such as the sun or a star; another in height, such as the sea.

Thus it is plainly seen that no element is God.

That they were made is shown by their mutability, which cannot belong to eternity. That they did not make themselves is also clear: for if they made themselves, they already existed before they were made, so that they could make themselves—which is utterly absurd to say.

When they change, alter their arrangements, and yield to one another, they show that they were made by one author and that they do not perform their own will but that of their Lord, whose command they cannot transgress.

For God manifested it to them.

His hidden power is judged from the things that are evident. If the things that are seen were made by him so magnificently that some people considered them gods and attempted to make them eternal, how much more could they understand that their maker is everlasting, almighty, and boundless!

This agrees with the Book of Wisdom, which says: “Compared with whose greatness, creation, the creator of these things may be seen,” and so forth.

For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made.

They were understood so evidently that they are said to have been perceived.

His eternal power and divinity also are so evident that they are without excuse.

Because, although they knew God—whether through nature, or through his work, or through reason—

they did not glorify him as God or give thanks.

This was despite having been made such that, if they wished, they could recognize God.

But they became futile in their thoughts.

Thinking that they could comprehend God’s greatness in their own thought, they became futile in their natural slumber, worshiping creatures in place of the Creator.

And their foolish heart was darkened.

They withdrew from the light of truth.

For while claiming to be wise—

as though they had discovered how the invisible God could be worshiped through the visible form of idols—

they became fools.

And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for a likeness.

They did not understand that mortal cannot have the likeness of immortal, nor corruptible the likeness of the eternal.

[Col. 0651B] Of the image of corruptible human beings, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of reptiles.

Not merely of a human being, but of the image of a human being; and not only of that, but also of animals.
