Here he refers to the worshipers of Jupiter, who assert that he was transformed into such creatures because of his most shameful loves, and therefore consecrated images of those forms to him, in which he satisfied his lust.

Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts.

When Scripture says that God gave sinners over to their own desires, it shows that he is not himself the cause, but that through forbearance and patience, by not bringing punishment upon them, he allows them to act according to the will of their hearts. He does this because he wishes them to turn to repentance.

Again, in the Scriptures God is said to “give over” when he does not restrain those who sin, on account of the freedom of their will, as the Psalm says: “And he gave them over to the desires of their heart.”

To impurity.

This is found in the shameful services of idols.

So that they dishonor their bodies.

When, in their rites, they inflict upon themselves cauteries and burnings.

In themselves.

So that, like madmen, they themselves become the avengers of their sins against themselves.

Because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie.

They exchanged the worship of the true God for the lie of idols, which they worshiped falsely through prodigies; and in a way they foolishly claim that something is what it is not.

And they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.

They not only loved it but also served it. For whoever is overcome by desire for some creature serves that creature. For everyone is the servant of the one by whom he has been overcome.

He who is blessed forever: amen. If they had served him, they could have become blessed forever. For whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as he himself remains forever.

Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions. For the reasons mentioned above, they have been abandoned to these shameful acts.

For their women exchanged natural use for that which is contrary to nature. Those who were perverse toward God perverted everything. For they did not preserve the order of nature, having abandoned the author of nature. [Col. 0652A] The worship of unspeakable idols is the cause, beginning, and end of every evil.

And likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of the woman, burned in their desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males. Unrestrained lust knows no moderation.

And receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error. The course of events proceeded in such a way that those who had forgotten God did not even recognize themselves.

And just as they did not approve of having God in their knowledge. They did not fail to know, but emphatically did not approve. For a person proves that he has God in his knowledge when, always having him present, he does not dare to sin.

God handed them over to a reprobate mind. They were not handed over to a reprobate mind in order that they might be rejected.

[Col. 0652B] To do things that are not fitting for a human being.

Filled with every kind of wickedness and malice. He shows wickedness and malice to be the principal causes of vices.

Fornication, greed, depravity. He joined fornication and greed together because idolatry is nearly equated with each of them as wickedness.

Full of envy and murder. Aptly he associated envy with murder, because the former itself is the first material of this crime.

Strife. Strife exists where something is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of mind, and where truth is no longer sought but one’s neighbor is wearied.

Deceit. Hidden malice adorned with flattering words.

Malignity. The desire or action of malice is called malignity.

[Col. 0652C] Whisperers. Murmurers who speak not to the face but into the ear.

Slanderers, hateful to God. For nothing is so hateful to God as idolatry; by comparison, the punishment of slander is joined to it in the writing, as though it were to be eradicated.

Insulting. Those who are quick to utter injurious words.

Proud, arrogant, inventors of evil. Whoever wishes to rise above what he is is proud, just as the devil destroys himself by aspiring beyond what he is. For whoever wishes to be above others will become beneath himself; and therefore “inventors of evil” follows, because pride always devises and discovers evil, just as the author of pride, through his arrogance, found for himself an evil that had not existed before. An arrogant person is one who is raised above his proper measure.

Disobedient to parents. True parents are those who, [Col. 0652D] through the seed of the word, beget children into the light for eternal life.

Foolish, disorderly. Those who have withdrawn from the fountain of wisdom must necessarily be carried along without order.

Without affection, without covenant. Affection is the fulfillment of charity.

Without mercy. When could they show mercy to others, since they did not wish to be merciful toward themselves? All these sins, arranged in order, are said of those who, abandoning God, have in turn been abandoned by him. Let us therefore beware lest, possessing some evil from among these, we too are similarly abandoned.

Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death. Here [Col. 0653A] he shows how each human being is to be judged by God according to his own actions: in this respect, the person himself judges and condemns another human being who sins. Again, when someone is displeased with himself because he has done evil, he is said to have recognized God’s justice; but such people did not understand that they would be punished by him, if not in the present, nevertheless in the future. For if they had understood, they would certainly have been afraid to commit such acts.

Not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them. So that no one might say that he had not done all these things, he added: those who approve of those who do them. But even one who did not approve these things, and who judged such conduct, nevertheless, by approving idolatry—which is the head and cause of all these things—seemed to have approved them all.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0653B]

Therefore you are without excuse, O every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself. For you do the very things that you judge. All such people who passed judgment are addressed, especially those who possess authority as judges and masters in reproving others. For by natural judgment each person pronounces a sentence worthy of his deeds; and everyone knows both that innocence deserves a reward and that wickedness has punishment.

For we know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things. But do you suppose this, O every human being who judges those who do such things and yet does them yourself—that you will escape God’s judgment? The judgment by which such people are judged will be according to truth: [Col. 0653C] they were unable to condemn in others what they did not fear to commit themselves. For if you, a sinner, judge a sinner like yourself, how much more will God, who is just, judge you, who are unjust? It must not appear that evil pleases him and good displeases him, since we read that he accepts no persons and has spared neither his friends nor his angels when they sinned. Human judgment, however, is corrupted in many ways. The integrity of judgment is often violated by love, hatred, fear, and greed; and sometimes mercy is bent contrary to the rule of justice.

Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? Here it is openly shown why God has allowed the sinner the desires of his heart: [Col. 0653D] although he can restrain the sinner or inflict punishment, he prefers that the sinner turn to repentance. Again, do you flatter yourself concerning impunity because God does not repay you in the present? Looking at the length of time and the abundance of his goodness, do you suppose that there is no judgment? Hear the judgment of Scripture: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promises, but acts patiently for your sake, not wishing anyone to perish but all to turn to repentance.” He is good in waiting; he is just in punishing. Hence the Prophet admonishes: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day; suddenly his anger will come, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” And again: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is a patient repayer.” [Col. 0654A] Many people deceive themselves through God’s patience, because he does not immediately punish sinners. He is thought either not to care at all for human affairs or to pardon faults because he postpones punishment. Many even bring accusations against him, asking why he does not repay in the present, without understanding that if this happened, scarcely any human being would remain, nor would the unjust ever become just. God therefore seems to people to wait a long time for sinners because, being of short duration, we consider a hundred years to be eternity. But for him, with whom a thousand years are as one day, a hundred years do not equal the span of a single hour; therefore this is short in his sight, even though human beings themselves commonly expect the correction of sinners to take a long time.

According to your hardness and impenitent heart. [Col. 0654B] But you, foolish sick person, apply the remedy itself more harmfully to your wounds, because, in accordance with the judgment of blessed Job, you abuse repentance as an occasion for pride. Thus unrecognized piety prepares a greater judgment for you, so that the one who disdained to experience mercy may experience vengeance. Again, every heart that does not feel is hardened. In this way God hardened Pharaoh’s heart.

You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who repays each person according to his works. For the day of judgment, you yourself store up wrath upon wrath, which will appear on the appointed day and at the determined time.

To those who, by perseverance in good work—. The reward of good work is awaited through perseverance, because it is not repaid in the present life. For we walk by faith and not by sight. And the work will then be complete [Col. 0654C] if it endures to the end, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Glory, honor, and incorruption. Glory, by which the saints will shine like the sun. Honor, the honor of the children of God, than which nothing is greater; through it they will also judge angels. Incorruption of perpetual life.

To those seeking eternal life. Whoever seeks eternal life through works of perseverance obtains all these things. And whoever has this hope sanctifies himself in it, just as he is holy.

But to those who are from strife. Let those who, often defeated, contend out of hostility hear this and fear remaining in their evil habit, lest all these things be counted against them. It has already been said above that the contentious person is specifically one who strives to defend something against his own conscience.

And to those who do not assent to the truth but believe in iniquity. They do not believe the truth of the Gospel and consent to iniquity, so that, abandoning the Creator, they may serve the creature.

Wrath and indignation. These are punishments in the judgment.

Tribulation and anguish. Of conscience and fruitless repentance, as it is written: “Then, practicing repentance, they will say within themselves and groan in anguish of spirit.” Up to this point the discourse is addressed to all who are subject to the natural law, among whom the Jews are also included. The Jew is placed before the Gentile because, in addition to the natural law, he possesses the written law.

[Col. 0655A] Upon every soul of a human being who does evil, of the Jew first and of the Greek. The Apostle threatens punishment to the soul because of heretics who say that only the flesh sins and deny that the soul can sin. Or “soul” is used for the whole human being, as in Genesis, where Jacob is reported to have entered Egypt with seventy souls.

But glory, honor, and peace to everyone who does good. Glory corresponds to wrath, honor to indignation. And what he called incorruption above, here he calls peace.

To the Jew first and to the Greek. What he called “soul” above, he has here named “human being.” He uses “first” in place of “indeed.” Or “first” refers to the time of believing, not to honor.

For there is no partiality with God. [Col. 0655B] Therefore let neither the Gentiles falsely flatter themselves concerning their ignorance, nor the Jews concerning the circumcision and privilege of the law.

For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. “Without the law of nature”: here “will perish” and “will be judged” are intended to mean one thing, because the one who perishes perishes through God’s judgment, and the one who is judged, as a sinner, perishes—as it is written, “because sinners will perish.” For he also makes them alike by saying that not merely hearers of the law but doers will be just. And a little later he says that the Gentiles will be judged on the day of the Lord. For who doubts that both those placed under the law and those living without the law will perish unless they believe in Christ?

For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, [Col. 0655C] but the doers of the law will be justified. He gives the reason why they are not better than the Gentiles. Therefore we too must fear lest, hearing the law but not doing it, we perish with the Gentiles, as he himself says elsewhere: “Lest we be condemned with this world.”

For when Gentiles, who do not have the law—. So that no one might perhaps say, “They do not have the law; by what standard can they be judged?”

By nature they do the things of the law. He is speaking either of those who were naturally just before the law, or of those who even now do something good.

Although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves. He shows that they are not without law, both to make the Gentiles inexcusable and to remove from the Jews their boast in their special possession.

They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them. Nature works the law in the heart through the testimony of conscience. Or conscience testifies that it possesses the law by fearing when it sins and rejoicing over conquered sins, even if the sinner himself has no fear of any human being.

And among themselves, their thoughts alternately accusing or even defending them on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings. He says that there are disputes among thoughts when, after prolonged deliberation, we decide what ought or ought not to be done; and according to this we will be judged on the day of the Lord, because we are shown not to have been ignorant of good or evil. Or our conscience and thoughts will be before our eyes on the day of judgment like histories to be examined: either they will accuse us or even defend us, as it is written: “I will reprove you and set it before your face.”

According to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ. According to what I proclaim through Jesus Christ, God will judge.

But if you are called a Jew. Here he turns to the Jews, teaching that one must be a Jew in deed, not in name only, and that the true Jew is the one whose hidden qualities are good:

And rest upon the law. You trust in it or are secure in it.

And boast in God, and know his will. You boast that you alone know God and recognize his will.

And approve what is more useful, being instructed by the law. You choose what is greater [Col. 0656B] and distinguish it from what is lesser. For whatever is judged more useful by nature is more useful through the law.

You are confident that you are a guide of the blind. Those whose heart has been darkened.

A light for those who are in darkness. The darkness of ignorance.

An instructor of the foolish. Those who do not possess the wisdom of God.

A teacher of infants. Of little ones in age or understanding.

Having the form of knowledge and truth in the law. By always looking to it, you cannot go astray.

Therefore, you who teach another, do not teach yourself. He had said similarly to the Gentiles: “You who judge another condemn yourself.” You who rest in the law, O Jew, why do you transgress the law? You who boast in God, why do you dishonor God? You who know his will, why do you not obey his will? You who approve what is more useful, why do you pursue what is useless? Guide of the blind: how do you not see the straight way? For if you saw it, you would certainly walk along it. If you are a light to others, why do you not cast off the works of darkness? Instructor of the foolish: why have you abandoned the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom? Teacher of infants: how are you childish in understanding? You who possess the form of the knowledge of truth in the law, why do you neither follow it yourself nor, by your worst example, allow others to follow it? Why does your life not correspond to your teaching, and why does your conduct destroy your faith? Thus the law, not observed by you, will not only benefit you nothing, but will also hold its contemptor guilty of a greater crime.

[Col. 0656D] You who preach against stealing, do you steal? Some say that by concealing Christ from human beings, you steal.

You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? Adultery is not of only one kind. For whatever the soul owes to God, if she gives it to anyone other than God, she commits adultery.

You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? Sacrilege is what is committed specifically against God, as a violation of what is most sacred. Again, he says that in the very act by which you commit sacrilege, you are shown to be an idolater.

You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? He explains the sacrilege, since he says:

For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written: in Isaiah. He placed the testimony before saying that it was written, in an inverted order. For the statement flowed forth in such a way that what he was saying from his own intention he found written with the same meaning. Or, in truth, the name of God had been blasphemed because of their unjust actions, as it is written: “They profaned my name among the Gentiles,” while they were called the people of God and dwelt among the nations to which they had been led captive because of their sins. Again, just as he says, “Through your good works God is blessed,” so now, when people do not live rightly, he is blasphemed.

Circumcision indeed profits if you observe the law. But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. How can it be nothing if it profits? It profits as a sign in its proper time; it profits if the justice of which it is the seal is present. Otherwise it will be superfluous, whether because it made a Jew live and caused infancy to be cut off before it could understand, or because it made him belong to the law, which, when examined, is found to teach that, once the circumcision of the flesh has ceased, the true circumcision of the heart would come. And he is a transgressor of the law when he does not follow what was foretold there.

Therefore, if uncircumcision keeps the ordinances of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? Visible things need invisible things; invisible things do not need visible things, because visible things are an image of invisible things, while invisible things are the reality of visible things. Therefore circumcision of the heart does not need circumcision of the flesh, because the reality does not need the image, whereas the image needs the reality. The question naturally arises: why was circumcision given if it does not profit by itself? First, so that God’s people might be recognized among the nations. Indeed, when they alone were in the desert, they were not circumcised. Or so that their bodies might be recognized in battle. The reason they are marked on such a member is first to prevent another member from becoming either weak or disgraceful and publicly visible. Again, it was because of the promise of grace, through which they were to please God by chastity. Or so that Christ might be signified as destined to be born from his seed, to whom this carnal circumcision would pertain, since it was to bring spiritual circumcision; bearing this type, Jesus son of Nave was ordered to circumcise the people a second time.

And uncircumcision, which is so by nature, fulfilling the law, will judge you, who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law. Either because, while pursuing the circumcision of the letter, you disdain to receive the circumcision of the spirit, or because, by not following what the law says, you have failed to receive true circumcision by believing in Christ.

For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly. He is the true Jew. For everything previously practiced concerning the outer person bore a figure of the inner person.

And circumcision of the heart. Of this it is written in the law: “In the last days God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God.” And again: “Circumcise yourselves for your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart.”

In spirit, not in letter; its praise comes not from human beings but from God. Not according to the letter of the law, but according to the [Col. 0658A] New Testament, which seeks the inner things that God alone sees.

## CHAPTER III

What, then, is greater in the Jew, or what is the advantage of circumcision? Much, in every way. This is said in the person of the Jew asking the question, with the Apostle replying: much indeed, in every way. The advantage is great not because they received circumcision in the flesh, but because the words of God were entrusted to them. Again, he explains that the law, when despised, is of no benefit, and that the privilege of carnal circumcision, unsupported by any works, is vain. He asks what greater advantage the Jew has. In his person the answer is given: much, in every way. For if the meaning is “much, in every way,” and “every human being is a liar,” how does he later contradict this by saying: “But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust?” Far be it from us, and so forth. Finally, how does he confirm that the Jews have nothing greater if here he recalls that they have much?

First, because the words of God were entrusted to them. This is what you will say first: that the words of God were entrusted to them, and to the Gentiles nothing.

For what if some of them did not believe? Did their unbelief annul the faithfulness of God? Far be it. He means the faithfulness of the promises, when it was said to Abraham: “In your offspring all the nations will be blessed.”

But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar. Here he uses “every” for “the greater part,” as in: “They all seek their own interests,” and “They all abandoned me; Luke alone is with me.”

As it is written: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” In the fiftieth Psalm. The opposing party placed this testimony as though it were saying: “I sinned for this reason, so that you might appear just by judging me.” But the true meaning is as follows: God had promised that he would exact punishment from sinners without partiality, and some judged his patience to be falsehood. He prevails when he judges, when he punishes their deeds—deeds in which no one would have thought that punishment would be exacted. Alternatively: You have shown that you care for human beings, since through the Prophet you revealed my hidden things, and you prevailed over those who pretend that you are unconcerned with human actions. Up to this point the objection has continued; now the Apostle begins to reply.

[Col. 0658D] But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust? It would be unjust if he exacted punishment from those who sinned for the purpose of appearing more just through them. Again, it is not that our iniquity adds anything to God’s justice; rather, at the time when we come to judgment with God, by not observing his commandments we deprive ourselves of the repayment of his promises. Thus God is shown to be truthful, because he does not give sinners what he promised to the saints.

Who inflicts wrath. As in the Flood and Sodom, so also in the judgment.

I speak in human terms: far be it from us. This is according to you, who think in such a way. Otherwise, how will God judge the world? For justice will condemn injustice, if, according to you, he is made more just by human iniquity.

For if the truth of God abounded through my lie for his glory. That is, increased.

Why am I still also—? That is, why am I additionally judged, I, whatever human being lies, who ought to be praised if God’s truth is confirmed by my lie?

Being judged as a sinner? And not as we are slanderously accused, and as some claim that we say. That is, why should the one who judges me judge me as a sinner, and not as some say that we teach: that the greater evils we commit, the greater goods we will receive?

Let us do evil so that good may come. They perhaps thought this because they did not understand what someone said: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.”

Their condemnation is just. For what is more just than that they should suffer the punishment which, by lying, they claimed we denied—the very punishment of God that we proclaim above all?

What then? Are we superior to them? Not at all. For we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin. We find no reason for us who are Jews to be greater. Reason has investigated this matter and found that both Jews and Greeks are under sin; we establish this not by reasoning alone but also by testimony concerning the Jews. Again, he shows that although the Jews possessed the Law and the Prophets, they had nothing greater than the Gentiles, because all sinned alike and lack the glory of God.

[Col. 0659C] As it is written: “For there is no one who is righteous.” In the thirteenth Psalm. The Psalm from which this testimony is taken speaks of the foolish person; it shows this testimony to have been especially fulfilled at Christ’s coming, namely at the time of his Passion, when, I think, no righteous person was found suffering with him.

There is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God. Whoever does not seek the foundation must necessarily turn aside.

All have turned aside. Whoever does not understand does not seek, or does not understand for this very reason: because he does not seek. God is sought when his will is investigated, because everyone who sins has not seen him or known him, since the one who sins does not know the will of his Lord. In ordinary speech as well, a person is said not to know when his will is unknown.

[Col. 0659D] Together they have become useless. Useless for the work for which they were created.

There is no one who does good, not even one. Not even the Apostle? Again, if there is no one who does good, how does he later accuse the people of devouring and confounding the counsel of the poor? The people of God would not be his people if they did no good, especially since a righteous generation is named in that very place. This pertains more to the interpretation of the Psalm than to the Apostle’s argument.

Their throat is an open tomb. By the stench of their teaching and the flattery of their speech, it contaminates and destroys those who hear. For this reason a tomb is carefully closed, lest, while people are still alive, its exhalation produce plague.

[Col. 0660A] They dealt deceitfully with their tongues. They promise one thing with their mouth while desiring another in their heart.

The poison of asps. He says that the poison of these snakes is especially deadly.

Under their lips. That is, in their heart.

Whose mouth is full of cursing. Cursing is not of one kind. Whatever is spoken with an evil wish is undoubtedly evil speech.

And it is full of bitterness. Bitterness is opposed to the sweetness of God’s words.

Their feet are swift to shed blood. He either simply calls them murderers, or those who kill souls through flattery. Hence Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “I am clean from everyone’s blood. For I did not shrink from proclaiming to you the whole [Col. 0660B] counsel of God.”

Ruin and misery are in their paths, and they have not known the way of peace. Their souls are crushed and made miserable either by their teachings or by the examples of their conduct.

There is no fear of God before their eyes. He concludes with the fear of God: if they had always had the fear of God before their eyes, they certainly would not have sinned. For a servant does not dare to sin in the presence of his master.

But we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law. So that they might not say that these things were spoken in the Psalm about the Gentiles, he shows that what is spoken in the law speaks to those who are under the law. The question naturally arises how the Jews said that God does not exist. They did not say this in words, but in their actions. For they profess to know him, but deny him by their deeds. Therefore here he does not mean the Gentiles, since he had already spoken such things about them in their own case.

So that every mouth may be stopped. Not only the mouths of the Gentiles but also those of the Jews, since they have nothing in which they can boast.

And the whole world may become subject to God. In the confession of sin.

Because no flesh will be justified before him by works of the law. “Is justified” in the present. Or by “works of the law” he means circumcision, the Sabbath, and the other ceremonies, which pertained not so much to justice as to the joy of the flesh. Again, the Apostle is not contradicting himself when he said above, “They show the work of the law in their hearts,” and now says that no flesh is justified by works [Col. 0660D] of the law. He accuses the flesh, which by its own inclination cannot submit to God’s law. For the law can show sin, but it does not show how it ought to be observed; and again, while punishing what is harmful, it does not grant pardon to the repentant. Christ, however, grants forgiveness of sins to believers and teaches how the vices of the flesh must be avoided and cut away by prudence.

For through the law comes knowledge of sin. It is not forgiveness of sin but knowledge. Through the law one recognizes what sin is because either the law of nature had been forgotten, or, before the written law, certain lesser matters were not recognized as sins—that is, things that did not harm others, such as desire, drunkenness, and other things of this kind.

But now the justice of God has been manifested apart from the law. This is what he means: the justice that was to be manifested in Christ was not known in the natural law. The testimonies of the law of Moses and of the Prophets are proclaimed through their announcements. Again, justice has been manifested apart from the written law: the justice freely given to us by God, not sought by our labor, and more clearly revealed through Christ’s examples—things that had lain hidden in the law.

Attested by the Law and the Prophets. Either this justice was proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets as destined to come in the last times, or the knowledge of sin received testimony from the Law and the Prophets.

[Col. 0661B] But the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ, for all and upon all who believe in him. The justice by which one believes in Christ.

For there is no distinction. Between Jew and Greek.

For all have sinned and lack the glory of God. Because they do not possess their own glory.

Justified freely by his grace. Without any action of works, through baptism, by which he freely granted forgiveness of sins to all who did not deserve it.

Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. By this redemption he redeemed us by his blood from death, to which we had been sold through sin, according to Isaiah’s statement: “You were sold because of your sins.” Christ conquered this death because he did not sin. We were all liable to death, but he handed himself over to it without owing it, so that he might redeem us by his blood. Hence the Prophet had foretold: “You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.” That is, you received nothing in exchange for yourselves, and you are to be redeemed by Christ’s blood. It should also be noted that he redeemed us, not purchased us, because previously we were his by nature, although by our sins we have been alienated from him. Our redemption will truly be fruitful if we cease to sin.

Whom God set forth. He placed him openly before the eyes of everyone, so that whoever wishes to be redeemed may approach.

As a propitiator through faith in his blood, for the showing of his justice. So that he might be gracious to those who believe that they are to be freed by his blood.

Because of the forgiveness of previous sins. Christ suffered for this reason: to appease God’s purpose, [Col. 0661D] by which he had finally determined to punish sinners.

In the forbearance of God, to demonstrate his justice at the present time. He wishes to show that God waited for this purpose: so that sinners might eventually correct themselves. But they, having misused God’s patience, fell into greater sins. Hence that most righteous Job, in his own time, says of the sinner: “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride.”

So that he himself may be just and the one who justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. He alone is found righteous, as is the one whom he himself has justified—not by works but by faith.

Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. He speaks to the Jew, so that you may not boast that you earned justice by works. Again, this is the Jew’s question. And the Apostle answers: It has been excluded. Again, the Jew asks:

By what law? Of works? That is, by the natural law. The Apostle rejects the works of the law.

No, but by the law of faith. By what law? Of works? “Is” is understood: No, but by the law of faith. By “law” he means the established order and principle of faith, that is, the New Testament.

For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. We are certain, or we judge. Some abuse this passage to destroy works of righteousness, asserting that faith alone is sufficient, although elsewhere the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.” In another passage he asserts that the fullness of the law is contained in this charity, saying: [Col. 0662B] “The fullness of the law is charity.” If these statements seem contrary to their understanding, we must believe that the Apostle said that a person is justified by faith without those works of the law—namely, circumcision, the Sabbath, and other things of this kind—not without works of righteousness, of which blessed James says: “Faith without works is dead.” Here, however, he speaks of the person who comes to Christ and is saved by faith alone when he first believes. By adding “works of the law,” he also shows that there are works of grace.

Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of Gentiles? Did God create only the Jews, or does he care only for them? For the Gentiles sinned, and so did you; and if you are converted, so are they. If Christ came to you as promised by the law, he came to them as well. For the Prophets frequently also spoke [Col. 0662C] about the calling of the Jews.

Indeed, also of the Gentiles. He preserved the order of the words beautifully. He said “indeed,” to show that the Gentiles were even more so included, although they had not been circumcised, and that Abraham was righteous before circumcision. He gives the reason so that he might not appear to exclude the Jews.

Since there is one God who justifies. You have believed in one God and one Christ alike.

Circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith. “By faith” and “through faith” mean the same thing. But the usage of Scripture here is to prefer changing the expression rather than repeating it when the subject is the same, as it is written in Daniel: “For the sake of Abraham your servant, Isaac your beloved, and Israel your holy one.”

Do we then overthrow the law through faith? Far be it from us. Rather, we establish the law. The Apostle is not contradicting himself when he said above that the shadow and type of the law were excluded by the present reality; now he says that he approves the law, in that he himself bears witness to it. Abraham was justified not by works of the law but by faith. Again, are we therefore to judge the law that commands circumcision superfluous? Far be it from us. Rather, let us make it stand, while we prove true what he said: that law would succeed law, covenant would succeed covenant, and circumcision would succeed circumcision.

## CHAPTER IV

What, then, shall we say that Abraham found? He brought them back to the beginning of circumcision, so that what had been established at the beginning might be applied to the whole.

[Col. 0663A] Our father. Our father according to the circumcision of the flesh. For faith resides in the mind.

According to the flesh. By saying “according to the flesh,” he shows that descent is of the flesh, not of the soul.

For if Abraham was justified by works of the law. If he was justified by circumcising himself, God gave him nothing, but he had glory from himself. Alternatively: If he fulfilled the commands, he has glory in himself, not before God.

He has glory, but not before God. By saying, “He has glory, but not before God,” he shows that he has glory from his own works and not from God.

For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God.” Abraham’s faith was so great that his former sins were forgiven, and faith alone, above every form of righteousness, was declared acceptable to him; thereafter he burned with such love that he prepared himself for works above all else.

And it was counted to him as righteousness. Therefore he has glory before God, in accordance with what the law approved.

But to the one who works, the wage is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt. For it is the debtor’s duty to do what is commanded; and unless he obeys, he is condemned. If he does obey, he has no grounds for glory, because he is still called an unprofitable servant who does nothing beyond what was commanded. Alternatively: Righteousness is not freely bestowed on such persons; rather, the reward of their former works is rendered.

But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. God justifies the ungodly who turns to him through faith alone, not through good works, which he did not possess. Otherwise he would have had to be punished for the works of his ungodliness. Notice also that he does not say that a sinner is justified through faith, but the ungodly; that is, he has just asserted the case of one who has recently come to faith.

According to the purpose of the grace of God. He purposed freely to forgive sins through faith alone.

As David also speaks of the blessedness of the human being. It is a great blessedness to obtain the Lord’s grace without the labor of the law and repentance, just as someone might receive some distinction freely.

To whom God reckons righteousness without works. Faith is first reckoned as righteousness for this purpose: that one may be absolved from the past, justified in the present, and prepared for the works of faith in the future.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.” What is repented of is not retained; what is covered does not appear, and therefore is not reckoned at all. Some say that sins are forgiven through baptism, covered through the labors of repentance, and not reckoned through martyrdom. Others say that, once sins have been forgiven through baptism, love for God is increased; this love covers a multitude of sins and thereafter prevents them from being reckoned, while past evils are overcome each day by good works.

Does this blessedness, then, remain only in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision? He wishes to assign this blessedness to three periods: nature, circumcision, and Christianity.

For we say that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. We all confess and agree that what reason discovers concerning Abraham, we should observe concerning the others.

How, then, was it reckoned to him: in circumcision or in uncircumcision? Let us see whether circumcision arose from righteousness, or righteousness from circumcision.

Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision. For he was righteous before he was circumcised.

And he received the sign of circumcision. Lest they should say, “Then he was circumcised to no purpose,” he says that it was a sign of righteousness, not an increase of it.

A seal of the righteousness of faith that was in uncircumcision. He received the seal of that righteousness which the faith of the uncircumcised man had earned. For his faith was perfect, so that it deserved a seal. A complete reality is always sealed. Or it was so that he might show how righteous and faithful was the one who did not hesitate to inflict pain upon himself at God’s command. Do not think it pointless that he was commanded by the Lord of all being, just as he did not believe parricide to be impious when it was commanded by the source of piety.

So that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them also; and the father of circumcision—not only of those who are from circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith that was in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham. Thus all who believe from the nations are Abraham’s children, since faith alone is reckoned as righteousness to them also. They will be circumcised, but in heart. Or, because he was righteous in uncircumcision, he was to be the father of the uncircumcised; and, remaining righteous after circumcision, he was to become the father of the righteous who were circumcised.

Not through the law was the promise made to Abraham or to his seed. Here he calls circumcision itself “the law,” since every commandment can be understood as law.

That he should be heir of the world—but through the righteousness of faith. Or, so that all the nations might be blessed in his seed, which is Christ, and were given to him by the Father as an inheritance. Or, so that the nations might recline with him in the kingdom of heaven.

For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished. If, as you wish, only the circumcised are heirs, God did not fulfill his promise to Abraham that he would be the father of many nations; and, if that is so, he will now appear to have believed God without reason.

For the law produces wrath. It was established for the unrighteous, and it burdened those who wished to sin more heavily than it absolved them, increasing their offenses through knowledge. For if you were blind, you would have no sin.

For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be secure according to grace for all the seed—not only for the one who is of the law, but also for the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written. Since faith cannot be emptied and the promise cannot be abolished, the inheritance is not from the law but from faith. For the law does not forgive sins but condemns them, and therefore it cannot make all nations Abraham’s children, since, insofar as all were found under sin, all were certainly subject to punishment. Faith, however, by forgiving sins through grace, makes all believers Abraham’s children—either because there is nothing to transgress where there is no law, or because there is nothing to be punished where the law is not necessary.

“I have appointed you the father of many nations” before God, in whom you believed. Before God, who is the father of all believers.

Who gives life to the dead. Here he speaks of the dead as being made capable of procreation, so that the statement may fit the present case.

And he calls those things that are not as though they were. Although at the beginning also he called into being things that did not exist, and they immediately began to exist, here he signifies the hopeless conception of a son, since their time for procreation had already passed.

Who against hope believed in hope. It was against the hope supplied by nature that a man of one hundred years, from a woman already exhausted and who had been barren even in youth, should believe that his offspring would be like the stars of heaven.

So that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea.” He who, by his own natural capacity, could no longer be the father even of one son.

And he was not weakened in faith. It is asked how Abraham, when his body had already become dead, fathered children by Keturah, although he had previously been unable to do so by Sarah. He did not father children by Sarah because he was both old and she was barren; but with Keturah, as though she were young, he could easily beget children according to the course of nature.

He did not consider his own body, already dead, when he was nearly one hundred years old, nor Sarah’s womb, already dead. Faith takes no account of nature, because it knows that the one who spoke is almighty.

He did not waver in disbelief at God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith. He doubted neither himself, nor the impossibility imposed by old age, nor the greatness of the promise.

Giving glory to God, fully certain that whatever God had promised, he was able also to accomplish. He gave thanks as though the promised gift had already been received.

Therefore it was also reckoned to him as righteousness, because he believed so perfectly and firmly.

Now it was not written only for his sake—that it was reckoned to him as righteousness—but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned. This was not so that we might merely know his faith, by which he pleased the Lord. He was tested so that he himself might know himself and so that we might follow him.

To those who believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead. If we believe as perfectly that Christ rose from the dead as Abraham believed that his already dead body could be made alive for procreation, then—

Who was handed over because of our offenses and rose because of our justification. By his death he abolished our sins; and, necessarily rising in the same condition in which he had died, he appeared in order to confirm the righteousness of believers.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, having been justified by faith. Having dealt with the reason why none of them was justified by works but all by faith—which he proves by the example of Abraham, whose children the Jews alone thought themselves to be—he shows by argument that it is not descent or circumcision but faith that makes people children of Abraham, who was justified by his first faith alone. Having concluded this argument, he urges them to have peace, because no one has been saved by his own merit, but all equally by God’s grace.

Let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Either, we are subject to both God and Christ; or, let us have the peace of God, not merely the peace of the world.

Through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace. Through him we have drawn near, although we were far away.

In which we stand. We who previously lay prostrate.

And we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. We glory because we hope to possess the glory of God’s children. What we hope for is so great that no one would dare to expect it on his own, lest it be thought not hope but blasphemy, since its greatness makes it seem incredible to many.

And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, and endurance produces testing. We glory not only in the hope of glory but also in the most beneficial tribulations, recognizing the greatness of the reward, as James says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers,” and so forth. For this reason we ought also to rejoice in suffering something for God’s name, so that from a tribulation that will end we may acquire an infinite reward. In view of the reward, we can judge no labor worthy of it. We know that people willingly consign themselves to wild beasts for the sake of gold, although they could not possess it forever; how much more ought we, following the example of the Apostles, to rejoice in tribulations! Although these tribulations are temporary, they acquire eternal salvation and free us from everlasting pains. Many have endured the greatest tortures for the hope of a small salvation and for the care of the body, yet they could not attain perfect health; and even if it came, it would soon be dissolved by the intervention of death. We therefore have something in which we may glory honorably and without danger. For it is a great glory to rise from the lowest things to the highest, to arrive from nothing at the greatest things, from clay to heaven, and from slavery to be called to a kingdom—provided that, having despised all the glory and pleasure of the world, we glory in that alone which is promised to us. If you do this, it is like someone who, having despised a lead coin, obtains a royal jewel—although the comparison is not even adequate, because however far the value of the two differs here, the corruption of both remains; there, however, corruptible things are exchanged for incorruptible and perishable things for eternal.

And testing produces hope, while hope does not disappoint. Hope for future things drives out all shame. Hence it is shown that the one who is put to shame by Christ’s commandments has no hope.

Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts. The greatness of benefits awakens in itself a corresponding greatness of love; when this love is perfect, it is confident and does not know fear. He also clearly demonstrates this, because whatever is given to human beings by God the Father is bestowed through the Holy Spirit.

Through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. We recognize from this how much God loves us: he not only forgave our sins through the death of his Son, but also gave us the Holy Spirit, who already displays the glory of future things.

For why did Christ die for us while we were still weak? Why did he die for us undeservedly, unless to make his love evident, when we were still oppressed by the sicknesses of sins and crimes?

At the proper time. At the time when we were weak, when righteousness had almost failed. Or because Christ suffered in the final period; or because he died for the period of three days, as had been foretold.

He died for the ungodly. He wishes to show that he died for the ungodly, so that by contemplating his benefits he might commend his grace and demonstrate, in the transaction concerning sin, how much we ought to love him. He also wishes us to see whether anything should be preferred to so great and holy a benefit, since he did not prefer even his own life to us, the ungodly, lest he deny us the death that was necessary for us.

For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person. For this reason someone dies with difficulty for a righteous person, because a righteous person has no need to die. Perhaps one person dies for another who is about to die.

For perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. The good person is himself the righteous person. For elsewhere he says: “The commandment is holy, righteous, and good.” “Perhaps,” however, means that someone might dare to do so just as readily, lest the good person suffer an injustice.

But God commends his love toward us. He makes himself lovable when he reveals how much he loves us. For when something is bestowed undeservedly, love is commended most of all. What could be more undeserved than that the sinless Lord should die for ungodly servants, and that the creator of the universe should deign to appear in human form and be despised for the restoration of his own creature?

For if, while we were still sinners according to the proper time—Christ died for us, then how much more, having now been justified— He notes that the Apostle often says that those who believe in Christ were sinners, thereby indicating that they are no longer sinners, so that they may recognize how they ought to conduct themselves.

We shall be saved from wrath through him, by his blood. Not by the blood of animals, as under the law. Let us therefore beware lest, by sinning, we call him polluted, as the Apostle himself says to the Hebrews.

For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Sinners are enemies because they despise God, as the Apostle says: “You know that friendship with this world is enmity with God. Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is regarded as an enemy of God.” They are enemies in their actions, not by nature. They are reconciled because by nature we had been brought into friendship.

Much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved in his life. If we have been saved through Christ’s death, how much more shall we be glorified in his life if we imitate it!

And not only that, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. We shall not only be given eternal life, but through Christ a certain likeness to divine glory is also promised, as the Apostle John says: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be, for when he appears, we shall be like him.”

Therefore, just as through one man— If sin entered the world through one man, Eve, those who say that sin was already in the world before the devil deceived Eve are insane. Here also he wishes to show that Christ suffered for this reason: so that we, who had departed from God by following Adam, might be reconciled to God through Christ.

Sin entered this world, and through sin, death. By example or pattern.

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Marius Mercator quotes this passage from Pelagius’ book as follows: “He used an example, or likeness,” he says, “because just as sin entered through Adam when it did not exist, so also, when righteousness had remained with almost no one, life was restored through Christ.”]

Just as, when sin did not exist, it came through Adam, so also, when righteousness had remained with almost no one, it was restored through Christ. And just as death entered through the sin of the former, so through the righteousness of the latter future life was restored, not present life.

And thus death passed to all human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0667D] The same Mercator reports this passage as follows: “When they sin in this way, they likewise die. For death did not pass to Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says: ‘They all live.’ He says that he calls all these people dead because, amid the multitude of sinners, the few righteous are not excepted, just as he says there: ‘There is no one who does good, not even one.’ And again: ‘Every human being is a liar.’ Or certainly,” he says, “it passed to all those who lived according to human custom, not heavenly.”]

While they sin in this way, they likewise die. For death did not pass to Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob, concerning whom the Lord says: “For all these are alive.” But he calls all dead here because, amid the multitude of sinners, the few righteous are not excepted, as in the statement: “There is no one who does good, not even one,” and: “Every human being is a liar.” Or it passed to all those who lived according to human custom rather than heavenly custom. Here the Apostle also signifies the death of the soul: Adam died when he transgressed, just as the Prophet says: “The soul that sins shall itself die.” It passed also to all human beings who transgressed the natural law.

In which all sinned. That is, all sinned in this respect: they sin after the example of Adam.

For until the law, sin was in the world. The law arrived as the avenger of sin; before its arrival, they enjoyed greater freedom, or the greater length of the present life. Sin certainly existed before the law, but it was not regarded as sin in the same way, because it had already been almost erased from nature. By saying “until the law,” he means the law of Moses. By adding, “sin is not reckoned when there is no law,” he again indicates the natural law, through which Cain transgressed and, after him, those who transgressed the natural law.

But sin was not reckoned when there was no law. How did death reign, if sin was not reckoned? Unless one understands that it was not reckoned in the present life.

But death reigned from Adam to Moses.

[Note: [Col. 0669C] In the same author’s account from Pelagius’ book: “Or,” he says, “when there was no one to distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous, death thought that it ruled over everyone; or it ruled over those who transgressed a commandment as Adam did—that is, the sons of Noah, who were commanded not to eat the soul with the blood, and the sons of Abraham, who were commanded to be circumcised—and also over those who, without a commandment, disregarded the natural law.”]

While there was no one to distinguish beforehand between the righteous and the unrighteous, death thought that it ruled over everyone. Or it ruled not only over those who transgressed a commandment as Adam did—that is, the sons of Noah, who were ordered not to eat the soul with the blood, and the sons of Abraham, who were commanded to be circumcised—but also over those who, without a commandment, disregarded the law of nature.

Even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. These are those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression: they transgressed through the natural law, and not, as Adam did, through a commandment.

Who is the pattern of the one to come.

[Note: [Col. 0669C] The same author had read this as follows: “For just as Adam was formed by God without sexual intercourse, so Christ proceeded from a virgin, with the Holy Spirit as maker; or, as some say, he was a pattern by contrast—that is, just as the former is the head of sin, so the latter is the head of righteousness. But not as the offense, so also the gift, lest equality be thought to exist in the pattern.”]

Either Adam was therefore a pattern of Christ because, just as Adam was made by God without sexual intercourse, so Christ proceeded from a virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit. Some say that he was a pattern by contrast, that is: just as the former was the head of sin, so the latter was the head of righteousness. Adam was also made a pattern of Christ. For just as the first Adam, transgressing God’s commandment, is an example for those who wish to transgress God’s law, so Christ, fulfilling the Father’s will, is an example for those who desire to imitate him.

But not as the offense, so also the gift. This is so that equality may not be thought to exist in the pattern.

For if the many died through the offense of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for the many.

[Note: [Col. 0669C] The author cited above found the passage explained differently by Pelagius: “The Apostle says that grace was more powerful in giving life than sin was in killing, because Adam killed only himself and his descendants, whereas Christ freed both those who were then in the body and those who were to exist afterward.” The same author adds this antidote to the poison in these words: “Here the careful Catholic reader should note what he says: that Adam harmed not only himself but also his descendants. By ‘descendants’ here, hold to his earlier definition: he does not mean that all human beings everywhere were entirely harmed by that sin, but only those who, through imitation, became guilty by their own sins and transgressions in the same way as Adam. These are undoubtedly found to be his great-grandchildren and descendants.”]

Here he clearly teaches that he is not speaking generally about every human being when he says, “Through the offense of one, many died,” because through the common and natural death not only sinners but also righteous people die.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Saint Augustine seems also to have had this passage in mind when he attacks it at the beginning of book 3, chapter 1, of On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins: “But,” he says, “after a very few days I read certain writings of Pelagius, a man, as I hear, holy and a Christian of no little advancement, containing very brief expositions of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. There I discovered, when he had come to the passage where the Apostle says that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus passed to all human beings, a certain argument of those who deny that infants bear original sin [lacuna] Thus the argument is set out: ‘These people,’ he says, ‘who oppose the transmission of sin try to attack it in this way: If Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe, because he says in the same way, indeed even more strongly, that through one person people are saved than through one person they previously perished.’” Mercator gives the same passage more fully: “Those who hold opinions against the transmission of sin try in another way to attack those who defend its transmission. ‘If Adam’s sin,’ he says, ‘harmed even those who did not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits those who do not believe, since the Apostle says in the same way, indeed more strongly, that people are freed through one person than they previously perished through one person.’ Then they say, he continues: ‘If baptism cleanses that ancient and long-standing sin, those who are born from two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin. For they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess at all.’ They add, he says: ‘If the soul is not transmitted by descent, as indeed it is not, but only the flesh has the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves the punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s mass, should bear another’s ancient sin; nor is it reasonable that God, who forgives one’s own sins, should reckon against someone an alien sin.’”]

And not as through one sin, so also is the gift. It is greater.

For judgment from one offense led to condemnation, but grace from many offenses led to justification. From one righteous man’s sin came the judgment of death.

For Adam did not find much righteousness to destroy by his example; Christ, however, dissolved the sins of many by his grace. Adam supplied only the pattern of offense, whereas Christ both freely forgave sins and gave an example of righteousness.

For if death reigned through the offense of one, through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Why did he forgive many sins? Because the gift of the Holy Spirit is abundant, since there are many gifts. Righteousness itself is given through baptism; it is not possessed by merit.

Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings. Death reigned; the implied meaning is that grace also reigned through justification.

He also says above: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” And he adds: “Certainly not.” How can he condemn all human beings through the offense of one, Adam, when all human beings have not been justified through the righteousness of one, Christ? When he says “all,” he does not speak universally but indicates the multitude of each particular group. Otherwise all human beings would be found justified in Christ just as they were condemned in Adam, and there would no longer be anyone to punish.

For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous. Many sinned by the example of Adam’s disobedience. For the crime of disobedience is great, since it killed so many.

But the law entered alongside, so that the offense might abound. Since the Hebrews and scribes, who possessed the natural law, received the written law as well, he says that it entered alongside. They received the law for a greater reward, but by their negligence they did not keep it and fell into a greater offense. They should not say, “The law was given to us to remove sin.” No, he says; it did not come to remove sins but to display them. And while people sinned knowingly, the offense began to abound—as though he were saying: “As I see it, the law did not take away sin but added to it,” not through any fault of its own but through theirs. It entered alongside, that is, it entered suddenly, and thus it happened that the offense abounded.

But where the offense abounded, grace abounded still more. As the Savior says: “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more.” The quantity of sin was made manifest so that the greatness of grace might be known and we might render the appropriate debt of love.

So that, just as sin reigned in death, grace might also reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Just as the kingdom of sin was abundantly established through contempt of the law, so the kingdom of grace may be established through the forgiveness of many sins and the continual practice of righteousness thereafter.

## CHAPTER VI

What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? Certainly not. For we who died to sin— He speaks of those whom faith found in this condition, not of us, who have now died to sin so that we might live by grace, lest people who did not understand should say: “If grace increases in proportion to the magnitude of sins, we ought to sin so that grace may abound more and more.”

How shall we still live in it? He wishes the baptized person to be so firm and so perfect.

Or do you not know, brothers? Or perhaps you do not know the very sacrament of baptism.

For all who were baptized into Christ Jesus— Scripture understands baptism in three ways: baptism of water; of the Holy Spirit, who is also called fire; and of blood in martyrdom, concerning which the Savior said: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized.”

Were baptized into his death. So that we might die together with him in baptism.

For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. He shows that we are baptized for this purpose: that through the mystery we may be buried with Christ, dying to our crimes and renouncing our former life. Thus, just as the Father is glorified in the resurrection of the Son, so he may be honored by all through the newness of our conduct, so that not even the signs of the old human being may be recognized in us. For we ought not to desire or pursue anything that those who have not yet been baptized desire and pursue, nor anything pursued by those who are still entangled in the errors of their former life.

For if we have been grafted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with him in his resurrection. If we have now been buried with him, then we shall also be able to share in his resurrection; and if we have become new and changed in our conduct, we shall likewise be new and changed in glory.

Knowing this, that our old human being— Those who sinned by imitating the earthly old human being, Adam—

Was crucified together with him. Understand that you were crucified through baptism, having become a member of his body. He hung an innocent body on the cross so that you might suspend your guilty body from its vices. In this mystery Moses hung a bronze serpent in the desert.

So that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we might no longer serve sin. This means that all vices are to be destroyed, since each individual vice is a member of sin, while all of them together constitute the whole body. Christ was crucified whole, not partially. Or it means that our body should be destroyed as a servant of sin and made a slave of righteousness, although it had been accustomed to belong to wrongdoing. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

For the one who has died has been justified from sin. That is, he has been separated from sin. A dead person does not sin at all. So also, the one who has been born from God does not sin. For one whose every limb is occupied by the pain of crucifixion can scarcely sin.

But if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him. If we have not died together with him, we shall not live together with him, because we are not his members.

Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him. Thus, if here we have died voluntarily, we shall not fear a second death. Or, you cannot be baptized a second time, because Christ cannot be crucified again for you, as he says to the Hebrews: “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened,” and so forth. He does not deny repentance to them but rejects the repetition of baptism.

For in that he died to sin, he died once. He himself bore our sins and suffered for us so that we would not sin thereafter.

But in that he lives, he lives to God. He lives in the glory of divinity.

So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus. Know that, as his members, you have died together with him once and must now always live to God in Christ, in whom our life is hidden with God. Put him on and follow his example.

Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Live in your mortal body as immortal people. He explains how sin reigns in the body: through obedience and consent.

Nor should you present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. Each member, if it turns its function to evil uses, becomes a weapon of unrighteousness for attacking righteousness. It should also be noted that, by the freedom of the will, a person presents his members to whichever side he wishes.

But present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead—as people who have already risen, because then one no longer lives carnally or in sin.

And your members as weapons of righteousness for God. Let the eye that previously looked in order to desire now look upon the naked in order to clothe them. Apply this same principle to the other members.

For sin will not rule over you. Sin will not conquer you. For you are not little children but mature, like a tutor in relation to a child. Do not commit a fault in speech; you are no longer listening to a grammarian but to an orator. Or, it means that sin ought not to rule. He does not say this because it is impossible for those who have received grace to sin; rather, he says that sin will not rule over you.

For you are not under the law but under grace. He knows well that those who are under grace are free from many different precepts and burdens of the law. These were given because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, as in the command to destroy a leprous house and cast it far from the city into an unclean place. Those who share in Christ’s grace have learned how they ought to overcome their passions and love God and their neighbor, as it is written: “You are not under the law but under grace.” Grace has provided an example of how to live and of teaching.

What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law? He says this lest they should say: “Then, since the law’s punishment has ceased, we may sin with impunity.”

But under grace? Certainly not. If you sin, you are not under grace.

Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness? If you wish to serve sin, you will begin to be subject to the sentence of the law, which takes vengeance on sinners. But if you obey righteousness, you are not under the law but under grace.

But thanks be to God that you were slaves of sin. “You were,” he says, “but you are not.”

But you obeyed from the heart the form of teaching to which you were handed over. “From the heart” means faithfully.

And having been freed from sin, you became slaves of righteousness. You became so through the teaching and example of Christ, who taught us to remove not only sins but also the occasions of sins.

I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. I speak in human terms because you are not yet able to hear divine things fully. Although you ought to serve righteousness much more than you formerly served sin, I nevertheless accommodate myself to your weakness, so that you serve righteousness alone. Or it means: I speak now in terms worthy of human reason, which everyone could share with me and no one reject.

For just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity, leading to iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness, leading to sanctification. Whatever the soul does carnally is reckoned as carnal; but if the flesh performs a spiritual work, the whole human being becomes spiritual, as in the saying: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul.” We presented our members to serve sin, not—as the Manichaeans say—with sin implanted in the nature of the body.

For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. That is, you served it in no respect at all. So now also be free from every sin.

What fruit did you have then from those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. There is certainly no fruit in something of which one is ashamed through repentance. Everyone who recognizes goodness is ashamed of his former actions; but whoever is ashamed of righteousness does not know its fruit. Thus those who sin have no fruit even in the present and will receive everlasting death in the future. Those who serve the Lord, however, have fruit in the present—the gift of the Holy Spirit—and eternal life in the future. Alternatively: Why did you have fruit in practicing that thing whose very recollection also brings shame?

But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification, and its end is eternal life. This itself is fruit, because you will live sanctified through baptism.

For the wages of sin are death. Whoever serves under sin receives death as his recompense. Likewise, the reward which it offers for our deception is death.

But the grace of God is eternal life. He did not say similarly, “the wages of righteousness,” because righteousness does not exist in us before it is rewarded. For it was not acquired by our labor, but granted freely as a gift of God.

## CHAPTER VII

Do you not know, brothers? For I am speaking to those who know the law. Here he begins to demonstrate the difficulty of the law, so that he may urge them to pass over to grace without fear of it. [Col. 0674D]

For the law rules over a person for as long as he lives. “The person,” or “the law over the person.”

For the woman who is subject to a husband is bound by the law while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband. By comparison with the law, he calls the commandment “the husband,” in order to show that the law, deprived of the effect of punishment and as it were dead, can no longer hinder us, now that we have been put to death, from passing over entirely to Christ, who rose from the dead. He would rightly live for us if he had found something in us that he could punish.

Accordingly, while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she belongs to another man. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she belongs to another man. [Col. 0675A] As long as her husband lives, she must live according to his will alone; but when, after his death, the woman has been joined to another man, she no longer has to live according to the custom of her former husband.

Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death with respect to the law. He did not wish to call the law “dead,” in keeping with the comparison; rather, what he did not dare to say to them in words he left to their understanding.

Through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another husband, who rose from the dead, in order that you may bear fruit for God. By dying with Christ, who condemned sin in the flesh.

For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which existed through the law, were at work in our members. When we were living in a carnal manner, the passion of desire was at work in the eyes, and other passions in the other members, although the law showed these passions to be sins. A person is also “in the flesh” when he is led by the will of the flesh and is prevented from obeying God’s law, because he cannot serve two masters. But now, taught by the grace of the Holy Spirit to overcome the passions, we are not in the flesh, because we have died to the law, which does not contain the teaching of grace.

So that we might bear fruit for death. So that the severity of the law might kill us.

But now we have been released from the law of death, in which we were held captive. By dying to the sin in which we were held captive by the law.

So that we may serve in newness of spirit. By the commands of spiritual grace, and not of the letter of the law. Likewise, this is a new form of service: not to love the world, nor the things that are in the world, and not to care for the flesh in its desires. For the law, by promising the good things of the earth, knows how to nourish the desires of lovers of the flesh. Here, rightly, the disciples of Jesus have died to the law, since they have renounced the world.

And not in the oldness of the letter. Here he makes mention of the written law and of the natural law, because the written law also contains the natural law. He goes on to say: “For I would not have known desire except through the law.” He assumes the role of a young person, wishing to show that as long as we are infants we have no knowledge at all of what desire is. But when we begin to grow, desire—which is forbidden by the law—begins to come within our awareness, once we are able to distinguish good and evil.
