What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Since he had always said that release from death came through it. Here again he wishes to show that the failure did not lie in the weakness of the law, but in the human will, because the law was not observed. By saying, “I did not know sin except through the law,” he assumes the role of a child who, because of the weakness of his age, is not subject to the law; but once he has grown up, he begins to be under the law and to know the commandments. [Col. 0675D]

By no means. This is directed against the Manichaeans. If they should say that he feared causing scandal, then he always feared it and never spoke against the law. From where, then, did you hear what he did not do?

But I did not know sin except through the law. Here he speaks in the person of the man who received the law, that is, who first comes to know God’s commandments while he has a habit of sinning. [Col. 0676A]

For I would not have known desire unless the law had said, “You shall not desire.” He did not say, “I did not have it,” or “I did not do it,” but “I did not know it”—that is, “I did not know that desire was sin.” Likewise, just as light reveals things in darkness, or shows an obstacle or a pit, so the law makes known that one must take precautions against and keep watch over sins; and for this reason we say that the law is holy and good.

But sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, worked in me. Here he calls the devil “sin,” as he is named in the Apocalypse—namely, the author of sin. He therefore speaks of the opportunity supplied by the commandment, which removed the excuse of ignorance. For he makes one sin more gravely than before, just as every envious person embraces an opportunity to do harm all the more eagerly when something is entrusted to the person against whom he is plotting. [Col. 0676B]

Every desire. Which had been forbidden by the law.

For without the law. The natural law, which suggested what sin is, had almost fallen into oblivion; therefore the written law was added, to remind those who had forgotten. Likewise, if sin was dead when the law did not exist, those who assert that sin comes down to us by transmission from Adam are insane. For this reason he says here that sin is dead: because in infants, who are without the law, it does not live—that is, it is committed with impunity. For when an infant curses his parents, the act appears to be sin, but it is not living sin; it is dead.

Sin was dead. Although a child sins, sin in him is dead, because he is not subject to the law. [Col. 0676C]

Now I was once alive without the law. I thought that I was living as a righteous and free person; or, “I was alive in the present life.” Likewise, when I was a child, I was not subject to the law.

But when the commandment came. Sin was recognized at the end of its oblivion, when the commandment arrived, so that everyone who committed it might know that he was dead.

Sin revived. When I grew up and began to be under the law, the offense that had been dead in me through ignorance when I was a child revived in me as the law ruled. Thus, he says, the commandment that had been given for life was found to bring me death, because of the habit and practice of sinning acquired in childhood. Likewise, because sin had lived through natural knowledge and had become dead through forgetfulness, it is said to have revived through the law. [Col. 0676D]

But I died. Because I transgressed knowingly.

And the commandment that was for life was found by me to be for death. When observed, it advanced one toward life; when neglected, it led to death. Likewise, he calls the punishment “death,” which sin acquired for us through its deception, displaying temporal and earthly things that are thought to be good and persuading us to transgress the law, which promises eternal life to those who fulfill it.

For sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me. Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good. This is directed against the opponents of the law and against those who separate righteousness from goodness: the law is called both holy and good and righteous. “Unless your righteousness abounds,” he says. But God, too, is sometimes called good in the Old Testament and righteous in the New. “Righteous Father,” the Lord says. This passage is directed against the Marcionites. [Col. 0677A]

Therefore, did what is good become death for me? By no means. It was not itself the cause of death for me, but I, who by sinning found death.

But sin, in order that it might appear to be sin, through what was good worked death in me. Through the goodness of the law sin is revealed and is punished by it. Likewise, he wishes to show how, when a child who had previously been without the law begins to grow up and is nevertheless forbidden things by his parents, sin begins to appear. It becomes apparent when he learns to avoid it. For if sin itself, at a more mature age, is not only not cut away but increases, the person becomes a sinner beyond measure, since he no longer deserves pardon. [Col. 0677B]

So that sin might become sinful beyond measure. Before the law, sin had a limit because of ignorance; it exceeds the limit when it is knowingly committed. Likewise, he says that when the adolescent was not yet liable to sin on account of his age, but, once the law came to rule him, the act he committed was reckoned as guilt: sin became beyond measure.

Sin through the commandment. Now the discourse is delivered from the perspective of one who has reached the legally responsible age. For the person who says, “The law is spiritual,” condemns himself by sinning through his own will. Hence he adds: “But I am carnal, sold under sin,” to show that, although he was free, he himself sold himself to sin. For what else does he say? “What I do, I do not understand”—that is, unwilling to discern the harm, I do harm willingly. I desire what belongs to others, wishing to defraud them of it: this is what he shows by saying, “For I do not do what I want”—that is, that good should be done to me—“but what I hate, that I do”; this is similarly understood as bringing evil upon me. For if I do what I do not want—evil to be done to me—I agree with the law, because it is good, commanding: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.”

For we know that the law is spiritual. It commands spiritual things.

But I am carnal. Whatever law I receive, I am accustomed to live according to it in a carnal manner. [Col. 0677D]

Sold under sin. “For what I do, I do not understand.” I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate. Once sin has been proposed, if I accept its counsel, I become its slave, voluntarily subjecting myself to it. Even as though intoxicated by the habit of sins, I do not know what I am doing. “For what I do, I do not understand.” Or it should be punctuated in this way: I do not understand that the evil which I admit unwillingly is evil, since I do not want to do the evil that I commit; nevertheless, I agree with the law, which both does not want evil and forbids it. It may also be understood thus: If I sin, I subject myself to the severity of the law. Likewise, the person who serves the will of the flesh is found to sin.

But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, because it is good. If I wish to keep, according to the flesh, the things that the law commands and that are contrary to the will of the flesh, I do what I do not want; but according to the will of the spirit, I agree with the spiritual and good law of God. [Col. 0678A]

But now it is no longer I who do it. Before the habit arose, I myself willingly did it. Likewise, by saying, “It is no longer I who do it,” he shows that a rational person ought not to live in the manner of irrational animals. Then, by adding that sin dwells in him, he teaches that he has handed himself over entirely to the passions of the flesh, which are hostile to God.

But the sin that dwells in me. It dwells like a guest and as one thing in another—not as one unified thing, that is, not as something natural, but as something accidental.

For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. He does not say, “My flesh is not good.” Likewise, this is spoken in the person of one who has a habit of sinning and is held captive by the vices of the flesh. [Col. 0678B]

For the will is present with me. There is a will, but not its accomplishment, because the carnal habit resists the will. Likewise, the will of the flesh is loved more than God’s will. Therefore he says, “The will is present with me,” so that I may not accomplish for my neighbor what I want to be done as good for me; for what I hate to suffer, that I do.

But I do not find how to accomplish the good. I do not see how to do it.

For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want. For example, if someone has already become accustomed to devouring, he falls into it even when he does not wish to.

But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me. Not I, who act unwillingly, but the habit of sin—which nevertheless I myself prepared for myself. [Col. 0678C]

I find, therefore, a law for me who want to do good. If I want to do good, I find in myself a law opposing the evil that is present. Likewise, this is what he says: according to the will of the soul, he wants to do good; evil lies close beside him, according to the desires of the flesh.

For evil lies close beside me. By saying, “For evil lies close beside me,” he shows that he does not sin by necessity, but is led to sin by his own will when he chooses to be a lover of the flesh.

For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person. I agree with the law according to the mind. Likewise, our inner person is the rational and intelligible soul, which agrees with the law of God. Its law is to live rationally and not to be led by the passions of irrational animals. The outer person, however, is our body. Its law is the prudence of the flesh, which teaches one to eat and drink and to make use of other pleasures that oppose reason. If these prevail, they subject one to the law of sin. Thus it is just as some understand it: we do what we do not want. [Col. 0678D]

But I see another law in my members. The customary desires, or the persuasion of the enemy.

Warring against the law of my mind. That is, against the natural conscience, or against the divine law that resides in the mind.

And taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members. Into the habit of offenses.

Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? I, who am held in this way—who will deliver me from this bodily, deadly habit? [Col. 0679A]

The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Admirably he added, saying, “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” because what Moses and the natural law did not teach, our Lord Jesus Christ taught: to despise the world and overcome vices. Hence the blessed Apostle teaches this when he says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” Likewise, the law could not set him free—but was Paul not yet liberated by the grace of God? From this it is proved that he is speaking here in the person of another.

Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind. He recapitulates in order to conclude, and again speaks in the person of the one who was under the law. [Col. 0679B]

But with my flesh I serve the law of sin. The carnal person is, in a certain way, double and divided within himself.

## CHAPTER VIII

Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. Here the Apostle says that there is nothing deserving condemnation in those who have crucified the works of the flesh.

For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus. It should be noted that he calls grace “law.”

Has set me free from the law of sin and death. Which puts sinners to death.

For what was impossible for the law. Here he shows that the law could not be fulfilled because of the weakness of the flesh. But in saying, “God, by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin,” he demonstrates that the Son existed before the incarnation and that, having afterward assumed flesh inclined toward sin, he nevertheless assumed it without sin. For this reason he is said to have come “in the likeness of sinful flesh”: having assumed flesh, he came and condemned sin in that same flesh, because he preserved the flesh he had assumed unharmed by every contagion of sin. Likewise, by “law” he does not mean the commands concerning sacrifices and the other things given as a shadow until the time of Christ, but the law which our Lord Jesus Christ also taught when he said: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.” “For this is the Law and the Prophets.” That law was weak because of us, because we were unwilling. The commandments were not impossible. Therefore the Son of God, taking the form of a servant and becoming human, condemned sin in the flesh and instructed us how sin ought to be condemned in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. [Col. 0679C–D]

In what was weakened through the flesh. It was weakened in them, not in itself.

God sending his Son. This is directed against Photinus, who denies that the Son existed before the flesh.

In the likeness of sinful flesh. By saying “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he shows that Christ bore the same flesh, but without sin. Likewise, here the likeness possesses reality, just as Adam begot offspring in his own likeness. Our Lord God Jesus Christ therefore assumed flesh like that of other human beings. [Col. 0680A]

And by sin he condemned sin in the flesh. It is as if you were to say, “From the enemy he conquered the enemy.” Or, just as the victims that they offered for sin under the law were called by the name “sin,” although they themselves knew no transgressions—as it is written, “And they shall lay their hands upon the head of their sin”—so Christ’s flesh, which was offered for our sins, received the name “sin.” Some, however, say that through the sin of the Jews, who killed the Lord, the devil’s sin—which had deceived the enemy—is condemned through a human being, as he says to the Hebrews: “So that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death.” Or he means that from the substance of that flesh which formerly served sin, Christ conquered sin by never sinning; and in that same flesh he condemned sin, to show that guilt belongs to the will, not to nature—which was made by God in such a way that it can refrain from sinning if it wishes. [Col. 0680B]

So that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. So that what the law could not fulfill in them, because of the opposition of the carnal habit, might at least be fulfilled in us, who will put the flesh to death by Christ’s example.

Who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the spirit attend to the things of the spirit. The human being is constituted from spirit and flesh. Therefore, when he performs carnal acts, he is called entirely “flesh”; but when he performs spiritual acts, he is called entirely “spirit.” For each substance, when it raises the other into its own dominion, loses, in a certain sense, its distinctive power and name. For each desires what is akin and close to it.

For the prudence of the flesh is death, but the prudence of the spirit is life and peace. It should be noted that it is not the flesh but the prudence of the flesh that is death. By calling its end “death,” he signifies eternal punishment. Likewise, elsewhere he says that human prudence consists in returning evil for evil. Such prudence therefore produces death by transgressing the commandment. The prudence of the spirit, however, has peace in the present, by not returning evil for evil, and life in the future. Prudence derives its name from foreseeing.

Because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. For it is not subject to the law of God. It is not the flesh itself, as the Manichaeans say, that is hostile to God, but the carnal understanding. Everything that is not subject is hostile, and whoever wishes to avenge himself sometimes even exceeds the measure of the old law. [Col. 0680C–D]

For it cannot. He called it impossible, in order by this means to recall them from the desires of the flesh.

But those who are in the flesh. Here it is proved that above he had accused not the flesh itself but the works of the flesh, because those to whom this is said were certainly living in the flesh.

Cannot please God. For it is impossible that someone devoted to the flesh should not at some time sin.

But you are in the flesh, yet in the spirit. That is, occupied with spiritual works. [Col. 0681A]

If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. Here he shows that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son. Likewise, the Spirit of God dwells in the person in whom its fruits appear, as he says to the Galatians: “But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy,” and so forth.

But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him. The Spirit of Christ is humility and patience and every virtue: Christ loved his enemies and prayed for them.

But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin. If you imitate Christ, the carnal understanding, as though dead, does not resist. Hence David also said: “I was like one who does not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth,” and so forth. [Col. 0681B]

But the spirit lives because of righteousness. Here he signifies our spirit, which is called life because of its righteousness, as though it were justifying the body for that blessed eternal life. Likewise, the spirit lives so that it may practice righteousness. For it is not enough merely to cease from carnal acts; we must also perform spiritual acts.

But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you. If you have indeed been purified so that the Holy Spirit may deign to dwell in you, God does not allow the temple of the Spirit to perish. Rather, just as he raised Jesus from the dead, so he will restore your bodies.

Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. He does all this to show them that the law given to carnal people is not necessary. Likewise, he now clearly shows that above he was not speaking of ordinary and natural death when he says: [Col. 0681C]

For if you live according to the flesh, you will die. He signifies the death of eternal punishment. He does not praise the spirit and blame the flesh because the human flesh is evil and the spirit good, since he himself teaches, saying: “The virgin thinks about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” He also knows how to accuse the mind, saying: “People corrupted in mind.” He says this in order to show that the greater part of the passions belong to the desires of the human body, which we share with the other irrational animals. For just as the other animals derive their origin from the earth, so do we with respect to the body. But our soul is a spirit, incorporeal, rational, and immortal. “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” According to the explanation given, carnal people cannot keep righteousness. [Col. 0681D]

But if by the spirit you put to death the works of the flesh, you will live. If you subject the works of the flesh through spiritual actions. It should certainly be noted that he is accusing the works of the flesh, not its substance.

For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. All who are worthy to be governed by the Holy Spirit. Conversely, those who sin are led by the spirit of the devil, who was a sinner from the beginning. Likewise, those who live according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit are the ones who are led by the Spirit of God.

For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God. It should be noted that although the Jews were sons of God, while they were under the law and acted as under a pedagogue, they nevertheless had the spirit of fear. Likewise, the Jews received a spirit that compelled them to slavery through fear. For it belongs to slaves to fear, but to sons to love, as it is written: “A slave will fear his master, and a son will love his father.” Therefore, those who were unwilling to act out of love were compelled by the necessity of fear. But let us do everything voluntarily, so that we may all prove ourselves sons, not slaves of fear. Likewise, you Romans have been called to adoption as sons, unlike the Jews, who were held in slavery, subjected to the authority of the law. [Col. 0682A]

In whom we cry, “Abba, Father.” Whoever calls him Father professes himself to be a son. He must therefore be found like his father in conduct, lest, having used the name in vain as well, he become subject to a greater punishment. [Col. 0682B]

For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. The testimony of adoption is that we have the Spirit through whom we pray in this way. For they could not receive so great a pledge unless they were sons.

But if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ. Whoever deserves to be a son deserves to become an heir of the Father and a fellow heir of the true Son.

If indeed we suffer with him. If, whenever necessary for his name, we endure sufferings such as he endured for us.

So that we may be glorified. As John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him.”

For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison. Here he wishes to commend the future glory, so that we may endure present pressures more easily. And truly, no human being could suffer anything worthy of heavenly glory, even if that glory were of the kind that the present life is. Whatever someone suffers through death is no more than he had already deserved for his sins. But now sins are forgiven, and then eternal life will be granted: fellowship with the angels, the splendor of the sun, and the other things that we read were promised to the saints. [Col. 0682C]

With the future glory that will be revealed in us. For now it is hidden with Christ in God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be—what the Lord promised to the saints.

For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God. Different people explain this passage in different ways. Either all creation awaits the time of the resurrection, because then it will be changed for the better, whether angelic or rational creation. For Peter says that the angels also desire the glory of the saints. Some also say it this way: Adam and Eve are the creation whom the serpent once subjected to vanity and made servants of corruption, after depriving them of the hope of divinity—not sinning of themselves, but through the serpent’s instigation and counsel. They too, they say, will be liberated, so that they may no longer serve corruption. They say that all creation consists of those who were righteous until the coming of Christ, because they too, not yet receiving what was promised, await it, while God provides something better for us. [Col. 0683A] Not they alone, but we ourselves as well, in whom these things have been completed—we do not yet possess them, but endure in hope, although we have seen many things that the righteous desired to see. Likewise, by saying, “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified,” and adding, “The expectation of creation,” he spoke about rational creation, not, as some think, about irrational or insensible creation, which was created for human service and will afterward perish when the sun is darkened, the moon gives no light, and the stars of heaven fall upon the earth. Then there will be a new heaven and new times. Creation, however, is Adam and Eve, who still await receiving adoption from God.

For creation was subjected to vanity. Everything that eventually comes to an end is vanity. Likewise, transgression is vanity: Eve was subjected to it, not by her own will, but deceived by the serpent through the hope in which she had heard, “And you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” The servitude is that of corruption, which Adam heard: “You are earth, and to earth you will go.” In the resurrection they will receive the incorruption of the sons of God. [Col. 0683B]

It was subjected. If angels minister to human beings.

Not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because creation itself will also be liberated from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God. It will no longer serve those who have corrupted the image of God.

For we know that all creation groans and is in labor until now. Just as the angels rejoice over penitents, so they grieve over those unwilling to convert. Likewise, here he calls the common creation—the righteous who existed until the time of Christ—“creation,” after Adam and Eve. They too groan together with Adam and Eve, who are called creation, desiring to receive the rewards of virtue that the Lord promised them. [Col. 0683C]

Not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we await the adoption of the sons of God. Not only the angels, who are kinder than we are, grieve over such matters, but we also, who already possess the Holy Spirit, groan over them, just as Jeremiah said in his lament: “Woe is me, my soul, for the one returning from the earth has perished,” and the rest. Likewise, by saying, “Not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit,” he clearly taught that he was not speaking about irrational or insensible creation, which does not share in the Holy Spirit, but about the saints who pleased God by the natural law, and likewise Moses. The disciples of Christ are said to have the first fruits of the Spirit, that is, the first and excellent spiritual gifts by which they enriched the whole earth. For such grace did not exist before the law or under the law of Moses. He teaches that the disciples of Christ are earlier than the others when writing to the Hebrews: “But all these, having been approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us.” [Col. 0683D]

Awaiting the redemption of our body. We have not yet received the promised reality itself, but we hope for it, as he says to the Corinthians: “For we walk by faith, and not by sight.”

For by hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what does someone hope for when he sees it? What is seen is not hoped for; rather, if it is one’s own, it is possessed. For Christians have no hope in visible things. What has been promised to us is not present things, but future ones. [Col. 0684A]

But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience. For this reason faith accompanied by patience is of great reward: it believes what it does not see and is so confident about things not yet received as though it had already received them, as he says to the Hebrews: “You need patience, so that, knowing the will of God, you may receive the promise.” For hope does not know how to exist without patience.

Likewise, the Spirit also helps our weakness. According to this hope it helps us, so that we may ask for heavenly things and not earthly ones. For our ability is weak unless it is assisted by the teaching of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0684B]

For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought. Because we still see through a mirror. Frequently the things we think will help us harm us, and therefore our requests are not granted by divine providence, as he himself says elsewhere: “For this I besought the Lord three times, that he might depart from me,” and the rest. Alternatively: It is difficult to express the desire of our prayer according to what we have conceived in our hearts; we can scarcely articulate it in words. Hence what follows:

But the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings. Therefore God, who searches hearts, even if we are not sufficient to comprehend it in speech, knows how far we wish to believe at present. Yet he knows that we ask for holy things, not worldly things, according to his own will.

But he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires. As the high priest.

Because he pleads according to God for the saints. Here he calls the grace of the Spirit “the Spirit,” just as elsewhere he says: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays,” and, “You are zealous for spirits.” But it is said to plead because it makes us plead with groanings that cannot be expressed, just as God is said to test us so that he may know—that is, so that he may make us know—what sort of people we are. Likewise, even a common action that the Lord commands is said to be performed by him: for example, “He built the house,” or “He made the book,” although he neither wrote it himself nor constructed it himself. Likewise, he calls the grace of the Spirit “the Spirit” that teaches us to plead with the Lord on our behalf, as Isaiah says: “The Spirit of wisdom and knowledge and understanding.” Writing to the Corinthians he also says: “Since you are zealous for spirits, seek the building up of the Church, so that you may abound.” [Col. 0684C–D]

But we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good. Everything that we do or suffer for the love of God increases our reward. For everything that the righteous person does will prosper.

For those who are saints, called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew. According to what he purposed—to save by faith alone those whom he had foreknown would believe—and those whom he freely called to salvation he will much more glorify as they work toward salvation. [Col. 0685A]

And he predestined them to be conformed to the image of his Son. To predestine is the same as to foreknow. Therefore, those whom he foresaw would become conformed in life, he wished to become conformed in glory. He “will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.”

So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. The firstborn from the dead into glory. Likewise, here, according to the fact that he became human, and according to the grace that was in him, the Son of God, the firstborn, intercedes for us—not as God does he intercede, but as the high priest. [Col. 0685B]

And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. Those whom he foreknew would believe, he called. Calling gathers willing people, not unwilling ones. Or certainly, the distinction lies not in persons but in time. He says this because of the enemies of faith, lest they consider God’s grace accidental. Therefore they are called through preaching, so that they may believe; believers are justified through baptism; and they are glorified through the virtues of grace.

What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He wishes to show that no one can prevent those who love God and are loved by God from attaining the glory that has been promised, because the perfect love that is in them drives out every cause of mortal fear.

He who did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all. He first said “handed him over,” so that freedom of choice might remain with those who handed him over, and so that an example of patience might be shown to us. By saying “for all,” it should be noted that he means not “for some.” [Col. 0685C]

How will he not also, together with him, grant us all things? What more precious thing could he withhold from us, who did not withhold his Son?

Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies? Who is the one who condemns? Those whom God chose as believers and showed to be righteous by signs and virtues—who would dare accuse them on account of their former offenses, or on account of their contempt for the commandments of the law?

Christ Jesus, who died—rather, who was also raised, who is at the right hand of God. He speaks according to the form of the human being that was assumed: the one who died and rose again.

Who also intercedes for us. So that we may be with him where he is. The Arians plainly customarily raise a calumny on the basis of the intercession, saying that the one who is interceded for is greater than the one who intercedes. They should be answered that God does not suffer forgetfulness, so that he must continually be reminded about those whom he himself chose. Rather, he is said to intercede in that he continually displays and offers to the Father the human being whom he assumed, as our pledge, as the true and eternal high priest.

Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword? As it is written. After such great and excellent benefits, or promises, what pressure could be so severe as to tear us away from his love? And in saying this he teaches everyone that those who belong to Christ ought to be such that not even dangers can separate them from him. [Col. 0686A] At that time, however, the Jews wished to separate them from Christ in such a way as to recall them to observance of the Law.

Because for your sake we are put to death all day long. Not because of any crime, but for your sake, who said: “Blessed will you be when they persecute you,” and so forth.

We are regarded as sheep for slaughter. This is fulfilled especially in us Christians, who are not permitted to defend ourselves; but, following the example of the Lord and Teacher, who was led like a sheep to the sacrifice, we must endure with the utmost patience everything inflicted upon us.

But in all these things we conquer, because of him who loved us. We regard all these tribulations as nothing because of him who loved us so greatly that he even died for us. And when we die for his name, then we triumph most fully—especially [Col. 0686B] since it is a light thing to suffer for him when Christ the Lord deigned to suffer for the sake of others.

For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither powers, neither height nor depth. I am firmly convinced that neither if someone threatens me with death, nor if he promises life, nor if he claims to be an angel sent by the Lord, nor if he falsely claims to be the prince of angels, nor if he confers honor in the present, nor if he promises the glory of future things, nor if he performs miracles, nor if he promises heaven and frightens with hell, or attempts to persuade us of the depth of knowledge—nothing will ever be able to separate us from the love of Christ.

Nor will any other creature be able to separate us from the love [Col. 0686C] of God. He has named almost every creature, and he was not content with these unless he added that even if there were some other creature, it too would not be able to separate us.

Which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. He loves God in Christ, whose love consists in keeping the commandments, as he himself also says: “If you love me, keep my commandments.” He likewise established the imitation of his love in brotherly love, saying: “By this people will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.” And John says: “If you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?”

## CHAPTER IX

I speak the truth in Christ Jesus; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit: for I have great sorrow and continual grief in my heart. Since he is about to deal with the Jews, he first assures them that he does not say this out of hatred but out of love, because he grieves that they do not believe in Christ, although he had come first to save them. When he says that he speaks the truth in Christ, he shows that he is a baptized man, who through participation in the body and blood of Christ remains in him, and he in him; whatever he does or says in Christ, he does or says as one whose member he is. And whatever injury is inflicted upon him is likewise inflicted upon Christ. For when he says that his conscience bears witness for him in this matter, he teaches that the man speaks the truth whose conscience attests him in all things. He does not establish him as guilty of falsehood through an inward accusation. Likewise, the Apostle says that he is very sad on behalf of his brothers according to the flesh, although he says that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ. He knew that when he was a persecutor and wished to be anathema from Christ, he had been called by Christ according to Christ’s mercy; and he wanted them to believe and to obtain that same mercy.

For I myself once wished to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh. At one time, when I was persecuting Christ, I did not merely wish this: I knew that all these things belonged to them. But after I came to know the truth, I abandoned those whom I had loved in such a way, and they still have not been converted.

[Col. 0687B] They are Israelites, to whom belongs the adoption as sons. For he said concerning them: “Israel is my firstborn son.”

And the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law. The promulgation of the old covenant, and the promise of the new.

And the worship and the promises. This is the mystery of the angels or prophets.

Whose are the fathers. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

And from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. Against Manichaeus, Photinus, and Arius: for he is from the Jews according to the flesh, and he is God blessed forever, just as Thomas also worships him and says: “My God, my God.” He confirms this by saying: “Because you have seen, you have therefore believed.”

But it is not as though the word of God had failed. Although the Apostle grieves that the Jews have fallen away from the grace of the promise, he nevertheless shows that the word of God was not empty, and that what was promised belongs not to those who were born from Abraham, Isaac, and Israel according to the flesh, but to those who preserve the faith of the patriarchs, from whose seed they are considered to descend. Likewise, because he had said above that he grieved that the nation of Israel was excluded from the kingdom through its own fault, although all these things belonged to it, here he shows that those who do not believe are not children of Abraham, lest he seem to prejudice all Jews and they object to him: “Has God, then, lied to Abraham?”

For not all who are Israel by circumcision are Israelites, nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children. If not all, nevertheless some are. And if not all Israelites are Israel, then some are from the Gentiles [Col. 0687D] in whom there is no deceit.

But “in Isaac shall your seed be called.” Even then the children of Abraham were called only in Isaac, not also in Ishmael, although he too descended from Abraham’s stock. Likewise, Isaac’s seed does not mean those who were born according to the flesh, but those who are according to the spirit—that is, according to Isaac’s faith. Whoever is such a person belongs to this promise and to the adoption as sons. For Esau was his firstborn, yet he was not loved by God, except Israel.

That is, not those who are children of the flesh are the children of God, but those who are children of the promise are regarded as the seed. For Ishmael was born according to natural carnal use from a slave woman, whereas Isaac was generated beyond nature from aged parents, by God’s promise. Thus now the promise makes Christians children of Abraham, a promise merited by faith, so that he might be the father of many nations.

For the word of promise is this. Here he shows that the later people, like Isaac, are a people of promise.

“At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” Before you were born—indeed, before Rebecca brought Esau and Jacob forth from her womb—I loved Jacob. I hated Esau, the Edomite. The Apostle Paul, unfolding this passage by a mystical argument, as is written in Romans, joins together two testimonies from Genesis and Malachi. Rebecca also had Isaac our father from one act of intercourse. For although they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from the one who calls—it was said to her: “The elder shall serve the younger.” As it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” What is said here, “as it is written,” refers both to the Book of Genesis and to the prophet Malachi. He not only says, “I loved Jacob” before he was born and “I hated Esau” before he was brought forth from his mother’s womb, but he also preserved his love and hatred toward their descendants. His hatred toward Esau is shown in the fact that he reduced his mountains, called Seir, to desolation, made his cities deserted, and allowed them to be inhabited by snakes and wild beasts.

And not only she, but also Rebecca. Not only Ishmael and Isaac—who, although generated from one father, were born from different mothers—are not one before God, but also Jacob and Esau, who were born from one act of intercourse with Rebecca. Before they were born, they were separated before God by the merit of faith, so that God’s purpose of choosing the good and rejecting the evil might remain even in the present. Thus also now he chose those among the Gentiles whom he foreknew would believe, and rejected the unbelievers from Israel.

Having Isaac our father from one act of intercourse. She is read to have given birth to twins first; and, terrified as though something new had occurred, she inquired of God.

For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain. Or this signifies that even now, among twins, the one who does not believe will be rejected.

It was said not from works, but from the one who calls. God’s foreknowledge does not prejudice sinners if they wish to convert. For he says through Ezekiel: “If I say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he turns and does righteousness, he shall live and shall not die.”

For the elder shall serve the younger. In the Book of Genesis it is said: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your body; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.” Therefore the prophecy does not concern those who are Jacob and Esau according to the flesh, but those who were destined to arise from works of good and evil, and who through those works would either incur God’s hatred or obtain his mercy.

As it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” This phrase, “as it is written,” belongs both to the Book of Genesis and to the prophet Malachi. In Genesis it is said to Rebecca: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples in your womb.” Thus the Apostle rightly shows that the promises do not belong to those who are children of Abraham according to the flesh, but to those who preserve and keep the faith of their fathers.

What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. He feared that, because he had said this in order to prove that the privilege of ancestry counts for nothing before God—or because it had already been signified that the later people would be better—people who did not understand might think he was saying that God made some good and others evil. According to their reasoning, it would be unjust to punish someone who had not sinned voluntarily. He therefore sets against himself the testimonies that they themselves customarily used to assert this, and answers these examples by brief replies, showing that they cannot be understood in that way.

For he said to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion.” In the correct sense, this is understood as follows: “I will have mercy on the one whom I foreknew would be able to merit mercy, so that even then I might have mercy upon him.”

On whom I will have mercy. This is the Jews’ contrary argument. “Therefore it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs.” And again: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens.” The Apostle does not abolish what lies within our own will, since above he says: “Do you not know that God’s goodness leads you to repentance?” And again he writes to Timothy: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed for honor, and some for dishonor. If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified.”

[Col. 0689C] Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy. Here the Apostle Paul assumes, up to the passage “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”, the role of an opponent who comes forward and says that it is not within us either to do good or to do evil, but that everything is established by God’s decision: he has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens. “Who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me this way?’” The Apostle now rebukes the one contradicting him above, showing that the very statement “He has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens—and why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” demonstrates that the person possesses free choice or will. If, as the opposing speaker says, “God has mercy on whom he wishes and hardens whom he wishes,” then there is no difference between what the potter handles in his hands—an object formed from clay cannot contradict the potter about what he wishes to make from it—and this person, who, because he contradicts, complains about God’s will. By daring to question God’s judgment, he shows that he possesses free choice. Likewise, if it is not of the one who wills or runs, as some think, why does Paul himself run, saying: “I have finished the race”? And why did he exhort others to run, saying: “Run in such a way that you may all obtain the prize”? Hence it is understood that here he uses the voice of one asking a question and, rather, refuting than denying.

For Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” They too put this forward wrongly. But this passage is explained in two ways by different interpreters: either that each person fulfills the measure and limit of his sins so that he may be punished, as happened with the Sodomites and Amorites. Pharaoh, then, had already exceeded the measure; and therefore God wished, as though dealing with one already destined to perish, to provide for others, so that his people might recognize his justice and power, neither sinning nor fearing their enemies. What happened in Pharaoh’s case is like a physician who, from the suffering of a condemned criminal, discovers the means of restoring health to many by investigating the causes of diseases. Or it is like a judge who, although he could immediately punish a criminal, subjects him to various punishments to instill fear in everyone. Alternatively, he was hardened by God’s patience. For when God’s plague ceased, he became harder; and although God knew that he would not convert, he nevertheless wished to demonstrate his clemency even in him.

Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens. If this is understood in this way—“He has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens”—it is sufficiently unjust, and your argument is brought to this conclusion: you say that you are not the cause of your own wickedness, but that the cause is the Lord’s will, which cannot be resisted. Yet the very nature of God’s justice resists your reasoning.

You will say to me, then: “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” The Apostle speaks against his opponents: “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault?’” And he immediately adds, confirming what he had said: “O man, he truly and justly finds fault all the more because of your own words.” No one who does not possess a will of his own can say to God, “Why does he still find fault?” Therefore, rightly rebuking his foolishness, he says: “Who are you to answer back to God?” For one who has been hardened by God, as you claim, cannot contradict his Creator, since he would have no will of his own—just as clay, an insensible material, cannot answer its maker, because it is placed under the potter’s power.

O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why have you made me this way?” Some think that this too is still spoken from the perspective of the opponents, since it amounts to saying that no one can contradict the will of God, who has mercy on one person and hardens another, and to add that no one can answer God. Others, however, say that from this point onward the Apostle is answering them: even if matters were as they maliciously allege, they ought not to answer back to their Maker, since in comparison with God they are to their maker what a formed object is to the craftsman who made it from clay. In Greek it reads, μενοῦνγε ὦ ἄνθρωπε, which means: “O man, all the more so!”

Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? According to those who explain these words of the Apostle in this way, by “lump” he means all those dwelling in Egypt, because Israel too had served idols there.

But what if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power. He endured him for a long time while he blasphemed and afflicted God’s people through various actions. Moreover, he had cruelly ordered innocent children to be killed. This is also an appropriate answer: his patience and goodness cause those who possess their own will for living to become either vessels of wrath or vessels of mercy.

He endured with much patience vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction. By filling up their sins, they were made worthy to be vessels of wrath and were prepared for destruction by themselves.

In order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory. They were worthy of mercy because they had committed lesser offenses and had been grievously afflicted.

Whom he also called—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. Some Egyptians had also gone out with the children of Israel; if God were a respecter of persons, Israel alone ought to have obtained salvation. Thus now too he called not only Jews but also Gentiles to the faith. According to those who think that these words are spoken not from the Apostle’s perspective but from that of the Jews, the meaning is: “He saved only those whom he wished to such an extent that he even chose idolatrous Gentiles who had never served God, while he called only a few from Israel, in accordance with Isaiah’s testimony.”

As he says in Hosea. He speaks of two tribes as “not a people,” and of the ten tribes as “not having obtained mercy.”

I will call “my people” those who are “not my people.” Here he signifies Judah.

And “beloved” the one who was “not beloved,” and “having obtained mercy” the one who had “not obtained mercy.” He means the Israelite people.

And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people.” He points to the Gentiles who would believe in Christ, just as the Lord speaks in the Gospel by means of the parable of the wedding banquet: when Israel refused to come, the Gentiles were called in its place.

There they shall be called sons of the living God. He signifies the calling of the Gentiles.

But Isaiah cries out on behalf of Israel. This is shown to be a sharing in their cause.

“Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved.” He shows that only a small number of them had come to faith.

For he will complete and abbreviate the word in righteousness, because the Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth. Historically, these words have this meaning: “Just as I abbreviate the word and quickly bring it to its conclusion, so God will accomplish this with all speed.” In prophecy, however, the abbreviated word is understood as the New Testament, because in it everything is briefly contained and brought to completion.

And as Isaiah foretold. He foretold it well, because it was written above.

“Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah.” He did not allow the few righteous to perish with the multitude of the ungodly in the faith, unless Christ, the seed of Abraham, had been sent to the people for their deliverance, since they would otherwise have fallen.

What shall we say, then: that the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness? If the preceding remarks are spoken from the Apostle’s perspective, he again raises the objection on his own behalf: “If matters are not as we say—if it is not of the one who wills or runs—how did the Gentiles find righteousness, when they had never previously sought it, whereas Israel, which had always sought righteousness, could not find it?” But if the whole preceding argument is directed against the objectors, the Apostle answers here and briefly recapitulates the question, saying: “What shall we say to the objections put before us, except that the Gentiles were called and believed, while the others refused to believe?”

The righteousness, namely, that comes from faith. Righteousness comes from faith, which they refused to believe.

But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. He gives the reasons why they did not find righteousness: because they falsely gloried in works and refused to believe, regarding grace as though it were righteousness. He says that the Jewish people, thinking that they were justified by works of the Law, could not attain the law of righteousness—that is, faith in Christ—because of their disdain.

For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” Whoever sees the stone does not stumble; but the blind person strikes against it. This happened to the Jews, whom their own wickedness blinded; they did not recognize Christ and crucified him. Christ was also foretold as the stone of stumbling and rock of offense because many are scandalized by his birth and passion, as it is written: “They will be scandalized in him.” And the Apostle says that Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are called, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Hence what follows here: “Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” Peter likewise says that to believers the stone is chosen and made the cornerstone, but to unbelievers it is a stone of offense.

And everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame. Not the Jew alone, but everyone who believes in him will not be ashamed of former sins.

## CHAPTER X

Brothers, the desire of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for their salvation. Here he shows that he prays for his enemies not only with his lips but also with his heart.

For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. They have knowledge for pursuing the Law, but they do not understand [Col. 0692D] that Christ came in accordance with the Law. And because they cannot be justified through the Law, they are truly in danger if their zeal is without knowledge, since it often turns into its opposite.

For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God. They do not know that God justifies by faith alone, and they think themselves righteous through works of the Law, which they did not keep. They refused to submit themselves to the remission of sins, lest they appear to have been sinners, as it is written: “But the Pharisees, rejecting the counsel of God concerning themselves, refused to be baptized with John’s baptism.” Likewise, because the sacrifices of the Law and the other things that were shadows of the truth, destined to be brought to completion through Christ, ceased when Christ appeared—and they refused to believe in him—the Apostle rightly says that it is their own righteousness, because it is no longer God’s but theirs.

For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The person who has believed in Christ is, on the day he believes, such as the person who has fulfilled the whole Law.

For Moses wrote concerning the righteousness that comes from the Law. Moses distinguished in Leviticus between the two kinds of righteousness—namely, that of faith and that of works—showing that one is attained through works and the other through the addition of faith alone. Likewise, wishing to show the difference between the righteousness of the Law and that of faith, the Apostle calls Moses as a witness. Moses teaches concerning the righteousness of the Law: “The person who does these things shall live by them.” But concerning the righteousness of faith he says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” That is, do not hesitate to believe the commandment that announces what is destined to happen: Christ, who is to come and give you righteousness from faith.

The person who does these things shall live by them. None of those people lives in this way, because in the present age no one fulfilled the Law without Christ; for this too belongs to the Law, that Christ be believed in. Some think from this passage that the Jews earned only the present life through works of the Law. The Lord’s words show that this is not true: when asked about eternal life, he sets forth the commandments of the Law, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” Hence we understand that whoever kept the Law in its own time possessed eternal life.

But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks in this way: “Do not say in your heart.” Historically, he said this about the Law; but the Apostle applies it to Christ, because the Law was neither in heaven nor in the abyss. Or the Law always commands that this be contemplated so that they may be able to find Christ there.

Who will ascend into heaven—that is, to bring Christ down? Or who will descend into the abyss—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead? Because Christ is God and man: insofar as he is God the Word, who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming man. Therefore he says: “Who will ascend into heaven?”—that is, to bring Christ down. “To bring down” is said according to the form of God; “to bring back from the dead” according to the form of a servant.

But what does Scripture say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart”—that is, the word of faith which we preach. In Deuteronomy. Namely, the New Testament.

[Col. 0693D] For if you confess the Lord Jesus with your mouth and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead. The confession of the mouth is the testimony of the heart.

You will be saved. From former sins together with future ones.

For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Therefore, if faith is sufficient for righteousness and confession for salvation, there is no distinction between a believing Jew and a believing Gentile.

For Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him.” In Isaiah. Not the Jew alone.

Will not be put to shame. Therefore do not shame them over their former deeds, since Scripture says that they cannot be put to shame.

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. There is one Lord of all, abounding in mercy and salvation, and possessing the means by which he may bestow them.

For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. How, then, will they call upon one in whom they have not believed? In Joel. This is the Jews’ objection concerning the Gentiles: that they cannot call upon God.

Or how will they believe in one whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? And how will they preach unless they are sent? For prophets were never sent to them.

As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” Their feet are beautiful who announce peace; but the feet of those who announce the course of this world are ugly and deformed.

But not all obey the Gospel. Therefore, if not even all those to whom these preachers were sent obeyed, how much less will those obey to whom no one was sent?

For Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” Who believes what they have heard from us, or what we heard from you so that we might announce it to others?

Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. This is the Apostle’s answer.

But I say: Have they not heard? Indeed they have. He confirms that they heard even before those others.

“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” By allegory he wishes this testimony to be understood of the voices of the prophets.

But I say: Did Israel not know? That the Gentiles were to be called to the faith.

Moses is the first to say this. Moses is called first because nearly all the prophets later spoke about the salvation of the Gentiles.

“I will provoke you to jealousy through a people that is not a people; I will anger you through a foolish nation.” In the Song of Deuteronomy. Before they believed in God, the Gentiles were not God’s people. It is as though he says: “I will call those who are not my people, and they will believe in me to your irritation, so that, although you ought to have been greater than they, you may rejoice to be made equal to them.” It is like someone who has a disobedient son and, in order to correct him, gives half his inheritance to his slave, so that the son may eventually repent and rejoice—or may deserve to receive as much. Alternatively, we were not a people because we were dead in sins.

[Col. 0694D] Isaiah, however, hears and says: “I was found by those who were not seeking me.” By the Gentiles, who did not seek the God whom they did not know in the Law, but sought him ignorantly in an idol.

“I appeared openly to those who did not ask about me.” They did not inquire of God but of demons, through augurs, haruspices, the diviners of idols, and astrologers.

But to Israel he says. Because he promised such things in anger to the Gentiles, behold what he threatens the Jews, so that you may know that both things were foretold.

“All day long I stretched out.” Throughout the whole period he displayed miracles or inflicted punishments, yet even so they refused to believe.

“I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe but contradicted me.” The stretching out of the hands allegorically signifies the cross.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0695A]

I say, then: Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. Because he had sufficiently humbled them, he now consoles them like a good teacher, lest he appear to provoke them excessively. He says that he has not rejected them all, nor forever, but only as long as they do not believe.

For I too am an Israelite. If he had rejected them all, he would not have accepted me.

From the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. Not from the seed of proselytes.

God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. He has not rejected that people whom he foreknew would believe.

Or do you not know what Scripture says in Elijah? In the Book of Kings, where the account of Elijah is written.

[Col. 0695B] How he pleads with God against Israel. He removes the Gentiles’ grounds for arrogance, lest they boast that only a very few from the Jews believed and that they alone remained with God.

“Lord, they have killed your prophets; they have torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.” All the prophets knew only those things that had been revealed to them by the Lord. Hence the king also asks Jeremiah uncertainly whether, at the hour when he was speaking with him, the word of the Lord was with him. Elisha likewise says: “How has the Lord hidden these things from me?” Thus Elijah too, in this passage, did not know that there were others besides himself who worshiped God.

But what does the divine response say to him? “I have left seven thousand men for myself.” If so many escaped the prophet’s knowledge, [Col. 0695C] how much more do you not know how many Jews have been saved and will be saved?

Who have not bent the knee before Baal. One serves idols not only by sacrificing to them but also by committing sins. For if God is denied by one’s actions, then demons are certainly honored as well.

Thus also in the present time. Just as not all perished then, so now too some are being saved.

A remnant has been saved according to the election of God’s grace. The election of grace is faith, just as the election of the Law is works. Otherwise, what election is there where there is no difference in merits?

But if it is by grace, then it is no longer from works. They might say of those concerning whom the account of Elijah speaks, “They were righteous, whereas these are sinners; how, then, have they been chosen?” He added that they too were saved freely, just as the Gentiles were.

Otherwise grace is no longer grace. For it is called a free gift.

What then? Israel did not obtain what it was seeking. Therefore all Israel did not obtain righteousness, because it did not seek it from faith but thought that it was justified solely by works of the Law, even while it especially disregarded the commandments of the Law. Hence the Savior rebukes them for straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel. He also says this because the promises belonged to the Jews, through which Christ was to come to save them from their sins; but because he came and they did not believe, he says that Israel did not obtain it.

But the elect obtained it. Those who were chosen through faith.

[Col. 0696A] The rest were hardened. The rest were hardened through unbelief, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

As it is written: “God gave them a spirit of compunction: eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear.” In Isaiah. “Life and death are set before a person; whichever pleases him will be given to him”—so that freedom of choice may not be taken away. Therefore, God’s giving means permitting. But they desired a spirit of compunction. For they had always been unbelieving toward God’s words; if they had wished to possess a spirit of faith, they would have received it. Likewise now, Christians who doubt the resurrection, the reward, and Gehenna have sought a similar spirit for themselves. In this passage the Prophet is speaking about unbelievers. Divine Scripture has this characteristic: although each person possesses the freedom to do good or evil, it says that God hands over or gives, because he is the one who gave freedom. His patience produces this result, since he does not immediately inflict vengeance on sinners or rewards on the good.

Until this present day. Until they are converted, as he says to the Corinthians concerning the veil of the heart.

And David says: “Let their table before them become a snare, a trap, a stumbling block, and a recompense to them. Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and keep their back continually bent.” Alternatively: “Keep them continually bent under the burdens of sin, so that they may not be released unless they believe,” because they are blessed in the passion of Christ as they eat the Passover. This is prophesied about those who gave the Savior vinegar and gall to drink; yet Peter says to them: “And now I know that you did this through ignorance. Repent, therefore, and let each one of you be baptized.” Paul himself shortly afterward says: “And they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in,” so that we may know that the spirit of compunction did not take away from them the ability to convert. Finally, he immediately resolves this in the words that follow. Likewise, the priests, supposing that if they killed Christ they would always possess the table of sacrifices and tithes, found it turned into a snare for them. For they lost the temple in which they had placed vain hope, and now they are accursed among the Gentiles.

I say, then: Did they stumble in this way? Now again he reveals a part concerning the Jews.

So that they might fall? Certainly not. They did not fall completely or irreparably [Col. 0696D].

But through their offense there is salvation for the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to jealousy. He loved them so greatly that the Gentiles were called for their salvation, so that, seeing them admitted to the kingdom of God, they might perhaps be converted more readily even in this way. Likewise, God’s plan was that through the death of Christ the whole human race might be saved, as the Lord himself says: “When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to myself.” Therefore he says: “But through their offense there is salvation for the Gentiles.” By saying “to provoke them to jealousy,” he shows that unless the Gentiles had believed in Christ, the remnant of the Jews would never have been saved.

Now if their offense is the riches of the world, and their diminution the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness? If their offense benefited you so greatly that, without the works of the Law, it caused you to cling to them, and if the few among them who believed called all of you to salvation, how much more could they benefit you if they all believed, through their teaching?

For I speak to you Gentiles. He wishes to show that he is hastening with the greatest eagerness toward the salvation of the Jews.

As long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry. As long as I remain established in the body, I will honor our ministry, striving by my example to save more of them.

If somehow I might provoke my flesh to emulation. That is, that I may present myself in every way as one whom they desire to imitate.

[Col. 0697B] And save some of them. Or “a certain number,” since they do not all wish to be saved.

For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world. He repeats what he said above.

What is their acceptance, except life from the dead? Whence came acceptance for the Gentiles, if not life out of their death? [The transmitted Latin here is grammatically uncertain.] From the Jews who were dead, Christ—or the Apostles—were life for the Gentiles. Or, if I have freed some from them, this will contribute to your life. He also says this: just as the Gentiles were accepted through faith, so the Jews too, if they believe, will pass from death to life.

And if the first portion is holy, so is the lump. If those few among them who have believed are holy, then all will be holy if they believe. Here he calls Christ the firstfruits, but the lump the Hebrew people, from whom Christ is according to [Col. 0697C] the flesh.

And if the root is holy, so are the branches. The root is the patriarchs; the branches are the Apostles. That is, both the first and the last are holy from them. In this passage he signifies Abraham as the root, since on account of his faith he is called the father of many nations. By the branches he means his descendants, who likewise retain the faith.

But if some of the branches have been broken off. They were not broken off on your account; rather, you were grafted in because they were broken off.

But you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted in among them. An olive, indeed, but uncultivated and wild. Here too he says that the Gentile people were grafted contrary to nature into the root—that is, into the faith of the patriarchs—and that, not according to the nature of trees, as though grafted in to bear the fruit of their own [Col. 0697D] kind, but they follow the goodness of the root into which they were grafted.

And you became a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive. The root means the fathers; the richness, Christ.

Do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root that bears you. Do not rejoice over their destruction; otherwise you will hear that they do not stand through you, but that you stand through them. Nor do you provide them life; rather, they provide it for you.

You will say, then: “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” They were broken off because of unbelief, certainly. You say that they were broken off for the sake of your being grafted in; let us see whether that was indeed the reason, or whether they fell rather because of their own unbelief.

[Col. 0698A] But you stand by faith. For God would not accept your person and cast them out without cause.

Do not be high-minded, but fear. Some, not understanding this passage and not considering the reason or the persons about whom and to whom the Apostle is speaking, think that wisdom is being forbidden here. If that were so, according to them he would be found contradicting himself: here forbidding what elsewhere he earnestly beseeches the Ephesians and the others to receive from the Lord. Therefore, “Do not be high-minded” means: do not be arrogant toward them.

For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either. If he did not spare them because of unbelief, although they are from the holy root, much less will he spare you if you sin.

[Col. 0698B] See, therefore, the kindness and severity of God. This is directed against those who assert that one God is just and another good, and against those who deny that God punishes sinners.

Severity toward those who fell, but God’s kindness toward you. For they were justly broken off, while you were mercifully grafted in.

If you remain in his kindness. That is, in the faith bestowed upon you by God’s kindness.

Otherwise you too will be cut off. But they also, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. Otherwise, you will experience severity, and they will experience kindness.

For God is able to graft them in again. Among human beings it is impossible to restore withered shoots, but with God all things are possible and easy.

[Col. 0698C] For if you were cut from the naturally wild olive. Their fathers had long ago forgotten the natural law and degenerated from nature; and, through successive sins, with the habit remaining, they began to be, as it were naturally, bitter and fruitless. Here too he says that the Gentile people were grafted contrary to nature into the root—that is, into the faith of the patriarchs—and that, not according to the nature of trees, as though grafted in to bear the fruit of their own kind, but they follow the goodness of the root into which they were grafted.

And if you were grafted contrary to nature into a cultivated olive, how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive? It is contrary to nature to graft a wild olive onto an olive, since ordinarily the branch is more accustomed to imitate the power of the root than the root to transform the branches into its own quality.

[Col. 0698D] For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. All this is directed against them, so that the Gentiles may not become proud.

This mystery. An arcane matter unknown to human beings: why the Gentiles were saved—because Israel’s blindness also provided them an opportunity for salvation.

So that you may not be wise in your own estimation. So that you may not say according to human wisdom: “God chose us and rejected them.”

For blindness has happened in part to Israel. Israel was so occupied by sins and unbelief that the time came when all the Gentiles would be admitted to life, and thus all Israel would be saved by faith alone. In this way the fullness of the Gentiles would be equal in life in Christ, since they had been unequal in sins.

[Col. 0699A] Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved. It remained so until the Gentiles who had been saved saw that all had been called to salvation—whether from Judah, from Israel, or, of course, through the law. He also shows here that, when the Gentiles’ complement enters into the faith of Christ, then the remaining Jewish people, moved by zeal and emulation, will believe in Christ and be saved. The Apostle sometimes places the Gentiles before the Hebrew people in faith for this reason: although some of them had believed in Christ, they nevertheless still observed the precepts of the Mosaic law. Later, therefore, following the example of the Gentiles, they too began to preserve the Christian faith completely. He does not say “fullness” on account of their number, but because they have been filled by our Lord, just as Paul himself says concerning believers: “And he gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

As it is written: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.” Some think that all these things are still future. They must be answered: then this testimony too—“He will come from Zion, the one who delivers Israel”—would still be future, so that Christ might come again to set them free. They have been blinded by God for a time, and they do not understand concerning themselves how they are perishing by not believing.

And this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins. The new covenant that he promised, which they will receive only once they have been made new and their sins have been abolished.

According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake. They are enemies to me on account of what I preach to you: they prevent Christ from being proclaimed to the Gentiles so that they may be saved.

But according to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. If they believe, they are beloved—commended in two ways.

For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable. If they believe, their sins cannot be charged against them, because God does not repent of having promised the offspring of Abraham. Or, without the affliction of repentance, they will be saved if they believe.

For just as you once did not believe God. When they still believed.

But now you have obtained mercy because of their unbelief. Not through your own merit.

So they too now have not believed because of the mercy shown to you. The mercy of the Gentiles is Christ.
