[Col. 0699D] So that they too may obtain mercy. They did not believe to such an extent that they too are not justified by their works, but by mercy, just as you are.

For God has enclosed all in unbelief. He did not enclose them by force, but by reason: those whom he found in unbelief—that is, he enclosed both Jews and Gentiles here, because previously the Jews were merely sinners and not also unbelievers; but after they did not believe in Christ, they became equal to the Gentiles, and all alike obtain mercy.

So that he may have mercy on all. For this reason.

O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! He praises God’s wisdom, who waited so long, according to his foreknowledge, until all stood in need of mercy, [Col. 0700A] so that every glorying based on the false boast of works might be removed from everyone.

How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways! The judgments of God are a great abyss. Some people cannot comprehend them.

For who has known the mind of the Lord? Formerly no one knew it; for at present Paul himself certainly knew it, since he was showing it to others. “But we have the mind of the Lord.” Or, no one by himself has known his law; and no one, instructed through some private conversation with God, has no need of the teaching of the law.

Or who has been his counselor? So as to know his mysteries.

Or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid? Who first did anything good and does not glorify God’s mercy, but boasts that he received it by his own merit?

[Col. 0700B] For from him and through him and in him are all things. From him every creature received its beginning; through him all things are governed; and in him all things are brought to their completion, while he himself is contained by nothing.

To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. He alone must be glorified, since what we are, live, and move is also from him. This passage also serves against the Arians, when it says that God is the one from whom all things are and through whom all things are shown to have been made. Since the Evangelist has declared that all things were made through the Word in the beginning, what the Evangelist testifies concerning the Son, the Apostle teaches us to understand and believe, through the mystery of unity, concerning the Father.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0700C]

I appeal to you therefore, brothers. Since he had spoken of the mind of the Lord, he now says what sort of people they must show themselves to be in order to deserve to possess the mind of the Lord. Up to this point he speaks about doctrines; from here onward he teaches morals.

Through the mercy of God. Than which nothing is greater, for through it we have been set free.

To present your bodies. How much more your soul—not like the bodies of animals in the law, which, although they were offered figuratively, were nevertheless offered spotless and alive.

A living sacrifice, holy. That is, chaste and separated from every death of sin.

Acceptable to God. Please the Lord, not merely human beings; or, such a sacrifice is pleasing to him.

Your rational service. Every good work pleases God if it is done rationally. Otherwise it loses its reward: for example, if someone fasts for the sake of human beings, he performs a good service foolishly. The same must be understood of all related matters.

And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind. Do not be like the children of the world, since you have become children of God; rather, renew your mind, through which the body is governed and all the members are directed, so that the actions of the body too may become new, and so that you may recognize the will of God and his mind. For these things are revealed only to a renewed mind.

So that you may prove what the will of God is: good, pleasing, and perfect. That is, what is good, better, and best.

[Col. 0701A] For I say, through the grace that has been given to me. He forbids the use of human wisdom that is outside the law; he says that he does not speak from his own judgment but by the authority of God’s grace.

To everyone who is among you. To those who are priests or teachers, whose example the others follow.

Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety. He wishes to think more highly who investigates what the law does not say. Hence Solomon also says: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not investigate what is greater than you; but always consider what God has commanded you.”

And to each as God has allotted. It should be noted that he calls the Holy Spirit “God,” just as he says to the Corinthians that he distributes gifts to each as he wills.

A measure of faith. The measure of faith is to be understood as the grace [Col. 0701B] of virtue, which only the faithful receive.

For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ. By comparing them to a body, he urges them to concord, so that they may not be disturbed by having received different gifts. For individuals could not have everything, lest they become proud, needing no one; nor could everyone have the same gifts, so that the likeness of Christ’s body might be displayed in us. He also says that there are many members in one body on account of the diversity of functions. The eye cannot hear, nor the ear see, and the rest must be understood similarly.

And individually we are members of one another. By supplying to one another what we have, let charity be confirmed in us more and more.

[Col. 0701C] And having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us. A gift depends not on our own choice but on the judgment of the giver. Glory is promised in the future to all believers; but whoever has so pure a heart as to be worthy of it receives the grace of virtues even in the present.

Whether prophecy, according to the proportion of faith. Of faith, not of the law; or because that faith merits it. For each person receives as much as he believes. Or, according to the faith that has been given and granted to each by God.

Or ministry, in ministering. Ministry means the priestly or diaconal office.

Or the one who teaches, in teaching. The one who exhorts, in exhortation. The one who teaches is greater than the one who exhorts. [Col. 0701D] Even the less learned can exhort according to their abilities. It should certainly be noted that he has used “whether” only three times; why he did so should be discerned by the spiritual reader.

The one who gives, in simplicity. He gives generously to all, believing that everyone is good and in need of what they request.

The one who presides, with diligence. Whoever presides over the Church or over the brothers must be diligent.

The one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. Especially by showing mercy toward the sick; or the title “mercy” is general and must be shown toward everyone with a tranquil spirit. For God loves a cheerful giver, and without doubt hates a sorrowful one, because a good word is better than the best gift.

[Col. 0702A] Love without pretense. Hating evil and clinging to good. There must be complete purity among Christians, just as God is a pure law. To pretend belongs to slaves. Let us love not only in word but in deed and truth, so that, if necessary, we may even die for one another.

Loving one another with brotherly affection. Love one another as though you had been born from one mother.

Outdoing one another in showing honor. If we always kept this and maintained charity and patience, as he says elsewhere—“considering one another better than yourselves”—then, if we judged ourselves inferior to everyone, we would neither voluntarily injure anyone nor consider an injury inflicted upon us [Col. 0702B] a serious matter.

Not sluggish in diligence. Do not become sluggish and inactive in God’s work through worldly concerns.

Fervent in spirit. The Lord does not love those who are cold, and he is disgusted by those who are lukewarm. We are truly fervent in spirit if we are cold toward the world.

Serving the Lord. Not the world or vice, but God.

Rejoicing in hope. In hope, not in what is present. For hope that is seen is not hope.

Patient in tribulation. Endure everything for the joy of future hope, as he says: “Consider it all joy.”

Devoted to prayer. Constancy in prayer provides us help in adversity.

[Col. 0702C] Sharing in the needs of the saints. Minister to those who, having rejected all their possessions for Christ’s sake, temporarily need the assistance of others. Some manuscripts read: “Sharing in the memories of the saints,” which is understood as remembering the circumstances in which the saints won God’s favor, or the works by which they did so, that you may become participants in them by continually imitating them. Finally, what follows is:

Pursuing hospitality. For the saints also did this, as Abraham and Lot did; they even detained unwilling guests. Of this it is said: “For by this some pleased God, receiving angels as guests.”

Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. We must not think that we ought to do both. Blessed Peter also says: “Not repaying a curse with a curse, but blessing instead.”

Rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep. So that if one member suffers, all the members may suffer with it. As Job says: “If I did not groan or weep when I saw people in distress.” And the Lord is moved to weeping by Mary’s tears, to give us an example. For we must not think that he wept for Lazarus, whom he was about to raise, or because of the unbelief of those who had often failed to believe him when he performed miracles. We, however, now weep with those who rejoice in a perverse manner, and rejoice with those who weep. If someone is praised, we are distressed; if someone falls, we rejoice. Thus we show that those who do such things are not of the body of Christ [Col. 0703A], since we do not grieve over a member that has been cut off; rather, we are enemies of our own side and friends of the opposing side. We do not grieve when we see the strongest men of our own line running into battle, nor rejoice when we see them fighting bravely, although we ourselves may not be equally strong in combat.

Having the same mind toward one another. So that you may think toward another as you do toward yourselves.

Not being concerned with high things, but associating with the humble. That person is proud who wishes to avenge his own injury by himself and does not consent to humble matters—that is, to humility.

Do not be wise in your own estimation. Do not glory in human wisdom, but be foolish to the world so that you may be wise in the Lord, as it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law.”

Repaying no one evil for evil. It is human wisdom to seek to repay one’s enemies in kind. It is folly in this world if you wish to offer the other cheek to one who strikes you. But if you possess such patience and humility, you will be able to appear approved not only before the Lord but also before all human beings.

Providing what is good, not only before God but also before all people. Take care only that you do not do this in such a way that you desire to please not God but human beings alone.

If possible, so far as it depends on you, living in peace with all people. As far as it is your responsibility, keep peace with [Col. 0703C] everyone, and say with the Prophet: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable”—that is, desiring their conversion and salvation, as far as this may be possible for you.

Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to anger. Either by fleeing or by allowing the other person to do harm.

For it is written: “Vengeance is mine.” “I will avenge the injury,” says the Lord, “as my own, not as yours,” since the Prophet says: “Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of his own eye.”

And I will repay, says the Lord. He promises to repay the one who does good.

But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. Do not deny him what God denies to no one, [Col. 0703D] even though he may be blasphemous and impious.

For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head. When he realizes that coals have been heaped upon him through your undeserved mercy, he may shake them off—that is, he may be converted and love you, whom he had once hated. Otherwise, it is not mercy but cruelty if you do this so that something worse may happen to him, for which you would bid God to be entreated. Here too he teaches us that we ought to imitate God, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil. By feeding and giving drink to an enemy, we urge him toward peace or reconciliation; but if he persists in wickedness, he heaps fire upon his own head.

Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. The one [Col. 0704A] who leads another over to his own side is said to have conquered him, as in the case of a heretic or pagan. If, therefore, he has made you repay him in kind, he has conquered you by making you like himself. But if through your patience you make him cease from his injury, you have conquered.

## CHAPTER XIII

Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. This was stated against those who thought that they possessed Christian freedom in such a way that they either owed honor to no one or paid no taxes. In whatever manner, therefore, he desires to humble them, lest they suffer insult because of pride rather than for God’s sake. Thus he teaches them to redeem the time through [Col. 0704B] humility. Alternatively, “higher authorities” may be understood as ecclesiastical dignities.

For there is no authority except from God. And how does God say through the Prophet: “They reigned, but not from me”?

And those that exist have been established by God. If he seems to be speaking of the authorities of the world, they will not therefore be just, even if they received their beginning from God. They are given according to the desire of each person. For Solomon says: “For authority has been given to us by God. But although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly. Terribly and swiftly he will appear to you,” and so forth. Authority is established by God so that it may judge justly and so that sinners may have something to fear, lest they sin.

Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. [Col. 0704C] And those who resist will acquire condemnation for themselves. As it is said to Rahab: “Whoever goes outside will himself be guilty.”

For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. The evil person ought to fear authority; the good person has nothing to fear. If he is unjustly killed, he rejoices.

Do you wish not to fear authority? Take my advice, and you will never fear.

Do what is good, and you will have praise from it. The condemnation of the wicked is the praise of the good.

For it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, fear. It is concerned for your peaceful security. By saying here that it is a servant for your good, he shows that judges must be obeyed in matters that are right, but not in those contrary to religion.

[Col. 0704D] For it does not carry the sword without cause. For it is God’s servant. It has a duty against you if you sin; nor does it profit you for a reward. Or, priests carry the spiritual sword, as Peter struck Ananias and Sapphira, and Paul struck the magician.

An avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. For God does not love the wicked; he hates all who work iniquity.

Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. Not only because authorities can become angry even without cause, but also lest you be condemned on account of the consciousness of some sin. Or, not only lest priests become angry, but also because you owe honor to those holy and just persons. [Col. 0705A] Likewise, those who do evil and live contrary to the commandments are subject to authorities because of punishment; those who live rightly are subject because of conscience, since what is commanded is good and just.

For this is also why you pay taxes. For they are God’s ministers, serving precisely for this purpose. These may also be understood as the taxes of priests, which have been established for them by God. Or, this is why you pay taxes to kings: because you have chosen, by possessing the world, to be subject to it. He calls them God’s ministers so that in this way too they may repay them what they owed them, lest Christ appear to have taught pride.

Therefore repay everyone what is owed. To whom tax is owed, tax. Almsgiving too can be called a debt. Scripture [Col. 0705B] says: “Incline your ear to the poor, and repay your debt.”

To whom revenue is owed, revenue. Our revenue is that we give to those who pass by, or to those who do not pass by but sit beside the road, and give generously to those who come from there.

To whom fear is owed, fear. How, then, is it written elsewhere: “No one is to be feared except God”? But, he says, act in such a way that you fear no one. For fear of God drives out human fear. But since you still have reasons for fear, it is necessary for you to fear.

To whom honor is owed, honor. Fear also belongs to superiors, but only honor to equals.

Owe no one anything. The Apostle spoke excellently: what is owed must be repaid to each person, and we must be bound to one another by love [Col. 0705C] alone. If we always owe love to the brothers, let us preserve it, so that we may be joined to perpetual charity. For “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,” and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word. Alternatively, owe no one a debt that you do not repay.

Except to love one another. This alone must always remain, because it can never be fully paid.

For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. According to the Lord’s parable, which commands mercy to be shown to all without distinction, every human being must be considered one’s neighbor. Alternatively, he put love first because he was writing to believers and was discussing a life of righteousness.

[Col. 0705D] For “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet,” and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” All righteousness is recapitulated in love of one’s neighbor; and injustice arises when we love ourselves more than others. Whoever loves his neighbor as himself not only does him no harm but also does him good, because he desires both to be done for himself as well.

Love of one’s neighbor does no evil. Not doing good also is evil. For if someone sees another in danger from hunger, does he not himself kill that person if, while he has abundance, he does not give him food, even though he has not taken away his possessions? Whoever can come to the aid of someone dying in any kind of need [Col. 0706A] and does not do so kills him.

Therefore the fullness of the law is love. That is, perfection.

And do this, knowing the time: it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep. That is, you must strive toward more perfect things. You must not always remain children and infants, as he says elsewhere: “For when you ought to be teachers,” and so forth. The Apostle also exhorts us, leaving behind works darkened and weighed down by the torpor of sleep, to walk in the light—that is, in good works. Let us also rise from the sleep of inertia and ignorance. For knowledge is already shining.

For our salvation is nearer now than when we believed. As knowledge progresses, salvation is nearer [Col. 0706B] than when we first believed.

The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. He compares knowledge to day and ignorance to night, in accordance with Hosea, who says: “I have likened your mother to night; my people have become like one without knowledge.”

Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. With ignorance, let us cast off also the works of ignorance; and let us put on the armor of light—that is, works of illumination. For whoever does evil hates the light, but whoever does the truth comes to the light.

Let us walk honorably as in the day. Just as the light of day prevents each person from doing what he freely committed at night, so knowledge prevents us from despising the commandments of the law, since we know that we are always seen by [Col. 0706C] God.

Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and sexual indecencies. A revelry is a gathering at table. We, however, have a spiritual banquet, saying: “When you come together, let each one have a psalm,” and so forth. We know that drunkenness is destructive and an occasion of debauchery from the fact that he added indecency. Elsewhere he says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.”

Not in quarreling and jealousy. Many other examples also prove that quarrelsomeness and envy are criminal, as James says: “For if you have bitter zeal,” and so forth.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Let Christ alone be seen in you, not the old person. [Col. 0706D] For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked, in whom all virtues are found.

And do not make provision for the flesh in its desires. As Solomon says: “Do not go after your desires.” And again: “If you give your soul its desire, you will bring yourself into the joy of your enemies.”

## CHAPTER XIV

But receive the one who is weak in faith. Here he begins indirectly to rebuke those who considered themselves strong because they ate meat without restraint. Here he also calls weak those believers who thought that the meats sold in the market at that time were offerings connected with idolatry; and because they thought this, they ate vegetables so as not to be [Col. 0707A] defiled. Hence the Apostle commands that the uninstructed, holding this opinion, should not judge those who have faith and eat without dispute everything sold in the market, since every creature of God is good and nothing created by God for human consumption is to be condemned.

Not for disputes about thoughts. Do not judge according to your own thoughts what the law does not judge.

For one person believes that he may eat everything. He has such great faith that he is not troubled either by being weakened through abstinence or by old age.

But the one who is weak should eat vegetables. Weak either because of age or because of the body’s heat. Here too it is demonstrated [Col. 0707B] that he is not speaking of Jews, as some think, but of those who abstain. For they did not eat meat according to the law, but only vegetables. Alternatively: If weakness of soul arises in you for this reason—because you happen to know another of the same purpose who shudders at eating meat on account of his faith—do not judge another’s will, nor demand anything from anyone. Each person has been left free in his own will; but if it is a stumbling block to you, and you do not wish to eat meat, impose the limit upon yourself and, doing what is better, eat only vegetables. Let each person be moved toward abstinence by your equanimity, rather than, being provoked, become a stumbling block to you in this matter. Rather, let him be strengthened in eating meat, since you cannot reproach it as a fault in another if each person undertakes it either faithfully or perhaps because the severity of illness or old age [Col. 0707C] requires it.

Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat. They had stumbling blocks between them: the latter judged the former as carnal, while the former mocked the latter as foolish and judged them superstitious.

And let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. For God has accepted him. God called them in the same way he called you.

Who are you to judge another’s servant? What authority do you have to judge someone whom the law does not judge? Hence James also says: “Whoever judges his brother,” judging himself wiser, “judges the law.” Yet Paul himself judged those who acted contrary to the commandment and granted others the ability to judge. The statement is directed to the one weak in faith: he must not judge the one who eats. Everything sold in the market—[Col. 0707D] the one who is strong in faith recognizes as clean for the clean.

He stands or falls before his own master. Whether he lives or dies: the one abstains for God’s sake, and the other eats according to God.

But he will stand. For God is able to make him stand. God, who caused the three boys fed on legumes to appear better than those who ate from the king’s table, can also make them remain longer in the body.

For one person judges one day different from another, while another judges every day alike. Let each person abound in his own understanding. The Jews could not judge one day different from another with regard to foods. Therefore he is speaking of fasting and abstinence, which have not been reduced to a fixed rule of the law, so that each person may do as much [Col. 0708A] as he can—as much as he wishes to have as a reward. Hence what follows: in such a matter, let each person do what he judges to be better. He also means that some have determined to abstain from eating meat at particular times of the year, while others have determined to abstain throughout the whole time of their lives.

The one who regards the day, regards it for the Lord. He regards it for the Lord who fasts for God’s sake and not for human beings.

And the one who eats, eats for the Lord. For he gives thanks to God. The one who eats for the Lord, so that he may have strength to preach the Gospel, does not devote himself to his own appetite but to the salvation of others, so that those who are converted may give thanks to God.

And the one who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. For many are saved through his example and give thanks to God. Whoever [Col. 0708B] gives thanks with the voice gives thanks alone; whoever does so also in deed gives thanks in many.

For none of us lives for himself, and none dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. No believer lives for himself, and no believer dies for himself, because Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him. Conversely, we must beware lest we live for ourselves by eating, or die for human beings by fasting.

For Christ died and rose for this purpose, so that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead. Christ’s coming will find some alive and will raise the dead. Therefore it makes no difference [Col. 0708C] whether he raises you or finds you alive; only strive to appear righteous before him.

But you, why do you judge your brother? By what authority do you condemn him as a glutton?

Or you, why do you despise your brother? Despising him as weak, or as fasting needlessly.

For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. Then the Lord will judge our consciences: what we have done and with what intention.

For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.” By this testimony he proves that we shall all give an account of our actions to the Lord alone.

Therefore each of us will give an account of himself to God. This concerns matters about which the law is silent. Otherwise, if someone sees [Col. 0708D] a sinner and does not rebuke him, he will also give God an account for him.

Therefore let us no longer judge one another. What you have done up to now is enough.

But judge this instead: not to place a stumbling block or an occasion of offense before your brother. Here he subtly turns to commend abstinence and says that they ought to abstain, even though they are strong, lest the weak suffer offense through their example.

I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him. I do not say this because I think that anything is common. For through Christ I know that all things have been cleansed. “Common” is what is considered unclean in Jewish food.

[Col. 0709A] But for the one who considers something to be common, it is common. It becomes common through his conscience, because he still supposes that something in such matters is unclean according to the Jewish rite, even after faith in Christ.

For if your brother is distressed because of food. He did not say “because of fasting,” but so that you may neither provoke nor compel him by your example.

You are no longer walking according to love. For he eats unwillingly what is not good for him. You do not love your neighbor as yourself if you do not consider his benefit as you consider your own.

Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. He did not say, as some wish, “by your abstinence.”

Therefore let not our good be blasphemed. We possess freedom in the Lord, so that all things may be clean for us; but we must not use it in such a way that we seem to live for gluttony and banquets. Or it is blasphemed if we quarrel over such matters.

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink. We are not justified through food. It should also be noted that he did not say, “Fasting and sobriety are not the kingdom of God,” but “food and drink.” This also clearly shows that the kingdom of heaven does not have temporal food and drink, but that there one lives spiritually.

But righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. These are more easily preserved through abstinence. Where there is righteousness, there is also peace; where there is peace, there is spiritual joy, because dissension always produces sadness and distress.

For whoever serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by human beings. No one can doubt concerning such a person that he is holy.

Therefore let us pursue what makes for peace, so that we may not judge one another concerning such matters.

And let us watch over one another in matters that make for edification. Abstinence is edification. Food, on the other hand, even if it destroys no one, edifies no one.

Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food—that is, the human being created by God.

All things indeed are clean. He repeats what he said above, lest he seem to condemn the creature.

But it is evil for the person who eats through an occasion of offense. The very clean thing becomes evil for them if, through it, they offend another.

It is good not to eat meat and not to drink [Col. 0709D] wine. He explains what he meant by offending the weak. Here he does praise abstinence from meat and wine, but he much more strongly admonishes that, for the sake of a brother’s stumbling, one should abstain from the food and drink sacrificed to idols.

Nor anything by which your brother is offended, made to stumble, or weakened. He is weakened with respect to chastity. For wine and women make even the wise apostatize.

Keep the faith that you have before yourself before God. If you consider yourself faithful in this matter, eat in such a way that no one is weakened by your example.

Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves. For he does not consider his own weakness by approving it, but the salvation of the other who is weak.

[Col. 0710A] But whoever discriminates: if he eats, he is condemned. If someone discriminates concerning another and says, “If this person eats, he must certainly be condemned,” this is not faith, and therefore what follows is added.

Because it is not from faith. It is not from faith if you condemn another for this reason: that while you are fasting, he eats. Alternatively: “Whoever judges himself in this way.” For discrimination and judgment are the same thing, since judgment is made by discriminating, and discrimination by judging.

But everything that is not from faith is sin. Not from the faith that works through love. Therefore whatever destroys another is not from faith, and for that reason is sin.

## CHAPTER XV

But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak. If you are truly strong, act as I do, who became weak in order to win the weak.

And not to please ourselves. Let each of you please his neighbor. Let us be commended not by ourselves but by our neighbors, just as elsewhere he sets forth his own example for us, saying: “Just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking what is useful for myself but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved.” No one can edify another if, through a good life, he has not first become pleasing. But there are also people who please themselves: seeking their own advantages, they do their own will.

For the good, for edification. He shows the manner and reason for pleasing, so that we may not please for empty glory. At the same time, by saying “for good edification,” he shows that there is also bad edification, as in the saying: “He will be edified for eating idol-food.”

For Christ did not please himself. The disciple of Christ imitates this: he does not seek his own advantage. Christ died for the salvation of others and endured the bitterest insults from those who said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple,” and so forth.

But as it is written: “The insults of those who insulted you fell upon me.” Whatever is reproached not only to Christ but also to the saints for God’s sake is said to be reproached to God, as in: “Where is your God?”

For whatever was written was written for our instruction. Nothing was written without purpose. The merits and trials of the righteous also contribute to our edification, because they were completely known to God.

So that through endurance and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope. Through the consolations of the Scriptures we await future hope with the greatest patience, as it is written: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them.” That is, those who make use of the consolation of the law cannot be shaken by any trial. Through the examples of the endurance and consolation contained in what has been written, we hope for consolation even amid present trials. It is a great source of comfort if we know that our Lord Jesus Christ and his saints endured what we suffer.

Now may the God of endurance and consolation. Here “the God of endurance” signifies the Holy Spirit, who grants us, according to Christ, to glorify with one accord the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise, it signifies that endurance which consists in conversion and consolation, not in anger or dissension.

Grant you to have the same mind toward one another according to Jesus Christ. Let each person seek the salvation of the other as his own, just as Christ by his death saved everyone from death.

So that with one mind and one voice you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is truly honored when he is praised with one mind and a harmonious voice. For if two of you agree on earth about anything, whatever they ask will be done for them.

Therefore welcome one another. For the honor of God, bear one another’s burdens; thus you will fulfill the law of Christ, because he received us into himself when we were ungodly. How much more, then, ought we to bear one another, since we are alike? Here again he urges both peoples toward unity. “I agree with you, Jews, that Christ, who was promised to you, came first to you, and that the Gentiles were called through the mercy of God; nevertheless, you have become one body.”

Just as Christ also received you for the honor of God. Either for the glory of his divinity, or for the honor of God.

For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God. Here he shows that Christ, according to the flesh, was born from them in accordance with the promises made to the fathers, so that he might fulfill the precepts of the law. Moreover, he did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

[Col. 0711C] To confirm the promises made to the fathers. For he had promised Christ to them, as he himself says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

But the Gentiles are to honor God for his mercy. For to whom more is forgiven, that person loves more.

As it is written: “Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles, Lord, and I will sing to your name.” He removed Jewish arrogance by teaching that the salvation of the Gentiles had been foretold, although Christ himself had not been announced among the Gentiles. He confesses that they had obtained mercy, because they too are in his body.

And again he says: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people.” You who, together with them, have been brought to salvation.

And again: “Praise the Lord, all Gentiles, and magnify him, all peoples.” And again Isaiah says: “There shall be [Col. 0711D] a root of Jesse.” Jesse was the father of David, from whose seed—that is, from Mary—Christ was born.

“And the one who rises to rule the Gentiles—in him the Gentiles will hope.” He is not speaking of proselytes, but this also resembles the passage: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins.” From this it is proved that Christ has truly already come, in whom it is evident that all the Gentiles hope.

Now may the God of hope. In him we all hope. This shows how God does not at any time fill a nation with grace without the power of the Holy Spirit, since the Father and the Holy Spirit have one gift.

Fill you with all joy and peace. The peace of the faithful ought to be in future hope. And there is complete joy wherever there is peace. There is no joy in dissension, but universal sadness.

In believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit. Abundance in hope consists in the Spirit, in virtues, and in signs.

I am confident, then, my brothers, and I myself concerning you. A good teacher urges people toward progress by praising them, so that they may be ashamed not to be what the Apostle thinks them to be.

That you yourselves are also full of love. He took care that he should not seem ever to have rebuked them too harshly or contentiously. Or he shows that Christians who disagree or are foolish must always admonish one another.

Filled with all knowledge, so that you may be able to admonish one another. This means knowledge of the New and Old Testament.

[Col. 0712B] But I have written to you rather boldly, brothers, in part. Rather, I had greater confidence to write because I know that, being prudent, you quickly accept a reasoned argument, as it is written: “Reprove a wise person, and he will love you.” Alternatively, here the Apostle speaks by humbling himself; or, since they already had Peter’s preaching, he dares to preach himself.

As though bringing you back to remembrance. Knowing that you are prudent, or not ignorant, I do not teach you but remind you, as people who know.

Because of the grace that was given to me by God. Not because of earthly gifts or praise, but so that I may fulfill the office I received.

So that I may be a minister of Christ Jesus among the Gentiles. Serving the Gospel—that is, calling back to it certain runaway servants.

[Col. 0712C] Sanctifying the Gospel of God. Demonstrating by my example that it is holy, since I carry it out with such great fear. Some people, because they despise what is human, regard what they preach as divine; and thus a holy matter comes to seem unholy when it is not performed in a holy manner. Hence it is said: “Sanctify a fast,” that is, “make it holy,” or “demonstrate it to be holy.”

So that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit. So that, by my example, the Gentiles may become an offering acceptable to God—not sanctified or received by fire, but by the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “For he sat upon the Apostles like fire, and various tongues appeared to them.”

Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus before God. “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” I have glory before God, even though among human beings I am defamed and disgraced.

For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ accomplishes through me for the obedience of the Gentiles. Here he shows that Christ and the Holy Spirit have one power and one might. Alternatively, I have not dared to say that in these matters I accomplished anything by my own power and that God did not work everything through me.

In word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders. That is, in teaching and signs. Here he was not speaking of ordinary works but of powers.

In the power of the Holy Spirit. They have one power and one might.

So that from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum I have filled the Gospel of Christ. The Gospel is filled when the Gentiles also believe.

Thus I preached this Gospel, not where Christ had already been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation. Not everyone who builds upon another’s foundation does wrong, provided he builds with gold and the other materials. Here he touches upon the false apostles, who always went to those who had already believed and never to the Gentiles, because they could not perform acts of power. He shows that he labored perfectly: he both laid the foundation and built the structure upon it.

But as it is written—in Isaiah. He shows that his labor had already been foretold.

“For those to whom nothing was announced concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.” Christ is manifested in the Apostles and through the powers performed in his name.

For this reason I was very often hindered from coming to you. He explains what he had said at the beginning of the letter.

And I have been prevented until now. But now I have no further place in these regions. Since everyone here is already firmly established, he denies having a reason to lay the foundation.

But having a desire to come to you. It should be noted that desire can also be good, as in: “I desire to depart and be with Christ,” and: “My soul has desired to long for your ordinances.”

For many years already. He shows what necessity there was that kept him occupied for many years.

When I begin to set out for Spain, I hope to see you as I pass through. Whether he was in Spain is uncertain.

And to be escorted there by you, if I may first enjoy you in part. You so conduct yourselves that I will have neither reason nor need to remain longer among you; therefore he says that he will enjoy them only in part, because they did not need to believe but only to be strengthened. Or he says “in part” because no length of time can produce love.

Now, therefore, I will set out for Jerusalem. This remains for me to do next: to come.

To minister to the saints. There were saints in Jerusalem who, after selling all their possessions and laying them at the feet of the Apostles, devoted themselves to prayer, reading, and teaching. What sort of people they were is shown by the fact that the Apostle himself went to minister to them and desired his offering to be acceptable to them—that is, he wanted them to deem it worthy of acceptance—showing that this benefited not so much those who received as those who gave. He says this against those who attack the glory of perfection.

For Macedonia and Achaia approved of making a contribution. They approved this as beneficial to themselves, if they made some contribution of expenses for the saints.

For the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. For it pleased them. They wished to be poor for the sake of the edification of the saints. Or simply understand “the poor among the saints.”

And they are their debtors. By their example he urges the Romans toward a similar work, showing that this rightly pleased them.

[Col. 0714A] For if the Gentiles have become participants in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things. Since they had teachers from among them and had become partners in the root and richness of the olive tree, each person ought to share with another what he possesses in abundance.

When I have completed this and delivered this fruit to them, I will set out for Spain through your region. If you conduct yourselves well, good teaching concerning you will abound for us, because as the disciple progresses, the teacher is equally encouraged to teach. As he says elsewhere: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians.” Or: “Christ is abundantly blessed in you at my coming.”

I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ. The Apostle knew that, because of preaching Christ, he would be led to Rome in chains; nevertheless, he says that he will come in an abundance of blessing. Or perhaps because he was conscious that he also possessed grace from the other Apostles.

I appeal to you, therefore, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ. He asks that the whole Church pray for him earnestly, because he knows that the prayers of many offered together have great power. After James was killed, Peter was freed from prison by the prayers of the brothers, who thereby provided the benefit not so much to him as to themselves, so that they might be strengthened by his teaching.

And through the love of the Holy Spirit, that you may assist me in your prayers to God on my behalf. Spiritual love causes you to pray for one another.

That I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem. Either so that all may believe, or so that, while ministering to the faithful, I may not fall into the hands of unbelievers, lest I be unable to come to you.

That I may come to you with joy through the will of God and be refreshed with you. I shall come with joy if my offering is accepted by them and, secure, I speak the word of God more abundantly. For sadness of mind greatly hinders teaching.

Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen. The God of peace is present only among peaceful people. He ended beautifully, having recalled the two peoples to harmony.

## CHAPTER XVI

I commend to you Phoebe, our sister. [Col. 0714D] As though the text of the Letter were already finished, he appended, as is customary, a commendation. Here also the Apostle shows that a person’s sex—man or woman—is not to be accepted or chosen as a criterion, since he is said to send the letter to the Romans through a woman. In the same Letter he sends greetings to other women.

Who is in the service of the Church that is in Cenchreae. Even now, in the East, deaconesses appear to minister within their own sex at baptism or in the ministry of the word, for we find that women taught privately, such as Priscilla, whose husband was called Aquila.

So that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you. For she too has assisted many, including me personally. Help her, whether with financial resources or with comfort, because as long as she had the means, she herself helped many.

Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus. They are said to have conformed themselves to the Apostle in faith. He calls them fellow workers because, in the work of teaching where he labored, they too helped.

Who risked their own necks for my life. Not only I give thanks to them, but all the churches of the Gentiles. By confirming my teaching, they exposed themselves to danger; for this reason all the churches give thanks to them, because through them I was preserved.

And their household church. He shows that a congregation of the faithful is called a church.

Greet Epaenetus, beloved by me, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ Jesus. Greet Mary, who labored greatly among you. We understand all those whom he greets as firstfruits of the church of Asia to have been foreigners by origin, judging from their names. Through their example and teaching, we reasonably suppose that the Romans believed.

Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are notable among the Apostles and who were in Christ before me. Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ Jesus, and Stachys, my beloved. Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, the most beloved, who labored greatly in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. Greet her as a mother because of age, not because she gave birth to me. These were Jews, and because they had suffered together with Paul and had not been frightened, they were considered notable on this account. They had been assigned, among others, to promote the Romans’ progress, and Paul’s testimony reports that they believed before him.

Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympias, and all the saints who are with them. By his own example he teaches us what sort of friends we ought to greet in our letters: not the rich of this world, honored for their wealth or dignities, but those enriched by grace and faith.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you. Not falsely or deceitfully, like the kiss Judas gave the Savior. For this reason peace is announced first in the Church: to show that the person who is about to share in the body of Christ is at peace with everyone.

I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and occasions of stumbling contrary to the teaching that you learned, and to avoid them. Such people do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly. He speaks of those who at that time came from the circumcision, destroying fasting and abstinence. For the sake of their belly they preached new moons, [Col. 0716A] Sabbaths, and the other festivals, dissenting from apostolic teaching and preparing occasions of stumbling for the brothers.

And by pleasant speeches and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. Through flatteries and acts of adulation composed in polished speech.

For your obedience has become known everywhere. If you obeyed those whom you ought not to have obeyed, how much more ought you to obey us! They came to you for this very reason: they knew that through your simple obedience you could quickly be led astray.

I rejoice, therefore, in you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil. Now may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet speedily. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Timothy, my fellow worker, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, greet you. I, Tertius, who wrote this Letter, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, my host, and the whole Church greet you. Obedience is good, provided that it is reasonable; therefore I want you to be wise in what is good, so that, knowing nothing of evil, you may place the enemy beneath the feet of innocence. For the Lord has given us power to tread upon scorpions and serpents and upon all the power of the enemy—that is, so that he may not prevail over us and so that we may be able to walk freely and unimpeded over all his members.

Erastus, the treasurer of the city, greets you, and Quartus, the brother. Here he calls him “treasurer” from the word “treasury,” just as he often called Gentiles who believed “from the Gentiles,” following the custom of the law, which still calls Abigail the wife of Nabal even though, after Nabal’s death, she had married David.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen. This is his handwritten subscription in all the Letters, so that in it he might also remind them of Christ’s benefits.

Now to him who is able to strengthen you. By signs and teachings. Here too he indicates the person of the Father. Then, when he says that this was manifested through the prophetic Scriptures according to the command of the eternal God, he signifies the Holy Spirit. He adds: “Made known to the only wise God through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever.” Here he clearly speaks of the Father and the Son. When he says, “Made known to the only wise God,” he signifies the Trinity in the common gift of the mystery.

[Col. 0716D] According to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. Live in such a way as I preached Christ to the Gentiles by example and authority.

According to the revelation of the mystery. The mystery concerning the calling of all the Gentiles had long been hidden in the Law; now the Gospel has been clearly revealed through Paul in Christ by the testimonies of the Prophets. Although he had said many things about the Gentiles beforehand, no one had understood so openly how they would become one in Christ, together with the Jews. They could have supposed that certain people were to be admitted to the faith as proselytes.

Kept silent through eternal times, but now revealed [Col. 0717A] through the Scriptures of the Prophets. By saying “revealed,” he explains what had been hidden.

According to the command of the eternal God. God commanded that all the Gentiles obey and acknowledge God. He alone knew beforehand that this would one day happen, since he alone is wise by nature, just as he is good by nature. Human beings too are called good, but we can become good or wise through instruction; he is so by nature. To him, through Jesus Christ, be glory and honor for ever and ever.

For obedience to the faith among all the Gentiles. He signifies the Holy Spirit. He adds:

Made known to the only wise God through Jesus Christ: to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

# INTO THE FIRST LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0717]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0717A]

Paul. The name “Paul,” which he places first in his Letters, should be understood as expressing authority. Alternatively: “Paul the Apostle,” joining the name of the brothers in the Letter, either signifies his humility or shows that he was a fellow worker in apostolic preaching.

Called an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God. Everyone is called to faith by the will of God, but each person believes voluntarily and by his own choice, as he says in the Acts: “I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.”

And Sosthenes, a brother of the Church of God. He says “brother,” not “apostle.” He introduces him as writing with him because he was a teacher from among them and was greatly concerned for them.

Which is in Corinth. He shows who are the Church of God: the holy and blameless, since the Church has neither stain nor wrinkle. Therefore he writes to those who still preserved their integrity, not to those who had lost holiness. He honors the former with a letter and commends the latter by his authority.

Sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints. Sanctified through baptism. With all who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is properly the duty of priests to invoke the Lord. They are told: “Thus bless the children of Israel, invoking my name over them.” And the Psalmist says: “And Samuel among those who invoke his name.” That Samuel was a priest is proved by the fact that he succeeded a priest and offered sacrifices. Concerning him it is also said according to the historical account: “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest.” Although he was not of the family of Aaron, he is nevertheless read in Chronicles as being from the tribe of Levi, because he established him just as he established the other. For Aaron was chosen in such a way that he did not afterward lose the power to choose others.

In every place belonging to them and to us. Because priests serve both in their own place and in that of the Apostles. For this reason they are also called apostles of the churches. Alternatively: He shows that he is sending this Letter to all the churches of the province of Achaia.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Peace preserves grace, which some did not wish to have.

I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus. First, as usual, he urges them toward progress by praising them. He says that he rejoices in their knowledge, but that they must know that true wisdom does not puff up and does not produce dissension.

[Col. 0718A] Because in every respect you have been enriched in him. In every virtue, through wisdom, which established the friends of God and the Prophets. Alternatively: By saying this, the Apostle shows that when they came to the faith of Christ they were then enriched with every grace; but now, because they are not living according to the faith, he shows that the grace they received has been emptied.

In every word and in every knowledge. That is, not only of the New but also of the Old Testament.

As the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you. The testimony that says: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

So that you lack nothing in any grace. Hence Solomon says: “All good things came to me together with her,” that is, with wisdom.

Awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0718C] Christ. The person who is prepared in every respect truly awaits Christ’s coming. The Lord’s coming is called a revelation because it is now hidden from us.

Who will also strengthen you to the end, without blame, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Through teaching, as David says: “Strengthen me in your words.” And again: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them.” Alternatively: He prays that they may remain irreproachable until the end of their lives, for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Christ our Lord. John explains this fellowship when he says: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie.” And Paul says: “If we have died together, we shall also live together; if we endure, we shall also reign together.” This passage works against the Arians, who wish the Son to be lesser because all things are said to have been made through him, although this also applies to the Father, through whom he calls believers into fellowship with his Son. Alternatively: This also works against the Arians, who say that the Son is the minister of the Father’s commands, since it is written: “All things were made through him.” Here, however, it is shown that through God the Father they were called into communion with Jesus Christ our Lord. Thus far the preface has been praise.

I appeal to you, brothers. He calls them back to unity of thought and urges them all to speak the same thing. Alternatively: Here he now takes up the case against dissension.

By the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In whose name you were saved and saw signs being performed.

That you all say the same thing. That you think and say one thing.

And that there be no divisions among you. Divisions always arise from contention.

But that you be perfected in the same mind and in the same knowledge. If you think and speak the same thing, then you can truly be perfected.

For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you. It may be asked how the Apostle believed something about absent people, since it is written: “You shall not believe a vain report.” And again: “Speak of what your eyes have seen,” and so forth. But he possessed the grace of knowing, while absent, what was happening in each church. As he says to the Colossians: “Although I am absent in body, I am present in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order,” and so forth. Since, therefore, he knew that the Corinthians were acting as he had heard, he did not believe without reason concerning absent people, whose conduct he knew in the spirit.

Now I mean this: each of you says, “I belong to Paul,” or “I to Apollos,” or “I to Cephas,” or “I to Christ.” Under the names of the Apostles he touches upon the false apostles, who had ensnared them through the wisdom of the world, so that each person said he belonged to whichever teacher’s doctrine he had chosen, even though they taught opposing things. If he does not permit this to be said even of the true Apostles, [Col. 0719C] how much less will it be permitted concerning the false ones?

Is Christ divided? The body is divided when the members disagree.

Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul? This may also be said to those who, abandoning Christ’s example, desire to imitate the saints of the Old Testament solely in their wealth: “Was Abraham crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Job?” And there is also that saying of the Lord, where we are taught not to ask what is commanded to another disciple, when he says to Peter: “What is that to you? You follow me.”

I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. I also baptized the household of Stephanas; apart from that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else among you. This happened in such a way that I baptized those few who do not say that they were baptized in my name. Alternatively: I baptized none of those people themselves except those whom I have listed.

For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize. He did not arrogate to himself the lesser task, since he was able to fulfill the greater offices. In the same way today a bishop or priest, if he wishes, can fulfill the ministry of a deacon.

Not in wisdom of speech. Although the Apostles could also preach discourses of wisdom, they teach simply, so that prudence may not be attributed to the cleverness of preaching and the cross of Christ be emptied.

[Col. 0720A] So that the cross of Christ may not be emptied. For those who charm the ears with rhetorical display empty the power of the cross.

For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. The preaching of the cross seems foolish to those who do not understand the power of God: to say that the Son of God was crucified. But believers understand it to be the power of God, through which death became life and the devil was overcome.

But to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. Their faith saves them.

For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.” He asserts that this was fulfilled at the Savior’s coming, that is, “I will reduce it to nothing.”

And I will reject the understanding of the understanding ones. By choosing fishermen, he rejected rhetorical and philosophical skill. It may plainly be asked where this wisdom that God rejects comes from. For it is written that all wisdom is from the Lord God—that is, it derives its beginning from a good nature. The human mind has this capacity: wherever you direct it, it follows, and through gradual reflection it advances. Hence many uneducated people compose poems so refined that highly learned men admire them. God had given this faculty so that human beings might know him from created things and seek his will, but they turned it toward the investigation of vain and curious matters. The same may be understood of wealth, strength, and everything else that we use badly.

Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? That is, the teacher.

Where is the investigator of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish? The one who acquires secular wisdom, or anyone who investigates obscure matters of other kinds.

For since the world, through its wisdom, did not know God in the wisdom of God. The making of the world was fashioned by the wisdom of God; in it, through the natural wisdom that had been given and created for this purpose, the one who had made it ought to have been recognized. But since human beings did not acknowledge him, another remedy is provided for them. Alternatively: In this passage he shows the wisdom of God through the ordering of the visible creatures, from which they ought to have revered and recognized God as their author.

It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. Not because the preaching of the cross is truly foolishness, but because it was regarded as such among them.

For Jews indeed ask for signs. Following the custom of the [Col. 0720D] Prophets, the Jews ask for signs; yet even when they saw them, they refused to believe.

And Greeks seek wisdom. The principles of dialectical art and human wisdom.

But we preach Christ crucified. He shows that his teaching differs greatly from their understanding.

To Jews indeed a stumbling block. They are scandalized when they hear that Christ was crucified by them. Or it is a stumbling block for them to hear that Christ could have died, since they await him as virtually immortal. Hence they said: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever,” not understanding that he first had to suffer and then enter into his glory.

[Col. 0721A] But to the Gentiles foolishness. According to worldly wisdom, believing that God was crucified appears foolish.

But to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Here he does not call Christ’s divinity the power and wisdom of God, but the arrangement of the cross. Alternatively: When the Jews and Gentiles themselves have believed, they understand that it is the power of God that, after conquering death, restored the human being to life, and the wisdom that freed us from the dominion of the devil—something they had previously been unable to understand because of unbelief.

For what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings. What is considered foolish of God surpasses all human wisdom, because those who have been saved through the mystery of the cross could not be liberated by their own wisdom.

And what is weak of God is stronger than human beings. The weakness of the crucified one overcame death, which not even giants could escape.

For consider your calling, brothers. He takes his example from those who had believed, to show that fleshly boasting does not benefit faith but rather harms it, since people inflated by pride in wisdom and nobility refused to submit to the wisdom of God.

For not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. Here he indirectly attacks those who boasted that they were learned in the Law, stronger than the apostles, and descended from a more noble priestly lineage.

But God chose what is foolish in the world to confound [Col. 0721C] the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to confound the strong; and what is ignoble and contemptible in the world God chose. Because they did not trust in themselves, they believed more readily. For the glory of the wise, the rich, and the strong is always rebuked, as the Prophet says: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches.” But the Lord himself fulfilled for our example what he had said through the Prophet. By being born of a poor mother, he rejected riches. By not learning letters, he rejected worldly wisdom. When he was handed over, he did not resist but patiently endured the cross, forbidding glorying in human strength. Let such people, therefore, humble themselves before God, if they too wish to be freed along with the rest.

[Col. 0721D] And things that are not, so that he might destroy things that are. Things that are not: wisdom, strength, and nobility; so that he might overthrow things possessing these qualities.

So that no flesh might glory in his presence. “All flesh,” not the spirit, because this boasting is carnal.

But from him you are in Christ Jesus. If, then, you are from him, do not admire what he rejects.

Who was made wisdom for us by God, and righteousness. He was made these things for us; for himself he always was, so that he might make us wise, righteous, and holy. Another exposition: Although Christ is the wisdom of God the Father, nevertheless, when someone believes in him, Christ becomes wisdom for that person.

[Col. 0722A] And sanctification, and redemption. The redemption of our salvation.

So that, just as it is written: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” Not in himself, nor in the things mentioned above.

## CHAPTER II

And I, when I came to you, brothers. Since he had shown that they ought not to admire human wisdom, he confirms this by his own example, because he himself had not preached through human wisdom.

I did not come with superiority of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ. I did not wish to parade an ornate style of eloquence in divine preaching.

[Col. 0722B] For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ. That is, I did not glory in anything except Christ.

And him crucified. Something that appears foolish to human beings.

And I was with you in weakness, fear, and much trembling. For God ought not to have been preached in any other manner: not with boasting or fleshly glory.

And my speech and my preaching. Since the Corinthians were dialecticians, he did not wish to engage them in disputation, lest this too should appear to them some new philosophy; instead, he demonstrated to them powers and miracles.

Not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power. For rhetoric has persuasive devices in every subject.

[Col. 0722C] So that your faith might not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God. Human wisdom is temporal and benefits one only briefly. But the power of God, being eternal, grants progress without end.

But we speak wisdom among the perfect. Do not suppose that we too lack wisdom: we possess divine wisdom, but at that time you were quite unable to grasp it; it is now disclosed to those who believe.

Yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. Whether kings or philosophers, who appear in this age to hold primacy in wisdom. Through our Gospel they are being destroyed together with their wisdom.

But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom. In the Gospel, which contains Christ’s birth, passion, and the rest.

[Col. 0722D] Which God predestined before the ages. Whether in the present age or in the Law before the times. For many prophets desired to see it and did not see it.

For our glory. For us who believe in Christ.

Which none of the rulers of this age knew. Pilate, Caiaphas, and the others, whose ignorance is also condemned, because they ought not to have been ignorant.

For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory and majesty. At this point two heresies—those of Apollinarius and Arius—abuse the passage in defense of their perverse doctrine. One does so in order to destroy the complete nature of the humanity assumed; the other, in order to assert that the Word of God is passible, and [Note: [Col. 0723D] “ea” must absolutely be restored in place of “erat,” to which “neque ista” corresponds. But since books commonly print it thus [Col. 0724D], and Martianay did not remove any error of the older editions, it is enough to have warned the reader.], not understanding [Col. 0723A] that the Lord of majesty was also called “the assumed human being,” nor knowing that the passible nature is not the divine but the human nature. Another exposition: The Lord of majesty suffers in the flesh, is crucified in the flesh, and dies in the flesh, while the substance of his divinity is impassible. In the same way the apostle Peter also testifies in his Epistle that Christ suffered for us in the flesh, saying: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree.” Elsewhere as well: “Christ, therefore, having suffered in the flesh.”

As it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him.” The minds of the rulers mentioned above were unable to see these things, because they refused to believe. Some indeed say: “The eye has not seen a virgin give birth, nor has the ear heard: ‘Then the righteous will shine like the sun.’” “The one who has ears to hear,” he says, “let him hear”; and what has not entered into the human heart is that human beings would become co-heirs with Christ.

[Col. 0723B] But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit. To us, who by faith have deserved to receive the Spirit of God, which shows us his will.

For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. Even those things that rest in the secrecy of God’s counsel.

For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God. What thoughts are at work in a human being. Another exposition: This is a splendid passage against heretics [Col. 0723C] who say that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Here it is shown not only that he is not a creature, but also that he alone searches the innermost and deepest things of God, since he is of the same nature and substance as Christ.

But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God. Whoever has a worldly disposition does not seem to possess the Spirit of God but the spirit of the world.

So that we may know the things given to us by God. So that we may know how much has been bestowed on us by God through Christ’s coming.

And we speak these things not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit. These things also we proclaim to you, instructed not by philosophers or grammarians but by the Spirit of God.

Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. Saying these things to those who are able to hear; for such things can be grasped only through what is known and similar to them.

[Col. 0723D] But the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. One who does not have the Spirit of God is natural, because he conducts himself in the manner of animals, thinking that nothing exists after death. Therefore, like an animal, he gives himself over to his belly and his lust, destined to perish by eternal death.

For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand it, because it is examined spiritually. First, it seems foolishness to him that the one who suffered, died, and rose again should now be proclaimed Lord of the whole creation. [Col. 0724A] Second, he regards as foolish the commandments of Christ: to despise one’s own goods, offer the other cheek, and other things of this kind.

But the spiritual person judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one, as it is written. He judges to be empty the things in which carnal people delight. And he conducts himself in such a way that he is judged by no one. Or: The spiritual person discerns and understands all things, and his understanding is not understood by a natural human being. Another exposition: By “all things” he means spiritual things. For the natural person cannot know even the arts and disciplines of this world unless he understands them spiritually.

For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has instructed him? No one without the Spirit of God has known the mind of the Lord, which is in spiritual people. Here “mind” signifies understanding.

[Col. 0724B] But we have the mind of Christ. We who have received the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER III

And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people. He is now concerned that they might think that they alone possess the mind of the Lord, because they had heard it as children. “The mind of the Lord,” he says, “did not fail in me; rather, you lacked the power to hear.” Another exposition: The Apostle rebukes the Corinthians because they had lost the grace they had received when they first believed. It appears that here he rebukes everyone collectively, since those who do not live according to the faith are being reproved.

As to infants in Christ. Not infants in bodily age, but in Christ.

I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able, and indeed even now you are not able, since you are still carnal. Blessed Peter says the same: “Therefore, laying aside all malice and deceit, as newborn infants desire rational and guileless milk, so that by it you may grow unto salvation.” If, then, those who have cast away all malice and are not yet perfect in virtue are still infants, what should be thought of those whom every form of malice dominates?

For since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal? Here he shows by what vices carnal people are judged: these things are not performed directly through the flesh, but such conduct descends from a carnal understanding.

[Col. 0724D] And are you not walking according to the human being? Whoever has nothing more than other human beings is said to walk according to the human being; but in this passage, because of the defense of particular people, they are called human beings.

For when someone says, “I indeed belong to Paul,” and another, “I to Apollos,” are you not human beings? He wants us to be more than human beings.

What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants of the one in whom you believed. If we are nothing, whom he himself appointed as servants, how much more are those who glory in carnal things nothing!

[Col. 0725A] And each according as the Lord gave. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” This itself does not come from us but is God’s gift: that signs should be performed through my hands to arouse you to faith, and that Apollos should strengthen you by his teaching. For just as a plant withers without water, so faith withers without teaching. If both the planting and the spring belong to God, why do you attribute anything to us, as though we had done something by our own power?

Therefore neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one. Each will receive his own reward according to his labor. For unless God gives the growth, we labor in vain. We are hired workers in another’s field. We use another’s tools; we possess nothing of our own except the reward of our labor.

For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field; you are God’s building. We help cultivate God’s field and construct the temple, not by power but by the word.

According to the grace of God that was given to me. Not according to my own power. Or: I received the grace to lay the foundation, so that I might preach where Christ had not been announced.

As a wise architect I laid the foundation. An unskilled architect cannot lay a foundation.

But another builds upon it. Another teacher instructs upon the faith that I founded.

But let each one watch how he builds upon it. Let him be concerned that the courses of the walls rise strong and straight.

[Col. 0725C] For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. There is no other Christ whom anyone can preach to you besides Jesus, in whom you have believed with the firmest faith. The only concern is that, through the negligence of teachers, you should not begin to become liable to Gehenna.
