But if anyone builds upon this foundation. The one who builds upon it practices the same craft, although he may be lesser in the work, as the one who laid the foundation. Therefore it is not each person who builds upon his own faith, but each teacher, since walls cannot ever rise by themselves unless they have been constructed by a workman. Alternatively: Here he means teachers and instructors, who correctly or wrongly establish people upon the foundation, which is Christ. The teaching of these teachers will be revealed in fire on the day of judgment, when, after sinners have been consumed, those who have been proved will remain. The teachers will receive the reward of recompense for those who have been proved; but in the case of those whom the fire consumes, they will suffer loss, because they have labored in vain. Yet these same teachers, when they come to judgment, will be saved, provided that they themselves were not the cause of the lost.

When he says, “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss,” the works are not, as some think, to be burned in the fire of flame, but the people who have acted in such a way as to deserve assignment to the fire. If works—that is, crimes—are punished while the one who committed them is saved, this will not be loss but gain for him. [Col. 0726A] Hence it is clearly shown, as was explained above, that the people are the gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, and straw, because, having received instruction from teachers, they either observe the commandments or neglect them.

Gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw: each one’s work will become evident. For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire. In the Church there are three kinds of good: good, better, and best. He placed gold first so that the wording might be more elegant, or he compared it with strength rather than appearance. Since silver is stronger than gold, it is assigned the better place. Conversely, there are three kinds of evil: evil, worse, and worst. These are compared with wood, hay, and straw.

[Col. 0726B] And the fire will test what each one’s work is like. If anyone’s work remains, what he built upon it, he will receive a reward. Gold and silver not only do not burn, but through fire they will shine more brilliantly. Wood and the rest, however, will be consumed. Or he wished to compare the examination of judgment with fire, according to the customary language of Scripture.

If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss. If anyone teaches negligently, whether by word or by example, he will lose his labor, because he completed a dry and weak work.

He himself will be saved. By his own righteousness.

Yet so as through fire. If the one who is righteous in himself will be saved only through fire because he built his disciples negligently, what will happen to those who neither build by their speech nor, in addition, cause scandal by their example?

Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Do you not know whose temple you are, whether individually or in the Church as a whole?

If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. This means either his own body, by sinning, or the Church, by turning it toward false teaching or certainly destroying it by his own example. The Novatians customarily use this passage to exclude repentance. They should be answered by asking why this very passage was written: they will have no hope of pardon.

Let no one deceive you. Deceived either by his own flattery or by that of another.

[Col. 0726D] If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise. Here he specifically rebukes the wise of the world, whom human wisdom did not allow to perceive divine things. Alternatively: If anyone thinks himself wise in returning an injury, should he do the same thing, let him become foolish. In this age the person who wishes to fulfill the commandments of the Gospel is foolish; for whoever offers the other cheek to the one striking him is foolish by choice, not by nature.

For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. Nothing is more foolish than for someone who cannot avenge himself to wish to do so and not reserve his injury for God. Thus he will lose vengeance for the insult with God, and also the reward for patience.

[Col. 0727A] For it is written: “I will seize the wise in their cunning.” No cunning helps to escape the hand of God.

And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.” They contribute nothing useful to salvation.

Therefore let no one glory in human beings. That is, in false apostles, who think only worldly thoughts; indeed, one must not glory even in us, but in the one to whom we ourselves belong.

For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death. All things were created for the saints, who, though they possess nothing, possess everything. We can also refer these words to freedom of choice, so that they may choose what they wish, whether death or life.

[Col. 0727B] Whether things present or things future. For all things are yours. This signifies that both present and future things have been divinely assigned to the saints; alternatively, it refers to Christ’s life and death, since he both died and rose again for us.

But you are Christ’s. Christ is God’s just as elsewhere God is called Christ’s, if you wish to understand this as referring to his divinity. Otherwise, here he is discussing the form of the assumed human being, according to which he is also called anointed.

And Christ is God’s. As a human being.

## CHAPTER IV

Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the ministries of God. Not as Christ’s equals.

[Col. 0727C] Here the question is already being asked among stewards, that someone be found faithful. This is the voice of one asking: that is, do you now think that consciences are being judged here?

But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human day. By “human judgment” I mean a matter of no importance, in which truth and justice are often frustrated. “For I have not desired the day of man,” says Jeremiah.

But I do not even judge myself. I, who know my conscience best, judge myself to be nothing. Nor do I judge myself.

For I am conscious of nothing against myself. Those who say, “No one can avoid sin,” think wrongly.

But by this I am not justified. He says this out of humility: “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” by which I might glory over other people. If Paul says this, we must consider what ought to be said of us. But by this I am not justified.

The one who judges me is the Lord. This is not because certain people praise me in this way: just as someone is not justified by another’s praise, so he is not stained by another’s disgrace. For before God each person is credited with what he is, not with what is said about him.

Therefore, brothers, do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts. A human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.

And then each one will receive praise from God. That person alone is praiseworthy who is praised by God’s testimony, before whom all hidden and unseen things are known.

[Col. 0728A] Now, brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake. So that you may take from us an example of humility, lest anyone dare, beyond the discipline of Scripture, to become inflated against another on behalf of someone else, once the teacher of evil contention has been overthrown.

So that in us you may learn not to become inflated, one against another on behalf of someone else, beyond what is written. This is what he means: let no one, proclaiming his own teacher, incite one person against another.

For who distinguishes you? Here he turns his words to those inflated by eloquence: who distinguishes you; of what importance are you?

And what do you have that you did not receive? What good do you have from yourself that you learned from no one or did not receive at all as a gift from God?

[Col. 0728B] But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it? As though you gloried in what was your own.

Already you are filled; already you have become rich. This should be read or pronounced in a rebuking manner.

You reign without us. You have no need of us in anything.

And would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you! Would that you had not been deceived by false boasting! Perhaps we would reign together.

For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the very last, as destined for death. He sent us, the last of all, to the Gentiles as if to death.

For we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. Everyone publicly watches our injuries—whether “angels and human beings” means literally, or holy people and sinners.

[Col. 0728C] We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are noble, but we are ignoble. We, like fools for Christ’s sake, endure everything, while you wish to be Christians in such a way that you retain worldly wisdom. We are weak because we do not wish to return injury for injury, while you glory in returning it and call yourselves strong. We, cast down in voluntary poverty and possessing nothing, while you even claim for yourselves the nobility of earthly descent.

Until this present hour. From the beginning of our preaching until the present time.

We are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten, and homeless. We do not remain in fixed dwellings but are driven everywhere by the necessity of the Gospel.

And we labor, working with our own hands. Yet they worked in such a way that they fulfilled the duty of teaching all the more.

[Col. 0728D] We are cursed, and we bless. We endure persecution and bear it. We are reviled, and we entreat. We pray to God for those who revile us.

We have become like the refuse of this world. As it is written: “The righteous person is unclean in the eyes of the wicked.”

The refuse of all things to this very day. The most humble and subject of all.

I do not write these things to shame you, but I admonish you as my most beloved children. They could have been shamed by their own glory if he had not lifted them up. For he did not seek their destruction but their progress.

For if you have ten thousand tutors in [Col. 0729A] Christ, yet not many fathers. All who minister to those already born through another cannot be called fathers.

For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you. You remember that you were reformed into new life when I first preached.

Therefore I urge you: be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ. It belongs to good children to imitate good parents in everything.

For this reason I sent you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord. The more faithful he is than the rest, the dearer he is to all.

He will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus. He will remind you through both my letters and his own example, for one without the other could not benefit you.

[Col. 0729B] As I teach everywhere in every Church. How my example always agrees with my teaching, everywhere and always.

As though I were not coming to you. Here he begins to rebuke the matter of fornication.

Thus certain people have become inflated. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. Someone boasts of false knowledge only until the preacher of true knowledge arrives.

And I will know not the speech of those who are inflated but their power. I will examine not the pomp of eloquence but the effect of their conduct, where the power of faith is shown to exist.

For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in [Col. 0729C] power. Here he shows that teaching without works of righteousness benefits nothing the person who does not do what he persuades others ought to be done.

What do you want? A kindly teacher leaves the correction of his disciples in their power, so that, if they wish to repent, the most merciful consoler may be present; but if they do not wish to repent, a harsh avenger may confront the sinners.

Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? With what sort of rod Peter came to Ananias and Sapphira, and Paul himself to the magician.

## CHAPTER V

It is reported everywhere. He shows why he made the preceding threat.

There is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. [Col. 0729D] In the Church over which you appear to preside.

And you have become inflated, and have not rather mourned. You are inflated by empty knowledge and have no concern for those who are perishing, whether they should be corrected or separated from the Church. Yet we always read that good shepherds mourned the sins of the people, as Jeremiah did when he said: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” He showed that he lacked not the feeling of grief but the tears.

So that the one who has done this deed may be removed from your midst. Either the person who sinned is removed, or Satan is expelled, provided he has no one through whom to work.

I, though absent in body but present in [Col. 0730A] spirit, have already judged, as though present. He says that he is present in spirit, lest anyone think that he condemned an absent person merely on the basis of hearsay, in accordance with the words of Elisha to Gehazi: “Was not my spirit with you on the way?”

The one who has acted in this way, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled and my spirit is present with the power of the Lord Jesus. He was present on my behalf, whether through the authority of my letters, by which the power of the Lord also assists.

To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. So that he may have the power to seize him bodily. When he sees that he will have rest neither for his flesh here nor for his spirit in the future, let him repent of his deed so that he may be saved. Or: In this way each person, according to his merits, is driven from the Church and handed over to Satan’s power, so that, while his flesh suffers a kind of [Col. 0730B] destruction through repentance, his spirit may be preserved. Scripture has the custom of understanding the whole person through a part. Or: This is also a Scriptural usage, namely, that carnal acts are shown to perish in the flesh, while a spiritual way of life is shown to be saved in the spirit. Alternatively, here he shows that one expelled from the Church is to be torn apart by the rabid mouths of demons if he persists in refusing to mortify the vices of the flesh, so that he may recover holy life.

So that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since Satan cannot be given power over the spirit, it is reserved for the Lord’s judgment.

Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Do you not know that many can perish through a bad example? We also read that through the offense of one person the anger of God came [Col. 0730C] upon the whole Jewish people.

Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened. Leave nothing of your former way of life in yourselves that could corrupt the purity of your nature.

For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Not in figure, but in truth. The Jews ate unleavened bread for seven days; we, however, do so always, if we live simply and purely. For the world was made in seven days and always revolves in its ordered course. Every day the lamb is slain for us, and every day we celebrate Passover, if we do not possess the leaven of malice [Col. 0730D] and wickedness. For what else is leaven than corruption of nature? It too, having first departed from natural sweetness, has been corrupted by an adulterated acidity.

I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators. Certainly not with the fornicators of this world, or with the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols. I wrote this very thing in the letter so that you would separate yourselves not from the Gentiles but from those who sin within the Church; otherwise you would have had to die. For this reason above all God wished them to live for the time being: so that unbelievers might make progress through living together with you.

Otherwise you would have had to depart from this world. Or: otherwise it would have been better for you to depart from this life [Col. 0731A] than to need admonition in order to be separated from association with the Gentiles.

But now I wrote to you not to associate. Rather, this is what I wrote: that you should not join yourselves to such people.

If anyone who is called a brother among you is a fornicator, greedy, an idol-servant, a reviler, a drunkard, or a rapacious person. He is not to be avoided merely on the basis of an opinion. But if someone is called a brother in name only, while he is exposed as a fornicator or a thief, we are commanded to separate ourselves from him, as it is written: “Whoever joins himself to fornicators is wicked; decay and the worm will inherit him.”

With such a person not even to eat. He did not permit even the sharing of a common meal with such people.

[Col. 0731B] For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? That is, unbelievers.

Are you not to judge those who are inside? For those who are outside God will judge. Surely you judge only those who are within the Church?

Remove the evil person from among yourselves. So that you may more easily teach those who are outside.

## CHAPTER VI

Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Does anyone dare to act against the Lord’s command, which says: “If anyone wishes to go to court with you,” and so forth? It should be noted that sometimes the Apostle inserts certain ideas in the middle of the case he is presenting and throws them in from the side; after explaining them, he returns to the case.

Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? This is what the Lord promised his disciples when he said: “You will sit, and you also will judge the twelve tribes of Israel,” promising the same to all who would imitate them. For one of them perished, and another succeeded to his place, though nothing had been promised to him. Paul and Barnabas, too, were appointed apostles by the Holy Spirit.

And if the world will be judged among you. Either through you or by your example.

[Col. 0731D] Are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we will judge angels, how much more matters of this life? Therefore those who will judge the whole world and the angels are unworthy to judge trivial matters. Those angels who, although they did not possess flesh, wished to sin will be judged by those who wished to be holy in the flesh.

If, then, you have judgments concerning matters of this life. Matters that arise from the affairs of the world.

Appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church. Even those who are least in the Church can judge such matters. Alternatively, by “contemptible in the Church” he means those judges whom below he calls unbelievers.

I say this to your shame. Is there really no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? You ought to be ashamed that there is no one among you wise enough to discern cases between brothers, so that it is not necessary to litigate publicly.

But brother goes to court against brother, and that before unbelievers. It is a double sin: both that you go to court and that you provoke yourselves to quarrels before unbelievers.

Now, indeed, it is altogether a fault among you. The mere fact that you act against Christ’s command is already a fault.

That you have lawsuits among yourselves. You who ought always to preserve peace, even at the cost of temporal possessions.

Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you yourselves inflict injury and commit fraud. Although, according to the commandment of the Gospel and the example of the Lord, you ought patiently to endure what is inflicted, you do the opposite: not only do you refuse to suffer it, but you inflict it even on those who have not done it.

And this against brothers. You do not hesitate to do to your brothers what you ought not to return even to your enemies.

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? They will not possess the kingdom of God unless all sins are washed away through the grace of baptism.

Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God. Do not be deceived, thinking that faith alone is sufficient for your salvation, when every persistent sin excludes one from the kingdom. Thus he says to the Galatians: “The works of the flesh are manifest, namely fornication, uncleanness, quarrels, anger, and things like these, which I proclaim to you: for those who do such things will not attain the kingdom of God.” He therefore added “and things like these,” so that no one might deny that, besides these, there are other sins that prevent entry into the kingdom of God.

And such were some of you at one time; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified. Do not fear your past sins; only take care not to sin after baptism. Or, if someone has been overtaken—as commonly happens—let him turn to repentance. Again, all sins are washed away by the grace of baptism. Another explanation: He says this against the heretics who try to separate Christ and the Holy Spirit from God the Father. Here it is shown that, just as the Father does, so Christ and the Holy Spirit wash away sins, justify, and sanctify.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. Washed in the name of Christ, sanctified through the Spirit of God.

Everything is permitted to me, but not everything is beneficial. In discussing fornication, he wished to show that gluttony and lack of self-control provide material for fornication, and at the same time to destroy them. He also says this: “Since I am free in my will, and it is permitted me to do what I wish, I must not nevertheless become subject to any sin.”

Everything is permitted to me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. [Col. 0733A] Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food. We are permitted to eat and drink, but if we become excessively subject to the stomach, what is itself permitted draws us toward what is not permitted, that is, toward fornication. The same is to be understood of everything which, although not itself sin, can nevertheless become an occasion of sins.

But God will destroy both the one and the other. That is, both these things—food and the stomach—and the human being subject to them and serving pleasures. Another explanation: At the resurrection of the dead, the substance of the stomach will not be destroyed, but the eating of food and the functions of the stomach will cease. For, as the same Apostle says to the Romans, the kingdom of heaven is neither food nor drink.

But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body. Let it be offered not to fornication but to the Lord, and the Lord will be joined to the body. For the Lord is with us as long as we remain with him; if we abandon him, he too will abandon us.

But God both raised up the Lord and will raise us up through his power. Because he raised up our Head, he will also raise us up, provided that we deserve to be his members through holiness.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? The whole Church is the body of Christ; individuals, however, are members.

Therefore, taking away the members of Christ. He takes away Christ’s members—that is, he cuts himself off from the body of Christ—who is joined to a prostitute.

Shall I make the members of Christ members of a prostitute? Certainly not. He did not say “of a fornicator,” in order to show that the man shares both her crime and her designation. Among human beings, the man’s act appears less shameful than the woman’s.

Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body? “For,” he says, “the two will be one flesh.” Just as lawfully with a wife, so unlawfully with a prostitute, one flesh is made through love.

But the one who clings to God is one spirit. Just as through the works of the flesh one becomes flesh, so through the works of God one becomes spirit.

Flee fornication. You see that its crime is exceedingly grave.

For every other sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. Every other sin can be committed by one person, who may be called a member but not nevertheless the body. In fornication, however, two perish, including the body. It is therefore a more serious evil in which two souls die. He wishes to make the cause of fornication appear weightier, since by habit they regarded it as very trivial. Another explanation: The Apostle takes an example from those who are married. “As it is written,” he says, “‘the two will be one flesh’: that is, a man and a wife become one body. Therefore, if one of them has committed fornication, he sins against the other as against his own body. The remaining sins, however, belong specifically to each individual and do not condemn the other.”

Or do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God? By committing fornication, you inflict the gravest injury upon him.

[Col. 0734A] And you are not your own. For you were bought at a great price. One who is not his own must not serve his own will, but that of the one by whom he was bought, according to his command, which says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” For if a person buys a slave for a small sum of money, he demands continual service; how much more does the one who redeemed us by his death! As Peter says: “Knowing that you were not redeemed from your futile conduct inherited from your fathers with corruptible things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of an unblemished and undefiled lamb.” Alternatively: Whoever violates the right of the testament rescinds the agreement of purchase; and one who is not hindered in the freedom of his will is not subject to a servile condition.

Glorify and bear God in your body. Glorify [Col. 0734B] God by your deeds, and bear him by preserving his image, as he says elsewhere: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.”

## CHAPTER VII

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me. He begins concerning marriage; for he first attacked what was unlawful before speaking about what was lawful.

It is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the due affection to his wife; likewise, the wife to her husband. What I preached to you at the beginning was good: namely, according to the use of marriage, not to touch a woman. But since you have written that many incontinent people oppose this teaching, let a remedy be granted, lest they perish by committing fornication. Thus, by this example of the Apostle, virginity and continence are preached above all. And if someone is not ashamed to confess himself incontinent, let him who cries out under the sickness of incontinence not be denied the remedy of marriage. It is as when a skilled physician grants something to a restless patient who says that he cannot abstain from all fruit, lest he presume something harmful. Incontinence is indeed restricted by circumstance, age, place, and weakness; chastity, however, can be preserved continually. We ought therefore to seek what we can preserve more easily and without any impediment, and possess forever.

But lovers of luxury are accustomed to object: “Why, then, did God’s first blessing grant, ‘Increase and multiply’?” So that the earth might be filled, naturally; once it has been filled, we ought to restrain ourselves from incontinence. “But,” you say, “he could have formed all human beings from the earth if the use of marriage had not always been pleasing to him.” But the question is not what he could do, but what he did; and all things are possible for him. Finally, he did not wish to make Eve from the earth, but from a rib. If, however, you think that the ancient times are in every respect applicable to us, imitate Adam, who—so to speak—took his daughter as his wife. Likewise Cain, if you are not ashamed, and the others who married their own sisters. But if this ought not to be done, let us believe that the Lord ordered everything according to his foreknowledge and for its proper times: he who then wished the earth to be filled now loves chastity more, and promises it a great reward. It must also be said that, even according to the Old Testament, we do not see that certain men had wives. For there they were permitted to have wives for the sake of children, not to exercise excessive lust. Those who are known to be worse than animals in this respect prove, by killing their children, that they did not marry for the sake of children. But whoever unites for that reason alone immediately abstains after conception. And when childbirth has ceased because of age, sexual intercourse also ceases.

A woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise, a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Everything that is touched is called a body. Therefore, just as a woman is called the body of the husband, so the husband is called the body of the wife. Therefore, even if the woman wishes to oppose him, the husband will be able to exercise mastery over his own body, that is, over his wife. There is no doubt that, much less against the husband’s will, can the woman prevail over the husband. Since he is speaking of two incontinent people, the Apostle grants, out of necessity, that they return to one another, because both are incontinent: if any cause of disagreement intervenes, both admit the crime of fornication, because both are incontinent. But if one of the two, considering the reward of chastity, wishes to remain continent, he ought not to accommodate himself to the incontinent partner. Rather, he should act so that, by seeing the other’s continence, the incontinent partner may be stirred to it; for luxury ought to pass over to continence, not continence decline into luxury. Although very many women oppose chastity, the one who wishes to remain continent ought to act in such a way that the incontinent partner consents to mutual abstinence, lest while he remains continent she should sin. “The soul that sins shall itself die.” For neither brother nor sister is subject to servitude in such a matter. For God did not call us to uncleanness but to sanctification. Alternatively: Because he wished the woman to be subject to the man, she alone forfeited her freedom.

Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and return again to one another. He seems to deny that the incontinent can devote themselves to prayer, which is in any case less than the communion in which catechumens and penitents pray, since they cannot communicate. Not only in the New Testament, but also in the Old, they keep themselves holy by abstaining from a woman, so that they may deserve to stand beside the Lord as he descends upon the mountain. Here it is demonstrated what perpetual continence can accomplish, since continence for three days had such force. Hence, in the Book of Kings, only those who are continent receive the priestly bread. For this reason, necessity could be excused for relaxing the law through the aid of charity. Hence Peter also urges that our prayers ought by no means to be hindered.

Lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence. It should be noted that, while he is addressing two incontinent people, he does not prejudice the one who is continent. Also, lest when one withdraws, the other commit fornication.

But I say this by way of indulgence, not by command. Yet I wish all of you to be as I myself am. I grant this to the weak; I do not command it to the perfect. For I wish all people to be found like me. I know how highly chastity is valued as a reward. The Apostle would never have wished this if it were altogether impossible.

But each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that. That is, he has received a gift corresponding to his own will.

Now I say to the unmarried and to widows. He begins another discussion concerning the unmarried.

It is good for them if they remain as I am. [Col. 0736B] What is praised by so great a teacher ought to be sought with the greatest eagerness.

But if they do not remain continent, let them marry. It should be noted that marriage is granted to the incontinent.

For it is better to marry than to burn. That which is punished by fire is better than the evil of fornication, as Judas pronounces concerning his daughter-in-law in Genesis.

But to those who are joined in marriage. Again he discusses marriages that are by no means to be dissolved for some cause.

I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not leave her husband. He forbids separation for any reason, lest they join themselves to others according to the custom of the Jews, which the Lord prohibited, saying: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery.” Alternatively: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not leave her husband.” He does not say this because Christ, speaking in him, was absent, but to show that the Lord himself spoke about this in the Gospel.

But if she does leave, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not divorce his wife. If she has left for some reason, let her not marry another; or, if she wishes, let her be reconciled to her own husband, since it is clearly better than marrying another.

But to the others I say—I, not the Lord. I give advice that seems useful to me.

If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not divorce her. And if any woman who believes has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not divorce her husband. If only one of the two has believed—not that he permitted a believer to unite with an unbeliever. For he did not say, “If someone takes a wife,” but “If someone has an unbelieving spouse.”

For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband. The example [Note: [Col. 0735D] Saint Augustine, Book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, near the end, after adducing this passage of Paul, says: “Or it should be understood in the manner in which we too explained it elsewhere (*On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, Book I), and Pelagius explained it when he reexamined the same Epistle to the Corinthians. [Col. 0736D] For examples had already preceded: men whom their wives had won for Christ, and women whom their husbands had won, and so forth. Nor does it seem doubtful that he had this passage before his eyes.”] He reports that it has often happened that a husband was won through a wife. Hence blessed Peter also says: “So that if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of the women,” [Col. 0737A] that is, when they see them changed for the better, they may recognize that God’s law could thus be changed by long-established custom. Likewise, husband and wife are sanctified by one another because, by God’s ordinance, marriage is holy.

Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy. If it were not as I say, your children would still remain unbelievers. For it would often happen that children followed those parents who had believed. Under this hope he wished it to be believed that one spouse could be saved, both by the example of the children and by that of the spouse.

But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. For neither husband nor wife is to be preferred to the Lord.

For the brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such a matter. He is not so bound in such a case [Col. 0737B] as though it were truly necessary for him to serve the other and perish on the other’s account.

But God has called you to peace. We were not called to dissension; therefore we ought not to depart of our own accord.

For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? He has placed this in doubt; but doubtful matters should always be believed to turn out for the better. At the same time, one must ask how the unbeliever is called sanctified above, when his salvation is here doubted—unless it is according to the understanding we have explained.

Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? That is, whether she will believe through you and be saved?

Except that each person should live as the Lord has assigned to him. Let each person walk as God has called him, and as I teach in all the churches. Whether with an unbelieving spouse or even with a believing [Mart.: unbelieving] one; whether uncircumcised or circumcised; slave or free.

Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not restore the foreskin. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. Let him not think that his circumcision was superfluous, nor repent of it; for it was necessary in its own time. Or in this sense: Let him not restore the foreskin in order to live without the ceremonies of the law, because at that time the Apostles permitted some people to observe the legal practices, lest, suddenly withdrawn from the law, they should suffer scandal. Another explanation: It is evident that in this passage the Apostle is not speaking of the circumcision of the flesh or of the foreskin. For it cannot happen that someone circumcised could restore the foreskin. Rather, he is speaking to those who are [Col. 0737D] married. This is what he says: If someone comes to faith in God without having a wife, he ought not afterward to take a Gentile spouse. But if someone established in such a union is called to the faith, he ought not dissolve the marital bond.

Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the observance of God’s commandments. At the present time, neither can it benefit nor harm.

Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned. A servile condition cannot harm the Christian religion. Do not say, “How can I please God, since I am a slave?” For God does not look at one’s condition, but seeks the will and the mind.

[Col. 0738A] But if you can become free, make use of it all the more. To such an extent does freedom not benefit and slavery not harm. Likewise, the Apostle speaks to those who are joined in marriage, saying: “But if you can become free, make use of it all the more”—provided that it is not burdensome to you when you wish to serve God chastely, since perhaps through your companionship even she may be converted to God.

For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave. The one who is the slave of a human being is free before God; and the one who is free among human beings is Christ’s slave. Thus both are one. For there is no partiality with God.

You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Therefore, let each brother remain with God in the condition in which he was called. [Col. 0738B] You were bought at a price—that is, purchased with Christ’s blood. Therefore, do nothing on account of human beings, as he says elsewhere: “Not serving by eye-service, as those who please human beings, but as Christ’s slaves, doing the will of God from the heart,” and so forth.

Now concerning virgins. They had also consulted him about this, where virginity was commanded.

I have no command of the Lord. What is under command brings punishment if it is not fulfilled. Once fulfilled, it is free only from death, because it gives nothing of itself but pays what is owed.

But I give advice. This is the advice of the Savior, who says: “There are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”

As one who has obtained mercy from the Lord. By his own example he teaches that one should glory only in the Lord.

[Col. 0738C] So that I may be faithful. Always occupied in the service of my Lord.

I therefore consider this good. Here “I consider” does not express doubt but certainty, as in: “For I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

Because of the present necessity. That is, the solitude of the present life, which can greatly hinder righteousness and by which those especially who are joined in marriage become entangled.

For it is good for a person to be so. It is a twofold good: to be free from the anxieties of the world and to await the reward of virginity.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. Thus he does not wish those who are free to become bound, just as he does not allow those bound by marriage to be released through separation.

But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Since you possess free will, if you do not wish to be greater, be at least lesser. Marriage is not a sin, but those who marry can scarcely keep the law because of the anxieties of the world. Alternatively: He says that those who marry do not sin if they have not yet vowed chastity to God. But whoever has promised it, even in his heart, incurs condemnation if he does otherwise, because he has invalidated his first faith. What was lawful he has made unlawful for himself through his vow, as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira, who were not permitted to retain any part of the price of their property; for this reason they were struck down by sudden death.

[Col. 0739A] Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh. By subjecting themselves to Eve’s curse, or they will endure the anxiety, tribulation, and sorrow of worldly affairs.

But I spare you. I spare you virgins, so that with less labor you may fulfill greater righteousness.

Now this I say, brothers. Here he exhorts even those who have wives to continence with every earnestness, so that he may all the more strongly persuade those who do not have wives not to marry.

The time is short; it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none. He asserts that the time of our life is brief, to teach that pleasure, which quickly ends, should not be eagerly sought, but that the eternal reward of chastity should be desired more.

And those who weep as though not weeping; and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing; and those who buy as though not possessing; and those who use this world as though not using it. For this too will soon pass away; there is a season for everything under the sun, a season for weeping, and so forth.

For the form of this world is passing away. This age passes by like a shadow. Therefore, do not be excessively concerned about it, lest by possessing it you lose what is eternal, and, while seeking its appearance, begin to lose the truth. This world is an image of the future. If the image is such, what must the reality itself be? Therefore, if you love this world so intensely, how much more intensely ought you to love that one! Daily examples of those who die testify that we shall leave this age behind. Or do we perhaps believe that we are immortal, as though we were generated from human beings? Hence the wise person is always corrected by the misfortunes of others, as Scripture says: “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning.” For this is the end of every human being; and to whom he wishes, he will give goodness in his heart.

But I wish you to be without anxiety. We too ought to wish what the Apostle says he wishes, lest we appear to act against his will by remaining incontinent.

The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world. It is greatly advantageous for us to be free from worldly anxiety, lest perhaps the thorns choke the seed and we begin to say: “I have bought a farm, I have purchased oxen, I have married a wife; I cannot come to the dinner.”

How he may please his wife. What is it like to wish more to please a wife [Col. 0739D] than God?

And he is divided. What is divided cannot be one, because unity admits no division at all.

The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit: in body, by abstaining from marital intercourse; in spirit, by freedom from worldly anxiety, while she gives herself wholly to divine service.

But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband. He says that a wife pleases her husband by thinking about worldly things, whereas the unmarried woman pleases God because she has no concern for the age. What, then, if a woman has no husband and yet thinks about worldly things—whom does she desire to please? Will she not begin to prefer the married woman, who by thinking about worldly things pleases either her husband, or—since [Col. 0740A] she has no husband—neither her husband nor God?

Moreover, I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what grants the ability to entreat the Lord without impediment. He seems to impose a necessity upon them: he says that he is reminding them of what is beneficial for them. At the same time, observe that if what the Apostle advised was useful for them, what they wanted was less useful.

But if someone thinks that he is acting shamefully with regard to his virgin, because she is beyond marriageable age. He may appear shameful if he does not permit his virgin to marry when she desires it and she commits fornication. Here, however, he is not speaking of the parents of virgin daughters. For the decision concerning another person’s continence cannot belong to their authority; rather, each person has control over his own flesh and may preserve it undefiled.

And so it ought to be done: let her do what she wishes; she does not sin if she marries. If this is necessary because of the daughter’s will—for parents ought to guard her until the lawful age and teach her what is better; but if she does not wish it, let what is necessary be done.

For the one who has firmly resolved in his heart, having no necessity, but possessing control over his own will, and has decided in his heart to preserve his virgin, does well. He is firm in his decision when the girl’s consent has strengthened the father’s will. The necessity of the daughter does not compel him to do what he did not want, as it compelled the one of whom he spoke above.

[Col. 0740C] Therefore, both the one who joins his virgin in marriage does well and the one who does not join her does better. Thus he concludes the matter of virgins in such a way as to make them better in every respect. Hence prudent people should always pursue what is better and more perfect, since even in secular and transitory matters they do not know how to be content with what is merely moderate.

A woman is bound by the law for as long as her husband lives. Here he begins concerning those married twice and widows.

But if her husband has died, she is released from the law. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. According to the law, she has been freed from the bond of marriage. If she does not then wish to remain continent, a second marriage is also granted to her, provided that she does not marry according to the custom of unbelievers.

But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice. Happy is a woman with a husband if she preserves chastity. Happier is the widow, because with less labor she will attain greater chastity. Happiest is the virgin, who can reach the highest reward without labor.

But I think that I too have the Spirit of God. Do not despise my advice as though it were merely human.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now concerning things sacrificed to idols. He begins concerning food offered to idols, about which he had also said that some people ate in temples, saying that an idol was nothing and that they ought to make use of God’s creation. They were deceived by an argument that seemed plausible. The Apostle says that this must be rebuked in those who possess the knowledge to judge that what is sacrificed to idols is nothing. This, then, is what he says:

[Col. 0741A] We know that we all have knowledge. That is, knowledge is not possessed by everyone. We all know, as you do, but there are some who are ignorant.

Knowledge puffs up. This is the knowledge that proceeds from one’s own human judgment; it puffs up those who do not possess divine knowledge beyond it, and it relies more on conjectures than on examples. But if divine knowledge puffs up, as some think, why does he wish to puff them up further by teaching them? At the beginning of this Epistle he also says that he gives thanks to God because they have been filled with all knowledge. Elsewhere he likewise offers his own example, saying: “Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not in knowledge.” He often also reproves the ignorant. He compared ignorance with darkness. Likewise, he brands the Galatians as foolish, and he earnestly prays for the Ephesians to receive the light of wisdom.

[Col. 0741B] But love builds up. For it does not seek what is its own, but what builds up the brothers.

If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know how he ought to know. If anyone seems wise to himself, he is a fool; for the truly wise person considers himself more foolish than everyone else. Hence Solomon says: “I saw a man who seemed wise to himself, and the fool had more hope than he.”

But if anyone loves God, he is known by him. He loves God who builds up the brothers, as it is said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep.”

Now concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one. He repeats what he said above that he knows, and shows more clearly what it is.

For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—for indeed there are many gods and many lords—in heaven there are angels, and on earth there are saints, concerning whom it is said: “I said, You are gods.” And there are lords, namely his saints, whom they will judge, concerning whom it is said: “They will judge nations and rule over peoples.”

Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things were created by his power out of nothing. Heretics interpret this passage by separating the persons of the Father and the Son, saying that there is one God and Father, from whom all things are, and that the Lord—that is, Christ—is greater, through whom all things are. But the same Apostle teaches in his Epistle to the Romans that these things are common to the Son as to the Father, saying: “For who has known the mind of the Lord?”—that is, of Christ, not of God the Father—as he says and adds: “For from him and through him and in him are all things.” Likewise, by whom, he ascribes the same thing to God the Father in this same Epistle, saying: “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.”

From whom all things are, and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ. The Arians raise a charge from this passage, claiming that, since the Father alone is called God, the Son has been separated from deity. They must be answered: if the Son is not God because the Father is the one God, then the Father will not be Lord because Christ is the one Lord. But if the Father is not excluded from lordship, neither is the Son excluded from deity; rather, both attributes are common to both.

[Col. 0742A] Through whom all things are, and we through him. Through the Son all things were made, and through him we too have been saved.

But knowledge is not in everyone. Not everyone knows that you eat by despising idols, and not rather for the sake of venerating them.

But some, with consciousness still attached to the idol, eat the food sacrificed to idols as such, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Some ignorant people still retain in their conscience the practice of eating as they did before they believed.

But food does not commend us to God. As the prophet Haggai says: “And if you ate and drank, did you not eat and drink for yourselves?”

For neither if we eat shall we abound, nor if we do not eat shall we lack. Who could doubt that no one becomes prosperous by eating or needy by not eating? On the contrary, poverty should be more greatly feared by those who do not know how to restrain their appetite. But because they attributed to the greatness of their faith the eating of what had been sacrificed to idols, the Apostle therefore testifies that neither abundance of faith lies in eating it nor poverty in refusing to eat it.

But take care lest this freedom of yours. Take care lest what you believe is insufficient for yourselves harm others. This may also be said of those who destroy by their example what they build by their speech.

Become an offense to the weak. Lest through you they take offense and fall.

For if someone sees the one who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be emboldened to eat food sacrificed to idols? And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, by sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be cast into the depths of the sea.” How much more severe a punishment awaits those people, so that, by comparison with it, what is most severe may be considered light! It should also be noted that he says that the person who sins against a member of Christ sins against Christ.

Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble. Not only food, but everything that may cause a brother to stumble.

## CHAPTER IX

Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? As are the others? He repeats to them the same form of question, because he too has renounced what was lawful, lest others be weakened by his example.

Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? And if I am not an apostle to others, yet I am to you. He means those to whom he was not sent by the Lord—that is, the Jews.

For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. You are the proof of my apostleship, because through me you came to believe in the Lord, moved by signs and mighty works.

[Col. 0743A] My defense before those who question me. From this I defend my claim to be an apostle.

This is my answer to those who question me. In the Greek it reads “judge.”

Do we not have authority to eat and drink? We have authority granted by the Lord to live from your support, without our own labor.

Do we not have authority to lead about a sister, a woman? He did not say “to take wives,” lest people think he was speaking of wives; rather, he says “to lead about” through the provinces women who would provide what was necessary from their own resources.

As do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas lack the authority to do this? He does not condemn them, but gives his own [Col. 0743B] example. For they preached to people who were more faithful; and among the Jews there was an ancient custom of providing teachers with necessities from their disciples. This could scandalize the Gentiles, who were still inexperienced.

Who serves as a soldier. He proves by other examples also that this was owed to him.

At his own expense? At his own, and not at public expense or at the expense of those for whom he serves.

Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk? Through the comparison of the vineyard and the flock he wishes the people to be understood, as in: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” And again: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with discipline.”

Do I say this merely from a human standpoint? That is, am I speaking only from my own judgment?

Or does the law not say this as well? For it is written in the law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? For it was certainly written for our sake. How, then, is he concerned about animals? And concerning Nineveh it is said to Jonah: “In which there are many human beings and animals”? But he is concerned about them for the sake of the human being, for whom they were created; for when the human being perishes, they too perish. Nevertheless, they do not themselves deserve God’s particular care.

For the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of receiving a share of the harvest. He ought to receive the fruit of his labor; and the one who threshes ought to eat from the threshing floor itself.

[Col. 0743D] If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? If we have sown spiritual and divine things for you, will we burden you if we wish to receive from you what is necessary for the flesh?

If others share in your authority, why not we rather? If they received from you—those to whom nothing is at all owed, namely the false apostles, whom you know to have conferred nothing certain upon you—how much more may we receive, if we consider ourselves useful to you?

But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure everything, lest we give any occasion for offense to the Gospel of Christ. That is, we most willingly endure hunger and thirst and nakedness, lest, when our adversaries have received an opportunity through us, you should be offended by those who devour you. Or lest our preaching [Col. 0744A] should appear in any respect blameworthy, stained by the suspicion of greed.

Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary? And that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? Among the Jews, according to the custom of the Old Testament, he confirms this example also by repeating the same point.

So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But I have used none of these privileges. He says: “The laborer is worthy of his wage.”

I have not written these things so that they might be done in my case. I do not write this for the purpose that what has not previously been done should now be done in any way; rather, I offer you examples both from my own situation and from that of others, teaching you—at least—to abstain from what is unlawful, [Col. 0744B] since you see that, for the sake of the salvation of others, I have despised things owed to me no less than things permitted.

For it is better for me to die than that anyone should empty my glory. And even if I should die of hunger, my purpose—which I glorify before God—can never be changed.

For even if I preach the Gospel, there is no glory for me: necessity is laid upon me. When you have done all the commands, say that you have paid what you owed. For you have done nothing more by which you could glory.

For woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel. I would be condemned.

For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. It will then appear more voluntary when permitted things are despised out of love for him.

[Col. 0744C] What, then, is my reward? That, in preaching the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel without charge, so that I do not abuse my authority in the Gospel. As though he were asking how he could obtain a greater reward, he himself answers: if I announce it freely and do not exercise the authority I have received.

For although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win the greater number. Although I could have used my freedom and cared nothing for the others, I nevertheless sympathized with all, so that I might save them.

And I became to the Jews as a Jew, so that I might win the Jews. When he purified himself in the temple, although he knew this to be superfluous in the time of grace.

To those who are under the law, as though I were under the law. He shows [Col. 0744D] how he himself was with them as a Jew. It may also be understood in this way: that he calls the Samaritans those who are under the law, since they appear to accept only the law of Moses.

Although I myself was not under the law, so that I might win those who were under the law. He is not under the law of the letter, which is described as having been given to sinners.

To those who were without the law, as though I were without the law. Without the law of the letter. From the Gentiles especially he sought faith alone, as though he did not have the precepts of Christ’s law by which he could teach them to observe them; or else because he summoned them to belief in the faith not so much by legal teachings as by rational arguments. This is said to have been what he did at Athens, urging philosophers and pagans through philosophy and by appealing to the inscription on the altars, [Col. 0745A] when he says: “I went around your altars, and, as some of you said…”

Although I was not without the law of God, but was under the law of Christ, so that I might win those who were without the law. Against the Arians and Photinians: that Christ is God. This too should be noted: that the New Testament is called a law.

I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak. For the sake of the weak I ate vegetables, although I could safely eat all kinds of meat.

I became all things to all, so that I might save all. Not seeking anything for myself, nor what is useful to me, but what is useful to many. Another interpretation: In the matters mentioned above, this does not mean, as some wrongly suppose, that he consented even to unlawful things.

[Col. 0745B] I do everything for the sake of the Gospel, so that I may share in it. So that I may deserve to have a share in it together with the saints.

Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. Here he compares the race in the stadium with righteousness or faith: for just as there, although all run within the stadium, only the one who has run well is judged worthy of the prize, so here, although all believers are contained within the bounds of faith, only those who have lived righteously will receive the heavenly reward. Alternatively, in this passage, by speaking of one among those who run in the stadium receiving the palm, he signifies everyone who holds the faith correctly and keeps the precepts.

For everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-restraint in all things. [Col. 0745C] From all foods that are accustomed to hinder their running.

And they do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. I therefore run in this way, not as though toward an uncertain goal; I fight in this way, not as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into servitude. I do not run in vain, nor merely pretend to compete; rather, I discipline my body and subject it to servitude through abstinence, affliction, and labors, as he says elsewhere: “In many fasts, in vigils, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in labors, in prisons,” and so forth. Likewise, in the Letter to the Hebrews, he recalled many such sufferings of the prophets and other holy people.

Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected. By failing to do what I say.

## CHAPTER 10

[Col. 0745D]

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea. He sets before them the example of their fathers, to show that no one should trust merely in having been baptized, or in spiritual food or drink, and think that God will spare him if he sins; these things will benefit him deservedly only if the precepts are kept.

And all were baptized into Moses. Into Moses, who bore the type of Christ. Alternatively, these things were happening at that time as though in shadow and type, not in reality; afterward, however, they are fulfilled in the presence of Christ.

In the cloud and in the sea. For the cloud too carries its own moisture.

[Col. 0746A] And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. The manna was a figure of the body of Christ.

And they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. The apostle shows that, for as long as the people of Israel were in the desert, the rock followed them throughout their entire journey. From it, streams supplied the people with all their needs, until, when they reached the land of Moab, they dug a well of water, with the land of promise now nearby.

And the rock was Christ. Because Christ was afterward going to follow them, and the rock at that time bore his figure. Therefore he aptly said, “the rock that followed them.”

But God was not pleased with most of them. [Col. 0746B] For they were struck down in the desert. Thus it will also be for you if, by sinning, you wish to imitate them.

Now these things happened as a figure for us, so that we might not be desiring evil things, as they desired them. Those things that were figures of ours truly happened to them, so that we might fear doing such things lest we suffer such things. For everything that happened at that time among the people of Israel occurs now among us in reality. Just as they were freed from Egypt through Moses, so we are freed from the world through whatever priest or teacher. Then, having become Christians, we are led through the deserts, so that through the discipline of contempt for the world and abstinence, the pleasures of Egypt may become forgotten to us, until we no longer know how to return to the world. When we cross the sea of baptism, then the devil, together with his army, is drowned for us like Pharaoh. Then we are nourished with manna and receive the drink flowing from Christ’s side. The radiance of knowledge too is shown, like a pillar of fire, in the night of the world, and in the heat of tribulation we are sheltered by the cloud of divine consolation. After all this, if we sin, these things alone will not be able to help us, as it is also said in the Letter to the Hebrews: “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses is punished without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God?” and so forth.

Nor become idolaters, as some of them did; as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” By referring to those reclining in the idol-shrine, he so greatly intensifies the matter that he declares them to have been idolaters.

Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them fornicated, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. It should be noted that it is not only idolaters who are said to perish.

Nor let us test Christ, as some of them did. Here too Christ is shown to be God, because we read that God said: “They tested me ten times.”

They tested him and perished by serpents. Saying, “Can God prepare a table in the desert?”

Nor murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer. In tribulations endured for Christ.

All these things happened to them in a figure, but they were written for our correction. Everything [Col. 0747A] that happened to them they received according to their deeds; nevertheless, it was written for this reason: so that we should not think that we may sin with impunity. For if he did not spare them, though they were still little ones and inexperienced, how much less will he spare us, who have received the law of perfection, if we do such things!

Upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Upon whom the whole fulfillment of time has run its course.

Therefore, let the one who thinks that he stands take care lest he fall. Let him beware lest he fall precisely through this: that he boasts of standing firmly; or let him beware lest he be deceived.

Let no temptation seize you except what is human. No temptation has seized you except a human one. This temptation does not come upon you from outside; you generate it voluntarily, although even if you were compelled by tortures, you ought not to admit it. He says this because [Col. 0747B] they were eating what had been sacrificed to idols of their own free will.

But God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear. He has promised that, for the sake of his name, he will be present with those who suffer tribulation, as in the passage: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous,” and so forth.

But with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure it. He will not permit a greater tribulation to come upon you than you can bear.

Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I speak as to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say. This is because of all that I have set forth above.

The cup of blessing which we bless. He mentioned the cup first so that he might discuss the bread more fully.

[Col. 0747C] Is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? As the Savior himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

And the bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Since we, though many, are one bread and one body. Thus the bread of idolatry is also shown to be a participation in demons.

For we all share in the one bread and the one cup. Therefore, if we eat from one bread with idolaters, we become one body with them.

Consider Israel according to the flesh. Carnal Israel offered carnal sacrifices, just as spiritual Israel offers spiritual sacrifices to Christ. Alternatively, “according to the flesh” because they served not spiritually but according to the letter.

[Col. 0747D] Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? Just as those who ate the sacrifices became participants in the divine altar, so these likewise become participants in the altar of idols.

What then? Do I say that something sacrificed to idols has any significance, or that an idol has any significance? Rather, what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. But I do not want you to become partners with demons. He forestalls anyone who might say: “Then do you claim that an idol has some power, or that it can defile?” No, he says; it is not the insensible idol that defiles, but the demons who preside over the temples in order to corrupt human beings and enslave them to their service.

You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord [Col. 0748A] and the table of demons. You cannot be participants both in God and in demons.

Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Other manuscripts have: “They themselves provoked me to jealousy in the Lord,” that is, “they provoked me to jealousy.”

Are we stronger than he? He did not do these things; for if he had known that faith would be most firmly established by this, he would have given an example in this matter as well.

Everything is permitted to me, but not everything is beneficial. Everything that is not prohibited by the law is permitted, because in itself it does not contain sin; but it is not always beneficial, because it sometimes gives rise to an opportunity for wrongdoing.

Everything is permitted to me, but not everything builds up. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another. Everything beneficial is permitted; not everything permitted is beneficial. But [Col. 0748B] we apostles, following the example of Christ, must consider not only what is permitted, but rather what is beneficial to us and builds up the brethren, so that we do not seek what benefits us alone temporarily and perhaps harms others.

Whatever is sold in the meat market, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. If you wish to eat meat, at least buy it in the meat market; only do not eat in an idol-shrine, and do not ask whether it was sacrificed, lest, knowing you, they answer that everything has been sacrificed and you be unable to eat on account of conscience.

The earth belongs to the Lord, and its fullness. If they belong to the Lord, then all things are clean for those who use them simply.

If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go, [Col. 0748C] eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone says: “This has been sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who disclosed it and for the sake of conscience. He permitted them to go if they wished. A Christian should indeed go to an unbeliever when he knows that it will be beneficial, as the Savior did, who went for this purpose either to perform signs or to teach. Thus, at the Pharisee’s house, he first taught him that one should not feed the rich but the weak. Then, while reclining at table with them, he taught that humility must also be maintained at table. Finally, he rebuked the teachers of the law for their arrogance, because they neither rebuked arrogance themselves nor allowed others to do so.

Now by conscience I mean not your own but another’s. Let no one suppose that you eat those things as though they were holy.

For why is my freedom judged by another’s conscience? [Col. 0748D] That is: what benefit is there in my using my freedom in such a way that another person criticizes me?

If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks? We are not under grace for the purpose of giving unbelievers an opportunity to blaspheme under the appearance of freedom.

Therefore, whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do everything to the glory of God. Nothing should be more characteristic of a Christian than that God’s glory be proclaimed in all his works, and that he do nothing by which the teaching of Christ could in any respect be criticized.

Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God. For the Jews, taking offense as though at idolatry, did not dare to believe; the Gentiles were confirmed in [Col. 0749A] the worship of idols; and Christians were destroyed by such an example.

Just as I also please everyone in every way, not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved. I conduct myself in such a way as to please everyone for their advancement. If someone wishes to hate me without cause, I am not at fault. The apostle never praises himself in order to exalt himself; rather, by his example he urges them toward advancement. Therefore we too should wish to please only for this purpose: so that, as God alone knows our conscience, it may be clear that we do this not for favor but for the salvation of human beings.

## CHAPTER 11

Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ. Christ [Col. 0749B] did and suffered nothing for himself, but for the salvation of many. Likewise, whoever does not seek what is beneficial only to himself but also to many, so that they may be saved, is an imitator of Christ, who both suffered and died for us.

Now I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything. He begins to speak about veils and, by praising them, urges them toward sound reasoning, because in this matter he does not have the authority of the law that he cites. The apostle says this ironically, because they were hardly keeping his commands.

And, as I delivered them to you, you hold fast to my commands. As though he were saying: You hold my commands as law, knowing that the Spirit who spoke in the Law and the Prophets speaks through me.

But I want you to know. I also wish to instruct you in this, so that you may likewise hold to it.

[Col. 0749C] The head of every man is Christ. A man is subject to no one except Christ, who is both human and God. But a woman ought to be subject both to Christ and to her husband.

But the head of a woman is the man. According to the natural order. Nevertheless, in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female, but he willed them to be subject.

But the head of Christ is God. According to the form of the assumed human being. Again, Christ’s head is God because, according to his humanity, the divinity dwelling in him governed the incarnation that he had assumed, as the same apostle says elsewhere: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

Every man praying or prophesying. Whether teaching or proclaiming future things.

With his head covered, dishonors his head. He comes to the issue at hand: men were growing their hair, and women were entering the Church bareheaded, boasting in their hair. This was not only immodest, but also provided fuel for desire. A man, therefore, as a free person, ought not to have a veil, since Christ is his head. A woman, however, ought to be veiled, so that it may be shown that she should be humble and subject.

But every woman praying or prophesying with her head unveiled dishonors her head. For it is one and the same as if she were shaved. For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head. In her own sex, or in her own household.

A man indeed ought not to cover his head. Therefore neither should he grow his hair.

[Col. 0750A] For he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man. The man was made in the image of God and therefore is free. The woman, however, was formed in the likeness of the man; hence she is commanded to be subject.

For man is not from woman, but woman from man. From the man’s rib, of course.

For man was not created on account of woman, but woman on account of man. Man was made for himself, whereas woman was created as a helper for man.

Therefore the woman ought to have a veil over her head. He declares that the veil is a sign of authority.

And because of the angels. Here too he calls the angels those who preside over the churches, just as the prophet Malachi also testifies that the priest is an angel, saying: “For the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law [Col. 0750B] from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” Or truly, because of the honor of the angels who are said to attend the Church.

Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord. He comforts them, lest he seem to have burdened them too heavily; and neither can man be born without woman, nor woman without man.
