For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman. This is in the beginning. It may also be said in this way: Just as Eve was from Adam, so, according to his humanity, Christ was from Mary.

But all things are from God. Against the Manichaeans, who deny that the flesh was made by God.

Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled? He leaves it to their own judgment, so that they may be convicted by their own conscience.

[Col. 0750C] Does not nature itself teach you? One may say: if this is natural, why is it not observed by all nations? Because they have fallen away from nature, as is proved by many other examples. In short, they live without the law, and if the apostle were speaking among them, he would use other arguments.

That if a man grows his hair, it is a disgrace to him; but if a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her. The Nazirites grew their hair with the utmost devotion, in accordance with God’s command.

Because her hair has been given to her as a covering. He explains what he had said: that if she is not veiled, she should be shorn.

But if anyone seems to be contentious. He forestalls them, lest someone say, “Where is this written?” or resist this reasoning with other arguments.

[Col. 0750D] We have no such custom. Whether of arguing or of doing such things.

Nor does the Church of God. The Church devotes itself to gentleness rather than to disputes.

Now this I command. One should consider what that servant heard from the Lord who guarded only the talent he had received. Therefore the person who does not continually grow toward what is better is not to be praised, because faith ought to be more perfect the older one becomes. It is pitiable if someone is always fed milk like an infant, or if one who studies letters has only what he received in his earliest rudiments. How much more hopeless, then, is the person who not only makes no progress but even declines, and completely forgets what he received!

[Col. 0751A] I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse. What is implied is: I condemn you because you advance toward what is worse.

First of all, when you come together in the Church. He begins to speak about the sacraments.

I hear that there are divisions among you, and I believe it in part. Either according to what was revealed to me by the Lord, or because I know that you are contentious.

For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become evident among you. Because you have such disputes, it is necessary that you proceed even to heresies. It is like saying: “One who drinks so much necessarily becomes drunk.” Alternatively, the apostle does not say this because there ought to be heresies, but because they had divisions among themselves; therefore he says, “This must happen,” and [Col. 0751B] “there must be heresies.”

When you come together, then, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each person takes his own supper beforehand to eat. It is no longer the Lord’s supper but a human one, when each person, as though invading his own supper alone, takes possession of it and does not share with another who has not made an offering; so that you appear to come together more for satiety than for the mystery. Otherwise, the Lord’s supper ought to be common to all, because he handed the sacraments equally to all his disciples who were present. It is called a supper because the Lord handed over the sacraments at supper. Alternatively, he says this because, when they came together in the Church, they offered their offerings separately; and after communion, whatever remained of the sacrifices they consumed together in the Church at a [Col. 0751C] common supper.

And one person is hungry, while another is drunk. Whoever had not made an offering did not share, because those who had made offerings consumed everything by themselves. Some refer this passage to those who held banquets in the Church. Another interpretation: one is hungry and another is drunk; he says this because, when people of modest means arrived and wished to receive the sacraments, none remained, since everything had been consumed at the common banquet by those who had made the offerings.

Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? If you wish to be satisfied, eat at home. Sanctification consists even in a small amount.

Or do you despise the Church of God? By making it a dining room for banquets.

[Col. 0751D] And do you shame those who have nothing? They were put to shame, marked out by everyone, although they ought to have shared in such a way that no one would know who had made the offering.

What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you. Just as I praised you in other matters where you acted commendably, in this I do not praise you at all.

For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you. What I delivered to you is not my own; I received it from the Lord, just as he says elsewhere that he learned everything not from human beings but from God.

That the Lord Jesus. From this point he recalls, as though they had forgotten, how great is the sacramental mystery of this rite.

On the night when he was betrayed. That is, by Judas.

[Col. 0752A] He took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat.” That is, blessing it, even though he was about to suffer, he left us a final commemoration, or memorial. It is like someone departing on a journey who leaves a pledge with the person he loves, so that whenever the latter sees it, he may remember his benefactor’s kindness and friendship. If he loved that person deeply, he cannot see it without immense longing or tears.

This is my body, which will be delivered for you. Do this in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: “He who eats my body and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Therefore everyone who either eats Christ’s body or drinks his blood ought to recognize himself, lest he do [Col. 0752B] anything unworthy to the one whose body he has become.

This cup is the New Testament. For the old testament foreshadowed this through the blood of animals.

In my blood. Both the old and the new are consecrated through blood, because a testament cannot be firm without death.

Do this, whenever you drink, in remembrance of me. The Savior handed over this sacrament for this reason: so that through it we might always remember that he died for us. Therefore, when we receive it, the priests also remind us that it is the body and blood of Christ, so that we may not prove ungrateful for his benefits.

For whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord. Either you announce it through the mystery itself, or you acknowledge it in your hearts.

[Col. 0752C] Until he comes. The memorial is necessary for as long as it takes, until he deigns to come himself.

Therefore whoever eats this bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily. As it is written: “Everyone pure shall eat.” And again: “The soul that eats while unclean shall be cut off from his people.” The Lord himself also says: “If, before the altar, you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go to be reconciled with your brother.” Therefore the conscience must first be examined, to see whether it reproaches us in anything; and then we ought either to offer or to communicate. Some indeed say that he recalls not the unworthy person but the one who receives unworthily, keeping him away from the holy thing. If even a worthy person approaching unworthily is held back, how much more an unworthy person who cannot receive worthily! Therefore the idle person must cease from vices, so that he may receive the holy body of the Lord in holiness.

He will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Because he has despised the sacrament of so great a mystery as something worthless.

But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat from that bread and drink from the cup. If he does not dare to place it on a dirty cloth or in a filthy vessel, how much less should he place it in a polluted heart! God abhors this impurity above all things, and it alone constitutes an injury to his body. For that righteous Joseph also buried the Lord’s body, wrapped in a clean linen cloth, in a new tomb, prefiguring that those who are to receive the Lord’s body ought to have a mind as clean as a new thing.

For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks [Col. 0753A] judgment upon himself. Having become guilty in two ways: of presumption, that is, and of sin.

Not discerning the Lord’s body. Not distinguishing it from ordinary food.

For this reason many among you are weak and ill, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. Correction was present then and is present now; but because many suffer such things, we suppose that what is actually guilt is merely customary. Bodily illnesses arise for three reasons: either from testing, as in the case of Job and Tobit; or from sin, as in the case of King Asa and those whom the apostle is rebuking here; or from some lack of moderation, as in the case of Timothy and those who are commanded to honor the physician. Only this last cause can be relieved by human medicine. Alternatively, he signifies that the Corinthians, [Col. 0753B] because of the sin mentioned above, were rebuked by the Lord through illness, weakness, and death.

But when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world. This correction is the mercy of a father, so that we may repent and not be condemned eternally with the unbelievers of the world.

Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home. For no one was waiting for another so that the offering might be made in common.

So that you do not come together for judgment. They were coming together not for sanctification but for judgment.

The remaining matters I will arrange when I come. The remaining matters concerning the sacrament of the mystery itself.

## CHAPTER 12

[Col. 0753C]

Now concerning spiritual things. He begins to speak about spiritual sacraments. As faith increased, the gift of tongues—which they had received for the sake of unbelievers—was already ceasing. Hence many were saddened and envied those who still possessed this grace, thinking it greater than all the other gifts.

I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. I do not want you to be unaware of the meaning of this mystery.

You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led to mute idols. That is, to irrational things, according to the prophet who says: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them.”

As you were led, going along. By magicians or diviners of idols.

[Col. 0753D] Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus.” Would that you were not irrational and easily moved! For with religious devotion you ought also to change your conduct and understand the reasoning of your faith.

And no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit. How, then, will the Lord recognize workers of iniquity if, even though they have performed miracles, God is denied by their evil works? No one can call Jesus Lord in the Holy Spirit unless he confesses him both in words and in deeds. Alternatively, he teaches the Corinthians that unless they call Jesus Lord in the Holy Spirit—that is, while conducting themselves in good works—it cannot benefit them, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ [Col. 0754A] will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father.”

There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord. There are varieties of works, but the same God, who works all things in all. Here he wishes to show that the varieties belong to the grace of the Holy Spirit, not to the Spirit himself. Although this passage is directed especially against the Macedonians, who deny that the Holy Spirit is God—by saying “the same” throughout, he declares that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit in every case—shortly afterward he also says: “The one and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things,” demonstrating that he is both God and Lord. Nevertheless, this is also a substantial argument against the Arians, who customarily make this a point of accusation, that the Father is named first, [Col. 0754B] the Son second, and the Holy Spirit third. Here he reverses that order. It is also an explicit proclamation that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one divinity and substance, since, as Lord and God, he distributes the gifts of grace to each individual as he wills.

But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good. So that it may become evident that he has received the Holy Spirit.

To one, indeed, a word of wisdom is given through the Spirit. The word of wisdom is to speak wisely, appropriately, and rationally, and to be able to explain or teach what one knows correctly. The person who possesses wisdom as a gift speaks without his own effort or labor, and no one can prevail against him, as against the blessed Stephen. It is for the benefit of unbelievers, [Col. 0754C] so that they may believe, and of believers, so that they may be strengthened.

To another, a word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit. So that he may know how to explain the mysteries of the law, or so that he may know the past and form judgments about the future.

To another, faith in the same Spirit. Here “faith” means faith for performing miracles, faith that can move mountains. He uses the thing metaphorically for its effect.

To another, gifts of healings in one Spirit. So that he may cure the sick.

To another, the working of miracles. The work of power is to drive out demons or raise the dead.

To another, prophecy. That is, so that he may proclaim future things.

To another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues. So that he may understand what sort of person is coming or speaking, or by what spirit he does so.

[Col. 0754D] To another, the interpretation of speeches. One person could interpret what another was saying.

But one and the same Spirit works all these things. If one Spirit works all things, why are you saddened because you have received a different grace, and why do you envy another as though he had seized a greater portion, when this rests not in our power but in the power of the giver?

Distributing to each as he wills. Here too he calls him the Spirit of the Lord, since he works voluntarily, not under compulsion.

For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are nevertheless one body, so also is Christ. By the comparison with the body, [Col. 0755A] he shows that it is not the nature of the members but their functions that are different, and that no one should be concerned about what function he has, so long as all are animated by one and the same Spirit. He takes the example from the human body in order to teach that the churches are likewise one body in Christ, just as the members are one body in a human being, so that one member should not be puffed up against another.

And so is Christ. It should be noted that Christ is here called the Church through his body.

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free. So that we might become one body in Christ. Therefore, since spiritual and heavenly things are common to them, they ought also to possess earthly and bodily things in common, according to the prophet’s saying: “Is there not one Father of us all?” This is also plainly shown here: those who are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit are baptized into one substance, because the Trinity of the Godhead has no diversity, as the apostle says:

And we were all called in one Spirit. As though they had been given to drink of the Spirit, whom those who are baptized receive through the laying on of hands.

For the body also. He returns to the example.

It is not one member but many. The whole body cannot perform one function; rather, each of the members performs the task for which it is suited.

If the foot should say. The foot of the Church may be understood as the one who goes forth to intercede.

Because I am not a hand. The hand is the one who works.

[Col. 0755C] I am not part of the body: is it for that reason not part of the body? And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I am not part of the body,” is it for that reason not part of the body? For he was saying that he was not part of the body because he did not possess the grace that others had received.

If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If all were knowledgeable, where would the listeners be?

If the whole body were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? If all were listeners, who would distinguish what is of good or bad odor, so that we might become one body in Christ?

But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he wished. Just as the members are arranged suitably and orderly in the body, so in the Church each person is appointed by God to that for which he is suited.

[Col. 0755D] But if they were all one member, where would the body be? If all had one grace, where would the others be? They could no longer be a body, but only members.

But now there are many members, yet one body. That is, the human body, which displays many members.

But the eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of your work.” Therefore we need one another, so that charity may be confirmed more and more. For if one person possessed everything, he would become arrogant toward the others.

Or again, the head cannot say this to the feet. The priest is the head; the weak are the feet of the Church. If the little ear, which is the wise listener—for Isaiah the prophet says that the ear is among the other things taken away from Judah—should say, “I am not an eye, I am not part of the body,” is it for that reason not part of the body?

[Col. 0756A] You are not necessary to me. The eye is the one who understands; the mouth is the one who teaches or speaks in tongues.

But much more necessary are those members of the body that seem to be weaker. The members that you despise in the Church are shown to be of greater usefulness: just as one can live in the body without hands and feet, but without the intestines one cannot live at all.

And those members of the body that we think are less honorable. Not that they truly are such.

We surround these with greater honor. For they are covered more carefully and diligently with clothing.

And those parts of us that are unseemly have greater modesty, whereas our seemly parts need none. [Col. 0756B] Those that are beautiful in themselves need no covering to enhance their beauty, as do the head and hands.

But God has harmonized the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it. He grants greater gifts to the lesser, so that the one who was lesser in honor might abound in grace.

So that there may be no division in the body. So that we may be concerned for one another: since we need one another, lest anyone follow after one who is deprived both of grace and of honor.

But the members should be concerned for one another in the same way. Just as the eyes look ahead on behalf of the feet, and the hands work for the whole body, so all the members serve one another.

And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. If one member is in pain, the whole [Col. 0756C] body is afflicted, and all the members work together for its healing.

Whether one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. As Solomon says: “With a joyful heart, the face flourishes.” But we turn compassion and rejoicing into their opposites.

Now you are the body of Christ. That is, the Church from his flesh and from his bones, as he says to the Ephesians.

And members from a member. Together they are the body; individually, members.

And God has appointed some. He now wishes to demonstrate the order of the members themselves.

In the Church, first apostles. Not in the synagogue, lest we think that he meant the ancient prophets, such as Agabus; otherwise he ought also to have mentioned the patriarchs.

Second, prophets; third, teachers. Prophets are those who explain the obscure things of the prophets, and those who exhort people, as he says elsewhere: “The one who prophesies speaks to people for building up, exhortation, and consolation.”

Then miracles, thereafter gifts of healings. Here “miracles” signifies greater signs.

Helps. That is, assistance. Hence, in a vision, a Macedonian man says to Paul: “Come, help us.”

Governments, kinds of tongues, interpretations of speech. Those who know how to govern individuals according as they are suited to do so.

[Col. 0757A] Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Do all possess the gift of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? This is what he had said above: “If they were all one member, where would the body be?”

But earnestly desire the better gifts. That is, pursue the prophets.

And [I show] a still more excellent [way]. In Greek it has, “beyond measure.”

I show you a way. Charity, by which one reaches God. He wishes us to seek more eagerly those things that arise from us and benefit us for life than signs, which have not been placed within our power.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0757B]

If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels. Not only in the tongues of all human beings, but also, if there are any, in those of angels.

But do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. That is, something which, not acting from itself but merely struck by another, produces only a sound and pleases the hearing. Charity, however, comes from us and possesses every fruit.

And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries. Here, to foretell future things is prophecy; knowledge of mysteries means knowledge of all secrets. Knowledge properly so called is to know all things that have been and that are. If all these things, so great, are nothing without charity, how much more are they nothing without abstinence, fasting, and similar practices, in which, having abandoned charity, [Col. 0757C] many boast!

And have all knowledge. Here too the knowledge is great, because it is counted among these things, even if it is lesser than charity.

And if I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. Here a great faith is understood, one that in the Gospel is compared with a mustard seed—not because of its smallness, but because of its completeness or vigor. It should certainly be noted that even all faith, which removes mountains, is of no benefit without charity.

And if I distribute all my possessions for feeding the poor. In treating of the supreme good of charity, the Apostle must certainly be understood [Col. 0757D] to have preferred it to great things; for great things could not be compared with what is supreme, as is recognized from the very examples. For who does not know that speaking in the tongues of human beings and angels, having prophecy, knowing all mysteries, possessing all knowledge, having all faith, and delivering oneself to be burned in the fire are great things? To these is also added contempt for the world: who would not regard that as great, and as comparable with the supreme reality, namely charity, and therefore as belonging among great things? This destroys the opinion of those who wish renunciation of worldly affairs to be regarded as a command given only at a definite time, when persecution compels it, so that they may also take away the apostles’ glory, since they do not wish them to have done it voluntarily but unwillingly, and may make the perfect people of our own age worthless, [Col. 0758A] because they have now wished in vain to practice what belonged to another time. Alternatively: It should be noted that contempt for the world is compared with martyrdom, against those who strive by various arguments to explain it away in the Gospel passage where it is said to the rich man: “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor.”

And if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing. This is when it is done not for God but for human glory. Or certainly, if someone during martyrdom itself retains anger against a brother, despising the one who commanded us to forget the malice of our neighbor, and thus remains a transgressor even in death.

Charity is patient; it is kind. It always wills what is good. He now describes all the members and forms of charity. [Col. 0758B] Parents, because they love their children greatly, also willingly endure injuries from them.

Charity does not envy; it does not act wrongly; it is not puffed up. No one envies the person whom he truly loves, whatever glory or honor he sees that person possessing; rather, he willingly embraces all that person’s happiness as though it were his own.

It is not ambitious. It does not seek to be greater than others, nor desire to rule over its brothers.

It does not seek its own interests. It does not seek what is useful only to itself, but what is useful to many.

It is not provoked. It is not stirred up to quarrels by the one whom it loves.

It does not think evil. It not only does not do evil, but does not even think it.

It does not rejoice over iniquity. It is saddened if it sees someone either committing or suffering something unjust. [Col. 0758C]

But it rejoices with the truth. That is, with good works or with the truth of faith.

It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. It bears injuries; it believes the one who makes amends; it hopes for his correction and patiently waits until he reforms.

Charity never fails. That is, it alone remains in the future. Or certainly, what is true does not come to an end.

Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed. For we know in part and prophesy in part. We do not know everything, nor do we prophesy everything. And thus, so that we may advance toward what is greater, [Col. 0758D] these things will be destroyed; for through them we come to perfection.

But when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished. This is what has been promised to the saints in the future.

When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. By the example of bodily growth, he wishes to demonstrate spiritual progress.

But when I became a man, I abolished the things that belonged to the child. He has explained how the things mentioned above will be abolished.

We see now. Like children, who cannot perfectly behold the light of truth with the clear light of the heart.

[Col. 0759A] Through a mirror in an enigma. Through the mirror of the law, we contemplate something like an image of realities.

But then face to face. That is, in his presence.

Now I know in part; then I shall know just as I also have been known. Just as God knows me perfectly, so I too shall know the things that are divine.

But now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity. Everything that we hope for, we believe; but not everything that we believe, we hope for. In the present there are these three; in the future, only the charity of God, of the angels, and of all the saints will remain. Therefore what will always exist is greater than what will at some time cease. Again, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, faith is stable, for it needs no addition. But he says that hope remains [Col. 0759B] which concerns things that we do not see. Charity is greater than all for this reason: the one who loves also believes and hopes.

## CHAPTER XIV

Pursue charity. Follow it with every effort, because it lies within your power.

Earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. I do not forbid you to desire and seek spiritual gifts; rather, I exhort you to make greater progress.

For the one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God. For no one hears. No one receives understanding through the hearing of the ears concerning what is said, except God and the one who receives the gift of interpreting, or one who speaks the same language.

[Col. 0759C] But the spirit speaks mysteries. Again he means a tongue.

For the one who prophesies speaks to people for building up, exhortation, and consolation. The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself; but the one who prophesies builds up the Church of God. It should be noted that he calls teaching prophecy; he has explained in how many ways prophecy is to be understood. Whoever possesses this gift should be regarded as a prophet.

Now I want all of you to speak in tongues, but especially to prophesy. I do indeed want the former, but I prefer the latter. I do not forbid the one; I exhort you to the other.

For the one who prophesies is greater. Because this is a great work of charity, through which many make progress.

Than the one who speaks in tongues. This is what you consider pre-eminent.

Unless he interprets, so that the Church may receive building up. If he interprets, he may be equal to the one who prophesies.

Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching? He sets his own example before them: you will have only amazement, not progress, unless I either interpret for you, or make plain to you the hidden things of the law that I know, or explain prophecies, or teach you through moral instruction.

Nevertheless, things without a soul that give a voice, whether a flute or a lyre, if they do not produce distinct sounds, [Col. 0760A] how will what is being played be known, or what is being played on the lyre? If these lifeless things, unless they have distinction, cannot produce a melody and are rejected as useless, how much more should you, who are spiritual, seek sweetness not to caress the ears but the minds!

For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless through the tongue you give a clear utterance, how will what is said be known? If the trumpet’s sound is uncertain, whether it is for a festival or for war, no one will fight. Therefore your speech must likewise be intelligible, so that it can prepare the soldiers of Christ for spiritual battle.

For you will be speaking into the air. There are, so to speak, so many kinds of languages in this world. Even if you speak as [Col. 0760B] many languages as there are kinds of languages, what benefit will it be when everything dissolves into the air and benefits no one?

And nothing is without a voice. Nothing that possesses a tongue is without a voice.

Therefore, if I do not know the force of the voice, I will be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak. Every speech that is not understood is judged barbarous.

And the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts for the building up of the Church, seek to abound in them. Since you pursue spiritual gifts, seek especially those that build up the hearers.

And therefore let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. Here “prayer” means the utterance of the mouth. Let him therefore speak in such a way that the words of grace he says can be understood; [Col. 0760C] or let him pray that the gift of interpretation may be granted to him.

For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays. He says this because if someone speaks in languages unknown to others, his mind is not without fruit for himself, but it is without fruit for the hearer, who does not understand anything that is said. Again, if I speak in a tongue, it is not I who speak, but the spirit that is in me. But if “spirit” is required for prayer, the speech that is not understood must not be intended—although sometimes one prays while the mind is occupied with another thought.

But my mind is without fruit. Because I do not understand what I am saying.

What, then? I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind. For the one who interprets must first understand what he is going to say to others. Likewise, one must speak in such a way that others understand.

[Col. 0760D] Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit. Everything that is truly and according to God is said as a blessing.

Who fills the place of the unlearned? He means the layman, who holds no ecclesiastical rank. Alternatively: Who fills the emptiness of knowledge in the heart of the ignorant?

How will he say “Amen” over your blessing? Because he does not know what you are saying. How can he give witness to, or assent to, your blessing?

For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not built up. What he had said above concerning blessing, he explains here.

I give thanks to my God that I speak in a tongue more than all of you. Do not think that I do not possess this grace as well, and that I therefore forbid you and do not speak in tongues.

[Col. 0761A] But in the Church I prefer to speak five words with my understanding. I prefer to speak a very few words for progress rather than many that benefit no one. Some indeed ask what the five words are; conversely, one must ask them what the ten thousand are.

So that I may instruct others, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue. That is, with personal understanding and simple reasoning.

Brothers, do not become children in your understanding. You ought to know how long tongues will exist, or why they were given.

But be children in malice and mature in understanding. You ought to be children in malice, not in understanding. At the same time he shows that no one is perfect in understanding unless he is a child in malice, because the spirit of wisdom will not enter a malicious soul.

[Col. 0761B] For it is written in the law: “Because in other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even then they will not hear me, says the Lord.” I shall also give this sign: I shall speak through my holy ones in an unusual speech, and even then they will not understand the one speaking.

Therefore tongues are for a sign, not for believers. Here it is shown that, as faith increased, signs ceased, since it had been foretold that they were to be given for the sake of unbelievers.

But for unbelievers. So that they might at least be moved by their amazement.

But prophecy is not for unbelievers, but for believers. Therefore prophecy is greater and more useful, since it benefits believers and is always necessary.

Therefore, if the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in tongues. This is if it could be granted [Col. 0761C] to you, who all desire this.

But unlearned people or unbelievers enter. Here “unlearned people” means recent believers.

Will they not say, “You are insane”? Just as the Jews said about the apostles: “These people are full of new wine.” Alternatively, as at the beginning, when the apostles received the Holy Spirit, they appeared to be drunk.

But if all prophesy and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all. For the secrets of his heart become manifest when his conscience is struck by the teaching.

And thus, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you. Just as Nebuchadnezzar worshiped Daniel, saying, “Truly your God is himself God,” after he had heard the dream that he had forgotten and its interpretation.

[Col. 0761D] What then, brothers? What, then, should be done, or what shall we determine must be maintained?

When you come together, each of you has a psalm; he has a teaching. That is, he understands a psalm.

He has a revelation, he has a tongue, he has an interpretation. A revelation of some mysteries, which is what “revelation” means.

Let everything be done for building up. Let there be nothing among you that does not build one another up.

If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be two, or at most three, and in turn, and let one interpret. That is, let them speak prophesying in turn, and let one interpret gradually.

[Col. 0762A] But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the Church; let him speak to himself and to God. Let him keep this grace to his own conscience and to God.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be exhorted. Not while standing, but with the prophets sitting.

And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace. Either the grace of the spirit has agreed with another prophet, so that they yield to one another, or prophets ought to possess a spirit of humility and charity. For the God who is in them is not a God of dissension or arrogance. He says this also because the one in whom the spirit of prophecy is present is subject through the fellowship [Col. 0762B] of grace, in which he does not compete to prophesy when something has been revealed to another.

As I teach in all the churches of the saints. This is done everywhere, so that you may not think that I am imposing something new upon you.

Let women be silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but are to be subject, as the law also says. For it is contrary to the order of nature or of the law that women should speak in an assembly of men. It is therefore asked how he can say elsewhere that women ought to teach prudence and chastity. But this is within their own sex. Here too he identifies the place where they must be silent; elsewhere he permitted them to speak, as the law also says.

But if they wish to learn anything. Because the man was made first, and Sarah called Abraham “lord.”

[Col. 0762C] Let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church. Lest he seem to have forbidden them even to learn, he commanded them to do at home what was not proper for them publicly.

Did the word of God proceed from you, or did it reach you alone? Is the teaching of Christ either from you or confined among you? The same must be said concerning knowledge.

If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write to you are the Lord’s commandments. But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored. You test whether someone is a true prophet by whether he recognizes that what I say are the Lord’s commandments. But whoever is ignorant of these things will be ignored both by us and by the Lord, who says to those who claimed to have prophesied in his name, “I do not know you.”

[Col. 0762D] Therefore, brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. Pursue the one; do not forbid the other.

But let everything be done among you decently and according to order. Do nothing in a perverse order, or through contention, or for empty glory.

## CHAPTER XV

Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you. He begins the argument for the resurrection. Among other things, some of the Corinthians had even dared to deny the resurrection of the flesh, relying presumptuously on their former learning; the Apostle refutes them here.

Which you also received. So that they would not appear not to have believed it, or all to have rejected what had been believed.

[Col. 0763A] In which you stand, through which you are also saved. You stand in its teaching, and through it you hope for salvation; even at present you are often saved from various weaknesses.

In what manner I preached it to you. The whole purpose of our preaching is this: that you believe in the resurrection. For this is the first principle of all who serve Christ; otherwise all the labor of prayers and fasts that you endure in this life is pointless, since here you seem to share prosperity or adversity with unbelievers, just as the pagans themselves are accustomed to say: “What more do we have than they?” And it is true: if we have no reward for these labors in another life, we are worse off than they, because they at least appear to have the consolation of pleasures and luxury in the present.

[Col. 0763B] If you hold fast to it—unless you believed in vain. If you do not hope for the reward of your faith and labor, you have believed these things to no purpose.

For I delivered to you first of all. At the beginning, or above all.

What I also received. Either from the law, or from those who came before, or through the revelation of Christ.

That Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried. The apostles’ preaching, together with the performance of many signs of power, could indeed have won belief that the one whom they were proclaiming was Christ. But so that the blessed Apostle might establish with greater authority that this was Christ, the Savior of the world, whom Moses and the prophets announced, he recalls that this had been foretold according to the Scriptures; [Col. 0763C] as, among other things, the prophet Isaiah says: “As a sheep he is led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he is silent.” Again, below, the same prophet says: “And he will give the impious for his burial, and the rich man for his death.” Likewise, the prophet Hosea announces that Christ’s resurrection would take place on the third day, saying: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence.”

And that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures. As Hosea says: “He will revive us in two days, and on the third day we shall rise.”

And that he was seen by Cephas. What is said in the Gospel: “He appeared to Simon.”

And afterward by the eleven. Again, by Peter and the other ten.

[Col. 0763D] Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep. You see that not all the visions are recorded in the Gospel, but only those sufficient for faith. Here, because he had spoken of the apostles, he added this as well, lest the apostles, as his intimate companions, be thought to have lied. And so that greater credibility might be given to the multitude of witnesses, he also says that many were still alive and could, if questioned, declare what they had seen.

Then he was seen by James. He appeared to James separately.

Then by all the apostles. Either again, or by the apostles whom he sent to preach beyond the Twelve.

Last of all. So that they would not think that he was reporting things heard rather than seen.

[Col. 0764A] As though to an untimely birth. One whose life had been despaired of.

He was seen also by me. Namely, on the road or in the temple.

For I am the least of the apostles. Least in time, not in labor.

Who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. “My son, you have sinned; do not add again,” and also pray concerning your former sins. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you remember them.” For it is better to remember sins that have been forgiven than to forget sins that remain.

But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty. It has not been without fruit, like the one who buried the Lord’s talent in the ground.

But I labored more abundantly than all of them. Because I labored longer than they did.

[Col. 0764B] Yet not I, but the grace of God with me. Not from myself, but from the grace of God. Nor does he say that he labored in the Gospel without grace, lest he seem to claim that something was given to him contrary to what he had said above; nor does he say that grace acted without him, so as to preserve free choice.

Whether, then, it was I or they, thus we preached, and thus you believed. Why, then, did we preach in this way, and why did you likewise believe? Because Christ rose first for this reason: to open the way of resurrection. He recalls this to them so that they cannot deny what necessarily follows.

But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead. This follows by reason. For the very fact that Christ rose from the dead is already the resurrection.

[Col. 0764C] How can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead. One depends upon the other: either both must be denied, or both must necessarily be confessed.

Neither has Christ risen. Otherwise he ought not to have given an example of something that would not occur in the future.

But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and your faith is also empty. Therefore we too have preached these things without cause, if he truly did not rise, and you have believed in him in vain. Some heretics wish to assign resurrection to the soul, not to the flesh; but nothing is said to rise again unless it has fallen and rises. Therefore neither did the soul fall by death, nor did the body always lie there; otherwise it would be called rising rather than rising again.

And we are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we have borne testimony against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if the dead do not rise. We are found to have been not merely vain but also false against God, if indeed the dead do not rise.

For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. But since no one doubts this concerning him, let no one doubt it concerning us.

And if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain. For you are still in your sins. If he lied when he said that he would rise after three days, he also lied when he said that he forgives sins. Or alternatively: We are all baptized into his resurrection so that our sins may be washed away. If therefore he did not rise, neither have our sins been forgiven.

[Col. 0765A] Therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ have also perished. He speaks especially of those who have died for Christ: for they lost this life without reason if they will have no other.

If we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings. For they at least glory in the present, whereas we endure tribulations here every day.

But now Christ has risen from the dead. This is certain to everyone, because it was established first of all.

The first fruits of those who sleep. Because he was the first to rise in incorruption. If therefore the head has risen, the other members must also follow.

[Col. 0765B] For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also came through a human being. Just as death entered through Adam, because he himself was the first to die, so resurrection came through Christ, because he was the first to rise. And just as the former is the pattern of those who die, so the latter is the pattern of those who rise. Alternatively: Wishing to show the hope of resurrection, he says this: just as we are mortal in Adam, so we shall be immortal in Christ.

And just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. All indeed will rise, but only those will be made alive in Christ who deserve to be joined to Christ’s body. Again, he speaks both of the common death and of the resurrection.

But each in his own order. Whether of time or of honor.

[Col. 0765C] Christ the first fruits; then those who are Christ’s, who believed at his coming. Then the end. Then the end of everything, including death, will come, when all rise.

When he has handed the kingdom over to God and the Father. He asserts that the kingdom of the human race, according to the Epistle of Peter and the Apocalypse of John, is to be handed over through the Son to the Father, so that God may reign there through glory, where the devil formerly reigned through vices. To God and the Father: to God according to his humanity, to the Father according to his divinity. At this point the Arians commonly bring accusations, saying that the Son is lesser. “For if he will hand the kingdom over to the Father,” they say, “then he will certainly cease to reign.” To them one must first say that here he is not confirming a matter concerning the substance of the Trinity, [Col. 0765D] but concerning the resurrection. Therefore he speaks according to the substance of the one who rose from the dead. Yet if Christ will not reign for the reason that the kingdom will be handed over to the Father, then neither did the Father reign before it was handed over to him by the Son. But if the Father did not first begin to reign at that time, although he then receives the kingdom, neither does the Son lose it, although he appears then to hand it over. Alternatively: Christ hands the kingdom over to God the Father in this respect: no one can come to the Father unless he has believed in Christ, as he himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

When he has abolished every principality, authority, and power. Once sins have been abolished, all opposing powers will be abolished from us, inasmuch as they rule over us as we follow them, by the power with which they had conquered us. For their power is our sins.

But he must reign until he has placed them. That is, together with all that belongs to him. “Until” does not always indicate an end, as in the saying: “I am your God until you grow old,” and other such passages. Alternatively: He says that Christ must reign over all until he subjects to himself and to the Father the enemies and unbelievers. But there is not only one kind of subjection: he subjects the righteous, who come to him through faith and belief. But he will [Col. 0766B] subjugate unbelievers and impious people by destroying them and assigning them to eternal punishment.

All enemies under his feet. When some will be subject willingly and others by necessity.

But last of all, death, the enemy, will be destroyed. For he has subjected all things under his feet. When he says that all things are subject to him, he means the devil, who in the Apocalypse is called sin and death, because he is the author of sin and death.

Except for the one who subjected all things to him. The Apostle carefully says that all things have been subjected to the Son by God the Father, who subjected all things to him, lest we believe that he too, together with all the things that have been subjected, is subject, since he sits at the Father’s right hand and will judge with equal power with the Father.

But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also [Col. 0766C] be subject to the one who subjected all things to him. Here too the Arians bring their accusation, saying that after the resurrection of all and the end, the Son will be subject to the Father, as the lesser to the greater. They must be answered that subjection does not always concern a diminution of honor, but also the duty of charity, especially since the spirit of prophets is also said to be subject to prophets, so that God may not be a God of dissension but of peace. And the Lord himself is written to have been subject to Joseph and Mary. Many, indeed, have held different opinions about this passage. For some say that, just as he hungered in his hungry members, or is nourished in them, so also in the Church—which is his body—he himself is subjected. Others say that the human nature that he assumed is always subject in thanksgiving to the divinity, [Col. 0766D] to which he subjected all things by making them one with himself. Many others say different things as well, but it would be lengthy to insert and enumerate them.

So that God may be all in all. Then God will be all in all, when death has been abolished and every evil or error destroyed, and he alone will reign in everything.

Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? All of us who have been baptized in Christ were baptized into his death.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] Concerning these words of the Apostle, Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 28, discusses the custom of vicarious baptism for the dead. In preference to his opinion, the view of our author is closer to the truth, since he explains “baptized in the death of Christ.” Compare the Apostle’s other Epistle to the Romans [Col. 0766D] 6:3. Cosmas Indicopleustes, Book VIII, p. 280, gives a somewhat different account: “We are baptized more mystically on behalf of our dead bodies by immersing ourselves in the holy water and emerging from it, imitating death and resurrection.” Isidore of Pelusium likewise, Book I, Letter 221: “We are baptized on behalf of the bodies naturally subject to death, believing that they are transformed into incorruption.” Tertullian, *Against Marcion* V.10, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others have similar statements.]

[Col. 0767A] That is, we who have been baptized are already as though dead together with him. What benefit, then, is it for us to die to this world if eternal life does not follow this contempt for pleasures? Again, this is what he says: they are baptized not only for the forgiveness of sins, but also for the resurrection of our flesh. He calls our flesh dead because the soul does not die by this death. Hence, rebuking them, he says: “Or what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?” That is, why is it necessary to baptize the flesh if it does not rise?

If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for them? Why are we also in danger every hour? If there were nothing in the future, we would not be so foolish as to endure such great tribulations for them.

I die daily. I am always ready for death, and every day I expect to die for your [Col. 0767B] glory.

By your glory, brothers. “By” does not always signify an oath. For if I say, “I sent by the boy,” it would not immediately be correct to think that I swore by the boy.

Which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. I have the reward of my labors in you—even if you should be unwilling to make progress.

If, speaking in human terms, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what benefit is it to me if the dead are not raised? If I hope for no reward from God for this contest, why did I fight, merely perhaps to please human beings? Alternatively: Here he calls “beasts” those who at Ephesus stirred up a popular uprising against him because of the idol of Diana, whose worship he was overthrowing through apostolic preaching. That the beasts with whom the Apostle fought must clearly be understood as human adversaries is likewise recalled in another Epistle, where he says: “And I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.” By this he shows that he escaped Nero’s savagery when he was brought to Rome in chains for the first time. By saying, “What benefit is it to me if the dead are not raised?” he refutes the doctrine of those who say that souls were created in heaven before bodies and had carried on a certain course of their own conduct. Alternatively: Many things are said in the Epistles that are not contained in Acts, and many things in Acts that are not written in the Epistles. Allegorically, however, “beasts” may be understood as hostile powers, as he says in the Psalm: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you”—against whom he says here that he fought.

[Col. 0767D] “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” He rebukes those devoted to gluttony, through the example of the Prophet, because of their despair regarding the future; and it is denied that the guilt of this offense will be remitted to them until they die.

“Do not be deceived.” By those who speak such things.

“Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” So that they would not say, “Then do you judge us to be the sort of people who are easily deceived?” He does not say, “I am afraid for you,” but, “I fear their way of life.” Yet just as evil conversations corrupt good morals, so, conversely, good conversations build up evil morals.

[Col. 0768A] “Awake, righteous ones, and do not sin.” The righteous person is the one who does not sin.

“For some have ignorance of God.” They are ignorant of God’s power who think that he cannot raise the dead, judging his power by their own weakness.

“I speak to your shame.” So that you may blush at these words, as though you were still being instructed as little children.

“But someone will say.” He raises the objection himself, adopting the persona of those who contradict him. Alternatively: Here the Apostle takes the example of seeds to make a splendid argument about the resurrection of the flesh. Although seed is sown naked, it does not grow again in the same form in which it is committed to the earth; rather, just as in the beginning, according to the order proper to each seed, God ordained what sort of body it should have and commanded the earth to produce it according to his ordering, so it endures and persists. Likewise, in the resurrection he will restore to each human being the flesh that he specially assigned to each at the beginning of birth. By saying, “He gives it a body as he wills,” and not, “as he willed,” he shows that God’s original constitution remains unchangeable.

“How will the dead rise? With what sort of body will they come?” Many customarily ask whether weak bodies, such as those of the dead, will rise. They must be answered that in the resurrection not the defect of weakness but the integrity of nature is restored. For the body is never so weak as when it has been dissolved into dust. If, then, God is believed able to restore the whole, why should it be doubted that he can restore it in part? That is, for example, why should he not restore the eyes, since he will restore the whole body?

[Col. 0768C] “Fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it first dies.” Although you ought also to have been instructed by examples from nature, you nevertheless remain unbelieving regarding the divine promises.

“And what do you sow?” You do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain—for example, of wheat or of some other kind. Just as a more fertile ear rises from the grain, with grains in it, so the corruptible body rises in glory, with increase.

“But God gives it a body as he wills.” As from the beginning he ordained that all seeds, once they have decayed, should be re-formed into something greater.

“And to each of the seeds its own body.” Observe that he says “its own body,” not another’s.

“Not every flesh is the same flesh, but one belongs to human beings, another to animals.” At his command, in the beginning, the earth—which had not received them—gave forth such great and diverse living bodies. What wonder, then, if at his command he restores the human being whom he received?

[Col. 0768D] “Another belongs to birds, and another to fish.” Understand the same thing concerning the waters, which produced such a great diversity of birds and fish.

“And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies.” He who made such bodies of the elements—why should he not be able to restore the small human body?

“But one is the glory of the heavenly bodies, and another of the earthly.” [Col. 0769A] “One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars.” The whole diversity of this comparison serves the purpose of making you believe that the one who made so much out of nothing can easily restore one kind of thing.

“For star differs from star in brightness: so also is the resurrection of the dead.” He compares the diversity of the stars with the difference among the righteous, whom degrees of virtue, not sins, will make different in glory. For there will be no diversity of sinners in heaven, but only in punishment.

“It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption.” So that they may no longer suffer fevers or the other forms of corruption. Alternatively: The resurrection of the flesh is common to saints and sinners, but the bodies of the saints will be clothed with eternal glory, with incorruption [Col. 0769B] and immortality.

“It is sown in dishonor.” What is as dishonorable as a corpse?

“It will rise in glory.” In the glory of splendor, like the sun.

“It is sown in weakness.” In human frailty.

“It will rise in power.” In the power of eternity.

“It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written. Here the body is called “animal” because it does not always possess the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0769D] Everything that follows from this point to the end of this work, and the beginning of the next, in the commentary on verse V of the following Epistle, was formerly found in precisely the same words in the ancient editions of Saint Ambrose, before the Parisian Benedictines prepared their edition.] Then, however, it will always remain in the saints. Alternatively: He calls it an animal body because it is formed from the earth and is subject to corruption; a spiritual body, however, is one that rises incorruptible, so that it can pass through the air, hastening toward the heavens. The first Adam was made only for the purpose of living. The last Adam, that is, Christ, therefore assumed a human being in order to give life.

“The first man, Adam, became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.” It should be noted that when God calls both of them “Adam,” he demonstrates that they are of the same nature. This stands against the Manichaeans and Apollinarists, who deny that a complete human being was assumed by the Word of God.

“But not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward the spiritual.” The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly. He is called heavenly because he was conceived and born not according to the pattern of human frailty but by the will of divine majesty. For he possessed our nature to such a degree that he is called the second Adam and a human being. Alternatively: Here he speaks of the first and second human being according to their works, the earthly and the heavenly. For Christ also, according to the flesh, came from our stock.

“And as was the heavenly, so also are the heavenly.” If, as the heretics wish, the human being assumed was not of our kind because he is called heavenly, then neither do those who are called heavenly belong to our nature. But if no one doubts this concerning them, there must be no uncertainty concerning the others either.

“Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” The sinner bears Adam’s image [Col. 0770A]; the righteous person bears Christ’s image. Therefore, just as we bore the old human being before baptism, so after baptism let us bear the new.

“Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption.” Scripture frequently uses “flesh” to mean the works of the flesh, as in the passage: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit.” Alternatively: Flesh, as it is, will not possess the kingdom of God unless it is clothed with immortality.

“Behold, I tell you a mystery.” By naming it a mystery, he signifies something obscure.

“We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” All human beings will rise, but only those who are to reign in glory will be changed. Or in this sense: We shall all rise who are found dead at Christ’s coming. Not all who are found in the body will be changed, because only the saints will attain the glory of blessedness. Alternatively, in certain Greek manuscripts it is written: “For we shall all sleep; we shall not all be changed.” In others, however: “For we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.” This agrees better with the Apostle’s meaning, because here the statement is not made about everyone generally, but only about the saints.

“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” By the striking of the eye he wishes to signify the extreme brevity of the moment, so that from the swiftness of the resurrection you may recognize how great God’s power is.

“At the last trumpet.” “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” The last [Col. 0770C] trumpet signifies Christ’s final coming. “The dead” may mean sinners, who are also said to be dead while living, so that they may rise for punishment either immortal or without any diminution of their members. Or he may simply mean that all the dead will rise, while only the saints, together with those righteous people who are found alive, will be changed into glory.

“For this corruptible must.” It is necessary that what has been promised should come to pass.

“Put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality.” There is that which puts on, and there is likewise the garment.

“But when this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory.’” Once the causes of death have been abolished, through divine [Col. 0770D] victory death, itself swallowed up, will no longer appear.

“Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” The Prophet speaks in the person of the righteous, who mock death.

“Now the sting of death is sin.” Sin is the arrow of death, by which souls are slaughtered.

“But the power of sin is the law.” Through knowledge, sin becomes stronger and greater.

“But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” The victory is over that sin in which the law had been weakened through our carnal will [Col. 0771A], and which Christ destroyed by the cross and by his example.

“Therefore, my beloved brothers.” Having given the reasoning concerning the resurrection about which they were uncertain, he urges them to remain in God’s work, now assured of the future recompense.

“Be steadfast and immovable, abounding always in every work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord.” Let no one move you any further from the level of future hope.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Now concerning the collections that are made for the saints: as I ordained in the churches of Galatia, so you also should do.” He speaks of the funds collected throughout the individual churches and sent to Jerusalem for the poor saints.

“On the first day of the week.” The first day of the week is the Lord’s Day, as the Gospel says that the Lord rose on the first day of the week. [Col. 0771B]

“Let each of you put something aside privately, storing up whatever he has been pleased to give, so that collections may not take place when I come.” By setting something aside gradually, they should not think themselves burdened all at once, since God loves cheerful givers.

“And when I am present, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. But if it is worthy that I should go, they will go with me. I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia. For I shall pass through Macedonia. Perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now merely in passing. I hope to remain with you for some time [Col. 0771C], if the Lord permits.” The Macedonians conduct themselves in such a way that there is no need for me to remain with them longer; with you, however, it is necessary that I remain or spend the winter. For there are many things in you that must be corrected, just as a physician stays where more people are sick.

“But I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” I will remain there because a clear opportunity to preach has been given to me, though there are very many who resist.

“If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you. For he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. Therefore let no one despise him.” Let him be free from fear of tribulation and also from your contempt.

[Col. 0771D] “Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me. For I am expecting him with the brothers.” Let nothing be done that might injure his soul.

“Now concerning our brother Apollos, I inform you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers [Col. 0772A], but it was certainly not his will to come now. He will come when he has an opportunity.” Be watchful; stand firm in the faith. Watch with the eyes of the mind, so as to guard against the devil’s cunning. Stand firm, because when people are standing, sleep has difficulty creeping upon them.

“Act manfully.” Every instability and changeability is judged womanly.

“And be strengthened.” Let everything you do be done in love. Hurry to do everything not for the sake of empty glory but for the sake of love, so that there may be progress in your strength.

“Now I appeal to you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, that they are the first fruits of Achaia, and that they have appointed themselves to the service of the saints, so that you also may submit to such persons and to everyone who cooperates and labors.” I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas [Col. 0772B], Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking in you. They are present among you, and through them you can make great progress. Or because they came to me to perform for you the service of love.

“For they refreshed both my spirit and yours.” They refreshed my spirit through their love for you, and yours through my joy.

“Therefore acknowledge those who are such.” Hence elsewhere also he says: “Recognize those who walk in such a way that you have our example.” Recognize this: honor them by recognizing their zeal and labor.

“The churches of Asia greet you.” Aquila and Prisca greet you greatly in the Lord, together with the church in their house, with whom I am lodging. All the brothers greet you. [Col. 0772C] Greet one another with a holy kiss. He called the household gathering of the brotherhood a church.

“The greeting is by the hand of Paul.” “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed.” Just as Christ will come as redemption for those who love him, so whoever does not love him is to be accursed—that is, let him be detested and destroyed by him.

“Maranatha.” It is more Syriac than Hebrew, although, because the two languages border one another, it has something that sounds Hebrew. It is interpreted: “Our Lord has come.”

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.” The customary subscription written in his own hand.

“My love be with you all.” Just as I love you, so may you love one another in Christ.

[Col. 0772D] “In Christ Jesus.” Not according to the love of the world.

“Amen.” This word confirms the blessing, as he himself demonstrates above when he asks: “How does he say ‘Amen’ over your blessing?”

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0771]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0771D]

“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, through the will of God.” It is asked why, contrary to the custom of letters, he places his own name first in all his Epistles, before the name of those to whom the letters are addressed [Col. 0772D]. This is because of the authority of the apostolic office, since he wrote to people of lesser rank; even the judges of this world customarily direct writings to those whom they govern. “Through the will of God,” that is, not through the will of human beings [Col. 0773A]. At the same time, he wishes to show that Christ did not send him without the will of the Father.

“And Timothy, a brother, to the church of God that is at Corinth.” He did not say “Paul and Timothy,” because both are not apostles. To the Philippians, however, where such authority was not necessary, both are called servants.

“With all the saints who are throughout Achaia.” Here “saints” may be understood as priests, who are mentioned first in the invocation of the Lord, and in the Epistle to the Philippians together with bishops and deacons. They are named afterward so that those who understood less might not think they had been omitted. They are included in the church of Achaia, whose metropolis is Corinth.

“Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” This is the customary greeting. Here he gives thanks [Col. 0773B] to God, rejoicing that he is comforted for the purpose of comforting others.

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies.” Because every mercy comes from him.

“And the God of all consolation, who consoles us.” That is, of perfect consolation, because consolation is not less than tribulation.

“In all our tribulation.” That is, not in some tribulations but in all.

“So that we may also console those who are in every distress, through the exhortation with which we ourselves are exhorted by God.” That is, we are liberated for this reason: so that we too may console others and free them from sorrow. Or he gives us a pattern for consoling others, so that through the exhortation by which we ourselves are consoled by God we may recognize that God abandons no one who fears him, and that in the future he will reward even more greatly those whom he does not forsake in the present.

“For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us.” That is, on account of the name of Christ.

“So also through Christ our consolation abounds.” As Peter was freed from prison, and Paul was strengthened in the temple by a vision and voice of the Lord.

“Whether we are afflicted for your exhortation and salvation, or whether we are consoled for your consolation, or whether we exhort for your exhortation and salvation.” Because we exhort you toward salvation, or so that we may offer you an example of endurance.

“Which produces the endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer, so that our hope for you may be firm.” That is, we are liberated for this reason: so that you may be strengthened by the reality itself not to fear sufferings, or so that we may urge you patiently to bear those things that pertain to present and future consolation.

“Knowing that, just as you are partners in the sufferings, so you will also be partners in the consolation.” That is, this is our firm hope for you.

“For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation that occurred in Asia.” He recounts his sufferings so that they may recognize that what they suffer is small by comparison—especially since those who had been appointed in Christ’s place suffer such things. It is as if a disciple were distressed over an injury to himself, but, when he heard that his teacher had endured greater things, received consolation and ceased to grieve.

“For we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength.” We were weighed down beyond our strength by the burden of sufferings.

“So that we were even weary of living.” So that we desired death with every longing.

“But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we would not trust in ourselves.” That is, in our own prudence or caution.

“But in God, who raises the dead.” Death itself taught us that every human resource had failed and that a remedy must be hoped for from him alone, for whom it is also possible to raise the dead.

“He delivered and delivers us from such great dangers; in him we have hoped that he will also continue to deliver us.” Whoever hopes that he will continue to be delivered knows that he will still suffer much.

“With you helping us.” No one is said to be helped by another unless he is laboring.

“Through prayer for us.” The prayer of the whole Church has great power; it liberated Peter from prison.

“So that, on account of the gift bestowed upon us through many persons, thanks may be given for us by many.” That is, so that, because we have been given to you, thanks may be returned to the Lord by the gathering of many; or because we have been given to many, those converted through us give thanks.

“For this is our glory.” We glory in these very sufferings because conscience does not condemn us at all, since we do not appear to teach for the sake of glory or profit.

[Col. 0774C] “The testimony of our conscience.” That is: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”

“That we conducted ourselves in simplicity of heart and the sincerity of God.” Just as God is simple and sincere.

“And not in carnal wisdom, but in the grace of God, we conducted ourselves in this world.” We did not teach deceitfully or craftily, like carnal wisdom, which is sold for payment, but freely, as we received from God, or for the sake of God alone.

“And more abundantly toward you.” From whom we have not even accepted the food that is rightfully owed to us.

“For we do not write anything else to you.” I am not ashamed, because you know that what I say is certain.

“Than what you have read and recognized.” That is, what you have read in the Epistle and recognized in your conscience.

[Col. 0774D] “But I hope that you will recognize fully to the end.” That is, I am certain that my purpose will not change.

“As you have also recognized us in part.” Because the end has not yet come; when it does come, you will recognize us completely.

“Because we are your glory, just as you are also ours.” Disciples glory in a good teacher, just as a teacher glories in good disciples.

“On the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” When true teachers and good disciples alike will be tested.

“And with this confidence I wanted to come to you first.” That is, I sought nothing from you except your salvation.

“So that you might have a second grace, and that through you I might pass into Macedonia, and again come to you from Macedonia, and be sent on my way by you into Judea.” You had the first grace at my first arrival [Col. 0775A], or so that after the letter you might have the second grace of my presence.

“When I had therefore intended this, did I use fickleness?” Because he had not fulfilled his promise, he excuses himself lest he be accused of fickleness.

“Or do I make my plans according to the flesh?” That is, according to carnal will. For it is carnal, when no greater reason exists, not to do what one has promised.

“So that with me there should be ‘yes’ and ‘no’?” I do not think according to the flesh, so that I may not be found a liar or double-minded.

“But God is faithful.” So are we, through whom he speaks: while imitating him, we are not unfaithful.

“For the word that was among you, our word, was not ‘yes’ and ‘no,’ but ‘yes’ in him.” There is no ambiguity in him, nor have we ever lied to you.

“For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not ‘yes’ and ‘no,’ but ‘yes’ in him.” When he had promised to go to the centurion’s servant, why did he not go? He was present by spiritual grace, although he was not present bodily. “Yes” in him was “was”: that is, unchangeable truth, as he says to Moses: “He who is has sent me.” For he truly is who is always the same.

“For however many promises of God there are, in him is the ‘yes.’ Therefore through him we say ‘Amen’ to God, for our glory.” Every truth of the promise is in Christ, and through us it is proclaimed to the glory of God.
