“Now he who confirms us with you in Christ.” Through grace [Col. 0775C] and teaching. Since he had said “through us,” he now shows that God does everything, since he worked all these things in them.

“And God is the one who anointed us.” With the Holy Spirit, or with chrism.

“And who sealed us.” That which contains something precious within is sealed.

“He gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.” That is, the grace of the Spirit as a pledge. Every pledge is ordinarily given in proportion to the value of the price. How great, then, is the price whose pledge is so great?

“But I call God as a witness against my soul.” He gives the reason why he did not fulfill his promise; he asserts that this should be attributed not to his fickleness but to their weakness.

“Against my soul.” Its secrets are known by him alone.

[Col. 0775D] “That, sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth.” So that I might not exercise harsher punishment among you.

“Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy.” It is not that you believed for the purpose of our ruling over you, as priests do under the law, and therefore terrifying you. Rather, we do everything for your correction, so that you may rejoice here in conscience and forever, lest you use that very freedom for the worse.

“For you stand by faith.” By faith, not by the law—that is, you began to stand by believing in Christ.

## CHAPTER II

“But I decided this within myself: not to come to you again in sadness.” I considered or resolved not to come a second time in sadness [Col. 0776A]. When you first believed, I was with you in joy.

“For if I make you sad, who is there to make me glad?” I do this for the purpose of being able to rejoice over you.

“Except the one who is made sad by me.” Whoever is made sad understands that he has sinned, just as a sick person who feels pain can perceive his own condition and belongs to the physician’s joy.

“And I wrote this very thing to you.” I write now—or wrote earlier—for this reason: so that, corrected by the letter, you may cause me to rejoice when I am present.

“So that when I come I may not have sadness upon sadness.” I am sad because you sinned; this sadness will increase if I do not see you completely corrected.

[Col. 0776B] “Those over whom I ought to have rejoiced.” Over whom I ought always to have rejoiced, or over whose correction I ought to have rejoiced.

“Having confidence in you all, because my joy is the joy of you all.” “For out of much tribulation and anguish of heart.” That is, I am confident that you understand that your joy is genuine if I rejoice. Or, I am confident that you love me so much that you say my joy is yours.

“I wrote to you with many tears.” The first Epistle, in which I rebuked you; from this it should be understood how concerned he was for the salvation of all.

“Not that you might be made sad, but that you might know the love that I have.” I do not mention this so that you may again be saddened, but so that you may know that I did everything in love.

[Col. 0776C] “More abundantly toward you.” Recognize that my love is more abundant because of my greater concern.

“But if anyone has caused sadness, he has not caused sadness to me.” Through his sin you too were corrected and made greater progress. Or: The one who corrected me did not completely sadden me.

“But in part.” That is, only in the respect in which he harmed himself, since it is necessary for him to repent.

“So that I may not burden all of you.” I write that he should be received so that you may not be burdened if, because of your harshness, he despairs of salvation.

“This rebuke by the many is sufficient for such a person.” He is not speaking only about the one who polluted his father’s marriage bed, but about every sinner; for the first Epistle shows that many there had sinned.

“So that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive.” In contrast to the rebuke, grant forgiveness.

“And console him.” With the words of the Prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner”; and: “On whatever day the wicked person turns back, his sins will not be remembered.”

“Lest perhaps such a person be swallowed up by excessive sadness.” Lest, through despair of forgiveness, he be swallowed by the whirlpool of vices and, persuaded by the devil, be driven into greater plunges of unbelief and blasphemy.

“Therefore I appeal to you to confirm your love for him.” So that he may recognize fully that he has obtained forgiveness.

[Col. 0777A] “For this reason I also wrote to you, so that I might learn by experience whether you are obedient in everything.” So that I might see whether, just as you obeyed in punishing, you also obey in forgiving. For that obedience is true and perfect which despises nothing.

“To whomever you forgive anything, I forgive also.” Just as I punished together with you, so I forgive together with you.

“For what I have forgiven.” Not in my own person but in Christ’s, who said: “Whatever you loose on earth will also be loosed in heaven.”

“If I have forgiven anything, it was for your sake.” So that you may not be burdened or saddened.

“In the person of Christ.” Because we act in Christ’s place.

“So that we may not be outwitted by Satan.” “For we are not ignorant of his thoughts.” Nor are we ignorant of his tricks [Col. 0777B]. He similarly outwits sinners through excessive harshness, so that they perish by despair, just as through excessive leniency he fails to correct them. Hence Solomon says: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left.” Although the whole Epistle is directed against Novatian, it is shown here most clearly that those who deny repentance have been outwitted by the devil. This is his trick: to deceive the unwary under the appearance of justice.

“When I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit because I did not find my brother Titus.” He now wishes to prove to them how much more he loves them: he was so concerned for their sake that, although everything had prospered for him, he had no rest because he did not find Titus, whom he had sent to see them. He feared that he had not corrected them at all, since Titus had not yet reported anything to him.

“But taking leave of them, I departed.” I quickly left there, although I had an opportunity to preach.

“To Macedonia.” Titus was certainly to return from you by way of Macedonia. Macedonia is nearer to Achaia than to Troas; indeed, when he was there, he says that Titus later arrived.

“But thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus.” He makes us triumph through Christ, or he himself triumphs in us.

“And manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place.” The fragrance of the knowledge of God is manifested through teaching and signs. It is called a fragrance because it is sensed rather than seen, and because those who first believed were able to sense something as though through a slight fragrance.

“For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” To some we are the fragrance of death leading to death; to others, the fragrance of life leading to life. Some explain it in this way: Our labor is always pleasing to God, because we preach in every circumstance, whether they wish to believe or not. But here he is speaking specifically of those who were healed through them or among whom punishment was carried out. Thus the fragrance is good in both groups, because it is just.

“And who is sufficient for these things?” Who can be so sufficient to do these things as we, who were chosen for this purpose?

“For we are not like the many who adulterate the word of God.” He touches upon the false apostles, who mix human understanding into divine preaching. Hence Isaiah says: “Your wine merchants mix water with wine”—that is, they mix soft words of flattery into pure teaching, by which people do not so much become intoxicated and fervent as waste away in delight.

“But from sincerity, as from God, before God, in Christ, we speak.” The teaching proceeded from God, and we know that, with him present, we speak in the person of Christ—that is, just as he preached.

## CHAPTER III

“Are we beginning again to commend ourselves?” We do not wish to praise ourselves by saying these things, as though we were commending ourselves to you; but we are compelled to recall them so that you may not be deceived by others.

“Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you or from you?” Those whom the grace of their virtues does not commend are rightly commended by letters from friends.

“You are our letter.” Through your faith we are commended to everyone, as he says elsewhere: “You are the seal of my apostleship.”

“Written in our hearts, known and read by all human beings, made manifest.” In our consciences, and in the fact that you believed when we preached to you. Or: The preaching by which you were made our letter is in our heart; it is known, read by all human beings, and made manifest.

“For you are a letter of Christ.” It is manifest to everyone that through our teaching you believed in Christ, while the Holy Spirit confirmed its power. Or: You are truly recognized here as belonging to Christ because you have received his Spirit.

“Ministered by us.” That is, prepared by the Holy Spirit.

“And written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.” Here he introduces a distinction between law and grace. The Jews had received the law on hard material, signifying the hardness of their mind; just as the veil over Moses’ face foreshadowed the veil of ignorance over their hearts. Although we have the law of Christ written in the Gospels, nevertheless, at the beginning we received the Lord’s words in our hearts through hearing, not as though he were absent and they were present on written tablets. The Gospels were written later for the memory of those who came afterward. Therefore, if those who received the law on stones are without excuse, how much more are we, who received Christ’s words, if we sin? As it is written to the Hebrews: “For if they did not escape when he spoke to them on earth,” and so forth.

“Now we have such confidence through Christ toward God.” Because we know that you believed through us; or because divine grace, not a human letter, commends us.

“Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves.” He wishes to show that he does nothing through his own prudence or power, since a few uneducated men could never have saved the whole world without God’s grace.

[Col. 0779A] “But our sufficiency is from God.” He said this beforehand because he was about to say that he had received a ministry so much greater than Moses’ as the New Testament is greater than the Law, in order to recall them from the false apostles who were disparaging him.

“Who also made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament.” Although we would not have been sufficient to fulfill this task.

“Not of the letter but of the Spirit.” We minister not the letter of the law but the Spirit of grace.

“For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” Elsewhere he says that the law is spiritual for spiritual people. In other respects, it kills sinners, while grace gives life to the impious person who turns back. Some say that the historical interpretation kills, not knowing that neither history nor allegory can be preserved everywhere. For just as certain things were spoken figuratively, so, if you wish to understand the commandments allegorically, you have opened the way for everyone to sin, emptying them of all their force. But the true spiritual interpretation is the one that does not paint a beautiful lie with plausible colors; rather, through the power of realities, it expresses the reality itself in truth.

But if the ministry of death, set forth in letters engraved on stones, was in glory. It is what puts sinners to death; yet elsewhere he himself calls it holy, just, and good.

So that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses. That is, against the Manichaeans. For the Apostle could never make a comparison with something contrary to it—that is, say that the glory of the ministers of the New Testament was greater than that of Moses—if there were not understood to be some communion between them.

[Col. 0779C] Because of the glory of his face, which is being brought to an end. The glory of the Law is brought to an end by the glory of the Gospel, but it is brought to an end in such a way that it makes progress, just as he himself says that an infant is brought to an end when he reaches the age of a mature man. Seed, too, is brought to an end in fruit: the fruit is better than the seed, but it cannot exist without it. The fruit does not perish; rather, the seed is multiplied in the fruit and is brought to an end in the same way as prophecy and knowledge will be destroyed.

How much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory? In our glory, which, being perfect, cannot be brought to an end.

For if the ministry of condemnation is in glory. He has explained what he said above, that the letter kills: the ministry is one of death, since it already condemns sinners.

Much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. [Col. 0779D] It is what ministers righteousness by admitting sins.

For even that which was glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. In comparison with the glory of the Gospel, the glory of the Law is overshadowed: just as, when the sun has risen, the light of the moon is dulled, although in its own time it possesses great radiance. The Lord also demonstrates this when, ascending the mountain alone, he was seen to shine with the splendor of the sun, although Moses and Elijah are reported to have appeared in glory; and therefore the Father’s voice from above commanded that he alone be heard.

For if that which is being brought to an end was given through glory, much more will that which remains be in glory. If the Testament that was to be brought to an end was given through glory, how much more glorious will that be which remains?

[Col. 0780A] Therefore, since we have such a hope. Such a hope of glory, because we have been saved in hope.

We use great confidence. In God, who made us fit for this.

And not as Moses used to put a veil over his face. We do not act in this way, because now all Christians see the glory of the Lord, as the Holy Spirit reveals it.

So that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face. Until its end—that is, until the end of his life. Likewise, the Law is not understood until its end—that is, until one believes in Christ.

Which is being brought to an end. The veil is now brought to an end in Christ.

But their minds were dulled. Until the present day. For unless they believe, they cannot understand at all, according to the Prophet.

That same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament. [Col. 0780B] He bore its figure upon his face.

Which is brought to an end in Christ. He who is the end of the Law.

But until the present day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. The veil of ignorance lies over the heart of those to whom Moses is read—that is, over the hearts of the Jews.

But whenever it turns to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. When the Jew turns, just as Moses turned toward the Lord in order to listen to him.

Now the Lord is Spirit. There is nothing obscure or veiled in him.

But where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. The Spirit is free, and for that reason cannot receive a veil, since it is rather he himself who reveals all things. For whoever has the Spirit of God has everything naked and open before him, because the Spirit searches all things.

But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord. We contemplate the glory of the Lord openly and clearly.

Are being transformed into the same image. The image that the Lord displayed on the mountain, as he says elsewhere: “He transformed the body of our lowliness, making it conform to the body of his glory.” Or, we are transformed daily and strive to be transformed.

From glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord. That is, through the Spirit of the Lord at work, we advance from this glory to the glory that is to come.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, since we have this ministry, according as we have received mercy. Because we were not fit of ourselves for so great an office.

We do not fail. In all our tribulations.

But we renounce the hidden things of shame. That is, the hidden things of vices. For it is shameful for a Christian [or, according to the variant, “Christ”] to sin.

Not walking in craftiness. Not preaching for the sake of sordid gain.

Nor falsifying the word of God. By flattering people and excusing sins, as some, in order to make the human heart glad, mix worthless speech with the word of God and creep along upon the earth.

But by the manifestation of truth, commending ourselves to every human conscience. But what we say is so clearly manifested among human beings as true that their conscience bears witness for us, even among those who resist.

Before God. Not before human beings—that is, we do not commend ourselves to them for their own sake.

But if our Gospel is also veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing. As though someone had objected to him that not everyone understands this truth; but, he says, it is veiled among unbelievers—or among the deceitful, not the faithful. Even many of the Jews were ignorant of it.

Among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ might not shine. “The god of this age” may be understood as “the ruler of the world,” because he claims sovereignty for himself among unbelievers. Or, because of the slander of heretics, it should be understood in this way: God blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age on account of the merit of their unbelief, just as the Savior says: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” The Apostle himself also says elsewhere: “Because they did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity, God sent them a spirit of error”—that is, he permits it to be given, because they were unwilling to believe. It is as when a physician abandons a disobedient sick person: the physician is said to have prolonged the illness, although the entire fault belongs to the sick person, because he scorned to listen. Yet if he asks again and obeys, he can recover his health.

Who is the image of God. The expressed substance of God, as it is written to the Hebrews.

For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus [Col. 0781C] Christ our Lord. Whoever seeks his own advantage preaches not Christ but himself, like those who serve their own belly.

But ourselves as your servants through Jesus. Because we provide for your benefit in all things, after the example of Christ, who took the form of a servant; we do not teach for the sake of glory or greed.

For the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness.” This is directed against all the enemies of the Old Testament, because it was given by the Father of Christ.

He himself shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God. He first shone in our hearts through Jesus Christ, so that we might be able to illuminate others.

[Col. 0781D] In the face of Jesus Christ. What charity is greater in the face of Christ than in that of Moses? Or, in the person of Christ we illuminate human beings with knowledge.

But we have this treasure. Here he begins to show why they suffer such great and numerous things: because the false apostles were disparaging him to them on this account.

In earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may belong to God and not come from us. We carry the treasure of spiritual grace in a fragile body; even when we heal others, we ourselves are sometimes weakened, so that it may be recognized that what we do belongs not to our own power but to God.

In every way we are afflicted, but not crushed. We suffer persecution, but through the consolation [Col. 0782A] of future hope we are not crushed; rather, we rejoice all the more.

We are perplexed, but not abandoned. We suffer persecution, but are not forsaken. We are humbled, but not put to shame. We endure slaughter and reproaches, but are not deprived of divine assistance.

We are struck down, but do not perish. We come as far as the point of despair concerning life, but we do not die; and even if we die, we do not perish.

Always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. Through tribulation, as he says elsewhere: “We die daily for your glory”; therefore, he says, “if we die with him, we shall also live with him.” But those who are unwilling to die with him will not live with him either.

[Col. 0782B] For we who live are always being handed over to death. For as long as we are in the body.

For the sake of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. We suffer not because of evil deeds, but for his body—that is, the Church—what he suffered for us, so that his life, that is, eternal life, may be manifested in our mortal flesh, so that it may become immortal. For what we shall be has not yet appeared in us.

Therefore death is at work in us, but life in you. Will death, then, always be in us and life in you, both the future and the present?

But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written. He rebukes those who believed the false apostles, who therefore thought that Paul was subject to sufferings because he was deficient in faith. If, then, one could not suffer tribulation through faith, he shows conversely that he endures such things because of faith, whereas they have no grounds for hatred except through flattery and dissension. Hence he says to the Galatians: “Those who wish to please in the flesh only, so that they may suffer the persecution of the cross of Christ as little as possible.”

“I believed, and therefore I spoke”; and we also believe, and therefore we speak. By this testimony he proves that he believes. For if that man spoke because he believed—for no sane person affirms to another what he himself does not believe—then we too, he says, who speak, believe; and for that very reason we also suffer tribulation.

Knowing that he who raised Jesus. Holding firmly to this faith, from which not even death can tear us away.

Will also raise us with Jesus and establish us with you. [Col. 0782D] Just as he raised him, so also will he raise us if we die for him.

For everything is for your sake. We suffer everything because we faithfully seek and desire your salvation.

So that abundant grace, through many, may abound in thanksgiving to the glory of God. This is the meaning: through the multitude of believers, because grace abounds, thanksgiving may also abound to the glory of God.

For this reason we do not fail. For your sake and for the glory of God, we do not cease amid all tribulations and reproaches.

But although our outward person is being corrupted, yet our inward person is renewed day by day. Although the body is corrupted by the injuries of suffering, the soul is nevertheless [Col. 0783A] strengthened daily by hope in future things to endure everything.

For this momentary and light affliction of ours. The present tribulation, however long it may continue, is brief and easy in comparison with the immense glory that is eternal, as he says to the Romans: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory.”

Beyond measure, in sublimity. Because there can be no comparison.

It produces for us an eternal weight of glory. Since he had called it light, he therefore places here “weight,” preserving the metaphor of the balance; or, the weight of tribulations, which at present are beyond measure, brings the sublimity of eternal glory to perfection.

[Col. 0783B] While we do not contemplate the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal. We are moved neither by good nor by evil visible things, because both come to an end.

## CHAPTER V

For we know that if our earthly house, this dwelling, is dissolved, we have an edifice from God. As though someone had said to him, “When will this be, since I know that I am mortal?” Therefore he introduced the resurrection of glory. “Our house,” he says, “is the earthly body in which we still dwell bodily in this age. If, before the Lord’s coming, it is dissolved either by sufferings or by the condition of nature, we shall receive heavenly incorruption from God, when the body comes to life again.”

A house not made by human hands, but eternal in the heavens. For the animal body, which is said in a certain sense to have been formed by the hand of God himself, will become spiritual through the Spirit.

For in this also we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven. This groaning is understood as labor, because one labors with groaning, just as childbirth is also used for labor. For this purpose, therefore, we labor, so that we may deserve to be clothed over with that dwelling.

If indeed, once clothed, we are not found naked. Through faith or through the work of piety.

For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over. For those who are found alive will labor for this: not to be [Col. 0783D] stripped by the fire together with sinners when all the elements begin to be consumed, but to deserve to be clothed over with immortality together with the righteous.

So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. What is swallowed up does not appear, although it exists, just as, if iron is thrown into fire, while its substance remains, it becomes entirely fire; for it also assumes the brightness and heat of the fire itself.

Now the one who prepares us for this very thing is God. He says that God does this so that it may not seem impossible to anyone.

Who gave us the pledge of the Spirit. He gave us the pledge of the Spirit so that we may know that he does not permit the temple of his Spirit to perish.

Therefore, being confident always and knowing. We dare to ask for this because, as long as we are in the body in this life, we are tossed about by uncertain events, not knowing the end of our departure. But when we have departed from the body, then we know that we are drawing near to the Lord, because we have been freed from the hostile and uncertain troubles of the world.

For while we are in this body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith and not by sight. But we are confident, and we have good will. We are away from him because we are not yet in our paternal inheritance. As strangers, therefore, we ought not to care greatly about the affairs of this age; but, content with what is necessary, we should have every desire and zeal to reach our homeland, because for now we hope through faith and do not yet possess it by sight. But we are confident and consent, and we read this with complete boldness, as he says elsewhere: “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is much better.”

Rather to be away from the body. He rightly says “to be away from the body,” because we are to return to it again.

And to be present with the Lord. Although no creature is absent from its Creator, we shall then in some manner be more present to him, even perfected, when we have been separated from the frailty of the flesh. Or, we shall be present with God according to our own condition, because according to his condition we can never be absent from him.

And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. Even now we strive to be in action such as we shall be in the kingdom—without doubt, incorruptible by nature and perfect. He says this: as long as we are placed in the world and are away from the Lord, let us act in this way through good conduct, so that we may be able to please him in the future—not, as some think, that after we have departed from the body we may merit God by doing something there.

For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ. From the greatness of the power of the one seated, one must estimate the greatness of the tribunal and the terror of the judgment.

So that each may receive what belongs to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil. Since he had mentioned the time of the resurrection, he wishes to show that the soul has accomplished everything through the body, whether good or evil: “Come to me, blessed ones”; and, “Depart from me, accursed ones.”

Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings; but we are manifest to God. Knowing how great the fear of divine judgment is, we persuade human beings to beware; but we are manifest to God, provided that we ourselves are not also afraid.

I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences. Although evil has been suggested to you about us, I nevertheless think that your conscience does not accept any suspicion about us other than what it knows; nor can it place greater faith in others than in itself.

We do not commend ourselves to you again. Because above he had said: “We are beginning to commend ourselves.”

But we give you an occasion to boast on our behalf. This is against the false apostles, who first sought, through disparagement, to implant hatred of us in them, so that they might more easily be believed.

So that you may have something to say to those who boast in appearance and not in heart. So that you may have something to say to those who boast in carnal and visible things, and not in their consciences. You can respond to the things they fabricate in their disparagement of us, so that they may also be refuted by the testimony of their own heart.

For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God. If, he says, we pervert what is right into vices through our own judgment, we ourselves fall away from God and are alienated from him. But if we think soundly and soberly, our preaching is for you. He was saying concerning them that, if they had remained mindful of God, they would never have suffered such things. Some interpret it differently: whether we are in ecstasy, it is for God; whether we speak with sound judgment, it is for you.

Whether we are sober, it is for you. Whether we abstain, it is for your sake.

For the love of Christ compels us. We must in some measure repay his love in return—that is, suffer for his body, since he deigned to die for us by death.

Judging this: that if one died for all, then all died. And Christ died for all. He alone was found who could be offered as an immaculate sacrifice for all who were dead in sins.

So that those who live may no longer live for themselves. We owe our life to the one who preserved it for all by his death. Therefore, if anyone does his own will rather than God’s, he lives for himself, not for him. Hence the Lord himself says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and so forth.

[Col. 0785C] But for him who died and rose again for their sake. Because of the slander, he always joins resurrection to death. This concerns the abolition of the old things, the renewal of creation, and our reconciliation to God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. That is, circumcised according to the flesh and observing carnal ceremonies; nor do we imitate the example of any of the ancients.

And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way. “We knew Christ,” he says, “according to the flesh” when, having been made a curse, he accepted the cross’s gibbet for our salvation. But now we do not know him in this way, for he who once died for all and rose again will no longer suffer for us. Alternatively: “Even if we knew Christ when we were still according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way.” Because he was proposing the examples of the ancients to them, he says that Christ, circumcised according to the flesh, celebrated everything with the Jews. But now we no longer know these things, because after his resurrection the Testament is new. Alternatively: Those who are weak believe in Christ according to the flesh; but the perfect understand that after his resurrection there is no longer anything weak or frail in him according to the flesh.

Therefore, if there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, everything has become new. If anyone believes in Christ, he is a new creation, understanding that the old things were separated in their own time and that from now on one must live in a new manner.

[Col. 0786A] But everything is from God. For the commandments also have been renewed; nevertheless, both the new and the old have been dispensed by one God according to the diversity of times.

Who reconciled us to himself. Because by sinning we had turned away from him.

Through Christ. Through the teaching and example of Christ alike.

And gave us the ministry of reconciliation. So that we too might be able to reconcile others.

For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. We read of God’s being present in three ways: according to his infinity, to every creature, as he says through the Prophet: “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” According to sanctification and a special indwelling in the saints, in accordance with this: “And I will dwell in them.” According to the fullness of divinity in Christ, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily”—reconciling the world to himself.

Not counting their trespasses against them. That is, knowing them through faith alone.

And he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ, so that in Christ’s place we may reconcile human beings to God, whose ambassadors we are in the place of Christ.

As though God were exhorting through us. That is, we do not speak from ourselves but from God.

We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. What he says is this: “We do not plead for Christ, but because of what he suffered for us, [Col. 0786C] so that, believing in him, you may be reconciled to God”—that is, in Christ’s place.

He who knew no sin he made sin for us. In accordance with this: Christ, who was without sin, is said to have been made sin for us because he died for our sins. The Father made Christ, who knew no sin, sin for us—that is, just as the victim offered for sin was called “sin” in the Law, as it is written in Leviticus: “And he shall lay his hand upon the head of his sin,” so Christ, offered for our sins, received the name “sin.”

So that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Not our righteousness, nor righteousness belonging to us.

## CHAPTER VI

But as fellow workers, we also exhort. We assist you by our word.

That you not receive the grace of God in vain. Whoever is not new in the New Testament receives the grace of God in vain; that is, it profits him nothing.

For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The acceptable time for hearing and having mercy unto salvation is the present life, as the Savior says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.”

Behold, now is the acceptable time. As he says elsewhere: “While we have time, let us do what is good.” This life is called a day because it is suitable for working, and it is closed by the night of judgment. That [Col. 0787A] day will be darkness for sinners, not light, in which no one will then be able to work. This time is also likened to summer, in comparison with which the ant is said to hope for the coming winter.

Behold, now is the day of salvation. Now alone can we find salvation, because, according to the testimony of the Prophet, no one will confess in hell.

Giving no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be reviled. Let no one be offended by our example, lest the fault be thought to belong not so much to us as to the Law.

But in everything. Not merely in some things.

Let us present ourselves. Everything concerning this matter lies within our power.

As ministers of God. The ministers of God ought, as far as possible, to imitate God, so that they may be recognized by their conduct as worshipers of God. Hence he says elsewhere: “Bear God in your body.” He allows himself to be blasphemed by everyone and yet, in this present life, does not deny his benefits even to the ungrateful.

In great patience, in tribulations. Every injury is a tribulation.

In necessities. Let us endure everything that is necessary, as necessity requires.

In distress. Every want is distress.

In blows, in prisons, in seditions, in labors. The labors of the hands or of journeys.

In vigils. Of the mind no less than of the body.

In fastings. It should be noted that fasts are counted among the virtues.

[Col. 0787C] In chastity. That is true chastity which is not polluted even in the mind.

In knowledge. It should be noted that knowledge is counted among the kinds of virtue.

In long-suffering. That is, prolonged endurance.

In gentleness. So that we generate bitterness for no one by our words, and it may be said of us: “His jaws are sweetness, and he is altogether desirable.”

In the Holy Spirit. While we prepare ourselves as a worthy dwelling for him.

In unfeigned love. Let us do for others everything we wish to be done for us, so that we may love not in word but in deed and in truth.

In the word of truth. That is, in the word of Christ: if it is spoken suitably and truly, so that truth does not become falsehood.

[Col. 0787D] In the power of God. Through the weapons of righteousness. Let us fight against the devil in the power of God, or of the Law.

On the right and on the left. Let us not be lifted up by prosperity, nor broken by adversity.

Through glory and dishonor. The glory of virtues and the dishonor of prison.

Through bad report and good report; as deceivers, and yet truthful. By some we are praised as truthful; by others we are branded as deceivers, just as the Savior himself was called a deceiver by the Jews. We endure all these things equally, so that praise may not exalt us, nor disparagement cast us down, because both sides must at some point lie. Therefore, returning to our conscience, [Col. 0788A] we ought not to place greater faith in others than in ourselves.

As unknown, and yet known. Unknown to the faithless and ungrateful, but known to the faithful and just.

As dying, and behold, we live. That is, reaching as far as death, as when he was stoned and, having been thought dead, rose and taught at Lystra.

As chastened, and not put to death. “The Lord has chastened me severely, but has not handed me over to death.”

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Sorrowful in the severity of our countenance, but rejoicing in heart even amid tribulation.

As poor, yet making many rich. In the very thing in which we lack, we abound for others, while alms are performed through us; or, being in need of earthly things, we make others rich in heavenly goods. At the same time, one must observe how he says that he suffers everything “as if,” but does not actually suffer it, to show that these things are merely images of sufferings in comparison with the everlasting reward.

As having nothing, yet possessing everything. As Solomon says: “The whole world of riches belongs to the one who is faithful.” For, apart from the fact that everything belonging to us belongs to God, no one has more than the one who needs nothing. That person needs nothing who seeks nothing beyond what is necessary. Concerning the separation of the faithful from the unfaithful, and the fact that all the saints are God’s temple.

Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. We have been so moved by your progress that we cannot remain silent at all. For the progress of the disciple opens the mouth of the teacher and enlarges and expands the heart—that is, makes it abound in understanding. As it is written about Solomon: “For God gave him breadth of heart, like the sand of the sea.”

You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections. You are not restricted by any narrowness of speech coming from us; rather, because you cannot hear a stronger teaching, the cause of the restriction proceeds from you.

But, having the same recompense. If you endure the same labor. Or certainly, if you take in as much as we are able to say.

I speak as to children: be enlarged also yourselves. As children, be enlarged by my example, so that you may receive greater things. Or, priests in their teaching command that people be enlarged by their example.

Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Do not join yourselves to them or make yourselves equal to them, because a yoke is drawn together only by equals. That is, do not associate with the false apostles or with those who reclined at an idol’s table.

For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity, or what fellowship between light and darkness? None, just as darkness has no fellowship with light. He simultaneously shows that no one can be both righteous and unrighteous, setting forth examples that are strongly opposed to one another.

And what agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? There can be absolutely no agreement between them. By Belial he names the devil, or the Antichrist, under the designation of an idol.

And what agreement does the temple of God have with idols? For you are the temple of the living God. He calls the people themselves idols, [Col. 0789A] those who worship idols, because they are temples of demons, just as the righteous are the temple of God.

As God says: “For I will dwell in them.” Although God is everywhere, he says that he dwells properly in those who enjoy his grace and prepare for him the hospitality of their heart.

And I will walk among them. I will possess or traverse all their senses.

And I will be their God. God is the God of all by nature, but of few by will; for he is not the God of the dead but of the living.

And they will be my people. Those who are servants by their will, not merely by nature.

Therefore, “Come out from their midst and be separate,” says the Lord. In action, conduct, or association, [Col. 0789B] not in physical location.

And do not touch what is unclean. Everyone who sins is unclean, for every unrighteous person is unclean before God.

And I will receive you. If they cast you out.

And I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me. If your unbelieving parents disown you, you will have me as your everlasting father.

Says the Lord Almighty. He added “Almighty,” so that nothing might seem impossible to anyone.

## CHAPTER VII

Therefore, since we have these promises, beloved. Since we have such great and such splendid promises, with how much zeal must the house that is to receive such a guest be cleansed? And how ought the children of God to imitate their father in all works of righteousness?

Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Defilement of the flesh is what is admitted through the flesh; defilement of the spirit is what is sinned through thought alone.

Perfecting holiness. Holiness will then be perfect if both are kept clean.

In the fear of God. Not in human praise or fear.

Receive us. We have harmed no one. Accept what we say, or what we live, so that you may hold to our example.

We have corrupted no one. Through evil teaching.

We have defrauded no one. In order to take something from him.

I do not say this for your condemnation. For we have already said that you are in our hearts, to die with us and to live with us. I am not exposing you as such in order to excuse myself; for I cannot think this about you whom I love, as I mentioned above.

I have great confidence in you. You have given me great confidence to speak, because you obeyed in everything; or because I do not fail to know that you love me greatly.

I have much ground for boasting about you. Among the other churches, I applaud myself for your correction.

I am filled with consolation. After much sadness. Or, my speech supplies me with consolation, stirred up by your example and progress.

I overflow with joy in all your tribulation. I rejoice so greatly in all your tribulation that I forget all my pressures.

[Col. 0790A] For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest. He wishes to show them how greatly the magnitude of his joy surpassed his distress.

But we suffered every kind of tribulation. We experienced no kind of tribulation that we did not undergo.

Battles outside, fears within. Battles against unbelievers, and fear concerning false brothers; or, we feared lest the weak should be scandalized.

But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us. That is, those who had been humbled and afflicted by sufferings.

At the arrival of Titus. Not only at his arrival, but also through the consolation he brought. Not only because the man whom we desired arrived, but also because he reported those things for which we were especially awaiting his arrival.

In which he was comforted among you. After the grief that he shared with us [Col. 0790B] on your account.

Reporting to us your longing, your weeping. On account of our sadness and the sins of certain people.

Your zeal for me. Because in my place you were zealous with God’s zeal against those who were sinning. Or, there are three kinds of zeal: imitation, envy, and the kind at issue here.

So that I rejoiced all the more. Because you not only corrected yourselves but also made greater progress.

For even if I made you sorrowful in the letter, I do not regret it. Even if I had regretted it when I saw that the letter, although it made you sorrowful for an hour, I now rejoice—not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance. Even if I had regretted having rebuked you too harshly, your progress makes it so that I do not regret it, [Col. 0790C] as though a physician were saying: even if I had been sorry that I used such a burning cautery, now I rejoice, not because you suffered pain, but because that pain benefited you unto salvation.

For you were made sorrowful according to God. Not according to the world.

So that you might suffer no loss through us. Either through our negligence, or because we might come and condemn one of you.

For godly sorrow produces repentance unto steadfast salvation. There is also a demonic repentance opposed to salvation, if someone regrets a good work. It produces steadfastness—that is, steadfast or enduring salvation—or a repentance that persists. Concerning the forgiveness of sins, we must not be without fear.

[Col. 0790D] But worldly sorrow produces death. Worldly sorrow is either grieving over the loss of one’s own possessions, grieving because one has not seized another’s possessions, or being tormented by another’s happiness. Godly sorrow, on the other hand, is mourning either one’s own sins or those of another.

For behold, this very thing—your being made sorrowful according to God—what earnestness it produces in you. This very event that has now taken place can teach you what the difference is between the two kinds of sorrow.

But defense. Some manuscripts have “but excuse”; in Greek, ἀπολογίαν (*apologian*), that is, a satisfaction of the commandment, he says. Some say that in this passage the preposition *sed* (“but”) is superfluous in Latin; among the Greeks, however, it belongs to the syntactical sequence of the expression.

But indignation. Against those who sinned, not negligence.

But fear. Fear of the Lord, not security.

But longing. Not aversion, but our longing.

But zeal. Against those who sinned, so that they would not sin further; not leniency.

But vengeance. Not a harmful pardon, but a salutary vengeance.

In every respect you have shown yourselves to be pure in the matter. You have proved yourselves free from guilt; for one who is polluted has no authority to exact vengeance.

Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not on account of him who committed the wrong, nor on account of him who suffered it. I did not write merely because of the one who wronged the father, nor solely because of the father himself. It can also be understood this way: I did not write on account of the one who was expelled; for this matter was not corrected or rebuked by me alone.

But to make manifest our concern, which we have for you before God. So that you may not think that anything can be hidden from us while we are deeply concerned for you.

For this reason also we were comforted. Because you have proved yourselves pure in the matter.

In our consolation, however, we rejoiced all the more abundantly over Titus’s joy, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. In this we rejoiced still more: that Titus’s spirit was so refreshed by you that you can never depart from his mind. For the progress of disciples is the spiritual joy of teachers.

And if I have boasted somewhat to him about you. He acts like a skilled physician who encourages a wound already nearly healed with gentle applications, so that it may more easily be healed by the cautery’s burning.

I have not been put to shame, but just as we have spoken everything to you in truth. Boasting about progress is not subject to shame.

So also our boasting, which was made to Titus, has become truth. Boasting about just matters is not vanity but truth.

And his affections are more abundantly directed toward you, as he remembers your obedience. All the members of his affections long for you: his eyes await your presence, his ears your speech, and his mouth your conversation.

How you received him with fear and trembling. He described faithful obedience: for one who obeys out of love fears to grieve the person he loves.

I rejoice that I have confidence in you in everything. You have made me rejoice, because I have never been able to doubt your obedience and your service to the saints.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia. He begins his discussion of the collections and, by the example of those churches, urges them to repentance and almsgiving, so that they would not regard as burdensome what they see the poorer believers have already done.

For in the midst of much testing through tribulation, the abundance of their joy was great. They rejoice most of all when they have been afflicted, knowing that the Apostles, after suffering insult before the council for the name of Christ, rejoiced with public gladness.

And their extremely deep poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity. In earthly resources they are indeed very poor, but in great simplicity they are rich, desiring to give more than they possess. Therefore God tests the disposition more than what the right hand offers; for one who does as much as he can has done everything. The same applies to rich and poor alike, although the rich may appear able to give more.

For I bear them witness according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing. He says this in an inverted order of words: “I bear them witness,” namely, that while acting according to their means, they were willing beyond their means.

With much exhortation they begged us for the grace and fellowship of the ministry performed for the saints. Urging us insistently, they asked us to receive gladly what they were offering for the service of the saints.

And not as we hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us. They did more than we had hoped: not content merely to give what was theirs, they first handed themselves over to the Lord and then to us. That is, God sees their intention, while we see its result.

According to the will of God. They did not act merely to please us without the Lord’s will.

So that we urged Titus that, just as he had begun, so he should also complete this grace among you. Their devotion moved us to send him to you, so that by his teaching and direction he might also complete this matter among you, lest you should have less than the others. He is dealing with the Corinthians’ commendation, their equality according to what each possessed, and the ministry performed for the saints.

But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, all diligence, and also in your love for us—so may you abound in this grace as well. He notes that their faith and knowledge are praiseworthy.

So that you may abound in this grace also. Lest, while you surpass others in other matters, you should be surpassed by others in this one.

I do not say this as a command, but by means of the diligence of others I am also proving the genuine quality of your love. I do not command or demand it, but I give advice: just as you provide an example to others in many matters, so should you do in this work. For you have such inborn devotion that you have no need at all to learn it from others.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that although he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich; and I give counsel in this matter. This is useful for you. You do not fail to know that the Son of God became poor for your sake, although he was the Creator and Lord of all, so that by his example you might be enriched with heavenly goods. If, then, he despised all temporal things for your sake, how much more ought you to give small things—not your own, but rather to return his own to him. For whatever is offered for his sake is given to him. At the same time this passage opposes Photinus: before Christ became poor, he was rich, because he dwelt in the Father.

You who began not only to do but also to desire it in the previous year. He shows that some are able to act without being willing, when either the persistence of the one asking or the authority of the one commanding requires it.

But now complete the work as well, so that just as the willingness of your intention is ready, so also may your completion be, from what you have. Complete what you began willingly. For the end of every good work is to be sought. Just as a deed done unwillingly is not acceptable, so willingness is fruitless when those who possess it do nothing.

For if the willingness is ready, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. Do not suppose that I am forcing anyone beyond his ability, or asking as much from the poor in this matter as from the rich. All will give equally if each gives only as much as he can, not according to what he does not have. Tobias said the same to his son: “According to what you have, my son, give alms.”

For this is not so that there may be relief for others but affliction for you, but that there may be equality at the present time. I am not saying that you should preserve nothing for yourselves, but that there should be sufficiency for both sides.

Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need, and thus there may be equality, as it is written. Give them material things, so that they, being free for spiritual matters, may be able to return spiritual things to you. These two levels cannot exist without one another: for one who thinks about material things will no longer be perfect, however merciful he may be, if he has no one to whom he can give or no one to teach him how to give.

The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little. This is said about the manna that the people received in the wilderness; by its example we are taught that every excess produces worms. It is also shown that what God gives ought to be equal for all. Because of the authority of this testimony, the Apostle wants all present goods to be held in common, so that the perfect do not conceal their teaching and those who possess the world’s goods do not deny them food. For the laborer is worthy of his food.

But I give thanks to God, who put the same diligence for you into Titus’s heart, because he received the exhortation, but, being even more diligent, went to you of his own will. By the grace of the exhortation and by his own will he hastened, so that he might have a reward, not unwillingly, as though this administration had been entrusted to him merely as a duty.

We sent with him our brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. This is understood of Luke, because he seems to have particular praise for writing the Gospel; he also wrote the Acts of the Apostles in addition to the Gospels.

And not only that, but he was also appointed by the churches as our traveling companion in this grace, which is administered by us. He demonstrates, on the testimony of the churches, that this man was suitable and approved.

For the glory of the Lord and our declared intention. That is, our proposed or prepared intention.

Avoiding this, so that no one may blame us in this abundance that is administered by us for the glory of the Lord. Lest anyone say, “How did Christ fulfill the law, when we see Christians not giving as much alms as the law commanded?”

For we provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings. We do nothing for human glory, yet we do not want anyone, with good reason, to suffer scandal because of us; rather, we want all who see our good works to glorify our Father.

We also sent with them our brother. Some assert that this was said about Apollos.

Whom we have often proved to be diligent in many matters. He gives him this testimony so that he may be heard more readily.

Now he is shown to be much more diligent, with great confidence in you. We now prove him much more diligent because of you: either because your obedience has been aroused, or because, helped by Titus, he has proved himself independently.

Whether concerning Titus, who is my companion and your helper, or concerning our brothers, the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ. What he says is this: whether for the sake of Titus, who had commended their obedience, or for the sake of those who had likewise been sent to them, they should so conduct themselves that, before everyone, they might demonstrate both the sincerity of their love and the truth of the apostolic glory that exists for them.

Therefore, in the presence of the churches, show them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you. Let them see that what is said about your progress in all the churches is true. Or, alternatively: show them your love, of which we boast before all the churches.

## CHAPTER IX

Now concerning the ministry performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your ready disposition, on account of which I boast about you among the Macedonians. Here the word “saints” seems to change the meaning; therefore some say that above he spoke about laypeople, but here about holy priests. Others say that until this point he has been discussing almsgiving, but now he is reminding them about the ministry of the word, which is offered to those sanctified through baptism. Here both interpretations must carefully be followed to the end of the argument.

For Achaia has been ready since the previous year. The whole province, whose chief city you are, has been urged by us to this ministry.

And your zeal has stirred up very many. Here “zeal” is used for imitation.

But we sent the brothers so that our boasting about you in this matter might not be emptied of meaning. He referred to this above: “Those who may remind you, lest they find you otherwise,” in the matter of doctrine or ministry, as I thought.

So that, as I said, you may be ready; lest, when the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—and I do not say you—should be ashamed in this undertaking. If we are ashamed, as though we had boasted falsely, how much more will you be ashamed, both because of your negligence and because of our embarrassment? For it is a great disgrace if someone is ashamed on behalf of a person who loves him.

Therefore I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go to you beforehand and prepare this promised blessing, so that it might be ready. Either it is called a blessing because it blesses, or because through their kindness God’s blessing arises.

Thus, as a blessing and not as greed. But I say this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will also reap in blessings. Let each person give as he has resolved in his heart, not from sadness or compulsion. It will be a blessing if it is given with a grateful spirit.

For God loves a cheerful giver. But the greedy person does not know how to give cheerfully. In knowledge also, the greedy person is one who does not wish to fulfill the understanding he has begun to possess. Hence the Lord commanded no one to greet anyone on the road—that is, not to announce the word of salvation to anyone only in passing. This is what is meant by “whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” This passage also works against Jovinian, since it shows that there are degrees of merit. “Whoever sows in blessings will also reap in blessings.” Conversely, therefore, the one who sows in cursing will reap from it as well, as it is written: “Do not sow evil in the furrows of injustice, and you will not reap it sevenfold.” “Let each person give as he has resolved in his heart,” that is, willingly and not under compulsion, not from sadness or necessity. For God loves a cheerful giver, according to Solomon’s wisdom: “In every gift make your face cheerful.” But if this is understood of knowledge, he wants the teacher to be cheerful in his labor, as he says elsewhere about himself: “For if I do this willingly, I have a reward,” and so forth.

Now God is able either to prevent them from fearing poverty or to provide the free gift of wisdom.

To make every grace abound in you. This is the grace of increase, because from it thanksgiving is returned to God through your works. “From the fruit of his grain, wine, and oil they have been multiplied.”

So that, always having all sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work, as it is written. Thus you may complete both the good work of material mercy and that of spiritual things, that is, teaching, as it is written:

“He distributed; he gave to the poor.” This may refer either to the poor in understanding or to material goods, as he said above: “Let their abundance be the supply of your need.”

“His righteousness remains forever.” Temporal goods are compared with eternal righteousness.

And the one who supplies seed to the sower will also provide bread for eating. He says this: God, who has granted them the will, will also bring the deed to completion in you. That is, God, who has given you the means to distribute, will not allow the hungry person to suffer. But if you refer it to the seed of the word, then the one who gave you the office of teaching will also provide you food, provided only that you wish to devote yourself to this.

And he will multiply your seed. Either the seed of humility or of speech.

And he will increase the harvest of your righteousness. The harvests of righteousness are resources when justice is done with them. But when they are gathered unjustly or possessed for greed or pride, they become harvests of iniquity. For one who makes wheat expensive is cursed by the people. Or the harvests of righteousness are the words of God, for “the wise person will be satisfied with the fruit of his lips.”

So that, enriched in everything, you may abound in all simplicity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God. So that you may give simply to all who are in need, without discrimination—not asking to whom you should give, but why you should give.

For the ministry of this service not only supplies what the saints lack, but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord. You can have a double reward: the perfection of the saints and their thanksgivings to the Lord. Alternatively: it not only teaches the saints, but gives thanks to the Lord, who has instructed us with such great wisdom.

By the testing of this ministry, glorifying God through the obedience of your confession in the Gospel of Christ. Through this ministry you are proved to be Christians, magnifying God through the confession expressed in your works, just as, conversely, others are said to deny him by their deeds. Alternatively: you teach perfectly and show that what you magnify God through obedience is divine.

And through the simplicity of your fellowship with them and with all, and through their supplication for you. Giving simply to everyone, or teaching the good things that you share rather than merely give, confident that you will receive them back with multiplied interest. The administration of this service accomplishes all these things, and it abounds in this respect as well.

While they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Who would not long for people so distinguished from others by the grace either of knowledge or of mercy?

Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift. He has deigned, in his goodness, to bestow such great grace upon us. He now turns to carnal and spiritual weapons, to the Apostle’s authority, and to those who try to commend themselves.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0796D]

I myself, Paul, beg you by the gentleness and modesty of Christ. I ask you with the gentleness with which Christ, although he could have taken vengeance on those who injured him, refused to do so, so that they might correct themselves, even if late.

I who am humble in person among you, but when absent am confident toward you. The presence of the saints, because of their excessive humility, can be held in contempt by those who understand little. When absent, however, if necessary, they boldly display their authority. When present, they are as though they possessed no power at all—provided they find no offense in those subject to them.

But I beg you not to make me bold when I am present. Act in such a way that I do not need to display my power.

[Col. 0797A]

By that confidence by which I am thought bold against some. For every opinion has been formed according to the facts. But I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

Those who consider us to be walking according to the flesh. Those who think we possess no greater virtue than other human beings.

For although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but powerful through God. We appear to walk in a body, but as ministers of God we wage spiritual warfare. Indeed, the weapons of our warfare are not made of iron or fashioned by human hands, but are the power of God, by which one accomplishes more through the word than other human beings do with carnal weapons.

For the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments. False teachers fortify and surround their doctrine with the arguments of cunning; the Apostle destroys these aerial powers by the strength of spiritual grace, just as Paul blinded the magician who was overturning the ways of the Lord with perverse arguments. He likewise says that opposing theories, which make suggestions against Christ, must be destroyed.

And every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. What is more arrogant than to oppose divine doctrines?

And taking every understanding captive into the obedience of Christ. We destroy those who, under the name of obedience to Christ, wish to make every understanding captive to their own opinion.

And being ready to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience has been fulfilled. We are ready to avenge every disobedience when obedience has been fulfilled. The Apostle says that he is now ready to avenge every disobedience once they have fulfilled what is commanded. Alternatively, when your obedience through us has already been fulfilled, those people are not to be listened to: they claim to have received from the Lord the power to take vengeance, but they lie.

Look at what is according to outward appearance. That is, beware of those who boast in outward appearance. The proof of the matter is so evident that it is very easy to understand. Or: beware of those hypocrites who boast in their presence.

If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: that just as he himself belongs to Christ, so do we. No one is so foolish as one who boasts that he alone belongs to Christ.

For even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for building you up, I will not be ashamed. Even if I say that I received from Christ more authority than the others, as an Apostle, I will not be ashamed, because I speak the truth and do this not for boasting but because I am compelled for the sake of building you up.

And not for your destruction: I will not be ashamed. For they desire to exercise an authority that they have both usurped and use for destruction.

Lest I appear to be terrifying you through letters, since, they say, the letters are severe and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible. I say this so that no one may think that I am threatening to do what I cannot accomplish, as the deceivers boast about me.

Let the person who is such consider this: that what we are in word through letters when absent, we are also in deed when present. Let the one who thinks this know that I can do everything, if necessary, that I promise. For toward the obedient I am weak through humility, but toward sinners I am strong through severity.

For we do not dare to insert or compare ourselves with certain people who commend themselves. That is, we ought not to despise God so far as to make ourselves equal to people who prefer to be commended by their own praises rather than by God’s grace; nor can we boast greater things about ourselves than we actually are.

But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves. We do not go beyond the limits of our measure.

[Col. 0798B]

And comparing ourselves with ourselves. Not with those who are inferior, as when they, though nothing, make themselves not merely equal to the Apostles but even superior to them.

But we will not boast without measure; rather, according to the measure of the rule by which God measured out to us a measure extending as far as you. We do not extend ourselves beyond you as though we had not reached you. We do nothing beyond the human measure, but within the grace of the apostolate, as far as the Lord has deigned to grant us, we preach to you Corinthians. We did not do this by usurpation but by command.

For we reached you in the Gospel of Christ. Not in our own gospel, as those who, by preaching themselves, make the Gospel their own.

Not boasting without measure in the labors of others. It is without measure to boast in another’s labors. But they always went to believers who sought no signs at all.

But having hope that, as your faith grows, we shall be magnified among you according to our rule. We do not await gifts from you but a reward from God for your faith.

In abundance—even to evangelize in the regions beyond you. That is, it is not enough for us to reach you; but when your faith has grown, we shall go on to another place.

Not boasting in another’s rule about things already prepared. As they foolishly boast about things already prepared by others.

But whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord. He now urges boasting in the Lord, whose powers have worked in him.

For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends. The person who commends himself is the one who praises himself; the one whom the Lord commends is commended by the powers of his signs.

## CHAPTER XI

I wish that you would bear with a little of my foolishness—but indeed, bear with me. Bear with me, you who are accustomed to bearing with my great imprudence. He calls himself foolish because he had to say certain things about himself, although they were true, in order to show how truly foolish those are who falsely praise themselves. But indeed, bear with me.

For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ. That is, I am not inflamed by the goad of envy; rather, like a father, I guard you with divine jealousy, so that I may join you to Christ undefiled. You should conduct yourselves with all the greater devotion the better the bridegroom is to whom you are to be joined.

But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted. The serpent deceived Eve by lying about God, asserting that God had merely threatened death and would not actually bring it upon her. So also the false apostles claimed that the precepts of the Gospel had been added so that the ancient law might in this way be preserved, and zealous imitators seek to maintain that law alone as sufficient. Now the serpent similarly deceives certain people who assert that hell is mentioned only to inspire fear, claiming either that it does not exist at all or that it is not eternal, contrary to the authority of all the Scriptures.

And fall away from the simplicity. For simply to believe the word of God is not characteristic of perverse people.

Which is in Christ Jesus. A pure understanding that is joined to Christ, the one husband; and the promises made once to him alone are sufficient.

For if the one who comes preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or if you receive another spirit which you did not receive, or another Gospel which you did not accept, you rightly put up with him. If something more of grace were preached to you than you received through us, you might perhaps rightly tolerate their being preferred to us.

For I think that I have done nothing less. Do not suppose that I have done less than these people, who are not insignificant.

Than the great Apostles. How much more do Peter and the others preach that they received something less.

For even if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge. For I am like those who, although unskilled in knowledge, boast in inflated speech.

But in every respect I have been made manifest to you. He shows his integrity, by which he did everything through God, since he never sought greed, gluttony, or glory from them.

Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted? If this alone was perhaps my sin: that for your sake I even despised things that were lawful and permitted.

Because I freely preached the Gospel of God to you. We accepted neither the daily bread that the Lord ordained.

[Col. 0799D]

I robbed other churches, receiving support for your service. When I preached to you, the Macedonians ministered to me.

And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone. This was the true way of bearing with the weakness of little ones: even when in need, he did not wish to receive.

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked. They did not come forward by worshipfully honoring brothers whom they knew to be false, nor had they accepted false apostles; indeed, they prevailed over them.

And in everything I kept myself from being a burden to you, and will continue to do so. This is so when you are weak.

The truth of Christ is in me. Just as Christ established this once and did not deny it, so I must at some time act in this way without lying.

That this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. He does not abandon the boasting granted to him for God’s sake, especially if he suffers poverty.

Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. He himself knows whether I love you or not. Rather, it is because I love you greatly that I do not accept anything from you.

And what I do, I will continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity of those who desire an opportunity, so that in the matter of which they boast they may be found to be like us. Here he explains why he himself did not accept anything and why his adversaries taught gluttony and greed: they sought to find even the smallest opening for profit, so that he might accept bread here while they might demand gold more freely there. Therefore the Apostle removes the opportunity, so that in this matter those who teach for God’s sake may be shown to do so if they ask nothing from their disciples.

For such people are false apostles. They say, “Thus says the Lord,” although he himself did not send them, and they speak visions from their own heart.

Deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. A deceitful person is one who pretends to be one thing while doing another, so that under the appearance of evangelical preaching he may conceal his rapacity. Such preachers, in order to please human beings, must flatter; by flattering they please, and by pleasing they receive. They say what is praised, not what builds up the hearer. Most of them desire honor more than money, thinking themselves richly endowed if everyone praises them. Yet they do not reject money because they lack it, but because they possess it in hidden places. True and simple teachers, however, imitate the Apostles, saying: “For we have never been found in flattering speech, nor in an opportunity for greed, nor seeking glory from everyone, nor from you.”

And it is no wonder. For Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. One must not too easily put faith in dreams or in certain beings appearing as angels of light, lest Satan disguise himself as an angel of light and deceive and mislead the unwary.

Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. It is no wonder if Satan’s ministers, for the sake of greed—that is, glory—pretend to preach righteousness.

Their end will be according to their works. A bad end awaits bad works.

Again I say, let no one think me foolish. Otherwise, accept me as a foolish person, so that I too may boast a little. Above he said: “Bear with a little of my foolishness,” and he had given the reason: he was jealous for them with the jealousy of God and was not going to say something about himself out of a desire for glory, lest they turn against him and follow false apostles. If, then, his foolishness is so wise, how wise will wisdom itself be? It should also be noted that it should not be surprising if false teaching prevails for a time, since vengeance is promised to its authors at the end.

[Col. 0801A]

What I say, I do not say according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this matter of boasting. If here, compelled by the necessity of the people, he denies that he boasts according to the Lord, what should be thought of those who boast merely from empty display in the matter of boasting? For there is another true substance in which one may boast.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. To boast in the nobility of an earthly lineage is carnal.

For you gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise. I see that, although you have been instructed, you have easily agreed with fools who are worth nothing.

For you tolerate it if someone enslaves you. To the law or to the Pharisees, who exercised domination over the people.

[Col. 0801B]
