What Adomim signifies, I, 701. Much blood was shed there through the attacks of robbers, ibid. The Lord mentions this place in the parable of the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, III, 149.

Adonis, Venus’s lover, I, 320.

The gardens of Adonis, IV, 774.

The grove of Adonis, I, 322.

The custom of worshiping, I, 1023. Another custom of worshiping among the ancients, IV, 952. Each person worships what he loves, IV, 953. The Jews worshiped facing the temple, wherever they might have been, V, 90. What does it mean to worship by falling down? V, 638. It is not permitted to worship statues and images of kings, 641. True worshipers worship God everywhere, I, 320.

What Adorea or Adoria was among the ancients, I, 907.

Adrammelech, an idol of the Assyrians worshiped by the Samaritans, III, 162.

The islands of the Adriatic, I, 638. Their waves, 727.

The Adriatic Sea, I, 695. Its tides, 409.

Hadrian, trained in the arts of philosophy, consecrated Antinous as a god, etc., IV, 35.

The coming of Christ, I, 927. Christ’s second coming in glory is to be demonstrated, VII, 193. What is its sign? 194 and following. Jewish tradition concerning Christ’s coming at midnight, 202.

In adversity and prosperity alike, let God’s will be praised, I, 179. What can a person say who glories in God’s mercy amid adversity? ibid.

The powers opposed to us are stronger by nature, but we are stronger through faith, IV, 1062.

Flattery is always treacherous, crafty, and pleasant, I, 222. Where there is no flattery, 501.

A flatterer is a pleasant enemy, I, 89. We readily favor our flatterers, 107. Flatterers must be avoided, 324. The rebuker who heals loves more than the flatterer who anoints the head, 304. The nature of flatterers and cowards, 240. How is a flatterer defined? II, 709. To flatter properly belongs to heretics, II, 723. What is said about those who reject the austerity of teachers and favor flatterers, IV, 407. To flatter the wicked because of their power and despise the good because of their poverty is a widespread vice, V, 82. The impious must not be flattered, 637. Flatterers of royal eminence, VI, 332. Flatterers are not to be believed, 515. Let us not be foolish flatterers of God, 604.

In Jerome’s time adultery was customarily punished by death, I, 3. It is condemned even among pagans, 459. The apostle [Col. 0915] Paul takes care that children born of adultery not be killed for fear of childbirth, I, 901.

An adulterer is called one who violates holy things, corrupts the chaste, etc., V, 206.

Forensic advocates who lie in conducting other people’s cases, I, 768.

We build as though we were always going to live, I, 965.

God’s building, V, 756. The devil’s building, ibid.

The word “building up” is used of small works, VII, 627.

The aediles restrained the rage of sellers, I, 944. The Greeks call them ἀγορανόμοι (*agoranomoi*), “market overseers,” ibid.

You rebuke with difficulty what you allow to become habitual, I, 685.

Who ought to attend a sick person? III, 258. Clemency and diligence toward the sick, 707. Many sick people prefer death to life, II, 483. The sick who prefer death to life, VII, 658.

Egypt is always understood as this world, I, 204. It cherished the little Christ and defended the adult with the warmth of faith, 581. Egypt and Parthia know the hospice at the Roman harbor, 466.

The individual cities of Egypt worship individual animals, II, 335. They derive their names from them, ibid. In Egypt and Palestine the cow is not eaten, 334.

Egypt is called Mesraim in Sacred Scripture, III, 13. In Jerome’s time the language of the Egyptians was called Ham, 316. Low-lying Egypt is watered by waters coming from Ethiopia, 399. In what respects is Egypt most fertile? IV, 203. The Egyptian desert is fertile in poisonous animals, 781. What are the idols of the Egyptians? 165. No nation was so devoted to idolatry as Egypt, 540. The Egyptians call their regions *nomoi*, “districts,” 165. How great is the lust of the Egyptians? 848. The Egyptians are called flies, and the Assyrians bees, 113. Egypt is blessed through its association with Israel, 300. Among the Hebrews, Egypt, Egyptian, and Egyptians are called by one word, Mesraim, 198. God built houses for the Egyptian midwives, 792.

Among the Egyptians, a husband is taken only once for the rites of Taurus, I, 906.

The Egyptian priests used linen garments, V, 547.

Aelia Jerusalem, V, 695 and 891.

Aelius Hadrian overcame the rebellious Jews, V, 695.

Good and bad rivalry, VII, 463, 464. We scarcely lack it, 507.

What is said about Aeneas, I, 401. The resurrection of Aeneas and Dorcas, 696.

Riddles are proper to dialecticians and philosophers, I, 426.

A riddle and a parable present one thing in their words and another in their meanings, V, 190.

What is an *aenigmatiste* among the Greeks? II, 285.

Aeolic is the fifth language of Greece, III, 318. From where the Aeolids come, ibid.

Aeon, or Αἰών, the span of human life, V, 302. The thirty aeons of Valentinus, VI, 257.

The difference between equality and likeness, V, 331.

Few are guided by equity, VI, 51.

The air is called heaven, IV, 142.

The harshness of the air permits nothing to be covered except the private parts, II, 44. Corrupted air and pestilence from the stench of dead locusts, VI, 195.

The heresy of the Aerii, II, 416.

Mount Hermon, which the Phoenicians called Sanior and the Amorites Sanir; on its summit was a notable temple of idols, III, 145.

Bronze from Cyprus on which monstrous figures were sculpted, II, 23.

The substance of bronze is more sonorous than all metals, V, 465.

Aeschines lived in exile at Rhodes, I, 272. What he is then reported to have said, ibid. His speech, 308.

Asclepius, II, 622. The prophets of Asclepius were consulted, 23. The poets’ fables boast that Asclepius revived Virbius, IV, 352. The shrine of Asclepius was celebrated for dreams of future events, 775.

Aesop’s fable, I, 501. Aesop’s crow, 705.

Esther, amid purple and jewels, overcame pride with humility, I, 502.

The moments of our life diminish with every action, I, 346. The various conditions of this life are not perceived, ibid. Desired old age promises us not nearness to death, but a span of years, 913. A fragile sex and a weak age should not use its own judgment, 290. The ardor of youth is quenched by God’s mercy and the rigor of fasts, 987. To admonish a slippery age is an act of piety, 504. One should not readily believe whatever is said about advanced age, when a person’s past life defends it and the title of dignity honors it, 946. If one of mature age and independent status is imputed to the parents, how much more one who is nursing and frail? 684. The order of age is commended, II, 279. What is said about the differing ages of the two sexes, 789. The flourishing age soon falls, IV, 494. The age of the old is venerable even among enemies, [Col. 0916] 551. Mature age seeks prudent counsel, V, 78. Mature age condemns the errors of youth, 457.

The priestly age among the Hebrews, V, 4. Before priestly age, which portions of the Old Testament are not permitted to be read? ibid., in the prologue.

Compared with eternity, all time is brief, V, 359. The eternity of ages and times, VII, 691. God has one time: eternity, ibid. Compared with eternity, all time is brief, 758.

The Ethiopians were subject to the Medes, VI, 710. In Scripture those immersed in vices are called Ethiopians, ibid. Examples of Ethiopians pleasing to God, 674.

The Ethiopian woman, Moses’ wife, I, 480.

The Ethiopian changes the color of his skin against nature, and the leopard its spots, I, 420. Ethiopians are ironically called “silver-colored,” 187.

Ethiopia is called Cush by the Hebrews, III, 319. Ethiopia is near Egypt, V, 356.

The fires of Etna, I, 287.

The Stoics teach that affections should be eradicated, I, 1026. The affections of the soul were created for the good, III, 508. What order exists in affection? VII, 65.

Affliction in the world is the material of rewards, I, 711. The saints willingly endure afflictions, IV, 979. Every affliction is dispensed by God as judge, VI, 181.

Africans are accustomed to eat green lizards, II, 334. The Africans altered the Phoenician language in part, VII, 429.

Africanus, a historian of the ages, VII, 11. His exposition of the Seventy Weeks, V, 682.

What is reported about the grammarian Afer, II, 556.

Agamemnon destroyed Troy after a ten-year siege, I, 691.

Agamnestor, commander of the Athenians, I, 46.

What is *agape*? I, 117. The plague of the Agapetae, 98.

Agape, a blind woman, led the blind Elpidius into a pit, I, 1032.

Hagar and Sarah signify the two Testaments, I, 910. Whether Hagar carried a grown son on her shoulders, I, 166. Hagar is the same as Keturah, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, III, 342. The interpretation of Hagar, VII, 472. Nearly everyone gives the same explanation concerning Hagar and Sarah, ibid. Another explanation is given concerning them, ibid.

The Hagarenes, called Saracens, in the vicinity of Jerusalem, I, 972. The same, IV, 217.

Agatho, bishop, I, 536.

The pride and debauchery of Agathocles, the brother of a female harpist, whom Ptolemy appointed commander of Egypt, V, 707.

The city of Agenor, VII, 427.

The concepts of agent and patient, VII, 570.

The meaning of the name Ageruchia, I, 900. A noble crowd of relatives surrounds her, ibid. She was brought up by her paternal aunt, ibid. Ageruchia does not preserve monogamy for her family, but restores it, ibid. She had a posthumous son named Simplicius, ibid. Her husband bore the same name, ibid. Ageruchia avoids many nobles of the palace, ibid. The devil inflames these men in rivalry so that they may test her chastity, ibid. Her nobility, beauty, age, and wealth make her desirable, ibid.

A watered and pleasurable field, II, 337. No one possesses a field securely, 196.

Haggai is interpreted as “festive and joyful,” I, 278. What he prophesied about, ibid. Whether he was an angel clothed in a human body, VI, 751.

Blessed Agnes overcame both age and the tyrant, I, 979. She consecrated the title of chastity through martyrdom, ibid.

The sacrifice of the mystical Lamb, I, 265.

How recognition differs from knowledge, II, 614. What is recognition? VII, 563.

Our judge of the contest, Christ, is not envious, I, 432.

In the field of good earth, three fruits are found, I, 393.

A kind of grass, *agrostis*, VI, 108.

Aila, a city overlooking the Red Sea, II, 21.

The letter *Ayin* is a vowel among the Hebrews, III, 11. It is read as G by the Septuagint interpreters, ibid., and 17, 35, 42, 130, 218.

Akiba, the teacher of Aquila, IV, 122.

What are the wings of ships? IV, 285.

The six wings of the two Seraphim, I, 49.

Alanus, I, 344.

Albina, mother of Marcella, I, 950.

She urges her daughter toward a second marriage, 951. She is called a common mother, 153. The death of Albina, the mother of St. Marcella, is announced to Jerome, VII, 367.

Albinus, in place of Albina, I, 677. Whom he greets, 1067.

Albinus, successor to Festus in the administration of Judaea, II, 831.

Alcaeus, I, 279.

They say that Alcestis died voluntarily for Admetus, II, 311.

Alcibiades, II, 241. By whom he was killed, 311. The love of his concubine for him, ibid.

The adultery of Alcmene, II, 397.

The Alemanni, I, 914.

Alentius the deacon, I, 1047.

[Col. 0917] Alethius the presbyter, I, 851.

Alexander, king and high priest of the Jews, V, 686. After her husband’s death, his wife Alexandra obtained rule over the Jews and distributed it among her sons, 687.

Alexander of Macedon, conqueror of the world, I, 682. In character and bearing he could not be free from the vices of his teacher Leonidas, ibid. He perished by Babylonian poison, 689. Alexander’s barriers restrain savage peoples, 464. The same Alexander the Great, II, 567. What Alexander is reported to have said at the tomb of Achilles, 13. Why Alexander was called a leopard, IV, 872. Alexander the Great was called a he-goat, 212. He perished by poison, and his kingdom was divided into parts, ibid. Why is the kingdom of Alexander the Great made of bronze? V, 634. The victories and death of Alexander the Great, 703. His successors, ibid. Alexander’s swift victory, 668. Alexander besieged and captured Tyre, 305. He also defeated Darius in Lycia, ibid.

The commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias, I, 237, and II, 476 and 635.

Alexander the monk, I, 799.

Alexander the emperor, II, 893. He was the son of Mammaea, 899.

Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, II, 879. His letter survives, ibid. He governed the Church with Narcissus, ibid. He slept in prison for confessing Christ, 595.

A work of Alexander the heretic, VII, 369.

Alexandria was formerly called No, I, 704. It boasted that it shared in the Roman faith, 535. A standard of the cross was erected at Alexandria, and the crowd of peoples looks upon the shining trophies against heresy, ibid. Alexandria is called Diospolis, or the city of Jupiter, III, 84. Alexandria, which was previously called No, received its name from Alexander of Macedon, VI, 94. It is the metropolis of Egypt, ibid.

The Alexandrian decree, I, 39.

The custom of the Alexandrian Church, II, 875. Its martyrs, 492. Alexandria and Egypt praise Hesychius as the author of their Septuagint, 522. What was established at the Alexandrian Synod, 193. The West gave its assent to it, ibid.

The Hebrew alphabet, I, 146 and following. Which things in Sacred Scripture begin in order with its letters, ibid.

Jerome says that he explained the Hebrew alphabet, III, 73. How the alphabet was read among the Greeks and Hebrews, IV, 1019.

Alien sons, those generated in the error of idols, VI, 50.

Public laws forbid coveting what belongs to others, I, 112.

God spares those alienated from him because of his own gentleness, V, 877.

Allegory: what is it? VII, 471. The books of orators and poets are full of allegories, ibid. It is called spiritual understanding, ibid. The clearest prophecy in Scripture must not be weakened by the uncertainties of allegory, VI, 952.

Alleluia. See Epistle XXVI. It was customarily sung at the funerals of Christians, I, 466. A signal for the gathering, II, 622.

The Roman army was defeated at the Allia, I, 914.

The Jewish interpretation of the word *Almah*, II, 287. The true meaning is given from the Hebrew, 288. In Hebrew Scripture *Almah* always signifies a hidden virgin, not a married young woman, III, 342 and 343.

The Julian Alps, I, 914. Different names of the Alps according to the variety of places, 344. Whatever lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees was devastated by various enemies, 913.

With what reverence one should serve in the ministry of Christ’s altar, I, 759. Horses were stabled at Christ’s altars, 344. The Church has one altar, not many, IV, 207. One altar, just as there is one faith and one Church, 208. The Church has one altar, VI, 262. Heretics have many altars, ibid. They have as many altars as schisms, ibid. Heretics boast that they have one altar, ibid.

The temple altar was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, I, 381. God’s altar was constructed from unhewn stones, IV, 779. The crown of the altar in the form of a lily, V, 530. The Lord’s two altars, one golden and one bronze, 94. It is not understood how the altar on which the fire was to be kindled could suffer nothing from it, 503. Why are a grove and trees not planted beside the Lord’s altar? VI, 40.

The strait of Altinum, I, 337.

Alypius had seen Jerome, I, 301. Jerome greets him, 634.

Amabilis the bishop, IV, 167.

Haman is interpreted as “iniquity,” I, 105.

Amalek and the Canaanite are called Amorite in Deuteronomy, III, 202. The ancestors of the Amalekites, 350.

After God, children and relatives are to be loved, III, 411. The judgments of lovers are blind, VI, 109. It is necessary to love something, I, 100. Lovers are granted nothing, 124. What are the sweet words of lovers? 260. Loving and being loved sometimes happen to certain people through magical arts, VII, 506.

Bitterness that should not be rejected, I, 474. Bitterness and fury are forms of anger, VII, 635. It is opposed to sweetness, 636. God is changed into bitterness by our vices, although by his nature he is sweet and kind, V, 30.

[Col. 0918] Amathas, a disciple of Antony, II, 2. He buried his body, ibid.

The self-lover deceives himself, VII, 522. We are kind when God is dishonored, but exercise hatred when we ourselves are concerned, 141.

The Amazons, II, 328.

The Ambiani, I, 914.

Ambition that does not cease amid mourning and tears, II, 14.

Ambrose, Origen’s ἐργοδιώκτης (*ergodióktēs*), “taskmaster” or “driving worker,” I, 192. He is accused of rashness, 532. A just criticism of him as a wealthy man, II, 897 and 901.

Ambrose the brother brought Jerome small gifts and letters, I, 270.

St. Ambrose, I, 41, 230. St. Ambrose’s book *On Widows*, 225. Much is quoted from it, 226. Jerome weighs and praises his words, ibid. He wrote three little books on virgins, ibid. They are praised, 106. Ambrose’s books *On Duties*, 774. He compiled Origen’s *Hexameron*, 529. He followed the opinions of Hippolytus and Basil, ibid. He followed Origen, 753. Praises of Ambrose, II, 647, 648. Ambrose’s books are full of Origen’s sermons, 644. He is called a pillar of the Church, ibid. Rufinus wished Ambrose to be torn apart by Jerome, 647. He was an interpreter of Origen, 504.

Ambrosia and nectar of the pagans, IV, 438.

Amen, an approval of what has been said, IV, 787. What does “Amen” signify? VII, 35, 380, 535.

A friendship that can end was never true, I, 13. A true friend should not conceal what he thinks, 511. The fickleness of human friendship, 761. Every suspicion must be removed from it, 638. To will and not will the same things: that finally is firm friendship, 988. That friendship is true which is brought about not by the usefulness of household property, nor merely by bodily presence, but by fear of God and devotion to the Scriptures, 270. It is better to endure the lasting hostility of human beings than to provoke God’s offense through harmful friendships, 719. Under pretext of conversation, someone may seek the friendship of powerful people, 498. What are Christian friendships? 779. False friendships, 195. The friendship of good people should be sought, 456. From what do firm friendships arise? II, 539. There is no greater hostility than to join friendships out of necessity, 753.

Amici are rare who are good and faithful, II, 756. Their plots must be guarded against, 776. It belongs to a prudent person, even after a quarrel with a friend has been reconciled, to avoid slight suspicions, 459. If a friend has spoken on your behalf, he will be considered not a witness or judge, but an advocate, 410. One must never boast of the judgment of friends. A friend judges what is wrong as right, 409. The loyalty of friends proved by example, VII, 142. A friend is sought for a long time, found with difficulty, and preserved with difficulty, I, 13. In friends it is not the thing but the intention that is sought, 409. Charity joins friends no less than nature does, 17. They may hold different opinions and yet not injure one another on that account, 640. The vices of friends are not to be praised, 523. Even in friends we fear what is safe, 537. A friend strikes in one way, an enemy in another, IV, 1056. What is a friend? VI, 516. The rich have many friends, the poor none, ibid. He is sought for a long time, found with difficulty, and preserved with difficulty, ibid. Friends are called brothers, 233. In what does true friendship consist? 517. When is the same friendship delicate? ibid.

Aminadab: what does the name signify? II, 287.

Ammana, the name of a city which is also Philadelphia, VI, 572.

Ammonius condemned, I, 1030.

Ammon, bishop of Berenice, II, 911.

The Ammonites were born from the stock of Lot’s descendants, VI, 236. They dwell in Arabia, where Philadelphia now stands, ibid. Rabbah was their metropolis, ibid.

Beautiful and elevated places were always dedicated to idols, IV, 849.

Love knows no order, I, 21. What does the love of Christ accomplish? 124. What bonds the love of God and fear of Gehenna break, 31. Holy love has no impatience, 290. What does an unchaste man do? 1090. Negligence can be corrected more easily than love can arise, 18. Injured love ought to grow angry, 29. Great devotion toward one’s own is impiety toward God, 184. Love driven out by love, 942. Illicit loves cannot be uprooted in an old man, 787. Holy love has no impatience, II, 401. The whole attack on love is set forth in Plato, 318. Lysias explains its disadvantages, ibid. No one can be possessed by two loves: if you are a lover of the flesh, you do not grasp the love of the spirit, III, 505.

The pure love of charity, VII, 750.

The Amorites were expelled after their sins had reached completion, VI, 213.

Amos, while gathering blackberries from brambles, suddenly became a prophet, I, 35. Concerning whom he prophesies, 277. It cannot be explained in a few words, ibid. The tomb of the prophet Amos at Tekoa, III, 206, 283. The name Amos is written among the Hebrews with different letters and interpreted in different ways, IV, 7, 8. Amos, the father of Isaiah, is not the third of the Twelve Prophets, 8. Amos the shepherd of livestock uses in his prophecy expressions from his own craft, VI, 225. Amos preaches not at all to Jerusalem, but to Israel and in Samaria, 221.

Amphiaraus betrayed by his wife, II, 317.

Amphilochius, I, 66.

[Col. 0919] Amphimallum, I, 435.

Amulius, king of the Latins, I, 46.

What Ana found in the desert: hot springs, or a pool, or exceptionally swift asses? III, 363.

The Anabasii, who… II, 533.

The way of life of the anchorites, I, 120.

Anacletus III, bishop of Rome, II, 853.

Anagogy: what is it? I, 851.

*Anamartetos*—the same as “without sin,” I, 1028.

Ananias and Sapphira: why were they condemned? I, 990. They are punished not by the cruelty of the sentence, but as an example of correction, ibid. Ananias and Sapphira timidly kept what was theirs, 324.

The Hebrews relate that Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael, returning from captivity, brought gold and silver as gifts for the Temple, and the crowns of the high priest and the commander, VI, 828.

Anastasius condemned Origen, I, 583. Rome did not deserve to retain him long; why? 958. He is praised, 992. Anastasius, bishop of the city of Rome, II, 491, 515, 546, 550, 553, 560, 564. He declares Origen a heretic, 465. A letter of Pope Anastasius, 549. One to John of Jerusalem, 505.

Anathema: what is it? I, 839 ff.

Anathoth: what does it signify? V, 816. How far it is from Jerusalem, IV, 923.

Anatolius, priest of the church of Laodicea, I, 429.

The opinion of Anaxagoras, I, 334.

The second book of Anaxilides on philosophy, II, 309.

Anchira, the metropolis of Galatia: by how many schisms was it torn apart? VII, 427.

You should know that maidservants who attend upon their mistress are lying in wait for you, I, 936. The baser their condition, the easier their downfall, ibid. A virgin maidservant who comes forth more adorned than her mistresses: why is she worthy of mourning? 802. Others are noted, ibid.

The Andabatae’s manner of fighting, II, 210. What does it mean to fight in their manner? 294.

The goodwill of the apostles Andrew and Philip, I, 890. The bodies of Saints Andrew, Luke, and Timothy translated to Constantinople, II, 301.

Andromeda fastened to the rock, I, 966.

Anea, a village in which all the inhabitants were Christians, III, 151.

Among the angels there is neither male nor female, I, 213. The joy of the angels over sinners doing penance, 896. The guardian angel, 1090. Guardian angels of places, 453. We shall be like the angels in heaven, ibid. The likeness of angels is promised to us, but not their nature, 817. The Lord promises us not the substance of angels, but their manner of life and blessedness, ibid. When we are said to become like angels, the nature of bodies is not removed, but the greatness of glory is shown, 453. By what means is the life of angels obtained in a human body? 987. “Angels” is the name of an office, II, 423. According to their nature they are invisible, 415. They are read to be immortal by grace, not by nature, 750. Nowhere is it heard that spiritual powers celebrate weddings in heaven, 439. The merits of angels differ, 369. The army of angels is called the camp of God, 790. There is subordination among them, 479. They have different kinds of offices and merits, 480. They can receive sin, 329. In what does the likeness of angels consist? 439. A fallen angel, 482, 612. The abandoned charity of the angel of Ephesus is charged against him, 198. In the angel of the church of Pergamum, the eating of sacrifices offered to idols and the teaching of the Nicolaitans are condemned, 198. Angels preside over this world, III, 487. An angel accompanies each of us, by whom our words are carried to God, 428. Angels go around the earth and are ministering spirits who, like birds, carry our words and thoughts to heaven, 479. Angels set over human beings surpass human power and can prevent injuries to their clients, 429. Where the angels sang at the Lord’s birth, 361. The protection of angels, IV, 1055. Guardian angels, 673. Angels who preside, 550. Angels preside over the gates of the Lord’s city, 344. Angels preside over individual nations, 264, 441. Angels preside over the human race, 246. Everyone has a guardian angel, 822. Angels stand in God’s presence, 950. Heaven is the dwelling place of angels, 537, 650. Angels are called birds, 547. Angels are fiery stones, 638. In what sense are angels said to have wings? 92. Angels and holy men are called vehicles by which human beings are brought to faith, 821. The entire multitude of human beings, compared with the multitude of angels, is counted as nothing, 488. We imitate angels through the virtues, 702. What angels do in heaven must be done on earth, 586. The Spirit of the Lord is to be understood as an angel, 754. Good and evil angels designated, 236. Evil angels preside over provinces, 337. Angels preside over all things, V, 818. The offices of angels, 669. The principal kingdoms entrusted to four angels, 663. An apostrophe to the guardian angel, 889. Angels are often called gods, 643. We imitate the offices of angels, 647. Evil angels are placed over punishments, 362. Angels are administrators of human affairs, VI, 500. They are praised and accused according to the virtues or vices of those over whom they preside, ibid. Angels designated for the governance of the world, 662. Angels ministered to Christ on earth, 785. The mind illuminated by God is our angel, 808. The protection of angels, 17. Some think that John the Baptist, Malachi, and Haggai were angels, 751. The worst angels are called the army of God, 190. Angels and apostles are changeable by nature, VII, 383. The help and protection of angels, 21, 140. Guardian angels, 446. They preside over the four elements, 447. The various ministries of angels toward Christ, 241. The powers of heaven—angels, 197, 198. God speaking in angels and through angels, 442. In what sense do angels have fathers in heaven? 601. A fallen angel, 619. Apostate angels, 576.

A corner is used for a kingdom, IV, 205.

In straits and hardships: what should be read? I, 124. The glory of the future age alleviates present hardships, 620. What should be said for consolation in hardships? IV, 884. God crushes us in various hardships so that he may thresh out the straw, 306. What are we accustomed to say when placed in hardships? VI, 301.

Annianus succeeded Marcus, II, 845. Anicetus governing the Church, II, 857. He was the tenth bishop of Rome after Peter, 863.

The soul is immortal and continues to exist after death, I, 334. Some have philosophized about it, ibid. It knows no distinction of sex, 900. Some churchmen think that souls were created long ago and are kept in God’s treasury, 948. Others think that they are made by God each day, ibid. Where Jerome wrote about the origin of the soul, 949. The opinion of most Westerners concerning it, 948. Various other views are noted, ibid. What is thought concerning its name? 598. If it is without mind and sensation, it is compared with animals, 588. Every sorrowful soul is separated from the body, 127. How the treasury of souls is emptied, 617. Prudence of the soul cannot itself be called the soul, 588. Disembodied souls are not called man and woman, but bodies are, 624. The nourishment of Christian souls is to meditate on the law of the Lord, 15. The true temple of Christ is the soul of the believer, 324. It must be adorned so that it may deserve to receive Christ, ibid. What is more beautiful than a soul called the daughter of God and seeking no adornments from outside? 283. How must she be educated who is to become the Lord’s temple? 681. A soul devoted to God’s sacrifices ought to be free from every affection, 182. Its enemies are various, 31. Let us fortify it with the wall of continence, 605. Let us protect its freedom by the daily exercise of virtues, ibid. With all our strength let us cleanse our souls from every defilement, 585. The soul’s freedom is oppressed by vices and healed by meditation on the virtues, 608. The cleanliness of the body and clothing is its uncleanness, 713. What is sought in us is not the adornment of the body but the vigor of the soul, etc., 288. Take care not of your household property but of your soul, 936. By what summit is the soul’s edification protected? 719. Spare no one, so that you may spare the soul alone, 936. Let the little body not rest before the soul has been fed, 121. It wavers midway between the works of the flesh and of the spirit, 506. The soul desires one thing, while the flesh is compelled to do another, 896. Those who have sold their souls to various desires are called servants of those to whom they have surrendered themselves, 605. By preserving the commands of the laws, it is separated from the contagion of evil people, 614. By what means does the usually barren soil of souls become fertile? 933. The goods of the flesh are not to be sought in its praises, 336. The Lord seeks the souls of believers more than their wealth, 433. How it is carried headlong into the depths of ungodliness, 605. God received no soul that is separated from the body against his will, 180. The soul is not of God’s substance, II, 426. The church’s opinion concerning the origin of souls, 557. Three origins of souls are noted, 497. Three opinions concerning the same subject, 558. God fashions rational souls every day, 427. We share the soul with the gods, and the body with beasts, 339. The body is called the child, the soul the pedagogue, ibid. The body is the soul’s bond, 481. Comparisons of soul and body, 339. God is the creator of both, 428. Compacted from soul and body, we derive the nature of both substances, 794. Just as a body is called healthy if it is afflicted by no illness, so the soul is healthy if shaken by no disturbance, ibid. What is demanded is not polish of tongue, but piety of soul, 224. From where does its great exultation arise? 341. The soul’s refreshment must be sought before that of the body, 27. It endures the assault of thoughts and disturbances: why? 704. The soul enters the bodies of infants, III, 482. Those who think that souls are sown together with bodies and generated not by God but by the parents of bodies are to be laughed at, 492. The soul was created in the image of God, IV, 594. The soul’s ornaments: what are they? 872. The virtues are the soul’s goods; the vices, its evils, 645. The souls of the saints are always in God’s heart, 570. The souls of the saints are called hills and mountains according to the variety of their virtues, 653. Our soul is called God’s vineyard and a paradise of fruits when reason presides and has God as its guardian, 18. The soul’s freedom must be preserved, 700. The desolation and misery of souls that have fallen from their former holiness, 16, 17. After the night’s rest, the soul is more vigorous for hearing and doing what is said, [Col. 0921] 893. Disturbance of the soul is called drunkenness, 76. A shameless soul is never satisfied with its error, 662. The affection of all souls for their offspring is innate, 810. What living creatures dwell in desert lands? 444. Pure souls created by God, V, 257. The desolation and misery of souls that have fallen from their former holiness, 171. The foulness of the soul when it prostitutes itself to vices, 267. The tripartite soul, 898. The beauty of the soul, 951. The soul placed midway between virtues and vices, VI, 375. All souls belong to God, 175. What is the true cause of the soul’s joy? 728. By its nature every soul is God’s tabernacle, not the devil’s, 597. The soul becomes like the one to whom it clings, either God or the world, 578. Where is the soul led when separated from the body? 348. It cannot escape God’s hand, ibid. The soul is invisible and incorporeal, VII, 62. It will be punished together with the body, ibid. The soul’s principal faculty is in the heart, not in the brain, 114. The soul is placed in a certain middle position between flesh and spirit, 505. It stands midway between the strife of flesh and spirit, 502. The great dignity of souls, 139. It has its own senses and members, as the body does, 420, 678. For what purpose did we receive a soul and understanding? 620. Where, according to some, do souls released from bodies dwell? 676. How the Christian soul loves and nourishes the flesh, 658. There is no greater gain than if someone wins a human soul, 705.

Brute animals follow their guides, I, 942. They do not fall into the same nets, 283. The desert of this age nourishes such creatures, 934. An animal cannot live unless it is capable of growth, II, 340. Brute animals, although on a long journey, know the byways on a second journey, 486. Dumb animals perceive that God exists, 12. A multitude of poisonous animals suddenly boiling up, 32. Brute animals cured, 25. Poisonous creatures are noted, 47. Different living creatures are likenesses among human beings of different kinds of behavior, IV, 259.

What the four animals in Ezekiel signify, I, 368. The animals assigned to the Evangelists, VII, 6.

The human mind divided into three parts, I, 505. The human mind’s change into different states, II, 737. Nothing overwhelms it so much as a full belly, 341. The different appearance of minds within one person, I, 193. Some recovered in body and began to be sick in mind, 25. Let both body and mind be stretched toward the Lord, 939. To have laid aside one’s mind is more than to have laid aside one’s dress, 458. What ought we to anticipate in our minds? 342. The softness of the mind must be overcome, 343. Let it not swell with pride, 936. The charity of minds, not bodies, is commended, IV, 766. Joy of mind alleviates bodily pain, 15. The four disturbances of the mind, VI, 171. See *Mens*, *Ingenium*, *Pectus*.

The Anicii, a family of illustrious blood, I, 977. In it there was either no one, or scarcely anyone, who had not deserved the consulship, ibid.

Anna is interpreted as “grace,” I, 292. What does she fear? ibid. She changed barrenness of the womb into fertility, ibid. Formerly barren, she became more fruitful than Peninnah in her abundance, 680. She bore Samuel not for herself but for the tabernacle, 508. After offering the son whom she had vowed to God, Anna never took him back, 937, 689. After conceiving, she did not dare approach the Temple until she had first returned what she owed, ibid. Why was she deemed worthy to have many children? 689. Anna is to be imitated by widows, 508. She first received the Savior of the world, conscious of future mysteries, ibid. Her ardor becomes an object of wonder, 978.

What the Hebrew word *Anna* signifies, VII, 766.

The years of the ancient Fathers before the Flood, I, 255. The cycle of the year, 368. The seventh year begins to blush, etc., 964. The years of the present age signify future ages, IV, 276. The thirtieth year is the strongest in human beings, the third in cattle and beasts of burden, 187. Where does the word “year” come from? V, 11. Six thousand years had not yet been completed in Jerome’s time, VII, 691. The calculation of the years from Abraham to Moses sought by many, 440.

The Jewish Year of Jubilee, IV, 50. The true Year of Jubilee, 690. In the year of remission, or Jubilee, every purchase returned to the seller, V, 69.

Annianus, pseudo-deacon of Celeda, I, 1067. A few things are said about him, ibid.

A very good saying of Annia, II, 312.

A gold seal-ring, I, 953.

The book entitled The Ring, by Sextus the Pythagorean, attributed to Pope Sixtus, IV, 993.

What the preposition *ante* often indicates, II, 207.

The Anthropomorphites, II, 418. Their heresy, 589.

The Antichrist pretends to be Christ, I, 123. The Antichrist’s veil, 286. The expected coming of the Antichrist, II, 889. The true preaching of the Antichrist, 357. His synagogue: what is it? 201. The people of Israel will receive the Antichrist in place of Christ, III, 426.

The Antichrist will perform many signs, IV, 241. The devil is the parent of the Antichrist, 271. According to some, the Antichrist will be destroyed on the Mount of Olives, 341. The Antichrist, the Christ of the Jews, V, 468. Just as Christ had saints as types, so does the Antichrist, 715. In what does the Antichrist’s pride consist? [Col. 0922] ibid. Many of our people think that Domitius Nero will be the Antichrist, 715. The Antichrist will fight against the saints of the Lord, VI, 214.

An extremely bitter antidote is given by physicians to a nauseated stomach, IV, 596.

Antigonus of Carystus, II, 821.

A reconciliation of contradiction, V, 577.

Antimus, a false monk, I, 112.

Antinoüs: from where did the city receive its name? II, 336.

Antinoüs, the slave of Hadrian Caesar, II, 863. A gymnastic contest was held for him, and there is a city called Antinoüs after his name, ibid.

The church of Antioch split into three parties, I, 43. Antioch was formerly called Reblatha, IV, 169. Antioch, Laodicea, and Apamea were enlarged after the empire of the Macedonians, 192.

Antioch is besieged, I, 345. Antioch, the metropolis of the entire East, II, 447. It is a city of Syria, 41.

Antiochus, a name of kings among the Syrians, V, 341.

Antiochus the Great, king of Syria, made war on Ptolemy Philopator and was defeated, V, 707. He was defeated by A. L. Scipio and ordered to reign within the Taurus, 710. His war against Ptolemy Epiphanes was conducted with varying success, 709. He betrothed his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy Epiphanes, 710. While fighting against the Elymaeans, he was destroyed together with his entire army, ibid.

Antiochus *Theos*—“God”—was killed by poison through his wife Laodice, V, 705.

Antiochus Epiphanes, an exceedingly cruel king, II, 779. Antiochus Epiphanes, who was also called Philopator, V, 674. A certain faction of the Jews incited him to persecute the people, 49. The same man, while a hostage at Rome, seized the kingdom by deceit, 674. He desired to plunder the temple of Diana, 675 and 712 ff. A type and figure of the Antichrist, 673 and 711. How cunning he was in subjugating and devastating Egypt, 713. He besieged the two Ptolemaic brothers at Alexandria, 715. He compelled the Jews and Samaritans to worship the idols of Greece, 716 and 719. He was so luxurious that he publicly consorted with prostitutes and mime-actors, 719. He fought against Artaxias, king of Armenia, 667, 668 and 722. He ordered his statue to be placed in God’s Temple, 718. His death, 676. Why he was punished, 719.

Antipatris, a small town: from where does it get its name? I, 696.

Antipater wanders among thorns, II, 371.

What did Antisthenes do? I, 433, 399. The history of Antisthenes, II, 345.

M. Antoninus, II, 857, 865.

Antoninus Verus, ibid. He was a pupil of Fronto the Orator, 865. A book in defense of Christian doctrine was presented to him, ibid.

Antoninus Caracalla, II, 875.

The emperor Antoninus Pius, I, 428. The emperor Antoninus Pius, II, 857, 865.

Antonius joined to Cleopatra, I, 5. After defeating Antonius and Cleopatra, Augustus Caesar subdued Egypt, IV, 203.

A saying of Antonius the Orator, I, 212. Antonius the Orator, II, 271. Tullius resounds in praise of Antonius the Orator, 802. He says that he had seen many eloquent speakers, but as yet no truly eloquent man, ibid.

Antonius, the illustrator of the life of the anchorites, I, 121. He never saw Jerusalem, 321. His Life translated, 310. His history and that of Didymus, 410.

Antonius is popularly called the head of the monks’ way of life, II, 2. What is the order of Antonius’s life? 14. Why do crowds of people flock to him? ibid. Description of his dwelling and cell, 30. His labors and exercises, ibid. He rebukes wild asses, and they obey him, ibid. Why his tomb was unknown, ibid. He had ordered it to be concealed, ibid. Antonius rejoices in Christ’s glory and Satan’s destruction, 7. He wore Paul’s tunic on the days of Easter and Pentecost, 12. The mutual letters of Antonius and Hilarion, 26. Antonius’s humility, 10. His age, 6. His death became known to Hilarion before it was announced, 29. The elements are said to mourn Antonius’s death, 32. His memory is transmitted in Greek and Roman style, 3. Antonius’s monastery occupied by the Saracens, 10.

Antonius, VII, 738.

Anubis, the barking one, IV, 544.

The Church supported many old women, I, 260.

The Aonian mountains, I, 325.

Apadno, the name of a place near Nicopolis, V, 723.

Some maintain *ἀπάθειαν* (*apatheia*), I, 1040.

Apelles had Philumen as a companion in his teaching, I, 1031. Apelles, II, 431. Why was he ineffectual? 877. The same, VII, 1, 743, 749. Apelles and his virgin Philumen, 220.

Apelles, bishop and successor of Timothy, I, 405.

Aper of Erimanthus, II, 388.

Apher, one of Abraham’s descendants, led an army against Libya; after defeating the enemy there, he settled in the land. His descendants called it Africa after the name of their ancestor, III, 344.

The islands of Aphrodisias, VII, 427.

Aphroditon, a small town, II, 30.

[Col. 0923] Apis, worshiped by the Egyptians in the form of a bull, VI, 44. He was killed by Cambyses, V, 352.

The laws of Apicius and Paxamus, II, 304.

The Apocalypse was written long after the Lord’s Passion, I, 203. It is difficult and obscure, 274. It is opened only by Christ, ibid. The Apocalypse contains as many mysteries as words, 280. Many understandings lie hidden in each individual word. In proportion to the worth of this volume, all praise falls short. The Apocalypse contains infinite mysteries of future things, II, 280. Who interpreted the Apocalypse? 845. The word “Apocalypse” properly belongs to Scripture, VII, 387.

Apocryphal books, that is, hidden books, I, 579. They must be avoided, and how they are to be read, 688. Many faulty things have been mixed into them, ibid. Apocryphal books not received by the Church are not to be read, II, 394. Books rejected among the Apocryphal Scriptures, 839. Many, through ignorance, follow the ravings of the Apocryphal books, 420. Apocryphal books and fabricated revelations, 394. The Church knows nothing of the Apocrypha, 403. The ravings of the Apocrypha, 214. The nonsense of the Apocryphal books is to be left to heretics, VII, 5. Testimonies that have been cited are not immediately to be referred to the absurdities of the Apocrypha, 660.

Apollinaris, priest of the church of Hierapolis, I, 428, and II, 867.

Apollinarius of Laodicea, I, 223, 235, 347. Whom he overturned by his writings and his doctrine of the Incarnation, 589. He understood and wrote perversely concerning Christ’s soul and therefore was a heretic, ibid. He was Jerome’s teacher at Antioch, 523. He departed from the Church, 740. He wrote on the Epistle to the Galatians, ibid. The same man wrote against Porphyry, 523. How many volumes? 427. His impious doctrine concerning Christ, 523, 526. His opinion concerning the soul, 949. He wrote on the Psalms, 733. How he should be read, 352. Theophilus stabbed him after wrenching a sword from his hands, 583. What is said against him and his disciples, 587. Their doctrines, ibid. and following. Jerome followed Apollinarius in some places, II, 469. His translation was sewn together from various scraps, 528. He constructed the sequence of Scripture not according to the rule of truth but according to his own judgment, ibid. He wrote against Porphyry, 527. His little commentaries, 477. There is great diversity of style and doctrine between Apollinarius and Didymus, 543. He could please neither Jews nor Christians, because he is far removed from the Hebrews and disdains to follow the Seventy Translators, III, 491, 492. Apollinarius wrote not so much commentaries as chapter headings on Isaiah, IV, 5. In his customary manner he runs over everything, ibid. His little commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, VII, 541. They are not approved, 195.

Apollo of Delphi uttered oracles for Croesus and Pyrrhus, I, 526. The perpetual virginity of Apollo’s virgins, 906. Apollo of Delphi, Loxias, Delius, Clarius, IV, 503.

Apollo, a bishop in Achaea, I, 405.

Apollo, Paul’s disciple: who was he? VII, 739.

Apollonius the Greek, I, 211. Apollonius the magician, or philosopher: what regions did he travel through? 271. He heard Iarcas teaching about nature, morals, and the course of the stars, ibid. He went to Ethiopia to see the Gymnosophists and the most famous table of the sun in the sand, ibid. Everywhere he found something to learn, and always progressing, he became better, ibid. Apollonius the Greek is suddenly recorded not to have appeared while standing in the court before Domitian, II, 444.

Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome, published a little work, I, 429. By whom was Apollonius betrayed? II, 881.

The apostles passed from catching fish to catching human beings, I, 937. They carried their cross daily, ibid. The Holy Spirit suggested to the apostles whatever exercise and daily meditation on the law usually provide to others, 273. They are called *θεοδίδακτοι* (*theodidaktoi*), “taught by God,” ibid. The eleven were not broken by Judas’s betrayal, 122. In them the greatness of holiness excused simplicity of speech, 318. Each of them spoke in the language of all nations, 188. The apostles’ virtues are to be imitated before the simplicity of their words, 318. Whoever strayed by a different path from the apostles’ rule is expelled as unworthy of Christ’s choir, 592. The apostles were either virgins or continent after marriage, 233. As pilgrims and poor throughout the whole world, what could they have said? 913. Not weighed down by the burden of riches, they could enter through the narrow opening of a needle, ibid. As far as riches were concerned they left nothing; as far as willingness was concerned, they left the whole world, 402. No one was poorer than the apostles, and no one abandoned so much for the Lord, 1080. In what do the apostles glory? 725. They are crowned by the testimony of the future Judge, ibid. Offering themselves, they had abandoned everything they possessed, ibid. They gloried when they suffered insult for Christ, 709. A veil was placed not only on Moses’ face but also on the Evangelists and apostles, 325. The seventy palms of the apostles are watered by the sweetened streams of the law, 419. The poverty of the apostles, 423. They are to be treated differently from other interpreters, 515. The apostles and Evangelists brought forth the meaning of Scripture, not its words, 315. A praiseworthy matter, to be made equal to the virtues of apostolic times, 433. [Col. 0924] The apostles’ words are called little sparks; Christ’s lamp is exceedingly bright, II, 752. This did not destroy their faith, 396. Through the mouth of the apostles Christ sounds forth to us, 421. They are read to have been placed before the prophets among the spiritual gifts, ibid. They are humbled so that they may be exalted, 801. In what sense were they not perfect? 704. They were not without sin, ibid. The apostles overcome by the frailty of the flesh, 757. As the cross approached, they contended about rank, 760. They were sinners above all human beings, 783. Without destroying their friendships, they disagreed among themselves, 532. The apostles’ boat is in danger, 191. The apostles, prophets, and saints lament that they are sinners, 357. They are preferred to the Seventy Translators, 520. The apostles follow the Seventy where they do not disagree with the Hebrew; where they differ, they placed in Greek what they had learned from the Hebrews, 529. The apostles and apostolic men often make use of testimonies that had already been widely circulated among the gentiles, III, 371. Through the apostles, as through little cups, wisdom was poured out to believers throughout the whole world, 401. The apostles and Evangelists, and also our Savior, often bring forth things as if from the Old Testament that are not in the copies of the Seventy Translators, 303. The grace of the prophets came upon the apostles, IV, 714. The apostles are counted, 194. The apostles divided among different provinces, 445. The apostles are commanded to raise up the sign of the Lord’s cross, 235. The apostles’ preaching, 511. The apostles are strengthened against persecutions, 517. The apostles are commanded to regard their persecutors as brothers, 802. How the apostles release those who are bound, 255. The apostles and Evangelists recited testimonies from the Hebrew, 1064. In testimonies from the Old Testament they follow the meaning, not the words, 110. They translated from Hebrew into Greek without damage to the meanings, 396. The choir of apostles is called a worm on account of humility and contempt, 500. The apostles are called farmers, 70. Who are the sons of the apostles? 595. Whoever was freed from the sea by the apostles ought to live in the hills, V, 857. The apostles and martyrs are called the foundations of the earth, VI, 501. The names of the apostles are magnified daily, 733. That benefits us, ibid. The preaching and works of the apostles, 785, 786. The keys of the Church entrusted to the apostles, 445. The apostles are commanded to walk barefoot, 242, 260. Why the apostles spread their garments over the colt of the she-ass, 244. The apostles recited the Scriptures from memory, 489. The apostles performed greater signs than Christ himself, 527. The apostles’ courage and unconquered steadfastness, 496, 497. “Apostle” is properly a word of the Hebrews, VII, 374. The apostles are called the pillars of the Church, especially Peter, etc., 404. Believers and the Church itself can likewise be called this, ibid. The majesty and breadth of wisdom from the apostles, 487. Why authority to heal the sick, etc., was given to the apostles, 58. They are sent naked to preach, ibid. The patriarchs stood upon the foundation of the apostles, just as we are founded upon the prophets, 446. Who are called apostles? 374. There are four kinds of apostles, ibid. Why, apart from the Twelve, are many called apostles? 396. The apostles and Evangelists bring forth only the meaning of the Old Testament, 228. There was no rivalry among the apostles, 749. Apostolic clothing, 161.

Appio, an Alexandrian grammarian, noted, I, 428, and II, 847. He was sent as an envoy under Caligula, ibid. He wrote against Philo, ibid.

A saying of Appius, I, 1040.

How someone can draw near to God, IV, 394. Drawing near to God concerns not place but disposition, 686.

The true season of the month of April, VI, 271.

Plato’s apsides, I, 1028.

Water is by nature extremely cold, I, 288. The waters above the heavens are set apart for the praises of God, 419. The mysteries of the waters are held in God’s hands, ibid. Their praises and those of baptism are proclaimed, ibid. The Lord cleansed by his baptism the waters polluted by the Flood and stained by the slaughter of the entire human race, 702. All waters and streams return through hidden channels to the matrix of the abyss, III, 316. How the Jews prepared water for a siege, IV, 222. Water frozen into ice is called *crystallus*—crystal—among the Greeks, V, 20. How waters are understood in a good and a bad sense, 587. The diversity of waters, some eternal and others brief, VI, 650.

Hot springs erupted at Amanta, III, 147. The earth itself brings them forth at Beelmaus, 170. Hot springs also erupted at the foot of the mountain-city of Galatia, with baths built above them, 227.

What kind of interpreter Aquila was, I, 316. He is rejected by Christians, ibid. Aquila’s edition helps strengthen the Christian faith, 152. Jerome fears that, out of hatred for Christ, the synagogue may have altered something in it, ibid. Aquila’s first edition, IV, 879. Aquila’s second edition, 903. Aquila, a highly learned man, either feigned ignorance or was deceived by the Pharisees’ interpretation, 564. Aquila, a careful and inquisitive interpreter, VI, 25.

Eagles perceive corpses across the sea, II, 445. The nature of eagles toward their young, IV, 810. The old age of eagles becomes youthful again through the change of their feathers, 495. They gaze upon the brilliance of the sun’s rays with their flashing eyes, ibid. How they test their young, ibid. The eagle holds sovereignty among birds, as the lion does among beasts, V, 664. The nature of the eagle, VI, 268 and 447. It is called the queen of birds, 447. The eagle surpasses everything in flight, 595. Eagles and vultures are said to perceive corpses across the seas, VII, 197.

The addition of the church of Aquileia to the Creed, II, 577.

The north wind is exceedingly harsh and cold, I, 472. It is called “right-hand,” or falsely assumes the name of the right hand, ibid. The land of the north, IV, 862. The north wind is exceedingly harsh and makes the hearts of its inhabitants exceedingly hard, VI, 796.

All Aquitania was laid waste, I, 914. Aquitania boasts of Greek origin, VII, 427.

What do the Arabs and Saracens eat? II, 334. They consider it unlawful to eat pork, ibid. The Arabs, devoted to brigandage, used to beset the roads of Jericho, IV, 857. Arab women, like those of Mesopotamia, covered with cloaks, 62. “Arab” is understood in a favorable sense, 245.

Arabia abounds in flocks, V, 317. What does Arabia signify? VII, 429, 472.

Arach, that is, Edessa, III, 330.

The island of Aradus is noted, V, 309.

Aracus and Antaradus, near Tyre, ibid.

The tomb of Aram, Abraham’s brother, in Ur of the Chaldeans, III, 287.

Ararat is Armenia, in whose mountains the remains of Noah’s ark survived, III, 126. Ararat, a level region in Armenia, IV, 466. The Araxes flows through it, ibid.

Aratus is called a witness by the Apostle, I, 426. Aratus, VII, 647, 648. A hemistich of Aratus, 471, 706. He wrote about heaven and the stars, ibid. From whom the *Phaenomena* of Aratus were translated, ibid.

Arbee, in which four were buried: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam himself, the first ancestor of the human race, III, 340.

The arbitrator’s judgment, I, 995.

Assertion of free will, I, 613. It always needs God’s help, 1029. It lies within our free choice whom we wish to follow, either Lazarus or the rich man, 234. Who destroys free will? 104. Let him be condemned who condemns it, 1034. Those destroy the freedom of choice who readily misuse it against the beneficence of the giver, 1034. To will and to run is ours, but this very “ours,” without God’s constant help, will not be ours, 1033. God created us with free will; we are driven by no necessity either toward virtues or toward vices, II, 326. God’s foreknowledge together with free will, 788. We pray always in vain if it lies within our free choice to do what we wish, 760. Once this is removed, the sect of the Manichaeans is constructed, 787. Free will consists only in this: that we wish, desire, and give assent to what pleases us, 793. What is attributed to God and to free will in our works. The grace of free will was not bestowed in such a way that God’s assistance in each matter is removed, 699. In our will and in our running, free will is preserved; but in the completion of the will and the running, everything is left to God’s power, 700. It is not solely within our power to do what we wish, but also within God’s clemency, 749. What breaks the freedom of choice when it grows proud? 792. He cannot proceed to Christ unless he is drawn by God, ibid. Where mercy and grace are present, free will partly ceases, 793. Human free will is demonstrated, IV, 563, 873, 985. Why free will is preserved for humanity, 1023. It lies within our choice to select good or evil, 671. There is no power of free will without grace, 970. Those are condemned who praise the power of choice in such a way that God’s mercy is removed, 910. The freedom of choice must be preserved in such a way that the grace of the giver excels in everything, 969. Free will in all things, V, 395, 885, 892. Human free will together with God’s foreknowledge, 24. Human free will, VII, 487, 500, 558. The freedom of free will: from whom? 577.

Arboc, a city, III, 340.

The tree prefigures Abraham’s hospice, I, 401.

A tree is recognized by the sweetness of its fruits, II, 417. Some things are said about the seed and growth of trees, wheat, and so forth, 432. So long as it perseveres either in its goodness or in its wickedness, neither does a good tree bear evil fruit nor an evil tree good fruit, 366. How deeply the roots of trees descend into the depths, VI, 160.

Arcadius Augustus, I, 914. Arcadius and Honorius, highly religious emperors, ibid.

Peter interprets Noah’s ark typologically as the Church, I, 909. In it there is found neither remarriage among men nor double mating among animals, ibid. In it there were not only clean but also unclean animals, ibid. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he will perish when the Flood reigns, 39. Noah’s ark, a type of the Church, II, 359. Its sacraments together with those of the Church, 195. It was endangered in the Flood, ibid. Why the animals entered the ark of Noah by sevens, [Col. 0926] 267. All who wrote barbarian histories remembered Noah’s ark, III, 126. Noah’s ark was carried to the mountains of Taurus, IV, 467.

To know the secrets of the heart does not belong to man, even if he is a saint, V, 143.

God’s secrets are not to be related to just anyone, III, 451.

Arcesilas removed truth from life, II, 498. Founder of the Middle Academy, ibid.

The archangel is the first among the angels, II, 479.

Count Archelaus was praised, II, 440.

The burial mound of Archelaus, king of Judaea, was shown near Bethlehem, III, 16.

A physician was called an *archiater*, VII, 282.

The archdeacons of the individual churches, I, 942.

Archippus, a listener of Pythagoras, held schools at Thebes, II, 565. Retaining his teacher’s precepts in memory, he used his intelligence in place of books; some of these precepts are reported, ibid. Archippus: who was he? VII, 748.

The archpriests of the individual churches, I, 942.

A saying of Archytas of Tarentum when angry, I, 506. He was visited by Plato, 220. Archytas of Tarentum wrote about odd numbers, 232. Archytas of Tarentum, II, 567.

Arcturus, VI, 289 and following.

What the deceptive bow signifies, VI, 162.

The Areopagus is the council-house of the Athenians, VII, 706.

Areopolis, a city named by some after Mars, III, 162. This derivation is rejected, IV, 184. The walls of Areopolis collapsed in an earthquake during the night, 185.

Aretas ruling Damascus, IV, 570.

The fifteen silver pieces that Hosea promised the adulteress, explained mystically, VI, 30.

Argentoratum, I, 914.

Silver, to which everything is subject, signifies the talents of the Gospel, III, 478. Divine Scripture always places silver and gold above speech and meaning, 400. The inferior material of silver is the adornment of peasants and maidservants, V, 157.

The hundred eyes of Argus, I, 287.

Arguments, I, 237. What is learned in an argument, 222. A complicated argument, VII, 449.

A clear matter must not be made doubtful by arguments, II, 503.

The doctrine of the Arians, II, 184? They bring forward a slander to which the Church replies, 861. Their conventicles are the camps of the devil, 172. An Arian bishop is an enemy of Christ, 176. The Arians and Semi-Arians blasphemously assert that the Holy Spirit was created, 423. They do not grant to the Son of God what Pelagius attributes to every human being, 716. The Arian bishops and clerics who subscribed to *homoousion* at the Council of Nicaea, 193. They pretended to condemn the name *homoousion*, 410. Letters and books of the Arians published before the Council of Nicaea, 193. Various things are said about the Arians, 173, 189. The Arian heresy, IV, 877. The Arian error is refuted, 787. The Arian heresy is noted, V, 670. A passage to be understood of Arian bishops, 545. The Arians boast in vain of the testimony of Scripture, VII, 595. Jerome argues against the Arians, 609. Arian madness, supported by the resources of the world, rages, 41. The Arians cause no labor for teachers, 1034. What Jerome demands from the Arians and the Campenses, 38. The authors of the Arian heresy, ibid. The whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian, 191. The persecution of the Arians was most savage, 789. Arius, I, 40. To deceive the world, he first deceived the emperor’s sister, 1032. Arius is refuted, II, 412 and 508. His impious doctrine concerning Christ, 512. Arius says that all things were created through the Son, 423. He is called the noonday demon, 509. He is the head of the Arians and the cause of their evils, ibid. He subscribed to the Council of Nicaea, 193. The heresy of Arius is noted, VI, 429. He does not deny that the Son is Creator, ibid. Arius, Aetius, and Eunomius, heretics, 229. In what sense Jerome calls Arius the door, but Aetius and Eunomius the bars, ibid. Arius, VII, 610, 737. He preaches that Christ is a creature, 108, 238. He was called a serpent, 724. A spark, 489. Why do Arius and Eunomius rejoice? 199. The same men are questioned, 170.

Ariel, a city also believed by some to be called Areopolis, I, 696.

Ariel is interpreted as “Lion of God,” I, 697. Jerusalem was once called Ariel, “most powerful,” IV, 388.

The battering ram, a weapon of war, I, 30, and V, 81.

Who are the rams among the people? IV, 1023 and following.

The Acts of the Council of Ariminum, II, 188 and following. What happened in the Church at Ariminum? 189. The churches kept the Acts of the Council of Ariminum in strongholds, 190. The bishops ensnared by the tricks at Ariminum testify that they suspected nothing in their faith, ibid.

The learning of Aristarchus, I, 237.

Aristeas says nothing about the cells of the Seventy Translators, II, 520. Aristeas and Josephus assert that only the five books of Moses were translated by the Seventy, V, 53 and following.

Aristaenetus the consul, I, 725.

Aristaeneta wishes to go to Antony, but is prevented, [Col. 0927] and how, II, 29. She was the wife of Elpidius, 19. Concerned about the health of her sons, she goes to Hilarion, ibid.

Aristides presented Hadrian with an *Apology for the Christians*, I, 428, and II, 861. The same man was an Athenian philosopher; why was he called “Justus”? II, 316.

Aristion, II, 859.

Aristippus, I, 341, and II, 569.

Aristobulus wrote against the Gentiles, II, 879.

Aristobulus was the first to assume the diadem, the insignia of royal power, together with the honor of the high priesthood, V, 686.

Aristocles, tyrant of Orchomenus, II, 308.

In what respect Aristomenes of Messenia was most just, II, 308. He is acquitted through the deeds and prayers of virgins, ibid.

Aristophanes, II, 183.

Aristotle, I, 222. Teacher of Alexander the Great, 682. Aristotle’s *Categories* [Greek: *katēgoriai*], and so forth, 36. Arguments, 37. Aristotle’s syllogisms, 237. Aristotle was the chief of philosophers, II, 707. He wrote in prose, 332. In his books he develops Pythagorean precepts, 566. The Arians used Aristotle’s arguments, 183. He wrote about marriage, 318. His opinions, 558. *Spineta*, 206. What is learned from reading Aristotle? 476.

Aristotle, chief of dialecticians, VII, 735. He was neglected after the preaching of the Gospel, 487.

Christ is our armor, I, 737.

Armenius laid down his quivers, I, 679.

What bracelets signify, I, 151.

Arnobius, I, 338. He published seven books against the Gentiles, 429. How he should be read, 352. He is uneven and excessive, confused without division of his work, 326.

Aroer is explained as “tamarisk,” IV, 192.

Many spices come from India, IV, 888.

A pledge is defined, VII, 560, 561. From the pledge it is estimated what the future purchase will be, ibid.

We are without arrogance only with greater difficulty than we are without gold and gems, I, 458. Flight from arrogance and thanksgiving, V, 631.

The kings of Persia were called Arsacids, V, 341.

The hand of Arsenius was amputated, II, 569.

Arses, son of Ochus, king of Persia, V, 665.

Arsinthius the bishop, I, 640.

Arsisius, a pillar of Christ, I, 705.

No art is learned without a teacher, I, 942. The arts practiced by hand, 275. They cannot be mastered without instruction, ibid. From old and worn material we devise the raw material of an art, 900. The arts would be fortunate if artists alone judged them, 400. Things made by hand and visible to the eyes prove the artists more convincingly, ibid. God gave the human race all the arts as possible accomplishments, II, 716. No one, however gifted, can comprehend them all, ibid. The arts that the Greeks call *banausoi* [Greek: *banausoi*], that is, mechanical or menial arts, ibid. Many others are noted, ibid. One thing is the arts, another is what exists through the arts, 702. What is the most precious art among the barbarians? IV, 1012.

The *artaba*, an Egyptian measure, makes twenty *modii*, IV, 75.

Artabanus was king of Persia for seven months, V, 40 and 665.

Esther corrects the judgment of Artaxerxes, II, 792.

Artaxerxes Longimanus, king of Persia, V, 665.

Artaxerxes Mnemon was king of Persia for forty years; he is called Ahasuerus by the Hebrews, V, 43 and 665.

Artaxerxes Ochus, king of Persia, V, 665.

Artaxias, king of the Armenians, V, 890.

The celebrated chastity of Artemisia, the wife of Mausolus, II, 311. She was queen of Caria and is praised by poets and historians, ibid. She always loved her dead husband as though he were alive and built him a tomb of extraordinary size, ibid.

Artemis is Diana, III, 99.

The doctrine of Artemon revived, II, 913.

The best artists are the best judges of the arts, IV, 666. The art of craftsmen inlaying gold and gems is most precious among the barbarians, 1011. All artists speak of their own art by examples, VI, 224.

Kinds of magical arts, IV, 127.

The Artotyrites, heretics, VII, 429.

What does it mean “to break the bruised reed and extinguish the smoking flax”? VII, 78.

Babylon and all Chaldaea cultivated the pursuit of soothsayers, diviners, and enchanters, IV, 553.

Although Asa is just, he is said to have gone astray, II, 767.

Asclepiades of Cyprus, II, 919, 343. The ordination of Asclepiades the Confessor, 879.

The Ascodrobi, VII, 429.

Asella, a notable example of chastity and virginity, I, 198. She is burdened by her own praises, 128. Her way of life is a model of perfect living, ibid. She is blessed in her mother’s womb, ibid. How great were her virtues? ibid. and following. She sold little moray eels and, dressed in a dark tunic, consecrated herself to the Lord, ibid. Her love of solitude, ibid. She did not know conversation with a man, ibid. Continual fasting, doubled during Lent, did not harm her health, [Col. 0928] ibid. Through the roughness of camel hair, her knees became calloused from frequent prayer, ibid. In everything she was so modest that she is proposed to all as an example for imitation, ibid.

An ass on the road, when it has become tired, seeks side paths, I, 687.

Asher is rendered as “into blessedness” or “into riches,” I, 292.

Asian swelling is dried by Attic salt, I, 935.

In what respect Balaam’s she-ass was fortunate, VII, 288.

Regarding the colt of the she-ass when it is loosed, VII, 359.

What was the burial of asses? IV, 992.

Asinius Pollio, II, 485.

Asor, metropolis of all the kingdoms of Philistia, III, 145.

No appearance is safe, even in the house, I, 96.

The commentaries of Asprius on Virgil and Sallust, II, 472.

Assa, a city, I, 344.

The prophet Asaph, I, 494.

God’s likeness in the hands of the prophets, VI, 140.

What the asterisks and obeli signify in the interpretation of Scripture, I, 752. Asterisks and obeli in Jerome’s version, II, 565.

Ahasuerus is called Artaxerxes by the Septuagint, II, 792. Why sleep is taken from his eyes, ibid. Various things are related about the same man, ibid.

The Assyrians and Chaldaeans are in the northern region, adjacent to the position of Judaea, IV, 87. The kingdom of the Assyrians was most ancient and once extremely powerful, 425. For 1,300 years the Assyrians possessed the empire of Asia, Egypt, and Libya, 114. For seventy years the Assyrian kingdom was in Jerusalem, 231. A list of the Assyrian kings who conquered the people of Israel, 455. Greek authors described the wars of the Assyrian nation, 227. The ancient Assyrians are called Syrians, 209. The Hebrews report that the bodies of the Assyrians were burned while their garments remained unharmed, 147. According to the same authorities, only ten of their army survived, ibid. What regions the Assyrians and Babylonians held, VI, 377. The Assyrians and Babylonians occupy the northern land, 795.

Asterius of Scythopolis, I, 429. He wrote on the Psalms, 753. The books of Asterius and Apollinarius against Marcellus of Ancyra, II, 925.

Asserius the subdeacon, I, 634.

Ashtaroth, the idol of the Sidonians, VI, 84.

The stars derive their names from the Gentiles, I, 367. Some think that they are rational beings, IV, 539. The order of the heavenly stars cannot be changed, 1076. There is an observance of the stars among the Chaldaeans, 476.

Who are the astrologers? IV, 553. They are numerous in Chaldaea, 16.

Astyages, the maternal grandfather of Cyrus, king of the Medes, V, 673. Some call Astyages “Darius the Mede” in Greek volumes, 653.

What the myths relate about Atalanta of Calydon, the virgin, II, 306.

The comic performances of the Atellanae, I, 255.

Various things are related about Quintus Aterius, II, 419.

Athanasius the deacon, I, 536.

Athanasius of Alexandria, bishop, I, 429. He fled to Rome to avoid the persecutions of the Arians, 954. In that city he proclaimed the discipline of the monks and the life of Saint Antony, ibid. His letters are praised, 688. What is falsely attributed to Athanasius, II, 568. Athanasius the victor returns to his church, 191. He defends the error of Dionysius, 509. Athanasius and Paulinus were the only Catholics in the East, 411. A book of Athanasius, 649.

Athanasius of Athribis, bishop and successor of Isidore, I, 630.

What Pope Athanasius approves, VII, 738.

What is an Athenaeum? I, 400. The same, VII, 483.

Atherbius, stirred up against Rufinus, II, 561. From Jerome’s friendships he denounced Jerome as a heretic, ibid. He barked against Rufinus, ibid.

The city of the Athenians was devoted to idolatry, IV, 604, 980. The inscription on the altar of the Athenians, VII, 706. Paul altered some things concerning it, ibid.

Athenodorus, the brother and companion of Theodore, II, 905. They were disciples of Origen, ibid.

What is *Athenogeron*? II, 536.

Are athletes stronger than their own trainers? Yet the weaker man urges the stronger to fight, I, 798. No athlete is crowned without sweat, 37. What Galen says about athletes, II, 340. The custom of Palestine and Greece in training athletes, VI, 896. When the strength of athletes is praised, VII, 522.

The Lord glories in his athletes, VI, 733. The athlete of the Lord and the athlete of luxury are noted, 373.

Athyr is the name of an Egyptian month, the eighth month for the Hebrews, corresponding to November among the Latins, VI, 779.

What is an atom? I, 802.

The atoms of Democritus and Epicurus, IV, 468.

King Attalus, I, 18.

What is an *attelabus*? VI, 576. The difference between an *attelabus* and a *bruchus*, 581, 582. Heresies compared to an *attelabus*, 583.

The Atticoti had wives in common and children in common, [Col. 0929] I, 413. The Atticoti eat human flesh, II, 335.

Atys and his worship, VI, 41.

Read non-orthodox authors in such a way that you judge them rather than follow them, I, 688.

What is boldness? I, 605. Where does unbridled boldness not burst forth? II, 554.

Great matters are always placed at the discretion of the hearers, I, 398. Simple and pure praise is not so concerned about the faith of the hearers, 512.

The tears of hearers are the praises of the teacher, I, 263. A prudent hearer is necessary in the Church, VI, 51. A vicious hearer is noted, VII, 114. Things heard are reported one way, things seen another, II, 521. Enemies and friends do not listen equally, 409.

In the Holy Scriptures, hearing is perceived not by the ear but by the heart, VI, 169. Spiritual and earthly people hear in different ways, ibid.

The virtue of the Aufidii was no less in mourning than in wars, I, 335.

Many Chaldaean augurs, IV, 553.

Augustine urges Jerome to a recantation, I, 407. He seems to boast of his learning, 640. Augustine’s letters to Jerome were answered only with difficulty, 752. Augustine uses a new syllogism against Jerome, ibid. The holy Doctor answers him, 753. In what honor he was held by Jerome, 949. Jerome refers questioners about the origin of the soul to him, ibid. Jerome considers him to have injured friendship and violated the rights of their relationship, 640. Jerome’s friends accused Augustine of vainglory, 638. Why Augustine does not want Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew to be read in the churches, 781. He prefers that in the prophet Jonah *cucurbita* (“gourd”) be read rather than *hedera* (“ivy”), ibid. He praises Jerome’s writings, 404. What he says about Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, 408. Augustine praises Jerome’s translation of the Gospels, 637. Why Augustine accepts him in the correction of the New Testament, 753. What he asks from him, 301. Augustine wishes to discuss the Scriptures seriously with Jerome rather than in play, 762. Augustine dedicates two books to Jerome, 1043. They shine with every splendor of eloquence and are praised; Jerome celebrates Augustine’s genius, ibid. Jerome could not answer them, ibid. Each discusses for the sake of learning, ibid. Jerome’s attitude toward Augustine, ibid. What honor Augustine accorded the canonical books, 762. If anything in them seems contrary to the truth, he attributes it either to a corrupt manuscript or to an interpreter who did not understand what was said, ibid. What sense he assigns to other interpreters, ibid. He extinguished the factions of heretics, 1065. He is celebrated throughout the world, and Catholics venerate him as the founder of the ancient faith, ibid. All heretics detest him, ibid. Augustine laments the cause of the disagreement between Jerome and Rufinus, 732 and following, 759. In that matter he neither reproved Jerome nor recognized any fault in him, 303, 771, 780. He wrote against Faustus the Manichaean, 771. He confirms Jerome’s words, ibid. Augustine’s love of peace and brotherly affection, 782. The people venerated him, 751. Augustine’s true opinion, 175. It does not differ greatly from Jerome’s opinion, 782. Once Augustine’s opinion has been set forth, no one after the earlier writers will dare to speak and write, 783. Augustine’s books of *Soliloquies* and commentaries on the Psalms, 640. Some things are criticized in them, ibid. His praises, 150. Also his books to Marcellinus and Hilary, ibid. The Coelestian heresy was put to death through the work of Augustine and Alypius, 1067.

Augustus honored by Herod, I, 703. The world serves the tables of the emperors, and lands and seas are subject to them, 502. Where Augustus defeated Antony and Cleopatra, VII, 738. See *Caesar*.

Aulon, the name of a plain among the Palestinians, I, 446. Aulon is not a Greek word but a Hebrew one, III, 139.

Popular favor is a very bad guide, I, 572. How the more prosperous “breeze” of circumstances is moderated, 608.

What is a *aurata*? I, 431.

The histories of Aurelius Victor, I, 24.

Aurelian, II, 903.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus succeeded Macrinus, II, 903.

Lucius Aurelius Commodus, II, 857.

Uncircumcised ears: what do they signify? IV, 884. We are taught to hear both with the ears of the body and with the understanding of the soul, 586.

“Ears” is taken to mean gates, VI, 440.

The golden age of Saturn compared with the fables of the Jews and Judaizers, IV, 149.

The charioteer of Gaza, struck by a demon, is healed, II, 20.

To lay down gold is the act of beginners, not of the perfect, I, 433. By whom it is despised, 795. The difficulty of finding gold, II, 254. What the hunger for gold compels one to do, 4. Gold is the god of the greedy, IV, 40. Possessing gold and silver does not free a person, 74. What it signifies in sacred matters, 75. The ancient custom of burying gold and ornaments in tombs, 898. There is a place in India where the finest gold is produced, 242.

What Jerome says about Ausonius, I, 791. What is said about the same man, [Col. 0930] 799.

The south wind is hostile to flowers, I, 341. It is pestilential to human bodies, ibid.

Autolycus, II, 867.

Auxentius the Arian, I, 741.

Help. Those whom we cannot aid in deed we ought to assist with advice and support with consolation, III, 445.

Greed is the root of all evils, I, 118, 933. Greed is lust, fraud, and idolatry, 31. It is satisfied by no deeds, 713. The more it has, the more it demands; neither abundance nor want diminishes it, ibid. It despises laws and scorns the flames of Gehenna, and so forth, 627. Greed imitates hell, ibid. Whatever it has, it will demand more, ibid. It considers everything it possesses less than what it desires, ibid. At banquets it devours not food but injustice, ibid. In lawsuits it mixes quarrels and discord, ibid. It gives birth to envy and, as though drunk, surges about, ibid. It has one measure: always to seek beyond measure, ibid. It is compared with the luxurious, and the evils it perpetrates are enumerated, ibid. We burn with greed, and while arguing against money we open our bosoms to gold; nothing is enough for us, 913. It is better not to have something to give than shamelessly to seek something to hoard, 264. Greed must be avoided, 116 and following. Fear of God restrains insatiable greed, 617. Let us avoid it as though it were the worst moneylender, 608. What kind of guards greed has is demonstrated, 934. Even a robber can accuse greed, 262. The root of greed is the concern of the Gentiles, 116. For many, the name “poor” is an occasion of greed, II, 21. Luxuries and varieties of feasting are fuel for greed, 341. Greed is diminished neither by want nor by abundance, III, 430. Greed is condemned among idols, IV, 36. The greedy and rapacious are servants of Mammon, 576. Jerome condemns the vice of greed, V, 283. Good and evil greed, VI, 618. Greed, signifying uncleanness, VII, 640, 643.

The greedy man is always in need, I, 627. He lacks what he has as much as what he does not have, ibid. What befits the greedy who refuse alms, 118. The greedy man is always in need, III, 430. He tortures himself by the most foolish thrift, preserving things for others to devour, 433. The greedy man is called an idolater, VII, 643.

“Aversion” is taken to mean punishment, I, 1087.
