Wandering birds do not fall into the same snares and nets, I, 283. Choice birds for eating, 504. Pheasants and birds carried in litters, 618. What birds do to defend their young, IV, 423. Birds and beasts devour not branches cut from trees but corpses, 200.

Female avidity, VII, 155.

Avienus, VII, 706.

The cruelty of Hazael, king of Damascus, VI, 226, 227.

Azotus, a most powerful city of Palestine, IV, 211.

## B

Baal, the idol of the Sidonians, IV, 407. The idol Baal placed in the Temple, 672. The statue of Baal was called the idol of Jealousy and was placed by the northern road, V, 84. Baal is interpreted as “the higher one” and “devouring,” VI, 17. It is also interpreted as [Greek: *echōn*], “having,” 24. Baal, a shrine in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, IV, 974. Baal, or Bel, an idol: the religion of the Assyrians, consecrated by Ninus in honor of his father Bel, V, 264. The worship of Baal introduced by Ahab, VI, 122. Baal is called the image of Jealousy, VI, 679. It is an idol of the Sidonians, ibid. The Sidonians and Phoenicians call him Baal and Beel, ibid. The idol Baal near Jerusalem, VII, 62.

Babylas, bishop of the Church of Antioch, died in prison, II, 895. He suffered at Antioch and was led to Caesarea, 903.

Babylon received its name from the confusion of languages, IV, 143. It was overthrown by the attack of the Medes and Persians, 169. It was founded by the Chaldaeans, 549. It was the metropolis of the Chaldaeans, 169. The circuit of Babylon, the height of its Capitol, and the magnificence of the things contained in it are described, 180. In Hebrew it is called Babel, 234. It is called “virgin” and “daughter,” 549. Its nature is not condemnable, as heretics wish, ibid. Babylon and the region of the Chaldaeans are called the misty mountains, 933. Why Babylon is called the sea, 212. The Babylonians were cruel, 203. There were royal hunting grounds in Babylon, 175. Fire and burning are much more useful to Babylon than astrologers and so forth, 554. What is said against Babylon pertains to the confusion and destruction of this world, 235. Why the Babylonian kingdom is called a lioness, V, 664. Semiramis, wife of Ninus, built the walls of Babylon, VI, 24.

*Bacellus* for *baculus* (“staff”), II, 67.

The Bactrians expose their old men to dogs, II, 335.

The Bactroperitae, philosophers, VII, 58.

Baisanes the deacon: in what respect he is to be praised, II, 30.

Balaam openly prophesied the future mysteries of Christ, I, 463. Balaam, from the stock of Buz, is called Elihu in the Book of Job: at first a holy man and prophet of God, later, through disobedience and desire for gifts, he is called a diviner, III, 339. He was from the city of Fathura, 214.

Who is a buffoon? I, 534.

Bale is otherwise called Salissa, III, 326.

The more a ballista is drawn back, the more forcefully it shoots, II, 240.

The heat of the baths must not inflame the young woman’s fresh blood, I, 505. Let him who wishes to extinguish the body’s heat by the chill of fasting not seek their comforts, 936. Fires lulled to sleep by the comforts of baths are rekindled, 687. When you bathe in baths, filth is removed, 787.

“Balsamus” is a name devised by heretics, I, 453. What is *balsamus*? II, 393.

Balsam and dates grow near the city of Balam, III, 167.

King Belshazzar was not the son of Nebuchadnezzar, V, 651. What Josephus writes about King Belshazzar, 656.

Baptism without the Holy Spirit is not sufficient for salvation, I, 420. From the time when we are reborn in Christ we are counted as belonging to him, 336. The waters in baptism are consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, 595. Baptism is the day of our military training, 29. In baptism the child is released from the bond of the parent, 413. It makes a new person and creates one entirely anew, ibid. All crimes are cleansed in Christ’s font, 415. The redemption of former sins is found in the waters of baptism, 700. Through baptism we have been buried with Christ into death, 421. Very many things pertaining to the power of baptism, 422 and following. In baptism we swear by the words of the sacrament, 29. By what words Christians renounced the devil in it, 984. Origen’s opinion concerning its effect, 199. Why infants are baptized, ibid. The apostles are commanded to baptize in the mystery of the Trinity, 420. Imperfect baptism without invocation of the Holy Spirit, II, 530. The true and legitimate baptism of the Church, 180. Nothing can be called perfect unless it is in the cross and resurrection of Christ, 179. In baptism the head was immersed three times, 180. After emerging, they tasted milk and honey beforehand; why? ibid. For water does not wash the soul, but is first itself washed by the spirit, 177. What a person is through baptism, ibid. It is conferred in the name of the Holy Trinity, ibid. There is no baptism without the Holy Spirit, 177, 179. From what we have been freed through it, 742. It cuts away old sins but does not bestow new virtues, 719. Baptism forgives past sins; it does not preserve future righteousness, 781. In what sense it does not make those who receive it equal, 289. No one can be as free from fault as those who immediately emerge from Christ’s font, 800. It was customary in the bath to ask about one’s religion, 184. The effects of baptism, 489. What those about to communicate drink after baptism, 800. When someone attributes more to John’s baptism than it possessed, he destroys the Lord’s baptism, 179. The raven and dove sent out from Noah’s ark are a type of baptism, 195. The Psalmist’s words appropriate to those rising from the baptismal font, 800. The sacrament of baptism alone remits sins, IV, 22. Baptism and martyrdom are consecrated in the water and blood of Christ’s side, 651. In baptism there is no distinction of persons, 602. In baptism a human being contributes the water, but God the Holy Spirit, 66. Those reborn in baptism are compared with green herbs, 525. Some are baptized with the baptism of fire, others with the baptism of the Holy Spirit, V, 868. We are cleansed in baptism by faith in Christ, 441. The saving grace of baptism is shown, 588. Nothing is to be changed in baptism, 949. In what sense baptism and penance are called gates, VI, 686. True baptism is in the Holy Spirit and in the mystery of the Holy Trinity, 202. The effects of baptism, 907. Once the baptismal chrism has been lost, one must not therefore despair, 655. Baptism is conferred at Easter and Pentecost, 921. What is commanded us in baptism, 683. The apostles baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 415. Baptism is given in the name of the Holy Trinity, VII, 19, 243, 610. Triple immersion in baptism because of the mystery of the Trinity, 610. The covenant in baptism, 28. In the second generation we receive the seal of the Creator, 560. The efficacy of the sacrament of baptism even in infants, 287. Why infants are baptized, ibid.

The custom of baptizing in the Church, II, 419. Hands were laid upon those baptized for the invocation of the Holy Spirit, 180. A presbyter and deacon have no right to baptize without the bishop’s command, 182. When necessity compels, laypeople may baptize, ibid. Anyone knowingly baptized by heretics does not deserve pardon for his error, 184.

Among the Hebrews, *bar* has different meanings, II, 475.

Baraciba, a teacher of the Hebrews, whom the Jews in Jerome’s time admired above all others, III, 424.

Some incompetently think that a certain Barak was the son of Deborah, I, 293, and II, 469.

Baranina, Jerome’s teacher, I, 524.

The cruelty of the barbarians, sparing no one, I, 464. The attack of the barbarians upon various regions, 949. Why the bodies of the barbarians were straighter than Roman bodies, V, 14.

The Greeks call the beard of the upper lip a *mystax*, III, 3.

[Col. 0932] The beauty of the beard is an indication of manliness, IV, 114. Shaving the beard and head was an indication of mourning, 185. The beauty of the beard is an indication of manliness, V, 49.

Barbelon, a portentous name, I, 453.

What is Barbelus? II, 393.

Barce, a town, I, 972.

Barchochabas, the author of the Jewish revolt, II, 559. He waved a burning straw in his mouth so that he might be thought to breathe out flames, ibid.

Bardesanes of Babylon, I, 428. What does Bardesanes of Babylon relate? II, 346. The same, ibid., 871. Bardesanes, whose intelligence even philosophers admire, VI, 196.

What does Barjona signify? II, 475.

Barnabas was gentler than Paul, II, 763. Barnabas of Cyprus, 839. His letter was counted among the apocryphal Scriptures, V, 480.

The interpretation of Bartholomew, II, 475. The same man preached Christ in India, according to Matthew’s Gospel, 875.

What does Barabbas signify? VII, 229. Again, what does it mean? VII, 123.

The little book of Baruch is joined to the edition of the Seventy, but is not found among the Hebrews, IV, 833. The Hebrews say that Baruch escaped the impending captivity of Egypt by death, 450. The interpretation of Baruch, VII, 546.

Bashan, a region of Arabia, IV, 39.

Basilicas adorned with flowers and little branches, I, 340. Basilicas built from the resources of private individuals, 207.

The heresy of Basilides, the teacher of luxury, raging throughout Spain, I, 453. The same man, a teacher of luxury, II, 381. The monstrous verbal inventions of Basilides, 197. His impious fabrications, ibid. The twenty-four volumes of the heretic Basilides, 861. What were his mysteries? ibid. He died in Alexandria, ibid. Basilides the heretic, V, 784, 818. His error, VII, 1 and 685. Basilides and the other heretics do not possess the Gospel of God, ibid.

Basil, bishop of Cappadocia, I, 429. The same Basil, 529. The commentaries of Saint Basil on Isaiah are cited, IV, 237.

What are the Basternae? I, 99, and IV, 823 and following.

Why Porphyry was called Bataneotes, VII, 371.

A *bathus* is used for liquids, an *ephah* for dry measures, IV, 75.

Baum, the name of an Egyptian monastery, II, 95.

Blessedness must not be enclosed by any limit of time, I, 620. Who is happy and worthy of every blessedness? 798. Eternal joy is diminished by no weight of vices, 569. How great is heavenly blessedness? VII, 561. No condition is excluded from it, 721. Perfect blessedness is to complete in deed what one has taught in speech, 26. In what place did Christ teach the Beatitudes? 23. The eighth Beatitude ends in martyrdom, 24. The individual advances of the Beatitudes in the teaching are demonstrated by the example of a vineyard, 461. The end of blessedness is to know God, V, 460. See *Heaven*, *Paradise*.

Who is called blessed? I, 92. It is impossible for anyone to be blessed and happy both in this world and in the future one, 798. Those called blessed not because of virtue but because of gifts will be precipitated into death, 141. Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness, IV, 755.

Beel-shephon, I, 472.

Beeri is explained by some as “my light,” but is more correctly translated “my well,” VI, 1. The father of the prophet Hosea, ibid.

Bel, an idol, is called Belus by the Greeks and Saturn by the Latins, IV, 544. Human victims were sacrificed to him, ibid. The idol Bel was the religion of the Assyrians, V, 264. Ninus consecrated it in honor of his father Bel, ibid.

Belial, for which many read *Belian*, VII, 629.

Beel-phegor, the idol of Moab, surnamed Baal, whom the Latins call Priapus, III, 170. Beel-phegor, an idol consecrated on Nebo, IV, 185. What is the idol Beel-phegor? VI, 98. Those who serve lust worship it as a god, ibid.

Bella and ruins the spirit of Jerome shudders to recount, I, 344. Jerome cannot run through all the names of those slain in the wars, 345. It is dangerous to relate what happened in them, ibid. In the East, barbarian wars are surpassed by civil wars, 464. Internal war is more dangerous, 402. By what means Diogenes says that civil and foreign wars are stirred up, II, 40. From where do wars and quarrels arise? 764.

A good war sent by Christ, VII, 64.

Belzebub, or Beelzebub—not Belzebul should be read, III, 97. The idol of Ekron, VII, 61. Its interpretation, ibid.

To bless used in place of “to curse,” I, 794.

Blessing and punishment are far apart in name and in deed, I, 625. The blessing of bread and oil, II, 29. Earthly and spiritual blessings, VII, 546, 547.

What we do not understand through benefits, we perceive through torments, V, 79. The greatness of God’s benefits makes God our own, VI, 412.

Benjamin: what does it signify? I, 395. The tribe of Benjamin was preserved because of Paul, 698. It precedes the rape of the Sabine women by Romulus, 703.

[Col. 0933] The kindly mother of Ageruchia, I, 900. She completed the years of her widowhood, ibid.

Definition of kindness, and how it differs from goodness, VII, 511.

The Samaritans who had crossed over from the region of Babylon built Benith, III, 179.

Benoni is interpreted as “son of my sorrow,” I, 698.

The Dialogue of Berillus, II, 899.

Mount Beris in Armenia, where certain traces of Noah’s ark were found, III, 126.

The city of Beersheba, “city of the oath,” takes its name from its springs, I, 419.

Berosus wrote a history of the Chaldaeans, V, 651.

Berytus, a Roman colony, I, 695.

The ferocity of the Bessi, I, 334. The laughter of the Bessi, II, 332.

Some adopt images of different beasts, V, 136.

Ignatius fought with beasts at Rome, VII, 262.

Beasts are understood as savage nations, IV, 1030. The worst beasts are introduced into lands laid waste, V, 55. The foolish religion of the Gentiles worshipped every kind of beast, 86. Images of all beasts were consecrated in Egypt for divine worship, 670.

Beta, a kind of very cheap vegetable, IV, 598. It is food for the sick, ibid. The various conditions of the faithful are represented by it, ibid.

Bethacharma, a village near Jerusalem, IV, 881.

Bethany, “house of obedience,” VII, 164, 211.

Bethaven, “house of iniquity” and “of uselessness,” VI, 43. Some have wished it to mean “house of the sun,” that is, the Church of Christ, 44. Why the Septuagint translated it “house of [On]” [Greek as printed: ῶν], ibid.

Betharam, called Bethramtha by the Syrians and renamed Livias by Herod in honor of Augustus, III, 172, 174.

The power and efficacy of the pool of Bethesda, II, 117.

Bethel, that is, “house of God,” I, 798. Bethel, which was formerly called “house of God,” was later called Bethaven, that is, “house of uselessness and of the idol,” VI, 43.

Bethfogor, a mountain of the Moabites, III, 214.

Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread,” I, 698. The most august place in the world, 321. Bethlehem more august than Rome, ibid. Pious exercises in Bethlehem, 208. Bethlehem in the tribe of Zebulun, and Bethlehem in the tribe of Judah, III, 177. A city more august than Rome, 381. Little Bethlehem possesses the glory of holiness from which Jerusalem has fallen, IV, 676. Bethlehem and Ephrathah are two names for the same place, 1064. There are two Bethlehems, VII, 14.

Lower and upper Beth-horon, cities founded by Solomon, I, 696. They were destroyed by various storms of war, ibid.

Bethphage, “house of jaws,” on the Mount of Olives, I, 701. What it signifies, VII, 159. Its location, ibid.

In what sense Bathsheba is written as sanctified, I, 535.

Bethsaida: what does it signify? V, 339. Bethsaida, a city of Galilee, VII, 72.

Bethzur, a village in the tribe of Judah, I, 700.

Bethulia, II, 30.

Who was Biarchus? II, 425.

The Hebrew Bible translated corruptly by the Seventy Interpreters, II, 929. How it was translated by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, 528. How the Greek Bible was revised by Origen, I, 642. See Scripture.

What are the Biblinae Epistles? I, 242. They fly across the rivers of Ethiopia, II, 741.

The libraries of the churches, I, 235. Who is compelled to condemn all the libraries of the churches? 752. The Caesarean library, 545, 774. What was in it, 825. The same library is praised, VII, 734.

What is the divine library? II, 915.

Polybius and Diodorus write histories of libraries, V, 718.

Who was the first bigamist? I, 507. See Digamy, Bigamist.

Bilia, an example of chastity, III, 312. In what else she is praised, ibid.

They used to remove bitumen from the remains of Noah’s ark, and those who were purifying themselves used it, III, 126.

Blasphemy is apparent at first sight, I, 1040. Enmity can be restored, but blasphemy does not merit pardon, 533. They do not need to be convicted of what is blasphemous by their own profession, 1040. Blasphemy does not merit pardon, II, 467. Open blasphemy demands indignation, 402. At the hearing of blasphemy it was customary to tear one’s garments, IV, 459. The nature and origin of blasphemy, VII, 637. It must be avoided by all, 730. One ought not to blaspheme Christ’s disciples, ibid. Blasphemy is not to be forgiven at any time, 81.

Blastus, II, 875.

Blesilla, the widowed sister of Eustochium, became a widow in her seventh month, I, 98. Amid the ardor of her beginning faith, she received the crown of a completed work, 180. For thirty days she continually burned with fevers, 174. Her conversion thereafter, ibid. and following. Her exercises and clothing, ibid. At Blesilla’s death all virtues failed, 176. A widow of twenty years, she is called a young woman, [Col. 0934] ibid. What were her natural gifts? ibid. She excelled perfectly in the use of languages, ibid. Her humility and other virtues, ibid. As she was soon to die, she commended herself to the prayers of those assisting her, ibid. Noblewomen led the funeral procession, and a golden veil was spread over the bier, ibid. What she seemed then to have cried from heaven, ibid. In the short span of her life Blesilla completed many seasons of virtue, 282. She is said to have reproached the tears of her mother Paula, 182. Jerome was Blesilla’s father in spirit and her nurturer in charity, 177. Jerome’s devotion to her, 184. When Jerome wrote concerning Blesilla’s falling asleep, 457. The people’s murmuring at her death, 184. Blesilla, the mother of Paula, 691. She was descended from the Scipios and Gracchi, ibid. What Blesilla urgently requested from Jerome, II, 633. What Blesilla also requested from him, VII, 245.

Beroea, II, 43. It is a city of Syria, 833.

The neck-collars of condemned persons were commonly called boiae, III, 43.

Everything good that we have is a taste of the Lord, I, 1034. To know the good belongs to judgment; to do it, to labor, 106. The former is common to many, the latter to few, ibid. In some people good qualities are evident; in others we learn them through long practice, 287. Good must be done so that we may turn away from evil, 941. It is not enough to know what is good, unless what has been chosen is guarded more attentively, 106. Only with difficulty, laboring and sweating, can we change evils into goods, 613. Unless we hate evil, we cannot love good, 941. We must provide what is good even before human beings, 912. It is impossible for anyone to enjoy both present and future goods, 798. We are commanded to return good for evil, 522. Indifferent goods, 793. In their loss and contempt there is not perfect virtue, ibid. We ought not to receive another’s goods in such a way that we are also compelled to accept his evils, 347. Every good that we do is God’s good, II, 777. Let each person, according to his strength and as much as he can, extend himself toward the good, 713. Nothing is contrary to the good except evil, 216. Goods and evils are attributed to their own author, 563. Change from good things to better belongs to the right hand and power of God, 765. The Lord is not unjust, condemning sins alone and not remembering good works, ibid. Indifferent goods, 317. Every good and truth is enclosed by a definite end, whereas wickedness and falsehood are without end, III, 466. According to God’s arrangement, each thing is good when it is needed, 412. We can indeed call everything in this world good in itself; but compared with God, it is reckoned as nothing, 386. What goods God has given human beings in this life, 449. Nothing is good except virtue, and nothing evil except vice, IV, 159. Philosophers call goods indifferent, 607, 645. What are indifferent goods? 159. Whatever is good cannot be given without God, 943. What are goods, evils, and the visitation of the Lord? 1000. True goods are not born in the accursed earth, but in heaven, V, 859. It does not immediately follow that what is not good is evil, 231. The good need a constant teacher, 34. The good of union, 960. What are false goods? VI, 514. God’s blessing is present when he removes them, ibid. Not to love good is a sin; how great a crime, then, to hate it? 465. What does it mean to seek good and reject evil? 296. It is not enough to seek good and reject evil, 279. Where are love of good and hatred of evil placed? ibid. The reward of one who loves good, ibid. The end of punishments is the beginning of goods, 525. Who performs good? VII, 631. No one does so without virtues, 552. Nothing can be called good unless it is voluntary, 751. Let every good come from Christ, the source, 754. To be absolutely like God is good, 757. In good things, not beginnings but the end is more worthy of praise, 461. In what are goods and evils placed? 524. For what reason should good be done? 255.

The good and the evil seem to rage against one another, I, 196. Why are the good praised and the evil condemned? 126. Good and evil are found in every rank and sex, 260. In praising the best, the endeavors of the good are stirred up toward virtue, 128.

In what matter is goodness regarded with suspicion? II, 251. Our goodness is from God; sins are from us, V, 865. Definition of goodness, and how it differs from kindness, VII, 512.

The praises of Bonosus, I, 18. His solitude, 11. Why was he called “son of the fish”? ibid. He was brought up together with Jerome, 12. Jerome was always expansive in his praises of Bonosus, ibid.

The constellation Boötes, IV, 240.

The Borborites, VII, 429.

Borith, a fuller’s herb which, according to Palestinian practice, grows in green and moist places, IV, 850. The same herb, and what it signifies, VI, 972.

Where the Ox and the Ass are read together in Scripture, IV, 12. What the Ox and the Ass signify, 432.

Bosor: what does it signify? II, 442.

Bosra is interpreted as “flesh,” II, 774.

Bosra in the land of Moab, IV, 442. Bosra signifies Idumaea “fortified” [Greek: ὠχυρωμένην], and “protected,” VI, 235.

The people of Israel desired the head of the Egyptian ox, IV, 556.

What are the arms of God? IV, 587.

“Arm” is used for “work,” I, 355.

[Col. 0935] What do the arm and breast customarily given to the priest from the victims signify? I, 354.

Who are the Brahmans? I, 271. What do they observe concerning foods? 685.

Brennus took only what he had found, I, 983. After routing the army at the Allia, he entered Rome, 914.

“Brief,” that is, a catalogue, I, 15.

Britain, a fertile province of tyrants, I, 1038. It learns that there is a hospice in a Roman harbor, 466. Britain and Mauretania were Christian in Origen’s time, V, 917.

In what is the virtue of the Bruti praised? I, 334.

Brutus, II, 471. Brustus married Portia, 312. What doctrines are learned in Brutus, 565.

Untamed wild oxen, VI, 319.

Bubastis, a city of Egypt, V, 398.

The difference between bugles and trumpets, VI, 53. When the use of bugles and trumpets began among the people of God, IV, 190.

Bucolia of Egypt, II, 38.

Budda, chief of the Gymnosophists, was generated from the side of a virgin, II, 273.

The Burgundians, I, 914.

The horses of Buricus, I, 399.

Boxwood is an incorruptible wood, IV, 406. In boxwood they trained the hand of a child, VI, 610.

Byssus used for earth, I, 368. Byssus grows in Egypt, V, 306. The finest threads of byssus are woven into the high priest’s garment, 153.

## C

Virgil describes Cacus, II, 787.

From where is “corpse” derived? VII, 347.

Kadesh, a desert, I, 488. Its interpretation, 489. Cadesa, that is, “prostitute,” ibid.

What falling on one’s face and falling backward signify, V, 23.

At Cannae many thousands of Romans were killed, I, 980.

The blind prefigured the sacraments of both peoples, I, 702.

Caecilius translated the old comic poets, I, 309.

The presbyter Caecilius converted Cyprian to the faith, II, 907.

To strike is one thing when done with a parent’s affection, another when one rages against adversaries, II, 724. No one is bravely struck by himself, 412. He who strikes is not greater, but stronger, than the one who is struck, IV, 977.

The likeness of cemeteries, I, 625.

Caesar Augustus was honored by Herod, I, 696. What Tullius said about Caesar, 398. A saying of Caesar Augustus, II, 419. By the names Caesar and Augustus the royal dignity among the Romans is indicated, V, 341. The Romans retained the ancient name “Caesar” for their rulers even among barbarian nations, VI, 716. Caesar, VII, 530, 478. Roman kings were called Caesars after Gaius Caesar, 177. Augustus Caesar, 688. Pilate placed an image of Caesar in the Temple, 194. See Augustus.

From where did Caesarea receive its name? I, 696. What was seen there, ibid. Caesarea is the metropolis of Palestine, II, 447. It provided examples of virgin girls, 301. The Church at Caesarea was dedicated through Cornelius the centurion, ibid. Caesarea, the name given to Mazaca, the metropolis of Cappadocia, by Augustus Caesar, V, 311.

Caesarea Philippi is today called Paneas, IV, 507. From where Caesarea Philippi received its name, and by whom it was founded, VII, 121. It is now called Paneas and is in the province of Phoenice, ibid. Why, and by whom, the Tower of Straton was called Caesarea, 121, and II, 883.

Caesarius, brother of Gregory of Nazianzus, II, 943.

White hair shows the length of life, IV, 338. Hair and beard are an indication of manhood, V, 49.

The Cainite heresy raises its crushed head like a viper, I, 411. It overturns the whole sacrament of Christ, ibid. It asserts that there are certain sins which Christ cannot cleanse with his blood, ibid. It does nothing else but make Christ’s death useless, 412. The Cainite heresy restored, II, 396.

The Cainites, II, 197.

How Cain is understood to have been avenged through seven generations, I, 161 and following. By what sign Cain knew that Abel’s offerings pleased God, III, 310. He wandered in the earth, roaming and an exile, 312. Cain first built a city, VI, 229. 424. Gaius Caligula, II, 847.

A reed writes on parchment, paper, or any other material suitable for writing, I, 376.

What a broken reed mystically signifies, I, 856.

Calamity. Those who are unjustly oppressed by the powerful cannot find a comforter, III, 418.

To trample earthly things belongs to wisdom, knowledge, and virtue, III, 405.

Mourners customarily cast off their shoes, V, 282.

The feet of Christians shod, IV, 301.

A creaking little shoe, I, 286.

Christ did not have shoes, I, 103. What a shoe signifies mystically, ibid. Shoes were forbidden to the apostles, 346.

[Col. 0936] A calculus is a kind of stone, I, 61. It signifies the word of God, ibid.

The cup of unmixed wine [Greek: ἀκράτου] is an indication of the Lord’s fury, IV, 1017.

The cup signifies mortification of the flesh and a spirit always prepared for martyrdom, I, 194.

With what reverence chalices and sacred veils should be handled, 759.

The cup of punishment and the cup of blessing, V, 822, 829. What the cup signifies in Scripture, VII, 155. See Affliction, Distress.

Callides, II, 566.

Callimachus uses a half-line of heroic verse, I, 426. Callimachus of Cyrene, the poet, VII, 707. What is attributed to him? ibid. He wrote on the praises of Jupiter, ibid.

Callirrhoe, a city from which hot waters burst forth and flow into the Red Sea, III, 321.

Sudden heat overcomes prolonged lukewarmness, I, 17.

Calpe, a mountain, VII, 427.

Calvary: from where is it so called? I, 201. The site of Calvary, VII, 232. Some suspect that Adam was buried there, ibid.

Baldness is a sign of mourning, IV, 952, and V, 73, 322, and VI, 340.

A new kind of slander, II, 554. Every iniquity arises from slander, IV, 640. The vice of slander is described, VI, 801. The zeal and lies of slanderers, 331.

Cambyses, son of Cyrus, devastated Egypt as far as Ethiopia, V, 352. After capturing Egypt he carried the images of the gods to Persia, 710. Driven into madness, he was pierced by his own dagger after falling from his horse, 352.

The camels of Midian and Ephah, in the typology of the goods of the rich, I, 500. Dromedary camels that chew the cud, II, 48.

“Camel” is a word of ambiguous meaning, VII, 150. The camel’s hump signifies sins, I, 821.

The Camilli, I, 323.

Camilla, queen of the Volscians, is called a virgin on account of her exceptional chastity, II, 306. She provided Turnus with assistance, ibid.

The military garment called the camisia, I, 361. A military item of clothing, ibid.

The Campenses, heretics, I, 39, 41.

Cana and Capernaum, familiar witnesses of Christ’s miracles, I, 703. “Canna,” Latin for “reed,” is taken from the Hebrew language, III, 39.

Cancer, the disease, V, 927.

A candidate of the emperor Constantius was freed from demonic possession, II, 24. His rustic simplicity, ibid.

Candidus, a follower of Valentinian, II, 509. The Dialogue of Candidus and Origen, 511. He asserts that Christ was brought forth by the Father and that the demon was of the worst nature, ibid.

Dogs bark on behalf of their masters, II, 569. Dogs, the most keen-scented of animals, IV, 12. How dogs are said to become rabid, VII, 116.

The battle at Cannae, I, 18.

The dignity and perfection of those who sing the Lord’s praises, V, 490.

The cantharus in which there is a figure of the heretics, VI, 619.

Some are allowed to enjoy Gallic cart-horses, I, 135.

Cantherius accuses Saint Jerome of sacrilege, VI, 425. The holy Doctor proves his innocence, ibid.

The songs of the world must be ignored, I, 681. The songs of those serving idols are called howlings, VI, 80.

Whether it is fitting to pray with a song, VI, 633.

When the Song of Songs should be read, I, 688. Care must be taken lest, failing to understand spiritual things beneath carnal words, we be wounded, ibid. The Song of Songs contains the mysteries of virginity, II, 285. It does not signify carnal love, 286. Explained by Origen, 500. It consists of four voices, 502. The Song of Songs properly speaks of those who desire only heavenly things, III, 384. The shorter the Song of Songs is, the more difficult it is, VI, 364. Who sings a spiritual song? VII, 651.

The fault of singers, I, 17.

What are ecclesiastical chants? VII, 652. What must be avoided and desired in singing, ibid.

Caphar-Barucha is interpreted as “Village of Blessing,” I, 701.

The field of Capernaum, I, 490. What Capernaum signifies, VII, 23.

Women’s ambition concerning their hair is bound by a diadem, V, 156. Among the ancients it was customary for mourners to cut their hair, IV, 896.

The headpiece of the high priest in the Old Testament, I, 366.

Baldness of the head is a sign of mourning, V, 73.

The gilded Capitol lies grimy, I, 678.

The Cappadocians lived in Gaza after killing its former inhabitants, III, 218.

Wounded does seek dittany, III, 444. What the doe signifies, ibid. It sees with the greatest precision, ibid.

The Commentaries of Caprio, II, 897.

What are capsaces? I, 292.

Nothing is more cruel in captivity among the hands of enemies and under harsh necessity than separation of parents from their children, I, 694. Extreme captivity knows neither shame nor weakness, IV, 186. Why Israel’s captivity occurred especially in the time of King Hoshea, VI, 106 and following.

The bonds of captives seem to bind us, I, 579. Troops of captives being dragged along, 345.

The head holds the principal place among all the limbs and senses, IV, 15. When it suffers, they are weakened, ibid.

When the head is healthy, all the senses are vigorous, I, 326. Whatever praise belongs to the limbs is all referred to the head, 201. Movement of the head as a sign of one who is burning with anger and envy, IV, 160. The adornment of the head is the dignity of the whole body, V, 156.

Caracalla, a type of garment, I, 361.

A coal of desolation, I, 61.

What does “heap coals on the head of one’s enemy” mean? I, 821 and following.

Where the carbuncle and emerald are found, I, 934. What is a carbuncle stone? IV, 94.

Humanity should support those shut up in prison by daily assistance, I, 580.

The Persians used cardamom and salt in their stew, V, 697.

Mount Cardueni in Armenia, III, 126.

Cariath-Sepher is interpreted as “little village of letters,” I, 700.

Caricus, II, 881.

Mount Carmel in Galilee, covered with wooded groves, IV, 147, 191. There are two Carmels, 397. The two Carmels, VI, 225.

A song belongs to the just, I, 1087.

When are we called carnal, or spiritual? VII, 501, 504.

The little book of Carneades, I, 334. What did Carneades do? 237. Carneades, a disciple of Philo, II, 309. He removed truth from life, 498.

The eating of meat was unknown until the Flood, II, 267. It is rejected by many, 343 and following. Rotten flesh is treated with iron and cautery, 777. Those who serve the flesh commend meat, I, 504. Its consumption is permitted to some and forbidden to others, ibid. It is prohibited during fasts, 617.

The flesh draws the soul through certain enticements toward deadly pleasures, I, 506. It is a great virtue not to live carnally in the flesh, 287. Fragile and destined to become ashes, it fights alone against many, 89. Love of the flesh is overcome by love of the spirit, 100. The vigor of the soul becomes stronger through the weakness of the flesh, 288. The soul fluctuates between the works of the flesh and those of the spirit, 506. Which flesh is to be loved? 531. The fragility of the flesh is one thing, the strength of the spirit another, 1037. Its fragility leads to death, 1038. In the Creed, the resurrection of the flesh is believed, 527. What the weakness of the flesh cannot endure, the spirit conversing with God in faith overcomes, 620. The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God and is death, 588. It cannot be called the soul, ibid. The works of the flesh are condemned, not its nature, II, 436. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God, 273. The definition of flesh differs from that of body, 435. Flesh and spirit oppose one another, IV, 348. The nature of the flesh is not condemnable, 603. Very many reign with Christ in it, ibid. The flesh rejects hunger, that is, shuns it, VII, 502. Victory in the flesh is difficult, 519. The fruits of the flesh and of the spirit, 510. As much as we trust in the ardor of the mind, so much should we fear the fragility of the flesh, 220. Who does not trust in the flesh? 479. The desires of the flesh and of the spirit, 501, 502. It is one thing to be in the flesh and another to live in the flesh, 415. How many are prepared to endure exile, martyrdoms, and poverty, yet are nevertheless overcome by the suffering of the flesh, 684. By what aid is weak flesh to be strengthened? 277.

Iron-bound carts, by which threshing is completed in Palestine, IV, 342 and 385.

Even the unskilled can pluck and disparage, VI, 429.

Carpocrates, II, 197.

The praise of Carterius, I, 425. Various matters are reported concerning Carterius, bishop of Spain, 412.

Carthage was founded by Dido, II, 310. It was founded and brought to its end in praise of chastity, ibid. It is burned, ibid. The queen of Carthage preferred to burn rather than marry King Iarbas, 900. Carthage is thought to be Tarshish, III, 286. Carthage is a colony of the Tyrians, IV, 227. Who were the founders of Carthage? VII, 427.

The emperor Carus, II, 913.

What is cassia? I, 384.

The little work of Casianus Valentinianus, II, 879.

Casium, a city of Egypt, IV, 207.

The Caspians throw their dead elders to the beasts, II, 335.

Cassandra, the virgin prophetess of Apollo and Juno, II, 307.

Chastity cuts off lust, and woman conquers men, I, 293. It is purchased by fasts and abstinence, 616. Chastity and holiness are the most secure possessions, 628. The lover of chastity, intent upon the praise of modesty, catches it with a watchful ear, 230. While the law of marriage is preserved, it is cut down by evangelical chastity, 909. Companions for guarding chastity, 619. The tongue falsely proclaims chastity when the whole body displays immodesty, 286. Its dangers, 786. The devil finds chastity destructive to him, 905. Those who did not remain virgins are said to be polluted in comparison with the purest chastity, 226. A young woman whose body is heated by foods is not secure concerning chastity, 287. False chastity, ibid. One must not trust in one’s former state, 259. To make the chastity of many one’s own gain, 992. Chastity has always been preferred to marriage, II, 256. Its privilege, II, 484. The chastity of the devil, V, 947. Chastity and incorruption, VII, 720. What is perfect chastity? 716. It is pleasing in itself, 147. The enemy fights against chastity more fiercely in the flowering of youth, 719. See Modesty and Continence.

Castorina, Jerome’s maternal aunt, I, 27.

Camps were customarily fortified with rampart and ditch, I, 29.

In what is Castrutius’s good will toward Jerome recognized? III, 406.

The origin of the Cataphrygian heresy, II, 881. The Cataphrygians, VII, 429.

What are cataracts? VI, 145.

Who were called catechists among Christians? I, 237.

Catechumens are candidates for the faith, I, 415.

A purgative drink, IV, 1017 and following. Purgatives are given so that harmful humor may be expelled from the bodies, V, 269.

“Chair” is used for doctrine, VII, 182.

The first victory of Catholics is to expose the secrets of the heretics, VI, 370.

A saying of Catiline, II, 540.

Catina, the author, and his saying, V, 12.

Cato the Censor learned Greek literature when already an old man, I, 252. Various things are said about the same man, 989. The virtue of the Catos in mourning, 335. The empty names of the Catos, 324. Cato, a martyr of foolish philosophy, 180. A notable saying of Cato, 400.

The wife of Cato the Censor, II, 316. Catonian severity, 469. Pride, 726. An example of Cato, 335. Cato, the husband of Marcia, 312. Cicero did not benefit Cato’s glory by praising him, nor did Caesar harm it by criticizing him, VI, 53.

Catullus, I, 279.

The crags of the Caucasus, I, 464. The same crags, II, 300.

How innkeepers can be doctors, IV, 25.

Centumviral cases, I, 237.

What is a cautery? I, 262.

An unjust and false guarantee, IV, 690.

Cedar: what does it signify? I, 690. What are Cedar and Nebaioth? IV, 722. Cedar is a region of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, 846. The inhabitants of Cedar are especially skilled in the art of warfare, 218.

Cedar and cypress have the finest fragrance, IV, 502. Cedar wood is incorruptible, ibid.

Celerinus, father of Ageruchia, II, 894. His sister remained a widow for twenty years, ibid. He raised Ageruchia from infancy and received her, when born, into his own bosom, ibid.

“Celeuma,” the word used by sailors exhorting one another, I, 36.

Regard your little cell as paradise, I, 936.

The impiety of Celsus, I, 313. He wrote against Christians, and Origen replied to him, 427. By whom Celsus and Porphyry were attacked, 223. Celsus, an enemy of Christ, II, 823. Many wrote against Celsus and Porphyry, 569.

Who is an unjust censor? II, 502.

The fable of the centaurs, VII, 651.

The praises of the number one hundred, IV, 790.

What are centones? I, 275.

Centumviral cases, I, 237.

From where are centurions, tribunes, quinquagenarii, and decani so called? IV, 48.

The faith, humility, and prudence of the centurion, VII, 44.

Onions and the rumbling of the belly were part of the religion of Pelusium, IV, 544.

Cephas is interpreted as Peter, I, 890. Cephas and Peter have the same meaning, VII, 409. Some admit a double Cephas, 408. Yet Jerome knows no other than Peter, ibid.

Wax is the lodging-place of honey and was despised in sacrifices, I, 961.

Cherries: from where are they so called? I, 151. Lucullus is said to have first brought this fruit to Rome from Cerasus, ibid.

Cerberus, II, 387.

The Cereales, II, 536.

The consul Cerealis seeks Marcella in marriage, I, 951. He says various things to her when she refuses, 952.

Unless the brain is healthy, all the limbs will be diseased, I, 422. In some people the health of the brain was disturbed through excessive abstinence, 994.

Lighted candles were carried at the funerals of the dead, I, 722. For what purpose may they be lit? 194. Why are candles lit in churches? II, 394. Why are they lit for the reading of the Gospel? ibid.

The ceremonies of the Jews are harmful to Christians, I, 743. Why the Jews received the ceremonies of the Law, V, 228.

The heresy of Cerinthus, I, 746. Cerinthus, II, 843, 200. He had Ebion as his successor, 197. He mangled the Gospels, ibid. The doctrine of Cerinthus, VII, 3.

What is ceroma? I, 257.

Certainties must not be abandoned in pursuit of uncertainties, II, 400.

We should not think the contest perpetual and therefore grow weary, I, 616. Its end is the crown of righteousness, ibid. It is ours to choose, if we wish to be crowned in the contest and struggle, 990. Whoever removes the contest removes the crown, II, 784. As long as we live, we are in contest, II, 747. See Battle.

Stags draw serpents from their caves, IV, 938. Snakes are food for stags, I, 979.

Hardening of the neck, IV, 230. Raising of the neck, VI, 658.

By the islands of Kittim either Italy or the western regions are understood, IV, 846. Various opinions concerning Kittim, 227.

The Hebrews believe that Keturah is the same as Hagar, with the name changed, III, 343.

Chalanne, or the tower of Babylon, II, 88.

Among the Greeks, Chalceterus was a very prolific writer, I, 153. The multitude of his books, 237.

Chalcioecus, a virgin, II, 306.

Chaldaea, the land of Canaan, V, 170.

The Chaldaeans are interpreted as “demons,” I, 88. “Chaldaeans” means demons, IV, 529. Who are the Chaldaeans? V, 890.

Can Canaan be called the Promised Land? I, 966. The ten tribes are called Canaan, VI, 137. Canaan can be interpreted as “those who move,” 138.

The Canaanite language is the same as Syriac, IV, 207. What does it mean to speak in the Canaanite language? 296.

Charity is the mother of all virtues, I, 521. Its prerogative, 347. It has no measure, 199, 200. It can do everything, 3. Charity cannot be bought and has no price, 13. No necessity is greater than charity, 18. Let us prefer nothing in the world to charity toward God and neighbor, 626. Let it be inclined toward mercy, not insulting sinners, 580. Those whom charity joins, let not the length of the earth separate, 435. It makes absent persons present, 347. The dignity of charity, II, 491. Let charity of spirit, the bond of faith, and the harmony of the priesthood be preserved by us patiently and gently, 199. The charity of many is disordered: what they ought to love in the first place, they love in the second, III, 524. If a son is bad and a household servant good, let the servant be placed in the charity owed to the son; and thus the charity of the saints will be ordered, 525. True charity, violated by no envy: the more it increases in number, the more it grows in strength, 422. Charity holds the primacy among the virtues, VII, 510. Its duties, 607. The good of charity, 497, 510. Charity is fitting for angels, 407. It alone is without labor, 498. It is attacked in us by the devil, ibid. Its possession is rare, ibid. Without charity there would be public robbery among human beings, 501. Charity toward one’s neighbor is not the same as charity toward one’s wife, 661. The health of charity, 715. Fervent and chilled, ibid. See Love and Affection.

The scarcity of paper in the desert, I, 25. The trade in paper in Egypt, 18. Paper was made from reed, IV, 191. Bundles of papers containing the slanders of moneylenders, a principal cause of sedition, 689.

The archive of the Roman Church, II, 559.

Charybdis, I, 695, 933. Carybdis, II, 563. An insatiable whirlpool, 551.

Chavonae, or cakes or pastries, which idolaters prepared for the army of heaven, IV, 671.

Hebron, a city, III, 361.

Cherubim is interpreted as “multitude of knowledge,” I, 280.

Chaeremon relates many things about the priests of Egypt, II, 342, 343.

Who are the Chiliasts? VI, 925 and following. What kinds of pleasures they dream for themselves, 930, and IV, 646. They are refuted, 828 and following.

The monster Chimera, II, 387.

By what names are promissory notes called by the prophet? IV, 642 and following.

Surgeons are considered cruel and are wretched, I, 186.

Chnum, the name of an Egyptian monastery, II, 89.

What is Chobar? V, 5.

Chochebas, leader of the Jews, overcome by the Romans, V, 666.

Jerome does not know what Chodchod signifies, V, 313.

What is the choerogrilus? I, 670.

Chorazin, a city of Galilee, VII, 72.

A chorus of those singing psalms, I, 1090.

The use of chrism, VI, 654. It is called a spiritual ointment, ibid.

Christians become Christians, they are not born Christians, I, 678. Christ bestowed the dignity of the Christian name upon the saints, 623. They were anointed with oil, 182. Nothing is happier than the Christian, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised, 932. Nothing is more laborious, since he daily risks his life, ibid. Nothing is stronger, since he conquers the devil, ibid. Nothing is weaker, since he is overcome by the flesh, ibid. There are very many examples of these things, ibid. The life of a Christian is a military service, 29. To offer oneself to God belongs properly to Christians and apostles, 433. They receive more than they offer, 979. It is a great thing to be a Christian, not merely to seem one, 325. What is the first virtue among Christians? 207. It is humility, 705. Among them, not the one who suffers but the one who inflicts insult is wretched, 43. In all the judgments of the Lord, let the Christian rejoice, 179. What suspicion must be far removed from Christians, 501. Christ’s disciple ought to surpass the philosopher of the world, 399. Jerome teaches what he ought to desire who is destined to be Christ’s servant, 798. Christ’s servant does not swell with riches, nor shrink through poverty, 267. He despises things that are joyful and things that are sorrowful, ibid. Let Christians who are senseless take note of what is said, 233. In them beginnings are not sought, but the end, 285. They all wish to be without sin, 1036. How he walks, 267. The doctrine of Christians is to hold aloft the banner of humility, 210. The contest over this virtue among the first Christians, 207. To forgive belongs to Christians, 1091. They must flee Jewish practices, 265. The mourning of the Jews is the joy of Christians, 335. Food and clothing are the riches of Christians, 281. What sort of adornment the Lord seeks in them, 267. Neither affected squalor nor elaborate cleanliness befits them, 113. We ought to love the homes of Christians as though they were our own, 262. Let them know us as comforters in their sorrows, ibid. The profit of Christians, 346. What they ought to say at the loss of their own people, 796. In vice there is not much difference between being able to deceive a Christian and being deceived, 324. How the honor of the Christian name commits fraud more than it suffers it, 944. He is not at fault if a pretender to religion is vicious, 935. Where has the triumph of Christian glory been heard? 980. Who is called by the name “Christian”? 197. They regard it as a remedy for their punishment if there is a crowd of those perishing, and so forth, ibid. It was the custom of Christians to contemplate heavenly things and always pray to God, II, 849. What ought to be far removed from their conduct, 569. Jerome approves no accusation of one Christian against another, 711. What Rome could not reproach Christians with, 309. Among Christians it is a great vice to relate or do something shameful, 224. They should speak not for display but for edification, 535. To be struck by the sword is the wish of Christians, 3. Fortitude does not befit a Christian, 341. Health without excessive strength is necessary for him, ibid. The punishments of Christians who are saved, 712. Everything that is not permitted to a Christian is equally common to bishop and layman, 174. When you call someone a heretic, you deny him to be a Christian, ibid. Most Christians were baptized in the living stream at Bethabara, III, 182. The Christian people is called God’s people, IV, 739. The concord and unity of Christians, 160. Everything that the Jews do carnally is fulfilled spiritually by Christians, 21. In comparison with Christians, the pagans are like women, 206. What the teachers of the churches proclaim to Christians, 482. Christians are so through necessity, not through willingness, 727. Christians alone pollute the Lord’s name, V, 523. Why Christians are called Jews in Scripture, 871. The imitators of Christ are rocks, 858. In what does the duty of Christians consist? VI, 458. Torments will not overcome the Christian name, 478. A Christian ought to be temperate in prudence and simplicity, 76. Persecutions against Christians and the peace of the Church, 841. Christians fight against the Church during persecution, 897. How the number of seven thousand pertains to the name of Christians, 855. What befits a Christian, VII, 641. The multitude of Christians and the small number of Jews, 474. The distinctive virtue of Christians is to return thanks to God in adversity, 653. The dogs of the Gentiles bark against Christians, 166. The persecution of the Jews against Christians, 476.

Christ the model of perfect humility, I, 347. His soul possesses every virtue, 589. He lies hidden, enclosed in the letter, 274. He was predestined and prefigured in the Law and in the prophets, ibid. Christ is born as a treasure in the field of the Scriptures, 399. He is likewise the jewel purchased at the price of many pearls, ibid. He is sanctification, ibid. Likewise redemption, Redeemer, and price, 400. He is everything in us, ibid. He is not confined within a place, 520. Christ’s humility, 26. His obedience, 783. They revered the Mother whose father he himself was, ibid. He honored his foster-father, whom he had nourished, ibid. Christ is not deceived by secrets, 286. If Christ cannot give life to some, he died in vain, 412. The one voice of the whole world is Christ, 334. For our salvation Christ assumed flesh of human frailty, 586. When he began to be what we are, he did not cease to be what he had been, ibid. Although he was human, he was not changed into flesh, since he did not cease to be God, ibid. He assumed the whole human being without sin, ibid. By what means Christ shows himself to be the giver of laws and the true God, 563. His divinity is not circumscribed by any spaces of place, ibid. The narrowness of a human body did not confine the ineffable power of his majesty, ibid. The greatness of his works proves him to be the Son of God, ibid. Perfect God, of his own will he assumed everything belonging to the human condition and nature, ibid. Contrary to the error of some, he was not divided into two Saviors, 564. Whatever he once assumed, he never laid aside, ibid. He was truly God and man, ibid. To foolish minds, only that was believed of Christ which the eyes displayed, 622. The invisible God was discerned by the wise from his works, ibid. Him whom his face showed to be man, his powers signified to be God, ibid. He met death without fear, to give an example of courage and constancy, ibid. The Lord of glory was shown in his very passion, ibid. He remained impassible in his divinity, while passible in the flesh, ibid. Had he feared the cross, who would willingly have fought for religion? ibid. He who subjected the world to his faith is mocked by unbelievers, ibid. He bestowed the dignity of the Christian name upon the saints, ibid. Coming from heaven, he brought with him nothing belonging to our condition, 591. Christ was in the womb of blessed Mary for ten months, 123. How great were the indignities and reproaches that he endured, ibid. He saved the human race not by flashing lightning and thundering, but by wailing in a manger and remaining silent on the cross, 512. By his coming he destroyed the tricks of magicians, 576. He is for the ruin of sinners and the resurrection of the penitent, 897. Whatever belongs to the perfection of human nature was assumed by Christ, 591. He became man for us, not for brute animals, 588. He did not have an airy and spiritual body, 718. Nothing imperfect was assumed by him, 591. The Son of God and his soul are of different natures, 599. It is impious to say that his soul was without mind and sense, 587. He did not empty himself by the soul that he assumed, 233. He is proclaimed as born of a virgin, and she as his mother, 597. He left us examples of the virtues, 986. A virgin in the flesh, a monogamist in the spirit, 908. The age of thirty years is perfect in Christ, 518. The devil lays a snare for him through food, 986. Why was he tempted? ibid. By his washing he cleansed the waters, 702. After baptism and the sanctification of the waters of the Jordan, he preaches the kingdom of heaven, 419. He performs the first sign from water, ibid. Questioning the elders about the questions of the Law, he teaches, 273. He wept through the force of love and charity, 201. Why did he weep for Lazarus? 335. Holy women ministered to him from their own resources, 954. In a crown of thorns he bore the sins of the world, 291. In flesh capable of suffering he displayed the power of his own majesty, 564. Christ’s humility and passion surpass every virtue, 981. From Christ’s side flow the sacraments of baptism and martyrdom, 421. His tomb is more venerable than the Holy of Holies, 202. At the resurrection Christ received his soul, 590. After his body had been buried, this soul descended to the underworld, ibid. He neither brought flesh down from heaven, nor was his soul created before his flesh, 591. After the resurrection he possessed all his limbs, 718. What he did so that the reality of his body would not be thought a phantom, 233. In his resurrection he gave our bodies a pledge of salvation, 575. He slaughtered death, 332. Through Christ’s blood the gates of paradise were opened, 333. The voices and writings of the nations resound with his passion and resurrection, 334. He established a new family for himself on earth, 104. He gave us the eternal joy of his victory, 569. The gate of paradise had not yet been broken open by Christ, 181. Everything belonging to us died with Christ, 421. Whoever believes in him lives, 283. Before Christ, Abraham was in the underworld; after Christ, the thief was in paradise, 333. He will be judge, 1088. He saved the whole human being, 594. In the present he grants what he promised his servants, 692. This is proved by an example, ibid. A poor man dedicated the poverty of his house, 265. He desires all his athletes to be crowned, 432. Whoever believes in Christ must believe his words as well, 29. What is rightly understood in Christ, 273. He loves nothing intermediate, 151. Our likeness in Christ was not changed into the nature of divinity, nor was divinity [changed], etc., 565. On the gibbet he appears victorious, ibid. Some think that Christ was changed into another, ibid. Origen brings his kingdom to an end, ibid. If it must have an end, it follows that Christ ceases to be God, 567. What Abraham showed to strangers, he showed to his disciples and servants, 401. He is not deceived by artifice, 446. He is honored in his servants, 453. Whoever is not his belongs to the Antichrist, 39. Without Christ, everything we live is vain, 340. What does it mean to make Christ’s enemies and nourish his adversaries? 1042. Those desiring Christ with their eyes deem nothing else worthy of their gaze, 936. The perfect servant of Christ has nothing besides Christ, 33. What things seem harsh to those who do not love Christ? 123. He follows Christ who forgives sins and is the companion of the virtues, 399. Whoever belongs to Christ is more truly ours, 782. For whom he was of no benefit, 331. Whoever is first in the world should be first in Christ’s household, 795. Naked, follow the naked Christ, 948. His adversary is the one displeased by his commandments, 175. It is the same impiety to say that the Son of God and his soul are one, and to deny that the Father and the Son are one, 599. The same impiety is directed against him, 595.

Christ was never without the Holy Spirit, II, 179. He is called the second and heavenly Adam, 373. There is one Christ and one God for all the orders of Christians, 173. His folly despises the wisdom of the ancients, 425. He alone was without sin, 321. To be able to do all things belongs to him, and is preserved for him, 760. He alone possessed all the virtues, 719. His arm brought salvation, 774. Christ was in the womb of blessed Mary for ten months, 206. He alone opened the closed gates of the virgin womb, 745. Born in the flesh, he planted the Church, 195. The reality of the assumed human being in Christ, 758. It is related that he was unable to do something in the flesh and on account of the flesh, ibid. Certain Fathers spoke less cautiously about Christ’s divinity before the Arian heresy, 509. In what does he indicate the reality of the human being? 447. He assumed flesh and a soul of human nature, 493. The demons confess him, ibid. His soul is made a subject of inquiry, ibid. Christ is a virgin from a virgin, incorrupt from the incorrupt, 249. Let us imitate his manner of life, whose birth we cannot imitate, ibid. Christ is bright in virginity and ruddy in martyrdom, 287. The herald of virginity, 268. A virgin in the flesh, a monogamist in the spirit, 265. By his washing he cleansed the waters, 179. All, except a few, considered him the son of Joseph, 209. Why could Christ’s flesh not exceed the measure of its frailty? 758. He did not suffer the losses of the flesh, 795. He overcame both its injury and its frailty, 786. He feels pains, 778. He did not know the day and hour of the final consummation, 758. How he was transfigured on the mountain, 437. He is held back by the stupor of another’s unbelief, 757. Why did Christ follow the Jewish manner of life with the rest? 305. Although he was often present at meals, he is not said to have served either gluttony or his belly, 352. Insofar as he is the son of man, he moderates the sentence, 757. What does he say under the persona of the assumed human being? 347. He used the Hebrew Scriptures, 528. Christ expressed a mystery as a type of his passion, 352. As a man destined to suffer, he speaks in human words, 758. How he prayed on the cross, 799. The Jews mocked this crucified man, and the Gentiles honored him, 195. We were redeemed by his blood and passion, 255. Whatever Christ did after his resurrection, he did truly and in reality, 444. The fact that he suddenly vanished from their eyes is a work of God’s power, not of a shadow or phantom, ibid. Afterward he ate, to prove the reality of his body, 352. The answer to those asking why Christ was not recognized after his resurrection, 445. Recognized and unrecognized, he was always the same, ibid. He saved all, so that the whole world might be subjected to God and preserved by his mercy, 774. He must be subjected to the Father according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, 713. How are we one with him? 371. The humbler the things he suffered for us, the more we owe him, 226. Christ’s brothers should be regarded in the same way as Joseph was regarded as father, 224. Everything will tremble at his coming, 774. His glory and Satan’s destruction, 7. Christ the true Solomon: what sort of armor-bearers does he have? 285. To whom does he go? ibid. Under Christ the emperor, who is more glorious? 293. He drew back the end of time to the beginning, 268. He desires nothing of the things that are seen, 857. Naked, follow the naked Christ, 756. This is no game or jest, ibid. The heresy denying Christ before the Incarnation, 899. Heretics have erred by not understanding the mystery of Christ’s birth, 745. Why does Marcion assert that Christ’s birth occurred only as a phantom? 444. Heretics asserting that Christ’s resurrection occurred only as a phantom and that his birth was merely apparent, 431. The blasphemies of the Arians against the Son and the Holy Spirit, 181, 184.

Before Christ could be seen in the body, he was already named in the Scriptures and known to the prophets and saints of God, according to the human nature in which he is less than the Father, III, 435. Christ’s birth takes its beginning from a shadow, 523. His body is a great mixing-bowl, in which there is not unmixed divinity but divinity tempered by an intermediate humanity, 401. Called a Nazarene from Nazareth; and among the ancients we too were called Nazarenes, as though reproachfully, whom they now call Christians, 255. Both at the beginning of Genesis and at the opening of John the Evangelist, he is acknowledged as the creator of heaven and earth, 305. The servant of Abraham swore by the seed of Abraham, that is, by Christ, 341. In combat he becomes in a certain way stronger as we strive with him through free will, 423. He whose head is Christ will always have his eyes fixed upon Christ and, lifting his face on high, will never think about lower things, 403. No good is complete until Christ is manifested, 432. When Christ has drawn everything to himself and illumined all things with his rays, the original restoration will occur, and God will be all in all, 389.

Christ is God by nature, not by progress, IV, 981. His divinity, 528. In the Old Testament he is called almighty, 18, 44. The radiance of glory and the form of the Father’s substance, 648. He contains in himself all the virtues of the Father, 509. The arm of the Lord, 591. How great is his strength therein, ibid. The fountain and source of every virtue, 157. One person in Christ, 946. The Holy Spirit remained in him in eternal habitation, 156. In him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily, ibid. In him are all virtues, 507. Christ the leader of the penitent, 48, 49. All the desires of the prophets depended upon Christ’s coming, 12. Christ conceived from the Virgin alone, 1054. Christ’s Incarnation from the Virgin is established, despite the Jews’ resistance, 108, 109, 202. He was born in Judaea in the forty-first year of Caesar Augustus, ibid. His birth is called a creation, 1096. Human speech cannot explain the mysteries of Christ’s birth, 117. When the Lord Savior arose, all wars ceased, 34. At his arrival, the idols of Egypt fell, 202. The infancy of a human body in him did not prejudice divine wisdom, 111. His anointing was spiritual, 731. He was likewise anointed by the Holy Spirit, 732. The period of Christ’s preaching is the acceptable year, ibid. Christ teaches that Moses and the prophets prophesied everything concerning him, 118. Christ’s mercy, 624. He descended into the furnace of hell, 643. Christ’s blood is the price of redemption, 571. The Savior of all human beings, especially of believers, 572. We are nourished by his flesh and drink his blood, 571. No one can know the mysteries of his passion, body, and blood in accordance with the majesty of the matter, 537. Christ diminishes among those who curse and grows among those who bless, 847. Christ also descended to the saints before he assumed a body, 801. Christ leaves all that is his for us, ibid. Whoever sins leaves Christ, 797. We can follow Christ without labor, 99. Christ is the treasure of treasures, 800. He is given different names according to the variety of circumstances, 580. Christ’s mission from God to earth, VI, 796. Why he is called almighty, ibid. He is likewise proclaimed God, ibid. He assumed a soul together with a body, 410. His flesh did not see corruption, 411. Whenever he appeared in the Old Testament, he had one body, 608. The Law and the prophets prophesied about him, 70. In Christ alone the Holy Spirit remained, 741. He is truth, 646. How he is greater than the angels and less than they, 461. Christ is the new man; in him all things are new, 626. What does it mean to put him on? ibid. Why did he receive baptism? 19. Christ remained the same after being transfigured, 129, 130. The Law and the prophets announced Christ’s passion and resurrection, 130. In how many ways was Christ handed over? 415. In Christ’s cross and passion all things were recapitulated, 557. Why Christ was placed in a new tomb, 240. In what sense he was in the heart of the earth for three days, etc., 83. Why he descended to the underworld, 613. How he ascended above the heavens, 614. Christ’s blood benefited the angels and those who were in the underworld, ibid. He is considered differently according to the diversity of effects, 623. Christ always mingles sorrow with joys, 135. What does it mean to learn Christ? 623, 624. It is one thing to imitate him according to the human nature, another according to the divine, 639. Who has put on Jesus Christ? 444. In what sense do all love him? 553. What does it mean to err and stumble in Christ’s body? 753. Christ’s injury is our glory, 438. Everything was empty before his coming, 614. The Jewish tradition concerning him, 203. Christ’s coming, the salvation of the whole world, 160. Christ’s second coming will be in glory, 197. His sign, 194. In whom does Christ live? 415. How he is formed in the hearts of believers, 467. The kinds of Christs: what are they? VI, 654.

**B. Chromatius**, I, 21, 512. Chromatius excluded Arius’s doctrine, etc., 20. Praise of his sisters, ibid. Blessed Chromatius’s steadfastness at the death of his brother, 347. Blessed Chromatius, II, 460, 514, 526, 535. Jerome’s brief preface to the same, 521.

Chrysippus’s twisted subtleties, I, 318. His sophism, 413. Chrysippus’s acuteness, 349. Chrysippus wanders among thorns, II, 471. His twisted subtleties, 487. Why did he prescribe marriage? 318. Frugality is useful to the soul, 936. What food is suitable for monks? 324. Simplicity of food is praised, 94. Things that provide harmless food, 194. Luxuries must be avoided among them, 166. A scar that has badly skinned over bursts with unripe pus, II, 191.

*Ciceion* is expressed in different ways, I, 755. What is it? ibid.

The city that ought to be desired and praised, I, 320. Why the cities of refuge are passed over in silence in Ezekiel’s description of the Holy Land, V, 607 et seq. “City” used for its inhabitants, VII, 333.

Claudius, II, 847.

The nails of the Lord’s cross, from which Constantine Augustus made bits for his horse, VI, 935.

Clement of Alexandria, Origen’s teacher, I, 428. In Jerome’s judgment he is the most learned of all, ibid. His works, ibid. There is nothing unlearned in them, ibid. Origen imitated him, ibid. Clement of Alexandria, likewise Origen’s teacher, II, 877. What is reported about his books, ibid. He contains some heretical material, ibid. He is defended, 509. Clement, a disciple of the apostles, II, 329. Clement was bishop of Rome after the apostles and a martyr, 839, 507. He wrote Epistles, 258. The style of Clement’s Epistle to the Corinthians agrees with the character of the Epistle to the Hebrews, 853. A church was built at Rome in his name, ibid. Clement, an apostolic man, wrote to the Corinthians, IV, 612. Clement’s Epistle to the Corinthians, VII, 571, 606.

Mercy is more savage than cruelty, I, 586. All hardness of heart toward another is broken by Clement’s reflection upon ourselves, 458. Let us bear toward everyone an image of God’s goodness, 573. God’s mercy consists in the sinner’s being visited here for his offense, III, 315.

Cleobulina, II, 320.

Cleodemus Malchus, author of the *History of the Barbarians*, III, 334.

Cleombrotus, a martyr of foolish philosophy, I, 180.

The Egyptian kingdom was destroyed at Cleopatra’s death, IV, 164, and V, 341. Cleopatra, VII, 738.

The clerical office is a burden, not an honor, I, 937. Whoever desires the clerical office should learn what he may teach and offer a reasonable sacrifice to God, 259. The office of the clergy should not be regarded as a kind of ancient military service, ibid. What does the usefulness of the clerical office consist in? V, 809.

Interpretation of “cleric,” I, 258. Clerics succeed to the apostolic rank, 34. The duties of clerics, 268. The Lord is their portion, 258. Let them possess nothing apart from God, ibid. and following pages. Let them be supported by the offering of the altar, 259. The duty of clerics in burying the dead, 6. Their dignity in the consecration of Christ’s body and the absolution of sins, 34. What is proposed to them for avoidance or pursuit, 258 and following pages. Sacred reading should never be taken from a cleric’s hands, 261. Let him always be ready to give an answer to anyone who asks him for an account, ibid. Clerics must avoid the banquets of secular people, 265. Let them shun the powerful: secular people venerate their holiness more than their wealth; let the cleric be subject to the bishop and revere him as a parent of his soul, 262. It is the duty of clerics to visit the sick, 268. Let them keep their eyes and tongue chaste, ibid. Should a cleric arrange marriages? 946. He is a preacher of continence, ibid. He should not be a steward of another’s property, ibid. Clerics praised, 268. The worldly judge gives greater respect to a continent cleric than to a rich man, 268. They are commanded to despise their own possessions, ibid. The duty of clerics is one thing, that of monks another, 34. Jerome is careful not to speak anything unfavorable about them, ibid. The book to Nepotian teaches how they should live, 937. They are fathers of monks, 285. Clerics and monks are disinherited, 260. Abstinence from wine is prescribed for them, 266. Discord of character among clerics, 259. Let them flee women, ibid. Let them give no occasion for suspicion, ibid. Their shameful servitude, 261. Luxuries, 262. Vices, 99. A cleric who, though often invited to dinner, does not refuse to go is easily despised, 265. It is shameful for a provincial governor to dine more comfortably with a cleric than in the palace, 259. A trader and a poor man who has suddenly become rich should be avoided like a plague, 261. The arts of avarice among clerics, 262. The Church ought to be their heir, ibid. The celibacy of clerics, II, 388. The Church admits no one unless he is a virgin or continent, ibid. Let him not seek worldly profits in the military service of Christ, 264. Let him be hospitable, ibid. Some are tavernkeepers, 229. Clerics and monks should be received as guests with greater honor, 63.

Burning ovens: by this metaphor devotion to idolatry is signified, VI, 72.

The sick who are confined to bed, I, 694.

What did Clitomachus write about? I, 334.

The scarlet color in the pontiff’s garment: what does it signify? I, 366.

Codrus, VII, 553.

The heavenly follow the mystical understanding; the earthly, the literal history, IV, 11.

The Coelestian heresy was strangled, I, 1067.

The kingdoms of heaven desire inhabitants who are unencumbered and supported by the lightness of wings, 795. After the great perils of the sea, let us hasten to enter the safest harbor of heaven, 584. Unless you use force, you will not obtain the kingdoms of heaven, 125. There is no sin in heaven, 450. We must fly there naked, 1080. According to the Hebrews, “heaven” derives its name from the waters, 419. Heaven is not promised in the Old Testament, II, 728.
