Heaven and earth will not pass away, 588. The transformation of heaven and earth for the better, 589, 788. What does it mean that the heavens are rolled up like a book? 441. “Heavens” is expressed in the plural but understood in the singular, 10. Heaven signifies the angelic powers; earth, the mortal race, ibid. Heaven is affirmed to be round and to revolve in the form of a sphere, VII, 603. Some falsely claim that collapses occur in heaven every day, 34. It is taken for the air, 571. How the name “heaven” is to be understood, 675. How the heavens will pass away, 198, 199. The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel, 92. It is understood in three ways, 80.

Who are the celibates, and why are they so called? II, 381.

Celibacy praised, VII, 60.

Cenobites are called *Sauses* in the language of the Gentiles, I, 118. Their way of life: what is it? 119 and following pages. The life of the cenobites is approved and commended, 938, 942. They are commended, 1086.

“Coenomyia”: *Cynomyia* should be written instead, I, 676.

To think evil is criminal; it is worse to wish to carry out evil thoughts, I, 943. When someone passes from one thing to another, and one task succeeds another, he thinks only of that one thing, etc., ibid.

Silent thought is the mind’s secret speech, I, 604. When it resounds outwardly through the tongue, it expresses the judgment of the mind, ibid. Let us not allow evil thoughts to grow, 92. We shall give an account in judgment of thought, speech, and deed, 604. To keep the mind from wandering among destructive thoughts requires effort, 940. The worst thoughts and the mind’s decision are punished in evil deeds, 985. Our judgment lies at the center: either to reject thoughts or to admit them, 506. Frequent prayers are commended for driving away evil thoughts, ibid. Thought and perception are given by God, II, 777. Speech often does not express the thoughts of one’s own mind, 407. Silent thought is not hidden from the knowledge of God, 731. When is our thought confirmed? 791. Among many zealous people who toil in daily meditation, a pure thought, worthy of the name of a man, is scarcely found, III, 449. God alone knows the secrets of thoughts, IV, 960. Some say that there is no sin in thoughts, 865. The breast is the treasury of evil thoughts, V, 205. God does not punish the first and second impulses of thoughts, 200, 201. The depravity of human thought is noted, VI, 145. Evil thoughts will pay the penalty, 38. Thoughts arise from one’s own will, VII, 115. They are not sent by the devil but kindled, ibid. An evil thought is the precursor of the devil’s coming upon us, 630.

One who is always thinking about God cannot do wrong, VI, 551.

The knowledge of God is not of one kind, VI, 295.

Whence good or evil kinds of knowledge arise in us, VII, 280.

Everyone worships what he loves, I, 95.

The verb “to know” used of the act of marriage, II, 210.

[Col. 0948] The assembly of the brothers gathered together in one place, II, 58 and 72. Also, the name of the place itself, 71. Collections were held on Sunday, 398.

The bond of iniquity: what is it? VI, 150.

What is *collyba*? VII, 162.

Female money-changers, VII, 132.

*Collyra*, a kind of bread and pastry, I, 95.

Colossae, a city of Asia, VII, 762.

The serpent was wiser than all the beasts, I, 113. Serpents are food for stags, 985. Serpent skin alleviates earache, II, 332.

The dove of the Holy Spirit flies down to Noah as though to Christ in the Jordan, I, 419. With the branch of refreshment and light it announces peace to the world, ibid. The dove announces peace to the earth, II, 195.

Let us have the simplicity of doves, so that we may plot no deceit against anyone, I, 324. From a flock of doves the hawk often separates one to tear apart, 997. Two dove chicks were offered for Christ, 307. The solitary dove does not grieve for its separated chicks, VI, 77.

The pillars of Christ, I, 705. Where a pillar stained with the Lord’s blood was displayed, to which He is said to have been bound and scourged, 697. It supported the portico of the church, ibid.

Hair was customarily cut in mourning, V, 280. To let one’s hair grow is characteristic of the luxurious and the barbarians, 547.

One should eat in such a way that afterward one can pray and read, I, 289. Let a person eat so that he is always hungry and can read and sing psalms immediately after food, 686. No one can eat—or abstain when necessary—without God, III, 406. Whether we eat clean or unclean things lies with us, VII, 711.

The ending of a certain comic poet, I, 288.

A comic poet’s maxim, II, 336, 650.

To what was God’s threat directed? V, 33.

The duty of a commentator, I, 329. The same duty, II, 477. The commentator’s duty is to clarify obscure matters, VI, 388, 837. The same duty again, VII, 485.

The custom and rule of commentaries, II, 541. What sort of work do they contain? ibid. 471. Writers of commentaries, 472. Commentaries on Terence’s comedies, 471. On Cicero’s speeches, ibid. What are the laws of commentaries? IV, 833.

“Communicate” properly belongs to the language of Scripture, VII, 112.

The blessed transformation of things, I, 715.

What is the difference between acquiring and buying? II, 537.

Comparison of an inferior is an insult to a superior, II, 239.

A crossroads is a fork in the road, where a traveler must look more carefully to determine which path to take, III, 365.

The method of counting on the fingers among the ancients, I, 907 and II, 240.

The license of old comedy in censuring particular persons, I, 935. Comedies should not be read by priests, 78.

To attempt is one thing, to act another, I, 342.

What are shellfish? I, 682.

The meeting places of heretics are the lairs and dens of wild beasts, etc., VI, 80.

It is difficult for an outsider to reconcile those whom neither son nor brother could reconcile, I, 782.

Sermons in the Church, I, 263.

The tears of preachers should be the praises of their hearers, I, 263. Let them be skilled in the mysteries and most learned in the sacraments of God, ibid. Some are rebuked, ibid. What Tully says about the same men, ibid.

Seven modes of conclusions, II, 486.

Concord holds together what rivalry was about to scatter, I, 465. The good of concord and the evil of discord, VII, 79.

Concordia, a town of Italy, II, 311.

A new kind of concubines, I, 98. The fidelity of concubines, II, 311.

Even the most famous philosophers of Greece publicly kept male concubines, IV, 35.

The tombs of desire persist, II, 353.

Whenever we desire, we commit fornication, I, 937.

Scarcely anyone fails to feel the titillation of desire, V, 590.

No one is condemned for what he could not do, II, 741.

We learn our condition from history, II, 777. Let each thing not begrudge its Creator its own state and condition, 715. What is the human condition? VI, 448. The word “condition” is used of great matters, VII, 627. Whence forgetfulness of one’s condition creeps in, I, 907.

The twofold error of heretics concerning the Creator, VII, 377.

Where are confession and beauty found? I, 895. Confession of guilt is a second plank after shipwreck, 528. A frank and modest confession is to praise in others what one lacks oneself, 232. Confession and repentance are the remedy for sin, III, 474. “Confession” is taken for praise, IV, 630. Confession of sins and confession of praise, V, 680. Confession of offenses in conversion, VI, 157. Confession of sins is commended, VII, 125. “Confession” signifying thanksgiving, 73.

[Col. 0949] The Egyptian confessors, I, 30. Exiled confessors under Athanasius’s name, II, 191.

We must trust neither in our own wisdom nor in any virtues, but in the Lord alone, II, 791.

What some people fabricate with audacious rashness, II, 226.

What is believed simply must be confessed simply, I, 903.

We must confess our vices, II, 765. Those who confess their sins simply deserve, through their humility, the Savior’s mercy, 754.

How cast and sculpted images differ, VI, 627.

One kind of shame leads to life, another to death, VI, 528.

The marriages of pagans are cut off, I, 459. The pitiable shadow of marriage, 61. It would have been better to have entered into human marriage than, while striving for higher things, to fall into hell, 106. Whoever fulfills the marital obligation cannot pray, ibid. The bondage of marriage, 226. We are accustomed to overlook the vices of children and spouses while the neighbors sing, 1093. The Church approves and regulates marriages, II, 306. Heretics condemn marriage, 306.

Married men taken into the apostolate leave behind marital duties, II, 277. Counsel is given to married people, V, 206. After conception, married people ought to devote themselves to prayer, not intercourse, VII, 657. The causes of sterility and fertility among married people, 466. See *Marriage*.

What difference is there between the union of God and human beings? VI, 26. Joined to a virgin, a man makes her a woman; joined to a prostitute, God makes a virgin, ibid.

When does Scripture use the word “conjuration”? IV, 919.

Alms may be given to blood relatives as to the poor, but not otherwise, I, 990.

Conscience as a mirror, I, 422. A good conscience escapes no one’s eyes, 789. Let us fear the true judgment of conscience, 611. The goodness of conscience forbids tormenting oneself, 4. The crosses of conscience, II, 765. The tortures of conscience in sinners, IV, 239. Conscience is the undying worm of sins, 828. Happy the conscience that has sinned only in speech, 93. Happy the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord, 981. Happy the conscience that endures reproach for God, 948. Happy the conscience that, in a time of affliction, remembers good works, 468. The conscience of sins shines in the face, V, 73. Whoever is tormented by his own conscience carries his own torment, 183. Conscience bites after sin, IX, 296. To suffer the torments of conscience, VII, 623. Everything should be done with counsel, VII, 646.

The difference between counsel and command, II, 256. How great is the difference between God’s counsels and those of human beings? IV, 650.

Cousins are called brothers in Scripture, VII, 86.

The best comforter is not one overcome by his own groans, etc., I, 177.

Examples of consolation, and those who have written about consolation, I, 335. Many false consolations by which people are deceived, IV, 682. What consolation is there in misery? V, 650.

One who is secure in the companionship of his own people should not dangerously seek the company of outsiders, I, 506. Some, under the names of piety, seek suspicious associations, 935.

Constans, prince of Gaul, II, 925. Constantia, a holy woman, went to the sick Hilarion, II, 39. Her daughter and son-in-law were cured by anointing with oil, ibid. She died of grief because this saint’s body had been stolen, ibid. She was accustomed to spend sleepless nights at his tomb, ibid.

Constantinople, I, 344. It approves the copies of the martyr Lucian, II, 522.

The emperor Constantine removed an image of Jupiter from the place of the Resurrection and a statue of Venus from the rock of the Cross, I, 321. Under the emperor Constantine, while the Gospel was shining forth, the unbelief and depravity of all nations were destroyed, IV, 36.

King Constantius, favoring the Arian heresy, I, 343, and II, 844. He was indicated by the beast, 191. What happened under King Constantius? 188. Who was Constantius’s successor? 191.

A certain Constantius, an Origenist, I, 506.

The idolatrous custom in many cities of inaugurating the fertility of the years, IV, 782.

Good custom makes everything delightful and always strives toward greater things, I, 944. The worst custom, 290. Custom is like a second nature, VII, 403.

The deaths of the three consulars, I, 344.

The consulship was transferred through patrician hands, and only the nobility possessed it, I, 398. The honor of the consulship is annual, ibid. The consulship ennobles men, II, 319.

Whence are consuls so called? IV, 49.

There is a twofold consummation, III, 359.

Consus, the god of counsels, II, 22.

Things must not be despised as small, without which great things cannot stand, I, 682, and II, 353.

Contemplation. The human soul cannot always be engaged in contemplation of heavenly things, III, 410.

Where there is contempt, there is frequent injury, I, 33. Twofold contempt, VII, 728.

What does it mean to quarrel childishly? I, 640. We contend here so that we may be crowned elsewhere, 89.

Perfect continence: what is it? I, 604. It is good in itself, 905. What kind of continence is safer? 685. The contest of continence is greater than that over money, 402. Continence should be imitated, 750. What is reckoned as indifferent between continence and luxury? 908. Some, after baptism or marriage, have embraced continence out of the fervor of faith, 620. Through continence great and eternal rewards are obtained, 750. Frugality and continence are companions of chastity, 287. At what time should the sails of continence be spread? 619. Continence preserves bodies beautiful and strong, 749. It prevents infirmities from arising and restores illnesses to health, 614. In insult to continence, wines of different taste and color are sought, 618. Perfect continence sustains and protects all virtues, II, 300. Continence and modesty are commended, 269. Continence must be practiced during mourning, VI, 905. The concept of continence, VII, 513. It is not perfect in this life, ibid. How does it differ from moderation? ibid. It is necessary, 719. See *Chastity, Modesty, Abstinence, Food,* and *Fasting*.

Contraries cannot exist simultaneously, IV, 790.

What do brave men do in controversies? I, 224.

Convenae, a city, II, 390.

Every assembly that does not offer spiritual sacrifices is abominable to God, IV, 21.

The suspicion of bad conduct must be avoided, I, 912. Innocent conduct without speech benefits by example as much as it harms by silence, 423. Let us put off our former conduct and take up a new one, II, 300. Happy is the conduct in which enemies find no opportunity, V, 658. The example of bad conduct corrupts many, 183.

Those who are converted are compared to a fruitful olive tree, VI, 160.

Conversion is never too late, I, 42, 177, 678. By our conversion we change God, VI, 354.

An insult against a brother is the guilt of homicide, I, 36.

The daily banquet of the soul, I, 80. At a banquet a person is compelled, as though unwillingly, to eat meat, 265. Banquets are to be avoided by clerics, 265. Whence is *convivium* derived? IV, 26. The luxury of banquets affects not only the belly but also the ears, 332.

The twelve baskets, I, 706.

Cooks soothe the belly’s madness with various flavors of food, I, 618.

In Scripture, “heart” is taken for understanding and soul, IV, 868. What does “to speak to the heart” mean? 479. God loves those whose hearts and lips agree, 873. In Scripture, what are called the breast and breasts? V, 145. The secrets of the heart are indicated by bodily movement and gestures, 85. The new heart of Israel and the new heart of the Gentiles: where are they situated? 217. We must not return in heart to Egypt, 360. What does “to speak to the heart” mean? VI, 21. The heart of an animal is in the middle, VII, 539. The heart must be guarded with all diligence, 716.

The sacred *coracina*, I, 678.

*Corban*, the gift of God, I, 904.

Core, that is, the skull, I, 375. The sons of Core, ibid.

Why does Paul mourn the Corinthians? I, 893. Barbarians rule over the Corinthians, Athenians, etc., 345. The Corinthians’ propositions addressed to the Apostle, II, 245. The Corinthians polished by Attic eloquence, VII, 706. They were neighbors of the Athenians, 707. The points for which the Corinthians were condemned by the Apostle, 427. There is a great distance between the Corinthians and the Ephesians, 655.

Cornelia, an example both of chastity and fertility, I, 284. She bore the Gracchi, ibid. Cornelia’s chastity equaled that of Gracchus, II, 319.

Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian cohort, I, 431. Still a pagan, he was cleansed by the gift of the Holy Spirit, 35. The house of Cornelius is the Church of Christ, 696. What is said about the same man? 499. Cornelius dedicated a church in Caesarea, II, 301.

Cornelius and Asinius Pollio, I, 754.

Cornelius, father of the monastery of the Muchansians, II, 83.

At what time did Pope Cornelius die as a martyr? II, 3.

The defense of the seditious tribune Cornelius, II, 419.

Cornelius Nepos: what is reported? II, 419. See *Nepos*.

Cornutus, I, 429.

The horn signifies kingdom and power, IV, 68. Horns are used for kingdoms, VI, 639 and following, 790.

No horned animal is placed among the unclean animals, VI, 640.

Corojatha, a village flourishing with all Christians, III, 183.

No age of the world corrupts the crown of righteousness, I, 616. He will receive a crown who proves victorious in this world, II, 782.

The crown of the altar in the form of a lily, V, 527.

The body is composed of members, I, 718. Bodies are not fashioned because of the ruin of souls, but for the sake of…, etc., 623. They flow, grow, or diminish daily, 719. Differences of age do not change their nature, ibid. Different members make one body, 264. Everything done through the body becomes weaker when the body is broken, 721. Silent speech, silent eyes, and the bearing of the whole body sometimes speak, 789. We console those who mourn the absence of bodies, 194, 456. The body does not remain in one and the same natural condition, II, 340. The whole body is tortured by the pain of one member, 713. Although healthy and robust, it is rarely free from infirmities, 794. Sometimes it suffers the annoyance of phlegm so that it may become very strong, ibid. Nothing exists that is free from every infirmity, ibid. Without taste and food it is impossible for the human body to subsist, 339. Bodily evils and illnesses, VI, 564. Some note their causes, ibid. Why are the bodies of barbarians more upright than those of Romans? V, 147.

The condition of bodies is the same as that of beasts and animals unless the soul’s eternity is promised, I, 706. The body that has indulged in many luxuries must be afflicted, 507. It is much better to rule it than to serve it, 789. What is the body of death? II, 481. The heavenly body and the earthly body, 435. The bodies of believers are the temple of God, IV, 1040. The body is called a tabernacle, 452. Affliction of the body pleads for the forgiveness of sins, 690. There is no shame in naming a bodily member by its proper name, 550. The worst error concerning the condition of bodies after the resurrection, 828. The resurrection of bodies is established, 589. Not only souls but bodies also will be changed, 588. The substance of the glorified body is not denied, 702. The strength of the body is the weakness of the soul, and conversely, VI, 291. The weakness of the body draws the powers of the mind along with it, 263. The scourges of the body, ibid. To serve the needs of the body is not a sin, VII, 743. The true resurrection of bodies, 45. See *Resurrection*.

Correction, or reproof: moderation must be observed in it, I, 947. Correction from anyone, however inferior, must not be avoided or disdained, 780. Let the patient person be approached with reproof, the angry person with blandishments, I, 713. Reproof is a bringing to life, II, 802. In reproving, we are flatterers of the rich, 773. It is not necessary to expose to the scandal and ruin of many what can be reproved or corrected privately, 534. Straight things receive ornament; crooked things, correction, III, 394. Reproof is bitter for the present, IV, 840. One kind of reproof is directed at adversaries, another at children, V, 126. The reproof of the wicked does not condemn the good, VI, 719. When is reproof useful and good? 708. Hatred of reproof is noted, 292. Whoever is loved by God is reproved; whoever is neglected is abandoned to his sins, 42. Gentleness and mildness must be used in correction, VII, 518, 519. The agreement of many is effective for correction, 375. Who does not need correction? 376. Everything that is corrected is imperfect, 693. When is a rod necessary for the one who reproves? 519.

Whom reprimand does not correct, shame sometimes reforms, I, 713. It is more praiseworthy willingly to accept one who corrects than boldly to correct one who is going astray, 774.

Who and in what manner are said to corrupt their brothers by sins? V, 183.

A woman who has been corrupted should marry openly, I, 784. Let her at least mitigate by this remedy what she began badly, ibid. See *Prostitute*.

To what do corruption and incorruption pertain? II, 298. What is salutary corruption? VI, 458.

“Corrupt” and “incorrupt” according to common speech, VII, 684, 419, 420.

The *corus*, a measure of both dry and liquid substances, containing thirty *modii*, V, 563.

What is a *corymbus*? I, 393.

*Cossi*, worms, II, 334.

The Alps of King Cottius, I, 727.

The volume of Crantor, I, 334.

An attack against drunkenness, II, 339.

“Tomorrow” and “tomorrow’s” are used of the future, I, 295. What is “tomorrow” in Scripture? VII, 38.

Crassus, I, 20, 989. He is said to have laughed once in his life, ibid. and II, 486, 471, and 536.

Crassus the commander was captured and the Roman army massacred at Carrhae, a city of Mesopotamia, III, 190.

In what respect were the Crassi praised? I, 335.

Crates of Thebes, going off to philosophize, threw away a great weight of gold, I, 319. He did not think that he could possess both virtues and riches at the same time, ibid. What else did the same man do? 319. Crates of Thebes threw gold into the sea, II, 338.

What does creation signify in Scripture? I, 392. We were created good by God but fell through our own fault, II, 284. Everything was created for human use, 330. To restore what has existed is less than to make what has not existed, 440. In Scripture, creation does not always signify the making of things that did not exist, but sometimes grace bestowed upon those who have merited it, IV, 166. The name “creation” is used of the Savior’s conception and birth, 1069. What does “creation” signify among Greeks and Latins? VII, 626. This word is never used except of great works, ibid. What is the difference between creation and possession? 578.

Without knowledge of his Creator every human being is a beast, I, [Col. 0952] 334. We venerate the Creator’s skill equally in small and great things, 340. Who removes the variety of the Creator-Artist, the diversity of things and of graces, and their distinctions? II, 715. What is greater is attributed to the Creator; what is lesser is denied to Him, 446. From the equality, course, order, and constancy of things we understand the Creator, III, 413. The Creator’s great mercy, IV, 1084. We learn the Creator’s mercy from the example of mothers, 810. When the Creator is neglected, every creature rises against sinners, 944. The salvation of the creature is the Creator’s gain, 947. The Creator of the world is despised by heretics who do not accept the Old Testament, V, 6. Every creature is unclean in comparison with the Creator, 575. From the order and constancy of creatures we know the Creator, 493. The Creator is understood through creatures, 624.

Every creature of God is good, I, 504. If you compare it with God, it does not subsist, 224. The beauty of creatures consists in the order of their dignities, 594. They were created good by God, 224. The lowliness of creatures is demonstrated so that God’s incomparable sublimity may appear, 601. Some assert that rational creatures fell into bodies because of sins, 716. They maintained that, according to the diversity of their sins, they were generated in this or that condition, ibid. Every creature, except God, is subject to defect, II, 377. It is subject to sin and needs God’s mercy, 744. Every creature was created good and perfect by God, V, 335. Every creature flashes forth knowledge of God, 16. Are rational creatures all equal, so that none of them will perish? VI, 418. All creatures perceive the Creator, VII, 47. They have their existence from God, and why they are called good, 600.

We were all made from the same clay, formed from the same beginnings, I, 507.

For the believer the whole world is a wealth, I, 281. By what are the fields of believers customarily made fertile? 299. Whoever believes purely ought to speak purely, II, 409. What kind of simplicity is it not to know what one believes? 327. Four kinds of believers, IV, 72. By what means do believers come to faith? VII, 279. Who disturbs believers? 382.

Crescens the Cynic, a follower of lusts and an enemy of Christians, II, 865.

In Scripture, “to grow” is used in two ways, VII, 275.

The characteristics of the Cretans, VII, 416. The Cretans boasted that they could show the tomb of Jupiter, 708.

What is the difference between crime and error? I, 305. If old crimes are changed by a new conversion, God does not judge them, 897. Everything has been forgiven us in baptism, 416. Accusations of crimes should be contained in a judgmental petition, not in an ecclesiastical document, II, 596. Whoever accuses crimes becomes criminal, 776. Mortal crime, VII, 38. See *Sin*.

It is extremely foolish for someone accused by another to bring accusations, I, 308.

Why did virgins and widows in monasteries have their hair cut? I, 1089. Small animals commonly arise between the skin and the hair, ibid. Women’s hair is censured in opposition to the Apostle, 113.

Who was the tutor of Crispus Caesar, Constantine’s son? II, 905. This Crispus was killed by his father, ibid.

A saying of Crispus Sallustius, II, 13. The same is cited, VI, 617. His maxim, VII, 662.

The wealth of Croesus, I, 318, 339. Croesus is censured, II, 536.

Every contrivance of cruelty was overcome in the martyrs, I, 619. What surpasses the cruelty of all brigands? 269. To use cruelty as though it were piety, II, 5.

Indigestion is the parent of lust, I, 936. Let us follow the naked Cross naked, I, 259. The naked man following the naked Cross climbs Jacob’s ladder more freely and lightly, 319. Let us think of Christ’s Cross, and we shall regard riches as mud, 265. The image of the Cross adorns the purple robes and diadems of kings, 679. The standards of soldiers are insignia of the Cross, ibid. In every action, let the hand depict the Lord’s Cross, 121. Why should this be done frequently? 986. The standard of the Cross and the severity of preaching destroyed the temples of idols, II, 367. By it we triumph over enemies, 226. It is the object of our profession and faith, ibid. Christ’s Cross is not easy, 756. The sign of the Cross, praised, arms the forehead, 6. An impious utterance empties Christ’s Cross, 186. The sign of the Cross exalted among the nations, IV, 572. Why is the title of Christ’s Cross called in three languages? 486. The uneducated multitude of the nations accepted Christ’s Cross, not the wise of the world, 13. Why is the title of Christ’s Cross called in three languages? V, 568. Strength is hidden in the Cross, VI, 638. The mystery of the Cross prefigured in Moses, 139. Amalek was defeated under the standard of the Cross, 367. Constantine is said to have made bridle-bits for his horse from the nails of the Lord’s Cross, 935. Christ’s Cross possesses the whole universe, VII, 604. It purified both earthly and heavenly things, 568. It benefited angels and human beings, 582, 594. The Cross must always be borne, 65. The cause of Christ’s Cross is envy, 229. How was it a stumbling block to the Jews? 492. The demons immediately perceived the power of the Cross, 234. Can he glory in the Cross? 531.

To crucify and to crucify again, VII, 514.

[Col. 0953] Those who heal and correct seem cruel, IV, 384.

Underground crypts containing the bodies of buried martyrs, V, 468. Jerome frequently entered them at Rome with his contemporaries, ibid.

Nothing is purer than crystal, IV, 639. In the Alps, waters are said to congeal into crystal, ibid.

Ctesiphon and Seleucia, cities of the Persians, became famous in place of Babylon, IV, 174.

A speech on behalf of Ctesiphon, II, 520.

The meeting places of heretics are the lairs and dens of wild beasts, VI, 78.

*C u b i t u m* and *cubita* are neuter; elsewhere they are *cubiti* and *cubitus*, V, 472.

The monks’ hoods bore signs identifying monasteries and houses, II, 68 and following.

The ridiculous question of the gourd, I, 754. Gourds and ivy need the support of reeds and stakes, 754. The gourd is of the same nature as ivy, VI, 426. Both signify the people of Israel, 427.

It is not dignity that makes guilt, but the will, I, 459. Forgiveness must be granted for faults, VII, 143.

Superstitious worship must be avoided, I, 267.

What desire ought to hold us? I, 180.

Healing is not blessedness but consolation, VI, 525.

Curiosity about knowledge is condemned, III, 441. It contains useless torment, 457.

Curius, II, 37. The poverty of Curius, 342.

We must run in such a way that we do not fall on the road, I, 687.

What is the chariot of God? IV, 813.

Curtius, VII, 553.

The guardian whom we call by that name is called *Samarites* by the Hebrews, I, 198.

Keepers of vineyards and cucumber gardens were placed in shelters and huts, IV, 17.

Guarding of the heart praised, VI, 640.

Shining skin reveals a dirty mind, I, 787.

Trembling Cybele, I, 133.

The Cyclades, II, 551.

The river Cydnus, I, 345.

A voice sweeter than the swan’s song, VII, 331.

A shameful maxim of a certain Cynic, VII, 640.

The Cynics possessed nothing except a cloak, staff, and wallet, I, 399.

*Cyniphes*, small gnats, VI, 198.

The cypress, of excellent and imperishable fragrance, IV, 502.

### Saint Cyprian

Saint Cyprian, I, 223, 230, 232. His teaching is called an antidote, 25. It proceeds like a fountain of the purest water, sweet and calm, 326. He is wholly devoted to the exhortation of the virtues, ibid. Occupied with the hardships of persecution, he did not discuss the Scriptures at all, ibid. He was a man distinguished by eloquence and martyrdom, 427. Why is he criticized by Flaminius? ibid. He wrote against Demetrianus, ibid. Learnedly he exposed idols as not being gods, 430. A saying of his, ibid. The reading of Cyprian’s works is recommended, 688. He wrote on virginity, 106, 996. Some of his letters concern the faith, 159. He wrote to Fortunatus about the number seven, 232. He wrote about the power and rewards of almsgiving, 397. Cyprian always remained in communion with Stephen, the Roman pontiff, II, 198. Several passages are cited from him that prove this, ibid. He never anathematized those who refused to follow him, ibid. He wrote to Jubaianus about rebaptizing heretics, 199. Blessed Cyprian, rejecting the baptism of heretics, convened an African synod on this matter, 196. He shed his blood at Carthage, 4. What he says about the persecution of this time, ibid. What has been said about Saint Cyprian? 891. A saying of his, 410. His eight letters to Cornelius, 891. Cyprian’s letters in which Stephen is attacked, 200. His work addressed to Quirinus, 729. The story of Cyprian the martyr, 513. Cyprian and Hilary are praised, IV, 727. The praises of Blessed Cyprian, VI, 420. Saint Cyprian the martyr, I, 538. He left writings on zeal and envy, 508.

Cyprian the deacon, I, 729.

### Cyprus

Cyprus, an island near Judaea, from which Zeno, the leader of the Stoics, came, IV, 846.

Cyrene, near the Syrtes, VIII, 352.

Cyrenius is better and more accurately pronounced by the Latins with the letter Q, so that it is said *Quirinius*, III, 94.

Saint Cyril, I, 45.

### Cyrus

Cyrus was foretold before he was born, IV, 532. Josephus reports that the Jews loved him, ibid. He was the first to destroy Babylon and the Chaldaeans, 531. Under his reign the Temple began to be built, ibid. He is called “Christ,” ibid. He was a figure of the ecclesiastical man, 536. Cyrus ruled in Persia after overthrowing Astyages, king of the Medes, V, 41. He captured Babylon and Croesus, 226. Cyrus destroyed the empire of the Chaldaeans, VI, 778. His piety toward the Jewish people, ibid. He was killed among the Massagetae after thirty years of rule, ibid. His successors, ibid.

## D

[Col. 0954]

Dacia, a region, I, 344.

Dadan, a people of Ethiopia, III, 320.

### Demons

Demons are tormented before the tombs of the saints, I, 703. They are expelled from possessed bodies before the Lord’s tomb, 205. In what respect are people possessed by demons worthy of pity? 703. Demons believe in one God and tremble, II, 322. The roaming of demons, 392. They are deceitful and cunning, 24. They do not wish to wound the wicked, but those who are upright in heart, 766. The voices of demons resounded in the most ancient temple, 38.

Demons move about in the air, IV, 412, 577. They have no blood, 749. Nothing is more savage than demons, 291. They have no power over human beings, 869. Demons have sometimes been granted power to do harm, 504. They prefer to perish in flames rather than lose their prey, 131. In what sense they do not subsist, 774. Whatever we sin, is the dominion of demons, 953. Most people are accustomed to worship demons so that they may not do harm, 911. The error of certain people concerning the love of demons for women, 633. Demons, the enemies of Christians? VI, 75. Each troop of demons has its own leaders, 659. They rejoice in the destruction of human beings, 145. They cause people to admire the beauty of the world, 643. The confusion of demons at the end of the world, 554. Demons observe the times of the moon, VII, 22. The air is full of demons, according to the opinion of all the learned, 674. Their power comes from God, ibid. They have different ministries, ibid. The torments of demons in the presence of the Savior, 49. The Apostle teaches who demons are, what they can do, and so forth, 541. Some think that demons know the Son of God, while the devil is ignorant, 49. They are worshiped through vices, 505. See *Devil*.

A demoniac speaks in pure Syriac, although he does not know the language, 25.

Dagon, the idol of the cities of the Philistines, IV, 544.

The Dalmatians are fierce, VII, 416.

The devastation of Dalmatia, I, 344. The islands of Dalmatia, II, 535.

Nicolaus of Damascus wrote about the Flood, III, 126. His histories are praised, V, 297.

Damascus, a royal city, IV, 192. The threefold interpretation of the name Damascus, 278 ff. The origin of Damascus, and from whom it was so named according to Hebrew traditions, V, 316. By whom it was founded, III, 322. By whom it was captured, IV, 292 ff. Under whom it was restored, 292.

Pope Damasus is praised, I, 230. He wrote in verse and prose about virginity, 106. Pope Damasus, II, 415. Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, VII, 160.

The eternal punishments of the damned, IV, 828, 830. Some maintain that the torments of the damned will end, 829.

The heads of the condemned were severed outside the city, VII, 233.

### Daniel

Daniel, I, 307. Why he is called “a man of desires,” 95. And “a friend of God,” 218. Daniel, while still a boy, condemns the immoral elders, 319. Daniel and the three boys presided over Babylon’s wealth in such a way that they served God in spirit, 500. They were united in family and in faith, 618. Their hard servitude did not alter their nobility, ibid. They are commended because of their fasts, ibid. Daniel’s counsel proves the power and reward of almsgiving, 397. What matters does Daniel discuss? 279. Daniel, while still a boy: how was he known to the people? II, 534. Through fasting he became terrifying to lions, 340. What has been said, according to the hypothesis, about Daniel, Noah, and Job? 276. The churches of Christ read Daniel according to the edition of Theodotion, 527. Daniel and his companions were made eunuchs, according to the Hebrews, IV, 479. Daniel was of the sons of Judah, not a priest, V, 623 ff. Of all the prophets, he spoke most openly about Christ, 621. Daniel and his companions learned Babylonian teaching not in order to follow it, but to refute it, 624. Daniel built a lofty tower, constructed of square marble, in the city of Susa, 672. To understand the final parts of Daniel, a wide range of Greek history is necessary—and whose? 621. Daniel the eunuch, 920. In what languages the book of Daniel was written, 627. The calumniators of Daniel’s history are rejected, 671. A calumniator of the Church attacks Daniel and is refuted, 635. Why are Noah, Daniel, and Job alone named, while the others are omitted? 137.

The frontier of the Danube was breached, I, 914.

The place received the name Daphne from Cnaeus Pompey, who planted it with military force; and why? V, 599. The spring of Daphne, from which Antioch enjoys an abundant water supply, ibid.

Dardania, bordering Thrace, I, 344.

The comparison of Dares and Entellus, I, 633, 729.

Darius, king of the Medes, I, 464. The wealth of Darius, 339. Darius, the wealthy king of the Medes, II, 534. Darius was the first to destroy the Babylonian empire, IV, 173. After Babylon was overthrown, he returned to his kingdom and took Daniel with him, V, 637.

In the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, the Temple was built, V, 39.

Darius, son of Hystaspes, was appointed king of the Persians by the decision of the seven families, VI, 777. Under him Haggai prophesied, 737.

Darius Nothus was king of the Persians for nineteen years, V, 40. Both Greek and barbarian histories describe this Darius as the richest and most powerful of all, 673. He was defeated by Alexander the Great, 670, 673.

The three Dariuses, V, 677. Darius and Cyrus overthrew the empire of the Chaldaeans, 651. Under Darius and Cyrus there was one kingdom of the Persians and Medes, 659.

Everything must be referred to the glory of the giver, IV, 534. The giver who does not feel his abundance feels his want, VI, 18.

### David

With what weapons David the king advances to battle, I, 737. He preferred to be subject to enemies rather than to the envious, 708. Our Simonides, Pindar, Alcaeus, and others, 279. He makes Christ resound upon the lyre and raises Christ as he rises from the underworld, ibid. He desires the most difficult task rather than presuming to undertake it, 952. If he confesses the darkness of ignorance, by what night of ignorance should we suppose ourselves surrounded? 325. He was overcome as a human being—why? 504. A seven-day fast corrected the homicide and adultery of David, the holy man, 460. He wallowed in ashes and, forgetting royal power, sought light in darkness; he who had previously taught through virtues how a person should not fall, taught through repentance how one who had fallen should rise again, ibid. David advanced so far that, having once been a sinner and penitent, he became a teacher, 895. David’s virtue was gentleness of spirit, II, 713. Many kings were preserved through the virtues of David their father, 767. For a short time he was abandoned to his weakness, 764. He compensated for his faults with many other good qualities, ibid. In what respect was he a man of blood? 274. David, displeasing to Saul’s daughter, pleased God all the more, III, 409. The tomb of David and Jesse, 167. David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” IV, 715. Few from David’s line pleased God, 986. David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” VI, 33. How great was David’s gentleness? VII, 512.

We belong not to the one from whom we are born, but to the one from whom we are reborn, II, 336. See *To be*.

“Debile” is the name of a single infirmity, VII, 117.

Deblatha, the name of a city later called Epiphanea of Syria, V, 62.

Some incompetently number Deborah among the widows, I, 293. She was a prophetess and received the name “bee,” ibid.

Ten decades in a square form possess solidity, IV, 790. In the number of ten decades there is a full and perfect number, V, 497.

The Decalogue is not solid food but milk, V, 952. Each commandment of the Decalogue should be called the first, VII, 694. The Pharisees wrote the Decalogue on parchment strips, 183.

Who the decans are, IV, 49.

Ten tribes are sometimes referred to in the prophets, especially in Hosea, as heretics, VI, 8. The captivity of the ten tribes in the cities of the Medes, V, 262. By what names the kingdom of the ten tribes is designated, VI, 8.

The various kinds of tithes, V, 565. The Hebrew tradition concerning them, ibid.

Those who deceive themselves, II, 358.

Decius and Valerian, persecutors of Christians, II, 3. They wished to slaughter souls, not bodies, ibid. Decius, Valerian, and Maximian, persecutors, VI, 549.

The mice of Decius, VII, 553.

### Declamation

“Declamation.” It is a sign of folly, both in the speaker and in those who listen in church. To stir up applause by means of a certain seductive charm and elegance of words, III, 467.

The final age of the decrepit, IV, 885.

The decurions marked out, II, 24.

What is ridiculous and full of disgrace, I, 264.

“Failing” is explained in various ways, VI, 675 ff.

Who spoke the praises of the dead, and where, I, 332. Examples of the dead in various kinds of death, 343. It was once customary to crown the pyramids of the dead, 345.

Do not enter upon the slippery and soft path of pleasures, I, 613. Miseries are exchanged for pleasures, and pleasures for miseries, 234. To live amid pleasures and not be held by the vices of pleasures is impossible, II, 338. Those who enjoy the prosperity and pleasures of this age should not be thought blessed, 335.

What the pleasures of matrons did, VII, 147.

Sins committed through ignorance, II, 730. For these the Church commands offerings to be made, ibid., 741. See *Ignorance*, *Sin*, *Crime*.

The ravings of certain people, VII, 196.

Delphidius, a Gallic poet, I, 818.

Demaratus, II, 334.

Cyprian attacked Demetrianus, I, 427. He said that the testimonies of the prophets were fabricated and fictitious, ibid. He should have been attacked by the authority of philosophers and poets—why? ibid. Whose student was Demetrianus? II, 919.

The nobility of Demetriad’s great-grandmother, made more distinguished, I, 977.

Demetrias, a virgin of Christ, was first in the Roman world in nobility and wealth, I, 976. Jerome fears to speak about her—why? [Col. 0956] ibid. She surpassed her maiden years through the ardor of faith, ibid. She began where it is the mark of perfected and consummated virtue for others to have left off, ibid. Jerome did not know her according to her bodily appearance, ibid. When he wrote to her, ibid. She receives the bridal veil of virginity, ibid. Her family and nobility, 977. She despises all these things, including wealth, ibid. She marveled at the conduct of holy men and women, ibid. Her austerities, ibid. By what thoughts she withdraws herself from marriage, 977. She casts away the vanities of the world and shows that she chooses virginity, ibid. Many follow her purpose, and it is celebrated in various regions of the earth, 980. She receives more than she offered, ibid. Various counsels and instructions are given to her, 982 ff. She is commanded to be subject to her grandmother and mother, 988. The practices she is instructed to maintain, 989. With whom she ought to communicate in order to be safe from heretics, 989, 995. Women whom she must avoid or have in her company are set before her, 996. The happiness and blessedness of virginity, and in what they consist, are demonstrated to her, 991.

Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, condemned Origen, I, 154. He sent Pantaenus to preach Christ, 428. Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, II, 875. He was offended by Origen’s ordination, 893. He is assailed by Origen, 509.

Demetrius the Jewish writer against the Gentiles, II, 879.

Democritus: what he does not believe about the soul after death, I, 334. The wisdom of Democritus, 256.

Demosthenes, I, 222. The twisted and sharply struck maxims of Demosthenes, 979. His torrential river, 1089. The Philippics of Demosthenes, 318. What he did not know, 271. Demosthenes’ speech *For Ctesiphon*, translated by Tully [Cicero], 520. Demosthenes and Aeschines hurl thunderbolts against each other, 471. Demosthenes, VII, 485.

Demotion, chief of the Areopagites, II, 307. His virgin daughter killed herself, ibid.

What one denarius signifies, II, 374. The number ten is perfect, IV, 75. It is a mystical number, 1082. The denarius has the figure of a king, VII, 153. The denarius was reckoned as ten coins and bore the image of Caesar, 176.

Some people habitually deny with closed eyes what they do not believe happened, because they do not want it to have happened, II, 193.

Kissing as an act of veneration among the Hebrews, II, 475.

Deportation to the islands was formerly a kind of punishment, I, 695.

The customs of the Derbices toward elderly parents, II, 335.

How God is said to abandon, although he is everywhere, I, 330.

What does Desiderius ask of Jerome? II, 419. Desiderius, 389.

Desiderius the presbyter, I, 210. What was he grieving over? 391.

Desire is extinguished by desire, I, 101. The Lord’s desire is not in the flesh but in the soul, IV, 347.

Whatever is forbidden is desired all the more, VI, 152.

Despair must be avoided and shunned, I, 891. The only crime of despair is one that cannot be healed, 1087. Nothing so offends God as clinging to worse things out of despair of better ones, 891. Despair is a sign of unbelief, ibid. Despair must be avoided, IV, 663, and VI, 191.

Whoever despairs of salvation does not think that there will be a judgment, I, 891. The soul destined for destruction should not despair of applying a remedy to its wound, ibid. The unbelieving mind should not despair of the promise of good things, ibid. Those who despair think that everything ends with death, ibid. We must not despair even if we sin after baptism, II, 323.

What does the name of the betrothal, repeated three times, indicate? VI, 26.

### Detraction

Detraction must be avoided, I, 268, 946. It is common in most provinces, 207. What kind of detraction redounds to our praise, 785. No one willingly reports words of detraction to an unwilling listener, 268. Those who speak of other people’s sins to individuals as though they had told no one else are condemned, 947. A malicious tongue attacks the saints as a consolation for sinning, 712. It is no great achievement to chatter in corners and pass judgment on others, 240. It is difficult to pass through the course of this life in a slanderous city without picking up some tale of sinister rumor, 952. Deceitful lips and the tongues of the wicked are not to be feared, 710. No one can pass through the course of this life without suffering the bite of others, 290. Detraction must be avoided, V, 694. Detraction is easy, VI, 452.

Let the detractor learn, when he sees you, that you do not willingly listen and do not easily slander, I, 266. When he sees the listener’s sad face, he falls silent, 946. Detractors should not be listened to, 268. Let us pray for them, 579. Detractors are called the Scyllaean dogs, II, 14. The malice of detractors, 524. The detractor and the serpent are equals, III, 474. Our detractors should be forgiven, 446. Jerome rebukes those who slander and remain idle, VII, 537.

Do not slander anyone or tear others to pieces, I, 945. Whoever slanders, and whoever listens to the slanderer, will perish together, 946. We must neither disparage the good qualities of our adversaries nor praise the vices of our friends, 523. The saints must not be slandered, because the angels carry our words and thoughts to God, III, 479. To disparage a good person or praise an evil one is the same crime, V, 82. It belongs to the ignorant to disparage and to the learned to help, VI, 429.

### God

God is not composed of diverse members, I, 602. God has one single nature, the only nature that truly exists, 40. Other things that have been created do not properly exist; God alone does, ibid. He is not confined by measure or number, 600. God is good, and everything that the good God makes must be good, 178. He does not fail in giving, ibid. God’s omnipotence must not be confined within a narrow place, 320. Far be it from us to believe of the omnipotent God that he is impotent in anything, 412. He is shown when something occurs contrary to nature, 718. He knows the future beforehand, 129. We are ignorant of many things that must be left to his knowledge, 1038. God is one thing and the human being another, 1037. Everything is in God, 586. God alone is immortal, II, 749. He alone is truthful, 780. He alone is truthful; every human being is a liar, 799. God alone is without sin, 771. He alone is wise, 750. Everything is governed by his will, 698. Everything depends upon the judgment of him who is Creator of all, 698, 751. Everything is possible for God, 720. For God to will is to have done, 427. God’s power is commended, 440. He can do whatever he wishes, 783. He is the Creator of all, 697. He is the maker of souls as well as bodies, 497, 559. He is not the craftsman of superfluous things, 332. God’s works are in truth and justice, 779. All things live to God, 11. God’s foreknowledge, 477. God alone is always what he was, III, 386. As kind and merciful, he remembers even the least and all things, 392. God has no beginning, IV, 528. He has no partners in his nature, 731. The natural and written law bear witness to one God, 490. He is confined by no place, because he encloses all things in his fist and span, 799. He is the Creator of all visible and invisible things, ibid. No creature has seen God’s face according to the property of his nature; rather, he is seen by the mind when he is believed to be invisible, 20. God’s majesty and power are demonstrated, 487, 492. In what does God’s omnipotence prevail? 597. In God, to have spoken is to have done, 425. The greatness of God’s strength makes everything serve according to its order, 492. God makes things contrary to one another, 533. “The hand of God” signifies power, 811. God’s promise is constant and firm, 134, 633, 651. No one can weaken God’s plan, 261. We must believe God even when he does not swear, 181. His knowledge, immensity, and providence are noted, 494. God’s great love of justice, 872. When his justice is known, 384. Repentance in God—what does it mean? 871. In comparison with him, all wisdom is counted as nothing, 914. In what sense God is said to have limbs, 546. Divine majesty cannot be made by human hands, 528. God’s foreknowledge knows future things beforehand, 191, 1025. Nothing is hidden from God, 494. We can hide nothing from God, 23. No one knows the future except God, 547, 1044. What does God’s knowledge accomplish? 606. God says that he does not know things unworthy of his knowledge, 974. In what sense he is said to rise in the morning, 893. The name “Lord” added to God signifies knowledge of the person, 615.

God is kind and severe, V, 872. By wisdom God stretched out heaven, 795. By strength God founded the earth, 793. By wisdom God founded the earth, 795. God is a consuming fire, 861. In what sense God is called fire and light, 868. God’s name of four letters is ineffable, 327. He is confined by no place, because he encloses all things in his fist and span, 485. What heretics call cruelty in God signifies mercy, 236. There is nothing bodily in God, 82. It belongs to God’s mercy to overthrow false things, 362. Where the likeness of God is, there too is the fullness of wisdom, 339. Knowledge of the future belongs to God alone, 628. Why are the high and deep things of God not to be proclaimed publicly? 549. He wishes all to be saved, 205. What do “sleeping” and “waking” mean when attributed to God? 679. Even to speak truly about God is dangerous, 891. What the divine name *Tetragrammaton* properly signifies, 922.

God is truth, VI, 391. Merciful by his nature, 413. For the Lord to command is to have done, 379, 477. God is the author and giver of all benefits, 637. Creator of the whole human being, 896. God is equally the God of all, 850. He cares for all nations, 240. The Maker of the universe is briefly shown, 400. He does not change, 849. In what sense he is said to be changeable, ibid. Why does he change his promises? 354. His will is fulfilled through his enemies, 107.

The essence of God, VII, 600. God alone is immutable by nature, 383. Apart from him nothing can exist from itself, 600. His providence toward human beings, 63. His foreknowledge, 584. Nothing is hidden from God, 64. Good by nature, he makes the saints through participation in himself, 546. He wishes all to be saved, 558. He is everywhere, and wholly everywhere, 580. God is in individuals by parts, 569. He is the Creator of all things, 547. He created everything from nothing, 548. For God to have spoken is to have done, 124. What are the true works of God? 517. In what sense he works all things according to the purpose of his will, 558. In him all things are measured and ordered, 636. Knowledge of God is naturally present in everyone, 391, 704. He can be recognized from created things, 419. To assert that God’s substance is of one sort and another is the cause of error, 537. How he alone is truthful, and every human being a liar, 690. What does God’s sitting signify? 565. Whom is God said to know? 455. He does not know those who perish, 41. What especially provokes his anger, 644. What are anger and fury in God? 636. He swears in order to make us more secure, 690. He confirms his words by a certain custom of swearing, 535. We are ignorant of God’s judgments, 73. What do God’s right and left hands mean? 565.

God is always a giver, always a donor, I, 1033. How great is God’s mercy? 894. God is patient and merciful, 1087. Why does he not immediately become the avenger of crimes? ibid. God’s power is greater than the things that have been made, 600. He did not make creatures as great as he could have, but made them as great as they ought to have been, 601. His judgments are just and good, 178, 690. God’s hand is raised up for a long time and the blow is held back, so that it may strike more powerfully, 536. His name was spread everywhere after Christ’s resurrection, 333, 334. No rashness is greater than to claim equality with him, 1025. Do not regard God’s mercy and excessive kindness as an occasion for sins, 1094. If God’s justice and truth frighten you, let mercy and peace summon you to salvation, 895. What does it mean to possess the Lord? 259. He is not pleased by our hunger, 95. In God, falsehood is praised with a greater crime than truth is blamed, 303. God, who cannot be overcome by any forces opposed to him, is conquered by prayers, 42. He can be restrained from doing what he has threatened—how? 965. Grant God the power that belongs to him; he has no need of you as a defender, 1038. What is the true worship of God? 267, 268. We ought to be greedy in receiving God’s benefits, 1033. He judges each person as he finds him, 896. He considers not the past but the present, if old crimes are changed by a new conversion, ibid. We once feel that we have offended God and do not please him, 345. If we do not believe God when he promises, let us at least believe him when he swears for our salvation, 891. He gives more than is asked, 9. Imperfect service of God does not please him when it is delayed, 337. With how much fear must what has been consecrated to God be preserved? 683.

By God’s mercy we are preserved, II, 752. We can hide nothing from God, 697. God’s anger is just, 747. God’s threat sometimes conveys mercy, 724. In comparison with God no creature can be perfect, 710. No one has seen God in this age, 797. God’s will is one thing and his indulgence another, 298. God’s will is not to be scrutinized but endured with thanksgiving, 766. We cannot know God’s judgments and, according to our own choice, prejudge his sentence, 284. Why did he wish victims to be offered to him? 776. He commanded them not by his will but by comparison with idols, ibid. He permits impieties to be committed in order to punish sins, 780. How will God be all in all? 713. When the likeness of God and true contemplation are promised, 798. He does not dwell equally in everyone, 376. He always desires greater things in us, ibid. How are we one in him? 370. God’s words are exceedingly persuasive, 771. Not submitting to them is sin, 770. What does he crown in us? 787. At the fulfillment of the ages he recapitulated all things, 267. God judges the present, not the future, 788. He does not condemn from foreknowledge someone whom he knows will become such, but who later displeases him, ibid. He is so good that he chooses one whom he knows will become evil, ibid. The substance of the Lord must be guarded, 563.

We must speak and think soberly about God, III, 427. Whoever wishes to discuss more matters concerning divinity will fall into folly, ibid. God’s great mercy is praised, IV, 409, 632, 651. God’s mercy is overcome by the magnitude of sins, 756. We always need God’s mercy, and there is no end to his kindness, 299. God’s mercy and punishments have their own measure, 276. It belongs to God’s mercy that one nation should perish so that all may be saved, 99. God’s mercy is hidden and his anger displayed so that people may cease sinning, 229. God’s patience is unbelievable, 985. He administers the human race in various ways, 386. Everything is governed by his judgment, 493, 926. The order of God’s providence is described, 211. It is not his work to destroy those whom he created, 383. God’s labor is to defend sinners, 522. Everyone who is made upright in God is the scepter of his inheritance, ibid. Knowledge of the one God is possession of all virtues, 1075. It is great folly not to know God and to despise him when present, 870. He calls everyone to faith, 639. We are saved not by our merit but by God’s help, 22. Unless God draws us, we cannot be saved, 883. Everything contrary happens to those whom God wishes to save, 326. To see God is perfect joy, 811. By whom is God seen? 761. In what sense the patriarchs and prophets saw the Lord, 90. He must always be sought, and how, 307. By whom he is found, 685. When God opposes, rest is not found, 231. He draws near to his saints, 313, 649. We draw near to God in mind, not in body, 394. Drawing near to God is not a matter of an idle mind but of laborious action, 686. To serve the Lord and dwell before him depends not on place but on merit, 233. What does it mean to render to God and to Caesar? 629. We do not withdraw from God by place but by will, 944. The way of returning to God, 649. The source of forgetfulness in invoking God, 676.

In what sense God is said to rage, 83, 776. His vengeance is holy and just, 359. All things agree with God’s anger, 937. He delays his anger in order to show mercy, 377. Inanimate elements and living creatures feel God’s anger, 870. He strikes offenders in order to correct those who have been struck, 14, 679. He disciplines us like children when he visits our iniquities with the rod, 262. He shows mercy and spares so that his mercy may be exalted, 410. Those who do not feel God through benefits feel him through punishments, 71. His consolation is upon his enemies: those who did not perceive benefits are corrected by punishments, 27. Why does he visit iniquities? 241. Why does he overlook sins? ibid. Why will he come with glory and fury? 419. How is he fire? 812. He is shown in the attire of a judge and conqueror, 813. He comes to judgment, not to judge, but to be judged at the same time, 56, 522, 523. He calls heaven and earth as witnesses, 10. How he dwells on high, 678. The holier places are called God’s dwelling, 755. Wherever his will is done, there is his dwelling and house, ibid. God’s refreshment is that he may rest in us, 377. God’s name is blasphemed because of our evil works, 606. He speaks according to our feeling, 21. Who has resisted his anger? 699. We should not think it a small thing to fear the Lord, 582. Whoever desires the Lord desires nothing else, 347. He abandons for a short time in order to compel us to pray, 752. Who do not deserve to be heard by him? 865. He loves the poverty of the righteous more than the gifts of the rich, 736.

God impressed his image upon our soul; afterward the devil impressed his own through sin, V, 865. God begins with sorrows and ends with joys, 756, 767. God speaks through an angel, 858. God is not the God of all, 805. God first strikes, then heals, 861. God is the teacher of the sacred writers, 813. God is slow in punishing, 744. We must serve God in mind and speech, 501. God’s presence prevents us from sinning, 88, 255. The source of forgetfulness of God, 182. All things that are without God are nothing, 302. He is angry not with human beings but with vices, 649. He strikes offenders so that those who have been struck may be corrected, 23, 64, 68, 276. Every place in which he finds lodging is his place, 31. He does not consider the words of speakers but their hearts, 135.

He is the most merciful physician, VI, 591. His great mercy, 26. He foretells the future so that he may not be compelled to inflict punishments, 256. Severe on the day of judgment, he will be merciful toward his people, 214. He wishes all to be saved, 133. God saves some in truth and others in mercy, 531. Because of many sins he does not forget a few good deeds, 744. How repentance in God is to be understood, 325. It is not surprising if he is said to swear, 340. He does many evils, not by punishing but by granting an opportunity for repentance, 48, 49, 61, 269, 270. To whom is he good? 453. His benefits toward his people, 125. He threatens severe things in order to have mercy on the repentant, 63. He moderates the severity of the judge with the compassion of the Father, 129. God’s blow is visitation and healing, 252. What is the cause of God’s anger? 530. In his anger God does not forget, 636. He has his own measures, ibid. In what sense his anger must be understood, 780. How he becomes bitter, 143, 915. In what sense God thinks evil, 451, 534, 689. God gave Israel a king in his fury and afterward took him away in his indignation, 150. He seems to abandon us so that, when we do not feel him present, we may seek him as absent, 61. He wishes to be judged together with his people, so that he may not appear to pass sentence unjustly, 34, 257. He repays sinners in kind, 42, 836. He threatens that he will repay the sins of the fathers, 230. In what he commands, he himself seems to strike, 318. God commands nothing except what is honorable, in the Preface to Hosea. It is blasphemous to say that anything happens without God, 603. God’s power is demonstrated in small living creatures, 187, 198. How does God now love the Jews? 29. Whenever we do anything good, we confess God, 712. Whoever believes in God also believes in his saints, 752. What does it mean to deny God? 712. God’s will must be consulted in every work, 650. He is far from the wicked and near to the saints, 580. Whoever is without God has no god; what does it mean to be near God and to withdraw from him? 565. Human beings and angels are God’s dwelling, 584.

Jerome’s suspicion concerning the addition “of God” to the word of God, VII, 437. Heretics who disparage God the Creator, 454. They admit two gods, 31.

### Gods

The names of the pagan gods must not be used, I, 76. The opinion that there are many gods is condemned, IV, 527. Those who are fellow workers with Christ are called gods, 913. The authors and gods of the Egyptians, 205. The gods of Egypt have names derived from beasts, 544.

### Deuteronomy

Deuteronomy is called the second law and a prefiguration of the evangelical law, I, 276. It contains the earlier things in such a way that everything from the old things is nevertheless new, ibid. The book of Deuteronomy [Col. 0960] is an enumeration of past events, II, 735. It was found in the Temple under Josiah, 244. Moses wrote that volume near the Golden Mountains, III, 184. To the west of Moab, beside the Jordan opposite Jericho, 198. He read that book in Lobon, 238. He wrote it in Taphol, 281.

Dexter asked Jerome for a catalogue of ecclesiastical authors, II, 416. Dexter, 816.

How the right and left are understood in Scripture, IV, 629. What it means to turn to the right or to the left, 604. How difficult it is to turn neither to the left nor to the right, 82.

The devil fell through pride, I, 111. The devil’s judgment and ruin consist in arrogance, 424. His cunning and craftiness, 792. He has associates, 225. Because he perished from God, he is said not to exist; whatever belongs to the devil is idolatry, 31. He fights everywhere against God’s servants and goes before them to every place, 709. The devil’s food is those who deny God, 571. He grants health to the ungodly so that they may sin, 24. In what does the devil’s power against men and women consist? 96. The devil’s burning arrows: by what remedies are they to be extinguished? 286. Whom he seeks, 90. He does not seek unbelieving people, but hastens to snatch them from Christ’s Church, ibid. Whatever belongs to the devil is hostile to God, 31. The devil and his daughters are insatiable, II, 282. He spoke certain things from the Scriptures, 202. Nothing is safe with him: his ambushes are unspeakable, 44. He never reveals himself with an open face, 43. He even attacks animals for the sake of human beings, 25. Christ’s antidote against the devil’s poisons, 242. The devil falls through an abundance of good things, III, 396. The night of vices and sin works destruction in us, 451. Always desirous of new things, 476. A supporter of errors, 411. At the devil’s instigation, sins are heaped upon sins, 394. All the devil’s steps are wickedness and deceit, 309. Everything is full of his nets, 529. The number of those led astray by the devil cannot be grasped by reckoning, 394. The devil’s sin is pride, IV, 52. He is evil not by necessity of nature but by the choice of his mind, 641. In what respect is he like Christ? 252. He hastens to seize even the perfect, 260. His power compared with dust, 270. Those who say that the devil can be cleansed and repent are condemned, 257, 283. For the defeated there is destruction, and for the victors a cause of rewards, 641. Error concerning the devil’s father, 259. In what sense he is called an axe, a saw, and a rod, 146. The devil called a lion, bear, and serpent, VI, 301. The fountain of the dead, 156. The devil’s various scourge, 564. There is scarcely anyone—or no one—whom the devil has not deceived, 584, 586. Some think that the devil will repent, 418. The devil is given the name “world” and “age,” VII, 572. He insinuates sins into human beings, ibid. His various meanings, 679, 670, 721. He is called a mountain, 166. Why is the devil called “the enemy man”? 96. He became destruction by his own will, not by nature, 573. The opinion of the ancients concerning the devil, 28. He does not probe the secrets of the heart, 115. The devil’s tricks and devices, 670, 671. He can persuade but not cast down, 21, 22. He interprets the Scriptures badly, ibid. When are we most fully given into the devil’s power? 630. This lies within our own will, ibid. Those who think that the devil does not incite to sin are refuted, 672. Those who serve the devil’s passions and other vices, 671. In what sense they dwell in the heavenly places, 612. We were captives of the devil, 673. How and from where the devil tempts, 340. The extent to which we assume the form of the devil, serpents, vipers, a lion, a dragon, a fox, a goat, and pigs, 267. See Demons.

Deacons used to read the Gospel repeatedly, I, 1090. What makes deacons worthy of honor, 1083. Some equated deacons with presbyters; the response to them, 1081 and following. What did they do at Rome when presbyters were present? 1083. Why deacons were instituted, ibid. The deacon publicly recited the names of those making offerings, V, 209.

A royal diadem, I, 372. A diadem and purple are given only to emperors, IV, 532.

The art of dialectic, V, 287.

The snares of dialecticians, II, 206.

The fifth dialect of the Greeks is called Aeolic, III, 318. What dialecticians study, VII, 735.

The perpetual virginity of Diana and Minerva, I, 906. Diana remained a virgin, II, 307. The temple of Diana was burned, 223. What is reported concerning the author of this burning? ibid. The priests of Taurian Diana and of Vesta, 307. Antiochus wished to plunder Diana’s temple in Elymais, V, 718. Two Dianas are noted: one the huntress, the other *mulcimammia*—“many-breasted,” 541. The Ephesians worshiped the latter, ibid.

What does *diapsalma* signify? I, 436 and following, and VI, 637.

Dibon and Dimon are names of the same city of Moab, IV, 188.

Dibon-gad, I, 992.

What does Dicaearchus report in his books of Antiquities? II, 342.

Several styles of speaking are noted, I, 222. There are those who think that whatever they say is the law of God, 275. To win admiration for oneself through speed of speech before an uneducated crowd is characteristic of unlearned people, 263.

The rashness of dictation turns into ruin, I, 737. See *I write*.

An ancient saying, I, 281. A common saying, 994. A distinguished saying of a noble Roman, II, 317. A saying of a Greek orator, IV, 483. A saying of a man of outstanding gravity, VII, 723. Another saying of a certain orator, 516. Sayings of Latin historians, 416.

The didrachm is called *baca* in Hebrew; it is half an ounce, III, 341.

Dido, queen of Carthage, I, 906. The history and praises of Dido, II, 310.

Didymus, Jerome’s teacher at Alexandria, I, 524. His catechist, 237. He was a defender of Origen, 531. Didymus’s knowledge of the Scriptures, 237. He interpreted the Psalms, 751. He wrote on the Epistle to the Galatians, 738. A history concerning him and blessed Antony, 410. Didymus, 232, 235. Didymus is praised, II, 106. His book on the Holy Spirit, 107 and following. Jerome’s teacher at Alexandria, 103. He was a defender of Origen, 462, 507. He is Catholic in regard to the Trinity, ibid. He published a book on the Holy Spirit, which Jerome translated, ibid. In it some things are praised and others condemned, 556. Didymus on Hosea, 558. He explains and expounds the translations of the Jews, 528. Didymus’s book to Rufinus, ibid. Didymus, 469. Didymus, Jerome’s friend, published eighteen volumes on Isaiah, V, 5. Didymus of Alexandria, VII, 5, 539. His commentary, 357, 525. Didymus wrote three books on Hosea, VI, 777.

Day and night succeed one another at fixed intervals of hours, I, 621. Gradually diminishing, they recover, contribute, and give back what they lose, ibid. Twice a year they meet at the same measure, yet do not remain in the same condition, ibid. The alternating succession of day and night, ibid. By their brevity and length they distinguish the moments of the hours, so as to make the diversity of times useful to the world, ibid. Six days are assigned to the labor of this age, II, 366 and following. Those who live for a long time do not prolong their days; rather, those make their days great through the magnitude of good works, III, 455. “Day” is taken to mean “time,” IV, 208. The day of a human being, or human day, 962. What is the evil day? 963. In what sense is it called cruel? 171. The day of the Lord means either the consummation of the whole world or each person’s departure from life, 23. Day and night signify prosperity and adversity, 307. What meditation on the shortness of days works in us, V, 359. Which are the days of wrath? 258. Every seventh day is critical, VI, 283. The day of Jezreel is interpreted as the day of Christ, 11. Why the day of retribution is incurable, 181. In what way is Christ said not to know the day of the final judgment? 30. The preparation and effects of the day of judgment, 918. No day is evil, 312. It lies within our power to make a good day or an evil one, ibid. What does it mean to preach the day of retribution? VII, 352. All days are equal for Christians, 457. In what sense are they most evil? 377. What are the evil days? 676, 677. How are clear and rainy days foreknown? 119.

Whatever we do unwillingly is always difficult, V, 239.

Digamy is, in a certain sense, not good, I, 905. It does not arise in good soil, 907. The plant of digamy was at once overturned by the punishment of the Flood, 507. In digamy there is consolation for miseries; in prostitution there is punishment for sin, 902. To those slipping through lack of self-control into the abyss of sexual immorality, a hand is extended toward digamy, 905. In whom digamy is not found, 909. It is preferred to fornication, 902. Let the widow not know the indulgence granted to digamy, 507. Jerome does not condemn digamy, trigamy, and so forth, 231. Digamy is placed after first marriages, II, 262. What has been said about it? ibid. and following. It is rejected by many birds, 285. Although digamy is permitted, it is nevertheless said not to be expedient, IV, 784. Digamy and trigamy belong not to law but to indulgence, 951. Digamy is condemned in a bishop, presbyter, and deacon, VII, 302. See Bigamy.

A digamist cannot be chosen for the priesthood, I, 904. Digamists are not expelled from the Church, but monogamists are urged toward continence, 907. A digamist cannot be chosen for the clergy, II, 203. See Bigamist.

The joining and inequality of the fingers, II, 240. The ancient custom of counting on the fingers, 240. From the fingers, one is called a taster, IV, 487.

Among good men, dignity becomes more unworthy when many unworthy people possess it, II, 456. The order of dignities among human beings differs according to the variety of labor, II, 480.

The gods of the nations remained with the owls on the rooftops, I, 679. The gods who are called gods, V, 552. Who are the gods of the Egyptians? VI, 44. The gods of the ancients are dead gods, VII, 123. Some are listed, ibid.

Delay is not a loss when victory is made more certain by delay, II, 240.

Love has no order, I, 200. True love loves in faith, VII, 740. Many have considered love of enemies impossible, 31. The contrary is maintained, ibid. Danger and measure in love, ibid. 323. See Love and Charity.

What difference is there between “beloved” and “worthy of love”? VII, 749.

A dilemma against the Jews who killed Isaiah, I, 48. A dilemma produced from the workshop and reflection of executioners, II, 535.

A dilemma falling into the great abyss of blasphemies, II, 787.

Those whom we call diligent, II, 481.

Excessive diligence arouses suspicions, II, 409. Someone who does everything with diligence and caution can nevertheless say that all things are worthless, III, 402. What benefit do the diligence of priests and soldiers provide us? VII, 234.

It is difficult to be loved by those whom one surpasses in honor, I, 502. Everyone worships those whom he loves, IV, 953. What does it mean to love the good? VI, 296. To love each person as much as he deserves, VII, 323.

To fight: it is better to do so for a short time than to serve perpetually through the impatience of a single hour, I, 124. See Battle.

To dismiss: it is better to do so voluntarily than to lose that for which everything must be abandoned, I, 912.

Diocletian, II, 915.

Diodorus the Socratic is said to have had daughters of distinguished chastity, II, 309. The dispute between Diodorus and Chrysippus, 702.

A little work of Diogenes, I, 334. What Diogenes was famous for, II, 344, 345. Why did he trample on Plato’s couches with muddy feet? 338.

Dimon and Dibon are so called, IV, 188.

Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, I, 428, and II, 867.

Dionysius of Alexandria, bishop, I, 232, 235, 429. Dionysius’s four volumes against Sabellius, II, 508. He slips into Arian doctrine, ibid. He is defended, ibid. Dionysius of Alexandria wrote against Irenaeus, IV, 769. Apollinarius replied to him, ibid.

Why did Dionysius receive the name “Translated”? VII, 381.

Dionysius, a presbyter at Rome and later a bishop, II, 909.

Dionysius, bishop of Diospolis, II, 452.

Dionysius the philosopher, I, 534.

Dioscorus the physician, attacked by Hilary, I, 430.

Dioscorides, II, 332.

The Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, III, 100.

Diospolis was formerly called Lydda, I, 696.

Diospolis, a small city of Egypt, V, 357.

The wretched synod of Diospolis, I, 1067.

The Hebrew language has diphthongs, III, 58.

Pilgrimages were undertaken out of zeal for learning, I, 271. Learn for a long time what you are to teach, 945. Let us learn on earth those things whose knowledge will remain with us in heaven, 281. Some remain uneducated wise men because they do not wish to learn what they do not know, II, 473.

To discern. It is difficult to find someone able to distinguish a wise man from those who appear to be wise, III, 450.

A teacher does not correct a pupil unless he sees in him a more ardent intelligence, I, 410. It is one thing to teach a pupil and another to defeat an adversary, 223. No one can first be a pupil before hearing a teacher preach, II, 186. It is absurd that a pupil who goes to a teacher should be an artisan before he is taught, 184. The adversary is defeated; the pupil is taught, 185. A pupil imitating the vices of his teacher, 556. After much silence, we ought to become teachers from pupils, III, 412. The salvation of pupils is the reward of teachers, V, 560. Pupils should provide the necessities of life for their teachers, VII, 524. They offer false excuses so that they may be free from this duty, 525.

Christ had few disciples; the Pharisees had many. What follows from this? II, 380.

How great are the evils of discord? VI, 254.

The honorable stewardship of the apostles, I, 745. A prudent administration of household affairs, returning to an accounting, is not quickly laid aside, 432.

The best steward is the one who reserves nothing for himself, I, 269.

To displease. Everything under the sun is vain, while we mutually displease one another concerning the ends of good and evil, III, 393.

To instruct the person disputing against oneself more than to defeat him, I, 336.

The order of disputation and the method of truth, II, 699. What should the fruit of disputation be? 202. In ecclesiastical disputation, whether the ravings of old women’s quarrels should be avoided, 552. No Catholic, in a disputation among sects, has charged the person against whom he disputes with disgrace, 569.

Dissent contains something of human frailty, II, 763. The definition of dissent, VII, 507.

What is suitable for people who are dissolute, II, 338.

There is diversity between them wherever the distinct property of each is preserved, II, 249.

Divination is not taken in a favorable sense, VI, 472.

In divine matters, not possibility but intention must be considered, I, 2.

Who are diviners and dreamers? IV, 1043. Diviners and dreamers will take comfort in vain, VI, 871.

The divinity of the Father and the Son is one, VII, 614.

Wealth does not harm a rich person if he uses it well, I, 498. How it is possible for such people to be saved, 500. In Jerome’s time, someone who did not need bread was considered sufficiently rich, 947. The wretched condition of the rich, II, 12. What wickedness belongs to the rich man of the Gospel, V, 966. Many are tested by wealth and poverty, 320. The pride of the rich man condemned before judgment, VI, 687. The pride of the purple-clad rich man, 307. The choice of the rich, with the poor neglected, is condemned, 679, 680. The marks by which the rejection of the rich is recognized, ibid. 43. Wealth was hidden in the tombs of the rich, VII, 239. The vanity of the rich, 621.

By what means are riches scattered? I, 797. Like waves and billows, they are seized by successive masters, ibid. Whether you wish it or not, you will leave them behind at death, ibid.
