Let riches not exalt us; they commonly depress or elevate the most foolish of human beings, 626. Concern for them interrupts the sweetest sleep, ibid. Riches fight against the virtues no less than adversaries fight against their enemies, ibid. They should be regulated by reason and mercy toward one’s neighbors, ibid. In cities they are preferred to nobility, and they give a new man an ancient family, ibid. The desire for riches can never be satisfied by any riches, ibid. The evils they produce, ibid. Riches can be lost and found in a moment, 399. What is endured for the sake of riches, 934. Where riches are superfluous, 501. They must be abandoned for Christ, 284. They are compared with the crookedness of camels, 1080. What should be said about riches in the overthrow and destruction of one’s household property? 710. Although many were extremely vicious, they despised riches, 309. There is no perfect virtue in despising them, 793. Contempt for riches is strengthened by examples, 108. As long as our soul is bound to the management of possessions and revenues, we cannot think freely about God, 433. Possessing riches is not a matter of praise; despising them for Christ is, 692. The testing of virtues in the possession of riches, 506. Riches that are distributed daily and never fail, 326. Let them contribute to the redemption of the soul and the nourishment of the poor, 795. What are riches? 433. Riches are foreign to us, 116. Why riches are sought and their use, II, 341. It is no wisdom to gather earthly riches, III, 405. It does not lie within our power to possess riches, which the unjust often possess in greater measure, 440. It is a gift of God to be able to enjoy riches, 432. They are burdensome to a holy man, 325. It is the worst sickness to be tormented in thought over riches and to seek perishable wealth through sadness, groaning, quarrels, and futile labor, 431. Riches are not accumulated except at another’s expense, IV, 437. Worldly people gather riches through robberies and the tears of the wretched, 26. They receive their consolation in this world, 981. Stealing what belongs to others, 961. Many are tested by riches and poverty, 556, 675. The greater the authority among the rich, the greater the insolence of their sins, 873. The crime of the purple-clad rich man, 954. Riches are born from iniquity, VI, 509. Multiplied riches are dense mud, 613. How riches deliver from death, 687. Truth produces poverty; falsehood produces riches, 509. The slippery possession of riches, VII, 90. See Wealth.

To teach what one does is the foundation of the art, I, 423. It is most foolish to teach what the person being taught already knows, 111. Because of the fault of the ages daily sliding toward worse things, we now teach in the Churches what we do not know, III, 411. Can someone teach after sinning, and how? VI, 468.

The treatises of the Church’s teachers should be read after the sacred Scriptures, I, 289. Let them belong to those whose faith is known, ibid. Christian teachers ought to bark for Christ, II, 569. A false teacher flatters and deceives; he does not seek the conversion of his hearers but applause and praise, IV, 437. He teaches the same things that delight the people to hear, flattering sinners in their vice and stirring up the audience’s applause, 478. He seeks riches, food, and possessions through pleasing promises, ibid. He prepares his hearers for the future fire and binds them more tightly in the chains of sins, 437. Who are the false teachers? IV, 901. What is the reward of a teacher’s speech? 950. Teachers who promise prosperity to the rich are rebuked, 885. Greek and Latin theological teachers who Judaize, V, 422. The difference between a learned holy man and a simple holy man, 733. False teachers and designated prelates, VI, 338. The slightest fault in a teacher brings him down from the highest rank, VII, 26.

New doctrine must be suppressed, I, 536. What is delicate doctrine? 222. Foreign doctrine must not be accepted, 992. For even distinguished doctrine is ashamed when one’s own conscience reproves it, 953. Filthy doctrine found people in Rome whom it could deceive, 957. Formerly it circulated in wicked Egypt and the regions of the East, 993. Great men in every kind of learning, 237. The doctrine of the Pharisees is the overthrow of truth, IV, 707. False doctrine does everything for profit, 276. The bread of doctrine is not eaten unless we open the eyes of the heart, 651. It is better to devote oneself to secular disciplines than to die from a lack of doctrine, 984. Old and new doctrine are to be cultivated together, V, 552. The doctrine of teachers must be considered more than their life, 498. Through the truth of doctrine, different gods are worshiped, VI, 307. Virtues perish if there is no doctrine in the Churches, 343. The doctrine of God is, as it were, a standard of speech, VII, 533. Who adorns the Lord’s doctrine and brings it into disrepute? 723. This doctrine is commended when accompanied by the example of life, 697, 720. It is one thing to speak sound doctrine and another to teach things that accord with sound doctrine, 713. The leaven of false doctrine, 489.

Learned. Even a learned man debates with heretics not without danger, III, 473. The learned in the Church seize the wise men of the world in their own cunning, 400. A learned man who is not righteous should be trampled in the dung, VII, 633. According to the progress of his knowledge, his punishments are greater, ibid.

Doeg, or Doech, commander of the mules, V, 312.

The contagion of perverse doctrines violates the beauty of souls, I, 603. Those who contradict the Church’s divine doctrines cannot receive the sacraments of heavenly words, 585. In discussing doctrines and questions, one must seek not the person but the case, II, 781. The doctrine of the Gentiles, partly Platonic, 424. Doctrines of falsehood are called idols, IV, 41. Every doctrine contrary to the truth worships the works of its own hands, 37. All doctrines contrary to the truth are bitter, and truth alone is sweet, 82. Who are the teachers of perverse doctrines and disgrace? V, 174. As many false doctrines as there are, so many Antichrists are there, VI, 558. A new hidden doctrine is brought to light, VII, 523.

God’s “hewing” in the prophets, VI, 63.

It is disgraceful to strike an enemy by deceit rather than by strength, I, 223.

Pain that is cured neither by time nor by reason, I, 581. Moderation must be applied to pain, 183, 335. Pain that is to be lessened by time must be overcome by reason, 183. In pain of the flesh and limbs, it is difficult not to groan, 794. What hurts sufficiently is driven out by greater pain, 783.

What does *doma* signify? I, 1079.

Who is “of the household of faith”? I, 820.

Mistresses are judged by the behavior of their maidservants, I, 506. The wantonness of girls is often also judged by the behavior of their mistresses, 953. Each person delights in the company of those like herself, ibid. The crowd of female servants followed the example of their patroness and mistress, 980.

Masters are not to be obeyed if they command wicked things, VII, 668. Whatever returns to the Lord is counted among the members of the household, I, 690.

“Lord,” a word often added in the Greek version of the Psalter, I, 647.

The holy Lord is with the one who is holy and is perverted in the presence of one who was already perverted by his own will, III, 441. In what does the greatness of the Lord consist? VII, 259. By whom is the Lord found? 247.

In what sense is Christ called “the Lordly man”? II, 157.

Domitian, the emperor, I, 695. Domitian, the same man, II, 280. He banished John the Evangelist, 280. Domitian’s persecution, 845. He was killed, and his acts were rescinded by the senate, ibid.

The exile of Flavia Domitilla under the emperor Domitian, I, 695. The little cells in which she had endured a long martyrdom were shown, ibid.

A witty saying of the orator Domitius, I, 262.

Domninus turned toward the Jews, II, 883.

Domnion is called the Lot of his own time, I, 211. What Jerome received from him, 236. What Jerome indicated to Domninus, II, 634.

The house of God is the Church and each believer, VI, 97. Israel was expelled from the house of God—that is, the holy land—98.

Houses built with the sufferings of the wretched and the toil of the condemned, I, 208. In a great house there are various vessels, 907. In a house there is one master, 942. No one should remain in a house in which he must daily either perish or conquer, 784. Whatever is fabricated at home becomes public rumor, 788. We are the last to know the evils of our own household, 1093. Luxuriously furnished houses, IV, 331. Winter and summer houses, VI, 261 and following.

Christ’s gifts are diverse, II, 250. It is evil and sinful to wish to satisfy God not through obedience and good works but through victims, gifts, and sacrifices, III, 426. Spiritual gifts become less valuable if reward is placed between them, VII, 68. The gifts of the perfect and of beginners, 693.

Gifts strip the giver and kill the receiver, VI, 514. Gifts are shamelessly demanded and received even more shamefully, ibid.

A military donative, an enlistment bounty for soldiers, I, 29.

The commentaries of Donatus, Jerome’s teacher, II, 472. Donatus, Jerome’s teacher, had expounded Terence, III, 390.

Donatus, from whom the Donatists derive their name, aided by Lucilla’s wealth, I, 1032. What Donatus accuses Christians of, II, 929. Africa and Numidia were deceived by his persuasion, ibid.

The adverbs “until” and “up to” in Helvidius’s interpretation, II, 210. They are explained in the same way by Jerome, ibid.

Dor, once a very powerful city, I, 896.

The resurrection of Dorcas and Aeneas, I, 896.

Dorcas—that is, “doe”—received this name from the innate power belonging to her. Because she sees more sharply, she was called *Doreas*, III, 528.

Why does the Apostle forbid grieving over those who sleep? I, 450. See The Dead.

One should sleep more often with an empty stomach, I, 324.

How and of whom God is said to sleep, IV, 939.

Death is called “sleep,” IV, 250.

Sleeping in the shrines of idols on the skins of victims, so that the future may be learned through dreams, IV, 774 and following.

Dositheus, I, 703. Dositheus, leader of the Samaritans, rejected the prophets, II, 197. Dositheus, the heresiarch of the Samaritans, VII, 367.

The endowments of body and mind are different in different people, II, 720.

The drachma is lost and is found in dung, I, 896.

Eight drachmas make a Latin ounce, V, 43.

Dracontius, the bishop, where he was in exile, II, 30. He was visited by Hilarion, ibid.

The nature of the dragon, VI, 438. The terrible hissing of dragons when they are overcome by elephants, ibid. The dragon’s strength is in its loins, 557.

How far the Ishmaelites could flee in one day with dromedary camels, IV, 218.

The two women in Hosea represent the persons of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, VI, 2 and 3.

The duality of pontiffs, while Christ suffers, displays the split error of their religion, V, 96.

Duellius was the first at Rome to triumph in a naval battle, II, 312. What is said about him? ibid.

To pronounce on what is doubtful as though it were certain is rash, VII, 758.

Simulated sweetness conceals the worst poison, II, 463.

Duma, a region of Idumea that faces south and lies twenty miles from Eleutheropolis, IV, 216. Near it are the mountains of Seir, said to have been named from Esau, ibid.

Twelve, a perfect number, V, 373.

The number two is not good, and why, II, 268.

What is a dupondius? II, 260.

Dura, a plain in the land of Shinar, V, 623.

How great is our hardness? I, 894. Through hardness of heart we turn our backs in insult to God, 893.

E

The Ebionites are neither Jews nor Christians, I, 769. The Ebionites, who pretend to be Christians, 746. The doctrine of the Ebionites, II, 843. The doctrine and dwelling-place of the Ebionites, Hebrews of this sort, III, 190. The Ebionites are noted, IV, 823. The Ebionites rejected Paul, VII, 75. The Ebionites’ error concerning Christ, 399.

Ebion, Cerinthus’s successor, rejected the Gospels, II, 197. He is attacked by ancient writers, 225. Ebion, 200. Ebion, worthy of the poverty of his name, IV, 12. He plowed with an ox and a donkey, 21. Ebion, VII, 375, 737. He was half-Christian and half-Jewish, 435. His translation of certain Hebrew words, ibid. Ebion’s heresy is blunted, 375. Jerome constrains him and his followers, 480. A passage is directed against Ebion, 614. His doctrine is crushed, 385.

*Ebiymius*, or *Ebiymium*, an Egyptian or Coptic word, the name of a place or of the platform of the one who led the singing, II, 58.

Slices of ivory are used for various remedies, II, 331.

Drunkenness and gluttony drain the treasury of souls, I, 617. It is a feature of the Hebrew language to use “drunkenness” for “satiety,” III, 368. “Drunkenness” is taken in a favorable sense, IV, 1072. It is approved in the apostles, 1063. The spiritual drunkenness of priests, ibid. In drunkenness the condition of the mind is overturned, V, 551. Drunkenness is displayed not only in drinking wine but in all things, ibid. The drunkenness of the mind: what is it? VI, 277. “Drunkenness” taken for abundance of things, 160. Drunkenness arises from various causes, VII, 507, 508. Lust is always joined to it, ibid. Its effects, 699. Where there are drunkenness and satiety, there is lust, 700.

A drunkard is described, IV, 335. A drunkard is never chaste, VII, 700. A saying of a not insignificant orator about a drunkard, 509.

The Church is the one mother of all Christians, I, 908. Christ’s Church was founded by shedding blood and by enduring rather than inflicting insults, 519. It grew through persecutions and was crowned by martyrdoms, ibid. The Church was prefigured in the Law, 910. The cherubim migrating from the Temple founded the Lord’s Church, 701. It was founded on Peter with a firm mass, 188. It is shaken neither by the force of a river nor by any storm, ibid. The first Church was gathered from the remnant of Israel, 416. The Church of Christ rising among the nations is signified, 201. What does the Church gathered from the nations deserve to hear? 897. What did the beginnings of the nascent Church demand? 393. Paul instructed the inexperienced Church of Christ and provided for every order, 503. In the one body of the Church there are different members, 264. The Church’s just judgments must by no means be destroyed by irrational clemency, 630. The Church’s brightness polluted by the filth of the Gentiles, 426. It dislikes everything perverse, 936. The Jews, heretics, and Gentiles are foreigners and outside the Church, 425. Jerome’s grief over its condition, 909. The Churches are like standards erected for the Lord’s victories, 209. The flowers and ornaments of the Church are monks and virgins, 208. Why did all the Churches throughout Africa rejoice with a kind of exultation? 986. A very bad custom in certain Churches, 262. The handmaid of Christ must be brought forth not from the nobility of ancient history but from the humility of the Church, 456.

The Church ought to be universal, not established in a corner, II, 186. The tabernacle, a figure of the present and future Church, 186. In the body of the Church, Christ is the head, 713. When certain members resist, the body is not subject to the head, ibid. It was founded on Peter with a firm mass, 707. It is shaken neither by the force of a river nor by any storm, ibid. The diversity of the chambers of Noah’s ark prefigured the variety of the Church, 267. Just as the ark contained every kind of animal, so in the Church there are human beings of every nation and character, 195. The Church’s greatest elements, 885. Lighter commandments were given to the Church while it was still inexperienced, 290. In the Church of God there is simplicity and pure confession, 192. In the one body of the Church there are different members, 711. The Church has become greater in riches and lesser in virtues, 41. One must remain in that Church which was founded by the apostles and continues to this day, 201. The orders of the Church, 369. Its ranks, 195. The Church of believers in Christ was of the kind that monks now strive to be, 847. It is endangered in the world, 195. What adversaries does it have? 398. What should one think about the whole Church? 194, 195. The Church has always had very great and learned men, 823.

The Church: in it there are more herds than people, more sheep than servants, female servants, and slaves, III, 399. Through the negligence of its leaders, the entire height of the Church collapsed, 477. Christ is eaten in the Church alone, IV, 815. Nothing is more beautiful than it, 362. Founded upon a rock, 31. The doors of the Church are continually open to those who desire to be saved, 725. They ought to be engraved with every virtue, 729. In it are the doctrines of truth, 315. And true solemnity, 439. First gathered from the Jews, 1075. Founded in Jerusalem, it scattered Churches throughout the whole world, 33. The people of the nations built Christ’s Church, 725. The Church’s trophies in Egypt, 204. Founded with a firm mass, 750. Multiplied throughout the whole world, 315. From throughout the world the Churches of the Gentiles sent support to the Jews, 710. Those who were once inhabitants of idolatry became tenants of the Church, 640. The Lord’s glory is proclaimed in the Church’s desolation, 481. The leaders of the Churches were taken from the nations, 734. The leaders of the Church know the mysteries of God and the sacraments of the Scriptures, 236. Who are the guardians of the Church? 741. The assembly of presbyters is the senate of the Church, 50. It grows and declines through peace and persecutions, 826. As long as the devil lays waste to the Church, God’s anger is evident, 866. How does the Church of God become a den of robbers? 892. A negligent Church teaches its adversaries how to seize it, 935. God often abandons the Church because of negligence, 725. Christ will abandon his Church because of the impiety increasing day by day, 320. Why are Churches called islands? 540. In it there is fire and a furnace, 425. Blessed is the person who possesses such great merit and virtue that he is called an ornament of the Church, 571. The burden and confusion of ecclesiastical dignities, 229.

The Church contains good and evil people, V, 892. No one outside the Lord’s Church can possess purity, 74. It did the Gentiles and heretics no good to insult the Church during the persecution, 423, 429. How God’s secret is violated in the Church, 76. Images are found in the Church, 205. How one lives in it while content with simple faith, 61. Its leaders are accustomed to oppress the common people, 207. The pride of superiors drives many out of it, 412. It is dangerous to judge the opinions of the Church’s teachers, 682.

The origin of the Church, VI, 772, 793. Redeemed by Christ’s blood, 717. Why it is called “Dove,” ibid. It is joined by the unity of the Spirit, 444. It has its own cities, ibid. It possesses the mystery of the Holy Trinity, 445. It is fortified by the protection of angels, 861. Far better than the synagogue, 758. Why it is handed over to persecutions, 358, 788. Through the Lord’s help peace is restored to the Churches, not through the doctrine of teachers, 900. The Church alone is watered by everlasting rain, 273. In it hope, faith, and charity abound, ibid. It seems blasphemous to say that the Church is given over to evils, 713. Everyone who is saved is saved in the Church, 208. How the judges of the Church abhor judgment, 471. The life and avarice of the Church’s rulers drive many out of it, 750. The Lord does not spare a sinful Church, 713, 714. Which are the chosen Churches? 757.

Churches entrusted to angels, VII, 281. What is the twofold Church? 321. Christ’s Church gathered from a base common crowd, 485. It was barren before Christ’s coming, 472. Its fruitfulness, 474. It has four corners and rings, 1. The Church is understood in two ways, 376. It does not separate the Fathers of the Old Testament from the children of the New, but joins them together, 446. Manifold wisdom in the Church, 595. The Catholic Churches, 197.

The adornment of the Church, I, 240. They are noted, 991. Although they are judged good, they are placed after almsgiving, ibid. Gold and gems in Churches are not approved, 264. Churches are overthrown, 344. Sacred buildings once collapsed into ashes and embers, 965. Many thousands of people were slaughtered in the Churches, 914.

The Church is Christ’s house, IV, 999. It is a house of prayer, 659. Called “the Lord’s house,” 739. In the Churches of the West, wine and milk are given to those reborn in Christ, 644. A learned description of the building of the Church, 634 and following. What is said about it, 719 and following. The Church has many places, 1079. Why new names are imposed on Churches, 745. Abuse of the Church’s goods is noted, 57. Abuse of the property of the Temple and the Church, VII, 242.

Praise of the Roman Church, I, 208. Outside the Roman Church, built upon the rock, there is no salvation, 39. Churches of Christ built in Tyre, IV.

Ecclesiastical men who meditate on the law of God day and night cannot be deceived, I, 1028. The walls and towers are called the Church, 893. Let them move the hard hearts of sinners to weeping by their tears, ibid. Let every ecclesiastical rank be ashamed to purchase estates under the empty titles of monks, 981. It relies upon its own rulers, 943. The ecclesiastical ranks, 260. Ecclesiastical dignity does not make a Christian, 35. The white garment of ecclesiastics, II, 727. The Church, consisting of many ranks, ends with presbyters and bishops, 195. An ecclesiastical soul is better than all souls; if it is not better, it is not ecclesiastical, III, 514. An ecclesiastical man learned in the heavenly Scriptures always desires to learn, 434. What an ecclesiastical teacher ought to be, IV, 55. What works of an ecclesiastical man are involved in bringing back those deceived by heresy? 692. No ecclesiastic possesses as much zeal for the good as heretics do for evil, 286. Ecclesiastics are not secure from the terror of heretics, V, 391. They sin more seriously, 180. Ecclesiastical men, if they sin, will be subjected to the torments of Sodom and Gomorrah, VI, 130. The ecclesiastical ranks in Jerome’s time, VII, 162. They are censured, 728. Who ought to be promoted to the ecclesiastical rank? 694.

The book of Ecclesiasticus, from which we learn to trample underfoot the things of the world, I, 688. The book of Ecclesiasticus offers much concerning the nature of things, 564. Concerning it there is no ambiguity, II, 731. *Ecclesiastes* is called in Greek the one who gathers an assembly, that is, the Church; the Latins call him a preacher, III, 383. The book of Ecclesiasticus deserved authority, according to the judgment of the Hebrews, because of its final chapter, so that it might be included among the divine Books, 496. It is the book of Solomon doing penance, 392. Some wrongly think that we are summoned by this book to pleasure and luxury, 385. He would never have preferred the sadness of mourning to the festivity of a banquet if he had thought that anyone’s drinking and eating were of any importance, 433. It does not summon one to luxury, nor does it collapse into the doctrine of Epicurus, 486.

In ecstasy, no one can freely remain silent or speak, VI, 589.

Eden, the location of paradise, is in the East, III, 199 and 307.

Edessa, II, 43. Edissa, the same city of Coelesyria, III, 320, and VII, 57.

Some boldly explain to others what they do not understand, I, 275.

The Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Editions, II, 893. Where and by whom the Fifth Edition was discovered, ibid. The editions of the Jewish translators were purchased at great expense, 328. The Fathers expounded these, ibid. Origen found the Fifth Edition on the Actian shore and expounded it fully and openly, III, 499. The editions explain one another, IV, 561. The Vulgate translation of the Septuagint differs from the Hebrew truth and from the other editions, 130, 276. It overturns the strongest testimony, 565. The Septuagint edition rejected by the teachers of the Church, V, 645. The Fifth Edition of Scripture, VI, 213. Two editions without the names of their authors, 593. Besides the five editions, Jerome found two concerning the Twelve Prophets, VI, 618. The Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Editions of certain books of Scripture, VII, 735. They acquired authority without the names of their translators, ibid. The Vulgate edition, 95, 514. In what respect the editions agree with Jerome’s opinion, 642. See *Versions*.

Edom is interpreted either as “earthly” or “bloody,” II, 442. Edom, that is, “red” or “ruddy,” III, 346. Edom, Seir, and Esau are one man’s name, 362. Edom is not the name of a place but the name of blood, IV, 747. Edom, ruddy, VI, 364. Why the name Edom was imposed on Esau, ibid. The Jews understand Edom as the Romans and think that their empire was destroyed according to the prophecy of Malachi, 945.

How the education and instruction of children ought to be arranged, I, 680.

The term “outpouring” is taken in both a good and a bad sense, V, 978. “Outpouring” indicates the generosity of a gift, VI, 202 and 902.

The outpouring of the Holy Spirit, I, 834 and following, and VI, 203.

Who does not fear poverty? I, 290. See *Poverty*.

What does it mean for the Lord to go out from his place? IV, 357.

[Col. 0968] Those expelled from the assembly of the brethren because of some sin ought not to resist, V, 195.

Who venerates the tomb of Eleazar, son of Aaron, and where does it lie? I, 702.

Elam, from whom came the Elamite princes of Persia, III, 322.

Elam, a region of Persia beyond Babylon, IV, 1018.

An Elamite brother, from whom Jerome learned about royal hunting, etc., at Babylon, IV, 175.

The elect in Christ existed in earlier ages, before the foundation of the world, III, 329. There is great diversity among the elect, VII, 689.

Electrum, more precious than gold and silver, V, 8 and 812.

How much power and how many rewards almsgiving possesses, I, 397. In almsgiving there is not a diminution of substance but an exchange, ibid. Whatever you take from your possessions for expenses, count as profit, 281. To have practiced almsgiving is a great thing, 501. Alms are preferred to the building of churches, 991. Christ’s substance must not be poured out thoughtlessly, 324. Prudence in giving alms ensures that none of the poor is sent away empty-handed, 707. With the oil of almsgiving let us wash away the filth of sins, 579. Whenever you stretch out your hand, think of Christ, 290. When you give alms, let God alone see it, 110. What must be considered in almsgiving? 290. Many give alms for the sake of vanity, 117. To whom should alms be given? 289, 794. They should be given to individuals not for luxury but for necessity, 324. Give so that necessity may be supported, not so that wealth may be increased, 398. Nothing should be given anyone beyond necessities, ibid. Let the entrails of the hungry praise you, not the wealthy banquets of those who belch, 990. One kind of almsgiving is called hunting, 264. Not everyone who stretches out his hand to the poor immediately lends to God, II, 188. In almsgiving we seek empty glory, 754. Rare is the person who does not give with that intention, ibid. The practice of almsgiving among Hebrews and Christians, 399. To whom alms should chiefly be given, ibid. No one spends more generously than the one who keeps nothing for himself, 21. One should not choose the person to whom to do good, III, 482. Good should be done indiscriminately, and given to everyone who asks, 479. The person who considers whom he should benefit and does not give to everyone who asks often passes by the one who deserves to receive, 481. The person who gives to the needy sows not a grain of seed but the bread itself, awaiting its multiplication in a kind of interest and receiving on the day of judgment much more than he had given, 479. Whatever we can possess beyond food and clothing must be spent on nourishing the poor and giving to the needy, 413. There is nothing good in this life except what makes a person rejoice in his work when he gives alms and prepares future treasures for himself in the kingdom of heaven, 418. Almsgiving is commended, IV, 236. To whom alms should be given, V, 208. Almsgiving should not be done for the sake of the future, ibid. Almsgiving and humility, if they are genuine, are reckoned in place of sacrifices, VI, 65. Not every almsgiving pleases God, 298. What is unfailing almsgiving? VII, 31.

Scholarly elegance, VII, 709.

The elements serve God, I, 1085. There are four elements, from which all things are composed, II, 431. All the elements together rage against those who offend God, IV, 203.

The elements of the Hebrew alphabet, I, 140 and following. The very sound of the letters and the first formation of words are pronounced differently by the mouth of an educated person and by that of a peasant, 990.

The raising of the hand is the posture of one striking, V, 229.

Eleutheropolis, a city of Idumea, IV, 217, and VI, 381 and following.

What is the Eleutheropolitan diocese? I, 518.

At Eleusis it was customary to abstain from certain foods, II, 344. Three precepts in the temple of Eleusis, ibid.

Eleutherus, deacon of Anicetus and later bishop of Rome, II, 863.

Eli the priest: why did he suffer death? VII, 668.

Elijah remained a virgin, I, 102. The same man was taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot by a forty-day fast, 986. He could not go up to heaven with his cloak, 795. He left his *melote* on earth, 947. He is called the prince of monks, 323. Elijah’s little tower on the shore of Sarepta, 695. The apocryphal *Apocalypse of Elijah*, 314. Elijah is interpreted as “the strong one of the Lord,” II, 408. Elijah’s virtue was zeal, 713. Elijah and Elisha were foolishly placed in a catalogue of married men, 275. He was immortal before he died, 348. What did he merit by fasting? 349. He was taken up bodily, 437. Elijah and Enoch are not yet dead, 794. They remain at the same age at which they were taken up, 440. He was not free from fault, 767. The Hebrews are persuaded from apocryphal writings that Phinehas is Elijah, V, 813. Elijah and John: in what are they equal? VII, 70. The Pharisees’ tradition concerning Elijah, 132.

Of two evils, the lesser should be chosen, I, 305. What is expedient should be chosen, IV, 784.

Elimais, the last province of Persia, a region toward the East, V, 722.

The Elissaean islands, islands of the Ionian Sea, V, 306.

[Col. 0969] Elisha was a virgin, I, 104. He turned the oxen and yokes of his former occupation into vows, 433. He is called the leader of monks, 324. Elisha was buried in Samaria, 205. Elisha’s double spirit, II, 370. The mausoleum of the prophet Elisha, VI, 362.

Elizabeth and Zechariah are inferior in holiness to blessed Mary, II, 712.

The most frequent kind of expression, II, 567.

Antony used to say that he had seen no eloquent person but many articulate speakers, II, 783.

Sad eloquence is not eloquence, I, 610. The presses of eloquence should overflow not with the leaves of words but with the expressions of meanings, as with grapes, 935. It is much better to possess holy rusticity than sinful eloquence, 264. The force and precision of eloquence, II, 420. It offers a name for eternity, 319. Eloquence varied with Attic flower, 501. We cannot express everything that we feel, III, 395. Secular eloquence intoxicates, VI, 420. The sources of the rivers of eloquence, 538. Secular eloquence is preferred to the simplicity of the apostles, VII, 483.

ἝΛΛΗΝ signifies both “Greek” and “heathen,” VII, 445.

Elpidius is deceived by the woman Agape, I, 1032.

Elpidius, prefect of the praetorium, II, 18.

Elusa, a half-barbarian city, II, 26.

Eluza, a city situated in the parts of Moab, IV, 186.

Emmaus, or Emaus, was called Nicopolis, I, 695, and II, 903. Emmaus is the same as Nicopolis, V, 612, and VI, 381.

Greater Emath is Antioch; lesser Emath is Epiphania near Edessa, III, 209. The Syrians call Epiphania Emath, IV, 143, and V, 598. There are two Emaths: one great, now called Antioch, and one lesser, called Epiphania, VI, 311, 319. The Jews perform ἐμβολισμούς—intercalations of three months—over eight years, V, 683.

How buying and acquiring differ, II, 537. What is meant by buying and redeeming? VII, 434.

How the sending forth of God’s hand differs from its extension, V, 168.

Empedocles, I, 528. The same Empedocles, II, 575, 567. His doctrine, 331.

All purchasing returned to the seller in the fiftieth year, according to Hebrew custom, V, 69. Custom in purchases, IV, 1084.

From where is the term *Encaenia* derived? I, 62.

The flight of Enceladus, IV, 361.

From where were the Encratites so called? II, 869. Their error, 274. Tatian, the leader of the Encratites, VI, 180. The same, 247.

Ennius, I, 21. His opinion, 342. An Ennian saying, 784.

Engada, a Jewish village from which balsam was brought, III, 206.

Engaddi, fertile in palms and balsam, III, 328. What Engaddi and Engallim are and signify, V, 591.

Why was Enoch translated? II, 266. He was translated in the flesh, 437. Enoch and Elijah are not yet dead, 794. They are also inhabitants of paradise, 437. What food do they eat? ibid. The apocryphal book of Enoch, 833. The apostle Jude took his testimony from it, ibid. Enoch and Elijah taken up into heaven, VI, 347, 813. The apocryphal book of Enoch, VII, 708. The apostle Jude took testimony from it, ibid.

The hope of Enos is praised, VII, 426.

Entellus and Dares are mentioned, I, 633, 729.

The story of Epaphra, VII, 762.

What is an *ependytes*? I, 363 and following.

The *epha*, or *ephi*, is a tenth of a *cor*, a kind of measure for dry goods, IV, 75. What are the ephi, bathus, cor, shekel, mina, or *mna*? V, 563.

The ephod, a priestly garment, VI, 32. The ephod is either simple and common also to other men, or more ornate and peculiar to priests alone, I, 361 and following.

What is the ephod *bad*? I, 140 and following, and 363 and following.

The Ephesians’ love for Paul, VII, 541. The great consolation of the Ephesians and Colossians, 682. The good and evil angel of the Ephesians, 281.

Ephesus, the metropolis of Asia, VII, 541. Its idolatry and magical arts, ibid. What does it signify? 633.

The writings of Saint Ephrem were read in certain churches, II, 943. He is praised, ibid.

Scripture testifies that Ephraim is a type of the nations, IV, 1062.

Ephratha is interpreted as “fruitful,” I, 343. Ephratha and Bethlehem are names of the same city, III, 360. Ephratha, the region of Bethlehem, is in the tribe of Judah, not in the tribe of Benjamin, 202. Ephratha is also called Bethlehem, VI, 385.

The Epicureans despise logic, II, 487. The Epicureans, VII, 737.

Epicurus, I, 241. Epicurus, an advocate of pleasure, recalls people from marriage, II, 317. What does he teach concerning foods? 340. Epicurus’ condemned opinion, 333. Luxury, 387. Epicurus, 241, 463, 558. Epicurus asserted that through innumerable cycles the same things were made in the same places and by the same agents, III, 391. Epicurus’ opinion, IV, 474, 788.

Epidaurus, a town of Dalmatia, II, 35. What does it proclaim to this day? 36.

The poet Epimenides is cited by Paul, I, 424. We are said to be sleeping the sleep of Epimenides, 153. Epimenides, VII, 647, 648. His heroic verse, 471. It is approved by the Apostle, 416, 706. Why does Paul call him a prophet? ibid. He wrote a book entitled *Oracles*, ibid.

“Epiphanes” was the surname of Antiochus, the most cruel tyrant, V, 598.

Epiphania is the name of a city among the Syrians, formerly called Emath, IV, 143. It received its name from Antiochus Epiphanes, V, 598.

Epiphania of Syria was formerly Deblatha, V, 62.

The day of Epiphany was venerable in Jerome’s time, V, 6.

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, shone among the bishops as a distinguished star in the world, I, 757. The necessity of the Church drew Epiphanius to Rome, 955. There he was received as a guest by Paula, 693. What did he try to persuade Paula’s mother to do? 714. Epiphanius detained Paula for ten days, 695. Through love for her he had brought many people to himself, ibid. Where is the old monastery called Saint Epiphanius situated? 518. Epiphanius’ letters to John the bishop, 241. Epiphanius, a distinguished priest of the Church, knew five languages, II, 416, 537. He is called the father of bishops and a relic of ancient holiness, 419. Epiphanius’ patience, 420. His prudence, 450. His humility and charity toward John of Jerusalem, 414. Epiphanius, by approving John of Jerusalem’s words, clears himself of suspicion of heresy, 418. The people’s veneration for Epiphanius, ibid. He is praised, 411. He came to Jerusalem, 561. Jerome’s letters to him, ibid. Where did he receive Jerome? 551. Epiphanius, speaking against Origen, is mocked by some, 417. Epiphanius injured by Rufinus, 552. What is he accused of? 504. Letters against Epiphanius, 545. He wrote praises of Hilarion, 13. Certain words of Epiphanius are reported, 553. One of his letters was stolen, ibid. Epiphanius was read both for his subject matter and for his words, 951. Several letters of his: to whom were they written? 434. Epiphanius’ letter to Siricius, 421. Against Origen, 468. Epiphanius and Pliny the Younger wrote about the nature of stones and gems, IV, 637. The same men, V, 334. Both are praised, ibid.

Epirus, part of Acroceraunia, I, 344.

The episcopate is a task, not a dignity; labor, not luxury, I, 422. According to the terminology of honors, the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate, 780. There is no difference in the episcopate, 1083.

Bishops occupy the place of the apostles, I, 189. They act in the stead of Peter and Paul, 36. Let them know that they are fathers, not masters, 521. Let bishops take the apostles as their example, 323. Possessing their honor, let them strive to possess their merit also, ibid. What Aaron and his sons were, that are the bishop and presbyters, 262. From where the name “bishop” is derived, 1081 and following. As Paul’s imitator, let him serve the salvation of all impartially, 520. He is a father, not a master, 262. Let him honor priests and clerics, ibid. Let him diminish through humility, not swell with eminence, 422. Bishops must drive away the rage of wolves by the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s staff, 659. The glory of a bishop is to provide for the poverty of the poor, 262. How his ordination was carried out, and who was chosen, 1081. Bishops or presbyters are commanded to be monogamous when chosen for the clergy, 415. Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are chosen either as virgins, widowers, or men chaste after entering the priesthood, 233. A man who has had luxurious and disobedient sons cannot become a bishop, 683. Letters were written to ordained bishops, and ecclesiastical letters were received from them, 756. Everyone’s eyes are directed toward him, 342. His household and conduct are a teacher of public discipline, ibid. In the description of a bishop’s virtues, he is set forth as a mirror of the priesthood, 658. Not all bishops are bishops, 35. Individual bishops of the churches, 942. Their transfers are prohibited, 417. What difference exists among them, 262 and following. Among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same, 415. The former name denotes dignity, the latter age, ibid. The difference between a bishop and a king, 342. One must fear lest a bishop, instead of being a minister, perish incurably as an ὀπισθότονος—“one pulled backward” or “strained backward” [term uncertain], 1093. Ordained bishops, 756. Ordained bishops are announced, 609. The savagery of peoples toward bishops and matrons, 345. God wishes bishops and presbyters to be such as Paul teaches, II, 717. They are not therefore to be rejected if they are blameworthy in certain matters, ibid. and following. Virtue alone makes bishops and presbyters blessed, not dignity, 293. What is fitting for them? 718 and following. It belongs to a bishop to lay hands upon the baptized, 181. Why such laying on of hands is reserved to him, ibid. It is reserved rather for the honor of the priesthood than by a law of necessity, 181. The bishop is the light of the Church, 175. He is the seasoning of the whole world and of his own Church, 174. He is appointed in the Church so that he may restrain the people from error, 176. The zeal and love of peoples toward bishops, even to the point of almost killing those who depose them, II, 192. A bishop should not shine only for himself but benefit everyone, ibid. It does him no good to enjoy the consciousness of virtues unless he can instruct the people entrusted to him, 292. What his chastity ought to be, ibid. It is not enough for a bishop to possess chastity himself unless the chastity of his sons, companions, and ministers adorns him, 718. Let him fear incurring the punishment of Eli the priest, ibid. There is no bishop, or hardly one, who possesses everything he is taught to possess, 719. If one or two items from the catalogue of virtues are lacking in him, he will not for that reason lack the title of righteous, ibid. If a bishop falls, he obtains pardon with difficulty, 175. Then he is of no benefit to the people, 176. Bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not names of merits but of offices, 292. What is fitting for them? ibid. What bishop, conscious of his own goodness, tolerates being deposed? 192. Jerome does not judge the decisions of bishops, nor does he desire their decrees to be rescinded, 546. When he is called a disciple of Antichrist, 176. When a bishop returning from heresy is received, the whole province over which he presides is joined to the Church, 174. Bishops who do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives, 388. Deceived by others, 189 and following. Accusation against a bishop is difficult: for if he has sinned, he is not believed; and if he has been convicted, he is not punished, III, 454. The dignity and visitation of bishops: in what do they consist? IV, 728. The distinction between bishops and presbyters, 56. Let bishops, presbyters, and deacons understand what is said, 987, 988. Bishops and the entire ecclesiastical order are forbidden to introduce into the Church those uncircumcised in heart and flesh, V, 541, 542. Their arrogance and vices are condemned, 410. The office and duties of bishops, VI, 72. Let them act carefully lest they violate holy things, ibid. It is not dignity but work that saves them, ibid. What are the virtues of bishops? 760, 761. Let them possess knowledge so that they may instruct others, ibid. Let them learn from laymen what they do not know, ibid. Reading the Scriptures is commended in them, ibid. The episcopal name will be taken away without the work, 680. What bishop should be chosen? VII, 698. What is required in a bishop? 696 and following. Let him be learned and of holy life, 703. His words should be the rule of truth, ibid. What innocence and chastity are required of him, 696, 702. How far the bishop’s justice differs from that of a layman, 703. Let him not be proud but a good steward, 699. Let him live from the altar, not become rich, 701. His house should be common, ibid. The people are not the bishop’s slaves but fellow servants, 699. Presbyters and bishops were ordained by the apostles throughout the individual provinces, 207. From where and why is he established in the Church? 694. They are greater than presbyters only by the custom of the Church, not otherwise, ibid. and 696. They offer unblemished sacrifices daily, 702. In conduct and speech they should surpass the whole people, 728. Bishops and presbyters are servants of their own servants, 653. Let bishops who have the power to establish presbyters listen, 694. Let them not confer the ecclesiastical rank on blood but on life and merits, ibid. Very many who act otherwise are condemned, 695. Bishops and presbyters assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, 125. It is their duty to pass judgment on the truth of sins, ibid. The arrogance of bishops, 458. Let them learn humility from the Apostle, ibid. Their pride is brought low, 598. Laymen as judges of bishops, 70. Their envy of holy laymen, ibid. Why are fathers prevented from the episcopate because of their sons’ vices? 698. Let bishops and presbyters who educate their sons in secular letters read this, 666. See *Prelate, Pontiff, Presbyter, Priest*.

The bishops of the East and West were summoned to Rome because of certain dissensions among the churches, I, 693. Imperial letters compelled the bishops to come to Rome, ibid. African bishops assembled for ecclesiastical matters, II, 417. Exiles return to the churches through Julian’s clemency, 191. Bishops received by some into their former rank after blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, VII, 81.

A letter reserved for slander, I, 524. Love letters, 828.

The apostles’ letters are mystical and concise, I, 280. They are both brief and long, ibid. Rare is the person who does not stumble in reading them, ibid. The whole of the Apostles’ Letters resounds with the grace of Christ, 412. The Catholic Epistle of blessed Peter is noted, IV, 841. Jerome calls the Second Epistle of blessed Peter canonical, 779. The Epistle of blessed Barnabas is among the apocryphal Scriptures, 531. The Apostolic Epistles explain the ancient law, VI, 763.

The Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Romans: to whom and why was it written? VII, 478. It contains nothing contrary to the Epistle to the Galatians, ibid. and 479. The Epistle to the Galatians was subscribed by Paul’s hand but written by another, 529. The Epistles to the Galatians and to the Romans have the same subject matter, 369. A certain distinction between the two is noted, ibid. In them are contained the ending of the ancient law and the introduction of the new, 390. The Epistle to the Ephesians is obscure above all others, 622. It is called intermediate, 539. In mysteries it surpasses the others, 588, 633. From where was the Epistle to Titus written? ibid. Some reject the Epistle to Philemon, 741, 742. They are refuted, ibid. In what sense Paul’s Epistles are “great” in writing, 530. Some were written at a particular time, 752, [Col. 0972] 747. Why did Paul sign the Epistles with his own hand? 530. Epistles sent under Paul’s name, 529, 530.

The Epistle to the Hebrews is placed outside the number by most people, I, 280. To whom is the Epistle to the Hebrews attributed? II, 837. It was not held among the Romans, 899. The Epistle to the Hebrews was not accepted by the Latins, IV, 91. Why it is contradicted and doubtful, 97. It is not received among the canonical Scriptures, 125. The Epistle of blessed Paul to the Hebrews: why it is contradicted and doubtful, V, 335. The Epistle to the Hebrews was not accepted by everyone, VI, 838. Its author is unknown, 339. Both Epistles of Paul to Timothy, the Epistle to the Hebrews, and the Epistle to Titus are rejected by certain heretics, VII, 685. The Epistle to the Hebrews was not accepted by everyone, 583. The Latins doubt concerning it, 213. It is received among the ecclesiastical writings, 714.

Paul’s Epistle to the Laodiceans is rejected by everyone, II, 839. Paul’s letters to Seneca and Seneca’s to Paul, 851.

The commendatory letters of bishops, I, 1094. Letters make absent people present, 21. The more unexpected they are, the fuller they are of joys, 430. The letters of Biblina, II, 754. Some directed letters to the whole world in order to defame those whom they hated, IV, 1001.

An epitaph is properly inscribed for the dead, I, 738.

With colder banquets the heat of the body must be moderated, I, 288. The abundance of banquets weakens body and soul, II, 341. Wars and the destruction of cities are provoked by the delights of banquets, 340. See *Food*.

The province of Judaea did not possess herds of mares, IV, 385 and following.

The running of horses is made swifter by public favor, I, 977.

Circus horses were bred to celebrate the fortunate rape of the Sabine women, II, 22.

The Jewish people lacked knowledge of riding, IV, 455.

The army of the regions of Persia and Chaldaea rejoices in cavalry, IV, 926.

Praise of the eremitical life, I, 29 and following.

What do hypocritical hermits pretend among the uneducated? I, 938.

What Jerome saw in the Syrian desert, II, 5. The desert of Chalcis, 42.

The desert rejoices in being more closely attached to God, I, 36. To walk through paradise in the mind sweetens the desolation of the desert, 37. It loves the naked, 29. The vastest desert stretches from India to Mauretania, IV, 218. See *Solitude*.

Erichthonius was generated solely from the heat of lust, II, 247.

What kind of animal is the hedgehog? I, 984 and 985.

Why did Eriphyle betray her husband? II, 317.

The three kinds of Herodion, VI, 819.

What is the difference between error and crime? I, 305. To err is human, and to confess error is the mark of the prudent, 317. There is no error that cannot be caught, II, 748. It is human nature to defend one’s error, 191. How great is the error among the people when the very person who teaches is himself in error, 176. The errors of old men and children, IV, 206. Some fall through a pious error, 442. The error of many in reading the Epistle to the Romans, 707. The error of Latins and Greeks, 532. The danger of error must be avoided, VII, 516. The error of scribes corrected by Jerome, 95. See *Crime, Sin*.

The nature of the caterpillar, VI, 275. It is the extremity of all punishments, ibid. The caterpillar, locust, *brúchus*, and rust are expounded spiritually, 171, 172. Which peoples are designated under the names of the caterpillar, locust, *brúchus*, and rust? 170.

We ought to instruct others, V, 416.

The person who shuns the glory of learning is considered the most learned, I, 336. The learned man who has been instructed in the Scriptures finds that, the more he begins to know, the greater obscurity arises for him in them, III, 446. A learned man often lies hidden in obscurity and suffers persecutions, while the foolish gain the favor of the crowd, 465. The learned ought to bring forth the word of doctrine and ought not to be hindered, VI, 247. A learned man who spoke a ridiculous thing, VII, 530.

We ought to be content with the judgment of the learned, I, 400.

Isaiah begins with the letter I among the Hebrews, III, 101. See *Isaiah*.

Why did Esau degenerate? II, 428. Esau, because he was hairy, was called Seir, III, 267. Edom, however—that is, ruddy or tawny—because he sold his birthright for red food, 346. Esau and Elijah were hairy men, V, 416. The etymologies of the names of Esau, 291. Why is Esau so called? VI, 246, 364. Esau and Jacob are figures of the Jews and the Christian people, 235.

Esbus, a notable city of Arabia: by whom was it possessed? III, 202.

Escol is translated as “cluster of grapes,” I, 700.

Ezra and Nehemiah, I, 279. What the book of Ezra contains, 274. Ezra, restorer of the Pentateuch, II, 212. An apocryphal book is presented under the name of Ezra, 393.

To be. We do not belong to the one from whom we are born but to the one from whom we are reborn, who redeemed us at a great price with his blood, I, 284. It is one thing to be able to be, another to be, II, 701. Everything that is said to be or not to be must be counted among good or evil things, 699. It is better not to exist at all and not to possess the sense of substance than unhappily either to exist or to live, III, 419. Not to exist is better than to live amid punishments, IV, 982. Let us now begin to be what we shall be, VII, 659.

A gilded *essedum*, II, 313.

The Essenes are said to have observed the way of life of coenobites, I, 120. The life of the Essenes, II, 343.

Esther, as a type of the Church, frees the people from danger, I, 279. The subject of her book, ibid. After Haman was killed, she sent the portions of the banquet and the festival day to posterity, ibid. How Esther corrected the sentence of Artaxerxes, II, 474. Esther and Judith, a type of the Church, VI, 671. The history of Esther related to Artaxerxes, 784.

Esychius, a former consul, was condemned to death, I, 306.

The Etesian winds, II, 551.

What does Etham mean? I, 471.

The heathen prefer error and custom to truth, I, 625. How they blaspheme the invisible God, ibid. What were the heathen before the faith of Christ? IV, 277. The heathen receive a reward if they have done anything good, V, 353.

The Etruscan Sea, I, 462.

False etymologies of names must not be fabricated, IV, 300, and V, 319.

Eubulus, I, 535. Eubulus wrote a history of Mithras, II, 344.

The sacrament of the Eucharist is noted, I, 570. The mystery of the blood and body of Christ dedicated by Melchizedek, 200. Bread and wine in the sacrament of the Eucharist are sanctified through the invocation and coming of the Holy Spirit, 595. What does the sacrament of the Lord’s blood signify? 257. To whom the consecration of Christ’s body and blood belongs, 1081. Whether it should be received daily: see what the law says, 434. To receive the body of Christ is greater than to pray, 227. Delaying communion of Christ’s body does not make one holier, ibid. To receive the Eucharist always without our condemnation and without a pricking conscience is a thing to be desired, 434. Whoever approaches the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood, 35. The Roman Church and the churches of Spain are said to fast on Saturday and to receive the Eucharist daily, 434. What is reported concerning the Romans regarding communion in Christ’s body, 227. Whatever pertains to the preparation of the Lord’s body and blood is to be venerated with the same majesty as his body and blood, 759. The Lord’s body in the Eucharist in the Church, II, 191. Bishops handled it, 173. It was administered to the people from an elevated place, ibid. The hand was extended to receive the Eucharist, 508. Those receiving Christ’s body answered, “Amen,” ibid. The reception of Christ’s body, 800. The pure ought to receive it, 269. We receive it equally, although according to the merits of the recipients it is different, 364. The first communion of Christ’s body after baptism, 800. The Lord’s Eucharist must be received with caution, 734. The only good we possess in the present age is to feed upon the Lord’s flesh and drink his blood, not only in the mystery but also in the reading of the Scriptures, III, 413. In the sacrament of the Eucharist the truth and reality of Christ’s body and blood are affirmed, VII, 216. Christ’s body in the Eucharist is true and substantial, 702. It does not benefit the polluted, 711. Whoever hastens to reach the desired dwelling without the heavenly Bread is in danger, 116.

What is reported concerning the tyrant Eugenius, I, 344.

The Eumenides, or Furies: why were they so called? I, 187.

Eunomius, II, 508. He is the author of a heresy against relics, 395. His followers do not enter the basilicas of the apostles and martyrs, and they consider his books more authoritative than the Gospels, ibid. Eunomius’ doctrine concerning Christ, 512. What answer is made to him? 985. His doctrine, 507. The godless (ἀθέου) heresy of Eunomius, 416. Eunomius the leper, IV, 775. Eunomius, V, 380. The same man refuted, VI, 267. Eunomius and Eutyches, the bars of Arius, 229. Eunomius, VII, 737. His doctrine, 610. He arrogantly claims knowledge for himself, 74. He is called a serpent, 724.

The heresy of the Eunomians and Arians possessed the whole East, II, 411. The Eunomians, VI, 262.

Eunuchs do not diminish the courage of men, I, 687. Those eunuchs please God whom not necessity but will has castrated, II, 257. Who is a type of voluntary eunuchs? ibid. Eunuchs were overseers and priests of Heliopolis, III, 367. The eunuch of the New Law, guardian of the Sabbaths, IV, 657 and 658. The eunuchs who please God, VI, 674, 675. The threefold kind of eunuchs, VII, 146, 147.

The eunuch of Queen Candace, through Isaiah’s prophetic reading, is prepared for baptism, I, 420. Some things concerning him are reported, 274, 275. He was a lover of the law and of divine knowledge, ibid. In the desert he found more at the Church’s spring than in the gilded temple of the synagogue, ibid. The Ethiopian eunuch, prefiguring the peoples of the nations, changed his skin, 800. While rereading the Old Testament, he found the spring of the Gospels, [Col. 0974] ibid. The eunuch of Queen Candace obtained the name of “man” because of the strength of his faith, II, 257. The eunuch of Queen Candace was baptized in a spring near Bethzur, or Bethsoron, III, 175. The eunuch of Queen Candace: the Apostle was sent to the Ethiopian nation, IV, 617, 656.

Euphorbus is said to have been reborn, II, 388. Euphorbius, 566.

The Euphrates River, I, 345. The Euphrates, a river of Mesopotamia, rises in paradise, III, 201. According to Sallustius, the most reliable authority, it has its source in Armenia, ibid. The Euphrates is called a river within the boundaries of Judaea and a torrent within the borders of Egypt, IV, 368.

Euphra, II, 912.

Euphranor, II, 911.

What did Eupolemus the Jew write? II, 879.

What does Euripides report? II, 344. The tragedies of Euripides are curses against women, 317.

The pleasantness of the straits, I, 11.

Europe and Asia fought in a ten-year war, II, 317.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, I, 429. That he was an Arian, no one doubts; 1031. He composed an ecclesiastical history, 523. He was the most outspoken defender of Arius’s impiety, ibid. When Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Chronicle* was translated into Latin, 369. He interpreted the Psalms, 753. How many volumes did he compose against the same man? 427. He was a defender of Origen, 531. He strives to prove that Origen was a Catholic, 532. In his work he proves him to have held Arian doctrine, ibid. Eusebius, 223, 232, 236. Condemned, 1030. Eusebius, promising a historical exposition of Isaiah by its title, sometimes forgets his purpose, etc., IV, 168. Likewise, 170. He is criticized, 199, 220 and following. According to the historical explanation, he published fifteen volumes on Isaiah, 6. How Eusebius of Caesarea interpreted the seventy weeks, V, 687 and following. His confession concerning the histories of Susanna and Bel and the Dragon, 619. Eusebius’s book in defense of Origen, translated by Rufinus under the name of the martyr Pamphilus, 207. Eusebius of Caesarea wrote about the discrepancy among the Gospels, VII, 11. Three volumes of the same author, 195.

Eusebius of Cremona: what does he ask of Jerome? I, 306. He was ignorant of the Greek language, ibid. Eusebius of Cremona, II, 553, 561. He is sent to the West, 554. What does Eusebius’s letter contain? 418. A monk stole the letter from Eusebius’s bedroom, 534. The same Eusebius is defended, ibid. Eusebius of Cremona, VII, 3.

Eusebius of Emesa, I, 429. His commentaries, 739. Eusebius of Emesa, II, 927. Eusebius of Emesa wrote on the Apostle, VII, 369.

Eusebius of Vercelli translated Eusebius of Caesarea and Origen, I, 753. He translated the commentaries of a heretical man, 348. Eusebius of Vercelli returns from exile to Italy, II, 191. Eusebius of Vercelli, 194.

Saint Eusebius the brother, I, 21, 350, 1067. He doubles the grace, 281.

Eusebius, Jerome’s father, II, 953.

Eustathius of Antioch, bishop, I, 39. Sons are falsely attributed to Eustathius, II, 569. Where he was an exile and was buried, 923.

Eustathius of Sebaste, II, 927.

Eustochium, the first noble virgin of the city of Rome, I, 99. Her still tender age and inexperienced infancy, 184. The devil rages against her, ibid. Where Eustochium was brought up, 954. Her life is proposed for imitation, 689. Her speech, walk, and dress are a lesson in the virtues, ibid. Fortitude is praised in Eustochium, 394. She gathers the flowers of virginity, ibid. Her praises and virtues, 290. The humility of Eustochium and her mother Paula, 111. Who were her mothers? 125. She is called a virgin and a devoted daughter of Christ, 691. The life of her mother Paula is composed for her consolation, ibid. She is left far removed from noble birth, but rich in faith and grace alone, ibid. She was called Julia: why? 692. Eustochium is the precious jewel of virginity and the Church in the Holy Places, ibid. She was the companion of her mother’s purpose and pilgrimage, 694. How great were her virtues? 720. Eustochium’s constant devotion to her mother is demonstrated, 721. After her mother’s death she cannot be drawn away, 723. Eustochium accepts no consolation for her mother’s falling asleep, 616. Eustochium’s death is a cause of grief for Jerome, 163. When the book to Eustochium on virginity was written, 269. It is cited, 230. Eustochium, the unique example of nobility and virginity, IV, 535. Commentaries on Ezekiel dedicated to Eustochium, V, 2, etc.

Eutychius, II, 411.

Euthymius condemned, I, 1030.

The Euxine Sea, I, 3.

Euzonius, presbyter of Caesarea, I, 441.

Euzoius, a deacon and later, under Theodosius, bishop of Antioch, II, 192.

Eve is the one mother of all the living, I, 908. In paradise she was a virgin, 102. Through food she was expelled from paradise, 986. Eve as a type of the Church, II, 427. Eve is transferred into life, III, 310. She is called the mother of the living, ibid. Eve’s formation from Adam’s rib, VI, 349.

Evagrius, a presbyter known to Damasus, I, 142. He sent letters to Jerome, 18. His affection for him, ibid. The praises of Evagrius, 7. Evagrius, 10, 14, 16.

Evagrius of Pontus condemned, I, 1030. He wrote much, ibid. His book and sayings *περὶ ἀπαθείας* (*On Impassibility*), ibid. The impious opinion of Evagrius the Iberite, II, 693.

We have received the enduring grace of the Gospel in place of the grace of the Law, which has passed away, I, 748. We fear laws and despise the Gospels, as though the decrees of emperors were greater than those of Christ, 262. At the flashes of the Gospel every human understanding grows dull, 961. The Gospels should never be laid down from one’s hands, 788. It was contrary to the truth of the Gospel to think that believers could not be saved without the ancient sacraments, 765. What does the quadrangular vessel of the Gospels teach? 933. The Gospel did not exist before Christ’s cross, II, 277. It is consecrated by his Passion and Blood, ibid. It is preferred to the Law, 283. And why must it be preferred? 729. The grace of the Gospel succeeded because no one could be justified in the Law, 797. It is one thing to live under the Law and another in the Gospel, 274. The shadow is in the Law, the truth in the Gospel, 728. In the Law there is the wisdom of the flesh, in the Gospel the wisdom of the spirit, 283. We served Adam in the Law; let us serve Christ in the Gospel, 298. If ignorance is condemned under the Law, how much more conscience under the Gospel, 734. The heretics who tore the Gospels apart, 197. These words of the Gospel are explained: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle,” etc., 663. What is written at the end of the Gospel according to Mark in the Greek manuscripts? 758. What is found in the Greek and Latin texts according to Luke? 760. With the languages of believers divided, the whole world has been filled with the preaching of the Gospel, III, 139. The perfection of the Gospel, IV, 690, 918. Its truth is preferred to the shadow of the Law, 20, 801. The Gospel discourse, abbreviated, gave the briefest commandment of charity and faith, 149, 411. The seedbed of the Gospel proceeded from the fountains of Israel, 167. The Savior first preached the Gospel in the regions of the two tribes, 129. Apostolic men are commanded to leave Jerusalem and preach the Gospel throughout the whole world, 611. Its progress is expounded, 279. The preaching of the Gospel crushes the hostile powers, 500. The transformation of evils into good through the preaching of the Gospel, 796. The Savior’s fountains are evangelical teaching, 166. The Law is in the Gospel, and the Gospel is born from the Law, V, 511. The Gospels are joined to one another and cling mutually to one another, 13. There is nothing in them that does not shine, 18. In the Gospel there is an increase of virtue beyond the Law, 210. The Gospel discourse abbreviated, 364. Whoever observes the Law while violating the Gospel violates the name of God, 243. In the Gospel God cleanses those whom, as sinners under the Law, he had left unclean, 218. Only four ought to be accepted, VII, 3. They do not disagree, 28. The distinction between the Gospel and the Law, 30 and 74. In the Gospel the Law and the Prophets are recapitulated, 130. The Gospel is not in the words of the Scriptures but in their meaning, 386. In the words of the Gospel the spirit is always joined to the letter, 104. How the grace of the Gospel is easier than the grace of the Law, 74. One must pass from faith in the Law to faith in the Gospel, 753. Everything is recapitulated in the Gospel, 25. What its preaching accomplishes, 486 and 487. The Law is diminished and destroyed by the preaching of the Gospel, 454. It is called an axe, 18. Rare is the person who announces the Gospel with confidence, 682. Jerome’s opinion concerning the preaching of the Gospel, 194. Evangelical truth does not accept an oath, 30. The distinction between receiving the Gospel and learning it, 387. What those who wrote against the Gospels suspect, 236. The word of the Gospel is expressed more fully in Greek than in Latin, 727. What is read in the true copies of the Gospel, 168. What is discerned in the Gospel, 247. The four Gospels were selected from many and handed down to the churches, 247.

The Gospel according to the Hebrews, written in the Chaldaic-Syriac language but in Hebrew letters, II, 782. The Nazarenes use it, and some passages from it are reported, ibid. It is kept in the Caesarean Library, ibid. Jerome translated the Hebrew Gospel into Greek and Latin, 831. Origen frequently uses it, ibid. Certain passages from it are cited, ibid. The Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes, IV, 156, 485, and V, 158. The Gospel of Matthew written in Hebrew, VI, 123. The Gospel according to the Hebrews translated by Jerome, 520. Many people wrote Gospels, VII, 1. These became the beginnings of various heresies, ibid. False works were published by certain persons, ibid. The Gospel of the Nazarenes and Ebionites translated by Jerome, 77. A new reading is found in it, ibid. It is called by many the authentic Gospel of Matthew, ibid. What the Gospel of the Hebrews contains, 172, 236, 641. The Gospel according to the Egyptians, 248. The Gospel according to the apostles Thomas and Matthias, ibid. Many Gospels were written by many people, ibid. When the Gospel began to be preached, 313.

The four Evangelists, the Lord’s chariot and the true Cherub, [Col. 0976] I, 280. They hold one another and are mutually intertwined, ibid. Like a wheel, they revolve throughout the whole and go wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit leads them, ibid. What the Evangelists did in the sacred volumes, 310 and following. Why four living creatures are assigned to the Evangelists, II, 280. The four Evangelists, VII, 3. Why are forms of living creatures assigned to them? ibid. The harsh condition of the Evangelists, 65.

Evangelus, a presbyter, I, 442 and 1080.

The Hebrews gave names to things from their outcome, IV, 740.

Havilah, where the purest gold and the most precious gems—carbuncle and emerald—are born, III, 199.

A story is told about Evil-merodach, IV, 178. Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, V, 651.

Jerome greets Exodius [Exodium], I, 1066.

Who are “our exactors”? VII, 457.

“To answer [a prayer].” Why does God not always answer? VI, 591. It is beneficial for those who pray contrary to what is right, or who do not understand what is beneficial, not to be heard, 951 and following.

High and pleasant places are dedicated to idols, IV, 849. The irreligion of high places and sacred groves, VI, 40.

High places stand more dangerously, V, 645.

The exiles of Iberia, I, 1093. “Through an exile,” etc., I, 17.

Excommunication is not easily to be endured, I, 726.

An excuse is the companion of negligence, I, 23. Empty excuses must not be sought, nor opportunity given to the flesh for sinning, as though under compulsion we did what we do not wish to do, III, 428, 429.

Who are called “the shaken” in the Psalm? I, 155. The sons of the shaken, 156. It is necessary that individuals excel in certain things, II, 714.

To possess all copies of the Scriptures requires great expense and infinite difficulty, II, 524. The whole world conflicts within itself through the threefold variety of the copies of Scripture, ibid.

Latin and Greek copies confused through error, VII, 487.

An example is never taken from evil things, VI, 799. An example not to be imitated, 935. An example drawn from a ship’s pilot, 624. Example accomplishes more than words, VII, 720.

How powerfully an example from the sacred Scriptures strikes, VI, 868.

Monastic exercises, II, 712. The time occupied in devout exercises will seem short, 686. For those who labor and devote themselves to devout exercises, the days are never long, 991. The exercises and clothing of a woman converted to God, 275.

In a great army the signal of one man is awaited, I, 942. What armies consist of, II, 291, 293. The commanders of armies are called *archimagi* in Scripture—that is, chiefs of cooks, III, 364. What commanders of armies usually do in the assault of cities, VII, 670.

Exodus contains the ten plagues together with the Decalogue and mystical and divine precepts, I, 276. It is applied to the mysteries of the New Testament, ibid. and following.

The spies carried a cluster of enormous size as testimony to the fertility of the land and as a type of the Lord, I, 700. The spies of the Holy Land were geometers, V, 523.

A person converted from his sins must not investigate, V, 110.

A beautiful exposition of the words, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” IV, 751. Various expositions are described, 497. The expositions of Jews and others, 1065. The tricks of false interpretation must be avoided, 974. A false exposition, even when made with a good intention, 960. A heretical exposition is refuted, 654. A certain person’s ridiculous exposition is rejected, V, 323. Certain other interpretations are not approved, 218. A false exposition is not accepted in the Church, 640. A certain preacher’s exposition was not approved by Jerome, VII, 648. The various views of authors are noted, 544. An absurd meaning in the exposition of a certain scriptural passage, 629. Moral precepts require a prudent exposition, 681. See *Interpretation*.

The names of the interpreters are discreetly omitted, II, 480.

The faults of copyists, VII, 571.

The pomp of funerals among the Roman nobility, I, 177.

What does “to exterminate” mean? VII, 31.

The extension of the hand as the gesture of one striking, VI, 678. How do the extension of God’s hand and its sending forth differ? V, 268.

Some things are external and others internal, I, 792. What clings externally is easily cast off, 402.

Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, imitator of the widow of Zarephath, I, 956. While hungry he feeds others, and with a face pale from fasts he is tormented by another’s hunger, ibid. He distributed all his property to the poor, ibid. He carried the body of Christ in a wicker basket and the blood in a glass vessel, ibid. He drove avarice from the temple, etc., ibid. He is proposed for imitation, ibid. Toulouse is not destroyed through the merits of Saint Exuperius, 913. He is praised, 229.

Hezekiah, by doing penance, destroyed the Assyrians, I, 34 [Col. 0977]. He is terrified by approaching death, 174. Hezekiah is called God’s leader, II, 755. He is accused of unbelief, ibid. From where does he possess the name “just”? ibid. Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem in the twelfth year of Romulus, the founder of Rome, IV, 9. The humility and prudence of this king, 459. The cause of his weeping, 468. Why he was left to temptation, 476. The Hebrews report the cause of his illness, 478. What Isaiah does to heal Hezekiah, 467. His health is restored through harmful and adverse things, 476. The steps of Hezekiah’s house are shown in the Temple, 468.

Ezekiel, as a type of fornication-practicing Jerusalem, cuts off his hair, I, 427. He devours a book written inside and out, with lamentation, mourning, and woe, 891. These matters are explained, ibid. Why Ezekiel’s wife dies, 909. The difficult exposition of the same prophet, 449. Ezekiel has his beginning and end wrapped in obscurities, 279. These sections were not read among the Hebrews before the age of thirty, ibid. Ezekiel’s Temple is exceedingly difficult to explain, 976. The prophecy of Ezekiel is difficult, IV, 1096. Why Ezekiel is called “son of man,” V, 591. In the exposition of Ezekiel’s Vision, the synagogues of the Jews are mute, 7. Ezekiel and Habakkuk were transported not in spirit but in the body itself, 32. Ezekiel as a type of Christ, 884. The eight circumstances of Ezekiel’s Vision, 891. Ezekiel prophesies willingly and not under compulsion, 934. His prudence, 369.

What does Ezra signify? I, 279. Ezra and Nehemiah are compressed into one volume, ibid. What is contained in it? ibid. They present one thing in the bark and retain another in the marrow, ibid. See *Esdras*.

# F

Food of beans, detestable to the Pythagoreans, V, 44.

Fabian, bishop of the city of Rome, II, 330. He died in the persecution of Decius, 895.

Fabiola is called the praise of Christians, the miracle of pagans, the mourning of the poor, and the consolation of monks, I, 458. Her virtues were very numerous and distinguished, ibid. Who her parents were, ibid. A convert is not praised unless she is first absolved as guilty, 459. Because of her faults she withdrew from her husband, ibid. Through weakness of mind and ignorance of the law she married another while the first was still alive, ibid. After the death of her second husband she performs public penance, ibid. and 460. Her works of penance, ibid. She receives communion in the sight of the whole Church, 461. On the day of prosperity she did not forget the unfortunate, ibid. She was the first to establish a house for receiving the poor and caring for the sick, 764. She carried them on her own shoulders, washed the purulent discharge from their wounds, and washed their food with her own hand, ibid. Her generosity, ibid. Rome was too small for her mercy, ibid. She was devoted to the study of the Scriptures, ibid. What she asked of Jerome, 463. Her love of solitude brought her to Bethlehem, ibid. She returned to Rome in order to live there poor where she had been rich, ibid. Jerome praises the ardor of her spirit above her other virtues, ibid. She knew by heart Jerome’s letter to Heliodorus; hence she burned with the greatest desire for solitude, 465. She called the management and careful distribution of money a kind of unfaithfulness, ibid. She herself desired to receive alms for Christ, ibid. Since she was always preparing herself, death could not find her unprepared, ibid. Together with Pammachius she built a hospice, ibid. The fervor of both their spirits, 466. She dies, and the people of the entire city gather for her funeral, ibid. Alleluia is sung at it, ibid. She had fallen among robbers, but was carried back upon Christ’s shoulders, 467. Fabiola, II, 534.

Why does antiquity admire Quintus Fabius? I, 340. A saying of Fabius, ibid. 340. The family of the Fabii praised, 400.

Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, II, 905.

In the midst of fables—that is, conversations, I, 126.

What the fables of the pagans relate, I, 787. What fables about certain living creatures describe, IV, 444. The fable of a thousand years is to be rejected, 702. A pagan fable is explained, V, 88. In what sense Jerome calls the history of Susanna, Bel, and the Dragon a “fable,” 620 and 731 and following. The fable about the Ammonites and Moabites entering the opened Temple, 288.

Craftsmen practice crafts, II, 287.

The self-restraint of Fabricius, II, 341.

Fabricius considered it a crime to kill a betrayed king, I, 307. The Fabricii, 223.

Facidia, a small village of the city of Rhinocorura, II, 19.

The face is a mirror of the mind, I, 290. The face that was once painted contrary to the Lord’s command with rouge and white lead must be disfigured, 706. What does a veiled face signify? V, 135 and following. What does “to receive a face” in the Law mean? VI, 961.

A crime that neither a mime can devise, nor a buffoon perform, nor an Atellan actor utter, I, 1089.

Each person does what he is capable of, I, 194. What is done with an occupied mind is not done well, 535.

The nature of actions is one thing and that of the person who performs them another, I, 602.

Canine eloquence, I, 1043.

[Col. 0978] The sons of the Faliscans betrayed, I, 307.

Whatever is false can never come into being, II, 721. Everything false does not endure, VII, 382.

One must take care of a good reputation, I, 910. Although the conscience of a crime may not bear a wound, it sometimes bears the disgrace of reputation, 783. Through good and bad reputation one reaches heaven, 198.

Famine is sent by God’s judgment because of sins, V, 55 and following. What the famine of the Jews was, 817. Nothing is harsher than hunger, VI, 342. The spiritual hunger and thirst of the Jews, 343. Famine and want oppressing the world descend from God’s anger, as he complains that he is defrauded in the poor, 976 and following.

Familiarity produces contempt, I, 338. Constant association produces familiarity, 60.

An elderly servant of honorable character should be placed in charge, I, 505. See *Servant*.

Spelt: it is the custom of the Egyptians to call it *theran*, which in Jerome’s time they corruptly called *atheran*, III, 369.

Things happen not by the Fates but by the will of God, IV, 229.

Foolishness opposed to knowledge, V, 77, 778, 800.

What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, V, 800.

Fate is excluded, VII, 146.

What is *fatura*? VII, 577.

Fauns, II, 7. Others call them fig-fauns, IV, 175.

Faustina, Julian’s wife, I, 792.

Faustinus considers Origen worthy of rejection, I, 352.

Faustus the Manichaean, I, 771.

Fever ravages the whole body, I, 603. The heat of fevers warns that bodily pleasures must be rejected, 174. Fever consumes the bones in the likeness of a lion, IV, 472. The nature of fever, VII, 45.

Gall, the seat of savagery, anger, and violence in the lion, V, 10. A drink of gall in proportion to the magnitude of evils, IV, 902.

Participation in eternal happiness, I, 185. It is sometimes a great happiness not to deserve mercy in the present, V, 97.

Saint Felicitas, I, 198.

Felix is appointed bishop of Rome in place of Liberius, II, 931.

Felix: who is he? VII, 415.

The virtue of captive women, II, 45.

The judgment of women is changeable and wavering, I, 994. If they are left to their own will, they quickly fall into worse things, ibid. Women who hate their own are condemned, and those who are not caressed by the affection of their own, 935. Their impatience admits no excuse, ibid. The female sex should be joined to its own sex, 964. The ambition of noblewomen burns with regard to certain things, 934. Shameful things are said about noble women, 965. In them a tender matter is the reputation of chastity, 505. The steadfastness of one woman in abandoning her homeland and leaving behind children and relatives, 693.
