Jerome makes no distinction among holy women, 652. The virtues of women and widows are brought forward, 292, 293 and following. No saint, except very rarely, is said to have fathered daughters, III, 400. The jewels of women are described, and through them the emblems of virtues, IV, 61. “Daughter of women” is a pleonasm, V, 710. The nature of women, VI, 518. The most learned pagan women, 671. In holy women sacred affection is sometimes weakened and leads to death, VII, 715. See *Woman*, *Wife*.

What are *femoralia*? I, 361.

What is the thigh? I, 96. Mystically it is taken for the acts of marriage, 361. Striking the thigh with the hand is an indication of grief and mourning, IV, 1066.

Jacob’s thigh healed, III, 356.

Whether a lender may receive more than he gave, V, 210 and following.

What are “poisonous windows”? V, 476.

Phenon, where bronze ore is mined for the punishments of the condemned, III, 214.

The scarcity of hay in many provinces of the East, IV, 182.

Wild beasts that have tasted blood always thirst for it, I, 4.

What does leaven signify mystically? I, 471. Leaven of false doctrine, VI, 80.

If iron is without tin, it is burned and consumed, VI, 813.

The idolatrous custom of inaugurating the fertility of the years, IV, 782. The same custom among the Egyptians, ibid.

“Fervent” is taken for “good,” IV, 883.

Fervor arising from the love of God, I, 339.

The Fescennine song, I, 914. Bold or shameless, 909.

Festivals should be celebrated not in wine, VI, 549. Whose festivals does God cast away? 302.

How a feast should be celebrated, I, 151. The feast of the apostle Peter, ibid. For Christians every time is a feast, 881.

Festus ruled Judaea, II, 823.

He succeeded Felix, 827.

The offspring of the Aenean sow, VII, 378.

Spring offspring is better than autumn offspring, III, 354.

What is the use of figs? IV, 475.

[Col. 0979] Interpretations by certain persons concerning the two baskets of figs, IV, 1116.

What does resting under a fig tree signify? I, 799. The barren fig tree as a figure of the Jews, VI, 669.

Whence is faith so called? I, 774. The Catholic faith and the rules of the Church must be preserved, 536. Nothing is more ancient than preserving Christ’s rights, not transferring the boundaries of the Fathers, and always remembering the Roman faith, etc., 353. The inheritance of faith preserved among the Romans, 38. The victory of faith over heretics, 435. What great faith despises, 462. What full faith endures, 694. It does not fear hunger, 36. It conquers every deformity, 619. A house that lacks the solid foundations of faith collapses in the devil’s whirlwind, 899. It is rare among human beings, 323. It must not be weighed according to the times, 319. It is most foolish to make one’s faith depend on another’s judgment, 199. The battering ram of impiety by which faith is shaken must be blunted against the wall of the Gospel, 30. Pure and open confession of faith seeks neither tricks nor verbal arguments, 517. Those who contradict the ecclesiastical faith are held by a twofold sickness, 602. Let us adorn faith with our manner of life, 579. What is small, since it cannot preserve greater things, at least preserves lesser ones, 890. Individual believers are assessed not by differences of place but by the merit of faith, 320. The person surrounded by a believing crowd of sons and grandchildren is a candidate of faith, 678. It does not grow weary, although the torturers grow weary, 620. The spirit strengthened by faith conquers the weakness of the flesh, ibid. May that which unbelief displayed in others be displayed in us, 335. Through faith the sleeping understanding is awakened to vigilance, 616. The fragile and transitory nature of mortals—unless the faith of Christ raised us to heaven, 721. The faith praised by the apostolic mouth is violated by many, 958. If you perceive someone weaker in faith, receive, console, and encourage him, 113. It is no harm for prudent and learned men to be admonished out of concern for the faith, 335. Faith makes present those who are absent in body, 899.

The faith of the Church, II, 429. It belongs properly to Christians, 256. If it has no works, it is dead, ibid. What perfect faith is, 189.

It is perfect to believe God from God, ibid. What zeal for the faith should be, 415. The Roman faith admits no tricks, 542. It cannot be changed, ibid. It belongs to Catholics, 461. Its truth cannot be overturned by empty arguments, 752. Purity does not tolerate delay, 415. Nothing is greater than faith in the sacrament and purity of soul, 387. The house of certain faith, 436. Perfect faith, which is difficult to find even among those who believe correctly, 187. Faith directed without doubt toward God is difficult to find, ibid. If Peter has little faith, it is unknown in whom there is great faith, 188. What perfect faith does in one who prays, 189. Scrupulousness concerning faith, 444. Its free confession, 428. The Holy Spirit does not become an inhabitant of a temple that does not have as its bishop one of true faith, 181. Eroded faith—that is, neither sound nor whole, 415. Under the name of unity and faith, unbelief is written, 188. It is arrogance not to answer those who ask about the faith, 410. When a priest preaches the true faith, darkness is dispelled from everyone’s heart, 175. It is ridiculous to dispute about faith before believing, 184. The faith and devotion of the simple possess a reward, 394. Many things are proposed for belief under penalty of anathema, 90.

One must believe that he came who is written of, but one must not inquire how, how great, or of what kind he came, III, 436. Faith founded the Church after the Lord’s Passion, IV, 28. The faith of Christians, 434, 896. It is rare, 562. The brevity of faith’s worship, 432. It must not be idle, 809. Without works it is insufficient, 345. It is commended by past things, 510. All human beings are equally called to faith, 657. The calling of the whole world to faith is demonstrated, 163. The faith of the nations was in a certain sense forced from them by miracles of signs, 796. Roman leaders pass over to the faith of Christ, 719. The different faith of Christians and Jews, 1051. Each person will be crowned for his faith and condemned for his impiety, V, 216. Faith in the Holy Spirit is commended, VI, 202. Someone may receive the fruit of a good work before faith, 768. The calves and victims of faith, 158. What faith is rare? 517. Faith in Christ, the beginning of confidence, VII, 596. The sacrament of our faith is revealed only through the Scriptures and the coming of Christ, 592. The faith of the Church established amid the shipwrecks of false doctrines, 375. The kingdom of the Father is the faith of believers, 217. It is not a matter of our will but a gift of God, 577. There is no faithful affection among those whose faith is different, 61. The faith of the saints praised, 713. Evangelical faith is small at the beginning, etc., 92. All people are justified by the faith of Christ, 413. Soundness of faith and doctrine, 710. Faith and sanctification: from what source? 345. The working of faith through love contains all the commandments, 483. Faith is commended together with works, 759. Each person is better or worse than others according to the quality of his faith, 445. Faith differs according to the variety of minds, 692. Who lives by faith? ibid. The just person does not live without faith, ibid. The works of the Law and faith are to be sought together, 434. Without works faith is dead, 483. The faith of the apostles and believers is defended, [Col. 0980] 134. According to the diversity of faith, the order of names is changed, 116. Faith is judged according to devotion of mind, 445. By what means believers come to faith, 282.

To whom faith should be entrusted more, I, 517. If prudence does not extort faith, let modesty at least extort it, 676. Faith must be kept even among enemies, V, 193.

Trusts by which we mock the laws, I, 261.

Fidus, a bishop, I, 200.

What gives us confidence before God? VII, 595.

Certain monks’ fictions about the battle with demons, I, 983. Jerome reports certain fictions and tales of the ancients, IV, 923. The fictions and tales of the ancients, V, 658.

A round figure is more beautiful, V, 498. Small villages and towns are called “daughters,” IV, 60, and V, 54.

Sons do not always correspond to their lineage, I, 284. Examples of those who endured the death of their sons with great steadfastness, 334 and following. The firmness of a son redounds to the father, 412. It is not a small merit before God to educate children well, 504. Love of children is despised in comparison with greater love of God, 688. To love children is to fear servants, 262. Nothing is so dutiful as for a holy mother to guard her holy son, 937. Sons consecrated to God are firstborn offerings presented in the Law, 680. How sons and heirs become a cause of sadness to their fathers, II, 315. Every son, in comparison with his parents, is called an infant and a little child, among Romans as among Hebrews, III, 336. All sons are called infants at Rome, ibid. The distinction between sons and servants, IV, 780. Who are “the sons of the prophets”? ibid. Nothing is more painful than losing one or an only son, 889. For the sake of the holy fathers God has mercy on sons, 844. How the sons of darkness are wiser than the sons of light, 1049. Sons of pestilence, sons of Belial, 359. Many holy parents have wicked sons, and conversely, V, 201. Whether sinful sons can be freed from the fire of Gehenna through the merit and virtues of their parents, 139. No history reports that sons ate their fathers, 55. Because of the necessity of famine, mothers ate their sons, 51. In Holy Scripture a son and a servant become so by will, not by nature, VI, 945 and following. The name “son” is taken in a good and a bad sense, ibid. Sons and daughters in the Scriptures: what are they? VII, 573, 644, 699. They are the bowels of their parents, 756. Sons obey their parents, 662, 663, 665. The education of sons, ibid. Sons are commanded obedience, while parents are commanded moderate authority, 666. What does it mean to love sons? 718. How are we all sons of wrath? 573. Where “sons of pestilence” occur in the Old Law, *Beliat* is read in the Hebrew volumes, 629. See *Children*.

The Son of God is a consoler, I, 834. Those who assert by a subscription of their hand that the Son of God is a creature, V, 545.

“Son of man” is read in the singular in a good sense and in the plural in a bad sense in Scripture, V, 360.

Who are the sons of Joseph, the husband of Mary? VII, 265.

Who are the sons of the shaken? I, 156.

The end. Whoever is still running is lesser than the one who reaches the end, II, 797. Without God’s help we cannot reach our end, III, 464. It is the end, not the beginnings, that is sought, VII, 175.

Firmianus wrote a book on the anger of God, VII, 628. Firmianus’s ignorance of the Scriptures, 450. The books of letters concerning the same man, ibid. He erred concerning the Holy Spirit, ibid. See *Lactantius*.

Firmus: where was he directed, and why? I, 1043. What is said about him? 754.

Flaccus’s letter to Florus, II, 459. A few passages are reported from it, ibid. Flaccus’s opinion, VII, 653. Flaccus mocks the images of the nations, IV, 528.

Flails, instruments for threshing, IV, 386. The shoots of vines are to be propped up with stakes and reeds, 70. What is the devil’s flail? VI, 560.

Every disgrace, once it has exceeded the limit of modesty, always proceeds toward worse things, VI, 241.

A priest of one wife is admitted to the priesthood, I, 905.

The wife of one husband, a *flaminica* (wife of a flamen), I, 905.

The deed of Flaminius, the Roman commander, VII, 102.

How shall we conquer the flames of Babylon, when we cannot endure threats, insults, or poverty? II, 696.

The bridal veil of the consecration of virgins, I, 1090.

Flavia Domitilla rejoices because of her faith, I, 195.

Flavianus the grammarian wrote on medical matters, II, 919.

Flavius wrote in verse, II, 32.

The magnitude of tears is compared with a flood of waters, I, 895. What is completed in one who weeps? ibid. Tears are an indication of excessive joy, IV, 1061.

Flowers quickly perish; swiftly a pestilential breeze corrupts violets, lilies, and saffron, I, 686. The varied beauty of flowers, 934.

No royal purple can be compared with flowers, VII, 37.

Florinus, II, 873.

[Col. 0981] Flaccus’s letter to Florus, II, 459.

The waters of rivers changed into human blood, I, 345.

What is the river of fire? VII, 359.

Rivers burst forth from earthquakes, VI, 648. Others were swallowed up, ibid.

A second covenant after God, I, 783.

One fountain is divided into four beginnings, I, 420. It makes bitter and dead waters alive, ibid. The water of a fountain is purer than that of streams, II, 213. The fountains of Judaea stopped up, VI, 648. The reverence for fountains among pagans, IV, 894. The scarcity of fountains in the region of Jerusalem, 567.

What does a pair of tongs signify mystically? I, 60.

An ant has six feet, II, 557. The labors of ants, 46.

The Lord the Savior in the furnace, with the three boys according to certain interpreters, V, 643. The iron furnace as a symbol of tribulation, IV, 910.

Let us avoid with watchful mind the seductive and slippery serpent of fornication, I, 608. According to certain interpreters fornication and immodesty are permitted to men, 459. Why fornication alone is a sin against the body, 296 and following. Spiritual fornication occurs in three ways, V, 172 and following. Fornication among the breasts of heretics, VI, 14. The sons of fornication taken by Hosea, IV and following. Fornication is the same as idolatry, 39 and following. The evil of fornication, VII, 506. It is one thing in an unbeliever and another in a believer, 506.

Examples of fortitude are to be imitated, I, 619. Let us raise up the spirit weighed down and prostrate through fortitude, 608. Fortitude always has rivals openly confronting it, III, 301. Strength of body, weakness of spirit, VI, 995. Fortitude, a virtue of the spirit, VII, 669. Among philosophers this is counted among the four virtues, ibid.

Powers, or virtues, on the right and left of God, VI, 198 and following.

The nature of a strong man, VI, 172. The strongest, like diamonds, are dissolved by lust alone, 330. It is beneficial that the worst powers do not agree among themselves, 626.

The commentaries of Fortunatianus, I, 24. In what respect Fortunatianus is detestable, II, 931. Fortunatianus, VII, 3.

Fortunatus, I, 233.

Fortune. Some wrongly judge that everything happens by chance and that varying fortune plays with human affairs, III, 461. What does it mean “to prepare a table for Fortune”? IV, 783.

Fratres (“brothers”) are spoken of in Scripture in four ways, II, 220 ff. We are all brothers in two ways, 222. Sons are called brothers in Holy Scripture, III, 345. He who does not forgive the sins of his brothers is more just than is just, 443. “Brother” and “neighbor” apply to the whole human race, VI, 835, 849.

Who the Lord’s brothers were, and why they are called so, II, 216 and 220.

“Cold” is taken in the sense of evil, IV, 882.

Every fraud displays one thing and is another, I, 566. It conceals vices under the appearance of virtue, ibid.

Where is no deception by fraud found? I, 614. Nothing should be driven away from oneself so much as the charge of fraud and faithlessness, II, 560.

By contraction of the forehead and sadness of countenance, the one who errs is reproved, I, 713. To strike forehead against forehead is sometimes an act of God’s grace, V, 33.

The gravity of the orator Fronto, I, 941. Fronto the orator, teacher of Antoninus Verus, II, 865.

The sweetness of fruits compensates for the bitterness of the root, I, 678.

The frugality of masters is the loss of little slaves, I, 284. The frugality of many has been praised, II, 332 ff.

What methods farmers employ to preserve grain from birds, II, 196. Scarcity of grain in Judaea, I, 293.

The prophet Uriah’s flight was not one of faithlessness but of prudence, IV, 1030.

What are we commanded to flee? II, 255.

Which are the cities of fugitives? V, 604. Why they are passed over in silence by Ezekiel, ibid. What is suitable for a fugitive, VI, 393.

“Lightning strikes the highest mountains,” I, 344, 707. Lightning is produced by the collision of clouds, V, 798.

What Fulvia did against Cicero, II, 569.

“Smoke” is taken for glory, IV, 66.

What is meant by the smoke filling the Temple (Isa. 6:4)? I, 52.

What are the foundations of the earth? VI, 470.

Funerals are joyful for the Thracians, childbirths sorrowful, II, 360.

A cord is a measure of a definite journey, especially for those who tow ships on the Nile with ropes, VI, 216.

What is the threefold cord mentioned in Ecclesiastes? I, 521.

Although the face of a thief is shameless, he blushes when caught in the theft, IV, 852.

What is the difference between a thief and a robber? VI, 69. Who are the thieves and robbers in the Church? 66.

The fury of the daughter-in-law of the consul Probus, I, 715. The great privilege of the Furian family and its ancestors, 195.

[Col. 0982] Furius triumphed over the Gauls, I, 466.

“Fury” is used for that which hardens the mind’s softness, V, 502. What is fury? VII, 636. The effect of fury, ibid.

How “fury” and “anger” are to be understood in relation to God, IV, 85.

Theft is to be detested as sacrilege, I, 713. To snatch something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege, 269. Theft and perjury are no small crimes, VI, 816. What is theft? VII, 631. In theft, attention is paid not to what was taken but to the thief’s intention, 723. Suspicion of theft should be foreign to every free person, ibid.

Spiritual theft, VII, 531, 632.

Future things succeed as past things slip away, I, 622. All future things are uncertain, especially those that have never happened, II, 702. There is one knowledge of future things, 444. For one who foretells the future, it makes no difference whether he announces what will happen after ten years or after a hundred, ibid. Future things must always be guarded against amid prosperity, IV, 547. God alone possesses knowledge of future things, ibid. and 1033, 1046.

G

Gaas means “commotion,” II, 272.

Gabaa and Rama, two cities of the tribe of Benjamin, VI, 54.

The Hebrews say that Gabriel means “the angel who strikes the army of the Assyrians,” IV, 434. What do Gabriel, Raphael, and Michael signify? V, 676. Gabriel and Michael are protectors of the Jews, VI, 665.

Galaad, σωρός (*sōros*), “a mound of testimony,” or “the transmigration of testimony,” IV, 688. The possession of half the tribe of Manasseh beyond the Jordan, ibid. What are Galaad and Auran? V, 600. Galaad, a mountain of Lebanon, ibid. Galaad, a city in the priestly tribe, VI, 65 ff.

The origin and region of the Galatians, VII, 425, 427. What was their language? 429. How Paul’s account was useful to the Galatians, 389. Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians attempted by Latin writers before Jerome, 369. Very few Greeks had undertaken them, ibid.

The view of Galen and the physicians concerning the use of foods, I, 287. What does Galen, the interpreter of Hippocrates, say about athletes? II, 340. What does ἐν ἁπλοῖς (“in simple things”) teach? 331. Galen, the most eloquent of physicians, VI, 283. His book *On Crises and Critical Days* (*περὶ κρίσεων καὶ κριτικῶν ἡμερῶν*), ibid.

Galgala means “revelation,” II, 270. Galgala, also called Golgol, where the principal precepts of the Mosaic Law are said to have been fulfilled, III, 219. That place was held in extraordinary honor, ibid. Galgala, a place of idolatry, VI, 102 ff. and 269 ff. How it began to become famous for superstitions, 44.

Galla, an associate of Priscillian, I, 1031.

The Gauls lay waste to everything, I, 914. The attack of the Gauls, 310. The ranks of the Gauls laid low, 980. The native soil of the Gauls is subjected to Roman rule, 914. The Gauls’ steadfastness in lamentation is preferred, 335. When the Gauls invaded, the patricians and the flower of Roman youth were preserved in the citadel, IV, 220. The Gauls were mutilated by the Romans as a mark of disgrace, VI, 41. The Gauls were called Galatians from the whiteness of their bodies, VII, 425. Hilary called the Gauls unteachable, 427. They are fertile in orators, ibid.

The Galli, priests of the Mother of the Gods, VI, 41. Why especially effeminate? ibid.

The boundaries of Gaul, I, 914. The pursuits of Gaul are exceedingly flourishing, 935. Victors from East and West settled in Gaul, 914. The most savage nations occupied all Gaul, 913. Gaul has always abounded in brave and most eloquent men, 387.

Gallic garments and *Gallicarii*, II, 55.

Gallienus, II, 907.

Gallus, II, 907.

*Gallus*, the title of a Dialogue published by Severus, V, 422.

Against whom the patriarch Gamaliel exercised his hostility, I, 307.

The river Ganges flows around the whole land of Havilah, I, 934. Holy Scripture calls the river Ganges the Pishon, ibid. It is said to carry many kinds of spices from the fountain of paradise, ibid. What grows in it, ibid. The river Ganges, II, 344. The Ganges is believed to be the Pishon, flowing around the land of Havilah, III, 199, 211.

Garizim and Gebal, two neighboring mountains near Jericho, III, 219. The Samaritans’ error concerning this matter, ibid.

Garumma, I, 454.

Let us redeem future joys with present weeping, I, 608. What difference there is between joy and gladness according to the Stoics and certain others, VII, 510, 511.

Gaza, a city of the Gentiles where Marnas is worshiped, II, 19. The people of Gaza are adversaries of God, 24. How Gaza became an everlasting tomb, III, 218.

In the language of the Persians, Gaza means “wealth,” IV, 477.

Gazanus, a disciple of Hilarion, II, 33.

Gazanus Majomites, a paralytic who was healed, II, 22.

Who the Gazarenes were, and what their pursuits were, IV, 553.

The region of Gebalene, VI, 364.

[Col. 0983] Gideon was called Jerubbaal, IV, 150.

To whom are the fires of Gehenna assigned? II, 753. From where Gehenna received its name, III, 223. From where Gehenna was named, IV, 897. The name “Gehenna” was invented by the Savior, VII, 62.

Gehennon, a place near Jerusalem so called, VII, 62.

Γεῖσος (*geisos*), a term used by the Septuagint, which Jerome admits that he does not know, V, 487.

Gelasius concealed his works, II, 951.

The gleam of a flawless gem shines even in mud, I, 397. The most distinguished writers on gems and stones, IV, 637.

How the genealogy of Christ is related differently by the Evangelists, VII, 335. No holy woman is listed in the Savior’s genealogy, VII, 9. Three kings are omitted from it, 10.

Four kinds of human generation are assigned, II, 440. The one nature of humanity does not differ amid this diversity, ibid. The end of an evil generation is most evil, IV, 796.

We ought not to boast of our lineage, I, 336.

In the genus, what is true is also held in the species, II, 743. Whatever is removed from the parts must necessarily be denied of the whole, 699.

What the Book of Genesis contains, I, 276. The opening of Genesis was not read among the Hebrews until thirty years ago, 279. Genesis offers much concerning the nature of things, II, 558. Genesis is the head of all the books, III, 305. Among the Hebrews it is called *Beresith*, 306. Genesis, the book of the righteous, IV, 524. The Book of Genesis is called the Law, VII, 469.

Gennesareth, VII, 109.

A nation between the Saxons and Alemanni, not broad but powerful, II, 24. Which were the strongest nations? V, 309. One nation called by five names, 291.

By the conversion of the Gentiles, the famine of the Jews’ unbelief is quenched, I, 933. What was the multitude of the Gentiles before and after the knowledge of God? IV, 481. Why was it called “flesh”? ibid. The conversion of the Gentiles is foretold, 542. The calling of the Gentiles is indicated, 369. It is signified by Damascus, 278 ff. What the conversion of the Gentiles accomplishes, 449. From all the nations one nation of Christians was made, 806. The error of the Gentiles passed over to us, so that we think religion consists in riches, 911. The religion of the Gentiles worships every kind of animal, V, 86. The calling of the Gentiles is indicated, 577. The calling of the Gentiles is described, VI, 857, 861, 920. How it is just, 888. The Gentiles were cast out at the assumption of Israel, 889. The repentance of the Gentiles is the ruin of the Jews, 392. The Gentiles are said to possess certain idioms because of their former works, VII, 417. The complete salvation of the Gentiles was reserved for the time of the Passion and Resurrection, 115. The faith of the nations is secretly preferred to that of Israel, 84.

By no means should either Gentile or Jew be lamented, I, 893. It is the confusion of the Gentiles when they see that those things displease the churches which do not please all good people, 936. The people of the Gentiles earned the greatness of their rewards through the difficulty of faith, II, 374. The highest virtue of the Gentiles was not to seize what belonged to another, 290. The Gentiles were never excluded from the calling, IV, 631. The error of the Gentiles, who think that everything above them is a god, V, 646. The hearts of the Gentiles are called stones, VII, 423. The virtues of the Gentiles serve to condemn Christians, 528. Very many Gentiles gloried in their own disgraces, 505.

The solitude of paganism, I, 679. Paganism deceived by the error of those whom it worships, II, 7. Paganism did not fail to recognize the majesty of God, V, 156.

To kneel is an indication of anxious and humble prayer, I, 574. The soul’s concern frequently rouses one to bend the knees, 991. To bend the knee to Christ is the custom of the Church, which the Jews do not practice, IV, 542. At what times the knees should be bent, V, 659. With the knee placed on the ground, the custom of praying, VII, 427. How angels and souls bend the knee, 598. At what time we do not bend the knees, 541. Kneeling in prayer is commanded, 599. What it means to bend the knee to the Savior and to sin, ibid.

Josephus testifies that those sent by Joshua to survey the land were geometers, V, 524.

Geometry is an art proper to philosophers, V, 524. To possess knowledge of the geometric art is not absurd, ibid.

Geon, also called the Nile among the Egyptians, rises in paradise and circles all Ethiopia, III, 215.

The *geranopepa*, a fattened bird, I, 112.

Gerasa, a name of Arabia, VI, 381.

Geryon, three-formed, II, 388.

What Gergesa signifies, V, 751.

Very many cities and peoples were transferred into Germany, I, 913. In Jerome’s time Germany had cultivators of the sacred language, 642. Germany, now called France, II, 24.

Germanicus Caesar, VII, 706.

In Origen’s time the Gospel had not yet been preached to the German inhabitants of the Ocean coast, VII, 273.

The army of the Getae carries its tents around the churches, I, [Col. 0984] 679. In Jerome’s time the Getae were studying Holy Scripture, 642.

Geth, the metropolitan city of Palestine, VI, 441, 443. Now a fairly small village, 389. The tomb of Jonah is shown there, ibid.

Geth of the Palestinians, VI, 311.

Gethsemane is at the foot of the Mount of Olives, where a church had been built, III, 227. Gethsemane, the place where Christ was betrayed, IV, 371. What Gethsemane signifies, VII, 218.

The impiety of the giants brought about the shipwreck of the whole world, I, 23. The giants are called Anakim, left behind at Azotus, III, 146. In Gaza they were the mightiest of the Philistines, 218. “Giant” is taken in both a good and a bad sense, IV, 46, 47. Giants are understood differently according to the custom of the pagans and according to ours, 250. The devil is strong and gigantic, 574.

Claudian’s *Gigantomachia* is cited, IV, 361. The *Gigantomachia* was written in praise of the gods, VI, 289.

Gildo held Africa, I, 715.

The Gepids, I, 913.

What the sword means in Scripture, IV, 814. What a “holy and hard” sword means, 360. It is taken for punishment, 782. The sword that will pierce Mary’s soul, VII, 301.

The torpor of dormice, II, 559.

Vainglory must be fled, I, 110, 111. It must be guarded against, 266. The evil of vainglory, 110. Few are free from it, 111. The soul inwardly rejoices in its own praise, 107. It is better to have God as one’s supporter than the gaze of human beings, 268. It is difficult to surpass glory by virtue, 502. Let us slay the desire for vainglory as an insatiable beast, 608. Sometimes we swell with pride in glorious rags after casting away gold and gems, 458. Those who flee glory deserve it, 692. Abandoning those who seek him, he seeks those who despise him, ibid. Glory follows virtue like a shadow, ibid. It is rare to find a faithful soul that does nothing from desire for glory, II, 188. It is difficult to be content, in works of piety, with God alone as judge, ibid. It is a mark of modesty and prudence to conceal what one hears said gloriously about oneself, 560. “Glory” is spoken in the sense of disgrace, IV, 193. The innumerable books of philosophers on glory, VII, 515. Definitions of vainglory, ibid. The desire for vainglory destroys all works, ibid. and 516. Most people write books for the sake of glory, ibid.

How glory should be given to God, V, 832. What true glory is, VII, 747. What “glory” denotes in Scripture, 516.

On what matters it is fitting to glory, V, 810, 811.

Arrogant boasting was immediately punished, V, 650.

The Gnatonici, I, 240.

The Gnostic heresy, I, 1029.

The Gnostics arose from Basilides, II, 861. The Gnostics and their origin, IV, 761.

Gog and Magog are not the Goths, as some thought, but rather the Getae, III, 318. Gog is not a Goth, as a man of no little distinction in Jerome’s age, writing to the emperor, believed, V, 406. Gog and Magog are exceedingly savage nations, VI, 213.

The interpretation of the name Gomer, VI, 6. The name of the prostitute whom Hosea took, ibid. What children she bore, 8 ff.

Some interpret Gomer and Togarmah as the Galatians and Phrygians, V, 444.

Who were the people of Gomorrah? VI, 19.

Gordian succeeded Alexander in the imperial office, II, 899.

What flows from the springs of Gorgias? I, 222. Why philosophers and orators tear apart Gorgias of Leontini, II, 419. He is noted, 559.

Gorgunte, II, 320.

Gortyna, a city, II, 869.

The land of Goshen, or Gesen, III, 369.

The stock of the Gracchi, I, 690. Whose sons were the Gracchi? 284. It is said that their mother’s speech contributed to the eloquence of the Gracchi, 682. Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, is praised, VI, 671.

Gracchus, distinguished by nobility, held the urban prefecture, I, 678. He destroyed the cave of Mithras and its monstrous images, ibid. After sending these hostages ahead, he obtained Christ’s baptism, ibid. Gracchus, II, 320, 419.

Priestly ranks were established among the Jewish people to distinguish prophets from false prophets, IV, 52.

The steps of the house of Ahaz, within the enclosure of the Temple, shown by guides to the holy places, IV, 470.

What the most eloquent men of Greece were reading, I, 935. Exultant Greece borrowed something from the Latins through Jerome, II, 525. Greece attacked by Xerxes, V, 702. Conquered by Alexander the Great, 703.

The frivolity and vanity of the Greeks, I, 24. The custom of Greek writers to repay benefits received with the favor of language, 501. It is difficult in translating Greek to render word for word, 308 ff. The Greeks occupied nearly all the islands, the shores of the whole world, and lands near the sea, III, 319. We ought not to submit to the authority of Greek authors, V, 297. The frivolity and learned vanity of the Greeks, [Col. 0985] VII, 415. The Greek language is more expansive, 548. The breadth of the Greek language, 429.

What is better expressed in Greek, 518.

The opinion of grammarians, I, 30. What do the schools of grammarians proclaim? 232.

Grains are ground with various instruments, IV, 385. The pomegranate fruit, 366. It is taken in two ways in Scripture, 482. The drink of the pomegranate, VI, 905. The beauty of the pomegranate, ibid.

The necessity of grace and of God’s help is established, I, 1034. Believers are justified and saved by Christ’s grace alone, 769. Where there is grace, it is not the repayment of works but the generosity of the giver, 989. What God once gave us is not sufficient unless he continues to give it always, 1034. Let us know that we are nothing except insofar as God has given something to us and preserved it in us, ibid. Our weakness is strengthened by grace, 892. The multiplication of grace is promised, while our smallness is affirmed, 412. Equal grace should have an equal labor, 685. The privilege of God’s grace was granted to the three boys and to Daniel, 288. It is indeed ours to will and to run; but for our will to be fulfilled and our running to reach its goal belongs to God’s mercy, II, 700. A certain grace is called useless, III, 444. Without God’s grace we do not attain knowledge, 464. The grace of the Gospel is necessary, IV, 896. All things have been handed over to the human race through God’s grace, 1032. Christ’s grace, not merit, frees the poor, 981. It depends not on the possessor but on the will of the giver, 1081. Not only our works but also our will relies on God’s help, 1012. Whatever good we wish and accomplish, let us attribute it to God’s grace, 1026. We always need God’s help, 1014. No graces are lacking to the Church, 502. The variety of trees signifies the diversity of grace, ibid. Full perfection comes from grace, not merit, V, 577. Sometimes God’s grace consists in resisting shamelessness, 30. The graces of the Holy Spirit differ in those still led by the spirit of fear and in those who possess perfect love, VI, 203. The soul can do nothing without Christ’s grace, 748. Christ’s grace is commended, VII, 764. Through Christ’s grace we are all reconciled, 724. Who rejects God’s grace? 415.

Let us always give thanks to the giver, I, 1034. Those who have been taught and can teach others should give thanks to God and to their teachers, VI, 978 ff. Thanksgiving is taken in two ways, VII, 641. General thanksgiving and particular thanksgiving, 652. We must always render thanks to God, whether in prosperity or adversity, ibid.

The death of the emperor Gratian, betrayed by his own army, I, 343. The emperor Gratian, II, 943.

Gregory Thaumaturgus, a man of apostolic signs and virtues, I, 429. He was called Theodore, 419. Gregory Thaumaturgus was a disciple of Origen, II, 905. He performed very many signs and miracles, ibid. Gregory, bishop of Pontus and a hearer of Origen, wrote a paraphrase of Ecclesiastes, III, 424.

Gregory of Nazianzus was Jerome’s catechist, I, 237. He playfully mocked Jerome with elegance, 263. Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome’s teacher, II, 943. Praise of Gregory of Nazianzus, 469. What did he explain in Greek words? 160. Gregory of Nazianzus translated by Rufinus, 486. Praises of Gregory of Nazianzus, VII, 661. What he used to say to Jerome about a certain passage of Scripture, ibid.

Cranes follow one another in an ordered, letter-like sequence, I, 942.

The boys used to sing the *Testament of Grunnius Corocotta the Little Pig* in the schools, IV, 491.

Grunnius is mentioned; by this name Rufinus seems to be taunted, IV, 835. Wretched Grunnius opened his mouth to level accusations, 993.

A follower of Grunnian calumnies, IV, 1040. Heirs of the Grunnian faction, V, 401.

The Syrians call a cistern *gubba*, II, 3 ff.

Gluttony. Whatever is not perceived after the throat should be the same for you as bread and vegetables, I, 324. Many remedy the impatience of gluttony by vomiting, II, 340.

The Gymnosophists, I, 271. What the Egyptian Gymnosophists observe regarding food, 393. The Gymnosophists of India are divided into two doctrines, II, 344. Their abstinence, ibid. How greatly they are honored, ibid. What the Gymnosophists of India transmit concerning their prince Buddha, ibid. 309.

The Gymnesian islands, now called the Balearic Islands, VII, 427.

H

H is regarded by most people as an aspiration, not a letter, III, 34. Grammarians do not think it should be counted as a letter, 91. Three names are read with H, 106.

What Habakkuk signifies, I, 278. Its subject, ibid. His prophecy, V, 619. Elsewhere written Ambacum, VI, 587. At what time he flourished, ibid.

No one possesses anything good except what he distributes to the poor, I, 990. We felt more keenly what we had after we ceased to have it, 393. It is much more laborious not to enjoy what one has than to desire what one has lost, 908. Whatever you have must be credited to God’s beneficence, II, 700.

God’s dwelling place is wherever God’s will is done, IV, 775.

To dwell before God depends not on place but on merit, IV, 222.

Who are called “inhabitants of the earth”? IV, 481, 482 and 885, and V, 65. The distinction between the inhabitants and residents of the earth, VI, 35.

Hadrian calls Jerusalem Aelia, I, 697. He visited the Eleusinian rites, 428. Hadrian, 321. Hadrian spent the winter at Athens, II, 861. Nearly fifty years after Vespasian, Hadrian came to Judaea to plunder it, IV, 100. The Jews were forbidden by him to enter it, ibid. From the ashes of Jerusalem Hadrian founded a city named Aelia after himself, VI, 171. An equestrian statue of Hadrian standing in the Temple, VII, 194.

Hadrian, a disciple of Hilarion, announces to him that Julian has been killed, II, 33. The same man is called unfortunate; why? ibid.

Kids are taken in Scripture for sinners, I, 170.

The kid is an animal always hastening toward high places, V, 532.

Our inheritance is in Christ, VII, 764.

Heresy is defended more ardently by heretics than it is attacked by Catholics, I, 537. Origen explained heresies in many volumes; by whom they were explained, 429. The heresy called that of the Mineans, 746. One asserting that there are things Christ cannot cleanse with his blood, 412. A heresy pretending repentance so as to obtain the ability to teach in churches, 1043. A heresy drawing priests, monks, and laypeople into its agreement, 957. A heresy that is uncertain and promises great things, so as to remove what is certain and moderate, 454. A heresy that teaches pride through feigned humility, 1026. The heresies of the primitive Church, II, 197. Two are noted, 482. Heresy is subtle and easily deceives simple souls, 183. In heresy it is customary for the people to hear one thing and the priests to preach another, 410. Innumerable heresies already existed in Jerome’s time, 380. From where they had proceeded, ibid. The Latin language has its own heresy, 381. No one should be tolerant when heresy is suspected, 409. Those who follow the Catholic faith desire and wish heresy to be condemned and people to be corrected, 701. Heresies are divided among themselves, IV, 140. Prophetic discourse announced heresies, 285. No heresy is constructed except for the sake of the belly and the stomach, 860. He who attacks heresies can scarcely possess a complete victory, 144. The progress of the worst heresy, 966. Its authors and followers, 967. A new heresy is noted, 856, 860. The mutual clash of heresies is our victory, V, 451. Which is the most savage heresy? 331. From where all heresies come, VI, 582. With one tongue they bark against the Church, 659. Who are the patriarchs of the heresies? 267, 511. Pride is the mother of heretics, 49, 274, 706. The pretenses and pride of heretics are noted, 243, 244, 368. Among heretics he may be called king who first revives a heresy, 70. Heretics were flesh and a member of Christ, 102. They were expelled from the house of God, ibid. They differ in nothing from the Gentiles, 75, 80. They speak not the authority of Scripture but the sense of human reason, ibid. The most learned heretics, 106. Their speech is contrived, 229, 287, 293, 294. Whatever a heretic says is full of deceit, 138. What heretical doctrine is, 113, 625. What is heresy? VII, 737. From where heresies arise and receive their name, 507. They are referred to the works of the flesh, ibid. They are based on a carnal understanding of Scripture, 495. According to false faith, they possess all things falsely, 615, 616. Jerome does not wish to give occasion to heresy, 711, 712. The author of a new heresy, 737. What the new heresy maligns, 724, 725. The difference between heresy and schism, 738. A shameful heresy, 640.

Heretics are figuratively seen in Lamech, I, 909. Their churches are synagogues of the devil, not assemblies of Christ, ibid. Heretics are held by a twofold sickness, 603. Like snakes, they are wholly turned toward earthly things, ibid. They do not know the difference between vices and virtues, ibid. They reject the medicines of the Holy Scriptures, ibid. Like pregnant women, they suffer aversion to the truth, ibid. Like pigs, they wallow in filth, ibid. The patriarchs of the heretics have stained the purity of the Church with perverse doctrine, 1026. Heretics must be avoided like scorpions, 992. Whence their poisons come, 1026. Their eloquence is Babylon’s golden cup, ibid. The custom of heretics in commending their errors and their cunning in spreading them, 1029. By a knowledge falsely so called, they condemn the truth of doctrines, 585. Although they have written some things that do not conflict with the faith, they are nevertheless judged on account of their many impieties, 589. Heretics pervert the simple decrees of faith with the tricks of dialectical art, ibid. How the books of heretics should be read, 347. Monstrous names, 454. The multitude of associates does not prove a heretic to be Catholic, 199. The false questions and false doctrines of heretics, 714. Heretics exposed and refuted, 958. They criticize the lives of those whose faith they do not dare resist, 582. Women as assistants of heretics, 1030. Heretics condemned by bishops are noted, 1029. Heretics are not of Christ but of the devil, II, 187. One should speak of them as of the Gentiles; from Scripture they seem to affirm what they say, II, 301. Their arguments flowed from the fountain of the Gentiles, 439. The cunning of heretics, 435. The Apostle teaches us to avoid a heretic, not accuse him, 803. Those who wrote against heretics devoted themselves wholly to refuting heresy, not to casting insults, 569. He kills a heretic who allows him to be a heretic, 803. The faction of heretics was put to flight, 547. Their most impious judgment, 694. The enmity of friends is endured more lightly than friendship with heretics, 564. Heretics received into repentance by the supreme pontiffs, 300. They should be granted repentance without baptism, 198. Every heretic, and everyone defending a false doctrine, has an impudent face, III, 450. Heretics who acquiesce in false doctrines promise themselves joy and prosperity, 396. They are fruitless trees and groves without useful fruit, 473. They gather the riches of doctrines to their own harm, 431. The excessive speech and vanity of heretics are reproved, 475. Their net consists of agreeable speech, flattering eloquence, feigned or forced fasts, humble clothing, and imitation of virtues, 465. They labor and afflict themselves in the study of Scripture in vain because they walk in the desert and cannot find the city of truth, 475. They possess a false sacrament and a polluted baptism, 448. Heretics are noted, IV, 140, 141, 773, 859. How great is their pride? 272, 293. It is an injury to the truth, 241. Who are their angels? 286. Their princes are called lions, 843. They are sons of perdition, 670. Lying sons, 407. Makers of idols, 528. They worship their errors, 306. They glory in them, 856. Their heart is a treasure-house of perverse doctrines, 264. The invention of heretics is destruction, 312. They speak through demons, 1000. They prostitute their dwelling place to demons, 672. The doctrines of heretics must be utterly destroyed, 145. They fall quickly, 267. Their doctrine is compared to straw, 1005. They imitate leopards in their variety, 268. Among heretics there is nothing except the gleam of eloquence, a meaning constructed by devilish art, and dead speech, 40. They speak not from the mouth of the Lord but what they feign in their hearts, 1001. They promise many good things, 1005. They do not wish what they teach to be examined by reason, 411. Their speech creeps like cancer, 952. They steal the Savior’s words, 1006. They do not possess the fervor of the Holy Spirit, 253. They alone remained without the grace of the Holy Spirit, 957. On what their whole counsel rests, 429. They attack the Church, 119, and despise it, 137. They agree among themselves in order to destroy the Church, 102. They glory especially if they have insulted the Church, 236. Their pride, ibid. A heretic fears an ecclesiastical man and is terrified at the recollection of him, 295. They reject the doctrine of the Old Testament, 294, 315. They corrupt evangelical truth by perverse interpretation and are the worst tavern-keepers, 25. They misuse the testimony of Scripture, 936. They do not understand Scripture in a manner fitting its majesty, 432. They cannot digest the food of the Scriptures, 376. They have no knowledge of spiritual circumcision, 274. They possess the shadow of virtues, not the truth, 76. The shadows of heretics prevail for a time, 912. Whatever they say is the howling of demons, 246. They judge Christ, 946. If their wars rise up, may we hold Christ’s fortifications, 865. Every heretic contends and fights against the parent, 991. He does not feed on Christ’s body and blood, ibid. Whence his errors come, ibid. Heretics’ thought is to construct accusations against the saints, 971. They promise heavenly things, 286. They surpass the impiety of the pagans, ibid. They labor greatly to deceive the peoples, ibid. They do everything for the sake of payment, 372. They are the devil’s sweetest food, ibid. Samaritans, Jews, and heretics flee Christians as though they were unclean, 775. These flourish in Gaul, ibid. Their luxuries and pleasures, 1003. They do not hope for the future or believe in the resurrection, ibid. They are handed over to the desires of their hearts, 294. They are said to dwell in the Valley of Zion, 310. Their doctrine consists not in meaning but in excessive speech and shouting, ibid. They abandon the Church, 312. Who is their prince? ibid. How long they deceive the simple, 930. They claim for themselves Epicurus’ impious saying, 316. The more prudent someone is in heretical perversity, the farther he withdraws from the Lord, 312. How horrible the heretical people are, 286. Heretics are a leafy and barren tree, V, 873. Heretics are orators devoted to elegance of speech, not to the correction of their hearers, ibid. Heretics are noted, 362, 363. How great is their pride? 205, 476. They are called exceedingly powerful giants, 389. Their prince is the devil, ibid. All are insane, 391. They must be avoided, 393. Like foxes, 124. Why are they called birds and beasts? 459. They dwell in walls and deserts, 403. Their heart is a treasure-house of perverse doctrines, 56. The doctrines of heretics quickly collapse, 127. The conduct of heretics is dissolute, 908. A heretic of good life is more harmful, 947. Conversation with a heretic is dangerous, 954. Like a storm they come against the Church, 448. They perish outside the Church, 380. They imitate ecclesiastical men, 459. Their offering serves not the worship of God but food for demons, ibid. When heretics think that the teachers of the Church have been handed over to them to be devoured, 418. Their weapons must be set alight by teachers with the fire of the Holy Spirit, 455. They accuse God of cruelty, 67. They reject the doctrine of the Old Testament, 178, 199. They do not use testimonies of Scripture that cohere with one another, 380. They are called beasts made savage by vices, 381. As far as they can, they stain the Scriptures, 412. Their practice in the use of Scripture is reproved, 161. They blaspheme God with a shameful sound, 91. Their washings, 146. Heretics drive what should be concealed to be brought out publicly, 882. Their worship is turned into sin, VI, 625. Heretics do not have a voice explaining their judgments but only a sound, 121. The blindness of heretics, 303. God does not receive their gifts, 304. The varying judgments of heretics, 105, 304. Heretics do not care about works, provided that faith is maintained, 38, 468. What deceivers do, 209. They willingly fabricate many things as though by apostolic tradition, 479. They attempt above all to seize those who have been established in the Church, 145. Each heretic has his own gods, 123. They claim for themselves the dignity of the priesthood, 314. They confirm their doctrine by the wood of the cross, 620. They have their own solemnities, 73. The false mysteries of heretics, 80. Their worship is fornication, 43. They are severe toward the poor, not toward the rich, 295. A heretic rarely loves chastity, 78, 99. Some pursue continence and fasts, others pleasures, 262. They slander God, 273, 848. They all sin against the Trinity, 888. We free someone captured by pagans more easily than someone entangled by heretics, 376. Jews and heretics are much worse persecutors than pagans, 374. What is the tribulation of heretics? 529. Heretics should be mourned, 56. Their salvation is not to be despaired of but desired, 13. Heretics are worse than the Gentiles, VII, 84. Their hypocrisy, 40. Heretics are accustomed to claim that they are “gainers of men,” 705. If they perform some sign, they use it to prove the truth of their faith, 422. Heretics fighting against one another bring victory to the Church, 193. The leaven of heretics, 120. There are those who think that all things are animate, 47. The perverse doctrine of heretics and philosophers, 33. Heretics should be admonished only once and twice, 738. Who can be called a heretic? 508. Heretics asserting that Christ was not proclaimed by the prophets, 299. Heretics understood through the chariots of Ephraim, 336. Heretics have many Gospels, 247. Heretics who receive the Gospel of Luke, 298. What is the bread of heretics? 336.

Heresiarchs are called antichrists, VII, 193.

What Hagar signifies, III, 335 ff.

The Hagarenes, also called Saracens, IV, 308, and V, 285.

The name Haggai means “festive,” VI, 739. When Haggai prophesied, 737 ff.

Haila, or Aila, a place of Idumea, VI, 370.

The Halani, I, 913.

The river Halys, I, 345.

Hanes, the last city of Egypt near the Ethiopians and Blemmyes, IV, 403.

Hannibal descended from the Alps, I, 1095. His ranks were cut down, 18. Quintus Fabius Maximus broke Hannibal, exulting in youthful fashion, by his patience, 639. Hannibal devastated Italy but did not dare besiege Rome, 914. He found death by poison in Bithynia, ibid.

Through soothsayers future things are often foretold, IV, 47. It belongs to the Gentiles to listen to soothsayers, haruspices, and the like, 991.

The distinguished poet praises Harpalice, a Thracian virgin, II, 307.

Hasdrubal’s wife, and in her the love of chastity, I, 906. Seizing her children with both hands, she threw herself into the fire, ibid. The same deed was done by Hasdrubal’s wife so that she would not be captured by the Romans, II, 309. The same deed was done by Hasdrubal’s wife. VII, 656.

Hauran, a town of Damascus in the wilderness, V, 599.

The Hebrews read the letter *he* as *a*, and conversely. See under *A*.

Various interpretations by various authors of Daniel’s seventy weeks, VI, 682 and following.

Ebony wood, of black color and extremely precious, V, 313–314.

Hebion and the Hebionites. See *Ebion* and *Ebionites*.

Hebrew is interpreted as “one who crosses over” or “a passer,” I, 432. The Hebrew truth, 231, 311, 315, 518, 758. The Hebrew truth contains what is not found in the Latin and Greek texts, 894. Among the Hebrews there is a forest of ambiguous names and words, II, 475. Apostolic men and the Evangelists use the Hebrew Scriptures, 528. A proverb of the Hebrews when they are in distress, III, 339. Miracles of the Hebrews’ deliverance, IV, 520. Their observance, 96. It is a custom of the Hebrews to give things names from their outcome, 740. Hebrews believing in Christ, 13. The Hebrews’ tradition concerning Cain, V, 316. Their story about King Hiram, 337. Long stories, 658. One must rely on the Hebrews, 498. What is said about a fictitiously converted Hebrew? VII, 735. The opinion of Jerome’s Hebrew teacher concerning certain Hebrew words, 435.

The authentic books of the Hebrews, I, 317. The truth of the Hebrew Scriptures [Col. 0989], II, 527. Certain things are found in the books of the Hebrews that the Seventy do not have, 524. What is not read in the Hebrew volumes, 275. The Hebrews have this custom: they give their volumes names from their beginnings, III, 304. What the Hebrews did not read before the age of thirty, IV, 1095. What is the exposition of the Hebrews? 485. The Hebrews read against themselves, 1009. Some criticize the Hebrew truth, 957. Hebrew manuscripts have different readings, VI, 650. In the exposition of history, the Hebrew truth must be followed, 382. What is the Hebrews’ tradition? 823. The truth of the Hebrew volumes, VII, 15, 578. Translation of certain Hebrew words according to Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Seventy, and the Fifth and Sixth editions, 435, 725. Where the Old Testament reads “Son of man,” the Hebrew has “Son of Adam,” 122. In Hebrew and the other editions, where “Testament” is written, it does not mean Testament but “Covenant,” 439. What Jerome found concerning the Samaritans in the Hebrew volumes, 431. Jerome doubts the truth of the Hebrew codices, ibid. and 437. Why Jerome discusses all the editions of Scripture and the Hebrew volumes, 648–649. Why Hebrew names are pronounced corruptly by the Latins, 734.

The study of the Hebrew language is difficult, I, 906. Its idiom, 310. The truth of the Hebrew language, II, 475. It expresses in the feminine gender what we usually call absolutely and neutrally, 449. The Hebrew language does not have the Greek letter χ, 7. The riches of the Hebrew language, IV, 488. The idiom of Hebrew writing in the syllables *im* and *oth*, 10. The ambiguity of Hebrew speech, 124, 136. The Hebrew idiom, VI, 263, 452. The Jews portray everyone as destined to speak Hebrew, 722. Their language and custom in learning proper names thoroughly, VII, 735.

In Hebron four men were buried: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam—or Caleb, I, 694. Hebron, or Chebron, was founded seven years before Tanis, a city of Egypt, was founded, III, 190.

Ivy and gourds need the support of reeds and poles, I, 755. The nature of ivy, VI, 425. It grows in Palestine and in sandy places, ibid.

What Hedibia asked of Jerome, I, 890. A learned woman.

Helcesi, a village in Galilee, VI, 535.

The mausoleum of Helena, I, 691.

Helena, queen of the Adiabenians, helped the people during a famine with grain, ibid.

Helena, the prostitute who assisted Simon Magus, I, 1031.

Helenopolis, the burial place of Lucian, II, 903.

Eli the priest was holy, I, 1094. His sons fornicated with women in the tabernacle of God, ibid. By being excessively lenient toward his sons, he offended God, 1095. Their impieties and vices, 423. In what did he offend God? 683, 504. Why was Eli punished? II, 718. In what did he offend God? 293. Eli perished by an incurable *ὀπιστοτόνος* [a back-spasm or tetanus-like affliction], V, 14.

Elia, or Aelia, the name of a city built from the remains of the city of Jerusalem, VI, 171. See *Jerusalem*.

Who is the Elijah who was to precede Christ? VI, 970. He was taken alive into heaven, 984–985.

The peaks of Helicon, I, 335.

Heliodorus, I, 9, 15. Why did he leave the desert? 336. Jerome invites Heliodorus to pursue the solitary life, 36. He rebukes him, 15, 32. When the letter to Heliodorus was written, 254. What Jerome says about it, ibid. Heliodorus’s need was assisted, 13. He is brought forward as a witness, 17, 22. In his household there was a twofold dignity of the priesthood, 341. He was also the uncle of Nepotianus, 258. Heliodorus, Jerome’s dearest companion, II, 28. Jerome wishes to keep him in the desert, ibid. and following. What Heliodorus reported to Jerome about Rufinus’s zeal, 15. Heliodorus later became a bishop, II, 526. He is praised, VI, 362.

Another Heliodorus, a presbyter and assistant of Saint Hilary, II, 660.

The territory of Heliopolis, one of the nomes of Egypt, IV, 288.

Helios Mithras was worshiped at Rome, but his image was destroyed, I, 679.

Helcesaeus, according to the Hebrews the father of Nahum and himself a prophet, VI, 535. Helcesaeus, a village of Galilee, ibid.

The tomb of Elisha, I, 703.

Helvidius was at Rome, II, 224. He wanted virgins and married women to have the same glory, 229. He said that certain things had been falsified in the Greek manuscripts, 213, 224. Helvidius is proved to have said things contradictory to one another, 207. He calls Tertullian as a witness and presents the words of Bishop Victorinus, 225.

Heluza, or Eluza, the name of a city situated in the territory of Moab, IV, 186.

Hemath. See *Emath*.

Heopemptus, bishop, I, 630.

Heraclas governed the Alexandrian Church after Demetrius, II, 893, 907.

[Col. 0990] Heraclianus the tyrant, II, 804. Heraclianus, also governor of Africa, forgetting that his honor depended upon another’s command, V, 329. Accused of revolutionary designs, he lost both his honor and his life, ibid.

Heraclitus was obscure, II, 487. He is scarcely understood, 238.

What Heraclius the deacon reported to Jerome, I, 408.

Hercules was strong, I, 193. Hercules was born from adultery, II, 398. From this came his great strength, ibid. To wrench the club from Hercules’ hand requires great strength, III, 301.

Herennius, II, 471.

The hedgehog (*herinacius*) is a small, elusive animal, weighed down by the bristles of its spines, I, 983. The rich are compared to the hedgehog, or *hericius*, IV, 259. The hedgehog is a spiny animal, full of thorns, wounding whatever it touches, VI, 713. The nature of the hedgehog, VII, 42.

The timidity of Hermagoras, I, 281.

Hermacoras, II, 559.

What Hermione says about women, II, 317.

Hermippus the Peripatetic, II, 821.

Hermogenes, II, 867.

Hermotimus, II, 566.

Hero, bishop. Naseas succeeds him, I, 609.

Herod, son of Antipater, or Herod the Great, calls Strato’s Tower Caesarea. Why? I, 697. He calls Samaria Sebaste. Why? ibid. Herod names a town after his father, 679. He succeeded to the Jewish government after the rulers from the tribe of Levi, IV, 996. The same Herod, son of Antipater, was appointed king over the Jews by Augustus, VII, 175. The reason is explained, ibid. He was struck by an angel, 225.

Another Herod. What the ancient History relates about Herod, Herodias, and others, VII, 101–102. Certain Latins believed Herod to be Christ, 175. He was said to have crucified Christ, 133. Exiled to Lugdunum, he had his brother as successor to the kingdom, 16.

What Herodias did to John, II, 569.

Herodotus, I, 323. What he reports about the Huns, 264. Herodotus and Berossus relate that in Sennacherib’s expedition the Assyrians perished from pestilence, IV, 461. Herodotus wrote most fully about Cambyses and all of Egypt, V, 352.

The Heruli, I, 913.

Hesiod is praised, I, 256. While lamenting human births, he rejoices at a funeral, 342.

Hesychius, Hilarion’s friend, II, 28. He was devoted to Hilarion’s veneration, 29. He searches for Hilarion throughout the world, 35. At last he finds him, ibid. He is sent to Palestine, 38. Hilarion’s body is stolen, 40. Hesychius is praised, 523.

The Hebrew letter *heth* has a double aspiration and is represented by the Seventy with the Greek χ, III, 7, 317, 366.

The Etruscans: who were they? IV, 816. Colonists of the Lydians, ibid.

The Hexapla. See *Origen*.

The nocturnal rites called the Hyacinthian rites, II, 308.

Jebus, or Jebus and Salem, former names of Jerusalem, IV, 595.

Jeremiah. See *Jeremias*.

Jeroboam. See *Jeroboam*.

Hieria, a region of India, III, 199, 258.

Jerome was born to Christian parents and baptized at Rome, I, 29, 42. His golden intellect, 405. All Rome’s studies and interests were united in Jerome, 196. By the judgment of all, he was deemed worthy of the highest priesthood, ibid. Jerome’s solitude, 14, 29. The history of his solitude, 940. Jerome, doing penance of his own will in the desert, 42. He is harassed by heretics, ibid. Shut up in a little cell, he mourns his past vices and strives to avoid present ones, 782. Jerome’s temptations in the desert, 93. His austerities, fasts, and tears, ibid. He does not know whether his homeland still exists, 17. What he cries out against the barbarity of the place of his solitude, 45. Every day he sought food by his hands and his own sweat, ibid. A barbarous half-language prevailed in his solitude, 18. Jerome’s illnesses, 433, 610. His body was weak, 9. Consumed in the desert by bodily sickness and mental distress, 17. Jerome had lost his virginity, 232. He admits that he fell in adolescence, 19. To whom he entrusted his sister, ibid. Jerome rejoices in his sister’s perseverance in goodness, 17. He does not fear the judgment of those who slander him, ibid. He recounts the history of his misfortune, 114. His intense devotion to reading secular authors and his aversion to reading the prophets, ibid. With great labor he assembled a library for himself, ibid. He remembers what he had learned, 427.

Jerome and Pammachius were fellow students, I, 400. What did they laugh about? ibid. Jerome’s teachers, 523. Who were his catechists? 238. His praises, 762. In what is he better than others? 935. Jerome gives thanks to God that he is worthy to be hated by the world, 197. He calls Jerusalem his homeland, ibid. He came to Rome with Paulinus and Epiphanius, 955. What did he do at Rome with Damasus? 907. He lived at Rome for a full three years, [Col. 0991] I, 194. Jerome often disputed at Rome with a monk whom he ridicules, 239. There he endured a horned syllogism, 413. He considers himself much more glorious than a worldly philosopher, 535. Jerome built a monastery and a lodging house, 403. Why did he send his brother Paulinianus back to his homeland? ibid. The frequent arrival of pilgrims at Jerome’s dwelling, 433. He supported many brothers, 757. Seized by a very serious illness, he entered the threshold of death, ibid. He is called a falsifier, 307. What was more ancient than he? 534. His judicious judgment, 685. He used to seek the friendship of good men, 404. Jerome did not seek friendships with the powerful, 499. He could not endure impiety against God, 351. He publicly criticized all doctrines opposed to the Church, 348. At the urging of Saint Chromatius, Jerome wished to remain silent, 524. He learned the Scriptures from illustrious men of the Church, 720. He was always devoted to the Hebrew language, ibid. He followed the judgment of his predecessors, 519. By censuring vices, he became a criminal in the eyes of others, 782. The walls echoed curses against him, ibid. After sin, Jerome does not abolish repentance, 784. He was not a teacher of falsehood, 751. He does not wish to dispute with rancor in his heart, 632. How Jerome read books that had been condemned in certain respects, 347. He was not an Origenist, 524. Origen’s doctrines are brought against him, 348. He was always opposed to those doctrines, 523. Why does he persecute him? 532. He collected Origen’s books, 524. He translated from Greek a book against Saint John Chrysostom, 756. In the matter of the latter he was deceived, ibid. John of Jerusalem wanted to kill him, 958. He is falsely called a heretic, 43. His faith was shared with Peter of Alexandria and Damasus, ibid. He possessed zeal for the faith against all heresies, 540. He never yielded to heretical depravity, 349. The heretics did not love him, 346. Jerome could not patiently listen to the blasphemies of heretics, 727. The heretics pursue him with hatred, 1065. He is forced to leave the desert with his companions because of the heretics, 44. He was intensely averse to the Jews, 524.

Jerome patiently endured Rufinus’s incredible hostility, I, 735. Jerome wishes to be judged—or rather to err or stumble through affection—rather than deceive a friend by flattery, 327. He fears falling into the crime of agreeing merely to please, 610. Jerome did not deceive through flattery, nor overthrow anyone by slippery fraud, 794. He does not render verbal thanks because of any benefit received by himself, 501. Jerome is slandered in many matters, 195 and following. He excuses and defends himself modestly and religiously, ibid. He shows his detractors that he can say whatever comes into his mouth, 790. He wove his speeches with the flowers of Scripture, ibid. His tongue outruns the hands of the scribes, ibid. Jerome can bite back, but he prefers to be a disciple of Christ, 240. He fears his detractors, 269. He rebukes them, ibid. Jerome answers his detractors lest he be accused of pride, 132. For good counsel and instruction, he is marked by everyone’s finger, 134. He fears the hidden judgment of readers, 508. Jerome’s grief at the death of Saint Paula, 724. He invented nothing in describing her virtues, ibid. Jerome’s gifts to Lucinus, 435. He received a small cap from Paulinus, to whom he gives thanks, 535.

Jerome’s modesty, I, 190, 235, 280, 255. His humility, 19, 25, 210, 319. From childhood Jerome tried to avoid nothing so much as pride, 455. He is not guilty of boasting, 222. He preferred to be endangered in reputation rather than in faith, 533. His love of peace and silence, 519. Jerome’s pure faith and sincerity, 531. His adherence to the chair of Peter, 29. Jerome’s zeal for strengthening the Christian faith, 152. He always held in reverence not wordy rusticity but holy simplicity, 318. Jerome’s reverence for the ministers of the Church, 938. He does not venerate bishops unless they are orthodox in faith, 520. His virtue and constancy, ibid. He judges virtues not by sex but by the mind, 955. Meditation on the Scriptures had become Jerome’s true nature, ibid. In many matters he simply confessed his ignorance, 463. In comparison with whom Jerome admits himself most unlearned, 428. Jerome’s pure doctrine from adolescence, 1040. He always made it his concern to tell his hearers what he had learned publicly in the Church, ibid. He did not follow the arguments of philosophers but adhered to the simplicity of the apostles, ibid. He challenges his adversaries to examine all his writings in their entirety. Why? ibid. His mind was sincere and irreproachable, ibid. He preferred to correct an error rather than persevere in a corrupt opinion, ibid. Jerome possessed many codices of the sacred Library, 15. He had pupils devoted to the art of copying manuscripts, ibid. He asked that books he did not possess be copied and sent to him, 15. Jerome’s love of study, 524. He was considered eloquent in the Syriac and Greek languages, 44. Some of his works are listed, 349. The time of his writings is noted, 453.

Jerome’s policy in translating the Scriptures, I, 753. In translating the Scriptures he invented nothing of his own, 754. It is pure and sincere, ibid. Jerome translated not the words but the sense, 309. In his translation he preserves the truth of the meanings [Col. 0992] rather than the order of the words, 752. The prologue to the book of Hebrew Names, 523. Why does he refer the reader back to his little prefaces to the divine books? 753. He translated the canon of the Hebrew truth, 434. His little preface to Damasus on the homilies of the Song of Songs, 522. He interrupted his exposition of Ezekiel’s Temple in order to write to Demetrias, 976. He translated sixteen books of the prophets from Hebrew into Latin, 235. He translated Job into our language, ibid. He commends this translation, ibid. He sent Domnio certain works on the prophets, ibid. Jerome restored the New Testament to the authority of the Greek, 434. His interpretation containing prefixed asterisks and obeli, 751. He published another without these signs, ibid. He acted in the office of a commentator, 224. He desired to write commentaries on the Scriptures, 316. A disturbance arose among the people during the reading of Jerome’s interpretation, 106. He expounded the divine books to certain virgins, 196. He asks that an interpretation of David’s Psalms be transferred to him, 14. He carefully corrected the edition of the Seventy translators, 434. Through the speed of dictation he had omitted some words, 316. He wrote for the benefit of the Church, not to insult priests, 422. He despises the elegance of rhetorical art, 792. He kindled and assisted the zeal of holy men, 408. Jerome’s small works were immediately disseminated among the public, 233. Consequently he was unable to correct certain things, ibid. When he translated Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, 309. He wanted to write about avarice, 118. Jerome is asked why he places examples from secular literature in his small works, 424. How he used secular literature in his small works, 425. He wrote against Helvidius on the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Mary, 105. A book against him is cited, 231. Why did he not give this book a title? ibid. Some unlearned people are said to have inscribed it “On Authors,” ibid. A false rumor attributed the translation of certain works to Jerome, 433. Jerome’s book *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, 753. His books on preserving virginity are noted, 915. Jerome’s book to Heliodorus was learned by heart, 465. Two of his books were sent to Fabiola, 446. Many letters were demanded from him at once, 533. What Jerome observes in translating the Paschal Letters of Theophilus, 582. Theophilus’s letters were not returned to Jerome, 519. Jerome translated Epiphanius’s letters into Latin, 305. He marked the sense of the chapters at the side of the page, ibid. He translated Origen’s works, 348. Jerome does not reject everything Origen wrote, 534. He is accused of suddenly changing his opinion, ibid. He refused to translate Origen’s bad books, 530. He had delivered a declamation, 511. Jerome prays that, when he contends with Augustine, truth may prevail, 738. He feared answering a Catholic bishop insolently, 639. He retains in his mind nothing that differs from his lips, 640. His breast was sincere toward Augustine, ibid. He was careful not to injure Christian reputation, 633. Augustine praises Jerome’s writings, 404. What Augustine requests from Jerome’s works, 781. He asks Augustine for writings not of controversy but of charity, 760.

Jerome’s order of departure from the city of Rome, II, 551. His companions and the places through which he passed, ibid. He saw and learned many things on the journey, ibid. He was received by Epiphanius and enjoyed communion with Paulinus, ibid. Jerome as a young man stayed in Syria, 42. From adolescence he was enclosed in a monastery, 464. Jerome’s dreams, 486. He relates many things about himself, 650.

Jerome says that he remembers what he did as a boy, II, 486 and following. He was dragged from his grandmother’s lap to his teacher Orbilius, ibid. Jerome visited the monasteries of Nitria, 551. His choice, 13. He is compelled to become foolish, 295. Jerome invokes the Holy Trinity, 206. Jerome was ordained by Paulinus. What did he say to him? 485. His hospitality, 546. He did not receive heretics, ibid. Jerome and his companions are falsely called witnesses, 449. He admits that he had been deceived, 417, 541. Jerome speaks with fear of God and wishes to be heard, 418. His just excuses, 461. Jerome’s friends were sent to the West, 554. He cannot pass with a deaf ear over an injury to the apostles and prophets, 388–389. How he followed Origen, Didymus, and Apollinaris, 471. He was with Didymus for one month, 642. What he especially kept away from himself, 560. He is called Origen’s disciple and a traitor, 628. He is forbidden to enter the Lord’s Cave, 452. He clears himself of the charge that he was said to be tearing apart the Church, ibid. He refutes the accusation of heresy, 477. Jerome defends himself with all his strength against that suspicion, 539. He cannot obey heretics, 570. He proves this by examples, 695. Jerome does not hate people but errors, 695. His friends accuse him of hypocrisy, 562. While imprudently offering peace, he took up the Church’s internal wars, ibid. He is thought to be Rufinus’s fellow initiate, ibid. Of what crime is Jerome accused? 608. Rufinus spared this man; although he could have killed him, he did not, ibid. Jerome seeks not his condemnation but his conversion, 543. Jerome’s purpose is not to accuse others but [Col. 0993] to defend himself, 491. If Rufinus is to be believed, Jerome sought human favor, 600. In replying, he preserves the rights of friendship, 468. He despises his detractors, 13.

Jerome’s modesty, II, 563. His moderation, 468, 252. Jerome sometimes feared entering the basilicas of the martyrs, 389. There was no ambition or avarice in Jerome, 489. Jerome’s patience, 572. He yields to one who flatters him and does not fear one who threatens, ibid. Where there is one faith, there he has peace, ibid. He would rather be accused than accuse, and suffer injury than inflict it, 534. Though injured, Jerome preserves the rights of friendship, 563. It is lighter for him to endure a friend’s hostility than the friendship of heretics, ibid. He preferred to speak about the things of God rather than about injuries, 446. He cannot be accused of impatience, 408. Jerome’s pure faith and sincerity, 416. His zeal for the faith, 415. Jerome’s confidence, ibid. A story about Jerome, 632. From where did he draw what he said about marriage? 318. He is entrusted with copying a Hebrew volume, 833. He was trilingual, 416, 537. Jerome’s various kinds of knowledge, ibid. Theology, 427. His small works translated into Greek, 952. Jerome’s translations are pure, 464.

Jerome’s policy in translating the Scriptures, II, 555. Why Jerome’s prefaces to the Old Testament are cited, 419 and following. Why Jerome omitted part of the books of the Hebrew Questions, 613. He changed nothing of the Hebrew truth, 525. Why did he interpret the Books of Days [Chronicles]? 524. When Jerome wrote his commentaries on Ecclesiastes and the Epistle to the Ephesians, 424. He interpreted the words and names of the New Testament, 643. The Greeks accepted Jerome’s new translation, 418. When he wrote on the Epistle to the Ephesians, 479, 459. Rufinus censures Jerome’s translation, which is from the Hebrew, 613. He is forbidden to read the Scriptures because of the crowded place and the gathering of holy men, 487. Jerome corrected and translated the Seventy, 518. He expounds these matters at the gathering of the brothers and recites their Psalms through continual meditation, ibid. All his treatises are woven from testimonies of these sources; his commentaries on the prophets expound both his own edition and that of the Seventy, ibid. Jerome’s elegant reply, 556. He wanted to write against the volumes of Eusebius written under the name of Pamphilus, 416. He wanted to write a Church History, 41. He explains his plan for the order he intended to follow, ibid. He dares not expound the words of Scripture lest Helvidius slander him, 330. The epilogue of Jerome’s disputation against Jovinian, 382. He inveighs against him, 379, 382. Jerome’s books against Jovinian are criticized, 634. He wrote *On Illustrious Men*, from Christ’s Passion to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, 821. To whom Jerome wrote, 650. His letter to Rufinus was not returned in a friendly spirit, 564. What did he write to a certain Vincentius? 642. A letter falsely attributed to Jerome, 417, 545, 555. It contains falsehoods, 517. Letters translated by Jerome, 468. The translation of Theophilus’s letters made by him, 545. One book of Didymus translated by him, 939. Jerome, as Origen’s translator, removed many things, 653. He translated many things from the same author without envy toward others, 501.

How he interpreted him, 514. He translated his homilies, 417, 542. Jerome used to teach grammar to little boys in Bethlehem, 636. On the Mount of Olives, Cicero’s dialogues were copied out for him, ibid. Jerome often played in the schools with turns of satirical speaking, 160. He had learned fictitious controversies, 409.

Jerome’s childhood in the time of the emperor Constantius, III, 195. Jerome’s Hebrew teacher, under whose instruction he thoroughly read the sacred Scriptures, 393, 412, 424, 428, 438, 459, 466, 470, 471. Jerome does not approve his Hebrew teacher’s exposition, 428, 459. He often did not approve what he translated into Latin, 195, 207. Against his own conscience, he refused to follow the streams of opinions while abandoning the fountain of truth, 381. So as not to deter the reader’s zeal by excessive novelty, he sometimes followed the earlier interpreters, ibid. He does not criticize the errors of the Seventy translators, 303. He adapted himself to the usage of the Seventy in matters that did not differ greatly from the Hebrew, 381. At Rome he had read Ecclesiastes to the holy Blesilla in order to urge her to despise this world, 381.

Jerome’s practice in writing commentaries, IV, 994. His adversaries slander him for this, ibid. He does not approve Saint Basil’s commentaries on a certain passage of Isaiah, 98. About thirty years earlier he himself had written a treatise on the vision of this prophet, ibid. He testifies that he had Gregory of Nazianzus as a teacher in the sacred Scriptures, ibid. He wrote on the Epistle to the Ephesians, 833. He adds other volumes published against Rufinus and Jovinian, ibid. He had written on Matthew and a book to Algasia before expounding Isaiah, 506. He had written on Zechariah before expounding Isaiah, 630. He solves the question proposed to him by Eustochium concerning the eight verses of Psalm XIII, 665. He is constrained in understanding certain doctrines and the book of Revelation, 767. Jerome must labor so that a Latin reader may understand the Hebrew etymology briefly [Col. 0994], 840. He wishes to kill with the arrows of Scripture, 244. He argues against the Jews, 209. He rebukes Jewish critics, 396. He did not accept Hebrew traditions, 224. He rebukes the Seventy translators, 707. He doubts the translation of the Seventy, 1068. He doubts the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, 1073. He rebukes the false interpretation of certain passages, 532. Jerome’s humility and modesty, 206, 315. He seeks the testimony of a few, 493. An enemy of error, not of people, 967. He does not condemn in martyrs what he himself refuses to follow, 975. He inveighs against the Arians, 166. He avoids slander, 841. He marks out certain slanderers, 923. He lived in Palestine, 119. Jerome’s Hebrew teacher, 172, 220, 318.

While still a boy, Jerome used to enter and walk around the crypts of the martyrs, V, 468. He describes them beautifully, ibid. Jerome wrote against Helvidius, 538. He did not always translate in one and the same way, 527. He proposes and solves a question, 649. He does not concern himself with faults of expression, and so forth, 472. He admits the obscurity of Scripture, 475. He preserves the customary manner of speaking for the sake of the unlearned, 590. Concerning Jerome’s kinds of expression and his modesty, 201, 298, 452, 462. He disciplines himself, 469. He makes a Socratic saying his own, 510. He cites a work by an author of his own age who was not obscure. He avoids rivals and slanderers, 387, 587. He rebukes the envious, 410.
