Jerome prays for the remission of his sins, VI, 531. What he observes in interpreting the Scriptures, 447. His humility, 361, 386, 443, 452. Jerome’s devotion to the Hebrew language, 773. He does not speak from his own opinion, 550. He willingly endures illnesses, provided that he is free from lust, 263. He doubts the wickedness of the Jews, 474. He guards against the hatred of bishops, 719. He was an eyewitness to the overthrow of Judea, 692.

What Jerome as a young man devoted himself to, VII, 408. He was devoted to study from adolescence, 539. He went to Alexandria to question Didymus about the sacred Scriptures, ibid. The harsh sound of Hebrew reading sullied Jerome’s elegance of Latin, 483. His tireless devotion to the Hebrew language, ibid. What faith did he have concerning Christ? 724–725. How great was his love of truth? ibid. His modesty, 470. The cause for admiration in Jerome, 136. His illnesses, 485. His monastery, 585. Jerome’s choice: what was it? 635. He follows Origen, 369. His devotion to Origen’s Hexapla, 734. Jerome’s custom of returning to the original books of Scripture, 429. He is compelled to change the order of reading, 555. He is falsely criticized, 508. Jerome had ceased reading secular authors and did not wish to use them, 425. From what time did he cease reading Tully and the other authors? 485. Jerome expounded Leviticus orally, not in writing, to Paula and Eustochium, 723. He had decided to expound the book of Exodus, 211. Jerome does not wish his small works to be easily handed over to the malicious and envious, 539. What number of verses Jerome wrote each day, 587. At Rome he wrote a book on the virginity of the Blessed Mary, 395. A little book *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, 218. Jerome had not yet written on Zechariah when he published Matthew, 160. Jerome’s books of Hebrew Questions on the Old Testament, 245. His Hebrew Questions on Genesis, 672.

At Athens a hierophant becomes chaste through an everlasting weakness, I, 905. The hierophants of the Athenians, II, 320.

Hilarion saw Jerusalem for only one day. Why? I, 322. Where was Hilarion born? II, 14. His parents were devoted to idols, ibid. His natural and spiritual gifts, ibid. He goes to Antony and sets him before himself as an example to imitate, ibid. He distributes his possessions, ibid. Where did he withdraw? ibid. His fasting, temptations, and exercises, 16. Prostrate on the ground, he signed the cross of Christ on his forehead against the attacks of demons, ibid. His mind is drawn away from prayer, ibid. What sort of cell did he have? ibid. His austerities and food, 17. He knew the sacred Scriptures by heart and recited them, ibid. He does not fear robbers, ibid. and following. He was the founder and teacher of monastic life in Syria, 19. Walking with the brothers, he interpreted the Scriptures, 21. He scorns gifts and presents, ibid. He is demanded for punishment as a sorcerer, 23. His fame spread through distant provinces, 24. All the monks hasten competitively toward him, 26. What was he like in Antony’s estimation? ibid. The people, gathered in honor of Venus, encounter him and profess the Christian faith, ibid. From the odor of their clothing he recognized each person’s vices, ibid. He grieves over the crowds coming to him, 29. He recognized Antony’s death before it had been announced, ibid. His marvelous contempt for glory, ibid. He obtains rain and, with blessed oil, frees farmers from the bites of serpents, 29 and following. He is sought for execution, ibid. The people of Gaza had obtained from Julian the deaths of Hilarion and Hesychius, 33. As a young man Hilarion wrote a copy of the Gospel book in his own hand, ibid. He casts out a demon, ibid. In what did he rejoice? 34. He flees to the inland regions and, while hidden, is exposed by a demoniac, ibid. He is called the prophet of the Christians, ibid. He accepted nothing from anyone, [Col. 0995] ibid. He grieved that, while his own tongue was silent about him, miracles were speaking, 36. The swelling sea stands still at Hilarion’s prayers and gradually subsides again, ibid. At his command pirates are carried unwillingly to the shore, ibid. Nearly two hundred people were cured by him, 37. His flight from glory does not allow him to remain long in the same place—not from fickleness of mind, ibid. In place of a testament he wrote a brief letter to Hesychius, 39. Many religious people came from Paphos to the sick Hilarion, ibid. What does he command concerning his body? ibid. His hope and death, ibid. After ten months his body is found intact and his clothing unharmed, ibid. A marvelous dispute between the Palestinians and Cypriots concerning Hilarion, ibid.

Saint Hilary and his orthodox books, I, 688. Saint Hilary is elevated on the Gallic buskin, 325. He is adorned with the flowers of Greece, ibid. At times he is wrapped in long periods and is inaccessible to simpler readers, ibid. Saint Hilary’s lengthy book on the Synods, 14. Jerome copied the same book on the Synods in his own hand, ibid. He imitated Quintilian’s books in style and number, 430. In the little book he wrote against Dioscorus, he showed what his literary ability could achieve, ibid. What did Hilary translate from Greek? 310. Which works did he translate? 348. He translated Origen and Eusebius, 753. Hilary, Origen’s translator, 532. Hilary, 223, 232. Hilary is called a pillar of the Church, II, 460. When Hilary returned from exile and battle, the Church of Gaul embraced him, 392. Hilary’s falsified book and a story about him, 635. He is called a most eloquent man and the trumpet of the Latin language against the Arians, 504, 510. Saint Hilary translated a work of Origen, VI, 479. Hilary of Poitiers was born at Poitiers, VII, 427. His encomium, ibid.

Hilary, a cleric of the Roman Church, II, 194. The same Hilary is called the Deucalion of the world, 199. Before the Council of Ariminum he accepted those baptized by the Manichaeans and approved the baptism of Ebion, 200. Hilary’s pamphlets on rebaptizing heretics, ibid. What is related about the same man? 194, 200.

A kind of measure, V, 43–44 and 576 and following.

The neighing of a horse has a twofold meaning in the Scriptures, VI, 315–316.

A hippocentaur appears to Antony in the desert, II, 6. He is questioned and replies, ibid.

What Hippocrates demands from his disciples, I, 268. He prescribes many things for them, ibid. His bonds, ibid. Hippocrates is praised, 851. His oath, 268. What does Hippocrates teach about an obese body? II, 339. His bonds, 239, 390.

Whether and why the Seventy translated *Hippodrome* for *Ephratha*, III, 360.

Hippolytus, I, 232, 529. Hippolytus, a very eloquent man, concerning whom he wrote, 434. Hippolytus published a work of his own against the Gentiles, 907. Hippolytus, II, 431. Hippolytus’s opinion concerning the seventy weeks, V, 689 and following. His commentaries on Zechariah, VI, 788. Hippolytus the Martyr, VII, 2.

Hir means “watchful,” I, 453.

The Hebrews fabulously relate that Hiram lived a thousand years, V, 337–338.

Hyrcanus, prince of the Jews, IV, 28. Hyrcanus, likewise high priest, placed a diadem on his head, V, 251. He was beheaded by Herod, 688.

Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, brothers, fought in an internal revolt, V, 687.

The quarrel between Hyrcanus and Alexander, V, 49.

Hyrcanus’s old men cast the half-alive to dogs and birds, II, 335.

Hirtius proposes to Cicero that his sister be married, II, 315.

The goat, as a type of Christ, carries the people’s sins into the wilderness, II, 733. Why the goat is offered in sacrifices, V, 533.

The swallow knows how to treat its young with its own eye-healing celandine (*chelidonia*), III, 444.

To sing beside the Ismenus, II, 523.

Spain trembles daily from the incursions of enemies, I, 913. Whatever others have suffered once, Spain suffers continually through fear, ibid. Spain is called Iberia and Celtiberia, IV, 817. The heresy of Lusitania and Spain, 761.

Where the Spaniards come from, and why they are called Iberians, V, 311.

History is called “law” by Paul, I, 814. What is read in ancient histories, 210. What is the true law of history? II, 209. What the ancient History relates, 412. Sacred histories are older than profane ones, IV, 9. It is one thing to write history and another to write prophecy, 983. Who are the writers of natural history? 960. History proceeds along the same lines as tropology, V, 482. Who are the writers of barbarian histories? 651. History is sometimes woven metaphorically, VI, 658. The order of history is not always maintained in praises of God, especially in Psalms III and LI, 245. Not everything narrated in history can be taken tropologically, 395. When history contains impossibility or shamefulness, we are carried to higher meanings, VII, 160. Error [Col. 0996] arising from ignorance of history, 16.

Historians should set Thucydides, Sallust, Herodotus, and others before themselves as models, I, 322. The historians whose knowledge is necessary for understanding the final parts of Daniel, V, 621–622.

A single actor introduces different characters, I, 193.

The various interpretation of the word “today,” VI, 36.

*Hodoeporicon*, I, 692.

The difference between a holocaust and sacrifices, or offerings, IV, 660, and V, 568.

Homer was endowed with wisdom, I, 256. Homer invents Death and Sleep as brothers, 342. What he relates about Nestor, 258. Homer is the herald of Achilles’ merits, II, 13. A Homeric proverb, 568.

Who are called *Homerocentones*? I, 275.

He is a murderer who, although able to rescue a person from death, does not rescue him, II, 789. If you hate your brother, you are a murderer, 534. To punish murderers is not bloodshed but the administration of the laws, IV, 987.

Murder often arises from hatred, I, 27. Death is the worst of all things, II, 534. The murder of Judas is worse than all murders, VI, 301.

The human being fashioned from mud, I, 419. No human being is polluted by nature, 741. All are equally called to the grace of Christ, ibid. The perfect composition of the whole human being, 130. The misery of humanity before Christ’s coming, 333. What befits a prudent person, 349. The inner person is lifted by desire toward heavenly things, 629. He restrains every impulse of pleasure by reason, ibid. Through the outer person the vices of the inner person are shown, ibid. The life of people living in the world is described, 193. What does it mean to take a person out of a person and to be established in a body without a body? 1026. Crowds of people, and offices and greetings to be avoided, 502. Some preach that God gave the human being a part of his own nature, II, 422. The human being belongs to nature, but is a sinner by will, 743. Every human being is vanity, whether living in the body or living in virtues, 765. There are many faces among human beings, and likewise diverse hearts, 782. In the human being male and female are included, 283. He was expelled from paradise by the devil’s counsels, 241. The human being wavers in an uncertain condition, and while he fears nothing, suffers a storm in calm weather, 765. He is never secure, but always fears shipwreck in tranquility, 705. Humanity’s glory is increased in Christ, not its nature changed, 371. A person devoted to Christ can die but cannot be overcome, 48. All his strength withers and perishes if he is abandoned by God’s help, 891. Human labors are always uncertain, 418. Their pursuits have opposite ends, ibid. The human desire to know hidden things, 5. True human wisdom, 708. A human gift is not to be despised, 250. Human excrement is useful in medical treatments according to Galen, 331. Human life after the Flood was not shortened to one hundred and twenty years, III, 315, 318. The human being was not created by God insensible and foolish; rather, free choice is left to him for choosing good and avoiding evil, 442. The human being was born for this purpose: that, understanding his Creator, he should venerate him with fear and honor and by the performance of his commandments, 496. Humanity was appointed a tenant and guest of the world, to enjoy the brief span of its life and, with hope of a longer age cut short, to regard all that it possesses as though it were about to depart elsewhere, 412. The inner person arises within us after the fourteenth year of puberty, 424. The foolish person never thinks of the future, but delights in present and passing things as though they were great and everlasting, 425. People swept along by the error and whirlwind of the age do not understand the ruin of their sins, and rejoice in things more worthy of mourning, 396. We should not care what people say about us, 446.

The human being is defined as a rational animal, IV, 37. All human beings are by nature children of God, but by their own fault become strangers, 18. The first period of human wisdom is when we leave childhood and arrive at the rational age, 77. In Scripture this age is called “morning,” ibid. Among human beings the thirtieth year, and among animals the third, is the most vigorous, 187. All the people whom histories relate are reckoned as almost nothing, 492. People pass from one purpose to another, 325. Every person seems just to himself, 349. Their character is displayed through different living creatures, 259. Beasts are called those devoted to the world, 404. Human worthlessness is perceived through death, 177. Human frailty and continual mutability are compared with hay, 482. Strength even without Christ is considered weakness, 955. How great God’s help is, and how fragile human nature, 1066. Human perversity is prone to excuse itself, 853. Why does God abandon the human being to his own will? 969. Those who preach perfect justice in humanity are condemned, 999. A delirious old woman fabricating the claim that a human being can be without sin, 957. Certain wild human beings, 175. “Human beings who do not exist,” V, 911. The image of God was made in the human being at creation, and likeness in baptism, 331. Two inner persons, 951. Where no individual person is specified, “human being” signifies any person, VI, 761. The human being flees from God, 396. Human miseries and sins, [Col. 0997] 451. Their cruelty, 129. The formation of the human being in the womb over nine months, VII, 466. The inner and outer human being, 625. The members of the inner person, 563. The solution to the question why God did not make the human being necessarily good and upright, 756–757. The whole human race is discussed in the singular number, 452. People having a good testimony even among their adversaries, 721. The sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings, 75. Who are understood by “human beings and beasts”? 480. Human frailty cannot endure the sight of greater glory, 131. What is suitable for all the ages of human life, 713 ff. Two angels attend each individual person, 280. Human judgment is deceptive, 249.

Many things are honorable in reality but shameful in name, and conversely, IV, 550.

Honor taken for almsgiving or for a gift, I, 904. Where there is no honor, many inconveniences follow, 33. However illustrious, honor becomes worthless in the crowd, 398. Do not be puffed up by honors, but esteem them lightly for the sake of God’s faith, 691. With what honors the whole world is filled, 398. What is “honor” in Scripture? VII, 110.

We ought to honor those set over us, but not place our hope in them, VI, 518.

Honorius and Arcadius, highly religious emperors, I, 913.

Canonical hours, I, 121, 686, 712, 691.

Horace has nothing in common with the Psalter, I, 114. What he prescribes for the interpreter, 309. A remarkable saying of Horace, 1026. The poems of Horace, 17, 24, 283, 506. Horace mocks the appetite for food, II, 342.

Why barley flour was added to the drink of the *eligmos* (τοῦ ἐλιγμοῦ), VI, 342.

Hormiscus: a torque or necklace, III, 515.

How the steps of Ahaz’s sundial were constructed by mechanical art, IV, 469 ff.

Where the Horraeans lived, VI, 364.

How exhorting and persuading differ, I, 36.

The speech of Hortensius grew up in his father’s bosom, I, 682. Hortensius, husband of Marcia, II, 312.

The gardens of Adonis, IV, 774.

The place of Topheth, watered by the springs of Siloam, supplied the delights of gardens, III, 300.

Hosanna. See Osanna.

Hosea. See Osee.

The commendation and duties of hospitality, II, 546. The duty of hospitality should be one thing in a bishop and another in a layman, VII, 701.

We should invite guests not with light speech and superficial lips, but hold them with the full ardor of our mind, I, 942. They present themselves together with our profit, ibid. What is to be feared in rejecting guests, II, 546.

Kill the enemy while he is small, I, 92. Whether enemies should be deceived by fraud, V, 194.

Whoever offers a mutilated sacrifice is guilty of sacrilege, I, 684. The Lord wants you yourself as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God, 796. Why God sought sacrifices and the offering of victims, IV, 21. Human sacrifices offered to Saturn, 544. Those who lay upon the hides of sacrificial victims in order to learn the future through dreams, 774. What the priests received from the sacrifices, VI, 949 ff. Their allegory, ibid.

An exposition of Hulli the patriarch is reported from Origen, II, 469.

The misery of human life, I, 1057. The variety of human affairs, and the stability of nothing, 342. What is a human day? 886. The frailty of the human condition, IV, 473, and V, 72, etc. Human sacrifices offered to Saturn, IV, 544.

The shoulder signifies work, VI, 65.

The humbler someone is, the more exalted he is, I, 396. The least among all becomes the greatest of all, 692. The more someone casts himself down, the more Christ raises him up, ibid. We should neither wish to appear excessively religious nor more humble than necessary, 111. However much you abase yourself, you will not be humbler than Christ, 404. God raises the humble and despised into the kingdom, II, 779.

Humility is a Christian virtue, I, 210. It is commended, 36. False humility should be avoided, 112. By walking through the lowest places, we climb to the highest, 210. The least is recognized as greater, and humility is transformed into exaltation, II, 759. God changes the powerful through humility, 779. Through humility we ascend into heaven, IV, 251. What is affected humility? 687. In what does humility that deserves no praise consist? 673. Humility of heart is commended, V, 642. An arrogant mind offends God, while a humble one calls forth mercy, 522. However earnestly we strive toward higher things, we should consider ourselves placed among the lower, 530. The higher someone has been placed, the more he ought to fear falling, 160. Humility is foremost among the virtues, VI, 431. It arises from hope of the Lord’s inheritance, 697. Humility arises from the frailty of our condition, VII, 605. It resides in the mind, 607. Poverty of spirit is humility, 23. Through humility one reaches the summit of the virtues, 157.

What arises from the dryness of the humors, II, 794.

The Huns burst into the East, I, 464. According to Herodotus [Col. 0998], they held the East captive for twenty years and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians, ibid. They learn the Psalter, 679. The Huns eat half-raw meat, II, 334.

Huram. See Hiram.

The nocturnal sacred rites of Hyacinthus, II, 300.

Hyacinth is a most precious stone, I, 366. Philo compares the hyacinth in the high priest’s garments to air, ibid. It bears a likeness to the sky, V, 17.

The faction of Hydatius, II, 947.

The many-headed Hydra, II, 35.

Winter is to be spent by soldiers under hides, I, 29.

Hyena gall restores clarity to the eyes, and its dung cures putrefying wounds, II, 331. The nature of the hyena, IV, 928. The hyena is a harmful animal that lives on the corpses of dead bodies, IV, 928.

Hyginus, writer on illustrious men, II, 821.

Hylas, servant of Saint Melania, I, 10.

Hymetius was the husband of Praetextata, a most noble woman, I, 683. He was the uncle of the virgin Eustochium, ibid.

The hymn of the three young men is not found in Hebrew, II, 527. What is a hymn? VII, 651.

Hypatius the consul, II, 188.

It is said hyperbolically that birds and walls report what they have heard us say, III, 479.

To be without the stain of hypocrisy is characteristic either of very few or of no one, II, 757. Hypocrisy corrected by hypocrisy, VII, 404.

Who is a hypocrite? IV, 139, and VII, 32.

What *hypostasis* means in the school of secular letters, I, 49. What are “three hypostases”? ibid., 38.

Hyram, the name of a Tyrian craftsman, IV, 51.

## I

Iberia, Spain, so called from the river Iberus, IV, 817. Iberian dirges, I, 646.

What Ichabod signifies, I, 395.

The mysteries of the *ichthys*, or fish, I, 286.

Who are the ichthyophagi? II, 334. What food they live on, 335.

Ida, a mountain of Phrygia, IV, 639.

The statue of the Idaean goddess in a ford of the Tiber, II, 307.

Apostolic idiom, VII, 754.

What idols are, and what it means to serve idols, I, 31. Their service in vices and sins, ibid. Each person’s idol is whatever he loves, 96. Idols are said first to have been fashioned in the time of Enosh, III, 312–313. Idols are images of the dead, IV, 462. Their manufacture, 497. From what wood they are made, 489. Their various kinds are noted, 544, 911. An apostrophe addressed to idols, 504–505. After Christ’s coming they all fell silent, ibid. They did not foretell the future, ibid. Their answers were ambiguous, ibid. Why they are compared with moles and bats, 42. Prophetic speech is woven concerning their mockery, 527. The Israelites imitated this, ibid. The origin of idols, VI, 24. What are the idols of the nations? 207. The naming of the idols worshiped by Judas in Egypt, 240. What is found in idols, 230. An idol is called an abomination, VII, 195. Idols have those who uphold them, 528. Those who make and worship idols are like them, 283. To what extent idolaters have been turned into stones, ibid.

What an *idolium* (a little idol) is, VI, 227 ff.

Idolatry is sustained by magical art, I, 570. We all come from the error of idolatry, 396. How great idolatry is in Alexandria, II, 7. The ancient practice of idolatry in Egypt is described, etc., IV, 782.

Idrus, a mountain, VII, 427.

Idumaea was later called Gebalene, I, 696. Idumaea means “bloody” or “earthly,” II, 774. The Hebrews believe that under the name Idumaea the Romans are always signified, IV, 217 ff. Mountainous Idumaea, VI, 371. A village of Palestine, 369. Idumaea extends toward the southern region, 235. This province is called Theman, Sharon, and the Negeb, ibid.

What the region of the Idumaeans is like, VI, 370. The underground huts of the Idumaeans, ibid. The Idumaeans are reckoned as Romans by the Jews, 217.

Ignatius, an apostolic man and martyr: what he writes, II, 783. No one uses his testimonies as authoritative, ibid. He used the Hebrew Gospel, 855. Ignatius the martyr, VII, 32.

Eternal fire according to Origen, II, 496. According to the philosophers, everything we see will perish by fire, IV, 588. The fire of the Holy Spirit is the word of God, V, 455. The pagans used to pass their children through fire, or compel them to pass through it, 165. The nature of fire is twofold, VI, 203.

Ignorance punished by the Lord’s anger, II, 738. The Scriptures prove that ignorance is sin, 730 ff. New Testament testimonies by which ignorance is held culpable, 741 ff.

Forgiveness can be granted to the ignorant, VII, 422.

There are sometimes miracles unknown to us, II, 544.

The founders of Rome were born from Ilia and Mars, [Col. 0999] II, 310.

Virgins were customarily sent to Ilium, II, 308.

Temptations. Where the appearance of virtue was thought to provide a covering, there are the temptations of vices, III, 477.

Nighttime illusions from the enemy, V, 589.

An image hanging in a temple is torn apart by Epiphanius, I, 253. The custom of preserving images of slain tyrants, VI, 659.

Our soul bears the image of the heavenly from creation and, through repentance; the image of the earthly through sin, V, 865. There is no human being who does not bear some image, either of holiness or of sin, 86.

A sudden and excessive rain overturns fields headlong, I, 289.

Who are the undefiled in the way? I, 952.

The merciless are not heard, VI, 466.

The offering of human sacrifices and of children belonged to the worship of Saturn, IV, 544.

How immortality differs from incorruption, I, 800 ff.

We were all unclean, II, 760. Who is to be called unclean in soul? VI, 761. To the unclean nothing is clean, ibid.

God rejoices in an odd number, VI, 738.

Impatience knows no measure, I, 199, 202. Its effects are noted, 125. Human impatience is displayed in disputes, VI, 608.

Perpetual sinlessness is reserved for God alone and for Christ, II, 795.

The imperative mood is sometimes used for the optative in Scripture, III, 505.

The various deaths of many emperors, I, 343. The emperor’s speech inflames battle lines prepared for combat and drawn swords, 977. Roman emperors submit their necks to Christ’s yoke and defend his Church by their authority, IV, 725. The statues of emperors were worshiped, V, 638. Impious emperors were punished by God, VI, 659. Roman emperors brought back distinguished names from the subjected nations, VII, 746–747.

The Apostle teaches as imperfect what we human beings thought perfect, II, 708.

An imperial rescript, II, 546–547.

Inexperience is a familiar vice, I, 236. Inexperience is the cause of all evils, 573. Forgiveness is granted for inexperience, 221. What is meant by insolent inexperience? II, 563.

An inexperienced person accuses his own inexperience more forcefully when he writes, II, 562.

A unique empire was established, VI, 477.

To whom impiety belongs, II, 724. How impiety and iniquity differ, IV, 880. It is great impiety not only to fail to avoid sins but even to refuse to understand them, etc., 886.

The impious are often not afflicted with illnesses, while the saints are tortured by miseries and poverty, I, 409. How the impious differs from the iniquitous, II, 729. The impious person is without law, 725. The impious have been forejudged for destruction, 724. Who is impious? IV, 346. It is one thing to be impious and another to be a sinner, 386. The impious person is a bridle for peoples leading to ruin, 418. In the destruction of the impious, the Lord’s will and command are fulfilled, 1023. The impious who do not believe have been handed over to the everlasting sword, 1022. They are compared with a sea that never rests, 584. The impious hide themselves from the face of God, V, 859. The impious sow wheat and reap thorns, 809. The prosperity of the impious in this life, 818. The multitude of the impious is useful for nothing, VI, 102. Their dullness, 734. Why do the impious prevail over the just? 602–603.

Impenitence is the only crime that cannot obtain forgiveness, I, 1087.

The impenitent provokes the judge to anger, I, 1087. Nothing is so opposed to God as an impenitent heart, ibid. and II, 641.

The laying on of hands obtained the force of a precept through the agreement of the whole world, II, 180.

The impossible compared with the impossible, II, 603, 757. God appears to have commanded things virtually impossible because of their extreme difficulty, 753.

The impossibility of hearing, which proceeds from contempt and unbelief, is not without punishment, IV, 884.

The custom of impostors according to Justinian, II, 29.

Imprecation. Ecclesiastes curses those who do not have the fear of God and wishes that they not be long delayed from punishment, III, 455.

Among the ignorant, impudence is sometimes considered truth, and fury constancy, I, 537. Impudence is nourished by malice and envy, VII, 180.

Where earrings get their name, V, 155. Enchanters and enchantment are sometimes taken in a favorable sense, IV, 52. How enchanters, magicians, and sorcerers differ, V, 627. The activity of enchanters among the Chaldaeans, 553.

The mystery of the Incarnation is explained in full, IV, 155, 1069. What is its effect? 290. The mystery of the Incarnation, VII, 743.

Everything is now uncertain among human beings, including whether they endure through love of [Col. 1000] God, like Job, or through hatred, like most sinners; this is now uncertain, III, 457.

Kinds of incest, V, 254.

Who are uncircumcised and unclean? IV, 601.

The distinction between inhabitants and dwellers upon the earth, VI, 35.

Inconstancy does not deserve trust, II, 471.

How a certain incontinent young man was saved by the abbot of a monastery, I, 941.

Unbelievers will suffer different things according to the diversity of their merits, IV, 33.

Incubus spirits, II, 7, and IV, 175.

The Indians have many wives, II, 311. Among them there is a law that the beloved wife be burned with her dead husband, ibid. What is read about the same people, ibid. What the Indians, Persians, and Babylonians used to do, VII, 183.

The kingdoms of India are exceedingly wealthy, I, 271. By way of the Ocean one scarcely reaches India within a full year, 934.

Many spices come from India by way of the Red Sea, IV, 887.

Things indifferent, which are neither good nor evil, I, 750. Which things of this age are indifferent? IV, 159. The goods of the world are indifferent, varying according to the character of those who use them, 645.

Where there is indignation, there is no rest, I, 34. Where indignation comes from, VII, 636.

A certain philosopher preached freedom from pain, VII, 621.

Indulgence is beautiful, I, 228. Indulgence is attributed to our lack of self-control, 905. After indulgence, the severity of judgment is not to be feared, 416. A ruler’s clemency sometimes tolerates the slander of the accused, 411. Princely indulgence, II, 375. It is one thing to attribute indulgence to weakness and another to promise rewards to virtues, 299.

It is foolish to endure infamy without reason, II, 409.

Childhood does not know the difference between good and evil, I, 684. Childhood remembers many things perfectly, II, 612. The bodies of infants, as soon as they are brought forth from the womb, are customarily washed, V, 146. What does the age of infancy fear? VII, 447.

At the beginning of their birth infants do nothing except plead for mercy, I, 201. The salvation of infants is the gain of their elders, 684. Infants killed by barbarian cruelty, 464. An infant strikes his laughing mother with a tender hand, 962. He should love what he is compelled to learn, so that it may be not labor but delight, ibid. They should be sustained by eating meat, lest their feet fail before they begin to run, 685. Infants can neither sin nor wish to sin, II, 802. Infants are not to be excluded from baptism, 804. The question why infants die so quickly is answered, 558. Among the Hebrews every son is called an infant in relation to his parents, III, 336. At Rome also all infants are called sons, ibid. Infants will rise again at the stature of a perfect man, IV, 1065. Why infants are wrapped in swaddling clothes, V, 147. Midwives also customarily touch them with salt, 147. The care of newborn infants, ibid.

It is a great misfortune to learn songs of lamentation from women, IV, 367.

We ought not to insult the unfortunate over their calamities, I, 683.

What *inferiae* are and where the name comes from, I, 334. Human beings sacrificed by the Bessi as offerings for the dead, ibid.

The underworld is not filled by the dead; rather, the more it receives, the more it desires, I, 526. Before Christ’s coming it made little difference whether one perished with the body or was detained in the darkness of the underworld, III, 416. The underworld is beneath the earth, IV, 105, 179. It is said to have a soul, although it is not an animal, 79. It is a place of punishments and torments, 250. An angel is said to preside over it, ibid. The eternal burning of the underworld, 421. Just as a lake receives the waters flowing down into it, so the underworld receives souls, 252. What is the lowest underworld? 178. “The deep” signifies the underworld, and “the heights” the heavens, 106. The underworld is called a lake, VI, 340. The underworld is in the middle of the earth, VI, 408. What difference there is between the underworld and death, 152. No one will be brought back from the underworld before the day of resurrection, 347. Whatever separates brothers should be called the underworld, 152. The underworld is in the lower part of the earth, VII, 613. A question concerning it, 676. The gates of the underworld, 124.

Even an unbeliever needs a penny, I, 281. The devil is the father of unbelievers, 387. Among unbelievers the rewards of future things are uncertain, 979. A faithful household sanctifies one unbeliever, 678. The unbeliever possesses nothing in the world, V, 564.

The various illnesses and miseries of human beings, I, 461. They do not always come from sin, 409. Illness itself can have the fruit of almsgiving, 260. Illness is doubled when bodily sickness is accompanied by distress of mind, IV, 15. To waste away through a long illness is God’s anger, 987. Illness that is beneficial, VI, 690. We should have compassion on the illnesses of our brothers, VII, 520.

Whatever the sick person suffers, we too can suffer, I, 462. Let us consider his wounds our own, ibid. We must have compassion on our fellow sufferers who are sick, ibid.

Small intellects cannot bear great subjects, I, 331. Minds liberally educated overcome shame more easily than fear, 397. Brilliant intellects and a mind full of virtues overflow into elegance in various arts, [Col. 1001] 340. We should not greatly care what the mutterings of the ignorant say about our intellect, 700. Bodily weakness and sorrow of mind blunt the sharpness of the intellect, 759. A teachable intellect is praiseworthy, 272. The intellect smells of what it was once imbued with, II, 486. There are many things that ennoble brilliant intellects, 329.

The human race is ungrateful for benefits received, III, 466.

Enemies who rebuke are more useful than friends who fear to rebuke, I, 730. How far enemies are to be loved, 533. We are surrounded by great armies of enemies, 594. What the love of enemies should be like, II, 728. We ought not to love them as though they were blood relatives and friends, ibid. Paul’s beautiful interpretation concerning love of them, ibid. It is easier to guard against an avowed enemy than to endure a hidden enemy under the name of friend, 529. The enemy is always lying in wait, 783. He attacks and withdraws unconquered, ibid. The enemy looks for a knot in a reed, ibid., 409.

Useful enmity, VII, 506.

Where there is iniquity, there is also indignation, I, 33. How iniquity differs from impiety, IV, 880. Return from iniquity consists in thinking upon God’s truth, V, 679.

How the iniquitous person differs from the impious, II, 724.

In injuries, do not consider what the enemy deserves but what is fitting for you, II, 530. With what spirit the Israelites avenged the injury done to the Levite’s wife, VI, 114. To endure injury is not as great a virtue as not to inflict injury, VI, 551.

Who is innocent? I, 1096. The innocent receive a reward for blood poured out for Christ, IV, 1075.

Every injustice is a judgment of blood, IV, 438.

It is difficult not to grieve when innocence is oppressed by evils, I, 793. Innocence would perish if power were always joined to wickedness, II, 418. Nothing in a human being is safe if innocence is made criminal, ibid.

Innocentius, Jerome’s friend, I, 10.

The faith of Pope Innocent is proposed for adherence, I, 592.

Through poverty many are converted to the Lord, IV, 324.

It is much better to confess ignorance simply than to make others heirs of one’s own inexperience, IV, 998.

To lay traps is the devil’s work, II, 560. Traps are to be avoided, V, 659. Traps were set for those traveling to Jerusalem for the solemn feasts, VI, 66.

Kinds of grafting, I, 940.

Meditation on a dream, II, 765.

How we pursue with hatred the instruments that contribute to the death of human beings, VII, 377.

The islands of Dalmatia, I, 337. With what rumor are all the islands between Africa and Italy filled? 988. What “islands” mean in Scripture, IV, 508.

Why foolish people are called “insipid,” I, 148.

We must not insult those who have been handed over to punishments by God’s judgment, V, 110.

The difficulty of interpretation, I, 535. What ecclesiastical interpretation ought to avoid, 235. What kind of interpretation should be followed in the sacred Scriptures? 753. An abraded brow often interprets what it does not know, 311. When it has persuaded others, it also claims knowledge for itself, ibid., 311. No one can easily judge concerning interpretation, II, 527. The cause of differing interpretations, 476. In interpreting the Scriptures we ought not to sew together patches of opinions according to our own will, but preserve one continuous text and order of argument and the same meaning, II, 429. Simple understanding does not require interpretation, 427. Historical interpretation clings to the letter, IV, 176. A pious interpretation not approved by Jerome, 195. A dangerous interpretation, V, 118. A forced interpretation, VII, 63. A rejected interpretation, 143. Superstitious interpretations must be avoided, 204. The interpretation of certain persons, 91. See *Exposition*.

The interpreter should follow the meaning, not the letter, I, 647. The rule of a good interpreter, 643. The duty of a true interpreter, 307 ff. Rules prescribed for interpreters, II, 308 ff. It is sacrilege in an interpreter either to conceal or to ignore the mystery, 312. Jewish and Greek interpreters, 232. Interpreters of Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians, 235. In spiritual gifts, interpreters occupy almost the last rank, II, 521. The Greeks carefully read all the interpreters of Scripture, 527. The practice of setting out the opinions of different interpreters was mocked by Grunnius and his like, IV, 993. A deranged interpreter is noted, 934. The Latin interpreter was deceived, 779. The exposition of a certain depraved interpreter, 1017. The Latin interpreter, VII, 515, 560, 596, 704. He is censured by Jerome, 398. He inserted what is not found in the Greek, 494. The Latin interpreter was deceived, 702. His various reading, 487. Some interpret boldly what they do not understand, 466.

The interpreters of the Septuagint. See *Septuagint*.

The person to be questioned is one whom his life commends, age excuses, and reputation does not condemn, I, 113. A horned question, II, 225.

Through envy death entered the world, I, 325. Envy is self-biting, [Col. 1002] 197. It always follows virtues, ibid. It gnaws at itself and even falls upon the saints, 425. The spite of envy blazed up against the most learned men, III, 301. It finds even those who are hidden, ibid. Nothing is more vain or unstable than people who do not mourn their own miseries or grieve over their own sins, but envy those who are better, 420. The nature of envy, VII, 507. It is divided into a twofold passion, ibid. An elegiac meter on envy, 508. Cyprian wrote about it, 608. Envy is slow to become quiet, 181.

The envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, and the honored person lies open to plots, III, 420. The more someone envies his brother, the more he himself wastes away and perishes, ibid. The disparagements of the envious, IV, 369. The envious person is censured, VII, 417. He is especially harmful to infants, ibid. What difference is there between an envious person and one who is envied? 508. The envious and slanderers are censured, 539.

To invoke the name of the Lord belongs not to beginners but to the perfect, VI, 205.

Who is useless to himself and to everyone? IV, 49.

The Ionians are called after Javan, IV, 817. The eastern Iberians are called Ionians, V, 311. The Ionians are Greeks, VI, 716.

The Ionian Sea, IV, 817.

The blood of the virgin Iphigenia appeased the opposing winds, II, 395.

Anger imposes the character of a lion upon us, I, 193. A man’s anger proceeds from a disturbed mind, II, 747. No one can be without anger, ibid. Justice consists in calming anger through swift repentance, ibid. It is safer to endure the rage of a lion than that of a human being, 47. Anger is used for correction and instruction of inferiors, III, 439. Anger is always joined with pride, and if a wise person is angry, he is judged foolish, ibid. When raging and recent anger has been postponed, it is more easily calmed and can be removed, ibid. We should be angry with ourselves when we sin, and angry with others also, because through sadness of countenance the mind becomes better, 437. The nature of anger, VI, 173. Its magnitude is shown in feigned laughter, 289. What is anger? VII, 636. Anger is given a double name, 628. It is likewise defined in two ways, ibid.

The anger of God has its material not in the Lord’s will but in our vices, IV, 776. The anger of God is sometimes understood as the devil and wicked angels, who are sent to punish those deserving anger, V, 537. God’s anger is necessary, 879. God’s great anger is not to be angry, 168. There is scarcely anyone, or no one, who is not deserving of God’s anger, VI, 540. Brute animals perceive God’s anger, 676. God’s anger has measures, 635. All created things will suffer God’s anger, VII, 283.

Who is an angry person? VII, 699. How an angry and an irascible person differ, 507.

To become angry is human; not to inflict injury is Christian, I, 27, 608. Whoever becomes angry shows that he is not a Christian, 175. To become lightly angry is sin, II, 747. It is not permitted to become angry even with cause, ibid.

Saint Irenaeus, successor of the martyr Photinus, I, 428. Irenaeus was a disciple of the martyr Polycarp, II, 873. He was the successor of the martyr Photinus, ibid. Irenaeus explained the origins of many heresies, IV, 761.

Whoever is irreproachable is praised with harmonious voice not only by his household but also by outsiders, I, 425. There are few, or none, who are irreproachable, II, 718.

What is the rainbow? V, 22. It never appears except in rain, ibid.

Signs of mockery, I, 945.

Do not willingly accommodate yourself to mockers, I, 944.

Isaac had twice David’s years, I, 254. Before the Gospel he bore the evangelical cross, 398. Isaac and Rebekah were monogamous, 910. Where Isaac received his name, II, 536. “The husband of one wife” prefigures Christ’s Church, 268. Isaac was born at Gerar, not beside the oak of Mamre, III, 337. Either at the ninth hour or before sunset he offered spiritual sacrifices to God and devoted himself to prayer in the field, 343. Isaac always retained the same name and was content with one wife, IV, 756.

Isaac, interpreter of Antony, II, 31.

Isaias was more an evangelist than a prophet, I, 784. The visions of Isaias are exceedingly obscure, 435. Isaias, the demonstrator of the Virgin, succumbs in one question, II, 417. By the merit of his virtues he enjoyed the sight of God, and, conscious of his sins, confessed that his lips were unclean, 773. Isaias was called arrogant by Pelagius, 799. Isaias: who was he? IV, 211. He prophesied under four kings, 89, 90. The four prophets Isaias, Osee, Joel, and Amos prophesied at the same time, 7. The book of Isaias contains all the mysteries of the Lord, 3. He speaks chiefly of the tribe of Juda and Benjamin, 7. Prophecy is joined together with history in him, 460. The prophet is wrapped in many obscurities, 326. In explaining him, the ingenuity of the Greeks labored, not that of the Latins, 5. In the number of its verses it is equal to, or greater than, the twelve prophets, 5. There were 150 years between Isaias and Jeremias, 400. The Ascension of Isaias and the Apocalypse, 761. He calls himself not a prophet but the son of a prophet, 460. He does not dare to praise the Lord, 93. What was the cause of his mourning? 335. Why was he killed by the Jews, according to the opinion of the Hebrews? 19. His death and punishment according to Jewish tradition, [Col. 1003] 666. What is the difference between Isaias and Jeremias? V, 752. Isaias was sawn apart, VII, 204. The name of Isaias was added through a scribal error, 17.

Why Isachar was so called, III, 351. It is interpreted as “reward,” ibid. Why “bony ass”? 376.

The incursion of the Isaurians into the East, I, 757.

Isboseth is called righteous because he was killed without guilt, II, 737.

Isidorus, bishop and confessor, I, 704. Isidorus is condemned, 1029.

Isidorus the presbyter was sent by Theophilus of Alexandria to settle the dispute between John of Jerusalem and Hieronymus, II, 447 and following.

The gluttonous abstinence of the worshipers of Isis and Cybele, I, 687. Isis, IV, 205. The heads of the priests of Isis and Serapis were shaved, V, 547.

Ishmael, playing with Isaac, was either making idols or, in jest, claiming the rights of the firstborn, III, 335. Ishmael was not of the promise, VII, 470. A very difficult question concerning Isaac and Ishmael is proposed and resolved, 469 and following. Scripture calls Ishmael’s quarrel with Isaac “play,” 575.

The prosperity of the Ishmaelite merchants, I, 501. Their merchandise is the salvation of the world, ibid. The clothing and weapons of the Ishmaelites, II, 43. The Ishmaelites live in tents and flee through the vast wilderness, IV, 218. How far the Ishmaelites can flee in one day with dromedary camels, ibid. A description of that people, ibid. Asor is their capital, ibid.

How many years Isocrates completed in the labor of teaching and writing, I, 257. He debated in prison about the soul after death, 334.

Israel’s sons fight with their adversaries with a peaceful mind, I, 738. Israel hastened by the royal road toward the promised land, 946. He is called both a nation and a people, IV, 13. The Israelites are called firstborn, not only-begotten, ibid. The people of Israel received the promised land not through their own merit but through the virtues of their fathers, 1089. The ten tribes of Israel that were in Samaria were called Ephraim and Israel, 6. The difference between Israel and Juda, 72. Israel more righteous in comparison with Juda, 859. The people of the ten tribes are called the crown of pride, 372. Its glory is compared with a crown of various flowers, ibid. There was no kind of sin that did not exist among the people of Israel, 14. Israel always limped between idols and God, 143. It desired the head of the Egyptian ox, 556. The Israelites, devoted to idolatry, had household gods, 672. Israel’s hands were bloodstained, 736. Israel was ravaged not only by the Romans but by all nations, 808. Why does it lie pierced through and slaughtered? 16. Israel sinned first, then Juda, V, 869. Israel sinned less seriously than Juda, ibid. Israel is utterly rejected by God, 871. A bill of divorce was given to Israel, 871. Israel’s divorce did not correct Juda, 869. The Israelites worshiped idols in Egypt, 261. Those who perished in the wilderness were not blotted out of the book of the living, 229. The kingdom of Israel lasted 250 years, VI, 2. Israel is called Ephraim, Joseph, and Samaria, 8. In what sense the people of Israel are called a virgin, 281. Why God bestowed so many benefits upon Israel, 503. Israel’s idolatry, 285. The obstinacy of the people of Israel in their sin, 278, 311, 312. Rich in possessions, 261. Its acts of plunder, ibid., 293. It is instructed through scourges and torments, 275. It adopted the worship of idols through the fault of its rulers, 46. The cruelty of Israel’s rulers, 465. The Israelites were captives in Egypt for 530 years, 217. At the end of the world all Israel will be saved, 355. The Scriptures accuse Israel of a heavy heart and a stiff neck, VII, 416. The impious worship of the people of Israel, 62. It burns and initiates its sons for demons, ibid. See Hebrews and Jews.

Israel, scorning the angels’ food, longed for Egyptian meat, II, 347. Israel is interpreted as “a mind seeing God,” IV, 13. He is found to possess in Abraham the warmth of faith, 779. From what source Israel received the name “seeing God,” VI, 275.

Itabyrium and Tabor are the same mountain, I, 209, 325. Itabyrium is Mount Tabor in the great plain, III, 235.

Italy was once called Greater Greece, I, 270. The people of Italy are called “Cheese-eaters” by Ennius, 20. What Cicero said about them, ibid. Their custom in writing and sending letters, ibid. Civil wars in Italy, 464. Italy was once called Greater Greece, II, 565. Italy was formerly called Hesperia, IV, 87. Italy was formerly called Greater Greece, VII, 427.

Italicus, a Christian municipal official, was assisted by Hilarion, II, 22.

The journey of the Hebrews from Egypt signifies our journey from earth to heaven, I, 468. This is explained at length in the account of the stopping-places, 470 and following.

The faction of Ithacius, II, 947.

The region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, VII, 121.

## J

Jacob asked only for necessities, I, 117. By the prophetic Spirit he foresaw events far in the future, 409. The Church beside Jacob’s well, [Col. 1004] 703. Jacob obtained his father’s blessings through a contrived lie, II, 475. When he received the name Israel, 269. He wrestles with an angel in human form, 178. He is called perfectly righteous before God, ibid. He does not dare return to his brother unless strengthened by God’s help, ibid. Jacob proves himself human by mourning the death of his son Joseph, 731. Why Jacob was called Israel, III, 357. Jacob and Ephraim seized the rights of the firstborn, IV, 1062. Jacob endured hardships for the sake of one daughter, 805. In what sense his days are called few and evil, 982. From what source Jacob received the names Israel and Upright, VI, 136, 551, 552. He is strengthened by the angel so that he will not fear Esau, 142. He too is a type of Christ, ibid. What is said about Jacob’s wrestling, VII, 672.

James and John, although excessively fervent, were not without error, II, 759. Two apostles named James, 219. James, the brother of the Lord, is praised, 829, 301. His holiness and virginity are commended, ibid. James alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies, 829. Josephus’s testimony about him, 831. Testimonies of very many authors about the same man, ibid. James was known by the title until the siege under Titus and the final period of Hadrian, 833. A false opinion held by some concerning the place of his burial, ibid. Who was the mother of James the Less? 219. He is given various names, ibid. Saint James was thrown down from the Temple, VI, 692. James was beheaded, VII, 155. James was specially called the brother of the Lord, 396. He is praised, ibid. He presided over the Church that was the first among the Jews to believe in Christ, ibid. His holiness, 397. He was thrown down from the Temple, ibid.

The seedbed of boasting, I, 324.

Jaddus the high priest, during whose lifetime Alexander the Great came to Jerusalem, V, 685 and following.

The philosopher Iamblichus wrote a commentary on the doctrines of Pythagoras, II, 575.

The doors of the Temple at Jerusalem opened of their own accord before the destruction of the city, IV, 605. The doors of the Temple were made of juniper wood, V, 161.

To enter through closed doors is contrary to the nature of solid bodies, I, 717.

January contains the supremacy of winter cold, V, 341. Why it was so called, ibid. Our January corresponds to the fourth month of the Jews, 6. The month of January: why is it so called? VI, 852.

Japhet, the ancestor of the eastern nations, IV, 817.

King Jarbas of Libya sought Dido in marriage, I, 906, and II, 310.

Jarcas, seated on a golden throne and drinking from Tantalus’ spring, taught about nature, morals, and the course of the stars, I, 271.

The dispute between Jason and Papiscus, VII, 435. What Hieronymus read in it, ibid.

The stone jasper, I, 371. Where many kinds of jasper are found, IV, 638.

The city of Java overlooks the Dead Sea, IV, 186.

Javan, from whom the Ionians derive their name, V, 311. The etymology of Javan, ibid., 316.

Jechonias is interpreted as “the preparation of the Lord,” VI, 995. He was the grandson of Josias, 989. Jechonias was dishonored, VI, 86.

The liver, seat of pleasure, desire, and lust, I, 355, and V, 10.

Jehu, the bloodstained king, VI, 64. The avenger of Naboth’s blood, 7. The overthrow of Jehu’s house, ibid.

During a fast one must abstain from wine and meat, II, 619. Fasting is not perfect virtue but the foundation of the other virtues, 988. The gentle reins of fasts, 628. Ecclesiastical tradition concerning ending a fast, 120. Observance of God’s law adorns the precepts of fasting, 628. What is the strongest fast, and what kind is it? 266. What must be avoided in it? 100. Why fasts should be moderate, 266, 687, 936, 788. Superstitious fasts are to be avoided, 266. Long and immoderate fasts are condemned in tender years, 689. The history of Daniel teaches us to desire and honor fasts, 618. Chastity is redeemed through continence and fasting, 616. Care must be taken that hunger restore those whom satiety expelled from paradise, 96. It is no great thing to feign fasting, abound in the income from one’s possessions, and display a cheap little cloak, 319. Fasts are placed after frugality, 289. It is of no benefit, after passing two or three days, to carry an empty belly if the fast is compensated by overeating, ibid., 100. Let fasts be daily, and let nourishment avoid satiety, ibid. Fasting rejected by God, 180. There are books by many authors on fasting, to which Hieronymus refers, 988. The commendation of fasts, II, 348, 349 and following. Their sanctification, ibid., 353. Christ sanctified the fasting of Christians, 352. It is relaxed on Sunday and at Pentecost, 180. Through fasting we can return to paradise, 348. Human nature does not permit a fast of forty days, 443. Whoever can fast and live for forty days will be able to live eternally without food or drink, 444. The Lord left us solemn days of fasting, IV, 689. When fasts and prayers are beneficial, 940. What true and false fasting consist in, ibid., 687. Our fasting must not be a profit for the purse, 691. It involves affliction and humiliation of the soul, 690. That is accepted by God which is not idle of good works, 21. God must be moved by fasts and vigils, V, 661. The fasting of the Manichaeans, heretics, and especially the Encratites is worse than satiety and drunkenness, VI, 180. Why fasts were instituted, VII, 457. See Abstinence, Continence, Food.

When you fast, let your face be cheerful, I, 110. You should fast in such a way that you do not tremble and can scarcely breathe, 988. Those who fast receive much more than they offer, 1020. How those who fast may be worse than those who do not fast, 121. Not everyone who fasts fasts for God at once, II, 188.

Jephthah is included in the catalog of the righteous, I, 236. Why is he placed in this enumeration by the Apostle? 797. Jephthah is numbered among holy men, although he was the son of a prostitute, 439. He is censured for his rash vow, 275. In Jephthah’s sacrifice it was not the act but the intention that pleased God, IV, 897.

Jeremias was sanctified in the womb, I, 128. Jeremias did not take a wife, 104. Why he was forbidden to marry, 910. He mourns a people that does not repent, 893. Certain statements are attributed under Jeremias’ name that belong to Zacharias, 310. Jeremias was sanctified in the womb, II, 777. He was a virgin and a prophet, ibid. He fears the impious king, ibid. He dreads the prison, for which paradise was prepared for him, ibid. As a type of Christ, the Prophet is sent to the nations, 477. What are Jeremias’ prerogatives? IV, 999. The Hebrews say that Jeremias and Baruch escaped death from the impending captivity of Egypt, 405. How the Hebrews calculate the time of Jeremias’ birth, 982. Some suspect that he existed before his conception, 837. His prudence, humility, and patience, 1038. Jeremias and Ezechiel prophesied the same things and at the same time, 1053. As simple as he is in words, so profound is he in the majesty of his meanings, ibid. He wishes the false prophet to speak truth rather than himself, 1037. Cruel priests attacked him through envy of his holiness, 1027. Jeremias and Ezechiel prophesied the same things and at the same time, V, 116. When Jeremias began to prophesy, 623. Jeremias was holy from the womb, 791. Jeremias was a prophet from his cradle, 843. Jeremias was an outstanding prophet, 746. At what time Jeremias prophesied, 745. Jeremias as a figure of Christ, 747, 844. Most things said about Jeremias apply to Christ, 747. The difference between Jeremias and Isaias, 792. Jeremias wrote the Lamentations concerning Josias, VI, 904. The apocryphal book of Jeremias, VII, 394.

Jeria, a region of India, III, 322.

Jericho, at whose destruction the world was destroyed, II, 271. The first, second, and third Jericho, III, 230, 231. The mystery of the river of Jericho, V, 590. There were many robbers in Jericho, VII, 157.

Jerusalem is given three names, I, 202, 696. Their interpretations, 202. It is called Aelia by Aelius Hadrian, 696. Jerusalem is higher than all the cities of Judaea, ibid. It is called a cursed land because it drank the Lord’s blood, 205. From this it is inferred that it should be called blessed, ibid. It is called the Athens of the Christians, 206. Pilgrimages to Jerusalem are commended, 211. Their frequency and antiquity, 206, 211, 322. The swarms of monks who have not seen Jerusalem, ibid. It is praiseworthy not to have been in Jerusalem but to have lived well in Jerusalem, 319. Jerusalem is much worse than Sodom, II, 712. It was believed that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the death of James, 831. Jerusalem itself is also Salem, etc., III, 141. Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin, IV, 881. It was built on rocky mountains, 570. It is called the city of the sanctuary, 601. It alone in the world received the law, ibid. In Scripture, Sion and Jerusalem are understood in four ways, 569. It was devoted to idolatry, 668. In Jerusalem and Samaria the same idols were found as among the Gentiles, 144. By comparison with Jerusalem, Sodom receives the name of righteousness, 853. It is said that all demons dwelt in it, 445. In what sense it is a prostitute and adulteress, 673. The revolt of Jerusalem was divided into three factions, 52, 804. The Romans, Gauls, and Spaniards were called by God to besiege it, 87. It was captured forty-two years after the Lord’s Passion, 93. Hieronymus saw with his own eyes the overthrow of Jerusalem and the Temple, 17. Its utter desolation is described, 444. It was not struck as severely as it struck Christ and the Apostles, 364. It is called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian, 976. The Prophet testifies that Jerusalem is situated at the center of the world, V, 49. The glory of the Lord gradually departs from it, and how this happens, 112. How great were its impieties? 271. It sinned far more wickedly than Samaria and Sodom, 264, 779. In chapter 16 of Ezechiel it is expounded under the person of an adulteress and prostitute, V, 143. It is called a lioness, 218. The overthrow of the Temple and city of Jerusalem, 277. Jerusalem is situated among the mountains, VI, 23. It is called by three names, 861. Its ingratitude, 45. It was handed over to the Roman armies, 316, 694. Jerusalem, the metropolitan city of the Jews, VII, 400. It is called the holy city, 238. The three factions of the revolt in Jerusalem, 196.

[Col. 1006] Jesus is jealous, I, 108, 109. Jesus is the commander of believers, VII, 234. At times he signifies God the Word and the man separately, 623. What is the difference between Christ and Jesus? 125. These are names of the assumed man, 724. The excellence of the name Jesus, 286. In what sense Jesus was soiled, 286. How Jesus grew and became strong, 302. Who possesses Jesus? 304. Where and how Jesus is to be sought, 287. See Christ.

Jesus son of Nave is a type of the Lord in his deeds and in his name, I, 276. In what sense he describes the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem, ibid. The chastity of Jesus son of Nave is commended, II, 279. Jesus son of Nave is a type of the Savior, VI, 741.

Jesus Josedech, a type of the Savior, II, 328.

Jethira had all its inhabitants as Christians, III, 234.

Jezrael signifies “Seed of God,” I, 427. The vineyard of Jezrael, that is, of the Seed of God, 1093. Jezrael, the son of Osee, VI, 6. The name of a city, ibid.

Joacin was killed in the eleventh year of his reign in Jerusalem, IV, 1013. Joacin was to be buried with the burial of an ass, 992.

What Joanna signifies, VII, 124.

John the Baptist is sanctified in his mother’s womb, I, 128. He is said to have prophesied in his parent’s womb, 978. Before the day of judgment he was praised by the voice of the Judge, ibid. The Lord’s precursor in the waters of the springs prepares the people for Christ, 419. He was the chief of the anchorites, 126. The relics of John the Baptist were buried in Samaria, 209, 702. John is praised, II, 843. He is compared with the angels by the testimony of the Lord, 712. He is said to be less than the least in the kingdom of heaven, ibid. In his baptism he gave the Holy Spirit to Christ, not to others, 178. A question is proposed concerning his baptism, and an answer is given, ibid. He was both a faster and a virgin, 351. The relics of John the Baptist were buried in a Palestinian town called Sebaste, III, 272. The blessed John’s bones were buried at Sebaste, VI, 8. John the Baptist first preached the kingdom of heaven, VII, 17. The Pharisees consented to the death of John the Baptist, 133. He was beheaded in a town of Arabia, 103. John was the minister of Christ’s coming, 277. John’s teaching and freedom, and the fact that he did many things that were not written down, ibid. John was the last of the prophets, 335. How the power and spirit of Elijah were in John, 257. How John grew and became strong in spirit, 303. John was greater than Moses, 277. Where and when the word of the Lord came to John, 313.

John the Evangelist was known to the high priest because of his noble birth, I, 955. He did not fear the plots of the Jews, ibid. He alone of the apostles stood before the cross, ibid. The virgin son received the virgin Mother, the Lord’s virgin inheritance, ibid. He was not uneducated, 273. Why John did not describe Christ’s temptation, 339. Origen’s exposition of John, 248. John the Evangelist’s privilege is virginity, II, 280. John the Evangelist’s virginity is praised, IV, 658. John the Evangelist is interpreted from the Hebrew, VI, 903. The prerogatives of the apostle John, VII, 3. He was compelled by the bishops of Asia to write the Gospel, ibid. The reason is explained, ibid. Before its publication he prescribed fasting and prayers, ibid. What is the teaching of John the Evangelist? 529. John related the mystery of the Word’s birth, and from what source, 543. How he drank the cup of martyrdom, 155. He was likewise sent into a cauldron of boiling oil and exiled to the island of Patmos, ibid. An interpretation of one passage of the Gospel of Saint John, 166. John’s Gospel was written against the doctrines of Cerinthus and the Ebionites, II, 843. Disagreement (διαφωνία): how is the disagreement between John’s Gospel and the others resolved? 845. Which two Epistles are asserted to be his? ibid. John the Evangelist wore a golden plate on his forehead, 885. He fell asleep at Ephesus, ibid. Two memorials of him exist at Ephesus, 845. When John the Evangelist died, 279. The same man was an apostle, evangelist, and prophet; he was exiled to the island of Patmos, 280. What Tertullian reports about him.

John Chrysostom adorned the Church of Constantinople, I, 741 and 733. In his explanation of the Epistle to the Galatians he followed Origen, ibid. Heretics misuse his authority, ibid. Hieronymus reports certain unfavorable things about him, 757. He is said to have received Origenists into his intimate circle and promoted many of them to the priesthood, ibid. For this reason he is reported to have saddened Epiphanius, ibid.

John of Jerusalem is attacked, I, 512 and following. John called his own stomach the cause of the universal Church, 523. John of Jerusalem’s letter is full of insults, 516. John of Jerusalem is mocked by Hieronymus, II, 448, 449. He diminishes the dignity of his own name, 419. Eight questions concerning the faith were brought against John, 413. He is accused because he did not clear himself, 447. The monks did not communicate with John the bishop, 410. He regards them as public enemies, ibid. He is approved by Rufinus, 498. Did Epiphanius openly call John a heretic? 411. John ordered Epiphanius to be silent, 421. He wishes to make Epiphanius suspect of heresy, 418. He mocks the same man, ibid. His shamelessness toward him, ibid. Those whom he forbids to enter the Church, 452. His cruelty, ibid.

[Col. 1007] John the Elder is different from the Evangelist, II, 859. The two Epistles of John the Evangelist are said to belong to him, ibid.

John, superior of the monastery of Chnum, II, 90.

What were Joatham’s impieties? IV, 101.

Job is a model of patience, I, 276. In his own speech he embraces all the mysteries, ibid. Saint Job’s flesh is given into the power of the devil, while the health of his soul is preserved; why? ibid. After the trials of misfortune, the worst wife was reserved for blessed Job, and so forth, 792. Job’s patience is praised, 183. In him we follow examples of virtue and patience, 688. He is reproved by his own speech, 137. Although righteous, by God’s word he is accused as a sinner through his confession, 898. Job, victor over torments, consoles his miseries through the hope and truth of the resurrection, II, 438. No one spoke so openly about the resurrection of the flesh, ibid. He was an athlete of the Church, ibid. He seems to have written against Origen, ibid. With what end he is crowned with righteousness, 746. Job and the others are called righteous according to that righteousness which can be changed into unrighteousness, 809. Job was not of Esau’s lineage, as some wrongly judge, III, 339. His house was in Carnaim-Astaroth, 182. He is said to have reigned after Balac son of Beor, 195. At what time Job lived, V, 919. Job’s constancy in virtue, VII, 650.

The book of Job translated by Hieronymus, I, 235. The discourse is partly prose and partly metrical, in the Preface to the translation from the Hebrew. What kind of poem the metrical part contains, ibid.

Jobab is thought to be the same person as Job, 365.

How Christian jokes ought to be conducted, I, 151.

Jod and vav differ only in size, IV, 143.

What does Joel discuss? I, 227. Joel’s prophecy concerns the tribe of Juda, not the ten tribes, VI, 169. Joel, that is, “beginning,” or “he is God,” 167. At what time he prophesied, 169.

The praises of Jonadab’s sons, I, 936. It is written in the Psalm that they were the first to endure captivity, ibid.

The Port of Jona, I, 696, and II, 551.

Jonah is interpreted as “dove,” I, 278. By his shipwreck he prefigures the Lord’s Passion, ibid. He calls the world back to repentance and, under the name of Nineveh, announces salvation to the nations, ibid. Jonah is accused of unjust grief, II, 788. Jonah is accused by God of valuing a lie more than the ruin of Nineveh, IV, 1037. Where Jonah wished to flee, V, 698. Jona signifies “Dove” and “Greece,” VI, 716. It is the tradition of the Hebrews that Jonah was the son of the widow of Sarepta, 390. Why he grieved over his election, 392, 393, 423. He is accused by God, 393. A type of Christ, 140, 387.

In Jonah, a variant interpretation of a certain word, etc., I, 754. The interpretation of the ancients concerning Jonah is obscure, VI, 387. Where Jonah is mentioned in the Old Testament apart from his own book, 390.

Jonathan stood between David and Saul, II, 377.

Joppa, a maritime town of Palestine, I, 1047. Joppa, 696. One cannot sail from Joppa to India, IV, 141. Joppa, a port of Judaea, VI, 394. There the rocks are shown to which Andromeda was bound, ibid.

The river Jordan, I, 495. Where it flows, ibid. Its mystery, ibid. The river Jordan rises from the springs of Paneas and enters the Dead Sea, III, 139. It bursts forth from the stream of Dan and Jor, which signifies “river,” 195, 230. Dan and Jor are the springs of the Jordan, from which it also received its name, 328. What cities are situated on the banks of the Jordan? IV, 129. From what source the Jordan received its name, V, 317. Lions dwell beside the Jordan, VI, 884. The source of the Jordan, and the origin of its name, VII, 122.

The valley of Josaphat, I, 47.

In what is Josaphat censured? I, 1041. Josaphat was not without error, II, 768.

Josedec is interpreted as “righteous of the Lord,” II, 772.

Joseph was a virgin because of Mary, II, 226. He was her guardian rather than her husband, ibid. Why he is called the Father of the Lord, 209. In what sense Joseph is called Christ’s father, VII, 302.

Joseph was sold so that he might feed his father and brothers, I, 174. He preceded the Savior as a type, 727. Joseph’s bones were buried at Sichem, III, 274. His mausoleum could be seen at Sichem in Hieronymus’ time, 374. For what price Joseph was sold, VII, 213. The virtue of the patriarch Joseph was persevering and constant, 650.

Josephus is called the Greek Livy, I, 129. He is the Jewish writer in the vernacular, 213. His two books against Apion, 428. Hieronymus did not translate his books, 434. Josephus admits that Christ was killed by the Pharisees because of the greatness of his signs, II, 851. His testimony concerning this same Christ our Lord, ibid. Josephus, the writer of the history of the Maccabees: what does he think about the sufferings? 749. He says nothing about the cells of the Seventy translators, 520. He reports much about the Essenes, 343. His two books against Apion, ibid. What he wrote about James, 301. Josephus’ books on the Jewish captivity were delivered to the Roman libraries, 851. Josephus wrote about the Jewish captivity, IV, 766. He is refuted, 208. His error is noted, [Col. 1008] 288. Josephus explained all the names of the Hebrew peoples, V, 446. Josephus wrote about the triumphs of Vespasian and Titus, VI, 171.

In what is Josias condemned? I, 1041. The three sons of the righteous King Josias, IV, 989. Josias died in the sins of the sinful people, V, 138. Under Josias, the final kingdom of the two tribes, VI, 675.

A comparison of the burials of Josue and Moses, II, 272. The tomb of Josue was shown near Thamna, III, 223, 283.

Jovianus died suffocated by the stench of burning coals, I, 344. The reign of Jovianus, II, 926.

The monk Jovinianus, a dog returning to its vomit, II, 303. His name is derived from idols, 384. Jovinianus was at once an Epicurean and a Stoic, 357. He praises marriage in order to disparage virginity, 239. He is called the Epicurus of the Christians, 237. The faults in his speech, ibid. He is the common enemy of all, 241. He had many disciples, 380. Jovinianus’ opinion was condemned at Rome and in Africa, 781. Basilides is transformed into Jovinianus as into Euphorbus, 380. He was condemned by the authority of the Roman Church, 389. Jovinianus’ argument is refuted, IV, 951.

An image of Jupiter was placed at the site of Christ’s Resurrection, I, 321. An idol of Jupiter stood where the Temple of God had once been located, IV, 37. From Hadrian to Constantine, an image of Jupiter stood at the place of Christ’s Resurrection, I, 118. An image of Jupiter standing in the Temple, V, 716. Jupiter’s tomb, VII, 708. See Jupiter.

Jubal, inventor of the lyre, IV, 77.

The jubilee year, in which all debts owed to everyone were released and the seller returned to his former possession, II, 350. The Jewish jubilee year, IV, 49. At the arrival of the jubilee every harsh condition was released, VII, 379.

The misfortune of Judas the betrayer, I, 319. His beginnings are praised, but his end is condemned because of his betrayal, 285. The election of Judas, like the anointing of Saul, does not accuse God of ignorance but shows that he is judge of present things, V, 16. The death of Judas the betrayer, VI, 301. Judas cannot be said to have been snatched from God’s hands but to have fallen away, 60. Judas’s homicide was worse than all homicides, 301. Why Judas is called Iscariot, VII, 57. He is said to have been of an evil nature, 226. He thought Christ’s signs had been performed by magical arts, 221. Judas’s shameless confidence, ibid.

Juda is interpreted as “confession,” I, 179. The house of Juda is the Church of Christ, 616. The tribe of Juda, endowed with the most warlike men, held the chief place among all the tribes, III, 174. It boasts in vain of the leisure of the Sabbath, 307. The tribe of Juda is situated in the southern part, IV, 403. Juda sinned after Israel, V, 868. Juda sinned more seriously than Israel, 869. Juda is utterly rejected by God, 871. Why the tribe of Juda deserved to receive the kingdom, VI, 132. The twelve tribes are enclosed between Emath, Epiphania, and the borders of Egypt, 320. Juda’s entry into the Red Sea according to the Hebrew story, 122.

The doctrine of Judas the Galilean, VII, 729. Judas, the brother of James, II, 833. Judas and Joseph are types of Christ, VI, 875.

A description of Judas Maccabaeus, VI, 872.

Judaea is higher than the other provinces, I, 202. All Judaea borders on Moabitis, IV, 189. Its cities are called islands, 711. They were reduced to desolation, 916. Why? 281. Scripture speaks according to the geographical situation of the land of Judaea, 868. It is said to possess the shadow of piety, 282. Judaea is a very beautiful region, V, 225. Judaea was subjected to the Romans under Caesar Augustus, VII, 175. Having become tributary, a revolt arose, ibid. It became tributary after Caesar Augustus, 135. See Jerusalem.

Jews, having become servants of impiety through the killing of the Lord’s flesh, I, 622. Although his virtues shine forth to all, they do not cease blaspheming, ibid. The ceremonies of the Jews are harmful and deadly to Christians, 747. Their sacraments are not indifferent between good and evil, 750. A heresy flourishing among the Jews throughout the synagogues of the East, 746. The practice of Jewish mourners, 182. In the wilderness the Jews did not experience the growth of their hair, II, 440. Heretics among the Jews, 197. It is one thing to read psalms in the churches, another to answer the Jews who slander every individual word, 526. The Jews were handed over to the Romans because they provoked the Holy Spirit, 154. In what sense the Jews were called sons of God and sons of iniquity, IV, 14. The good things of the present age were promised to them, so that, invited at least by present benefits, they might do what was commanded, 24, 723. God demanded obedience from them, 522. God reproves them for having placed their trust in man, 224. They were always unbelieving toward the Lord’s commandments, ibid. The Lord, from being the protector of the Jewish people, became their adversary, 754. Their solemnities were types of future things, 276. Once their religion was removed, all their festivity perished, 389. By a very wicked custom they sacrificed on the mountains, 455. By sacrificing their children to idols, they make their wombs their children’s tombs, 975. By whom the Jewish people was ruled from Jehoiakim to Christ, 996. The Jews earned the friendship of the Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Romans, 15. How great were their impieties? 815, [Col. 1009] 709. The hardness of the Jews is censured in comparison with the faith of kings and princes, 889. Their blindness, 514. Their rashness—which? 685. Rejection and darkness, 709. Jews and millenarians are censured, 627. Their opinion refuted, 158. Their empty vows, 369. They defer their vows to the future, 232. They will receive Antichrist, the instrument of the devil, ibid. The one whom they promise to themselves in place of Christ, 704. Their tradition rejected, 318. Antichrist lies hidden in Jewish traditions, 705. The pride of the Jews is broken, 488. They follow a simple and merely literal history, 935. They possess neither knowledge of the Scriptures nor the leaves nor the fruits of words, 29 and 368. They strive to overthrow the sacraments of Christ and the Apostles, 434, 579. They interpreted an ambiguous Hebrew word in the worse sense, 43. What the Jews assert will take place carnally in the future has already taken place spiritually, 165. Jewish transgressors and the Apostles are distinguished by various expressions of Scripture, 524. Their interpretations, 248, 717. A Jewish fable, 361. In the name of Idumaea they understand the Romans, 218. They carried very old children in their arms and on their shoulders, 572. Jerome calls the Jews “the Circumcision,” 154. How certain people made a foreskin for themselves, 601. They have bread but without strength; they have waters but without vigor, 46. No nation is more avaricious than that of the Jews and Romans, 36. Under the name of the Holy Spirit they sold doves in the Temple, 660. Three times a year they came to Jerusalem, 573. After Christ’s killing, all grace and gifts were taken away from the Jews, 43. Few of them were saved, 149, 614. They sent letters to all nations so that they would not accept Christ’s Passion, 199. Three times each day they curse the Christian name, 81, 565, 604, 766. They have no judges of their own, but Roman ones, 47. They have no prophet or warrior in the law, ibid. They have no authority to bear arms, ibid. When the Romans conquered the Jews, the Lord is shown to have fought, 711. The day of the Jewish destruction—which is it? 971. Their final devastation occurred under Vespasian, Titus, and Hadrian, 430. Their devastation will continue until the end, 21. Their eternal captivity is expressed by the description of wounds that cannot be healed, 16. They were destroyed because they rejected the law of the Gospel, 87. They are forbidden by law to enter the holy City, 971. Compared with their former multitude, scarcely a tenth part remains, 100. Their confusion when they recognize Christ, 350. Judah is lovable and beloved in comparison with Israel, 72. The idolatry of Judah and Benjamin, 374. The Jews and their teachers bound the Decalogue around their heads, V, 280. Their festivals of Unleavened Bread and Booths, 388. When were they celebrated? ibid. They set up a statue of Baal in the Temple, 271. Certain men vainly claimed the Jewish kingdom for themselves, 251. The shamelessness of the Jewish people and God’s compassion toward it, 235. A catalogue of its impieties, 320. Their empty vows, 41. To this day they have a veil placed over them when the Old Testament is read, 27. Through the prophets they sought what they wished to know, 222. They listened to the prophets for the pleasure of their ears, not for the salvation of their souls, 404. They no longer deserve to have prophets, 69. They mocked the discrepancy of the words in the Latin manuscripts, 432. Their interpretations, 444, 453. On what food do they feed? 44. They act for the sake of the good things of this age, 46. God does not desire their death, 217. The distinction between the Jewish and Christian peoples, 602. If the Jews did not receive the land promised by God, the reason is their unbelief, 225. The Jews evade the prophecies concerning Christ, VI, 851. The Jews’ various captivities, 300. Their solemnities, 19. What was the affliction of the Jewish people? 692, 693. They are forbidden to enter Jerusalem, ibid. The fact that the Jewish people takes offense is part of God’s dispensation, 454, 455. The Jews worship one God but do not acknowledge the Trinity, 303.
