Although the Jews do not serve idols, nevertheless they do not possess God, 31. What foods do they eat? ibid. Christ’s compassion and love for the Jewish people, 394. In how many ways does the Lord come to the Jewish people? 665. The Jews of their own accord separated themselves from Christ, 345. They were rejected by God, 104. They were compelled to eat the bodies of their children, 178. The pride of the Jewish princes, 307. After the Lord had been offered, the kingdom departed from the Jews, 683. The Jews’ civil wars, 886. Forty years after Christ’s Passion they were overthrown, 666. Their final ruin, 337. Their crimes and the cause of God’s anger are recounted, 339. The Jews are wanderers throughout the whole world, 342. Their punishments in every place, ibid. The Jews are covered by eternal blindness, 927. Their teachers follow the killing letter, 231. There were few teachers among the Jews in Jerome’s time, in the Preface to Hosea. The Jews are called “the Circumcision,” ibid. The synagogue of the Jews is both a harlot and an adulteress, 14. The conversion of the Jewish people at the consummation of the age, 664. The boundaries of the land of Judah, 319. The dryness of the springs of Judaea, 272. The Jews are deprived of gifts, VII, 88. Their hardening is not of nature but of the will, ibid. Before Christ’s coming they possessed justice not fully but to some extent, 731. The solemnities of the Jews, 456. Exorcists among the Jews, 79. Clerics, 60. In what do they boast? 734. The Jews’ knowledge consists in vanities, ibid. [Col. 1010] They keep the precepts of men more than those of God, 351. Two heresies among the Jews, 177. How great is the Jews’ unhappiness? 421. How are they without excuse? 220. The error of the Jews is our salvation, 99. The Jews’ arrogance, 735. Their interpreters persecute the Church, 389. The Jews are turned from head into tail, 153. Their last state is worse than the first, 85. Jews and Gentiles are divided fourfold, 579. What do the Jews object to Christians? 435. Jerome refutes them, ibid. and following. The emperors’ laws concerning the Jews, 531. Their custom concerning handing over defendants to the judge, 226. The punishment for greater crimes among them, 138. The Jews’ very bad custom of swearing, 30. What they usually do to those who blaspheme against God, 225. Apostles sent by the Jewish patriarchs, 374. Jewish fables, 710. Who pay attention to them? ibid. See Hebrews and Israel.

Judaizers snore in a very deep sleep, IV, 159.

When the Lord is about to judge, the world will groan mournfully, etc., I, 37. What will then be of no avail, ibid. Human envy judges one way, Christ another, 26. Each thing must be judged not by the importance of persons but by the weight of the facts, 523, 479.

He who asks bends the judge, I, 1088. What the judges of the world do in order to appear more distinguished, VII, 688. The presence of the Judge is to be feared, 198. God alone is the just Judge, 250. The unjust judge is censured, VI, 512.

In the Book of Judges, as many leaders, so many figures, I, 277.

In judgments, consideration should be given not to persons but to facts, I, 579. The judgments of lovers are blind, II, 409. Judgment must be guarded at all times, IV, 654. One must not immediately submit to the judgment of the multitude, 53. Judgments were conducted at the gates of the Temple, 1027. The earlier judges of the Hebrew people, 28. Judgments took place at the gates of cities, 291. When true judgments take place, 53. What are the signs of true judgment? 850. Judgment turns into fury when an angry man judges, 321. We ought not to be disturbed by perverse judgments, 592. Human judgment is not certain, VII, 250.

At God’s judgment the just alone will rejoice; the rest will tremble, I, 37. The sentence of Christ’s tribunal is not the same as that of whisperers in a corner, 26. Whoever fears it certainly prepares himself for judgment through good works, 691. God’s judgment is measured and weighty, II, 764. The certain judgment belongs to God alone, 748. No one can claim Christ’s palm for himself before the day of judgment, 196. No one goes without fear to the Lord’s judgment, 769. No one may judge human beings before the day of judgment, 196. The whole earth needs judgment, 774. Many have been judged in this life before the day of judgment, III, 444. God does not now judge piecemeal and individually, but reserves judgment for the future, so that all may be judged together and there receive according to their will and works, 415. When the Lord begins to judge at the judgment, then there will be truth; now injustice rules in the world, 490. In what sense the time of judgment is at hand, 246. There will not be a time of repentance but of punishments, 239. He does not allow anyone to depart unpunished, 418. On the day of judgment the earth will bring forth into the open all blood, 359. Then every creature will perceive itself to be nothing, 38. Judgment must not be anticipated, 79. A splendid and terrifying explanation of the day of judgment, 238 and following. No one, however holy, should proceed to judgment secure, 1055. The day of judgment is to be feared, V, 359. Neither the angels nor the Son know the day of judgment, VI, 32. How great is the severity of the day of judgment? 181, 188, 213. The day of judgment is to be feared, 301. There is no soul that does not fear at God’s judgment, 540. On the day of judgment Christ will deny some and confess others, VII, 312. On the day of judgment there will be no place for repentance nor opportunity for denial, etc., 174. On that day neither other people’s virtues nor their vices will support anyone, 204. After the day of judgment there will be no opportunity for good works and justice, 205. Why it is not expedient for the Apostles to know the day of judgment, 200. What does it mean to bear judgment? ibid.

Judith, as a type of the Church, cut off the devil’s head, I, 507. Praises of Judith, ibid. She is proposed to widows as an example for imitation, 508. The Book of Judith was not accepted by everyone, 231. Judith overcame Holofernes by a prudent pretense in her words, II, 474.

He who is under the yoke must run in such a way that he does not leave his companion in the mud, I, 689.

Julia, a city, VII, 122.

Juliana, mother of Demetrias, I, 979.

Julian the Apostate, traitor to his own soul and slaughterer of the Christian army, perceived Christ in Media, I, 35. The emperor Julian vomited forth seven books against Christ, 427. According to the poets’ fables, he is said to have slashed himself with his own sword, ibid. He called Christ a Galilean, ibid. He received the reward of his foul tongue when he was pierced through by a spear, ibid. The emperor Julian, a most implacable enemy of Christ, II, 823. He succeeded Constantius, and through Constantius’s indulgence the exiled bishops returned to their churches, 191. The same Julian vomited forth certain volumes against the Christians, VI, 123. The calumny of that Apostate is refuted, ibid. A pagan’s saying at Julian’s death, 660. An objection of Julian Augustus, VII, 11. His calumny refuted, 50.

[Col. 1011] Julian lost two daughters and his wife within a short time, I, 792. His losses and a catalogue of his temptations, ibid. Those proposed to Julian for imitation, 796. His good works toward the saints and churches, ibid.

The communion of the pontiffs Julius and Athanasius, II, 925.

Julius Africanus wrote histories of the ages, 429.

Julius derives his name from the great Iulus, I, 692.

Great Iulus, I, 692.

The souls of beasts perish with their bodies and are dissolved into dust, I, 590. From what “beasts” (jumenta) derives its name, II, 328. Beasts are so called from the fact that they help human beings, IV, 12. See Animals.

The juniper and the power of its ash in preserving something in fire for a year, I, 481.

In what way Christ is like the juniper, VI, 161.

The virgins of one-married Juno continually withered in perpetual virginity, I, 906. The one-married virgins of Juno, II, 255. Juno has women married only once, VII, 528.

Jupiter Gamelius and Genethlius, II, 317. The temples and rites of Jupiter collapsed at Rome, 384. The abstinence of Jupiter’s prophets, 344. Jupiter Enyalius signifies Mars, III, 266. Jupiter Gamelius, ibid. Jupiter’s lover and catamite used to hand the cup to Jupiter himself, 356.

An oath is called a sacrament, I, 116. In what do an oath and perjury differ? IV, 864. “To swear” is used for “to confess,” 863. The inviolability of an oath’s faith, V, 194. It is the end of a dispute, 150.

What it means when God is said to swear, VI, 339.

When people swear, one must consider not by whom but through whom they have sworn, V, 193.

Those quarreling with one another are reconciled by very gentle speech, I, 713. See “I Contend.”

The highest law is the highest wickedness, I, 7.

A human being is not justified except through faith in Christ, II, 752. No one is justified before God’s sight, 780.

Justin the philosopher, whom he imitated, I, 428. He published a book against the Gentiles and offered it to Antoninus Pius, ibid. He defended the disgrace of the cross and proclaimed Christ’s resurrection, ibid. Justin the philosopher, II, 863.

There is a twofold justice in the holy Scriptures, II, 709. Justice is preserved through labor, diligence, and God’s mercy, 781. Justice lies not in human merit but in God’s grace, 750. The justice of the patriarchs and prophets was not perfect, 707. He who does not wish to distribute his possessions to the poor does not possess full justice, 757. Justice has rest, iniquity labor, III, 421. Justice is inhuman when it does not forgive the frailty of the human condition, 443. Justice and piety ought to precede the light of knowledge in us, 407. A great scale of justice is to give to the right person, the right amount, for the right length of time, and of the right quality, whether in deed or in counsel, 446. Justice embraces all virtues, IV, 665. Its parts are to turn away from evil and to do good, 23. Unhappiness exists where peace has been lost and there is no justice, 729. Human justice needs God’s mercy, 1068. The Lord alone knows how to test it, 981. What is the difference between the two kinds of justice? 762, 763. “Justice” and “works” are used ironically, 676. Justice must be preserved in all things, V, 564. How iniquity justifies and justice condemns, 964. God’s justice is enclosed by mercy, VI, 419. Justice satisfies; iniquity leaves empty bellies, 39. How the fruit of justice is turned into bitterness, 321. Justice must always be hungered for, VII, 24.

Let the just person not be secure in his own virtue, I, 912. In accordance with what justice are the just in Scripture so called? 898. Adam’s punishment for sin exists among the just, 333. They were not entirely without fault, 1041. They are troubled because of the prosperity of the wicked, 178. The condition of the just and the sinner is distinct, 127. The Lord does not kill the soul of the just through hunger, 117. The just person is one who flourishes in many virtues, II, 748. Why are they scarcely saved? ibid. No one is perfectly just, but is a sinner in some respect, 755. They are not free from every sin, 744. Some may be called just who are not just in comparison with others, 710. Those whom we think just are often found to be sinners, and so forth, 748. The just person does not have a left cheek in himself, but everything in him is right, III, 469. The things that ought to happen to the wicked frequently happen to the just, while the wicked live so prosperously in this world that you would think them most just, 456. Because of the uncertain and slippery condition of this life, both the just person falls and the sinner rises, 418. The just and the sinner will by no means have the same end: the one will proceed to refreshment, the other to punishment, 404. He is not just who does not sin, IV, 81. His impatience, 981. He is just who perishes in his justice, 762. In what sense is the just man God’s loincloth? 931. He does not fulfill all virtues, 1055. The just who are killed and tortured are regarded as wretched by the wicked, 433. The just man is a stranger upon the earth, VI, 695. His constancy and moderation, 171. The just man is praised because he is not overcome by poverty so as to do something unjust, 241. The just speak with God, 529. All the just are understood through Noah, Job, and Daniel, [Col. 1012] VII, 191. How great is the difference between the simple and the learned just person? 633.

Justus of Tiberias, II, 853.

Juvencus explained the history of the Lord in verse, I, 430. Juvencus the presbyter, VII, 14.

There are said to be very many eloquent and noble young men at Rome, I, 639. Young men with long hair and linen garments are described with girls, 786. What do wanton youths usually do, etc.? 964, 965. Against young men and girls our enemy takes advantage of the heat of their age, 986. A black and shining boot, by its creaking, calls young men to itself, 688. We have gone astray as young men; let us amend our ways as old men, II, 539. See Adolescent.

## K

Among the Latins, except in the word *kalendae*, K is considered a superfluous letter, III, 34. It is expressed by C, 91.

Description of the Labyrinth from Virgil, V, 561.

A protruding lip on the edge of the altar, V, 527.

Labor must be joined with piety, I, 991. Without labor the monasteries of Egypt receive no one—and why? 940. Great is the labor, but great also is the reward that the martyrs receive, etc., I, 123. The labor of the present age will come to an end, and everlasting joy will succeed it, 622. Limited labor is greater; unlimited labor is more moderate, 687. Life has given mortals nothing without great labor, 327. The greatest vanity among human beings is that one should enjoy another’s labor and that the sweat of the dead should be the delight of the living, III, 405. All labor is brief while one reaches the desired reward, IV, 219. Through sweat and labor we attain an abundance of fruits, 872.

For this we labor and struggle in the warfare of this age, so that we may be crowned in the age to come, I, 981. Human beings must labor so that the devil may always find them occupied, 939. For what do we labor on earth? VI, 901.

Labosorodach, king of Babylon after Neglisar, V, 623.

The frugality of the Lacedaemonians, II, 342. The Lacedaemonians were most ready for war, IV, 61.

Lachish, a city devoted to idols, VI, 442.

Laconian garments—which ones? IV, 62.

Tears to be detested and full of unbelief, I, 185. In what are we all worthy of tears and grief? ibid. We are permitted to have tears only in calamities, when we are oppressed by the powerful, III, 418. The custom of provoking tears in Judaea, IV, 908. See Lamentation.

Lactantius was a disciple of Arnobius, I, 429. What were his works? ibid. An *epitome* (ἐπιτομή) of Cicero’s dialogues is found in them, ibid. Lactantius was, as it were, a river of Tullian eloquence, 337. He did not so much affirm our own positions as easily destroy those of others, ibid. Lactantius’s error concerning the Holy Spirit, 528. He wrote most vigorously against the Gentiles, ibid. What is attributed to Lactantius, II, 497. A saying falsely attributed to him, 558. Jerome defends Lactantius, 500. In his splendid work, the *Institutes*, he mentions the letter Y and discusses most fully the right and left sides—that is, virtues and vices, III, 469. Lactantius, VII, 537. His volume to Probus concerning the Galatians, 425. See Firmianus.

A land flowing with milk and honey, IV, 918.

A very famous lake, II, 551. What is a lake? V, 661. The lakes of Tiberias, Larius, and Benacus, 390. “Lake” used for “cistern,” ibid.

What does Laelius forbid? I, 20.

The *laena*, a type of luxurious garment, I, 289.

Laeta was born from an unequal marriage, I, 678. She devoted herself to perpetual chastity, 720.

Joy is not merely a bodily temptation but also a spiritual one for the person who possesses it, so that he needs the correcting spur lest he become exalted, III, 396. In the joy of a banquet, if we seemed to possess any fear of God, we lose it, 436.

What is unsuitable for a layman? II, 173.

Lamech was the first bigamist, I, 507, 909. From Lamech’s offspring seventy-seven souls perished in the Flood, 163 and following.

Lamentations, song, and woe—to whom do they pertain? V, 27. Concerning what did Jeremiah write the *Lamentations*? VI, 904. What difference is there between lament and woe? 906.

Women who lament in Judaea, VI, 298 and following.

What the *lampenae* are and signify, IV, 823.

No one restores wool dyed purple to its original color, I, 682. No waters wash out wool dyed purple, II, 486. Milesian wool, V, 316.

Many poor people, though healthy, envy the sick, I, 462.

Laodamia is celebrated in the poets’ song, II, 311.

The Laodicean interpreter, VII, 369.

Lapetha, a town, II, 37.

What became of the twelve stones taken from the bed of the Jordan? I, 701. [Col. 1013] They were a type of the twelve Apostles, ibid. Various kinds of precious stones, 982. The fable of the Lapiths, VII, 651.

The devil has filled everything with snares, and all things are full of nets, III, 529.

Household gods, IV, 672.

What must be avoided in giving, VII, 528.

It is the nature of ghosts to terrify children and chatter in dark corners, III, 303.

The Lateran Basilica, I, 459.

Lateranus was beheaded by Caesar’s sword, ibid.

If Latin learning has not formed the tender mouth from the beginning, the tongue is corrupted into a foreign sound, I, 686. Which Latin authors translated Greek works? 309. The Latin language does not express Greek propriety, II, 261. The Latins were delighted only by the applause accorded to eloquence, IV, 6. Their ears were fastidious when it came to understanding the Scriptures, ibid. The Latin language does not express the sound of the Hebrew letter *ṣade*, 155. It is scarcely produced with clenched teeth by an impression of the tongue, ibid. Latinity changes daily according to regions and time, VII, 429. What the Latin language does not express, 551, 692.

The thief passes from the cross into paradise, I, 678. He exchanges the cross for paradise and makes the punishment of homicide into martyrdom, 319. A naked thief is not afraid, II, 18. The thief passes from the cross into paradise, IV, 654. When will the Church of God be turned into a den of thieves? 892. The thief entered paradise first with Christ, VI, 865. The thief—which one in the Temple? VII, 162.

The peoples of the Idumaeans, Ammonites, and others are more suited to brigandage than to battle, IV, 829.

Little thieves, that is, emissaries, VI, 443.

The Hebrews call the king’s side the queen, V, 674.

Health-giving baths at Betoaenea, III, 151, 175. The Gentiles promise many baths in their mysteries, V, 146.

Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, I, 1087. Human beings are excessive in praise or blame, 235.

Do not believe your praisers, I, 944. The praise of God benefits those who praise more than God himself, VII, 562.

People sometimes praise what they do not approve, II, 421. It is permissible, depending on circumstances, both to praise and to blame the same person, 943. It is not a fault to praise one person in some respects and accuse him in others, etc., 556. Many are frequently praised in the Church after death, and those who were blessed in things they had not done commendably are publicly celebrated either by their successors or by the people, III, 454.

Laurels lie hidden in the multitude, III, 398.

The Latin interpreter renders Λαξευτήριον (*Laxeutērion*, “place of hewing”) as *Ascia*, I, 676.

Lazarus’s tomb was displayed, I, 701. Lazarus’s poverty and refreshment, 798.

The death of Saint Lea was announced to Jerome, I, 127. Her remains were carried to Ostia, ibid. She was head of a monastery and mother of virgins, ibid. Her lot was far better than that of the consul Praetextatus, ibid.

A lioness attacking a man, II, 48.

The nature of lionesses, V, 664. Why the Babylonian kingdom is compared with a lioness, 670. Lionesses are fiercer and more eager for intercourse, ibid.

Sacred reading is commended, I, 100. In it God speaks to us, 109. Let sacred reading always be in one’s hand, 334, 939. Through constant reading and meditation, let our breast become Christ’s library, 339. It should not be for labor but for the soul’s delight and instruction, 991. Negligence in reading, 192. Let reading follow prayer and prayer follow reading, 686.

Variant readings of Latin and Greek manuscripts, I, 134. A variant reading is noted, V, 589. Variant manuscript readings, VII, 72, 95, 422, 552, 596, 626, 627, 632, 654, 659, 692, 702, 727, 745, 753. The reading of Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus, 641. Let the mind be nourished by divine reading, 734.

What is an unjust reader? I, 214. What should a prudent reader do? 221. A cautious reader quickly detects the underground passages and ambushes by which the truth is overturned, II, 410.

What must be read cautiously? VII, 511.

The Roman legion surnamed the Tenth was stationed at Aila, at the farthest boundaries of Palestine, III, 130. A legion consisted of six thousand men, VII, 222.

Legumes, taken sparingly and moderately, are harmless, I, 288.

Lenulus the writer of mimes, II, 513.

The Nemean lion, II, 387. With a lion as guardian and protector, no one dares approach, IV, 1024. Why was the rage of the lions shut up in a pit by an angel? V, 664. The lion does not roam in cultivated fields, but where there are forests and untilled ground, 254.

Leonidas, Alexander’s teacher, I, 682.

Leonidas, Origen’s father, crowned by martyrdom, II, 891. He left behind a wife with seven sons, ibid. The treasury seized his property, ibid.

Leontius the presbyter asks Jerome to translate the rule of Saint Pachomius into Latin, II, 53.

Leontia, wife of Metrodorus, I, 317.

The death of Leosthenes, II, 307.

What is the rock of hares? I, 984.

Leptis, a half-barbarian city, II, 307.

The Lernaean serpent, IV, 923.

The Lethean whirlpool, II, 486.

Leucate, a promontory of Epirus, II, 230.

The tribe of Levi was substituted for the tribe of Dan, II, 306.

Light things are compared with light things, and heavy things with heavy things, II, 714.

The dress of the Levites, II, 274. Spiritual Levites, or those who are hidden, IV, 825.

Forty-eight cities were given to the Levitical tribe for habitation, V, 603.

Almost every syllable of the Levitical books breathes heavenly mysteries, I, 276.

The *levitonarium*, a type of monastic garment, II, 66.

Leusibore, a ridiculous name, II, 393.

The Law and the Gospel have one and the same God, I, 916. He sows in the Law so that he may reap in the Gospel, ibid. The Law is spiritual, and revelation is needed for it to be understood, 474. Observing its ceremonies cannot be indifferent, 750. Paul reproves those who believed that they could be justified in the Law, 772. Whoever is under it does not have the Holy Spirit, ibid. No one fulfilled the Law, II, 752, 746. Its justice, in comparison with evangelical grace, does not appear to be justice, 709. The times of the Law were times of ignorance, 761. Some things in the Law must be observed and others omitted, 741. Knowledge of the Law is rarely found among the teachers of the Church, 721. From the beginning of the world until Noah, what did not prevail? 267. After the Flood and after Christ, certain things were permitted and the same things prohibited, 268. The ancient Law, rigid and unkind, sparing no one, kills the sinner. The grace of the Gospel has mercy and summons to repentance, III, 409. Why was the Law given through Moses? IV, 331. The pure and sincere Law of God was violated by the traditions of the Pharisees, 25, 141. The Law of the Lord was first translated in Alexandria, 108. The justice of the Law, in comparison with evangelical purity, is called uncleanness, 762. The opinion asserting that the ceremonies of the Law must be observed in the Church is rejected, 623. The apostolic command is manifest in the Law, V, 583. The Law was written under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, VI, 808. Only the five books of Moses were translated by the Seventy, 439. The reading of the Law without Christ is bitter, 573. The Law and the prophets proclaim Christ’s Passion, 809. Why was the Law given? VII, 440, 441. The elements of the world are the Law of Moses and the Old Testament, 447. It restores justice through retaliation, 499. The reward for observing the Old Law, 433. The curses of the Law are fulfilled, not with God as their author, 434. Moses and the Prophets did not live under the Law but as if under the Law, 503. The Old Law cannot save without faith in Christ, 411. Paul teaches that it has everywhere been laid aside, 369, 371. He hears the Law who looks into not its surface but its marrow, 469. A question is posed concerning the Old Law and resolved, 453, 454. The spiritual understanding of the Law is preferred to the literal, 446, 447. Its spiritual understanding is rich, 455. There are commandments in the Law that no one can fulfill, while others are performed by those who do not know the Law, 413. The commandments of the Law are summed up in the single commandment of love, 497 and following. The Law has no force after the Gospel, 421. The Old Law contains the shadow, and the Gospel the truth, 481. The difficulty of the ancient Law is changed by the completeness of the Gospel, 446. The Law cannot now be fulfilled, 444. Who fulfills the Law of Christ through charity? 521. He does not fulfill it who lacks mercy, ibid. It is one thing to die through the Law, another to die to the Law, 413. Being under the Law is not the same as being as if under the Law, 503. Whoever dies to the letter of the Law lives to God, 413. The conflicts over the Law arise not from a desire for truth but from ostentation of glory, 736. Who are servants and free people in the Law? 470. The Law, taken allegorically, was established not according to the reader’s will but according to the authority of the writer, 474.

Law. The benefit of observing laws, I, 614. What the Law of God is to the mind, that is what a law is to a ship’s pilot, 626. It must be obeyed as a very powerful commander, 616. Remembering it does not allow sins to arise, nor does it permit them to grow, 611. Tireless meditation on the Law of Christ arises from love of God and desire for him, [Col. 1015] 339. It is not a matter of repeating what has been written but of putting it into practice, 953. Human judgments must not be preferred to the Law of God, 629. Laws must maintain the standard of truth, 579. The laws of Caesar are one thing, those of Christ another, 447. In the midst of arms the laws are silent, 447. Who judges the law? II, 746. Reason is not sought in the law but authority, 747. The natural law was given to all, IV, 331. The natural law was restored, 590. What is the law of divorce? V, 871. What does it mean to hear the law secretly? 833, 834. Its interpretation is the priest’s duty, 78. Teaching sons and daughters according to the Law of God, 724. The Law was torn apart because of bribes, 593. The natural law speaks in our hearts, VII, 419.

Leah, fertile, prefigured the Synagogue, I, 910.

Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness,” II, 286. Lebanon, a mountain of Phoenicia, IV, 397, 726. In Scripture Lebanon is frequently called the Temple, 435. It is called Jerusalem, ibid. Lebanon is homonymous with frankincense—*homōnymos* (ὁμώνυμος), VI, 160. The trees of Lebanon are very tall and deeply rooted, ibid. In the Promised Land nothing is higher than Lebanon, 884.

By generosity generosity perishes, I, 334. Liberality and administration are the greatest virtues, IV, 674.

“Without Liber and Ceres, Venus grows cold,” I, 287. Liber was born from Jupiter’s thigh, II, 309. There is a twofold Liber, good and evil, V, 669.

Liberius, bishop, II, 919, 931.

The procreation of children was formerly blessed and considered, as it were, just, I, 105. A multitude of children is promised to the just as a blessing, 624. God is appeased by the virtues of children, 503. See Son.

The freedom of the mind is not destroyed even though we always turn to God and depend on his will, I, 1035. All people were in captivity and under a general siege, and they did not desire a freedom they did not know, 913. Freedom of human choice, V, 790.

Desire was implanted by God for the procreation of children, I, 287. If it goes beyond its limits, it overflows into vice, ibid. The inducements to lust and the signs of an immodest mind, 286. It rules equally in silk and in rags, 507. Lust when it subdues minds of iron, 787. It suffers greater hunger in virgins, while it thinks everything it does not know sweeter, ibid. Once acted upon, it always leaves regret behind, 911. Under whose protection does lust flatter itself? ibid. 901. A lustful mind pursues dishonorable things more ardently, 787. It suspects that what is not permitted is sweeter, ibid. Lust is safe in no age, 790. By what signs is a lustful spirit revealed? 713. Which young man’s Egyptian mistress did not hold his cloak? 501. From fulfilled lusts, triumphs and the palms of vices are lifted up, 1094. By the laws of the Caesars, except in the case of adultery, lust is permitted in brothels, 459. The misfortune of a dead wife is blamed, while the lust of a prostitute is crowned, 415. Let the one who served lust serve chastity with a good freedom, ibid. The eating of meat, drinking of wine, and fullness of the belly are the seedbed of lust, II, 336. No captivity is a greater calamity than being dragged into another’s lust, 319. See Luxury, Pleasure.

A part of Libya is full of Greek cities, VII, 427.

From what are scribes so called? I, 21. Unlearned scribes, who, while trying to correct others’ errors, display their own, 434. The duty of scribes, 688. The negligence of scribes produced variant readings in the Bibles, 646. A scribal error is noted, VII, 14.

## Books

The apocryphal books are to be avoided, I, 432. Almost all books are full of secular learning and instruction, 456. From style and “saliva” we recognize the author of a book, 632. Let books be written, so that the hand may work for food and the soul be satisfied by reading, 939. Just as the reliability of the ancient books is to be tested against the Hebrew volumes, so the new require the standard of the Greek language, 434. The material and decoration of books, 117. Books are not greatly to be feared when their author fears to publish them, II, 461. The books of the unlearned find readers, 474. A solemn warning concerning the transcription of books, 879. Many, through ignorance, prefer Iberian nonsense to authentic books, 520. The Hebrews give books their names from their beginnings, III, 306. Innumerable books are called one Law and one Gospel, 495. The books that people compose with the greatest labor they often hand over to the sluggish and idle, 404. The Hebrew books have not been corrupted, IV, 97. The apocryphal books must be avoided, 76. The sacred books are adorned with gold and purple, VI, 841. The Book of Judith was not accepted by everyone, 745. The doctrine of the apocryphal books is condemned, 604. Some statements from the apocryphal books, 751. The canonical books: whence their authority is derived, VII, 743.

From the bitter seed of letters sweet fruits are gathered, 941. Letters do not follow the purse, II, 473. They are companions of sweat and labor; allies of fasting, not of satiety; of self-restraint, not of luxury, ibid. The roots of letters are bitter, but their fruits sweet, IV, 840. One must sometimes necessarily depart from the letter, V, 905. The bitterness of literal understanding, V, 587. The Letter has the greatest usefulness if it is observed, ibid. 241. The arrogance and vanity of the letters of the world, VII, 487.

Letters made of boxwood or ivory for playing, I, 681. The Hebrew letters aleph, he, heth, and ‘ayin alter their aspirations and sounds, III, 3. Through the exchange of letters we always feel a friend to be present, I, 435.

What is said about the shore that stretches along Palestine and Egypt, II, 22.

## Mourning

Small works were written to calm mourning, I, 334. The virtue of very many was no less in mourning than in war, 335. The sinful people are described as mourning in black garments, III, 462. Maturity of character as well as of age must be looked for in the elderly, IV, 48 and following.

Maximinus, the most savage persecutor of all, IV, 954, and VI, 826.

Maximus the tyrant, II, 947.

Maximus the philosopher, II, 943.

Daily meditation and frequent reading are usually more a labor of the soul than of the flesh, III, 395.

What is said about the Megarians? I, 912.

Honey is not offered in sacrifices: why? I, 962. Honey, through excessive satiety, is turned into wormwood, V, 315. Honey is not offered in sacrifices, VI, 173.

Melania, II, 14, 87. Her true nobility among Christians, 183. Her patience and steadfastness, ibid. Her praises, 196. In what matter did she provide Rome with a spectacle? ibid. The stricter life of Melania and Paula, 197.

Melanthius replied to the rhetorician Gorgias, II, 316.

The *meli*, a priestly garment, I, 363.

The *melotes*, a type of garment, II, 55.

Why are parchment sheets called *membranae*? I, 18.

How human limbs and human affections are attributed to God, VI, 315 and following. The members are not one another except among the faithful alone, VII, 627.

**Memory.** It is of no benefit to have seen and heard something unless what is seen and heard is stored in the treasury of memory, V, 466.

Menander, a disciple of Simon Magus, II, 197.

Menander the poet, VII, 647, 648. His iambic trimeter, 471. Menander’s comedy, 707. Paul took an iambic verse from it, ibid.

Liars cause people not to be believed even when they speak the truth, I, 16. Liars ought to remember this, II, 543.

A lie strengthened by time, I, 586. The end of lies is destruction, 606. A lie does not hold together within itself, II, 536. An impudent person is not to be refuted, 3. According to some, lying is permissible, 474. Open enmity arouses suspicion of lying, 470. A lie imitates the truth, IV, 1006, 1039. The instability of falsehood and the stability of God’s word, 266. Some in the Church, through ignorance, defend falsehood in place of truth, 144. The habit of lying transformed into a nature, 905. The guilt of lying, VII, 592.

Many wealthy people have ended as beggars, worn out by poverty amid their weights of gold and silver, V, 76.

Menites, II, 642.

A mind devoted to Christ attends to lesser matters, I, 340. There is no guilt where understanding and the judgment of the mind are lacking, 794. A mind burdened with food is weighed down, 193. A mind joined to God calls forth his mercy, not proximity to the Church, V, 523. Obscurity of mind and vanity of perception are divided into two parts, etc., VII, 621. The blessing of the table and thanksgiving, I, 121.

The months Phamenoth and Pharmuthi, I, 630. The months Mechir and Pharmuthi, 609. Among the Hebrews the month is reckoned according to the course of the moon, V, 353. Nothing is more unclean than a menstruating woman, VI, 907.

The measure of divine mercy, IV, 272.

Consider lying sacrilege, I, 688. Where what is said comes to pass, there is no room for lying, 774. No one who lies weeps, 788.

The mercenary is censured, IV, 276.

Prostitutes should not be thought unmarried, II, 260. Examples of prostitutes and adulteresses specially raised up by God, VI, 19 and following. The Athenian prostitute, VII, 545.

The Hebrews report that Merodach was the father of Nebuchadnezzar, IV, 477.

The wife of Messalla, who married Corvinus for the third time, II, 316.

The books of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, VI, 406.

Metanaea, a monastery near Canopus, II, 53.

Elegant metaphors drawn from analogy, I, 603. If a metaphor is transferred word for word from one language into another, it becomes obscure, II, 476. Metaphor and allegory do not always correspond with history, VI, 658. A metaphor translated literally has obscure meanings, VII, 620.

The Metelli are praised, I, 335.

Methona, II, 35.

Michael, prince of the Israelite people, V, 328. Michael, avenger of Israel’s sins, VI, 784. Michael, prince of the Jews, VII, 282.

For a monk, the town should be a prison and solitude a paradise, 937. Why should one who is esteemed for solitude desire the crowds of cities? ibid. What a monk ought not to think about, 943. Such silence prevailed among the monks that no one dared look at another or spit, 119. The love of the heavenly homeland among certain monks, ibid. Their food and way of life, ibid. Their leaders, 323. Let monks imitate them, ibid. Their life is said to be harsh, 338. What is alien to the monks’ purpose? 208. What they must flee and pursue, 323. Since we have begun to be monks, let this not be an occasion of pride but of humility, 402. False and secular monks, 963. Some are turned toward melancholy: why? ibid. The discipline of the Egyptian monks, 16. The abstinence of some, 5. There were no monks in Syria before Hilarion, 19. Many monks were deceived, and how? 43. An excessively cautious monk expelled by Hilarion, 28. What is said about the frugal man? 27. His frugality is punished, ibid. Swarms of monks flourished in Egypt and Mesopotamia, III, 210.

The superior of a monastery should be feared as a master and loved as a parent, ibid. Learn the order and royal discipline of monasteries from the small animals, ibid. A monitor should not be despised, provided that he teaches what is right and just, I, 196.

Monogamy preceded in Isaac and Rebekah, I, 910. Monogamy is commended, 901 and following. Monogamy is placed after bigamy, VII, 697.

A monster born at Lydda, I, 437. Many kinds of monsters are noted, II, 299.

The Montanists, rigid while committing worse sins, I, 190.

The Montenses, or Campitae, II, 201.

The tombs were opened at the time of the Passion, I, 831 and following.

Nopsiviculus, where Constantine died, I, 343.

Morasthis, the tomb of the prophet Micah, I, 704. Morasthi, a village of Palestine, VI, 433.

From Gerar to Mount Moriah—that is, the site of the Temple—the journey was three days; but from the oak of Mamre to the same mountain, it was scarcely a full day’s journey, 338. Moriah, the mountain, VII, 62.

Maritime peoples, I, 914.

Everything mortal is corruptive, but not conversely, I, and following.

What is *morticinium*? V, 45.

Mortification bears the marks of the Lord, VII, 534.

Christian tradition concerning the recitation of Psalms and hymns over them, 466. The *Alleluia* is sung at the funerals of the dead, ibid. Wealthy people wrap their dead in gilded garments, II, 12. Christian tradition concerning the recitation of Psalms and hymns over them, 11. In the presence of a dead corpse we are reminded of our condition and human frailty, III, 436.
