The eyes confess the secrets of the heart, I, 290. The impure do not know how to contemplate the beauty of the soul, but only that of bodies, 107. Let not a mole despise the eyes of goats, 430. The right eye is taken for virginity, II, 286. The left for marriage, ibid. What is seen with the eyes is more firmly retained in the mind, IV, 969, 973. Through the gates of the eyes and ears, just as the greatest vices entered, so through those same gates the greatest punishment will be felt, VI, 684 and following. The eye of the flesh and of the mind, VII, 300.

When human hatreds are not to be feared, I, 533. Murder often arises from hatred, 27. We pursue our adversaries with undying hatred; toward those who blaspheme God we extend a merciful hand, II, 447.

Odolla, a city of Judah, VI, 443.

To whom is Christ’s good fragrance life, and to whom death? I, 843 and following. To whom the sweetness of fragrance is fitting, II, 337.

[Col. 1035] The story of Oedipus—by whom it was appropriated, I, 257.

Oenanthe, a herb, II, 513.

Oestrus, a kind of fly, I, 738.

Offellus, a bishop, I, 630.

A great offense is refusing to appease the person whom one has offended, IV, 856.

What is to be offered to the Lord? I, 791. If we offer wealth to Christ together with our soul, he will gladly receive it, 402. If we give to God what is outward and to the devil what is inward, the division is not equitable, ibid. The one who offered himself gave everything to God, 281. To offer lies within our power; to neglect what has been offered brings danger, 684. To offer what we can is ours; for God to fulfill what we cannot is his, II, 781.

The names of those making offerings were publicly recited, IV, 921. The names of those making offerings, which have been consecrated to the Lord, do not belong to those to whom they were given, but to the one in whose name they are possessed, V, 607. God regards not the gifts but the will of those making offerings, VI, 305.

An office is sometimes thought to be ambition, I, 497. The terminology of offices, 783.

Huldah the prophetess was a reproach to all men, II, 556. When Huldah the woman prophesied, V, 623.

Eating vegetables is greatly beneficial to young Christians, I, 288. They should be taken temperately, ibid.

Why oil, not wax, is burned in the temple, I, 962. Blessed oil heals the bites of poisonous animals, II, 32. It is the nature of oil both to feed a flame and to relieve the labor of the weary, III, 463. The power of oil, IV, 502. “Son of oil”—who is he? 69. The oil with which our Savior was anointed, V, 151. Some think that oil is not produced in Egypt, VI, 134. Samaria is exceedingly fertile in oil, ibid. The prophets were anointed with oil, ibid.

The usefulness of the fruit of the olive, VI, 162. Converts are compared to fruitful olives, 163.

Olive-grove trees are fruit-bearing, VII, 161.

Olybrius, father of Demetrias, I, 777. Rome mourned him, taken away by premature death, ibid. His praises, and in what respect he is proclaimed happy, ibid. The names of the Olybrii, ibid.

The Ommei, or Omnium, a powerful people in Save, III, 267.

The word “all” sometimes signifies the greater part, I, 85. “Every” is taken for the greater part, VII, 568.

On, in Greek Heliopolis, had been built before Jacob entered Egypt, III, 258. On, or Aun, a city of Samaria, ibid.

The wild asses obedient to Antony, II, 31.

Onasus of Segesta is censured, I, 187.

Jerome does not approve of bearing burdens beyond one’s strength, I, 688, 714.

What the difference is between “burden” and “vision,” IV, 184, 1067. “Burden” may be taken in a good or an evil sense, VII, 490.

Onesimus, a boy, I, 11. Onesimus was from Colossae, VII, 748. The history of Onesimus, 755.

Two kinds of pelicans, VI, 710.

The onyx stone, I, 371.

Oholibah is interpreted as “my tent is in her,” IV, 25. Oholah and Oholibah are sisters, the same as the women of Hosea, VI, 6.

Works. A work without faith is fleeting and weak, I, 604. The ointment of good works, 431. Works should not contradict the teacher’s speech, 262, 422. Many, although silent in speech, speak through their deeds, 118. The usefulness of labor and work, 991. For this reason one must labor, so that during the occasion of work one thinks of nothing except what pertains to the service of the Lord, ibid. Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied, 939. No one ought to cease from work because he lacks nothing, 991. God is the perfecter of good work; the devil is the perfecter of evil, II, 325. The saints seek God’s help in each matter and in each one, 700. In good works we rely on God’s help, in evil works on the devil’s, 698. Forgiveness should be granted to a new work, III, 303. The perverse seize seeds of heresies from the best works and slander the labors of others, 405. The error of certain people concerning the works of the dead, 459. After death human beings can perform no good work, ibid. Good works are signified by spikenard, 517. The works of God’s people do not grow old but are renewed daily, IV, 794. The reward is in the work, not in the promise, 1079. No work worthy of God’s righteousness will be found, 238. The holy person glories not in knowledge of the Scriptures but in works, 685. Good works alone are beneficial, V, 79. When do our works have no reward? VI, 844. Those works that are not done in Christ’s name are without reward, 846. Good works are of no benefit among unbelievers, 768. God changes his promises if people change their works, 421. God’s work is something different from human work, VII, 487. Care must be taken over good works, through which God’s inheritance is prepared, 733. Everything must be done in the Lord’s name, 528. Everyone is called the son of the one whose works he performs, 186. Good works without faith are counted as dead, 483. All works are assigned either to the flesh or to the spirit; it is difficult to find middle cases, 501. If they are done for love of empty glory, they bring punishment, not reward, 499. Whence zeal and sluggishness in good works? [Col. 1036] 464. More detestable is the person who performs the works of unbelievers than one who is a pagan, 141. The good works of pagans without faith, 391. See Labor.

We must work while it is day, V, 831.

The laborers sent into the vineyard, I, 86.

Let us love not uncertain riches but the firmest virtue, I, 627. It is not enough to despise riches unless we follow Christ, 299. Riches do not harm a rich man if he uses them well, 946. How riches should be distributed, 399.

Ophaz—what is it? I, 170 and following.

Ophir, a kind of gold, I, 386.

Ophir, a region of India so called from Ophir, one of the descendants of Eber, III, 258, 275.

The Ophites, II, 197, and VII, 429.

Oppian of Cilicia, a most learned poet, V, 595.

An opusculum, that is, a *syntagma*, a written poem, I, 378.

Or, condemned, I, 1030.

Hor, the mountain on which Aaron died, III, 258.

A yellow color covers the face, II, 794.

The false oracles of demons and their cures of diseases, VI, 597.

We should pray with the body bent and the mind raised to the Lord, I, 334. We ought to have appointed hours for prayer, 121. To pray is ours; to grant what is requested belongs to God, II, 781. On the Lord’s Day and at Pentecost let us pray standing, 180. We should pray in secret, with the chamber of the heart closed, IV, 689. No one is worthy to pray for sinners, 944. It is foolish to pray for sinners unto death, 940. Many, although kneeling, do not pray; many others, standing upright, pour forth prayers, VII, 599.

Prayer is commended and commanded, I, 121. In it we speak to God, 109. Popular applause breaks the straight path of prayer, 267. The Apostle commands us to pray without ceasing, 106. Where are the weapons of prayer to be taken up? 121. As we leave our lodging, let prayer arm us, ibid. As we return from the street, let prayer meet us before we sit down, ibid. At night we should rise twice or three times for prayer, ibid. Daily prayer, 28. Prayer is a discourse of the mind, II, 17. Every prayer and supplication draws forth the Creator’s mercy, 793. The Lord’s Prayer is recited by the faithful during the altar sacrifice, 800. What they ask through it, ibid. How far it differs from Pelagius’ prayer, ibid. Continuous prayer ought to be in our mouth, IV, 741. Perseverance in prayer is commended, 920. The prophet’s persevering prayer is noted, 738. Certain impious people join days and nights together in prayer, yet are not heard by God, 22. The necessity of prayer, V, 499. Ecclesiastical tradition understands three times of prayer, 680. A conclusion once added to the Lord’s Prayer, 604. The efficacy of prayer, VII, 761. Through our fault we do not receive what we ask, 134. We often ask for things against ourselves in prayer, 603. It is of no benefit to invoke with the voice one whom we deny by our works, 205. A conclusion added to the Lord’s Prayer, 220. What bread we ask for in it, 726. What prayer ought to be like, 248.

A prayer in which only the words are praised is lifeless, I, 335. Some praise with a mercenary prayer, 982. Prayer must not be wasted on trifles, II, 22. A composition not polished by the author’s hand betrays negligence, VI, 881. A composition must be refined and completed by the author’s hand, VII, 485.

Definition of an orator, I, 422. Orators should imitate Lysias, the Greeks, Demosthenes, etc., 323. A saying of a renowned orator, 976. There is no bombast here among orators, whose definition is to speak suitably for persuasion, II, 707. The ears of the inexperienced are commonly deceived by the flowers of orators, 802. Pagan and Christian orators praised for the flow of their eloquence, IV, 329. An excellent saying of a most eloquent orator, 665. Orators and philosophers were regarded as kings of human beings, VI, 410. Their precepts are received almost as oracles of the gods, 420. They find it difficult to believe in God, ibid. Orators summarize briefly at the end what they previously discussed at greater length, VII, 556. Orators, often setting aside the business at hand, turn to personal insults, 408.

Orbilius the grammarian, I, 486.

The world has four regions, IV, 568. The devastation of the world in Jerome’s time, 810. The condition of the world before and after Christ’s Passion, VI, 404. There is much difference between the inhabited world and the earth, 356.

With what ordinances the whole world is filled, I, 412. The more credible the bishop who ordained a minister is, the more detestable is the ordained man if he has deceived him, 1093. The ordination of clerics is fulfilled not only by verbal invocation but by the laying on of hands, IV, 696. It ought to be given to saints and to those most learned in the Law, not to others, etc., ibid. Just as, in the ordination of wicked people, the one who appoints such persons shares in their sins, so, in the ordination of saints, the one who chooses good men shares in their righteousness, ibid.

The orgies and mysteries of the heretics, V, 130, and VI, 628.

Easterners commonly eat locusts, II, 334. Among Eastern peoples October is the first month of the year, V, 6.

The calamities of the East, I, 396. Its condition and that of the West concerning the faith, [Col. 1037] 38. Why do intellects in the East smell of barbarous stupidity? VII, 427. The inhabitants of the East have arrived to take their seats in the West, ibid.

Our Origen is the Chalcenterian, whence he received the name Adamantius, I, 153. His works are listed, ibid. He surpassed Greeks and Latins alike through his labor, ibid. He was condemned by Demetrius and by the Roman Church: why? ibid. Origen’s praise and life, 530. The time and place of Origen’s death, 529. Popular favor bestowed the name upon him, 569. He interpreted many things well, 347. He interpreted the Psalms, 753. He confirms the doctrines of our religion from the philosophers, 429. What is approved and disapproved in Origen, 517. How should he be read on account of his learning? 352. Why? 524. What did he add from Theodotion’s edition? 752. Origen’s commentaries, which he usefully published on the Holy Scriptures, are not to be rejected, 352. Although he surpassed everyone in his other books, in the Song of Songs he surpassed even himself, 529. His works on the Epistle to the Galatians, 739. He wrote eight books against Celsus, 427. What does his letter to Fabianus contain? 531. In the sixth book of the *Stromata* he taught perjury and lying, 525. It is foolish to assert that his books were tampered with, 531. He deceived the ears of the simple by his persuasion, 623. What is said against him, ibid. Many were deceived by his error, 352. Some things from Ezekiel are spoken against Origen, 568. He was condemned by Anastasius, 583. He was a participant in pagan impiety, 597. He is called a many-headed hydra of heresies, 582. He is heretical, 582. How his disciples exempt him from this charge, ibid. Catalogue of Origen’s principal heresies, 592 and following. They are refuted, ibid. They are described throughout the Epistle, 917 and following. He is called the fountain of Arius, 526. Origen’s manifold madness and insanity, 568. He asserts that Christ ought to be crucified for demons; this is refuted, ibid. Origen is more unjust toward Christ than Pilate and the Jews, 565. He renders Christ’s passion ineffectual, ibid. He puts an end to Christ’s kingdom, 565. This is refuted, ibid. He turns Christian doctrine into a game and jest, ibid. and 565. Origen’s doctrine concerning Christ’s soul is attacked, 591. He wishes bodies, after the resurrection, to be seized again by death, 572. He likewise writes that the Son ought not to be prayed to, 573. His error concerning bodies is worse than the preceding one, ibid. Origen’s blasphemous utterance concerning the Holy Spirit, 595. Origen’s heresy concerning souls, 592. His opinion concerning the soul, 948. He gives patronage to magical arts, 575. He contradicts himself, 599. He surpasses all heretics in the magnitude of his blasphemy, ibid. He confined God’s power in creating, ibid. Those who wrote against Arius and Eunomius are to be believed to have answered Origen’s impieties, 931. Origen was Clement’s disciple, II, 879. Under the pretext of secular literature, he instructed those who came to him in the faith of Christ, 895. A hundred and fifty years after his death he is brought to trial, 330. Origen’s library restored, 941. In him knowledge of the Scriptures is praised, but the falsity of his doctrines is not accepted, 556. He is praised by Jerome, 521 and following. Origen’s little works on the whole of Scripture are threefold, ibid. Lists of his books in the third volume of Eusebius, 416. Which of Origen’s works are praised? 521. He composed the *Hexapla* of four editions and mixed Theodotion’s edition into the edition of the Septuagint, 522. What Philo, as a Jew, omitted, Origen, as a Christian, supplied; ibid. He wrote that he had found a fifth edition on the Actaean shore, 523. Origen’s three volumes on the Epistle to the Ephesians, 477. His homilies and books in which moral matters are treated and obscure passages of Scripture are disclosed, 514. His books are almost full of errors, 511. In his books he transferred Plato, 567. Origen’s learned letter, 903. His little book to Fabianus, 330. Origen’s letter to Demetrius, 510. Origen’s dialogue, 889. Origen’s dialogue with Candidus, 511. In it he denies Christ’s divinity, ibid. Six thousand books of Origen never existed, 504, 417. What they usually write when approving what he says, 470. His caution in putting forward his opinions, 605. Origen’s little works and the errors in them, 431. Eight errors of the same man, 413. He removes the truth of history, ibid. In our view he was an Arian, 464. What he teaches through Jacob’s ladder, 425. His doctrine woven from pagan fables, ibid. He asserts that all rational creatures were created on equal terms, 715. He did not say that souls are made from angels, 423. Origen teaches that lying is permissible, 474. Origen’s “Principal Indulgence,” 503. Origen is called a teacher of the Churches after the Apostles, III, 4. In his homilies he followed the common edition; in his books he sought assistance from the Hebrew language, 303. In the book of Hebrew Names he supplied what Philo the Jew had omitted, ibid. He surpassed everyone in his other books; in the Song of Songs he surpassed himself, 499. Origen, an allegorical interpreter, IV, 1031, 1034, 1039, 1046. He makes the mysteries of the Church conform to his own ingenuity, 167. His volumes, homilies, and excerpts, 6. Many volumes on Isaiah, ibid. Two books to Grata were thought spurious, ibid. What were Origen’s and Eusebius Pamphilus’s interpretations of Scripture like? 167. What is Origen’s exposition? 994. He is censured, 981. Origen the presbyter, V, 810. Origen suffered the hatred and envy of many, 800. Origen acknowledges that he was regarded as learned, 801. Origen hears Hebrew, 925. His allegories are rejected, ibid. He is criticized, 667. He is censured, 644. Origen wrote on the Song of Songs, VI, 361. And three volumes on Malachi, 441. He is wholly occupied with allegorical interpretation, ibid. His interpretation is condemned, 814. Origen’s three volumes on the Epistle to the Ephesians, VII, 543. Jerome follows him, ibid. The different kinds of his commentaries, 369. His exposition, 494 and following. The tenth book of the *Stromata*, 494, 505. How many volumes did he write on Matthew? 3. Origen’s *Hexapla*, 734. Origen’s reading, 513. Errors, 548, 551, 665. Origen’s error concerning souls after the resurrection, 288.

The slippery impiety of the Origenists, I, 623. The hatred of Origen’s disciples toward the faithful, 605. They evade signing the subscription and seek evasions, 525. The madness of their heresy, 956 and following. What is said about the same matter? ibid. Jerome refutes an Origenist, 716. The Origenists bind themselves together among themselves by orgies of lies, II, 474. Imperial decrees against the Origenists, 468. What was said about a certain Origenist, 425.

Orion, a distinguished and very wealthy man, is healed by Hilarion, II, 20.

Orion has twenty-two stars, IV, 240. Orion and Arcturus, VI, 289.

What is *oriza*? I, 685.

What should adornment be like? I, 264. Ornament and dress are filthier than dirt, 423. Ornament and filth are to be avoided equally, 264. The one suggests luxury, the other glory, ibid. Ornament and the jewels of worldly women, 982. Many, not understanding what it means to be adorned, rush into vices, 422.

Oros, the god of the Egyptians, IV, 205.

The river Orontes, I, 345.

Orpheus detests the eating of meat, I, 346. At the sound of Orpheus’s lyre, trees, beasts, and the hardness of stones were softened, I, 786.

A polluted mouth is forbidden even to mention the name of God, VI, 44.

What does “Hosanna” signify? I, 64 and following. “Hosanna,” a Hebrew name, VII, 160. Its interpretation, ibid. It was said to saints and bishops, 164.

In former times greeting was given with a kiss, I, 268.

What does Hosea contain? I, 277. He is joined not only to a prostitute but also to an adulteress, 909. What does his taking a prostitute as wife represent? 427. According to Jerome’s opinion, Hosea does not seem to have had a prostitute as wife, IV, 125. Hosea was formerly the proper name of Joshua, VI, 1. The name of the last king of Israel, 4. It denotes “Savior,” 2. He is wrongly called Ause, ibid. Under which king Hosea began to prophesy, 2. Hosea prophesied before and after Israel’s captivity, 3. He was the first of the prophets who prophesied in the time of King Uzziah, 2. Hosea was more patient in proportion as the wife whom he took was more degraded, 3. Hosea’s wife of fornications signifies the people serving fornication and lust, ibid. Hosea’s love for the adulteress signifies God’s love for the children of Israel, 29. Hosea’s prophecy concerns the ten tribes, not the tribe of Judah, 169. Greek authors who interpreted Hosea, in the Preface to Hosea. To understand his prophecy is not impossible, but it is difficult, ibid. The writer himself testifies to the obscurity of the book, ibid.

Why Israel was captured especially under King Hosea, VI, 107. What does “the bones were attacked” mean? IV, 697. The dry bones come to life again, V, 433. The bones of the king of Edom were burned by the Moabites, VI, 237.

Osroene, a region of Syria, VII, 57.

A door opened to Paul, I, 834.

Ostracine, a city of Egypt, IV, 207.

Sitting is suitable for the idle, I, 194.

Idleness must be avoided, V, 183.

Leisure and laziness are the rust of wisdom, III, 473.

A little verse of Ovid, I, 902. Ovid’s books of the *Metamorphoses*, VI, 406.

Diseased sheep leave their shepherd and are devoured by the jaws of wolves, I, 995. All the limbs of the sheep were carried, 412. Italian and Mesopotamian sheep are said to have one nature, III, 355.

Although Uzzah wished to support the Ark as though it were falling, he was struck down, I, 1093.

The history of King Uzziah is explained, I, 45 and following. Uzziah himself is Azariah, under two names, IV, 7.

## P

The Hebrews do not have the letter *P*. Their names are improperly written with *F* among the Latins, III, 96, 101. The Hebrew language does not have the letter *P*, but uses the Greek phi in its place, IV, 35.

Pachomius’s monasteries are praised at Rome, I, 954. Pachomius learned the knowledge of the mystical language from an angel, II, 56. Pachomius’s precepts, ibid. and following. His Institutes, 73 and following. His judgments, 77 and following. His laws concerning evening prayers, etc., 79. His admonitions, 81 and following. His letter and mystical words, 83 and following, 97 and following.

The Pactolus is richer in mud than in flowing water, I, 816.

“Covenant” and “Testament” are the same, IV, 1074.

What should a governess be like? I, 764.

The best tutor is one who gives warning and frightens by the sternness of his face, I, 789. What is a tutor? VII, 442. Why is one assigned to little children? ibid.

Winnowing shovels were commonly called *ventilabra*, III, 96.

Palestine is part of Syria, I, 345. The perfect Christian life in Palestine, 207. Palestine did not belong to the bishop of Alexandria, II, 447. The Palestinian practice in threshing straw, IV, 342. Palestine is near Egypt, V, 166. What resources it abounds in, 314. In Palestine they customarily anoint their heads on feast days, VII, 35.

The Palestinians were captured and devastated by the Babylonians, IV, 1018. The five cities of the Palestinians, ibid. and VI, 231 and 311.

Perverse doctrine is compared with straw, IV, 105. The practice of the Palestinians in threshing straw, 342.

To sing a palinode in the manner of Stesichorus, II, 467.

The art of Pallas, II, 540.

Palladius, Rufinus’s friend, is censured, II, 560. What heresy did Palladius, in his servile wickedness, attempt to restore? 695. He contrives a slander against Jerome, ibid.

The palm of one person does not prepare disgrace for another, I, 431. By unequal running but with equal courage one strives toward the palm, 394. What does the carving of palms in Ezekiel signify? V, 477. In the branches of palms: a sign of victory and the reward of virtue, VI, 932.

The measure of a palm, V, 478 and following.

Palmyra is the name of a city which is also called Tamar, V, 601 and 613.

Pambo and Isidore, monks, I, 118.

Pammachius, a noble and learned man, I, 236. Jerome’s friend, 232. Pammachius’s devotion to sacred literature, 235. Pammachius is considered by everyone worthy of the priesthood, ibid. At Rome Pammachius attempts to reproduce what Paula accomplished at Jerusalem, ibid. 716. His life and virtues, 394 and following. Pammachius offered not only his riches but himself also to God, 796. Pammachius built a hospice together with Fabiola, 465. Pammachius’s dream, II, 554. The deaths of Pammachius and Marcella are announced to Jerome, V, 1. What does the name Pammachius signify? VI, 223.

Pamphilus did not publish Origen’s *Apology*, I, 532. It is believed to belong to whom? ibid. The martyr Pamphilus completed the Caesarean Library, II, 833. Where the life of Pamphilus is written, 416. Jerome kept copies written in Pamphilus’s hand as a precious treasure, ibid.

Vine leaves in place of words, I, 935.

Pancratius, a cleric of the Roman Church, II, 929.

Paneas is the name of the city formerly called Caesarea Philippi, IV, 507. Paneas was once Caesarea Philippi, V, 317.

Israel despised the heavenly bread and desired the meat of the Egyptians, III, 138. In Scripture “bread and water” is taken for every kind of food and drink, IV, 45. The bread of mourning was assigned to heretics, VI, 15.

The showbread: the twelve loaves signify the months in the Tabernacle, I, 360. The priests themselves had to sow, reap, grind, and bake the showbread, VI, 948. It was offered from the new crops at the feast of Pentecost, 779. The loaves were always exchanged, new for old, 953. Those removed passed into the priests’ use, ibid. Lay loaves, VII, 75.

The Pannonians, I, 913.

The regions of Pannonia and Dalmatia were devastated, VI, 676.

Pantaptes, the daughter of Cambyses and wife of Smerdis, married Darius after Smerdis was killed, V, 702.

Pantaenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, is sent by Demetrius to preach Christ, I, 428, and II, 861.

Panthea, the wife of Abradatas, II, 311.

Jerome did not translate the volumes of Papias, I, 434. Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, II, 859.

Paphos, a famous city of Cyprus celebrated in the poets’ songs, was overthrown by an earthquake, II, 37.

The jurist Papinianus prescribes one thing, our Paul another, I, 459. He permits fornications and brothels, ibid.

Papirius triumphed over the Samnites, I, 466.

The Blessed Papirius: where he lies, II, 887.

Papyrus vessels used for letters, or for ships, IV, 199.

Spots on the lips after an illness are a sign of recovery, VI, 556.

The meanings of parables and riddles, V, 190. Parables are familiar to the Syrians and Palestinians, VII, 142. Parables and riddles do not contribute to the authority of doctrines, 94.

The gate of Paradise is open to everyone, I, 321. Paradise is planted in Eden, 419. A woman drove the inhabitant of Paradise from his possession, 259. Paradise is said to have been created before heaven and earth, III, 307. What should be thought about Paradise and its rivers, on the authority of Sallust, the most reliable author, 202. Paradise is the mountain of God, V, 336.

The book of Chronicles is called the *epitomē* (ἐπιτομή) of the Old Testament, I, 279. If someone wishes to claim for himself knowledge of Scripture without it, he mocks himself, ibid. Through individual names and verbal connections, the histories omitted from the books of Kings are touched upon, and innumerable questions concerning the Gospel are explained, ibid.

The Fates are so called because they do not spare, I, 187.

Why Alexander the Great was called a leopard, II, 13.

What the *parentalia* are, IV, 552. From where they derive their name, VI, 93.

Parents are not to be loved above Christ, I, 30. When are parents to be honored? 282. How are parents to be honored by their children? 904. The scribes and Pharisees were overturning this commandment, ibid. Piety toward a parent is considered the greatest inheritance, 720. The great reward of one who forgets a parent, 283. The indulgence of a parent and the piety of a son contend with each other, 425. For parents and children to be separated is nothing, 694. Let parents learn that children can be taught more by examples than by words: why? 686. It is not children who store up treasure for parents, but parents for children, 738. Whoever is a child, until he reaches the years of wisdom, has both his good and his evil attributed to his parents, 684. Parents commonly dedicate disfigured daughters to virginity, 476. Jerome attacks them for this, ibid. Those who are joined to us in Christ we should regard as our parents, brothers, and relatives, 432. In common speech, parents were called relatives and kinsmen, 352. Parents should beware of provoking their children to anger, II, 909. False piety causes disagreement between parents and children, 334. What does it mean to be defiled through parents and relatives? V, 553. Parents are to be loved after God, ibid. To injure parents merely by one’s expression is a crime, VI, 519. Children are to be subject to their parents, following Christ’s example, VII, 312.

“Parish” is used for “diocese,” I, 726.

What does it mean to seek a share with Christ, with the prophets, and with the apostles? V, 851–852.

What do *particeps* and *comparticeps* mean? VII, 644.

Nothing is more grievous than the pain of women in labor, IV, 889.

A small tool for removing thorns that become lodged in the feet while walking, II, 67. *Parvula mordax* means a small pair of pincers, ibid.

Little children are instructed in the morning hours, IV, 579.

Concerning Passover, or the Paschal book, I, 610. What is required for the celebration of Passover, 608, 579. The bishops of Asia celebrate Passover with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, II, 883. The solemnity of Passover in monasteries, 92 and following. “Passover” signifies crossing over, IV, 424. The Lord came to Jerusalem during three Passovers, 390. From whom Passover received its name, VI, 530. Where does the name Passover come from? VII, 210. What is the Passover of the Jews? 254.

Pashhur: one is the son of Immer, IV, 997. Another is the son of Malchiah, 982.

The disgrace of Pasiphae, the king’s wife, II, 317.

The Passalorincitae, VII, 429.

The sparrow is never read in Scripture in a bad sense, III, 489.

We are subject to human passions, I, 597. There are two passions: one of evil, the other of good, II, 748. What does it mean to exceed in passions? 749. Opinions of some concerning the passions of the soul: whether anyone can be without them or not, ibid. In anger all disturbances of the soul are included; in the malice of the flesh, all bodily pleasures, III, 486. Passions are called disturbances, IV, 83. Those who rule ought to be free from them, ibid. Four passions are noted, V, 12. Cicero wrote about them most fully, ibid. The four virtues opposed to them, concerning which the Author argues, ibid. The three passions of the soul and their seats, VII, 94. The use of the passions, ibid. Evangelical doctrine surpasses this, ibid. They become occasions for triumphs, 528. Those devoted to passions have a god of their own, 37. The difference between passion and pre-passion, 28, 29.

The Law and the entire chorus of the prophets proclaim Christ’s passion, VI, 977.

What is a *pastophorium*, or παστοφόριον? IV, 318, and V, 490 and 504.

The Shepherd’s book was read in some Churches of Greece, II, 897. Many cited testimonies from it, ibid. Among the Latins it was almost unknown, ibid. The Shepherd’s book, VI, 75.

A fine description of negligent shepherds, IV, 661. The same men are censured, 696 and following. Because of bad shepherds the Lord’s inheritance is trampled, 928. Negligent shepherds are censured, VI, 884, 894. Who is the good shepherd, and what is his office? VII, 277. An exhortation to the shepherds of the Church, 168. Whoever is a shepherd must also be a teacher, 615. The harassment of the sheep is the shepherds’ fault and the teachers’ vice, 55. False shepherds in the Church, 616.

A father is not punished for a son, nor a son for a father, I, 1093. A father educates only the one whom he loves, 410. In Scripture “young men” and “fools” are those who depart from ancient authority and despise the venerable teachings of their fathers, III, 476. Sons who resemble their fathers are punished both for their own crime and for that of their parents, 854. No history relates that fathers ate their sons or sons their fathers, V, 52. Our fathers are of two kinds, 807. Every father bears the title of son, VII, 200, 217. In what sense are human beings called fathers and teachers? 185. They receive from God the right to be called fathers, 601.

“Father” is properly a name of God, IV, 1088. The name “Father” was hidden before Christ’s coming, VI, 635. From where comes the acknowledgment of the Father and the Son? 636.

Pathuel: “the breadth of God,” or “God opening,” VI, 167.

Patience must be displayed in adversity, I, 178. Like a very strong athlete, one should endure the injuries inflicted, 628.

An example of patience in a woman, 708–709. By enduring injuries, the fury of a raging heart is calmed, 712. Christian patience, II, 727. Since we are merciful toward ourselves, let us not maintain severity against others, 408. Patience is necessary not only in difficulties but also in more joyful circumstances, lest we become more elated than is fitting, III, 439. It is appropriate for a just person to have a little simplicity and, by reserving vengeance for God because of excessive patience, to seem foolish, rather than to practice malice immediately while hiding it under the guise of prudence, 468. God’s patience is hidden: it permits the saints to suffer now and does not visit sinners according to their crime, so that he may restore eternal good things to the just and bring perpetual evils upon sinners, 443. Through our patience the name of God is glorified, IV, 803. The health of patience, VII, 716.

We suffer not by chance but by God’s will, VI, 547.

The word *patria* is Greek, not Latin, I, 220–221. To love one’s homeland is natural, IV, 891.

The patriarchs and apostles were not without sin, I, 898. The patriarchs had very many wives and concubines, 909. The twelve tombs of the patriarchs are pointed out, 703. The righteousness of the patriarchs was not perfect, II, 707. The etymologies of all the patriarchs’ names are given, III, 350.

Those called patricians at Rome, I, 285.

*Cousin*, πατράδελφος, IV, 1708. Christ is called Isaiah’s cousin, 67.

Paula treads the laborious threshing floor of widowhood, I, 394. Paula had renounced the whole world and wished to leave her homeland, 183. While still alive, she distributed all her possessions to the poor and her children, ibid. Righteousness is proclaimed in Paula, 394. After distributing her wealth among her children, she teaches them to despise riches, ibid. Paula enjoyed Marcella’s friendship, 954. Paula and Eustochium, flowers of the Furian family, 182. The softness of Paula and Eustochium, and afterward their virtues, 402. They do not wish to be surpassed by others in bodily labors, whom they themselves surpass in strength of soul, 485. Paula’s virtues, 197. The younger Paula is reserved for Christ’s bridal veil, 720. Jerome wished to be her teacher and foster father, 689. Paula and Pammachius passed through the eye of the needle, IV, 724. Both are praised by Jerome, ibid. Paula, lover of monasteries and of Scripture, VI, in the Preface to Hosea. Jerome’s promise to explain certain prophets for Paula, 224. Paula and her daughter Eustochium were *philoponōtatai*—most devoted to labor, 310. Why Jerome dedicated books to Paula and Eustochium, 572.

Paulina, Pammachius’s wife, is mourned, I, 393. She is praised, ibid. and following.

Paulinianus, presbyter and Jerome’s brother, I, 350. Paulinianus’s ordination gave rise to what enmities? ibid.

Paulinus of Nola offered not only his riches but himself also to God, I, 796.

Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, travels to Rome, 692.

Lucius Paulus entered the city triumphantly during the funeral rites of his sons, I, 335.

Paul learns the Law of the Lord and the prophets at Gamaliel’s feet, I, 272. Why is Paul called the vessel of election? 273. He was a treasury of the Law and the sacred Scriptures, ibid. The words of the Apostle Paul are thunderbolts, 223. He argues in various ways in his Epistles; Paul is last in order but first in merits, 319. Christ resounded in Paul’s mouth, 937. He sees the natural ardor of the flesh resisting his judgment, ibid. Paul enters Rome in chains so that he may free those bound by the errors of superstition, 431. He remains in a lodging for two years so that he may make for us an eternal house of both Testaments, ibid. Praise of rightful freedom in Paul, 775. The Apostle Paul’s prudence deserves attention, 224. Paul demands almost something contrary to nature, 422. What the Apostle wishes is one thing; what he is compelled to wish is another, 905. He has two wills concerning the precepts of continence and marriage, ibid. Paul’s journeys, 272. Paul began badly but ended well, 285. Paul provided what was good even before human beings, 912. In what sense did Paul undertake the lawful observances of the Jews? 764, 766. Why did Paul circumcise Timothy but not Titus? 768. In what was Paul an imitator of the Gentiles? 751. Paul used a verse of Epimenides, 425. He employs a senarius of Menander, 426. Arguing among the Athenians in the court of Mars, he calls Aratus as a witness, ibid. The Apostle Paul did not have a wife, 103. In Paul there is a warning of human weakness, in the likeness of triumphant men, 179. Paul restrains his body because of the thorns of the flesh, 91. Under his own persona Paul confessed the frailty of the human body, 504. Paul was inflamed by bodily passions as a representative of the human race, 985. Paul is ignorant of many things and concedes them to the knowledge of God, 1038. Paul wrote to seven Churches, 280. Why did Paul mourn the Corinthians? 891. Paul and Samuel mourned sinners with merciful piety, 1084. A comparison of Origen and Paul, 402. Paul thought about those things necessary for the body’s use, II, 785. He seems to be accused of impatience, ibid. Paul withstood Peter to his face, 534. He calls him a pillar of the Church, ibid. Paul was compelled to wish many things that he did not wish, 264. Paul makes progress daily, 376. What was Paul’s humility? 249. Paul’s charity, 599. Paul’s beautiful interpretation concerning love of enemies, 728. Paul, not yet perfect, reaches toward greater things, 707. He takes testimonies from poets, 250. Paul was stricter than Barnabas, 763. The disagreement between Paul and Barnabas contains something of human weakness, ibid. Why did Paul despise or conceal Greek eloquence? 473. Nearly all Paul’s Epistles: what beginning they have and with what conclusion they are closed, 750. Where Paul wrote the Epistle to the Ephesians, 481. There are different copies of Saint Paul, 708. We should care not what Aristotle teaches but what Paul teaches, 714. The prophecy concerning the Apostle Paul in the blessing of Benjamin is most evident, III, 379. From where the Apostle Paul received his name, IV, 278. The preaching of the Gospel was multiplied through the Apostle Paul, 130. His preachings, 355. He follows the Hebrew truth, 608, 760. He uses testimonies of poets, 580. Where the authority of the Apostle Paul takes precedence, let every other interpretation cease, 149. His exposition must be followed, 567. He praises and rebukes the Corinthians according to the diversity of their inhabitants, 756. Paul is understood by the name Benjamin, V, 920. The Apostle Paul calls a Greek poet a prophet, 121. Paul, the ravening wolf, VI, 55. His conversion, 290. Why he was called the vessel of election, 86. He heard the mysteries of the Trinity, 349. He wrote to seven Churches, 855. Paul is foolish and disobedient, VII, 734. His malice and envy toward Christians, ibid. He had a keen and sharp intellect, 517. He was instructed at Gamaliel’s feet, 475. Paul was skilled in Hebrew and highly learned in the Law, 429. He was highly learned in the vernacular language, not in Greek, 520. He knew secular literature, but not perfectly, 471. From whom he received the apostolate, 375. In Hebrew, Paul sounds marvelous, 147. Why was he so named, when he was called Saul? 745 and following. He was likewise called Saul, not Saulus, ibid. He discloses secrets from the traditions of the Hebrews, 566. In what was Paul greater than everyone? 592. His humility, 398, 681, 733. His prudence, 371, 384. His magnanimity and fervor, 756. Paul’s anxiety and parental affection, 466. He prophesied, 490. He was afflicted with a very severe headache, 460. The Apostolic error arising from an affect of piety, 127. His speech is a rule of life and conduct, 714. The weight of Paul’s words must be observed, 389. He does not seem to have agreed with the secret intention of his mind, 592. The order of the history concerning Paul does not seem coherent to him, 392. He changes his appearance in the manner of actors, 468. He does not explain profound meanings in Greek, 468. Certain fictitious errors concerning the Apostle Paul, 350. Out of excessive love for Christ Paul named him frequently and unnecessarily, 559. An army of demons fought against Paul, 596. The devil’s fury and madness against him, 635. He was sent to prison by Caesar, 748. He converted Caesar’s household to the faith, ibid. He wrote Epistles to all the faithful of Galatia, 375. He used lowly language when writing to the Galatians, 439. Why did Paul place neither his name nor the title “Apostle” at the beginning of the Epistle to the Hebrews? 374. Some think that he should be criticized, 591. He is defended and excused, 493. Unskilled in speech, 596. He made a grammatical error, 587. Jerome does not attack him but rather defends him, ibid. He used the language of the common people, 417. He uses a common word, 641. He used verses of poets, 647. He did not therefore believe that what they had written was holy, 648, 709. Jerome defends Paul, 708. He marks out each province by its own peculiarities, 427. He gave greater weight to the sense of the testimony than to the words, 431, 437. The Apostle’s text has been corrupted, 488. What was added in Paul? 487. Paul’s numerous differences, 692.

Paul the elder, a disciple of the martyr Peter, II, 640.

Paul of Concordia: what he reports having heard from the notary of Saint Cyprian, 889.

In what respects Paul of Samosata and Photinus were accursed, IV, 958.

P. Paulus entered the city triumphantly seven days between the funeral rites of his two sons, I, 335.

Poverty, when sought, has glory; when inflicted, it has torment, I, 938. The love of a certain woman for the poor, 693. The harshness of poverty should not humble us, 627. In vain does one preach poverty and almsgiving with his tongue who swells with the riches of Croesus, etc., 953. At times we offer ruinous poverty to popular acclaim, 458. Feigned poverty is condemned, IV, 473. The Jews do not praise poverty, 50. God loves the poverty of the righteous more than the gifts of the rich, which come from plunder, ibid. People are tested through poverty, ibid.

Whoever is poor with Christ is rich, I, 29. Poverty does not make a poor man more commendable if, amid filth and want, he does not avoid sins, 498. Gifts are to be given to the poor, not to the rich or the proud, 399. The property of the poor is not to be assigned, through excessive judgment, to those who are not poor, 334. Let the bishop know whom to appoint over the care of the poor, 264. Some give a little to the poor so that they may receive more, ibid. It is no small thing for a nobleman to avoid the company of the powerful in the streets and cling to the poor, 397. What benefit is there in walls shining with gems while Christ is endangered by hunger in a poor man? 324. Evil and perverse poor people, II, 400. Who are called blessed? ibid. The poor of holy places were helped before others, 399. Partiality toward the poor and the rich is condemned, IV, 57. One must lend to Christ in the poor, 946. It is dangerous to demand repayment from a poor man who cannot pay, 687. To convert the property of the poor to one’s own uses is sacrilege, VII, 136. Whoever gives to the poor lends to God, 638. Who are the holy poor whom Paul mentions? 577. Among nobles and needy people there is no difference in divine matters, 68.

Peacock dung eases the heat of gout, II, 332.

It is not enough to seek peace unless, once found and fleeing, we pursue it with every effort, I, 941. A feigned peace should not take away what war preserved, II, 696. What was preserved in battle is often lost in peace, 45. There is no peace for the impious, IV, 683. The one who is subjected to insults is filled with peace, VI, 493. What peace did the Lord send upon the earth, and when did he take it away? VII, 280. Who dies in peace? 292. What is true peace? 24, 611. Peace is among God’s principal gifts, 683. Those who do not seek God rightly cannot find peace, 733.

To sin belongs to the human being; to lay snares belongs to the devil, II, 560. We all sin every day and stumble in some respect, 408. We remain children of God so long as we do not sin, 322. A person can refrain from sinning, if he wishes, for a time and in a place, as long as his mind is attentive, 785. If someone deviates even slightly, he must either go astray or fall headlong, 794. Sinners are to be rebuked by priests, 722. To sin in thought is one thing, and to sin in deed another, III, 470. Whoever has sinned and done evil is dead; for in the very act of sinning he immediately died, 454. One must not sin either in word or in deed, IV, 700. The ease of sinning and the difficulty of escaping from sins, 81. It is a lesser evil to sin openly than to feign and fabricate holiness, 277. Whoever sins believes wrongly, V, 691. Whoever sins is born of the devil, 807. Everyone who sins loves darkness, 424.

The sinner is compared to an actor on the theatrical stage, I, 193. Let the sinner not despair of salvation, nor the righteous be secure in his own virtue, 912. After a shipwreck, let the sinner hold onto the plank by which he can be saved, 1087. The sinner’s heart is often hardened because he is not struck immediately and is long spared for punishment, 1084. It is great wrath when God is not angry with sinners, 412. The multitude of sinners does not diminish the crime, 542, 565. We must not insult sinners but grieve with them, 579. It is one thing for sinners to desist from sin and iniquity, and another for them to perish forever, II, 724. The sinner, ignorant of spiritual contemplation, bars his heart from true joy, 402. God’s anger is against the sinner who spends his days and nights accumulating wealth and, using none of it, leaves it to those who are righteous in God’s sight, 406. Because sinners are not immediately convicted and corrected, they think that judgment will never come and persist in crime, 453.

The remedy for sins arises from good conduct, not from swelling and excessive dignity, 470. The later the vengeance for sins, the more just it is, IV, 1088. To punish those who sin is foreign and alien to God, 383. In what does their hope of salvation consist? 327. They refer their faults back to God, 757. They are punished so that unavenged sin may not harm others by its example, 937. Torments are applied to them so that they may be purified by divine fire, 148. Their execution signifies that wrath has reached its consummation, 946. The divine word urges sinners to repentance, 409. Through stages of repentance, Moabites become Israelites, 271. They die in the midst of their days, 471. It is harmful to live with sinners, 93. Indulgence must not rashly be promised to sinners, V, 649. Torments and their remedies, 269. Each person prepares punishments for himself when he does not wish to correct his errors? 136. What benefit is there for sinners? 525. Two kinds of sinners, 990. The pride of sinners, ibid. Sinners are separated and scattered by God, 824. The sinner’s rank brings a greater punishment, 184. They are not freed from the fires of Gehenna by the merits of their parents, 138. They are saved by the Lord’s propitiation, 529. What happens in the sinner’s conversion? VI, 690. The sacrifices of God are the conversion of sinners, 65. Sinners are expelled from the Church, 484. [Col. 1044] Sinners should compensate for the pleasures of their former life by austerity, 180. Nor is it enough to weep and assume the clothing of a mourner unless they sanctify the fast, ibid. God binds the feet of sinners so that they may not flee from him, 126. God’s patience is an opportunity for their salvation. How he strikes them for salvation, 129. The just ruin of sinners, 254. One must not insult those who fall, 454. The reason is given, 524.

Sin has no substance, I, 564, 622. Our death is sin, 18. Every sin, even in an idle word, deserves condemnation, 422. Original sin, 182, 199. There is no Christian who does not wish to be without sin, 1032. If there was sin in heaven, how much more on earth? 898. Let us be the accusers of our own sins, 608. Freed from sins, they demonstrate Christ’s power, 412. The cessation of sin is the beginning of virtue, 613. Just as sins produce negligence, so diligence produces virtues, ibid. The excuses that are advanced to excuse sins, 945. Those who leave the Church through crimes and sins are to be mourned, 893. How these words are explained: “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” 984. Light and serious sins, II, 373. We are subject to sin, not through a defect of nature but through frailty, 780. All sins cannot be avoided simultaneously, 792. There is no soul that can be without sin, 794. A person can be without vice, but cannot be without sin, 744. One who is cautious can avoid sins for a time, 772. It belongs to God alone to be without sin, 745. God can preserve a human being without sin, 720. Pride consists in referring the sins of one’s own will to an injury against the Creator, 775. Sin has the odor of something rotten; virtue breathes perfumes, III, 305. Because of one sin, many acts of righteousness perish, 468. Sin is most foul-smelling, IV, 256. It is a wall dividing God and human beings, 703. Through excessive habit it is transformed into nature, 636. Each person is sold into slavery by his own sins, 575. The order of judgment is arranged according to the diversity of sin, 248. As many kinds of sins as we have, so many sentences of judgment do we deserve, 308. God cannot be harmed by our sins, 894. All our sins are open to God’s eyes, 777. Nothing so offends God as an erect neck after sins have been committed, 223. Those who do not wish to acknowledge their sins provoke God’s anger all the more, 856. Whoever dies in sin perishes from God and does not continue to exist, 774. Our sins are not loosed unless we receive them from the hand of the Lord, 480. Every creature grieves over human sins, 847. Sins are various, 262. By what remedies are light and serious sins cleansed? 850. Lighter sins are washed away; serious ones are burned out, 66. As long as they are lesser, God acts patiently, etc., 235. To have sins loosed is not the same as to have them forgiven, 480. However serious the sin may be, if someone turns back, he can be healed, 99. Those who wish to turn back are preserved not by their own merit but by God’s clemency, 711. The forgiveness of sins is a cause of consolation, 479. The beginning of salvation is to understand and mourn one’s sins, 266, 863. All their remedies were sought from the Temple, 988. “Excuses in sins” are words of murmuring, 695. Someone who is not overcome by the bonds of sin is found only with difficulty, 694. Each person kindles a fire for himself according to the quality of his sin, 584. The more frequent the admonition, the greater are the sins of those who despise it, 1024. Sin signifies death, V, 725. Our sins are the cause of all evils, 55. In what sense God punishes the sins of the fathers in the third and fourth generation, 199, 224. Sins are not equal, against certain people and especially the Stoics, 99. Light sins on account of the necessities of the flesh, 551. How do those dead through sins rise again? V, 436. Comparison of sin and virtue, 959. Unequal sins, 962. Our sins are inscribed upon our souls, 864. Our sins are from ourselves; our goodness is from God, 865. Different sins are to be cured by different remedies, 867. Some sins are cured by *poa* and natron, others by the spirit of burning and punishment, 867. Some receive their sins twofold, others singly, 863. The four stages of sin, VI, 228. The kingdoms of the devil are different sins, 647. The exceedingly heavy burden of sins, 818. They are veins of death, 155. Nothing worthy can be offered to God for sin, 505. One’s own blood is worthily offered for sin, ibid. He asks for other things that may benefit those who give them, etc., 506. The order of punishments corresponds to the order of sins, 437. Great indignation is directed against great sins, 127, 836. It is a great sin to hate the one who corrects, especially if he corrects out of love, 292. It is a great sin not only to do evil but also to love it, 296. The difference between iniquity and sin, 89. Sin is the death of the soul, VII, 571. It is called the corruption of that same soul, 684. No one is without the sin of his parents, 667. Their punishments are eternal, 644. The opinion of certain people concerning the punishments of sinners, ibid. Sins of the flesh and of the mind, 572. The sins of heretics are sins of the mind, ibid. Small sins, 38. The necessity of forgiving sins, 141. Their forgiveness is called a gift, 738. The excuse of sins is condemned, 66. A fall into sin does not destroy one’s earlier works of faith if one returns to that faith and to one’s former zeal, 421. The difference between sins and offenses, 571.

[Col. 1045] With what riches the storeroom of the breast should be enriched, I, 688. A wound of the breast is made ulcerous by recollection, 393. The breast is a treasury of evil thoughts, II, 712.

The breast-piece and arm of the victims, set apart for the priests, I, 355. Why the breast-piece from the sacrifices was assigned to the priests, IV, 855.

For what purposes should money be spent? I, 701. Another’s money must not be accepted for distribution, 324. The administration and careful distribution of money is called a kind of unfaithfulness, 465. Where it is shown that money must be trampled underfoot, 990. The money laid at the apostles’ feet showed that greed must be trampled underfoot, 413. In view of the ambiguity of the Greek term, *argyrion* (“silver”) can also be translated as “money,” III, 430. Money and silver are the same, VII, 207.

Those who originally had more *peculia*, that is, cattle, are said to have been called wealthy, III, 430.

Whose feet the Seraphim cover, and why, I, 51. Why did Christ wash the apostles’ feet? 512.

Pelagius, a new apostle, decrees for the whole world what must and must not be done, I, 1038. His false humility, ibid. He threatened Jerome lest he write, 1039. Pelagius’ heresy contains the poisons of all heretics, 1026. Pelagius’ teaching is a little branch of Origen, 1030. It is close to Jovinian’s error, ibid. Pelagius’ heresy alone blushes to speak publicly, 1038. The fury of his disciples brings forth his silences, ibid. Pelagius’ statements contradict one another, 1031. Pelagius, the heir of Jovinian, II, 772. Pelagius attributes to every human being what the Arians do not grant to the Son of God, 716. Pelagius’ prayer is full of swelling and pride, 798. It far surpasses the arrogance of the Pharisee’s prayer, ibid. Jerome attacks this, ibid. and following. Pelagius urges women to possess knowledge of the Law, 722. He delights in their speech and songs, ibid. Pelagius flatters a widow, 801. He attributes to her what the angels do not dare to claim, ibid. A book of Pelagius is cited, 721.

The sect of the Pelagians abolished prayer, fasting, and continence, I, 1033. The Pelagians exclude a large part of Christians from righteousness, II, 721. Pelagian grace, ibid. The Pelagians are censured, IV, 916 and 1014.

Fur-clad peoples, I, 333.

Pelusianus, a monk of Antony, II, 31.

Part of the religion of Pelusium consisted of onions and the rumbling of the belly, IV, 544. Why the poet called the lentil “Pelusian,” V, 354.

Why the Pelusiots were so called, I, 525.

Pelusium is called the bulwark of Egypt, V, 353. It has a very safe harbor, ibid. Why the poet calls it “Pelusian lentil,” ibid.

Penelope’s chastity is a poem of Homer, I, 311.

The wings of the winds, IV, 92.

Moses is the author of the Pentateuch; Ezra is believed to have restored it, II, 212.

One must not fast at Pentecost, I, 184. The time of Pentecost is a time of joy and victory, VII, 541.

*Πεπληροφορημένον* (*peplērophorēmenon*), “fully assured”: what does it mean? VII, 249.

Fear of poverty becomes an occasion of unfaithfulness, I, 398.

Pepuza, an obscure village of Phrygia, from which the patriarchs of Montanus came, I, 189.

God’s striking is not so much punishment as correction, IV, 10 and following.

The nature of the partridge, IV, 961. The partridge is a cunning animal, V, 782. The partridge is lustful and impure, 785. The partridge is a symbol of the devil, ibid. The partridge protects its young from the heat, ibid.

Whether the word “perdition” always signifies abolition forever, IV, 669.

Not content with their own destruction, many wish to have more people share in death, I, 539.

Human perfection cannot attain the perfection of God and Christ, I, 1035. This is the only perfection available to human beings: that they know themselves to be imperfect, 1031. It is better to have walked on level ground than, while reaching toward higher things, to fall into the depth of hell, 92. Whoever disgraces himself, 199. Perfection comes not from nature but from grace, II, 750. This demonstrates that those who seem perfect are imperfect, ibid. The way of perfection according to the apostle Paul, 707. How the divine word calls us to perfection, 713. True perfection is reserved for the heavenly realm, 708. Perfection and true righteousness are to be attributed solely to the virtues of God, ibid. Perfection is not found on the way, IV, 845. In what does perfection consist? V, 537. What are the steps toward perfection? 588, 589. An exhortation to perfection, 577. The Apostle speaks of a twofold perfection, ibid. What must be done to attain perfection, VII, 148, 149.

The rudiments of perfect warfare, I, 796. To refuse to be perfect is to transgress, 34. The perfect person is one who follows the perfect and one God, II, 736. God commanded the most perfect things, 754. In what sense was the one who walked in the law of the Lord called blameless and perfect? 797. No creature can be perfect according to true and complete righteousness, 710. [Col. 1046] What someone considers perfect today, while he is stretching toward better things, proves tomorrow to have been imperfect, 708. What frees from Gehenna is perfect, 379. Among the perfect and those perfected in love, teacher and disciple are equal, III, 385. Who are the perfect and the beginners in the Church? IV, 736. Perfect and imperfect, VI, 215. It is in our power whether we wish to be perfect, VII, 148. Who are perfect men? 215.

The origin of the name of Pergamene parchment, I, 18.

Pergamius, after the body of Saint Antony had been removed, wished to build a shrine, II, 32.

What Pericles did after losing his sons, I, 334.

Perictione, Plato’s mother, II, 309. How she conceived him, ibid.

Everything is full of dangers, I, 934. It is safer to be unable to perish than, standing beside danger, not to have perished, 783. We always stand in danger, IV, 84. We avoid dangers through God’s mercy, VI, 789. When the danger is shared, the prayer should also be shared, 398. It is not permissible to perish by one’s own hand, 402.

The foulness of perjury, V, 193. Some consider perjury and theft minor crimes, but wrongly, VI, 816.

*Periosius*, what does it mean? VII, 725.

The Peripatetics descend from the source of Aristotle, I, 1026. They are opposed by those who wish the passions of the soul to be eradicated, ibid. The dispute between the Peripatetics and the Stoics, 1041. According to the Peripatetics, it is impossible to be free of passions, II, 749. The authority of Scripture agrees with them, ibid. The Peripatetics, VII, 737.

Some take “to perish” and “to grow old” as meaning abolition, IV, 588.

The skill of youth and that of old age differ greatly from each other, VI, 361.

To allow a person to remain in his crimes is a great offense, V, 176.

Nothing is perpetual in human affairs, V, 68 and following.

The Persians are situated in the east, IV, 568. Before Cyrus they were obscure, 215. They founded the cities of Seleucia and Ctesiphon in place of Babylon, 174. Before Cyrus the Persians were obscure and of no valor, 552. The Persians were a very powerful nation, V, 309. They use perfumes instead of baths, 697. Fourteen kings, 664, 692, 702. The Persian kings: which were merciful and which cruel, VI, 784. After Cyrus’ victory, the Persians and Medes formed one kingdom, 790.

There is no Christian who does not suffer persecution, I, 30. Persecution was stirred up against the Christians in the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, II, 891 and following. The fourth persecution after Nero, 857. The seventh persecution under Decius, 903. The eighth persecution under Valerian and Gallienus, 907. A savage persecution against Christians, 3. A great persecution in Egypt and the Thebaid, 5. At that time it was the Christians’ desire to be struck by the sword for Christ, ibid. Persecution concerns not the denial of believers but their testing and crown, IV, 208. In a time of persecution no one is to be trusted, 905. In a time of persecution, in what should one place one’s confidence? 855. The saints were killed by hunger during the persecution, 785. We are purified through persecutions and distress, 905. The persecutions of the Church from Nero to Maximian, 955. The persecutions of Christians, IV, 285. There was persecution throughout the world under Diocletian and Maximian, V, 423. During the persecution many Christians were compelled to fight against the Church, VI, 897. The gravest persecution of the Church occurred under Valerian, Decius, and Maximian, 549. The Lord’s Churches endured persecutions from the Gentiles and from Arian heretics, 789. Persecutions do not occur without God’s will, 408. Persecution is not to be feared, VII, 62. What must be done during persecution, 61. The occasion of persecution becomes a seedbed for the Gospel, ibid. To deny Christ amid many tribulations is less serious than to collapse at the first persecution, 90. Many suffer, but are not righteous, 24.

Persecutors should be flattered, I, 630. Persecutors are not to be feared, IV, 593. Their fury and cruelty, 283. Their pride is scattered, 593. All their reproach will pass away, 590. How the Lord frees his own from persecutors, 838. Persecutors are punished by God in this world, VI, 925. Heretics and Jews are much worse persecutors of Christians than Gentiles are, 374 and following. The rage and savagery of persecutors, 841. The punishments of persecutors, 826.

Perseus, the liberator of Andromeda, VI, 394.

Verses of Persius are cited, I, 187, 633.

Persia and Chaldaea take pleasure in cavalry, IV, 926. The kings of Persia after Cyrus, V, 665, 691.

A change of persons makes the prophets obscure, IV, 214 and following. A change of persons makes understanding especially difficult in the prophets, 902.

The beginnings of disturbances are called “pre-passions,” I, 506. [Col. 1047] We can govern disturbances of the soul, but cannot cut them away, 989. Let your mind not be empty of various disturbances, 939. If they take their seat in the breast, they lead to the greatest offense, ibid. More people are found to be strangers to disturbances of the soul, 110. The Stoic and Peripatetic view of disturbances of the soul, 1041. The four disturbances by which the human race is troubled, II, 746. Two belong to the present and two to the future, ibid. Two concern good things and two evil things, ibid. The four disturbances of the soul are to be governed by the judgment of the four virtues, V, 12. Four disturbances are observed in a human being, VI, 171. Nothing intoxicates in such a way as disturbance of the soul, 173.

Perversity can never overcome what is right, IV, 121.

A perverse person, unless corrected beforehand, cannot be adorned, III, 394.

Pestilence follows God’s indignation, creates diseases of the soul, and lays waste regions, IV, 203. Pestilence always follows famine and poverty, V, 138. It is sent upon us because of our sins, 55. Pestilence, 212.

A pestilential person lays waste everything, V, 212.

*Petesatus*, what does it mean? VI, 825.

No traces of a serpent are found on the rock, I, 984. Who are the rocks? V, 852. “Rock” is understood in both a good and a bad sense, IX, 368.

Petra, a city of Arabia, also called Jactael and known to the Syrians as Rekem, III, 259.

Peter dismissed his wife and everything he possessed, I, 795. He erased his threefold denial by a threefold confession, 460, 893. Peter announces God’s judgment by a prophetic spirit, so that the punishment of two men may be the instruction of many, 990. Praise of holy humility in Peter, 775. How great was his authority? 743. The cause of his transgression was fear of the Jews, ibid. He correctly understood the abolition of the Mosaic Law, ibid. How he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, 767. Peter and Paul, commanders of the Christian army, 205. They were killed by Nero, 409. The place of his burial, ibid. The chair of Peter, 583. The chair of Peter is to be consulted, 38. Peter, the chief of the apostles, II, 279. Why one was chosen among the Twelve, 279. He presided over the Roman Church for twenty-four years, 661. He was not irreprehensible, 718. Peter is celebrated with the veneration of the whole world, 827. The Roman bishop offers sacrifices over the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul, 395. Peter’s letters are called Catholic, 827. The second is denied by most to be his, ibid. Eusebius refuted the dispute between Peter and Appion, 853. Peter and James, pillars of the Church, VI, 534. Their authority must be followed, ibid. Peter’s unbelief was a heavy burden, 556. Peter possessed a most ardent faith, VII, 107. This is demonstrated by its effects, ibid. Why he was left to temptation, ibid. He was the first bishop of the Church of Antioch and transferred the See to Rome, 409. According to Clement, Peter had baldness on his head, 394 and following. Some frivolously defend him in his denial of Christ, 225. According to certain people, he was called *Barjonna*, not *Barjona*, 124. Paul truly rebuked him, 755. He was constrained by blessed Paul with an irrefutable argument, 411. Satan and Peter are not condemned by the same sentence, 21. The dispute between Paul and Peter was a matter of administrative dispensation, 406 and following. Jerome proves this with strong arguments, 407 and following. Peter was the first bishop of Antioch, 262.

Peter of Alexandria, I, 44, 954.

Socrates transferred Phaedo, who was serving lust, to the Academy, VI, 5.

Whether *phantasia* (“imagination” or “appearance”) is understood in a good sense in sacred matters, VI, 651 and 652.

Pharan, a place near Mount Sinai, VI, 637.

Pharaoh endured the ten plagues not as though from an angry God but as though from a father giving admonition, I, 1084. He repented in a perverse manner, ibid. He could be taught only by means of the seas; one must fear him to whom even the elements are subject, ibid. Among the Egyptians, Pharaoh is the name of royal power, IV, 402. His royal house was at Tanis, ibid. Jerome discussed the hardening of Pharaoh after the apostle Paul, 757. Pharaoh and Herod were persecutors of male children, 805. The etymology of Pharaoh, V, 341.

What does Phares, the son of Judah, signify? I, 256.

Christ was crucified because of the zeal of the Pharisees, I, 707. In what do the Pharisees place meditation on the Law? 449. The righteousness of the Pharisees perishes through pride, 897. Why were the Pharisees separated from the Jews? II, 197. They received their name from division, ibid. The arrogance of the Pharisees, ibid. The Pharisees were called “separated from the people,” VII, 177. The Pharisees and Sadducees, opposed to one another, agree with one mind in testing Jesus, 180. The scribes and Pharisees turn the Temple money toward the redemption of falsehood, 242. Their vices have passed over to us, 183. The worst tradition of the Pharisees, 111. Superstition, 183.

Phasian birds cooked in gentle vapors, I, 424.

Phatures, the metropolis of Egypt, V, 348.

[Col. 1048] *Pheduth*, “redemption,” I, 64.

The daughters of Phidon, in order to preserve their virginity, threw themselves into a well, II, 307.

The goodwill of Philip and Andrew, I, 890. The little chapels and rooms of Philip’s four virgin prophet-daughters were visible at Caesarea, 696. Where Philip and his daughters slept, 885. Some think that Philip was carried away by an angel, IV, 754, 755.

Philippi, a city of Macedonia, VI, 695.

Philip, king of the Macedonians, expelled by his wife, II, 318, 869.

The virtue and zeal of Phinehas, II, 713.

Phogor is translated as “disgrace.” Among the Hebrews it is Priapus, II, 272.

Photinus, a martyr, I, 428. Photinus, VII, 375. His doctrine refuted, 385. Where the heresy of Photinus is refuted, 375. A passage works against him, 614.

A distinguished work against the Phrygians, II, 877. All poets tear the Phrygians apart with insults, VII, 416.

Phud, or Phul, Libya, IV, 816 and following.

The river Pison is very broad, I, 271.

The greatest duty of piety, II, 772. There is a time for hating in martyrdom, when piety, hostile to us, attacks us for the confession of Christ, III, 411. Piety and true religion are the royal road, IV, 674. Piety is an abomination to the sinner, VI, 293.

The round priestly cap, I, 362. Such as we see depicted on Ulysses, ibid.

The *pilum*, a Roman spear, I, 344.

A winged house, VI, 262.

*Pipi*, or *πιπί*, read in place of [uncertain/illegible], I, 131.

Mount Pirene, VII, 427.

The sheep-pool (*piscina probatica*, literally “pertaining to sheep”) is elegantly described, III, 182.

The vice of Piso, I, 413. The steadfastness of the Pisones in lamentation, 335.

What is the pistachio? I, 332.

What is phlegm? I, 231.

To refuse to appease someone whom one has offended is a great offense, IV, 855.

The four quarters of the world, V, 33.

What is a plagiarist? I, 14.

The plantations of sinners, V, 753.

What is *plasmatio*? VII, 577.

Plato’s journeys, I, 270. A short work, 335. Plato’s *Politeia*, 415. His age, 356.

The threshing cart, IV, 499 and following. Iron-bound carts for threshing, VI, 226.

Plautus translated the comic poets, etc., II, 397.

The common people can easily be deceived, I, 263.

Lead is customarily mixed with adulterated metals so that it may be separated from foreign matter, IV, 890.

*Poa*, a grass, V, 865.

[Col. 1050] A remedy for gout, II, 332.

Punishment associates people in hell, ibid. Human frailty cannot pass judgment concerning punishments and their measure, 337. The order and usefulness of punishments and the fruit of repentance, 758. Fear of punishments is praised, 941. The whole of punishment is not to see God reigning in his majesty, 349. The longer God’s forgetfulness lasts, the greater the punishment of sin, 855. The crown of repentance is woven from the flowers of Scripture, 899. An example of perfect repentance, 460. If someone who sins seventy-seven times turns to repentance, his sins are forgiven, 897. Amid the evils of captivity and shipwreck, the plank of repentance must be held fast, 899. Repentance is never too late, 1092. Let us not flatter ourselves with the resources of repentance, which are remedies for the unfortunate, 507. One does not lose the name of “righteous” if one continually rises again through repentance, 897. The fiftieth Psalm displays the sinner’s complete repentance, 896. Some do not accept repentance, 461. While the repentance of a few is awaited, the boldness of the lost is sometimes nourished, 353. Penitents fill the heavenly realms with joys, 890. Repentance imitates baptism, II, 730. The medicine of repentance is offered to sinners, III, 444. God does not immediately avenge human crime but delays punishment while awaiting repentance, 453. At the voice of a bishop or presbyter, sinners rise through repentance, 489. When all have been restored through repentance, the devil alone will remain in his error, 394. Repentance is praised against Novatian’s will, IV, 327. It wounds, 538. Without God’s help we cannot perform repentance, 1066. Through repentance every person, even the impious, can be saved, V, 395, 397, 398. We are summoned to repentance for former sins, 540. The suitable place for repentance and confession is the church and the altar, 193. Continence is required in works of repentance as necessary, ibid. Repentance is compared with death and the underworld, 282. Scripture urges repentance, although forgiveness is not granted to everyone, 191. No one should feel secure about repentance, 525. Repentance leads to salvation, VII, 171. The reform of repentance against the Novatians, 467.

The order of penitents, 175. The Church’s weeping for penitents, ibid. The doors of the Church are opened to penitents, 249. God receives penitents, provided that they return in weeping, IV, 217 and 863. Victory is granted to penitents by the Lord’s grace, 592. In what does their joy consist? ibid. What is the concern of the true penitent? VI, 505 and 577. His progress, 597. The penitent gladly suffers, provided that he deserves forgiveness, 657. God receives penitents to such an extent that he calls them his people, etc., 200. He answers them, 136. The penitent must match the multitude of his sins with a multitude of virtues, 580. Christ is raised daily in penitents, VII, 563.

Poem by a certain poet, I, 261. Some poets advanced in years, 257. Saying of a pagan poet, 505. Some passages of poets are cited, II, 238. The poets’ fables boast that Virbius was revived by Aesculapius, IV, 352. Their fables and license in the wings of the winds, 92. The poets’ fables: ridiculous and monstrous lies, VI, 288. Famous poets, 224. A pagan poet stole a saying from the prophet Amos, 290. The comic poet, VII, 40.

[Col. 1051] Polemo: Xenocrates made him, from a most dissolute youth, into a very wise man, VI, 5. Polemo, VII, 485.

Who are said to profane the name of God? V, 523.

Polygamy in the Old Testament, I, 417.

The Pontic Sea, I, 913.

The duality of high priests, while Christ suffers, shows the divided error of their religion, 109. The succession of high priests after the Babylonian captivity according to Eusebius, 682 and following.

The deed of Marcus Popillius Laenas, V, 715.

The pores of the body, VII, 114.

Porphyry, a rabid dog, II, 913. His wickedness, 596. A special enemy of Christ, 635. He accuses Christ of inconsistency, 761. He wrote much against Daniel, ibid. The usefulness of harbors, I, 627.

Rabsaces—who was he? ibid.

When the angel Raphael is sent by God, V, 676.

The region of Reblatha, VI, 311.

For sinners to withdraw from God is not a matter of place but of will, IV, 311.

The commandment of reconciliation is difficult, II, 753. The harsh necessity of reconciliation, VII, 27.

The usefulness of remembering God, VI, 412, 413.

To accept what is right but not sharply refute what is wrong, I, 338.

Let us minister with solicitous care to those suffering from jaundice, I, 579. Having been destroyed by jaundice, he survives his own corpse, 396.

Some exclude second marriages from the kingdom of God, 302.

The basilisk seeks out everything dry, I, 419. No bird can pass beyond the gaze of the basilisk, IV, 182.

The progress of the Christian religion, I, 679. The magnitude of bereavement is an occasion of religion, 498. The fault of a few does not prejudice religion, II, 396. Our religion instructs the seeker of wisdom, 333. From where “religion” is derived, VI, 350. To suppose religion consists in riches is an error, 911.

The religion of the pagans worships every kind of beast, V, 86.

The veneration of relics is established, I, 205. How we venerate the holy relics, 725. Jerome establishes this veneration, ibid. The veneration of relics is established, II, 392. The translation of the holy relics took place under the emperor Constantius, 391.

To curse back and bite in retaliation accomplishes nothing, I, 552.

Upon whom the preaching of remission is directed, VII, 345.

The year of remission among the Jews, V, 455.

The Remoboth, the worst kind of monks, I, 118.

A very powerful city of the Remi, I, 913.

In what perfect renewal consists, VII, 625.

Mourning of the kidneys, V, 280. By the designation “kidneys” all works pertaining to sexual intercourse are indicated, VI, 259.

The renunciation made in the mysteries to the one who is in the West, VI, 322.

When God appears to repel us, VI, 732.

Why the law concerning the recovery of extorted property was established, IV, 36.

To rebuke, I, 750. It is more difficult to establish one’s own position than to criticize another’s, 750. Far be it from us to do in others what we criticize, II, 552. One is not at fault who, concerning the same people, both proclaims what deserves praise and censures what deserves blame, 556. Why a bill of divorce was permitted, VII, 146.

Why everything should not be demanded from everyone, II, 784.

A thing that no eloquence can explain, I, 1089. The use of things is beneficial, not their possession, 495. The use of things makes them good or bad, IV, 646. New names are invented for new things, V, 154. What happens at the sight of something new and unusual, 60. The loss of secular goods ought not to be mourned with lamentations unbecoming and inappropriate for a man, VI, 967.

Resep, a demon, VI, 641.

In Scripture, the resin of Gilead is used for repentance, IV, 904. A gentle resin suitable for bodies and accepted as medicine, V, 315.

Not every answer proceeds from reason; sometimes it proceeds from contentiousness, VI, 980.

The restoration of all things, V, 855.

We shall rise again in our own sex, I, 719. In the heavenly Jerusalem the bodies of those who rise again are alive, 333. We shall rise again in our own sex, II, 296. What retribution is worthy of God? I, 124.

We must not walk backward, V, 840.

To reveal. To know what we know by the equality of nature is one thing; to know it through the condescension of the one who reveals it is another, VII, 74.

Leave laughing and being laughed at to worldly people, I, 582.

The ruin of an initially holy soul, V, 300. The falls of others are examples for the righteous, 301.

False rumor is quickly suppressed, I, 290.

The oath of Rusticus, I, 899. His wife’s concern for his salvation, ibid.

Why is the great priest forbidden to approach dead relatives? I, 182. How those who do not obey priests are punished, 34. Why priests are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, 422. If the daughters of priests were widows, they ate priestly foods; but they became excluded from them if they took another husband, 905. There is no Church that does not have priests, 194. The priest’s duty in the reconciliation of sinners, 175. Why chastity is required of priests, 291. Let them read attentively what is said, 549, 550 and following. Chastity is commended to those serving at the altar, 549. The name Saddai is explained, I, 131.

The doctrine of the Sadducees, II, 197. The heresies of the Sadducees, VII, 365. The Sadducees are interpreted as “just,” 177. They thought that the soul perished with the bodies, ibid. They are refuted, ibid. Their opinions, ibid. They accepted only the five books of Moses, rejecting the prophecies of the prophets, ibid.

Avoid the company of secular and powerful people, I, 325.

There is no security in the world, I, 32. Its tranquility is a storm, ibid. Everything in this world is full of enemies, 89. The duration of a single age is demonstrated, V, 324.
