Paul, the arrow of the Lord, I, 388. What is the arrow flying by day? II, 776. The arrows of God are many, although only one is called chosen, II, 562.

Every region of Persia and Assyria uses arrows, IV, 113.

The Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians were skilled in archery, IV, 877.

The Greeks founded Saguntum from the island of Zacynthus, VII, 427.

If salt becomes tasteless, it not only loses the dignity of its name but is not even useful for the dunghill, I, 932. The usefulness of salt, II, 176. Christ is heavenly salt, V, 147. Why it became customary to touch the bodies of newborn children with salt, ibid. There is no sacrifice that lacks salt, 534. What a city sprinkled with salt after its destruction signifies, 595.

What was being shouted at Salamis? II, 37. Salamis of Cyprus is now called Constantia, VII, 746.

Salem, whose king was Melchizedek, I, 445. Salem is called Shechem and Jerusalem, III, 358, 359.

What willow seed does, IV, 267. Willow seed taken in food makes people sterile, 525. The nature of the willow according to the physicians, VI, 932.

Salissa, formerly called Bale or Segor, III, 326.

The Histories of Sallust, I, 430. Sallust, an enemy of Cicero, II, 316. The wife whom he married, ibid. Commentaries on Sallust, 472. Sallust’s opinion, VII, 499.

Salmana, prince of the Midianites, was killed by Gideon, or Jerubbaal, VI, 120.

Salmoneus, II, 559.

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” I, 279. He proposed certain matters to the philosophers of Tyre and answered some of theirs, 425. Solomon, beloved of God, was overcome as a human being—why? 504. Cities founded by Solomon, 696. Solomon’s virtue and wisdom, II, 713. When he built the Temple, 275. He departed from God through love of women, 328. Solomon had three names, III, 383. He was wiser not than Abraham, Moses, and the other saints, but than those who had been before him in Jerusalem, 394. According to the number of his names, he published three books in which he teaches children, men of mature age, and those who are perfect and complete, 384. Solomon did not have a son like himself in Rehoboam, 404. Many of Solomon’s writings became obsolete and did not endure in memory, 496. Solomon assumed the kingdom in the twelfth year of his age, IV, 51. Solomon repented, V, 524. Solomon preceded Christ as a type, VII, 511. He spoke about the natures of beasts, birds, and plants, 590.

Wise people are called “salty,” fools “tasteless,” V, 147.

Why Jerusalem is called a “woodland,” IV, 986.

When and in what things the greatness of the Savior was revealed, VII, 362.

All human beings can be saved, I, 933. Why many are not saved, IV, 753. Let the one who could not be saved by shame be saved by reproaches, VII, 141.

Salvina, daughter of Gildo, I, 915, 498.

If we wish to share in salvation, what must we do? I, 584. It is better for one’s property to diminish than for the soul’s salvation to perish, 912. God desires the salvation of all, 795. Make the salvation of others the gain of your soul, 322. Simpler people sometimes attain the salvation that more learned people lose, III, 417. We ought not be content with our own salvation, IV, 309. The more merciful is the one who shows the way of salvation after sin, the more wretched is the one who, and so forth, 858. For the salvation of God’s servants, kings rise up against others, V, 367. The salvation of all is promised on the third day, VI, 61. There are two ways of salvation, VII, 72.

Which province in Palestine is called Salutaris? III, 337.

Mary’s greeting by the angel was new, VII, 362. The greetings of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, 60.

Where Samaria comes from, and why it is called Augusta, I, 703. Samaria is called Sebaste, IV, 203. In what period the kingdom of Samaria and Syria ended, ibid. When Samaria was captured, 104. Why Samaria is called “greater” and “older,” V, 261. Samaria, the capital of the ten tribes, VI, 7 and 8. Samaria is extremely fertile in olives, 134. Samaria is situated in a very fertile place, 442. Why and by whom it was called Sebaste, 363. The bones of Saint John were buried in Samaria, 437.

The Samaritan woman, thirsty, is invited to drink, I, 420.

The Samaritans were intensely hostile to the Jews, I, 862. The Samaritans and Jews avoid contact with Christians, IV, 775. The Samaritans use the ancient Hebrew letters, V, 895 and following. What does “Samaritan” signify? VII, 349.

[Col. 1065] Shammai and Hillel, founders of the scribes and Pharisees, lived not long before Christ was born, IV, 122.

Samson as a type of the Savior, II, 273. From where Samson and Delilah came, III, 277. Samson as a type of Christ, V, 550. Samson and Delilah as figures of Christ and the Church, VII, 557. The history of Samson is called a fable, 752.

Samuel was brought up in the Temple, I, 680. Why he mourned Saul, 890, 1084. Samuel’s sons went after greed and iniquity, 1094. Samuel’s relics were transferred—by whom? II, 391.

The sanctification of the slayer and his weapons differs from that of priests, IV, 989.

Who enters the Holy of Holies? II, 378. Except for the high priest, no one else dared enter the Holy of Holies, V, 76. The Holy of Holies was defiled by the profane entry of enemies, 77.

Sanctus, no one is holy before God, I, 1227. The saints and the elect before birth, 128. The life of the saints is a long martyrdom, 723. No saint is crowned without a struggle, 124. All the saints who are virgins express in themselves, in this age, the life of angels, 717. Holy men were not without sin, 898, 1027. For the saints, sleep itself is prayer, 121. Holy men are sometimes mistaken, 1089. After death the saints are with Christ in heaven, 335, 450, 397. Their promises are fulfilled even in the present, ibid. In heaven the saints favor those who live and labor on earth, 185, 450. Holy men fathered sinners, 336. In what sense are the children of the faithful called holy? 535. How are the saints chosen? II, 478. There is no time at which mercy is not built up in each of the saints, 766. No saint, so long as he is on the way, can possess all the virtues, 714, 720. One must not form rash judgments about holy men, 226. There is a manifold and infinite diversity between saints and angels, 367. The prayers of the saints benefit us, 392. For the saints, sleep itself is prayer, 792. Before Christ’s coming, all the saints were detained in hell; but not after the Lord’s resurrection, because they are with Christ, 464. Every holy one is a throne of God, IV, 943. The saints are not inhabitants of earth, 841. They need God’s mercy, 578. They complete their days, 471. They have the wings of an eagle and a dove, 253. They ask that God not spare them in this age, 962. Power is given by God to the wicked, so that the faith of the saints may be displayed, 977. God shows that he is held back by their prayers, 1036. God protects the descendants of the saints out of love of justice, 466. What is their joy at the consummation of the world? 334. The saints do not know the children whom God does not love, 756. Holy men fathered very wicked children, 796. Many build houses and do not live in them, 793. Every saint is loved by God, V, 698. No one digs a cistern, 390. There is nothing sinister in the saints, 506. The people of this age rejoice at the ruin of the saints, 287, 295. The saints are gathered by God, 824. The saints are written in heaven, 790. The saints are subject to afflictions, 752. The saints do not hide themselves from the face of God, 859. The saints are not debtors, but give each person his due, 842. A saint is begotten by God, 806. A saint full of bitterness, 854. Each saint is a cloud, 797. Holy men are called angels, VI, 803. They are called stones because of the harshness of their tribulations, 867. The steadfastness of holy men, 521. The heart of a holy man rests under God’s protection, 640. A holy man desires to be exercised, 592. The saints will not be without fear at the judgment, ibid. A saint is not good in comparison with God, VII, 148. It is understood in two ways, 703. Every saint who is with God is greater than one who still remains in the battle, 70. The saints are called eagles, 197. They are tested in this age while the wicked flourish, 597. Into what sin do they frequently fall? 493. It is fitting for holy men to weep and mourn, 641. No distinction is to be made among the merits of the saints, 90. Whatever God has granted to the whole human race, he has always granted to each of the saints, 454. What is the difference between “holy” and “immaculate”? 649.

The saints of the Old Testament were rich not for themselves but for others, II, 703. They used their riches for good works, ibid. They should be called stewards of God rather than rich men, ibid. What kind of righteousness did they have? 777. They prayed for themselves, contrary to the opinion of certain persons, 780. All the saints of former times had the same merit as Christians now, 327. The saints of the Old Testament were justified by faith in Christ, VII, 412.

How blood corrupted by bile becomes inflamed, II, 794. What is the judgment of blood? IV, 442 and following. The nature of shed blood, V, 275. How blood is understood in Scripture, VI, 695. The blood of a human being, ζωτικόν—that is, vital—by which he is invigorated and sustained, etc., ibid. Once they have tasted blood, wild beasts always thirst for it, 607.

Sanir means “tooth of a lamp,” II, 286. Literally, Sanir is a mountain, etc., V, 305.

What good health possesses, illness shows, I, 393, 891. A great swelling is contrary to health, 400. Health is more welcome once illness has been driven away, IV, 1053.

Santra, a writer on Illustrious Men, II, 821.

[Col. 1066] “He who is wise by himself is blessed first; second is he who listens to a wise man,” a saying of a Greek poet, IV, 50.

A wise man can never be alone, II, 315. In Scripture the wise man labors and composes books, which come into the hands of fools and are often exposed to slander, III, 405. The wise man always thinks about the future age, which leads to the right; the foolish man, however, thinks about the present, which is placed on the left, 469. Why is a wise man with riches better than one who is merely wise? 440. The wise man goes to a man’s house in order to rebuke himself when he sins, bring himself to tears, and provoke himself to weep over his own sins, 437. What is the grief of the wise and the perfect? 395. By the example of many it is proved that sometimes the wisest men are in need of necessities, while the most ignorant in the Church flourish and consider themselves prudent, 465. It belongs to a wise man to follow wisdom as his guide and to pay no attention to empty rumors, 446. The perfect wise man needs no reproof and is disturbed by no slander, 438. The wise are called “seasoned” (*salsi*), but fools “unseasoned” (*insulsi*), V, 147. The wise men of the age find it difficult to believe in God, VI, 429. The wise are called by two names, VII, 411.

Wisdom is always giving birth and remains incorrupt, I, 258. Wisdom is warm and burns with divine reading, 259. When wisdom works good in us, 613. Those who have devoted their souls to the disciplines of wisdom will obtain eternal rewards, 620. Wisdom is almost suffocated in the young, 256. Sometimes wisdom flourishes in the young and withers in the old, ibid. How secular wisdom is to be used, 399. The more someone has attained wisdom, the more he is indignant at being subject to vices and far from the virtues he seeks, III, 395. Wisdom comes to us through certain torments and intolerable labor, through continual meditation and study, 390. It lies hidden in a secret and profound place and does not present itself to minds as light does to the eye, ibid. It is proved by seeking good things and avoiding evil ones, ibid. It is the tree of life; unless it is planted in the midst of virtues, the other trees will dry up, 398. It can do more for one placed in distress than any greatest powers can do, 445. What wisdom is to be pursued, IV, 645. True wisdom, joined to the fear of God, 870. It is not sufficient without the other virtues, 1042. He is wise in vain who thinks that he can accomplish anything without God’s wisdom and protection, 396. Secular wisdom has been overthrown by the preaching of the cross, 613. It is foolish, and its teachers are fools, 293. “Wisdom” is taken to mean malice, 1042. The distinction between wisdom and prudence according to the Stoics, 83. True wisdom cannot perish, ibid. Everyone, even the wicked, says that he loves wisdom and justice, VII, 552. The definition of wisdom according to the Stoics, 554. How Christ was filled with the wisdom of God, 302.

The Book of Wisdom is contradicted, II, 731. The Book of Wisdom is inscribed with Solomon’s name, IV, 753, and V, 155. Why the Book of Wisdom is inscribed with Solomon’s name, VI, 902.

A saying of one of the Seven Wise Men, I, 988.

Where Sarah’s cells were displayed, I, 704. Sarah and Hagar signify the two Testaments, 910. Sarah was not Abraham’s sister, VII, 223. The name Sarah means “princess,” IV, 570. The meaning of Sarah, VII, 473.

Among the Chaldaeans, *saraballa* are called the legs and shins of a man, V, 639.

The Saracens wander here and there, II, 43, 46. They worship Lucifer, 27. The mountain and desert of the Saracens is called Pharan, III, 191. They wander and attack all peoples from uncertain settlements, and are attacked by everyone, 330. The Saracens worshiped Lucifer, VI, 305.

Sarai’s name was changed to Sarah. The errors of the Greeks concerning the change of this name, III, 331.

Saras, a presbyter of Libya, II, 192.

The Hebrews maintain that Sarasar and Regemmelech were Persians, commanders of Darius, and God-fearing men, VI, 832.

The riches of Sardanapalus, I, 318. His marriages, 290. Sardanapalus was more disgraceful in his vices than in his name, VI, 223.

Sardius, a precious stone, I, 365.

Sardonyx, a precious stone, I, 365.

The *mastruca* of the Sardians, II, 171.

Zarephath, a city of the Sidonians, VI, 383.

Sargon, king of the Assyrians, was called by seven names, IV, 211.

The Sarmatians, I, 913.

What are Sharon and Bashan? IV, 436. All Sharon, near Joppa and Lydda, is an exceedingly fertile region, ibid.

A Gallic *sarracum* [wagon], IV, 824.

How Satan entered Judas’s heart, II, 565. “Satan” means “adversary,” III, 347. Satan will dwell bodily in the Antichrist, V, 712. Satan is avenger and accuser, VI, 800. What does Satan signify? VII, 126.

What is a *satum*? VII, 94.

Saturninus the heretic, II, 197.

The faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, 933.

How great was the worship of Saturn among the ancients, IV, 544.

[Col. 1067] Satyrus, a learned man, II, 345.

Satyrus was brought alive to Alexandria in the time of Constantine, and then to Antioch, II, 8. A little man called a satyr appeared to Antony, and they spoke together, ibid. Who are the satyrs? IV, 174 and following.

What is *saucomaria*? VI, 425.

Saul is mourned by Samuel because of his impenitence, I, 890. Under Saul, Jerusalem was not yet being ruled, III, 390. Saul was deceived by desire for plunder, IV, 353. Why Saul killed every male, and only the males, among the Amalekites, 353. Saul was anointed king at Gilgal, VI, 44. He was made king not by God’s will but through the people’s error, 82. Saul means “desired,” VII, 474.

The Saxons, I, 913.

The mystical ladder seen by Jacob, I, 585.

Where the word “scandal” gets its name, II, 476. What is scandal? VII, 112, 113.

The scarab, a worm of dung, VI, 619.

The virtue of the Scauri, I, 335.

The Scaevolas are praised, I, 533.

The daughters of Scedasus avenge, by their own deaths, the violation of their chastity, II, 308.

Crimes do not remain hidden for long, II, 191.

Among the Hebrews, the festivals of Tabernacles and Unleavened Bread are of the greatest importance, V, 388. The Feast of Tabernacles, a Jewish festival, VI, 139.

In what does schism differ from heresy? VII, 738.

What did boys sing in the schools? II, 358.

Knowledge without works is weak and fleeting, I, 604. Joined to works, it is a sign of perfect virtue, ibid. The sciences are most useful to human beings, 275. They are divided into three parts, ibid. Holy men possessed only that knowledge which had been revealed to them by the Lord, 169. What are the branches of philosophy? II, 717. God’s knowledge is not unaware of what we think secretly, III, 479. It is part of knowledge to know what one does not know, V, 510. The truth of knowledge should be sought more from the source than from the streams, VI, 850. Useless knowledge, VII, 736.

What do the minor scholars do? I, 230, 736.

Scipio triumphed over Numantia, I, 464. What did he earn beyond his years for his virtue? 396. Publius Scipio wrote about the odd number, 231. The Scipio brothers, V, 710. Why Scipio took the name Africanus, VI, 747.

To know. We more often suppose than know what is true, III, 401. Excessive care and anxiety, tormenting human beings through various channels, was given by God so that they would desire to know what they are not permitted to know, 393. We are commanded that a person should not wish to know more than Scripture attests, 435. A human being cannot know the wisdom of the Creator so clearly and purely as the one who is the creator knows it, 403. The more we seek to know, the more we display our vanity and our superfluous words, 435.

The rending of the Temple veil while Christ suffered, IV, 605. The rending of the Temple veil explained mystically, VI, Preface on Hosea.

The rending of garments upon hearing blasphemy, IV, 459. The rending of garments in sorrow and adversity, VI, 191.

Scopas of Aetolia, Ptolemy’s commander, was defeated by Antiochus the Great, V, 708.

Dross, the dirt and refuse of metals, V, 256.

Scorpions pursue whatever is dry, I, 430. The stings of scorpions, 5, 30.

The customs of the Scots and Atticoti, I, 415. The Scottish people have no wives of their own but indulge in lust like animals, II, 335. Scottish porridges, IV, 835.

The scribes and Pharisees, together with Herod, slaughtered many thousands of infants, IV, 112. They are called mockers and pestilent men, 785.

One should not rush too quickly into writing or be carried away by a light-minded madness, I, 944. What does it mean to be written in heaven and on earth? V, 169.

What was written nearly four hundred years after Christ, II, 614. There are many kinds of diction and writing, 471.

Scripture has one and the same author, I, 903. Holy Scripture cannot contradict itself, 203. The words of Scripture are divinely inspired, 134, 1041. The Scriptures were handed down to the churches as the fullest instrument of faith, 764. The history of Scripture is said to be the foundation of truth, 720. If deliberate falsehoods are admitted into Scripture, no authority will remain in it, 405, 774. The order of words in Scripture is a mystery, 508. What Jerome observed in translating it, ibid. The mysteries of Scripture are to be admired in simple words, 182. Scripture is difficult to understand, 235, 325, 640. Everything we read in the divine books shines and gleams even on the surface, but is sweeter in the marrow, 325. Only the saints and the apostles have deserved possession of Scripture, 410. No one can enter into the sacred Scriptures without a teacher, 275. A faulty method of teaching is to corrupt meanings and draw a resistant Scripture toward one’s own will, [Col. 1068] ibid. Who should be praised or blamed in interpreting them? 230.

No one should interpret the law of Christ according to personal hatreds and private hostilities, 425. Learned men have more often conjectured the meaning of Scripture’s words than expressed it, 134. We should take care to say not what each person can or wants to say, but what the Scriptures command, 228. Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh, 939, 997. Through continual meditation on the Scriptures we erase the stains of the soul, 664, 561. Study and reading of the Scriptures are commended, 262 and following. In the Scriptures the penitent is mourned, the holy man is sung, and the despairing man is cursed, 1088. The book that Ezekiel devours is the entire sequence of the Scriptures, ibid. In the midst of arms, the studies of Scripture are silent, 446. What assistance and security do they require? ibid. One must advance to the battle of Scripture with a peaceful mind, 738, 761. Wicked men try to criticize the Scriptures, 640. The only art that everyone everywhere claims for himself is the art of Scripture, 275. Different medicines from the Scriptures must be applied according to the diversity of persons, 457. Certain things were taken into the holy Scriptures from the books of the gentiles, 425. To hear willingly about the Scriptures and to answer modestly, 338. Some, with raised eyebrows, philosophize about sacred letters among little women, 275. The Scriptures must be learned by heart, 688. A daily task from the Scriptures, 686. The usage of Scripture, 535. The Scriptures were handed down to the churches as the fullest instrument of faith, II, 661. They consist not in reading but in understanding, 201. The Scriptures must be used against adversaries, so that if they despise human things, they may at least not neglect divine things, 570. Those who weaken the meaning of Scripture with little rhetorical flowers are censured, 183. If we follow the letter of Scripture, we can compose a new doctrine, 201. Because of the variety of regions, different copies of the Scriptures are circulated, 642. In what does Scripture agree with the Peripatetics? 748. The canon of the Scriptures, 278. Three books of sacred Scripture offer much information about the nature of things, 158. The usage of Scripture, 208, 210, 212, 219, 366, 369. The rule of the Scriptures, 276. Scripture habitually names one thing in the plural and many things in the singular, 370. Divine Scripture is compressed into a brief compass: as much as it expands in meaning, so much is it constricted in speech, III, 495. The true food and drink taken from the Word of God is knowledge of the Scriptures, 413. Knowledge of them is the riches of Christ, 303. Wisdom must be pursued, and knowledge of the Scriptures joined to it as in marriage, 463. Knowledge of the Scriptures cannot be possessed together with the riches of the world, 303. We cannot know the meaning of the Scriptures unless we learn it through the words, 394. Although there are many who say that they can unlock the hidden things of Scripture, few are those who find the true solution, 450. We do not learn any art without a teacher; only the teaching of Scripture seems so cheap or easy to many that it does not need a teacher, 411. All things are learned with difficulty and great labor, contrary to those who think that knowledge of the Scriptures comes to the idle and to those who merely make requests, 390. The poverty of the historical account, or the simple meaning, must not be passed over while we pursue the anagogical meaning in the Scriptures, 409. It is the custom of Scripture, although there are many books, to call them one volume when they do not disagree with one another and are written about the same subject, 495. They use the imperative mood in place of the optative, 506. All the Scriptures are inspired by the Holy Spirit, IV, 393. They are called one book, ibid. Christ is the foundation of the meaning of Scripture, 3. The majesty of divine Scripture is to be admired, 728. It is wrapped in the mysteries of future things, 284. The authority of the Scriptures must be followed, 126. Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ, 1. Knowledge of the Scriptures among the gentiles, 512. Jerome encourages understanding of the Scriptures, 284. Blessed is the one who sows in the utterances of the Scriptures, 13. A person learned in the holy Scriptures is a bulwark of the Church, 638. The teaching of Scripture is pure silver, 25. In the exposition of the Scriptures, truth rather than contention must be sought, 44. The meaning of Scripture weakened through allegory. After the historical truth, everything in the Scriptures is to be understood spiritually, 3. In the Scriptures the letter must be trampled down and the fruit of the life-giving Spirit gathered, 13. The simple words of Scripture are straw; its inner meaning is wheat, 157. One must not flatter princes so far that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected, 431. One must follow neither the error of parents nor that of ancestors, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God who teaches, 907. Scripture wishes the people to be taught not only through the ears but also through the eyes, 973. Those who receive them otherwise than the Holy Spirit speaks are called false prophets, 1053. Those who do violence to Scripture are censured, 1922. The Scriptures give Jews and heretics an occasion for error, 313. Who is the false teacher and corrupter of the Scriptures? 25. It is the custom of Scripture to summon people to repentance, 271. Many things are said in Scripture according to the opinion of the time in which the events are reported to have occurred, 1038. What the apostles observe when reciting testimonies from the Scriptures, 622, 665. The apostles took the testimonies of Scripture according to the Hebrew text, 378, 394. The propriety of holy Scripture is praised, 509. What is the custom of Scripture? [Col. 1069] 201. The idiom of sacred Scripture, 171, 191, 205. The mysteries of the understanding of Scripture are expounded, V, 515. In the divine books the interpreter must remove nothing; why? 15.

The threefold manner of understanding the Scriptures, 172. Human nature cannot grasp all the treasures of Scripture, 27. Human speech cannot explain the mysteries of Scripture, 503. The words of Scripture must be turned into deeds, 79. Some promise themselves an understanding of the Scriptures without God’s grace, 724. The abuse of testimonies from Scripture builds a brothel, 172. The purpose of Scripture is not to weave an external history without the Jews, but, etc., 704. The rule to be observed in the Scriptures, 394. The custom of holy Scripture, 652. Scripture is a spring to some and a well to others, 166. The Scriptures were produced by the Holy Spirit, VI, 520. Their threefold understanding, 270. Whatever is said in the holy Scriptures is a trumpet, penetrating the ears of believers with a loud voice, 255. Simplicity is sought in the exposition of the Scriptures, 309. What assistance must be used in opening the secrets of Scripture? 25, 441. The custom of Scripture and our own custom, 596. It is impious to say that Scripture lies, 543. The teaching of the Scriptures is the firmest wall, 580. The learning of the Scriptures produces virgins, 869. In reciting the Scriptures the apostles follow not the words but the meaning, 306. Why the Apostle used a testimony of Scripture according to the Septuagint, 612. Nothing strikes so forcefully as a testimony taken from the Scriptures, 868. Why holy Scripture is difficult, 574. Abuse of testimonies from Scripture is condemned, 271. Reading the Scriptures is paradise, 935. Various flowers are gathered from it, ibid. When the Scriptures benefit the reader, 454. They benefit only the one who acts, ibid. Heretics approve some Scriptures and reject others, 314. A forced exposition of the Scriptures, 459, 467. The literal meaning is outside; the spiritual meaning is in the marrow, 281. Scripture is the kingdom of heaven, VII, 80, 92. Sacred Scripture is the kingdom of God, 170. Knowledge of the Savior is stored within it, 97. Through the Scriptures God made all the mysteries known, 554, 555. It is full of allegories, 471. In the Scriptures, what seems plain is full of questions, 113. Everything is also full of meanings, 191. The spirit of Scripture and its fruit are found through much labor and worthy cultivation, 496. When is Scripture useful to listeners? 386. Those things that do not have the authority of Scripture are despised, 190. The fruit of meditation on the Scriptures, 537. They must be read with every effort, 637. The idle who do not read are censured, 703. Divine Scripture builds up when read, but it is more beneficial when turned into speech, 467. It is not the author of sin, although it encloses everything under sin, 443. It is a great danger to interpret the Scriptures in the Church, 486. Superstitious understanding of them must be avoided, and how this is to be done, 63. Some prefer to follow the Jews rather than the apostles in interpreting the Scriptures, 463. A carnal understanding of Scripture is the occasion of many evils, 496. The literal sense does not help, 495. Examples prove this, ibid. The one who follows Scripture according to the letter is consummated in the flesh, 420. Those who learn the Scriptures not merely in a Jewish but in a spiritual manner wage war in the flesh, but not according to the flesh, ibid. Some do not wish to understand them spiritually, 515. Some dispute among themselves about the Scriptures, 518. Contention must be avoided in interpreting them, 514. Among heretics they are full of scandals, 114. The devil and all heresies speak about the Scriptures, 386. In disputation one must flee from one testimony of Scripture to another, 61. It is the custom of Scripture to speak of the future as though it were past, 575. It is customary for Scripture often to place a Hebrew word together with its interpretation, 451. A rule for interpreting the Scriptures, 207. The custom of Scripture, ibid., 11, 13, 14, 41, 55, 102. Poor in faith and knowledge of Scripture, 405. Jerome reconciles this, 212. He rejects the interpretation of certain words of Scripture, 449. In reciting the Scriptures the apostles and evangelists present the meaning, not the words, 424, 490. Matthew takes not the words of Scripture but its meaning, 17.

The testimonies of Scripture: by whom and for what purpose they were cited is considered, 340. How Marcion, Basilides, and Valentinus read the Scriptures, ibid.

Non-orthodox writers should be read so that we select what is good in them and avoid what is contrary, I, 352. Very many writers are noted, 233, 234. Ecclesiastical writers are praised in some respects and condemned in others, II, 556. Writers on Illustrious Men among the Greeks, 821. Among the Latins, ibid. A series of ancient writers against Ebion, 225. The judgment of writers belongs not to themselves but to their readers, 468. Many ecclesiastical writers are noted, IV, 451. In what sense does Jerome call them teachers of the Church? ibid. Certain things were altered by unlearned writers, 644. An addition by bad writers, 642. The fault of writers is demonstrated, 995. The writers of psalms, hymns, and songs of God are to be called prophets, VII, 95. Several are listed, ibid.

Vendors of baskets, V, 313.

How sculpture differs from casting, VI, 627, 628.

[Col. 1070] Knowledge of vulgarity, and its distinction from foolish talk, VII, 641. This must be driven away by holy men, ibid.

A certain shield-bearer, possessed by a demon, reveals Hilarion while he is in hiding, II, 34.

*Scybala*, that is, refuse, VII, 400.

The Scyllaean shore, II, 551.

The Scythians eat half-raw meat, II, 335. They bury alive those who were loved by the dead, ibid.

Sebaste, the name of Samaria, IV, 113. Samaria was called Sebaste from the name of Augustus, VI, 156. Sebaste was formerly called Samaria, 363. There was the burial place of Obadiah, the prophet Elisha, and John the Baptist, ibid.

Sebesius pleased more by being corrected than he had harmed by erring, I, 129.

Secrecy and silence must not be violated, I, 268. The secrets of the heart are revealed through bodily movement and gestures, V, 85.

The number two is unclean and pertains to the union of the flesh, VI, 337 and 782.

Security and despair are to be avoided, IV, 1042. Security produces negligence, and negligence produces contempt, 354, 1089.

Nothing is secure when God is opposed, VI, 396.

How can any one of us be secure, if Paul is afraid? I, 504. Never be secure, II, 772. No one should now consider himself secure; rather, he must handle his weapons in this time of war, so that once victorious he may rest in peace, III, 411.

*Sedec* is a Hebrew word that more properly means “just” than “justice,” IV, 25.

Zedekiah was blinded and put into a cage, IV, 169. Zedekiah abandoned the covenant of the king of Babylon through perjury, 184. Zedekiah is surnamed Seilum; and why? 989. Zedekiah was led away to Babylon, V, 220. How Zedekiah was treated as a disgrace at Nebuchadnezzar’s banquet: the tale of a certain Hebrew, VI, 623. Whether Zedekiah’s captivity preceded as a type of the Savior, V, 115.

To sit is the posture of one judging, IV, 58.

Segor was previously called Bala, I, 701. It means “little one,” 890. Lot’s faith saved all Segor, ibid. Segor, the fifth city after Sodom, etc., was preserved through Lot’s prayers, IV, 187.

By whom were the mountains of Seir named? III, 348. What region is Seir? VI, 371.

What Sela signifies, I, 137 and following. What it signifies mystically, ibid.

Seleucia was situated on a promontory of Syria, I, 695. Seleucia was formerly Chalanne, III, 320. Seleucia, a city of the Persians, IV, 174.

Seleucus Callinicus, king of Syria, V, 795.

Seleucus Ceraunus, king of Syria, V, 706. Seleucus Nicator, the first king of Syria after Alexander, V, 704.

Seleucus, after subduing Babylon, placed the diadem of all Asia and Syria upon his own head, V, 700.

A *sellula*, a reclining seat for sleeping, II, 69.

Sellum, Zedekiah’s surname; and why? IV, 989.

Salmona, a station of the children of Israel, I, 914.

The Hebrews think that Shem, Noah’s son, was Melchizedek, I, 444. The Hebrews consider Shem to be Melchizedek, IV, 497.

The plural form *semina* is found nowhere in the sacred books, VII, 439.

Semiramis, wife of Ninus, built the walls of Babylon, VI, 124.

“Always,” signifying “eternally,” I, 569.

The senate of the Church, an assembly of presbyters, IV, 51.

Seneca wished to be among his own people what Paul was among Christians, II, 851. What Seneca says about love of women, 318. He wrote about marriage, ibid. Whose doctrines are learned from him? 565.

Old age that has trained its youth in honorable arts reaps the sweetest fruits, I, 256. It should neither seek nor accept luxuries, 639. The disadvantages of old age, 291. A description of perfect and sound old age, 25. In old age we live more moderately, II, 17. Good must be done at every age, both in prolonged old age and in youth, because frugality in youth is of no benefit if old age is spent in luxury, III, 483. Old age brings many good and bad things with it, VI, 263.

Old men suffer from phlegm and cold, I, 287. Warm foods and old wines benefit them, ibid. Wisdom grows in the old and is almost suffocated in the young, 256. Old men are to be honored, but openly rebuked if they sin, 945. Sometimes, contrary to the maturity of our years, we fall into the faults of children, ibid. Distinguished old men in wisdom, 256. What is said about an immodest old man? 786. By which peoples were old men customarily devoured? II, 334. Old men lose their understanding through excessive age, 206. Old men are so called because of merit and wisdom, not age, 48. What place old men and rulers had among the people of God, 53. The age of old men is venerable even among enemies, 548. Old age is close to death and to mature judgment, VI, 180. No one before Abraham is called an old man, 839. What is fitting for old men? VII, 713 and following.

[Col. 1071] Many elders were rejected and younger men chosen, V, 308.

Shinar is a plain of the Chaldaeans, VI, 820.

The sense must be alert and not open to empty thoughts, I, 939. Our senses are uncertain, especially sight, II, 445. Our sense is drawn toward the desire for that thing whose pleasure captivates it, 338. Through the five senses there is an entrance for vices into the soul, 336. What they take delight in, ibid. The kingdom of the five senses, 271. Through the senses the strength of the soul is softened, IV, 334. Through all the senses death enters for the destruction of the soul, 908. Those who indulge their senses are condemned, 332. Through all the senses one reaches understanding, 968. By natural sense we must understand what is right, 879. Human beings abuse the gift of sense and speech, which was given so that they might sense and hear God, 41. To argue about the words of God according to human sense is sacrilege, 1069. Enemies desire to enter the soul through the senses, VI, 190, 374. The five senses are the gates of Nineveh, 579. The pleasure-lover opens these gates, ibid.

We ought to follow the meaning more than the words, III, 495. The meaning is clearly disclosed by comparing statements, VII, 560.

What is the ancient opinion? II, 789. A bold opinion, V, 531. The opinion of a certain person swollen with pride, VII, 728. A noble poet among the Romans, 462. The opinion of a wise man, 421.

Boys construct clever little maxims at the ends of sentences, I, 400.

Sihon, king of the Amorites, VI, 244.

The Hebrews call Apamea Sephama, V, 599.

What sort of region is the Shephelah? VI, 381.

Zipporah means “bird,” II, 268. Zipporah kept the strangling angel away from her husband, VII, 482.

Among the Hebrews, seven is understood to mean many, IV, 626. The seventh number is holy, 1083. The mysteries of the number seven, VI, 283.

The number seven is complete and perfect, III, 461. The numbers seven and seventy signify perfect repentance, IV, 327. Why are the numbers seven and ten familiar to the Jews? 64. The number seven represents the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 64 and 65. The mystery of the number seven, V, 479. The power of the number seven in fevers, VI, 283.

What do northern peoples not eat? II, 334. The northern quarter according to the Hebrews, V, 597.

The seventieth year of the desolation of the Jewish Temple was completed in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, VI, 283.

The seventy-two disciples are represented in the seventy-two psalms, I, 474.

Allowance must be made for the Seventy Translators, I, 312. Whatever they did in the sacred volumes, etc., 310 and following. They added very much of their own and left other things out, 316. Why did the Septuagint version prevail in the churches? 302. A corrupted translation, 637. The Seventy Translators are said to have gathered in the basilica and compared their work, not prophesied, II, 520. Their cells were falsely invented, ibid. Why did they not wish to disclose clearly the mysteries of their faith? 527. What they did not know, they expressed in doubtful statements, 520. The usefulness of the Septuagint version, 528. It was strengthened by the antiquity of its readers, ibid. A corrupted translation, ibid. The Septuagint version in Daniel differs greatly from the truth and is rightly rejected by the churches, 527. The Septuagint Translators were corrected and translated by Jerome, 518. He spoke well of them, ibid. and following. The authority of the apostles and of Christ is greater than that of the Septuagint Translators, 520, 528. The Seventy Translators did not wish to disclose the mysteries of Scripture to King Ptolemy, III, 303. Jerome did not reproach them for these errors, ibid. They translated only the five books of Moses into Greek, ibid. Those books agreed more closely with the Hebrew than did the others, ibid. Jerome vindicates them, 340. The Septuagint version is disseminated throughout the whole world, IV, 792. They translate the name *Sabaoth* in two ways: either “Lord of hosts” or “Lord almighty,” 18. They did not wish to translate a clear prophecy about Christ into Greek, 43. They did not dare to interpret openly that the child should be called God, 133. They alter the meaning of prophecy, 565, 945. In very many places they disagree with the Hebrew truth, 269. They placed not the words of Scripture but their own meaning, 341. An addition by the Septuagint: “pierced through with a spit,” 120. They added things of their own, 143. They omit certain things, 956. The reason for an omission in the Septuagint, 1056. A verse was not in the Septuagint, 1017. An error of the Septuagint Translators, 461. Jerome defends the Septuagint Translators, 415. Jerome is compelled to interpret the Septuagint version, 420. The Septuagint imitates the fables of the gentiles in its interpretation, 245. The Septuagint and Theodotion name many things in the likeness of gentile fables, 236. What the Septuagint version lacked in the Latin and Greek texts, 1008. Many things are missing in the Greek and Latin copies of the Septuagint, 1035. Things added by Origen in the Greek copies, taken from Aquila’s version, 42. The Alexandrian copies contain things that are not in the Hebrew and Septuagint copies, 696. What was added to the church copies from the Hebrew and from Theodotion, 100. The Septuagint version rejected by the teachers of the Church, [Col. 1072] V, 645. The Septuagint was deceived by similarity of letters, 600. The Septuagint translation was corrupted through the fault of writers and readers, 54, 401, 474. The entire school of the Jews maintains that only the five books of Moses were translated by the Septuagint, 53. The Septuagint altered the Hebrew names as it pleased, 474. Certain things are omitted in the Septuagint Translators; why? 159. The Septuagint does not agree with itself, II, 453. Through the Septuagint the divine law was translated into Greek, VII, 734. They represented letters by other letters, ibid. and following. The Septuagint Translators coined new words, 387.

The sellers of tombs are chastised, following the example of Ephron the Hittite, III, 340, 341. The custom of burying gold and ornaments in tombs among the ancients, IV, 898. The tombs of the apostles and martyrs at Rome, V, 468. The ornaments of tombs, VII, 188.

Sepulcher of Christ, to be venerated, I, 209.

Interpretation of the two Seraphim by Origen and Jerome, I, 294, 524.

The Seraphim and the meaning and explanation of their name, I, 50, 56. They attend upon God with praises and, according to the opinion of a certain writer, are sent to cleanse human beings, 53. God should not be said to sit upon the Seraphim, 60. They are treated at length in Letter 18, while Isaiah’s vision is being explained. The two Seraphim of Isaiah signify the two Testaments, 284. The Seraphim, angelic powers, IV, 93. Certain persons, understanding the two Seraphim as the Son and the Holy Spirit, are refuted, 92. Others wish the Old and New Instrument to be signified by them, 93. The two Seraphim celebrate the mystery of the Trinity, VI, 634.

Serapion the Confessor, I, 424, 705. Serapion, II, 640. He acquired the surname “the Scholastic,” 933.

Serapis the Egyptian became a Christian, I, 679.

The praise of Desiderius’s sister—or wife—Serenilla, I, 210.

Serenus, I, 279.

Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, II, 835.

A good discourse does not seek secrets; rather, it delights in its own praises and in the testimony of many, I, 964. A discourse often drawn out at length lacks understanding, 748. Discourse is the vestibule of action, 604. Discourse, reason, knowledge, and faith without works are empty and unstable, ibid. One’s conduct and speech should not disagree, 936. When discourse has been completed by action, an end is put to knowledge and thought, 604. The native language is sullied by foreign vices, 686. The richness and polish of Gallic speech, 935. If someone’s speech does not sting but is merely pleasing to its hearers, it is not the speech of a wise person, III, 494. Why the end of a discourse is better than its beginning, 438. Divine discourse, conceived in the mind, burns in the breast, IV, 890. Why divine discourse is divided into sections, 560. It uses the words of human usage, 487. For what three reasons may someone keep silent about the words of God? V, 33. The manner of divine discourse in expressing historical truth, VI, 115. In what does contempt for the word of God consist? 835. When the words of God are good, 455. Good and evil discourse, VII, 632. The word of God flows from the Holy Spirit, 681. Its effectiveness, ibid. The context and sequence of a discourse, 84. The discourse of the Gospel is superior to the voice, 247. The apostles are ministers of the word, 240. Who see the word of God, and who do not, 247.

“Late” (*sero*) is explained as “belatedly” in the Gospel of the Resurrection, I, 826.

Let us possess the serpent’s cunning, lest we be supplanted by the plots of others, I, 324. No one enters safely among serpents and scorpions, 89. The serpent was more prudent in wickedness than all the beasts, II, 338. No one enters safely among serpents and scorpions, 401, 35. Serpents of extraordinary size, called boas, 36. What is related about them? ibid. One is burned up at Hilarion’s command, 36. The serpent’s cunning, VII, 60.

Among slaves, character should be chosen, not elegance of face, I, 989. Whatever slaves have not endured, they think has been taken away from them, 284. Their rumors, ibid. The class of little slaves is querulous, and however much you give them, it is always too little for them, 788. They do not consider from how much is given, but how much is given, ibid. They console their grief only with slander, ibid. Sold slaves—those whose price was paid for them—are called servants and scourgers, 605. Slaves sometimes, suddenly puffed up by the devil with rank, wear down the public roads with their horses, while every noble and prudent person, oppressed by poverty, walks along the road and performs the service of slaves, III, 471. It is characteristic of slaves not to love but to fear, VI, 400. What is appropriate for slaves? VII, 722 and following. Fear and trembling are appropriate to them, 661. Let them be subject to their masters, provided that what is commanded is not contrary to God, 722. It is a vice of slaves to contradict their masters and to steal, 723.

What is the inheritance and reward of the servants of God? IV, 642. What is necessary for the servants of God? VII, 41. Christian slaves are bound to their masters by a double law, 758. In these subjected persons the Lord is subjected, 722.

Servius, Valeria’s husband, II, 313.

Whoever is free from conjugal servitude is truly a servant of Christ, IV, 657. The servitude that does not demand its payment immediately is more acceptable to God, VI, 950.

[Col. 1073] The posture of sitting is the characteristic posture of a judge. See “To Sit.”

Setta and Settim, what are they? IV, 502.

The Setthoites, II, 197.

Settim: the solidity, beauty, and smoothness of wood, IV, 502. What is Settim? VI, 215, 502. It is read that God’s Tabernacle was constructed from Settim wood, ibid. Press-vessels are made from the same wood, 215. These woods are not found in cultivated places or in Roman soil, except in the desert of Arabia, ibid.

The Severian heretics, II, 969.

Affected severity seeks popular glory, I, 989.

Severus, Apollonius’s servant and his betrayer, II, 883.

The emperor Severus, II, 875.

The book of Sextus the Pythagorean, a most distinguished pagan, published under the name of Xystus, I, 1030. The same book, translated into Latin by Rufinus, is falsely accused, IV, 993. A saying from the same book, etc., V, 206, 207.

There is no sex among the heavenly beings, V, 20, 94. It is not sex that is taken into account, but merit, VII, 751.

Whistling, an indication of a miracle and astonishment, IV, 1015.

The ten Sibyls according to Varro, II, 306. Their distinguishing mark is virginity, and the reward of virginity is divination, ibid. The Sibyl is called *theoboulē* (θεοβούλη, “divinely counseled”) in the Aeolian form of speech, ibid. The Cumaean Sibyl, ibid. The Erythraean Sibyl, ibid.

Drought in the churches, IV, 939. A description of a great drought, ibid.

What is *sicera*, and in how many ways is it made? I, 266. Among the Hebrews, *sicera* means anything capable of causing intoxication, III, 96. What is *sicera*? IV, 76, 374.

Sychar, or Shechem, is Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans, III, 541.

The funeral pyre of Sychaeus, Dido’s husband, II, 310.

Shechem is now called Neapolis, I, 703. Most people, in error, read “Sychar” for “Shechem,” ibid. Shechem signifies *ōmous* (ὤμους), that is, “shoulders,” VI, 67.

The *siclus* in Latin, called *sekel* in Hebrew, has the weight of an ounce, III, 341. The *siclus*, drachma, and *hiu*: what are they? V, 44. How many obols does a *siclus* contain? VI, 472.

The adverb *sicut* explained, VII, 661.

The stars that are called wandering stars, II, 697.

Sidon, an ancient city, I, 695. Sidon, a city of Phoenicia, IV, 1018.

*Sigala*, a kind of grain, V, 43.

Sigaris, bishop and martyr, laid to rest at Laodicea, II, 887.

In the magnitude of signs, it is not a change of nature but God’s omnipotence that is demonstrated, I, 718. Many are those who received signs, etc., IV, 106. A sign of great sterility: in what does it consist? 938. Why signs are performed among barbarian nations through the servants of God, V, 662. How is Christ a sign that is opposed? VII, 299.

Silas and Judas are named as apostles, VII, 396.

A prohibition of speech reforms a cursing tongue, I, 287. It is incongruous for the body to remain hidden while the tongue wanders throughout the whole world, 782. The silence of the Jews, VI, 337. It has been cast forth throughout the whole world, ibid.

The pods of pigs, mystically, I, 75.

At Shiloh, a demolished altar was shown in Jerome’s time, V, 703. Shiloh, the site of God’s Tabernacle, IV, 893.

The spring of Siloam at the foot of Mount Zion, IV, 119. The scarcity of its waters, 937. The river Siloam, VII, 62.

A forest as a figure for the multitude of believers, I, 488.

Silvester, II, 198.

The tribe of Simeon is not blessed by Moses, I, 496. The tribe of Simeon dwelt among the tribe of Judah, III, 174. Simeon and Levi did not receive a separate inheritance, 375.

Simeon, Jacob’s successor, VII, 397. He is said to have been crucified for the Lord, ibid.

Simeon the leper invites the Master with his disciples and is not despised, I, 432. Why Simeon was called a leper, VII, 211.

What is *simila*? I, 266.

Likeness and equality differ, V, 331. The likeness feared as punishment should prevent the likeness of committing an offense, VI, 567 and following.

By whose aid did Simon Magus establish his heresy? I, 1031. Simon Magus was baptized with water alone and not with the Spirit, II, 321. His doctrine, 197. Simon Magus was baptized in water, but not unto salvation, V, 146. Simon and Elymas, magicians resisting the apostles Peter and Paul, IV, 641. The errors of Simon Magus, VII, 191.

Simon Peter, II, 827.

The wisdom of Simonides is praised, I, 257.

Simplicity without reason is foolishness, VI, 76. The simplicity of doves must be tempered by the cunning of the serpent, ibid.

Simplicius, the posthumous son of Ageruchia, I, 900.

Images derive from likeness, and the Latin noun *similitudo* (“likeness”) derives from the Hebrew *semel*, III, 86.

[Col. 1074] Pretended holiness is a lighter evil than sinning openly, IV, 277.

Pretence is the protection of a lie, I, 301. Pretence is sometimes useful and should be adopted, VII, 407.

*Sin*, the hissing element among the Hebrews: Isaac inclined slightly and pronounced *samekh* in its place, III, 348.

Sin, which is also Kadesh, another desert, I, 475.

Sinai and Zion signify the two Testaments, I, 1000.

According to Jerome, Mount Sinai is sometimes called Mount Horeb, III, 191. Mount Sinai is situated in the southern region, IV, 568.

What are the left and the right? I, 218.

What is *sinōpis* (Σίνοπις)? I, 981.

“Bosom” is explained in two ways, IV, 777. It is sometimes called “head,” ibid. “Bosom” as affection and love, ibid. What are “bosom” and “breast”? VI, 81.

David captured Zion and rebuilt it at the same time, I, 696. What is written about it? ibid. Zion and Jerusalem are one city, IV, 506. Zion, the mountain on which Jerusalem was built, was called the City of David, 24. Why is Zion called a virgin and a daughter? 463, 464, 744. Why is it called a valley rather than a mountain? 220. There is no other Zion except the people of God, 594. No one dwells in Zion except one who is holy, 410.

Sior is interpreted as “turbid,” I, 704.

The song and stories of the Sirens, I, 290, 787, and II, 242, 551. The nature of the Sirens, IV, 521. By their deadly song they plunge souls into the depths, 246. What does Jerome understand by them? 175.

The letter of Siricius, IV, 550, 553. Letters to Siricius, 421.

Sisinius hastens to Egypt for the refreshment of the saints, I, 632, 638.

Sixtus the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church, I, 1029. See “Sextus.”

Where the emerald and carbuncle are born, I, 934.

Smerdis the Magus took as his wife Pantaptes, the daughter of Cambyses, V, 702.

Shebna, governor of the temple, and the Scribe are distinct, IV, 459 and following. Shebna, high priest and betrayer of a large part of Jerusalem, 224, 225, and 462. Shebna’s ambition in preparing a tomb for himself, 225.

The rule of sobriety, II, 293.

The sober and simply dressed are mocked, I, 176.

The Samaritans founded Soccoth, III, 274.

Association with sinners is harmful, IV, 93.

Choose as companions those whose fellowship will not disgrace you, I, 260.

Socrates, I, 334. Socrates had two wives, II, 316. They frequently quarreled with one another, ibid. How many hardships he suffered because of them, ibid. Socrates’ frugality, 344. His elegance and wit, 567. What philosophers falsely boast about Socrates, 782. Socrates did not write books, 567. Socrates is falsely praised, IV, 508.

A Socratic saying, I, 317. The disciples of Socrates, 222. The Socratic practice in writing, 1042. A Socratic saying, II, 472, 557. Socratic mockery, 379.

All mothers-in-law hate daughters-in-law, II, 317. Mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law hate one another, VI, 519.

Sodom is said to be righteous in comparison with Jerusalem’s wickedness, II, 712. In what did it sin? ibid. According to the Hebrews, Sodom is to be restored to its former state in the thousand-year reign, V, 181. Which Sodom is the younger? 179. Sodom and Gomorrah were leaders in sin, VI, 130.

The sun and moon are the two eyes of the world, I, 584. What is said about the sun’s cycle? 621. Concerning the sun, moon, and stars, 593. The famous table of the sun, 271. An eclipse of the sun around the days of Pentecost, II, 452. By its rising every day the sun indicates the world’s destruction, and by its setting, III, 387. When it travels through the south, it is nearer the earth; when through the north, it is raised aloft, 389. One and the same action of the sun melts wax and dries clay, 441. The sun is called by three names, IV, 336. The courses of the sun, moon, and other stars are defined, 492. The sun and moon will receive the rewards of their courses, 415. The course of the sun and of the other stars is defined, V, 17. The sun completes its annual course in twelve months, VI, 272. The sun did not dare to look upon its Lord hanging on the cross, 340. The eclipse of the sun, VII, 400.

A house’s upper room, I, 667.

In what does consolation amid evils consist? IV, 337.

The solemnity is not everyone’s, but that of Christ’s Church, I, 585. How solemn days are to be celebrated, 151. The holy and heavenly solemnity is bounded by no intervals, 616. Perfect men here taste in advance the solemnity of eternity, 622. Two solemnities are noted that are not in the Mosaic Law, V, 569. The solemnities of Christians, VII, 456. Their observance and institution, ibid. How greatly they differ from Jewish solemnities, ibid. and 457.

What solitary life is to be condemned? VI, 527, 528.

The praise of solitude and its advantages, I, 32. The vices of solitude, 938. The solitary life is preferred to the communal life, 993. Yet it is dangerous, not only for men but especially for women—why? ibid. Jerome often praised the solitary life, 938. Those who seek it should leave the monastery’s training ground, ibid. Let them not be frightened by the harsh beginnings of the desert, ibid. The sign of the most remote solitude is noted, VI, 113.

The cause of anxiety and distraction is not in God but in the one who previously sinned of his own accord, III, 407.

What is the difference between having sins loosed and having them forgiven? IV, 207.

Who should sit alone? V, 853, 854.

It is permissible for sleep to steal upon a long task, I, 530. The sleep of Jonah, as also that of Christ’s disciples, was not one of security but of grief, VI, 397.

Dreams are not to be believed, II, 487. Things that happen then, whether good or bad, neither benefit nor harm, ibid. Their illusions, ibid. One should not boast of another’s dream as though it were a great testimony, 560. Whoever believes dreams gives himself over to vanity and foolishness, III, 429. Why the impious saw dreams, IV, 1004. Prophetic dreams are open to God alone, V, 635. Dreams are often revealed by God to the Gentiles, VII, 394.

Dreamers in the Church, proclaiming their errors, IV, 1004.

Sonthomphanec, or Saphanet Phanee, is interpreted by the Egyptians as “Savior of the world,” III, 17. See above, “Psonthonphanech.”

The frauds of sophisms, II, 861.

What is related about Sophocles? I, 257.

When Sophocles flourished, V, 702.

Zephaniah is interpreted as “watchman” and “knower of the Lord’s secrets,” I, 278. What matters does he address? ibid. Zephaniah prophesied after the deportation of the ten tribes, VI, 674. His genealogy, ibid.

Sophronia, I, 954.

Sophronius, a false monk, I, 112.

Sophronius disputing with a Hebrew, II, 525.

Dirt is cleaner than all the world’s forms of worship, I, 293. Dirt deliberately sought in condemnation of silk clothing, 458. All the lights of others are stained by some dirt, II, 749. In Scripture, dirt conveys something different from sin, VII, 286.

*Sorec*, a kind of excellent vine, IV, 69, 850.

The stages of sorites, II, 487.

One should not immediately believe in lots, VI, 398. The will of God governs uncertain lots, 399.

Soter, bishop of the Romans, II, 869.

The friendship of the Spartans and Messenians, II, 307.

The steadfastness and chastity of Spartan maidens, II, 307. A serious war was stirred up on their account, ibid.

Each nation calls distances along roads by its own names, VI, 215.

The seven stages of human life, VI, 314.

Spectacles are condemned, V, 226.

Ezekiel is appointed as a watchman, V, 33. The ministers of the Church are called watchmen, IV, 662.

The philosophers’ spheres, VII, 613.

The caves in which Obadiah fed one hundred prophets with bread and water, I, 703.

Hope is more deserving of praise than reality in the praise of a little girl, I, 961. The mystery of our hope and faith, II, 287. Hope in God is commended, IV, 583. Through hope of future things, we endure tribulation, 680. The defenses of those who have no hope in God are quickly scattered, 873. Our hope is certain, VI, 731. Vain hope among the many, 747.

To hope for as certain what often proves uncertain is ridiculous, I, 230. No one is to be trusted, nor is hope to be placed in anyone, even though we submit to others, VI, 519, 520.

Speusippus, Plato’s sister’s son, II, 309.

Spiritual things are to be preferred to carnal things, I, 629. Spiritual things are considered through bodily things, II, 719. The spiritual person never persecutes the carnal person, VII, 476. The spiritual person according to Jerome, 472. His formation, 466. A carnal sign is made so that the spiritual may be proved, 49.

All things are contained in the Holy Spirit and surrounded by his majesty, I, 595. He was borne over the waters almost in the manner of a charioteer, 419. He was bringing forth the nascent world in the figure of baptism, ibid. The place of the Holy Spirit’s descent was shown, 698. Let us bear the Holy Spirit with the measured and composed gait of riders, 507. Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, II, 107, 167. The substance of the Holy Spirit is unknown to philosophers, 107. That he is not a creature, 109 and following. The same Spirit existed before the Lord’s coming and in the apostles, 108. In what sense he is blameworthy and not receptive, 110 and following. Although the Holy Spirit is in many, he does not possess a circumscribed substance, 112 and following. It is impossible for anyone to obtain the grace of God if he does not have the Holy Spirit, 115. In the power of the Holy Spirit God will fulfill the hope he promised, 217. How the Holy Spirit inspires human beings with his will, 123. Love is the fruit of the Holy Spirit, 125. How the Holy Spirit is to be understood as proceeding from the Father, 133 and following. The prophets possessed the Holy Spirit, 136. The Holy Spirit came in the name of the Son, 133. The Holy Spirit is the Creator, 140. Through the Holy Spirit certain knowledge of future things is granted to holy men, 145. The fellowship that the Holy Spirit has with the Father and the Son, 147. The Father and the Son are called Spirit, 160. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of Jesus, 789. The Holy Spirit dwells only in a pure faith, 181. He is not opposed to himself, 692. Merchants of the grace of the Holy Spirit, 21. The Holy Spirit cannot be conferred by heretics, 177. Heretics acting against the Holy Spirit, 749. Heretics blaspheme by saying that the Holy Spirit was created, 423. The Holy Spirit from the beginning is life-giver, Creator, and God, III, 306. The Holy Spirit is of the same nature as the Father and the Son, IV, 753. His riches, 681. Among the Hebrews he is designated by the feminine gender, 485. The Spirit is incorporeal, 574. He keeps watch toward God, and how, 348. Certain heretics wish the Holy Spirit to be created, VI, 260. The Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought, 472. Spirit, soul, and body are brought together into one Holy Spirit, 58. In the name of the Savior, the gifts of the Holy Spirit descend, 204. The Holy Spirit is Christ’s vicar, VII, 313. What is the Holy Spirit like? 332. The Holy Spirit is the third person from the Father and the Son, 324. How is his promise fulfilled? 438. The seal of the Holy Spirit, 632. There is no strength without him, 602. He is bestowed upon the worthy at every moment, 422. The grief of the Holy Spirit, 632. By what works he is grieved, 743. Error concerning the Holy Spirit, 450. According to certain persons, the Holy Spirit did not always speak through Paul and the prophets, 741.

The bonds of the spirit are stronger than those of bodies, I, 352. What things does “spirit” signify? II, 261 and following. Among the Hebrews, both *spirit* and *scent* are similarly called *ruha*, III, 439. How “spirit” is taken in a good and a bad sense, VI, 461, 629. Evil spirits and opposing powers are ministers of God, 199. The Lord summons opposing powers to judgment and disputes with them on behalf of his people, 207. The baptism of the Spirit, VII, 276. In what way was the Lord strengthened by the Spirit? 302. Three spirits named in Psalm 50 are demonstrated, 451. Paul names three spirits, ibid. The name “Spirit,” without qualification, is taken in a good sense, 651. The spirit of a human being is always taken in a good sense, 648. The death of the Spirit is nowhere read of, ibid. To emit the Spirit is an indication of divine power, 236. “Spirit” is taken for “soul,” 237.

The Bride of Christ, the Ark of the Testament, I, 108. Let her flee wine as poison, 923. Scripture calls wives brides, II, 208. A bride is called a wife, VII, 12, 13.

Marriage contracts, I, 292.

A guarantor is not at fault if the person to whom a promise is made has made himself unworthy of the promise, V, 225.

Among whom is the Bridegroom feeding? I, 109. The Bridegroom cannot be found in the streets, ibid. How we are joined to the embraces of the divine Bridegroom, III, 319.

A Saturnalian dole, VII, 667.

The nature of tin, VI, 812. Tin separates metals mixed and adulterated with one another by means of fire, ibid.

We do not read of a sinner standing in sacred Scripture, V, 23.

What is a *stater*? VII, 136.

Statues of emperors were worshiped, V, 638. Statues and inscriptions: what are they? VI, 105.

Compared with the moon, a star is blind, I, 224. Each star is perfect in its own light, though, in comparison with a greater one, it lacks perfection, II, 697. Various names of the stars, 362. That stars exist in the sky by day is proved by the eclipse of the sun, IV, 240. God called the stars by their names, ibid. The stars have their own names among the Hebrews, ibid. The orders, movements, and courses of the stars in heaven, 492.

Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, was the twenty-sixth after blessed Peter, II, 196. The words of Stephen the martyr are defended, VI, 305.

Sterility is said to be caused by taking willow seed in food or drink, IV, 268 and 525.

Stesichorus is praised, I, 257. He vacillates between blaming and praising Helen, 632.

What is *stibium*? I, 286.

Why the prophets are said to “drip,” VI, 334.

“Dripping” taken as eloquence, VI, 452.

The *stiva*, the part of a plow, II, 180.

Zeno, founder of the heresy of the Stoic school, IV, 900.

The impious doctrine of the Stoics, I, 569. The Stoics’ spheres, 718. They maintain that the soul is from God’s own substance, 948. The Stoics describe four virtues, 394. The dispute between Stoics and Peripatetics, 1042. The Stoics, II, 558. Why they lingered in the colonnades of temples, 338. They claim logic for themselves, 487. According to the Stoics, a person can be free of passions and reach perfection, 734. They argue that sins are equal, 701. The Stoics agree with us in defining good and evil, IV, 159. The Stoics, VII, 554, 737. They distinguish among words with greater subtlety, 511, 728.

[Col. 1077] What does the robe signify mystically? I, 79.

Everyone serves his own stomach, I, 511, 520. Why doctors customarily give the bitterest antidote to a nauseated stomach, IV, 596.

Strato, ruler of Sidon: how and why he was killed by his wife, III, 311. She afterward took her own life, ibid.

The tower of Straton, called Caesarea by Herod in honor of Caesar, I, 695.

A New Year’s gift, VII, 666.

Strophes in a subscription, I, 527.

What are *strophomata*? IV, 239.

The nature of ostriches, IV, 245. The ostrich is born and nourished in the deserts, 916. The nature of the ostrich, VI, 438.

Whatever a fool says must be called shouting and clamor, I, 727. To lack wisdom is the first folly; but no one can be free from folly unless he has understood it, III, 395. Folly wages war against wisdom, and whatever prudence it sees in a learned man, stimulated by jealousy, it does not accept, 474. Fools judge everyone by their own character, 469. A fool sees himself as learned in the very matter in which he thinks himself wise, if he multiplies words, 475. In this world fools are lifted up before the face of the devil, while princes walk in the lowliness of slaves, 395.

What is foolish speech? VII, 640, 641. It flourishes among the wise men of the world and in the Church, ibid. How does it differ from buffoonery? ibid.

The Stymphalides, II, 387. The virginity of a Stymphalid marked by death, 308. All Arcadia avenges this, ibid.

What is “to persuade”? VII, 385.

Voluntary and unwilling subscription are condemned, I, 348.

The rule concerning what follows and what precedes, VII, 81, 205.

Not to subsist is better than to subsist badly, VII, 215.

Different substances possess different power and condition, I, 602.

The suburban estates of priests, IV, 1081. They could not be sold except to one whom kinship required, ibid.

Where amber congeals, IV, 496. The power of amber, VII, 50.

The interpretation of the verb *sufflaminare*, “to check” or “to hinder,” II, 419.

The testament of Suis, II, 473.

The interpretation of “Shunamite,” I, 257.

What is holy pride? I, 99. Pride has God as its adversary, 27. A swelling spirit and an uplifted neck provoke God’s hatred against themselves, 455. Pride in angels, in the Jewish people, and in sophists is punished, 27. Pride is broken by humility, 708, 608. There is nothing in this world worse or emptier than every vain wind than pride and a self-satisfied person who is pleased with nothing except what he himself has done, III, 435. What is the voice of pride? IV, 177. It must be avoided with every effort, 224. Ruin follows pride, and glory follows humility, 241. Many fall into pride through an opinion of their virtues, 877. Pride is understood as power and glory, 735. Pride is the devil’s distinctive sin, V, 181. Every pride offends God, 77. The material of divine pride, 963. Ruin follows pride, and glory follows humility, 238. What is holy pride? VI, 687. Pride is displayed in the stretching out of the neck, 718, 719.

Every proud person is ready to inflict injury, IV, 241. To whom does the designation “proud” apply? 139. The confidence of the proud as they await the day of judgment, VI, 300. It benefits the proud to be humbled, 614. Before Christ’s coming, almost everyone was proud, 642. How greatly it offends God to pride oneself on sins, IV, 224.

The high priest’s shoulder garment, I, 363. What it signifies mystically, 363.

The superstition of the impious concerning knowledge of the future, IV, 755. The superstition of Christian women, VII, 184.

Punishment and blessing are far apart in name and in action, I, 624. Punishments produce holiness, V, 818. The punishments of the impious benefit others, 825. Eternal punishments, VII, 210. Among sinners punishments differ, 60. The punishments of things, 674.

The Hebrews’ reckoning of the lunar year, V, 683.

Sur, a desert, IV, 151.

How can the deaf receive the Gospel? VII, 420.

Whose is it to rise? VI, 500.

The story of Susanna is approved, I, 5. The story of Susanna is not found in Hebrew, II, 527. It is approved, 276. Why was Susanna’s story not accepted by the Hebrews? IV, 1048.

Susa, metropolis of the Elamites, V, 672. In it Daniel built a lofty tower where the bodies of the Persian and Median kings are buried, ibid. Its guardian and priest is a Jew, ibid.

Let us beware of all suspicions, and whatever can plausibly be invented, let us avoid inventing beforehand, I, 260.

Whisperers, the most pernicious kind of people, I, 712.

The *sycamina*, a kind of tree in the plains of Palestine, bearing wild figs? VI, 334.

Sycamore wood is cheap; cedar wood is imperishable, IV, 136.

[Col. 1078] What is slander? IV, 883. Slander is the greatest sin of the Jewish people, ibid.

Syene, a tower situated at the extreme borders of Egypt, V, 356, 360. Its description, 345.

What is reported about Lucius Sulla? II, 316.

A Hebrew lengthens syllables, IV, 733.

What is syllepsis? VII, 211, 235.

Syllogisms, I, 237. The syllogism in Scripture, IV, 1077. The inevitable syllogism, VII, 81. The resolution and consequence of syllogisms, 416.

The Creed of faith handed down by the apostles, II, 435. It is not written on paper and in ink, ibid. How it concludes at the end, ibid. The forehead is signed at the end of the Creed, 577.

Symmachus translated the Scriptures in his usual manner, more explicitly, IV, 7. Symmachus was an Ebionite, VI, 656. Symmachus does not ordinarily follow verbal *kakēzēlia* (κακοζηλία, “affected imitation”), but the order of meaning, 258.

The synagogue was first taken from the idolaters through Abraham and Moses, I, 910. After adultery and the denial of Christ, it sits without an altar and awaits the return of its former husband, ibid. After the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then it will be saved, ibid. By whom it was prefigured, ibid.

Christ spoke by synecdoche, VII, 83.

What is necessary for a Church synod? II, 513.

What is a *synthema*? I, 791. When the *synthema* was dismissed, the public horse was saddled, ibid.

Syrian merchants, I, 982. The Syrians eat land crocodiles, II, 334. The language of the Syrians and Chaldaeans is largely related, Preface to the Books of Kings. The Syrians possess an inborn passion for trade, V, 313.

The kings of Syria after Alexander the Great, V, 703. Syria is called “high” and “lofty,” VII, 397.

The language called Syriac is Chaldaic, V, 624.

Syrus, father of the monastery of Chnum, who receives the grace of the angelic language, II, 85. Some maintain that the Syrians were called *Assurim*, III, 344.

The name *Syrtis* is derived from its physical character, according to Sallust, III, 104.

## T

Tabeel means either “man” or “idol,” IV, 203.

Why messengers are so called, I, 21.

Examples of the monks of Tabenna, I, 57.

The mystery of the sacred Tabernacle is explained, I, 360. Why God formerly spoke to Moses at its entrance, 52. The measurements of the Jewish Tabernacle, IV, 628.

The end of the Tabernacles is possession of the eternal dwelling, IV, 628. The origin of the Feast of Tabernacles, VI, 931.

Marriage tablets and dowry rights, I, 418.

The second writing of the tablets, II, 348.

It is sometimes fitting for a Christian to be silent, I, 234. Much more is signified by silence than by speech, 782. Whatever he has kept silent, the accused confesses when he is charged with many things and omits some of them, II, 412.

Silence is sometimes a dispensation, not consent, I, 535.

Tacitus, II, 899. Tacitus wrote the lives of the Caesars, VI, 914.

“Touch” taken to mean affliction, VI, 799.

Women’s headbands, IV, 60.

The mole: an animal without eyes, harmful to crops, IV, 42.

The icy Tanais, I, 466.

Virtue commends Tanaquil, II, 320.

Tanis was the metropolis of Egypt, IV, 205. Tanis, Pharaoh’s royal city, 402.

Tantalus, I, 271.

Taphnis, a royal city, V, 359.

Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh king of the Romans, VI, 737. He was expelled by Brutus, ibid.

The founders of Tartessus, VII, 427. It is now called Carteia, ibid.

Tarsus of Cilicia, and Tharsus, I, 162 and following. Tharsus, a city of Cilicia, V, 698. Tharsus, a region of India, ibid.

The virtues of Tatiana, mother of Furia, I, 282.

The doctrine of Tatian, I, 213. Tatian taught at Rome, IV, 869. He condemns and rejects marriage and foods, 239. Tatian, leader of the Encratites, VI, 247. He maintained that wine ought not to be drunk, ibid. Tatian, patriarch of the Encratites, VII, 685. He rejects some of Paul’s Epistles, ibid. The errors and arguments of Tatian, 526. They are refuted, ibid. His syllogism deceives the hearer by a sophism, ibid.

The letter *tau*, in the ancient Hebrew script, resembles a cross, V, 96.

Taurus, prefect of the praetorium, was present at the Council of Ariminum at the king’s command, II, 189.

Mount Taurus, V, 597.

A roof is called *doma* and *maenianum*, I, 667.

[Col. 1079] King Tiglath-pileser, while Pekah was reigning in Samaria, transferred the Israelites to Assyria in the fifty-second year of the reign of Uzziah, king of Judah, V, 7.

The saying of Telamon is praised, I, 334.

Telesphorus, II, 911.

Where does unrestrained rashness lead? II, 517.

The age, wisdom, and sayings of Themistocles, I, 256.

Why oil was burned in the Temple, I, 962. In what sense is it called the sanctuary? 535. What is the true Temple of God? II, 289. All the temples at Rome are covered with soot and spiders’ webs, 686. Christ avenges those who violate his temple, 591. Entering the house of God is not a matter of praise, but entering without offense, III, 426. The Temple situated on Ornan’s threshing floor, IV, 216. Angels as guardians of the Temple, 605. A voice is said to have gone forth from its sanctuary, etc., ibid. The Temple of Jerusalem was built more splendidly under different rulers, 15. A statue of Hadrian and an idol of Jupiter were placed in the Temple of Jerusalem, 37. What was the overthrow of the Jewish Temple? 766. The Temple of the Lord on the summit of Gethsemane, 372. Lebanon is called a temple, V, 190. A voice is said to have gone forth from its sanctuary, etc., 110. Nothing was made in God’s Temple without reason and measure, 502. All its walls were painted with various images of idols, 85. The idol of Antiochus in the Temple, 712, 722. The Temple polluted for three years, 721. The Temple described by Ezekiel, much more splendid than Solomon’s Temple, 464. What does it mean to enter the Temple through the northern gate and leave through the southern gate, and conversely? 578. At what time did the Temple’s overthrow take place? VI, 880. It is always time to build the Temple of the Lord in good works, 742. What the angels guarding the Temple are said to have proclaimed, VII, 401. The Temple of God, the Church: from what was it constructed? 291.

Time considered in three ways, II, 784. The definition of time according to the Stoics, VI, 743. What does it mean to buy time? VII, 649. Some do not think that the present exists, but only the past or the future, 681.

The farther the outer darkness separates us from Christ, the true light, the more it surrounds us with horror, I, 983. The Cimmerian darkness, II, 453. Darkness as a figure for tribulation, IV, 347. In sacred Scripture darkness signifies ignorance, V, 630. Why is it called “outer” darkness? VII, 45.

Temptation is human life, I, 937. God warns us through various temptations, 790. How they are to be overcome, 126. Good things sometimes come from them, ibid. The shield of faith must be taken up against temptations of the flesh, 100. We are either proved as righteous or sustained as sinners, etc., 183. You are attacked most of all when you do not know that you are being attacked, 31. Temptation is human life, II, 328. Since we are composed of flesh and Spirit, we must suffer the wars of each against the other, 324. The devil’s temptation under the pretext of an honorable matter, 43. What is a great temptation? 29. In temptations, when the Lord turns his face away from us, we are dashed to pieces, IV, 764. Temptations and injuries are applied as remedies, VI, 580. God seems to reject us when he abandons us to temptation, 733. What is the great temptation of human beings? VII, 597. Why did John not describe Christ’s temptation? VII, 254.

It is impossible for a human soul not to be tempted, II, 220.

Who is the tempter who asks questions? VII, 180.

What does *tenupha* signify? I, 355.

God hates the lukewarm, and they make him nauseated, I, 285.

The terebinth market is detestable to the Jews, IV, 1065.

Terentia, Cicero’s wife, II, 316.

Terentius translated Menander, I, 309. A saying of Terentius, II, 317. Terentius presented the prologues of his comedies on the stages in his own defense, III, 301. Luscius Lanuinus accused him as though he were a thief of the public treasury, ibid.

What does “to turn one’s back” mean? IV, 853. Whoever turns his back indicates by the gesture of his body that he disregards the one threatening him, 1093.

Each one of us has his own limits, II, 258.

The Holy Land is more august after Christ, I, 202. The places of the Holy Land in which remarkable and memorable things are seen, 209 ff. The Promised Land: nothing is more fertile, IV, 69. Its boundaries, ibid. No region is found equal to the Promised Land, 457. How great was the terror of the inhabitants of the Land of Promise at the arrival of God’s people? 194. The Promised Land is bounded on the southern side, along the borders of Egypt, by Rhinocorura and the torrent, V, 613. How it was divided among the tribes, 612. To what extent the land was exterminated, 809.

The foundations of the earth are the will and power of God, by which all things are contained, IV, 242. They are borne by angelic powers, 529. The earth is called a point, and human beings are called locusts, 474. What does “to work one’s land” mean? 324. What is “the land of the living”? 701. “Earth” is taken for the soul, 359.
