No one possesses this earth through gentleness, but through pride, VII, 23.

The earthquake of the whole world after the death of Julian, II, 36. What it does in the sea, ibid. The earthquake in the time of King Uzziah, VI, 223.

[Col. 1080] All earthly things will pass away, I, 320.

Tertullian is abundant in maxims but difficult in expression, I, 326. He is to be mourned, 352. His *Apologeticus* and books *Against the Nations* contain the whole discipline of the age, 429. Tertullian’s books on virginity, ibid. He asserts that the soul is produced by transmission (*ex traduce*), 948. He is said to have been Cyprian’s teacher, 523. Tertullian is called a heretic, II, 225. In him his talent is praised, while his heresy is condemned, 556. He was still a young man about whom he wrote, 260. He wrote seven books against the Church on behalf of Montanus, 867, 881. He replied to Apollonius, ibid. What he reports concerning John the Evangelist, 280. What he relates about a presbyter, 845. Tertullian’s volume *Scorpiace*, 395. The epitome of Tertullian’s work is believed by many to be Cyprian’s, 911. A story about Tertullian, 513. Tertullian, IV, 478. Tertullian wrote against Marcion, VI, 361. Tertullian, VII, 537. He is praised, 383. He wrote a heretical book *On Monogamy*, 697.

By whom were the two Testaments prefigured? I, 910. The figures of the Old Testament preceded evangelical truth, 205. The Lord Christ is the author of both Testaments, II, 522. Many things concerning the old books are found in the New Testament that are not found in the Septuagint, 529. The heretics who tear apart the Old Testament, 787. How the Old and New Testaments should be read, III, 483. We are commanded to believe in both Instruments—that is, in the Old as well as the New—with equal reverence, 480. Eternal punishments are prepared for those who by no means join the two Testaments together, 482, 483. The two Testaments are joined by unity, IV, 95. The New Testament is strengthened by testimonies from the Old, 316. Nothing succeeds the New Testament, 795. We were once strangers to God’s Testament, having no hope and being without God, 720. Both Testaments belong to one God, VI, 619. The two Testaments are more closely related than united, 916. Reading the Old and New Testaments is the way of the Lord, 163. The heretics who deny the Old Testament, 199, 787. The God of the New and Old Testaments is the same, VII, 594. There is one providence of both, 416. In true visions of the Old and New Testaments, fear is first driven away, 407. The New Scripture preserves the custom of the Old Testament, 377. The history of the Old Testament, 752. The prophets of the New Testament, 615. Those who bark against the Old Testament are refuted, 494, 663. Some reject it, 54. Heretics tearing apart the Old Testament, 686. Which Scriptures of the New Testament do the same people reject? ibid.

Testament-hunters are condemned, I, 261. Those claiming false testaments for themselves, IV, 1083.

A testimony is faithful when it has no reason to lie, I, 501.

Testimonies deserve reverence because of their antiquity, II, 783. That testimony is true which is uttered by an enemy’s voice, 409. It is not the number of testimonies but their authority that matters, 178. Christ and the apostles produce many testimonies from the Old Testament that are not read in the books of the Septuagint translators, III, 383.

One witness is not believed, II, 640.

Who is a false witness? VII, 223.

A tortoise does not so much walk as move, VI, 142.

Origen’s *Tetrapla*, II, 893. The order of the same, 527.

Teuta, queen of the Illyrians, flourished in chastity, II, 310. She ruled over very brave men and often defeated the Romans, ibid.

Thabatha, a village, II, 13.

Mount Tabor in Galilee, III, 283. Mount Tabor in Galilee, V, 612. See above, Itabyrium.

What history records about Thaddaeus, VII, 57. He had three names, ibid.

What did Tamar’s childbirth prefigure? I, 910.

Tamar is today called Palmyra, V, 601. Solomon built it with marvelous works, ibid. and 613.

What does Thamnatz Sare signify? II, 271.

Thamuz stands for Adonis, I, 321.

The Tharsensian heretics, I, 39.

The region of Tharsis, III, 286. The whole open sea was called Tharsis, 299. In Hebrew, Tharsis is called “sea,” IV, 816. Josephus thinks that Tharsis was the city of Cilicia, Tarsus; others think it was a region of India, 40.

Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, glorious through the apostle Paul, III, 318. Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, IV, 816, and VII, 762.

The Theban maiden killed her violator and then took her own life, II, 309.

The city of Thebestis, VII, 427. What it was formerly called, and by whom it was built, ibid.

Thecla is said to have come into the embrace of virgins, I, 125.

The village of Tekoa, separated from Jerusalem by twelve miles, IV, 881. Tekoa, a town six miles south of Bethlehem, VI, 221. The greatest expanse of desert lies beyond Tekoa, ibid. The prophet Amos was from this town, ibid.

Among the Hebrews, Theman denotes every southern region, III, 282.

Themistocles, as it is written, when he died at the age of one hundred and seven, regretted that he was departing from this life just when he had begun to become wise, I, 256. The death of Themistocles, V, 702.

Theoctistus, bishop of Caesarea, II, 893.

Theodora, the wife of Lucinius, is commended, I, 456.

The charity of the monk Theodore, I, 538. He saw all the monasteries, ibid.

The letter of Theodore, or Theodoric, concerning Easter, to all the monasteries, II, 10.

Theodore of Heraclea, I, 739, 753. The same Theodore praised, VII, III. His commentaries, 369.

Theodore, later called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, brother of Athenodorus, II, 905. He was a disciple of Origen, ibid.

The emperor Theodosius, I, 307, 211. Theodosius praised by Paulinus, 325. The same emperor Theodosius, II, 935, 192.

Theodosius the bishop: whom did he succeed? I, 630.

The edition of Theodotion, I, 752. Theodotion agrees in many places with the Septuagint translators, III, 396. Theodotion, the Greek translator, V, 624. Theodotion and Symmachus were Ebionites and semi-Christians, VI, 656. Theodotion was a Judaizing heretic, ibid. He was not a trustworthy translator of Scripture, ibid. Theodotion was truly poor, ibid.

Theodore of Byzantium opposed, II, 225.

Theogonus, bishop of Nicaea, II, 192.

Theonas, bishop of Alexandria, II, 501.

What happened when the presbyter Theon preached the Holy Spirit? II, 414.

The eloquence and learning of Theophilus, I, 610. In his Paschal letter he borrowed nothing from secular sources, ibid. Concerning whom and against whom he acts in his Paschal letters, 582. The victories of Theophilus over the heretics, 535. Almost all Italy was freed from heresy by Theophilus’s letters, 537. He drove Origen out of the whole world, 581. The letter of Theophilus to Pope Anastasius, 537. Some letters of Theophilus translated by Jerome, II, 545. Theophilus praised, 867. What does Theophilus mean? VII, 249. The commentaries of Theophilus, 3.

Theophrastus’ book *On Marriage*, II, 313. He wrote in prose, 332. Theophrastus, a writer of natural history, IV, 960. Theophrastus wrote three volumes *On Friendship*, VI, 517. Cicero also has a book on this subject, ibid.

Nothing is sweeter than theory and knowledge, V, 466.

The Latins use *theorica* for logic, I, 146. What is theory? III, 384. The discipline of contemplation, ibid.

Theoseba, deacon of the Church of Thira, II, 453.

*Teraphim*: images or figures, III, 70, 355. What are *teraphim*? VI, 32.

*Theriace* is made from the flesh of a viper, II, 331.

The *theristrum* mentioned in the *Song of Songs*, signifying chastity, I, 685. The *theristrum* is a type of Arabian garment with which the women of that province are veiled, III, 343. *Theristra*, women’s clothing, IV, 62.

The Thermodon River, IV, 638 ff.

The various treasures of God, V, 798.

Thespesius the rhetorician, II, 941.

The invasions and victories of the Germanic people, I, 906.

Theogorma, that is, Phrygia, whence horses come, V, 311.

Thomyris, queen of the Massagetae, VI, 778. She killed Cyrus, ibid.

Tophet, the name of hell, IV, 421.

Trachonitis and Ituraea are the same region, III, 279.

Thraseas, martyr and bishop of Smyrna, II, 887.

Many thousands of Romans were killed at Lake Trasimene, I, 980.

Thubal: some wished “Iberians,” others “Italians” to be understood, V, 387.

Thucydides is praised, I, 323, 345.

Thummim: see Urim.

Frankincense (*thus*) grows among the Sabaeans, III, 319. Frankincense comes from Sheba, IV, 887. Frankincense is a symbol of spiritual incense, VI, 626.

The Etruscans were once highly skilled at shooting arrows, IV, 817.

The tiara of the high priest, I, 362. *Tiara* is a Greek word transferred into Latin usage, V, 639. It is a kind of cap worn by the Persian and Chaldean peoples, ibid.

The elders of the Tibareni hang up those whom they love on gallows, II, 335.

Tiberias was formerly called Chinnereth, V, 612. Tiberias, VI, 389.

Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, VII, 177. He succeeded to his place, ibid. Christ suffered under him, ibid. The same is noted, 530, 688.

The Tigris and Euphrates rise in Armenia, III, 202. The Tigris was so called because of its swiftness, 279. The Tigris and Euphrates are rivers of the region of Chaldea, V, 5.

What does Timaeus relate? II, 309, 567. Plato’s *Timaeus* is extremely obscure, VI, 283.

Timasius was suddenly hurled down from the highest rank of dignity, I, 344.

[Col. 1082] To fear belongs to slaves, not to those who love, VI, 400.

Timoclia, II, 320.

What did Timon do at Athens? VI, 528.

The fear of God enables us to despise all other fears, I, 199. It must be preserved, 89. Let no one learn to hear or say anything except what pertains to the fear of God, 680. A mind fortified by the fear of God despises the pains of torments, 620. There are two kinds of fear in the Holy Scriptures, II, 709. There are two kinds of dread and fear of God: that of beginners and that of the perfect, III, 497. Whoever fears God is neither uplifted by prosperity nor crushed by adversity, 445. As an imitator of his Creator, he hastens to do good to all without regard to persons, 444. Whence human fear arises, IV, 593. It is more grievous to see the one whom we hold than to endure the torment of punishments, 1081. What fear preserves the souls of the saints whole and pure? 582. God protects those who fear Him in religion, ibid. The age nearer to death embraces the fear and worship of God more fully, VI, 180. The fear of the perfect, VII, 662. Servile fear does not make people perfect, ibid. Fear of wife and servant, 667. The two meanings signified by the verb of fearing, 662.

Timothy, I, 272. Timothy’s bones were transferred to Constantinople, II, 391.

To what is the moth referred? VI, 57. In what sense is God called “moth and rottenness”? ibid.

What the bells on the high priest’s garment signify, I, 366.

What Typhon signifies, IV, 205.

The fable of the Titans, extremely famous among the pagans, IV, 289.

The titles of the Psalms are examined, I, 1049 ff.

Titus, bishop of Bostra, I, 429.

Livy is a source of milky eloquence, I, 271. Why did some people come to him from the farthest boundaries of Spain and Gaul? ibid.

Titus and Vespasian offered the spoils from the vessels of the Temple to the Capitol, IV, 390. Titus, the son of Vespasian, VII, 528. How great was his goodness? ibid. He is offered to us as an example, ibid.

Titus, Paul’s disciple, remained a virgin, VII, 720. Titus receives great praise because through Paul he is greeted by all, 740.

The Book of Tobit is not found in the Canon, XVI, 389. See the Preface to that book.

Jerome cannot mention Toulouse without tears, I, 913. It was not devastated because of the merits of Saint Exuperius, ibid.

How can the winepress be compared with the altar? IV, 69. In Scripture the winepress stands for vengeance and the gathering of fruits, 748. It signifies the Lord’s Passion, 155. Which psalms are entitled “of the winepresses”? V, 566.

The torments of some are remedies for others, IV, 858. The magnitude of torments is displayed, VII, 175.

Tournai, I, 913.

Jerome was reproached because he translated *torquem* in the feminine gender, etc., V, 653 ff.

In Scripture, “torrent,” without an added qualification, is never read in a good sense, III, 389. The torrent of Shittim, or of thorns: where is it? VI, 216.

*Totihioc*, that is, a prefect, I, 57.

Toxotius, Paula’s husband, traces his descent from the blood of Aeneas and the Julians, I, 692.

Toxotius, Paula’s son, was his father’s desire, 693.

One commentator can explain the same passage differently while preserving the faith, I, 780. The ancient commentators of the Church scarcely explained one question in many discourses, II, 714.

Let us take delight in the treatises in which the piety of faith does not falter, I, 688. The authority of ecclesiastical treatises is commended, II, 513.

Ecclesiastical traditions, provided they do not oppose the faith, should be observed as they were handed down by our ancestors, I, 434. One person’s custom should not be overthrown by another’s contrary practice, ibid. Ecclesiastical tradition, II, 196. Its authority, 180. Many practices are observed in the Churches through tradition which have claimed for themselves the authority of written law, ibid. Apostolic tradition, VII, 203.

Trajanopolis in Thrace, a place of exile and the burial place of Eustathius, II, 923.

Suetonius wrote *On Illustrious Men*, II, 825.

“Let us depart from these dwellings”: the voice of the heavenly Powers heard in the entrances of the Temple, I, 33 and 832.

To carry over what has been said in the divine books, even if you do not understand it, is better than to remove what you do not know, V, 15.

The difficulty of translations, I, 610. In translations one must not count the words but weigh the meanings, 759. Many use a false translation, IV, 93. Jerome speaks about the causes of differing translations, VI, 226.

One translated by God is secure, VII, 379. Who are those called “translated”? ibid.

The prudent money-changer, VII, 646. Who is the best? 753.

Many thousands of Romans were killed at the Trebia, I, 980.

[Col. 1083] At Trier, Jerome copied Hilary’s book *On the Synods*, I, 25.

To endure tribulation upon tribulation belongs to the perfect, I, 709. Let us help those placed in tribulation, 580. Although we are hemmed in by various tribulations, we must say nothing blasphemous and think nothing impious, III, 479. Tribulations correct us, IV, 354. Present tribulation is compensated by future joy, 642, 679.

The tribunician power, II, 340. A tribunician riot on account of debt, IV, 400.

The city and Temple were situated between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, V, 612. Why are the two tribes called Judah? VI, 286, 287. A large part of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin believed in Christ, 12. The ten tribes, because of the multitude of the people, retained the former name Israel, 221, 287. The captivity of the ten tribes has never been dissolved, 9.

At the age of thirty, priests approached the ministries of God, VI, 767.

What is *trichaptum*? V, 154. What is your *trichaptis*? VI, 928.

How the three days of Christ’s death are to be reckoned, VI, 405.

Thirty years is the perfect age in a human being, V, 3.

The true faith of the Most Holy Trinity, II, 39, 189. One divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 189. In what sense the Father and Son are one, 999. The mystery of the Trinity was unknown to the ancients, II, 500. The sacraments of the Trinity were made manifest after Christ’s resurrection, 801. The true faith of the Most Holy Trinity, 187, 415. Wherever Scripture testifies to any sacrament concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Septuagint either translated it differently or was altogether silent: why? 520. Whatever is said of seeing and being seen among bodily natures is said to be known and recognized between the Father and Son, 590. The unity of the Trinity: by what it is taught, 126 ff. The Trinity surpasses all material substances, 144. The confession of the Trinity among Christians, III, 469. The mystery of the Trinity in one divinity, IV, 92, 397. Unity of substance and fellowship of majesty in the divine Persons, 90. The Father, saying, “I will not give my glory to another,” does not exclude the Son, 509. The correct confession of the Most Holy Trinity is ignorance of knowledge, 767. At the Lord’s command, the Trinity commands, 95. The Most Holy Trinity dwells in the Church, 356, 766. The confession of the Trinity: the holy mountain and doctrine of truth, 659. While sin reigns in us, we cannot know the mysteries of the Most Holy Trinity, 89. The mystery of the Trinity in one divinity, V, 492, 511. One substance and power of the Father and Son, 208. The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity prefigured, 488. The Trinity surrounds and protects all things, 518. In the Most Holy Trinity true propitiation is given, 530. Every understanding, both of the letter and of the Spirit, etc., pertains to the sacraments of the Most Holy Trinity, 481. The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity praised, VI, 273, 756. Known, 666. In the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity there is nothing obscure, 415, 753. True purity in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, 753. Those who deny the Trinity and admit two gods are refuted, 96. The Most Holy Trinity is injured by the Jews, 487. The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, VII, 451, 732. Its eternity, 691. In the Most Holy Trinity there is one divinity, 130, 244, 563. A splendid exposition of the Most Holy Trinity, 611. Eternity is coequal in the Father and Son, and the nature of both is the same, 551. Equality in both, 609. The operation is the same, 639. The Father and Son have one nature, 751. The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity, 732.

The threefold interpretation of the Scriptures, V, 172.

The laws of Triptolemus, II, 344.

If the purest wheat had mixed chaff, what could be said of us? I, 898.

Who the Tristatae are, V, 266.

The various methods of threshing, IV, 386.

Threshing by cows, VI, 116.

A companion clung to a triumphing man, saying in each acclamation of the citizens: “Remember that you are a human being,” I, 177.

Triumphs are sometimes stained by the filth of the triumphant, I, 398.

The food of the Troglodytes consists of half-raw meat, II, 334.

The ten-year siege of Troy, I, 691.

Tropology in Scripture, I, 848. How, in a tropical sense, the Church can be transferred to the soul, 395. Tropological interpretation requires historical truth, and conversely the latter requires it, V, 504. The difference between tropology and history, 490. The order of tropology and history is not always the same, VI, 393.

The Trosuli, or Torosuli, as they were formerly called, I, 788.

The trowel is a mason’s tool, VI, 328.

Tryphillius, bishop of Ledra in Cyprus, I, 429.

Tryphon, a leader of the Jews, II, 865.

The blast and sound of trumpets, V, 500. The use of the trumpet is described in different ways in the Holy Scriptures, VI, 187, 188. The difference between trumpets and horns, 54 ff. The trumpet in the throat signifies the raising of the voice, 82. What is said in Scripture by way of threat with the trumpet, 253. Trumpets used in mourning, 692.

In what Tullius and Demosthenes were mute, I, 1090. The most beautiful eulogy of Marcus Tullius, 263. His speech on behalf of Quintus Gallius, [Col. 1084] ibid. Whom he proposes in his book *Consolation*, 334. What Greek works Tullius translated, 308. Tullius’s judgment concerning the Greeks, 24. The river of Tullius’s genius, 980. What does Tullius explain in the *Tusculan Disputations*? II, 693. Tullius’s words concerning the preservation of friendship, 159. Tullius, king of orators and illuminator of the Latin language, is accused by the Greeks of extortion, III, 301. Tullius translated Plato’s *Timaeus*, which discusses the harmony of the world, IV, 491. The obscurity of this author is noted, ibid. Tullius the philosopher and orator, VI, 538. He wrote on the cardinal virtues, 792. Tullius, VII, 537. His twofold speech, 416, 417. A saying, 517. See Cicero.

What is tumult? VI, 468.

A burial according to Christian custom, II, 12.

A cheap tunic demonstrates contempt for the world, I, 936.

Adam’s tunics of skins, mystically understood, I, 101 ff. Origen’s opinion on this matter, 218 ff.

The crowd is always changeable, VII, 172.

Turnus is said to have praised Camilla, II, 306.

Many things are shameful in reality that are expressed in honorable words, IV, 550.

The comic poet Turpilius treated the alteration of letters, I, 21.

Whether it is shameful to call a human body part by its proper name, IV, 550. What is shamefulness? VII, 642.

For what purpose a tower is built, IV, 140.

The turtledove is a most chaste bird, always dwelling in elevated places, II, 285. The turtledove is a type of the Savior, ibid.

The *Tusculan Questions* and monstrosities of wording, VII, 387.

The image of the guardian deity, which in Rome was customarily worshipped in each house with lamps and candles, IV, 672.

The lake of Tiberias was sanctified when the Lord sailed upon it, I, 703.

Tiberias was built by Herod in honor of Tiberius Caesar, III, 191. It possessed knowledge of the Law and was therefore called “well-watered land,” according to the opinion of the Hebrews, 378.

Hyrcanian tigers, I, 393.

How type and history differ, VI, 124. Some types can precede in other things what is referred to Christ according to truth and fulfillment, 123. If the whole thing precedes in the type, it is no longer a type, 624.

What the tyrants of Athens are said to have done, II, 307.

Tyre is used to signify the Gentiles, I, 389. Wishing to tear itself away from the mainland, Tyre sought the ancient island: why? 464. Tyre is called *Sor* in Hebrew, III, 46, 93. Tyre was founded in the land of Canaan, IV, 230. Histories report that it was a colony of Sidon, 228. It was the marketplace of the whole world, ibid. It is pressed by the borders of Galilee and Damascus, ibid. The Nile flows into it from nearby, ibid. It is said to be crowned, 229. Tyre was made a peninsula by Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander, 226, 228. What the histories of the Assyrians relate about the flight of the Tyrians, 229, 230. Tyre, the metropolis of Phoenicia, V, 294. Its devastation, 296. A question concerning it is raised and resolved, 297. It was changed from an island into a peninsula, 299. The beauty and wealth of Tyre’s ships, 306, 307. What each province sends to Tyre is described, 307. To this day commerce among all nations is carried on in Tyre, 303, 311. Alexander changed Tyre from an island into a peninsula, VI, 596. A question is posed concerning Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom, VII, 73. See above, *Sor*.

The Tyrians, under siege, boarded ships and fled to Carthage, IV, 233 ff. The Tyrians are called brothers of the Jews, VI, 233. The conversion of the Tyrians and Sidonians, 858.

## U

Elm and poplar are customarily joined for training vines, IV, 50.

Why is all God’s vengeance holy and just? IV, 100. To what the vengeance for the blood of Jezreel can be referred typologically, VI, 130.

Howlings are songs of those who serve idols, VI, 177.

Ulysses, or the Ulyxeum, I, 362.

Scripture calls women’s genitalia by the respectable name “navel,” V, 200. Fetuses are nourished through the navel in the womb, ibid.

What does the navel signify mystically? I, 96.

The custom of sacrificing to the shades of dead people, I, 333. The difference between “shadow of death” and death, IV, 129.

Among the Hebrews, anointing is the insignia of royal power, VI, 655. There are three kinds of anointing: priestly, royal, and prophetic, ibid.

The same person is often found to have been anointed, VI, 655.

Magdalene’s ointments signify good works, I, 432. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call good ointment “oil,” III, 436. The Persians and Indians use ointments in place of baths, V, 160.

Nails mystically signify dead works, I, 399.

Mary, fruitful through union in the likeness of God, I, 103. The number one, which is a perfect number, imitates God through its unity, V, 470. The number held together in unity is the most perfect number, VI, 520.

The hoopoe is a most filthy bird, VI, 819.

The frequency of visiting in cities, I, 193. What harm results from it? [Col. 1085] ibid. Cities are mentioned in which there were once substantial kingdoms, 344. The adornments of cities, IV, 58. The names of Palestinian cities explained, VI, 231, 698, and 858.

Uriah fears death, II, 777. Uriah the prophet, IV, 1030. The flight of Uriah the prophet was not due to infidelity but to prudence, VI, 980.

Urim and Thummim, I, 369 ff.

The pains and difficulties of urination, II, 736.

The nature of bears, VI, 148.

Ursacius boasts of victory, II, 191. The two bears of Elisha—Titus and Vespasian—are interpreted mystically, I, 833.

Ursicinus was set up against Damasus as bishop, I, 39.

One divinity in three Persons, I, 38. The name “Usia,” as though it were new, is rejected, II, 189.

A celebrated passage prohibiting usury in every form, V, 210.

Use. It is a gift of God to give a righteous man such a mind that he himself consumes what he has sought through cares and vigils, III, 406.

We are shut up for ten months in the womb, I, 783.

Every vessel will be filled with wine—and to what extent? V, 821.

An unripe grape is spoken of with reference to vices and sins, IV, 107.

A wife becomes a man’s servant, I, 908. A wife and husband do not have power over their own bodies, nor do they possess freedom concerning chastity, 903. In his wife’s salvation, the husband is a candidate for the faith, 899. The common use of wives among some peoples, 415. The use of many wives and concubines among the patriarchs, 909. What is commanded to one who has a wife, 962. A wife’s concern for her husband’s salvation, 899. The words “the husband of one wife” are explained, 417. Nothing surpasses the love of mother and brother except the affection of one’s wife, 786. A good and pleasant wife is rare, II, 325. Excessive love of one’s wife is condemned, 311. The reasons for which wives are taken, 314. The disadvantages of taking a wife, 283 ff. A servant of a wife cannot serve in the Lord’s army, 270. What happiness it is not to be the servant of a wife but of Christ, 255. Wealth is more often chosen in wives than chastity, 342. It is difficult to support a poor wife; to endure a rich one is torture, 313. Nothing is more pleasing to a man than a good wife, V, 206. How the scandalous acceptance of a prostitute as wife in Hosea is to be understood, VI, 2 ff. Wives are often found to be much better than their husbands, VII, 662.

## V

The red heifer was burned each year on the Mount of Olives, I, 701. No one eats cow in Egypt or Palestine, II, 334.

“Woe” pertains to those who despair, VI, 885, 1081. Woe is the final form of punishments, VI, 298. What does it mean to incur a double woe? ibid. Lamentation, song, and woe: to whom do they belong? 281, 282.

Valens, bishop of Mursa, II, 189.

The death of the emperor Valens after his defeat in Thrace, I, 343. The emperor Valens, II, 939. Valens’s law concerning the prohibition against eating veal, 334.

Valentinian was killed by vomiting blood, I, 343. His corpse was dishonored by hanging, ibid.

The doctrine of Valentinian, II, 591. The Valentinians are refuted, V, 898.

Valentinus the heretic, II, 225. Valentinus the heretic, V, 898. The impious doctrines of Valentinus and Basilides, VI, 545, 818. Valentinus, VII, 120, 737, 743. His error and doctrine, 88, 593, 602. What are Valentinus’s ravings? 378. He maintains that there are two baptisms, 610. He is refuted, 493. How Valentinus read the Scriptures, 340.

Valeria, sister of the Messallae, II, 315.

Valerian, II, 576.

The construction of a valley, IV, 51. The Valley of the Sons of Hinnom, 973. The Valley of Jezreel, VI, 5. The Valley of Jehoshaphat, 208. Near Jezreel there is a valley extending for more than ten thousand paces, 7.

All things are vain until what is perfect comes, III, 386. Nothing in this world is vainer than for the earth, which was made for human beings, to remain while the human being, its lord, suddenly dissolves into dust, 387. We should not eagerly pursue things which, while they are possessed, perish, 385.

The Vandals, I, 344, 913.

The Vangiones were destroyed by a long siege, I, 913.

How all things are vanity, I, 224.

A saying of the orator Geminius Varro, II, 282.

Marcus Terentius Varro, the most prolific writer among the Latins, I, 153. Some of his works, ibid. Marcus Varro praised, VII, 425. He wrote much about the Galatians, ibid.

Varus, who devastated Judaea, I, 974.

[Col. 1086] A clay vessel, an earthen vessel, V, 792. A useless or unclean vessel, VI, 86.

In what sense the vessels of the Temple are holy, I, 535. The Chaldeans placed the vessels of the Lord’s Temple in the temple of Bel, VI, 209. After the Temple of Peace was built at Rome, Vespasian and Titus dedicated the Temple’s vessels in that shrine, ibid.

It is one thing to be a prophet (*vates*) and another to be a translator, II, 520.

Human weakness cannot endure continual prophecy, V, 394.

How the sacred coverings and those pertaining to the worship of the Lord’s Passion should be handled, I, 759. How, and by whom, the veil of the Law was removed, VII, 270.

Willing and unwilling belong to us; yet even what belongs to us is not ours without God’s mercy, I, 989.

A veil hanging at the doors of a certain temple, because of an image painted on it, was torn by Epiphanius, II, 414. See Epiphanius.

Why the Temple veil was torn at the time of the Passion, I, 831. The outer Temple veil was torn, according to Jerome’s understanding, ibid. When and why the inner Temple veil was to be torn, ibid.

The dried fleece and dew poured out over the threshing floor: what do they signify? I, 320.

By whom was the frenzy of the sellers restrained? 943.

Royal hunts in Babylon, IV, 173.

“Hunter” is never read in a good sense, VI, 494.

Poisons are expelled by a serpentine antidote, I, 783. Poisons are not administered unless coated with honey, 684.

Everything sexual requires purification, V, 719.

A statue of Venus placed on the rock of Christ’s cross, I, 321.

Venerius, a bishop, II, 575.

The forgiveness you grant yourself is an act of your humanity; extend it also to others, I, 753. It is not easy to forgive having spoken evil of good things, 190. Forgiveness follows where mourning has preceded, II, 175.

A belly heated with unmixed wine soon foams over into lust, I, 423. Who is there who thinks more about his own belly than about another’s soul? 797. A full belly readily discusses fasting, 319. A fat belly does not produce a refined understanding, 266.

How winds are said to have storerooms, IV, 92. The treasuries of winds and spirits, V, 798. The wind that overthrew Job’s house was brought by the Lord, VI, 154. “He comes from the desert,” ibid.

Wind is understood in Scripture in three ways, IV, 763.

Venus with her offspring, I, 37, 797. A statue of Venus placed on the rock of the cross, 321.

Saint Vera is proposed for imitation, I, 799.

To utter half-formed words harms the tongue, I. A shameful and lustful word must never be spoken from a virgin’s mouth, 713. Never hear an indecent word, 989. Ambiguities of words are condemned, II, 408. The meanings of words must be considered, 257. Defects of speech are not censured among Christians, 498. We shall give an account for every idle word, and everything that does not edify the hearers becomes a danger to those who speak, III, 497. All pomp of words will be reduced to nothing, IV, 75. Among the Hebrews, “word” is used for “thing,” 1090. A great conflict can arise over a single word, 869. Words bursting forth from the inner person are a sign, V, 85. The words themselves, not merely the things, are discerned, 363, 364. What is an idle word? 82. Empty and full words, 644. Which are criminal? VII, 82. How a Greek word was interpreted by Jerome, 398. A certain rendering of words is not approved, 481.

The word of God destroys and builds, V, 755. Why the word of God is not perfected in the disciple, VII, 466.

Vercellae, a city of the Ligurians, I, 3. Its location, ibid.

Modesty is more easily overcome by generously educated talents than by fear, I, 397.

A courier, I, 112. Who couriers are and from where they received their name, VI, 397.

Truth must be loved, not the person, I, 589. Truth cannot favor falsehood, 407. It ought to prevail among disputants, 738. It does not love corners, nor does it seek whisperers, 945. Such is the nature of things that truth is bitter, while vices are thought pleasant, 186. Biting truth pleases God, 49. Few people are pleased by the judgment of truth, 757. Truth is owed to friendship, 779. Whoever possesses sincerity and truth will suffer persecution in the world, 962. Truth can suffer, but cannot be conquered, II, 821. The profit of truth, 195. Let truth be in us, and sincerity and bitterness immediately follow, 723. To have kept silent about the truth is a sin, 773. We must not depart from justice under the pretext of truth, 744. Let us seek not victory over an opponent but truth against falsehood, 715. We see truth through a hole and certain dark caverns, III, 488. Truth must always be loved, and the multitude of human beings must not be feared, IV, 842. Truth can be shut up and bound, but cannot be conquered, 1009. The light of both knowledge and truth drives away all errors, 693. There is one way of truth and many of falsehood, 674. In truth there is beauty; in falsehood, shame, 912. Once error has been perfected, we more readily accept the truth, 718. Truth and steadfastness must not be abandoned in distress, 1028. In the old law there is the shadow of truth, 736. The snares of truth, 540. Each of the two opponents considers truth to be on his own side, 105. One who asks with the intention of testing does not deserve to hear the truth, V, 134. Truth is quickly forgotten, 635. Some prefer to err rather than learn the truth from their rivals, 387. Truth is always above, VI, 134. When one truth rises, many falsehoods will be destroyed, 262. Truth is not found without the grace of the Holy Spirit, VII, 501. Truth was found in no one except Jesus alone, 624. A twofold truth, or knowledge, is assigned: one according to piety, the other, etc., 690. Those who speak the truth are not enemies, although, etc., 686. Those who persecute speakers of truth become enemies of truth, ibid. Courtesy wins friends; truth produces hatred, 462.

Worms are mentioned elsewhere where they are demanded as great revenues, II, 334. The little worm that the common people call a millipede, 557, 715.

Springtime is the chosen season of the year, III, 360.

Verres, successor of Silvanus as bishop, I, 609.

The Psalms and several other parts of Scripture are written in verse, I, 147.

How the versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion render the text of Scripture, II, 524. They are accepted by the Greeks, ibid. By crafty interpretation they concealed many mysteries of the Savior, ibid. They are contained in the *Hexapla* and explained by ecclesiastical writers, ibid. The version of the Septuagint (*τῶν LXX*): see Septuagint. The version of Hesychius: see the Preface to the Four Gospels. The version of Lucian, ibid.

Natural for the bladder to be loosened under the compulsion of fear, V, 245.

Vespasian and Titus, two bears, I, 833.

How “evening” is understood in the Gospel, I, 826. The word “evening” and the West receive different interpretations in Scripture, IV, 308. Whoever possesses the beginning of sins is dwelling in evening, ibid. “Evening” and “morning” signify the succession of day and night, V, 675.

The bat, a nocturnal bird, resounding less through voice and song than through screeching, IV, 42.

The virgins of Vesta, I, 906, and II, 254. Vesta has virgins, VII, 528.

What clothing ought to be like, I, 110, 264, 324. It is not without scandal that some admire silk and gold-embroidered garments in others, 786. Dirty garments are signs of a pure mind, 787, 936. Various opinions concerning the use of clothing by girls, 962. One should use garments that ward off the cold, not those which, by their thinness, display the body naked, V, 541. Egyptian priests use linen garments, 548.

The common garments of priests and of the high priest of the Old Testament, I, 360. The distinctive garments of the high priests, 361 ff. The garments of the high priest of the Old Testament explained, 362 ff. The same garments applied mystically to the renewal of the human being, 364.

The tearing of garments on hearing blasphemy, IV, 459. What the tearing of garments by the high priest signifies, VII, 678.

Ancient things appear fabulous to unbelievers, I, 678.

What is appropriate for old women? VII, 716 ff. Their conduct should be holy, ibid. In what respects certain women are reproved, ibid. They ought to correct young girls privately, not accuse them in public, ibid.

The Old Testament. See Testament.

Age consumes everything, V, 80.

The royal road: what it is, I, 319. For rulers, to do what is just is a good way, 611. Few find the road that leads to life, and far fewer enter upon it, II, 755. Our roads are made straight not by our own labor, but by God’s help and mercy, 791. What is the royal road? IV, 676. What are the right and left roads? VI, 900. Among the Latins, the length of a road: one thousand paces, 215.

Let each person prepare for himself the provisions necessary for a long journey, I, 291.

The difference between a victim and a sacrifice, IV, 660. Why victims were granted to the Jewish people, 718. Sacrifices and victims were not principally sought by God, but were given so that they would not be offered to idols, 21. Religion gradually passed from sacrifices of victims to praises of God, IV, 24. The difference between victims and burnt offerings, 660. Why God granted victims to the people of Israel, 718. When God did not accept victims, 521. After the Temple was destroyed, the Jews cannot offer victims, V, 165. Spiritual victims were to succeed carnal ones, VI, 952.

He is victorious who, in a dispute, recognizes and admits his own error, I, 738.

Letters to Victor, bishop of Rome, concerning Easter, II, 877. He had condemned many bishops of the East, ibid. A synodal letter against Victor, 885.

Where is victory certain? I, 584. In this life there is no certain victory, 90. Victory became for many an occasion of faith, II, 23. Our victory and the crown of victory are prepared by God’s protection and shield [Col. 1088], 781. In this life there is no certain victory, 747. A most wretched victory, 43. Human victory is not perfect, IV, 200. The palm is the emblem of victory, 759. No certain victory exists in this world, 1079.

In the books of Victorinus the martyr there is no learning, I, 326, 429. Interpreter of Origen, 529. Victorinus the martyr is called a pillar of the Church, II, 159. Victorinus’s commentaries, 472, 159. Victorinus the Martyr was unlearned in language, though not in knowledge, IV, 3. He wrote on Isaiah, ibid. Victorinus, VII, 3. Commentaries of Victorinus the Martyr on Matthew, 249.

The rhetorician Victorinus cited, II, 507.

Victorinus of Pettau followed Origen, I, 348.

Excessive concern for food must be laid aside, VI, 114.

The food of a single day signifies all the nourishment necessary for us, I, 823. The food of many nations, II, 334, 342 ff.

It is useless to see what we have despised, I, 324.

What does it mean to see the word of God? VII, 241. What a widow ought to be like, I, 175, 901, 705 ff. She is truly a widow whom both age and life prove to be one, 503. God should be the hope of widows, and their every work and prayer, 903. Whom and what should a widow avoid? 289, 505. Even things that are safe should be feared by a widow, 290. More distinguished widows in both the Old and New Testaments, 508. Widows honored by everyone, 911. Why does the Apostle wish young widows to marry and bear children? etc., 902. Many holy widows in the city of Rome, whose example is proposed for imitation, 294. Widows who are fed by the alms of the Church, 503, 903. Those who urge a widow to marry a second time, 911. Idle and inquisitive widows, 915. The Gospel widow richer than the entire Israelite people, 293, 796. Widows are placed in distress and tribulation, II, 240. Jerome does not disparage widows, 290. In what position he places them, ibid. Widows who are fed by the alms of the Church, 263. The steadfastness and chastity of pagan widows, 310. Widows supported by ecclesiastical provisions, IV, 51. The widow’s offering praised by the Savior, VI, 303. The prophetess Anna as an example of widows, VII, 307.

Vigilantius was stirred up by Rufinus against Jerome, 548. Vigilantius is called “Dormitantius,” I, 725. He attacks the veneration of the holy martyrs, ibid. ff. The method of Vigilantius, 349. Jerome rebukes and mocks him, ibid. and 351, 726. The blasphemies of Vigilantius in his interpretation of Daniel, 351. Vigilantius condemned the monastic life, II, 400. A very curious account of Vigilantius, 398.

Vigils and all-night watches in basilicas, I, 727. The Church proclaiming the Lord Christ during nocturnal vigils, 1089. Vigils and all-night watches in basilicas, II, 396.

The number twenty-five is never taken in a favorable sense, V, 107.

Why country estates belong to the rights of cities, V, 610. What use they have, ibid. ff.

Who the unjust steward is, and his entire history is explained, I, 893 ff.

Grape marc; raisins, VI, 29.

Vincent the presbyter, I, 349. What does he concelebrate? 537. Vincent the presbyter, II, 447, 451, 551. He is sent to the West, 553.

Bonds are frequently read of in Scripture as punishments for sins, IV, 80. The bonds of the Lord are one thing, those of the devil another, V, 42. “The Lord will not avenge except against the same” [reading uncertain], I, 417, 798. Whoever avenges himself does not deserve the Lord’s vengeance, II, 534.

Vengeance is sought under the pretext of peace, I, 518. The later the vengeance of sinners, the more just it is, IV, 1091. The circle of divine vengeance, VI, 377.

Although a vineyard is beautiful, if you remove its reeds, it withers in the heat, V, 221. Jerusalem is compared with a vineyard and with a vine, 142. What is the vineyard? VI, 438.

Wine should be used moderately, I, 266. For what reasons Paul permits the drinking of wine, 94, 953. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure, 94. The marrow of young men, full of wine, with what is it compared? 287. Whatever intoxicates and overturns the state of the mind, flee in the same way as wine, 266. Wines of different taste and color are sought to the injury of self-restraint, 618. The luxurious rich sigh for a cup of wine, 616. Wine generates virginity and love of chastity, II, 287. Wine was consecrated together with meat after the Flood, 268. Wine is drunk in the mysteries, VI, 357. How wine rages against the drinker, 613. Jerome taught that young men should shun wine, VII, 651. Its effects, 508, 509. In what sense Jerome condemns it, ibid. It is consecrated into the blood of Christ, ibid. The slavery of wine-drinking, 717. What does one possess who is filled with wine? 650, 651.

Drunkenness belongs to jesters and feasters, I, 422.

Violence toward the kingdom of heaven is praised, I, 125 ff.

What is holy violence? V, 202. What is great violence? VII, 70.

Beside the viper no one sleeps securely, I, 783.

History teaches that the authority of a man must not be preferred to Christ, [Col. 1089] I, 683. The downfall of brave men arising from women, 97. What is not permitted to women is likewise not permitted to men, 458. Would that men imitated the praises bestowed upon women, 282. What is the difference between *vir* and *homo*? 1049. When a man is subject to a woman, II, 288. What kind of marriage is prescribed between husbands and wives, 248, 265. Jerome does not disparage holy men, 274, 275. Why are men commanded to love their wives so greatly, while wives are to love with fear? VI, 518.

Why Eve was called *virago*, I, 3, 308.

Virbius, VII, 619.

The rod is used for the kingdom, I, 383. It signifies secular power, which is forbidden to the apostles, 127. The two rods among the prophets signify the Church and the synagogue, 448 ff. The mystery of the two rods is explained, IV, 630. The rod is understood as chastisement and visitation, V, 68. Who needs the pastoral rod? VI, 527. Why Moses was equipped with a rod, but not the apostles, 527.

What is Virgil doing with the Gospels? I, 114. He is likewise praised, 1026, 275. Virgil, II, 566. What is “Virgilian”? 238. Virgil was called a compiler of ancient writers, III, 301. He was both philosopher and poet, 469. Virgil was the first Homer among the Latins, VI, 520. What has been handed down about Virgil? 881. What is reported about Virgil? VII, 485. Verses of Virgil, 611.

A bishop who consecrates virgins, II, 424. Can a virgin be the Mother of the Lord? 122. The mother of a virgin is called the mother-in-law of God, 104. Virgins are jewels of the Church, 693. Virgins are to be called ladies, 88. The region of the virgin is paradise, 103. She walks amid snares, 113, 783. She should guard the privacy of her chamber, 109. She should not wish to appear eloquent, 114, 989. Gravity befits the person of a virgin, 989. There should be equality among virgins, not domination, 113. The reward of virgins and of chastity, 125. Virgins should shun wine, 93. A virgin’s appearance in public should be rare, 100, 995. Christ condemns gems and the most precious ornaments in a virgin, 683, 979. What does a girl who enjoys luxuries suffer? 93. God cannot raise up a virgin after her fall, 91. What companion ought to please a virgin? 100, 686. What sort of woman should the one preferred to her be? 994. The examples of certain virgins are not to be followed, 121, 122. False virgins are to be avoided, 113. A virgin should avoid the company of men, even when they are close relations and kinsmen, 181. Good and bad virgins, 91, 997. The falls and crimes of corrupted virgins, 97, 98. Some have lost the crown of chastity at the very threshold of death, 113. The type of virgins and figure of matrons, 195. The canonical hours and other exercises of virgins, ibid. The joy of the citizens of heaven at the reception of a virgin, 125. The garment proper to virgins consecrated to God was called the *flammeum*, 720. The virgins of heretics are to be regarded as prostitutes, 123. Why virgins and widows are tonsured in monasteries, 1090. The perpetual chastity of the virgins of Vesta, Apollo, Juno, etc., 906. Why virgins are loved more by Christ, II, 257. The definition of a virgin: holy in body and spirit, 227. It is of no benefit to have a virgin body if one has married in mind, 227. What others will be in heaven, virgins have begun to be on earth, 296. Which women are praised as virgins? 273. The reward of virgins and chastity, 260. Virgins were always held in honor among the Romans, 307. An example left for virgins, 309. The falls and crimes of corrupted virgins, 258. The pagans placed the virgin among the twelve signs of heaven, 307. The virgin’s conception and childbirth are shown to King Ahaz, VI, 259. Which are good and bad virgins? 323. A virgin who has gone astray has no one to raise her up, 283. She cannot be raised up for a slight sin, 282. Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist were virgins, 876. The soul of a virgin has one kind of purity, and another is possessed by one who has submitted to lust, 524. A virgin who has not been prostituted by her own will remains a virgin, 75.

Virginity is consecrated by the virgin Savior, I, 102, 233. From where the gift of virginity flowed more abundantly to women, 105. The palm of virginity and chastity, 969. What is blessed virginity? 996. Virginity perishes in the mind as well, 92. Rules are given for preserving the integrity of virginity, 107, etc. In this respect it is easier, because it does not know the incentives of the flesh, 908. How difficult it is to preserve it intact! 97. It was commended among pagan priests, 905. Virginity is natural; marriage came after sin, 103. Why no commandment is given concerning virginity, 986. Virginity is both against nature and beyond nature, 986. Many have written about virginity in both Latin and Greek, 107, 996. Virginity is consecrated by the virgin Savior, II, 275. Virginity is voluntary, 287. That virginity is Christ’s sacrifice whose mind no thought and whose song no desire has stained, 260. It does not die, 273. After death it begins to be crowned, 273. It fills paradise, 266. Violated virginity is considered a great crime, 307. To chaste minds virginity is more than a kingdom, 309. It is a difficult matter, and therefore rare, 204. Paradise consecrated virginity, and earth marriage, 284. Among the pagans it always held the chief place, 306. Two kinds of virginity, 227. It is the fruit of marriage, 240. Why no commandment is given concerning virginity, 229, 256. The imitation of the virgins of the devil does not prejudice true virginity [Col. 1090], 354. Virginity alone, without other works, does not save, 305. What are the beginnings of dying virginity? 23. False virginity is condemned, IV, 892. What does the word of God accomplish in a virginal soul? 118. Virginity is not demanded but offered, V, 579. In what does the virginal privilege consist? 554. The reward of virginity, VII, 145. Why does it have greater rewards? 761.

Virbius, II, 622.

What is great virtue? I, 287. The desire for virtue sustained by God’s mercy, 619. Whoever has once given himself to virtue tramples upon and despises whatever may come, 620. Virtue governs the soul like a charioteer, 629. As though standing in a chariot, it orders its various desires, ibid. When we think that we have reached the finish line of virtues, then we shall have the beginning, 103. Virtue is always exposed to envy, 982. Just as sins spring from negligence, so diligence produces virtues, 613. Nothing is more precious than the cardinal virtues, 268, 394. Outside the Church there are no rewards for virtues, 123. While someone fears reproaches, he is not summoned to virtue, 283. Virtue is always rare, II, 341. Whoever possesses one virtue seems to possess them all, 714. No possession of virtues is certain or secure, 326. We cannot possess all the virtues at once, 717. It is a great matter of faith and a great matter of virtue to be holy in body and spirit, 257. It is the work of our labor to prepare different rewards for ourselves according to the diversity of virtues, 376. Among the pagans virtue is preferred to pleasure, 242. No one can always think about virtues, 786. The particular virtues of the saints, 714. Among philosophers the virtues are placed in the middle, and everything excessive, whether above or below, is reckoned as a vice, III, 332. They are in the middle, and every excess is a vice, 469. They follow one another, and whoever possesses one possesses them all, 468. There is no rivalry among virtues, 509. They make the days good for one who lives by them; vices make them bad, 439. They breathe forth perfumes, 509. Whoever restrains himself after vices and pursues virtues is praised by Ecclesiastes, 398. All the virtues follow one another and adhere to one another, IV, 275, 655. Unless vices withdraw, virtues do not enter, 412. The gates of righteousness are works of virtue, 344. Under the heading of righteousness all virtues are understood, 636. We cannot immediately, however much we may wish it, grasp perfect virtue, 275. Vain glory in virtues must be avoided, 936. The people of God is understood through virtues, 736. According to the diversity of virtues, there are differences of dwellings, 256. The temple of the Lord is that in which the chorus of all virtues dwells, etc., 881. Whoever imitates a certain virtue is called its son as well, 702. Virtue is rare, V, 388. Possession of virtue is not certain, 609. Virtues are always opposed, 602. Through virtues we attain the name and dignity of a leader, 574. What is the first entrance into virtue? 480. Whoever lacks one virtue lacks them all, 14. A catalogue of the virtues of the righteous, 203. Christ is the virtue of God, and in what respects? VII, 261. The connection of the virtues, 645. The way of virtues is praised, 461. They are denied through vices, 712. Virtues are understood in two ways, 376. What is the greatest virtue? 653. It is virtue not to have begun but to have completed, 60. A certain seed of righteousness and of the other virtues is present in those who are born, 391. Each person is named from the virtue that he possesses most fully, 425. What lies between virtues and vices is neither to be done nor desired, 481. It is not the virtue but the cause of virtue that receives a reward from God, 32. It is one thing to compose books about vices and virtues, and another to enter into the meaning of the prophets and apostles, 539.

“Virtues” is used to mean miracles, IV, 750.

The poisons of the Egyptians, I, 479.

What it means to violate one’s own inward parts, and what “the inward parts of mercy” means, VI, 239. What are the inward parts? VII, 756.

What kind of prophecy is called a vision? IV, 1007. The difference between a vision and an oracle, or burden, ibid. ff. Ezekiel’s famous vision of the dry bones, celebrated in the reading of all Christians, V, 432. What the use of the word “vision” for prophecy signifies, VI, 591.

“Visitation” signifies consolation and punishment, IV, 1081. “Visitation” is understood not as a remedy but as a blow, 188.

The life of mortals is uncertain, I, 899. The long life of the ancient fathers was like a second immortality, 23. Long and short life compared with one another, 342. Why the length of this life is burdensome and troublesome, 783. The life of mortals ends with a screech, 722. How one must run in this life so that eternal things may succeed transient ones, 127. Later life judges the earlier, 290. After the rules of Scripture, it is good to learn the course of one’s life from others, 994. We are taught to imitate the life of angels amid the titillations of the flesh, II, 256. This is our portion and the fruit of our labor: if in this shadowy life we are able to find the true life, III, 463. A peaceful death is preferred to a wretched life, IV, 982. Everlasting life is the promise of all good things, 646. The seven periods of human life, VI, 314. Few despise the present life, 811. Those who are willing to die for others deserve life more, 592. In what respects the solitary life is praiseworthy [Col. 1091], 528. Perpetual life has no fear of ruin, VII, 210. The Lord accepts the good life of philosophers and pagans, 208.

The Greeks and Latins wrote the lives of illustrious men, I, 738. By what title they named these books, ibid.

Vitalis the presbyter, I, 38, 41.

Vices are the causes of calamities, I, 107. What is the palm of vices? 344. They deceive only under the appearance and shadow of virtues, 684. By the fear of eternal fire let us consume vices as they grow, 611. Unless vices are restrained, they grow proud and drive those who obey them down to hell, 612. The fall into vices is easy, 579. Few are those who, having trampled upon vices, keep to the path of truth, 692. Cessation from vices draws one near to God, 612. The incentives of all vices tickle the mind, 506. Some cure one vice with another, and one sin with another, 941. From our vice we put on many roles, 193. The testimonies of Scripture are like the armor of God against all vices, 711. Vices must be opposed at their beginnings, lest they grow, 92. External vices are easily cast aside, but pleasure is not so easily abandoned, 287. The inner person fluctuates between vices and virtues, 92. No one is born without vices, 506, 1026. Those who cunningly conceal their vices are recognized from their subsequent conduct, 287. Whoever censures vices offends many people, 183. The ages slide daily into vices, 23. Some take a general discussion of vices as a personal insult, 935. When they grow angry with the one arguing, they reveal their own conscience, ibid. The barbarians are strong because of our vices, 344. We pursue vices more than virtues, II, 380. They are close to virtues, 794. We are not ashamed to hold out the names of piety as a pretext for our vices, 402. It is one thing to be cleansed by God, another to be without vice through oneself, 336. Through our vice we daily slide into worse things, III, 448. Vices bear the images of beasts, IV, 576. According to the diversity of vices among the proud, some are mountains and others hills, 40. Vices and sins are an unripe grape, 1074. Peace follows the cleansing of vices, 867. Vices do not follow one another, but virtues do, in which all things are balanced, 611. It is our vice that we are overwhelmed by the waves of the sea, 302. Our vices make God bitter and cruel, V, 113. Greater things are shown through lesser vices, 85. Whoever does not rebuke vices slaughters, 409. Some think that our vices do not pertain to God, 88. Vices are sweet, VI, 173. There are four by which we are attacked, 565. From these many others derive their origin, ibid. Vices are our idols, 240. They appear beautiful and delight us, 313. We readily applaud our own vices, 108. How vices are changed into virtues, 929, 930. The four cardinal virtues are shields against vices, 565. The connection of the virtues, 34. Persecution is the advancement of virtues, 707. Former virtues do not benefit one who possesses vice, 183. Names are assigned from virtues, as also from vices, 431. Into what likeness do virtues and vices make us? 687. Human frailty is never safe, and the more we grow in virtues, the more we must fear vices, 196. Every time in which we do not serve the virtues is reckoned as vice, 743. Vice is not shown except by comparison with virtue, VII, 62. Whenever we are conquered by vices, so often we deny God, 712. It is of no benefit to have withdrawn from vices unless the best things are grasped, 461. Vices come to an end and perish in themselves; virtues abound in fruits, 505.

The heifer that is three years old, being of mature age, IV, 187 ff.

What is the fattened calf mystically? I, 80. Where is there wrongdoing in eating the flesh of calves? II, 334. Who are the “calves of the lips”? VI, 158. The Hebrews report that the golden calves were secretly carried away by the priests and bronze ones set in their place, 159.

The first of living creatures emerged from the waters in creation, V, 9 ff.

By living long, many carry their own funerals, I, 319. No one is so broken in strength and so decrepit with old age that he does not think he will live one more year, 912.

It is one thing to live while destined to die, another to die while destined to live, I, 342. Is living in the body a commendation? IV, 471. In what sense God alone is said to live, V, 181. The priest is permitted to live from the altar, not to live luxuriously, VI, 472 ff.

What God has made alive cannot be killed by him or by another, V, 755.

Each person receives a name according to his character, V, 300.

The Hebrews very rarely use vowel letters in the middle of words, I, 445.

The time of the various callings, II, 374.

In the Old Testament it is said that the people saw the voice of God, IV, 8.

The province of the Volscians, I, 462.

A person’s will before God receives the reward of his intention, I, 515, 176. The human will is uncertain, wavering, and changeable, II, 780. It is better to do everything according to understanding, which is the eye of the soul, than to follow the will of the heart, III, 485. We are evil by will, not by nature, IV, 258. One should follow the will of the teacher, not his indulgence, 784. It lies within our power either to do something or not to do it, [Col. 1092] 890. By our own will we do not receive the word of God, 884. By his own will each person is trampled down by vices, 669. The freedom of the will to do good is within us, VII, 311.

*Volvola*, a herb, VI, 544.

Pleasure fears neither the purple of kings nor the squalor of beggars, I, 507. Whatever is a seedbed of pleasures, consider it poison, 288, 612. A human being cannot be without incentives to pleasure and luxury, 92. Pleasure is difficult to conquer, 287, 502. The chains of pleasures, 323. Who entered the king of Babylon’s furnace without being burned? 501. Some think it is a greater virtue to despise present pleasure, 685. One is persuaded to despise the body itself and to enter upon a harsher but better life than present pleasures, 628. Many give alms, but contribute nothing from their own bodies, overcome by fleshly pleasure, 707. Burning pleasure dominates and is not conquered by punishments, II, 274. Why did philosophers abandon things that favor pleasure? 337. Pleasure and desire are compared with drunkenness, which overturns the vigor of the mind, III, 397. Past pleasure does not help the present, and what has been exhausted does not satisfy, 396. The more wealth and pleasures increase, the more wisdom is lacking among human beings, 297. People give themselves wholly to luxury and pleasures and seek riches that do not free them in necessity, 467. Those whom love of pleasure and riches surrounds are reproved, IV, 322. Pleasure is insatiable, VI, 39. It is called drunkenness, 173. It perverts the senses, 39. There is little strength in men devoted to pleasure, 577. A purse is despised more easily than pleasure, VII, 149.

Volusianus, II, 907.

Although many corpulent people endure continual vomiting, etc., VII, 114.

He offers and fulfills a vow to God who is holy in body and spirit, IV, 298. What is the vow of a righteous man? 629.

The living voice of teachers is more beneficial than books, I, 272. A spoken word does not know how to return, 234. The sweetness of the voice wounds the soul through the ear, 954. The living voice has great power, VII, 467.

The commentaries of Vulcatius, II, 47.

The old Vulgate edition and its divergence from the Septuagint, I, 642 ff. See Edition.

The uneducated crowd easily changes its opinion, IV, 104.

Who is difficult to wound? VII, 67.

May the wound of others be our warning, I, 290. To efface old wounds with new charity, 516.

Innumerable peoples delight in the flesh of foxes, II, 334.

We cannot always have the same expression, II, 782.

Vultures sense corpses across the sea, II, 445. In the vulture there are as many cures as there are limbs, 332.

Countenances that the Creator does not recognize, I, 286. The redness of the face is an indication of modesty, V, 73. A hardened expression is an indication of severity, 38. Whence comes pallor of the face? VI, 274.

## X

Xantippe, the wife of Socrates, II, 316.

What does the philosopher Xenocrates write? II, 344. Xenocrates wrote about the nature of gems and stones, VI, 328. Xenocrates transformed Polemo, a most disgraceful young man, into a most wise philosopher, 5.

A hospice built by Pammachius in the Roman harbor, I, 401.

What does Xenophon report? I, 222, 334, and II, 311, 343 ff. Xenophon wrote a history of Cyrus, IV, 522, and V, 651.

The xerophagy of Tatian and Mani, VI, 262.

Why did Xerxes weep? I, 345. The origin and victories of Xerxes, V, 702.

The book of Xystus the Pythagorean, bearing the name of Saint Sixtus the martyr, I, 1029. It has nothing suggestive of Christianity, ibid. A saying of Xystus, II, 318. A beautiful saying of Xystus the Pythagorean, V, 280.

Xystus succeeded Stephen, II, 909.

## Y

What the letter Y signifies for philosophers, III, 424, 469.

## Z

Zacchaeus, I, 432, 701. Why he was not among the twelve apostles, 402. Zacchaeus restored fourfold what he had taken by robbery, VI, 302.

Zechariah is interpreted as “mindful of his Lord,” I, 278. Zechariah the prophet is obscure and the longest of the Twelve, VI, 777. Zechariah the prophet and priest, VII, 259. What does Zechariah’s silence signify? 260. The praises of Zechariah and Elizabeth, 251. A verse of Zechariah cited under the name of Jeremiah, 227, 228.

[Col. 1093] Zacynthus, an island, VII, 427.

The torrent of Zared and its mystery, I, 493.

Zebennus, bishop of Antioch, II, 905.

Jealousy gnaws at its own author, I, 712. Jealousy is understood in a favorable sense, VI, 535. Jealousy is manifold, VII, 465. One kind is close to envy, ibid.

Zeno the martyr of foolish philosophy, I, 180. From Zeno, the leader of the Stoics, the poisons of heretics flowed, 1026. The opinions of Zeno, II, 558, 740. What Zeno and the Stoics conjecture about God and creatures, VII, 611.

Zenobius, I, 45.

[Col. 1094] Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, II, 893.

The Cilician town of Zephyrium is today called Zephrona, V, 598.

What does the Hebrew word *zo* mean? I, 698.

The signs of the zodiac, I, 679.

The priestly belt, I, 361. What it signifies mystically, 398.

Zoroaster the Great, I, 1032.

From where Zorobabel received his name, V, 219. Zorobabel as a type of the Savior, VI, 74.

Zythum is a kind of drink made from grain and water, IV, 292. In Dalmatia it is called *sabaia*, ibid.
